text: Aaron was the son of Amram and Jochebed, of the tribe of Levi, the brother of Moses and Miriam, and Israel's first high priest. Because he spoke well, God appointed him to speak for Moses before Pharaoh, and the two brothers led Israel out of Egypt (Exod 4:14; 7:1). At Sinai he went partway up the mountain with the elders. While Moses was away, he gave in to the people's demand and made the golden calf, and Moses prayed for him. He and his sons were then consecrated as priests, wearing holy garments and offering sacrifices at the tabernacle. After a challenge to his authority, his rod was kept before the testimony as a sign of his appointment. He married Elisheba and had four sons: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar. He died on Mount Hor at age 123, and his descendants formed Israel's priesthood.

Abana was one of the two "rivers of Damascus" that Naaman, the Aramean army commander, named with the Pharpar when Elisha told him to wash in the Jordan to be cured of his skin disease. Naaman protested that these rivers were better than all the waters of Israel and left in anger (2 Kgs 5:12). The Hebrew margin gives the name as Amanah, and Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary take it to mean "perennial" or "stony." Both dictionaries identify the Abana with the modern Barada River, which the Greeks called the Chrysorrhoas, or "golden stream." It rises in the Anti-Lebanon range about 23 miles northwest of Damascus and flows through the city and across its plain, making that land fertile. The location shown here follows this Barada identification.

Abiel (meaning "God is my father," according to Hitchcock's Bible Names) was a Benjamite, the son of Zeror and an ancestor of King Saul. 1 Sam 9:1 calls him the father of Kish, Saul's father, and 1 Sam 14:51 calls him the father of Ner, whose son was Abner, Saul's commander. However, 1 Chr 8:33 and 9:39 say that Ner was the father of Kish, so the generations are hard to align. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes "father" in 1 Sam 9:1 to mean grandfather, making Abiel the father of Ner. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat Kish and Ner as brothers, both sons of Abiel. This entry follows the STEPBible identification of Abiel with Jehiel, the "father of Gibeon," who lived in Gibeon with his wife Maachah (1 Chr 9:35). That passage goes on to list his ten sons, including Kish and Ner. Several other people in the Bible share the name.

Ashur was a man of the tribe of Judah, the son of Hezron and his wife Abiah. He was born after his father died at Caleb-ephratah (1 Chr 2:24), which makes him a brother of Jerahmeel, Ram and Caleb, and a half-brother of Segub. He is called "the father of Tekoa," which Smith's Bible Dictionary takes to mean the founder of that town in Judah, probably near modern Khirbet Tequ'a south of Bethlehem. He had two wives, Helah and Naarah (1 Chr 4:5). The verses that follow, 1 Chr 4:6–7, name his sons: Naarah bore Ahuzam, Hepher, Temeni and Haahashtari, and Helah bore Zereth, Jezoar and Ethnan. This entry also counts Coz among his sons, by inference from his place in the list at 1 Chr 4:8. Some reference works, such as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, spell the name Ashhur.

Atad was the site of a threshing floor "beyond Jordan" where Joseph and the funeral party from Egypt stopped on their way to bury Jacob. There they held a great and bitter mourning for seven days (Gen 50:10). The local Canaanites, watching this, called it "a grievous mourning to the Egyptians," so the place was renamed Abel-mizraim. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as a wordplay meaning "mourning of Egypt" or "meadow of Egypt" (Gen 50:11). The name Atad means "thorn" or "buckthorn." Its location is unknown. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it east of the Jordan and north of the Dead Sea. Smith's Bible Dictionary puts it west of the river, between the Jordan and Jericho, and links it with Beth-hogla. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it was near Hebron. No location is shown in this entry.

Baal-zephon was a place in Egypt near the sea, mentioned only as a landmark for the Israelite camp just before they crossed the Red Sea. The Israelites turned back from Etham and camped before Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, facing Baal-zephon. There Pharaoh's chariots and army overtook them (Exod 14:2, 14:9; Num 33:7). By inference from context, this was about 1491 BC. The name means "lord of the north," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that a god called Baali-Zapuna appears in an Egyptian papyrus, so the place was probably a shrine or town dedicated to that deity. Its exact position is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on the western shore of the Gulf of Suez, possibly at Jebel Deraj or Kulalah, while other scholars consider the site unknown. The location shown here follows a placement near the northern end of the Gulf of Suez.

The Birth of Simeon was the birth of the second son of Jacob and his wife Leah, following Reuben (Gen 29:32). After conceiving again, Leah said that the LORD had heard that she was unloved and had given her this son as well, so she named him Simeon (Gen 29:33). The name echoes the Hebrew verb for "hear," matching her explanation. From the surrounding narrative, the birth took place while Jacob was living with his uncle Laban in Haran, during the years he served Laban for his wives Leah and Rachel. Simeon later became the ancestor of the Israelite tribe that bore his name. This entry dates the birth to about 1757 BC, an estimate inferred from context rather than stated in the text.

Cherith was a brook or seasonal stream in a ravine where the prophet Elijah hid at God's command after announcing a drought to King Ahab (1 Kgs 17:3, 5). The same chapter says that ravens brought him food there and that he drank from the brook until it dried up for lack of rain. The text places it "before Jordan," which Easton's Bible Dictionary takes to mean that it opened toward the river and flowed into it. The exact site is uncertain. Easton's notes that some identify it with the Wadi el-Kelt behind Jericho, west of the Jordan. Easton's, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also point to a ravine east of the Jordan in Gilead, since Elijah was told to turn eastward. The location shown here follows the eastern view, roughly where a stream from the Gilead hills meets the Jordan valley.

The Creation of all things is the Bible's opening account, in which God makes the heavens and the earth over six days and rests on the seventh (Gen 1:1–2:3). The earth begins formless and dark, with the Spirit of God moving over the waters. By speaking, God creates light on the first day and the sky dividing the waters on the second. Dry land, seas and plants follow on the third, the sun, moon and stars on the fourth, and sea creatures and birds on the fifth. On the sixth day come land animals and humankind, male and female in God's image. God calls each stage good, gives humans dominion over other creatures, and blesses the seventh day. Later passages such as John 1:3 and Col 1:16 present Christ as the agent of creation. The date of about 4004 BC follows the traditional chronology of James Ussher and is an estimate based on biblical genealogies.

Delilah was a woman from the valley of Sorek whom Samson loved (Judg 16:4). The Philistine lords offered her silver to learn the secret of his great strength and how he could be bound (Judg 16:5). Three times she asked, and three times Samson gave false answers. She tied him with new ropes and even wove his seven locks of hair into a loom while men lay in wait, and each time he broke free. When he finally told her everything, she summoned the Philistine lords, who came with the money in hand (Judg 16:18). Later in the chapter his hair is shaved while he sleeps, and he is captured. The text does not state her nationality. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take her to be a Philistine, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that this is presumed rather than stated and that she is not called Samson's wife.

The Deliverance by Ehud was Israel's rescue from Moabite rule, which had followed a period of domination by Eglon king of Moab. When Israel cried to the LORD, he raised up Ehud son of Gera, a left-handed Benjamite. Sent to bring Israel's tribute to Eglon, Ehud strapped a double-edged dagger to his right thigh under his clothing. After the tribute was delivered, he returned from the quarries near Gilgal, claimed a secret message from God, and stabbed the very fat king in his private summer room, locking the doors behind him. The servants waited, assuming the king was relieving himself, and Ehud escaped to Seirath. Blowing a trumpet in the hill country of Ephraim, he led the Israelites to seize the Jordan fords, where about ten thousand Moabites were killed. The land then had rest for eighty years. This entry dates the event to about 1360 BC, by inference from context.

Fair Havens was a harbor on the south coast of Crete where the ship carrying Paul to Rome stopped after a difficult passage along the island, near the city of Lasea (Acts 27:8). Easton's Bible Dictionary says the ship waited there a considerable time for a favorable wind. The ship's master and owner then chose to sail on against Paul's advice, because the harbor was not suitable for spending the winter (Acts 27:9–12). The ship was later wrecked on Malta. By inference from context, this happened about AD 56. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that no other ancient writing mentions the harbor, but it is still known by its Greek name, Kaloi Limenes. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it about 5 miles east of Cape Matala, in a bay open to the east and sheltered by two small islands. The location shown here matches that modern site.

Haggith was one of King David's wives and the mother of Adonijah, David's fourth son. She is named only as Adonijah's mother. He was born in Hebron during the years David reigned there, before he moved his capital to Jerusalem (2 Sam 3:2–5; 1 Chr 3:1–4). Her son is repeatedly called "Adonijah the son of Haggith," including in the account of his attempt to make himself king as David grew old, which the prophet Nathan reported to Bathsheba, the mother of Solomon. Adonijah's later visit to Bathsheba after Solomon became king also uses this name. Nothing else is recorded about Haggith herself. Her name is usually taken to mean "festive" or "festal" (Easton's Bible Dictionary; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia).

Hezron was a landmark on the southern border of Judah, named in the boundary description between Kadesh-barnea and Adar (Josh 15:3). The border ran past the Ascent of Akrabbim and the wilderness of Zin, up to Kadesh-barnea, on to Hezron, then up to Adar and around to Karkaa. The name probably means "enclosure." In the parallel boundary list in Num 34:4 the place appears as Hazar-addar, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Hezron and Adar may have been close together. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as a plain west of Kadesh-barnea, and the surveyor Conder proposed that the name survives in Jebel Hadhireh, a mountain northwest of Petra. Its exact site is uncertain. The location shown here corresponds to the site of Hazor in northern Galilee, a different identification from the southern setting the verse describes.

Jahath was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:2. He was the son of Reaiah and the grandson of Shobal, and he was the father of Ahumai and Lahad. The verse identifies these descendants as the families of the Zorathites, a name that probably links them with the town of Zorah in the lowland of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about his life. The name Jahath is also borne by several other men in the Bible, mostly Levites, and they should not be confused with this descendant of Judah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may mean "he (God) will snatch up," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "broken in pieces" or "descending."

The event of Jesus in Capernaum was his move from Nazareth to Capernaum, a town on the shore of the Sea of Galilee in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali. Matthew presents the move as fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy that the people of "Galilee of the Gentiles," who sat in darkness, would see a great light (the passage quoted is Isa 9:1–2). From that time Jesus began preaching, "Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand." Luke's account says he came down to Capernaum and taught the people there on the sabbath days. In this entry it follows his rejection at Nazareth, and Luke places the two episodes side by side. It is dated about AD 27, by inference from context. Capernaum is usually identified with the site of Tell Hum on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee.

Joseph (son of Judah) is a name in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, listed as the son of Juda and the father of Semei (Luke 3:26). Nothing else is recorded about him. Many Greek manuscripts and modern translations spell the name Josech, as the STEPBible proper-names index notes. Two other men named Joseph appear in the same genealogy (Luke 3:24, 30), as Easton's Bible Dictionary points out. The next verse continues the line back through Joanna and Rhesa to Zerubbabel, which suggests he lived a few generations after the return from the Babylonian exile. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him somewhere between 536 and 410 BC, an estimate drawn from his position in the list. His name is usually taken to mean "increase" or "addition."

Lahmam was a town in the lowland district (the Shephelah) of the tribe of Judah. It appears only once, in the list of Judah's towns in Josh 15:40, where it is named between Cabbon and Kithlish. By inference from its surrounding entries, it belonged to the group of towns in the region around Lachish. Nothing else is recorded about it. Some manuscripts spell the name Lahmas, and the Revised Version margin notes this reading. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the modern site of el-Lahm, about 2.5 miles (4 km) south of Beit Jibrin, and the location shown here follows that identification. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "provisions."

The Lifetime of Arphaxad covers the 438 years of this descendant of Shem, as given in the genealogy from Shem to Abram in Genesis 11. Arphaxad was 35 years old when he fathered Salah (Gen 11:12). He then lived another 403 years and had other sons and daughters (Gen 11:13). The total of 438 years is not stated in the text but comes from adding these two figures. The verse just before says Arphaxad was born to Shem two years after the flood (Gen 11:10). This entry dates the start of his life to about 2346 BC, an estimate inferred from the chronology of the genealogy. Luke 3:36 places a Cainan between Arphaxad and Sala, following the Greek Old Testament, while the Hebrew text of Genesis names Salah as Arphaxad's son. This entry follows the Genesis account.

Michael was a Levite named in the ancestry of Asaph, one of the leading singers David appointed for the music of the house of the Lord. In the genealogy in 1 Chr 6:40 he is the son of Baaseiah and the grandson of Malchiah. His son Shimea appears in the line that leads down to Asaph, so Michael was one of Asaph's forefathers. Because Asaph's line is traced back through Gershom, Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify Michael as a Gershonite Levite. Smith's gives the meaning of the name as "who is like God?" Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name Michael, and this one should not be confused with them.

The Mission to Iconium was the stay of Paul and Barnabas in the city of Iconium during their first missionary journey. They had arrived after being driven out of Antioch in Pisidia (Acts 13:51). They spoke together in the Jewish synagogue, and a large number of both Jews and Greeks believed. Jews who did not believe stirred up Gentiles against the new believers. The two men still stayed a long time, speaking boldly, and signs and wonders were done through them. The city became divided, with some siding with the Jews and others with the apostles. When Gentiles, Jews and their rulers moved to mistreat and stone them, they fled to Lystra and Derbe, as the next verse, Acts 14:6, relates. This entry dates the mission to about AD 46 and estimates it lasted around five months, both by inference from context. Iconium is generally identified with modern Konya in Turkey.

Mount Shapher (spelled Mount Shepher in some modern translations) was a mountain where the Israelites camped during their wilderness journey after leaving Egypt. It appears only in the list of camping places in Numbers 33, where Israel moved there from Kehelathah and then left it to camp at Haradah (Num 33:23–24). Nothing else is recorded about it. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "brightness." Its exact location is unknown, and none of the neighbouring stations has been firmly identified. The location shown here is only a rough estimate, placing it in the mountainous region of what is now southern Jordan, east of the Arabah valley.

Peter's Confession "Upon this Rock" was the occasion near Caesarea Philippi, probably the modern site of Banias at the foot of Mount Hermon, when Jesus asked his disciples who people said he was. They reported that some thought he was John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah or another prophet. When he asked who they themselves said he was, Simon Peter answered, "Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God" (Matt 16:16). Mark and Luke record shorter forms of the answer, and Luke places the question after Jesus had been praying alone. In Matthew alone, Jesus calls Peter blessed, says the answer was revealed by his Father, declares that on "this rock" he will build his church, and promises Peter the keys of the kingdom of heaven with power to bind and loose. All three accounts end with Jesus ordering the disciples to tell no one. The date, about AD 29, is inferred from context.

Reaiah was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem. The family is named in both lists of returning exiles (Ezra 2:47; Neh 7:50), and Smith's Bible Dictionary places the return with Zerubbabel, before about 536 BC by inference from context. Nothing else is recorded about Reaiah himself, and the name may stand for a family or clan rather than a single known individual. The name means "the Lord has seen" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other people in the Bible share the name, and this Reaiah should not be confused with them.

Rehoboth was the home city of Saul (or Shaul), who succeeded Samlah as one of the early kings of Edom, reigning before Israel had kings (Gen 36:37; 1 Chr 1:48). It is called "Rehoboth by the river," and the name means "wide places" or "open spaces." Its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary take "the river" to mean the Euphrates, as the phrase often does in the Bible, and place the city there. Others look for it within or near Edom, with the river being a local stream. The location shown here follows the Edom identification, in present-day southern Jordan, and is only approximate. This place should not be confused with the well called Rehoboth dug by Isaac near Gerar (Gen 26:22) or with Rehoboth-Ir in Assyria (Gen 10:11), which share the name.

The Reign of Hezekiah was the rule of Hezekiah son of Ahaz over Judah from Jerusalem. It began in the third year of Hoshea king of Israel, about 726 BC by inference from context, and lasted about twenty-nine years. Hezekiah is described as doing right as David had and keeping the commandments given through Moses, and he defeated the Philistines as far as Gaza. In his reign Assyria deported the northern kingdom of Israel. In his fourteenth year Sennacherib of Assyria captured Judah's fortified cities. Hezekiah paid him silver from the temple and palace, yet the Assyrian official Rabshakeh still demanded Jerusalem's surrender. Hezekiah prayed and consulted the prophet Isaiah, who announced the city's deliverance, and Sennacherib went home to Nineveh. Later Hezekiah recovered from a serious illness, given the sign of the shadow moving back on the dial of Ahaz, and received envoys from Babylon. His son Manasseh succeeded him.

The Reign of Jehoshaphat was the twenty-five-year rule of Asa's son over Judah from Jerusalem. It began in the fourth year of Ahab king of Israel, when Jehoshaphat was thirty-five, about 914 BC by inference from context. His mother was Azubah daughter of Shilhi. He followed his father's ways and did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, though the high places remained in use for sacrifice and incense. He made peace with the king of Israel and removed the male cult prostitutes left over from Asa's time. Edom then had no king, only a deputy. Jehoshaphat built ships of Tarshish to sail to Ophir for gold, but they were wrecked at Ezion-geber, and he refused Ahaziah son of Ahab's offer to send his own crews along. He was buried in the city of David, and his son Jehoram succeeded him. The parallel account in 2 Chr 17–20 gives a fuller narrative of this reign.

Simeon was a man living in Jerusalem at the time of Jesus' birth. Luke describes him as just and devout, waiting for "the consolation of Israel," and says the Holy Spirit was upon him (Luke 2:25). When Mary and Joseph brought the infant Jesus to the temple, Simeon took the child in his arms and praised God. His words of praise are traditionally known as the Nunc Dimittis, from their opening words in Latin. He then blessed the parents and told Mary that her child was set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel and would be a sign spoken against (Luke 2:34). According to Hitchcock's Bible Names, his name means "that hears" or "that is heard." Several other people in the Bible share the name Simeon, including a son of Jacob, and they are distinct from this man.

Tabor (Mountain) is a prominent, isolated mountain in Lower Galilee, rising from the northeastern edge of the Jezreel Valley (the plain of Esdraelon). It is identified with the modern Jebel et-Tur (Mount Tabor), about 1,843 feet high according to Easton's Bible Dictionary, and the location shown here follows that identification. Josh 19:22 names it on the border of Issachar's territory. The Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna killed Gideon's brothers at Tabor (Judg 8:18). The earlier account in Judg 4:6–14 has Barak gather his forces there before defeating Sisera. Poets and prophets used it as a landmark. Ps 89:12 pairs it with Hermon, Jer 46:18 points to how it stands out among the mountains, and Hos 5:1 speaks of Israel's leaders as a net spread upon Tabor. A Christian tradition traced to the fourth century places the transfiguration of Jesus on this mountain.

event: Zaccheus Converted and Parable of the Pounds
text: The Zaccheus Converted and Parable of the Pounds event took place as Jesus passed through Jericho on his way to Jerusalem, probably in AD 30 (a date inferred from context), after he healed blind Bartimaeus. Zacchaeus, a rich chief tax collector, was too short to see over the crowd, so he climbed a sycamore tree. Jesus called him down and said he would stay at his house, and the crowd complained that he was the guest of a sinner. Zacchaeus pledged half his goods to the poor and fourfold repayment to anyone he had defrauded. Jesus declared that salvation had come to his house. Because people expected God's kingdom to appear immediately, Jesus then told a parable. A nobleman left to receive a kingdom and gave ten servants a pound each. On his return he rewarded those who had traded profitably, took the pound from the servant who had hidden it, and ordered his enemies killed. Jesus then went on up to Jerusalem.

The 2nd Rejection at Nazareth was a return visit by Jesus to his hometown, recorded in Matthew and Mark, probably about AD 29 by inference from context. Accompanied by his disciples, he taught in the synagogue on the Sabbath. His hearers were astonished at his wisdom and mighty works but took offense, asking how a local man could have such things. They identified him as the carpenter (or the carpenter's son), the son of Mary, and the brother of James, Joses, Simon and Judas, with sisters living among them. Jesus replied that a prophet is honored everywhere except in his own country and household. Because of their unbelief he did few mighty works there, healing only a few sick people by laying hands on them. He marveled at their unbelief and went on teaching in the surrounding villages. Luke 4:16–30 describes a similar rejection. Some take it as the same visit, but this entry treats it as an earlier one.

The 3rd Tour of Galilee was a preaching circuit in which Jesus went through the cities and villages of Galilee, teaching in synagogues, proclaiming the kingdom and healing the sick. Seeing that the harvest was plentiful but the workers few, he sent out the twelve apostles, who are named in Matt 10:2–3, in pairs with authority over unclean spirits and disease. He told them to go only to Israel, not to Gentiles or Samaritans, to take no money, bread or extra clothing, to stay in one house in each town, and to shake the dust off their feet where they were rejected. He warned of coming persecution, divided households and the cost of following him. The apostles went through the towns preaching, casting out demons and anointing and healing the sick. It is dated to about AD 29, by inference from context, and follows the second rejection at Nazareth.

The 7 years of famine was the period of severe food shortage that followed the seven years of plenty, beginning as Joseph had foretold when he interpreted Pharaoh's dreams (Gen 41). It struck all lands, but Egypt had bread because Joseph had stored grain, and he opened the storehouses to sell it. When Jacob learned there was grain in Egypt, he sent ten of his sons to buy food. Joseph recognized his brothers, accused them of being spies, held Simeon, and demanded that they bring their youngest brother, Benjamin. On the way home they found their money returned in their sacks. As the famine grew worse, Judah pledged himself as surety for Benjamin, and the brothers went back with gifts, double money and Benjamin. Joseph received them at his house and held a meal for them. The famine's start is dated to about 1708 BC by inference from context.

The 7 years of plenty were the period of abundant harvests in Egypt that Joseph had foretold when he interpreted Pharaoh's dreams. They followed his appointment as Pharaoh's chief administrator. The land produced crops "by handfuls," and Joseph collected the surplus food of each region and stored it in the nearby cities. He gathered so much grain that he stopped counting, comparing it to the sand of the sea. During these years, before the famine began, his wife Asenath, daughter of Potipherah priest of On, bore him two sons. He named the firstborn Manasseh, saying God had made him forget his hardship and his father's house, and the second Ephraim, saying God had made him fruitful in the land of his affliction. The period ended as predicted and gave way to seven years of famine. This entry dates it to about 1715 BC, an estimate inferred from context.

The 70 Sent Out was the occasion, recorded only in Luke, when Jesus appointed seventy followers besides the twelve apostles and sent them ahead in pairs to every town he planned to visit. It followed a Samaritan village's refusal to receive him, probably about AD 29, by inference from context. He told them to pray for more workers, to travel without purse, bag or sandals, to stay in one welcoming house, to heal the sick and to announce that the kingdom of God had come near. Towns that rejected them were to be warned by wiping off their dust, and Jesus pronounced woes on Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum. The seventy returned rejoicing that even demons submitted to them in his name. Jesus told them to rejoice instead that their names were written in heaven. Some ancient manuscripts read seventy-two; this entry follows the King James reading of seventy.

Abagtha was one of the seven chamberlains, or eunuchs, who served in the presence of King Ahasuerus of Persia. He is named only in Esth 1:10, alongside Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, Zethar and Carcas. On the seventh day of the king's feast, when Ahasuerus was merry with wine, he gave these seven men a command. The following verse shows the command was to bring Queen Vashti before him. Easton's Bible Dictionary also links him to Esth 2:21. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies Ahasuerus as Xerxes and notes that the name is Persian, one of many Persian features in the Book of Esther. The meaning of the name is uncertain. The same encyclopedia suggests "fortunate one," Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "God-given," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "father of the wine-press." Nothing more is recorded about him.

Abarim was a mountainous region east of the Jordan, in the land of Moab, facing Jericho. The name means "regions beyond" or "the parts across," probably because, seen from Canaan, these highlands lay across the Jordan and the Dead Sea. Israel camped in "the mountains of Abarim, before Nebo" and then went down to the plains of Moab by the Jordan (Num 33:47–48). God told Moses to climb this range to Mount Nebo and view the land promised to Israel (Num 27:12; Deut 32:49). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Nebo as one of its summits. In Jer 22:20 the King James Version translates the word as "the passages," but the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reads it there as the name Abarim, a region listed alongside Lebanon and Bashan. How far north the name reached is uncertain. The location shown here is in the hills near Mount Nebo, in present-day Jordan.

Abda was the father of Adoniram, one of King Solomon's chief officials. He is known only as a name in the list of Solomon's officers, where his son Adoniram is said to have been "over the tribute" (1 Kgs 4:6). Easton's Bible Dictionary explains this as the forced labour, which the Revised Version calls the "levy". Nothing else is recorded about Abda himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may be a shortened form meaning "servant of Yahweh", and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "servant" or "servitude". Another man named Abda appears among the Levites in Nehemiah's time, but he is a different person from Adoniram's father.

Abdeel was the father of Shelemiah, one of three men King Jehoiakim ordered to seize Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet, though the LORD hid them (Jer 36:26). He is known only as Shelemiah's father and appears in this single verse. The king is not named in the verse itself, but the surrounding chapter identifies him as Jehoiakim, who had just burned the scroll of Jeremiah's prophecies. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of his name as "servant of God," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a vapor; a cloud of God."

Abdi was a Levite of the clan of Merari, the son of Malluch and the father of Kishi. He appears only in the genealogy of Ethan, the Merarite singer who stood on the left hand in the temple music that David organized (1 Chr 6:44). That makes Abdi Ethan's grandfather. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that this would place him around the time of King Saul. His name probably means "servant" and is perhaps short for "servant of the LORD." Several other men in the Bible share the name, so this Abdi should not be confused with them.

Abdi was a Levite of the clan of Merari and the father of Kish, one of the Levites who rose up at King Hezekiah's call to cleanse and rededicate the temple at the start of his reign (2 Chr 29:12). Abdi himself is known only as Kish's father. He probably lived a generation before Hezekiah. His name means "my servant" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), probably a shortened form of "servant of the LORD" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). The name is shared by several people. Another Merarite Levite called Abdi appears in the singer Ethan's ancestry (1 Chr 6:44). Some identify him with this man, but the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats them as two people, and this entry follows that view.

Abdi was a man of the family or clan of Elam who lived in the time of Ezra, after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears only in the list of men who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:26). The surrounding chapter shows that these men agreed to send those wives away. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that he was not a Levite but a layman, "of the sons of Elam," and takes the name as probably a shortened form of "servant of the Lord." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "my servant." The name Abdi is also borne by other people in the Bible, including a Levite of Merari's line, so this Abdi should not be confused with them. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Abdiel was a man of the tribe of Gad, the son of Guni and the father of Ahi, named in the Gadite genealogy of 1 Chronicles. The verse calls Ahi, or possibly the family line as a whole, "chief of the house of their fathers." The surrounding passage places the Gadites in Gilead and Bashan east of the Jordan. It says their genealogies were recorded in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel (1 Chr 5:16–17), so Abdiel probably lived in or before that period. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 758 BC, an estimate drawn from that context. His name means "servant of God." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Abdon was a judge of Israel, the son of Hillel, from the town of Pirathon. He succeeded Elon as judge (Judg 12:13). The verse between the two cited here, Judg 12:14, says he had forty sons and thirty grandsons who rode on seventy donkeys, and that he judged Israel for eight years. When he died he was buried in Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites (Judg 12:15). His judgeship is dated to about 1129 BC, an estimate inferred from context. Easton's Bible Dictionary counts him as the tenth judge of Israel and suggests he is probably the Bedan named in 1 Sam 12:11. The name Abdon belongs to several people in the Bible, and this entry concerns the judge.

Abdon was a son of Shashak and a member of the tribe of Benjamin. He appears only once, in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 8:23, where he is listed with his brothers Zichri and Hanan. The full list of Shashak's sons in that passage also includes Antothijah, Elam, Eliel, Hananiah, Heber, Iphedeiah, Ishpan and Penuel. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places him among the Benjamites said to have lived in Jerusalem, possibly in Nehemiah's time, though it notes that the date is unclear. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "servile," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "service." Several other people in the Bible share the name, including a judge of Israel, and there was also a Levitical town called Abdon in Asher. This Abdon should not be confused with them.

Abdon was a Benjamite named as the firstborn son in the family that settled at Gibeon, listed in the genealogies of 1 Chr 8:30 and 1 Chr 9:36. His father is called Jeiel, "the father of Gibeon," in the surrounding verse (1 Chr 9:35), a name also given as Abiel. His mother was Maachah. His younger brothers included Zur, Kish, Baal, Nadab, Ner, Gedor, Ahio, Zacher and Mikloth. Ner appears among them only in the second list. Since the same genealogy makes Ner the grandfather of King Saul (1 Chr 8:33), Abdon was by inference Saul's great-uncle, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. Nothing is recorded about his life beyond his name and place in the family. The name, perhaps meaning "service," is shared by several other people in the Bible, including a judge of Israel, and should not be confused with them.

Abdon was a city in the territory of the tribe of Asher that was assigned, together with its surrounding pasturelands, to the Levites (Josh 21:30; 1 Chr 6:74). The surrounding passages place it among the towns given to the Gershonite clan of Levites, and Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries say the same. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it is probably the same town as Ebron ("Hebron" in the King James Version) in Asher's boundary list in Josh 19:28, where some manuscripts read Abdon. The name may mean "service" or "servile." The site is generally identified with the ruins of Abdeh (Khirbet Abdeh), about 8 to 10 miles northeast of Acco in northern Israel, a few miles inland from the Mediterranean. The location shown here follows that identification. Abdon is a different person from the judge Abdon and the other men of that name.

Abel was the second son of Adam and Eve, the brother of Cain and of Seth, who was born after Abel's death. He kept sheep, while Cain farmed the land (Gen 4:2). When the brothers brought offerings to the LORD, Abel brought firstborn animals from his flock and their fat, and the LORD looked with favor on him and his offering (Gen 4:4). Later, while they were in the field, Cain attacked and killed him, then claimed not to know where he was (Gen 4:8–9). Eve named her next son Seth as one appointed in Abel's place (Gen 4:25). In the New Testament Jesus calls him "righteous Abel," the first in a line of innocent people killed (Matt 23:35; Luke 11:51). Hebrews says he offered a better sacrifice than Cain by faith (Heb 11:4). Easton's Bible Dictionary explains his name as meaning "breath" or "vanity."

Abel was a fortified city in the far north of Israel, near Dan, where Sheba son of Bichri took refuge after his revolt against David. In 2 Sam 20:14–15 it is also called Abel of Bethmaachah, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the short form as an abridgment of the fuller name Abel-beth-maacah. The name means "meadow." Joab's forces besieged the city, built a siege ramp against it and battered its wall. A wise woman of the city then spoke with Joab, recalling an old saying that people would "ask counsel at Abel" to settle disputes, which suggests the town had a long reputation for wisdom. According to the rest of the chapter, the townspeople handed over Sheba's head and the siege ended. The city is usually identified with Tel Abel Beth Maacah (Abil el-Qamh), near present-day Metula, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Abel-beth-maacah, meaning "meadow of the house of Maacah," was a fortified city in the far north of Israel, in Naphtali near Ijon and Dan. When King Asa of Judah persuaded Benhadad of Damascus to turn against Israel, Benhadad's forces struck it with other northern towns (1 Kgs 15:20). The parallel account in 2 Chr 16:4 names Abel-maim instead. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes this as another name for the same city, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia allows it may be a nearby place. In the days of Pekah, Tiglath-pileser of Assyria captured the city and deported its people (2 Kgs 15:29), about 734 BC according to Easton's. In 2 Sam 20, Joab besieged the rebel Sheba there. A wise woman called the city "a mother in Israel," and the townspeople ended the siege by executing Sheba. It is generally identified with Abil el-Qamh, a few miles west of Dan, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Abel-keramim was a town in the region of Ammon, east of the Jordan River. Its name means "meadow of vineyards," and the King James Version translates it as "the plain of the vineyards" rather than treating it as a proper name. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the Revised Version gives it as a place name. It appears only once, in Judg 11:33, as the furthest point of the campaign in which Jephthah (the "he" of the verse, by context of the chapter) struck the Ammonites from Aroer to Minnith, taking twenty cities, until Ammon was subdued before Israel. The exact site is unknown, and several locations in the hills of Ammon have been proposed. The location shown here is a rough one in the area of modern Amman, Jordan.

Abel-maim was a town in the far north of Israel, in the territory of Naphtali. Its only mention is in 2 Chr 16:4. There, Ben-hadad of Damascus, persuaded by King Asa of Judah, sent his army against Israel and struck Abel-maim along with Ijon, Dan and the store cities of Naphtali. The name is usually understood as "meadow of waters," though Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "mourning of waters." The parallel account in 1 Kgs 15:20 names Abel-beth-maacah in its place. For this reason Smith's Bible Dictionary treats Abel-maim as another name for that city. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia allows that it may instead be a separate town nearby. The location shown here follows the identification with Abel-beth-maacah, at modern Abil al-Qamh. The site lies on a height a few miles west of Dan, near the sources of the Jordan.

Abel-meholah, meaning "meadow of dancing," was a town in the Jordan Valley and the home of the prophet Elisha son of Shaphat. God told Elijah to anoint Elisha from there as his successor (1 Kgs 19:16). The following verses describe Elijah finding him plowing, probably near the town. Earlier, the Midianite army routed by Gideon fled toward the border of Abel-meholah (Judg 7:22). Under Solomon, the town marked a limit of Baana's district, which ran from Beth-shean to Abel-meholah (1 Kgs 4:12). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Eusebius and Jerome placed it about ten Roman miles south of Beth-shean. It links the site with the area where Wadi el-Malih or Wadi Helweh enters the valley, and Easton's Bible Dictionary names 'Ain Helweh. Some scholars place it east of the Jordan instead. The location shown here follows the west-bank identification south of Beth-shean.

Abel-mizraim was the name the Canaanites gave to the threshing floor of Atad, where Joseph, his brothers and the Egyptians traveling with them held a solemn mourning for Jacob on their way to bury him in Canaan (Gen 50:11). The surrounding passage says this mourning lasted seven days (Gen 50:10). The name is a wordplay: the local people called it "a grievous mourning to the Egyptians," and Abel-mizraim sounds like "mourning of Egypt," though it can also mean "meadow of Egypt." The verse places it "beyond Jordan." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary take this to mean east of the Jordan, north of the Dead Sea. Easton's Bible Dictionary reads it as west of the Jordan, and Smith's notes suggestions near Jericho or Hebron. The site is unknown, and this entry shows no location.

Abel-shittim, meaning "meadow of the acacias," was a place on the plains of Moab, east of the Jordan River and roughly opposite Jericho. Israel camped there in the last stage of the wilderness journey, along a stretch of the Jordan running from Beth-jeshimoth to Abel-shittim (Num 33:49). This full name appears only in this verse, but Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with the place more often called simply Shittim, the camp where the episode with Moab occurred, from which Joshua sent out the spies, and the last stop before the crossing of the Jordan (Num 25:1; Josh 2:1). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Josephus knew a later town there called Abila, and that scholars of its time placed the site near Kefrein, at the mouth of the wadi of that name. The location shown here follows the Kefrein identification.

Abiah was the second son of the prophet Samuel. He and his older brother Joel served as judges in Beersheba, where their father had appointed them (1 Sam 8:2). The following verse, 1 Sam 8:3, says the brothers did not follow their father's ways but took bribes and perverted justice. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that this caused the discontent that led Israel's elders to ask Samuel for a king. 1 Chr 6:28 lists him among the Levites as Samuel's son, naming the firstborn "Vashni" rather than Joel. Joel is named in 1 Chr 6:33, so Vashni is probably a textual variant or alternate name for the elder brother. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "the Lord is my father." Several other people in the Bible bear this name or its variant Abijah.

Abiah was the wife of Hezron, a grandson of Judah, in the genealogy of Judah's descendants. According to 1 Chr 2:24, after Hezron died at Caleb-ephratah, Abiah bore him a son, Ashur, described as the father of Tekoa. This suggests the child was born after his father's death. "Father of Tekoa" probably means Ashur was the founder or leading figure of the town of Tekoa rather than the father of a person named Tekoa. This is the only verse that mentions her, and the Hebrew of the verse is difficult, so some details of the passage are uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of her name as "the Lord is my father." The same name is borne by several other people in the Bible, and she should not be confused with them.

Abiah was a member of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the nine sons of Becher listed in the Benjamite genealogy at 1 Chr 7:8. Becher was himself a son of Benjamin, so Abiah was Benjamin's grandson. His brothers were Zemira, Joash, Eliezer, Elioenai, Omri, Jerimoth, Anathoth and Alameth. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in this list. The Hebrew name is often written Abijah, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "the Lord is my father." Several other people in the Bible share the name, and this Abiah should not be confused with them.

Abiathar was a priest, the son of Ahimelech son of Ahitub, and the only one of his father's house to escape when Saul had the priests killed. He fled to David carrying the ephod, which David used through him to seek guidance (1 Sam 23:9; 30:7). Under David he served as priest alongside Zadok, helped bring up the ark, and is named among the king's counselors. During Absalom's revolt he stayed in Jerusalem with the ark, and his son Jonathan carried news to David. He later backed Adonijah's bid for the throne. Solomon spared his life for his past service but banished him to Anathoth and put Zadok in his place, fulfilling the word against Eli's house. His son Ahimelech also served as priest. Mark 2:26 places David's eating of the sacred bread "in the days of Abiathar"; Easton's Bible Dictionary reads this as meaning during his lifetime.

Abida was one of the five sons of Midian, listed alongside his brothers Ephah, Epher, Hanoch (also spelled Henoch) and Eldaah. Midian was a son of Abraham by Keturah, so Abida was Abraham's grandson. Both genealogies that mention him count these descendants among "the children of Keturah" (Gen 25:4; 1 Chr 1:33). Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes him to have been, apparently, the head of an Arab tribe, since the names in this list are generally understood to stand for peoples descended from Midian. His name is commonly explained as meaning "father of knowledge" or "my father knows." The King James Version spells it Abidah in Genesis and Abida in Chronicles.

Abidan, son of Gideoni, was the leader of the tribe of Benjamin during Israel's time in the wilderness after the Exodus. He was one of the tribal heads named to help Moses take the census at Sinai (Num 1:11). In the arrangement of the camp, he was captain of Benjamin, which camped on the west side with Ephraim and Manasseh (Num 2:22). When the tribal leaders brought offerings at the dedication of the tabernacle's altar, Abidan presented Benjamin's gifts on the ninth day. These included peace offerings of two oxen, five rams, five male goats and five year-old lambs (Num 7:60, 65). When Israel set out from Sinai, he commanded Benjamin's company on the march (Num 10:24). His name is usually explained as "father is judge" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "father of judgment" (Hitchcock's Bible Names).

Abiel the Arbathite was one of David's mighty men, the elite warriors listed in 1 Chr 11:32. The parallel list in 2 Sam 23:31 calls him Abi-albon, and Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary treat the two names as referring to the same man. "Arbathite" probably means he came from Beth-arabah, a town on the border between Judah and Benjamin near the Jordan valley. This is an inference from the form of the name. His name is usually explained as "God is father" or "my father is God" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in the list of David's warriors.

Abiezer is the name of a clan of the tribe of Manasseh, used here for the clan's home district west of the Jordan. In Judg 8:2 Gideon, himself an Abiezrite, calms the angry men of Ephraim with a proverb: Ephraim's 'gleaning', its capture of the Midianite princes, was worth more than Abiezer's whole 'vintage', his own clan's victory. Elsewhere, Josh 17:2 lists Abiezer among the families of Manasseh, and Judg 6:11, 24 and 34 place Gideon's town of Ophrah among the Abiezrites and show the clan rallying to him. The district's exact extent is not given. The location shown here lies near modern Afula at the edge of the Jezreel Valley, one proposed site for Ophrah, though other sites have also been suggested. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as 'father of help.'

Abiezer was a man from Anathoth, a town of Benjamin, who is listed among David's mighty men, the elite group of warriors known as "the thirty" (2 Sam 23:27; 1 Chr 11:28). The King James Version spells his town-name in several ways (Anethothite, Antothite, Anetothite), all referring to Anathoth. He also appears as the captain of the army division that served David in the ninth month of each year, a rotating course of twenty-four thousand men, and is identified there as a Benjamite (1 Chr 27:12). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the warrior and the divisional captain to be the same man, and this entry follows that view. His name means "father of help." Several other men in the Bible share the name Abiezer, so he should not be confused with them.

Abiezer was a member of the tribe of Manasseh, named in its genealogy as a son of Hammoleketh and a brother of Ishod and Mahalah (1 Chr 7:18). By inference from the surrounding verses, Hammoleketh was the sister of Gilead, Machir's son, which would make Abiezer a great-grandson of Manasseh through his mother's line. STEPBible Proper Names also places him among Manasseh's descendants. He is probably the ancestor of the Abiezrite clan of Manasseh, which Josh 17:2 lists among the tribe's family groups and to which Gideon later belonged (Judg 6:11), though this link is drawn from those connected passages rather than stated in 1 Chr 7:18. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names renders "father of help," is shared by several people in the Bible, including one of David's warriors from Anathoth.

Abiezer was a descendant of Manasseh son of Joseph and the founder of a clan within that tribe. In Num 26:30 he appears as Jeezer, a son of Gilead, whose descendants were the Jeezerites. Josh 17:2 lists the children of Abiezer among the Manassite families that received a share of land. Easton's Bible Dictionary, drawing on 1 Chr 7:18, makes him instead a son of Hammoleketh, Gilead's sister. This entry follows the listing as a son of Gilead. His clan later produced the judge Gideon. When Gideon blew the trumpet, Abiezer gathered to him (Judg 6:34), and Gideon spoke of the "vintage of Abiezer" while calming the men of Ephraim (Judg 8:2). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as "father of help." Several other men in the Bible share this name.

Abigail was the wife of Nabal, a wealthy and harsh man of the house of Caleb living at Carmel in Judah. She is described as intelligent and beautiful. When Nabal insulted messengers sent by David, a servant warned her. She quickly loaded donkeys with bread, wine, meat, grain, raisins and figs, rode out to meet David, and bowed before him. David blessed God for sending her. About ten days later Nabal died, by inference from the wider chapter, and David sent for Abigail to marry him. She went with five maidservants and became his wife. She lived with David at Gath, was taken captive at Ziklag, and moved with him to Hebron. There she bore his second son, called Chileab in 2 Sam 3:3 and Daniel in 1 Chr 3:1. Another Abigail, David's sister, also appears in the Bible.

Abigail was a sister of Zeruiah, a half-sister of King David, and the mother of Amasa. She is a different person from Abigail the wife of Nabal, who later married David. 1 Chr 2:16 counts her among the sisters of Jesse's sons, while 2 Sam 17:25 calls her the daughter of Nahash. This entry therefore treats her as David's half-sister, probably sharing a mother with him but having a different father. Her husband is called Ithra an Israelite in 2 Sam 17:25 and Jether the Ishmaelite in 1 Chr 2:17. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes these as the same man and reads "Ishmaelite" in both places. Her son Amasa was made commander of Absalom's army in place of Joab, who was Abigail's nephew through Zeruiah. Hitchcock's Bible Names explains her name as meaning "the father's joy."

Abihail was a Levite, the father of Zuriel. In Moses' time Zuriel was chief of the families descended from Merari, one of Levi's sons. During the census of the Levites in the wilderness, Zuriel's clan was assigned to camp on the north side of the tabernacle (Num 3:35). Abihail is known only through his son, and nothing more is recorded about him. By inference from the setting, he lived around the time of the Exodus, and Smith's Bible Dictionary places him as a contemporary of Moses. The name means "father of strength" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other people in the Old Testament share it, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts five, so this Merarite should not be confused with the others.

Abihail was the wife of Abishur and the mother of his sons Ahban and Molid, named in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah (1 Chr 2:29). The surrounding genealogy places Abishur in the line of Hezron and Jerahmeel, so she belongs to the Jerahmeelite branch of Judah, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes. Nothing more is recorded about her. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names explain as "father of strength," is borne by several people in the Old Testament, both men and women. This Abihail should not be confused with the others, such as the father of Queen Esther.

Abihail was a member of the tribe of Gad, named in the Gadite genealogy of 1 Chronicles as the son of Huri. His ancestry is traced back through Jaroah, Gilead, Michael, Jeshishai and Jahdo to Buz. His seven sons were Michael, Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Jachan, Zia and Heber. The surrounding passage places these Gadite families in Gilead and Bashan, east of the Jordan. It says their genealogies were recorded in the days of King Jotham of Judah and King Jeroboam of Israel (1 Chr 5:17). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts him among the heads of the tribe of Gad. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as "father of strength."

Abihail was a woman of the tribe of Judah named in 2 Chr 11:18 in connection with King Rehoboam's marriages. She is called the daughter of Eliab son of Jesse, David's eldest brother; Smith's Bible Dictionary takes 'daughter' here to mean descendant. Readings of the verse differ. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary treat her as a second wife of Rehoboam, and this entry follows that view. On this reading, the sons listed in the next verse, Jeush, Shamariah and Zaham (2 Chr 11:19), are hers. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and the Tyndale House proper-names index instead take her as the mother of Mahalath, so that she was the wife of Jerimoth, David's son. Either way, the verse shows marriage within David's extended family. The name is shared by several other people in the Bible.

Abihail was the father of Esther, the Jewish woman who became queen to the Persian king Ahasuerus, and the uncle of Mordecai (Esth 2:15). Since Mordecai is described as Esther's cousin and as having taken her as his own daughter, Abihail had probably died while she was young. Esth 2:7 says that both her parents were dead. He is named only to identify Esther, both when she went in to the king and when she and Mordecai wrote to confirm the observance of Purim (Esth 9:29). Nothing else is recorded about him, though Esth 2:5 traces Mordecai's family to the tribe of Benjamin, so Abihail likely belonged to it too. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as "father of strength," is shared by several other people in the Old Testament, and this entry concerns only Esther's father.

Abihu was the second son of Aaron and his wife Elisheba, and brother of Nadab, Eleazar and Ithamar, of the tribe of Levi. His name means "he is my father" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). With his father and older brother Nadab, he went part of the way up Mount Sinai with Moses and seventy elders of Israel to worship at a distance. He and his brothers were set apart to serve as priests alongside Aaron. Abihu and Nadab later offered "strange fire" before the LORD in their censers, fire the LORD had not commanded, and both died before the LORD in the wilderness of Sinai. They had no children, so Eleazar and Ithamar carried on the priestly office. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggest the brothers may have been drunk, since a ban on priests drinking wine follows soon after in Leviticus 10.

Abihud was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named as one of the sons of Bela in the genealogy of 1 Chr 8:3. Bela was Benjamin's firstborn, which made Abihud a grandson of Benjamin. In that list he appears alongside Addar and Gera, and the wider genealogy counts several brothers, among them Abishua, Naaman and Ahoah. The name is usually taken to mean "father of majesty" or "my father is majesty." Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he is the same man as the Ahihud named a few verses later, in 1 Chr 8:7. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with the Abiud of Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, a different person.

Abijah was the mother of King Hezekiah of Judah and the daughter of a man named Zechariah. She is named in 2 Chr 29:1, while the parallel account in 2 Kgs 18:2 gives her name in the shorter form Abi. Her name means "the Lord is my father" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). She was the wife of King Ahaz, Hezekiah's father and predecessor. Through her son she belongs to the royal line of David, which the Gospel of Matthew traces in its genealogy of Jesus. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests her father may be the Zechariah whom Isaiah called as a reliable witness (Isa 8:2), but this identification is uncertain. Several other people in the Bible, both men and women, share the name Abijah.

Abijah was a son of Jeroboam, the first king of the northern kingdom of Israel, and a brother of Nadab, who later succeeded their father on the throne. He is one of several people in the Bible with this name, which means "the Lord is my father" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). 1 Kgs 14:1 records that he fell sick. The surrounding narrative in 1 Kgs 14 says Jeroboam sent his wife in disguise to the aged, blind prophet Ahijah to ask whether the boy would recover. Ahijah recognized her and foretold the boy's death. He said Abijah alone of Jeroboam's family would be buried and mourned, because in him "some good thing toward the Lord" was found. The child died as his mother returned home, and all Israel mourned him. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as dying in childhood.

Abijah was a priest whose name was given to the eighth of the twenty-four priestly divisions. These divisions were assigned by lot to take turns serving at the sanctuary (1 Chr 24:10). The surrounding chapter places the arrangement in David's reign. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a descendant of Eleazar, son of Aaron. His name means "the Lord is my father" or "Yahweh is father." Centuries later, in the days of Herod king of Judea, the priest Zechariah, husband of Elizabeth, is said to belong to "the course of Abia," the Greek form of the name (Luke 1:5). Zechariah is known from the same chapter as the father of John the Baptist. Several other people in the Bible are also called Abijah, including a king of Judah and a son of Jeroboam. This entry refers only to the priest who headed the eighth division.

Abijah, a name meaning "the Lord is my father" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), was a priest or priestly family of the period after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears among the priests who returned with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:4, read with Neh 12:1). In the next generation, under the high priest Joiakim, a priestly household called by his name was headed by Zichri (Neh 12:17). An Abijah is also listed among the priests who set their seal to Nehemiah's covenant to keep God's law (Neh 10:7). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia tentatively treats these as one man, and this entry follows that view. Because the lists span many decades, Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the name may stand for a priestly family, perhaps linked to the earlier priestly division of Abijah (1 Chr 24:10). Several other people in the Bible share this name.

Abijah, also called Abijam and Abia, was king of Judah, the son and successor of Rehoboam and the father of Asa. His mother was Maachah, called the daughter of Absalom (2 Chr 11:20). 2 Chr 13:2 names her Michaiah, daughter of Uriel of Gibeah. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Michaiah as a variant of the name and 'daughter' as meaning granddaughter. Rehoboam made him chief among his brothers, intending him to be king. He began to reign in Jeroboam's eighteenth year and ruled three years in Jerusalem, about 958–956 BC by inference from context. Chronicles describes his war with Jeroboam of Israel. He addressed the northern army from Mount Zemaraim, then defeated it and took Bethel, Jeshanah and Ephrain. He had fourteen wives, twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters. He was buried in the city of David. Matthew lists him in the genealogy of Jesus. Several other people share the name.

Abilene was a district on the eastern slope of the Anti-Lebanon mountains, northwest of Damascus. It appears in the Bible only in Luke 3:1, where it is named as the tetrarchy of Lysanias in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, the year John the Baptist began preaching. The region took its name from its chief town, Abila. According to Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries, Abila stood about 18 miles from Damascus in the gorge of Suk Wady Barada, beside the Barada River. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a Greek inscription found there that mentions a "freedman of Lysanias the tetrarch." The same work records that Abilene was later granted to Agrippa I and afterward to Agrippa II. The location shown here follows the identification with the Suk Wady Barada area.

Abimael was a son of Joktan, named in the Table of Nations in Gen 10:28 and in the matching genealogy in 1 Chr 1:22. He is listed between Obal (called Ebal in Chronicles) and Sheba, ninth of Joktan's thirteen sons. Neighboring verses in these lists, outside the passages given here, make Joktan a son of Eber and a descendant of Shem. Nothing else is recorded about Abimael himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains his name as "my father is God" and regards it as South Arabian, like several names in the list. Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "a father sent from God." Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take it as "father of Mael," and Smith's suggests he was probably the ancestor of an Arabian tribe. As with his brothers, his name may stand for a people as well as an individual.

Abimelech (King of Gerar) was a Philistine ruler of Gerar who dealt with both Abraham and Isaac. After Abraham called Sarah his sister, Abimelech took her, but God warned him in a dream that she was a married woman. He had not touched her. He rebuked Abraham, returned Sarah with gifts of livestock and servants, and invited him to settle in his land. God then healed his household of barrenness (Gen 20:17–18). Later, with his army commander Phichol, he made a covenant with Abraham at Beersheba after a dispute over a well. In Isaac's time Abimelech discovered that Rebekah was Isaac's wife, not his sister, and ordered that no one harm them. He later asked Isaac to leave and then came to make peace with him. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries treat Isaac's Abimelech as a later king, probably a son, and suggest the name may have been a royal title. This entry treats both accounts under one name.

Abimelech, one of several men of this name in the Bible, was a son of Gideon (also called Jerubbaal) by a concubine from Shechem. Backed by his mother's relatives, he won over the men of Shechem, used seventy pieces of silver from the house of Baal-berith to hire followers, and killed his seventy brothers "upon one stone." Only Jotham escaped (Judg 9:5). The Shechemites then made him king, about 1218 BC by inference from context. Jotham warned that Abimelech and Shechem would destroy each other. After three years Shechem turned against him under Gaal son of Ebed. Abimelech defeated Gaal, destroyed Shechem and sowed it with salt, and burned about a thousand people in its tower. While attacking the tower of Thebez, he was struck on the head by a millstone thrown by a woman. According to Judg 9:54, he then had his armor-bearer kill him.

Abimelech, son of Jerubbesheth, is the man Joab mentions in 2 Sam 11:21. There Joab anticipates David's anger at soldiers who went too close to the wall of Rabbah, and recalls that Abimelech died at Thebez when a woman threw a piece of a millstone down on him from the wall. Jerubbesheth is another form of Jerubbaal, the name given to Gideon, so this is Gideon's son Abimelech. Judges 8–9 tells his story, and Smith's Bible Dictionary summarizes it. He was born to Gideon's concubine from Shechem. After his father's death he killed his brothers, leaving only Jotham alive, and the people of Shechem made him king. After a three-year reign he put down a revolt in Shechem and then attacked Thebez, where the woman struck him. The name means "father of the king," and several other men in the Bible bear it.

Abinadab was a man of Kirjath-jearim whose house sheltered the ark of the LORD after the Philistines sent it back. The men of the town brought the ark to his house "in the hill" and consecrated his son Eleazar to look after it (1 Sam 7:1). According to 1 Sam 7:2 it stayed there twenty years. When David later moved it, Abinadab's sons Uzzah and Ahio drove the new cart that carried it from the house, with Ahio walking ahead (2 Sam 6:3–4; 1 Chr 13:7). The following verses record that Uzzah died after touching the ark. The "Gibeah" of 2 Samuel is probably not a separate town but the Hebrew word for "hill," pointing to the same hilltop house. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries describe him as a Levite. Several other men in the Bible share his name, including a son of Jesse and a son of Saul.

Abinadab was the second son of Jesse of the tribe of Judah and an older brother of King David. When Samuel came to Bethlehem to anoint a new king, Jesse had his sons pass before the prophet. Abinadab followed his elder brother Eliab, and Samuel declared that the LORD had not chosen him either (1 Sam 16:8). Later, he and his brothers Eliab and Shammah, Jesse's three eldest sons, followed Saul to war against the Philistines. This was the campaign in which Goliath issued his challenge (1 Sam 17:13). The genealogy of Judah also names him as Jesse's second son (1 Chr 2:13). His name is usually taken to mean "my father is willing" or "father of willingness" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia; Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a son of Saul.

Abinadab was the father of one of King Solomon's twelve district officers, who in turn supplied food for the king's household, as the surrounding list in 1 Kings 4 explains. That son is called simply "the son of Abinadab" in the King James Version, or Ben-Abinadab in the Revised Version. He governed the whole region of Dor on the Mediterranean coast and married Solomon's daughter Taphath (1 Kgs 4:11). Nothing else is recorded about Abinadab himself. This entry follows Smith's Bible Dictionary in treating him as the officer's father. Easton's Bible Dictionary applies the name to the officer himself. The name is usually taken to mean "father of willingness" or "my father is willing." Several men in the Bible bear this name, so it is uncertain whether he is the same as any other Abinadab.

Abinadab was a son of King Saul, listed among Saul's sons in the genealogies alongside Jonathan, Malchishua and Eshbaal (Ish-bosheth). He was killed by the Philistines together with his father and his brothers Jonathan and Malchishua. The surrounding narrative places this battle on Mount Gilboa (1 Sam 31:1). 1 Sam 14:49 names Saul's sons as Jonathan, Ishui and Melchishua but does not mention Abinadab. For this reason many, including the STEPBible names index, take Ishui (Ishvi) to be another name for Abinadab, and this entry follows that view. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats Ishvi under a separate heading. His mother was Ahinoam, Saul's wife (1 Sam 14:50). His sisters were Merab and Michal. Armoni and Mephibosheth were his half-brothers, Saul's sons by his concubine Rizpah (2 Sam 21:8). The name is generally explained as "my father is willing." Several other men in the Bible share it.

Abinoam was the father of Barak, the Israelite commander who, with the prophetess Deborah, led the army that defeated the Canaanite forces under Sisera. He is known only through his son, who is called "Barak the son of Abinoam" each time the name appears (Judg 4:6, 12; 5:1, 12). Barak was summoned from Kedesh-naphtali, so the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes Abinoam as a man of that town, a reasonable inference from the passage. Twice the phrase comes in the Song of Deborah, which celebrates the victory (Judg 5:1, 12). Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "father of kindness," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "father of pleasantness." Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the period to about 1300 BC, an estimate.

Abiram (son of Eliab) was a member of the tribe of Reuben and a brother of Dathan and Nemuel. With Dathan, On son of Peleth, and the Levite Korah, he led a revolt against Moses and Aaron during Israel's time in the wilderness (Num 16:1; 26:9). When Moses summoned the two brothers, they refused to come (Num 16:12). Moses then went to them, followed by the elders. The congregation was told to move away from their tents, and Dathan and Abiram stood at their doors with their wives and children (Num 16:24–27). The earth opened and swallowed them along with their households, tents and possessions (Deut 11:6; Ps 106:17). This was distinct from the rest of Korah's company, for Num 26:11 notes that Korah's sons survived. Later passages recall the event as a warning to Israel. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "high father."

Abiram was the firstborn son of Hiel the Bethelite and the brother of Segub, Hiel's youngest son. He is mentioned only in 1 Kgs 16:34, which reports that during Ahab's reign Hiel rebuilt Jericho, laying its foundation "in Abiram his firstborn" and setting up its gates "in his youngest son Segub." The verse presents this as fulfilling the word spoken through Joshua, whose curse in Josh 6:26 warned that whoever rebuilt Jericho would lose his eldest and youngest sons. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take Abiram's death as the outcome of that curse. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mentions a possible alternative, that Hiel offered his sons as foundation sacrifices. This entry follows the more common reading, that Abiram died when the foundation was laid. He is a different man from Abiram son of Eliab, who joined Korah's rebellion in the wilderness.

Abishag was a young woman from Shunem, a town that Smith's Bible Dictionary places in the tribe of Issachar. She was chosen after a search throughout Israel for a beautiful young woman to attend King David in his extreme old age. She served as his personal attendant, and she was present in the king's chamber when Bathsheba came to urge him to name Solomon as his successor. The surrounding passage (1 Kgs 1:4) adds that David did not have sexual relations with her. After David's death, his son Adonijah asked Bathsheba to request Abishag from Solomon as his wife. Solomon treated the request as a bid for the throne. He replied that his mother might as well ask the kingdom for his elder brother, and the account that follows (1 Kgs 2:25) records that he had Adonijah put to death. Nothing further is said of Abishag.

Abishai was a son of Zeruiah and brother of Joab and Asahel. 1 Chr 2:16 places Zeruiah among David's sisters, making him David's nephew. He volunteered to go with David by night into Saul's camp and urged him to kill the sleeping king, but David refused. With Joab he pursued Abner after Asahel's death and later joined in killing him. He led troops against the Ammonites, and 1 Chr 18:12 credits him with killing eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt. During Absalom's revolt he twice asked to kill Shimei for cursing David, and he commanded a third of David's army in the decisive battle. He pursued the rebel Sheba and rescued David by killing a Philistine giant, named Ishbi-benob in 2 Sam 21:16. He was chief among a group of three of David's warriors after killing three hundred men with his spear.

Abishua was a Levite priest, the son of Phinehas and grandson of Eleazar, Aaron's son. He appears only in genealogies of Aaron's descendants, where he is named as the father of Bukki, who in turn was the father of Uzzi (1 Chr 6:4–5, 50). Ezra 7:5 traces Ezra's own priestly ancestry back through Abishua to Aaron. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him in the line of the high priests, and because his father Phinehas and grandfather Eleazar held that office, he is probably to be counted among them, though the verses themselves do not say he served as high priest. Nothing else is recorded of his life. The name is shared by another man, a Benjamite descendant of Bela, who is a different person. The meaning of the name is uncertain; suggestions include "father of deliverance" (Smith's) and "father of wealth" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia).

Abishua was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, listed in 1 Chr 8:4 among the sons of Bela, Benjamin's firstborn, which makes him Benjamin's grandson. Nothing is recorded about him beyond his place in this genealogy, where he is named alongside Addar, Gera, Abihud, Naaman and Ahoah. The brothers listed with him here combine this list with a different list of Bela's sons in 1 Chr 7:7, which names Ezbon, Uzzi, Uzziel, Jerimoth and Iri. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "father of deliverance", Hitchcock's Bible Names "father of salvation", and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "father of wealth". The same name belongs to another man, a priest descended from Aaron through Phinehas, who should not be confused with this Benjamite.

Abishur was a man of the tribe of Judah who appears only in the genealogy of Jerahmeel's descendants in 1 Chronicles. He was a son of Shammai, son of Onam, and his brother was Nadab (1 Chr 2:28). His wife was Abihail, and she bore him two sons, Ahban and Molid (1 Chr 2:29). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts him as a great-grandson of Jerahmeel and Atarah, tracing the line through Onam, Atarah's son in the surrounding verses. Nothing else is recorded about his life. His name is usually explained as "my father is a wall" or "father of the wall." Easton's Bible Dictionary takes this to mean "mason."

Abital was one of the wives of King David and the mother of his son Shephatiah. She appears only in the parallel lists of the sons born to David at Hebron, where Shephatiah is counted as the fifth son (2 Sam 3:4; 1 Chr 3:3). By inference from the context of those lists, she married David during his seven-year reign at Hebron, before he moved his capital to Jerusalem. Nothing else is recorded about her family or life. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls her David's fifth wife, following her son's place in the list. Her name is usually explained as "my father is dew" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "father of dew" (Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary).

Abitub was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named once in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles. He was a son of Shaharaim by his wife Hushim, and his full brother was Elpaal (1 Chr 8:11). From the surrounding verses (1 Chr 8:8–10), Shaharaim also had sons by another wife, Hodesh, while living in the country of Moab: Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcham, Jeuz, Shachia and Mirma, who were Abitub's half-brothers. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes Abitub to have been born in Moab, though the passage does not say clearly where Hushim's sons were born. Nothing else is recorded about him. Through his brother Elpaal, the genealogy goes on to name descendants who built the towns of Ono and Lod (1 Chr 8:12). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names give the meaning of his name as "father of goodness."

Abiud was a man of the tribe of Judah named in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus as the son of Zerubbabel and the father of Eliakim (Matt 1:13). Nothing else is recorded about him, and Matthew is the only book that uses this name. The children of Zerubbabel listed in 1 Chr 3:19–20 include Meshullam, Hananiah, their sister Shelomith, Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah and Jushab-hesed. This entry counts Abiud among those children, although his name does not appear in that list. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him with Juda in Luke's genealogy (Luke 3:26) and with Obadiah in 1 Chr 3:21. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names give the name's meaning as "father of praise," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "my father is majesty."

Abner, son of Ner, was commander of King Saul's army. 1 Sam 14:50–51 can be read to call him Saul's uncle or, since Ner and Saul's father Kish were both sons of Abiel, Saul's cousin. This entry follows the cousin reading, as does the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Abner brought David before Saul after Goliath was killed, sat beside the king at meals, and was rebuked by David for failing to guard Saul. After Saul died, he made Saul's son Ishbosheth king at Mahanaim. When David's men defeated his forces at Gibeon, he killed Joab's brother Asahel.
