Later he quarrelled with Ishbosheth over one of Saul's concubines (Rizpah, named in 2 Sam 3:7) and met David at Hebron, offering to bring all Israel over to him. Joab then killed him at the city gate to avenge Asahel. David buried him in Hebron and mourned him. His son Jaasiel later led the tribe of Benjamin.

Abraham, first called Abram, was the son of Terah and brother of Nahor and Haran (Gen 11:26). God brought him out of Ur of the Chaldees and renamed him Abraham (Neh 9:7; 1 Chr 1:27), a name Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as "father of a great multitude." He settled in Canaan while his nephew Lot moved toward Sodom (Gen 13:12). His wife Sarah bore him Isaac in old age (Gen 21:7). Sarah's maid Hagar bore Ishmael, and Keturah bore six more sons. God promised that all nations would be blessed in him (Gen 18:18) and swore to give the land to his descendants (Exod 33:1). He was tested by being told to offer Isaac (Heb 11:17) and bought a burial cave from the sons of Heth (Gen 23:20). Later Scripture calls him God's friend (2 Chr 20:7) and an ancestor of Israel and of Jesus (Matt 1:1). He lived about 1996–1821 BC, by inference from context.

The separation of Abraham and Lot was the parting of Abram (later called Abraham) and his nephew Lot after they returned from Egypt to the area between Bethel and Ai. Both men had grown wealthy in livestock, and the land could not support their combined flocks, so their herdsmen quarreled. Abram proposed that they part peacefully because they were family, and he offered Lot first choice of land. Lot chose the well-watered plain of the Jordan and settled among its cities, pitching his tent toward Sodom, whose people the passage describes as very wicked. Afterward the LORD told Abram to look in every direction and promised to give him and his descendants all the land he could see, with offspring as countless as dust. Abram then moved to the oaks of Mamre at Hebron and built an altar there. This entry dates the event to about 1920 BC, by inference from context.

The entry of Abraham into Canaan was the journey in which Abram (later called Abraham) left Haran for the land God promised to show him. His father Terah had earlier set out from Ur of the Chaldees toward Canaan with Abram, Sarai and Lot, but settled and died in Haran. In response to God's call and promise to make him a great nation and a blessing to all families of the earth, Abram departed at age seventy-five with Sarai, his nephew Lot, their possessions and the people they had acquired. He passed through to Shechem, to the plain of Moreh, while Canaanites still lived there. The LORD appeared to him and promised the land to his descendants, and Abram built an altar. He then camped between Bethel and Ai, built another altar, and continued south toward the Negeb. The date of about 1921 BC is an estimate inferred from context.

The episode of Abraham going to Egypt (Gen 12:10–20) took place soon after Abram, as he was then called, entered Canaan. A severe famine drove him south to stay in Egypt for a time. As they neared the border, he feared the Egyptians would kill him to take his beautiful wife Sarai, so he asked her to say she was his sister. Pharaoh's officials praised her to the king, and she was taken into Pharaoh's household. Pharaoh treated Abram well for her sake and gave him sheep, oxen, donkeys, camels and servants. The LORD then struck Pharaoh and his house with great plagues because of Sarai. Pharaoh confronted Abram for not saying she was his wife, returned her, and had his men send them away with all their possessions. The date of about 1921 BC is an estimate inferred from context.

The Abrahamic Covenant was God's call and promise to Abram, later named Abraham, recorded in Gen 12:1–3. God told him to leave his country, his relatives and his father's household and go to a land God would show him. God promised to make him into a great nation, to bless him, to make his name great, and to make him a blessing. God would bless those who blessed him and curse those who cursed him, and through him all the families of the earth would be blessed. This entry dates the event to about 1921 BC, an estimate inferred from context. That fits Gen 12:4, which says Abram was seventy-five when he left Haran. The word "covenant" does not appear in these verses. Later passages, such as Gen 15 and Gen 17, describe God formally making a covenant with Abraham, expanding these promises of land and descendants.

Abronah was one of the places where Israel camped during the wilderness journey. It lay between Jotbathah and Ezion-geber, the station just before Ezion-geber at the northern end of the Gulf of Aqaba (Num 33:34–35). The King James Version spells the name "Ebronah," while the Revised Version uses "Abronah," as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it on the march from Sinai toward Kadesh. Its exact site is unknown. Because Ezion-geber was near the head of the gulf, Abronah was probably somewhere in the Arabah valley a short distance north of modern Eilat and Aqaba. The location shown here is a rough estimate in that area.

Absalom was David's third son, born at Hebron to Maacah, daughter of Talmai king of Geshur (2 Sam 3:3; 1 Chr 3:2). He was praised above everyone in Israel for his beauty. After his half-brother Amnon wronged his sister Tamar, Absalom waited two years. He then had his servants kill Amnon at a sheep-shearing feast at Baal-hazor and fled to his grandfather in Geshur. Joab later brought him back to Jerusalem. Absalom gathered chariots and followers, courted people who had grievances, and launched a revolt from Hebron that forced David to flee Jerusalem. Ahithophel advised him, but Hushai, secretly loyal to David, undermined that advice. In the battle that followed, Absalom's head caught in an oak. Joab killed him, he was buried under a heap of stones, and David mourned him deeply. He is also called Abishalom, and his daughter Maacah married King Rehoboam (1 Kgs 15:10; 2 Chr 11:20).

Accad was a city in the land of Shinar, named in Gen 10:10 as one of the first cities of Nimrod's kingdom, along with Babel, Erech and Calneh. This is its only mention in the Bible. This entry dates the start of that kingdom to about 1822 BC, an estimate inferred from context. Shinar is generally understood as southern Mesopotamia, in present-day Iraq. The STEPBible proper-names index takes Accad to be the ancient city of Akkad, which gave its name to the Akkadian people and language. The exact site of that city has not been found. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls its position quite uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions an identification with the mounds of Akker Kuf, north of Babylon, and places the city near the Euphrates, opposite Sippar. The location shown here is a general placement in central Iraq, south of modern Baghdad.

Acco was a coastal city on the Mediterranean, a few miles north of Mount Carmel on the northern side of the bay now shared with Haifa. It lay within the territory assigned to the tribe of Asher, but Judg 1:31 records that Asher did not drive out its inhabitants, listing it with Sidon, Achzib and other towns that stayed in Canaanite or Phoenician hands. Its harbour and its position on the coast road gave it lasting importance. According to Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, it was later renamed Ptolemais after the Ptolemaic kings of Egypt. Under that name it is probably the port where Paul stopped on his last journey to Jerusalem (Acts 21:7). During the Crusades it became known as Acre. The location shown here is the modern city of Acre (Arabic Akka) in northern Israel.

Achaia was the Roman province covering southern Greece, including the Peloponnesus, with Corinth as its main city. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the name once meant a narrow strip on the northern Peloponnesus, but the New Testament always uses it for the larger province. It was governed by a proconsul, rendered "deputy" in the King James Version, and Gallio held that office when Jews in Corinth brought Paul before his judgment seat (Acts 18:12). Apollos later went there and helped the believers (Acts 18:27). Paul addressed 2 Corinthians to the church at Corinth and to all the saints in Achaia, and he called the household of Stephanas its firstfruits (2 Cor 1:1; 1 Cor 16:15). Achaia is often paired with Macedonia, the province to its north, so that the two together cover all of Greece. The churches of both gave money for the poor believers in Jerusalem (Rom 15:26; 2 Cor 9:2).

Achaicus was a Christian from Corinth who, with Stephanas and Fortunatus, came to the apostle Paul. Paul wrote that he was glad of their coming, because they had supplied what was lacking on the Corinthians' part (1 Cor 16:17). This probably means that their presence made up for Paul's absence from the church. By inference from the context, Paul was writing from Ephesus (1 Cor 16:8). Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests the three men came to consult him about the church's affairs and probably carried the Corinthians' letter that Paul mentions in 1 Cor 7:1. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia infers from 1 Cor 16:15–18 that Achaicus was among the church's leaders, whom Paul urged the believers to recognize. His name means "belonging to Achaia," the Roman province that included Corinth. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Achan, son of Carmi, was a man of the tribe of Judah, descended through Zabdi from Zerah. He took items from the spoil of Jericho that had been devoted to God, and the Lord's anger fell on Israel (Josh 7:1). After Israel's defeat at Ai, Joshua brought the tribe forward group by group and household by household, and Achan was singled out (Josh 7:18). Urged by Joshua to confess, he admitted his sin (Josh 7:19–20). He was brought with the silver, a garment, a wedge of gold, his family and all his possessions to the valley of Achor (Josh 7:24), where, as the account goes on to say, he was stoned and burned. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the text is not explicit about what happened to his family. Later passages recall that his sin brought wrath on all Israel (Josh 22:20), and 1 Chr 2:7 calls him Achar, “the troubler of Israel.”

Achbor was the father of Baalhanan, one of the kings who ruled Edom before Israel had kings. Baalhanan took the throne after the death of Saul (called Shaul in 1 Chr 1:49) and was followed by Hadar (Gen 36:38–39). The text says nothing about Achbor himself and names him only to identify his son. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts Baalhanan as the seventh of the eight Edomite kings in the list and gives the meaning of Achbor's name as "mouse." Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Achbor as an Edomite king. The same name belongs to a different man, an official in the court of King Josiah of Judah, who is a separate person.

Achbor son of Michaiah was an official of King Josiah of Judah. He was one of five men, along with Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Shaphan the scribe and Asahiah, whom the king sent to ask the Lord about the book of the law found in the temple (2 Kgs 22:12). The group went to the prophetess Huldah in Jerusalem and consulted her (2 Kgs 22:14). The parallel account in 2 Chr 34:20 calls him Abdon son of Micah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he is probably the same Achbor named in Jer 26:22 and 36:12 as the father of Elnathan, an official under King Jehoiakim. The name Achbor is shared by other people in the Bible, including the father of an Edomite king.

Achbor was the father of Elnathan, an official at the court of King Jehoiakim of Judah. He is mentioned only through his son, who was sent to Egypt to bring back the prophet Urijah (Jer 26:22) and who later sat with the princes in the scribe's chamber when Jeremiah's scroll was read (Jer 36:12). Several men in the Bible bear this name. Many readers identify him with Achbor son of Michaiah, the court official whom King Josiah sent with others to consult the prophetess Huldah (2 Kgs 22:12, 14). That would place him in the royal service a generation before his son, but the identification is an inference and is not stated in the text. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a rat" or "bruising."

Achim was an ancestor of Jesus named in Matthew's genealogy, the son of Sadoc and the father of Eliud (Matt 1:14). He is mentioned nowhere else in the Bible. He belongs to the part of the line that follows the return from exile in Babylon, so the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a descendant of Zerubbabel. That places him in the royal line of the tribe of Judah. Nothing is recorded about his life beyond his place in the list. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests that the Hebrew form of his name would be Jachin, a short form of Jehoiachin, meaning "the Lord will establish." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meanings "preparing," "revenging," or "confirming."

Achish was a Philistine king of Gath, called son of Maoch (1 Sam 27:2) or Maachah (1 Kgs 2:39). David first fled to him from Saul, but when Achish's servants recognized David as the hero of Israel's victory songs, David pretended to be mad and Achish sent him away. The title of Ps 34 calls this king Abimelech. Later David returned with six hundred men and their households, and Achish gave him the town of Ziklag. David raided neighboring peoples while telling Achish he had attacked Judah, and Achish trusted him, even making him his bodyguard. When the Philistines marched against Israel, the other Philistine lords refused to let David fight, and Achish reluctantly sent him back. Shimei's runaway servants later fled to Achish early in Solomon's reign. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes this as the same king, still ruling decades later.

Achsa is the form of the name Achsah used in the King James Version at 1 Chr 2:49, where she is named as the daughter of Caleb in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah. The verse closes a list of Caleb's descendants by his concubine Maachah, and the brothers grouped with her here are sons of Caleb by several mothers. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat her as the same woman as Achsah, the daughter of Caleb whom Josh 15:16–17 and Judg 1:12–13 describe as given in marriage to Othniel after he captured Kirjath-sepher. Because the Caleb of 1 Chronicles 2 is traced through Hezron, while the Caleb of Joshua is called the son of Jephunneh, how the two Calebs relate is not certain. This entry follows the reference works in identifying her with Achsah.

Achsah was the daughter of Caleb. Her name probably means "anklet," according to Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries. Caleb promised her as a wife to the man who would attack and capture Kirjath-sepher, also called Debir. Othniel the son of Kenaz took the city and so received her in marriage. Othniel is described as Caleb's younger brother, though the wording may also be read as making him a younger kinsman, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia puts it. The account appears twice, in Joshua and again in Judges. The verses that follow in both books (Josh 15:18–19; Judg 1:14–15) tell how she asked her father for land and springs of water, and he gave her the upper and lower springs. Her brothers Iru, Elah and Naam are named in a genealogy of Caleb's family (1 Chr 4:15).

Achshaph was a Canaanite royal city in northern Canaan. Its king was one of the rulers Jabin king of Hazor summoned to join a coalition against Joshua and Israel (Josh 11:1). He later appears in the list of kings Joshua defeated (Josh 12:20). The city was then named among the border towns of the tribe of Asher (Josh 19:25). The name is usually explained as meaning "sorcery" or "fascination." Its exact site is uncertain, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that explorers have not agreed on an identification. Other proposals include Tell Keisan. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies Achshaph with the ruined village of Kesaf or Yasif, northeast of Acco, and the location shown here follows that view, near modern Kafr Yasif in the western Galilee.

Achzib was a town in the Shephelah, the low hill country of Judah. It is listed among the towns given to the tribe of Judah, grouped with Keilah and Mareshah (Josh 15:44). The prophet Micah mentions it in a lament over the towns of Judah, saying that "the houses of Achzib shall be a lie to the kings of Israel" (Mic 1:14). This is a play on the name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names take to mean "lying" or "false." Easton's and Smith's dictionaries probably identify it with Chezib, the place where Judah's son Shelah was born (Gen 38:5). Easton's places it at Ain Kezbeh. The location shown here lies in the western foothills southwest of Jerusalem, in that general area. A different Achzib lay on the coast in the territory of Asher.

Achzib was a coastal city in the territory given to the tribe of Asher. It is named near the end of Asher's boundary description, where the border runs to the sea "from the coast to Achzib" (Josh 19:29). Judges records that Asher did not drive out its Canaanite inhabitants, along with those of nearby Accho and Sidon (Judg 1:31). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as a Phoenician city that its original people always kept, known in Greek as Ecdippa. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it appears in Assyrian inscriptions as Aksibi, among the Phoenician towns Sennacherib took. It is generally identified with es-Zib (ez-Zib) on the Mediterranean coast, about 8 to 9 miles north of Acre, and the location shown here follows that identification. The name is shared with another Achzib in Judah, which is a separate place.

Adadah was a town in the far south of Judah, listed among the cities of the tribe's southernmost district alongside Kinah and Dimonah (Josh 15:22). It is mentioned nowhere else in the Bible. Its location is uncertain. The older copies of the Greek translation read "Arouel" here, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some scholars adopt this reading and place the town at Ararah, about seven miles southeast of Beersheba. This is probably the site often linked with the Aroer of 1 Sam 30:28. Others identify it with a site eight or nine miles southeast of Arad. The location shown here follows the Ararah identification southeast of Beersheba, and its coordinates are only approximate. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "testimony of the assembly". Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "festival" or "boundary".

Adah was one of the wives of Esau. She was a Hittite woman, the daughter of Elon (Gen 36:2), and she bore Esau's son Eliphaz (Gen 36:4, 10). Through Eliphaz she was the ancestor of several chiefs ("dukes") of Edom, including Korah, Gatam and Amalek. Amalek was born to Eliphaz by his concubine Timna but is still counted among Adah's descendants (Gen 36:12, 16). Gen 26:34 calls Esau's Hittite wife, the daughter of Elon, Bashemath. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries therefore treat Adah and Bashemath as the same woman, and this entry follows that view. The lists of Esau's wives differ between Gen 26:34, Gen 28:9 and Genesis 36, where Bashemath is the name of a different wife, Ishmael's daughter. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that there is too little evidence to settle this. Another Adah, the wife of Lamech, appears in Gen 4:19.

Adah (wife of Lamech) was the first of the two wives of Lamech, a descendant of Cain; the other was Zillah. She bore Jabal, described as the father of those who live in tents and keep livestock. Her other son was Jubal, whom Gen 4:21 names as Jabal's brother and the father of those who play the harp and pipe. Adah and Zillah are the wives Lamech addresses in his short poem, in which he tells them he has killed a man for wounding him. Her name is usually explained as meaning "adornment" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "ornament, beauty" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). She should not be confused with the later Adah who was one of Esau's wives.

Adaiah was a Levite of the Gershonite branch who appears in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 6. In the list of Gershom's descendants he is called Iddo, son of Joah and father of Zerah (1 Chr 6:21). In the ancestry of Asaph, the singer whom David set over temple music, he appears as Adaiah, father of Zerah, with his own father named as Ethan (1 Chr 6:41–42). The two lists line up generation for generation, so Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat Iddo and Adaiah as the same man, and this entry follows that view. On the same reasoning Joah and Ethan would be two names for his father. Nothing beyond his place in these lines is recorded. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name Adaiah as "adorned by the LORD". Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Adaiah was a man of Boscath and the father of Jedidah, the mother of King Josiah of Judah. That made him Josiah's maternal grandfather (2 Kgs 22:1). He is mentioned only in this one verse, which gives Josiah's age at his accession and the length of his reign. Boscath is usually taken to be the same as Bozkath, a town in the lowlands of Judah listed in Josh 15:39. Smith's Bible Dictionary places that town there. Because Josiah appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matt 1:10–11), Adaiah belongs to that family line through his daughter. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as "adorned by the LORD," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the witness of the Lord." Several other men in the Bible share the name Adaiah. Nothing else is recorded about this one.

Adaiah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in its genealogy as one of the sons of Shimhi, listed alongside Beraiah and Shimrath (1 Chr 8:21). His other brothers named in the same list are Jakim, Zichri, Zabdi, Elienai, Zilthai and Eliel. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes his father Shimhi to be the same man as Shema in 1 Chr 8:13. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia goes further and traces this Shema through Elpaal to Shaharaim, whose family is listed among the Benjamites. Nothing else is recorded about Adaiah beyond his name and family. The name means "Yahweh has adorned" according to Smith's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Several other people in the Bible share the name, so this Adaiah should not be confused with them.

Adaiah son of Jeroham was a priest who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. He is one of several men in the Bible with this name. His family line runs through Pashur to Malchijah (1 Chr 9:12). The fuller genealogy in Neh 11:12 adds Pelaliah, Amzi and Zechariah between Jeroham and Pashur, so the Chronicles list is probably abbreviated. Nehemiah counts him among the priests' kinsmen who did the work of the house of God, a group numbering 822. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "adorned by Jehovah." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the witness of the Lord."

Adaiah was the father of Maaseiah, one of the captains of hundreds whom the priest Jehoiada brought into a covenant in the seventh year, as he prepared to act (2 Chr 23:1). The surrounding chapter shows this was the plot to remove Queen Athaliah and crown the young Joash as king of Judah. Adaiah himself is known only through his son and does nothing in the narrative. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him Maaseiah's "ancestor" rather than his father, since "son of" in Hebrew can mean a more distant descendant. The name, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders "Yahweh has adorned," belongs to several men in the Bible. This Adaiah should not be confused with the others of the same name.

Adaiah was one of the descendants of Bani listed in Ezra 10:29 among the men of Israel who had married foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon. The surrounding chapter describes how these men agreed, at Ezra's urging, to send away their foreign wives. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that he was a layman rather than a priest or Levite, since he appears among the 'sons of Bani' and not in the priestly or Levitical lists. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the episode to about 459 BC. The name means 'Yahweh has adorned' according to Smith's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives 'the witness of the Lord.' Several other men in the Bible share the name Adaiah. Nothing more is recorded about this one.

Adaiah was one of the Israelite men in Ezra's time who had married foreign wives, named in the list of those who agreed to send them away (Ezra 10:39). He appears only once, in a run of names with nothing else said about him. The setting is inferred from the surrounding chapter, where Ezra led the returned exiles to give up such marriages. Which family group he belonged to is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place him among the descendants of Bani, possibly a second Bani in the list. The STEPBible names list from Tyndale House describes him as a priest descended from Harim. Several other men in the Bible share the name Adaiah, and it is not clear whether he is the same as any of them. The name is usually explained as "the Lord has adorned."

Adaiah was a man of the tribe of Judah who appears only in the family line of Maaseiah, one of the Judahites who lived in Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time (Neh 11:5). He was the son of Joiarib and the father of Hazaiah. By that genealogy he was Maaseiah's great-great-grandfather, so he probably lived several generations before the return from exile. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place him in the line of Perez, son of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "adorned by the LORD," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the witness of the Lord." Several other people in the Bible share the name Adaiah and should not be confused with him.

Adalia was one of the ten sons of Haman, the Persian official who plotted to destroy the Jews in the reign of Ahasuerus. He appears only in the list of Haman's sons at Esth 9:8. By inference from the surrounding passage (Esth 9:6–10), he was killed with his brothers in Shushan when the Jews defended themselves on the day set for their destruction. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him as the fifth son and gives the meaning "a fire-god." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia regards the name as probably Persian, with its meaning unknown. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Adam was a city in the Jordan Valley, mentioned once in the Bible. It was the point upstream where the Jordan's waters stopped and 'rose up upon an heap' when the Israelites crossed the river opposite Jericho under Joshua. Downstream, the flow toward the Dead Sea was cut off (Josh 3:16). The verse places Adam 'beside Zaretan', probably the same place as Zarethan. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on the west bank of the Jordan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connects the name with the Damieh Ford, near where the Jabbok joins the Jordan, about twenty miles above Jericho. That work notes that the river's narrow gorge there could easily be blocked, and cites an Arab historian who reported a landslide damming the Jordan at that spot around AD 1265. The location shown here follows the Damieh identification, at the modern Tell ed-Damiyeh. The name may mean 'red' or 'earthy'.

Adam was the first man in the Genesis account, formed by God and placed in the garden of Eden. His name is the ordinary Hebrew word for 'man,' which Hitchcock's Bible Names glosses as 'earthy' or 'red.' He named the animals, and God made a woman from one of his ribs. Adam called her Eve. After both ate from the forbidden tree, they hid from God, who cursed the ground for Adam's sake and clothed them in skins. Adam fathered Cain, Abel and Seth, the last at age 130, as well as other sons and daughters, and he died at 930. The genealogies in 1 Chr 1:1 and Luke 3:38 begin with him. Paul contrasts Adam, in whom all die, with Christ as 'the last Adam' (1 Cor 15:22, 45). The date of about 4004 BC for his creation is an inference from the genealogies.

Adamah was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Naphtali, listed between Chinnereth and Ramah, just before Hazor (Josh 19:36). The list it belongs to opens in Josh 19:35 with the words "the fenced cities," so Adamah is understood to have been a fortified town. It is mentioned nowhere else. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "red earth." Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Damieh, west of the Sea of Galilee, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia prefers 'Admah, a ruin on the plateau about 10 miles north of Beisan (Beth-shean). The location shown here is only approximate. It places Adamah in the hills of lower Galilee southwest of the Sea of Galilee, between these two proposed sites, and does not settle the question.

Adami-nekeb was a town on the boundary of the territory of the tribe of Naphtali, named once in the description of that border (Josh 19:33). The King James Version prints it as two names, "Adami" and "Nekeb." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that scholars have long debated whether one place or two is meant, and that most Greek texts read two names. It gives the meaning as "the ground of the pass." The site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary favors Seiyadeh, a ruin between Tiberias and Mount Tabor. Others place Adami at Damieh, northwest of the Sea of Galilee. The survey maps cited by the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia put Adami at Khurbet Adamah, several miles south of where the Jordan leaves the lake. The location shown here follows that southern identification.

Adbeel was the third son of Ishmael, Abraham's son by Hagar, named after Nebajoth and Kedar in the list of Ishmael's twelve sons (Gen 25:13; 1 Chr 1:29). That made him a grandson of Abraham. Nothing else is said about him in the Bible. The siblings shown here include Bashemath, who appears elsewhere as Ishmael's daughter and a wife of Esau. Like his brothers, Adbeel was probably the ancestor of an Arabian tribe, as Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary suggest. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that a north Arabian tribe of this name appears in Assyrian records, living somewhere southwest of the Dead Sea. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Suggestions include "miracle of God" (Easton's), "offspring of God" (Smith's), "God's discipline" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) and "cloud of God" (Hitchcock's Bible Names).

Addar (spelled "Adar" in the King James Version) was a place on the southern border of the tribe of Judah's territory. Joshua 15:3 traces the boundary from Maale-acrabbim past Zin and Kadesh-barnea, then on to Hezron, up to Addar, and around to Karkaa. Addar therefore lay somewhere in the dry region near Kadesh-barnea, on the edge of the Negev and the Sinai. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with Hazar-addar, which appears at the same point in the parallel description of Israel's southern border in Num 34:4. There, Hazar-addar seems to combine Hezron and Addar into one name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "high" or "eminent." The exact site is unknown, and the location shown here is only a rough estimate.

Addar was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named first among the sons of Bela, Benjamin's firstborn, in the genealogy at 1 Chr 8:3. That makes him a grandson of Benjamin. His name probably means "glorious" or "mighty." Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper-names list identify him with Ard, who appears as a son of Bela in Num 26:40 and as a son of Benjamin in Gen 46:21. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that he is sometimes counted as one of Benjamin's own sons. This entry lists Ard among Addar's brothers, along with Gera, Abihud, Abishua, Naaman, Ahoah and others drawn from the different lists of Bela's sons. On that view the two names refer to separate people, though the equation of Addar with Ard is widely held.

Addi is a man named only once in the Bible, in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, which traces the line back from Joseph to Adam. He appears as the son of Cosam and the father of Melchi (Luke 3:28). In Luke's list he stands three generations above Salathiel, the father of Zerubbabel. By inference from his position in the list, which runs through David's son Nathan rather than through the kings, he would have lived some generations before the Babylonian exile and belonged to the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "ornament."

Addon was a place, probably in Babylonia, from which some exiles set out to return to Judah after the captivity. Neh 7:61 lists it with Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub and Immer. The returning families from these places could not prove their father's house or show that their descent was from Israel. The parallel list in Ezra 2:59 spells the name Addan, and Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat the two as the same place. Easton's Bible Dictionary reads Addon as one of the people who could not trace their ancestry, not as a place. This entry follows the reading of it as a place, as the STEPBible proper-names index also does. Its location is unknown. The neighbouring names Tel-melah and Tel-harsha begin with "tel", meaning a mound, which suggests settlements in the Babylonian lowlands, but no site has been identified.

Ader was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named once in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 8:15. He is listed among the sons of Beriah, alongside Zebadiah, Arad, Michael, Ispah, Joha and others. Nothing further is recorded about his life. The surrounding passage describes Beriah as one of the heads of the families living in Aijalon, so Ader probably belonged to that community, by inference from context. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "flock" and notes that the Hebrew form is more accurately Eder. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia likewise treats "Ader" as the King James spelling of Eder, the form used in most modern translations. He is distinct from other men named Eder in the Bible.

Adiel was a leader in the tribe of Simeon, named in a list of Simeonite family heads in 1 Chr 4:36. The surrounding passage, which continues past this verse, describes these men as princes in their families whose households grew large. In the days of King Hezekiah they went to the valley of Gedor, attacked the people living there, including Hamites and Meunites, and settled in their pasture lands. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him a family head of Simeon. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both take part in the Gedor raid as his, and Smith's dates it to about 711 BC, an estimate drawn from context. The name is usually explained as "ornament of God." Several other men in the Bible share the name Adiel, and this one should not be confused with them.

Adiel was the father of Azmaveth, the official in charge of King David's treasures (1 Chr 27:25). He is known only through his son's name in the list of David's administrators. Nothing else about his life or tribe is recorded. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him an ancestor of Azmaveth, since "son of" can refer to a more distant forebear. It dates the period to about 1050 BC, an estimate inferred from the timing of David's reign. Smith's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the name's meaning as "ornament of God," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the witness of the Lord." Several other men in Chronicles bear the same name, including a Simeonite leader and a priest's ancestor. This Adiel is distinguished from them only by his connection to Azmaveth.

Adin was the ancestor of a family whose descendants returned to Judah from exile in Babylon. The list of those who came back with Zerubbabel gives the children of Adin as 454 (Ezra 2:15), while the parallel list in Nehemiah gives 655 (Neh 7:20). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the difference by suggesting that one copy of the list was made later and brought up to date. A later group of 50 men from the same family came with Ezra, led by Ebed the son of Jonathan (Ezra 8:6). Smith's Bible Dictionary adds that an Adin is named among the leaders who sealed Nehemiah's covenant (Neh 10:16), probably representing the family as a whole. Little is known of Adin himself beyond the family that bore his name. The name is usually taken to mean "adorned" or "delicate."

Adin was one of the leaders of the people who sealed the written covenant in the time of Nehemiah, when the community in Jerusalem pledged to keep the law of God after returning from exile. His name appears in Neh 10:16 within the list that begins with "the chief of the people" in Neh 10:14, alongside Adonijah and Bigvai. The text gives no further details about him. The name also appears elsewhere as the head of a family whose descendants returned from Babylon (Ezra 2:15; Neh 7:20). Bigvai is a family name in those same lists, so this Adin may stand for that family rather than for a single individual. Whether he is the same person is uncertain, and the name is shared by several people in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "adorned" or "dainty."

Adina was a Reubenite, the son of Shiza, named among David's mighty men in 1 Chr 11:42. He is described as a captain, or chief, of the Reubenites, with thirty men under him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that he appears in the part of the Chronicler's list that adds names not found in the parallel list of David's warriors in 2 Samuel 23. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him among David's captains east of the Jordan, which fits the territory of the tribe of Reuben. His name is usually explained as meaning "slender" (Easton's Bible Dictionary) or "adorned" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Nothing else is recorded about him.

Adino the Eznite is named in 2 Sam 23:8 as the first and chief of David's mighty men, called the Tachmonite who "sat in the seat," chief among the captains. He is credited with killing eight hundred men with his spear at one time. The Hebrew of this verse is difficult, and its reading is debated. The parallel list in 1 Chr 11:11 names the chief warrior Jashobeam, a Hachmonite, says he lifted up his spear, and gives the number slain as three hundred. Many scholars therefore take "Adino the Eznite" as a garbled form of that phrase rather than a personal name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint keeps the names Adino and Eznite, and it suggests judgment be suspended. This entry follows the King James reading, which treats Adino as another name for the same chief warrior. Neither name appears anywhere else in the Bible.

Adithaim was a town allotted to the tribe of Judah, named only once in the Bible, between Sharaim and Gederah, in Josh 15:36. That verse closes a list of fourteen towns with their villages. By inference from the start of the list (Josh 15:33), the group lay in the lowland, or Shephelah, the foothills between the Judean hills and the coastal plain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "double ornament," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "assemblies" or "testimonies." The exact site is unknown. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the same place as Adida, a town near Lod. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the western Shephelah near the other towns of the same list, not at Adida.

Adlai was the father of Shaphat, one of the officials over King David's property. He is mentioned only once, in a list of David's stewards, where Shaphat son of Adlai is named as the man in charge of the royal herds that grazed in the valleys. A different official, Shitrai the Sharonite, oversaw the herds in the plain of Sharon (1 Chr 27:29). Nothing else is recorded about Adlai himself. By inference from the list, he lived in or before the time of David. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "justice of Jehovah," the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "lax, weary," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "my witness; my ornament."

Admah was one of the cities of the plain, always named alongside Zeboim and grouped with Sodom and Gomorrah. Gen 10:19 lists it at the edge of Canaanite territory. In Abraham's time its king, Shinab, joined the kings of Sodom, Gomorrah, Zeboiim and Bela (Zoar) in battle against an alliance of eastern kings in the Vale of Siddim (Gen 14:2, 8). Deut 29:23 says the LORD overthrew it in his anger together with Sodom, Gomorrah and Zeboim, leaving a land of brimstone and salt. Hos 11:8 uses Admah and Zeboim as examples of total destruction. Its exact site is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes a suggestion that it is the Adam of Josh 3:16, near the Damieh ford of the Jordan. The location shown here follows a placement near the southern end of the Dead Sea. The name probably means "red" or "earthy."

Admatha was one of the seven princes of Persia and Media at the court of King Ahasuerus, listed third in Esth 1:14 among Carshena, Shethar, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena and Memucan. These men "saw the king's face" and "sat the first in the kingdom." In other words, they had direct access to the king and held the highest rank under him. From the surrounding passage, they were the advisers the king consulted when Queen Vashti refused his summons. Nothing else is recorded about Admatha himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint gives only three names in this list. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "given by the highest," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a cloud of death."

Adna was a man of the family of Pahath-moab who appears in the list of Israelites found to have married foreign wives in Ezra's time (Ezra 10:30). The surrounding chapter describes how, after the return from exile in Babylon, these men agreed to send away their foreign wives as part of Ezra's reforms. He is one of eight men named from Pahath-moab. The events fall in the mid-fifth century BC; Smith's Bible Dictionary dates them to about 459 BC, an estimate drawn from context. The name is usually explained as meaning "pleasure" or "delight" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several people in the Bible share this name, including a priest in Nehemiah's day, and this Adna should not be confused with them. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Adna was a priest in Jerusalem after the return from exile. He is listed as head of the priestly family of Harim in Neh 12:15. The surrounding list in Nehemiah 12 places him in the days of Joiakim, son of Jeshua the high priest, a generation after the first exiles returned from Babylon. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 500 BC; that date is an estimate drawn from context. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as meaning "pleasure" or "delight," is shared by several people in the Bible, including a man of the family of Pahath-moab who had married a foreign wife (Ezra 10:30). This entry concerns only the priest of Harim's family.

Adnah was a man of the tribe of Manasseh, one of the "captains of the thousands" of Manasseh who came over to David as he went to Ziklag (1 Chr 12:20). The surrounding passage places this when David was leaving the Philistine camp, and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Adnah as deserting Saul to join David and fighting with him against the Amalekite raiders; the next verse speaks of these men helping David against the band, which is read as that pursuit. Smith's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of the name as "pleasure." The name Adnah is shared by more than one person in the Bible, and this entry concerns only the Manassite captain. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Adnah was a commander from the tribe of Judah in the army of King Jehoshaphat. He is named first among the captains of thousands from Judah and is called "the chief." Under him were 300,000 "mighty men of valour" (2 Chr 17:14). The context places him in Jehoshaphat's reign over Judah, as part of the king's organized military force. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he may have been the commander-in-chief of the army. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "pleasure," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "eternal rest." The name is shared by another man in the Bible, a warrior of Manasseh who joined David. This entry concerns only the commander under Jehoshaphat, who is known from this single verse.

Adoni-bezek was a Canaanite ruler at Bezek, whose name means "lord of Bezek." After Joshua's death, the men of Judah, with Simeon according to the surrounding passage (Judg 1:3), fought him at Bezek and defeated the Canaanites and Perizzites there. He fled but was caught, and his captors cut off his thumbs and big toes. He then said that seventy kings whose thumbs and big toes he had cut off had gathered scraps under his table, and that God had paid him back for what he had done. He was brought to Jerusalem and died there. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint confuses him with Adoni-zedek, king of Jerusalem, and treats the two as different names. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 1425 BC.

Adoni-zedek was the king of Jerusalem when Joshua led Israel into Canaan. His name means "lord of righteousness" or "lord of justice." He heard that Joshua had destroyed Jericho and Ai and that the people of Gibeon had made peace with Israel. He then sent to four other kings, Hoham of Hebron, Piram of Jarmuth, Japhia of Lachish and Debir of Eglon, and called on them to join him in attacking Gibeon (Josh 10:1, 3). The rest of the chapter tells what happened next. Joshua came to Gibeon's aid and routed the allied armies. The five kings hid in a cave at Makkedah, and Joshua later had them taken out, put to death and hung on trees. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that his name closely resembles that of Melchizedek, an earlier king of Salem in Abraham's time.

Adonijah was the fourth son of David, born to Haggith at Hebron (2 Sam 3:4; 1 Chr 3:2). When David was old, Adonijah declared, "I will be king," gathered chariots, horsemen and fifty runners, and won the support of Joab and the priest Abiathar. Zadok, Benaiah, Nathan and David's mighty men did not join him. He held a sacrificial feast by the stone of Zoheleth near En-rogel, where guests hailed him as king. Nathan and Bathsheba reminded David of his oath that Solomon would reign, and Solomon was made king. Adonijah's guests scattered, and he grasped the horns of the altar, asking Solomon to swear to spare him. Later, through Bathsheba, he asked to marry Abishag the Shunammite. Solomon treated this as a claim to the kingdom and ordered his death. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him heir-apparent after Amnon and Absalom died. Several other men share this name.

Adonijah was a Levite in the reign of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. He is named in a list of Levites whom Jehoshaphat sent out, together with several officials and the priests Elishama and Jehoram, to teach the people (2 Chr 17:8). The surrounding passage says they carried the Book of the Law and went through the cities of Judah giving instruction. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia dates this mission to Jehoshaphat's third year. His name means "my lord is the LORD" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with other men of the same name, such as David's son Adonijah, who tried to claim the throne.

Adonijah was one of the men who set their seal to the covenant made under Nehemiah after the return from exile, pledging to keep the Law of God. He appears in Neh 10:16 between Bigvai and Adin. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place him among the "chiefs of the people" listed in that part of the chapter, while the STEPBible proper-names index describes him as a Levite. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him with Adonikam, whose family appears among the returned exiles, which would make the name stand for that clan. His name means "my lord is the LORD." Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with other men of the same name, such as David's son.

Adonikam was the ancestor of a family group, the "children of Adonikam," who returned to Jerusalem from exile in Babylon. The list of returnees who came with Zerubbabel counts them as 666 in Ezra 2:13 and as 667 in the parallel list in Neh 7:18. A later group of his descendants came up with Ezra, led by Eliphelet, Jeiel and Shemaiah, with sixty males (Ezra 8:13). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia leaves open whether that later group is counted within the earlier total or is in addition to it. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the Adonijah who seals the covenant in Neh 10:16 may be the same family name. The name is usually understood to mean "my lord has risen up" or "the Lord is raised." Nothing else is recorded about Adonikam himself.

Adoniram, son of Abda, was the royal official "over the tribute", meaning the forced labor levy, in Israel. He is also called Adoram and Hadoram. Most reference works, including Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, take these as one man who held the office under David, Solomon and Rehoboam, and this entry follows that view. Under David he appears as Adoram in the list of officials (2 Sam 20:24). Under Solomon he directed the 30,000 laborers sent to Lebanon in rotating shifts of 10,000, each working one month there and two months at home (1 Kgs 4:6; 1 Kgs 5:14). When the northern tribes rebelled against Rehoboam, the king sent him to them, and the Israelites stoned him to death. Rehoboam then fled to Jerusalem in his chariot (1 Kgs 12:18; 2 Chr 10:18).

Adoraim was a town in Judah that King Rehoboam fortified after the kingdom divided. It appears in a list of his defensive cities alongside Lachish and Azekah (2 Chr 11:9). The surrounding passage presents these as cities built up for defence. The name is usually explained as "pair of mounds" or "two knolls" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "strength of the sea." Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both take it to be the Adora mentioned in 1 Maccabees and Josephus. Smith notes that Adora might instead be Dor on the coast. Both works identify Adoraim with the village of Dura, about five miles west-southwest of Hebron, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Adrammelech was a god worshipped by the people of Sepharvaim, named together with Anammelech as one of the two gods of that city. According to 2 Kgs 17:31, after Assyria resettled foreigners in Samaria, the Sepharvite settlers kept up his worship there and burned their children in fire to him. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a form of the sun-god. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that his rites resembled those of Molech, and suggests he represented the male power of the sun, with Anammelech as the female counterpart. The name is usually explained as meaning something like "splendor" or "glory of the king." The same name belongs to a different person, a son of the Assyrian king Sennacherib who helped kill his father (2 Kgs 19:37; Isa 37:38). That man is a separate figure from this god.

Adrammelech was a son of Sennacherib, king of Assyria. With his brother Sharezer he killed their father with the sword while Sennacherib was worshipping in the house of his god Nisroch. The two brothers then escaped to the land of Armenia (the region of Ararat), and another brother, Esarhaddon, became king in his father's place (2 Kgs 19:37; Isa 37:38). Both accounts place the murder after Sennacherib's failed campaign against Jerusalem and his return home. Smith's Bible Dictionary places the temple at Nineveh, the Assyrian capital, and gives the name's meaning as "splendor of the king." The same name also belongs to a god worshipped by the people of Sepharvaim, who is a different figure from this son of Sennacherib.

Adramyttium was a port city on the northwest coast of Asia Minor, in the region of Mysia within the Roman province of Asia. It stood at the head of a gulf facing the island of Lesbos. It appears in the Bible only once, when Paul, travelling as a prisoner to Rome, boarded a ship that belonged to this city (Acts 27:2). From the surrounding narrative, he boarded it at Caesarea. The ship planned to sail along the coast of Asia, and Aristarchus of Thessalonica went with him. The following verses show that Paul stayed on this ship only as far as Myra in Lycia, where he moved to an Alexandrian ship bound for Italy. The voyage dates to about AD 56, by inference from context. The name survives in the modern Turkish town of Edremit, slightly inland from the ancient harbor, and the location shown here matches that area.

Adria, called the Adriatic Sea in modern translations, is the sea across which the ship carrying Paul to Rome was driven by a storm. On the fourteenth night of being tossed about there, the sailors sensed around midnight that they were nearing land, shortly before the shipwreck (Acts 27:27). Today the name refers to the sea between Italy and the Balkan coast. According to Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary, in Paul's time it covered a much wider area, the whole central Mediterranean between Greece and Italy, reaching south from Crete to Sicily. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that ancient writers extended the name as far as the waters between Crete and Malta. Since the ship approached the shore of Malta (Acts 28:1), the storm was probably in this southern part. The location shown here is a point in the modern Adriatic.

Adriel was the son of Barzillai, a Meholathite, probably meaning a man from Abel-meholah. Saul's daughter Merab had been promised to David, but she was given to Adriel as his wife instead (1 Sam 18:19). Later, five sons connected with Adriel were among the seven descendants of Saul whom David handed over to the Gibeonites (2 Sam 21:8). The Hebrew text of that verse says that Michal, Saul's other daughter, brought up these sons for Adriel. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains this in two ways: either Michal raised them as though they were her own, or "Michal" should read "Merab." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the second view and treats the sons as children of Adriel and Merab. The name is usually explained as "flock of God" or "my help is God." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia regards it as an Aramaic form of the Hebrew name Azriel.

Adullam was a city in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, listed with Jarmuth, Socoh and Azekah. It was once the seat of a Canaanite king defeated by Joshua, and Gen 38:1 already mentions it in the story of Judah. Rehoboam later fortified it, and Jews resettled it after the return from Babylon. Micah names it among towns of Judah facing judgment. It is best known for the nearby cave of Adullam, where David took refuge and his family joined him. Later, three of his chief warriors came to him there while the Philistines camped in the valley of Rephaim. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify the city with the ruin of 'Aid el-Ma, about 13 miles west-southwest of Bethlehem. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it near Deir Dubban. The location shown here follows the 'Aid el-Ma identification.

Adummim was a hill pass, called "the going up to Adummim," on the road climbing from the Jordan valley near Jericho to Jerusalem. It appears only as a landmark on the boundary between the territories of Judah and Benjamin. Josh 15:7 places it opposite Gilgal and south of the stream, and Josh 18:17 uses it again when describing Benjamin's southern border. The name probably means "red ones," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links it to red streaks in the local rock. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify the ascent with the road along the south side of the Wadi Qelt gorge, at a spot called Tal'at ed-Dumm, roughly halfway between Jerusalem and Jericho. The location shown here follows that identification. Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia add that this stretch of road is traditionally taken as the setting of the parable of the Good Samaritan in Luke 10:30–37.

Aeneas was a man living at Lydda who had been bedridden for eight years with paralysis. Lydda is named in the surrounding passage (Acts 9:32) and in Smith's Bible Dictionary; it is probably the modern town of Lod in Israel. While Peter was traveling among the believers there, he found Aeneas and said to him, "Aeneas, Jesus Christ makes you whole: get up and make your bed," and Aeneas got up at once. The account that follows (Acts 9:35) says the healing led people of Lydda and Sharon to turn to the Lord. Soon afterward Peter went on to nearby Joppa, where he raised Dorcas. These events are dated to about AD 38, by inference from context. Nothing else is recorded about Aeneas, including whether he was already a believer. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "praised" or "praiseworthy."

Aenon was a place near Salim where John the Baptist was baptizing because there was much water there, and people came to him to be baptized (John 3:23). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the name's meaning as "springs." The surrounding passage suggests it lay west of the Jordan, unlike Bethabara where John first baptized. It was here, probably around AD 27 by inference from context, that John spoke about his role in relation to Jesus. Its exact site is uncertain. Eusebius's Onomasticon places it eight Roman miles south of Scythopolis (Beth-shean), and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links this to springs near Umm el-'Amdan in the Jordan Valley. Easton's suggests the springs at the head of Wadi Far'ah, near Mount Ebal. The location shown here follows the Jordan Valley identification south of Beth-shean.

Agabus was a Christian prophet from Judea in the early church, mentioned twice in Acts. At Antioch, where he had come with other prophets from Jerusalem, he stood up and, moved by the Spirit, foretold a great famine across the world. Acts notes that it happened in the reign of the emperor Claudius (Acts 11:28), and Smith's Bible Dictionary points out that the historian Josephus records a severe famine in Judea under Claudius. Years later, while Paul was staying at Caesarea on his way to Jerusalem, Agabus came down from Judea to meet him (Acts 21:10). The following verses describe him binding his own hands and feet with Paul's belt to show that Paul would be bound in Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he was probably one of the seventy disciples sent out by Jesus. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "a locust."

Agag is a king named in Balaam's oracle over Israel, which says that Israel's king "shall be higher than Agag" (Num 24:7). The verse does not say who he was, but Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him as a king of the Amalekites living at the time of the Exodus. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggest that Agag may have been a title used by Amalekite kings, much as Pharaoh was used in Egypt. This entry covers only the Agag of Balaam's oracle. A different Agag, also an Amalekite king, was later spared by Saul and then put to death by Samuel (1 Sam 15). Some readers take the name in Balaam's oracle as pointing ahead to that later king. The meaning of the name is uncertain, and older works offer readings such as "flame" or "violent."

Agag was a king of the Amalekites in the time of Saul. When Saul attacked the Amalekites, he took Agag alive and killed the people. Saul and his army spared Agag, along with the best of the sheep and cattle, instead of destroying everything as commanded (1 Sam 15:8–9). Saul then told Samuel he had obeyed the Lord and brought back Agag (1 Sam 15:20). Samuel had Agag brought to him, and Agag came saying, "Surely the bitterness of death is past." Samuel answered that as Agag's sword had made women childless, so his own mother would be childless, and he cut Agag in pieces before the Lord at Gilgal (1 Sam 15:32–33). The name is also used of another Amalekite ruler in Num 24:7, and Easton's Bible Dictionary treats Agag as a name borne by more than one Amalekite king. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "roof" or "upper floor."

Agee was a Hararite, the father of Shammah, one of David's three most prominent mighty men (2 Sam 23:11). He is named only in that verse, which introduces Shammah's stand against the Philistines in a field of lentils after the rest of the people had fled. The epithet "the Hararite" may describe Agee or his son, and probably points to a home in the hill country or to a family or clan name. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the name the meaning "fugitive." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a textual puzzle. 1 Chr 11:34 names "Jonathan the son of Shagee the Hararite," while the parallel list in 2 Sam 23:32–33 has "Jonathan, Shammah the Hararite." On one reading Agee was Jonathan's grandfather. On another, "Agee" and "Shagee" are the same name, which would make Jonathan and Shammah brothers.

Agrippa was the king who came with Bernice to Caesarea to greet the new Roman governor Festus (Acts 25:13). He is usually identified as Herod Agrippa II. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him the son of Herod Agrippa I, born at Rome about AD 27, brother of Bernice and Drusilla, and ruler of the former territories of Philip and Lysanias. Festus told him about Paul, a prisoner he could bring no clear charge against, and Agrippa asked to hear Paul himself. The next day, amid great ceremony, Festus brought Paul before him so that he would have something to write to the emperor (Acts 25:23–26). Paul addressed his defense to Agrippa and asked whether he believed the prophets. Agrippa replied, "Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian." He later told Festus that Paul could have been freed if he had not appealed to Caesar. This entry dates the hearing to about AD 56, by inference; Easton's places it in AD 59.

The meeting of Agrippa and Bernice with Festus took place when King Agrippa and Bernice came to Caesarea to greet Portius Festus, the newly arrived Roman governor (Acts 25:13). The king is generally identified as Herod Agrippa II, and Bernice as his sister. During their long stay, Festus described the case of Paul, a prisoner left behind by Felix. He explained that the chief priests and elders in Jerusalem had asked for a judgment against Paul, but he had insisted on the Roman practice of letting the accused face his accusers. At the hearing he found no charge of the kind he expected, only disputes about their religion and about a dead man named Jesus whom Paul said was alive. When Paul appealed to the emperor, called Augustus here, Festus held him for transfer to Caesar (Acts 25:21). This was about AD 56, by inference from context, and it led to Paul's hearing before Agrippa.

Agur was the son of Jakeh, named in Prov 30:1 as the author of the sayings collected in Proverbs 30. The verse calls his words "the prophecy" (or "oracle") and says he addressed them to Ithiel and Ucal, who are otherwise unknown. Nothing else is recorded about him, and his time and place are not stated. The meaning of his name is uncertain: Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give "gatherer" or "collector," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also allows "hireling." Smith's describes him as an unknown Hebrew sage who spoke or collected the sayings. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that his chapter includes a well-known prayer asking for neither poverty nor riches (Prov 30:7–9) and several numerical proverbs.

Ahab was the son of Omri and succeeded him as king of Israel, ruling from Samaria (1 Kgs 16:28). By inference from context his reign began about 918 BC. He married Jezebel, and Kings says he did more evil than all the kings before him (1 Kgs 16:30). The prophet Elijah announced a drought to him and confronted him repeatedly (1 Kgs 17:1; 18:17). Ahab defeated Ben-hadad of Syria and released him under a treaty (1 Kgs 20:34). When Naboth refused to sell his vineyard, Jezebel arranged Naboth's death using Ahab's name. Elijah then pronounced judgment on Ahab's house, and Ahab fasted in sackcloth (1 Kgs 21:8, 20, 27). He allied with Jehoshaphat of Judah against Ramoth-gilead (2 Chr 18:3), where, according to Easton's Bible Dictionary, an arrow killed him. His sons Ahaziah and Joram reigned after him, his daughter married Jehoram of Judah, and Jehu later destroyed his house (2 Kgs 8:18; 10:17). The name is shared by other people in the Bible.

Ahab, son of Kolaiah, was a prophet among the people of Judah exiled in Babylon. He is a different person from the better-known King Ahab of Israel. In his letter to the exiles, Jeremiah condemned Ahab and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah for prophesying lies in the LORD's name. He announced that God would hand them over to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who would kill them in front of the exiles (Jer 29:21). Their fate would become a curse used among the captives: "The LORD make thee like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire" (Jer 29:22). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes this to mean he was burned to death. The next verse, Jer 29:23, also accuses the two men of adultery. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that nothing more is known of him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "uncle" or "father's brother."

Aharhel was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the genealogies of Judah as the son of Harum (1 Chr 4:8). The verse says that Coz fathered Anub and Zobebah, and then mentions "the families of Aharhel the son of Harum." That wording suggests Aharhel founded a clan known by his name. How he and Harum relate to Coz is unclear. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls the passage an obscure fragment of Judah's genealogies. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "behind the breastwork," while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers several possibilities, including "another host" and "a brother's sheep."

Ahasbai was the father of Eliphelet, one of the warriors listed among David's mighty men in 2 Sam 23:34. The verse calls him "the son of the Maachathite," which probably means Ahasbai himself was a Maachathite, someone from Maacah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests this could be either Abel-beth-maacah in northern Israel or, more probably, the Aramean kingdom of Maacah east of the upper Jordan. Nothing else is recorded about him. The parallel list in 1 Chr 11:35 gives different names at this point, "Eliphal the son of Ur." Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both explain the difference as damage to the text in copying. The name is usually taken to mean "blooming." By inference from David's reign, he lived about 1050 BC.

Ahasuerus was the Persian king of the Book of Esther, who reigned from Shushan over 127 provinces stretching from India to Ethiopia (Esth 1:1–2). He removed his queen Vashti from her position when she refused his summons during a feast (Esth 1:15–19), and in his seventh year he took Esther as queen (Esth 2:16). He promoted Haman, who sent out a decree in the king's name to destroy the Jews (Esth 3:1; 3:12). After Esther intervened, Ahasuerus gave Haman's house to her and made Mordecai second only to himself (Esth 8:1; 10:3). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify him as probably Xerxes I, who reigned about 486–465 BC. The name also appears in Ezra 4:6 and in Dan 9:1, where Ahasuerus is the father of Darius the Mede. Smith's treats these as separate kings (Cambyses and the Median Cyaxares). This entry groups all these mentions under one name.

Ahava was a river, or possibly a town or district that a river flowed toward, in Babylonia. Ezra gathered the exiles there before leading them back to Jerusalem. The company camped in tents for three days while Ezra reviewed the people and priests. He found no Levites among them (Ezra 8:15) and sent for some. He also proclaimed a fast there to ask God for a safe journey for the families and their goods. The group left the river on the twelfth day of the first month and reached Jerusalem safely. The phrase "the river that runneth to Ahava" suggests the name may belong to a place rather than the stream itself. The site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia thinks it was probably one of Babylonia's many canals, while Smith's and Easton's Bible Dictionaries mention the modern town of Hit on the Euphrates. The location shown here follows the Hit identification.

Ahaz was king of Judah, the son and successor of Jotham. He became king at twenty and reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem, beginning about 742 BC by inference from context, and the text says he did not do right as David had. When Rezin of Syria and Pekah of Israel besieged Jerusalem, Isaiah met him, but Ahaz declined to ask for a sign. Instead he sent temple and palace silver and gold to Tiglath-pileser of Assyria for help. After meeting Tiglath-pileser in Damascus, he had the priest Urijah copy an altar he saw there and rearranged the temple furnishings. According to Chronicles, he also broke up the temple vessels and shut its doors. A sundial bore his name. He was buried in Jerusalem but not in the royal tombs, and his son Hezekiah succeeded him. Matthew lists him as Achaz in the genealogy of Jesus.

Ahaz was a Benjamite descendant of King Saul. He was the son of Micah and the brother of Pithon, Melech and Tarea (spelled Tahrea in 1 Chr 9:41). He appears only in the two parallel genealogies of Saul's family in 1 Chronicles. The surrounding verses trace Micah back to Merib-baal, son of Jonathan, so Ahaz was Jonathan's great-grandson. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him Jonathan's grandson. His son is called Jehoadah in 1 Chr 8:36 and Jarah in 1 Chr 9:42. Both lists give the same descendants, Alemeth, Azmaveth and Zimri, followed by Moza, so the two names probably refer to one person spelled differently. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is a different person from the better-known Ahaz, king of Judah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "one that takes or possesses."

Ahaziah was a king of Israel, the son and successor of Ahab and Jezebel. He reigned two years from Samaria, beginning in the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat of Judah (about 897 BC, by inference from context). He proposed that his sailors join Jehoshaphat's in a shipping venture. 1 Kgs 22:49 says Jehoshaphat refused, while 2 Chr 20:35–37 says the two kings did join forces, and the prophet Eliezer declared that the ships would be wrecked. They were broken before they could sail to Tarshish. Chronicles says Ahaziah acted very wickedly. After falling through a lattice in his upper room, he sent messengers to ask Baalzebub, the god of Ekron, whether he would recover. The following narrative tells how Elijah intercepted them and foretold the king's death. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that Moab revolted during his reign. His brother Joram succeeded him. He is distinct from the later Ahaziah, king of Judah.

Ahaziah was king of Judah for one year, the son of King Jehoram and Athaliah, and the youngest son of his father. He is also called Jehoahaz and Azariah. After raiders killed his older brothers, the people of Jerusalem made him king. His age at accession is given as 22 in 2 Kgs 8:26 and as 42 in 2 Chr 22:2. While visiting his wounded uncle Joram, king of Israel, at Jezreel, he rode out with him to meet Jehu and was caught up in Jehu's revolt against the house of Ahab. Kings says he was struck near Ibleam and died at Megiddo. Chronicles says he was found hiding in Samaria and killed. His death was about 886 BC, by inference from context. Athaliah then destroyed the royal family, but his sister Jehoshabeath hid his son Joash. He is distinct from Ahaziah, Ahab's son, king of Israel.

Ahban was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles. He was the son of Abishur and his wife Abihail, and Molid was his brother (1 Chr 2:29). The surrounding genealogy traces Abishur's line back through Shammai and Onam to Jerahmeel, a descendant of Judah through Perez and Hezron. Nothing else is recorded about Ahban's life. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes his name to mean "brother of the wise" or "discreet," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "brother of an intelligent one," marking that meaning as uncertain.

Aher is named once in the Bible, in 1 Chr 7:12, as the father of Hushim. The verse comes at the end of a list of Benjamin's descendants, and Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat him as a Benjamite. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name means "another" and may be a shortened form. Both works suggest he may be the same man as Ahiram, a son of Benjamin in Num 26:38, or Aharah in 1 Chr 8:1. The STEPBible proper-names index, by contrast, links him to the tribe of Asher as a son of Shemer. The brief and compressed wording of the verse leaves his exact place in the genealogy uncertain. This entry follows the Benjamite reading suggested by the verse's context and records only what the verse states: that Hushim was his son.

Ahi was a member of the tribe of Gad, named in the Gadite genealogy of 1 Chronicles as the son of Abdiel and grandson of Guni. He is described as "chief of the house of their fathers", meaning the head of a family clan (1 Chr 5:15). The surrounding passage places the Gadites in Gilead and Bashan, east of the Jordan, and says their genealogies were recorded in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel. Smith's Bible Dictionary accordingly dates him to about 758 BC, an estimate drawn from that context. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "my brother". The name Ahi is borne by more than one person in the Bible. This Ahi should not be confused with the Asherite of the same name in 1 Chronicles 7. Nothing further is recorded about him.

Ahi was a man of the tribe of Asher, listed in the Asherite genealogy as the first of the sons of Shamer, with his brothers Rohgah, Jehubbah and Aram (1 Chr 7:34). Shamer is probably the same man called Shomer, son of Heber, two verses earlier in 1 Chr 7:32. The STEPBible proper names index identifies him the same way. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "my brother." Because the Hebrew word can also be read as an ordinary noun, some translations render the verse as "the sons of Shamer his brother" rather than treating Ahi as a personal name. This entry follows the King James reading, which takes Ahi as a son. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is distinct from another Ahi, a man of the tribe of Gad named in 1 Chr 5:15.

Ahiah was one of the officials of King Solomon. He and his brother Elihoreph served together as scribes, or royal secretaries, and both are called sons of Shisha (1 Kgs 4:3). Shisha is probably the same man as Shavsha, David's scribe (1 Chr 18:16), who is also called Seraiah (2 Sam 8:17) and Sheva (2 Sam 20:25). If so, the office passed from father to sons. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him among Solomon's princes, since he is named in the list of high officials. His name is often spelled Ahijah. Smith's gives its meaning as "friend of Jehovah," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "brother of the Lord." Several other people in the Bible share this name. Nothing more is recorded about this Ahiah.

Ahiah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 8:7 alongside Naaman and Gera. The surrounding passage, which lists "the sons of Ehud" (1 Chr 8:6), indicates that he was a son of Ehud, and this entry follows that reading. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries instead describe him as a son of Bela, Benjamin's firstborn, since Bela's line opens the chapter. The verse also notes that "he removed them" and then names Uzza and Ahihud, who are listed here as his brothers. The wording is compressed, and who carried out the removal is not clear. The Revised Version spells his name Ahijah, which Smith's Bible Dictionary renders "friend of Jehovah" and Hitchcock's Bible Names renders "brother of the Lord." Several other people in the Bible bear the same name. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Ahiam was one of David's mighty men, the warriors known as "the thirty." He appears only in the two parallel lists of these heroes. In 2 Sam 23:33 he is called the son of Sharar the Hararite, while 1 Chr 11:35 gives his father's name as Sacar; this entry follows the name Sharar. "Hararite" probably refers to a place or clan, perhaps in the hill country, though its exact meaning is uncertain. In the Samuel list his name follows Shammah the Hararite, which may suggest a family or regional connection, though the text does not say so. The name is usually taken to mean "mother's brother" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia; Easton's Bible Dictionary). Nothing further is recorded about his deeds.

Ahian was a son of Shemida in the genealogy of the tribe of Manasseh, one of the two tribes descended from Joseph. He is named first among Shemida's four sons, with Shechem, Likhi and Aniam, in 1 Chr 7:19, and nothing more is recorded about him. The chapter places Shemida among the descendants of Manasseh. Num 26:32 and Josh 17:2 also list Shemida as the founder of a Manassite clan, which suggests that Ahian belonged to that family line. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "brotherly." Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "brother of wine."

Ahiezer the son of Ammishaddai was the leader of the tribe of Dan during Israel's time in the wilderness. He was named as Dan's representative to help Moses take the census (Num 1:12). In the arrangement of the camp he served as captain of Dan, whose standard was on the north side (Num 2:25). On the tenth day of the offerings for the dedication of the altar, he brought Dan's gifts as prince of the tribe, including peace offerings of oxen, rams, goats and lambs (Num 7:66, 71). When Israel marched, Dan's camp went last as the rear guard, with Ahiezer over its host (Num 10:25). His name means "brother of help" or "my brother is help." The name is shared by another man in the Bible, a warrior who joined David at Ziklag, who is a different person.

Ahiezer was the son of Shemaah the Gibeathite and the brother of Joash. He is named as the chief of a group of warriors who came to David at Ziklag (1 Chr 12:3).
