The surrounding passage describes these men as kinsmen of Saul from the tribe of Benjamin, skilled with bow and sling, who joined David while he was still kept away from Saul. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him the chief of the Benjamite slingers, while Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as leading a body of archers. "Gibeathite" probably means he came from Gibeah, Saul's hometown in Benjamin. His name is usually taken to mean "brother is help." He should not be confused with the other Ahiezer, the leader of the tribe of Dan during the wilderness period.

Ahihud, son of Shelomi, was the prince, or leader, of the tribe of Asher. He appears in the list of tribal leaders whom the LORD named to Moses to divide the land of Canaan west of the Jordan among the tribes (Num 34:27). The surrounding passage shows that these men were to work with Eleazar the priest and Joshua in assigning each tribe its inheritance. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "brother is majesty" and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "brother of renown." Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the Hebrew spelling differs from another Ahihud in the Bible, a Benjamite named in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles, so the two should not be confused.

Ahihud was a member of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the Benjamite genealogy at 1 Chr 8:7. This entry treats him as a son of Ehud, whose sons are listed as Naaman, Ahiah and Gera, followed by Uzza and Ahihud. The verse is hard to follow, however. It says of the first three that "he removed them," probably referring to a forced move of these families, and then that "he begat Uzza, and Ahihud." Some readers therefore take Gera as Ahihud's father. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls the passage obscure and probably damaged in transmission. Easton's Bible Dictionary links him with the line of Bela, Benjamin's son. The name is usually explained as "brother is majesty." Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with others of the same name, such as the Asherite leader in Num 34:27.

Ahijah was a prophet from Shiloh, called "the Shilonite," active in the days of Solomon and Jeroboam. This is one of several men named Ahijah in the Bible. Meeting Jeroboam alone in a field outside Jerusalem, he tore his own new garment into twelve pieces as a sign that the kingdom would be divided and Jeroboam would rule part of it (1 Kgs 11:29–30). Rehoboam's refusal to listen to the people is presented as the fulfilment of this word (1 Kgs 12:15; 2 Chr 10:15). Later, when Jeroboam's son fell sick, Jeroboam sent his wife in disguise to Ahijah, who was by then blind with age. Forewarned by the LORD, Ahijah recognized her and gave her heavy news: the child's death and the destruction of Jeroboam's house, both of which came to pass (1 Kgs 14:2–6, 18; 15:29). Chronicles cites a written "prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite" as a source for Solomon's reign (2 Chr 9:29).

Ahijah was the father of Baasha, the man who seized the throne of the northern kingdom of Israel. He is known only through his son, who is repeatedly called "Baasha the son of Ahijah." The family belonged to the tribe of Issachar (1 Kgs 15:27). Baasha conspired against King Nadab, killed him at Gibbethon, and then reigned over Israel from Tirzah for twenty-four years, beginning in the third year of Asa king of Judah (1 Kgs 15:33). Ahijah's name appears again when prophets compare the coming downfall of Ahab's house to the fate of "the house of Baasha the son of Ahijah" (1 Kgs 21:22; 2 Kgs 9:9). Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this one should not be confused with Ahijah the prophet of Shiloh. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of the name as "brother of Yahweh."

Ahijah was one of the sons of Jerahmeel, of the tribe of Judah. He is mentioned only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:25, which names Jerahmeel as the firstborn of Hezron and lists his sons as Ram the firstborn, Bunah, Oren, Ozem and Ahijah. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe Jerahmeel as a great-grandson of Judah. The next verse, 1 Chr 2:26, says Jerahmeel had another wife, Atarah, who was the mother of Onam, so Onam was probably Ahijah's half-brother. Because that verse speaks of "another wife," some interpreters have suggested that "Ahijah" here may be the name of Jerahmeel's first wife. This entry follows the usual reading, which treats Ahijah as a son. The name, often explained as "brother of the LORD," belongs to several different people in the Bible. Nothing more is recorded about this one.

Ahijah the Pelonite was one of David's mighty men. He is named in the list of David's warriors at 1 Chr 11:36, next to Hepher the Mecherathite. Nothing else is recorded about him. The parallel list in 2 Sam 23:34 has "Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite" at roughly the same place, and Easton's Bible Dictionary treats Ahijah and Eliam as the same man. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes the correspondence between the two lists, which probably arose from differences in how the names were copied. The name Ahijah means "brother of the Lord" or "my brother is the Lord." Several other men in the Bible share this name, so this Ahijah should not be confused with Ahijah the prophet of Shiloh or with others called Ahijah.

Ahijah was a Levite who was in charge of the treasuries of the house of God and of the treasuries of the dedicated things (1 Chr 26:20). The surrounding chapter describes how the Levites' duties were organized, and Smith's Bible Dictionary places him in the reign of David. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he is one of several men in the Bible named Ahijah. The name is usually explained as "brother of the Lord" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). That encyclopedia also notes that the Greek translation of this verse reads "and their brethren" instead of a personal name, a reading many scholars accept. This entry follows the Hebrew text as translated in the King James Version, which names Ahijah.

Ahijah was one of the men who set their seal to the covenant made under Nehemiah, in which the community returned from exile pledged to keep the law of God. He is named only in Neh 10:26, alongside Hanan and Anan. The verse falls within the list that begins at Neh 10:14 with "the chief of the people," so he was probably a lay leader, and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of the "heads of the people." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts him as a Levite, and the Tyndale House proper-names list calls him a priest. This entry follows the reading as a head of the people. Nothing else is recorded about him, and several other men in the Bible share his name. The name is usually explained as "brother of the LORD" or "my brother is the LORD."

Ahikam was a royal official of Judah, the son of Shaphan and the father of Gedaliah. When the book of the law was found in the temple, King Josiah sent him with Hilkiah the priest, Shaphan the scribe and others to consult the prophetess Huldah (2 Kgs 22:12–14; 2 Chr 34:20). His father is probably that same Shaphan the scribe. Later, when priests and prophets demanded Jeremiah's death in Jehoiakim's reign (the setting given in Jer 26:1), Ahikam's support kept the prophet from being handed over to the people (Jer 26:24). After Jerusalem fell, the Babylonians made his son Gedaliah governor of those left in Judah, based at Mizpah, and placed Jeremiah in his care. Gedaliah was later murdered by Ishmael son of Nethaniah. Elasah and Gemariah, named elsewhere as sons of Shaphan (Jer 29:3; 36:10), were his brothers. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives his name's meaning as "my brother has risen up."

Ahilud is known only as the father of two officials in the royal administration of Israel. His son Jehoshaphat served as recorder, the official chronicler of the kingdom, under David and continued in that post under Solomon (2 Sam 8:16; 2 Sam 20:24; 1 Kgs 4:3; 1 Chr 18:15). A Baana son of Ahilud was one of Solomon's twelve district officers, responsible for a region including Taanach, Megiddo and Beth-shean (1 Kgs 4:12). Whether the two fathers are the same man is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary leaves the question open, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia assumes they are one person. This entry follows that identification and treats Jehoshaphat and Baana as brothers. Nothing else is recorded about Ahilud himself. His name is usually explained as meaning something like "brother of one born" or "child's brother."

Ahimaaz was the father of Ahinoam, the wife of King Saul. He is mentioned only once, in 1 Sam 14:50, which names Saul's wife and her father alongside Abner, the commander of Saul's army. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with others of the same name, such as the son of Zadok the priest. The meaning of the name is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "my brother is rage" or "brother of rage", Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "brother of anger", and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a brother of the council." Smith's Bible Dictionary places him before 1093 BC, an estimate drawn from his connection to Saul's reign.

Ahimaaz was the son of Zadok the priest, a Levite, and one of several men in the Bible with this name. During Absalom's revolt, David sent Zadok back to Jerusalem with Ahimaaz and Jonathan son of Abiathar so the two could relay news to him (2 Sam 15:27, 36). Waiting at En-rogel, they received word through a servant girl and escaped Absalom's men who searched for them (2 Sam 17:17, 20). After the battle in which Absalom died, Ahimaaz pressed Joab to let him run, outran the Cushite messenger, and told David of the victory. When asked about Absalom, he said only that he had seen a great tumult (2 Sam 18:19–29). The genealogies place him in the priestly line as father of Azariah (1 Chr 6:8–9, 53). Easton's Bible Dictionary treats him as Zadok's successor as high priest. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia regards his later career as unknown.

Ahimaaz was one of the twelve district officers King Solomon appointed to supply food for the royal household, each for one month of the year. His district was Naphtali (1 Kgs 4:15). The surrounding passage lists these officers, which is why he is understood as a governor or commissary officer there. He married Basmath, a daughter of Solomon, and so was the king's son-in-law. Several people in the Bible are called Ahimaaz. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that this man may possibly be Ahimaaz the son of Zadok the priest, though nothing in the text confirms it. This entry treats him as a separate person. The name is usually taken to mean "brother of anger" or "my brother is rage" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a brother of the council."

Ahiman was one of the three sons of Anak, along with Sheshai and Talmai, who lived at Hebron when the Israelite spies explored Canaan (Num 13:22). The Anakim were remembered as people of great size, and Easton's Bible Dictionary describes the three brothers as giants. Joshua 15:14 says Caleb drove them out of Hebron, and Judges 1:10 says the men of Judah killed them when they attacked the Canaanites of Hebron, formerly called Kirjath-arba. The two accounts probably describe the same conquest from different angles, with Caleb leading Judah's forces. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "brother of the right hand." The name is also borne by at least one other man in the Bible, a Levite gatekeeper in Chronicles, who is a separate person.

Ahiman was one of the gatekeepers ("porters") named in 1 Chr 9:17, listed with Shallum, Akkub, Talmon and their relatives, with Shallum as their chief. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a Levite porter. The setting is open to two readings. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place him among the temple guardians after the Exile, since the surrounding chapter lists those who lived in Jerusalem. The STEPBible proper-names index places his service in David's reign, reading the list alongside the chapter's later reference to gatekeepers appointed by David and Samuel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia compares the parallel list in Neh 11:19, which names Akkub and Talmon but not Ahiman. He is a different person from Ahiman the son of Anak at Hebron. His name is often explained as "brother of the right hand" or "my brother is fortune."

Ahimelech was a priest at Nob in Saul's reign, the son of Ahitub. When David arrived alone while fleeing Saul, Ahimelech was afraid. David claimed to be on secret business for the king and asked for a weapon (1 Sam 21:1–8). The same chapter says Ahimelech gave him the consecrated bread and Goliath's sword. Doeg the Edomite reported this to Saul, who summoned Ahimelech and the priests of his family. Ahimelech defended David as Saul's most faithful servant, but Saul condemned him and his whole house to death. His son Abiathar escaped and fled to David with an ephod. Following Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries, this entry treats him as probably the same man as Ahiah son of Ahitub, a great-grandson of Eli, who wore the ephod in Saul's camp and was told to bring the ark. Some instead take Ahiah to be his brother.

Ahimelech was a Hittite who was among David's companions while David was hiding from Saul in the wilderness. He is mentioned only once. When David found Saul's camp in the wilderness of Ziph, he asked Ahimelech and Abishai son of Zeruiah which of them would go down with him into the camp at night. Abishai volunteered, and nothing more is said of Ahimelech (1 Sam 26:6). His presence shows that David's band included foreigners, as did his later forces, which counted Uriah the Hittite among them. The name is usually explained as "my brother is king" or "brother of a king" (Hitchcock's Bible Names; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several people in the Bible share this name. This Ahimelech should not be confused with Ahimelech the priest of Nob, who helped David earlier in his flight from Saul.

Ahimelech, also called Abimelech, was a priest under King David, named as a son of Abiathar. He is listed with Zadok son of Ahitub as one of David's priests (2 Sam 8:17; 1 Chr 18:16), and he represented the priestly line of Ithamar when David organized the priests into divisions, while Zadok represented the line of Eleazar (1 Chr 24:3). He witnessed the recording and casting of lots for these divisions (1 Chr 24:6, 31). His brother is named as Jonathan, known from later passages as Abiathar's son. Elsewhere Abiathar is himself called the son of an earlier Ahimelech, the priest of Nob (1 Sam 30:7). For this reason Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that many scholars read 2 Sam 8:17 as "Abiathar the son of Ahimelech." This entry follows the text as written and treats him as Abiathar's son. Several people in the Bible share this name.

Ahinadab, son of Iddo, was one of the twelve district officers King Solomon appointed over Israel. According to 1 Kgs 4:7, which introduces the list, each officer provided food for the king and his household for one month of the year. Ahinadab's district was Mahanaim, a town east of the Jordan in Gilead, and by inference the surrounding territory as well (1 Kgs 4:14). Nothing else is recorded about him or his father. The meaning of his name is understood in different ways: Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "brother of liberality," Smith's Bible Dictionary "noble brother," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia "brother of willingness" or "my brother is willing."

Ahinoam was the wife of King Saul and the daughter of Ahimaaz. She is named once, in 1 Sam 14:50, in a brief summary of Saul's family and court that also names Abner as commander of his army. The preceding verse lists Saul's children, and by inference from that context she is taken as the mother of Jonathan, Malchi-shua, Merab and Michal. Abinadab, a son of Saul who died with his father in battle according to 1 Sam 31:2, is also counted among her children here. Nothing else is recorded about her life. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains her name as "my brother is pleasantness." She is a different person from Ahinoam of Jezreel, one of David's wives. Her father Ahimaaz is also distinct from the later priest of that name.

Ahinoam was a woman from Jezreel who became one of David's wives during the years he was fleeing from Saul (1 Sam 25:43). This Jezreel is probably the town in the hill country of Judah rather than the northern city of that name. She and Abigail lived with David at Gath under King Achish (1 Sam 27:3). Both were taken captive when the Amalekites raided Ziklag, and the following account in 1 Sam 30:18 says David recovered his two wives (1 Sam 30:5). She went with him to Hebron when he became king of Judah (2 Sam 2:2). There she bore Amnon, David's firstborn son (2 Sam 3:2; 1 Chr 3:1). Her name is always listed before Abigail's, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes 1 Sam 25:43 to mean David had married her earlier. The name is shared with Saul's wife, a different woman.

Ahio was a son of Abinadab, in whose house at Gibeah ("the hill") the ark of God had been kept. When David first tried to bring the ark to Jerusalem, Ahio and his brother Uzzah drove the new cart that carried it. Ahio walked in front of the ark, probably guiding the oxen, as Easton's Bible Dictionary describes. The parallel account in 1 Chr 13:7 tells the same story. By earlier passages such as 1 Sam 7:1, the house was at Kiriath-jearim, and his brother Eleazar had been set apart to keep the ark there. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that about a century may have passed since the ark arrived, so "sons" may mean descendants. Ancient Greek translations treat the name as a common noun meaning "his brother" or "his brothers." The name is shared by several other people in the Bible.

Ahio was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, listed in the genealogy of 1 Chr 8 among the sons of Beriah, alongside brothers such as Shashak and Jeremoth. By inference from the surrounding verses, Beriah and Shema were family heads of the inhabitants of Aijalon who drove out the people of Gath (1 Chr 8:13), and 1 Chr 8:16 closes the list as 'the sons of Beriah.' The Tyndale House proper-names index (STEPBible) instead counts Ahio as a son of Elpaal, Beriah's father. This entry follows the reading that makes him Beriah's son. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name probably means 'brotherly' or 'his brother.' The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Old Testament renders it as an ordinary word, 'his brother.' Other men bear the same name, including the son of Abinadab who walked before the ark (2 Sam 6:3).

Ahio was a Benjamite listed among the sons of the founder or leader of Gibeon and his wife Maachah in the genealogies of 1 Chr 8:31 and 1 Chr 9:37. The parallel list in 1 Chr 9:35 calls the father Jehiel. This entry identifies him with Abiel, whom 1 Sam 9:1 names as the father of Kish. Ahio's brothers included Kish and Ner, so he belonged to the extended family of King Saul, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. Nothing is recorded about his life beyond his place in these lists. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "his brother." According to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, Greek copies often translate the word as an ordinary noun rather than a name. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including the son of Abinadab who walked before the ark (2 Sam 6:3).

Ahira was the son of Enan and the leader of the tribe of Naphtali during Israel's time in the wilderness after the Exodus. He was named as Naphtali's representative to help Moses and Aaron take the census of the fighting men (Num 1:15). In the arrangement of the camp he was captain of Naphtali, which camped on the north side with Dan and Asher (Num 2:29). At the dedication of the altar he brought his tribe's offering on the twelfth and last day, including the peace offerings described in Num 7:83. When Israel set out from Sinai, he commanded Naphtali's troops on the march (Num 10:27). The meaning of his name is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "brother of evil" (that is, unlucky) or "my brother is friend," and Hitchcock's Bible Names adds "brother of the shepherd."

Ahiram was a son of Benjamin and the ancestor of the Ahiramites, one of the Benjamite clans counted in the census taken in the plains of Moab (Num 26:38). He is third in that list, after Bela and Ashbel. His name is usually taken to mean "exalted brother" or "my brother is exalted." The lists of Benjamin's sons in other books do not match exactly, and Ahiram may appear there under other forms. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both connect him with Ehi in Gen 46:21, possibly a shortened form of the name. They also note that Aharah in 1 Chr 8:1 and Aher in 1 Chr 7:12 may be the same man, though this is uncertain. This entry lists Ehi separately among his brothers.

Ahisamach was a man of the tribe of Dan, known only as the father of Aholiab (Oholiab), the craftsman who worked with Bezalel on the tabernacle in the wilderness. He appears only in the phrase "Aholiab, the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan," which comes up three times in Exodus. In those passages his son is named as appointed to help make what God commanded, as gifted to teach others, and as an engraver, skilled workman and embroiderer in blue, purple, scarlet and fine linen. Nothing else is said about Ahisamach himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "my brother supports." Smith's Bible Dictionary gives it as "brother of help." Smith's dates him to about 1490 BC, an estimate drawn from the setting of the Exodus.

Ahishahar was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, the last-named of the seven sons of Bilhan in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:10. His brothers were Jeush, Benjamin, Ehud, Chenaanah, Zethan and Tharshish. Bilhan was a son of Jediael, and the surrounding passage traces Jediael back to Benjamin, son of Jacob. That makes Ahishahar a great-grandson of the tribe's founder, though Smith's Bible Dictionary calls Bilhan Benjamin's grandson. The brother named Benjamin shares his name with the patriarch but is a different man. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of the name Ahishahar as "brother of dawn." He appears only in this one verse, and nothing else is recorded about him. By inference from the context, which counts men of valor by their fathers' houses, he was the head of one of the family groups within this branch of Benjamin.

Ahishar was one of King Solomon's chief officials. He was "over the household," meaning he managed the royal palace and its affairs. He appears only once, in the list of Solomon's high officers in 1 Kgs 4:6, where he is named alongside Adoniram, who was in charge of forced labor. Nothing else is recorded about his family or career. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take his name to mean "brother of song" or "my brother has sung," while Hitchcock's Bible Names also offers "brother of a prince." Later passages show that the office of the one "over the household" carried considerable authority in the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, so Ahishar probably ranked among the most important figures at Solomon's court.

Ahithophel was a man of Giloh who served as King David's counsellor and later joined Absalom's revolt. His advice was regarded as if it came from the oracle of God, under both David and Absalom (2 Sam 16:23). David prayed that his counsel would be turned to foolishness and sent Hushai back to Jerusalem to defeat it. Ahithophel advised Absalom to take David's concubines and to pursue David that night with twelve thousand men, but Absalom preferred Hushai's plan. Seeing his counsel rejected, Ahithophel went home, put his household in order, hanged himself, and was buried in his father's tomb. His son Eliam was one of David's mighty men. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies this Eliam with Bathsheba's father (2 Sam 11:3), making Ahithophel her grandfather. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia considers two different men named Eliam more likely.

Ahitub was a priest of Eli's family, the son of Phinehas, the grandson of Eli, and the brother of Ichabod (1 Sam 14:3). His son Ahiah wore the ephod in Saul's camp, and his son Ahimelech was the priest at Nob. Saul summoned Ahimelech and all the priests of his father's house after Doeg the Edomite reported that David had been helped there. Only Ahimelech's son Abiathar escaped (1 Sam 22:9–20). Smith's Bible Dictionary treats Ahiah and Ahimelech as the same man and traces the family through Eli to Ithamar. Easton's Bible Dictionary says Ahitub became high priest when Eli died, though the verses here do not state this. His name means "brother of goodness," according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Ahitub was a Levite of the priestly line, the son of Amariah and the father of Zadok, who served as one of the priests under King David (2 Sam 8:17; 1 Chr 18:16). The genealogy of the priests in 1 Chronicles traces his descent through Meraioth and Amariah, and continues through Zadok to Ahimaaz (1 Chr 6:7–8, 52). Smith's Bible Dictionary places him in the house of Eleazar, the son of Aaron, which follows from that same line of descent. Nothing is recorded of his own life or service. The name means "brother of goodness," according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Several other men named Ahitub appear in the Bible, including a priest of Eli's family who was the father of Ahimelech, and a later Ahitub in the same genealogy. This entry concerns Zadok's father.

Ahitub was a Levite in the high priestly line descended from Aaron. He was the son of Amariah and the father of Zadok, and through Zadok an ancestor of Shallum (1 Chr 6:11–12). Ezra 7:2 traces Ezra the scribe's ancestry back through this same line, so Ahitub was one of Ezra's forebears. This Ahitub comes later in the genealogy than the better-known Ahitub whose son Zadok served as priest under David (1 Chr 6:7–8). Because the names Amariah, Ahitub and Zadok repeat in the list, the two are probably separate people bearing family names that were reused, though some readers take the repetition as a copying duplication. This entry treats him as a distinct person. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "brother of goodness."

Ahlab was a town in the territory of the tribe of Asher whose Canaanite inhabitants the Israelites did not drive out. It appears only once, in a list of coastal and northern towns, including Accho, Zidon and Achzib, that Asher failed to conquer (Judg 1:31). The name probably means "fatness" or "fertile," according to Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mention its common identification with Giscala (Gush Halab), the modern village of el-Jish in upper Galilee, northwest of the Sea of Galilee. Others place it nearer the coast close to Tyre, a site sometimes linked with Helbah in the same verse. The location shown here follows the el-Jish identification.

Ahlai was a member of the tribe of Judah, descended through Jerahmeel, Onam, Appaim and Ishi, and named in 1 Chr 2:31 as the child of Sheshan. That verse says only "children," but 1 Chr 2:34 adds that Sheshan had no sons, only daughters, so Ahlai is understood as his daughter. STEPBible's proper-names index takes her this way, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes both readings. The same passage says Sheshan gave a daughter in marriage to his Egyptian servant Jarha, and she bore Attai, through whom the family line continued (1 Chr 2:34–35). That daughter is probably Ahlai, by inference from the passage. The name is shared with another Ahlai, the father of Zabad, one of David's mighty men (1 Chr 11:41). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "beseeching; sorrowing; expecting."

Ahlai was the father of Zabad. He is known only from 1 Chr 11:41, where Zabad son of Ahlai appears in the list of David's mighty men, the elite warriors of his army, named immediately after Uriah the Hittite. Nothing else is recorded about Ahlai himself. The same name belongs to another person in the Bible, a daughter of Sheshan in the genealogy of Judah (1 Chr 2:31, 34). The two are distinct, and this entry concerns the father of Zabad. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the Hebrew name as meaning "O would that!", while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "beseeching; sorrowing; expecting."

Ahoah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the sons of Bela, Benjamin's firstborn. He appears only once, in the list of Bela's sons at 1 Chr 8:4, with Abishua and Naaman. His name may mean "brotherly." Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take Ahiah in 1 Chr 8:7 to be the same man. Easton's also identifies him with Iri, who is named among Bela's sons in 1 Chr 7:7. Both dictionaries connect him with the Ahohites, a clan named after an Ahoah (2 Sam 23:9, 28; 1 Chr 11:12, 29; 27:4). Members of that clan included Dodo, father of Eleazar, and Zalmon (also called Ilai), two of David's mighty men. By inference, these men descended from this Benjaminite. Beyond his place in the genealogy, nothing more is recorded about him.

Aholah is a figurative woman in Ezekiel's allegory of two sisters, the elder of the pair, with Aholibah as her younger sister. Ezekiel 23:4 states plainly that Aholah stands for Samaria, capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, and Aholibah for Jerusalem. Both sisters are said to belong to the LORD and to bear sons and daughters. Aholah is then accused of playing the harlot by doting on the Assyrians, her neighbours, which pictures Samaria's political and religious ties with Assyria. Later the prophet is told to judge both sisters and declare their abominations, and they are called lewd women. The name appears in modern translations as Oholah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "his tent" or "his tabernacle." She is a symbolic figure, not a historical person.

Aholiab, son of Ahisamach of the tribe of Dan, was a skilled craftsman appointed to help Bezaleel make the tabernacle and its furnishings during Israel's time in the wilderness (Exod 31:6). He is described as an engraver, a designer, and an embroiderer in blue, purple and scarlet yarn and fine linen (Exod 38:23). Along with Bezaleel, he was given the ability to teach others the work (Exod 35:34). Moses called the two of them, together with every skilled worker willing to take part, to carry out the work on the sanctuary as the LORD had commanded (Exod 36:1–2). Modern translations spell his name Oholiab. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names give its meaning as "tent of the father."

Aholibah is a symbolic name for Jerusalem in Ezekiel's allegory of two sisters (Ezek 23:4). She and her elder sister Aholah, who stands for Samaria, are pictured as women who belonged to the Lord and bore him sons and daughters. Later in the chapter both are condemned as unfaithful wives who took foreign lovers. Aholibah is described as watching her sister's fate and then becoming even more corrupt than she was (Ezek 23:11). The Lord announces that he will turn her former lovers against her and bring them on her from every side (Ezek 23:22). Ezekiel is told to declare the abominations of both sisters (Ezek 23:36), and they are called "the lewd women" (Ezek 23:44). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names give the name's meaning as "my tent is in her," and the STEPBible names list takes her to represent the southern kingdom of Judah.

Aholibamah was a daughter of Anah and the sister of Dishon. She appears in the genealogy of the Horites, the earlier inhabitants of Seir (Edom). Gen 36:25 names her as Anah's only daughter. By inference from the verse before it (Gen 36:24), her father is Anah the son of Zibeon. Esau's wife Aholibamah is described in Gen 36:2 and 36:14 as the daughter of Anah, the daughter of Zibeon, so she is probably the same woman. Through that marriage the Horite line would have joined Esau's family. Because several people in the Bible carry this name, including an Edomite chief in Gen 36:41, the identification is likely but not certain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "my tabernacle is exalted."

Aholibamah is a name listed among the chiefs ("dukes") of Edom, the descendants of Esau, in Gen 36:41 and the matching list in 1 Chr 1:52. It appears alongside Elah and Pinon, with no further detail. The introduction to the list (Gen 36:40) says the chiefs are named by their families and places, so many readers take Aholibamah here as the name of a clan or district rather than an individual. The same name belongs to one of Esau's wives, the daughter of Anah (Gen 36:2, 14). The chiefdom may have taken its name from her line, which would explain why this entry treats the name as female, but the link is an inference and not stated in the text. Because several people share the name, the identification is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "my tabernacle is exalted."

Aholibamah was one of the wives of Esau. Genesis 36 calls her the daughter of Anah, the daughter of Zibeon the Hivite. This entry reads that phrase as making Anah her mother, a daughter of Zibeon. She bore Esau three sons in Canaan, Jeush, Jaalam and Korah, who later became chiefs ("dukes") among the Edomites. This entry also identifies her with Judith, the daughter of Beeri the Hittite, whom Esau married at forty (Gen 26:34). That would make Beeri her father. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests Judith may have been her original name. The two lists of Esau's wives differ in names and ancestry, so the match is an inference. STEPBible traces her to Seir the Horite, following the Horite genealogy later in Genesis 36. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "my tabernacle is exalted." The name is also borne by an Edomite chief in the same chapter.

Ahumai was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:2. He was a son of Jahath and a brother of Lahad. His grandfather was Reaiah, son of Shobal. The verse says these were "the families of the Zorathites," so Ahumai and Lahad were apparently founders or heads of clans linked with Zorah, a town in the lowland of Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to be the head of one of these families. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia tentatively gives "brother of water," and Hitchcock's Bible Names offers both "a meadow of waters" and "a brother of waters."

Ahuzam was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:6 as the first of four sons born to Ashur by his wife Naarah. His full brothers were Hepher, Temeni and Haahashtari. Ashur also had another wife, Helah, whose sons Zereth, Jezoar, Ethnan and Coz were Ahuzam's half-brothers, according to the verse that follows in the same genealogy. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the spelling Ahuzzam and identifies Ashur as the father or founder of Tekoa, drawing on the opening of this family list (1 Chr 4:5). Smith's renders the name as "possession," and Hitchcock's Bible Names as "their taking or possessing vision." Nothing more is recorded about him beyond his place in this family line.

Ahuzzath was one of the friends of Abimelech, king of Gerar, mentioned only once. He went with Abimelech and Phichol, the commander of Abimelech's army, to meet Isaac after Isaac had moved away from Gerar (Gen 26:26). By inference from the surrounding passage, the meeting took place at Beersheba, where the two sides swore an oath and made a covenant of peace. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that the title "friend" may mean a royal adviser or minister, and that his name, meaning "possession," ends in a way that recalls Philistine names such as Gath and Goliath. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the event to about 1877 BC, an estimate drawn from context.

Ai was a Canaanite city east of Bethel, "beside Bethaven," whose name is usually taken to mean "the ruin" or "heap." Abraham camped and built an altar between Bethel and Ai (called Hai in the KJV) when he entered Canaan and again on his return from the south. Under Joshua, Israel's first small attack on Ai was driven back with thirty-six dead. A second assault used an ambush on the west side of the city. It drew the defenders out, then took and burned Ai. Twelve thousand inhabitants were killed, and the king was hanged and buried under a heap of stones at the gate. The city was left "an heap for ever" (Josh 8:28). After the exile, men of Bethel and Ai were listed among the returnees. Easton's Bible Dictionary places Ai at Haiyan; the location shown here follows the alternative identification with the mound et-Tell.

Ai was a city in Ammonite territory, named only in Jeremiah's prophecy against the Ammonites. There Heshbon is told to wail because Ai has been plundered, and the daughters of Rabbah, the Ammonite capital, are told to put on sackcloth because their king, priests and princes will go into captivity (Jer 49:3). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it to have been closely linked with Heshbon. It is a different place from the better-known Ai near Bethel west of the Jordan. The name probably means "the ruin" or "heap." Some scholars, as noted in Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, think the text originally read Ar or "the city" rather than a place-name. This entry treats it as an Ammonite town. Its site is unknown, and the location shown here is only a rough placement east of the Jordan.

Aiah was the father of Rizpah, a concubine of King Saul. He appears only as part of her name, "Rizpah the daughter of Aiah". Nothing is said about his own life, family line or home. His daughter comes into the account twice. First, Ishbosheth accused Abner of sleeping with her after Saul's death (2 Sam 3:7). Later, her two sons by Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth, were handed over by David and put to death. Rizpah then guarded their bodies on a rock from the beginning of harvest until the rains came, and David was told what she had done (2 Sam 21:8–11). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the name to mean "falcon" and lists a different Aiah, an Edomite son of Zibeon, elsewhere in Genesis.

Aiath was a town north of Jerusalem, named once in Isaiah's poetic description of an invading army, understood from the surrounding chapter to be Assyria, advancing on Jerusalem. Isaiah 10:28 says the invader reaches Aiath, passes on to Migron, and leaves his baggage at Michmash. The name is a feminine form of Ai, and Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both take Aiath to be the same place as Ai, the city Joshua captured. The similar name Aija in Neh 11:31, also listed near Michmash, probably refers to the same town. Ai is commonly identified with et-Tell, east of Bethel, though other nearby sites have been proposed. The location shown here follows the et-Tell identification.

Aija was a town where people of the tribe of Benjamin lived after the return from exile in Babylon. It appears only in Neh 11:31, listed with Michmash, Bethel and their villages. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat Aija, like Aiath in Isa 10:28, as another form of the name Ai. That city stood near Bethel and is best known from Joshua's conquest in Josh 7–8. The pairing with Bethel supports this, as does Ezra 2:28, which counts returned exiles from "Bethel and Ai." Ai is commonly placed at et-Tell, a mound east of Bethel north of Jerusalem, and the location shown here matches that site. Whether the town settled after the exile stood on exactly the same spot as the older city is uncertain.

Aijalon was a town in the low hills northwest of Jerusalem, allotted to the tribe of Dan and given to the Kohathite Levites (Josh 19:42; Josh 21:24; 1 Chr 6:69). The valley of the same name is where Joshua called on the moon to stand still (Josh 10:12). Amorites held on there, though the house of Joseph made them pay tribute. Saul's army drove the Philistines from Michmash to Aijalon. Benjamite clan heads living there drove out the people of Gath. Rehoboam fortified it, and the Philistines captured it in the reign of Ahaz. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with modern Yalo, and the location shown here follows that view. The Aijalon in Zebulun where the judge Elon was buried (Judg 12:12) is probably a separate town. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it at Jalun in Galilee.

Ain was a landmark on the northeastern boundary of the land of Canaan as described to Moses, mentioned only in Num 34:11. The border was to run down from Shepham to Riblah "on the east side of Ain" and then descend to the eastern side of the Sea of Chinnereth (the Sea of Galilee). The name means "spring" or "eye" in Hebrew, so the place was probably named for a notable spring. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with 'Ain el-'Asy, the main source of the Orontes River, southwest of Riblah in present-day Lebanon. The ISBE also notes a view that, because the border reaches the Sea of Chinnereth, this Riblah and Ain lay farther south. The location shown here follows the Orontes-spring identification. This Ain is distinct from other places with the same name.

Ain (meaning "spring" or "eye") was a town in the far south of Judah, in the Negev region. It is listed among the southernmost cities of Judah's territory (Josh 15:32) and was later counted among the towns given to the tribe of Simeon, whose land lay within Judah's (Josh 19:7; 1 Chr 4:32). It was also one of the towns, with their surrounding pasturelands, assigned to the priestly descendants of Aaron (Josh 21:16). Because Ain is repeatedly named immediately beside Rimmon, the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes the view that the two names may form a single place, En-rimmon (Ain-Rimmon). STEPBible's Proper Names takes the same view. The location shown here, north of Beersheba, follows that En-rimmon identification. The name Ain is also used for at least one other place in the Bible, so references need to be read in context.

Ajah was a son of Zibeon and a brother of Anah, part of the Horite clans of Seir listed alongside the descendants of Esau in Edom. Genesis 36:24 gives the King James spelling Ajah, while the parallel genealogy in 1 Chr 1:40 spells it Aiah. Nothing is recorded about him beyond his place in these lists. By inference from the surrounding chapter, Zibeon was a son of Seir the Horite, and Ajah's brother Anah was the father of Aholibamah, one of Esau's wives. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "falcon", and Smith's Bible Dictionary as "clamor". Smith's also suggests that Ajah probably died before his father, since the line is traced through Anah. He is a different person from Aiah, the father of Saul's concubine Rizpah.

Akan was a son of Ezer and a brother of Bilhan and Zavan (Zaavan), listed among the Horites, the people who lived in the land of Seir before Esau's descendants settled there. He appears only in genealogies. Genesis 36:27 calls him Akan, while the parallel list in 1 Chr 1:42 gives the name as Jakan. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take the two names as the same person, and some English versions spell the Chronicles form Jaakan. His father Ezer is named in Genesis 36 as one of the sons of Seir the Horite and as a Horite chief. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "he twists," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "twisted." Nothing more is recorded about him.

Akeldama, meaning "Field of Blood" in Aramaic, was a plot of land near Jerusalem connected with the death of Judas. Matthew says the chief priests used the thirty pieces of silver Judas returned to buy "the potter's field" as a burial place for strangers. He adds that it was therefore called the field of blood "unto this day" (Matt 27:6–8). Acts gives a related account: the field Judas acquired with his reward, where he fell and died, became known to the people of Jerusalem by the Aramaic name Akeldama (Acts 1:18–19). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a tradition going back to about the 4th century that places the field on a level terrace on the southern slope of the Valley of Hinnom, near where it meets the Kidron Valley. A ruined charnel house long stood there. The location shown here follows that traditional identification, given only roughly.

Akkub was one of the seven sons of Elioenai, listed in the genealogy of David's royal line in the tribe of Judah (1 Chr 3:24). His brothers were Hodaiah, Eliashib, Pelaiah, Johanan, Dalaiah and Anani. The surrounding genealogy traces this family through King Jehoiachin and Zerubbabel, so Akkub belongs to the generations after the Babylonian exile. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia call him a descendant of Zerubbabel. Easton's Bible Dictionary simply describes him as a descendant of David. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his name and place in the list. Several other men in the Bible share the name Akkub, including Levite gatekeepers and the head of a family of temple servants, but this entry refers only to the son of Elioenai. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "pursuer."

Akkub was a Levite gatekeeper ("porter") at the temple in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. He is listed with Shallum, the chief, and with Talmon and Ahiman among the porters who lived in Jerusalem (1 Chr 9:17). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places him on duty at the east gate. The "children of Akkub" appear among the gatekeeper families who returned from Babylon (Ezra 2:42; Neh 7:45). Akkub and Talmon also lead the 172 gatekeepers in Nehemiah's day (Neh 11:19), and Akkub is named among those guarding the storehouses at the gates (Neh 12:25). Because these references span several generations, the name probably stands for a gatekeeping family as well as an individual. Other men named Akkub appear elsewhere in the Bible. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "pursuer."

Akkub was the ancestor or head of a family of Nethinim, the temple servants, whose descendants are listed among the exiles who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem and Judah (Ezra 2:45). The list in Ezra 2 records the groups who came back with Zerubbabel. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this return to about 536 BC. Nothing else is said about this Akkub himself. He appears only as a family name. Notably, the parallel list in Nehemiah 7 does not include his family. The name Akkub is shared by several other men in the Old Testament, including a gatekeeper and a descendant of David, and this entry is distinct from them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives meanings for the name such as "footprint" or "supplanting."

Akkub was one of the men named in Neh 8:7 who helped the people understand the law when Ezra read it publicly in Jerusalem after the return from exile. He is listed with Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah and others, and the verse groups them with "the Levites" who explained the reading while the people stood in their places. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Levite who assisted Ezra in expounding the law. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name Akkub is shared by several people in the Bible, including a gatekeeper family and a descendant of David. Whether this Akkub is connected to any of them is uncertain, so this entry treats him as a distinct individual known only from this passage.

Akrabbim, meaning "scorpions", was an ascent or mountain pass on the southern edge of the land of Israel. It always appears with the word for "ascent", and Josh 15:3 gives the full form Maaleh-acrabbim, "Scorpion Pass". It was one of the landmarks on the southern border of the promised land, running toward the wilderness of Zin and Kadesh-barnea (Num 34:4), and it also marked the southern border of the tribe of Judah (Josh 15:3). Judg 1:36 names it as a point on the border of the Amorites. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries place it between the southern end of the Dead Sea and Zin and explain the name by the scorpions common in the district. Easton's links it with the pass of es-Sufah. The exact pass is uncertain. The location shown here lies in the Negev, southwest of the Dead Sea.

Alameth was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the nine sons of Becher listed in the genealogy at 1 Chr 7:8. His brothers were Zemira, Joash, Eliezer, Elioenai, Omri, Jerimoth, Abiah and Anathoth. Becher was himself a son of Benjamin, which makes Alameth a grandson of Benjamin, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes. Nothing is recorded of his life beyond his name. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name more properly as Alemeth, meaning "covering," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "concealment." The ISBE also suggests that his name survived as that of a town near Anathoth, the Levitical city called Alemeth (Allemeth) in 1 Chr 6:60. His brother Anathoth likewise shares his name with that nearby town.

Alemeth was a Benjamite named in the genealogy of King Saul's family. He was a son of Jarah and a brother of Azmaveth and Zimri. Zimri's line continued through his son Moza. The two copies of this genealogy differ on his father's name. 1 Chr 9:42 calls him Jarah, while 1 Chr 8:36 calls him Jehoadah. Easton's Bible Dictionary treats these as two names for the same man, and this entry follows Jarah. In both lists his grandfather was Ahaz, who descended from Saul through Jonathan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts Alemeth as the fifth generation after Jonathan. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name probably means "concealment" or "covering." The same name is used for a Levitical town of Benjamin, also spelled Alameth or Almon, but that is a place, not this person.

Alemeth was a city in the territory of Benjamin, given with its surrounding pasture lands to the priestly descendants of Aaron. It is listed alongside Geba and Anathoth among the thirteen cities assigned to the priestly families (1 Chr 6:60). The parallel list of Levitical cities in Josh 21:18 names the same town Almon, and Easton's Bible Dictionary treats the two names as one place. Easton's identifies it with the ruin of Almit, about a mile northeast of ancient Anathoth, northeast of Jerusalem. The location shown here follows that identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives several possible meanings for the name, including "hiding" and "youth." A man named Alemeth also appears in Benjamite genealogies, and the town may share his name, though the text does not connect them.

Alexander was a son of Simon of Cyrene, the man who was passing by on his way in from the country when the soldiers made him carry Jesus' cross (Mark 15:21). His brother was Rufus. Mark names the two sons without explaining who they were. By inference, they were probably known to Mark's first readers, since he identifies Simon through them. Some have linked Rufus with the Rufus greeted in Rom 16:13, but nothing in the text confirms a connection, and nothing further is recorded about Alexander himself. Several other men named Alexander appear in the New Testament, and there is no clear reason to identify this Alexander with any of them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "one who assists men."

Alexander (Son of Simon) was a man in Jerusalem who was present when Peter and John were questioned by the Jewish leaders, about AD 30 by inference from context. Acts 4:6 lists him with Annas the high priest, Caiaphas, John and "as many as were of the kindred of the high priest." Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take him to be a relative of Annas, a member of the high-priestly family who sat in on the hearing before the Sanhedrin. Nothing more is recorded of him. The title of this entry calls him a son of Simon, but Acts 4:6 does not name his father. Mark 15:21 mentions an Alexander whose father was Simon of Cyrene, and whether that is the same man is uncertain. Several other men named Alexander also appear in the New Testament. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "one who assists men."

Alexander (Jew of Ephesus) was a Jewish man who took part in the riot at Ephesus. The riot was stirred up by Demetrius the silversmith against Paul's preaching, about AD 53 by inference from context. During the uproar, the Jews of the city pushed Alexander forward from the crowd, and he motioned with his hand, intending to make a defence before the people (Acts 19:33). Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests that he was probably meant to show that the Jews had no connection with Paul. According to the next verse, the crowd recognized him as a Jew and drowned him out by shouting for about two hours in praise of the goddess Artemis (Diana), so his speech was never given. Easton's also notes that he may be the same person as Alexander the coppersmith mentioned in 2 Tim 4:14, though the name was common and the link is uncertain.

Alexander was a man named by Paul in his letters to Timothy as an opponent. In 1 Tim 1:20 he is paired with Hymenaeus as one of those who had abandoned faith and a good conscience. Paul says he has "delivered" both men "unto Satan" so that they would learn not to blaspheme, which Easton's Bible Dictionary understands as excommunication from the church. In 2 Tim 4:14 Paul writes that "Alexander the coppersmith" did him much harm and leaves his punishment to the Lord. Whether these two passages refer to the same man is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests they may, and this entry treats them together. The name was common, and the New Testament mentions other men called Alexander, including a son of Simon of Cyrene and a Jew put forward during the riot at Ephesus. Their link to this Alexander is unclear.

Alexandria was a major Egyptian port on the Mediterranean, founded by Alexander the Great about 332 BC and still a large city with the same name today. Apollos, an eloquent Jew well versed in the scriptures, was born there before he came to Ephesus (Acts 18:24). Alexandrian ships twice carried Paul toward Rome, about AD 56 by inference from context. At Myra a centurion put the prisoners aboard one bound for Italy (Acts 27:6). After the shipwreck they sailed on in another that had wintered at the island, bearing the sign of Castor and Pollux (Acts 28:11). Smith's Bible Dictionary calls the city one of Rome's chief grain ports, which fits the wheat cargo mentioned in Acts 27:38. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes its large Jewish community, its famous library, and that the Greek Septuagint translation of the Hebrew Bible was made there.

Allammelech was a town in the territory given to the tribe of Asher. It appears only once, in the list of Asher's boundary towns in Josh 19:26, where it is named together with Amad and Misheal, just before the border runs west to Carmel and to Shihorlibnath. The King James Version spells it Alammelech. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as meaning "oak of a king" and says its location is not known. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the inland hills of western Galilee, east of Acco. It is inferred from the town's place in the boundary list among Asher's towns rather than from any identified site.

Allon was a man of the tribe of Simeon, the son of Jedaiah and the father of Shiphi. He appears only in the genealogy of his great-grandson Ziza, which traces the line back through Jedaiah, Shimri and Shemaiah (1 Chr 4:37). Ziza was among the Simeonite leaders who, in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, moved into the area of Gedor and took over pastureland there. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Ziza as a prince of his tribe in Hezekiah's reign. The name means "oak." The same word appears in Josh 19:33, in the border list of Naphtali, but there it is a place name, or possibly just the word "oak" (the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia prefers this reading). It refers to a different thing, not to this man.

Allon-bacuth, meaning "oak of weeping," was an oak tree below Bethel where Deborah, the nurse of Rebekah, was buried (Gen 35:8). The name probably recalls the mourning for her death. According to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, the narrative implies that Deborah was living with Jacob's household after his return from Paddan-aram, while they were staying at Bethel. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that large trees were rare enough in the land to serve as landmarks, and it suggests this tree may be the same as the "palm tree of Deborah" mentioned in Judg 4:5, though that Deborah was a different woman. The exact spot is unknown. The location shown here is a rough placement near Bethel, which is usually identified with modern Beitin, north of Jerusalem.

Almodad was the first-named of the thirteen sons of Joktan, listed in the genealogy of the nations descended from Shem (Gen 10:26; 1 Chr 1:20). His brothers included Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah, Ebal, Abimael, Sheba, Ophir, Havilah and Jobab. Nothing is recorded about him beyond his place in these lists. Like several of Joktan's sons, his name is usually taken to stand for a people as well as a person. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him the founder of an Arabian tribe, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes the name as south Arabian. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Easton's gives "immeasurable," Smith's Bible Dictionary "measure," Hitchcock's Bible Names "measure of God," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia "the beloved" or "God is beloved."

Almon was a city in the territory of Benjamin that, along with its surrounding pasturelands, was assigned to the priests. It is named in Joshua 21:18 beside Anathoth as the last of four Benjamite cities given to the descendants of Aaron. The surrounding verses name the other two as Gibeon and Geba. The name means "hidden" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia all identify it with Alemeth, the name used for the same priestly city in the parallel list at 1 Chr 6:60. Almon is probably the modern ruin of Khirbet Almit, a short distance northeast of Anata (ancient Anathoth), northeast of Jerusalem. The location shown here matches that identification.

Almon-diblathaim was a city in Moab, east of the Dead Sea, and one of the last camps of the Israelites near the end of their wilderness journey. They came to it from Dibon-gad and went on from it to the mountains of Abarim, opposite Mount Nebo (Num 33:46–47). The name may mean "Almon of the double fig-cake," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the site was named for two hills that looked like lumps of pressed figs. That work also notes the Hebrew may be read "Almon toward Diblathaim." Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat it as probably the same place as Beth-diblathaim, named in Jeremiah's oracle against Moab (Jer 48:22). Its exact site is uncertain. The location shown here lies on the Moabite plateau between Dibon and the Nebo range, which fits the order of the itinerary.

Alphaeus was the father of James, one of the twelve apostles, who is called "James the son of Alphaeus" in every list of the Twelve to tell him apart from James the son of Zebedee. Nothing is recorded about Alphaeus himself. This entry also counts Lebbaeus Thaddaeus as his son. That follows from reading "Judas the brother of James" in Acts 1:13 and Luke 6:16 as the same apostle called Thaddaeus in Matthew and Mark. His name appears in the Acts list of apostles gathered in the upper room before Matthias was chosen to replace Judas. Several people share the name. Mark 2:14 calls Levi, also known as Matthew, a son of Alphaeus, and STEPBible's proper-name index treats both apostles as his sons. Easton's and Smith's Bible dictionaries identify Alphaeus with Clopas, the husband of the Mary mentioned in John 19:25.

Alphaeus was the father of Levi, the tax collector whom Jesus called to follow him as he sat at his tax booth (Mark 2:14). The parallel account in Matthew 9:9 names the tax collector Matthew, so Alphaeus is identified as the father of the apostle Matthew, as Easton's Bible Dictionary also states. Nothing further is recorded about him. The same name belongs to the father of another apostle, James "the son of Alphaeus," in the lists of the Twelve. Whether these are the same man is uncertain. The Gospels never call Matthew and James brothers, and many readers treat them as two different men named Alphaeus. This entry concerns Matthew's father.

Alush was a desert campsite of the Israelites on their journey from Egypt to Mount Sinai. It appears only in the itinerary of Num 33, where the people traveled from Dophkah to Alush and then moved on to Rephidim, where there was no water to drink (Num 33:13–14). That makes it the last recorded stop before Rephidim. The shorter account of this stretch in Exodus 17:1 does not name Alush, so nothing else is known of it. Its location is not certainly known, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it was probably on the shore of the Red Sea. The location shown here is a rough placement in the southwestern Sinai Peninsula, between the proposed sites of Dophkah and Rephidim. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "a crowd of men," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "mingling together."

Alvah was one of the chiefs (the King James Version says "dukes") of Edom who descended from Esau. He appears in Gen 36:40 among chiefs named "according to their families, after their places." The parallel list in 1 Chr 1:51 spells his name Aliah, a minor shift in Hebrew spelling noted by the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Because the list is arranged by families and places, the name may stand for a clan or its district as well as for one man. Tyndale House's STEPBible proper-names list places him in the line of Esau's son Eliphaz. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also suggests he may be the same as Alvan, a descendant of Seir (Gen 36:23). This entry treats Alvah as a separate person. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Alvan was a son of Shobal and is listed with his brothers Manahath, Ebal, Shepho and Onam in Gen 36:23. The parallel genealogy in 1 Chr 1:40 spells his name Alian. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains this as a small change in one Hebrew letter. The surrounding passage in Genesis 36 names Shobal as a son of Seir the Horite, one of the peoples who lived in the land of Seir, later Edom. By that context Alvan belonged to the Horite clans there, as Smith's Bible Dictionary also describes him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "tall," though the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia marks that meaning as uncertain. Nothing is recorded about him beyond his place in these two lists.

Amad was a town in the territory given to the tribe of Asher when Joshua divided the land. It is named only once, in the list of Asher's towns, between Alammelech and Misheal, in a passage tracing the tribe's boundary toward Mount Carmel on the west and Shihor-libnath (Josh 19:26). Nothing else is recorded about it. Its exact site is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats it as unknown, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the ruin called Amud near Accho (modern Acre). The location shown here, in western Galilee northeast of Acre, follows that suggested identification. Older name lists give differing meanings for the name: Smith's offers "enduring," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "people of witness" or "a prey."

Amal was a man of the tribe of Asher, named once, in the Asherite genealogy, as one of the four sons of Helem, along with Zophah, Imna and Shelesh (1 Chr 7:35). The verse calls Helem the brother of the man named just before. The earlier list in 1 Chr 7:32 names Shomer and Hotham as brothers, sons of Heber. So Helem is probably another form of the name Hotham, and this entry follows that identification in treating Hotham as Amal's father. Nothing else is recorded about Amal. His name means "labor" or "toiler" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Hitchcock's Bible Names also gives the meaning "iniquity."

Amalek was a son of Eliphaz, Esau's eldest son, by his concubine Timna, making him a grandson of Esau and his wife Adah (Gen 36:12). He is listed among the chiefs ("dukes") of Edom descended from Eliphaz (Gen 36:16). The list in 1 Chr 1:36 places Timna among Eliphaz's sons alongside Amalek. His name also stands for the people descended from him, the Amalekites. As a people, Amalek attacked Israel at Rephidim after the exodus and was defeated by Joshua while Moses held up his hands (Exod 17:8–13). The LORD then declared lasting war against Amalek (Exod 17:14–16; Deut 25:17–19). Amalek later joined Moab against Israel (Judg 3:13). Saul struck Amalek and captured its king Agag (1 Sam 15:2–20), and David took spoil from it (2 Sam 8:12). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the name's meaning as "dweller in a valley."

Amalek is the name of a nomadic people and of the desert region they roamed south of Canaan. Amalek attacked Israel at Rephidim soon after the exodus. Joshua defeated them while Moses held up his hand on a hill, and the LORD declared war with Amalek "from generation to generation." Deuteronomy tells Israel to remember that attack and blot out Amalek's memory. Saul later came to "a city of Amalek" and captured its king Agag, but he was rebuked for not fully carrying out the command. David took spoil from Amalek. Easton's Bible Dictionary places them between the Dead Sea and the Red Sea, "from Havilah until thou comest to Shur." Their origin is debated. Tyndale House's proper-names index traces them to Esau's family, while Easton's notes that they already appear in Abraham's day (Gen 14:7). The location shown here is a general marker in the central Negev.

Amam was a town in the far south of Judah, in the Negev, listed among the cities given to the tribe of Judah in the allotment of the land. It appears only once in the Bible, in Josh 15:26, where it is named alongside Shema and Moladah in the group of towns lying toward the border of Edom. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "gathering place." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes the site as unidentified, and no other passage mentions it. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the Negev, south of Hebron, based on the town's position in Judah's southern list rather than on an identified site.

Amana was a mountain named once in the Bible, in a love poem where the bridegroom calls his bride to come with him from Lebanon and look from the tops of Amana, Shenir and Hermon, a wild region of lions' dens and leopards' mountains (Song 4:8). The verse pairs it with peaks of the Lebanon and Hermon ranges, so it was probably a summit in that area. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it as the southern part of the Anti-Lebanon range, near the sources of the Abana, the river of Damascus mentioned in 2 Kgs 5:12. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes a possible link with Mount Amanus in far northern Syria. The location shown here follows the Anti-Lebanon identification, near the headwaters of the modern Barada River. The name probably means "firm" or "constant."

Amariah was a Levite in the priestly line descended from Aaron through Eleazar. He was the son of Meraioth and the father of Ahitub (1 Chr 6:7). He appears only in genealogies, in the list of Levi's descendants and again in the list of Aaron's line (1 Chr 6:52). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him the grandfather of Zadok, who served as priest in David's time, since both lists continue from Ahitub to Zadok. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he was probably the last high priest of Eleazar's line before the office passed to Eli, of the line of Ithamar. His name is usually taken to mean "the Lord has said." Several other men in the Bible share this name, including a later Amariah in the same priestly genealogy, so the references need to be kept apart.

Amariah was a Levite of the priestly line of Aaron, the son of Azariah and the father of Ahitub (1 Chr 6:11). His father Azariah is described in the preceding verse as the one who served as priest in the temple Solomon built, which places Amariah in the line of chief priests after Solomon's time. Ezra 7:3 names him among the ancestors of Ezra the scribe. That list is shortened and skips several generations found in 1 Chronicles, so it names his father as Azariah son of Meraioth. The STEPBible proper-names index (Tyndale House) identifies him as the high priest under King Jehoshaphat, by inference the chief priest Amariah mentioned in 2 Chr 19:11. This entry follows that identification, though several men in the Bible share the name and the link is not certain. The name means "the LORD has said."

Amariah was a Levite, listed as the second of the four sons of Hebron, after Jeriah and before Jahaziel and Jekameam. His name appears in two lists in 1 Chronicles that set out the Levitical families in the time of King David (1 Chr 23:19; 24:23). Hebron was one of the sons of Kohath (1 Chr 23:12), so Amariah belonged to the Kohathite branch of the tribe of Levi. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat him as the head of a Levitical house when David organized the Levites into divisions. Because "son" in these genealogies can also mean a later descendant, he may have lived several generations after Hebron. The name, meaning "the Lord has said," was borne by several people in the Bible. Nothing else is recorded about this one.

Amariah was the chief priest in Judah during the reign of King Jehoshaphat. When Jehoshaphat appointed judges in Jerusalem, he named Amariah as the one over them "in all matters of the LORD". Zebadiah son of Ishmael, ruler of the house of Judah, handled "all the king's matters", and the Levites served as officers (2 Chr 19:11). Amariah therefore had charge of religious cases within the king's judicial reforms. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he is probably the Amariah named in the priestly genealogy at 1 Chr 6:9, and Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him the son of Azariah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats that identification as possible. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which is usually taken to mean "the LORD has said".

Amariah was a man who served during the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah, one of six assistants named under Kore, the Levite in charge of the freewill offerings (2 Chr 31:14–15). Working in the cities of the priests, these men handed out the offerings brought to the temple to their fellow priests and Levites by their divisions, giving fairly to young and old alike. The surrounding passage sets this in Hezekiah's reorganization of temple worship and support. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and the Tyndale House proper-names index treat him as a Levite, while Easton's Bible Dictionary lists him among the high priests of Hezekiah's time. This entry follows the Levite reading, which fits his place under Kore. His name means "the Lord has said." Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, and nothing else is recorded about this one.

Amariah was one of the Israelite men listed in Ezra's time as having married foreign wives, who agreed to send them away during Ezra's reforms after the return from exile. He is named only once, alongside Shallum and Joseph, in Ezra 10:42. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place him among the descendants of Bani, the family group whose list begins earlier in the same chapter. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, meaning "the Lord has said" or "the Lord promises," is shared by several other men in the Old Testament, and he should not be confused with them.

Amariah was a priest, or a priestly family named after him, in the period after the return from exile. Neh 12:2 lists Amariah among the priests who came back to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel. Neh 10:3 names Amariah among the priests who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah's day. Neh 12:13 records that a man named Jehohanan headed the house of Amariah when Joiakim was high priest. Because these mentions span several generations, many readers take the later ones to refer to a priestly house carrying the founder's name rather than to the same man. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats them as one priest and calls him Jehohanan's father. The name means "the Lord has said." Several other men in the Bible share it.

Amariah was a man of the tribe of Judah, from the clan of Perez, named only in a genealogy in Neh 11:4. He was the son of Shephatiah and the father of Zechariah, and an ancestor of Athaiah, one of the Judahites who lived in Jerusalem when the city was resettled in Nehemiah's time. Amariah himself therefore probably lived some generations before the return from exile. His name means "the Lord has said" or "the Lord promises." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia compares this line with the similar list of Judahite settlers in 1 Chr 9:4, which names an Imri, and suggests Amariah may belong to the same family. Several other men in the Bible share the name Amariah, and this one is known only from this single verse.

Amariah was an ancestor of the prophet Zephaniah, named only in the genealogy that opens Zephaniah's book (Zeph 1:1). He was the son of Hizkiah and the father of Gedaliah, making him Zephaniah's great-grandfather. Zephaniah prophesied in the days of Josiah king of Judah, so Amariah probably lived two or three generations earlier. Hizkiah is the same Hebrew name as Hezekiah, and many interpreters take him to be King Hezekiah of Judah. If so, Amariah was a son of that king and Zephaniah was of royal descent, though the verse does not call Hizkiah a king. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as "the Lord says."

Amasa was the son of Jether and Abigail, and a cousin of Joab, whose mother Zeruiah was Abigail's sister. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Abigail as David's sister, which would make Amasa David's nephew. His father is called Ithra an Israelite in 2 Sam 17:25 but Jether the Ishmeelite in 1 Chr 2:17. During Absalom's revolt, Absalom made Amasa commander of his army in place of Joab. After the revolt failed, David promised Amasa command of his own army instead of Joab. Sent to gather the men of Judah against the rebel Sheba son of Bichri, Amasa took longer than the three days he was given. At the great stone in Gibeon, Joab greeted him as a brother and stabbed him to death. David later charged Solomon to avenge this killing, and Solomon called Amasa captain of the host of Judah. Others in the Bible share this name.

Amasa son of Hadlai was one of the leaders of the tribe of Ephraim in the northern kingdom of Israel during the reign of Ahaz, king of Judah. After Pekah's Israelite army defeated Judah and brought a large number of captives to Samaria, the prophet Oded warned the returning soldiers against enslaving their kinsmen. Amasa and three other heads of Ephraim, Azariah, Berechiah and Jehizkiah, then stood up against the returning troops (2 Chr 28:12). The surrounding passage records that they refused to let the captives be brought in, and that the captives were clothed, fed and returned to Jericho. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a prince of Ephraim. He is a different man from the better-known Amasa who commanded Absalom's army, since the name is shared by several people in the Bible.

Amasai was a Levite of the family of Kohath, named in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 6 as a son of Elkanah and brother of Ahimoth (1 Chr 6:25). He was the father of Mahath, and through this line an ancestor of the prophet Samuel. The singers' genealogy traces Heman the singer back through Samuel, and in it Amasai appears as the father of Mahath (1 Chr 6:35). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both identify him as part of Samuel's ancestry, and Smith's places him among the Kohathites. Nothing is recorded about his life beyond these family links. Several other men in the Bible share the name Amasai and should not be confused with him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "strong," while Smith's gives "burdensome."

Amasai was the leader of a group of men from Benjamin and Judah who came to David while he was an outlaw fleeing from Saul. When David questioned their loyalty, the spirit came upon Amasai, described as chief of the captains, and he declared that they belonged to David and were on his side. He wished peace to David and to his helpers, because David's God was helping him. David then accepted the men and made them captains of his band (1 Chr 12:18). Sources differ on where this happened. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it at Ziklag, while Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests the stronghold, probably of Adullam. This entry treats the place as uncertain. The name is shared by several men in the Bible. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "burdensome," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "strong."

Amasai was a priest, one of seven named in 1 Chr 15:24 who blew trumpets before the ark of God when David had it brought up to Jerusalem. The other trumpeters were Shebaniah, Jehoshaphat, Nethaneel, Zechariah, Benaiah and Eliezer. Obed-edom and Jehiah served as doorkeepers for the ark on the same occasion. Easton's Bible Dictionary places this during the ark's move from the house of Obed-edom, where it had been kept for a time. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Amasai, and this priest should be kept distinct from them. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "burdensome," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "strong."

Amasai was a Levite of the Kohathite clan, known only as the father of Mahath. His son was one of the Levites who came forward when King Hezekiah called for the temple to be cleansed and its worship restored, as described in 2 Chr 29:12. Amasai himself does not take part in the account, and the verse records nothing else about him. Mahath is listed as a Kohathite, so Amasai probably belonged to that clan as well. The same pairing of names, Mahath son of Amasai, also appears in the much earlier Kohathite genealogy of 1 Chr 6:35.
