That suggests these names ran in the family, though the two men are probably different people. Several other men in the Bible are also called Amasai. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "strong," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives it as "burdensome."

Amasiah, son of Zichri, was one of the military commanders of Judah during the reign of King Jehoshaphat. He appears only in 2 Chr 17:16, in a list of the king's army chiefs stationed in Jerusalem, where he is named next after Jehohanan. He commanded two hundred thousand "mighty men of valour." The verse singles him out as one who "willingly offered himself unto the LORD," a phrase Easton's Bible Dictionary compares with the volunteers praised in Judg 5:9. The text does not say what form this self-offering took. His name is usually explained as meaning "Yah bears" or "sustained by the LORD" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia; Easton's Bible Dictionary). Nothing else is recorded about him, and his father Zichri, a common name in the Old Testament, cannot be identified with any other person of that name.

Amaw was the land where Balaam son of Beor lived, in the town of Pethor "by the river," taken to mean the Euphrates. Balak king of Moab sent messengers there to summon Balaam to curse Israel (Num 22:5). The name does not appear in the King James Version, which translates the Hebrew phrase as "the land of the children of his people." Some modern translations read the same words as a place name, "the land of Amaw." STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) follows that reading and describes Amaw as a place near the Euphrates where Balaam lived. The area is otherwise unknown, and its location is only approximate. The location shown here places it on the upper Euphrates in what is now northern Syria, the region usually associated with Pethor.

Amaziah was a king of Judah, the son and successor of Joash and the father of Uzziah, also called Azariah. His mother was Jehoaddan of Jerusalem. He became king at twenty-five after his father was murdered. He reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem, roughly 839–810 BC by inference from context. He mustered Judah's army and hired Israelite troops for a hundred talents. At a man of God's word he sent them home, and the dismissed soldiers raided cities of Judah. He defeated the Edomites in the Valley of Salt, but then set up and worshipped Edom's gods, and a prophet rebuked him. He challenged Jehoash king of Israel, was defeated and captured at Beth-shemesh, and part of Jerusalem's wall was broken down. He outlived Jehoash by fifteen years. A conspiracy drove him to flee to Lachish, where he was killed. Several other people in the Bible share his name.

Amaziah was a man of the tribe of Simeon, known only as the father of Joshah, who appears in a list of Simeonite clan leaders in 1 Chr 4:34. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 4:38–41) describes these leaders as princes of their families who, in the days of King Hezekiah of Judah, moved toward Gedor in search of pasture and settled there. By inference, Amaziah lived a generation before that time, but nothing else is said about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies Joshah as one of the Simeonite chiefs in Hezekiah's time. Hitchcock's Bible Names and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of the name as "the strength of the Lord." Several other people in the Bible share the name Amaziah, including a king of Judah. This Amaziah should not be confused with them.

Amaziah was a Levite named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 6:45, where he is listed as the son of Hilkiah and the father of Hashabiah. The surrounding passage traces the ancestry of Ethan, one of the Levite singers David appointed for the music of worship, back through Merari, son of Levi. Easton's Bible Dictionary accordingly places Amaziah among the descendants of Merari in Ethan's family line. He would therefore have lived several generations before Ethan. STEPBible's proper-names index links him with the time of David. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as "the strength of the Lord," was borne by several other men in the Bible, including a king of Judah. This Levite should not be confused with them.

Amaziah was the priest of Bethel in the northern kingdom of Israel during the reign of Jeroboam II, and the opponent of the prophet Amos. He sent word to King Jeroboam accusing Amos of conspiring against him and saying the land could not bear his words (Amos 7:10). He then told Amos, whom he called a seer, to flee to Judah, earn his living there, and prophesy there instead (Amos 7:12). Amos answered that he was not a prophet or a prophet's son but a herdsman and a gatherer of sycamore fruit (Amos 7:14). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries describe him as a priest of the golden calf worship at Bethel, which by inference connects him with the shrine Jeroboam I set up there. The name, meaning "the strength of the Lord" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, is also borne by several other people in the Bible, including a king of Judah.

Amittai was the father of the prophet Jonah. He is known only through his son, who is called "Jonah the son of Amittai" both in the account of Jeroboam II's reign and at the opening of the book of Jonah (2 Kgs 14:25; Jonah 1:1). The text says nothing else about him. Since 2 Kgs 14:25 describes Jonah as being from Gath-hepher, Amittai's family probably lived there too. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places Gath-hepher in the tribal territory of Zebulun. By inference from his son's ministry under Jeroboam II, Amittai probably lived in the northern kingdom of Israel in the early eighth century BC. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of his name as "true," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "faithful."

Ammah was a hill near Gibeon in the territory of Benjamin. It is mentioned once, in 2 Sam 2:24, as the place Joab and his brother Abishai reached at sunset while chasing Abner after the battle at the pool of Gibeon. The verse places it "before Giah by the way of the wilderness of Gibeon," but Giah is otherwise unknown, and the exact site of the hill has not been identified. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it east of Gibeon, and the rough location shown here follows that view. The Hebrew word can mean "cubit," "mother" or "beginning." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same word forms part of Metheg-ammah in 2 Sam 8:1, though that is probably a different place.

Ammiel, son of Gemalli, was the man from the tribe of Dan among the twelve spies Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan (Num 13:12). By inference from the wider account, he was not Joshua or Caleb, so he was one of the ten spies who brought back a discouraging report. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that these ten died by a plague (Num 14:37). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as meaning "my kinsman is God," while Smith's and Hitchcock's dictionaries give "people of God." The name Ammiel belongs to several different men in the Old Testament, and this entry refers only to the spy from Dan.

Ammiel was the father of Machir of Lo-debar, and he is known only through his son. Machir sheltered Mephibosheth, the lame son of Jonathan, in his house at Lo-debar until King David sent for him (2 Sam 9:4–5). Later, when David fled from Absalom to Mahanaim, Machir was one of the men who brought him supplies (2 Sam 17:27). Lo-debar lay east of the Jordan in Gilead. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes Ammiel as a Benjamite, though the verses themselves do not name his tribe. The name means "my kinsman is God" or, according to Smith's and Hitchcock's dictionaries, "people of God." Several other men in the Bible share the name, so this Ammiel should not be confused with them. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Ammiel was a Levite named as the sixth of eight brothers in the list of temple gatekeepers in 1 Chr 26:5. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 26:4) presents these brothers as the sons of Obed-edom, and Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify Ammiel that way. This entry records his father as Shimei. His brothers were Shemaiah, Jehozabad, Joah, Sacar, Nethaneel, Issachar and Peulthai. The chapter belongs to the account of the duties assigned to the Levites in David's time, so he probably served as a doorkeeper during David's reign, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia states. The verse closes the list with the remark that God had blessed the family. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share his name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names takes to mean "the people of God."

Ammihud was a man of the tribe of Ephraim, one of the two tribes descended from Joseph. He was the father of Elishama, who led Ephraim during the wilderness journey after the Exodus. Elishama helped take the census, commanded Ephraim's camp on the west side of the tabernacle, brought the tribe's offering on the seventh day of the altar's dedication, and led its host when Israel set out (Num 1:10; 2:18; 7:48, 53; 10:22). In the Ephraimite genealogy Ammihud is the son of Laadan and father of Elishama (1 Chr 7:26). The next verse continues the line to Non and his son Joshua, so Smith's Bible Dictionary counts Ammihud as an ancestor of Joshua. The name is explained as "my kinsman is glorious" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "people of praise" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Ammihud was a man of the tribe of Simeon and the father of Shemuel. He is named only once, in Num 34:20, where his son Shemuel appears in the list of tribal leaders chosen to divide the land of Canaan among the tribes after Israel entered it. Nothing else is recorded about Ammihud himself. The name was shared by several other people in the Old Testament, such as the Ephraimite father of Elishama and the Naphtalite father of Pedahel, and this Simeonite should be kept distinct from them. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as "my kinsman is glorious," while Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names give its meaning as "people of praise."

Ammihud was the father of Pedahel, the leader of the tribe of Naphtali named in Num 34:28. Pedahel was one of the tribal leaders chosen to help divide the land of Canaan among the Israelites, and the surrounding passage describes that appointment. Ammihud himself is known only as Pedahel's father, and nothing more is said about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Ammihud, including fathers of leaders from the tribes of Ephraim and Simeon, so this one should not be confused with them. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as "my kinsman is glorious," while Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names give "people of praise."

Ammihud was the father of Talmai, king of Geshur, a small Aramean kingdom northeast of Israel. He appears only once, at 2 Sam 13:37, which says that Absalom fled to Talmai son of Ammihud after killing his brother Amnon. A connected passage, 2 Sam 3:3, says David's wife Maacah was the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur, so Ammihud was probably the great-grandfather of Absalom through his mother. Some Hebrew manuscripts spell the name Ammihur, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia prefers that reading. It gives the meaning "my kinsman is glorious," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "people of praise." Several other people in the Bible are also called Ammihud. Nothing more is recorded about this one.

Ammihud was a man of the tribe of Judah, descended through Pharez (Perez), son of Judah. He was the son of Omri and the father of Uthai. He appears only in a genealogy in 1 Chr 9:4, which traces Uthai's line back through Ammihud, Omri, Imri and Bani to Pharez. The surrounding chapter lists people who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile, so Uthai was probably one of those settlers. Ammihud himself may have lived somewhat earlier, but the text does not say. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "people of praise." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "my kinsman is glorious." Several other men in the Old Testament share the name, and this Ammihud should not be confused with them. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Amminadab was a man of the tribe of Judah, the son of Ram and a descendant of Judah through Perez and Hezron (Ruth 4:19; Luke 3:33). His son Nahshon was the leader of Judah during the wilderness journey. He headed the tribe's census, led its camp and march, and brought the first offering at the dedication of the altar (Num 1:7; 2:3; 7:12; 10:14). His daughter Elisheba married Aaron and bore him Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar (Exod 6:23). Amminadab appears in the line leading to David (Ruth 4:19–20; 1 Chr 2:10). Matthew and Luke include him, spelled Aminadab, in the genealogy of Jesus (Matt 1:4; Luke 3:33). The name, explained in Hitchcock's Bible Names as "my people is liberal," is borne by other men in the Bible as well. This entry concerns the ancestor in Judah's line.

Amminadab was a Levite in the time of King David, chief of the descendants of Uzziel, whose group numbered 112 men (1 Chr 15:10). Uzziel was a son of Kohath, so Amminadab belonged to the Kohathite branch of the Levites, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. David summoned him with other Levite leaders and the priests Zadok and Abiathar when he prepared to bring the ark of the covenant up to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:11). By inference from the following verses, these leaders were told to purify themselves and to carry the ark. Several other men in the Bible share the name Amminadab, and this one should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "my people is liberal."

Ammishaddai was a man of the tribe of Dan, known only as the father of Ahiezer, the tribe's leader during the wilderness journey after the Exodus. Every mention of him occurs in the phrase "Ahiezer the son of Ammishaddai." His son was named as Dan's representative at the census (Num 1:12) and as captain of the Danite camp, which was stationed on the north side of the tabernacle (Num 2:25). Ahiezer also brought Dan's offering on the tenth day of the altar's dedication (Num 7:66, 71), and he led the Danite host, which marched last as the rear guard of all the camps (Num 10:25). Nothing is recorded of Ammishaddai himself. His name contains Shaddai, "Almighty." Easton's Bible Dictionary renders it "people of the Almighty," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "Shaddai is my kinsman."

Ammizabad was the son of Benaiah, the warrior who was mighty among David's thirty champions and ranked above them. He is named only in 1 Chr 27:6, in the list of the twelve army divisions that served King David in monthly rotation. Benaiah commanded the division for the third month, and the verse says that in his course was Ammizabad his son. This is usually taken to mean that Ammizabad served under his father in that division, perhaps as his second-in-command or as his successor in the post, as the STEPBible Proper Names suggest. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary explain the name as "people of the giver," meaning God. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "my kinsman has made a present." Nothing more is recorded about him.

Ammon was the land of the Ammonites, east of the Jordan River and north of Moab, near the upper Jabbok River. On the way from Egypt, Israel was told not to take it, because it had been given to the descendants of Lot (Deut 2:19, 37). Easton's Bible Dictionary traces the people to Ammon, or Ben-ammi, Lot's son. The Ammonites, ruled by a king (Jer 27:3), later fought Israel. Jephthah subdued them, striking twenty cities from Aroer to Minnith (Judg 11:27, 33). In Jehoshaphat's day they joined Moab and Mount Seir against Judah, but the allies turned on one another (2 Chr 20:10, 22–23). Prophets list Ammon among the nations facing judgment, and Ezekiel foretold that its city Rabbah would become a stable for camels (Ezek 25:5). Nehemiah objected to Jews marrying Ammonite wives (Neh 13:23). The location shown here is Rabbah, the capital, at modern Amman in Jordan.

Amnon was David's firstborn son, born in Hebron to Ahinoam of Jezreel (2 Sam 3:2; 1 Chr 3:1). He became so infatuated with Tamar, the sister of his half-brother Absalom, that he made himself ill over her. His cousin Jonadab, son of David's brother Shimeah, advised him to pretend to be sick. Amnon then asked David to send Tamar to prepare food for him. When she came, he sent everyone out, forced her, and then turned on her with intense hatred and drove her away. Absalom said nothing to Amnon but hated him for what he had done. According to 2 Sam 13:23, two years later Absalom invited the king's sons to a sheep-shearing feast. There he had his servants kill Amnon once he was merry with wine. Jonadab assured David that only Amnon had died. The same name belongs to a different man, a descendant of Judah, in 1 Chr 4:20.

Amnon was a son of Shimon, named with his brothers Rinnah, Ben-hanan and Tilon in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah (1 Chr 4:20). Nothing else is recorded about him, and Shimon's own place in the family line is not stated. Because the surrounding list in 1 Chronicles 4 traces the descendants of Judah, he is generally taken to be a Judahite, as the STEPBible proper names index describes him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "faithful." He is a different person from the better-known Amnon, the eldest son of King David.

Amok was a priest listed among the chief priests in the days of Jeshua the high priest (Neh 12:7). The surrounding list in Nehemiah 12 names the priests who came back from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel and Jeshua, so Amok was probably one of that first group of returnees. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the return to about 536 BC, an estimate drawn from context. A generation later, in the time of the high priest Joiakim, the priestly family named after Amok was headed by a man called Eber (Neh 12:20). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes Amok to be Eber's forefather. The name is usually understood to mean "deep," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a valley" or "a depth." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Amon was the ancestor of a family listed among the descendants of "Solomon's servants" who returned from exile in Babylon. Nehemiah's list names him Amon (Neh 7:59). The parallel list in Ezra calls him Ami (Ezra 2:57), and the two are generally taken as the same person. Both lists place his family next to those of Shephatiah, Hattil and Pochereth of Zebaim. The surrounding passages count Solomon's servants together with the Nethinim, the temple servants, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. Nothing more is recorded about him. He should not be confused with others of the same name, such as Amon the king of Judah, son of Manasseh. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "faithful" or "true," and Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "builder."

Amon was the governor of the city, probably Samaria, in the time of Ahab king of Israel. When the prophet Micaiah predicted that Ahab would die in the battle at Ramoth-gilead, contradicting the court prophets, the king ordered that he be taken back to Amon and to Joash the king's son (1 Kgs 22:26; 2 Chr 18:25). In the following verse the king orders that Micaiah be held in prison on bread and water until the king returns safely, so Amon was apparently responsible for keeping him in custody. The passage does not name the city, but the setting at Samaria leads Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia to call him governor of Samaria. He is mentioned only in this account, and he is a different person from Amon king of Judah, the son of Manasseh.

Amon was a king of Judah, the son and successor of Manasseh and the father of King Josiah. Several other people in the Bible share the name. His mother was Meshullemeth, daughter of Haruz of Jotbah. He became king in Jerusalem at twenty-two and reigned two years, about 642–640 BC by inference from context. Chronicles says he did evil as his father had, sacrificing to the carved images Manasseh had made. Unlike Manasseh, he did not humble himself before the LORD. His servants conspired against him and killed him in his own house. The people of the land then executed the conspirators and made Josiah king. According to 2 Kgs 22:1, Josiah's mother was Jedidah, which makes her Amon's wife, and Josiah was eight when he took the throne. Jeremiah and Zephaniah name Amon as Josiah's father, and he appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus.

Amorite is named in the table of nations as a son, or more likely a descendant people, of Canaan, listed alongside the Jebusite and the Girgasite (Gen 10:16; 1 Chr 1:14). The name stands both for an ancestor and for the nation traced to him, one of the peoples living in the land before Israel. Amos recalls the Amorite as a people as tall as cedars and strong as oaks, whom God destroyed before Israel. He calls Canaan "the land of the Amorite" that Israel came to possess after the exodus and forty years in the wilderness (Amos 2:9–10). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries explain the name as "highlanders" or "mountaineers." They place the Amorites in the hill country west of the Dead Sea and toward Hebron, and east of the Jordan in the kingdoms of Sihon and Og. Easton's adds that the name was sometimes used broadly for the inhabitants of Canaan in general.

Amos was a prophet whose words make up the Book of Amos. He came from Tekoa in Judah, which Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies with modern Tekua, about 12 miles south-east of Bethlehem. He prophesied concerning the northern kingdom of Israel during the reigns of Uzziah of Judah and Jeroboam son of Joash of Israel, "two years before the earthquake" (Amos 1:1). His ministry is dated here to about 788 BC, by inference from context. He described himself as no professional prophet or prophet's son but a herdsman and a gatherer of sycamore fruit. He recorded visions such as a plumb line and a basket of summer fruit, each announcing judgment on Israel. Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, reported to Jeroboam that Amos had conspired against him by predicting the king's death and Israel's exile, and told Amos to go back to Judah. Several other men in the Bible share this name.

Amos is an ancestor of Jesus listed in Luke's genealogy, the son of Naum and the father of Mattathias (Luke 3:25). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places him eighth before Joseph, the husband of Mary. Since Luke's line runs through David and Judah, he belongs to the tribe of Judah by inference from the genealogy. He lived in the period after the Babylonian exile, judging by his position in the list. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is a different person from the prophet Amos, whose book appears among the Old Testament prophets, and the name is shared by others in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "loading" or "weighty."

Amoz was the father of the prophet Isaiah. He is known only through the phrase "Isaiah the son of Amoz," which appears in the headings of Isaiah's prophecies (Isa 1:1; 2:1; 13:1) and in the accounts of Isaiah's dealings with King Hezekiah in 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles and Isaiah. Since Isaiah prophesied in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, Amoz presumably lived in Judah in the eighth century BC. The Bible records nothing else about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "strong" and notes a view that he was the "man of God" of 2 Chr 25:7–8. Smith's Bible Dictionary reports a rabbinical tradition that he was a brother of King Amaziah of Judah. He should not be confused with the prophet Amos, whose name is spelled differently in Hebrew.

Amphipolis was a city of Macedonia that Paul and Silas passed through on their way from Philippi to Thessalonica, along with Apollonia (Acts 17:1). The verse only mentions it as a stop on the journey, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the wording suggests they did not stay long. According to that work, the city stood on a terraced hill on the east bank of the Strymon River (the modern Struma), about three miles from its mouth. It was an important station on the Via Egnatia, the main Roman road across Macedonia, and after 168 BC it served as capital of the first district of Roman Macedonia. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary place it about 33 Roman miles from Philippi. The location shown here matches the ancient site near the modern village of Amfipoli, in northern Greece.

Amplias was a Christian in Rome whom Paul greets near the end of his letter to the Romans, calling him "my beloved in the Lord" (Rom 16:8). He is mentioned nowhere else in the Bible, and nothing more is known of him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains that Amplias, the form used in the King James Version, is a shortened form of the Latin name Ampliatus, which is how the Revised Version renders it. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "large" or "extensive." Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the letter, and so this greeting, to about AD 55. The warm description suggests a close personal tie to Paul, though the text does not say how they knew each other.

Amram was a Levite, a son of Kohath and brother of Izhar, Hebron and Uzziel, and the father of Aaron, Moses and Miriam. He married Jochebed, his father's sister, described as a daughter of Levi born in Egypt. According to Exod 6:20 he lived 137 years, and Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that he died in Egypt. His line held a distinguished place among the Levites: Aaron and his sons were set apart to handle the most holy things and burn incense, and later lists of Levites still trace families back to him through Shubael. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that "son of Kohath" may mean a more distant descendant, because other genealogies of the same period show more generations. This entry follows the text as it reads. The name, meaning "exalted people," is also borne by other people in the Bible.

Amram was one of the descendants of Bani listed in Ezra 10:34, in the time of Ezra. He appears in the roll of Israelite men who had married foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon. By inference from the surrounding chapter, those named agreed to send these wives away as part of the reform Ezra led. Smith's Bible Dictionary places the event around 459 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with Amram the father of Moses, Aaron and Miriam, who has the same name. The name is usually explained as meaning "exalted people."

Amraphel was king of Shinar, the lowland region of southern Mesopotamia later known as Babylonia, in the time of Abram. Genesis 14 names him first among four eastern kings, alongside Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam and Tidal king of nations (Gen 14:1). These four fought against five kings of the cities of the plain, including Sodom and Gomorrah, in the vale of Siddim (Gen 14:9). In that list Chedorlaomer comes first, which suggests he led the alliance. The wider chapter tells how the eastern kings won the battle and carried off goods and captives, among them Abram's nephew Lot, until Abram pursued and defeated them. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify Amraphel with the Babylonian king Hammurabi. The latter notes that the different form of the name and the absence of this campaign from Hammurabi's known records leave the identification open. Amraphel is not mentioned elsewhere in the Bible.

Amzi was a Levite of the family of Merari, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 6:46. He was the son of Bani and the father of Hilkiah. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 6:31–47) traces the ancestry of Ethan, one of the Merarite singers David appointed to lead music at the tabernacle. By inference from that context, Amzi was an ancestor of Ethan, several generations back, and descended from Merari through Mahli and Shamer. The STEPBible proper names index describes him as a temple musician, a role tied to his family line. Nothing else is recorded about his life. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "strong, mighty." The name Amzi belongs to more than one person in the Bible. Another Amzi appears in the priestly genealogy of Neh 11:12 and is a different man.

Amzi was a priest named in the family line of Adaiah, one of the priests living in Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time after the return from exile. Neh 11:12 lists him as the son of Zechariah and the father of Pelaliah, and traces the line back through Pashur to Malchiah. Adaiah's family belonged to the 822 priests who 'did the work of the house', meaning the temple. Nothing else is recorded about Amzi himself. Because he appears several generations before Adaiah, he may have lived well before the exile ended, though the text gives no dates. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as 'my strength'. The name is shared by at least one other man, a Levite in the genealogy of 1 Chr 6, and this entry treats the two as different people.

event: An angel rescues Peter from prison
text: An angel rescues Peter from prison is the episode in Acts 12 in which Peter escaped Herod Agrippa I's custody the night before Herod meant to bring him out. Peter was asleep, chained between two soldiers with guards at the door, when an angel appeared in a light and woke him, and his chains fell off. Thinking it a vision, Peter followed the angel past two guard posts to an iron gate that opened by itself. The angel then left him in the street. Peter went to the house of Mary, mother of John Mark, where many were praying. The servant girl Rhoda knew his voice but ran to tell the others instead of opening the gate. Peter told them what had happened, asked them to inform James, probably the brother of Jesus, and the other believers, and left. Herod had the guards executed. The date, about AD 40, is inferred from context.

event: An Angel Speaks to Joseph in a Dream
text: An Angel Speaks to Joseph in a Dream is the episode in Matt 1:19–25 in which Joseph, the husband of Mary, learns how her pregnancy came about. Finding her with child, Joseph, described as a just man, decided to end the marriage quietly rather than expose her publicly. While he was thinking this over, the angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream. The angel addressed him as son of David, told him not to be afraid to take Mary as his wife because the child was conceived by the Holy Spirit, and instructed him to name the son Jesus, since he would save his people from their sins. Matthew presents this as fulfilling the prophecy that a virgin would bear a son called Emmanuel, meaning "God with us." When Joseph woke, he did as he was told and took Mary home. He had no sexual relations with her until she gave birth, and he named the child Jesus. The setting is probably Nazareth, and the date about 5 BC, both inferred from context.

Anab was a town in the hill country of Judah. Joshua drove the Anakim out of it, along with Hebron, Debir and the other mountain towns of Judah and Israel, and destroyed them and their cities (Josh 11:21). It was later listed among the hill-country towns given to the tribe of Judah, named in the same group as Eshtemoh and Anim (Josh 15:50). The name is usually explained as meaning "grapes" or "grape-town." Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the site still keeps its ancient name and lies among the hills about 10 miles south-southwest of Hebron. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it about twelve miles southwest of Hebron, a short distance southwest of Debir, and identifies it with the ruin called Khirbet 'Anab. The location shown here follows that identification in the southern Judean hills.

Anah was the mother of Aholibamah, one of Esau's wives, and the daughter of Zibeon the Hivite (Gen 36:2). Through Aholibamah she was the grandmother of Jeush, Jaalam and Korah, who became chiefs (“dukes”) in Edom (Gen 36:14, 18). The Hebrew text calls Anah “the daughter of Zibeon,” and this entry follows that reading in treating her as a woman. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint, Samaritan Pentateuch and Syriac versions read “son.” That reading would make Anah the same person as the son of Zibeon who found hot springs in the wilderness (Gen 36:24), and Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Anah as male. This entry names her husband as Beeri. That probably rests on identifying Aholibamah with Judith, “the daughter of Beeri the Hittite,” whom Gen 26:34 names as Esau's wife. Several people in the Bible share the name Anah.

Anah was a son of Seir the Horite, one of the early inhabitants of the land of Seir, later Edom. His brothers were Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Dishon, Ezer and Dishan, and Timna was his sister (Gen 36:20; 1 Chr 1:38). He is listed among the chiefs, or "dukes," of the Horites (Gen 36:29). His children were a son, Dishon, who had the same name as one of Anah's brothers, and a daughter, Aholibamah (Gen 36:25). Dishon's sons were Amram, Eshban, Ithran and Cheran (1 Chr 1:41). Several men in the Bible are named Anah. Another Anah in the same chapter is a son of Zibeon (Gen 36:24), and Esau's wife Aholibamah is called the daughter of an Anah (Gen 36:2), so it is uncertain which Anah is meant in some passages. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats Seir as the land itself personified as the ancestor of its tribes.

Anah was a son of Zibeon and brother of Ajah (spelled Aiah in 1 Chr 1:40). He belonged to the Horites, the descendants of Seir listed in Genesis 36 alongside the family of Esau. Genesis 36:24 remembers him as the Anah who found "the mules" in the wilderness while he was feeding his father's donkeys. The Hebrew word translated "mules" appears only here and its meaning is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it is often rendered "hot springs," and that Jewish tradition took it to mean mules, crediting Anah with first breeding them. The name was shared by other Horites, including a brother of Zibeon (Gen 36:20), and it is debated which Anah was the father of Esau's wife Aholibamah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "one who answers" or "afflicted."

Anaharath was a town in the territory given to the tribe of Issachar when the land was divided under Joshua. It appears only once, in the list of Issachar's towns at Josh 19:19, alongside Hapharaim and Shion. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it in the eastern part of the Jezreel Valley and identifies it with the modern village of en-Na'ura, where it holds the old name to have survived. The location shown here follows that identification, near the Hill of Moreh in northern Israel. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "gorge or pass," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "dryness, burning, wrath." The text records nothing about the town beyond its place in the tribal list.

Anaiah was one of thirteen men who stood on a wooden platform with Ezra the scribe when Ezra read the Book of the Law to the people gathered in Jerusalem. He stood on Ezra's right, between Shema and Urijah (Neh 8:4). The verse does not give his role. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to be probably a priest, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him a Levite who helped Ezra with the reading. The same encyclopedia suggests he may be the Ananias named in the parallel account in 1 Esdras 9:43. His name means "Yah has answered." The name is shared by more than one person. An Anaiah also appears among the leaders who sealed the covenant in Neh 10:22. That man may or may not be the same person, and the text does not say.

Anaiah was one of the men who set their seal to the written covenant made in Nehemiah's time, when the community returned from exile pledged to keep the law of God. His name, meaning "Yah has answered," appears only in a list of names (Neh 10:22). From its place in the chapter, the list seems to belong to the section headed "the chief of the people" (Neh 10:14). Smith's Bible Dictionary accordingly calls him one of the heads of the people, while the Tyndale House STEPBible proper-names list describes him as a priest. This entry follows the reading of him as a lay leader. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he may be the same Anaiah who stood beside Ezra during the public reading of the law (Neh 8:4). Nothing else is recorded about him, and because several people share the name, his identity is uncertain.

Anak was the son of Arba, after whom the city of Hebron was first called "the city of Arba" (Josh 15:13; 21:11). He was the ancestor of the Anakim, a people remembered for their great height. His descendants Ahiman, Sheshai and Talmai are called his children or sons, though the phrase may mean descendants rather than immediate sons. They lived at Hebron when the twelve spies explored Canaan. The spies reported that beside these "giants" they felt like grasshoppers (Num 13:33), and a saying arose: "Who can stand before the children of Anak!" (Deut 9:2). After the conquest Hebron was given to Caleb, who drove out the three sons of Anak (Josh 15:14; Judg 1:20). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "long-necked", while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a collar" or "ornament".

Anamim is named as one of the sons of Mizraim, the son of Ham, in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:13) and in its repeated genealogy (1 Chr 1:11). His brothers are listed as Ludim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim, Pathrusim, Casluhim and Caphthorim. The plural ending "-im" suggests the name stands for a people rather than a single individual. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both describe the Anamim as a tribe descended from Mizraim, the Hebrew name for Egypt. On that basis they were probably a people living in or near Egypt, although the text gives no location and their exact identity is unknown. Nothing else is recorded about them beyond their place in these two lists. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives possible meanings of the name as "a fountain," "answer" or "affliction."

Anammelech was one of the gods of Sepharvaim, worshipped by the Sepharvites after the king of Assyria settled them in Samaria in place of the deported Israelites (see 2 Kgs 17:24). 2 Kgs 17:31 names him alongside Adrammelech and says the Sepharvites burned their children in fire to both gods. The name is usually explained as "Anu is king" (Easton's Bible Dictionary) or "Anu is the prince" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), linking it to the Mesopotamian sky god Anu. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him Adrammelech's companion god, worshipped with rites like those of Molech. Easton's describes Anammelech as a female moon deity paired with Adrammelech as the sun, while this entry treats the god as male. Where the god came from is uncertain, because some identify Sepharvaim with Sippar in Babylonia and others with a Syrian city, possibly Sibraim near Damascus.

Anan was one of the Israelites who put their seal to the written covenant made under Nehemiah after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears only once, in the list of signers at Neh 10:26, between Hanan and Malluch. The surrounding list groups the signers into priests, Levites and "chiefs of the people," and Anan falls in this last group of lay leaders, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. Nothing else is recorded about his family or his role. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both give the meaning of his name as "cloud." Smith's dates the sealing of the covenant to about 410 BC, an estimate rather than a date stated in the text.

Anani was the seventh and last-named son of Elioenai, listed in the genealogy of the royal line of David in the tribe of Judah (1 Chr 3:24). His brothers were Hodaiah, Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub, Johanan and Dalaiah. The genealogy places him among the descendants of Zerubbabel, so he probably lived several generations after the return from the Babylonian exile, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he is often taken to be the last generation the Chronicler records in this line. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may be a shortened form of Ananiah, meaning "Yah has covered". Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "protected by Jehovah", and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a cloud".

Ananiah is named only as the grandfather of Azariah, who repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall beside his own house when the city was rebuilt under Nehemiah (Neh 3:23). Ananiah's son Maaseiah was Azariah's father. Nothing else is recorded about Ananiah himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he was probably a priest, perhaps because priests are mentioned among the nearby workers in the same chapter. By inference from the setting, he lived some generations before the rebuilding, which took place around the mid-400s BC. His name, meaning roughly "the Lord has covered" or "protected by the Lord," should not be confused with the town of Ananiah, which is mentioned elsewhere in Nehemiah.

Ananiah was a town of the tribe of Benjamin, named only once in the Bible. It appears in the list of places resettled by Benjamites after the return from exile in Babylon, alongside Anathoth and Nob (Neh 11:32). The following verse names Hazor next, so Ananiah lay among these towns north of Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "protected by the Lord," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia as "Yah has covered." Both works identify the town with the modern village of Beit Hanina, about three to four miles north-northwest of Jerusalem. The location shown here follows that identification, though the placement is approximate. Nothing else about the town is recorded.

Ananias (Husband of Sapphira) was a member of the early church in Jerusalem. With his wife Sapphira he sold a piece of property (Acts 5:1). He kept back part of the price and brought the rest to the apostles, presenting it as the full amount. Peter confronted him, asking why Satan had filled his heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to keep back part of the price of the land (Acts 5:3). On hearing these words Ananias fell down and died, and great fear came on everyone who heard about it (Acts 5:5). The surrounding passage adds that Sapphira, who knew of the deception, died the same way about three hours later. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that his offense was pretending to give everything, not keeping part, since giving was voluntary. His name is a Greek form of the Hebrew Hananiah, meaning "Yah has been gracious."

Ananias (Disciple at Damascus) was a follower of Jesus living in Damascus who was sent to Saul (later Paul) after Saul's encounter with Jesus on the road, about AD 32 by inference from context. In a vision the Lord told him to go to Saul, who in turn had seen a vision of a man named Ananias coming to lay hands on him so he could see again. Ananias objected that he had heard how much harm Saul had done to believers in Jerusalem. He went anyway, laid his hands on Saul, called him "Brother Saul," and said Jesus had sent him so that Saul would regain his sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit. Recounting the event later, Paul described him as devout according to the law and well regarded by the Jews of Damascus. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes a tradition that he later became bishop of Damascus and died a martyr.

Ananias (High Priest) was the Jewish high priest in Jerusalem when Paul was arrested there. When Paul stood before the Council and began his defence, Ananias ordered those standing beside him to strike Paul on the mouth (Acts 23:2). Five days after Paul had been sent to the governor Felix at Caesarea, Ananias went down there with some of the elders and a speaker named Tertullus to bring charges against him (Acts 24:1). The verses here do not describe the rest of his life. Smith's Bible Dictionary adds that he was the son of Nebedaeus, was appointed high priest by Herod king of Chalcis in about AD 48, was removed from office shortly before Felix left the province, and was later killed by the Sicarii at the start of the Jewish war against Rome. He is a different person from the other men named Ananias in Acts.

event: Ananias and Sapphira lie to God
text: The Ananias and Sapphira lie to God event took place in the early church in Jerusalem, probably about AD 30 by inference from context, soon after the believers began sharing their possessions. Ananias and his wife Sapphira sold a piece of land, secretly kept back part of the money, and brought the rest to the apostles as if it were the full price. Peter asked Ananias why Satan had filled his heart to lie to the Holy Spirit. He pointed out that the land and the money had been his to keep, so the lie was told not to people but to God. Ananias fell down and died, and young men buried him. About three hours later Sapphira came in, unaware of what had happened. She confirmed the false price, and Peter said the two had agreed to test the Spirit of the Lord. She also died at once and was buried beside her husband. Great fear came on the whole church.

Anath was the father of Shamgar, who came after Ehud and delivered Israel by killing six hundred Philistines with an ox goad (Judg 3:31). He is known only through his son, who is twice called "Shamgar the son of Anath." The second mention, in the Song of Deborah, uses "the days of Shamgar the son of Anath" to date a time when the highways were deserted and travelers kept to side paths (Judg 5:6). Nothing else is recorded about Anath himself. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary take the name to mean "answer." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it matches the name of Anat, a Canaanite and Phoenician goddess who was also worshipped in Egypt and is paired with the war goddess Astarte in Egyptian inscriptions of the 18th Dynasty.

Anathoth was a son of Becher and a grandson of Benjamin, named in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin in 1 Chr 7:8. He is listed as one of nine sons of Becher, alongside Zemira, Joash, Eliezer, Elioenai, Omri, Jerimoth, Abiah and Alameth. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "answers to prayer," while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "answer," "song" or "poverty." The same name belongs to a Levitical town in Benjamin, the hometown of Jeremiah, and to a man who signed the covenant in Nehemiah's time. Because he and his brother Alameth are listed together, and Alameth's name resembles the nearby town of Alemeth, some suggest these names may be linked to Benjamite settlements, but the text does not say so.

Anathoth was one of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the covenant made in the time of Nehemiah, after the return from exile in Babylon (Neh 10:19). His name appears in a list of signers alongside Hariph and Nebai. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is shared by others in the Bible, including a Benjamite listed in the genealogies of Chronicles, and it is also the name of a priestly town in Benjamin, the home of Jeremiah. Whether this signer had any connection with the town or its family is not stated. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the covenant to about 410 BC. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "answer," "song" or "poverty," while Smith's renders it "answers to prayer."

Anathoth was a town in the territory of Benjamin that was given, with its pasturelands, to the priestly descendants of Aaron (Josh 21:18; 1 Chr 6:60). Solomon banished the priest Abiathar to his fields there (1 Kgs 2:26). Abiezer, one of David's monthly army commanders, came from Anathoth (1 Chr 27:12). Isaiah names it among the towns on the route of an army advancing on Jerusalem (Isa 10:30). It is best known as the home of the prophet Jeremiah, who came from a priestly family there (Jer 1:1). Men of Anathoth threatened his life (Jer 11:21–23). While imprisoned, he bought his cousin Hanameel's field there for seventeen shekels (Jer 32:7–9). After the exile, 128 men of Anathoth returned, and Benjamites resettled it (Ezra 2:23; Neh 11:32). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the village of Anata, northeast of Jerusalem. The location shown here follows that identification.

Andrew was one of the twelve apostles of Jesus, the brother of Simon Peter and, like him, a son of Jonas. He came from Bethsaida and fished on the Sea of Galilee, where Jesus called the two brothers to follow him. John's Gospel says he first followed Jesus after hearing John the Baptist speak, and the next verse says he then brought his brother Simon. The brothers shared a house, probably in Capernaum by inference from the context. At the feeding of the five thousand Andrew pointed out a boy with loaves and fishes. With Philip he brought to Jesus some Greeks who wanted to see him. He joined Peter, James and John in questioning Jesus privately on the Mount of Olives, and he was with the apostles in the upper room after the ascension. Smith's Bible Dictionary records traditions that he preached widely and was crucified at Patrae in Achaia.

Andronicus was a Christian greeted by Paul at the close of his letter to the Romans, named together with Junia (Rom 16:7). Paul calls the two his "kinsmen," which may mean relatives or, more broadly, fellow Jews; Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Andronicus as a Jewish Christian. Paul also calls them his fellow prisoners, so they had evidently been imprisoned at some point, though the verse does not say when or where. They were "of note among the apostles," a phrase read either as well known to the apostles or as outstanding apostles themselves. Paul adds that they were in Christ before him, meaning they became believers earlier than he did. Since the greeting is sent to Rome, he was probably living there when the letter was written. Junia may have been his wife or another relative, but the text does not say. His name is Greek and is usually given as meaning "man-conquering."

Anem was a city in the tribe of Issachar, listed with Ramoth among the towns given with their surrounding pasturelands to the Levites (1 Chr 6:73). By inference from the surrounding list, it went to the Levite clan descended from Gershom. The name is usually taken to mean "two springs." The parallel list of Levitical cities in Josh 21:29 names En-gannim ("spring of gardens") where Chronicles has Anem, so Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat the two as the same place, the modern town of Jenin at the southern edge of the Jezreel Valley. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also records other suggestions: Eusebius linked it with Aner, and the explorer Conder proposed a village called Anim in the hills west of the plain of Esdraelon. The location shown here follows the Jenin identification.

Aner was an Amorite living near Hebron in the time of Abram, the brother of Eshcol and Mamre. The three brothers were allies of Abram (Gen 14:13). When a fugitive brought news that Lot had been taken captive by an invading coalition of kings, Abram set out to rescue him. By inference from Gen 14:24, Aner and his brothers went with him. After the victory Abram refused any share of the plunder for himself, but he asked that Aner, Eshcol and Mamre be given their portion. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Canaanite chief. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the names Mamre and Eshcol are also place names in the Hebron area, and suggests that Aner may likewise be linked to a local place, possibly a range of hills. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Aner was a city in the territory of the western half-tribe of Manasseh. It was given, with its surrounding pasturelands, to the Levites of the Kohathite family, together with Bileam (1 Chr 6:70). It is mentioned only once. The parallel list of Levitical towns in Josh 21:25 names Taanach and Gath-rimmon from the same half-tribe, so many scholars, Gesenius among them, treat Aner as another form of Taanach, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. That encyclopedia adds that there is no agreement about the site. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it west of the Jordan. The location shown here follows the Taanach identification, probably the modern Tell Ta'annek on the southern edge of the Jezreel Valley. The town should not be confused with Aner the Amorite, an ally of Abram.

The Angle was a point on the wall of Jerusalem where the wall turned, rendered in the King James Version as "the turning of the wall." The Hebrew word means a corner or angle. According to 2 Chr 26:9, King Uzziah built towers there, as well as at the Corner Gate and the Valley Gate, and fortified them. STEPBible's proper names index, from Tyndale House, treats the Angle as a fortified tower that Uzziah built. The same Hebrew term appears in Nehemiah's account of rebuilding the wall, where "the turning of the wall" marks sections repaired near the armoury and the king's house (Neh 3:19–20, 24–25). That passage probably refers to the same angle or to a nearby one, but this is an inference. The exact position is uncertain. The location shown here places it within the ancient city of Jerusalem, and that placement is approximate.

Aniam was a son of Shemida and a member of the tribe of Manasseh, one of the two tribes descended from Joseph. He appears only once, in the genealogy of Manasseh in 1 Chr 7:19, which lists him with his brothers Ahian, Shechem and Likhi. Nothing else is recorded about him. Shemida himself appears elsewhere as a son of Gilead, whose family formed one of the clans of Manasseh (Num 26:32; Josh 17:2). Aniam therefore belonged to that clan, though the text gives no details of his life or descendants. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explain the name as "sighing" or "lament of the people."

Anim was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed among the cities given to the tribe of Judah in the allotment recorded in Josh 15:50, where it is named alongside Anab and Eshtemoh. The Bible mentions it only in this list and records nothing else about it. The name is usually taken to mean "springs" or "fountains" (Easton's Bible Dictionary; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the double ruin of el-Ghuwein, south of es-Semu'a (ancient Eshtemoa) and roughly 10 miles south-west of Hebron. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the visible remains there are Byzantine and that a Christian town called Anem stood on the site in the 4th century, though the site appears to be much older. The location shown here follows the el-Ghuwein identification.

Anna was a prophetess in Jerusalem, the daughter of Phanuel, from the tribe of Asher. Luke describes her as very old. She had been married for seven years before she was widowed (Luke 2:36). The following verses, Luke 2:37–38, add that she was a widow of about eighty-four, that she never left the temple, and that she worshipped there with fasting and prayer night and day. They also say that when the infant Jesus was presented in the temple, she came in at that moment, gave thanks to God, and spoke about him to everyone in Jerusalem who was looking for redemption. Easton's Bible Dictionary places her alongside other women called prophetesses in the Bible, such as Miriam, Deborah and Huldah. Her name is the Greek form of the Hebrew Hannah and means "grace."

Annas was a Jewish high priest and the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest in the year Jesus was crucified (John 18:13). Luke dates the start of John the Baptist's ministry to the time when "Annas and Caiaphas" were high priests (Luke 3:2). After Jesus' arrest he was taken first to Annas, who questioned him and then sent him bound to Caiaphas (John 18:13, 24). Only John records this hearing. Annas appears again among the high priest's family at Jerusalem when Peter and John were brought to trial, about AD 30 by inference from context (Acts 4:6). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries place his own term as high priest at AD 7–14, before Roman officials removed him. They explain his continued title in different ways. He may have kept the title because the office was held for life under the law of Moses, or he may have led the Sanhedrin or served as Caiaphas's deputy.

Anointed by a Sinner Woman is the episode in Luke 7:36–50 in which Jesus, dining at the house of a Pharisee named Simon, is approached by a woman of the town known as a sinner. She weeps at his feet, washes them with her tears, wipes them with her hair, kisses them, and anoints them with ointment from an alabaster box. Simon privately doubts that Jesus is a prophet. Jesus answers with a parable of two debtors forgiven unequal debts, then contrasts Simon's lack of hospitality with the woman's actions. He declares her many sins forgiven, prompting the other guests to ask who this is that forgives sins, and he sends her away in peace, saying her faith has saved her. The town is not named. It is placed in Galilee by context, about AD 28 by inference. Similar anointings at Bethany appear in the other Gospels, and opinions differ on whether they describe the same event.

Antioch (Syria) was a major city on the Orontes River, capital of the Roman province of Syria and, according to Easton's Bible Dictionary, the third city of the Roman empire after Rome and Alexandria. It is the modern Antakya in southern Turkey. Believers scattered by the persecution after Stephen's death brought the gospel there, and some preached to Greeks. Jerusalem sent Barnabas, who brought Saul, and the two taught there for a year. It was here that the disciples were first called Christians. Nicolas, one of the seven chosen in Jerusalem, was a proselyte from Antioch. Its church sent Barnabas and Saul on their first missionary journey and welcomed them back, and it received the Jerusalem leaders' letter to Gentile believers. Paul returned there after his second journey, and in Gal 2:11 he describes confronting Peter there. This entry treats Galatians as written from Antioch, one of several proposed places.

Antioch (Pisidia) was a city in the interior of Asia Minor, distinct from Antioch in Syria. Paul and Barnabas came there from Perga on their first missionary journey, about AD 45 by inference from context, and spoke in its synagogue on the sabbath (Acts 13:14). Later in the chapter, opposition forced them to leave. Jews from Antioch and Iconium then followed Paul to Lystra, where he was stoned and left for dead (Acts 14:19). Afterward the missionaries passed back through Antioch on their way home (Acts 14:21), and Paul later recalled the persecutions he endured there (2 Tim 3:11). Smith's Bible Dictionary says Seleucus Nicator founded the city, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it became a Roman colony in the province of Galatia. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it at the modern Yalvaç (Yalobatch) in Turkey, which matches the location shown here.

Antipas was a Christian at Pergamum (Pergamos) who was put to death for his faith. He is named only once, in the message to the church at Pergamum in Rev 2:13. There the risen Christ calls him "my faithful martyr," a phrase that can also be translated "my faithful witness." The verse says he was killed among the believers there, in the city described as the place "where Satan's seat is." The church is praised for holding fast and not denying the faith even in the days when Antipas died, so his death evidently happened some time before Revelation was written. Nothing more is known of him for certain (Easton's Bible Dictionary). Smith's Bible Dictionary records a tradition that he was bishop of Pergamum. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name is a shortened form of Antipater.

Antipatris was a city on the road from Jerusalem to Caesarea. Roman soldiers brought Paul there by night after a plot against his life was uncovered in Jerusalem, on the way to sending him to the governor Felix (Acts 23:31), about AD 56 by inference from context. The next verses say the foot soldiers returned to Jerusalem from there while the horsemen took Paul on to Caesarea. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia say Herod the Great built the city and named it after his father, Antipater. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its earlier name as Capharsaba and links it with the village of Kefr-Sabba. Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia instead place it at Ras el-Ain, at the springs of the Aujeh (Yarkon) River northeast of Jaffa. The location shown here follows the Ras el-Ain identification.

Antothijah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named once in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. He is listed with Hananiah and Elam in 1 Chr 8:24, and the next verse groups these names among the sons of Shashak. His brothers include Ishpan, Heber, Eliel, Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Iphedeiah and Penuel. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in this family list, which belongs to the line of Elpaal's descendants living in or near Jerusalem. His name is also spelled Anthothijah in some reference works, such as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "answers" or "songs of the Lord." The name probably resembles that of Anathoth, a town in Benjamin's territory, though no link between the two is stated.

Anub was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the genealogy of Judah as a son of Coz (1 Chr 4:8). The same verse names Zobebah and "the families of Aharhel the son of Harum" in the same line of descent, and this entry treats Harum as Anub's brother. Smith's Bible Dictionary connects Coz with the family of Ashur, the father of Tekoa, from the surrounding verses, though the passage does not state the link directly. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the father's name as Hakkoz and suggests the name Anub means "ripe," while Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "confederate." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Apelles was a Christian at Rome whom Paul greets in his letter to the Romans, calling him "approved in Christ" (Rom 16:10). The phrase suggests he had been tested in some way and proved faithful, though the text does not say how. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Apelles was a common name in the period. Nothing else about him is recorded in the Bible. Smith's Bible Dictionary reports a later tradition that he became bishop of Smyrna or of Heraclea. In the same verse Paul goes on to greet the household of Aristobulus, but the text does not say whether Apelles was connected with that household.

Aphek was a city on the northern edge of Israel's promised land, one of several places in the Bible with this name. Joshua 13:4 names it as a point on the boundary of the land not yet conquered, near the Sidonians and "the borders of the Amorites." Joshua 19:30 lists an Aphek among the cities allotted to the tribe of Asher, and Judg 1:31 probably refers to the same town as Aphik, whose Canaanite inhabitants Asher did not drive out. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the two Joshua references as one place and identifies it with classical Aphaca, modern Afqa, near the source of the Nahr Ibrahim (the ancient Adonis River) in Lebanon. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes a temple ruin there. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia accepts Afqa but notes it lies farther north than expected. The location shown here follows the Afqa identification.

Aphek was a Canaanite royal city whose king was among those defeated by Joshua (Josh 12:18). Later the Philistines camped there before the battle near Ebenezer (1 Sam 4:1), and they gathered all their armies at Aphek before the battle in which Saul died, while Israel camped by a spring in Jezreel (1 Sam 29:1). Several places in the Bible share this name, so it is uncertain whether all three passages refer to the same town. Easton's Bible Dictionary places this Aphek in Issachar near Jezreel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reads Josh 12:18 as "Aphek in Sharon" and suggests that 1 Sam 29:1 may describe only a Philistine rallying point before they moved north toward Jezreel. The location shown here follows the Sharon identification. That places Aphek near later Antipatris, probably the modern Tel Aphek (Ras el-Ain) at the source of the Yarkon River, northeast of present-day Tel Aviv.

Aphek was a city east of the Jordan where the Syrian (Aramean) king Benhadad gathered his army to fight Israel in the year after an earlier defeat (1 Kgs 20:26). When the Syrians were beaten, the survivors fled into the city, where a wall fell on 27,000 of them, and Benhadad hid in an inner room (1 Kgs 20:30). Later the dying Elisha told King Joash of Israel that he would defeat the Syrians at Aphek (2 Kgs 13:17). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes this may be the same place. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary place it on the road from Damascus into Israel and identify it with modern Fik (Afiq), about six miles east of the Sea of Galilee, and the location shown here follows that identification. Several other biblical places share the name Aphek, which means "strength" or "fortress."

Aphekah was a town in the territory of the tribe of Judah, named only once, in the list of towns in Joshua 15:53 between Beth-tappuah and Humtah. The surrounding list places it in the hill country of Judah, in the group of towns around Hebron (Josh 15:48, 15:54). Its name probably means "strength" or "stronghold." Its site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as unidentified. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests it is probably the same place as Aphek, the Canaanite royal city whose king Joshua defeated (Josh 12:18). The location shown here follows that link to Aphek and places it at Tel Aphek, near modern Rosh HaAyin at the source of the Yarkon River. That site lies on the coastal plain, well northwest of the Judean hill country where the list in Joshua 15 places the town.

Aphiah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin and an ancestor of King Saul, Israel's first king. He appears only in the genealogy that introduces Saul's father Kish, where the line runs from Kish back through Abiel, Zeror and Bechorath to Aphiah (1 Sam 9:1). Bechorath is named as his son. The verse ends by calling the man "a Benjamite, a mighty man of power." Grammatically this description could refer either to Aphiah, the last name in the list, or to Kish, who opens the verse. Most readers take it to describe Kish. Nothing else is recorded about Aphiah. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "refreshed," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "speaking, blowing."

Aphik was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Asher. Judg 1:31 lists it among the places whose Canaanite inhabitants Asher did not drive out, alongside Accho, Zidon, Ahlab, Achzib, Helbah and Rehob. Its name probably means "stronghold." Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary treat it as the same place as the Aphek named in Asher's allotment (Josh 19:30), and Easton's also links it with the Aphek on the northern border in Josh 13:4. Its site is uncertain. One view places it on the coastal plain near Accho, at a mound such as Tel Afek. Another identifies it with Afqa in the Lebanon mountains, at the source of the Adonis River (modern Nahr Ibrahim). The location shown here follows the Afqa identification.

Aphses was a priest whose family received the eighteenth of the twenty-four divisions of priests, assigned by lot to serve in turn at the sanctuary (1 Chr 24:15). The surrounding chapter places this arrangement in the time of King David, who organized the descendants of Aaron into these rotating courses with the help of Zadok and Ahimelech. Aphses is probably the head of a priestly family rather than someone known for any personal deeds, since he is mentioned only in this list. Aphses is the King James spelling, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Revised Version renders the name Happizzez. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "the dispersion."

Apollonia was a city of Macedonia that Paul and Silas passed through, after Amphipolis, on their way to Thessalonica (Acts 17:1). The text does not say they stopped or preached there. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it in the district of Mygdonia, just south of Lake Bolbe (modern Lake Volvi), on the Via Egnatia, the main Roman road across the region. Smith's Bible Dictionary, citing an ancient Roman itinerary, gives its distance as about 30 Roman miles from Amphipolis and 37 from Thessalonica, roughly a day's journey from each. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds that coins show the town existed by the 4th century BC, and that its name may survive in the modern village of Pollina. The location shown here fits that position near Lake Volvi in northern Greece. Its name means "belonging to Apollo."

Apollos was a Jew born at Alexandria, described as eloquent and "mighty in the scriptures," who came to Ephesus (Acts 18:24). The verses that follow say he knew only John's baptism until Priscilla and Aquila explained the way of God to him more fully (Acts 18:25–26). He then went on to Achaia and was working at Corinth when Paul arrived in Ephesus. In 1 Corinthians, Paul notes that the believers at Corinth had split into groups, some claiming to follow him and others Apollos or Cephas. Paul describes Apollos and himself as servants through whom the Corinthians believed: "I have planted, Apollos watered." Paul urged him to visit Corinth again, but Apollos chose to wait for a better time. He is last mentioned traveling with Zenas the lawyer, whom Titus was asked to help on their way. According to Smith's Bible Dictionary, later tradition made him bishop of Caesarea.

Apollyon is the Greek name, meaning "destroyer," given in Rev 9:11 to the angel of the bottomless pit, whose Hebrew name is Abaddon. In John's vision he is king over the locust-like creatures that come up out of the pit when the fifth trumpet sounds. The Hebrew word abaddon means ruin or destruction. Elsewhere in the Old Testament, as Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note, it names a place: the realm of the dead, set alongside Sheol, death and the grave in passages such as Job 26:6, Job 28:22 and Prov 15:11. Revelation is the only place where the word becomes a personal name for the angel who rules that realm. Smith's Bible Dictionary observes that the Greek text makes clear Abaddon here is the angel, not the abyss. John Bunyan later used the name Apollyon for the adversary in The Pilgrim's Progress.

Apostles arrested, put on trial is the episode in Jerusalem, recounted in Acts 5, in which the apostles were jailed and brought before the Jewish council, about AD 30 by inference from context. After their healing work at Solomon's Portico, they were put in the common prison, but an angel opened the doors by night and told them to go on speaking in the temple. At dawn they were teaching there when the high priest gathered the council and sent for them. The officers found the prison still locked and guarded but empty. The captain of the temple then brought the apostles in without force, fearing the crowd might stone his men. The high priest reminded them of an earlier ban on teaching in Jesus' name, the order given in Acts 4:18. Peter and the others replied that they must obey God rather than men and testified to Jesus' resurrection. The council was enraged and wanted to kill them.

The Apostles Chosen was the occasion when Jesus selected twelve of his followers to be his companions and messengers. Luke says he went up a mountain and prayed all night, then in the morning called his disciples and chose twelve, whom he named apostles (Luke 6:12–13). Mark states their purpose: to be with him, to be sent out to preach, and to have power to heal and cast out demons (Mark 3:14–15). The lists name Simon, whom Jesus called Peter; his brother Andrew; James and John, sons of Zebedee, nicknamed Boanerges, "sons of thunder"; Philip; Bartholomew; Thomas; Matthew the tax collector; James son of Alphaeus; Thaddaeus, apparently Luke's "Judas the brother of James"; Simon the Canaanite, called Zelotes by Luke; and Judas Iscariot, the betrayer. The mountain is unnamed. This entry places it near Capernaum, about AD 28, by inference from context.

event: Apostles work signs and wonders in Solomon's Portico
text: The Apostles work signs and wonders in Solomon's Portico describes a period in the early Jerusalem church when the apostles performed many miracles among the people. It follows the deaths of Ananias and Sapphira. The believers met together in Solomon's Porch, a colonnade of the temple. Others were afraid to join them, yet the people held them in high regard, and large numbers of men and women became believers. People carried the sick into the streets on beds and mats, hoping that at least Peter's shadow would fall on some of them as he passed. Crowds also came from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those troubled by unclean spirits, and every one of them was healed. The high priest and his Sadducee associates were filled with indignation (Acts 5:17), which led to the apostles' arrest. The date of about AD 30 is an estimate inferred from context.

Appaim was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 2 as a son of Nadab and the brother of Seled. Because Seled died without children, the family line of Nadab continued through Appaim (1 Chr 2:30). His son was Ishi, whose son Sheshan was in turn the father of Ahlai (1 Chr 2:31). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place him in the house of Jerahmeel, a major clan of Judah. This follows from the surrounding verses of the same genealogy, which trace Nadab back to Jerahmeel. The name is usually explained as meaning "nostrils" or "face" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Nothing is recorded about him beyond his place in this family list.

Apphia was a Christian woman named in the opening greeting of Paul's letter to Philemon, where she is called "our beloved Apphia" (some manuscripts and the Revised Version margin read "the sister"). She is greeted with Philemon, with Archippus, and with the church that met in Philemon's house (Phlm 1:2). Because the letter deals with one household, many interpreters, including Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, consider her probably Philemon's wife and possibly the mother of Archippus, though the text does not say so. By inference from Col 4:9, 17, which mention Onesimus and Archippus, the household was at Colossae. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a Greek church tradition that commemorates her on November 22 and says she was martyred with Philemon under Nero. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "fruitful."

Appii Forum ("Forum of Appius" or "Market of Appius") was a town and way station on the Appian Way, the main Roman road running south from Rome. It lay about 43 Roman miles from the city, according to Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Christians from Rome heard that Paul was coming and travelled out along the road to meet him. Some went as far as Appii Forum, and others waited at the Three Taverns, closer to the city. When Paul saw them, he thanked God and took courage (Acts 28:15). This happened as he arrived at Rome as a prisoner, about AD 57 by inference from context. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that a canal began here and ran through the Pontine Marshes, which made the town a busy stopping point. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it at ruins near Treponti, south of Rome, and the location shown here matches that area.

Aquila was a Jew born in Pontus who, with his wife Priscilla, had recently come from Italy after the emperor Claudius ordered all Jews to leave Rome (Acts 18:2). Paul met them at Corinth and, according to Acts 18:3, stayed and worked with them because they shared the trade of tentmaking. When Paul left Corinth, the couple sailed with him, and Acts 18:19 says they remained at Ephesus. There they heard Apollos, named in Acts 18:24, speaking boldly in the synagogue and explained the way of God to him more accurately. Paul calls them his helpers in Christ Jesus and sends them greetings (Rom 16:3; 2 Tim 4:19). They also sent greetings along with the church that met in their house (1 Cor 16:19). The name means "eagle" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that when they became Christians is uncertain.

Ar, also called Ar of Moab, was a leading city or district of Moab on the border near the Arnon valley. During Israel's wilderness journey, God told Moses not to fight the Moabites, because Ar had been given to Lot's descendants (Deut 2:9). Israel passed through the region of Ar, and the Moabites living there were among those who dealt with Israel on the way (Deut 2:18, 29). An old song recalls the streams running down toward Ar, and another describes Sihon's forces from Heshbon burning it (Num 21:15, 28). Isaiah's oracle against Moab opens with Ar laid waste in a single night (Isa 15:1). Its site is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it at Rabba, between Kerak and the Wadi Mujib. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests a ruin on the floor of the Arnon valley, and notes a view that Ar was a district rather than a city. The location shown here follows the Arnon valley identification.

Ara was a man of the tribe of Asher, named as one of the three sons of Jether in the genealogy of Asher's descendants (1 Chr 7:38). His brothers were Jephunneh and Pispah. Nothing else is recorded about him; he appears only in this list. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Jether as the head of a family of Asherites. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "lion," Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "cursing" or "seeing," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the meaning as unknown.

Arab was a town in the hill country of Judah, named once, in the list of towns given to the tribe of Judah, where it appears alongside Dumah and Eshean (Josh 15:52). Nothing else is recorded about it. The name probably means "ambush," as Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explain it. Its towns in the same group lay in the hills around and south of Hebron. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the ruins of Er-Rabiyeh, south of Hebron. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it more generally near Hebron. The location shown here is only approximate and fits a site in that area southwest of Hebron. The exact site is uncertain.
