Arabah, called the Brook of the Arabah in modern versions, is a stream named in Amos 6:14, where the King James Version calls it "the river of the wilderness." Amos warns that a nation will oppress Israel "from the entering in of Hemath" in the north to this brook, which marks the opposite limit of the land. The STEPBible proper names index (Tyndale House) describes it as a boundary of King Jeroboam II's kingdom. This fits 2 Kgs 14:25, which says Jeroboam restored Israel's border from Hamath to the "sea of the plain," the Dead Sea. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains that "Arabah" refers to the deep valley of the Jordan and Dead Sea, so the brook was probably a stream running into that valley near the Dead Sea. Its exact identity is uncertain, and the location shown here is only approximate. Several other places in the Bible share the name.

Arabah is the Hebrew name for the deep rift valley that runs from the Sea of Galilee down the Jordan valley to the Dead Sea and on south to the Gulf of Aqaba. The King James Version usually translates it "the plain" and keeps "Arabah" only in Josh 18:18, which describes Benjamin's border. It is linked with Chinnereth and with the "sea of the plain," the Salt Sea (Deut 3:17; Josh 12:3). Its southern stretch is linked with Elath and Ezion-geber (Deut 2:8). Joshua lists it among the main regions of the land (Josh 11:16). Abner crossed it to reach the Jordan and Mahanaim (2 Sam 2:29), and Zedekiah fled toward it when Jerusalem fell (2 Kgs 25:4). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give its Arabic names as el-Ghor for the Jordan section and Wadi el-Arabah south of the Dead Sea. Because the name covers a long region, the location shown here marks the central Jordan valley.

Arabia was the broad desert region south and east of Israel, roughly the Arabian Peninsula and the Syrian desert to its north. In the Old Testament it is tied to kings and nomadic peoples. The kings of Arabia brought gold and silver to Solomon (2 Chr 9:14). Isaiah addresses an oracle to Arabia that mentions the travelling caravans of Dedan (Isa 21:13). Jeremiah lists its kings among the nations facing judgment (Jer 25:24). Ezekiel names Arabia and Kedar as traders in lambs, rams and goats with Tyre (Ezek 27:21). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew word strictly means the Arab people rather than a country. In the New Testament, Paul went into Arabia after his conversion before returning to Damascus (Gal 1:17), and he places Mount Sinai in Arabia (Gal 4:25). The location shown here is a general point in the northwestern Arabian Peninsula.

Arad was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the sons of Beriah, named in a genealogy alongside Zebadiah and Ader (1 Chr 8:15). His brothers were Ahio, Shashak, Jeremoth, Zebadiah, Ader, Michael, Ispah and Joha. In the surrounding passage Beriah appears among the descendants of Elpaal, and with Shema he is said to have driven out the inhabitants of Gath (1 Chr 8:12–13). For this reason the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places Arad among Elpaal's descendants. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a wild ass." He is a different figure from the Canaanite "king Arad" of the south who fought Israel in the wilderness (Num 21:1; 33:40). That phrase probably refers to the king of the town of Arad in the Negev.

Arad was a Canaanite city in the Negev, the dry south country of Canaan. When Israel approached near the end of the wilderness journey, the king of Arad attacked them and took some prisoners (Num 21:1; Num 33:40). The King James Version reads these verses as naming a king called Arad, but the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes Arad as the city's name, with the ruler being its king. Arad later appears among the cities whose kings Joshua defeated, listed next to Hormah (Josh 12:14). The Kenite relatives of Moses' father-in-law settled with the people of Judah in the wilderness south of Arad (Judg 1:16). The ISBE also notes that the Egyptian king Shishak listed the city among his conquests. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the ISBE identify it with Tel Arad, about 17 to 20 miles south of Hebron, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Arah was a man of the tribe of Asher, named first among the three sons of Ulla in the Asherite genealogy of 1 Chronicles, with his brothers Haniel and Rezia (1 Chr 7:39). Nothing else is recorded about him. Ulla does not appear elsewhere in the list, so his place in the family line is unclear. The STEPBible Proper Names index treats Ulla as another form of Shual, a son of Zophah named a few verses earlier in the same genealogy. The name Arah is usually explained as meaning "traveler" or "wayfarer" (Hitchcock's Bible Names; Smith's Bible Dictionary). Several other people in the Bible share the name, including the ancestor of a family that returned from exile with Zerubbabel, but they should not be confused with this Asherite.

Arah was the ancestor of a family whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Judah with Zerubbabel, probably about 536 BC, as Smith's Bible Dictionary dates it. The list of returning families in Ezra gives his descendants as 775 (Ezra 2:5). The parallel list in Nehemiah gives 652 (Neh 7:10). The difference is not explained in the text. He may be the same person as the Arah of Neh 6:18, whose son Shechaniah was the father-in-law of Tobiah the Ammonite, an opponent of Nehemiah's rebuilding of Jerusalem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes this identification, but it is not certain. Several people in the Bible bear this name, including an Asherite in 1 Chr 7:39. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "the way" or "a traveler."

Arah was the father of Shechaniah, a man of Judah in Nehemiah's day. He is mentioned only to identify his son, whose son-in-law was Tobiah, one of the opponents of Nehemiah's rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls. Because of this marriage tie, and because Tobiah's son Johanan had married into the family of Meshullam son of Berechiah, many in Judah were bound by oath to Tobiah (Neh 6:18). Several people in the Bible bear the name Arah, including the head of a family whose descendants returned from exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:5; Neh 7:10). This Arah may have belonged to that family or been its ancestor, but the text does not say. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the way" or "a traveler."

Aram (son of Shem) was one of the five sons of Shem named in the Table of Nations, along with Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad and Lud (Gen 10:22). His own sons were Uz, Hul, Gether and Mash (Gen 10:23). The parallel list in 1 Chr 1:17 names the same four directly after Aram among "the sons of Shem" and gives Mash as Meshech. By inference from Genesis, they are Aram's sons, listed in Chronicles as part of Shem's wider line. STEPBible's proper-names index presents Aram as the ancestor of the Aramean people. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains that the name, meaning "high" or "highlands," was also used for the upland region stretching from northeast of Palestine to the Euphrates, roughly the Syria and Mesopotamia of later Greek and Roman writers. Damascus eventually became its chief city. The Bible records nothing about Aram beyond these genealogies.

Aram (son of Kemuel) was a grandson of Nahor, Abraham's brother. He is named only once, in the list of Nahor's sons by his wife Milcah that was reported to Abraham after the near-sacrifice of Isaac (Gen 22:21). There his father Kemuel is called "the father of Aram." Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat him as distinct from Aram the son of Shem (Gen 10:22), the ancestor of the Arameans. Some readers note a possible link between this Aram's name and the Aramean peoples who lived around Nahor's family in Mesopotamia, but the text does not make that connection. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "high."

Aram (tribe of Aher) was a man of the tribe of Asher, listed as one of the four sons of Shamer, together with his brothers Ahi, Rohgah and Jehubbah (1 Chr 7:34). He appears only in this genealogy of Asher's descendants, and nothing else is recorded about him. His father Shamer is probably the same man called Shomer two verses earlier, a son of Heber, which by inference makes Aram a great-great-grandson of Asher through Beriah (1 Chr 7:30–32). He should not be confused with Aram the son of Shem or with the land of Aram (Syria), which share the name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "highness" or "magnificence."

Aram was the land of the Arameans, the highland region stretching from northeast of Israel toward the Euphrates, which the King James Version often translates as "Syria." Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "highlands" and notes that it roughly matches the Syria and Mesopotamia of Greek and Roman times. Balaam was brought from Aram, "out of the mountains of the east" (Num 23:7). Jacob fled there and kept sheep to win a wife (Hos 12:12), which Genesis places at Laban's home in Paddan-aram. The name also covered smaller Aramean states. David put garrisons in "Syria of Damascus" (2 Sam 8:6), Absalom stayed at "Geshur in Syria" (2 Sam 15:8), and Geshur and Aram took towns from the descendants of Machir (1 Chr 2:23). Because the term covers a wide area, the location shown here is only a rough central point in the Syrian interior toward the Euphrates.

Aram-maacah was an Aramean kingdom in Syria, called "Syriamaachah" in the King James Version. After Hanun of Ammon insulted David's messengers, the Ammonites paid a thousand talents of silver to hire chariots and horsemen from Mesopotamia, Aram-maacah and Zobah to fight against David (1 Chr 19:6). The parallel account in 2 Sam 10:6 mentions the king of Maacah, who supplied a thousand men. The STEPBible proper-names index likewise describes it as an Aramean kingdom allied with the Ammonites against David. By inference from other mentions of Maacah alongside Geshur and Bashan, it was probably a small state near Mount Hermon, east of the upper Jordan. Its exact borders are uncertain, and the location shown here is only a rough placement in southern Syria, south of Damascus.

Aram-naharaim, meaning "Aram of the two rivers," is the Hebrew name for the region of upper Mesopotamia, the land between the Euphrates on the west and the Tigris on the east. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the King James Version translates it as "Mesopotamia," as in Gen 24:10, where Abraham's servant travels there to find a wife for Isaac. The name also appears in the title of Ps 60. Easton's Bible Dictionary links it with the "field of Aram" (Hos 12:12, Revised Version), meaning the open country of Aram, and treats Padan-aram, the home of Abraham's relatives, as one part of it. The location shown here is an approximate point in northern Mesopotamia, in what is now northeastern Syria and northern Iraq. It stands for a broad region, not a single site.

Aram-zobah was an Aramean region named in the heading of Psalm 60, which places the psalm at the time when David fought "Aram-naharaim and Aram-zobah" and Joab struck down Edomites in the Valley of Salt. It is probably the same as the kingdom of Zobah. Other passages, such as 2 Sam 8:3 and 1 Sam 14:47, describe Zobah as an Aramean state whose king Hadadezer fought David. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it probably in the region between the Euphrates and the Orontes, in what is now Syria. Its exact extent is uncertain. The location shown here is only a rough placement in southern Syria near Damascus, and it does not mark a known site.

Aran was a Horite, a son of Dishan and brother of Uz, named in the genealogy of the descendants of Seir the Horite, the inhabitants of the land later occupied by Edom (Gen 36:28). The same pair of sons appears again in the parallel list in 1 Chr 1:42. Dishan was one of the sons of Seir and a chief among the Horites, so Aran belongs to one of the clans of that people. Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take the name to mean "wild goat," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that many Horite names in this genealogy appear to be animal names, though it also records that the meaning of this particular name is uncertain.

Ararat is a mountainous region in western Asia. Genesis says Noah's ark came to rest "upon the mountains of Ararat" as the flood waters went down. The plural points to a range of mountains rather than one peak. In Jer 51:27, Ararat is one of the kingdoms, along with Minni and Ashchenaz, called to attack Babylon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with Urartu of Assyrian records, a kingdom on the Armenian plateau around Lake Van. The same Hebrew name is translated "Armenia" in the KJV at 2 Kgs 19:37 and Isa 37:38. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the ISBE both suggest the ark's resting place was probably in the Kurdish range south of Armenia, and Kurdish tradition points to Jebel Judi. The location shown here marks the region at the peak now called Mount Ararat, in eastern Turkey near the Armenian and Iranian borders.

Arba was a leading figure among the Anakim, described in Josh 14:15 as "a great man among the Anakims" and twice called the father of Anak. The city of Hebron was earlier named Kirjath-arba, "city of Arba," after him. When the Israelites settled the land, this city in the hill country of Judah was given to Caleb son of Jephunneh as his share, and its surrounding pasturelands were later assigned to the priestly families of Levi (Josh 21:11). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia regard him as the ancestor of the Anakim, the tall people the Israelites feared, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also treats him as the reputed founder of the city. His name means "four," so Kirjath-arba can also be read as "city of four." Nothing else is recorded about his life.

Archelaus was a son of Herod the Great who ruled Judea after his father's death. Matthew mentions him once: when Joseph returned from Egypt with Mary and the young Jesus, he heard that Archelaus was reigning in Judea in place of his father. Joseph was afraid to go there, and after a warning in a dream he went instead to Galilee (Matt 2:22). His brothers included Herod Antipas and Philip. According to Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries, his mother was Malthace, a Samaritan, and he was brought up in Rome with Antipas. When Herod died, about 4 BC, the kingdom was divided among the brothers, and Archelaus received Judea, Samaria and Idumea. Smith's notes that his official title was ethnarch rather than king. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia records that the Romans removed him for misgovernment in AD 6, and Smith's adds that he was banished to Vienne in Gaul.

Archippus was a Christian known to the apostle Paul and mentioned only in two of his letters. In Philemon he is greeted alongside Philemon and Apphia and the church that met in their house, and Paul calls him "our fellowsoldier" (Phlm 1:2). At the end of Colossians, Paul asks the church to tell Archippus to take care to complete the ministry he had received in the Lord (Col 4:17). By inference from these letters he probably lived in or near Colossae and held some recognized role in the church there. Because he is named so closely with Philemon and Apphia, Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he was a member of Philemon's household, probably his son. His name means "master of the horse." A later church tradition describes him as bishop of Laodicea.

Ard is named as one of the sons of Benjamin, Jacob's youngest son, in the list of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt during the famine (Gen 46:21). He appears last among the ten sons given there and was part of the Tribe of Benjamin. Nothing else is recorded about him. The lists of Benjamin's sons in Num 26 and 1 Chr 7–8 differ from Genesis, which explains brothers named here such as Ahiram, Shupham, Jediael and Rapha. In Num 26:40 an Ard appears as a son of Bela, Benjamin's firstborn, and as the ancestor of the Ardites. That may be the same man counted as a grandson, or a separate person with the same name. The name is shared by more than one person, so the identification is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "one that commands" or "he that descends."

Ard was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, a son of Bela and so a grandson of Benjamin. He appears in the census of Israel taken in the plains of Moab, where he and his brother Naaman are named as the sons of Bela and the ancestors of two Benjamite clans. His descendants were the Ardites (Num 26:40). Other sons of Bela, including Gera, Abihud, Abishua and Ahoah, are named in the Benjamite genealogies of 1 Chronicles 7 and 8. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies Ard with Addar, listed among Bela's sons in 1 Chr 8:3. This entry treats Addar as a separate brother. Genesis 46:21 lists an Ard among Benjamin's own sons, so the name is shared, and how that Ard relates to this one is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "one that commands" or "he that descends."

Ardon was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:18 as one of the sons of Caleb, the son of Hezron. He is listed third after Jesher and Shobab. The verse names two women, Azubah, Caleb's wife, and Jerioth, and its wording leaves unclear which of them was the mother of these sons. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary take Azubah as his mother. This Caleb, a descendant of Judah through Perez and Hezron, is generally distinguished from the better-known Caleb son of Jephunneh. Nothing else is recorded about Ardon. The meaning of his name is uncertain: Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "fugitive," Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "ruling," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls it unknown.

Areli was a son of Gad and a grandson of Jacob, named last among Gad's seven sons in the list of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:16). His brothers were Zephon (Ziphion), Haggi, Shuni, Ozni (called Ezbon in Genesis), Eri and Arod (Arodi). In the wilderness census of Numbers his descendants appear as a clan of the tribe of Gad, the Arelites (Num 26:17). Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "heroic", Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the light or vision of God", and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests a form related to "God's lioness" or "God's hearth".

The Areopagus, meaning "hill of Ares" and called Mars' Hill in the King James Version, is a rocky hill in Athens just northwest of the Acropolis, above the ancient marketplace. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe it as the meeting place of Athens' oldest and most respected council, which still existed under Roman rule. In Acts 17, Athenians curious about Paul's "new doctrine" brought him to the Areopagus, where he stood and addressed the "men of Athens" (Acts 17:19, 22). Readers differ on whether he spoke before the council itself or simply on the hill. Smith's dictionary pictures the philosophers bringing him up from the marketplace to hear him more easily, and the location shown here is the hill. Among those who believed afterward was Dionysius "the Areopagite," probably a member of the council, along with a woman named Damaris (Acts 17:34).

Aretas was the king whose governor (ethnarch) held Damascus with a garrison in order to arrest the apostle Paul, who escaped by being let down through a window in the wall in a basket (2 Cor 11:32–33). The parallel account in Acts 9:24–25 describes the same escape but credits the plot to the Jews of the city. Aretas was a common name among Arabian rulers, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "agreeable" or "virtuous." This one is generally identified as Aretas IV, king of the Nabataeans, whose capital was Petra. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, drawing on Josephus, describe him as the father-in-law of Herod Antipas. Antipas left his daughter to marry Herodias, and war between the two followed. How Aretas came to control Damascus is unclear. Easton's holds that he seized it about AD 37. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia thinks it more probable that the emperor Caligula granted it to him.

Argob is a man named in 2 Kgs 15:25, in the account of how Pekah son of Remaliah, a captain of King Pekahiah of Israel, conspired against the king and killed him in the palace at Samaria with the help of fifty men of Gilead. Argob and Arieh are named alongside the king in that verse, but the wording is obscure. One reading, followed by STEPBible's proper names index and by this entry, takes them as men who were with Pekahiah, probably his officers, and who were struck down with him. Others read them as fellow conspirators with Pekah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Latin Vulgate treats both names as places, and that the Jewish commentator Rashi took Argob to be part of the royal palace. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Argob was a region in Bashan, east of the Jordan, belonging to the kingdom of Og. When Israel conquered Og it took all of Argob's sixty cities (Deut 3:4). Moses gave the region, with the rest of Bashan, to the half tribe of Manasseh (Deut 3:13), and Jair son of Manasseh took the whole area as far as the borders of Geshur and Maacah, naming it after himself (Deut 3:14). Under Solomon, Argob's sixty great cities, with walls and bronze bars, were administered by the son of Geber from Ramoth-gilead (1 Kgs 4:13). Smith's and Easton's Bible Dictionaries identify Argob with the later Trachonitis, the rugged volcanic Lejah south of Damascus. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the location is uncertain and suggests other fertile districts of Bashan. The location shown here follows the Lejah identification.

Aridai was one of the ten sons of Haman, the Persian official who plotted to destroy the Jews in the days of Queen Esther. He is named only once, in the list of Haman's sons at Esth 9:9. The surrounding passage, Esther 9, reports that the Jews killed these ten sons in Shushan on the day set for the Jews' destruction, and that their bodies were afterward hanged at Esther's request. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him as the ninth son and gives the meaning of his name as "the strong." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests a link to a Persian name meaning "delight of Hari," but notes that the text of the name is very uncertain. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Aridatha was one of the ten sons of Haman, the official who plotted to destroy the Jews of the Persian Empire in the reign of King Ahasuerus. He is named only once, in the list at Esth 9:8, where Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him as the sixth son. The surrounding passage reports that the Jews killed Haman's ten sons in Shushan on the day the decree against them was overturned, and that their bodies were later hanged at Esther's request. His brothers were Parshandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha, Poratha, Adalia, Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai and Vajezatha. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may come from the Persian Hari-data, meaning "given by Hari," and notes that the Greek Septuagint spells it Pharadatha. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Arieh is a man named in 2 Kgs 15:25 in the account of how Pekah son of Remaliah, a captain of King Pekahiah of Israel, conspired against the king and killed him in the palace at Samaria. Arieh and Argob are named alongside the assassination, but the Hebrew wording leaves their role unclear. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Arieh to have been one of the royal bodyguard killed with Pekahiah. Smith's Bible Dictionary allows either that view or that he was one of Pekah's accomplices, along with the fifty men of Gilead. This entry treats him, as the STEPBible notes do, as a man who was with the king at the time of the attack, probably one of his officials. Smith's dates the event to about 757 BC, an estimate drawn from context. The name means "lion." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Ariel was one of the "chief men" whom Ezra summoned at the river Ahava while he was gathering the exiles returning from Babylon to Jerusalem (Ezra 8:16). Ezra had found no Levites among the returning company, and the surrounding passage shows that he sent this group to Iddo at a place called Casiphia to bring back ministers for the house of God. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both describe Ariel as one of this delegation. Nothing else is recorded about his family or later life. The name is usually explained as "lion of God" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "lioness of God." The same word appears elsewhere in the Bible with other meanings, including a poetic name for Jerusalem and an "altar hearth," but those uses are unrelated to this man.

Ariel is a poetic name Isaiah uses for Jerusalem, identified in Isa 29:1 as "the city where David dwelt." In that oracle the prophet announces woe on Ariel despite its continuing round of yearly feasts and sacrifices. God will bring distress, heaviness and sorrow on the city (Isa 29:2). Yet the multitude of nations that fight against Ariel and its fortifications will vanish "as a dream of a night vision" (Isa 29:7). The meaning of the name is debated. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it as "lion of God" when applied to the city. Easton's Bible Dictionary links it with the related Hebrew word in Ezek 43:15–16 for the altar hearth of burnt offering, and that sense may lie behind the phrase "it shall be unto me as Ariel" in Isa 29:2. The location shown here is Jerusalem.

Arimathea was the home town of Joseph, the rich man and disciple of Jesus who asked Pilate for Jesus' body after the crucifixion and took it for burial (Matt 27:57; Mark 15:43; John 19:38). Mark describes Joseph as an honorable council member who was waiting for the kingdom of God. John says he was a secret disciple out of fear. Luke 23:51 calls Arimathea a city of the Jews (Smith's Bible Dictionary renders this as "a city of Judea"). The town is mentioned only in connection with Joseph, and its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary thinks it was probably Ramathaim, the birthplace of Samuel (1 Sam 1:1). Others place it at Ramleh, which Smith's Bible Dictionary favors, or at Ramah in Benjamin. The location shown here is a hilltop just northwest of Jerusalem associated with Samuel, which matches the Ramathaim identification.

Arioch (king of Ellasar) was one of four eastern kings, along with Amraphel of Shinar, Chedorlaomer of Elam and Tidal "king of nations," who made war together in the days of Abraham (Gen 14:1). Genesis 14:9 describes them as "four kings with five," meaning they fought a coalition of five local kings. The surrounding verses show that coalition was led by the rulers of Sodom and Gomorrah, and that Chedorlaomer was its overlord. Nothing else is recorded about Arioch himself. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify him with Eri-Aku, a king of Larsa known from Babylonian inscriptions, and take Ellasar to be Larsa in southern Mesopotamia, probably the site now called Senkereh. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "long, great, tall." He is a different person from the Arioch who served as captain of the guard in the Book of Daniel.

Arioch was the captain of the royal guard under King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, appearing in Daniel 2. When the king's wise men could not tell him his dream and its meaning, Arioch was appointed to carry out the order to kill all the wise men of Babylon. Daniel, who was among those to be killed, spoke to him with tact and asked why the decree was so hasty, and Arioch explained the matter. After the dream was revealed to Daniel, he went to Arioch, asked him to spare the wise men and to bring him before the king. Arioch hurried Daniel in, introducing him as a man from the captives of Judah who could give the interpretation. He is a different person from Arioch, king of Ellasar, who fought in Abraham's time (Gen 14:1).

Arisai was one of the ten sons of Haman, the official of the Persian king Ahasuerus who plotted to destroy the Jews. He is named only once, in the list of Haman's sons at Esth 9:9. By inference from the surrounding passage, he was killed by the Jews in Shushan when they defended themselves on the day Haman had set for their destruction. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him as the eighth son and gives the meaning of the name as "lion-like." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia instead treats the name as probably Persian, of unknown meaning. The wider chapter records that the bodies of Haman's sons were afterward hanged at Queen Esther's request. Nothing else is known about him.

Aristarchus was a Macedonian from Thessalonica and one of Paul's travelling companions. During the riot in Ephesus, the crowd seized him and Gaius and rushed them into the theatre (Acts 19:29). He was later among the group that went with Paul from Greece through Macedonia toward Asia (Acts 20:4). He also sailed with Paul on the voyage to Rome, which included the shipwreck and the stay on Malta (Acts 27:2). In Paul's letters to the Colossians and to Philemon, Aristarchus sends greetings. Paul calls him his "fellowprisoner" in Col 4:10 and his fellow worker in Phlm 1:24, so he was probably with Paul during his imprisonment, usually taken to be at Rome. His name means "best ruler." Smith's Bible Dictionary records a tradition that he became bishop of Apamea, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a tradition that he was martyred under Nero.

Aristobulus was a man living in Rome whose household Paul greets in Rom 16:10. Paul greets the members of his household rather than Aristobulus himself, so he may have died, been away, or not been a believer, though the verse does not say which. His name means "best counselor." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he was probably a grandson of Herod the Great and a brother of Herod Agrippa, a wealthy man close to the emperor Claudius. It notes J. B. Lightfoot's suggestion that his "household" were slaves who stayed together after his death and passed to the emperor while keeping their former master's name. Some of them were Christians. Smith's Bible Dictionary records a tradition that Aristobulus was one of the seventy disciples and preached the gospel in Britain. The Tyndale House proper-names index takes him to have been a prominent believer in Rome.

Arkite is the name given in the table of nations to one of the descendants of Canaan, son of Ham. He is listed among Canaan's offspring alongside Zidon, Heth, the Jebusite, Amorite, Girgasite, Hivite, Sinite, Arvadite, Zemarite and Hamathite (Gen 10:17; 1 Chr 1:15). Like most names in this list, it reads as the name of a people group rather than a single individual. It probably refers to the inhabitants of the town of Arka in northern Phoenicia. Easton's Bible Dictionary places Arka about 12 miles north of Tripoli, near the northern end of the Lebanon range. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds that the town appears in Assyrian inscriptions as Irkatah and was taken by Tiglath-pileser III in 738 BC. The two verses that mention the Arkite say nothing beyond the name and its place in Canaan's line.

Armageddon is the place named in Rev 16:16 where the kings of the world are gathered together, a site the verse says is called by this name "in the Hebrew tongue." The surrounding passage (Rev 16:14) connects the gathering with the "battle of that great day of God Almighty." The name is usually taken to mean "mount of Megiddo," and the Revised Version spells it Har-Magedon. Megiddo was an ancient city overlooking the plain of Esdraelon (the Jezreel Valley) in northern Israel. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that this plain was famous for Barak's and Gideon's victories and for the deaths of Saul and Josiah. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's both treat the name in Revelation as symbolic, drawing on that well-known battlefield. The location shown here follows the identification with Tel Megiddo.

Armoni was a son of King Saul by Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah, and the brother of Mephibosheth (not Jonathan's son of the same name). His name means "belonging to the palace" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, or "inhabitant of a fortress" in Easton's Bible Dictionary. He appears only in 2 Sam 21:8. There, during a famine in David's reign, the Gibeonites demanded seven of Saul's descendants because Saul had tried to wipe them out. David handed over Armoni and his brother Mephibosheth, together with five of Saul's grandsons. The surrounding verses say the Gibeonites put them to death and hung up their bodies at Gibeah. Rizpah then kept watch over the bodies until rain came. Ish-bosheth, who briefly ruled Israel after Saul's death, was also his brother, and Jonathan, Michal and Merab were among his half-siblings.

Arnan was a man of the tribe of Judah and a descendant of David through Solomon, named only once, in the royal genealogy of 1 Chr 3:21. He belonged to the line of Zerubbabel, who led Jews back from exile in Babylon. This entry treats him as a son of Hananiah, whom the preceding verse names as Zerubbabel's son, and as brother of Pelatiah, Jesaiah, Rephaiah, Obadiah and Shechaniah. The Hebrew wording is uncertain, though. It lists "the sons of Arnan" as one of several families without clearly linking them to Hananiah, so Arnan's exact place in the line is open. The Greek Septuagint reads the verse as a chain of fathers and sons and spells his name Orna. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning "joyous" and describes him as the founder of a family. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Arnon was the river, flowing through a deep valley east of the Dead Sea, that formed the border between Moab to the south and the Amorites to the north (Num 21:13; Judg 11:18). On their way to Canaan the Israelites went around Moab and camped beyond the Arnon. They then defeated Sihon, king of the Amorites, and took his land from the Arnon north to the Jabbok (Num 21:24; Judg 11:22). Sihon had earlier taken that territory from Moab (Num 21:26). Centuries later the king of Ammon claimed the same land, and Jephthah answered him (Judg 11:13, 26). Balak met Balaam at a Moabite city on the Arnon frontier (Num 22:36). The prophets mention its fords in oracles against Moab (Isa 16:2; Jer 48:20). It is the modern Wadi Mujib in Jordan, which enters the Dead Sea from the east, and the location shown here matches that identification.

Arod was a son of Gad, one of the sons of Jacob, and an ancestor of the tribe of Gad. Genesis 46:16 calls him Arodi and lists him among Gad's sons in the family that went down with Jacob to Egypt. His brothers were Ziphion (Zephon), Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon (Ozni), Eri and Areli. In the census of Israel's clans in Num 26:17 he appears as Arod, founder of the family of the Arodites. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts him as Gad's sixth son, and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "wild ass." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Aroer was a city on the northern edge of the Arnon gorge, east of the Dead Sea. It marked the southern limit of the kingdom of Sihon, the Amorite king of Heshbon (Josh 12:2). After Israel took his land, Moses gave the region running north from Aroer to the tribes of Reuben and Gad (Deut 2:36; Deut 3:12; Josh 13:16). Jephthah later cited Israel's long occupation of Aroer and its towns in his dispute with the Ammonites (Judg 11:26). The Syrian king Hazael's conquests reached as far south as Aroer (2 Kgs 10:33). By Jeremiah's time the city belonged to Moab (Jer 48:19). Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary identify it with the ruins of Ara'ir on the north rim of the Wadi Mujib, and the location shown here matches that site. Other places in the Bible share the name Aroer.

Aroer was a city east of the Jordan built by the tribe of Gad (Num 32:34). Joshua 13:25 describes it as "before Rabbah," the Ammonite capital, marking the edge of Gad's territory toward Ammon. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it to be the Aroer from which Jephthah struck the Ammonites as far as Minnith (Judg 11:33). Easton's Bible Dictionary links it to David's census, whose officers camped at Aroer (2 Sam 24:5). Several places share this name, so some passages are uncertain. The Reubenite home in 1 Chr 5:8 may be the Aroer on the Arnon. Smith's thinks "the cities of Aroer" in Isa 17:2 lie farther north. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that no matching name has been found near Rabbah, the modern Amman. The location shown here is only a rough estimate near Rabbah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "heath" or "tamarisk."

Aroer was a town in the far south of Judah, one of the places to which David sent gifts from the spoil he recovered from the Amalekites after the raid on Ziklag (1 Sam 30:28). It is a different place from the better-known Aroer on the Arnon River east of the Jordan, and several places in the Bible share the name. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it as the home town of two of David's warriors named in 1 Chr 11:44. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that the town called Adadah in Josh 15:22 may be the same place, read as Ararah. Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place it at Ar'arah, a ruin with ancient cisterns about 12 to 14 miles (19 to 23 km) southeast of Beersheba. The location shown here follows that identification.

Arpad was a city in northern Syria, always mentioned in the Bible alongside Hamath. Its name also appears as Arphad. In the Rabshakeh's speech to Jerusalem in Hezekiah's day, the Assyrians cited Arpad, its gods and its king as examples of peoples who could not withstand Assyria (2 Kgs 18:34; 19:13; Isa 36:19; 37:13). Isaiah uses it in a list of cities conquered by Assyria (Isa 10:9), and Jeremiah's oracle about Damascus pictures Hamath and Arpad dismayed at bad news (Jer 49:23). Easton's Bible Dictionary says Arpad fell to the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser after a three-year siege, dating this to 742 BC, and identifies it as Tell Erfud. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes it as apparently dependent on Damascus. The location shown here is a mound north of Aleppo, probably the site known today as Tell Rifaat.

Arphaxad (Arpachshad in the Revised Version) was a son of Shem, listed among his brothers Elam, Asshur, Lud and Aram. Gen 11:10 says he was born two years after the flood, when Shem was 100 years old, which this entry places at about 2346 BC, by inference from context. At 35 he fathered Salah (Shelah), and he lived another 403 years and had other sons and daughters, a total of 438 years. Through Salah and Eber his line leads to Abraham. Luke's genealogy of Jesus also includes him, but Luke 3:36 places a Cainan between Arphaxad and Salah, while Genesis and 1 Chronicles have Arphaxad as Salah's father directly. According to Easton's Bible Dictionary, he lived in Mesopotamia, and the Jewish historian Josephus regarded him as the ancestor of the Chaldeans.

Artaxerxes was a king of Persia to whom opponents of the Jews returned from exile sent letters of complaint about Jerusalem. Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel and their companions wrote to him in Aramaic (the "Syrian tongue"), and Rehum the chancellor and Shimshai the scribe sent a letter against the city on behalf of the men living west of the Euphrates (Ezra 4:7–11). The following verses of the chapter record his reply ordering the work to stop. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as the king who obstructed the rebuilding, and it and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify him with Smerdis, the usurper who briefly held the Persian throne about 522 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia considers it more likely that he was Artaxerxes I. Several Persian kings bore this name, and this entry treats the king of Ezra 4 as a person in his own right.

Artaxerxes was a king of Persia during whose reign Ezra and Nehemiah went to Jerusalem. In his seventh year Ezra led priests, Levites and other Israelites from Babylon to Jerusalem (Ezra 7:7; 8:1). Ezra carried a letter from the king that called him "king of kings" and ordered the treasurers west of the Euphrates to supply whatever Ezra needed (Ezra 7:12, 21). In his twentieth year Nehemiah, who served him wine, was allowed to go to Judah. He governed there until the king's thirty-second year and then returned to court (Neh 2:1; 5:14; 13:6). Ezra 6:14 also names him among the kings whose orders lay behind the temple work. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify him as Artaxerxes I Longimanus, son of Xerxes, who reigned about 464–425 BC. This entry follows that view. Several Persian kings bore the name, and the Artaxerxes of Ezra 4 may be a different ruler.

Artemas was a companion of the apostle Paul, named only in Titus 3:12. Paul tells Titus that he plans to send either Artemas or Tychicus to him in Crete, and that once one of them arrives, Titus should hurry to join Paul at Nicopolis, where Paul had decided to spend the winter. By inference from the passage, Artemas was trusted enough to take over Titus's work among the churches of Crete. Nothing more is recorded about him in the Bible. The name is Greek, probably a masculine form of Artemis or a shortened form of Artemidorus, a common name in Asia Minor (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). A later tradition, noted in Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, counts him among the seventy disciples and makes him bishop of Lystra.

Arubboth (spelled Aruboth in the King James Version) was a place or district that served as the base of one of the twelve officers who supplied provisions for King Solomon's household. According to 1 Kgs 4:10, the son of Hesed governed from Arubboth, and his territory also included Sochoh and "all the land of Hepher." The verse is the only mention of the name, so its exact location is uncertain. Many scholars place the district in the Sharon plain or the hills of northern Samaria, where Hepher was a clan area of Manasseh and another Socoh lay near modern Tulkarm. The location shown here is only approximate and sits near Socoh in the Judean lowlands (Shephelah), linking Arubboth to that better-known Sochoh.

Arumah was a place near Shechem where Abimelech, the son of Gideon (Jerubbaal), stayed during his conflict with the people of Shechem. According to Judg 9:41, after Abimelech defeated Gaal son of Ebed outside Shechem, he remained at Arumah, while Zebul, the ruler of the city, drove Gaal and his brothers out of Shechem. Judging from the narrative, Arumah was close enough to Shechem for Abimelech to attack the city again the next day. The name is usually understood to mean "height" or "lofty" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; Hitchcock's Bible Names). Its exact site is not known for certain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the ruins of El-Ormeh, about 6 miles southeast of Shechem, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Arvad was a small island city off the coast of Syria, named in Ezekiel's lament over Tyre. Ezekiel describes its people as rowers or sailors for Tyre, alongside the men of Zidon (Ezek 27:8), and as soldiers who manned Tyre's walls with its army (Ezek 27:11). Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the island of Ruad (modern Arwad), two or three miles off Tartus on the Phoenician coast, and the location shown here follows that identification. Smith's also links it with the Arvadites, listed among the descendants of Canaan with Zidon and Hamath in Gen 10:18 and 1 Chr 1:16. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "wandering" and notes that it appears as Aruada or Arada in the Tell el-Amarna tablets.

Arvadite is listed as a son of Canaan, son of Ham, in the table of nations in Gen 10:18 and its parallel in 1 Chr 1:16. He is named with the Zemarite and the Hamathite, just before the note that the families of the Canaanites later spread abroad. As with the other names in this list, the term probably refers to a people or clan rather than a single individual, presented as descending from Canaan. By inference, the Arvadites were the inhabitants of Arvad, a Phoenician island city whose men Ezek 27:8 and 27:11 describe as rowers and soldiers serving Tyre. Arvad is generally identified with the modern island of Arwad, off the coast of Syria. The Bible records nothing else about the Arvadite himself.

Arza was the steward in charge of the royal household at Tirzah, then the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel. He is mentioned only once. While King Elah was drinking himself drunk in Arza's house, Zimri, who commanded half of the king's chariots, plotted against him (1 Kgs 16:9). The surrounding passage shows that Zimri then killed Elah and seized the throne. The king is not named in the verse itself, but the context identifies him as Elah son of Baasha. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls Arza prefect of the palace. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the wording is not entirely clear, and that Arza could have been Zimri's servant rather than Elah's. This entry follows the more common reading that he served Elah. Nothing else is known of him, including whether he took any part in the plot.

Asa was the third king of Judah after the division of the kingdom, the son of Abijah (Abijam) and the father of Jehoshaphat. He also appears in the genealogy of Jesus (Matt 1:7–8). He became king in the twentieth year of Jeroboam of Israel and reigned 41 years, roughly 956–914 BC by inference from context. He destroyed idols, renewed the altar of the LORD, and removed Maachah from her position as queen mother, burning her idol at the brook Kidron, though the high places remained. He defeated an Ethiopian army at Mareshah. When Baasha of Israel fortified Ramah, Asa paid Benhadad of Syria with temple and palace treasure to intervene, then used Ramah's stones and timber to build Geba and Mizpah. The seer Hanani rebuked him for this, and Asa imprisoned him. In old age he had a severe disease in his feet and turned to physicians. Several other people in the Bible share his name.

Asa was a Levite, the son of Elkanah and the father of Berechiah, named once in the genealogy of 1 Chr 9:16. His son Berechiah appears in the list of Levites living in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. The verse says the family lived in the villages of the Netophathites, probably settlements around Netophah, near Bethlehem. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both describe Asa this way. Nothing else is recorded about his life. The name means "physician" or "healer" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several people in the Bible share this name, and this Asa should not be confused with the better-known King Asa of Judah.

Asahel was a son of Zeruiah and brother of Joab and Abishai. Because 1 Chr 2:16 lists Zeruiah among the sisters of Jesse's sons, he was David's nephew. He was famous for his speed, described as "light of foot as a wild roe." After David's men defeated Abner's forces near Gibeon, Asahel chased Abner and ignored repeated warnings to turn aside. Abner then killed him with the butt end of his spear. Asahel was buried in his father's tomb at Bethlehem. Later Joab, with Abishai, killed Abner at Hebron in revenge for their brother. Asahel is named among David's thirty mighty men, and as captain for the fourth month, "and Zebadiah his son after him." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests this honor may have been held through Zebadiah after Asahel's death. Other men in the Bible share this name.

Asahel was one of the Levites whom King Jehoshaphat of Judah sent out, together with princes and the priests Elishama and Jehoram, to teach the people in the cities of Judah. The surrounding verses describe the group taking the book of the law of the Lord with them as they went through the towns (2 Chr 17:7–9). Asahel is named only in this list, and nothing else is recorded about him. He is one of several men in the Bible who share the name, and he should not be confused with Asahel the brother of Joab, who belongs to the time of David. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this teaching mission to about 910 BC, and that date is an estimate. The name is usually explained as meaning "made by God" or "creature of God."

Asahel was a Levite in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah, one of ten overseers who served under Cononiah and his brother Shimei. They were appointed by the king's command and by Azariah, the ruler of the house of God (2 Chr 31:13). Going by the surrounding passage, their work was to look after the tithes, offerings and dedicated things that the people brought to the temple storerooms. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper-names index both describe him as having charge of these gifts. His name is usually explained as "made by God." Several other men in the Bible are also called Asahel, among them the brother of Joab and Abishai, but this Levite is mentioned only here and is a separate person.

Asahel was the father of Jonathan, a man of Ezra's time, after the return from exile. He is named only in Ezra 10:15. His son Jonathan and Jahaziah son of Tikvah had a part in the inquiry into the returned exiles who had married foreign wives. The Hebrew can be read two ways. The King James Version says the two men were "employed about this matter," meaning they oversaw it. Other readings, including the Revised Version text and STEPBible's proper names, have them opposing the plan. This entry follows the King James wording given in the verse. Nothing else is recorded about Asahel himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a priest and notes that 1 Esdras calls him Azael. The name means "God has made." Several other men in the Bible share this name, including a nephew of David.

Asahiah was a royal official of King Josiah of Judah, described as "a servant of the king's" (2 Kgs 22:12). After Hilkiah the priest found the book of the law in the temple, Josiah sent Asahiah with Hilkiah, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Achbor son of Michaiah and Shaphan the scribe to ask the LORD about the book's words. The group went to the prophetess Huldah, who lived in Jerusalem, and consulted her. The parallel account in 2 Chr 34:20 spells his name Asaiah and lists the same delegation, though it names Achbor as Abdon son of Micah. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both give the meaning of the name as "the LORD has made." Nothing else is recorded about him, and his exact office at court is not stated.

Asaiah was a leader of a family of the tribe of Simeon, named in a list of Simeonite chiefs in 1 Chr 4:36. The surrounding passage says these men were princes in their families whose households increased greatly, and that in the days of King Hezekiah of Judah they went to the region of Gedor looking for pasture for their flocks. There they attacked the people living in the area, including the Meunim, and settled in their place. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts Asaiah among those who took part in this incursion. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name means "the Lord has made" or "the Lord has wrought" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Simeonite should not be confused with them.

Asaiah was a Levite of the clan of Merari, named in 1 Chr 6:30 as the son of Haggiah. He appears only in a genealogy that traces the descendants of Merari, son of Levi, through Mahli, Libni, Shimei, Uzza, Shimea and Haggiah. Nothing is recorded about his life or activities. STEPBible's Tyndale House proper-names index describes him as an ancestor of Ethan the singer, one of the Levitical musicians of David's time. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the Lord hath wrought." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a Merarite leader in David's day, a Simeonite chief and an official of King Josiah. This entry treats this Asaiah as a separate person known only from this genealogy.

Asaiah was a man of Judah, named in 1 Chr 9:5 as the firstborn among the Shilonites, who lived in Jerusalem with his sons. The chapter lists people who resettled in Jerusalem, generally understood as the return from exile in Babylon. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 536 BC. "Shilonite" probably refers to descent from Shelah, son of Judah, rather than to the town of Shiloh. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify him with Maaseiah, son of the Shilonite, in the parallel list of Jerusalem's residents in Neh 11:5. His name means "the Lord has made." Several other men in the Bible share the name, so he should not be confused with them.

Asaiah was a Levite in the time of King David and the chief of the clan descended from Merari, one of Levi's three sons. He led 220 of his kinsmen when David gathered the Levites (1 Chr 15:6). David then called him, along with the priests Zadok and Abiathar and other Levite leaders, to take part in bringing the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:11). The surrounding chapter shows this was the ark's move from the house of Obed-edom to the city of David. The genealogy in 1 Chr 6:30 lists an Asaiah among Merari's descendants, and Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take him to be the same man. His name means "the Lord has made." Several other people in the Bible share the name.

Asaph is known only as the father of Joah, one of the three officials King Hezekiah of Judah sent out to meet the Assyrian envoy Rabshakeh during the siege of Jerusalem. Joah went with Eliakim, who was over the household, and Shebna the scribe, and the three later returned to Hezekiah with their clothes torn to report the envoy's words (2 Kgs 18:18, 37; Isa 36:22). The phrase "Joah the son of Asaph the recorder" can be read two ways. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the Tyndale House proper-names index give the title "recorder" to Asaph, while Smith's Bible Dictionary gives it to Joah. This entry presents both readings without choosing between them. Smith's also suggests that "son" may mean descendant, and that this Asaph may be the well-known Levite musician of David's time. Because several men bear the name, his identity is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "who gathers together."

Asaph (Levite) was a son of Berechiah from the tribe of Levi and one of the chief musicians in David's time. When the ark was brought to Jerusalem, the Levites appointed him with Heman and Ethan to sound bronze cymbals. He then led the musicians who served before the ark every day, and David handed a psalm of thanksgiving to him and his fellow Levites. His sons Zaccur, Joseph, Nethaniah and Asarelah (elsewhere Jesharelah) led groups of singers under his direction. Later passages call him a seer and name him alongside David as a leader of song. The 'sons of Asaph' served as temple singers through Hezekiah's reforms and after the return from exile. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests they may have been a guild of singers rather than strictly his descendants. Psalm 50 and Psalms 73–83 are attributed to him.

Asaph was a Levite named as an ancestor of Mattaniah, a Levite who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. In 1 Chr 9:15 the line runs Mattaniah son of Micah, son of Zichri, son of Asaph. The parallel list in Neh 11:17 gives the same line with Zabdi in place of Zichri, probably another form of the same name. There Mattaniah is described as the leader who began the thanksgiving in prayer, a role tied to the temple singers. Since several men in the Bible are called Asaph, it is uncertain who this one is. Smith's Bible Dictionary considers him most probably the same as Asaph the well-known Levite musician of David's time. If so, "son of Asaph" would mark Mattaniah as a distant descendant within that family of singers rather than a grandson. The name is usually taken to mean "gatherer" or "collector."

Asaph was the keeper of the king's forest under the Persian king Artaxerxes in Nehemiah's time. When Nehemiah got permission to go and rebuild Jerusalem, he also asked the king for a letter to Asaph ordering him to supply timber. The timber was for beams for the gates of the fortress beside the temple, for the city wall, and for the house Nehemiah would live in, and the king granted the request (Neh 2:8). The Hebrew word for forest here can mean a royal park or 'paradise', as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. Where this forest was is not stated. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Asaph as a Jew holding high office at the Persian court, probably because his name is Hebrew. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with the better-known Asaph, the musician of David's time, or with others who bore the name.

Asareel was a son of Jehaleleel, named in the genealogies of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chr 4:16. He is listed with his brothers Ziph, Ziphah and Tiria, and nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "whom God has bound (by an oath)," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the beatitude of God." Modern versions often spell the name Asarel. Jehaleleel's own link to the main lines of Judah's descendants is not stated in the passage, so Asareel's exact place in the tribe's family tree is uncertain.

Asenath was the Egyptian wife of Joseph, son of Jacob. She was the daughter of Potipherah, priest of On, a city usually identified with Heliopolis near modern Cairo. Pharaoh gave her to Joseph in marriage when he raised Joseph to authority over Egypt and gave him the Egyptian name Zaphnathpaaneah (Gen 41:45). She bore Joseph two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, before the years of famine began (Gen 41:50; Gen 46:20). Her name is Egyptian, and its meaning is explained in different ways. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "gift of the sun-god." Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connect it with the goddess Neith, meaning something like "belonging to Neith." Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "peril" or "misfortune." Apart from her marriage and her sons, the text records nothing more about her.

Ashan, a name meaning "smoke" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, was a town in the lowland of Judah, listed with Libnah and Ether among Judah's cities (Josh 15:42). It was later counted among the towns given to the tribe of Simeon inside Judah's territory (Josh 19:7; 1 Chr 4:32). It also appears among the towns with their pasturelands given to the priestly descendants of Aaron, alongside Beth-shemesh (1 Chr 6:59). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that "Ain" in the parallel list at Josh 21:16 is a copying variant of Ashan, and that Chor-ashan (1 Sam 30:30), probably a reservoir site in southwestern Judah, is the same place. The site has not been firmly identified, and the location shown here is only approximate.

Ashbel was a son of Benjamin, the youngest son of Jacob. In the list of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt, he is named third among Benjamin's sons, after Bela and Becher (Gen 46:21). The genealogy in 1 Chr 8:1 calls him Benjamin's second son, after Bela the firstborn. The census of Israel's tribes in the wilderness names him as the ancestor of a Benjaminite clan, the Ashbelites (Num 26:38). Nothing else is recorded about his life. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "reproof of God," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "an old fire."

Ashdod was one of the five chief cities of the Philistines, near the Mediterranean coast between Gaza and Joppa. Some of the Anakim still lived there after Joshua's conquest. It was allotted to Judah, though it was listed among the lands still remaining to be taken (Josh 13:3; 15:47). After capturing the ark of God, the Philistines placed it in the temple of their god Dagon at Ashdod. There Dagon's image fell before it, and the people were struck with tumors. King Uzziah of Judah later broke down its walls. Isaiah records its capture by the commander of Sargon, king of Assyria. Several prophets announced judgment on it. After the exile, Nehemiah found Jews married to women of Ashdod whose children spoke its language. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that it is called Azotus in Acts 8:40. The location shown here is the ancient mound of Esdud (Tel Ashdod), a few miles inland.

Ashdod's is a possessive form of Ashdod, a Philistine city near the Mediterranean coast, roughly midway between Gaza and Joppa. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as one of the chief centers of the worship of Dagon (1 Sam 5:5). It was assigned to the tribe of Judah (Josh 15:47), but Easton's notes that Judah never actually held it. Because it stood on the main road from Egypt into Palestine, it was strongly fortified. King Uzziah of Judah broke down its walls (2 Chr 26:6), and it was later taken by the Assyrians, with Sargon's capture of it mentioned in Isa 20:1. In the New Testament it appears under the Greek name Azotus, where Philip was found after leaving Gaza (Acts 8:40). Easton's identifies it with the village of Eshdud, and the location shown here follows that identification, at the ancient mound a few miles inland from the modern city of Ashdod.

Asher was the territory given to the tribe of Asher, named for Jacob's son, in the fifth lot of the land division (Josh 19:24). It ran along the Mediterranean coast from Mount Carmel northward toward Tyre and Sidon, with Manasseh to the south, Zebulun and Issachar to the southeast, and Naphtali to the east (Josh 19:26–29, 34; Josh 17:10). It held twenty-two towns with their villages. Manasseh also held certain towns that lay within Asher and Issachar (Josh 17:11). Asher did not drive out the Canaanites of coastal cities such as Accho, Sidon and Achzib and lived among them (Judg 1:31–32). The Song of Deborah pictures Asher staying by the seashore (Judg 5:17). Under Solomon, Asher formed part of an administrative district (1 Kgs 4:16), and Ezekiel's vision assigns it a strip of land and a city gate (Ezek 48:2, 34). Smith's Bible Dictionary describes its soil as among the richest in Palestine. The location shown here is in western Galilee.

Asher was the eighth son of Jacob and the second son of Zilpah, Leah's servant, making Gad his full brother. He was born in Paddan-aram, about 1752 BC by inference from context. Leah named him, saying "Happy am I," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "happiness." As one of Joseph's brothers, he would have shared in the events of Joseph's sale and the later journeys to Egypt during the famine. He went down to Egypt with his children Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi and Beriah and his daughter Serah (Gen 46:17; 1 Chr 7:30). Jacob's blessing promised Asher rich food, and Moses' blessing spoke of him dipping his foot in oil. He was the ancestor of the tribe of Asher, which settled along the northern coast. Anna the prophetess belonged to this tribe. The New Testament uses the Greek form Aser.

Ashkelon was one of the five chief cities of the Philistines, a seaport on the Mediterranean coast north of Gaza. Its location is not in doubt: it is the ancient site of Ashkelon in modern Israel, near the present-day city of the same name, and the location shown here matches that site. Judah is said to have taken it early in the period of the judges (Judg 1:18), but it was soon a Philistine city again. It was one of the five cities that sent a golden tumor offering when the Philistines returned the ark (1 Sam 6:17). Samson went down there and killed thirty men to pay off his riddle wager (Judg 14:19). David named it in his lament for Saul and Jonathan (2 Sam 1:20). Jeremiah, Amos, Zephaniah and Zechariah all announced judgment and desolation against it. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that it is also mentioned in Egyptian records.

Ashkenaz was a kingdom that Jeremiah's prophecy against Babylon summons, together with Ararat and Minni, to make war on Babylon (Jer 51:27). The KJV spells it Ashchenaz there. The name is the same as that of a son of Gomer in the table of nations (Gen 10:3), and Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the people to be descended from him. Because it is named alongside Ararat and Minni, Easton's places their original homeland in Armenia and suggests a link with the Black Sea. Many scholars connect Ashkenaz with the Scythians, who were active in the region south of the Caucasus in Jeremiah's time. The exact territory is uncertain. The location shown here is a rough one in the Armenian highlands, near Mount Ararat, which follows the Armenian identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a fire that spreads."

Ashkenaz (spelled Ashchenaz in 1 Chr 1:6) was a son of Gomer and grandson of Japheth, listed with his brothers Riphath and Togarmah in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:3; 1 Chr 1:6). His name also stands for a people or kingdom descended from him. In Jer 51:27 the prophet calls the kingdoms of Ararat, Minni and Ashchenaz to gather against Babylon. Because Ashkenaz is grouped there with Ararat and Minni, Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place the people in or near Armenia. Easton's adds that they probably lived near the Black Sea. Smith's Bible Dictionary links the name with Lake Ascanius in northern Asia Minor and mentions a view connecting it with the Germanic peoples. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "a fire that spreads."

Ashnah was the name of a town, or probably two separate towns, in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, listed in the territory allotted to the tribe of Judah. One Ashnah appears in the same group as Eshtaol and Zoreah (Zorah) in Josh 15:33, which places it in the northern lowland, west of Jerusalem. Another appears with Jiphtah and Nezib in Josh 15:43, in a group of towns farther south. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat these as two different places. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that the small ruin of Aslin, between Eshtaol and Zorah, may preserve the name of the northern town, and calls the southern site unknown. The location shown here is approximate and follows the northern town near Eshtaol and Zorah. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "change."

Ashpenaz was the master of the eunuchs, a chief court official, under the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar, who is named in Dan 1:1. The king ordered him to bring certain young Israelites of royal and noble families from among the captives so they could be trained for service in the palace (Dan 1:3). He is named only in this verse. The 'prince of the eunuchs' later in the same chapter, who gave Daniel and his companions Babylonian names and heard Daniel's request not to eat the king's food, is probably the same man, by inference from the passage. Easton's Bible Dictionary equates his office with the 'Rabsaris' title of the court. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as 'horse-nose,' while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name is more likely Babylonian than Persian in origin.

Ashriel was a man of the tribe of Manasseh, named at the head of the list of Manasseh's sons in 1 Chr 7:14. The verse says he was born to a woman it calls only "she," and it sets him apart from Machir, the father of Gilead, whose mother was Manasseh's Aramean concubine. This entry follows that reading and treats Ashriel as a son of Manasseh and a half-brother of Machir. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name more properly as Asriel and takes it to mean "vow of God." Num 26:31 and Josh 17:2 name an Asriel among the descendants of Gilead, and STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) identifies Ashriel with him, which would make him Manasseh's great-grandson rather than his son. The unclear wording of 1 Chr 7:14 leaves the exact relationship uncertain.

Ashtaroth was a city of Bashan, east of the Jordan, where Og king of Bashan lived and ruled alongside Edrei (Deut 1:4; Josh 12:4; Josh 13:12). Israel's defeat of Og under Moses was remembered as a well-known victory, and the Gibeonites mentioned it when they sought a treaty with Joshua (Josh 9:10). After the conquest the city was assigned to half of the clan of Machir son of Manasseh (Josh 13:31). It was later given, with its surrounding pasture lands, to the Levite family of Gershom (1 Chr 6:71). Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Beeshterah in the parallel Levitical list (Josh 21:27) as a shortened form of the same name. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the city was named after the goddess Ashtoreth. Easton's identifies it with Tell Ashterah in the Hauran region of southern Syria, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Ashteroth-karnaim was an ancient town east of the Jordan where Chedorlaomer and his allied kings defeated the Rephaim during their campaign in the time of Abraham (Gen 14:5). The name is usually explained as "Ashteroth of the two horns." Easton's Bible Dictionary links the horns to the crescent moon and suggests the town may be the same as Ashtaroth in Bashan. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note that a Carnaim or Carnion in Gilead, which had a temple, appears in 1 and 2 Maccabees as a town captured by Judas Maccabeus. Smith's and Easton's identify the site with es-Sanamein, about 25 to 28 miles south of Damascus. The location shown here follows a different identification. It places the town farther south in the Bashan region of southern Syria, near Tell Ashtara, the probable site of Ashtaroth.

Ashtoreth was a goddess of the Zidonians (Sidonians), the people of the Phoenician coast, whose worship King Solomon took up in his later years along with that of the Ammonite god Milcom (1 Kgs 11:5). Her worship is named among the reasons given for the division of Solomon's kingdom (1 Kgs 11:33). Solomon built a high place for her east of Jerusalem, on the "mount of corruption," and centuries later King Josiah defiled it together with the shrines of Chemosh and Milcom (2 Kgs 23:13). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes her as the chief female deity of the Phoenicians, often paired with Baal, and identifies her with the Assyrian Ishtar and the Greek Astarte. It links her with the "queen of heaven" mentioned in Jeremiah. Reference works differ on her character: Easton's calls her a moon goddess, while Smith's Bible Dictionary connects her with the planet Venus.

Ashvath was a man of the tribe of Asher, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 7:33 as one of the sons of Japhlet, with his brothers Pasach and Bimhal. Japhlet appears earlier in the same list as a son of Heber, a grandson of Asher through Beriah (1 Chr 7:30–32), which places Ashvath several generations down from Asher himself. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name appears only in this one verse, and he is known solely as part of Asher's family line.

Asia in the New Testament is the Roman province covering western Asia Minor, in present-day western Turkey, with Ephesus as its capital (Easton's Bible Dictionary; Smith's Bible Dictionary). Jews from Asia were in Jerusalem at Pentecost and later disputed with Stephen (Acts 2:9; 6:9). On his second journey Paul was forbidden by the Holy Spirit to preach there (Acts 16:6). He later stayed over two years at Ephesus, so that people across the province heard his message. This provoked a riot by craftsmen whose trade depended on the worship of Diana (Acts 19:10, 26–27). Jews from Asia later stirred up the crowd that seized Paul in the temple (Acts 21:27). The province held the seven churches addressed in Revelation (Rev 1:4). Easton's takes a few passages to mean wider Asia Minor. This entry follows the provincial sense, and the location shown here marks the general region.

Asiel was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named only in the Simeonite genealogy of 1 Chr 4:35. He was the father of Seraiah and, through Seraiah and Josibiah, the great-grandfather of Jehu. Jehu appears in a list of Simeonite clan leaders. By inference from the surrounding passage, these leaders lived in the reign of Hezekiah, when they expanded their families' grazing lands, so Asiel himself probably lived some generations earlier. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "created by God," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the work of God."

Asnah was the ancestor or head of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants, "the children of Asnah," appear in the list of exiles who returned from Babylon to Judah with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:50). Nothing else is recorded about him. His family is named alongside other temple-servant families, such as those of Mehunim and Nephusim. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of the name as "thornbush." His family does not appear in the parallel list of returnees in Nehemiah 7, which suggests it was either left out there or listed under another name.

Asnappar was the ruler called "the great and noble Asnappar" in a letter sent by officials in Samaria to the Persian king Artaxerxes. The letter says he had brought various nations over and settled them in the cities of Samaria and the region west of the Euphrates (Ezra 4:10). He is named only here. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper names index both identify him, probably, with the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal, son and successor of Esarhaddon. Easton's dates the start of his reign to about 668 BC and notes his great library of clay tablets at Nineveh. On that view, the passage refers to a later stage of the Assyrian resettlement of Samaria after the fall of the northern kingdom. The name appears as Osnappar in some modern translations.

Aspatha was one of the ten sons of Haman, the official of the Persian king Ahasuerus who plotted to destroy the Jews. He is named only once, third in the list of Haman's sons in Esth 9:7, after Parshandatha and Dalphon. His brothers were Poratha, Adalia, Aridatha, Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai and Vajezatha. From the surrounding passage, the ten sons were killed in Shushan when the Jews defended themselves on the day Haman had set for their destruction. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as Haman's third son, following the order of the list. The name is probably Persian, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a suggested meaning of "given by a sacred horse." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Asriel was a man of the tribe of Manasseh, son of Joseph, and the founder of the clan known as the Asrielites (Num 26:31). In the census list of Numbers 26 he appears among the sons of Gilead, alongside Abiezer, Helek, Shechem, Hepher and Shemida. This entry follows that view, which makes him a great-grandson of Manasseh through Gilead and Machir, as Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him. Joshua 17:2 names the same six as "the male children of Manasseh" in the broader sense of descendants, and records that their families received a share of land in the allotment to the rest of Manasseh. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that 1 Chr 7:14 presents an Asriel as born to Manasseh by an Aramean concubine. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "help of God."

Asshur is the Hebrew name for Assyria, the Mesopotamian power on the Tigris, and for its original capital city. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the name probably comes from Asshur son of Shem and that the old capital stood at Kalah Sherghat on the west bank of the Tigris, before the capital moved to Nineveh. In Balaam's oracle, Asshur will carry the Kenites away captive, and ships from Chittim will later afflict Asshur (Num 24:22, 24). Psalm 83 lists Assur among the nations allied with the children of Lot, meaning Moab and Ammon, against Israel (Ps 83:8). Ezekiel names Asshur among the trading partners of Tyre (Ezek 27:23). In these verses the name points to the nation more than to a single city. The location shown here is near Nineveh, opposite modern Mosul, and stands for the Assyrian heartland rather than the older city site farther south.

Asshur was a son of Shem, listed alongside his brothers Elam, Arphaxad, Lud and Aram in the table of nations (Gen 10:22; 1 Chr 1:17). Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him Shem's second son. In the King James wording of Gen 10:11, Asshur went out of the land of Shinar and built Nineveh, Rehoboth and Calah. Many translations instead read this verse as saying that Nimrod went out into Assyria and built those cities. This entry follows the King James reading, as Easton's does. Asshur is generally taken as the ancestor who gave his name to Assyria, and the name often stands for that people or nation. In Balaam's oracles, Asshur carries the Kenites away captive and is itself afflicted by ships from Chittim (Num 24:22, 24). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the Assyrians' chief god also bore the name Asshur.

Asshurim is named in Gen 25:3 as one of the sons of Dedan, alongside Letushim and Leummim. Dedan was a son of Jokshan, and the surrounding passage makes Jokshan a son of Abraham by his wife Keturah, so Asshurim belongs to the line of Abraham through Keturah, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. The name has a plural ending in Hebrew, as do the names of his two brothers. This suggests that the verse may be naming a tribe or people descended from Dedan rather than a single individual. The Bible gives no further details about him or his descendants. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "liers in want" or "beholders."

Assir was a Levite, a son of Korah, listed with Elkanah and Abiasaph (also spelled Ebiasaph) as the founders of the Korahite families in Exod 6:24. Through Korah he descended from Kohath, the son of Levi. 1 Chr 6:22 traces the same line from Kohath through Amminadab and Korah to Assir. Exod 6:21 names Korah's father as Izhar, so Amminadab there is probably another name for Izhar, though this is an inference. In Chronicles the names that follow Assir appear to run as a line of descent rather than as a list of brothers, so the relationship of Assir to Elkanah and Ebiasaph is presented differently in the two passages. This entry follows Exodus in treating them as brothers. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of his name as "captive." Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Assir was a Levite descended from Korah, named in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 6 as the son of Ebiasaph and the father of Tahath (1 Chr 6:23, 6:37). His name means "captive" or "prisoner" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names. He appears in the line that led to Samuel the prophet, and the second list traces through him the ancestry of Heman the singer, whose genealogy begins at 1 Chr 6:33.
