His brother Kore is probably the Kore named as a son of Ebiasaph in 1 Chr 9:19, an ancestor of the gatekeepers. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name was shared by several people, including another Assir who was a son of Korah and so this Assir's great-grandfather (1 Chr 6:22), so this man is told apart mainly by his place in the family line.

Assos was a seaport city in the district of Mysia in the Roman province of Asia, on the northern shore of the Gulf of Adramyttium, facing the island of Lesbos. During Paul's journey from Troas toward Miletus, his companions sailed ahead to Assos while Paul, by his own arrangement, travelled there on foot. They took him on board at Assos and sailed on to Mitylene (Acts 20:13–14). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the overland road from Troas was about 20 miles, compared with about 30 miles by sea. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes the city as built on a steep rock about 700 feet high, with a temple of Athena at its summit, and notes that Aristotle lived there for three years. The site is the modern village of Behramkale on the Aegean coast of Turkey, which matches the location shown here. This entry dates the voyage to about AD 54, by inference from context.

Assyria was a region on the upper Tigris River, probably in what is now northern Iraq, and the heart of a major Mesopotamian empire. Easton's Bible Dictionary derives the name from its early capital, Asshur on the Tigris. Genesis places the Tigris (Hiddekel) east of Assyria (Gen 2:14). Micah calls it 'the land of Nimrod' (Mic 5:6), which fits Gen 10:11 when read as Nimrod going out into Assyria. Its kings appear often as powerful adversaries of Israel and Judah. Pul and Tiglath-pileser exacted tribute and deported the eastern tribes. Shalmaneser besieged Samaria, and the king of Assyria resettled its cities with foreigners. Sennacherib invaded Judah and threatened Jerusalem under Hezekiah, and Assyrian captains took Manasseh to Babylon. Nahum and Zephaniah foretold Assyria's fall and the desolation of Nineveh. The location shown here marks its heartland near Nineveh.

Asyncritus was a Christian living in Rome whom Paul greeted near the end of his letter to the Romans (Rom 16:14). He is named first in a group of five men, together with Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas and Hermes, followed by "the brethren which are with them." That wording suggests these men belonged to the same circle of believers, possibly a house church meeting in Rome, though the text does not say so directly. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name is Greek and, according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names, means "incomparable."

Atarah was a wife of Jerahmeel and the mother of Onam. She appears only once, in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chr 2:26. That verse calls her Jerahmeel's "other wife," which sets her apart from the first wife, whose sons are listed in the verse before. She is therefore probably a second wife, though the text does not say which marriage came first. Through Onam, her descendants make up a separate branch of the Jerahmeelite line, traced in the verses that follow. Jerahmeel himself was a son of Hezron and a great-grandson of Judah. Her name means "crown," according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names. Nothing else is recorded about her.

Ataroth was a town east of the Jordan River. It was one of the places named by the tribes of Gad and Reuben when they asked Moses for the land of Jazer and Gilead as pasture for their livestock (Num 32:3). The Gadites afterward built, or fortified, Ataroth along with Dibon and Aroer (Num 32:34). The name means "crowns." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it seems to have lain in the area assigned to Reuben, even though Gad built it. It identifies the site with Khirbet Attarus, near Jebel Attarus in present-day Jordan, a mountain that keeps the ancient name, northwest of Dhiban (ancient Dibon). The location shown here follows that identification, east of the Dead Sea. Several other places in the Bible share the name Ataroth, and this entry covers only the town in this passage.

Ataroth, a name meaning "crowns" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), was a town on the border of the territory given to the descendants of Joseph. Joshua lists it twice. In Josh 16:2 the boundary runs from Bethel to Luz, past the Archites, to Ataroth. In Josh 16:7 it runs down from Janohah to Ataroth and Naarath, then to Jericho and the Jordan. Easton's Bible Dictionary treats both as one town on the Ephraim–Benjamin border, also called Ataroth-adar (Josh 16:5). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the Ataroth of Josh 16:7 as a separate, unidentified place on Ephraim's eastern frontier in the Jordan valley. Several places in the Bible share this name, so the identification is uncertain. The location shown here is approximate. It lies west of Bethel, matching the southern-border town rather than a Jordan-valley site.

Ataroth-addar was a town on the boundary between the tribal territories of Ephraim and Benjamin. Joshua 16:5 names it as a point on Ephraim's southern border, which ran from Ataroth-addar to Upper Beth-horon. The description of Benjamin's border in Josh 18:13 also mentions it, placing it near the hill south of Lower Beth-horon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "crowns of Addar," and Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "crowns of power." The exact site is uncertain. The location shown here is approximate and places it near the Beth-horon towns, northwest of Jerusalem, which fits the border descriptions. It is probably distinct from the other places called Ataroth in the Bible.

Ater was the ancestor of a family whose descendants, counted through a line called "of Hezekiah," numbered ninety-eight among the exiles who returned from Babylon to Judah with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:16; Neh 7:21). The phrase "Ater of Hezekiah" probably marks a branch of Ater's family descended through a man named Hezekiah, and this entry treats Hezekiah as his son. It may instead be a way of telling this Ater apart from others who share the name. Smith's Bible Dictionary adds that the family was also represented among the leaders who signed the covenant with Nehemiah (Neh 10:17). Nothing else is recorded about Ater himself. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "left hand" or "shut." Several people in the Bible bear this name, including a family of gatekeepers listed in the same return lists.

Ater was the ancestor or head of a family of temple gatekeepers ("porters" in the King James Version) whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem. He appears only in the parallel lists in Ezra 2:42 and Neh 7:45. There his family is named with those of Shallum, Talmon, Akkub, Hatita and Shobai, gatekeeper families that together numbered 139 in Ezra and 138 in Nehemiah. Smith's Bible Dictionary places this return under Zerubbabel, the leader named in the surrounding lists. Nothing else is recorded about Ater himself. The same name belongs to other men in the Bible, including the ancestor of another returning family listed in the same chapters, so this gatekeeper should be kept distinct from them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "left hand" or "shut."

Ater was one of the men who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, when the community in Jerusalem pledged to keep the law of Moses (Neh 10:17). He appears in the part of the list given to the leaders of the people, so he was probably a family or clan head rather than a priest or Levite. Because the name is placed next to Hizkijah, he may represent the family called 'the children of Ater of Hezekiah' among the exiles who returned from Babylon (Ezra 2:16; Neh 7:21). This is an inference from the names, not something the verse states. Several people in the Bible share the name, so other references may concern different individuals. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as 'left hand' or 'shut'.

Athach was a town in Judah, one of the places to which David sent a share of the spoil he took from the Amalekites while he was based at Ziklag (1 Sam 30:30). The surrounding verses show that these gifts went to towns where David and his men had moved about during his years as a fugitive from Saul. Athach is named only here, and its site is unknown, so no location is shown in this entry. Because the name appears nowhere else, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note a suggestion that it may be a copyist's variant of Ether, a town in the lowland of Judah listed in Josh 15:42. The name is usually explained as meaning "lodging place," though Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "thy time."

Athaiah was a man of the tribe of Judah who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. Nehemiah 11:4 names him first among the people of Judah who settled in the city. It traces his line through his father Uzziah and then Zechariah, Amariah, Shephatiah and Mahalaleel, back to Perez, the son of Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both take him to be the same man called Uthai in the parallel list at 1 Chr 9:4, although the ancestors named there differ. The meaning of his name is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "Yahweh is helper", Smith's gives "whom Jehovah made", and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the Lord's time".

Athaliah was the daughter of Ahab and Jezebel and the wife of Jehoram, king of Judah. She is called the daughter of Omri (2 Kgs 8:26; 2 Chr 22:2), which in context means his granddaughter. Her son Ahaziah reigned only one year. When he died, she killed the royal family of Judah and ruled the land herself. Her infant grandson Joash was rescued by Jehosheba (Jehoshabeath), Ahaziah's sister and the wife of the priest Jehoiada, and hidden in the temple for six years. When Joash was crowned there, Athaliah heard the noise, came into the temple, tore her clothes and cried "Treason, Treason." She was then killed with the sword beside the king's house. Chronicles adds that her sons had broken up the house of God and given its dedicated things to the Baals. By inference from context, her reign ran from about 886 to 879 BC.

Athaliah is a name in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin, listed in 1 Chr 8:26 among the children of Jeroham. Athaliah's siblings were Shamsherai, Shehariah, Eliah, Jaresiah and Zichri. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 8:27–28) describes Jeroham's family as heads of Benjamite households who lived in Jerusalem, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia accordingly describes this Athaliah as a Benjamite who lived there. Nothing else is recorded about this person. The name is shared by others in the Bible, most notably the queen who seized the throne of Judah (2 Kgs 11), and this entry should not be confused with her. The name's meaning is uncertain: Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the time of the Lord," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "whom Yahweh has afflicted."

Athaliah was a man of the family of Elam and the father of Jeshaiah. He is known only from the list in Ezra 8:7 of family heads who travelled from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra, where his son Jeshaiah is named as leading seventy men of the sons of Elam. The verse gives Athaliah only as Jeshaiah's father, so nothing more is known of his life. His name is the same as that of the better-known Queen Athaliah of Judah, and he should not be confused with her. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the time of the Lord."

Atharim is the name of a route in the Negev along which Israel was travelling when the Canaanite king of Arad attacked them and took some of them captive (Num 21:1). The Hebrew phrase is understood in different ways. The King James Version, following the Syriac and the Targum, translates it as "the way of the spies." The Revised Version, following the Septuagint, treats Atharim as a place name, "the way of Atharim." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes Dillmann's rendering, "the caravan path," from an Arabic word meaning a track or footprint. This entry follows the place-name reading. The route's exact course is unknown. By inference from the passage, it ran through the southern region near Arad's territory. The location shown here is a rough point in the Negev and should be taken as approximate.

Athens was the leading city of Attica in Greece, described in Easton's Bible Dictionary as the most celebrated city of the ancient world and a seat of Greek literature and art. It is the same city as modern Athens, the capital of Greece. Paul arrived there after being escorted from Berea and sent word for Silas and Timothy to join him quickly (Acts 17:15). While he waited, he was troubled to see the city full of idols (Acts 17:16). He spoke to the Athenians on Mars' Hill, the Areopagus, opening with the remark that they were very religious (Acts 17:22). From Athens he went on to Corinth (Acts 18:1). Paul later wrote that he had chosen to stay behind at Athens alone (1 Thess 3:1). The visit is placed about AD 48, an estimate inferred from context, during what Easton's calls his second missionary journey.

Athlai was one of the "sons of Bebai" named in Ezra 10:28. By context, this means he belonged to the family or clan descended from Bebai, not necessarily that he was Bebai's own son. He appears in the list of men who had married foreign wives and, after Ezra's reforms in Jerusalem following the return from exile, agreed to send them away. Three other men of the same family are listed with him: Jehohanan, Hananiah and Zabbai. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "whom Jehovah afflicts", and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "my hour or time".

Atroth-shophan was a town east of the Jordan that the tribe of Gad built or fortified after the land there was given to them (Num 32:35). It is named in a list of Gadite towns next to Aroer and before Jazer and Jogbehah. The King James Version prints "Atroth, Shophan" as two separate places. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both read it as a single name, Atroth-shophan, as the Revised Version does. This entry follows the single-name reading. Easton's gives the meaning of Shophan as "hidden" or "hollow." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that no firm identification of the site is yet possible. The location shown here is only a rough placement in Gadite territory, in the region of modern Amman, Jordan.

Attai was a descendant of Judah in the line of Jerahmeel, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 2. His mother was a daughter of Sheshan, who had no sons and gave her in marriage to Jarha, his Egyptian servant. She is probably Ahlai, the name listed as Sheshan's child in 1 Chr 2:31, and this entry follows that reading. Through this marriage Sheshan's line continued. Attai was the father of Nathan, and Nathan was the father of Zabad, after whom the genealogy goes on for several more generations. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies this Zabad with the Zabad listed among David's mighty men in 1 Chr 11:41. Several other men in the Bible share the name Attai, which Smith's renders as "opportune" and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia as "timely."

Attai was a warrior from the tribe of Gad who joined David before David became king. He is named sixth in a list of Gadite leaders (1 Chr 12:11). The surrounding passage, read in context, describes these men as experienced fighters with faces like lions and as swift as gazelles. It says they crossed the Jordan when it was in flood to come over to David at his stronghold in the wilderness, and that each became a captain in his army. Smith's Bible Dictionary places their joining in the wilderness. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connects it with David's time at Ziklag. The name may mean "timely." This name is shared by several people in the Bible, including a descendant of Judah and a son of King Rehoboam, but this Gadite is known only from this one verse.

Attai was a son of King Rehoboam of Judah and his wife Maachah, the daughter of Absalom. He is named second among her four children, after Abijah and before Ziza and Shelomith (2 Chr 11:20). Smith's Bible Dictionary therefore calls him Rehoboam's second son by Maachah. As Rehoboam's son he was a grandson of Solomon and a member of the tribe of Judah, and he was probably born in Jerusalem, the royal city. Through his father he also had half-brothers, Jeush, Shamariah and Zaham. His full brother Abijah was chosen to succeed Rehoboam as king, but nothing more is recorded about Attai himself. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and he should not be confused with them. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "opportune".

Attalia was a port city on the southern coast of Asia Minor in the region of Pamphylia. Paul and Barnabas came down to it from Perga near the end of their first missionary journey, after preaching in Perga (Acts 14:25). The next verse says they sailed from there back to Antioch in Syria, so Attalia was probably their port of departure. By inference from context, this was about AD 46. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says the city was founded by Attalus II Philadelphus, king of Pergamum (159–138 BC), and named after him. It stood on a limestone terrace near where the Catarrhactes River met the sea, and it long remained a main harbor for ships from Syria and Egypt. It is generally identified with modern Antalya in Turkey, which matches the location shown here.

Augustus was the title of the first Roman emperor, Gaius Octavius (Octavian), and of the emperors who followed him. Luke 2:1 says a decree from Caesar Augustus ordered a registration for taxation of "all the world," which Luke places at the time of Jesus' birth. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains that the name means "majesty" or "venerable." The Roman senate gave it to Octavian in 27 BC, and he ruled until his death in AD 14, when Tiberius succeeded him. In Acts 25:21 and 25:25 the governor Festus uses the same title for the emperor of his own day. He tells Agrippa and Bernice that Paul has appealed to Augustus and will be sent to Caesar. That ruler was not Octavian but a later emperor, probably Nero, by inference from the date of about AD 56. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats this second use separately, under the general title of emperor.

Aven, meaning "emptiness" or "wickedness," is the name Hosea uses for a center of idolatrous worship in Israel. He announces that its high places, called "the sin of Israel," will be destroyed, with thorns and thistles growing over their altars (Hos 10:8). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the name as a shortened form of Beth-aven, Hosea's mocking name for Bethel, home of one of the northern kingdom's royal shrines (compare Hos 4:15; 10:5). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same word is used elsewhere for other places, such as On (Heliopolis) in Egypt in Ezek 30:17 and a valley near Damascus in Amos 1:5. The location shown here follows the Bethel identification, near modern Beitin, north of Jerusalem.

Avith was the city of Hadad son of Bedad, one of the kings who ruled Edom before Israel had kings. Hadad succeeded Husham and is remembered for defeating Midian in the country of Moab (Gen 36:35; 1 Chr 1:46). Nothing else is said about the city. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "ruins," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "wicked, perverse." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint reads the name as Getthaim and that its site cannot be identified. Its location is therefore unknown. The point shown here is only an approximate placement in the Edomite highlands south-east of the Dead Sea, in present-day southern Jordan. It reflects the city's link with Edom rather than an identified site.

Avva (spelled "Ava" in the King James Version) was one of the places from which the king of Assyria brought people to resettle the cities of Samaria after the Israelites there were deported (2 Kgs 17:24). It is listed with Babylon, Cuthah, Hamath and Sepharvaim. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it to be probably the same place as Ivah, which Assyrian officials named among the cities whose gods had failed to protect them (2 Kgs 18:34; 19:13; Isa 37:13). Easton's also notes that it has been identified with Hit on the Euphrates in modern Iraq. Its exact site is uncertain. The location shown here is a rough one on the middle Euphrates, near modern Anah, somewhat upstream of Hit.

Avvim was a town allotted to the tribe of Benjamin, named only once, in the list of Benjamin's cities at Josh 18:23, where it appears alongside Parah and Ophrah. That list groups towns of Benjamin's eastern district, so Avvim probably lay in the hill country north of Jerusalem, near Bethel and Ophrah. Its exact site is unknown, and the location shown here is only a rough placement. Some scholars suggest the name may be another form of Ai, a town in the same area, but this remains uncertain. It should not be confused with the Avvim or Avites, a people who lived near Gaza before the Caphtorim displaced them.

Ayyah was a town named as one end of the territory held by the descendants of Ephraim, listed after Shechem in 1 Chr 7:28. The King James Version reads "Gaza" here, but the Hebrew word is closer to Ayyah, and many modern translations use that name. Its location is uncertain. Because the list describes Ephraim's lands in the central hill country, with Bethel, Naaran, Gezer and Shechem, many readers take Ayyah to be a town near Shechem, perhaps related to Ai or Aija, rather than the Philistine city of Gaza far to the southwest. Others follow the reading Gaza. The location shown here follows the Gaza identification, placing it on the southern coastal plain at modern Gaza. The verse gives no other details about the town.

Azal is a place named only once in the Bible, in Zechariah's prophecy of the day when the LORD comes to Jerusalem. Zech 14:5 says the newly formed "valley of the mountains" will reach as far as Azal, and that people will flee through it as they fled from the earthquake in the days of King Uzziah of Judah. By inference from the surrounding passage, this valley opens when the Mount of Olives splits in two, so Azal marked its far limit. The place has not been identified. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the word may not be a name at all and could be translated "very near." If it is a name, Easton places it near the western end of the valley, close to Jerusalem, while Smith's Bible Dictionary describes it as the limit of the ravine of the Mount of Olives. The location shown here is a rough position near Jerusalem.

Azaliah was the son of Meshullam and the father of Shaphan, the scribe who served King Josiah of Judah. He is known only through his son's genealogy. In Josiah's eighteenth year, the king sent Shaphan to the temple, and the Chronicles account adds that Shaphan went with Maaseiah the governor of the city and Joah the recorder to oversee repairs to the house of the Lord (2 Kgs 22:3; 2 Chr 34:8). In the Kings account, this errand led to the discovery of the book of the law. Nothing is recorded about Azaliah's own life. By inference from his son's career, he probably lived in Jerusalem in the generation before Josiah's reforms. His name is usually explained as meaning "the Lord has set aside" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "whom the Lord reserved" (Smith's Bible Dictionary).

Azaniah was the father, or possibly a more distant ancestor, of Jeshua, a Levite. He is known only from Neh 10:9, where "Jeshua the son of Azaniah" heads the list of Levites who put their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, after the return from exile. Nothing else is recorded about Azaniah himself, and it is not clear whether he was still alive at that time. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains his name as "whom the Lord hears," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives a similar meaning, "Yahweh has given ear."

Azarael was a musician who took part in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. He is named among the "brethren" of Zechariah, a descendant of Asaph, in one of the two great thanksgiving choirs that processed on the wall. These men played "the musical instruments of David the man of God", with Ezra the scribe leading them (Neh 12:36). The preceding verse names Zechariah as the son of Jonathan, and this entry treats Azarael as Jonathan's son too. However, "brethren" may mean kinsmen or fellow musicians rather than full brothers. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a Levite musician. STEPBible Proper Names describes him as a priest, since the group is connected with the priests' sons mentioned just before. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the name as a form of Azarel. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Azareel was one of the warriors listed among the Korhites who joined David, named alongside Elkanah, Jesiah, Joezer and Jashobeam in 1 Chr 12:6. The opening verses of the chapter place this list among the men who came to David at Ziklag while he was still in hiding from Saul. They were skilled with bow and sling, and many were Benjamites. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Korhite who joined David in his retreat at Ziklag, and dates this to about 1060 BC. "Korhites" may refer to descendants of a Korah, but which family is meant is not clear from this verse alone. His name means "help of God" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other men in the Bible share this name, and nothing more is recorded about this Azareel.

Azareel son of Jeroham was the leader, or prince, of the tribe of Dan during the reign of David. He appears only in 1 Chr 27:22, at the end of a list of officers placed over the tribes of Israel. Smith's Bible Dictionary connects the list with the time when David numbered the people, which the surrounding passage goes on to describe. Nothing else is recorded about him or his father Jeroham. His name means "God helps" or "help of God" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other men in the Bible share the name Azareel, and none of them can be identified with this tribal leader.

Azareel was one of the Israelites listed in Ezra 10:41 among the men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra, after the return from exile in Babylon. In the surrounding passage these men agreed to send away their foreign wives. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him among the descendants of Bani, inferred from the list's structure (compare Ezra 10:34), and dates the event to about 459 BC, an estimate drawn from context. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, meaning "God helps" or "help of God" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, is shared by several other men in the Bible, including a warrior who joined David and a temple musician. This Azareel should not be confused with them.

Azareel, also called Adiel, was a priest of the family of Immer and the father of Maasiai (called Amashai in Neh 11:13). The two genealogies list Maasiai among the priests who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. They trace the line differently. In 1 Chr 9:12 Adiel is the son of Jahzerah, son of Meshullam, son of Meshillemith. In Neh 11:13 Azareel is the son of Ahasai, son of Meshillemoth. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the two passages as describing the same family, and the STEPBible proper-names index identifies Adiel and Azareel as one person. This entry follows that view. The name probably means "God has helped" (Hitchcock's Bible Names: "help of God"), and Adiel is usually explained as "ornament of God." Several other men in the Bible are also named Azareel.

Azariah, also called Uzziah, was a Levite of the clan of Kohath who appears only in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 6. In the list of Kohath's descendants he is named Uzziah, son of Uriel and father of Shaul (1 Chr 6:24). In the parallel line tracing the ancestry of Heman the singer back to Kohath, an Azariah appears as son of Zephaniah and father of Joel (1 Chr 6:36). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the two as the same man, which places him among the ancestors of Samuel the prophet and of Heman. This entry follows that identification and gives his father and son as named in 1 Chr 6:24. The two lists name his neighbors differently, so how the lines line up is uncertain. His name means "the Lord has helped." Several other people in the Bible share this name.

Azariah was a Levite priest of the line of Zadok, the son of Ahimaaz and the father of Johanan in the priestly genealogy of 1 Chr 6:9. His name means "the Lord has helped." Since Ahimaaz was himself a son of Zadok (1 Chr 6:8), this Azariah was Zadok's grandson. 1 Kgs 4:2 lists "Azariah the son of Zadok the priest" first among King Solomon's chief officials. Views differ on whether that is the same man. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes "son" there to mean grandson and holds that Azariah succeeded Zadok as high priest under Solomon, perhaps because Ahimaaz had died first. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the official of 1 Kgs 4:2 as a separate son of Zadok. This entry follows the single-person identification. The name Azariah was common, especially among priestly families, so care is needed in telling its bearers apart.

Azariah, son of Nathan, was one of King Solomon's chief officials. He was placed "over the officers" (1 Kgs 4:5). These were probably the twelve district governors listed just after him, who each supplied the royal household with provisions for one month of the year. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia accordingly calls him captain of Solomon's tax collectors. His brother Zabud, also a son of Nathan, served as principal officer and "the king's friend." Which Nathan was their father is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he may have been David's son Nathan, which would make Azariah David's grandson. Others connect him with Nathan the prophet, who was closely tied to Solomon's accession. The name Azariah means "the Lord has helped" and was borne by several people in the Bible, so this man should be kept distinct from others of the same name.

Azariah was a man of the tribe of Judah, named as the son of Ethan in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:8. He is the only son of Ethan listed there, and nothing else is recorded about him. The surrounding genealogy places Ethan among the sons of Zerah, son of Judah, so Azariah belonged to the Zerahite clan by inference from context. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests that Zerahiah may be the better reading of his name in this verse. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links his father with Ethan the Wise. The name Azariah means "the Lord has helped" and was common in Israel, especially among priestly families, so this man should be kept distinct from the many others who bore it.

Azariah was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of Jerahmeel, the son of Hezron. He was the son of Jehu, the son of Obed, and the father of Helez, whose son was Eleasah (1 Chr 2:38–39). The surrounding passage traces this line back to the marriage of Sheshan's daughter to Jarha, his Egyptian servant (1 Chr 2:34–35), so Azariah descended from that union. Nothing else is recorded of him in these verses. Several other men in the Bible share his name, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders as "Yahweh has helped." Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he was probably the Azariah son of Jehu who was one of the captains of hundreds who joined the priest Jehoiada against Queen Athaliah (2 Chr 23:1). That identification rests on the shared name and father, and the genealogy itself does not confirm it.

Azariah was a priest of the tribe of Levi in the high-priestly line descended from Aaron through Zadok, listed as the son of Johanan and the father of Amariah (1 Chr 6:10–11). The Chronicler adds that he served as priest in the temple Solomon built in Jerusalem. Smith's Bible Dictionary places his high priesthood in the reigns of Abijah and Asa, after Solomon. Another view holds that the note about Solomon's temple belongs to the earlier Azariah, son of Ahimaaz, who served under Solomon (1 Kgs 4:2). This entry follows the reading that ties the note to Johanan's son. Ezra's genealogy names an Azariah as the father of Amariah and calls him the son of Meraioth (Ezra 7:3). That list is shortened and skips several generations, so it probably refers to this same man. The name is shared by several people in the Bible.

Azariah was a priest of the tribe of Levi, the son of Hilkiah and the father of Seraiah, in the line of high priests descended from Zadok (1 Chr 6:13–14). His father Hilkiah was probably the high priest of King Josiah's reign, and Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies his son Seraiah with the chief priest put to death by Nebuchadnezzar. Ezra the scribe traces his descent through Seraiah and Azariah to Hilkiah (Ezra 7:1). There "son" likely means descendant, since generations seem to be skipped. 1 Chr 9:11 names an Azariah son of Hilkiah as "ruler of the house of God," probably the same man. Jer 29:3 mentions a Gemariah son of Hilkiah, who is likely his brother. The name was common among priests, and this Azariah is easily confused with others who bore it.

Azariah son of Oded was a prophet in Judah during the reign of King Asa. 2 Chr 15:1 records that the Spirit of God came upon him. From the passage that follows, he went out to meet Asa after a military victory and urged the king and the people to seek the Lord, promising that God would be with them if they did. Easton's Bible Dictionary credits his message with prompting a great national reformation, in which Asa removed idols and renewed the altar of the Lord. In 2 Chr 15:8 the prophecy is attributed simply to "Oded the prophet," which Smith's Bible Dictionary takes as a shortened reference to Azariah himself. His name, which Smith's renders "whom the Lord helps," was common in Israel, and he should not be confused with the several other men called Azariah in the Bible.

Azariah was one of the sons of Jehoshaphat king of Judah and a brother of King Jehoram. He belonged to the tribe of Judah and was probably born in Jerusalem. The list in 2 Chr 21:2 is unusual because it names two different sons of Jehoshaphat called Azariah. This entry is one of them, but the text gives nothing that tells the two apart. The verse calls Jehoshaphat "king of Israel," which here means the king of Judah. The next verses (2 Chr 21:3–4) say that after Jehoram became king, he killed all his brothers with the sword. By inference, that is how Azariah died, in Jerusalem in about 889 BC, a date estimated from context. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "he that hears the Lord." Several other people in the Bible share the name.

Azariah was one of the sons of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, of the tribe of Judah, and a brother of King Jehoram. 2 Chr 21:2 lists two sons of Jehoshaphat named Azariah, so this entry refers to one of the two, and the text gives nothing to tell them apart. His other brothers were Jehiel, Zechariah, Michael and Shephatiah. The verse calls Jehoshaphat "king of Israel," though he ruled the southern kingdom of Judah. The surrounding passage says Jehoshaphat gave these sons gifts of silver, gold and fortified cities in Judah, but left the kingdom to Jehoram, the firstborn (2 Chr 21:3). When Jehoram had secured his rule, he killed all his brothers with the sword, so Azariah probably died then (2 Chr 21:4). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "he that hears the Lord."

Azariah son of Jeroham was one of the captains of hundreds whom the priest Jehoiada brought into a covenant with him in the seventh year (2 Chr 23:1). By inference from the surrounding passage, this was the plot to overthrow Queen Athaliah and crown the young Joash, the surviving heir of David's line, as king of Judah. He is named alongside four other commanders, one of whom, Azariah son of Obed, bore the same name. The seventh year refers, by context, to the seventh year of Athaliah's reign, during which Joash had been kept hidden in the temple. Nothing else is recorded about him, and several other people in the Bible share his name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of Azariah as "he that hears the Lord."

Azariah son of Obed was one of the military commanders, called captains of hundreds, who entered into a covenant with the priest Jehoiada in 2 Chr 23:1. The same verse names a second commander called Azariah, the son of Jeroham, so the two are told apart by their fathers. The pact took place in the seventh year, which by inference from the preceding passage (2 Chr 22:12) means the seventh year of Queen Athaliah's rule, while the young prince Joash was hidden in the temple. The following verses describe these commanders helping Jehoiada crown Joash and remove Athaliah. Nothing else is recorded about this Azariah, and because many men in the Bible share the name, he should not be confused with the others. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "he that hears the Lord."

Azariah was the chief priest of Judah during the reign of King Uzziah. When Uzziah entered the temple to burn incense, Azariah followed him in with eighty priests, described as valiant men (2 Chr 26:17). The surrounding passage, 2 Chr 26:16–19, records that the priests opposed the king because burning incense was reserved for priests descended from Aaron. While Uzziah was angry with them, leprosy appeared on his forehead. Azariah and the other priests saw it and drove him out of the temple, and the king himself hurried to leave, because the LORD had struck him (2 Chr 26:20). Easton's Bible Dictionary places him as a contemporary of the prophets Isaiah, Amos and Joel. The name, shared by many people in the Bible, is explained in Hitchcock's Bible Names as "he that hears the Lord."

Azariah, son of Johanan, was one of the leading men of Ephraim in the northern kingdom of Israel during the reign of Ahaz, king of Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him one of the captains of Ephraim. In 2 Chr 28:12 he stands up with Berechiah, Jehizkiah and Amasa against the soldiers coming back from war. From the surrounding chapter, those soldiers were Pekah's army returning with captives taken from Judah, and these leaders objected to making their own kinsmen slaves. By inference from the same passage, they helped see that the captives were clothed, fed and sent back to Jericho. His name is usually explained as "the Lord has helped." Several other men in the Bible are also called Azariah, and this one is known only from this single verse.

Azariah was a Levite of the Kohathite clan whose son Joel was among the Levites who came forward when King Hezekiah called for the temple to be cleansed (2 Chr 29:12). He is known only as Joel's father. Azariah himself does not appear to take part, and nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with another Azariah in the same verse, the son of Jehalelel, who belonged to the Merarite clan and served alongside Joel. The names Joel and Azariah also appear together in the earlier Kohathite genealogy of Heman the singer (1 Chr 6:36). Families often repeated names, so the two lists may refer to different men. The name is shared by many people in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "he that hears the Lord."

Azariah, son of Jehalelel, was a Levite of the clan of Merari who lived in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He appears only in 2 Chr 29:12, in the list of Levites who stepped forward when Hezekiah called on the priests and Levites to consecrate themselves and cleanse the temple in Jerusalem. He is named there alongside Kish son of Abdi as representing the Merarites, while other men stood for the Kohathites and Gershonites. Nothing more is recorded about him. He should not be confused with Azariah the Kohathite, father of Joel, named in the same verse, or with the many other men of this name in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "he that hears the Lord."

Azariah was the chief priest of the house of Zadok during the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. When Hezekiah asked about the heaps of offerings the people had brought, Azariah answered that since the giving began the priests had had enough to eat with plenty left over, and that the large surplus was the result of the LORD's blessing (2 Chr 31:10). He is also called the ruler of the house of God, and under his authority, with the king's command, Levites were appointed as overseers of the stored tithes and offerings (2 Chr 31:13). Smith's Bible Dictionary says he worked with Hezekiah in purifying the temple and restoring its services, and that he succeeded Urijah, high priest under Ahaz. Several other men in the Bible share the name Azariah, which was especially common in priestly families. Smith's gives its meaning as "whom the Lord helps."

Azariah, son of Maaseiah and grandson of Ananiah, was one of the people who rebuilt the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah. Like several others in the list of builders, he repaired the stretch of wall beside his own house. His section lay between the part repaired by Benjamin and Hashub and the part repaired by Binnui son of Henadad. Binnui's work ran from Azariah's house to the turning of the wall at the corner (Neh 3:23–24). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this work to about 446 BC, the period of Nehemiah. The name means "the Lord has helped" and was common in Israel, especially among priestly families. Several men in the Bible are called Azariah, so this one should be kept separate from others of the same name, including other Azariahs in Nehemiah.

Azariah, whose name means "the Lord has helped" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), is the name of a man, or possibly more than one man, in the book of Nehemiah. One Azariah is listed among the leaders who came back from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel and Jeshua (Neh 7:7). The parallel list in Ezra 2:2 has Seraiah in that place. An Azariah is named among the priests who sealed the covenant under Nehemiah (Neh 10:2). An Azariah also took part in the procession at the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt wall (Neh 12:33). Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the returning leader as a separate person and identifies the covenant-sealer and the man at the dedication as probably the same priest. STEPBible's Tyndale House names list treats all three mentions as one priest, and this entry follows that grouping. The name was common, so the identification is uncertain.

Azariah was one of the men who helped the people understand the law when Ezra read it publicly in Jerusalem after the return from exile (Neh 8:7). He is named in a list with Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah and others who explained the reading while the people stood in their places. The verse's wording leaves it slightly unclear whether every name in the list belongs to the Levites mentioned at its end. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat him as a Levite who assisted Ezra. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, usually explained as "the Lord has helped," was common in Israel, especially in priestly families, and he should not be confused with the many other men called Azariah.

Azariah was one of four young men from Judah, together with Daniel, Hananiah and Mishael, who were taken to Babylon and trained for service at the court of King Nebuchadnezzar (Dan 1:6). The chief of the eunuchs gave him the Babylonian name Abednego (Dan 1:7), the name by which he is better known. He was placed under the steward Melzar with his companions (Dan 1:11). When the king examined them, none of the other young men matched these four, so they entered the king's service (Dan 1:19). When Daniel needed to learn the king's dream, he told Azariah and the other two what was happening (Dan 2:17). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries describe him as probably of the royal family of Judah. As Abednego, he later survived the fiery furnace in Daniel 3. Several other people in the Bible share the name Azariah, a common Hebrew name meaning roughly "the Lord has helped."

Azaz was a man of the tribe of Reuben, named only in the Reubenite genealogy of 1 Chr 5:8. He was the son of Shema, the grandson of Joel, and the father of Bela. The verse says this family lived in Aroer and its territory reached as far as Nebo and Baal-meon, towns east of the Dead Sea in the land later held by Reuben. Nothing else is recorded about Azaz himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "strong," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "strong one." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "powerful."

Azazel is a Hebrew term found only in the Day of Atonement instructions of Leviticus 16. The King James Version translates it "scapegoat", while the Revised Version keeps it as a name. Aaron was to cast lots over two goats, one "for the LORD" and the other "for Azazel" (Lev 16:8). The second goat was kept alive and sent away into the wilderness (Lev 16:10). The man who released it had to wash his clothes and bathe before returning to the camp (Lev 16:26). The meaning of the word is debated. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that some Jewish interpreters took it as the name of a place in the wilderness about 12 miles east of Jerusalem. Others understand it as the name of an evil spirit, or as a word meaning "removal" or "separation". This entry treats Azazel as a place, following the first view, but its location is unknown.

Azaziah was a Levite musician in the time of King David. He was one of six men assigned to play harps "on the Sheminith" when David brought the ark of the covenant up to Jerusalem from the house of Obed-edom (1 Chr 15:21). "Sheminith" is probably a musical term, possibly referring to a lower pitch or an eight-stringed instrument, though its exact meaning is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that his name does not appear in the earlier list of Levites in 1 Chr 15:18. The name means "the Lord is strong" or "the Lord strengthens." Several people in the Bible bear this name. This entry refers only to the harpist named in this passage.

Azaziah was an Ephraimite, known only as the father of Hoshea, who led the tribe of Ephraim (1 Chr 27:20). The verse belongs to a list of the chief officers over the tribes of Israel during the reign of David. The surrounding passage links this list to the time David counted the people, so Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place Hoshea's leadership then. Nothing else is recorded about Azaziah himself. His name is usually explained as meaning "the Lord strengthens" or "strength of the Lord." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a Levite musician in David's time and a Levite overseer under Hezekiah. This Azaziah is a different person from them.

Azaziah was a Levite in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He was one of ten overseers who worked under Conaniah (spelled Cononiah in the KJV) and his brother Shimei. Hezekiah and Azariah, the ruler of the house of God, appointed them to look after the offerings, tithes and dedicated things the people brought to the temple (2 Chr 31:13). The surrounding passage describes how these gifts were stored in chambers prepared in the temple, so the overseers' work was probably to manage those stores. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both describe him as having charge of the temple offerings. His name is usually taken to mean "the Lord is strong" or "the Lord strengthens." Nothing else is recorded about him. Other men named Azaziah appear elsewhere in the Bible and should not be confused with him.

Azbuk was the father of a Nehemiah who ruled half the district of Beth-zur and repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall in the days of the governor Nehemiah. His son's stretch of the work ran to a point opposite the tombs of David, to the man-made pool, and to the "house of the mighty" (Neh 3:16). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that this son is a different man from the governor Nehemiah, though they lived at the same time. Smith's Bible Dictionary allows that Azbuk may have been a more distant ancestor rather than the immediate father, since "son of" can carry that wider sense. Azbuk is mentioned only in this verse, and nothing more is known about him.

Azekah was a fortified town in the Shephelah, the low hill country of Judah, listed among Judah's towns next to Socoh (Josh 15:35). Joshua's forces pursued the defeated Amorite kings from Gibeon as far as Azekah, and hailstones fell on the fleeing army along that route (Josh 10:10–11). Before David fought Goliath, the Philistines camped between Socoh and Azekah (1 Sam 17:1). Rehoboam fortified it (2 Chr 11:9). It was one of the last two fortified cities of Judah, with Lachish, still holding out when Babylon's army besieged Jerusalem (Jer 34:7). Jews returning from exile resettled it and its villages (Neh 11:30). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with Tell Zakariya (Tell Zaqareyeh), on the north side of the Valley of Elah about 3 miles northwest of Socoh. The location shown here follows that identification. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "dug over."

Azel was a Benjaminite descended from King Saul, named in the family line of Saul that appears twice in 1 Chronicles (1 Chr 8:37–38; 9:43–44). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "noble." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia traces his descent through Saul's son Jonathan, which matches the surrounding verses (1 Chr 8:33–36), where the line runs from Jonathan through Merib-baal and Micah down to Moza. The genealogy names Moza's son Binea, followed by Rapha (or Rephaiah), Eleasah and Azel, each called "his son." This wording can mean successive generations, but this entry treats Binea as Azel's father and Rephaiah and Eleasah as his brothers. Azel had six sons: Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah and Hanan. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Azgad was the ancestor of an Israelite family whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon. The list of those who came back with Zerubbabel numbers "the children of Azgad" at 1,222 in Ezra 2:12, while the parallel list in Neh 7:17 gives 2,322. The difference is probably due to copying variation between the two lists. A later group of 110 males from the same family, led by Johanan son of Hakkatan, returned with Ezra (Ezra 8:12). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also note that someone named Azgad, presumably representing this family, was among the leaders who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah's time (Neh 10:15). The name is often explained as "strong is Gad" or "strength of fortune." Because the name is shared by more than one person, the references cannot all be tied to a single individual with certainty.

Azgad was one of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the written covenant made in the time of Nehemiah, when the returned exiles pledged to keep God's law (Neh 10:15). He appears in a list of names with no further detail. In the surrounding passage this group is called the "chief of the people," and many of the names in it match families of returned exiles listed earlier. So Azgad here probably stands for the head or representative of the family of Azgad, whose descendants are counted among those who came back from Babylon in Ezra 2:12 and Neh 7:17. Because the name is used for more than one person or family, he cannot be identified with certainty. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a strong army" or "a gang of robbers."

Aziza was a man of the family of Zattu who lived in Judah after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears only once, in the list of men who had married foreign wives in Ezra's time (Ezra 10:27). The surrounding chapter shows that these men agreed to send their foreign wives away as part of the reforms Ezra led. He is named together with five others from the same family: Elioenai, Eliashib, Mattaniah, Jeremoth and Zabad. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a layman, as opposed to a priest or Levite, and gives the meaning of his name as "strong." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "the powerful" and notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:28 has the name Zardeus in his place. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Azmaveth was a town near Jerusalem. Forty-two of its people are listed among the exiles who returned from Babylon (Ezra 2:24). The parallel list in Neh 7:28 calls the town Beth-azmaveth. Later, at the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt wall, singers came from the fields of Geba and Azmaveth, where they had built villages around the city (Neh 12:29). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in the tribe of Judah. STEPBible's proper-names data places it in Benjamin, which fits its mention alongside the Benjamite town of Geba. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with el-Chizma, a village a little north of Anathoth, today known as Hizma, northeast of Jerusalem. The location shown here follows that identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "strong death."

Azmaveth was one of the warriors listed among David's mighty men, the elite group known as "the thirty." He is called "the Barhumite" in 2 Sam 23:31 and "the Baharumite" in 1 Chr 11:33. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes both forms to mean he came from Bahurim, a village near Jerusalem, and so was probably a Benjamite. Nothing else is recorded about his deeds or family. The name is shared by several other men in the Bible, including a son of Jehoadah in Saul's line and an official over David's treasuries. The two lists of David's warriors are the only places where this Azmaveth clearly appears, so whether he is the same man as any of the others is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "strong death."

Azmaveth was a descendant of King Saul, listed in the two genealogies of Saul's family in 1 Chronicles. He was a son of Jarah, a name given as Jehoadah in the parallel list (1 Chr 8:36; 1 Chr 9:42), and his brothers were Alemeth and Zimri. The surrounding verses trace this line from Saul through Jonathan, Merib-baal (Mephibosheth), Micah and Ahaz, so Azmaveth was a great-great-great-grandson of Jonathan. Nothing else is recorded about him, and the line continues through his brother Zimri rather than through him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including one of David's mighty men, and they should not be confused with this Azmaveth. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "strong unto death."

Azmaveth was the father of Jeziel and Pelet, two of the warriors who came over to David (1 Chr 12:3). The surrounding passage (1 Chr 12:1–2) places these men among the Benjamites, Saul's own tribe, who joined David at Ziklag while he was still in hiding from Saul. It describes them as archers and slingers who could use either hand. By inference, Azmaveth was also a Benjamite, and the STEPBible Proper Names index describes him that way. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several men in the Bible share the name, and some readers connect this Azmaveth with Azmaveth the Barhumite, one of David's mighty men (1 Chr 11:33). The text does not settle the question, so this entry treats him as a separate person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "strong death."

Azmaveth son of Adiel was the official in charge of King David's treasures, according to the list of royal administrators in 1 Chr 27:25. In the same verse, Jehonathan son of Uzziah oversaw the storehouses in the fields, cities, villages and fortresses. That suggests Azmaveth's charge was the king's central treasury, probably kept in Jerusalem, though the verse does not say where it was. Easton's Bible Dictionary places his service in the time of both David and Solomon. Several other men in the Bible bear the name Azmaveth, including one of David's mighty men. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some identify the treasurer with one or more of them. This entry treats him as the son of Adiel named in this verse. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "strong death."

Azmon was a place on the southern border of the land promised to Israel, later the southern border of Judah. The boundary ran from the ascent of Akrabbim past Zin and Kadesh Barnea to Hazar Addar and on to Azmon. From there it turned toward the river of Egypt and ended at the Mediterranean Sea (Num 34:4–5; Josh 15:4). It was therefore probably the last named point before the border reached the river of Egypt, which Smith's Bible Dictionary takes to be the Wadi el-Arish. Smith's left the site unidentified. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reports H. Clay Trumbull's identification with Ain el-Qaseimeh, northwest of Kadesh Barnea. The location shown here also lies northwest of Kadesh Barnea, near the modern border between Israel and Egypt, but the exact site remains uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "bone of a bone" or "our strength."

Aznoth-tabor was a landmark on the boundary of the tribe of Naphtali. It appears only in Josh 19:34, where the border turns west to Aznoth-tabor and then runs on to Hukkok. The name probably means "peaks of Tabor" (Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "the ears," possibly the summits, of Tabor). That suggests a spot near Mount Tabor on the western side of Naphtali's territory, where it met Zebulun. Smith's Bible Dictionary is unsure whether it was a town at all. Both it and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia say the exact site is unknown, while the STEPBible names list calls it a border town of Naphtali near Mount Tabor. The location shown here is a rough placement in the vicinity of Mount Tabor in Lower Galilee, not a firm identification with any known ruin.

Azor was an ancestor of Jesus who appears only in the genealogy in Matthew's Gospel. He was the son of Eliakim and the father of Sadoc (Matt 1:13–14). He belongs to the part of the list that runs from Zerubbabel (Zorobabel), after the exile to Babylon, down to Joseph, so he probably lived in the centuries after the return from exile. As a descendant of David, he belonged to the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he is not named in the Old Testament or in Luke's genealogy. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "a helper," and Hitchcock's Bible Names adds "a court."

Azotus was a city near the Mediterranean coast, named in the New Testament as the place where Philip the evangelist was found after he baptized the Ethiopian official on the road to Gaza. From there he preached in all the towns along his route until he reached Caesarea (Acts 8:40). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names identify Azotus as the Greek form of Ashdod, one of the five main Philistine cities of the Old Testament, where the captured ark of God was taken (1 Sam 5:1). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes the name in 1 Maccabees. The old city probably lay at or near the site of Isdud, close to the modern Israeli city of Ashdod, though no exact location is shown here.

Azriel was one of the heads of a father's house in the half-tribe of Manasseh that lived east of the Jordan. In 1 Chr 5:24 he is listed with Epher, Ishi, Eliel, Jeremiah, Hodaviah and Jahdiel, all described as mighty men of valour, famous men, and family heads. The surrounding passage places this half-tribe in the land from Bashan to Mount Hermon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links him with the people of his tribe whom the king of Assyria later carried into exile, as the following verses report. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 741 BC, an estimate drawn from that context. His name means "God's help." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Azriel is known only from this single verse.

Azriel was a man of the tribe of Naphtali and the father of Jerimoth. He is mentioned only once, in the list of tribal leaders during King David's reign, where Jerimoth son of Azriel is named as the officer over Naphtali (1 Chr 27:19). Nothing else is recorded about Azriel himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him Jerimoth's ancestor rather than his father, since "son of" in such lists can mean a more distant descendant. His name means "God's help" or "whom God helps". The same name belongs to other men in the Bible, and this entry covers only the Naphtalite.

Azriel was the father of Seraiah, one of three men whom the king ordered to arrest Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet. The order followed the king's burning of the scroll of Jeremiah's prophecies, but the LORD hid the two men (Jer 36:26). From the surrounding chapter, the king was Jehoiakim of Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary places these events about 605 BC. Azriel himself appears only as part of his son's name, and nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary translate as "God's help." Nothing links this Azriel to any of them.

Azrikam was a man of the tribe of Judah, one of the three sons of Neariah, along with his brothers Elioenai and Hezekiah (1 Chr 3:23). He appears only in the genealogy of David's royal line in 1 Chronicles 3, which traces the family through King Jehoiachin and Zerubbabel into the generations after the exile. This places Azrikam among the later descendants of Zerubbabel, as Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note. Nothing is recorded about his life beyond his place in this list. The name, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders "my help has arisen," is shared by several other men in the Bible, including a Levite and an official of King Ahaz. This Azrikam should be kept distinct from them.

Azrikam was a Benjamite and the first-named of the six sons of Azel. His brothers were Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah and Hanan. He appears only in the genealogy of Saul's family, which is given twice, in nearly identical form, in 1 Chr 8:38 and 1 Chr 9:44. In both lists Azel descends from King Saul through Jonathan and Merib-baal (Mephibosheth), which makes Azrikam a distant descendant of Saul. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him Azel's eldest son, apparently because he is named first. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "my help has arisen." Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Azrikam, and they should not be confused with this one.

Azrikam was a Levite of the clan of Merari, son of Hashabiah and father of Hasshub (spelled Hashub in Neh 11:15). He appears only in genealogies, as the grandfather of Shemaiah, a Levite listed among those who settled in Jerusalem after the return from exile (1 Chr 9:14; Neh 11:15). Nehemiah traces the line further back to Bunni, while Chronicles places it within the sons of Merari. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to before 536 BC, an estimate drawn from his place in these lists. His name is usually explained as "my help has arisen" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, and this entry concerns only the Levite.

Azrikam was an official of King Ahaz of Judah, described as "the governor of the house," probably meaning the officer in charge of the royal palace. He was killed by Zichri, a warrior from Ephraim, who also killed the king's son Maaseiah and Elkanah, who was "next to the king" (2 Chr 28:7). By context, this happened during the invasion of Judah by Pekah, king of Israel, in the reign of Ahaz. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates it to about 738 BC. The name is usually explained as "my help has arisen" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Bible share the name Azrikam, and this one is mentioned only in this single verse.

Azubah was the daughter of Shilhi and the mother of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. She is named only in the regnal summaries of her son, which record that he was thirty-five when he began to reign and that he reigned twenty-five years in Jerusalem (1 Kgs 22:42; 2 Chr 20:31). Since Jehoshaphat succeeded his father Asa, she was Asa's wife, probably one of his queens. Through this royal line she belongs to the ancestry traced in the genealogy of Jesus. Nothing else is told about her or about her father Shilhi. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of her name as "forsaken," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "desolation." The same name is borne by a different woman, a wife of Caleb son of Hezron, so the two should not be confused.

Azubah was a wife of Caleb son of Hezron, a descendant of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:18. The verse is hard to read. It mentions both Azubah and Jerioth, and says "her sons" were Jesher, Shobab and Ardon. Some read Jerioth as a second wife, and others read her as a daughter. This entry follows the common reading, given in the STEPBible names index, that these three were Azubah's sons. After Azubah died, Caleb married Ephrath, who bore him Hur (1 Chr 2:19). Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names give the meaning of her name as "forsaken." The name belongs to more than one person. A different Azubah, daughter of Shilhi, was the mother of King Jehoshaphat (1 Kgs 22:42).

Azur was the father of Hananiah, the prophet from Gibeon who confronted Jeremiah in the temple in the fourth year of Zedekiah king of Judah (Jer 28:1). He is known only from this one verse, which identifies his son by name and hometown. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a Benjamite of Gibeon, an inference from the town, which lay in Benjamin's territory. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Hananiah as a false prophet. Smith's gives the more exact form of the name as Azzur, and Hitchcock's Bible Names explains it as meaning "he that assists" or "is assisted." Several other people in the Bible bear the same name, and nothing links this Azur to any of them.

Azur was the father of Jaazaniah, one of the twenty-five men Ezekiel saw in a vision at the door of the east gate of the temple in Jerusalem. Jaazaniah and Pelatiah son of Benaiah are singled out there as "princes of the people" (Ezek 11:1), and the passage goes on to describe them as leaders whom Ezekiel was told to prophesy against. Nothing is recorded about Azur himself beyond his son's name. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name more properly as Azzur and explains it as "he that assists." The same name belongs to other people in the Bible, such as the father of the prophet Hananiah in Jeremiah 28 and a leader who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah 10. Nothing in the text links this Azur to either of them.

Azzan was a man of the tribe of Issachar, known only as the father of Paltiel. Paltiel was the prince, or leader, of Issachar named among the tribal representatives chosen to divide the land of Canaan among the tribes (Num 34:26). The context of the surrounding chapter, where God names these leaders to Moses, places this near the end of Israel's wilderness journey, before the crossing of the Jordan. Nothing else is recorded about Azzan himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "very strong," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "strong" or "thorn."

Azzur was one of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the covenant made under Nehemiah after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears only in the list of those who signed it, between Ater and Hizkijah in Neh 10:17. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he signed among the heads of the people rather than the priests or Levites. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the name probably stands for a family rather than a single individual. It notes that the Hebrew name is the same one elsewhere spelled Azur, and gives its meaning as "one who helps." Nothing else is recorded about him, and whether he is connected to the others who bear the name Azur is uncertain.

Baal was a place named as the limit of the villages belonging to the tribe of Simeon. In 1 Chr 4:33 their villages spread around their cities as far as Baal. The name means "lord" or "master" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both take it to be probably the same place as Baalath-beer, which Josh 19:8 lists among Simeon's towns and links with "Ramath of the south." On that view it lay in the southern country, the Negev, where Simeon's other towns were. Its exact site is uncertain. The location shown here lies east of the Jordan, so it reflects a different identification from the southern setting suggested by the surrounding list of Simeonite towns.

Baal, meaning "lord" or "master" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), was the chief male god of the Canaanites and Phoenicians, often worshipped alongside Ashtaroth (Judg 2:13). At Peor in Moab, Israel joined in the worship of Baal-peor, and those involved were put to death (Num 25:3–5; Deut 4:3). Gideon tore down his father's altar to Baal and was renamed Jerubbaal (Judg 6:25–32). King Ahab served Baal after marrying Jezebel, daughter of the Sidonian king Ethbaal. Elijah then challenged 450 prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel (1 Kgs 16:31; 18:19–26). Jehu destroyed Baal's temple in Samaria, and a house of Baal in Jerusalem was torn down when Athaliah fell (2 Kgs 10:19–27; 11:18). Jeremiah condemns the incense and child sacrifice offered to Baal (Jer 19:5). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a sun-god with many local forms, called the Baalim. The name Baal is also borne by other individuals in the Bible.

Baal was a man of the tribe of Reuben, named in the Reubenite genealogy of 1 Chr 5:5 as the son of Reaia and the father of Beerah. The following verse, 1 Chr 5:6, describes Beerah as a prince of the Reubenites whom Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria carried into exile. That would place Baal's life, by inference, in the generation or two before the Assyrian deportations of the eighth century BC. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name means "lord" or "master" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). It is the same word used for the Canaanite god Baal, and several people and places in the Bible share it. This Baal should not be confused with the Benjamite of the same name in Saul's family line.

Baal was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the family lists of 1 Chronicles as one of the sons of the "father of Gibeon" and his wife Maachah. He was fourth in the list, after the firstborn Abdon, then Zur and Kish. His other brothers included Ner, Nadab, Gedor, Ahio, Zacher (Zechariah) and Mikloth. The surrounding passage calls his father Jehiel (1 Chr 9:35), and Easton's Bible Dictionary names him that way. This entry identifies the father with Abiel, who appears as the father of Kish in 1 Sam 9:1. Because Ner and Kish belong to the line of King Saul in these lists, Baal was a member of Saul's extended family, though nothing is recorded about him beyond his name. The name means "master" or "lord" and is shared by several others in the Bible.

Baal-gad was a Canaanite city "in the valley of Lebanon under mount Hermon," marking the northern limit of Joshua's conquests (Josh 11:17; 12:7). The land he took stretched from Mount Halak near Seir in the south to Baal-gad in the north. Josh 13:5 also names it as the starting point of territory still unconquered, running from Baal-gad to the entrance of Hamath. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "lord of fortune" and says it probably comes from the worship of Baal. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's identifies it with Banias near the source of the Jordan and equates it with Baal-hermon, and notes that some have linked it to Baalbek. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it in the valley west or northwest of Hermon, distinct from Baal-hermon, and notes Conder's suggestion of Ain Jedeideh. The location shown here is a general point at Mount Hermon rather than any one of these sites.

Baal-hamon was the place where Solomon had a vineyard, according to Song 8:11. He leased it to keepers, and each was to bring a thousand pieces of silver for its fruit. This is the only mention of the place in the Bible, and its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "place of a multitude," and Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "who rules a crowd." Easton's records several proposed identifications: with Baal-gad, with Hammon in the territory of Asher (Josh 19:28), or with Belamon in central Palestine near Dothan. The location shown here, near the foot of Mount Hermon in present-day southern Lebanon, follows the Baal-gad identification. Because the verse appears in poetry, some readers also take the vineyard as part of the song's imagery, but the text presents it as a real holding of Solomon's.

Baalhanan son of Achbor was one of the early kings of Edom, listed among the rulers who reigned there before Israel had a king. He succeeded Saul (spelled Shaul in 1 Chr 1:49), and after his death Hadar, called Hadad in 1 Chr 1:50, took the throne (Gen 36:38–39). Unlike several other kings in the list, no city is named for him, and nothing more is recorded of his reign. The name means "Baal is gracious" or "the lord is gracious," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. The same name is borne by at least one other man in the Bible. This entry concerns the Edomite king.

Baalhanan the Gederite was the official who managed King David's olive trees and sycomore-fig trees in the "low plains" (1 Chr 27:28). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies these lowlands as the Shephelah, the foothills between the Judean hills and the coastal plain. He appears in a list of stewards in charge of the king's property, and in the same verse a man named Joash oversees the stores of oil. "Gederite" probably means he came from Geder or Gederah, though which town is meant is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "the Lord is gracious" and describes him as a gardener in David's service. The same name belongs to another person in the Bible, an early king of Edom, who is a different individual.

Baal-hazor was the place where Absalom held a sheep-shearing two full years after his sister Tamar was wronged by Amnon. It is described as "beside Ephraim," and Absalom invited all of King David's sons there (2 Sam 13:23). The following verses tell how Amnon was killed at this feast on Absalom's orders. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on the border of Ephraim and Benjamin and suggests it may be the same as the Hazor of Neh 11:33. Both Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with Tell 'Asur, a mountain about 4 to 5 miles northeast of Bethel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives its height as 3,318 feet above sea level. The location shown here follows the Tell 'Asur identification.

Baal-hermon was a place near Mount Hermon that marked the northern limit of the land settled by the half tribe of Manasseh east of the Jordan. According to 1 Chr 5:23, that tribe grew so numerous that it spread from Bashan to Baal-hermon, Senir and Mount Hermon. Judg 3:3 also speaks of a "mount Baal-hermon" in the same region. The name joins the god Baal with Hermon, which suggests a site linked to Baal worship. Its exact location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it to be probably the same as Baal-gad (Josh 11:17). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be Banias, near the springs of the Jordan. The location shown here does not follow either of these. It places Baal-hermon on Mount Hermon itself, at the area of its summit.

Baal-meon was a city east of the Dead Sea, in the tableland north of the Arnon. The Reubenites rebuilt it along with Nebo and Shibmah, and Num 32:38 notes that these towns were renamed. A Reubenite family line under Bela is said to have lived from Aroer as far as Nebo and Baal-meon (1 Chr 5:8). By Ezekiel's day it belonged to Moab and was named among the frontier cities, "the glory of the country," that would be laid open to invaders (Ezek 25:9). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it also appears as Beon, Beth-baal-meon and Beth-meon, and that the Moabite king Mesha claimed on his inscription to have fortified it. The site is usually identified with modern Ma'in, southwest of Madaba in Jordan, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Baal-peor was the name of a Moabite god, the "Baal of Peor," and is treated here as the place where he was worshipped. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the name from Mount Peor, where this cult was practised, and gives its meaning as "lord of the opening." The three verses here recall how Israel "joined" itself to Baal-peor and ate sacrifices offered to the dead (Ps 106:28). They also recall that the men who followed him were destroyed (Deut 4:3), and Hosea calls the episode a shameful turning away (Hos 9:10). The event itself is narrated in Num 25, set while Israel was camped at Shittim in the plains of Moab. Because the name can mean either the god or his sanctuary, the exact place is uncertain. The location shown here is a rough point in the hills of Moab northeast of the Dead Sea, in present-day Jordan, near where Mount Peor is usually placed.

Baal-perazim was the place where David defeated the Philistines early in his reign over all Israel. After the victory David said the LORD had broken through his enemies like a breaking flood of water, and the place was named for this. The name means roughly "lord of breakings through" (2 Sam 5:20; 1 Chr 14:11). The surrounding passages place the battle in or near the Valley of Rephaim, close to Jerusalem, where the Philistines had gathered. The Mount Perazim of Isa 28:21 is probably the same site. Its exact location is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Jebel Aly, west of Jerusalem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the heights just south of Jerusalem, near the so-called Mount of Evil Counsel, overlooking the valley often taken as Rephaim. The location shown here follows this second view and is only approximate.

Baal-shalishah was a town in Israel. A man from there brought Elisha, called “the man of God,” bread made from the firstfruits, including twenty barley loaves and fresh ears of grain. Elisha told him to give the food to the people so they could eat (2 Kgs 4:42). The nearby story in 2 Kgs 4:38 puts Elisha at Gilgal during a famine, so Baal-shalishah was probably not far from there. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note an identification with Khirbet Sirisia, about 13–15 miles north of Lydda, based on the ancient writer Eusebius. The encyclopedia also mentions Kefr Thilth, whose Arabic name matches Shalishah. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the hill country near that Gilgal, north of Bethel.

Baal-tamar was a place near Gibeah in the territory of Benjamin.
