There the main army of Israel drew up in battle order during the war against the Benjamites, while the troops hidden in ambush broke out from their positions near Gibeah (Judg 20:33). The name means "lord of the palm tree." Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it to have been a sanctuary of Baal and suggests the name may recall the palm tree of Deborah (Judg 4:5). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it between Bethel and Gibeah, inferring this from the roads mentioned in the same campaign (Judg 20:18, 31). It notes that Eusebius knew of the place but that all trace of the name has since been lost. Its exact site is unknown, and the location shown here is only a rough placement in the Gibeah area, north of Jerusalem.

Baal-zebub was the god of the Philistine city of Ekron. He is mentioned only in the account of Ahaziah, king of Israel. After Ahaziah fell through a lattice in his upper room in Samaria and was injured, he sent messengers to ask Baal-zebub whether he would recover (2 Kgs 1:2). The angel of the LORD sent Elijah to meet the messengers and ask whether there was no God in Israel, so that they had to consult the god of Ekron. Elijah announced that Ahaziah would not leave his bed but would die (2 Kgs 1:3, 6, 16). The name means "lord of flies." Easton's Bible Dictionary explains it as a title for a god believed to ward off plagues of flies. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the reason for the name as uncertain and notes only that he was known as a god who gave oracles.

Baalah was a town in the far south of Judah, listed in Josh 15:29 among the cities of Judah's southernmost district, near the border with Edom. The name is shared by other places, including Baalah, another name for Kiriath-jearim (Josh 15:9), and Mount Baalah on Judah's northern border (Josh 15:11). This southern Baalah should not be confused with them. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it to be the same town as Balah (Josh 19:3) and Bilhah (1 Chr 4:29), which appear in the lists of towns given to the tribe of Simeon inside Judah's territory. The STEPBible names index likewise treats it as a Simeonite town. Easton's identifies the site with Khurbet Zebalah. The location shown here is only approximate, placing it in the Negev region near Beersheba. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "her idol" or "a spouse."

Baalah was a city on the northern border of the tribe of Judah, identified in the text itself as another name for Kirjath-jearim (Josh 15:9; 1 Chr 13:6). The boundary description runs from the spring of Nephtoah to Baalah, then turns west toward mount Seir, Chesalon, Beth-shemesh and Timnah (Josh 15:10). David and all Israel went to Baalah, described as belonging to Judah, to bring the ark of God up from there (1 Chr 13:6). The name is often taken to mean "mistress" or "possessor" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several places in the Bible share this name, so this entry covers only the Judahite city. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Kuriet-el-Enab, or, as some think, with 'Erma. The location shown here is rough and lies nearer the 'Erma site, in the hills west of Jerusalem.

Baalath was a town in the territory given to the tribe of Dan. It is listed with Eltekeh and Gibbethon among Dan's cities in Josh 19:44, its only mention in this entry's verses. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it to be the same Baalath that Solomon later fortified (1 Kgs 9:18; 2 Chr 8:6), though because several places share this name, that link is not certain. Its exact site is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both mention a possible identification with Bel'ain, probably the present-day village of Bil'in west of Ramallah, and the rough location shown here follows that identification. The name is related to Baal, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "a rejoicing" or "our proud lord."

Baalath was a city that Solomon built or fortified as part of his building program. It appears in a list with Tadmor in the wilderness (1 Kgs 9:18). The preceding verse also names Gezer and lower Beth-horon. The parallel account places it alongside Solomon's store cities, chariot cities and cities for horsemen (2 Chr 8:6). Its location is uncertain, and the name is shared by several places in the Bible. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the town of Baalath in the territory of Dan (Josh 19:44) and mentions a suggested site at Bel'ain in Wadi Deir Balut. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links it with Beth-horon and suggests it may be the same as a nearby border town. STEPBible suggests it may have been in the Lebanon region. The location shown here follows the Danite identification and is only approximate, west of the hill country near Beth-horon.

Baalath-beer was a town on the edge of the territory given to the tribe of Simeon, named in Josh 19:8 together with the villages around it. The verse links it with "Ramath of the south," probably another name for the same place, which would put it on a height in the Negeb, the dry country of the far south. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "lady (mistress) of the well" and connects it with "Ramoth of the south" in 1 Sam 30:27. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it to be probably the same as Baal, a Simeonite town in 1 Chr 4:33. Its site is unknown. Conder suggested that the shrine Kubbet el Baul may keep the old name. The location shown here, east of the Jordan, reflects one proposed placement, while the verse's own setting points to the southern Negeb.

Baale-judah, meaning "lords of Judah" or "Baals of Judah," was a town in Judah. David and his people set out from there to bring the ark of God up to Jerusalem (2 Sam 6:2). The parallel account in 1 Chr 13:6 calls the place Kiriath-jearim, and Josh 15:9 says that Baalah is Kiriath-jearim. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat Baale-judah as another name for that town. This fits the earlier account in 1 Sam 7:1–2, where the ark was kept at Kiriath-jearim for many years after the Philistines returned it. Kiriath-jearim is usually placed in the hills west of Jerusalem, near modern Abu Ghosh. The location shown here is only approximate.

Baalis was king of the Ammonites at the time Jerusalem fell to Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon. After the fall, the Babylonians appointed Gedaliah son of Ahikam as governor over those left in Judah. Johanan son of Kareah and other army captains warned Gedaliah that Baalis had sent Ishmael son of Nethaniah to kill him, but Gedaliah did not believe them (Jer 40:14). The following chapter of Jeremiah records that Ishmael did murder Gedaliah at Mizpah and then tried to escape to the Ammonites. This supports the view, found in Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, that Baalis instigated the assassination. His motive is not stated. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a rejoicing" or "a proud lord," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be a form of Baalim.

Baana son of Ahilud was one of the twelve officers Solomon appointed over Israel. According to the surrounding passage (1 Kgs 4:7), each officer supplied food for the royal household for one month of the year. Baana's district included Taanach, Megiddo and all of Beth-shean near Zarethan below Jezreel, stretching from Beth-shean to Abel-meholah and beyond Jokneam. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes this as Jezreel and the north of the Jordan valley. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him one of Solomon's purveyors. He was the brother of Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud, whom 1 Kgs 4:3 names as Solomon's recorder. Several men in the Bible bear the name Baana. This one is distinct from Baana son of Hushai, another of Solomon's district officers (1 Kgs 4:16).

Baana was the father of Zadok, one of the men who repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah's leadership (Neh 3:4). He is known only from this single mention, which identifies his son. Nothing is recorded of Baana's own life or role, and he may not have been alive at the time of the rebuilding. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the work on the wall to about 446 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "son of oppression" and notes that a similar name belongs to two of Solomon's district officers (spelled "Baanah" in the King James Version). Because several people in the Bible bear this or a closely similar name, this Baana should not be confused with them.

Baanah was a son of Rimmon, a Beerothite of the tribe of Benjamin, and the brother of Rechab. He and Rechab were captains of raiding bands under Ishbosheth, Saul's son (2 Sam 4:2). The brothers came to Ishbosheth's house in the heat of the day while he lay resting at noon, entered as though to fetch wheat, struck him down, and escaped (2 Sam 4:5–6). They brought his head to David, probably hoping for a reward, but David answered them with an oath (2 Sam 4:9). The following verses of the same chapter, as Easton's Bible Dictionary summarizes, record that David had them put to death and their mutilated bodies hung up beside the pool at Hebron. The name Baanah is shared by several other people in the Bible, and this entry concerns only Rechab's brother.

Baanah was a man from Netophah, a town near Bethlehem in Judah, and the father of Heleb, one of the elite warriors known as David's mighty men. He appears only in the two parallel lists of those warriors, where his son is called Heleb in 2 Sam 23:29 and Heled in 1 Chr 11:30. The difference is probably a copying variation of the same name. The text says nothing more about Baanah himself. In both verses the description "the Netophathite" sits close to his name. Grammatically it most naturally describes the son, though it is often applied to the father as well (Smith's Bible Dictionary calls Baanah a Netophathite). Several other men in the Bible are also named Baanah. They include one of the assassins of Ish-bosheth and one of Solomon's district officers, and this Baanah should be kept distinct from them.

Baanah son of Hushai was one of the twelve district officers King Solomon appointed over Israel, responsible for Asher and Aloth (1 Kgs 4:16). By inference from the surrounding passage (1 Kgs 4:7), each of these officers supplied food for the king and his household for one month of the year. Easton's Bible Dictionary accordingly calls him one of Solomon's purveyors, and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a commissariat officer. Asher was the tribal territory in the northwest of the country, and Aloth was probably a place or district near it, though its location is uncertain. Some have suggested his father was Hushai the Archite, David's friend and counselor, but the text does not say so. The name Baanah is shared by several other men in the Bible, including a captain under Saul's son Ish-bosheth and another of Solomon's officers, Baanah son of Ahilud.

Baanah was one of the leaders who returned with Zerubbabel from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem. His name closes the list of leading men in Ezra 2:2 and in the parallel list in Neh 7:7, which come just before the count of the returning people of Israel. Nothing else is recorded about him in these passages. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the return to about 536 BC, and like the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia it suggests he may be the same Baanah who sealed the covenant in Neh 10:27. That identification is possible but not certain, because several men in the Bible share this name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "in the answer" or "in affliction."

Baanah was one of the chiefs of the people who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, when the returned exiles pledged to keep God's law. His name appears in the list of signatories, beside Malluch and Harim (Neh 10:27). By inference from the surrounding passage, the covenant was sealed after the public reading of the law and the confession recorded in Nehemiah 8–9. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Baanah, among them one of Ish-bosheth's murderers and one of Solomon's district officers. Some suggest this Baanah may be the man of the same name who returned from exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:2; Neh 7:7), or a family head of that name, but the text does not settle this. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "in the answer" or "in affliction."

Baara was one of the wives of Shaharaim, a member of the tribe of Benjamin, named once in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles. 1 Chr 8:8 says Shaharaim had children in the land of Moab after he had sent away Hushim and Baara, his two wives. The phrase "sent them away" is usually read as divorce. The next verse names Hodesh as the wife by whom he had children in Moab, and a later verse in the same chapter credits sons to Hushim. No children are named for Baara, and nothing else is recorded about her. The meaning of her name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "brutish," the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "the burning one," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a flame; purging."

Baaseiah was a Levite named only once, in the genealogy of Asaph the singer in 1 Chr 6:40. That verse makes him the son of Malchiah and the father of Michael. The surrounding passage traces Asaph's line back through Gershom, son of Levi, so Baaseiah belonged to the Gershonite branch of the tribe of Levi. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper-names index both describe him this way. Nothing else is recorded about his life. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "the Lord is bold." It also suggests the name may be a variant of Maaseiah, "the work of the Lord," a form that some Greek manuscripts support. Smith's dictionary dates him to about 1310 BC. That date is an estimate worked out from his place in the genealogy, not something the text states.

Baasha son of Ahijah, of the tribe of Issachar, was the third king of the northern kingdom of Israel and, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes, founder of its second dynasty. While Nadab son of Jeroboam was besieging the Philistine town of Gibbethon, Baasha conspired against him, killed him, and took the throne in the third year of Asa king of Judah. He reigned twenty-four years from Tirzah, beginning about 953 BC by inference from context. He was at war with Asa throughout and fortified Ramah to cut off movement into Judah. He abandoned the work when Asa paid the king of Syria to break his alliance with Israel. The prophet Jehu son of Hanani announced that Baasha's house would end like Jeroboam's. Baasha was buried in Tirzah and succeeded by his son Elah. Zimri later killed Elah and wiped out Baasha's whole family. Later prophecies cite Baasha's house as a precedent for the fate of Ahab's house.

Babel was a city in the land of Shinar, named in Gen 10:10 as the first of the cities where Nimrod's kingdom began, along with Erech, Accad and Calneh. Gen 11:9 explains the name: there the LORD confused the language of all the earth and scattered people across it. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "confusion" or "mixture." Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Babylon is the Greek form of Babel, and the city is generally taken to be the early Babylon on the Euphrates, in present-day Iraq. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects the tower of Gen 11 with the ruins of Birs Nimrud at ancient Borsippa, while others link it with a temple mound within Babylon itself. The location shown here follows the identification with the site of ancient Babylon, near the modern town of Hillah.

Babylon was the great city on the Euphrates that served as capital of the Babylonian (Chaldean) empire. Its ruins lie near Hillah in modern Iraq, about 50 miles south of Baghdad, which is where the location shown here is placed. Easton's Bible Dictionary treats the name as the Greek form of Babel. Its king Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem and carried the people of Judah and the temple vessels to Babylon (2 Kgs 24:11; Ezra 6:5; Dan 1:1). The exiled king Jehoiachin lived out his days there on the king's allowance. Zedekiah also died there, unable to see it, as Ezek 12:13 foretold. The exile lasted until Persia's rise, when captives returned to Judah (2 Chr 36:20; Ezra 2:1). The prophets announced Babylon's fall (Isa 13:1; Jer 50:23). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the Babylon of Revelation as a symbolic name for Rome. For 1 Pet 5:13, some readers also see Rome, while Smith's and Easton's take it as the literal city.

Babylonia was the region of southern Mesopotamia, the alluvial plain watered by the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, with Babylon as its chief city. It lies in what is now central and southern Iraq. In the verses shown here, the King James text says simply "Babylon," but the sense is the wider land where the exiles from Judah lived. Ezra 7:16 calls it "the province of Babylon," a district of the Persian Empire by that time. Sheshbazzar brought the temple vessels from there to Jerusalem (Ezra 1:11). Under Darius, the royal archives kept in Babylon were searched for an earlier decree (Ezra 6:1). Later Ezra the scribe led a group back from Babylonia to Jerusalem in the reign of Artaxerxes, a journey of about four months (Ezra 7:6, 9; 8:1). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes the land as a fertile, canal-irrigated plain bounded by Assyria, Elam, the southern marshes and the Syrian desert.

Baharum was the hometown of Azmaveth the Baharumite, one of David's mighty warriors, listed in 1 Chr 11:33. The place itself is not described, and it is known only from this title. The parallel list in 2 Sam 23:31 calls the same man "Azmaveth the Barhumite." For that reason Baharum is probably the same as Bahurim, a village near Jerusalem on the road to the Jordan Valley, which appears in the stories of David's flight from Absalom (2 Sam 16:5). The exact site is uncertain. The location shown here is a rough one, east of Jerusalem in the direction of the Jordan.

Bahurim was a village east of Jerusalem in the territory of Benjamin, on the road down toward the Jordan valley. Here Abner sent back Michal's husband, who had followed her weeping as she was returned to David (2 Sam 3:16). When David fled from Absalom, Shimei son of Gera, a Benjamite of Bahurim from the family of Saul, came out and cursed him (2 Sam 16:5). He later came down to meet David at the Jordan, and David spared him (2 Sam 19:16; 1 Kgs 2:8). David's messengers Jonathan and Ahimaaz hid in a well in a courtyard there (2 Sam 17:18). Azmaveth "the Barhumite," one of David's warriors, was probably also from Bahurim (2 Sam 23:31). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes the Talmud's identification with modern Almit, near Anata. The exact site is uncertain, and the location shown here is only a rough placement east of Jerusalem.

Bakbakkar was a Levite named in the list of those who lived in Jerusalem, recorded in 1 Chr 9:15. He appears alongside Heresh, Galal and Mattaniah. In the surrounding passage, this list describes the Levites who settled in Jerusalem, probably after the return from exile in Babylon, by inference from the context of the chapter. The verse traces Mattaniah's ancestry back to Asaph, the temple musician. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Bakbakkar to be apparently a descendant of Asaph as well. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain: Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "admirable," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "investigator." Some readers have linked him with Bakbukiah, a Levite in the similar list in Nehemiah 11, but the text does not make this identification.

Bakbuk was the ancestor of a family of temple servants, known as the Nethinim, whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel. The "children of Bakbuk" appear in the list of returning exiles in Ezra 2:51, and the same list is repeated in Neh 7:53. In both lists they are named among the temple servants, between the families of Hakupha and Harhur. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the return to before 536 BC. The name probably means "bottle." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may imitate the gurgling sound of liquid poured from a bottle, and notes that the same family appears as Acub in 1 Esdras 5:31. Nothing is recorded about Bakbuk himself beyond his name as the head of this family line.

Bakbukiah was a Levite in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. Nehemiah 11:17 names him "the second among his brethren," ranked after Mattaniah, who led the thanksgiving in prayer. Nehemiah 12:9 places him with Unni among Levites who stood opposite their fellow Levites "in the watches," probably singing in alternating groups. By the context of that list, this group came back with Zerubbabel. Nehemiah 12:25 lists him with Mattaniah and others as gatekeepers guarding the thresholds of the gates. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats these three mentions as possibly three different Levites. This entry follows the view that they are one man, since he appears with Mattaniah in both Neh 11:17 and Neh 12:25. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "the Lord pours out," while Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "wasting of Jehovah."

Balaam, son of Beor, was a soothsayer from Pethor in Mesopotamia, probably on the Euphrates. Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab, sent for him to curse the Israelites camped near his land. God at first forbade him to go, then allowed it on condition that he speak only what he was told. On the way his donkey turned aside from the angel of the LORD, and Balaam, after striking her, had his eyes opened to see the angel. At altars Balak built, including on the top of Peor, he blessed Israel three times instead of cursing them, and the two parted. Num 31:16 blames his counsel for Israel's sin at Peor and the plague that followed, and Israel later killed him with the sword. Later writers recall him as hired to curse Israel, as loving wages (2 Pet 2:15, which calls his father Bosor), and as teaching Balak to lead Israel astray.

Baladan was the father of Merodach-baladan (called Berodach-baladan in 2 Kgs 20:12), the king of Babylon who sent letters and a gift to King Hezekiah of Judah after hearing of his illness and recovery. He appears only in this identifying phrase in two parallel passages, and the Bible says nothing else about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explain the name as meaning "he (Merodach) has given a son," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "one without judgment." Assyrian inscriptions of Sargon call Merodach-baladan the son of Yakin. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes Yakin to be the founder of his dynasty rather than his father. It also suggests that "Baladan" may be a shortened form of the father's full name, possibly that of an earlier king also called Merodach-baladan.

Balah was a town in the territory given to the tribe of Simeon. It appears in Josh 19:3, in the list of Simeon's cities, between Hazar-shual and Azem. Simeon's towns lay within Judah's allotment in the Negev, the dry southern region around Beersheba. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies Balah with Bilhah in the parallel list of Simeonite towns (1 Chr 4:29) and with Baalah among the southern towns of Judah (Josh 15:29). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia accepts the link with Bilhah and calls the identification with Baalah possible. The site has not been identified. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the northern Negev, east of Beersheba, near the other towns in the same list.

Balak, son of Zippor, was king of Moab when Israel camped near his territory after defeating the Amorites. Alarmed, he sent elders of Moab and Midian with payment to summon the prophet Balaam from Aram to curse Israel. When Balaam refused, Balak sent more distinguished princes and promised him honour. He met Balaam at a city on the Arnon border and took him to the high places of Baal, then to other vantage points including the top of Peor, building altars and offering bulls and rams at each. Each time Balaam blessed Israel instead, and Balak angrily complained that he had blessed them three times. The two then parted. Later books recall the episode: Josh 24:9 says he warred against Israel, Micah urges Israel to remember his scheme, and Rev 2:14 says Balaam taught him (as Balac) to lead Israel into idolatry and immorality. His name is usually explained as meaning "one who lays waste" (Hitchcock's Bible Names).

Bamah is a Hebrew word meaning "high place", used as a name in Ezek 20:29. There God, speaking through Ezekiel, asks Israel's elders what the high place is that they go to, and adds that it is still called Bamah "unto this day." Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary take it as a general term for the hilltop sites where Israelites worshipped idols, not as the name of one town. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a possible wordplay in the Hebrew ("what" is mah, "come" is ba) and suggests that a prominent high place, such as the one at Gibeon, may be meant. It points to 1 Kgs 3:4 and 1 Chr 16:39 for that site. The location shown here follows the Gibeon identification, at the modern village of el-Jib north of Jerusalem. Because the passage does not name a specific site, any location is uncertain.

Bamoth was a stopping place of the Israelites on their journey through the land east of the Dead Sea, reached after Mattanah and Nahaliel and before the top of Pisgah (Num 21:19–20). Num 21:20 places it by a valley in the country of Moab. The name means "heights," and Easton's Bible Dictionary counts it as the forty-seventh station of the Israelites' journey. It is probably the same place as Bamoth-baal, mentioned later in Num 22:41 and Josh 13:17 as a height in this region, though the two names are not explicitly linked. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only approximate, on the plateau northeast of the Dead Sea near the Pisgah and Mount Nebo range, which fits its place in the itinerary just before Pisgah.

Bamoth-baal, meaning "heights of Baal," was a place in Moab east of the Jordan. The King James Version translates the name in Num 22:41, where the Moabite king Balak brought the prophet Balaam up to "the high places of Baal" so he could see the edge of Israel's camp. Later, Josh 13:17 lists Bamoth-baal among the towns near Heshbon and Dibon given to the tribe of Reuben. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests it is probably the same as Bamoth, a stopping place on Israel's journey, and is also mentioned in Isaiah 15:2. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on or near the Arnon River. Its exact site is uncertain. The location shown here is a rough one on the plateau near Mount Nebo, northeast of the Dead Sea in modern Jordan. That position fits a height overlooking the plains where Israel camped.

Bani was a man of the tribe of Gad who appears in the list of David's mighty warriors, the elite fighters known as "the thirty" (2 Sam 23:36). He is called simply "Bani the Gadite" and is named next to Igal son of Nathan of Zobah. Nothing else is recorded about him, his family or his deeds. The parallel list of David's warriors in 1 Chr 11:38 has "Mibhar the son of Haggeri" at this point, so some take the two names as variant forms of the same entry, though this is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of the name as "posterity", while Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "built". Several other men in the Bible are named Bani, mostly Levites and returned exiles in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah. This Bani is distinct from them.

Bani was a Levite named in the family line of Ethan, one of the temple musicians in 1 Chr 6:46. He was the son of Shamer and the father of Amzi. The surrounding passage traces Ethan's ancestry back through the Levite clan of Merari. In context, Ethan was one of the men David put in charge of singing at the place of worship (1 Chr 6:31–47). Smith's Bible Dictionary accordingly describes Bani as a Levite of the line of Merari and a forefather of Ethan. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Bani, and this entry refers only to the Merarite Levite of this genealogy.

Bani was a man of the tribe of Judah, descended from Pharez (Perez) son of Judah. He appears only in the genealogy of Uthai, one of the people of Judah who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile (1 Chr 9:4). There he is named as the father of Imri and an ancestor of Uthai through Imri, Omri and Ammihud. Bani himself probably lived several generations before the return. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Bani, and this entry concerns only the Judahite of the line of Pharez, as Smith's Bible Dictionary also identifies him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of the name as "posterity", while Smith's gives "built".

Bani was the ancestor of a family that returned to Judah from exile in Babylon, apparently with Zerubbabel. Ezra's list of returnees counts 642 "children of Bani" (Ezra 2:10). The parallel list in Nehemiah calls him Binnui and gives 648 (Neh 7:15). Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the two forms as variants of the same name, and the small difference in numbers is typical of these two parallel lists. Later, some men of this family were among those who had married foreign wives and agreed to send them away: Meshullam, Malluch, Adaiah, Jashub, Sheal and Ramoth (Ezra 10:29). Bani himself is known only as the head of this family line. Several other men in Ezra and Nehemiah share the names Bani and Binnui, including Levites, so it is not always clear which one a given passage means.

Bani is named in Ezra 10:34 as the head of a family whose members appear in the list of Israelites who had married foreign women after the return from exile in Babylon. Maadai, Amram and Uel are the first of the men listed under his name. By inference from the surrounding chapter, those named agreed under Ezra's leadership to send away their foreign wives. The STEPBible proper names index (Tyndale House) counts Bani himself among the men who had married foreign women and agreed to put them away. The verse does not make clear whether Bani was a living man or a more distant ancestor whose name marked the family. The name is shared by several people in the Bible, and another Bani family appears earlier in the same list (Ezra 10:29), so this entry treats him as a separate person, though the relationship between the two is uncertain.

Bani was an Israelite named in Ezra 10:38 among the men who had married foreign women in the time of Ezra, after the return from exile in Babylon. His name appears in a list that the surrounding chapter presents as men who agreed to send away their foreign wives. By inference from the list's structure, he seems to belong to a group introduced earlier as "the sons of Bani" (Ezra 10:34), and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him that way. In that case he would be a member of that family who shared its founder's name. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in Ezra and Nehemiah are also called Bani, and it is unclear whether any of them is the same person.

Bani was a Levite, known only as the father of Rehum, who led a group of Levites in repairing a section of Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah (Neh 3:17). The verse names him only to identify his son, so nothing else is recorded about his life. He is taken to be a Levite because his son is listed among the Levites; Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Levite. The work on the wall dates to the return from exile in the Persian period. Several other men in Ezra and Nehemiah share the name Bani, including Levites in the same period, and it is uncertain whether any of them is this same person. This entry treats him as a separate individual.

Bani was a Levite in Jerusalem in the time of Ezra and Nehemiah. He was one of the Levites who helped the people understand the law while Ezra read it publicly (Neh 8:7). He was also among the Levites who called the assembled people to stand and bless the Lord during the day of confession and prayer (Neh 9:5). A Bani appears in the list of Levites who sealed the covenant led by Nehemiah (Neh 10:13). This entry treats these mentions as one man, as Smith's Bible Dictionary does. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia separates the teacher of Neh 8:7 from the covenant signer of Neh 10:13. Because several Levites of this period were named Bani, and Neh 9:4 names a Bani as well, it is uncertain how many individuals these verses describe. The name is usually explained as meaning "built" or "posterity."

Bani was a Levite who stood on the stairs with other Levites and cried out loudly to the LORD during the assembly of fasting and confession held in Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah (Neh 9:4). The surrounding chapter places this after the return from exile, when the Israelites gathered in sackcloth to confess their sins and hear the law read (Neh 9:1–3). The verse names two Levites called Bani, one after Jeshua and another after Sherebiah, so it is not certain which of them this entry refers to. The two may also be easy to confuse with other men of the same name in Ezra and Nehemiah. Bani is one of the most common names of the period, and the text gives no family line or further details that would tell these men apart.

Bani was one of the chiefs of the people who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, when the community that had returned from exile pledged to keep the law of God. In the list at Neh 10:14 he appears among the lay leaders, after Parosh, Pahath-moab, Elam and Zatthu. Several of these names also appear as family names in the lists of returned exiles, so Bani here probably stands as the head or representative of a family group rather than as a private individual. This is an inference from the pattern of the list. The name, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains as meaning "posterity," is shared by several men in Ezra and Nehemiah, including Levites. Which of the other mentions, if any, refer to this same leader is uncertain, and nothing more is recorded about him.

Bani was a Levite descended from Asaph, named only in a genealogy in Neh 11:22. He was the son of Hashabiah and the father of Uzzi, who served as overseer of the Levites at Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. The same line traces his ancestry back through Mattaniah and Micha. Since the passage places this family among "the sons of Asaph," the singers who were in charge of the work of the house of God, Bani's household probably belonged to the Temple musicians. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible bear the name Bani, and this one should not be confused with them. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "posterity," while Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "built."

Barabbas was a prisoner held in Jerusalem during the Roman trials of Jesus, about AD 30 by inference from context. Matthew calls him a notable prisoner (Matt 27:16), Mark says he was bound with rebels and had committed murder in an insurrection (Mark 15:7), and John calls him a robber (John 18:40). At the feast, Pilate offered the crowd the release of either Barabbas or Jesus. Persuaded by the chief priests and elders, the crowd demanded Barabbas, and Pilate, wanting to satisfy them, released him and handed Jesus over to be crucified (Matt 27:20–26; Mark 15:11–15; Luke 23:18). His name is Aramaic for "son of the father," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, which also notes that a few ancient manuscripts of Matthew give his name as "Jesus Barabbas." Nothing more is known of him or of the uprising he took part in.

Barachel was a Buzite, of the kindred of Ram, and the father of Elihu, the young man who spoke to Job after Job's three older friends had finished (Job 32:2, 6). He is known only from these two verses, which name him to identify his son. Nothing else is said about his life. His name is usually explained as meaning "God has blessed" (Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary). "Buzite" probably links the family to Buz, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia points to that name and to Ram for comparison. In Gen 22:21 Buz appears as a son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, so the family was probably of Aramean descent. That connection is inferred and is not stated in Job.

Barak was the son of Abinoam, from Kedesh in Naphtali, who led Israel against the Canaanite commander Sisera. The prophet Deborah summoned him and told him the LORD commanded him to gather ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun at Mount Tabor. Barak agreed to go only if Deborah went with him. She went, but said the honor would not be his, because Sisera would fall into the hand of a woman. At her word Barak came down from Tabor, the LORD routed Sisera's chariots and army, and Barak pursued them to Harosheth of the Gentiles. Following Sisera, he found him already dead in the tent of Jael. Deborah and Barak then sang the victory song of Judges 5. Hebrews 11:32 names him among the people of faith. This entry dates the deliverance to about 1278 BC, an estimate inferred from context. His name means "lightning" (Easton's Bible Dictionary).

Bariah was a man of the tribe of Judah, one of the sons of Shemaiah, son of Shechaniah, in the genealogy of David's royal line in 1 Chr 3:22. His brothers were Hattush, Igeal, Neariah and Shaphat. The verse lists five names but gives the total as six, and Easton's Bible Dictionary explains this by counting the father Shemaiah along with his sons. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places him among David's descendants through Solomon. Because the surrounding genealogy follows the royal line after the exile, he probably lived in the post-exilic period, and Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him before about 410 BC. His name is usually taken to mean "fugitive." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Barkos was the ancestor of a family of temple servants, the Nethinim, whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel. The "children of Barkos" appear in the list of returning exiles, between the Nethinim families of Bakbuk-era names and those of Sisera and Tamah (Ezra 2:53; Neh 7:55). That the family belongs to the temple servants is inferred from where the name falls in the list. Nothing else is recorded about Barkos himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the return to about 536 BC, an estimate. The name is often explained as meaning "painter" (Easton's Bible Dictionary) or "party-colored" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), though the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia marks this meaning as uncertain. It also notes that the same family appears as Barchus in 1 Esdras 5:32.

Barnabas was the name the apostles gave to Joses, a Levite from Cyprus. Acts 4:36 explains it as “son of consolation.” An early member of the Jerusalem church, he brought the newly converted Saul to the apostles and vouched for him. Sent by Jerusalem to Antioch, he fetched Saul from Tarsus, carried famine relief to Jerusalem with him, and was listed among Antioch’s prophets and teachers. Set apart with Saul, he went on the first missionary journey (about AD 45, by inference) through Cyprus and Asia Minor. At Lystra the crowd called him Jupiter, and Acts calls him an apostle. He took part in the Jerusalem council, though Paul writes that he was once drawn into other Jews’ insincerity (Gal 2:13). After a sharp dispute with Paul over John Mark, he sailed with Mark to Cyprus. Col 4:10 makes Mark his sister’s son, and this entry follows that reading. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes Mark as his cousin.

event: Barnabas and Saul go to Cyprus
text: Barnabas and Saul go to Cyprus is the opening stage of the First Missionary Journey, dated to about AD 45 by inference from context. Sent out by the Holy Spirit, the two traveled to Seleucia, probably the port serving Syrian Antioch, and sailed to Cyprus. At Salamis on the island's east coast they preached in the Jewish synagogues, with John, identified elsewhere in Acts as John Mark, assisting them. Crossing the island to Paphos, they met a Jewish sorcerer and false prophet named Bar-jesus, also called Elymas, who was attached to the Roman governor Sergius Paulus. The governor wanted to hear their message, but Elymas opposed them and tried to turn him away from the faith. Saul, here first called Paul, denounced Elymas and declared that he would be blind for a time, and he immediately lost his sight. Seeing this, the governor believed.

Barsabas Justus, whose given name was Joseph, was one of two men put forward by the early believers in Jerusalem to replace Judas Iscariot among the twelve apostles (Acts 1:23). He bore two further names: Barsabas, often explained as "son of Sabas" (Smith's Bible Dictionary), and the Latin surname Justus. By inference from the surrounding passage (Acts 1:21–22), he had been among the followers who were with the apostles throughout Jesus' ministry, from John's baptism to the ascension, which made him eligible to serve as a witness of the resurrection. The other candidate was Matthias. After prayer the group cast lots, and the lot fell to Matthias, who was added to the eleven. This episode is set about AD 30, by inference from context. Nothing further is recorded of Joseph Barsabas. He is distinct from Judas Barsabas of Acts 15, though some have suggested the two were related.

Bartholomew was one of the twelve apostles chosen by Jesus. His name appears only in the lists of the Twelve (Matt 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:14) and among the eleven gathered in the upper room in Jerusalem after the ascension (Acts 1:13). As one of the Eleven he was presumably present when Matthias was chosen to replace Judas. The name means "son of Tolmai", so it is probably a family name rather than a personal one. In the first three Gospels he is always paired with Philip, while John's Gospel never mentions him but pairs Philip with Nathanael. For this reason many, including Easton's Bible Dictionary, identify Bartholomew with Nathanael, though the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes this has not been conclusively established. Later traditions, mentioned in Smith's Bible Dictionary, say he preached in India or Armenia.

Bartimaeus, son of Timaeus, was a blind beggar who sat beside the road outside Jericho as Jesus left the city with his disciples and a large crowd (Mark 10:46). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as Aramaic "bar" (son) joined to a Greek or Greek-like "Timaeus", so it may simply mean "son of Timaeus". The verses that follow in Mark (Mark 10:47–52) tell how he called out to Jesus and received his sight. The healing is dated to about AD 30, by inference from context, during Jesus' last journey to Jerusalem. Parallel accounts tell a similar story: Luke 18:35–43 places it as Jesus approached Jericho and does not name the man, and Matt 20:29–34 describes two blind men. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Bartimaeus to be one of those two, while some scholars read the accounts as separate incidents.

Baruch, son of Zabbai, was one of the men who repaired the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah after the return from exile. Neh 3:20 says he "earnestly" repaired a second section of the wall, running from the angle or turning of the wall to the door of the house of Eliashib the high priest. The text gives no further details about him, and he should be kept distinct from other men of the same name, such as Jeremiah's scribe. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the rebuilding to about 446 BC. The name means "blessed." He is probably the same Zabbai's son as no one else named elsewhere, though a Zabbai also appears among those who put away foreign wives in Ezra's time, and whether that man was his father is uncertain.

Baruch was one of the priests who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, when the community that had returned from exile in Babylon pledged to keep the law. His name appears in the list of priests at Neh 10:6, between Ginnethon and the next signatory. The heading of the list at Neh 10:8 identifies these men as priests, and Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the name may stand for a priestly family rather than a single individual. The name means "blessed." Nothing else is recorded about him. He should be kept distinct from other men called Baruch, most notably Jeremiah's scribe and Baruch the son of Zabbai, who repaired part of the wall of Jerusalem.

Baruch was a man of the tribe of Judah, known only from a genealogy in Neh 11:5. He was the son of Col-hozeh and the father of Maaseiah, and his ancestry is traced back through Hazaiah, Adaiah, Joiarib and Zechariah to Shiloni. His son Maaseiah is listed among the people of Judah who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. The surrounding passage suggests that the family belonged to Judah's clan of Perez, and Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both describe Baruch as a descendant of Perez. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including Jeremiah's scribe, and this Baruch should not be confused with them. According to Hitchcock's Bible Names, the name means "blessed."

Baruch son of Neriah, son of Maaseiah, was the scribe and companion of the prophet Jeremiah. During the Babylonian siege, Jeremiah handed him the deeds for the field bought from his cousin Hanameel and told him to keep them safe. In the fourth year of King Jehoiakim, Baruch wrote Jeremiah's prophecies on a scroll as the prophet dictated them. Because Jeremiah was barred from the temple, Baruch read the scroll there, then read it again to the royal officials, who told him and Jeremiah to hide. After the king burned the scroll, Baruch wrote a new, expanded copy. After Jerusalem fell, Jewish leaders accused him of turning Jeremiah against them, and he was taken with the remnant that went to Egypt (Jer 43:7). Jeremiah 45 records a personal message to him. Jer 51:59 names Seraiah son of Neriah, evidently his brother. Several other people in the Bible share his name.

Barzillai was a wealthy, elderly Gileadite from Rogelim, east of the Jordan, who supported King David during Absalom's revolt. When David fled to Mahanaim, Barzillai joined Shobi and Machir in bringing supplies to him and his followers. The text describes him as "a very great man" of eighty who had provided for the king throughout his stay there. After Absalom's defeat, Barzillai escorted David across the Jordan. David invited him to live at his court in Jerusalem, but he declined because of his age. The king kissed and blessed him, and Barzillai returned home. Later verses (2 Sam 19:37–38) show that he sent his son Chimham in his place. On his deathbed David told Solomon to show kindness to Barzillai's sons and let them eat at the royal table. Several men in the Bible share this name. The ISBE notes that the name probably means "man of iron."

Barzillai the Meholathite was the father of Adriel and is mentioned only once, in 2 Sam 21:8. His five grandsons, the sons of Adriel, were among the seven descendants of Saul whom King David handed over to the Gibeonites. The KJV text says Saul's daughter Michal "brought up" these sons for Adriel. Because 1 Sam 18:19 says Saul's daughter Merab was given to Adriel the Meholathite, the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Adriel's wife may have been either Michal or Merab. The STEPBible names index describes the boys as sons Michal adopted. The title "Meholathite" probably means he came from Abel-meholah. He is a different man from the better-known Barzillai the Gileadite, who supported David. The name is usually taken to mean "man of iron."

Barzillai was the ancestor of a priestly family whose descendants returned from the Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel. He married one of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite and took his wife's family name (Ezra 2:61; Neh 7:63). That Gileadite is probably the wealthy elder who supplied David during Absalom's revolt (2 Sam 17:27; 19:31–39). The verses that follow in each list (Ezra 2:62; Neh 7:64) say that this family searched for its genealogical record and could not find it, so its members were excluded from the priesthood as unclean. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that 1 Esdras 5:38 gives his original name as Jaddus (Addus in the King James Version). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "made of iron." Nothing else is known of him, and he should be kept separate from the other men named Barzillai.

Bashan was a fertile region east of the Jordan River, north of Gilead, stretching toward Mount Hermon and east to Salcah. Before Israel arrived it was the kingdom of Og, an Amorite king who lived at Ashtaroth and Edrei. Israel defeated him in battle at Edrei. Moses then gave Bashan to the half-tribe of Manasseh, and it was known as "the land of giants." Its towns included Golan, a city of refuge, the towns of Jair, and the region of Argob with sixty walled cities, which was later one of Solomon's administrative districts. Syria later took Bashan from Israel; the surrounding passage names Hazael as the conqueror. Psalms and the prophets use Bashan as a byword for richness: its strong bulls, fattened cattle, oak forests and pastures. It probably corresponds to the modern Golan Heights and the Hauran plain in southern Syria. The location shown here marks a point within that general area.

Bashemath was a daughter of Ishmael, the son of Abraham, and the sister of Nebajoth. She became one of Esau's wives. Genesis 36 calls her Bashemath, but the earlier narrative in Gen 28:9 calls her Mahalath. That verse says Esau married her in addition to the wives he already had. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that all three of Esau's wives have different names in the Edomite genealogy than in the narrative. Gen 26:34 also mentions a Bashemath who was the daughter of Elon the Hittite. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that name may be a mix-up with Adah or a textual variation. This entry follows the identification of Ishmael's daughter with Mahalath. She bore Esau a son, Reuel, whose sons Nahath, Zerah, Shammah and Mizzah became chiefs ("dukes") in Edom. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of her name as "fragrant" or "pleasing."

Basmath was a daughter of King Solomon and the wife of Ahimaaz, the officer responsible for the district of Naphtali (1 Kgs 4:15). Ahimaaz was one of the twelve district governors who each provided food for the king's household for one month of the year. Her sister Taphath was likewise married to one of these governors, which suggests that Solomon tied some of his officials to the royal family by marriage. Her brother Rehoboam later succeeded Solomon as king. Her name means "fragrant" or "pleasing," according to Smith's Bible Dictionary. She is mentioned only in this one verse. The English spelling Basemath is shared with a wife of Esau, but they are different women. It is uncertain whether her husband is the same Ahimaaz who was the son of the priest Zadok.

Bath-rabbim was a gate of the city of Heshbon, mentioned once in the Bible. In Song 7:4 the beloved's eyes are compared to "the fishpools in Heshbon, by the gate of Bath-rabbim," so pools apparently lay near this gate. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both take it as one of Heshbon's gates and give the meaning of the name as "daughter of many." That may refer to the crowds who passed through it, though this is only an inference from the meaning. Heshbon lay east of the Jordan, and it is generally identified with the modern site of Hesban in Jordan, southwest of Amman. The location shown here places the gate within that city. The exact position of the gate itself is unknown.

Bathsheba, also called Bath-shua, was the daughter of Eliam and the wife of Uriah the Hittite when King David asked who she was (2 Sam 11:3). The surrounding chapter tells how David lay with her, had Uriah killed in battle and then married her. Their first child died. She later bore Solomon (2 Sam 12:24), and 1 Chr 3:5 lists four sons born to her in Jerusalem: Shimea (Shammua), Shobab, Nathan and Solomon. That verse calls her father Ammiel, which Easton's Bible Dictionary treats as another name for Eliam. When David's son Adonijah claimed the throne, the prophet Nathan urged her to go to the aged king, and she secured David's promise that Solomon would succeed him. As queen mother she sat at Solomon's right hand and brought him Adonijah's request to marry Abishag. Matt 1:6 names her, as Uriah's former wife, in the genealogy of Jesus.

Bavai, son of Henadad, was ruler of half the district of Keilah in Nehemiah's day and helped rebuild the walls of Jerusalem. He is named only in Neh 3:18, which says he repaired a section of the wall after "their brethren," probably the Levites named in the verse before. Keilah was a town in the lowlands of Judah, so Bavai seems to have led workers from his own district. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this work to about 446 BC. Later in the same chapter, Neh 3:24 names another son of Henadad, Binnui, who repaired a different section. Some readers take Bavai and Binnui as two forms of one name. The usual reading treats them as brothers, and this entry follows that view.

Bazluth was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants returned from the Babylonian exile to Judah. His name appears only in the parallel lists of returning exiles, where "the children of Bazluth" are named between other servant families such as those of Mehida and Harsha (Ezra 2:52). Nehemiah's version of the same list spells the name Bazlith (Neh 7:54). Smith's Bible Dictionary places this return with Zerubbabel in about 536 BC, a date inferred from context. The surrounding lists suggest that these families served at the temple. Nothing is recorded about Bazluth himself beyond his name, and the text does not say when he lived.

Bealiah was one of the warriors who came to David at Ziklag while David was still in hiding from Saul. He is named only once, in a list of these men (1 Chr 12:5). The surrounding passage describes them as relatives of Saul from the tribe of Benjamin, men armed with bows who could sling stones and shoot arrows with either the right or the left hand. Easton's Bible Dictionary counts him among David's warriors of the sling and bow. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explain his name as meaning "the LORD (Yahweh) is Lord." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Bealoth was a town in the far south of Judah, in the Negeb. It appears only in the list of cities given to the tribe of Judah, between Ziph and Telem (Josh 15:24). Nothing else is said about it there. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it was probably the same place as Baalath-beer, a town assigned to Simeon within Judah's territory (Josh 19:8). The name is shared by other places. In 1 Kgs 4:16, where the King James Version reads "in Aloth," the Revised Version reads "Bealoth," a district that may be a separate location. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the Judahite town as unidentified. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the southern Judean region, matching its listing among the Negeb towns. The name's meaning is uncertain: Easton's gives "citizens," Smith's Bible Dictionary "ladies."

Bealoth was a place in northern Israel named in the list of Solomon's twelve district officers, who each supplied food for the royal household for one month of the year. Baanah son of Hushai governed the district of Asher together with Bealoth (1 Kgs 4:16). The King James Version reads "in Aloth" here, while the Revised Version reads "Bealoth," as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes. Nothing more is said about it, and its exact site is unknown. Because it is paired with Asher, it was probably in or near Asher's territory in western Galilee, and the location shown here is a rough placement in that area. This entry is distinct from the town of Bealoth in the far south of Judah (Josh 15:24), which Easton's Bible Dictionary treats as probably the same as Baalath-beer. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "cast under."

The Bearing Cross to Golgotha was the procession in which Jesus was led out from his Roman trials to the place of crucifixion, about AD 30 by inference from context. John says Jesus went out carrying his own cross. Matthew, Mark and Luke record that the soldiers compelled Simon of Cyrene, a man coming in from the country and, Mark notes, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry it behind him. Luke adds that a large crowd followed, including women mourning him. Jesus turned and told these "daughters of Jerusalem" to weep for themselves and their children because of coming days of distress. Two criminals were led out with him to be executed. At Golgotha, meaning "the place of a skull," he was offered wine mixed with gall or myrrh, which he tasted but refused.

The Beautiful Gate was a gate of the temple in Jerusalem. A man who had been lame from birth was carried there every day to beg for alms from people entering the temple (Acts 3:2). Peter and John met him there and he was healed. Afterward the people recognized him as the beggar who used to sit at the Beautiful Gate, and they were amazed (Acts 3:10). The event is dated about AD 30, by inference from context. Its exact position in the temple complex is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes the common view that it led from the Court of the Gentiles into the Court of the Women, and that it was a massive gate covered with plates of Corinthian brass. Others have placed it at an outer entrance to the temple. The location shown here is a point within the temple area rather than a precise identification.

Bebai was the ancestor and head of an Israelite family whose descendants returned to Jerusalem from exile in Babylon. The list of returnees in Ezra 2:11 counts the "children of Bebai" as 623, while the parallel list in Neh 7:16 gives 628. The difference is a variation between the two copies of the same register. Later, four men of this family, Jehohanan, Hananiah, Zabbai and Athlai, are named among those who had married foreign wives and agreed to put them away during Ezra's reforms (Ezra 10:28). Ezra 8:11 also names a Zechariah son of Bebai, who led another group back with Ezra, and the name appears among those who sealed the covenant in Neh 10:15. Bebai himself is known only through his descendants. The name is shared by more than one person, and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "fatherly."

Bebai was the father, or more likely the ancestor, of Zechariah, who led twenty-eight men of the family of Bebai back to Jerusalem with Ezra (Ezra 8:11). The verse speaks of "the sons of Bebai," so the name probably refers to the founder of a family clan rather than Zechariah's immediate father. STEPBible Proper Names describes Zechariah as a descendant of Bebai. A family group called the children of Bebai also appears among those who returned from exile earlier, as recorded in Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7. Nothing else is known about Bebai himself. The name is shared by several people in the Bible, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "void, empty."

Bebai was one of the leaders of the people who put their seal to the written covenant made in Nehemiah's time, in which the community in Jerusalem pledged to keep the law of Moses (Neh 10:15). He appears in a list of the chiefs of the people, between Azgad and Hodijah. Many names in this list, Bebai among them, match the family groups that returned from exile in Babylon (Ezra 2:11 counts a large group as the descendants of Bebai). So he probably signed as the head or representative of that family rather than only as an individual. Nothing else is recorded about him, and the name is shared by several people in the Bible. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of the name as "fatherly," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "void, empty."

Becher was a son of Benjamin, the youngest son of Jacob. He appears second in the list of Benjamin's sons in Gen 46:21, among the family who went down to Egypt with Jacob, and again in 1 Chr 7:6, where Benjamin's sons are given as Bela, Becher and Jediael. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that he is left out of the list in 1 Chr 8:1, and the clan list of Benjamin in Numbers 26 also does not name him. 1 Chr 7:8 names his nine sons: Zemira, Joash, Eliezer, Elioenai, Omri, Jerimoth, Abiah, Anathoth and Alameth. Anathoth and Alameth are also the names of Benjamite towns, which suggests that some of these names may stand for family settlements. The name, meaning "firstborn" or "young camel," is shared by others, including an Ephraimite in Num 26:35.

Becher was a son of Ephraim and the ancestor of an Ephraimite clan called the Bachrites (or Becherites). He appears in the census of Israel taken in the plains of Moab, where Num 26:35 lists him between his brothers Shuthelah and Tahan as the head of one of Ephraim's families. His other brothers, Ezer, Elead and Beriah, are named in the Ephraimite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:20–23. That genealogy does not name Becher, and Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both take him to be the Bered it lists there. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "first begotten" or "first fruits." The name is shared with others, notably a son of Benjamin (Gen 46:21), and this entry refers only to the Ephraimite.

Bechorath was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only in the genealogy of Kish in 1 Sam 9:1. He was the son of Aphiah and the father of Zeror, which makes him the great-great-grandfather of Kish. Since the next verse introduces Kish's son Saul, Bechorath was an ancestor of King Saul. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "first-born," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "first fruits." Smith's also links him with Becher, a son of Benjamin listed in 1 Chr 7:8, and treats Bechorath as Becher's grandson. That connection is not stated in the passage itself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia spells the name Becorath.

Bedad was the father of Hadad, one of the kings who ruled Edom before Israel had a king. He is known only from the list of Edomite kings in Gen 36:35 and its parallel in 1 Chr 1:46. Both passages say that Hadad succeeded Husham, defeated Midian in the territory of Moab, and ruled from a city called Avith. Nothing is recorded about Bedad himself, and the text does not say whether he was a king. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Hitchcock's Bible Names give the meaning of his name as "alone" or "solitary." Smith's Bible Dictionary places him sometime before 1093 BC, an estimate drawn from the chronology of the passage.

Bedan is a deliverer of Israel named by Samuel in his farewell speech, listed with Jerubbaal (Gideon), Jephthah and Samuel himself as leaders the LORD sent to rescue the people from their enemies (1 Sam 12:11). His name may mean "son of judgment." No judge called Bedan appears in the Book of Judges, so who he was is uncertain. The Septuagint, Syriac and Arabic versions read "Barak" here, and the Aramaic paraphrase reads "Samson" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). Easton's Bible Dictionary considers it most likely a shortened form of Abdon, the judge in Judg 12:13. This entry does not settle on any one of these identifications. The name is also borne by a different man, a descendant of Manasseh.

Bedan was a man of the tribe of Manasseh, named as the son of Ulam in the genealogy of 1 Chr 7:17. That verse ends by counting this family among the descendants of Gilead, the son of Machir, the son of Manasseh, so Bedan belonged to the Gileadite clans of the half-tribe descended from Joseph's son Manasseh. The preceding verse (1 Chr 7:16) makes Ulam a son of Peresh, whose mother was Maachah, Machir's wife. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "son of judgment." The name is also used of a different figure in 1 Sam 12:11, one of the deliverers of Israel named by Samuel, who is not the same man.

Bedeiah was an Israelite named in the list of men in Ezra's time who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:35). The list groups names by family. By inference from the context of Ezra 10:34, he belonged to the descendants of Bani, as Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both note. The surrounding chapter records that these men agreed to send away their foreign wives during the reforms led by Ezra after the return from exile. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 458 BC, an estimate inferred from context. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains his name as meaning "servant of Yah." Nothing else is known about him.

Beer was a stopping place of the Israelites on their journey through the region east of the Dead Sea, shortly before they entered Amorite territory. Its name means "a well," and Num 21:16 identifies it as the well where the LORD told Moses to gather the people so he could give them water. The following verses record a song the people sang there, praising a well dug by their princes and nobles with their staves. Easton's Bible Dictionary counts it as the forty-fourth station of the wanderings, in the wilderness of Moab, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it north of the Arnon River. The site has not been identified, and the location shown here is only a rough placement in that general region. The name is also used for at least one other place in the Bible, such as the town to which Jotham fled in Judg 9:21.

Beer was the town where Jotham, the youngest son of Gideon, fled and settled out of fear of his brother Abimelech (Judg 9:21). Abimelech had killed Gideon's other sons, and Jotham had just denounced him with a parable spoken from Mount Gerizim. The name means "a well" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), and several places in the Bible share it, including a well-station on Israel's wilderness route. The text gives no detail about this town's location. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both note that it may be the same place as Beeroth. The location shown here follows that identification and places it at Beeroth, probably near modern el-Bireh, north of Jerusalem. The site is uncertain because the passage itself names nothing nearby.

Beer-elim was a place in or on the border of Moab, named only once, in Isaiah's oracle against Moab, where the wailing of Moab is said to reach as far as Eglaim and Beer-elim (Isa 15:8). The name means "well of heroes" or "well of Elim" (Hitchcock's Bible Names suggests "well of rains"). The pairing with Eglaim suggests two places at opposite edges of Moab, so the verse probably pictures mourning across the whole land. Its site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary connect it with Beer, the well dug by Israel's leaders in Num 21:16. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it in northern Moab, opposite Eglaim in the south, and treats the link with Beer as possible but not certain. The location shown here is only approximate, in southern Moab, and does not settle the question.

Beer-lahai-roi was a well in the wilderness of the Negev, the dry south country of Canaan. Its name is usually explained as "well of the Living One who sees me." Genesis 16:7–14 presents it as the spring where the angel of the Lord met Hagar as she fled from Sarah, and places it between Kadesh and Bered on the way to Shur. Isaac was coming from this well when Rebekah first arrived to marry him, since he was living in the south (Gen 24:62). After Abraham's death, Isaac settled beside it (Gen 25:11). The exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mention its identification with 'Ain Muweileh (Moilahi), southwest of Beersheba and about 12 miles west of Kadesh-barnea. The location shown here follows that identification.

Beera was a man of the tribe of Asher, named as a son of Zophah in the tribal genealogy of 1 Chr 7:37. He is the last of the sons listed there. His brothers in the same list include Bezer, Hod, Shamma, Shilshah and Ithran, along with Suah, Harnepher, Beri, Imrah and Ulla. Jether, also counted here among his brothers, is probably the same person as the Ithran named in this verse, since the two forms of the name are closely related. Nothing else is recorded about Beera beyond his place in the genealogy. According to Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names, his name means "a well." He should not be confused with Beerah, a Reubenite leader taken captive by the Assyrians, whose name is spelled differently in English.

Beerah was a prince, or leader, of the tribe of Reuben. He was the son of Baal and appears in the Reubenite genealogy of 1 Chr 5. Tilgath-pilneser (Tiglath-pileser III), king of Assyria, carried him away captive (1 Chr 5:6). That places him in the eighth century BC, when Assyria conquered the Israelite territories east of the Jordan and deported their people. 2 Kgs 15:29 describes Tiglath-pileser taking Gilead and carrying its inhabitants to Assyria, and 1 Chr 5:26 names the Reubenites among those deported. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his captivity to about 738 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "expounder." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Beeri was a Hittite, the father of Judith, whom Esau married at the age of forty along with Basemath the daughter of Elon (Gen 26:34). The name is shared by several people in the Bible, and this Beeri is mentioned only in this one verse. The later list of Esau's wives in Gen 36:2–3 gives different names, and harmonizers have tried to match the two lists in different ways. One common reconciliation, which Smith's Bible Dictionary points to and this entry follows, takes Judith to be the same woman as Aholibamah and links Beeri with Anah, whom that list names as Aholibamah's parent. This is why Aholibamah is shown here as his daughter and Anah is connected with him. Easton's Bible Dictionary instead identifies Judith with Adah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "my well."

Beeri was the father of the prophet Hosea and is known only from the opening verse of the book of Hosea (Hos 1:1). That verse dates Hosea's prophetic work to the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel. By inference, Beeri lived in the eighth century BC; Smith's Bible Dictionary places him before 725 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him. Another man named Beeri, a Hittite and the father of Esau's wife Judith, appears in Genesis, and this one should not be confused with him. The name is usually connected with the Hebrew word for "well." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "my well," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "expounder."

Beeroth, whose name means "wells," was a city north of Jerusalem. It was one of four cities, with Gibeon, Chephirah and Kirjath-jearim, whose people made a peace treaty with Joshua after Israel's arrival. The wider passage identifies them as Hivites who won the treaty by deception (Josh 9:17). The city was later assigned to the tribe of Benjamin (Josh 18:25; 2 Sam 4:2). It was the home of Rimmon, whose sons Baanah and Rechab served as captains under Saul's son Ish-bosheth, and of Naharai, armourbearer to Joab (2 Sam 23:37). Men of Beeroth were among the exiles who returned from Babylon (Ezra 2:25; Neh 7:29). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with el-Bireh, about 10 miles north of Jerusalem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests a site northwest of Gibeon instead. The location shown here follows the el-Bireh identification.

Beeroth Bene-jaakan, meaning "the wells of the children of Jaakan," was a desert campsite of the Israelites during their wilderness journey. Deut 10:6 says they moved from there to Mosera, where Aaron died and was buried and his son Eleazar took over as priest. Easton's Bible Dictionary treats it as the same place as Bene-jaakan in Num 33:31. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Numbers places this camp after Moseroth, while Deuteronomy places it before Mosera. The Jaakan clan may be the Horite family of Seir listed in 1 Chr 1:42, which would place the wells near Edom, though this is an inference. The exact site is unknown. The rough location shown here is in the hills near Petra, close to Jebel Harun, which tradition identifies as Mount Hor, where Num 20 says Aaron died.

Beersheba was a city in the far south of Israel. Genesis explains the name as "well of the oath", recalling the covenant Abraham and Abimelech swore there (Gen 21:31–32). A second account links the name to a well dug by Isaac's servants (Gen 26:33). Abraham planted a grove, worshipped and lived there (Gen 21:33; 22:19). Jacob set out from it for Haran, and later offered sacrifices there before going down to Egypt (Gen 28:10; 46:1). It was allotted to Judah and to Simeon (Josh 15:28; 19:2). It marked the southern limit of the land in the phrase "from Dan even to Beersheba" (Judg 20:1). Samuel's sons judged there, Elijah fled there, and Amos named it alongside the shrines of Bethel and Gilgal (1 Sam 8:2; 1 Kgs 19:3; Amos 5:5). It was resettled after the exile (Neh 11:27). The location shown here follows the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia's identification with Tell es-Seba, east of the modern city.

Beeshterah was a Levitical city in Bashan, east of the Jordan. Joshua 21:27 lists it with Golan as one of two towns, each with its surrounding pasturelands, given to the Gershonite families of the Levites from the half tribe of Manasseh that settled beyond the Jordan. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as "house of Ashterah" and identifies it with Ashtaroth. That identification rests on the parallel list in 1 Chr 6:71, which names Golan and Ashtaroth as the Gershonite cities from eastern Manasseh. Beeshterah is probably a contracted form of Be-Ashtaroth. Ashtaroth is usually placed at Tell Ashtarah in southern Syria, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Bela was an older name for the city of Zoar, one of the five cities of the plain near the Dead Sea. Genesis explains the name as it goes: "Bela, which is Zoar" (Gen 14:2, 8). Its king, who is not named, joined the kings of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim against an alliance of four eastern kings, and they fought in the vale of Siddim. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both note that later in Genesis this city, as Zoar, was the only one of the five spared when the others were destroyed, because Lot asked to flee there (Gen 19:20–23). Its exact site is uncertain. Some scholars place the cities of the plain north of the Dead Sea, others to its south. The location shown here follows the southern view, placing Zoar southeast of the Dead Sea in the area of the modern Ghor es-Safi in Jordan.

Bela son of Beor was a king of Edom, the first named in the list of kings who reigned in Edom before any king reigned over the Israelites. His city was Dinhabah, a place not otherwise identified. When Bela died, Jobab son of Zerah of Bozrah succeeded him. The same brief account appears in Gen 36:32–33 and 1 Chr 1:43–44. Smith's Bible Dictionary places his reign about eight generations before Saul. Because his father shares the name Beor with the father of Balaam, some interpreters have linked the two, but the text makes no such connection. Several other people in the Bible are also named Bela, and this king should not be confused with them.

Bela was a man of the tribe of Reuben, the son of Azaz, son of Shema, son of Joel. He appears only once, in the Reubenite genealogy of 1 Chr 5:8. That verse says he lived in Aroer and that his people's territory reached as far as Nebo and Baal-meon, towns east of the Jordan in the region north of the Arnon River. The following verses, read in context, describe his family spreading eastward toward the Euphrates because their livestock had multiplied in Gilead. His tie to Reuben comes from the surrounding genealogy, though the exact link between Joel and Reuben's sons is not spelled out. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls his father Ahaz rather than Azaz. Several other men in the Bible share the name Bela, including a king of Edom and a son of Benjamin. This Bela should be kept distinct from them.

Bela, also spelled Belah, was the firstborn son of Benjamin and the head of the Belaite clan within the tribe of Benjamin. He appears among the family of Jacob that went down to Egypt, and in the census lists of Benjamin's clans. The lists of his sons differ. Num 26:40 gives Ard and Naaman. 1 Chr 7:7 names Ezbon, Uzzi, Uzziel, Jerimoth and Iri, heads of families with 22,034 fighting men. 1 Chr 8:3 begins another list with Addar, Gera and Abihud. Some of these names, such as Ard, Gera and Naaman, also appear as Benjamin's own sons in Gen 46:21. This probably reflects later clan groupings recorded as descendants of Bela, though the passages do not explain it. Several other people in the Bible share the name Bela.

The Believers pray for boldness is the prayer of the early Jerusalem church after Peter and John were released by the Jewish council. The two apostles returned to their companions and reported the threats of the chief priests and elders. The group then prayed together to God as the maker of heaven, earth and sea. They quoted David's words from Psalm 2 about nations raging and rulers gathering against the Lord and his anointed. They applied these words to Herod, Pontius Pilate, the Gentiles and the people of Israel, who had come together against Jesus. Rather than asking for protection, they asked God to notice the threats and to give his servants boldness to speak his word, while he healed and worked signs and wonders through the name of Jesus. When they finished, the meeting place shook, all were filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spoke God's word boldly. By inference from context, this was about AD 30.

The Believers share all things episode describes the common life of the early church in Jerusalem, set about AD 30 by inference from context, following the believers' prayer for boldness. The whole body of believers was united in heart and mind. No one claimed private ownership of possessions; they held everything in common. The apostles continued to testify powerfully to the resurrection of Jesus. No one among them was in need, because owners of land or houses sold them and laid the proceeds at the apostles' feet, and the money was distributed to each person as needed. As an example, the passage names Joseph (Joses), a Levite from Cyprus whom the apostles called Barnabas, meaning "son of consolation." He sold a field and brought the money to the apostles. The account that follows in Acts 5 contrasts his gift with the deceptive gift of Ananias and Sapphira.
