Belshazzar was king of Babylon, called king of the Chaldeans, in the book of Daniel. He held a great feast for a thousand of his lords. While drinking, he ordered the gold and silver vessels that Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the temple in Jerusalem to be brought so that he, his nobles, wives and concubines could drink from them (Dan 5:1–2). According to the same chapter, a hand then wrote on the wall, and the king was badly shaken (Dan 5:9). Daniel interpreted the writing and rebuked him for not humbling himself. Belshazzar rewarded Daniel with scarlet clothing, a gold chain and the rank of third ruler in the kingdom, and was killed that same night. Daniel dates two visions to his first and third years. Daniel calls Nebuchadnezzar his father, which Smith's Bible Dictionary takes to mean ancestor. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Babylonian inscriptions make him the eldest son of Nabonidus, probably ruling alongside his father.

Ben was a Levite named in 1 Chr 15:18 among the musicians and gatekeepers of the "second degree" whom the Levite leaders appointed at David's command when the ark of the covenant was brought up to Jerusalem. His name means "son." He appears in a list alongside Zechariah, Jaaziel, Obed-edom and others, and nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the text here may be uncertain, because the name is missing when the same group is listed again in 1 Chr 15:20 and does not appear in the Septuagint. On that reading, "Ben" may be part of a neighboring name rather than a separate person. This entry treats him as the individual Levite named in the verse.

Ben-ammi was the son of Lot and Lot's younger daughter, and the ancestor of the Ammonites (Gen 19:38). According to the surrounding account in Genesis 19, after Sodom was destroyed Lot lived in a cave with his two daughters. Believing no man was left to marry them, the daughters made their father drunk and each conceived a child by him. The older daughter's son was Moab, so Moab was both Ben-ammi's half-brother and his cousin. The name is usually explained as "son of my people" (Hitchcock's Bible Names, Smith's Bible Dictionary) or "son of my kinsman" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Genesis says he is "the father of the children of Ammon unto this day." The nation descended from him, Ammon, appears later in Ps 83:7 among the peoples allied against Israel, though Ben-ammi himself is named only once.

Ben-hadad, son of Tabrimon and grandson of Hezion, was a king of Syria who ruled from Damascus. Asa king of Judah sent him silver and gold from the temple and palace treasuries, and Ben-hadad responded by attacking northern Israel, striking Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maachah and the land of Naphtali. The accounts that follow describe a Ben-hadad who, with thirty-two allied kings, besieged Ahab in Samaria and demanded his wealth and family. He was drinking in his tents when Israel's forces routed his army, and he escaped on horseback. A year later he was defeated at Aphek, surrendered, and made a treaty with Ahab, promising to return captured cities. The name means "son of Hadad," a Syrian god, and several kings bore it. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes Ahab's opponent to be a later Ben-hadad, probably this king's son. This entry treats all these passages as one man.

Ben-hadad was a king of Syria (Aram) who ruled from Damascus in the time of the prophet Elisha. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him Ben-hadad II, son of an earlier Ben-hadad. The name means "son of Hadad" and was borne by several Syrian kings. He gathered his whole army and besieged Samaria, Israel's capital (2 Kgs 6:24). The account that follows tells of a severe famine in the city and the sudden overnight flight of the Syrian camp (2 Kgs 7). Later, when Elisha came to Damascus, Ben-hadad was ill. He sent his officer Hazael with a gift of forty camel-loads to ask whether he would recover (2 Kgs 8:7–9). The next day he was smothered with a wet cloth, and Hazael took the throne (2 Kgs 8:15). Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Hazael as the killer, while Smith's allows it may have been his servants. Both estimate a reign of about thirty years.

Ben-hadad, son of Hazael, was a king of Syria (Aram), ruling from Damascus. He is often called Ben-hadad III to set him apart from earlier kings of the same name. He succeeded his father on the throne (2 Kgs 13:24). Together with Hazael he is named as an oppressor of Israel (2 Kgs 13:3). After Hazael's death, Jehoash son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel, defeated Ben-hadad three times and recovered the Israelite cities that Syria had taken from his father Jehoahaz (2 Kgs 13:25). The prophet Amos announced fire on the house of Hazael that would consume "the palaces of Benhadad" (Amos 1:4). Easton's Bible Dictionary takes this as a reference to his defeats in war. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "son of Hadad," Hadad being a Syrian god.

Ben-hanan was a son of Shimon, named in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chr 4:20. His brothers were Amnon, Rinnah and Tilon. The verse belongs to a list of Judah's descendants, but Shimon's own link to the main family line is not stated, so his exact place in the tribe is unclear. Nothing else is recorded about Ben-hanan, and this is the only verse that mentions him. His name means "son of grace" or "son of the gracious one," according to Hitchcock's Bible Names and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia.

Ben-zoheth was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles as a son of Ishi and brother of Zoheth (1 Chr 4:20). His name means "son of Zoheth." Smith's Bible Dictionary reads it that way, which could suggest he was Zoheth's son and so Ishi's grandsonsuggested. The verse itself lists both Zoheth and Ben-zoheth among the sons of Ishi, and this entry follows that reading, as does the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "son of separation." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Benaiah son of Jehoiada was one of David's leading warriors and later commander of Solomon's army. Several other men in the Bible share his name. He came from Kabzeel. His recorded feats include killing two champion warriors of Moab and a lion in a pit on a snowy day, which made him famous among David's mighty men (2 Sam 23:20–22). David put him over the Cherethites and Pelethites, the royal bodyguard. He also commanded the army division that served in the third month, with his son Ammizabad in his division. 1 Chr 27:5 calls either him or his father a chief priest; Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries apply the title to Jehoiada. Benaiah did not side with Adonijah, and he helped bring Solomon to Gihon to be made king. On Solomon's orders he put to death Adonijah, Joab and Shimei, then replaced Joab as head of the army. Adonijah and Shimei are identified from the surrounding narrative.

Benaiah the Pirathonite was one of David's thirty mighty warriors, listed among them in 2 Sam 23:30 and 1 Chr 11:31. His title connects him with Pirathon, a town in the hill country of Ephraim that was also the home of the judge Abdon (Judg 12:13–15), and 1 Chr 27:14 confirms he was an Ephraimite. He commanded the division that served the king in the eleventh month of the year, a force of 24,000 men. His name means "the Lord has built" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). He should not be confused with the better-known Benaiah son of Jehoiada, the commander of David's bodyguard, who is listed separately among the mighty men. Several other men in the Bible also share the name.

Benaiah was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named in a list of Simeonite clan leaders in 1 Chr 4:36. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of the "princes" of the families of Simeon. By inference from the surrounding passage (1 Chr 4:38–41), these leaders' families grew large, and in the days of Hezekiah, king of Judah, they moved toward Gedor in search of pasture and attacked the people living there, including the Meunim. STEPBible's proper names index follows this reading and places Benaiah among the men who took part. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name is usually explained as "the Lord has built" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Bible share this name, including David's commander Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and this Simeonite should be kept distinct from them.

Benaiah was a Levite in David's time who took part in bringing the ark of God to Jerusalem. He is listed among the Levites of the second rank, alongside the gatekeepers (1 Chr 15:18), and among those who played psalteries "on Alamoth," a musical term of uncertain meaning, possibly a high register (1 Chr 15:20; 16:5). A Benaiah is also named among the priests who blew trumpets before the ark and who were afterward assigned to sound them there continually (1 Chr 15:24; 16:6). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat the Levite musician and the priestly trumpeter as two different men. This entry brings these mentions together under one name. The name means "the Lord has built." Several other men in the Bible share it.

Benaiah was the father of Jehoiada, who is named in 1 Chr 27:34 as one of King David's counselors, following Ahithophel in that role. Nothing else is said about Benaiah himself. This Benaiah is one of several men with the name, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains as "Yahweh has built." That dictionary links this entry to the better-known Benaiah son of Jehoiada, the commander of David's bodyguard. This suggests that the father and son may be the same family, with the names possibly appearing in reverse order here. Following the verse as written, this entry treats Benaiah as Jehoiada's father.

Benaiah was a Levite of the family of Asaph, known only from a genealogy in 2 Chr 20:14. He was the son of Jeiel and the father of Zechariah, which made him the grandfather of Jahaziel, the Levite on whom the Spirit of the LORD came in the assembly during the reign of King Jehoshaphat. The line continues back through Jeiel to Mattaniah. Nothing else is recorded about him, and since he is listed two generations before Jahaziel, he probably lived somewhat earlier than Jehoshaphat's time. Several other men in the Bible share the name Benaiah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives its meaning as "Yahweh has built."

Benaiah was a Levite in the time of King Hezekiah of Judah, called a Levite in Smith's Bible Dictionary. He was one of ten overseers who served under Cononiah and his brother Shimei, by order of Hezekiah and Azariah, the ruler of the house of God (2 Chr 31:13). The surrounding passage shows that Cononiah and Shimei were in charge of the offerings, tithes and dedicated gifts brought into storerooms prepared in the temple. Benaiah and the other overseers probably helped manage these stores for the priests and Levites. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with several other men of the same name in the Bible. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "made by the Lord," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "son of the Lord."

Benaiah was a man of Israel, a descendant of Parosh, named in the list of those who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra (Ezra 10:25). By inference from the surrounding chapter, he lived among the Jews who had returned from exile in Babylon, and he was among those who agreed to send away their foreign wives when Ezra led the community in a reform. He appears in the part of the list covering ordinary Israelites rather than priests, Levites, singers or gatekeepers. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Benaiah, including others in the same list, and this one should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "son of the Lord."

Benaiah was a man descended from Pahath-moab who is listed in Ezra 10:30 among the Israelites of the returned community who had married foreign wives. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was one of those who agreed to send away these wives during the reforms led by Ezra after the return from exile. He is known only from this list, and nothing else is recorded about him. The name Benaiah is shared by several other men in the Bible, including more than one in this same chapter of Ezra, so he should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "son of the Lord."

Benaiah was one of the men listed in Ezra 10 who had married foreign wives during Ezra's reforms after the return from exile. He appears only in Ezra 10:35. By inference from the surrounding verses, he belonged to the descendants of Bani (Ezra 10:34), and he was among those who agreed to send away their foreign wives and children (Ezra 10:44). Nothing else is known about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and he should not be confused with them, including other Benaiahs in the same list. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "son of the Lord."

Benaiah was one of the descendants of Nebo named in Ezra's list of Israelite men who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:43). By inference from the surrounding chapter, this was in the time after the return from exile in Babylon, when Ezra led the community to separate from such marriages, and those named agreed to send their wives away. The list says nothing more about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a well-known commander under David and Solomon, but nothing in the text links this Benaiah to any of them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "son of the Lord."

Benaiah was the father of Pelatiah, one of the leaders of the people in Jerusalem whom the prophet Ezekiel saw in a vision. In that vision Ezekiel was brought to the east gate of the temple, where twenty-five men were gathered, among them "Pelatiah the son of Benaiah" and Jaazaniah son of Azur, described as princes of the people (Ezek 11:1). As Ezekiel prophesied against these men, Pelatiah died, and the prophet cried out in distress (Ezek 11:13). Benaiah himself is known only as Pelatiah's father, and nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share his name, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders as "Yahweh has built." He is probably distinct from the others, though the text does not say so directly.

Bene-berak was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Dan, listed with Jehud and Gath-rimmon in Josh 19:45. This is its only mention in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of the name as "sons of lightning." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with the village of Ibn Ibraq, about an hour's journey southeast of Jaffa. The location shown here is in the coastal plain east of modern Tel Aviv, near the present-day city of Bnei Brak, which takes its name from the biblical town. This fits that general area, since Jehud and Gath-rimmon, the towns named with it, also belong to the coastal part of Dan's inheritance.

Bene-jaakan was a camp of the Israelites during their wilderness journey, reached after leaving Moseroth and followed by Hor-hagidgad (Num 33:31–32). The name means "sons of Jaakan," and Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it as a tribe whose name was attached to certain desert wells. Deut 10:6 calls the place Beeroth of the children of Jaakan, "the wells of the sons of Jaakan." Easton's Bible Dictionary treats the two names as one place. That passage places it before Mosera rather than after, so the camp may have been visited more than once or the route recorded differently. Jaakan is probably the descendant of Seir the Horite named in Gen 36:27 (as Akan) and 1 Chr 1:42, which would place the site near Edom. The exact site is unknown. The location shown here is a rough placement east of the Arabah, in the region of Edom.

Benhail was one of the princes, or officials, of Judah whom King Jehoshaphat sent out in the third year of his reign to teach in the cities of Judah (2 Chr 17:7). He is named alongside Obadiah, Zechariah, Nethaneel and Michaiah. By inference from the following verses, these princes travelled with a group of Levites and priests, taking the book of the law of the Lord with them. STEPBible's proper-names index describes Benhail as a Levite, while the verse itself counts him among the king's princes. His name is usually explained as meaning "son of strength" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia; Hitchcock's Bible Names), and Smith's Bible Dictionary also gives "son of the host." He is mentioned nowhere else in the Bible.

Beninu was a Levite named among those who set their seal to the written covenant made in the time of Nehemiah, after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears only once, in the list of Levite signatories, between Hodijah and Bani (Neh 10:13). That he was a Levite comes from the context of the list, which in Neh 10:9 begins naming the Levites who sealed the agreement. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both explain the name as meaning "our son." Nothing else is recorded about his family or his life.

Benjamin was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 7:10 as one of the seven sons of Bilhan. His brothers were Jeush, Ehud, Chenaanah, Zethan, Tharshish and Ahishahar. Bilhan was a son of Jediael, and the surrounding passage traces Jediael back to the patriarch Benjamin (1 Chr 7:6), so this man carried the name of his tribe's ancestor. The following verse (1 Chr 7:11) describes these descendants of Jediael as heads of their fathers' houses and men of valor, and Smith's Bible Dictionary accordingly calls him the head of a family of warriors. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with the patriarch Benjamin, Jacob's youngest son, or with other men of the same name. The name means "son of the right hand," according to Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Benjamin was an Israelite in the time of Ezra, listed among the men who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:32). He appears alongside Malluch and Shemariah in a group that, by the surrounding passage, belonged to the "sons of Harim" (Ezra 10:31), as Smith's Bible Dictionary also notes. The context of Ezra 10 shows that these men agreed to send away their foreign wives during Ezra's reforms after the return from exile. Nothing more is recorded about him. He is distinct from the more famous Benjamin, the youngest son of Jacob, and from other men of the same name. The name is usually explained as meaning "son of the right hand" (Hitchcock's Bible Names).

Benjamin was a man of Jerusalem who, together with Hashub, repaired a section of the city wall opposite their house during the rebuilding led by Nehemiah after the return from exile (Neh 3:23). The next section was repaired by Azariah son of Maaseiah. Nothing more is said about his family or background. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as meaning "son of the right hand," is shared by several people in the Bible, most famously Jacob's youngest son. A Benjamin is also named among those who took part in the dedication of the rebuilt wall (Neh 12:34), and he may be the same man, though the text does not say so.

Benjamin was one of the men named among those who took part in the procession at the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time (Neh 12:34). He appears in a list with Judah, Shemaiah and Jeremiah, in the company that walked along the wall behind Hoshaiah and half the leaders of Judah. The surrounding passage places the list just before the priests' sons with trumpets, and STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) identifies him as a priest, the view this entry follows. Some readers take "Judah and Benjamin" here as standing for the tribes rather than for individuals. Whether he is the same as the Benjamin who repaired part of the wall in Neh 3:23, or the Benjamin of Ezra 10:32, cannot be determined. The name, shared by several people in the Bible, means "son of the right hand" (Hitchcock's Bible Names).

Benjamin (patriarch) was the youngest son of Jacob and the second son of Rachel, making him Joseph's only full brother. Rachel died giving birth to him near Ephrath, about 1739 BC by inference from context. With her last breath she named him Ben-oni, which Smith's Bible Dictionary renders "son of my sorrow." Jacob renamed him Benjamin, meaning "son of the right hand" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names (Gen 35:18). He appears in the account of the brothers' journeys to Egypt, where Joseph gave him a portion five times larger than anyone else's (Gen 43:34). In his final blessing Jacob compared him to a ravening wolf (Gen 49:27). Genealogies name his sons, including Bela, Becher and Ashbel, and the Tribe of Benjamin descended from him. Its land lay between Judah and Joseph (Josh 18:11). King Saul and the apostle Paul both belonged to this tribe (Acts 13:21; Phil 3:5).

Benjamin (Territory) was the land allotted by lot to the tribe of Benjamin, lying between Judah to the south and the descendants of Joseph to the north (Josh 18:11). Its northern border ran from the Jordan past Jericho and up through the hill country toward Bethel (Luz). It then descended past Lower Beth-horon and turned to Kirjath-jearim, a city of Judah (Josh 18:12–14). The southern border ran from Kirjath-jearim to the waters of Nephtoah and along the valley of Hinnom just south of Jebus, then went down past En-rogel and En-shemesh to the northern end of the Dead Sea. The Jordan formed the eastern side (Josh 18:15–20). Its cities included Jericho, Gibeon, Ramah, Beeroth, Gibeath and Jebus, which is Jerusalem (Josh 18:21–28). This was a small strip of central hill country north of Jerusalem. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "son of the right hand."

Benjamin's Gate was a gate of ancient Jerusalem, probably on the northern or northeastern side of the city. Its name most likely comes from the road it opened onto, which led north into the tribal territory of Benjamin. The KJV uses the form "Benjamin's gate" in Zech 14:10, where it marks one boundary point of Jerusalem in a prophecy of the city's future. Under the name "gate of Benjamin" it appears in Jeremiah's time. There Jeremiah was arrested at it while trying to leave the city (Jer 37:13), and King Zedekiah was sitting in it when Ebed-melech appealed for the prophet (Jer 38:7). Jer 20:2 mentions a "high gate of Benjamin" by the temple. Some identify it with the Sheep Gate or another northern gate, but its exact position is uncertain. The location shown here places it on the northeastern side of the city, near the temple area.

Beno was a Levite of the clan of Merari, named as a son of Jaaziah in the list of Levite families in 1 Chr 24:26–27. He appears with his brothers Shoham, Zaccur and Ibri, who are counted among "the sons of Merari by Jaaziah." The name means "his son," according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names. Because the Hebrew word can be read either as a personal name or simply as "his son," the wording of these verses is somewhat unclear. This entry follows the reading that treats Beno as a personal name, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia does. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Beon was a town east of the Jordan, named in Num 32:3 among the places in the land of Jazer and Gilead that the tribes of Reuben and Gad asked Moses to give them because it suited their livestock. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes it as the same town called Baal-meon in Num 32:38, which Reuben rebuilt and renamed. It also identifies it with Beth-baal-meon, given to Reuben in Josh 13:17, and with Beth-meon, listed among the cities of Moab in Jer 48:23. The same work notes that Mesha, king of Moab, claimed to have fortified it. Following the early church historian Eusebius, it places the town at the ruins of Ma'in, about 4 miles southwest of Madaba in modern Jordan, though the visible remains there date only from Roman times. The location shown here matches that identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "in affliction."

Beor was the father of Bela, the first king named in the list of rulers who reigned in Edom before Israel had a king. Bela's city was Dinhabah (Gen 36:32; 1 Chr 1:43). Nothing else is recorded about Beor himself, and nothing in the text says whether he was a king. He should be kept distinct from another Beor, the father of the prophet Balaam (Num 22:5), since the name is shared by more than one person in the Bible. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "burning" or "torch", and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia tentatively suggests "destroyer."

Beor was the father of Balaam, the diviner from Pethor in Mesopotamia whom Balak king of Moab hired to curse Israel. Beor himself is known only through his son: every mention of him is the phrase "Balaam the son of Beor." It appears in Balak's summons, in Balaam's own oracles, in the account of Balaam's death among the Midianites, and in later recollections of the episode by Moses, Joshua and Micah. In 2 Pet 2:15 the name appears as Bosor. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains Bosor as the Greek form of Beor. The same name belongs to other people in the Bible, such as the father of Bela, an early king of Edom. They should not be confused with Balaam's father. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "burning" or "torch."

Bera was king of Sodom in the time of Abram, one of five kings of the cities of the plain who went to war against an alliance of four eastern kings led by Chedorlaomer of Elam (Gen 14:2). The same chapter says these cities had served Chedorlaomer for twelve years before rebelling. Their armies met in the Vale of Siddim, where the five kings were defeated and the king of Sodom fled. After Abram rescued his nephew Lot and recovered the captives and goods, the king of Sodom went out to meet him. He offered Abram the goods in exchange for the people, but Abram refused to keep anything (Gen 14:17, 21–24). Bera is named only once, in Gen 14:2, but he is probably the unnamed king of Sodom in these later verses. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "gift" or "son of evil."

Berachah was one of the warriors who came to David at Ziklag, named in a list in 1 Chr 12:3. The surrounding chapter describes these men as kinsmen of Saul from the tribe of Benjamin. They joined David while he was still hiding from Saul, and they were skilled with the bow and the sling. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both identify Berachah as a Benjamite on this basis. His name means "blessing." Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with the Valley of Berachah, a place named in a later period of Israel's history. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his joining David to about 1054 BC, an estimate drawn from context.

Beraiah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named once in the Bible, in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. He is listed as one of the sons of Shimhi, alongside his brothers Adaiah, Shimrath, Jakim, Zichri, Zabdi, Elienai, Zilthai and Eliel (1 Chr 8:21). Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a chief man of Benjamin, in line with the chapter's presentation of these names as heads of families. His name is usually explained as meaning "the LORD has created" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the choosing of the Lord." Nothing more is recorded about his life.

Berea was a city in Macedonia where Paul and Silas went after the believers in Thessalonica sent them away by night. On arrival they went into the Jewish synagogue to preach (Acts 17:10). When Jews from Thessalonica heard that Paul was preaching there, they came to Berea and stirred up the people against him (Acts 17:13). The surrounding passage says Paul then left for the coast and sailed to Athens, while Silas and Timothy stayed behind. This visit is dated about AD 48, by inference from context. Acts 20:4 names Sopater of Berea as one of Paul's later travelling companions, and Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he was probably converted during this visit. Easton's also identifies the city with modern Veria in northern Greece, which matches the location shown here. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists it under the spelling Beroea.

Berechiah (also spelled Berachiah) was a Levite, the son of Shimea and the father of Asaph, the leading musician appointed in David's time (1 Chr 6:39; 1 Chr 15:17). His name means "the Lord blesses." The genealogy he appears in traces Asaph's line back to Gershom, so Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Gershonite Levite. A Berechiah is also named as one of two doorkeepers for the ark, alongside Elkanah, when David brought it to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:23). Views differ on whether this doorkeeper is the same man. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia list him as a separate person. The Tyndale House proper-names index treats them as one Levite who served during David's reign, and this entry follows that view. Because several men in the Bible bear this name, the identification remains uncertain.

Berechiah was a son of Zerubbabel and a member of the royal line of David in the tribe of Judah. He appears only in the genealogy of David's descendants in 1 Chr 3:20, where he is named within a group of five brothers: Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah and Jushab-hesed. The previous verse lists Zerubbabel's other children, Meshullam, Hananiah and their sister Shelomith. Abiud is also counted as a sibling here because Matt 1:13 names an Abiud as a son of Zerubbabel. Since Zerubbabel led the return from exile in Babylon, Berechiah probably lived in Judah after the return, though nothing is recorded about his life. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "Yahweh blesses." Several other people in the Bible share the name, including the father of the prophet Zechariah, and they should not be confused with this Berechiah.

Berechiah, son of Asa and grandson of Elkanah, was a Levite named in the list of those who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears alongside Obadiah, a descendant of Jeduthun, among the Levites in that list. The verse says the family lived in the villages of the Netophathites. Netophah was a town near Bethlehem, so these settlements were probably in that area. It is not clear whether the phrase about the villages applies to Berechiah himself or to his ancestor Elkanah. STEPBible's Tyndale House name index calls him a Levite gatekeeper, while Smith's Bible Dictionary simply calls him a Levite. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several people in the Bible share the name Berechiah, which means "the Lord blesses," and this one should not be confused with the others.

Berechiah, son of Meshillemoth, was one of the leaders of the tribe of Ephraim during the reign of Ahaz, king of Judah. When the army of the northern kingdom of Israel came home from war against Judah with a large number of Judean captives, Berechiah and three other Ephraimite leaders stood up against the returning soldiers (2 Chr 28:12). The surrounding passage shows that they opposed keeping their fellow Israelites as slaves, and the captives were then clothed, fed and sent back to Jericho. Easton's Bible Dictionary counts him among seven Ephraimite chieftains. His name means "the LORD blesses." Several other men in the Bible share this name, and this Berechiah is known only from this one episode.

Berechiah was the son of Meshezabeel and the father of Meshullam, a man who helped rebuild the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah. He is known only through his son. Meshullam repaired one section of the wall next to Meremoth (Neh 3:4) and another section opposite his own chamber (Neh 3:30). Meshullam's daughter married Johanan, the son of Tobiah, Nehemiah's opponent. The surrounding context identifies Tobiah as the "him" of Neh 6:18, and this marriage was one of the family ties that gave Tobiah supporters in Judah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as meaning "Yahweh blesses." Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, and this Berechiah should not be confused with them.

Berechiah was the father of the prophet Zechariah and the son of Iddo, according to the opening of the book of Zechariah (Zech 1:1, 7). Nothing else is said about him. His son received his visions in the second year of King Darius, probably Darius I of Persia, around 520 BC by inference from context, during the rebuilding of Jerusalem after the exile. Elsewhere, Ezra 5:1 and 6:14 call Zechariah simply "the son of Iddo." This is usually explained by Hebrew "son" also meaning grandson, or by the possibility that Berechiah died young and Zechariah was linked directly to his better-known grandfather. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "blessed of Jehovah." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this entry refers only to Zechariah's father.

Bered was a place in the far south of Canaan, mentioned only once. Genesis 16:14 says the well Beer-lahai-roi, where the angel of the Lord found Hagar after she fled from Sarai, lay "between Kadesh and Bered." The wider story places this well on the way to Shur (Gen 16:7), so Bered was probably in the Negev or northern Sinai. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names give the meaning of the name as "hail." Its exact site is unknown. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Aramaic Targums render the name with terms for Shur and Chalutsah, and links it to the large ruin of Khalasa (ancient Elusa), southwest of Beersheba. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the region west of Kadesh, not a precise identification.

Bered was a descendant of Ephraim, son of Joseph, named only in the genealogy of Ephraim's line in 1 Chr 7:20. The verse lists him as the son of Shuthelah and the father of Tahath, which makes him a grandson of Ephraim, as Easton's Bible Dictionary also reads it. Eran, who is listed as a son of Shuthelah in Num 26:36, is shown here as his brother. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests Bered may be the same person as Becher in Num 26:35, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia points to Becher for comparison. The name probably means "hail" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Nothing else is recorded about his life.

Beri was a man of the tribe of Asher, named as one of the sons of Zophah in the genealogy of Asher's descendants in 1 Chr 7:36. His brothers listed with him include Suah, Harnepher, Shual and Imrah, and the list continues in the next verse with Bezer, Hod, Shamma, Shilshah, Ithran (or Jether) and Beera. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in this family line. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "a well," the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "wisdom," and Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "my son" or "my corn."

Beriah was a son of Asher and a grandson of Jacob, listed with his brothers Imnah, Ishvah and Ishvi and his sister Serah. He appears among the family members who went down with Jacob to Egypt (Gen 46:17). His sons were Heber and Malchiel, and 1 Chr 7:31 adds that Malchiel was the father of Birzavith. In the census of Numbers he is the ancestor of the Beriite clan of the tribe of Asher, and his two sons founded the Heberite and Malchielite clans (Num 26:44–45). Spellings of his brothers' names vary slightly between the lists. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "in evil" or "a gift". Several other men in the Bible share the name Beriah, including a son of Ephraim and a Benjamite, and they should not be confused with this son of Asher.

Beriah was a son of Ephraim, born after Ephraim's sons Ezer and Elead were killed by the men of Gath while raiding their cattle (1 Chr 7:21–22). Ephraim mourned them for many days. When his wife later bore him another son, he named him Beriah "because it went evil with his house," which links the name to the family's misfortune (1 Chr 7:23). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the Tyndale House proper-names index both explain the name this way. The following verses list his descendants. His daughter Sherah is said to have built the Beth-horons (1 Chr 7:24). Rephah and Resheph follow, though the text does not make clear whether they were Beriah's own sons. The line then runs down to Joshua son of Nun (1 Chr 7:25–27). Several other men in the Bible share the name Beriah.

Beriah was a Benjamite, a son of Elpaal, listed in the genealogy of Benjamin in 1 Chronicles 8. He and his brother Shema were heads of the families living in Aijalon, and they drove out the inhabitants of Gath (1 Chr 8:13). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes the two brothers as founders of Aijalon who expelled the Gittites. Michael, Ispah and Joha are named as his sons (1 Chr 8:16). Read as one continuous list, 1 Chr 8:14–16 also gives Ahio, Shashak, Jeremoth, Zebadiah, Arad and Ader as his sons, and this entry follows that reading. His other brothers, named in 1 Chr 8:12 and 8:17–18, include Eber, Misham, Shamed, Meshullam and Heber. Several other men in the Bible are also called Beriah, so this one should be kept separate from them.

Beriah was a Levite, the youngest of the four sons of Shimei, whose brothers were Jahath, Zizah (called Zina in 1 Chr 23:10) and Jeush. He appears only in the list of Levite families drawn up when David organized the Levites for service. From the surrounding chapter, this Shimei was probably a descendant of Gershon, so Beriah belonged to the Gershonite branch of the tribe. The STEPBible Proper Names index places him in David's reign. Because Beriah and Jeush had few sons, their descendants were not counted as separate households. They were reckoned together as a single father's house. The name is shared by several other men in the Bible, including sons of Asher and Ephraim and a Benjaminite, and this Beriah should be kept distinct from them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "in fellowship" or "in envy."

Bernice was a Jewish princess who came with King Agrippa to Caesarea to greet Festus, the newly arrived Roman governor of Judea (Acts 25:13). This was about AD 56, by inference from context. The next day she entered the hearing room with Agrippa "with great pomp," together with military commanders and the city's leading men, when Paul was brought out to make his defense (Acts 25:23). When Paul finished speaking, she rose with the king and the governor and left to discuss the case (Acts 26:30). Acts does not state how she was related to Agrippa. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify her as the eldest daughter of Herod Agrippa I and the sister of Agrippa II, and say she had earlier been married to her uncle Herod, king of Chalcis. Easton's adds that she later sided with the Romans in the Jewish war and lived in Rome. Her name means "bringing victory."

Berothah was a place on the northern boundary of the land of Israel described in Ezekiel's vision of the restored land. Ezek 47:16 lists it with Hamath and Sibraim, in the area between the borders of Damascus and Hamath. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the same as Berothai, a city of Hadadezer king of Zobah mentioned in 2 Sam 8:8. Its exact site is uncertain. Some have linked the name with Beirut. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it near the springs at Hasbeya. Others look to Wadi Brissa, north of Baalbek. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia prefers the village of Bereitan, a little south of Baalbek in Lebanon's Beqaa Valley. The location shown here follows the Bereitan identification.

Berothai was a city belonging to Hadadezer, king of Zobah, from which King David took a very large amount of bronze (the King James "brass") after defeating him (2 Sam 8:8). The parallel account in 1 Chr 18:8 names Cun instead of Berothai and Tibhath instead of Betah. Some connect it with Berothah on the northern border described in Ezek 47:16, though this is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "wells" or "a cypress." Its exact site is not certain. It is often identified with the modern village of Bereitan in the Beqaa Valley of Lebanon, south of Baalbek, and the location shown here follows that identification. A site in this valley would fit Zobah's position north of Israel, between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon ranges.

Besai was the ancestor of a family of temple servants, the Nethinim, whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Judea with Zerubbabel. "The children of Besai" appear in the list of returning families in Ezra 2:49 and again in the parallel list in Neh 7:52. Nothing else is recorded about Besai himself, and the name is known only as the head of this family group. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "sword", the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "downtrodden", and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a despising". The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes that the same family appears as Basthai in the apocryphal book of 1 Esdras.

Besodeiah was the father of Meshullam, who is known only from Neh 3:6. In Nehemiah's account of rebuilding Jerusalem's walls, Meshullam son of Besodeiah worked with Jehoiada son of Paseah to repair the Old Gate. They laid its beams and set up its doors, locks and bars. Nothing else is recorded about Besodeiah himself. He presumably lived in the generation before the rebuilding, which this account places in the Persian period after the return from exile. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes his name to mean "in the secret of the Lord," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reads it as "in the confidence or counsel of Yah." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "counsel of the Lord."

Besor was a brook or seasonal stream in the far south of Judah, named only in the account of David's pursuit of the Amalekites who had raided Ziklag. David set out with six hundred men, but two hundred were too exhausted to cross the brook and stayed behind while the other four hundred went on (1 Sam 30:9–10). On his return with the recovered people and goods, David met the men waiting at the Besor and greeted them (1 Sam 30:21). The following verses record his ruling that those who stayed with the supplies would share the spoil equally. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the Wadi esh-Sharia south of Gaza. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia prefers the Wadi Ghazza, which reaches the sea southwest of Gaza and into which the Sharia drains. The location shown here follows the Wadi esh-Sharia identification.

Betah was a city belonging to Hadadezer, king of Zobah. After David defeated Hadadezer, he took a great quantity of bronze ("brass" in the King James Version) from Betah and from Berothai (2 Sam 8:8). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "confidence." The parallel account in 1 Chr 18:8 calls the city Tibhath, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Syriac version reads the name as Tebah. That encyclopedia adds that the city may be the Tubihi named in Egyptian records alongside Kadesh on the Orontes, and that Chronicles presents this bronze as later used by Solomon for the temple furnishings. The exact site is unknown. It probably lay in the Aramean kingdom of Zobah, on or near the eastern slopes of the Anti-Lebanon range. The location shown here is a rough placement in the Beqaa Valley region of present-day Lebanon.

Beten was a town on the border of the territory allotted to the tribe of Asher. It is named in Josh 19:25 between Hali and Achshaph, in the list of places that marked Asher's boundary. Nothing else is recorded about it in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "belly," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "height." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Eusebius, in his Onomasticon, placed a town called Bethseten about 8 Roman miles east of Ptolemais (Acre). It suggests the site may be the modern village of el-B'aneh in western Galilee, though it adds that no certainty is possible. The location shown here follows the el-B'aneh identification.

Beth-anath was a fortified city in the territory allotted to the tribe of Naphtali in northern Galilee. It appears among Naphtali's nineteen cities with their villages, alongside Horem and Beth-shemesh (Josh 19:38). Judges 1:33 records that Naphtali did not drive out the Canaanites living in Beth-anath and Beth-shemesh. The Israelites lived among them instead, and these inhabitants were later made to pay tribute. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the name to mean "house" or "temple" of Anath, a Canaanite goddess, while Easton's Bible Dictionary renders it "house of response." Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both tentatively identify the site with the modern village of 'Ainata, a few miles west of Kedesh, in what is now southern Lebanon. The location shown here follows that identification, though the exact site remains uncertain.

Beth-anoth was a town in the hill country of Judah, named once in the list of cities given to the tribe of Judah (Josh 15:59). It belongs to a group of six towns with their villages that includes Maarath and Eltekon. By the surrounding verse (Josh 15:58), the group also includes Halhul, Beth-zur and Gedor, north of Hebron. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "house of answers", Smith's Bible Dictionary "house of echo", and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "house of Anath", after a deity. Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the ruin of Beit 'Ainun, about 3 miles northeast of Hebron and near Halhul. The location shown here follows that identification. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the visible ruins there come from later periods.

Beth-arabah, meaning “house of the Arabah” or “house of the desert,” was a town in the Jordan valley on the boundary between the tribes of Judah and Benjamin. Judah's northern border passed Beth-hoglah and then ran along the north side of Beth-arabah toward the stone of Bohan (Josh 15:6). It is listed among Judah's towns “in the wilderness” with Middin and Secacah (Josh 15:61). It also appears among the towns of Benjamin, alongside Zemaraim and Bethel (Josh 18:22). That fits a site lying right on the shared border. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the “Arabah” of Josh 18:18 to be the same place. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the site has not been identified and that the Judahite and Benjamite names may refer to different towns. This entry treats them as one town. The location shown here is a rough placement in the lower Jordan valley near the north end of the Dead Sea.

Beth-arbel was a place whose brutal destruction Hosea cites as a warning to Israel. Its fortresses would be plundered "as Shalman spoiled Betharbel in the day of battle," when mothers were dashed in pieces with their children (Hos 10:14). It is not mentioned anywhere else in Scripture, so both the place and the attacker are uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Shalman to be probably Shalmaneser, king of Assyria (2 Kgs 17:3). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes another view, that he was Shalamanu, a Moabite king who paid tribute to Tiglath-pileser. It also gives two possible sites: Arbela (Irbid) in Galilee, or Irbid east of the Jordan, southeast of Gadara, which Eusebius's Onomasticon called Arbela. The location shown here follows the eastern identification with Irbid in modern northern Jordan.

Beth-ashbea was a place, or possibly a family household, connected with the descendants of Shelah son of Judah. It is mentioned only in 1 Chr 4:21, which lists among Shelah's descendants "the families of the house of them that wrought fine linen, of the house of Ashbea." The Hebrew phrase behind "house of Ashbea" is Beth-ashbea. It can be read as the name of a town or as a household or guild named after an ancestor called Ashbea. The STEPBible Proper Names index treats it as a place associated with these linen-working families. Because other places in the same list, such as Mareshah and Lecah, are towns in Judah, Beth-ashbea was probably also in the territory of Judah, perhaps in the lowland near Mareshah. That is an inference from context. Its location is unknown, and no site has been identified.

Beth-aven, whose name means "house of nothingness" or "house of wickedness," was a place in the hill country of Benjamin, east of Bethel and near Ai (Josh 7:2). Its wilderness marked part of Benjamin's northern border (Josh 18:12). In Saul's time the Philistines camped at Michmash, east of Beth-aven, and the battle that followed Jonathan's attack spread as far as Beth-aven (1 Sam 13:5; 14:23). Its exact site is unknown. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mentions a suggestion of Khirbet An, west of Michmash, and the location shown here lies in that area between Bethel and Michmash. In Hosea the name appears alongside Gilgal and is linked with the calves worshipped there (Hos 4:15; 5:8; 10:5). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take these passages as a mocking name for nearby Bethel, the "house of God" turned into a "house of idols."

Beth-azmaveth was a town in Judah or Benjamin whose men, forty-two in all, are counted among the exiles who returned from Babylon in Nehemiah's list (Neh 7:28). The parallel list in Ezra 2:24 gives the same number under the shorter name Azmaveth, so the two names refer to one place, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also treats them. Nehemiah 12:29 later mentions the fields of Azmaveth as a place where the temple singers had settled near Jerusalem. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "house of death's strength." The town is commonly identified with the modern village of Hizma, a few miles northeast of Jerusalem near Anathoth. The location shown here follows that identification.

Beth-baal-meon was a town east of the Jordan listed among the cities on the plain near Heshbon that were given to the tribe of Reuben (Josh 13:17). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary treat it as the same place called Baal-meon, which Reuben rebuilt and renamed (Num 32:38), and Beon (Num 32:3). Later it appears as a Moabite city, called Beth-meon in Jer 48:23 and Baal-meon in Ezek 25:9. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes that the Moabite king Mesha named it among the towns he fortified. The name probably refers to a local shrine of Baal. Eusebius placed it near hot springs about nine miles from Heshbon. On that basis it is usually identified with the ruins of Ma'in, about 4 miles southwest of Madaba in modern Jordan, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Beth-barah was a place near the Jordan River, named only in Judg 7:24. After Gideon routed the Midianites, he sent messengers through the hill country of Ephraim calling the Ephraimites to seize "the waters unto Bethbarah and Jordan" ahead of the fleeing enemy, and they did so. The name is usually understood as "house of the ford" (Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries), and it was probably a main crossing point of the Jordan in that district. Its exact site is unknown. Easton's suggests it may be the ford Jacob used near the Jabbok and where Jephthah later killed the Ephraimites. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it where the Wadi Fari'ah meets the Jordan. Smith's links it with Bethabara, where John baptized. The location shown here follows that last view, placing it at a Jordan crossing east of Jericho.

Beth-biri (spelled Bethbirei in the King James Version) was a town of the tribe of Simeon in the Negeb, the dry region of southern Judah. It appears only in 1 Chr 4:31, in a list of the towns where the Simeonites lived, which the verse says remained theirs until the reign of David. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia (1915) takes it to be the same place as Beth-lebaoth, which appears at the matching point in the parallel list of Simeon's towns in Josh 19:6. STEPBible's proper-names index connects it instead with Bethul, another name in that list. The site has not been identified. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the northern Negeb, near Beersheba, based on the town's place among the other Simeonite settlements.

Beth-car was the place to which the men of Israel chased the Philistines after defeating them near Mizpah in Samuel's time (1 Sam 7:11). According to the surrounding chapter, the Philistines had attacked while Israel was gathered at Mizpah, and they were thrown into confusion before the pursuit began. Beth-car is mentioned nowhere else. Its name is usually explained as "house of the lamb" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; Hitchcock's Bible Names) or "sheep-house" (Easton's Bible Dictionary). Its site is unknown. Easton's and Smith's place it west of Mizpah, inferring this from the direction of a Philistine retreat toward their own coastal territory. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests 'Ain Karem, west of Jerusalem, if Mizpah is Nebi Samwil. The location shown here is only a rough placement near Nebi Samwil, northwest of Jerusalem.

Beth-dagon was a city in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, listed in Joshua's allotment of towns to the tribe alongside Gederoth, Naamah and Makkedah, in a district of sixteen cities with their villages. Its name is usually taken to mean "house of Dagon" (Smith's Bible Dictionary), probably after the Philistine god. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "house of corn, or of fish." Since it lay in the low country, it was probably near Philistine territory. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with modern Beit Dajan, about 5 miles from Lydda. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Beit Dajan, southeast of Jaffa, and nearby Khirbet Dajan are candidates, but suggests the list points to a site farther southeast. The location shown here is only approximate and lies in the coastal plain in the general area of these proposals. A different Beth-dagon appears on the border of Asher (Josh 19:27).

Beth-dagon was a city on the boundary of the tribe of Asher, named in Josh 19:27 as a landmark where Asher's border turned east toward Zebulun and the valley of Jiphthah-el. The name probably means "house of Dagon," after the god Dagon, and Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as a Philistine colony. Hitchcock's Bible Names instead gives "house of corn, or of fish." The name is shared by other places, including a town in Judah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name was widespread, which may reflect broad worship of Dagon. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it near the coast. Easton's and Conder identify it with Tell D'auk, near the mouth of the Belus River (the modern Na'aman) in the plain of Acre. The rough location shown here follows that identification.

Beth-diblathaim was a town of Moab, east of the Dead Sea. It appears once, in Jeremiah's oracle against Moab, where it is listed with Dibon and Nebo among the cities facing judgment (Jer 48:22). The name probably means "house of fig cakes," as Easton's and Smith's Bible dictionaries explain it. Several reference works, including Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, take it to be the same place as Almon-diblathaim, an Israelite camping site during the wilderness journey (Num 33:46). Easton's also links it with Diblath (Ezek 6:14). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that King Mesha of Moab claimed on the Moabite Stone to have fortified it. Its exact site is uncertain. The location shown here is a proposed spot in the Moabite highlands between Dibon and Medeba, in present-day Jordan.

Beth-eden, meaning "house of Eden," was a place named in Amos's prophecy against Damascus, where the LORD declares he will cut off "him that holdeth the sceptre from the house of Eden" (Amos 1:5). The King James Version translates the name rather than spelling it out. The verse links it with Damascus and the plain of Aven as a seat of Syrian (Aramean) rule, and says the people of Syria would go into captivity to Kir. Its location is uncertain. Some identify it with Bit Adini, a district on the middle Euphrates known from Assyrian inscriptions and probably the same as "the children of Eden" of 2 Kgs 19:12. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it was perhaps in Syria near Damascus. The location shown here follows the view placing it in the Damascus area.

Beth-eked was a place on the road between Jezreel and Samaria. The King James Version translates its name as "the shearing house"; the Hebrew name may mean "house of binding." Jehu passed it on his way to Samaria after overthrowing the house of Ahab. There he met forty-two relatives of Ahaziah, king of Judah, whom the surrounding passage (2 Kgs 10:13) describes as his brothers on their way to visit the royal family. Jehu ordered them taken alive. They were then killed at the pit of Beth-eked, and none were spared. Its exact site is uncertain. It is often identified, by inference from Jehu's route, with the modern village of Beit Qad near Jenin, at the southern edge of the Jezreel Valley. The location shown here is approximate and places it in that general area.

Beth-emek, meaning "house of the valley," was a town named once, in the description of the border of the tribe of Asher (Josh 19:27). The boundary ran east toward Beth-dagon, reached Zebulun and the valley of Jiphthah-el on the north side of Beth-emek, then went on to Neiel and Cabul. Because it lies where Asher's line meets Zebulun, the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts it within Zebulun, while Smith's Bible Dictionary places it on or near Asher's border. The ISBE describes the site as unidentified but says it should be sought east of Acre, not far from Cabul (modern Kabul). The location shown here follows a later identification with Tel Bet ha-Emek, near the former village of Amqa, which may preserve the name, about 9 kilometres (6 miles) northeast of Acre in western Galilee. That identification is probable rather than certain.

Beth-ezel was a town named only once in the Bible, in Micah's lament over the towns of Judah and the lowland facing coming judgment (Mic 1:11). The verse speaks of mourning in Beth-ezel, and Micah, as he often does in this passage, appears to play on the town's name, which means "house of nearness" or "adjoining house." Its people would offer no support or standing to others in the disaster. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it, from the context, in the plain of Philistia, alongside the other towns Micah lists. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the site has not been identified, and that some have linked it with Azel in Zech 14:5. Its exact location remains uncertain. The location shown here is only approximate and places it in the coastal lowland southwest of Jerusalem, in keeping with the towns named around it.

Beth-gamul was a city of Moab, named once in Jeremiah's prophecy against Moab alongside Kiriathaim and Beth-meon (Jer 48:23). It belongs to the list of towns of the "plain country" (the Moabite tableland) on which judgment is announced (Jer 48:21). The name probably means "house of the camel." Nothing more is recorded about it. Its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary links it with Umm el-Jemal, a deserted city in the Hauran near Bozrah, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Conder placed it at Umm el-Jamal on the plateau south of Medeba. Others, the encyclopedia reports, prefer Jemeil, about 6 miles east of Dhiban, the biblical Dibon. The location shown here follows the Jemeil identification, east of Dhiban in present-day Jordan.

Beth-gilgal, meaning "house of Gilgal," was a place where some of the Levite singers lived after the return from exile. The KJV translates the name as "the house of Gilgal." Neh 12:29 lists it with the fields of Geba and Azmaveth as places where the singers had built villages around Jerusalem. From these villages they gathered for the dedication of the rebuilt city wall, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats it as the same place as Gilgal. The location shown here follows that view and places it at the well-known Gilgal near Jericho in the Jordan valley. The verse itself gives no position beyond its link to villages around Jerusalem, so the exact site is uncertain.

Beth-haccherem, meaning "house of the vineyard," was a place in Judah near Jerusalem. After the exile it was the center of a district whose ruler, Malchiah son of Rechab, repaired the Dung Gate of Jerusalem under Nehemiah (Neh 3:14). Earlier, Jeremiah named it alongside Tekoa as a spot for raising a signal fire to warn of an invasion from the north (Jer 6:1), which suggests a high, visible site south of Jerusalem. Its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia favor ‘Ain Karim, west of Jerusalem, where ancient cairns on a nearby ridge may once have served as beacons. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes Jerome's remark that he could see the village daily from Bethlehem, which has led some to suggest the Herodium hill near Tekoa. The location shown here follows the Herodium identification.

Beth-haggan, meaning "house of the garden," was a place on the road Ahaziah king of Judah took as he fled from Jehu after Joram king of Israel was killed near Jezreel. The King James Version translates the name as "the garden house," but the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some read it as a proper place name. Jehu's men struck Ahaziah in his chariot at the ascent of Gur near Ibleam, and he escaped to Megiddo and died there (2 Kgs 9:27). The route suggests Beth-haggan lay south of Jezreel, toward Ibleam. Its exact location is uncertain. Many identify it with En-gannim, the modern town of Jenin, which lies on a route south from Jezreel. The location shown here is only approximate and is placed near Megiddo, where Ahaziah's flight ended.

Beth-haram (spelled Betharam in the King James Version) was a town in the Jordan Valley east of the river. Joshua 13:27 lists it with Beth-nimrah, Succoth and Zaphon among the towns of the territory given to the tribe of Gad, land that had been the rest of the kingdom of Sihon, king of Heshbon. Numbers 32:36 probably refers to the same place as Beth-haran, one of the fortified towns the Gadites built. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with Bethramphtha, mentioned by Josephus. In the first century Herod Antipas fortified it and renamed it Julias, and Eusebius says it was also called Livias. The same work places it at Tell er-Rameh in Wadi Hesban, about 6 miles (10 km) east of the Jordan, in present-day Jordan. The location shown here is in the Jordan Valley north-east of the Dead Sea.

Beth-haran was a fortified town east of the Jordan River, named in Num 32:36 among the fenced cities and sheepfolds the tribe of Gad built or rebuilt after Moses granted them land there. The surrounding chapter shows Gad and Reuben asking for this pasture country for their large flocks. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat it as the same place as Beth-haram, which Josh 13:27 lists among Gad's towns in the Jordan valley. Its exact site is uncertain. It is often placed at one of the mounds on the plain east of the Jordan opposite Jericho, such as Tell er-Rameh or Tell Iktanu. The location shown here places it in that area, northeast of the Dead Sea. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "house of grace."

Beth-hoglah was a town in the Jordan Valley near the northern end of the Dead Sea, on the boundary between the tribes of Judah and Benjamin. Judah's northern border ran up to Beth-hoglah and passed north of Beth-arabah (Josh 15:6). Benjamin's southern border passed along its north side before ending at the north bay of the Salt Sea, where the Jordan enters it (Josh 18:19). The town is listed among Benjamin's cities together with Jericho (Josh 18:21), so it probably belonged to Benjamin while marking Judah's edge. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "house of the partridge." It identifies the site with a spring between Jericho and the Jordan, near the ruins of a medieval Greek monastery called Kasr Hajlah, and notes that the area now lies several miles inland from the sea. The location shown here follows that identification, southeast of Jericho.

Beth-horon was a town in the hill country northwest of Jerusalem, on the route down from Gibeon toward the western lowlands. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries describe it as two villages, an upper and a lower Beth-horon, about 2 miles apart, linked by a steep ascent; Easton's explains the name as "house of the hollow" or "of the cavern." Joshua's army chased the Amorite kings from Gibeon along this road, and many fled down it and were killed by hailstones (Josh 10:10–11). It marked part of Benjamin's boundary (Josh 18:14) and was a Levitical city with its pasturelands (Josh 21:22; 1 Chr 6:68). A Philistine raiding company headed toward it in Saul's time (1 Sam 13:18), and Amaziah's dismissed soldiers raided towns as far as Beth-horon (2 Chr 25:13). The two sites are usually identified with the modern villages of Beit Ur el-Foqa and Beit Ur et-Tahta. The location shown here lies near the upper village.

Beth-horon, here Lower Beth-horon ("Bethhoron the nether"), was a town on the border between the tribal territories of Ephraim and Benjamin. It had a twin, Upper Beth-horon, and this name is shared by both towns. Lower Beth-horon marked a point on Ephraim's southern boundary as it ran west toward Gezer and the sea (Josh 16:3). A hill south of it was a landmark on Benjamin's northern border (Josh 18:13). Solomon rebuilt it along with Gezer, and he fortified both Beth-horons with walls, gates and bars (1 Kgs 9:17; 2 Chr 8:5). Easton's Bible Dictionary says the two towns stood about 2 miles apart on the road from Jerusalem to Joppa. The pass between them was the ascent of Beth-horon, where Joshua chased the Amorite kings. The lower town is generally identified with the modern village of Beit Ur et-Tahta, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Beth-horon was the name of a pair of towns, Upper and Lower Beth-horon, in the hill country northwest of Jerusalem. In 1 Chr 7:24, Sherah, a daughter in the line of Ephraim, is said to have built both towns along with Uzzen-sherah. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the name as "house of the hollow" or "of the cavern," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "house of wrath." Easton's places the towns in Ephraim's territory on the road from Jerusalem to Joppa, about 2 miles apart, with the upper town about 10 miles northwest of Jerusalem. The steep pass between them was the route down which Joshua drove the Amorite kings (Josh 10:10–11). Easton's identifies them with the modern villages of Beit Ur el-Foqa (upper) and Beit Ur et-Tahta (lower), and the location shown here lies in that area. Because the name covers two neighboring sites, references to Beth-horon can mean either one.

Beth-jeshimoth, meaning "house of the wastes" or "deserts" according to Easton's Bible Dictionary, was a town east of the Jordan near the northeastern shore of the Dead Sea, in the plains of Moab. Israel's last camp before crossing the Jordan stretched from Beth-jeshimoth to Abel-shittim (Num 33:49). It also marked a point on the border of the territory of Sihon, king of the Amorites, along the way toward the Dead Sea (Josh 12:3). It was later listed among the towns given to the tribe of Reuben (Josh 13:20). By Ezekiel's time it belonged to Moab and was named with Baal-meon and Kiriathaim as one of the frontier cities that were "the glory of the country" (Ezek 25:9). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it was Khirbet es-Suweimeh, about 3 miles east of the mouth of the Jordan. The location shown here matches that area.

Beth-le-aphrah was a town named only in Mic 1:10, in Micah's lament over the coming judgment on Judah. The King James Version renders it "the house of Aphrah." The name means "house of dust," and the prophet plays on it by telling its people to roll themselves in the dust as a sign of mourning. The verse sits among other wordplays on town names, beginning with Gath, so the place was probably one of several nearby towns threatened by the invasion. Its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in the Shephelah, the low country between Joppa and Gaza, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia puts it in the Philistine plain. Others link it with Ophrah in Benjamin. The location shown here follows that identification, probably the modern village of et-Taiyibeh northeast of Jerusalem.

Beth-lebaoth was a town in the territory given to the tribe of Simeon, named near the end of Simeon's list of thirteen cities and their villages in Josh 19:6. The name means "house of lionesses" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Because Simeon's towns lay within Judah's allotment, it was in the far south of the land, in the Negev region. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Lebaoth in Judah's list of southern towns (Josh 15:32). Both Smith's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take Beth-birei in the parallel list of Simeon's towns (1 Chr 4:31) as another name for the same place. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the northern Negev, north of Beersheba.

Beth-maacah was a city in the far north of Israel, closely linked with the town of Abel. Its name may mean "house of Maacah." In 2 Sam 20:14 the rebel Sheba son of Bichri passed through the tribes of Israel to Abel and Beth-maacah, and Joab's forces then besieged him in "Abel of Beth-maacah," building a siege ramp and battering the wall (2 Sam 20:15). Whether Beth-maacah was a separate place next to Abel or simply part of that town's fuller name is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it under Abel-beth-maacah. Easton's Bible Dictionary places that city in Naphtali near Dan and Ijon and identifies it with the modern village of Abil el-Qamh, about 6 miles west-northwest of Dan. The location shown here matches that identification, near the Israel–Lebanon border.

Beth-marcaboth, meaning "house of chariots", was a town in the far south of Judah that was allotted to the tribe of Simeon. It is listed next to Ziklag and Hazar-susah (Josh 19:5), and 1 Chr 4:31 counts it among the Simeonite towns held until the reign of David. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the parallel list of Judah's southern towns in Josh 15:31 has Madmannah in its place, and Tyndale House's STEPBible names list treats the two as the same town. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says the site had not been identified and mentions Guérin's suggestion of Khan Yunis, southwest of Gaza. It also links the name with the chariot cities Solomon later built. The location shown here follows the identification with Madmannah, in the northern Negev north-northeast of Beersheba. The exact site remains uncertain.

Beth-meon was a town of Moab named in Jeremiah's prophecy of judgment against Moab, listed alongside Kiriathaim and Beth-gamul (Jer 48:23). The verse gives no further detail about it. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat it as a shortened form of the same town elsewhere called Baal-meon (Num 32:38) and Beth-baal-meon (Josh 13:17). Those passages place it on the plateau east of the Dead Sea, a town the tribe of Reuben rebuilt after the conquest that later came back under Moabite control. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "house of the dwelling-place." The location shown here is probably the modern village of Ma'in, southwest of Madaba in Jordan, the site usually linked with Baal-meon.

Beth-millo, meaning "house of Millo," was a place or community associated with Shechem, translated "the house of Millo" in the King James Version. Its people joined the men of Shechem in making Abimelech king beside the pillar at Shechem (Judg 9:6). Jotham, in his fable from Mount Gerizim, called for fire to come from Abimelech and devour the men of Shechem and the house of Millo, and for fire from them to devour Abimelech, foreshadowing their later conflict (Judg 9:20). "Millo" probably refers to a rampart or earthwork fortification. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it as a rampart in Shechem, probably the same as the "tower of Shechem" mentioned later in the chapter (Judg 9:46, 49). It is distinct from the Millo in Jerusalem. The location shown here places it at or near ancient Shechem, by Tell Balata near modern Nablus.

Beth-nimrah was a fortified town east of the Jordan River, rebuilt by the tribe of Gad after the defeat of Sihon king of Heshbon. It was one of the fenced cities the Gadites built, alongside sheepfolds for their flocks (Num 32:36). In the allotment it is listed among the towns "in the valley" of the Jordan with Betharam, Succoth and Zaphon, part of the former kingdom of Sihon assigned to Gad (Josh 13:27). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note that it is probably the place called simply Nimrah in Num 32:3, and possibly the "waters of Nimrim" of Isa 15:6. The name means "house of leopards" (Hitchcock's gives "house of rebellion"). It is generally identified with Tell Nimrin, near the Wadi Nimrin in the Jordan Valley northeast of Jericho, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Beth-pazzez was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Issachar. It appears only once, in the list of Issachar's towns, where it is named alongside Remeth, En-gannim and En-haddah (Josh 19:21). Nothing else is recorded about it. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "house of the dispersion," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "house of dividing asunder." The site has not been identified. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it probably lay near modern Jenin, since it is listed with En-gannim, which is commonly linked to that area. The location shown here is a rough placement in that general region of the Jezreel Valley and the hills to its south, not a known site.

Beth-pelet was a town in the far south of Judah, in the Negeb region toward the border of Edom. It appears in the list of towns allotted to the tribe of Judah (Josh 15:27), where the King James Version spells it Bethpalet, and again among the places resettled by people of Judah after the return from exile in Babylon (Neh 11:26), spelled Bethphelet. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of the name as "house of escape" and places it among "the uttermost cities" of Judah toward Edom, following the heading of the list in Joshua 15:21. It also describes the site as unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the northern Negeb, near the other towns named with it, such as Moladah and Heshmon.

Beth-peor, meaning "house of Peor," was a place east of the Jordan in the land of Moab, opposite Jericho. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean a temple of Baal-peor, the god whose worship led Israel astray in Num 25:3. Israel camped in the valley facing Beth-peor while Moses gave the speeches of Deuteronomy. The area had belonged to Sihon, the Amorite king of Heshbon, whom Israel defeated. Moses was buried in a valley in Moab facing Beth-peor, though no one knew where his grave was. Later the town was assigned to the tribe of Reuben, listed alongside the slopes of Pisgah. Its exact site is uncertain. Eusebius placed it near Mount Peor, about six miles from Livias. Conder suggested el-Mareighat, an ancient worship site with standing stones, and the location shown here appears to follow that area, on the heights south of Mount Nebo.

Beth-rapha was a son of Eshton, named in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chr 4:12 alongside his brothers Paseah and Tehinnah. The passage groups these men as "the men of Rechah." Nothing else is recorded about him. Because the name begins with "Beth" (house), it may stand for a family, clan or settlement rather than a single individual, as other names in these Chronicles genealogies do. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes, however, that it cannot now be linked with any particular place or clan. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "house of health."

Beth-rehob was an Aramean (Syrian) town and small kingdom in the far north of Israel. Judges 18:28 places Laish, the city the tribe of Dan captured and rebuilt, "in the valley that lieth by Bethrehob," far from Sidon. In David's time, the Ammonites hired Syrian soldiers from Beth-rehob, along with troops from Zobah, Maacah and Ish-tob, to fight Israel (2 Sam 10:6). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as probably the same as the Rehob that marked the northern limit of the spies' journey in Num 13:21. The site is uncertain. Robinson, cited in Smith's Bible Dictionary, identified it with Hunin, west of Banias, while others favor Banias itself. The location shown here follows the Hunin identification, in the hills above the Huleh Valley near Dan.

Beth-shan was a city where the Philistines displayed the bodies of King Saul and his sons after defeating them on Mount Gilboa. They put Saul's armour in the temple of Ashtaroth and fastened the bodies to the city wall. The brave men of Jabesh-gilead marched all night, took the bodies down and burned them at Jabesh (1 Sam 31:10–12). Later David recovered the bones of Saul and Jonathan from the men of Jabesh-gilead, who had taken them from the street of Beth-shan (2 Sam 21:12). Other passages spell the name Beth-shean and place it in the territory assigned to Manasseh, near the Jordan Valley. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as "house of the tooth," "of ivory," or "of sleep." The site is generally identified with Tel Beth-shean, beside modern Beit She'an in northern Israel, and the location shown here matches that identification.

Beth-shean was a Canaanite city at the eastern end of the Jezreel Valley, west of the Jordan. It lay within the territory of Issachar but was assigned to Manasseh (Josh 17:11; 1 Chr 7:29). Its inhabitants had iron chariots, which the tribes of Joseph gave as a reason they could not take the valley (Josh 17:16), and Manasseh did not drive them out (Judg 1:27). In Solomon's time it gave its name to an administrative district under Baana son of Ahilud (1 Kgs 4:12). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes a shortened form, Beth-shan, in 1 Samuel and 2 Samuel, where the Philistines fastened the bodies of Saul and his sons to its walls. It says the city was later called Scythopolis. It is identified with modern Beisan (Beit She'an), about 12 miles south of the Sea of Galilee, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Beth-shemesh, meaning "house of the sun" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), was a city on the northern border of Judah, near the Philistine lowland (Josh 15:10).
