It was given with its pasturelands to the Levites (Josh 21:16; 1 Chr 6:59). When the Philistines sent back the ark of the LORD on a cart, the cows took the road straight to Beth-shemesh, where the people were reaping wheat. The cart stopped at a great stone in the field of Joshua, and offerings were made there. Many men of the town were then struck down for looking into the ark (1 Sam 6:12–20). Beth-shemesh lay in one of Solomon's supply districts (1 Kgs 4:9). Jehoash of Israel captured Amaziah of Judah there (2 Kgs 14:11–13), and the Philistines later took it under Ahaz (2 Chr 28:18). Several places share this name. The location shown here follows the identification with ʿAin Shems given by Easton's Bible Dictionary, about 14 miles west of Jerusalem.

Beth-shemesh was a city on the border of the tribe of Issachar, listed in Joshua 19:22 between Shahazimah and the Jordan, where Issachar's boundary ended. The name means "house of the sun." Several places in the Bible share this name, including the better-known Beth-shemesh in Judah and another in Naphtali, so this one should be kept distinct. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it between Dothan and the Jordan, near Issachar's southern border, about 7.5 miles south of Beth-shean, and identifies it with Ain esh-Shemsiyeh. The location shown here follows that identification, in the Jordan Valley south of Beth-shean.

Beth-shemesh, meaning "house of the sun," was a city in the tribal territory of Naphtali in Galilee. It is one of several places with this name, and it should not be confused with the better-known Beth-shemesh in Judah. It appears among the fortified cities assigned to Naphtali (Josh 19:38). Judges 1:33 records that Naphtali did not drive out its Canaanite inhabitants. Instead the tribe lived among them, and the people of Beth-shemesh and nearby Beth-anath were made to pay tribute. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it between Mount Tabor and the Jordan and identifies it with Khurbet Shema near Safed, while also suggesting it may be the same as the Beth-shemesh on Issachar's border. The location shown here is only a rough placement in Upper Galilee, somewhat north of Safed.

Beth-shittah, meaning "house of the acacia", was a place named in the flight of the Midianite army after Gideon's three hundred men blew their trumpets and the enemy camp turned on itself. The fleeing host ran toward Beth-shittah "in Zererath" and on toward the border of Abel-meholah and Tabbath (Judg 7:22). This is its only mention in the Bible. The route suggests it lay east or southeast of the Midianite camp in the Valley of Jezreel, toward the Jordan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with the modern village of Shatta (Shuṭṭa) in the Jezreel Valley, about 6 miles (10 km) northwest of Beisan (Beth-shean). The location shown here follows that identification, although the exact site remains uncertain.

Beth-tappuah was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed among the cities allotted to the tribe of Judah in a group of towns near Hebron (Josh 15:53). Its name means "house of apples" according to Easton's Bible Dictionary. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connect it with Tappuah, named as a son of Hebron in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:43, which probably reflects the founding or settlement of the town by a clan from Hebron. The ISBE also mentions a possible link with Tephon in 1 Maccabees 9:50. The town is usually identified with the modern village of Taffuh, a few miles west of Hebron, on a high ridge with fertile gardens, old cisterns and an ancient road. The location shown here follows that identification.

Beth-togarmah, meaning "house of Togarmah," was a northern region or people that Ezekiel mentions twice. In his lament over Tyre, the house of Togarmah traded horses, horsemen and mules in Tyre's markets (Ezek 27:14). In his prophecy against Gog, it appears among Gog's allies, described as coming "of the north quarters" alongside Gomer and its forces (Ezek 38:6). The name probably goes back to Togarmah, listed in Gen 10:3 as a son of Gomer, which would explain why the two are named together. Its exact location is uncertain. Some connect it with the ancient city of Tegarama (Til-garimmu) in eastern Anatolia, and others with Armenia, a region long known for breeding horses. The location shown here follows the Armenian identification, placing it in the highlands of modern Armenia.

Beth-zur, meaning "house of rock" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed with Halhul and Gedor among the tribe's towns (Josh 15:58). King Rehoboam fortified it as one of the defensive cities of Judah (2 Chr 11:7). After the exile, Nehemiah son of Azbuk, ruler of half the district of Beth-zur, repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall near the tombs of David (Neh 3:16). In the genealogy at 1 Chr 2:45, Maon is called the father of Beth-zur, which links the town with that clan. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that it commanded the main road from Hebron to Jerusalem, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes its importance as a fortress during the Maccabean wars. The location shown here is the site near the modern village of Beit Sur, a few miles north of Hebron.

Bethany was a village at the Mount of Olives, about fifteen furlongs (roughly 2 miles) from Jerusalem (John 11:18). It was the home of Lazarus and his sisters Mary and Martha (John 11:1), and the place where Jesus raised Lazarus from the dead. In his last week Jesus lodged at Bethany and went into Jerusalem by day (Matt 21:17; Mark 11:11–12). There, in the house of Simon the leper, a woman poured costly ointment on his head (Mark 14:3; Matt 26:6). John places Jesus at Bethany six days before Passover (John 12:1). It is named with Bethphage on the approach to Jerusalem (Mark 11:1), and Luke says Jesus led his disciples out as far as Bethany when he blessed them (Luke 24:50). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the modern village of el-Azariyeh, "place of Lazarus," which the location shown here matches. A different Bethany lay beyond the Jordan (John 1:28).

Bethany beyond the Jordan was the place east of the Jordan River where John the Baptist was baptizing and where the events of John 1:19–28 took place. The King James Version reads Bethabara here, but the oldest manuscripts, followed by the Revised Version, read Bethany (Easton's Bible Dictionary). It is a different place from the Bethany near Jerusalem that was home to Mary, Martha and Lazarus. Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Origen preferred the reading Bethabara on geographical grounds, that Grove suggested Beth-nimrah (modern Tell Nimrin), and that tradition places it at the ford east of Jericho. The location shown here follows that traditional site, probably the area now called Al-Maghtas in Jordan. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "house of song" or "house of affliction."

Bethel (of Palestine), meaning "house of God," was a town in the central hill country about 10 miles north of Jerusalem, west of Ai and south of Shiloh. Its earlier name was Luz (Gen 28:19). Abraham built an altar east of it on entering Canaan (Gen 12:8), and Jacob named the place and later returned to build an altar there (Gen 35:3). It lay on the Ephraim–Benjamin border and was taken by the house of Joseph (Judg 1:22). In the time of the judges Israel gathered there before the LORD, and Samuel included it on his circuit (1 Sam 7:16). After the kingdom divided, Jeroboam set up a golden calf and altar there (1 Kgs 12:29). Amos and Hosea denounced its altars, and Josiah later destroyed them (2 Kgs 23:15). Men of Bethel returned after the exile. The location shown here follows the identification with modern Beitin given in Easton's Bible Dictionary.

Bethel (of Judah) was a town in the south of Judah, distinct from the better-known Bethel north of Jerusalem. Its name means "house of God" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. In 1 Sam 30:27 it heads the list of towns whose people received a share of the spoil David sent after recovering the captives taken from Ziklag. It is grouped there with south Ramoth and Jattir, which places it in the southern hill country and the Negev. Easton's Bible Dictionary also takes the king of Bethel in Josh 12:16, listed beside the king of Makkedah among the defeated Canaanite rulers, as belonging to this southern town, though that verse may refer to the northern Bethel instead. Many interpreters identify it with Bethul or Bethuel, a town of Simeon (Josh 19:4; 1 Chr 4:30). Its exact site is unknown, and the location shown here is only approximate.

Bethesda was a pool in Jerusalem near the sheep market (or sheep gate) with five porches, or covered colonnades (John 5:2). The name is usually explained as "house of mercy". Some manuscripts call it Bethzatha or Bethsaida. The surrounding passage (John 5:3–9) describes many sick people lying in the porches, and Jesus healing a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years, about AD 28 by inference from context. The site has been identified in several ways. Smith's Bible Dictionary mentions the large Birket Israel north of the Temple area. Robinson and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia favour the intermittent spring called the Virgin's Fountain (Gihon) in the Kidron Valley. A third view, which Easton's Bible Dictionary notes was argued by Schick, places it at a rock-cut twin pool near St. Anne's Church, just inside St. Stephen's Gate. The location shown here follows the St. Anne's identification.

The Bethesda pool healing was Jesus' cure of a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years, recorded in John 5. During a Jewish feast in Jerusalem, Jesus came to the pool of Bethesda, near the sheep market, where many sick, blind and lame people lay in its five porches waiting for the water to be stirred. The man said he had no one to put him into the pool. Jesus told him to rise, take up his bed and walk, and he was healed at once. Because it was the Sabbath, Jewish authorities objected to his carrying his bed. Jesus later found him in the temple, and the man then told them who had healed him. The authorities sought to kill Jesus for working on the Sabbath and for calling God his Father. Jesus answered with a discourse on the Son's relationship to the Father and on the witness of John, his works, the scriptures and Moses. The event is dated to about AD 28, by inference.

Bethlehem was a town in the hill country of Judah, earlier called Ephrath, on whose road Rachel was buried (Gen 35:19; 48:7). It was the home of the judge Ibzan and of Elimelech's family. Naomi returned there with Ruth, and Boaz lived there. David's family lived there too. Samuel came to the town to anoint David, and his warriors broke through a Philistine garrison to bring him water from its well by the gate. Rehoboam fortified it, and people from Bethlehem were among those who returned from exile. Matthew and Luke call it the city of David, where Jesus was born, where shepherds and wise men came, and where Herod killed the young boys. It is the modern town of Bethlehem (Beit Lahm), about 5 miles south of Jerusalem, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "house of bread." Another Bethlehem lay in Zebulun, and this entry is the Judean town.

Bethlehem was a town in the territory given to the tribe of Zebulun. It appears only once, in Josh 19:15, as the last of twelve cities with their villages in Zebulun's allotment. It is a different place from the better-known Bethlehem in Judah, and several places in the Bible share the name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "house of bread." Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both identify it with Beit-Lahm, a village Easton places about 6 miles (10 km) west-northwest of Nazareth in Galilee. The location shown here matches that identification. Some scholars have suggested that the judge Ibzan of Bethlehem (Judg 12:8–10) came from this northern town rather than from Bethlehem in Judah, but the text does not say which one is meant.

Bethlehem Ephrathah is the name Micah uses for Bethlehem, the town in Judah. Micah 5:2 calls it small among the clans ("thousands") of Judah, yet foretells that a ruler in Israel will come from it, one "whose goings forth have been from of old." The added name Ephrathah sets it apart from another Bethlehem in Zebulun. Easton's Bible Dictionary treats Ephrath or Ephrathah as the town's ancient name, linked with Rachel's burial on the road there (Gen 35:16–19; 48:7). It also notes that Ruth 1:2 calls the place Bethlehem-Judah but its people Ephrathites. Bethlehem was David's hometown, and Matt 2:6 quotes Micah's prophecy as pointing to Bethlehem in the land of Judah. The location shown here is the town of Bethlehem, about 9 kilometers (6 miles) south of Jerusalem.

Bethphage was a village on the Mount of Olives, just outside Jerusalem and close to Bethany. It appears only in the accounts of Jesus' approach to Jerusalem. As he and his disciples drew near the city and reached Bethphage, he sent two disciples ahead (Matt 21:1; Mark 11:1; Luke 19:29). The following verses describe them fetching the animal he rode into the city. Mark and Luke name it together with Bethany. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary place it on the road between Jericho and Jerusalem. Easton's adds that it lay at the limit of a Sabbath-day's journey from the city. The name is usually explained as "house of unripe (or early) figs." The exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia prefers the village of Kefr et-Tur on the summit. Abu Dis has also been suggested. The location shown here is on the Mount of Olives east of Jerusalem.

Bethsaida was a town on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee. It was the hometown of Philip and also of Andrew and Peter (John 1:44), and John 12:21 calls it "Bethsaida of Galilee." Jesus fed the five thousand in a remote place belonging to the town (Luke 9:10). He sent his disciples across the lake toward it by boat (Mark 6:45), and he healed a blind man there (Mark 8:22). Along with Chorazin, it was rebuked for not repenting despite the miracles done in it (Matt 11:21; Luke 10:13). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it east of the Jordan where the river enters the lake, in the town that Philip the tetrarch enlarged and renamed Julias. Smith's Bible Dictionary records a view that there were two towns of the name, one on each side of the lake. The location shown here follows the identification with the ruins at et-Tel.

Bethuel was a town in the far south of Judah's territory where the descendants of Simeon lived. It appears in 1 Chr 4:30 in the list of Simeonite towns, named alongside Hormah and Ziklag, which places it in the Negev region. Both Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with Bethul in the parallel list of Simeon's towns at Josh 19:4. They also link it, the encyclopedia more cautiously as "probably," with the Bethel in southern Judah to which David sent spoil after recovering Ziklag (1 Sam 30:27). That Bethel is distinct from the better-known Bethel north of Jerusalem. The site has not been securely identified, and the location shown here is only a rough placement. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "filiation of God." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "destroyed of God."

Bethuel was the son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and his wife Milcah, which made him Abraham's nephew. He was the youngest of the eight sons Milcah bore to Nahor, and he was the father of Rebekah and Laban (Gen 22:22–23). When Abraham's servant came to find a wife for Isaac, Rebekah introduced herself as Bethuel's daughter (Gen 24:24). Bethuel speaks only once, together with Laban, agreeing that the match came from the LORD (Gen 24:50). Even there Laban takes the more prominent role, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains by the custom of a brother looking after his sister's welfare. It also notes that Josephus says Bethuel was already dead by then. He is called "Bethuel the Syrian" of Padanaram. Later Isaac sent Jacob to "the house of Bethuel" to find a wife among Laban's daughters (Gen 25:20; 28:2, 5). The name is often taken to mean "dweller in God."

Bethul was a town given to the tribe of Simeon. It appears in Joshua's list of Simeon's towns, between Eltolad and Hormah (Josh 19:4). Simeon's towns lay within Judah's territory, so Bethul was probably in the southern region near Beersheba. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it to be the same place as Chesil in Judah's town list (Josh 15:30) and Bethuel in the parallel list of Simeon's towns (1 Chr 4:30). The name is usually explained as meaning "dweller in God." Its exact site has not been identified, and the location shown here is only a rough placement.

Betonim was a town east of the Jordan that Joshua 13 lists among the places marking the territory given to the tribe of Gad. It appears only once, in Josh 13:26, in a line running from Heshbon to Ramath-mizpeh and Betonim, and then from Mahanaim to the border of Debir. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it to lie apparently on Gad's northern boundary, and it was in the region of Gilead. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the same as Batneh (Khirbet Batneh), about 3 miles (5 km) southwest of es-Salt in modern Jordan. The location shown here follows that identification. The exact site remains uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "bellies."

Bezai was the ancestor of a family group listed among the exiles who returned from Babylonian captivity to Jerusalem and Judah with Zerubbabel. Nothing is recorded about Bezai himself. Only his descendants are counted. Ezra 2:17 gives their number as 323, while the parallel list in Neh 7:23 gives 324. Small differences like this between the two lists are common. Bezai probably stands for the head of a clan or family house rather than someone who made the journey himself. The name is shared by more than one person. A Bezai is also named in Neh 10:18 among the leaders who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah's time, probably a representative of the same family. The meaning of the name is uncertain: Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "conqueror" and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia tentatively suggests "shining."

Bezai was one of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, when the community that had returned from exile in Babylon committed itself in writing to keep the law of God. He is named in a list of the chiefs of the people (Neh 10:18) and nothing else is recorded about him. The name also belongs to a family whose members returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:17; Neh 7:23). The Bezai who sealed the covenant was probably the head of that family, signing on its behalf, though the text does not say so directly. The meaning of the name is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia tentatively suggests "shining," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "eggs."

Bezaleel was the chief craftsman who built the tabernacle and its furnishings during Israel's time in the wilderness. He was the son of Uri and grandson of Hur, of the tribe of Judah (Exod 31:2; 1 Chr 2:20). God is said to have called him by name for the work, and Moses announced this to the people (Exod 35:30). Together with Aholiab and other skilled workers, he carried out all the work of the sanctuary as the LORD had commanded Moses (Exod 36:1–2; 38:22). He made the ark of acacia wood (Exod 37:1), and the bronze altar he made still stood before the tabernacle in Solomon's day (2 Chr 1:5). Easton's Bible Dictionary says he worked mainly in metal, wood and stone, while Aholiab, under him, oversaw the textiles. The name is usually explained as "in the shadow of God." Another man of the same name appears in Ezra 10:30.

Bezaleel was one of the sons, or descendants, of Pahath-moab named in Ezra's list of men who had married foreign wives after the return from exile (Ezra 10:30). By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was among those who agreed to send away these wives and their children under the reform led by Ezra. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 458 BC, and the name is usually explained as meaning "in the shadow of God." Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with the better-known Bezaleel, the craftsman of the tabernacle in Exodus, or with others who share the name.

Bezek was a Canaanite town where the tribe of Judah defeated the Canaanites and Perizzites after the death of Joshua, killing ten thousand men (Judg 1:4). It was the home of its ruler, Adoni-bezek, whose name means "lord of Bezek." Judah found him there and fought against him (Judg 1:5). By context it lay within the territory allotted to Judah. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in the hill country not far from Jerusalem and probably at the modern Bezkah, southeast of Lydda. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia tentatively links it with Bezqah, northeast of Gezer. The location shown here follows the Bezqah identification. The name is shared by more than one place: a different Bezek appears as the site where Saul mustered Israel (1 Sam 11:8).

Bezek was the place where Saul counted the men of Israel and Judah who had answered his call to arms. 1 Sam 11:8 records 300,000 from Israel and 30,000 from Judah. The surrounding chapter shows the muster was gathered to rescue Jabesh-gilead, across the Jordan, from Nahash the Ammonite. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both place it in the centre of the country near the Jordan valley, which suits a march to Jabesh-gilead. Easton's identifies it with the modern Ibzik, about 13 miles north-east of Shechem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Eusebius mentions two villages of this name on the road from Shechem to Scythopolis, and links them with Khirbet Ibziq and the nearby height Ras Ibziq. The location shown here follows that identification. The name is shared with another Bezek, connected with Adoni-bezek in Judges 1, which may be a separate place.

Bezer was a city of the tribe of Reuben east of the Jordan, described as lying "in the wilderness, in the plain country," the high tableland east of the Dead Sea. It was one of three cities of refuge set apart east of the Jordan, along with Ramoth in Gilead and Golan in Bashan (Deut 4:43; Josh 20:8). It was also given with its surrounding pasturelands to the Levites, and the surrounding passage (Josh 21:34) shows these were the Merarite families. Its site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions the ruins of Burazin, about 12 miles north of Heshbon, and Kasur-el-Besheir near Dibon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a suggested link with Bozrah. The location shown here follows a Bozrah identification and places Bezer at Bosra in southern Syria. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "vine branches."

Bezer was a man of the tribe of Asher, named in the Asherite genealogy of 1 Chronicles as a son of Zophah. He appears in a list of eleven sons that includes Suah, Harnepher, Beri, Imrah, Hod, Shamma, Shilshah, Beera and Ulla. The verse that names him also names Ithran, and the next verse in the chapter mentions Jether. This entry treats the two as the same brother. By inference from the surrounding genealogy, Zophah was a son of Helem, which places Bezer in a line descending from Asher through Heber. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him among the heads of the houses of Asher. Nothing else is recorded about him. Reference works explain his name differently: "strong" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), "gold ore" (Smith's) or "vine branches" (Hitchcock's). He is distinct from Bezer, the city of refuge east of the Jordan.

Bichri was the father of Sheba, the Benjamite who led a revolt against King David soon after Absalom's rebellion. He is known only through his son, who is called "Sheba the son of Bichri" throughout 2 Samuel 20. Sheba sounded a trumpet and called Israel to abandon David. Joab's forces pursued him to a walled city, where its people cut off his head and threw it over the wall to Joab (2 Sam 20:1, 20:22). The name means "first-born" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Smith's Bible Dictionary calls Bichri an ancestor of Sheba rather than strictly his father. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may mean "descendant of Becher," linking the family to Becher, a son of Benjamin. This entry treats Bichri simply as Sheba's father, as the phrase "son of Bichri" most directly reads.

Bigtha was one of the seven chamberlains who served in the presence of King Ahasuerus of Persia, according to Esth 1:10. On the seventh day of the king's feast, when he was merry with wine, Ahasuerus ordered these seven men, Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, Abagtha, Zethar and Carcas, to bring Queen Vashti before him. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe the chamberlains as eunuchs who had charge of the king's harem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies Ahasuerus with Xerxes, and Smith's places the event about 483 BC. Bigtha is mentioned only in this verse. Some take him to be the same man as Bigthan, a palace official who later plotted against the king (Esth 2:21). The names are similar, but this entry treats Bigtha as the chamberlain of Esth 1:10 alone.

Bigthana, also spelled Bigthan, was one of King Ahasuerus's chamberlains who guarded the door of the palace in Persia. Esth 2:21 says that he and another doorkeeper, Teresh, became angry and plotted to attack the king while Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate. Mordecai learned of the plot and reported it. The following verses of the same chapter say the two men were hanged and the matter was written in the royal chronicles. Later, when the king could not sleep and had those records read to him, he found the account of how Mordecai had exposed Bigthana and Teresh (Esth 6:2). This led to Mordecai being honored. The King James Version calls him a chamberlain, and Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a eunuch. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "gift of God."

Bigvai was one of the leaders who returned from the Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel. He is named among the men listed at the head of the register of returning Israelites, alongside Jeshua, Nehemiah, Mordecai and others (Ezra 2:2; Neh 7:7). Nothing more is said of him personally in these verses. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to be one of the chiefs of Zerubbabel's expedition and connects him with the Bigvai whose family later signed the covenant (Neh 10:16). The same name also heads a large family of returnees in the lists, so it is uncertain whether all these mentions refer to one man or to a clan bearing his name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "in my body," while Smith's gives "happy."

Bigvai was the ancestor of a large family group that returned to Judah from exile in Babylon. The list of returnees who came back with Zerubbabel counts 2,056 of his descendants (Ezra 2:14), while the parallel list in Neh 7:19 gives 2,067. A later group of his descendants, led by Uthai and Zabbud with seventy other men, traveled to Jerusalem with Ezra (Ezra 8:14). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the first return to about 536 BC. The name was shared by several people. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links this ancestor with the Bigvai named among the leaders who came back with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:2; Neh 7:7). The verses here, however, name him only as the founder of a family, so whether he is the same man is uncertain.

Bigvai was one of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the written covenant made in the time of Nehemiah, in which the returned community of Judah pledged to keep the law of God (Neh 10:16). His name appears in the list of the "chief of the people" that begins at Neh 10:14, between Adonijah and Adin. Nothing more is told about him personally. The name Bigvai is shared by several people. It belongs to a leader who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel and to a large family of returned exiles (Ezra 2:2, 14; Neh 7:7, 19). Since many names in this list match family names from those earlier lists, this Bigvai probably signed as head or representative of that family, though this is an inference. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "in my body."

Bildad the Shuhite was one of Job's three friends, along with Eliphaz the Temanite and Zophar the Naamathite. When they heard of Job's disasters, they arranged to come together from their own homes to mourn with him and comfort him (Job 2:11). Bildad speaks in each of the three rounds of debate with Job, in Job 8, 18 and 25. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes his speeches as severe and stern. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that his third speech is the friends' last. "Shuhite" probably links him to Shuah, a region east or southeast of Israel, or to his ancestor Shuah, a son of Abraham by Keturah (Gen 25:2). The exact place is unknown. At the end of the book, Bildad and the other two friends do what the LORD commands them, and the LORD accepts Job's prayer for them (Job 42:9).

Bileam was a town in the territory of the half tribe of Manasseh west of the Jordan. It was given, with its surrounding pasturelands, to the remaining families of the Kohathite Levites (1 Chr 6:70). Bileam is named only in this verse. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes it to be probably the same town as Ibleam (Josh 17:11) and identifies it with the modern site of Bel'ameh, about half a mile south of Jenin. The location shown here follows that identification. Smith's Bible Dictionary also equates it with Gath-rimmon, which appears in the parallel list of Levitical towns in Josh 21:25. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the ancient of the people" or "the devourer."

Bilgah was a priest in the time of David and the head of the fifteenth of the twenty-four divisions, or courses, into which the priests were organized for service at the sanctuary. The lots were cast to set the order in which these priestly families would serve, and the fifteenth lot fell to Bilgah, just before Immer (1 Chr 24:14). Nothing else is recorded about him personally. The name appears again for other men, including a priest who returned from exile with Zerubbabel and one who sealed Nehemiah's covenant, the latter spelled Bilgai in the KJV. These later bearers may represent the same priestly family or division, but they are distinct individuals. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "ancient countenance," while Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "first-born."

Bilgah, also spelled Bilgai, was a priest, or the head of a priestly family, after the Babylonian exile. He appears among the priests who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel and Jeshua (Neh 12:5; the list begins at Neh 12:1). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this return to about 536 BC. A generation later, in the days of the high priest Joiakim, the family of Bilgah was headed by Shammua (Neh 12:18). Bilgai is named among the priests who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah's time (Neh 10:8). This entry follows the STEPBible Proper Names and Smith's Bible Dictionary in treating Bilgai as the same name. Because the covenant was sealed decades after the first return, that signature probably represents the family rather than the original priest. The name is also borne by the head of the fifteenth priestly division in David's time (1 Chr 24:14), a different person.

Bilhah was a town in the far south of Judah where descendants of Simeon lived. It is named in the list of Simeonite towns in 1 Chr 4:29, alongside Ezem and Tolad. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes it to be the same place as Baalah in Josh 15:29 and Balah in Josh 19:3, which appear in parallel lists of towns in southern Judah allotted to Simeon. The site has not been identified. The location shown here is a rough placement in the Negev region of southern Israel, based on its listing among other Simeonite towns. The town shares its name with Bilhah, Rachel's servant and the mother of Dan and Naphtali, but the verse gives no indication of any connection between them.

Bilhah was the servant woman whom Laban gave to his daughter Rachel as her maid when Rachel married Jacob (Gen 29:29). Because Rachel had no children, she gave Bilhah to Jacob as a wife so that she could have children through her (Gen 30:3–4). Bilhah bore Jacob two sons, Dan and Naphtali, about 1755 and 1754 BC by inference from context (Gen 30:5–7; Gen 35:25). Elsewhere she is called Jacob's concubine, and Genesis reports that Jacob's eldest son Reuben slept with her (Gen 35:22). Later Jacob alludes to this in his final words to Reuben (Gen 49:4), and Easton's Bible Dictionary connects it with Reuben's loss of the birthright. Her sons and Naphtali's sons are counted as her descendants, seven persons in all, among those who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:25; 1 Chr 7:13). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of her name as "timid" or "bashful."

Bilhan was a son of Ezer, named first among his three sons alongside Zaavan (Zavan) and Akan (Jakan) in the genealogy of Gen 36:27, which is repeated in 1 Chr 1:42. From the surrounding chapter, Ezer was one of the sons of Seir the Horite, so Bilhan belonged to the Horite clans living in the land of Seir, later Edom, before and alongside Esau's descendants. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Horite chief dwelling in Mount Seir, and the STEPBible proper names index counts him among the chiefs of Edom. Nothing else is recorded about him. The spellings of his brothers' names differ slightly between the two lists. The name is shared by at least one other man, a Benjamite in a later genealogy, who is a different person.

Bilhan was a member of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 7:10 as the son of Jediael. That verse lists his seven sons: Jeush, Benjamin, Ehud, Chenaanah, Zethan, Tharshish and Ahishahar. His son Benjamin bears the same name as the tribe's ancestor, and his son Ehud should not be confused with the judge Ehud son of Gera. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes his sons as heads of houses within their tribe, by inference from the surrounding passage, which counts Jediael's descendants as fighting men. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name Bilhan is also borne by a Horite chief descended from Seir, a different person.

Bilshan was one of the leaders who returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel. He appears in the list of men at the head of the returning Israelites, given in Ezra 2:2 and repeated in Neh 7:7. In both lists he comes right after Mordecai. Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary explain the name as meaning "eloquent." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes other possible meanings and records that 1 Esdras calls him Beelsarus. It also notes that rabbinic tradition read Bilshan as a surname of the Mordecai named just before him. Smith's dates the return to about 536 BC.

Bimhal was a man of the tribe of Asher, named in 1 Chr 7:33 as one of the three sons of Japhlet, along with his brothers Pasach and Ashvath. He appears only in this genealogy of Asher's descendants, and nothing else is recorded about his life. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "circumcised."

Binea was a man of the tribe of Benjamin and a descendant of King Saul. He appears only in the two parallel genealogies of Saul's family, where he is named as the son of Moza (1 Chr 8:37; 1 Chr 9:43). Following the line back through these lists, Moza descended from Saul's son Jonathan through Jonathan's son Merib-baal, also known as Mephibosheth. After Binea the lists name Rapha, called Rephaiah in 1 Chr 9:43, then Eleasah, then Azel. This entry treats all three as his children. However, the repeated phrase "his son" can also be read as a chain of successive generations, with Rephaiah as Binea's son, Eleasah as Rephaiah's son, and Azel as Eleasah's son. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "son of the Lord". Nothing else is recorded about him.

Binnui was a Levite of the time of Ezra, known only as the father of Noadiah. According to Ezra 8:33, on the fourth day after Ezra's company arrived in Jerusalem from Babylon, the silver, gold and vessels they had brought for the temple were weighed in the house of God. This was done under the priest Meremoth son of Uriah, with Eleazar son of Phinehas, and with the Levites Jozabad son of Jeshua and Noadiah son of Binnui. The verse gives no further details about Binnui himself. Several other men named Binnui appear in Ezra and Nehemiah, and whether any of them is the same person is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats this Binnui as a separate Levite, and this entry follows that view. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "building."

Binnui was one of the descendants of Pahath-moab named in Ezra 10:30. He appears in the list of men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra, after the return from exile in Babylon. By inference from the surrounding passage, the men on this list agreed to send away their foreign wives as part of Ezra's reforms, and the STEPBible Proper Names index describes him this way. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah bear the same name, so he should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "building," while Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "familyship."

Binnui was an Israelite named in Ezra 10:38 among the men who had married foreign wives in the period after the return from exile in Babylon. By inference from the surrounding list, which is introduced as "the sons of Bani" a few verses earlier, he belonged to that family group. TIPNR describes him the same way and says he divorced his foreign wife during Ezra's reforms, which is what the men in this list pledged to do. Nothing else is recorded about him. Some translations read the words "Bani, and Binnui" in this verse as "of the sons of Binnui," which would make Binnui the head of a family rather than an individual. This entry follows the King James reading, which treats him as one person. Several other men in Ezra and Nehemiah share the name, and it is uncertain whether any of them is the same man. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "building."

Binnui was the son of Henadad and one of the workers who rebuilt Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah after the return from exile. Nehemiah 3:24 says he repaired a section of the wall running from the house of Azariah to the turning of the wall at the corner. Several men in the Bible bear this name, so his identity beyond this verse is uncertain. Neh 10:9 lists a Levite named Binnui "of the sons of Henadad" among those who sealed the covenant, and Neh 3:18 names a Bavai son of Henadad among the builders. Either or both may be the same man, which would suggest he belonged to a Levite family descended from Henadad, though this is only an inference. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "building."

Binnui was a Levite of the period after the return from exile in Babylon. Nehemiah 10 names him among the Levites who set their seal to the covenant made under Nehemiah, identifying him as one of the sons of Henadad (Neh 10:9). A Binnui also appears in the list of Levites in Neh 12:8, alongside Jeshua and Kadmiel. That list, by its context, names those who came up from exile with Zerubbabel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats both mentions, together with Ezra 8:33, as the same man, a Levite of Ezra's time, and this entry follows that view. STEPBible's proper-name index links him with Bani, a Levite who helped teach the Law and lead prayers in Nehemiah's day. Because several men bear this name, the identification is not certain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "building."

Birsha was the king of Gomorrah in the time of Abraham. He is named only once, in Gen 14:2, among five kings of the cities of the plain: Bera of Sodom, Birsha of Gomorrah, Shinab of Admah, Shemeber of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela, also called Zoar. The kings Chedorlaomer, Amraphel, Arioch and Tidal made war against these five. The rest of the chapter describes the battle in the vale of Siddim, the defeat of Sodom and Gomorrah, and Abram's rescue of his nephew Lot. By inference, Birsha was among the kings who fled that battle, though he is not named again. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "son of wickedness." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may have been altered in transmission, or chosen by the writer to mean "with wickedness."

The Birth of Abraham was the birth of Abram, later renamed Abraham (Gen 17:5), to Terah. Genesis lists him first among Terah's sons, alongside Nahor and Haran, the father of Lot (Gen 11:26–27). The family lived in Ur of the Chaldees, which they later left for Haran (Gen 11:28, 31), so he was probably born there. Gen 11:26 says Terah was seventy when he began fathering these sons, but they need not have been born in the same year. Terah died in Haran at 205 (Gen 11:32). Abram left Haran at 75 (Gen 12:4), and Acts 7:4 places that departure after his father's death. Reading these together, this entry has Abraham born when Terah was about 130. That puts his birth at about 1996 BC, a date inferred from context rather than stated in the text.

The Birth of Arphaxad is recorded at the opening of Shem's line of descendants in Gen 11:10. It states that Shem was a hundred years old when he fathered Arphaxad, two years after the flood. Arphaxad is the first son named in this genealogy, which traces Shem's descendants down to Abram, and he is the link through which that line continues. Elsewhere Arphaxad also appears among the sons of Shem in the table of nations (Gen 10:22), and Luke 3:36 includes him in the ancestry of Jesus. The date of about 2346 BC is an estimate inferred from the ages given in the genealogy, counting a hundred years from Shem's birth. It is not stated in the text.

The Birth of Asher was the birth of Jacob's eighth son, the second son borne to him by Zilpah, Leah's maid. Leah had given Zilpah to Jacob after she stopped bearing children, and Zilpah's first son was Gad, born just before (Gen 30:9–11). Because a son of her maid was counted as Leah's own, it was Leah who named the child. She said, "Happy am I, for the daughters will call me blessed," and called him Asher, a name usually understood to mean "happy" or "blessed" and matching her words. The birth took place while Jacob was living in Haran in the household of Laban, during the rivalry between Leah and Rachel over bearing children. Asher later became the ancestor of the tribe of Asher. This entry dates the event to about 1752 BC, by inference from context.

The Birth of Cainan was the birth of the antediluvian patriarch Cainan to his father Enos, the son of Seth. Genesis 5:9 records that Enos was ninety years old when he fathered Cainan. Counting from the birth of Enos, this places the event at about 3679 BC, a date inferred from the Genesis chronology rather than stated in the text. The same person appears as Kenan in the genealogy of 1 Chr 1:2, which lists him between Enos and Mahalaleel. Luke 3:37 includes him in the ancestry of Jesus as the father of Maleleel (Mahalaleel). He should not be confused with a second Cainan in Luke's genealogy, who lived after the flood.

The Birth of Caleb is not described in the Bible, but it is implied by his appearance as an adult in Numbers 13, where he is introduced as "Caleb the son of Jephunneh" of the tribe of Judah, chosen as one of the twelve men Moses sent to explore Canaan. He was therefore born into the tribe of Judah as the son of Jephunneh, probably during Israel's time in Egypt. Later, in Josh 14:7, Caleb says he was forty years old when Moses sent him out from Kadesh-barnea. That statement is the basis for estimating his birth year, placed here at about 1529 BC by inference from context. Nothing is recorded about his mother, his birthplace, or the circumstances of his birth.

The Birth of Dan was the birth of Jacob's fifth son, the first born to Bilhah, the servant of his wife Rachel. In the surrounding passage (Gen 30:1–5), Rachel has no children and gives Bilhah to Jacob so that she might have children through her. When Bilhah bears a son, Rachel names him and explains the name: "God hath judged me, and hath also heard my voice, and hath given me a son" (Gen 30:6). The name Dan is linked to the Hebrew word for judging, so Rachel's words act as a play on the name. The event took place during Jacob's years serving Laban in Haran, about 1755 BC by inference from context. Dan later became the ancestor of the Israelite tribe that bore his name.

The Birth of Dinah was the birth of a daughter to Leah, Jacob's first wife, recorded briefly in Gen 30:21. After bearing her sixth son, Zebulun, Leah "afterwards" bore a daughter and named her Dinah. Unlike the births of Jacob's sons, this one is not paired with an explanation of the name. By inference from the surrounding chapter, it took place during Jacob's years serving his father-in-law Laban in Haran, while his wives and their maids were bearing his children. The date given here, about 1750 BC, is an estimate inferred from context. Dinah is the only daughter of Jacob named in the narrative. She appears again in Gen 34, where her encounter with Shechem and her brothers' revenge on that city are told, and she is listed among Jacob's household that went down to Egypt in Gen 46:15.

The Birth of Eber was the birth of Eber to his father Salah, recorded in the genealogy of Shem's descendants. Genesis 11:14 states that Salah was thirty years old when he became Eber's father. The date of about 2281 BC is an estimate inferred from the ages given in this genealogy, placing the event thirty years after the Birth of Salah. The following verses of the same genealogy say that Eber later fathered Peleg and lived a long life afterward. Eber's name is often linked with the term "Hebrew," and the earlier Table of Nations calls Shem "the father of all the children of Eber" (Gen 10:21). He is also listed among the ancestors of Jesus as "Heber" in Luke's genealogy (Luke 3:35).

The Birth of Enoch was the birth of a son to Jared in the genealogy of Adam's descendants through Seth. Genesis 5:18 records that Jared was 162 years old when he fathered Enoch. This entry dates the event to about 3382 BC, an estimate inferred from the ages given in the genealogy. This Enoch is the father of Methuselah and should not be confused with Enoch the son of Cain, after whom Cain named a city (Gen 4:17). The verses that follow in the same chapter say that Enoch fathered Methuselah at 65, "walked with God," and after 365 years "was not; for God took him" (Gen 5:21–24). The birth itself is recorded only in the standard formula of the genealogy, with no further detail.

The Birth of Enos was the birth of a son to Seth, the son of Adam. Seth named the child Enos, and Genesis notes that from that time people began to call on the name of the LORD (Gen 4:26). The genealogy in Genesis 5 records that Seth was 105 years old when Enos was born (Gen 5:6). This places the birth about 3769 BC, an estimate inferred from the ages given in the genealogy and about 105 years after Seth's own birth. Enos appears as the third name in the line running from Adam through Seth, a line that 1 Chronicles repeats with the spellings Sheth and Enosh (1 Chr 1:1).

The Birth of Gad was the birth of Jacob's seventh son, born to Zilpah, the maid of Jacob's wife Leah. In Gen 30:10–11 Zilpah bears Jacob a son, and Leah names him Gad, saying "A troop cometh." The name is usually connected with good fortune or with a band of fighters. The surrounding chapter explains the background: Leah had stopped bearing children and gave Zilpah to Jacob as a wife, so that children born to her maid would count as her own, much as Rachel had done with her maid Bilhah. Gad later became the ancestor of the tribe of Gad, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. The event took place in Haran while Jacob was serving his uncle Laban, probably about 1753 BC by inference from context.

The Birth of Isaac was the birth of a son to Abraham and his wife Sarah, fulfilling a promise God had made to Abraham. In Gen 17:19 God told Abraham that Sarah would bear him a son, that he was to name the child Isaac, and that God would establish his covenant with Isaac and his descendants as an everlasting covenant. When the son was born, Abraham gave him the name Isaac, as he had been told (Gen 21:3). The surrounding chapters of Genesis describe both parents as very old at the time, Abraham about a hundred and Sarah about ninety, which made the birth remarkable within the narrative. This entry places the birth at about 1896 BC, a date inferred from context rather than stated in the text. The event begins the account of Isaac's life.

The Birth of Ishmael was the birth of a son to Abram and Hagar, recorded in Genesis 16. Earlier in the chapter Hagar, an Egyptian servant, was given to Abram by his wife Sarai because Sarai had no children, and Hagar later fled from Sarai's harsh treatment. Before the birth, the angel of the LORD met Hagar in the wilderness and told her she would bear a son and name him Ishmael, "because the LORD hath heard thy affliction." The angel also said he would be a "wild man," at odds with everyone yet living near his brothers. Hagar called the LORD "Thou God seest me," and the well where this happened became known as Beer-lahai-roi, between Kadesh and Bered. Hagar bore the son, and Abram named him Ishmael. Abram was 86 years old at the time, which places the birth at about 1910 BC by inference from context.

The Birth of Issachar was the birth of Jacob's fifth son by Leah, recorded in Gen 30:17–18. The text says God listened to Leah and she conceived. Leah explained the name by saying God had given her her "hire" (reward) because she had given her maidservant Zilpah to Jacob as a wife. The name Issachar sounds like the Hebrew word for wages or hire. The surrounding passage adds another sense of "hire": just before, Leah had bargained with Rachel, trading her son Reuben's mandrakes for a night with Jacob, and told him she had "hired" him (Gen 30:14–16). Counting the sons born to the maidservants Bilhah and Zilpah, Issachar was Jacob's ninth son. He became the ancestor of the tribe of Issachar. This entry dates the birth to about 1752 BC, an estimate inferred from context.

The Birth of Jacob and Esau was the delivery of twin sons to Rebekah, wife of Isaac. When her time came, she was found to be carrying twins. The first to be born was red and covered with hair "like a hairy garment," and he was named Esau. His brother followed, holding on to Esau's heel, and he was named Jacob, a name the surrounding narrative links with the heel. Isaac was sixty years old at the time. The verses just before this passage describe the twins struggling in the womb and a divine word to Rebekah that the older would serve the younger, which foreshadows their later rivalry. Esau later became the ancestor of Edom, and Jacob, renamed Israel, the ancestor of the Israelites. This entry dates the birth to about 1836 BC, an estimate inferred from context.

The Birth of Jared was the birth of Jared to Mahalaleel, a descendant of Adam through Seth, in the genealogy of Genesis 5. According to Gen 5:15, Mahalaleel was sixty-five years old when Jared was born. Jared is the sixth generation from Adam in this line, which runs from Adam through Seth, Enos, Cainan and Mahalaleel. The same chapter goes on to record that Jared became the father of Enoch and that his line later led to Methuselah and Noah. This entry dates the birth to about 3544 BC, an estimate reached by adding up the ages given in the genealogy, about sixty-five years after the birth of Mahalaleel. Systems for counting these years differ, so any such date is approximate.

The Birth of Jesus was the event, recounted in Luke 2, in which Mary gave birth to her firstborn son in Bethlehem, the city of David. A census ordered by Caesar Augustus, taken when Cyrenius (Quirinius) was governor of Syria, brought Joseph, a descendant of David, from Nazareth in Galilee to Bethlehem with Mary, who was pregnant. She wrapped the baby in swaddling clothes and laid him in a manger because there was no room in the inn. That night an angel announced to nearby shepherds that a Saviour, Christ the Lord, had been born, and a multitude of angels praised God. The shepherds hurried to find the child, then spread the news, while Mary kept these things in her heart. Matthew's account (Matt 2:1) also places the birth in Bethlehem, in the days of Herod. This entry dates it to about 4 BC, an estimate inferred from context.

The Birth of Job refers to the birth of Job, a son of Issachar and grandson of Jacob. He appears third among Issachar's four sons, after Tola and Phuvah and before Shimron, in the list of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:13). No account of the birth itself is recorded. That he is named in this list implies he was born before the move to Egypt, probably in Canaan. The date of about 1720 BC is an estimate inferred from context. In the parallel lists of Issachar's sons (Num 26:24; 1 Chr 7:1) the same son is called Jashub, so the two names probably refer to one person. He is a different person from Job of the Book of Job, whose name is spelled differently in Hebrew.

The Birth of John the Baptist is the account in Luke 1:57–80 of the son born to the elderly Elisabeth and her husband Zacharias, a priest. It is dated here to about 5 BC, by inference from context, and follows Mary's visit to Elisabeth. Neighbours and relatives rejoiced with her. At his circumcision on the eighth day they wanted to name the child Zacharias after his father, but Elisabeth said he would be called John. When they asked his father by signs, Zacharias wrote, "His name is John." At once he was able to speak again. Earlier in the chapter he had been made unable to speak for doubting the angel's message (Luke 1:20). News of these events spread through the hill country of Judea. Zacharias then prophesied, blessing God for redeeming his people and declaring that the child would be called the prophet of the Highest, going before the Lord to prepare his ways. John grew up and lived in the wilderness until he appeared publicly to Israel.

The Birth of Joseph was the event in which Rachel, Jacob's long-childless wife, gave birth to her first son. On delivering him she said that God had taken away her reproach, the shame of being barren, and she named him Joseph, adding, "The LORD shall add to me another son." The name sounds like the Hebrew word for "add," and it also echoes the word for "taken away" in her first remark. By inference from the surrounding chapter, the birth took place while Jacob was still serving his uncle Laban in Paddan-aram, since right after it Jacob asks Laban to let him return home (Gen 30:25). Rachel's hope for another son was later fulfilled in Benjamin, at whose birth she died (Gen 35:16–18). This entry dates the birth to about 1745 BC, an estimate inferred from context. Joseph's birth opens the story of his life, much of which was later spent in Egypt.

The Birth of Judah was the birth of the fourth son of Jacob and Leah, recorded in Gen 29:35. Leah conceived again and bore a son, and she named him Judah, saying, "Now will I praise the LORD." The name is linked in the text to praise. After his birth Leah stopped bearing children for a time. By inference from the preceding verses, Judah followed his brothers Reuben, Simeon and Levi, all born to Leah while Jacob was living in Haran and serving his uncle Laban. Later chapters record that Leah bore further children (Gen 30). Judah went on to become the ancestor of the tribe of Judah. The date of about 1755 BC is an estimate inferred from context and is not stated in the text.

The Birth of Lamech was the birth of Methuselah's son Lamech, recorded in the genealogy from Adam to Noah in Genesis 5. According to Gen 5:25, Methuselah was 187 years old when he fathered Lamech. This entry dates the event to about 3130 BC, an estimate inferred from the ages given in the genealogy rather than a date stated in the text. The surrounding passage goes on to say that Lamech later became the father of Noah (Gen 5:28–29). This Lamech, in Seth's line, is a different person from the Lamech descended from Cain who is mentioned in Gen 4:18–24.

The Birth of Levi was the birth of Leah's third son by Jacob, recorded in Gen 29:34. After bearing him, Leah said that now her husband would be "joined" to her because she had given him three sons, and so the child was named Levi. The name is linked to that hope of attachment, a wordplay on the Hebrew verb for "join". By inference from the surrounding passage, the birth took place in Haran while Jacob was serving his uncle Laban, after the births of Reuben and Simeon and before Judah. This entry dates it to about 1756 BC, an estimate inferred from context. Levi became the ancestor of the tribe of Levi, which later passages present as the priestly tribe of Israel, the line of Moses, Aaron and the Levites.

The Birth of Mahlaleel was the birth of Mahalaleel, son of Cainan, in the line of Seth recorded in the genealogy of Genesis 5. Gen 5:12 states that Cainan was seventy years old when he fathered him. The spelling varies: Genesis uses Mahalaleel, 1 Chr 1:2 lists him the same way, and Luke 3:37 gives the name as Maleleel in Jesus' genealogy. The date of about 3609 BC is an estimate made by adding up the ages in the Genesis 5 genealogy. On that count it came about seventy years after the birth of Cainan. The surrounding verses say Cainan lived another 840 years and had other sons and daughters. Mahalaleel himself later fathered Jared at sixty-five (Gen 5:15), continuing the line toward Enoch and Noah.

The Birth of Methuselah was the birth of a son to Enoch when Enoch was sixty-five years old, as recorded in the genealogy from Adam to Noah in Genesis 5. This entry dates it to about 3317 BC, by inference from the ages given in the genealogy, some sixty-five years after the birth of Enoch himself. The surrounding verses go on to say that Enoch walked with God for three hundred years after Methuselah was born and had other sons and daughters. Methuselah later became the father of Lamech and the grandfather of Noah. Genesis 5:27 gives his lifespan as 969 years, the longest recorded in the Bible.

The Birth of Moses is the account in Exod 2:1–10 of how Moses was born and saved in Egypt. A Levite man married a Levite woman, named in Exod 6:20 as Amram and Jochebed. His mother hid her healthy baby for three months, apparently because of Pharaoh's order to throw Hebrew boys into the Nile (Exod 1:22). When she could hide him no longer, she sealed a basket of bulrushes with tar and pitch and set him among the reeds at the river's edge. His sister, probably Miriam (Num 26:59), watched from a distance. Pharaoh's daughter found the crying child, recognized him as a Hebrew and pitied him. The sister offered to find a Hebrew nurse and brought the baby's own mother, who was paid to nurse him. Later the boy became the princess's son, and she named him Moses because she had drawn him out of the water. By inference from context, the birth is dated about 1571 BC.

The Birth of Nahor was the birth of a son to Serug when Serug was thirty years old, recorded in the genealogy of Shem in Gen 11:22. The passage says only that Serug lived thirty years and fathered Nahor. The following verses (Gen 11:24–25) say Nahor later became the father of Terah, which makes him the grandfather of Abram, Nahor, and Haran (Gen 11:26). He should not be confused with his grandson of the same name, Abram's brother. This entry dates the birth to about 2155 BC, thirty years after the birth of Serug. That figure is an estimate worked out from the ages given in the genealogy, not a date stated in the text.

The Birth of Naphtali was the birth of Jacob's second son by Bilhah, Rachel's maid. Rachel, who had no children of her own at the time, had given Bilhah to Jacob so that Bilhah's children would count as hers, and Bilhah had already borne Dan. When Bilhah conceived again and bore a second son, Rachel named him Naphtali, saying that she had wrestled mightily with her sister Leah and had prevailed (Gen 30:8). The name is generally understood to mean "my wrestling," reflecting that rivalry. Naphtali later became the ancestor of one of the tribes of Israel. The date of about 1754 BC is an estimate inferred from context, not stated in the text.

The Birth of Noah was the birth of a son to Lamech when Lamech was 182 years old, as recorded in the genealogy of Genesis 5. Lamech named the boy Noah, explaining that this son would bring comfort from the hard work and toil of farming ground the LORD had cursed. The explanation plays on the Hebrew name, which sounds like the word for rest or comfort. It also looks back to the curse on the ground after Adam's disobedience in Gen 3:17. This entry dates the birth to about 2948 BC, by inference from the ages given in the genealogy. That would be about 182 years after the birth of Lamech himself. Noah's birth begins his lifetime, which later includes the building of the ark and the flood narrated in the following chapters of Genesis.

The Birth of Peleg was the birth of Peleg to his father Eber, a descendant of Shem, recorded in the genealogy running from Shem to Abram. Genesis 11:16 states that Eber was thirty-four years old when Peleg was born. Counting through the ages given in this genealogy places the birth at about 2247 BC, an estimate inferred from context. That is thirty-four years after the Birth of Eber, which this entry dates to about 2281 BC. The earlier table of nations in Gen 10:25 explains the name. Peleg was so called because "in his days was the earth divided," and that passage also names his brother Joktan. Peleg's line continues through Reu and on toward Abram.

The Birth of Perez was the delivery of twin sons to Tamar, fathered by Judah, her father-in-law, as told in Genesis 38. During labor one twin, Zerah, put out his hand first, and the midwife tied a scarlet thread on it to mark him as the firstborn (Gen 38:27–28, by context). He then drew his hand back, and his brother came out first instead. The midwife exclaimed, "How hast thou broken forth?" so he was named Pharez, or Perez, which means "breach" or "breaking out" (Gen 38:29). Later passages trace Judah's line through Perez, including the genealogy of David in Ruth 4:18–22 and of Jesus in Matt 1:3. This entry dates the birth to about 1721 BC, an estimate inferred from context.

The Birth of Reu is recorded in the genealogy of Shem in Genesis 11. Gen 11:18 states that Peleg was thirty years old when he became the father of Reu. This places Reu in the line running from Shem to Abram, and the same chapter goes on to trace his descendants through Serug, Nahor and Terah. The verse gives Peleg's age at the birth but no other details about the event. The date of about 2217 BC is an estimate inferred from the ages given in the genealogy, about thirty years after the birth of Peleg. The name Reu appears again in the parallel genealogies of 1 Chr 1:25 and, as Ragau, in Luke 3:35.

The Birth of Reuben was the birth of the first son of Jacob and his wife Leah, recorded in Gen 29:32. Leah named him Reuben, explaining that the LORD had looked on her affliction and that now her husband would love her. The name sounds like the Hebrew for "see, a son," which matches her words about God seeing her. The surrounding passage explains her hope. Jacob loved her sister Rachel more than her, and the preceding verse says the LORD opened Leah's womb because she was unloved. Later passages such as Gen 35:23 and Gen 49:3 call Reuben Jacob's firstborn, so this birth began the family of twelve sons whose descendants became the tribes of Israel. It took place in Haran while Jacob was serving Laban, probably about 1758 BC by inference from context.

The Birth of Salah was the birth of Salah to Arphaxad, son of Shem, when Arphaxad was thirty-five years old (Gen 11:12). It is one link in the genealogy that runs from Shem after the flood down to Abram. This entry places it about 2311 BC, inferred from the ages given in the genealogy, roughly thirty-five years after the birth of Arphaxad. The surrounding verses say that Arphaxad lived 403 more years and had other sons and daughters, and that Salah later became the father of Eber (Gen 11:13–14). Salah also appears in the table of nations (Gen 10:24) and in 1 Chr 1:18. Luke's genealogy of Jesus names him Sala and places a Cainan between Arphaxad and Sala (Luke 3:35–36).

The Birth of Saul refers to the birth of the man who became Israel's first king. The Bible gives no account of the birth itself. It introduces Saul only as an adult, the son of Kish, a Benjamite named in the verse just before (1 Sam 9:1). He is described as a choice and handsome young man, the most impressive in Israel, standing head and shoulders above everyone else (1 Sam 9:2). This entry places his birth at about 1135 BC, a date inferred from the chronology of his later reign rather than stated in the text. Saul's exact age when he became king is uncertain, because the Hebrew text of 1 Sam 13:1 is unclear. His birth belongs to the background of the United Kingdom, the period when Israel was ruled by a single king, beginning with Saul.

The Birth of Serug was the birth of a son to Reu, recorded in the genealogy of Shem's descendants that leads from Noah's family to Abram. Genesis 11:20 states that Reu was thirty-two years old when Serug was born. By inference from the ages given in this chain of fathers and sons, the birth is dated here to about 2185 BC, roughly thirty-two years after the Birth of Reu. The surrounding verses go on to say that Serug later fathered Nahor, the grandfather of Abram, which places Serug in the direct line from Shem to Abraham. The parallel genealogy in 1 Chr 1:26 and the one in Luke 3:35, where the name appears as Saruch, also list him. The passage records nothing about the event beyond the father's age and the son's name.

The Birth of Seth was the birth of the third son of Adam and Eve named in Genesis, after the murder of Abel by Cain. Eve named him Seth, saying that God had appointed her another child in place of Abel (Gen 4:25). The Hebrew name sounds like the word for "appointed." Genesis 5:3 records that Adam was 130 years old when Seth was born, a son "in his own likeness, after his image," and here Adam is said to name him. From these figures the birth is dated to about 3874 BC, by inference from the chronology of Genesis. This entry places the event in the region of Eden, though the text does not name a location. Seth's line continues through his son Enosh, and he appears as "Sheth" in the genealogy of 1 Chr 1:1 and in Luke's genealogy of Jesus (Luke 3:38).

The Birth of Shem was the birth of Noah's son Shem, listed first among Noah's three sons in Gen 5:32, which says that Noah was five hundred years old and fathered Shem, Ham and Japheth. The verse gives Noah's age when his sons began to be born, but the three were not necessarily born in the same year. By inference from Gen 11:10, which says Shem was a hundred years old two years after the flood, and Gen 7:6, which places the flood in Noah's six hundredth year, Shem was born when Noah was about 502. That places the birth around 2446 BC, an estimate from the biblical chronology rather than a date the text states. The birth falls within the line of descent from Adam traced in Genesis 5 and begins the lifetime of Shem, whose descendants are followed in Genesis 10 and 11.

The Birth of Terah was the birth of Terah to his father Nahor, recorded in the genealogy of Shem's descendants in Genesis 11. According to Gen 11:24, Nahor was twenty-nine years old when Terah was born. This entry dates the event to about 2126 BC, an estimate reached by adding up the ages given in the genealogy rather than a date stated in the text. It follows the Birth of Nahor in the same line of descent. The surrounding passage goes on to say that Terah later became the father of Abram, Nahor and Haran (Gen 11:26). This made his birth a link between the line of Shem and the family of Abraham.

The Birth of Zebulon was the birth of Leah's sixth son by Jacob, recorded in Gen 30:19–20. After the birth, Leah said that God had given her a good dowry. She expressed the hope that her husband would now live with her, since she had borne him six sons, and she named the child Zebulun. The name is usually linked to the Hebrew word for "dwell" in her statement, and some also connect it with the word for "dowry." The account belongs to the wider story of the rivalry between Leah and her sister Rachel over Jacob's affection, carried on through the births of their children. The event is dated here to about 1751 BC, an estimate inferred from context. Zebulun later became the ancestor of one of the tribes of Israel.

Birzavith is named in the genealogy of the tribe of Asher as the child of Malchiel, who was a son of Beriah and grandson of Asher (1 Chr 7:31). She is mentioned only in this one verse, and nothing else is recorded about her. This entry treats Birzavith as a woman, Malchiel's daughter. Some readers take the name instead as a place. In the Chronicles genealogies, "father of" can mean the founder or leading figure of a town, and STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) notes that Birzaith may have been a town connected with Malchiel. Smith's Bible Dictionary simply describes it as a name in the genealogies of Asher. The spelling also varies, with Birzaith given as an alternative form.

Bishlam was one of the men who, in the days of Artaxerxes king of Persia, wrote a letter to the king with Mithredath, Tabeel and their companions (Ezra 4:7). The letter was written in Aramaic, which the King James Version calls "the Syrian tongue." From the surrounding chapter, which describes opposition to the Jews returning from exile, the letter was probably a complaint against them. The STEPBible Proper Names index describes him as a Samaritan official who opposed the rebuilding of Jerusalem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats him as one of three foreign colonists and notes that 1 Esdras gives the name as Belemus. The name may mean "in peace," and the Greek Septuagint renders the word as that phrase rather than as a name. This entry follows the reading of Bishlam as a personal name. Nothing else is known about him.

Bithiah was a daughter of Pharaoh who married Mered, a descendant of Judah, and appears only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:18. Her children are named as Miriam, Shammai and Ishbah the father of Eshtemoa. They are listed in the preceding verse, and by inference from the passage's phrase "these are the sons of Bithiah" that list belongs to her. Mered also had a wife called Jehudijah. The Revised Version renders this name "the Jewess," which sets her apart from the Egyptian Bithiah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that "Pharaoh" could mean an Egyptian king or could be a Hebrew personal name. This entry follows the more common reading of an Egyptian princess. Her name means "daughter of the Lord" (Hitchcock's Bible Names; Smith's Bible Dictionary), which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes to suggest she had adopted the worship of Israel's God.

Bithynia was a Roman province in northwestern Asia Minor, along the southern shores of the Black Sea and the Sea of Marmara, in what is now northwestern Turkey. On Paul's second missionary journey, after reaching Mysia, Paul and his companions tried to enter Bithynia, but the Spirit did not allow them (Acts 16:7). Bithynia is later one of the regions named in the greeting of 1 Peter, addressed to scattered believers in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia (1 Pet 1:1), which suggests Christian communities had formed there early. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the Roman governor Pliny, who ruled the province in the early second century, wrote to the emperor Trajan asking how to deal with the many Christians brought before him. Smith's Bible Dictionary names Nicaea as its chief town. The location shown here marks the general region rather than a single site.

Biziothiah (spelled Bizjothjah in the King James Version) was a town in the far south of Judah, listed in Josh 15:28 next to Hazarshual and Beersheba among the towns in the Negev given to the tribe of Judah. It appears nowhere else. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint reads "and her villages" (or "daughters") here, a difference of one Hebrew consonant. On that reading the word refers to the villages around Beersheba rather than a separate town, and the parallel list in Neh 11:27, which mentions "Beersheba, and in the villages thereof," fits that reading. This entry treats it as a place near Beersheba, following the Hebrew text. Its exact site is unknown, and the location shown here is only a rough placement in the Beersheba area.

Biztha was one of the seven chamberlains who served in the presence of King Ahasuerus of Persia, and the second named in the list in Esth 1:10. On the seventh day of the king's feast, when Ahasuerus was merry with wine, he sent these seven men to bring Queen Vashti before him. The word translated "chamberlains" usually means eunuchs, and Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both describe Biztha as a eunuch of the royal household. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies Ahasuerus with Xerxes and suggests the name may come from a Persian word meaning "bound," and so "eunuch." Smith's dates the event to about 483 BC. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Blastus was the chamberlain, or personal attendant, of King Herod in Acts 12:20. This Herod is identified as Herod Agrippa I by Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries. When Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon, they came to him together and asked for peace, because their land depended on the king's territory for its food supply. To do this they first won Blastus over as their friend, so that he could act as their go-between with the king. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests they probably gained his help with a bribe, though the text does not say how. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that such officials usually had great influence with their masters. Blastus is mentioned nowhere else in the Bible. His name is Greek and is usually explained as meaning "sprout" or "shoot."

event: Blind and Dumb Demoniac and Following Discourse
text: The Blind and Dumb Demoniac and Following Discourse was the occasion when Jesus healed a man possessed by a demon who could neither see nor speak, so that he both spoke and saw. Pharisees, and scribes who had come down from Jerusalem, claimed he cast out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons. Jesus answered that a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand, asked by whom their own followers cast demons out, and spoke of binding the strong man before plundering his house. He warned that blasphemy against the Holy Spirit would not be forgiven and that people would give account for every idle word. When some asked for a sign, he said only the sign of Jonah would be given. While he was still speaking, his mother and brothers arrived and stood outside. The setting is placed in Capernaum, and the date is about AD 28, both by inference from context. Luke's account may record a separate occasion.

Blind Man Healed is the account in John 9 of Jesus giving sight to a man blind from birth, dated to about AD 29 by inference from context. When his disciples asked whose sin had caused the blindness, Jesus said neither the man nor his parents had sinned. He then made clay with his saliva, put it on the man's eyes, and sent him to wash in the pool of Siloam, probably in Jerusalem. The man came back able to see. Because it was the Sabbath, the Pharisees questioned him and were divided about Jesus. They also questioned his parents, who answered cautiously for fear of being put out of the synagogue. The man insisted that Jesus must be from God, and they cast him out. Jesus then found him, and the man believed and worshipped him. The passage ends with Jesus' exchange with the Pharisees about who is blind.

Boaz (Greek form Booz) was a wealthy landowner of Bethlehem in the tribe of Judah and a relative of Elimelech, the late husband of Naomi. When Naomi's widowed Moabite daughter-in-law Ruth gleaned in his field, he welcomed her, praised her loyalty to Naomi, shared his reapers' meal with her and told his workers to let her glean freely through the barley and wheat harvests. After Ruth came to him at night on the threshing floor, Boaz went to the town gate, where a nearer kinsman gave up his right to redeem the family land. Before the elders, Boaz bought Elimelech's property and married Ruth, an arrangement Easton's Bible Dictionary links to the levirate law. Their son Obed was the grandfather of David. Boaz's father was Salmon, and Matthew names his mother as Rachab. He appears in both genealogies of Jesus. One of the pillars of Solomon's temple bore the same name.

Bocheru was one of the six sons of Azel, a Benjamite, listed with his brothers Azrikam, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah and Hanan. He appears only in a genealogy that is given twice in nearly identical form (1 Chr 8:38; 1 Chr 9:44). The surrounding verses trace this family back through Jonathan to King Saul, so Bocheru belonged to Saul's line many generations after him. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that he is a son of Azel "according to the present Hebrew text." The Hebrew letters of the name can also be read as "his firstborn," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "the first born." On that reading the word would describe Azrikam rather than name a separate son, which would sit oddly with the stated total of six. This entry follows the text as it stands and treats Bocheru as a son of Azel.

Bochim, meaning "weepers," was the place where an angel of the LORD, coming up from Gilgal, spoke to Israel early in the period of the judges. He reminded them that he had brought them out of Egypt and would never break his covenant with them (Judg 2:1). In the verses that follow (Judg 2:2–4) he rebukes them for making agreements with the people of the land, and the people weep aloud. They named the place Bochim for this and offered sacrifices there (Judg 2:5). No later place name resembling it has been found, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may not have lasted. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it probably at the head of a valley between Gilgal and Shiloh. Many, following the Greek Septuagint, identify it with Bethel. The location shown here follows the Bethel identification, near the modern village of Beitin north of Jerusalem.
