Bohan was a man called "the son of Reuben," known only because a boundary marker, "the stone of Bohan," was named after him. The stone marked the border between the tribal lands of Judah and Benjamin. It stood near the Jordan valley, between Beth-hoglah and Beth-arabah on one side and En-shemesh and the ascent of Adummim on the other (Josh 15:6; 18:17). He does not appear in the genealogies of Reuben's sons, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. So "son of Reuben" may mean a descendant of Reuben rather than a son, which is why Smith's Bible Dictionary simply calls him a Reubenite. Nothing else is recorded about him, and the site of the stone has not been identified. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "thumb."

Bor-ashan was a town in southern Judah, one of the places to which David sent a share of the spoil after defeating the Amalekites who had raided Ziklag. The list names the towns where David and his men had moved about while living as fugitives. The King James Version spells the name Chorashan. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both note that another reading of the Hebrew gives Bor-ashan, which later English versions adopt. Both works suggest it is probably the same place as Ashan, a town assigned to Judah and later to Simeon (Josh 15:42; 19:7; 1 Chr 4:32). Easton gives the meaning as "smoking furnace." The exact site is uncertain, and the location shown here is only approximate.

Bozez was one of two sharp rocks that stood on either side of the pass Jonathan crossed to attack the Philistine garrison; the other was called Seneh (1 Sam 14:4). The setting is the gorge of Michmash, known from the surrounding narrative. This is generally identified with the steep ravine now called Wadi Suweinit, northeast of Jerusalem, and the location shown here lies in that area. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places Bozez on the northern side of the gorge. It notes that this cliff catches the sun for most of the day while the southern cliff stays in shade, and suggests the name may mean "shining." Hitchcock's Bible Names instead gives the meaning "mud" or "bog." The name appears only in this one verse.

Bozkath was a town in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah. It appears in the list of towns given to the tribe of Judah, named between Lachish and Eglon (Josh 15:39). It is mentioned again as the home of Adaiah, whose daughter Jedidah was the mother of King Josiah (2 Kgs 22:1). The King James Version spells it "Boscath" there. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "rocky height," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "stony." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the site has not been identified. The location shown here is only approximate, placed near Lachish because of the town's position in the Joshua list.

Bozrah was a leading city of Edom, home of Zerah, whose son Jobab became one of the early kings of Edom before Israel had kings (Gen 36:33; 1 Chr 1:44). The prophets name it as a stronghold of Edom that would face judgment. Isaiah describes a great slaughter there, and also pictures a figure coming from Edom with garments dyed red from Bozrah (Isa 34:6; 63:1). Jeremiah says it will become a desolation and pictures an enemy spreading its wings over it like an eagle (Jer 49:13, 22). Amos speaks of fire devouring its palaces (Amos 1:12). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls it Edom's capital and gives the name's meaning as "sheepfold". Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with el-Busaireh (Buseirah), southeast of the Dead Sea, and the location shown here follows that identification. Other places in the Bible share the name.

Bozrah was a city listed among the cities of Moab in Jeremiah's message of judgment against that nation (Jer 48:24). It is distinct from the better-known Bozrah of Edom, because several places share this name. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it in the "plain country" mentioned a few verses earlier, meaning the high tableland east of the Dead Sea. The name is usually understood to mean "fortress" or "sheepfold." Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the same place as Bezer, the city of refuge, possibly at Qusur Bashair southeast of Dibon. Easton's Bible Dictionary links it with a modern Buzrah. The location shown here follows an identification with Bosra (Busra al-Sham) in the Hauran region of southern Syria, well north of Moab's usual heartland.

The Bread of Life Sermon was Jesus' teaching at Capernaum on the day after he fed the crowd with loaves (John 6:22–71). People who had eaten crossed the Sea of Galilee to find him. Jesus told them to work for food that lasts to eternal life, not food that perishes. When they asked for a sign and pointed to the manna in the desert, he said his Father gives the true bread from heaven and declared, "I am the bread of life." The Jews murmured, since they knew him as Joseph's son. They argued over his saying that they must eat his flesh and drink his blood. Many disciples found this hard and stopped following him. When Jesus asked the Twelve if they would also leave, Simon Peter answered that he had the words of eternal life. John 6:59 places the teaching in the Capernaum synagogue. The date of about AD 29 is inferred from context.

The Broad Wall was a section of Jerusalem's city wall that was repaired after the return from exile under Nehemiah. In the list of rebuilders, Uzziel, one of the goldsmiths, and Hananiah, son of one of the perfume makers, restored the stretch of wall leading up to it (Neh 3:8). At the dedication of the rebuilt walls, one of the two thanksgiving processions, with Nehemiah following it, walked along the top of the wall from the Tower of the Furnaces as far as the Broad Wall (Neh 12:38). Its name probably refers to the wall's unusual thickness. Its exact course is uncertain, but the surrounding passages place it on the western side of the city. Many scholars connect it with a very thick wall uncovered by excavations in the Jewish Quarter of the Old City, usually dated to the late 8th century BC. The location shown here follows that identification.

Brook Eshcol, also called the valley of Eshcol, was a valley in the hill country of Canaan explored by the twelve spies Moses sent ahead of Israel. There they cut a single cluster of grapes so large that two men carried it on a pole, along with pomegranates and figs, as samples of the land's produce. The place was named for that cluster, since Eshcol means "cluster." The spies' discouraging report after visiting the valley turned the Israelites against entering the land. Because the preceding verse, Num 13:22, says the spies came to Hebron, many place the valley near that city. Easton's Bible Dictionary, following Palmer, suggests the grape-growing valleys farther south near Beersheba, perhaps Wadi Hanein. The location shown here follows the identification near Hebron.

Brook Kidron, called the brook Cedron in John's Gospel and the Kidron Valley in modern versions, was the stream and ravine running below the eastern wall of Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "the black torrent." The stream flowed mainly in the rainy season, and the valley lies between the city and the Mount of Olives. During Hezekiah's Passover, the people removed the altars and incense altars that stood in Jerusalem and threw them into the Kidron (2 Chr 30:14). After speaking with his disciples on the night of his arrest, Jesus crossed the brook Cedron with them to a garden on the far side (John 18:1). By inference from other Gospel accounts, this was Gethsemane, on the slopes of the Mount of Olives. The location shown here is the valley immediately east of Jerusalem's Old City.

Bukki son of Jogli was the leader of the tribe of Dan named in Num 34:22 among the men chosen to divide the land of Canaan among the tribes. In the surrounding passage, the LORD tells Moses to appoint one leader from each tribe to assist Eleazar the priest and Joshua in giving out the land west of the Jordan. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him as one of the ten men chosen for this task, because Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh had already received land east of the Jordan. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with another Bukki, a priestly descendant of Aaron named in later genealogies such as 1 Chr 6:5.

Bukki was a priest of the tribe of Levi, the son of Abishua and the father of Uzzi, in the line of Aaron's son Eleazar. The genealogy in 1 Chronicles places him four generations after Aaron (Aaron, Eleazar, Phinehas, Abishua, Bukki) (1 Chr 6:5; 1 Chr 6:51). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible names index count him in the line of the high priests. He also appears in the ancestry of Ezra the scribe, listed between Abishua and Uzzi (Ezra 7:4). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that his name appears as Boccas in 1 Esdras 8:2 and as Borith in 2 Esdras 1:2. Nothing is recorded about his life beyond these genealogies. The name Bukki is shared by at least one other man in the Bible.

Bukkiah was a Levite, the first-named of the fourteen sons of Heman listed in 1 Chr 25:4. Heman was one of the leaders of music appointed under David. His sons were set apart to prophesy with harps, lyres and cymbals in the worship of the house of the Lord, according to the surrounding passage. When the temple musicians were divided into twenty-four groups by lot, the sixth lot fell to Bukkiah. His group, made up of him, his sons and his relatives, numbered twelve (1 Chr 25:13). Smith's Bible Dictionary places him among the Kohathite Levites, since Heman belonged to that clan. It gives the meaning of his name as "wasting from Jehovah," and Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "the dissipation of the Lord." He is not mentioned anywhere else.

Bunah was a man of the tribe of Judah, named second among the sons of Jerahmeel, the firstborn of Hezron, in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:25. His brothers listed there are Ram the firstborn, Oren, Ozem and Ahijah. The next verse, 1 Chr 2:26, says Jerahmeel had another wife, Atarah, who was the mother of Onam, so Onam was probably Bunah's half-brother. Through Hezron, Bunah belonged to the line of Perez, son of Judah, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. Nothing else is recorded about him, and no descendants are listed for him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "building" or "understanding."

Bunni was a Levite in the time of Nehemiah. He was one of eight Levites, listed with Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Sherebiah, a second Bani and Chenani, who stood on the stairs and cried out loudly to the LORD during the public gathering of fasting and confession after the return from exile (Neh 9:4). By inference from the surrounding chapter, these Levites led the people in prayer and confession of sin, and STEPBible Proper Names describes him in this way. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him simply as one of the Levites of Nehemiah's day. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "building me." The name Bunni belongs to more than one person in the Bible, and this entry covers only the Levite of Neh 9:4. Nothing more is recorded about his family or later life.

Bunni was one of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the written covenant made in Nehemiah's time, when the community in Jerusalem pledged to keep the law. He appears only in the list of signatories, between Bani and Azgad (Neh 10:15), and nothing else is told about him. Several of the names around his, such as Azgad and Bebai, also appear as family names among those who returned from exile (Ezra 2). So "Bunni" here may stand for a family or clan head rather than a single individual, though this is an inference. The name is also borne by Levites mentioned elsewhere in Nehemiah, and it is uncertain whether any of them is the same man. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "building me."

Bunni was a Levite named as an ancestor of Shemaiah, one of the Levites living in Jerusalem after the return from exile. The genealogy in Neh 11:15 traces Shemaiah back through Hashub, Azrikam and Hashabiah to Bunni, making Bunni Hashabiah's father and Shemaiah's great-great-grandfather. Because he stands several generations back in that line, he probably lived well before Nehemiah's day, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. Nothing else is recorded about him. The parallel list in 1 Chr 9:14 has "of the sons of Merari" where Nehemiah has "the son of Bunni," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the two readings as variants of the same text. This entry follows the wording of Nehemiah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "building me." Several other men in the Bible share the name, so he should not be confused with them.

Buz was an Arabian region or tribe named in Jer 25:23, where it appears with Dedan and Tema among the peoples made to drink the cup of the Lord's wrath, alongside "all that are in the utmost corners." Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as a district in Arabia Petrea. The people probably took their name from Buz, son of Nahor and brother of Huz (Gen 22:21). Elihu, Job's young companion, is called "the Buzite" in Job 32:2, which suggests he came from this people. Its exact location is unknown. Because it is listed with Dedan and Tema, it was probably in northwestern Arabia, and the location shown here is a rough placement near Dedan, around modern al-Ula in Saudi Arabia. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "despised" or "plundered."

Buz was the second son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and his wife Milcah. He is named in the list of Nahor's children reported to Abraham after the binding of Isaac, where he follows his elder brother Huz, the firstborn, and comes before Kemuel. Among his brothers was Bethuel, the father of Rebekah. Nahor also had sons by his concubine Reumah. Buz is probably the ancestor of the Buzites. Elihu, who speaks in the book of Job, is called "the Buzite" (Job 32:2), and both Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary take him to be a descendant of Buz. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names renders as "despised" or "plundered," is also borne by another man in the genealogies of Gad. A people or region called Buz appears in Jer 25:23 as well.

Buz was a man of the tribe of Gad, named only once, at the very end of a family line in 1 Chr 5:14. He was the father of Jahdo and the most distant ancestor listed for Abihail, whose descendants are traced back through Huri, Jaroah, Gilead, Michael, Jeshishai and Jahdo to Buz. The surrounding chapter places these Gadites in the region of Bashan and Gilead east of the Jordan, so his family probably belonged there. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him one of the chiefs of the tribe of Gad. Nothing else is recorded about his life. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "despised" or "plundered." The same name belongs to other figures in the Bible, notably a son of Abraham's brother Nahor, and this Gadite should not be confused with them.

Buzi was the father of the prophet Ezekiel and is known only from Ezek 1:3. There Ezekiel is introduced as "the priest, the son of Buzi" when the word of the Lord came to him in the land of the Chaldeans by the river Chebar. Because Israel's priesthood passed from father to son, Buzi was probably himself of a priestly family, and STEPBible's proper-names index describes him as a priest. The verse says nothing else about him, including whether he lived to see the exile in Babylonia that his son shared. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names give the meaning of his name as "contempt" or "my contempt."

Cabbon was a town in the Shephelah, the low hill country of Judah. It appears only once, in the list of towns given to the tribe of Judah, where it is named with Lahmam and Kithlish (Josh 15:40). The list places it in the same district as Lachish and Eglon, so it probably lay in the western foothills toward the coastal plain. Its site has not been identified. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the same place as Machbena, which appears in a genealogy of Judah (1 Chr 2:49). The location shown here is only an approximate point in the lowland district of Judah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "as though understanding."

Cabul was a town on the boundary of the tribe of Asher, named in the description of Asher's territory as a landmark the border reached after passing Bethemek and Neiel, toward Zebulun (Josh 19:27). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it on the line between Asher and Zebulun and links it with Chabolo, a place mentioned by the historian Josephus. It is generally identified with the modern village of Kabul, about 8 to 10 miles east-southeast of Acre (ancient Accho), near the edge of Galilee. The location shown here follows that identification. The same name is also given to the district of Galilean towns that Solomon gave to Hiram king of Tyre (1 Kgs 9:13). Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests this town was probably one of them, though that connection is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "displeasing."

Cabul was the name Hiram, king of Tyre, gave to a district of cities in Galilee that Solomon handed over to him. By the surrounding passage (1 Kgs 9:11–12), these were twenty cities given in return for Hiram's cedar, timber and gold. When Hiram saw them, they did not please him, and he called them "the land of Cabul," a name still used when the account was written. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "good for nothing," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "displeasing; dirty." Easton's places the district in northwest Galilee near Tyre and suggests that Hiram later returned the cities, citing 2 Chr 8:2. The name is shared with a town of Asher (Josh 19:27). The location shown here is approximate and lies near that town, probably the modern village of Kabul east of Akko.

Caesarea was a port city on the Mediterranean coast of Judea, about 70 miles northwest of Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary says Herod the Great built it on the site of an older town called Strato's Tower and named it after Caesar Augustus. It became the seat of the Roman governors. In Acts, Philip preached his way there and later lived there (Acts 8:40; 21:8), and believers sent Saul from it to Tarsus (Acts 9:30). The centurion Cornelius lived there and received Peter (Acts 10:1, 24). Herod Agrippa I stayed there and, as the account continuing in Acts 12 relates, died there. Paul landed there after his second journey. He was later held there as a prisoner before the governors Felix and Festus and King Agrippa until he appealed to Caesar. It is distinct from Caesarea Philippi. The location shown here is the coastal ruins at modern Caesarea in Israel.

Caesarea Philippi was a city at the foot of Mount Hermon, about 20 miles north of the Sea of Galilee, beside one of the main sources of the Jordan. It is the modern village of Banias. In its region Jesus asked his disciples who people said he was. That question led to Peter's confession of him as the Christ and to Jesus' first plain prediction of his death and resurrection (Matt 16:13; Mark 8:27). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries describe it as the northern limit of Jesus' travels. They say Herod Philip enlarged it and named it after the emperor and himself, which set it apart from the coastal Caesarea. Its earlier name was Paneas, after a cave linked with the Greek god Pan. Both dictionaries mention that some identify it with the Old Testament Baal-gad, though this remains uncertain.

Caiaphas was the Jewish high priest during the ministry, trial and death of Jesus. Luke 3:2 names him with Annas as high priest when John the Baptist began preaching, and John 18:13 says Annas was his father-in-law. The chief priests, scribes and elders met at his palace to plot against Jesus, and in council he said it was expedient for one man to die for the people (John 11:49; 18:14). After his arrest Jesus was brought to Caiaphas, where the scribes and elders had gathered, and was then taken from him to the Roman judgment hall (Matt 26:57; John 18:24, 28). Caiaphas also appears among the high priest's family gathered to examine Peter and John (Acts 4:6). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives his full name as Joseph Caiaphas. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia dates his term about AD 18–36, and Easton's Bible Dictionary gives AD 27–36.

Cain was the firstborn son of Adam and Eve. Eve said at his birth, "I have gotten a man from the LORD" (Gen 4:1). He farmed the ground, while his brother Abel kept sheep. When both brought offerings, Cain offered produce of the ground, but God did not accept his offering, and Cain grew angry. God questioned his anger. Cain then attacked Abel in the field and killed him. When God asked where Abel was, Cain answered, "Am I my brother's keeper?" (Gen 4:9). He was punished and complained that the punishment was more than he could bear. God set a mark on him so that no one would kill him and warned that anyone who did would be avenged sevenfold. Cain settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden. There he had a son, Enoch, and built a city named after him. Later passages present him as an example of wrongdoing (1 John 3:12; Jude 1:11).

Cain kills Abel is the account in Genesis 4 of the first murder. Cain, the firstborn of Adam and Eve, worked the soil. His younger brother Abel kept sheep. Cain brought produce of the ground as an offering to the LORD, and Abel brought the firstborn of his flock and their fat. The LORD accepted Abel and his offering but not Cain and his. Cain became very angry, and the LORD warned him that sin was waiting at the door and that he must master it. Cain then spoke with Abel, and when they were in the field he attacked and killed him. When the LORD asked where Abel was, Cain answered, "Am I my brother's keeper?" The LORD replied that Abel's blood cried out from the ground. The text says only "in the field"; this entry places it in the region of Eden. The date, about 3875 BC, is inferred from context.

Cainan (antediluvian patriarch), also called Kenan, was a descendant of Adam through Seth who lived before the Flood. He was the son of Enos, born when his father was ninety (Gen 5:9). At seventy he fathered Mahalaleel. He then lived another 840 years, had other sons and daughters, and died at the age of 910 (Gen 5:12–14). The genealogy in Chronicles lists him as Kenan (1 Chr 1:2), and Luke includes him among the ancestors of Jesus (Luke 3:37). Easton's Bible Dictionary counts him as the fourth patriarch before the Flood. By inference from the ages given in Genesis 5, this entry places his birth about 3679 BC and his death about 2769 BC. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "possessor" or "purchaser." He is a different person from the later Cainan, son of Arphaxad, named in Luke 3:36.

Cainan (son of Arphaxad) appears in Luke's genealogy of Jesus as the son of Arphaxad and the father of Salah, placing him three generations after Noah through Shem (Luke 3:36). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that he is not named anywhere in the Old Testament and that he is usually called the "second Cainan," which distinguishes him from the earlier Cainan son of Enos listed in the next verse of Luke's line. In the Hebrew text of Genesis 11:12, Arphaxad is the father of Salah directly, with no Cainan between them. Cainan does appear at that point in the Greek Septuagint translation of Genesis, which is probably where Luke's list draws the name from. Nothing else is recorded about his life. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "possessor" or "purchaser."

Calah was one of the ancient cities of Assyria named in the table of nations. Genesis 10:11 says that from the land of Shinar "Asshur" went out and built Nineveh, Rehoboth and Calah. The verse can also be read as Nimrod going out into Assyria, as the Revised Version and Easton's Bible Dictionary take it, which is why Calah is connected here with the beginning of Nimrod's kingdom. Resen lay between Nineveh and Calah, and the phrase "the same is a great city" (Gen 10:12) may refer to the whole group. Calah is probably the ancient Kalhu, the ruins now called Nimrud on the east bank of the Tigris near where it meets the Greater Zab, south of Mosul in Iraq. The location shown here follows that identification. According to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, Ashurnasirpal II rebuilt it about 880 BC, and it then served as a royal capital of Assyria.

Calcol was a man of the tribe of Judah, listed in 1 Chr 2:6 as one of the five sons of Zerah, alongside Zimri, Ethan, Heman and Dara. Since Zerah was a son of Judah by Tamar (1 Chr 2:4), Calcol was a grandson of Judah. Zimri is probably the same man called Zabdi in Josh 7:1, which is why Zabdi appears among his brothers. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both take Calcol to be probably the same person as Chalcol in 1 Kgs 4:31, one of the famous wise men, together with Ethan, Heman and Darda, whom Solomon surpassed in wisdom. That passage calls them sons of Mahol, so the identification is likely but not certain. The name is explained as meaning "sustenance" (Easton's, Smith's) or "nourishing" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Nothing else is recorded about him.

Caleb son of Jephunneh, called a Kenezite, represented the tribe of Judah among the men Moses sent to explore Canaan. When the others discouraged the people, he urged them to go up and take the land at once, and with Joshua son of Nun he tore his clothes in protest. Because he 'wholly followed the LORD,' he and Joshua were the only adults of that generation allowed to enter the land. He was later named to help divide it. At Gilgal he reminded Joshua of Moses' promise and received Hebron, driving out the three sons of Anak. He offered his daughter Achsah to whoever captured Kirjath-sepher. Othniel son of Kenaz, called Caleb's younger brother, took it and married her, and Caleb gave her upper and lower springs. His sons were Iru, Elah and Naam, and Nabal was of his house. Several men share this name, and 1 Chr 2 may refer to another Caleb. His birth is placed about 1529 BC by inference.

Caleb, also called Chelubai, was a man of the tribe of Judah. He was the son of Hezron and the brother of Jerahmeel and Ram (1 Chr 2:9, 18, 42), and he is known only from the genealogies of 1 Chronicles. His wife Azubah, along with Jerioth, bore Jesher, Shobab and Ardon. After Azubah died he married Ephrath, who bore Hur. His concubines Ephah and Maachah also bore him children, among them Shaaph and Sheva, and his daughter was Achsah. Several of his sons are named as the 'fathers', or founders, of towns such as Ziph, Madmannah and Gibea. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes the view that 'Carmi' among the sons of Judah in 1 Chr 4:1 stands for Chelubai, and this entry follows that view. He is a different person from Caleb son of Jephunneh, the spy. Smith's Bible Dictionary makes this Caleb the spy's grandfather through Hur.

Caleb-Ephrathah was the place where Hezron, son of Perez and grandson of Judah, died, according to 1 Chr 2:24. After his death his wife Abiah bore him a son, Ashur, who became the father of Tekoa. The name appears nowhere else, and no ancient site bearing it has been found. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that many scholars follow the Greek Septuagint and read the verse not as a place name but as "after the death of Hezron, Caleb came to Ephrath," Hezron's wife. The name probably joins Caleb, Hezron's son, with Ephrathah, the name of Caleb's wife Ephrath (1 Chr 2:19) and an old name for Bethlehem (Gen 35:19; Mic 5:2). The location shown here follows that link and places it at or near Bethlehem, though this is an inference.

The Call to Macedonia was the vision Paul received at Troas during his second missionary journey, in which a man of Macedonia stood and begged him, "Come over into Macedonia, and help us." Paul and his companions concluded that God was calling them to preach there and left at once. They sailed directly from Troas to the island of Samothrace, reached the port of Neapolis (probably modern Kavala in northern Greece) the next day, and went on to Philippi, described as a leading city of that part of Macedonia and a Roman colony, where they stayed for some days. The narrative switches to "we" at this point, which is usually taken to mean that Luke, the author of Acts, joined the group here. By inference from the surrounding chapters, Silas and Timothy were also with Paul. This entry dates the episode to about AD 47, an estimate inferred from context.

Calneh was a city in the land of Shinar (southern Mesopotamia), named in Gen 10:10 as one of the four cities where Nimrod's kingdom began, along with Babel, Erech and Accad. This beginning is dated here to about 1822 BC, an estimate inferred from context. Amos 6:2 also names Calneh, along with Hamath and Gath, as kingdoms Israel should look at and compare with itself. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies Calneh with Calno (Isa 10:9) and Canneh (Ezek 27:23), a town that traded with Tyre. Other interpreters take the Calneh of Amos and Isaiah to be a separate city in northern Syria. Its location is uncertain. The location shown here follows the identification with the mound of Niffer, ancient Nippur, east of the Euphrates and about 60 miles south-southeast of Babylon. Both Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note this view.

Calno was a city named in Isaiah's oracle against Assyria. In Isa 10:9 the Assyrian king boasts that Calno fared no better than Carchemish, just as Hamath fared no better than Arpad and Samaria no better than Damascus. The point is that each of these cities fell to Assyria in turn, so Jerusalem should expect the same. Calno is usually taken as another form of Calneh, a name found in Gen 10:10 and Amos 6:2. Its location is debated. Some place it in Shinar, in southern Mesopotamia, and connect it with the ancient city of Nippur in modern Iraq. Others identify it with Kullani, a town in northern Syria near Arpad, which suits the other Syrian cities in the list. The location shown here follows the southern Mesopotamian identification with Nippur. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "our consummation" or "altogether himself."

Cana, called "Cana of Galilee" in the Bible, was a village in Galilee where Jesus turned water into wine at a wedding. His mother was there, and John 2:11 calls it the beginning of his miracles. He later returned to Cana, where a nobleman asked him to heal his son, who was sick at Capernaum. It was also the home of the disciple Nathanael. The New Testament mentions it only in John's Gospel. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that "of Galilee" set it apart from Kanah in Asher. Its site is disputed. Church tradition places it at Kefr Kanna, about 4 miles northeast of Nazareth. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia prefers Khirbet Qana, a ruin about 9 miles north of Nazareth on the edge of the Beit Netofa plain, whose name may mean "place of reeds." The location shown here follows the Khirbet Qana identification.

Canaan, also called the Promised Land, was the region between the Jordan River and the Dead Sea on the east and the Mediterranean on the west. Terah's family set out from Ur for it (Gen 11:31), and Abraham lived there as a foreigner. Hebron, Shechem and Bethlehem lay within it (Gen 23:2; Gen 33:18; Gen 48:7). Famine drove Jacob's family to Egypt (Gen 47:4), but Jacob was buried in Canaan at Machpelah (Gen 50:13). God promised the land to Israel as a possession (Exod 6:4; Lev 25:38). Moses viewed it from Mount Nebo (Deut 32:49), and under Joshua Israel ate its produce and divided it by lot (Josh 5:12; Acts 13:19). Lands east of the Jordan were treated as outside it (Num 35:14; Josh 22:11). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the name first meant only the coastal plain around Sidon. Zephaniah applies it to the Philistine coast (Zeph 2:5). The location shown here is a central point for the whole region.

Canaan was a son of Ham and grandson of Noah, listed fourth among Ham's sons after Cush, Mizraim and Put (1 Chr 1:8). After Ham saw his drunken father's nakedness, Noah cursed Canaan, declaring that he would be Shem's servant (Gen 9:18, 26). This entry dates that episode to about 2346 BC, by inference from context. Canaan's firstborn was Sidon, followed by Heth and the ancestors of the Jebusites, Amorites, Girgashites, Hivites, Arkites, Sinites, Arvadites, Zemarites and Hamathites (Gen 10:15–18). Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as the forefather of the Phoenicians and of the peoples west of the Jordan before Israel arrived. His name became the name of their territory, the 'land of Canaan', where Abraham, Isaac and Jacob lived as foreigners and which was promised to Israel (Exod 6:4; Num 13:2). The Israelites later fought its inhabitants, the Canaanites (Josh 5:1; Judg 4:24). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as 'merchant' or 'trader'.

Canaanitish woman is the unnamed mother of Shaul, one of the six sons of Simeon, the son of Jacob. She is mentioned only in the family lists of Simeon's sons, in Gen 46:10 among those who went down to Egypt with Jacob and in Exod 6:15 among the families of Simeon. Shaul is the only son in these lists whose mother is singled out, and by inference she was probably Simeon's wife or concubine. Her people are noted because they set her apart from the other mothers in the family. Her name, her history and her exact relationship to Simeon are not recorded. Shaul's descendants later appear as one of the clans of Simeon.

Candace was the queen of the Ethiopians mentioned in Acts 8:27. Her treasurer, a eunuch of great authority who had charge of all her treasure, had gone to Jerusalem to worship. On his way home he met Philip, who baptized him, in an event dated here to about AD 32 by inference from context. Candace herself does not appear in the story and is named only as his ruler. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explain that Candace was not a personal name but a title held by a line of Ethiopian queens, much like "Pharaoh" or "Caesar." The Roman writer Pliny is cited for this. Easton's Bible Dictionary places her kingdom at Meroe in Upper Nubia, in present-day Sudan, a wealthy center of trade. Easton's also records a tradition that her treasurer converted her on his return, though Acts says nothing of this.

Canneh was a place named in Ezekiel's lament over Tyre as one of that city's trading partners, listed alongside Haran and Eden (Ezek 27:23). It appears only here, and its site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia sets out several views. Gesenius and others take it as another form of Calneh (Gen 10:10; Amos 6:2) or Calno (Isa 10:9). The Targums, Eusebius and Jerome identify it with Ctesiphon on the Tigris. Some scholars read the Hebrew as "the sons of Eden" rather than as a place name. Smith's Bible Dictionary also treats it as Calneh. The location shown here follows the identification with the Calneh of Gen 10:10, which Jewish tradition places at the ancient city of Nippur in southern Iraq. Its listing with Haran and Eden suggests it was probably a Mesopotamian trading center.

Capernaum was a city of Galilee on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, mentioned only in the Gospels. After leaving Nazareth, Jesus settled there, in the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali (Matt 4:13), and it became a main center of his ministry. He taught in its synagogue on the sabbath (Mark 1:21; Luke 4:31), and John 6:59 places the bread of life discourse there. Events connected with the city include the healing of a centurion's servant (Matt 8:5) and of a nobleman's son who lay sick there (John 4:46). Tribute collectors also questioned Peter there (Matt 17:24). Jesus pronounced judgment on the city despite the mighty works done in it (Matt 11:23; Luke 10:15). Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the name as "Nahum's town." The site has been placed either at Tell Hum or at Khan Minyeh, further southwest. The location shown here follows the Tell Hum identification.

The Capernaum Miracles were healings Jesus performed on a single day after he crossed back over the Sea of Galilee from the region of the Gadarene demoniacs (Mark 5:21). The setting is probably Capernaum, by inference from Matthew's mention of his own city (Matt 9:1). Jairus, a synagogue ruler, begged Jesus to come to his dying twelve-year-old daughter. On the way, a woman who had suffered bleeding for twelve years and spent everything on physicians touched his garment and was healed. Jesus told her that her faith had made her whole. Word came that the girl had died, but Jesus took Peter, James and John with her parents, said "Talitha cumi," and she rose. Matthew adds that Jesus then healed two blind men and freed a mute man from a demon, while the Pharisees credited his power to the prince of demons. The events are dated to about AD 28, by inference from context.

Caphthorim (also spelled Caphtorim) is listed among the descendants of Mizraim (Egypt) in the table of nations, alongside Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim, Pathrusim and Casluhim (Gen 10:14; 1 Chr 1:12). The plural -im ending marks the name as a people group, not a single individual. Later passages connect this people with a land called Caphtor: Deut 2:23 says the Caphtorim came out of Caphtor and destroyed the Avvim, who lived in villages as far as Gaza, and Amos 9:7 and Jer 47:4 say the Philistines came from Caphtor. In the genealogies, however, the note about the Philistines' origin follows Casluhim, so how the two peoples relate is not fully clear. Caphtor is commonly identified with Crete, though other locations, such as the Egyptian coast or southern Asia Minor, have also been proposed.

Caphtor was the land from which the Philistines originally came, according to Deut 2:23, Jer 47:4 and Amos 9:7. Deuteronomy says the Caphtorim, who came out of Caphtor, destroyed the Avims living in settlements as far as Azzah (Gaza) and took their place. Jeremiah calls the Philistines "the remnant of the country of Caphtor," and Amos sets God's bringing the Philistines from Caphtor alongside Israel's exodus from Egypt and the Syrians' migration from Kir. The Bible does not say where Caphtor was. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that it is commonly taken to be Crete, since the Philistines seem to be linked with the "Cherethites" (1 Sam 30:14). It also mentions a possible location in Egypt's northern Delta, and Smith's Bible Dictionary places it in or near Egypt. The location shown here follows the Crete identification.

Cappadocia was a large region in eastern Asia Minor, in what is now central Turkey. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls it the largest province of Asia Minor. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes it as mostly high, rather barren uplands bounded by the Taurus mountains to the south and the Euphrates to the east, with Caesarea Mazaca as its chief city. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes it was good grain and grazing country. Cappadocia came under Roman rule in AD 17. The New Testament mentions it twice. People living in Cappadocia were among those in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:9). It was also one of the regions, along with Pontus, Galatia, Asia and Bithynia, whose scattered believers Peter addressed in his first letter (1 Pet 1:1). This implies that Christianity reached the region early. The location shown here marks the general area of the region.

Carcas was the seventh of seven chamberlains who served in the presence of the Persian king Ahasuerus. On the seventh day of a royal feast, when the king was merry with wine, he ordered these chamberlains to bring Queen Vashti before him wearing her crown so that he could display her beauty (Esth 1:10). The Hebrew word for chamberlain usually means a eunuch, and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes the seven as eunuchs. Nothing else is recorded about Carcas. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "severe," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the covering of a lamb." The name is probably Persian in origin, so its meaning is uncertain.

Carchemish was an ancient city on the west bank of the Euphrates River, which commanded a main crossing of the river. Isaiah lists it with Calno, Hamath, Arpad, Samaria and Damascus as cities that had fallen to Assyria (Isa 10:9). It was the scene of a decisive battle. Pharaoh Necho of Egypt marched there to fight, and Josiah king of Judah went out to oppose him on the way (2 Chr 35:20). Later, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon defeated Necho's army at Carchemish (Jer 46:2). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this battle to about 605 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes it as a very old Hittite city and identifies it with Jerablus. Easton's and Smith's dictionaries place it at or near Hierapolis (Mabug). The location shown here follows the Jerablus identification, on the modern border between Turkey and Syria.

Carchemish is named in 2 Chr 35:20 as the target of a campaign by Necho king of Egypt, who "came up to fight against Carchemish by Euphrates." King Josiah of Judah went out to oppose Necho on his march, after he had finished restoring the temple. The KJV wording "fight against Carchemish" can be read as naming an opponent, and this entry treats the name as a person. Elsewhere in the Bible, however, Carchemish is a city on the Euphrates (Isa 10:9; Jer 46:2), and most readers take the name here as that city. Jeremiah links it with Necho's army and its defeat by Nebuchadnezzar. The city is generally identified with the ruins near modern Jerablus on the Turkey–Syria border. Nothing else is said about Carchemish as an individual.

Carmel was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed with Maon, Ziph and Juttah (Josh 15:55). After his campaign against the Amalekites, Saul came there and set up a monument before moving on to Gilgal (1 Sam 15:12). The wealthy Nabal, who lived in nearby Maon, kept his flocks at Carmel and sheared his sheep there. David sent young men to him there to ask for provisions, and after Nabal's death his widow Abigail, called 'the Carmelitess', became David's wife (1 Sam 25:2–40; 27:3). Hezrai (or Hezro) the Carmelite, one of David's mighty men, probably came from this town. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the ruins of Kurmul, about 10 miles south-southeast of Hebron, and the location shown here follows that identification. Several verses using the name, especially in the prophets, refer instead to Mount Carmel near the Mediterranean coast, which is a separate place.

Carmi was the fourth and last-named son of Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, and the brother of Hanoch, Pallu and Hezron. He is listed among the descendants of Jacob who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:9), and he appears again among the heads of the fathers' houses of Reuben (Exod 6:14) and in the Reubenite genealogy of 1 Chr 5:3. In the census taken in the wilderness he is named as the ancestor of the clan of the Carmites within the tribe of Reuben (Num 26:6). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "vine dresser," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "my vineyard." Nothing else is recorded about his life. The same name belongs to other men in the Bible, including a man of the tribe of Judah, so this Carmi should not be confused with them.

Carmi was a man of the tribe of Judah, the son of Zabdi and the father of Achan, who took forbidden plunder from Jericho and brought trouble on Israel (Josh 7:1, 18). His line ran back through Zabdi to Zerah, one of Judah's sons. Carmi himself appears only in these genealogies and plays no part in the narrative. In 1 Chr 2:7 his son is called Achar, "the troubler of Israel," a form that plays on the Hebrew word for trouble. The Chronicles genealogy names Zimri rather than Zabdi as a son of Zerah, and Easton's Bible Dictionary calls Carmi the son of Zimri. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Zimri and Zabdi are probably the same man, as the Greek Septuagint also takes them. His name may mean "vine dresser" or "my vineyard." Other men in the Bible also bear the name Carmi, including a son of Reuben.

Carshena was the first named of the seven princes of Persia and Media at the court of King Ahasuerus (Esth 1:14). These men "saw the king's face", meaning they had direct access to him, and they held the highest rank in the kingdom. From the surrounding passage, they were the advisers the king consulted when Queen Vashti refused to appear at his feast. Their spokesman in that episode was Memucan, and nothing further is recorded about Carshena himself. The name is probably Persian. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "illustrious", while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "a lamb" or "sleeping".

Casiphia was the place where Iddo, a leading man, lived with his relatives the Nethinim (temple servants). Ezra sent messengers there to ask for ministers for the house of God (Ezra 8:17). The surrounding passage shows this happened while Ezra's returning exiles were camped by the river Ahava and had found no Levites among them. The name may be connected with the Hebrew word for 'silver' or 'money', and the Septuagint translates it as 'the place of the treasury' (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Its site is unknown. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and the STEPBible names list place it in Babylonia, near the Ahava. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries describe it as lying somewhere between Babylon and Jerusalem. The location shown here is only a rough one in western Syria, which follows the 'between Babylon and Jerusalem' view.

Casluhim is a name in the Table of Nations, listed among the descendants of Mizraim (Egypt) alongside the Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim, Pathrusim and Caphtorim. The plural form suggests a people or tribe rather than a single individual, as with the other names in the list. Both Gen 10:14 and 1 Chr 1:12 add that the Philistines came from the Casluhim. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that this note may originally have belonged after Caphtorim, since other passages link the Philistines with Caphtor. Easton's Bible Dictionary places the original home of the Casluhim probably in Lower Egypt, along the coast toward the southern border of Palestine, and gives the name's meaning as "fortified." Nothing else is recorded about them.

Cenchreae was the eastern harbour of Corinth, on the Saronic Gulf side of the isthmus. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it about 9 miles from the city and calls it Corinth's outlet for trade with the eastern Mediterranean, while Lechaeum served as the western port. At the end of his long stay in Corinth, Paul had his hair cut at Cenchreae because of a vow, then sailed for Syria with Priscilla and Aquila. This marked his return from the second missionary journey, about AD 50 by inference from context (Acts 18:18). Romans 16:1 shows that a church existed there, and Paul commends Phoebe as a servant of that church. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia infers that she carried the letter to Rome. The site is generally identified with the ruins at modern Kechries, near Corinth, which the location shown here follows.

Chalcol was one of four men famous for wisdom in the days of Solomon. 1 Kgs 4:31 says Solomon was wiser than all of them: Ethan the Ezrahite, Heman, Chalcol and Darda, called "the sons of Mahol." Nothing else is said about him there, and his comparison with Solomon is his only role in the passage. The name is also spelled Calcol. The same group of names (Zimri, Ethan, Heman, Calcol and Dara) appears in 1 Chr 2:6 as sons of Zerah of the tribe of Judah, so Chalcol is probably the same man. If so, "sons of Mahol" may name a family line or guild rather than a literal father. This entry follows the verse in Kings and treats Mahol as his father, with Darda, Ethan and Heman as his brothers. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "who nourishes, consumes, and sustains the whole."

Chaldea was the region of southern Mesopotamia around Babylon, the alluvial plain formed by the Euphrates and Tigris near the Persian Gulf. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Chaldea proper as the southern part of Babylonia, though the name was commonly used for the whole Mesopotamian plain. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the prophets used the term for all Babylonia. In the Bible it appears mainly in Jeremiah and Ezekiel as the homeland of the Babylonians (Ezek 23:15). It was the land where the exiles from Judah lived, and Ezekiel was brought there in a vision to the captives (Ezek 11:24). Ezekiel also portrays Judah's political dealings with Chaldea as unfaithfulness (Ezek 16:29; 23:16). Jeremiah foretells that Chaldea will be plundered and repaid for the harm its people did in Zion (Jer 50:10; 51:24, 35). The location shown here is in present-day southern Iraq.

Chebar was a river or waterway in "the land of the Chaldeans" (Babylonia), where some of the Jews taken captive from Judah lived. The priest Ezekiel was among these exiles when he saw his first visions of God beside it (Ezek 1:1–3). Exiles also lived there at Tel-abib (Ezek 3:15). Ezekiel later compared other visions, including the glory of the LORD and the cherubim, to what he had first seen by the Chebar (Ezek 3:23; 10:15, 20, 22; 43:3). Its exact identity is uncertain. Some have linked it with the Habor (Khabur) River of northern Mesopotamia. Easton's Bible Dictionary favors Nebuchadnezzar's royal canal joining the Tigris and Euphrates. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia points to a navigable canal near Nippur, the modern Shatt en-Nil. The location shown here places it in central Mesopotamia near ancient Nehardea, in line with the royal canal view.

Chedorlaomer was a king of Elam in the time of Abraham, and the leading figure among four allied eastern kings: Amraphel of Shinar, Arioch of Ellasar and Tidal "king of nations". The kings of Sodom, Gomorrah and three neighbouring cities served him for twelve years and rebelled in the thirteenth. In the fourteenth year he and his allies marched west, defeating the Rephaim, Zuzim and Emim, and then met the five kings in battle, "four kings with five". The surrounding chapter says they carried off Abraham's nephew Lot. Abraham pursued and defeated them, and the king of Sodom met him on his return from "the slaughter of Chedorlaomer". Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him with Kudur-Lagamar of Babylonian inscriptions. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reads the name as meaning "servant of Lagamar", an Elamite deity, and notes that scholars are divided over the identification.

Chelal was one of the descendants of Pahath-moab listed among the Israelites who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra. He is named only once, in Ezra 10:30, in the list of men who agreed to put away these wives after Ezra's call for the community to separate from the surrounding peoples. Pahath-moab was a family group that had returned from exile in Babylon, and Chelal appears alongside seven other members of that clan. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of his name as "perfection," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "as night."

Chelluh was one of the Israelite men listed in Ezra 10:35 as having married a foreign wife. By inference from the surrounding passage, he belonged to the group called the sons of Bani (Ezra 10:34). The list records those who agreed, under Ezra's reforms after the return from exile in Babylon, to send away the foreign wives they had married. Nothing else is known about him. Some versions and reference works give his name as Cheluhi, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists him under that form. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "completed," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "all."

Chelub was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy at 1 Chr 4:11, which calls him the brother of Shuah and the father of Mehir, whose son was Eshton. He is linked here with Rechah as his ancestor, probably because the next verse ends this short family list with "these are the men of Rechah" (1 Chr 4:12). The name may be a variant form of Caleb. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some scholars have read the verse as referring to Caleb son of Hezron, and the STEPBible proper-names index treats Chelub as a brother of Caleb and a son of Hezron. This entry follows the link to Rechah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "a basket." He should not be confused with another Chelub, the father of Ezri, who appears later in Chronicles. Nothing further is recorded about him.

Chelub was the father of Ezri, the officer whom King David put in charge of the farm laborers who worked the royal fields (1 Chr 27:26). He is named only to identify his son in a list of the officials who managed David's property, and nothing else is recorded about him. The name is shared by other people in the Bible, including a man of Judah in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:11, who is probably a different person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a basket."

Chemosh was the national god of the Moabites, who are called "the people of Chemosh" in an old song quoted at Num 21:29 and again in Jeremiah's oracle against Moab (Jer 48:46). In Judg 11:24 Jephthah, answering the king of Ammon, speaks of the land "Chemosh thy god" gives. Smith's Bible Dictionary reads this as Chemosh appearing as an Ammonite god too, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connects it to the Moabite cities under dispute. Solomon built a high place for Chemosh on the hill facing Jerusalem, and this worship is named among the reasons for taking part of the kingdom from his line (1 Kgs 11:7, 33). King Josiah, the king in that chapter's context, later defiled the shrine (2 Kgs 23:13). Jeremiah foretold that Chemosh would go into captivity with his priests and princes, and that Moab would be ashamed of him (Jer 48:7, 13). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that on the Moabite Stone King Mesha credits his victories over Israel to Chemosh.

Chenaanah was the father of Zedekiah, one of the prophets at the court of Ahab king of Israel. He is known only through his son's name. When Ahab and Jehoshaphat king of Judah were deciding whether to attack Ramoth-gilead, Zedekiah son of Chenaanah made iron horns and announced that the king would push the Syrians until they were destroyed (1 Kgs 22:11; 2 Chr 18:10). When the prophet Micaiah predicted defeat instead, Zedekiah struck him on the cheek (1 Kgs 22:24; 2 Chr 18:23). Nothing else is said about Chenaanah himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary allows that he may have been an earlier ancestor rather than Zedekiah's immediate father. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia distinguishes him from another man of the same name, a Benjamite, and explains the name as related to "Canaan".

Chenaanah was a member of the tribe of Benjamin, listed fourth among the seven children of Bilhan, son of Jediael, in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:10. The verse names them as Jeush, Benjamin, Ehud, Chenaanah, Zethan, Tharshish and Ahishahar. The next verse (1 Chr 7:11) describes this family as heads of their fathers' houses and mighty warriors, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places them in the time of David. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the family probably belonged to the clan of Bela. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as a feminine form of "Canaan," noting that others read it as "toward Canaan." Nothing else is recorded about this person. The name is shared with others in the Bible, including the father of the prophet Zedekiah in the reign of Ahab (1 Kgs 22:11).

Chenani was a Levite named only in Neh 9:4. He was one of eight Levites who stood on the stairs, probably a raised platform, and cried out loudly to the Lord at the assembly where the returned exiles gathered to fast, confess their sins and renew their commitment to God in Nehemiah's time. The others were Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah and a second Bani. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "planted", while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "my pillar". The same encyclopedia notes that these names may stand either for individual men or for Levitical families. If they were families, they probably sang a well-known psalm. If they were individuals, they probably led the people in a special prayer. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Chenaniah was a chief of the Levites during David's reign who led the music when the ark of the covenant was brought up to Jerusalem. He was placed in charge of the song because he was skilled at it, and he gave instruction in it (1 Chr 15:22). In the procession he is named "the master of the song with the singers," walking with the Levites who carried the ark while David wore a linen robe and ephod (1 Chr 15:27). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew word rendered "song" can also mean "carrying," so he may have directed the carrying of the ark. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes him to be probably a Kohathite and distinct from the Chenaniah of 1 Chr 26:29, who held an outside office. The ISBE treats the two as one man. This entry covers only the Chenaniah of 1 Chr 15. His name means roughly "established by the Lord."

Chenaniah was a Levite of the Izharite clan, descended from Izhar son of Kohath. In David's organization of the Levites, he and his sons were assigned to "the outward business over Israel," serving as officers and judges (1 Chr 26:29). By inference from the context, this meant duties away from the temple service itself, probably administrative and judicial work among the people. The name is shared with another Levite, Chenaniah, who led the singing when the ark was brought to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:22, 27). Some readers identify the two as the same man, but the text does not say so, and this entry treats the Izharite on his own. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "preparation," "disposition," or "strength of the Lord."

Chephar-haammoni (ESV Chephar-ammoni; the KJV verse spells it Chepharhaammonai) was a town allotted to the tribe of Benjamin. It appears only once, in the list of Benjamin's cities in Josh 18:24, where it is named alongside Ophni and Gaba. That verse closes a group of twelve cities with their villages. The name means "village of the Ammonites," as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes, which may point to a settlement of Ammonites at some point, though the text says nothing about its origin. Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be Kefr 'Ana, a ruined site about two miles northeast of Bethel. The location shown here follows a similar identification with Khirbat Kafr Ana, in the hill country north of Jerusalem.

Chephirah was a city in the hill country northwest of Jerusalem, one of the four Gibeonite cities whose people tricked Israel into making a treaty with them (Josh 9:17). It was later counted among the towns given to the tribe of Benjamin (Josh 18:26). After the exile in Babylon its people returned and resettled it. The lists in Ezra and Nehemiah count them together with the men of Kirjath-jearim and Beeroth, 743 in all (Ezra 2:25; Neh 7:29). The name is often taken to mean "hamlet" (Smith's Bible Dictionary) or "little lioness" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with modern Kefireh, southwest of Gibeon, on high ground with many ancient remains. The location shown here follows that identification, the site known as Khirbet el-Kafira.

Cheran was a son of Dishon, named only in the genealogy of the Horites, the people descended from Seir who lived in the land later held by Edom. His brothers were Hemdan, Eshban and Ithran (Gen 36:26). The parallel list in 1 Chr 1:41 repeats the four names but gives Amram in place of Hemdan. Both lists follow a mention of Dishon as a son of Anah. The surrounding chapter also names a Dishon as a son of Seir and a Horite chief, so it is uncertain which Dishon is meant. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats Cheran as a Horite clan name as well as a personal one. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "lyre," Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "anger," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes Dillmann's derivation from a word for "lamb."

Cherub was a place in Babylonia named among the towns from which some exiles returned to Judea after the Babylonian captivity. It is listed with Telmelah, Tel-harsha, Addan and Immer (Ezra 2:59; Neh 7:61). The people who came from these places could not prove their family line or show that they were descended from Israel. Smith's Bible Dictionary links this group with the return led by Zerubbabel, which fits the setting of the list. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes the site as unidentified and notes that the parallel passage in 1 Esdras 5:36 seems to garble these place names. Its exact position is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in southern Mesopotamia. The place name is spelled the same in English as the winged figures called cherubim, but these verses use it only as the name of a town.

Chesalon was a landmark on the northern border of Judah. Joshua 15:10 identifies it with "the side of mount Jearim," on the north side, where the boundary ran west from Baalah past Mount Seir before going down to Beth-shemesh and on to Timnah. The name probably means "hopes" or "confidence" (Smith's and Easton's Bible Dictionaries). Easton's, Smith's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia all identify it with the modern village of Kesla (Kesalon), on a mountain ridge in the western hills of Judah, about six miles northeast of Beth-shemesh. The ISBE notes that it was still a very large village in the 4th century AD and gives its elevation as about 2,087 feet. The location shown here follows the Kesla identification. The Bible mentions Chesalon only in this one verse.

Chesed was a son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and his wife Milcah. He appears only once, in the list of Nahor's eight sons by Milcah that was reported to Abraham after the near-sacrifice of Isaac (Gen 22:22). His brothers were Huz, Buz, Kemuel, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph and Bethuel, the father of Rebekah. Nahor also had sons and a daughter by his concubine Reumah. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts Chesed as the fourth son and gives the name's meaning as "increase," while Easton's Bible Dictionary renders it "gain." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links the name with the Hebrew Kasdim, the people known in English Bibles as the Chaldeans, and suggests Chesed was probably their ancestor. The Bible says nothing further about his life.

Chesil was a town in the far south of Judah's territory, listed among the cities given to that tribe alongside Eltolad and Hormah (Josh 15:30). The name appears nowhere else in the Bible. In the parallel list of towns given to Simeon from within Judah's land, Bethul stands in the same position (Josh 19:4), and 1 Chr 4:30 has Bethuel. For this reason, Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary treat Chesil and Bethul as the same place. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the form "Chesil" may have come from a misreading of the text. Easton's identifies the site with Khelasa, and Smith's places it about 15 miles southwest of Beersheba. The exact site remains uncertain, and the location shown here is only approximate. The name is often taken to mean "foolishness" or "ungodly."

Chesulloth was a town listed in Joshua 19:18 among the places on or near the border of the tribe of Issachar, named between Jezreel and Shunem. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that its place in the list suggests a position between those two towns. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify it with Chisloth-tabor, which Josh 19:12 names on the boundary of neighboring Zebulun. That would make it a border town shared by the two tribes. They place it at the modern village of Iksal, on the northern edge of the Jezreel Valley (Esdraelon), about 3 miles (5 km) west of Mount Tabor. The location shown here matches the Iksal identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "fearfulness," while Easton's and Smith's render it "the loins" or "fertile places."

Chezib was a town in Canaan where Shelah, the third son of Judah by the daughter of Shua, was born (Gen 38:5). It is named only once. The surrounding chapter places Judah's household near Adullam, in the lowland hills west of Bethlehem, so Chezib was probably in the same area. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both identify it as probably the same town as Achzib, a town of Judah's lowlands listed in Josh 15:44 and mentioned in Mic 1:14. Some also link it with Chozeba in 1 Chr 4:22. Easton's gives the name's meaning as "deceitful." The location shown here follows the Achzib identification and places the town in the Judean foothills near Adullam. The exact site is uncertain.

The Chief Priests Conspire Against Jesus was the council meeting in Jerusalem, recorded in John 11:47–53, at which the chief priests and Pharisees decided Jesus should die. It followed the raising of Lazarus, and the council worried that Jesus' many miracles would lead everyone to believe in him. They feared the Romans would then come and take away both their place and their nation. Caiaphas, high priest that year, told them it was better for one man to die for the people than for the whole nation to perish. John comments that Caiaphas did not say this on his own. As high priest he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, and also to gather together the scattered children of God. From that day the leaders plotted to kill him. This entry dates the meeting to about AD 30, by inference from context.

The Childhood of Jesus is the period of Jesus' early life in Nazareth, summed up in a single verse in Luke's Gospel. After Joseph and Mary returned to Nazareth in Galilee, Luke reports that the child grew, became strong in spirit and was filled with wisdom, and that the grace of God was upon him (Luke 2:40). This entry dates its start to about 4 BC, an estimate inferred from context. Apart from this brief summary, the Gospels say almost nothing about these years. Luke goes on to tell of a visit to the temple in Jerusalem when Jesus was twelve, then repeats a similar summary of his growth in wisdom and stature (Luke 2:41–52). Matthew's account also places the family's settled home in Nazareth after their return from Egypt (Matt 2:23).

Chilion was one of the two sons of Elimelech and Naomi, Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah, and the brother of Mahlon. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him the younger son. During a famine the family moved to Moab and settled there (Ruth 1:2). After Elimelech died, the brothers married Moabite women named Orpah and Ruth (Ruth 1:4). Ruth 4:10 names Ruth as Mahlon's widow, so Orpah was by inference Chilion's wife, as Easton's also states. Both brothers died in Moab, leaving Naomi without husband or sons (Ruth 1:5). Later, at Bethlehem, Boaz formally acquired from Naomi everything that had belonged to Elimelech, Chilion and Mahlon, with the elders and people as witnesses (Ruth 4:9). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes his name to mean "pining" or "wasting away." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "finished, complete."

Chilmad was a place or region named once in the Bible, in Ezekiel's lament over Tyre, as one of the city's trading partners alongside Sheba and Asshur (Ezek 27:23). Nothing else is said about it, and its location is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls it a place or country unknown. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes several proposals: a link with Kalwadha near Baghdad; the Aramaic Targum's reading of the name as Media; and a different vocalization of the Hebrew that would make the word a phrase about Asshur rather than a place name. The location shown here is only approximate. It places Chilmad in northern Mesopotamia near ancient Nineveh, in the region of modern Mosul, Iraq, probably because the verse pairs it with Asshur (Assyria). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "teaching" or "learning."

Chimham was a man whom the aged Barzillai the Gileadite offered to King David in his own place when David crossed back over the Jordan after Absalom's rebellion. Barzillai asked to return home to die in his own city and asked the king to treat Chimham as he saw fit. David agreed and promised to do for Chimham whatever Barzillai wished (2 Sam 19:37–38). Chimham then went on with the king to Gilgal (2 Sam 19:40). The text calls him Barzillai's "servant," but Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take him to be probably Barzillai's son. Centuries later, Jer 41:17 mentions "the habitation of Chimham" near Bethlehem, where refugees stopped on their way to Egypt. From this, both dictionaries infer that David gave Chimham land at Bethlehem, which kept his name, possibly as the site of a lodging place.

Chinnereth is named in Deut 3:17 as the northern end of the territory Moses gave to the tribes of Reuben and Gad east of the Jordan. Their land ran along the Jordan valley from Chinnereth south to the Salt Sea (the Dead Sea), below the slopes of Pisgah. Here the name most likely stands for the lake later called the Sea of Galilee, Gennesaret or Tiberias, and the location shown here places it on that lake. The name is shared by several places. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects it with the Hebrew word for 'lyre' and notes that it was also the name of a fortified city near the lake's shore, which gave its name to the surrounding district, and it treats Chinnereth as probably an old Canaanite name that the Israelites adopted. The city is often identified with Tel Kinrot on the northwest shore.

Chinnereth was a fortified city in the territory of the tribe of Naphtali, listed with Ziddim, Zer, Hammath and Rakkath among the tribe's fenced cities (Josh 19:35). The same name is also used for the lake later called the Sea of Galilee (the Sea of Chinnereth) and, in the plural form Chinneroth, for a surrounding district. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "lyre", places the city near the lake shore a little south of Tiberias, and suggests the town gave its name to the district. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the city is named only here and that no later writer mentions it. Many modern scholars identify it with Tel Kinrot (Tell el-Oreimeh) on the northwestern shore of the lake. The location shown here is only approximate and places it beside the western shore of the Sea of Galilee.

Chinneroth was a region in northern Israel around the western shore of the Sea of Galilee. It is the plural form of Chinnereth, the name of a fortified town by the lake. Easton's Bible Dictionary places that town a little south of Tiberias and suggests it gave its name to the surrounding district. In Josh 11:2, the plains south of Chinneroth are among the areas whose kings joined the northern alliance against Joshua. In 1 Kgs 15:20, Benhadad of Syria, answering King Asa of Judah's appeal, struck Israel's northern cities, including "all Cinneroth" along with the land of Naphtali. That pairing suggests the district lay within or beside Naphtali's territory. The lake itself is also called the Sea of Chinnereth or Chinneroth, later known as Gennesaret or the Sea of Tiberias. The location shown here marks the general area near the lake's northwestern shore.

Chios is an island in the Aegean Sea, lying close to the coast of Asia Minor and separated from the mainland by a narrow strait of about 5 miles, according to Smith's Bible Dictionary. It still bears the name Chios and belongs to modern Greece. It appears once in the Bible, on Paul's voyage toward Jerusalem at the end of his third missionary journey, about AD 54 by inference from context. Sailing south from Mitylene, his ship came "over against Chios" the next day, then reached Samos and finally Miletus (Acts 20:15). The phrase probably means they passed or anchored opposite the island overnight. Easton's Bible Dictionary says they sheltered in a roadstead there. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests they anchored on the Asian coast facing it. No coordinates are given for the location shown here.

Chislon was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, known only as the father of Elidad. In Num 34:21, Elidad is named as Benjamin's representative among the tribal leaders chosen to help divide the land of Canaan among the tribes once Israel entered it. Nothing else is recorded about Chislon himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a prince of Benjamin, though the verse gives that role to his son. The name is usually understood to mean "strength" or "confidence". Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "hope, trust". Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the setting to about 1450 BC. Any such date is an estimate inferred from context rather than stated in the text.

Chisloth-tabor was a place on the border of the tribe of Zebulun in Lower Galilee. In Josh 19:12 Zebulun's boundary runs eastward from Sarid "unto the border of Chislothtabor" and then on to Daberath and Japhia. The name links it to Mount Tabor, and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "loins of Tabor," probably referring to the mountain's flanks. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as the same place as Chesulloth, a town on the border of Issachar mentioned later in the same chapter. That would fit a site on the line between the two tribes. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests it may be the village of Iksal, about 2.5 miles west of Mount Tabor, and the location shown here matches that identification, near present-day Iksal, southeast of Nazareth.

Chitlish (spelled Kithlish in the King James Version) was a town in the lowland region of Judah, the Shephelah. It appears only once, in the list of towns allotted to the tribe of Judah, where it is named alongside Cabbon and Lahmam (Josh 15:40). The next verse of that list goes on to name Gederoth and other towns of the same district, all within one group of settlements in the western foothills. Nothing else is recorded about the town. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with a place called Jelameh, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as unidentified. The location shown here is only approximate and places it in the Shephelah among the neighboring towns of its list.

Chloe was a woman mentioned only in 1 Cor 1:11, where Paul says that people "of the house of Chloe" had told him about quarrels and divisions among the believers at Corinth. The phrase probably refers to members of her household, such as family members, servants or slaves, who had traveled between Corinth and Paul, who was likely writing from Ephesus. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests she lived in either Corinth or Ephesus and that the messengers were probably Christian slaves. Whether Chloe herself was a believer is not stated, though it is commonly presumed. Her name means "green herb" or "tender shoot." Nothing else is known about her.

Chorazin was a town in Galilee, named in the Bible only in Jesus' woe against it. He paired it with Bethsaida and said that if the mighty works done in them had been done in Tyre and Sidon, those cities would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes (Matt 11:21; Luke 10:13). Matthew sets the saying alongside a similar rebuke of Capernaum, so Chorazin was probably one of the lakeside towns where Jesus often worked. Eusebius placed it 2 miles from Capernaum, and Jerome put it on the lake shore. Smith's Bible Dictionary treated the site as uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the ruins of Kerazeh, in the hills north of Capernaum (Tell Hum). The location shown here follows the Kerazeh identification.

Chushan-rishathaim was a king of Mesopotamia who ruled over Israel for eight years in the period of the judges (Judg 3:8). The text says the LORD gave Israel into his hand because of the people's wrongdoing. The oppression ended when Othniel, on whom the Spirit of the LORD came, went to war against him and won (Judg 3:10). Othniel is named in the surrounding verses as the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother. The date of about 1418 BC is an estimate inferred from context. "Mesopotamia" here translates Aram-naharaim, the region of the upper Euphrates. The name is variously explained: Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "chief of two governments," Easton's Bible Dictionary offers "Cush of double wickedness" or "governor of two presidencies," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "blackness of iniquities." He is otherwise unknown, and his identity outside the Bible is uncertain.

Chuza was the steward of Herod, the official who managed the ruler's household and property, and the husband of Joanna. He is mentioned only once, in Luke 8:3, where Joanna appears among the women who traveled with Jesus and supported him from their own means. The Herod meant is probably Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee, who ruled there during Jesus' ministry; Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies Chuza as his house-steward. The text says nothing more about Chuza himself. It does not say whether he shared his wife's support for Jesus. Joanna is named again in Luke 24:10 among the women at the empty tomb, which suggests her continued involvement, but Chuza does not appear there. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "the seer" or "prophet."

Cilicia was a Roman province on the southeastern coast of Asia Minor, between the Taurus Mountains and the Mediterranean, in what is now southern Turkey around Adana. Its chief city, Tarsus, was Paul's birthplace (Acts 21:39; 22:3), and the governor Felix noted that Paul came from this province (Acts 23:34). Jews from Cilicia belonged to a Jerusalem synagogue whose members debated with Stephen (Acts 6:9). Paul went to the regions of Syria and Cilicia soon after his conversion (Gal 1:21). Churches there received the Jerusalem council's letter to Gentile believers (Acts 15:23), and Paul later passed through, strengthening them, at the start of his second journey (Acts 15:41). On his voyage to Rome his ship crossed the sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia (Acts 27:5). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes the region was known for goat's-hair cloth used in tentmaking.

Clauda (Cauda in modern translations) was a small island south of Crete that the ship carrying Paul passed during a storm on his voyage to Rome. Driven by the wind, the ship ran under the island's shelter, and there the crew struggled to haul in the ship's boat (Acts 27:16).
