The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it about 23 miles west of Cape Matala. It suggests that in the calmer water south of the island the crew also undergirded the ship and adjusted the sails. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as about 7 miles long and 3 miles wide. It is today identified as Gavdos, the Greek island off the southwest coast of Crete, formerly called Gozzo. No coordinates are given for it in this entry.

Claudia was a Christian woman who, together with Eubulus, Pudens, Linus and "all the brethren," sent greetings to Timothy at the close of Paul's second letter to him (2 Tim 4:21). Because Paul appears to be writing from Rome, she was probably a member of the church there. Nothing more is known about her for certain. Later tradition adds details. The Apostolical Constitutions name her as the mother of Linus, whom Irenaeus and Eusebius list as a bishop of Rome. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions a conjecture that she was the wife of Pudens and a British princess, the daughter of King Cogidubnus. That theory rests on an epigram by the poet Martial about a couple named Claudia and Pudens. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that these identifications rest on very little evidence. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "lame."

Claudius (4th Roman Emperor) was the ruler of the Roman Empire during part of the apostles' ministry, reigning from AD 41 to 54 according to Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary. He succeeded Caligula. Acts names him twice. The prophet Agabus foretold a great famine "throughout all the world," which Luke says came to pass in the days of Claudius Caesar (Acts 11:28). Classical writers, cited by the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, also describe his reign as a time of bad harvests and scarcity. Claudius also ordered all Jews to leave Rome, which is why Aquila and Priscilla had recently come from Italy when Paul met them in Corinth (Acts 18:2). The Roman historian Suetonius links the expulsion to Jewish unrest. Its date is uncertain: Easton's gives AD 49, and others suggest about AD 50 or later.

Claudius Lysias was the Roman commander of the garrison in Jerusalem who sent Paul under guard to the governor Felix at Caesarea, with a letter that opens with his own name and greeting (Acts 23:26). The surrounding chapters, where he appears as the "chief captain", say he rescued Paul from a mob at the temple, bound him and questioned him. He let Paul speak to the crowd and stopped short of having him scourged once he learned Paul was a Roman citizen (Acts 21:31–40; 22:24–29). After a stormy session of the Sanhedrin and news of a plot against Paul's life, he sent him to Felix, by inference about AD 56. In Acts 22:28 the commander says he bought his citizenship. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both take him to be a Greek who adopted the Roman name Claudius when he became a citizen.

Clement was a Christian whom Paul names in Phil 4:3 as one of his fellow workers in spreading the gospel, whose names, Paul says, are in the book of life. He is mentioned alongside women who had worked with Paul, and Paul asks his "true yokefellow" to help them. Since the letter was written to the church at Philippi, he was probably a member of that congregation, as Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take him to be. The name means "mild" or "merciful." Ancient church writers such as Origen and Eusebius identified him with Clement, later bishop of Rome and author of a letter to the Corinthians. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name was common and that this identification can be neither proved nor disproved. This entry treats him simply as Paul's coworker at Philippi.

Cleophas is the name the King James Version uses in John 19:25 for the husband of Mary, one of the women who stood by the cross of Jesus. This entry treats him as the same man as Cleopas, one of the two disciples who met the risen Jesus on the road to Emmaus and asked him if he was the only visitor to Jerusalem who had not heard what had happened there (Luke 24:18). Whether the two are one person is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary allows that they may be, and also mentions a possible link with Alphaeus (Matt 10:3). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat them as different men, pointing out that Cleopas is a Greek name, a short form of Cleopatros, while Clopas (the Revised Version spelling in John) is Aramaic. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Cnidus was a city and harbor at the tip of a long peninsula on the southwest corner of Asia Minor, in the district of Caria within the Roman province of Asia. It is mentioned once, in the account of Paul's voyage to Rome, about AD 56 by inference from context. After leaving Myra, the ship sailed slowly for many days and only with difficulty came off Cnidus. The contrary wind then kept it from holding its course, so it turned south to shelter under Crete near Salmone (Acts 27:7). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that ships coasting along southern Asia Minor turned north at this point, that the city had two harbors and the status of a free city, and that Jews lived there by the 2nd century BC. Its ruins lie at the promontory Smith's Bible Dictionary calls Cape Crio, in present-day Turkey, and the location shown here marks that site.

Col-hozeh was the father of Shallun, who repaired the Fountain Gate of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. Shallun rebuilt and roofed the gate, set up its doors, locks and bars, and repaired the wall of the pool of Siloah by the king's garden as far as the stairs down from the City of David (Neh 3:15). The title "ruler of part of Mizpah" most naturally belongs to Shallun, though the wording could also be read as describing Col-hozeh. Nothing else is recorded about this man. The same name appears in Neh 11:5 for an ancestor of Maaseiah of the tribe of Judah, and it is unclear whether these are the same person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "every prophet."

Col-hozeh was the son of Hazaiah and the father of Baruch. He appears only in the family line of Maaseiah, his grandson, who was one of the people living in Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time after the return from exile (Neh 11:5). By inference from the surrounding passage, this family belonged to the tribe of Judah and traced its descent back through Joiarib and Zechariah to Shiloni. Nothing else is recorded about him. The same name belongs to the father of Shallun, who repaired the Fountain Gate (Neh 3:15). Whether the two are the same man is uncertain, and this entry treats Col-hozeh of Neh 11:5 on his own. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "every prophet."

Colossae (spelled Colosse in the King James Version) was a city in Phrygia in western Asia Minor. Paul's letter to the Colossians is addressed to the believers there (Col 1:2). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on the Lycus River, a tributary of the Maeander, about 12 miles from Laodicea and near the main road from Ephesus to the Euphrates. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it was also close to Hierapolis, that it was known for a distinctive wool, and that it declined as those neighboring cities grew. Both dictionaries infer from the letter that Paul had probably not visited the city himself, and that its church was founded through the work of Epaphras. The site was later called Chonae, and its ruins lie near the modern town of Honaz in southwestern Turkey, which matches the location shown here.

The Commandments and Tradition Discourse was Jesus' reply to scribes and Pharisees from Jerusalem who asked why his disciples ate without washing their hands, as the tradition of the elders required (Matt 15:1–2; Mark 7:1–5). Jesus said they set aside God's commandment to keep their tradition. As an example he cited the command to honor father and mother, which their practice of declaring property "Corban," a gift, allowed a son to avoid. He applied Isaiah's words about worship of the lips rather than the heart. He then told the crowd that what enters the mouth does not defile a person, but what comes out of the heart does. When the disciples said the Pharisees were offended, he called them blind leaders of the blind, and Peter asked him to explain the saying. This entry places it at Capernaum after the Bread of Life Sermon, about AD 29, by inference from context.

Conaniah was one of the chief Levites during the reign of King Josiah of Judah. According to 2 Chr 35:9, he and his brothers Shemaiah and Nethaneel, along with Hashabiah, Jeiel and Jozabad, gave the Levites 5,000 sheep and goats and 500 oxen for the Passover offerings. This was the large Passover that Josiah held in Jerusalem, which the surrounding chapter places in Josiah's eighteenth year. His name is usually explained as meaning "the Lord has established." A Levite with a very similar name, spelled Cononiah in the King James Version, was put in charge of the tithes and offerings in Hezekiah's time (2 Chr 31:12). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the two as separate men. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Conaniah as a Levite placed over the tithes brought into the temple. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Concubine the Aramitess is an unnamed woman mentioned once, in the genealogy of Manasseh in 1 Chr 7:14. She was a concubine, probably of Manasseh, the son of Joseph, since the verse lists the sons of Manasseh and then refers to "his concubine." She is called an Aramitess, meaning a woman from Aram, the region of the Arameans (Syria). She was the mother of Machir, who is described as the father of Gilead. Other passages, such as Num 26:29 and Gen 50:23, name Machir as Manasseh's son, which supports the inference that Manasseh was her partner. The wording of the verse is difficult. It says Ashriel was born to an unnamed "she" and then sets the Aramitess apart as Machir's mother, so the relationship between the two women, and between the two sons, is uncertain. Nothing else is recorded about her.

Cononiah was a Levite in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He was put in charge of the offerings, tithes and dedicated gifts that the people brought to the temple, and his brother Shimei served as his second in command. Ten overseers, including Jehiel, Azaziah and Mahath, worked under the two brothers. They were appointed by the king and by Azariah, the ruler of the house of God (2 Chr 31:12–13). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "appointed by the Lord" and dates his service to about 726 BC. The name also appears in the form Conaniah, the spelling used in the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and other reference works. That form is also given to a later Levite leader in Josiah's time, who is a different person.

The Construction of Solomon's Temple was King Solomon's building of a house for the LORD in Jerusalem, described in 1 Kings 5–7. With peace on every side, Solomon made a treaty with Hiram king of Tyre, who sent cedar from Lebanon by sea in return for food. Large work gangs quarried great stones for the foundation. Work began in Solomon's fourth year, in the month Zif, about 1012 BC by inference from context, and 1 Kgs 6:38 says it took seven years. The house measured sixty by twenty by thirty cubits. Its stone was dressed before delivery, so no iron tool was heard on site. Inside it was lined with carved cedar and overlaid with gold, and two large cherubim stood in the inner sanctuary. A craftsman also named Hiram, brought from Tyre, cast the bronze pillars Jachin and Boaz, the sea and ten stands in the Jordan plain. The account also describes Solomon's palace buildings.

The Conversion of Ethiopian Eunuch was Philip the Evangelist's meeting with a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, on the desert road from Jerusalem to Gaza. Sent there by an angel, Philip found the eunuch, who managed the queen's treasury, returning from worship in Jerusalem and reading Isaiah in his chariot. Prompted by the Spirit, Philip joined him and, starting from the passage about one led like a sheep to slaughter (Isa 53:7–8), told him about Jesus. At some water the eunuch asked to be baptized, and Philip baptized him. The Spirit of the Lord then took Philip away. The eunuch went on rejoicing, and Philip reappeared at Azotus and preached as far as Caesarea. The eunuch's confession in Acts 8:37 is missing from many early manuscripts. Ethiopia here probably means Kush, south of Egypt. The event followed Philip's work in Samaria, about AD 32 by inference.

Coos (spelled Cos in modern translations) was a small island in the Aegean Sea off the coast of Caria in southwest Asia Minor, northwest of Rhodes. It is now the Greek island of Kos, called Stanchio in older works. Paul's ship sailed straight there from Miletus on his return voyage to Jerusalem at the end of his third missionary journey, about AD 54 by inference from context. The next day it went on to Rhodes and then Patara (Acts 21:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary says the party spent the night there. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes Cos as a busy commercial center and a home of a Jewish community, known for its wine, fine cloth and medical school, and as the birthplace of Hippocrates. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both note that Herod the Great was one of the island's benefactors.

Corinth was a Greek city on the isthmus joining the Peloponnese to mainland Greece, about 48 miles west of Athens according to Easton's Bible Dictionary. The location shown here is the site of ancient Corinth, near the modern town. Its harbors made it a major trading center, and the city of Paul's day was a Roman colony rebuilt after its destruction in 146 BC. Paul came there from Athens (Acts 18:1) and founded a church, to which he later wrote 1 and 2 Corinthians, the second also addressed to believers throughout Achaia (2 Cor 1:1). Apollos later worked there (Acts 19:1), Paul delayed a return visit to spare the church (2 Cor 1:23), and Erastus stayed there (2 Tim 4:20). By inference, 1 and 2 Thessalonians were written from Corinth during Paul's first stay, dated here to about AD 49. Easton's places his arrival in AD 51 or 52.

The Corn on the Sabbath was an incident, recorded in Matthew, Mark and Luke, in which Jesus' disciples picked heads of grain while walking through fields on the Sabbath. ("Corn" in the King James Version means grain, probably wheat or barley.) They were hungry, and rubbed the ears in their hands and ate. Pharisees objected that this was unlawful on the Sabbath. Jesus replied by recalling how the hungry David ate the consecrated bread in the house of God, which only priests could lawfully eat (the episode told in 1 Sam 21). Matthew adds that priests work in the temple on the Sabbath without guilt, and quotes "I will have mercy, and not sacrifice." Mark adds that "the sabbath was made for man." All three end with Jesus saying the Son of man is Lord of the Sabbath. The setting is probably Galilee, about AD 28, by inference from context.

Cornelius was a Roman centurion of the Italian band, a military unit stationed at Caesarea (Acts 10:1). His messengers described him as a just man who feared God and was well regarded by the Jewish people (Acts 10:22). While praying at the ninth hour, he saw an angel in a vision. The angel told him his prayers and alms had been remembered by God and directed him to send for Peter (Acts 10:3, 30–31). He sent two household servants and a devout soldier to Joppa, where they found Peter (Acts 10:7, 17, 21). When Peter arrived, Cornelius had gathered his relatives and close friends, and he fell at Peter's feet (Acts 10:24–25). Later verses in the chapter (Acts 10:44–48) describe his household being baptized. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries treat him as the first Gentile convert to Christianity. The meeting is dated here to about AD 38, by inference from context.

The Corner Gate was a gate in the wall of Jerusalem, probably near a corner of the city's defenses, as its name suggests. When Jehoash king of Israel defeated and captured Amaziah king of Judah, he broke down 400 cubits (roughly 180 meters) of Jerusalem's wall, from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate (2 Kgs 14:13; 2 Chr 25:23). Since the Ephraim Gate faced north, the Corner Gate is usually placed at the northwest corner of the city, though its exact site is uncertain. Uzziah later built and fortified towers at the Corner Gate (2 Chr 26:9). The prophets used it as a landmark: Jeremiah foresaw the city rebuilt from the tower of Hananel to the Corner Gate (Jer 31:38), and Zechariah included it among the boundaries of a restored Jerusalem (Zech 14:10). The location shown here marks a general point within Jerusalem, not a precisely identified site.

Cosam was a man named only in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, where he appears as the son of Elmodam and the father of Addi (Luke 3:28). Luke traces this line backward from Jesus through Joseph, and Smith's Bible Dictionary places Cosam in the line of Joseph the husband of Mary. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that he stands five generations before Zerubbabel. By inference from the order of the list, he probably lived in the period of the kings of Judah, before the Babylonian exile, as a descendant of David through Nathan rather than through the royal line of Solomon. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of his name as "divining" or "a diviner."

Coz was a man of the tribe of Judah who is named only in 1 Chr 4:8, where he is the father of Anub and Zobebah and is linked to the families of Aharhel son of Harum. The verse does not state who his parents were. Because it directly follows the list of Helah's sons by Ashhur (1 Chr 4:5–7), he is probably a son of Ashhur and Helah. That would make Zereth, Jezoar and Ethnan his brothers, and Ashhur's sons by his other wife, Naarah, his half-brothers. This entry treats Harum as his son, by inference from the same verse. The name means "thorn" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). The Revised Version renders it "Hakkoz" (Easton's Bible Dictionary). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia distinguishes him from the priestly family of Hakkoz mentioned in 1 Chr 24:10 and Ezra 2:61.

Cozbi was a Midianite woman, the daughter of Zur, who was head over a people and of a chief house in Midian (Num 25:15). She was killed during the plague connected with Israel's worship of Baal of Peor, while the Israelites were camped at Shittim. The wider account in Numbers 25:6–14 tells that an Israelite named Zimri, son of Salu and a leader among the Simeonites, brought her into the camp, and that Phinehas the priest killed them both. God then told Moses to treat the Midianites as enemies, because they had led Israel astray at Peor and in the matter of Cozbi, 'the daughter of a prince of Midian' (Num 25:18). Her father Zur is probably the same Zur later named among the five Midianite kings killed in Numbers 31:8. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of her name as 'deceitful.'

Cozeba (spelled Chozeba in the King James Version) was a town of Judah, mentioned once in the genealogy of Judah's son Shelah. 1 Chr 4:22 lists "the men of Chozeba" alongside Jokim, Joash and Saraph, people linked with rule in Moab, and calls these records "ancient things." Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies Cozeba with Chezib, where Shelah was born (Gen 38:5), and with Achzib, a town in the lowlands of Judah (Josh 15:44). The Shelah connection makes this identification a natural inference. The location shown here places it in the Judean lowlands (the Shephelah) southwest of Jerusalem, in keeping with that view. Its exact site is uncertain.

The Creation of Adam and Eve is the account in Genesis 2 of how God made the first man and woman. The LORD God formed the man from the dust of the ground and breathed the breath of life into his nostrils, so that he became a living being. God planted a garden in Eden and placed the man there to tend it, forbidding him only the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Saying it was not good for the man to be alone, God formed the animals and brought them to Adam, who named them, but no suitable partner was found. God then put Adam into a deep sleep, took one of his ribs, and made a woman from it. Adam called her Woman. The name Eve is given later, in Gen 3:20. This entry dates the event to about 4004 BC, an estimate inferred from context.

Crescens was a companion and coworker of Paul, mentioned only once in the Bible. In 2 Tim 4:10, Paul, writing during his imprisonment, says that Crescens had gone to Galatia, a region in central Asia Minor, at the same time that Titus had gone to Dalmatia and Demas had left for Thessalonica. Unlike Demas, Crescens is not said to have deserted Paul, so he probably went to Galatia on church work, by inference from the context. His Latin name means "growing" or "increasing." Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he was probably a Christian from Rome. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionary both note a tradition that he was one of the seventy disciples sent out by Jesus. A later church tradition also links him with founding a church at Vienne in Gaul. Nothing more about him is recorded in the Bible.

Crete is a large, mountainous island in the Mediterranean that closes off the Aegean Sea to the south. The ship carrying Paul to Rome struggled against the wind past Cnidus and then sailed along Crete's southern side, in the lee of the island, rounding Cape Salmone on its eastern tip (Acts 27:7). Because the harbor where they had stopped was poorly suited for wintering, most of those aboard wanted to reach Phenice, another Cretan harbor, and they set out along the coast when a gentle south wind blew (Acts 27:12–13). A violent storm then drove them off course, and Paul later told them they should have listened to him and stayed at Crete (Acts 27:21). In his letter to Titus, Paul says he left Titus on Crete to put things in order and appoint elders in every city (Titus 1:5). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the island was once known for its "hundred cities."

Crispus was the chief ruler of the Jewish synagogue at Corinth during Paul's mission there. Acts 18:8 records that he believed in the Lord together with his whole household, and that many other Corinthians who heard also believed and were baptized. Writing later to the Corinthian church, Paul names Crispus as one of only two people there, along with Gaius, whom he baptized personally (1 Cor 1:14). His conversion took place about AD 50, by inference from context, around the time Paul wrote his letters to the Thessalonians. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Sosthenes appears as synagogue ruler soon afterward (Acts 18:17), probably as his successor, and records a tradition that Crispus later became bishop of Aegina. His name means "curled" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names.

The Crossing the Jordan into Canaan was the Israelites' passage over the Jordan River into the land promised to them, led by Joshua after the death of Moses. God commanded Joshua to take the people across and promised to be with him as he had been with Moses. Joshua told the people to prepare food for three days. The eastern tribes, already settled beyond the Jordan, agreed to send their armed men ahead of the others. From Shittim Joshua sent two spies to Jericho, where Rahab hid them in exchange for a promise to spare her family. When the priests carrying the ark of the covenant stepped into the river, the water coming from upstream stopped and piled up near the city of Adam. The priests stood on dry ground in the riverbed while all Israel crossed opposite Jericho. The date of about 1451 BC is inferred from context.

The Crucifixion and Burial was the execution of Jesus Christ at Golgotha, which Luke calls Calvary, and his burial the same day, dated here to about AD 30 by inference from context. All four Gospels record it. Soldiers crucified him between two criminals, divided his clothes by lot, and Pilate had a sign placed over him reading "The King of the Jews." Passers-by, priests and soldiers mocked him. Darkness covered the land from the sixth to the ninth hour, after which Jesus cried out and died. The temple veil tore, the earth shook, and the centurion declared him the Son of God. Women from Galilee, including Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, and Salome, watched from a distance. Because the sabbath was near, Joseph of Arimathea obtained the body from Pilate. He and Nicodemus wrapped it and laid it in a nearby tomb, which was then sealed and guarded.

Cun (spelled Chun in the King James Version) was a city belonging to Hadarezer, king of Zobah in Syria. After David defeated Hadarezer, he took a very large amount of bronze from Cun and from Tibhath, another of Hadarezer's cities. According to 1 Chr 18:8, Solomon later used this bronze to make the bronze sea, the pillars and the bronze vessels for the temple. In the parallel account in 2 Sam 8:8, the name Berothai appears in its place. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the two as the same city and connects it with Berothah in Ezek 47:16. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes the substitution. The exact site is uncertain. The location shown here follows the identification with Berothai at modern Bereitan in the Beqaa Valley of Lebanon, south of Baalbek.

Cush was a region south of Egypt, usually rendered "Ethiopia" in the King James Version. Ezekiel describes Egypt as stretching "from the tower of Syene" (probably modern Aswan) to the border of Cush (Ezek 29:10), and the prophets regularly pair it with Egypt (Isa 20:3–5; Ezek 30:4; Nah 3:9). Its king Tirhakah marched out to fight the Assyrian king, identified as Sennacherib from the surrounding chapter, in Hezekiah's time (2 Kgs 19:9; Isa 37:9). Isaiah and Zephaniah speak of the land "beyond the rivers of Ethiopia" (Isa 18:1; Zeph 3:10), probably the Upper Nile and its tributaries. It is also listed with Seba, the Sabeans, Libya and Persia. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that some also placed a Cush in Asia, but it identifies the African Cush with Nubia and Abyssinia. The location shown here follows the African identification, in what is now northern Sudan.

Cush (son of Ham) was the first-named son of Ham, listed before his brothers Mizraim, Phut (Put) and Canaan in the table of nations (Gen 10:6; 1 Chr 1:8). Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him probably the eldest. His sons were Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah and Sabtecha, and through Raamah he was the grandfather of Sheba and Dedan (Gen 10:7; 1 Chr 1:9). He was also the father of Nimrod, who "began to be a mighty one in the earth" (Gen 10:8; 1 Chr 1:10). In the surrounding passage, these descendants stand for peoples and regions. Easton's notes that the land of Cush seems to take its name from him. In the Old Testament that name usually refers to the lands south of Egypt, rendered "Ethiopia" in the King James Version. Some writers have also linked it with parts of Arabia and Mesopotamia. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "blackness."

Cushan is a place or people named once in the Bible, in the prayer-psalm of Habakkuk, where the prophet sees "the tents of Cushan in affliction" alongside the trembling "curtains of the land of Midian" (Hab 3:7). The parallel with Midian suggests a desert tent-dwelling people near Israel's southern lands. Its identity is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it as a poetic or lengthened form of Cush, meaning an Arabian Cush. The Septuagint translates it as "Ethiopians," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia sees it as Cush used loosely. Smith's Bible Dictionary mentions a possible link with Cushan-rishathaim, the Mesopotamian king who oppressed Israel in Judg 3:8–10. The location shown here follows the identification with Cush and places it along the Nile in present-day northern Sudan, as a marker for the surrounding region rather than an exact site.

Cushi was the messenger Joab sent to tell King David what had happened in the battle against Absalom's rebels (2 Sam 18:21). The name probably means "the Cushite," that is, a man from Cush (roughly ancient Nubia or Ethiopia), and the Revised Version renders it that way. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as apparently attached to Joab's household. After Cushi set out, Ahimaaz son of Zadok persuaded Joab to let him run too, took the route through the plain, and arrived first (2 Sam 18:22–23). When Cushi reached David he announced that the Lord had avenged the king on his enemies. Asked whether Absalom was safe, he answered indirectly that he wished all the king's enemies would be as that young man was, conveying Absalom's death (2 Sam 18:31–32). The name Cushi is also borne by other people in the Bible.

Cushi was the father of Shelemiah and the great-grandfather of Jehudi, the man the princes of Judah sent to bring Baruch and the scroll of Jeremiah's prophecies he had read to the people (Jer 36:14). He is known only from this genealogy. His lifetime would have been about three generations before Jeremiah's, by inference from the line of descent. The name means "a Cushite." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that with the article it marks a person of Cushite origin, as with the messenger in 2 Sam 18, and that it later came to be used as a personal name. The same name belongs to other people in the Bible, including the father of the prophet Zephaniah, and they should not be confused with this man.

Cushi was the father of the prophet Zephaniah and the son of Gedaliah. He is named only in the opening line of the book of Zephaniah, which traces the prophet's ancestry back four generations through Cushi, Gedaliah and Amariah to Hizkiah (Zeph 1:1). Since Zephaniah prophesied in the days of Josiah king of Judah, Cushi probably lived in Judah in the generation before, around the reigns of Manasseh and Amon, by inference from the passage. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Cushi is shared by several people in the Bible. Among them are the messenger who brought news of Absalom's death to David and an ancestor of Jehudi in the time of Jeremiah. This entry concerns only Zephaniah's father.

Cuth was a city of Mesopotamia whose people, after the fall of the northern kingdom of Israel, were among the foreigners the king of Assyria settled in the towns of Samaria. There they made an image of their own god, Nergal, alongside the gods of settlers from Babylon, Hamath and elsewhere (2 Kgs 17:30). The same place is called Cuthah in 2 Kgs 17:24, which lists it among the cities from which these settlers came. It is generally identified with ancient Kutha, a city known as a center of the worship of Nergal, at the site of Tell Ibrahim in central Iraq, northeast of Babylon. The location shown here follows that identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "burning." In later Jewish tradition the Samaritans were sometimes called "Cutheans" after this group of settlers.

Cuthah was a city in Babylonia, one of the places from which the king of Assyria brought settlers to repopulate the cities of Samaria after the people of Israel were deported (2 Kgs 17:24). The same chapter later calls it Cuth and says its people brought the worship of their god Nergal with them (2 Kgs 17:30), which fits Cuthah's known role as a center of that god's cult. Easton's Bible Dictionary attributes the resettlement to Shalmaneser. It mentions a suggestion that the Cutheans were the same as the Cossaeans of the hill country north of the Choaspes River, and it identifies Cuthah with Tell Ibrahim, about 15 miles northeast of Babylon in present-day Iraq. The location shown here follows the Tell Ibrahim identification.

Cyprus is a large island in the eastern Mediterranean, about 60 miles off the Syrian coast, and still known by that name today. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the Old Testament "Chittim" (Kittim), which the prophets mention as a place linked to Tyre's sea trade and as a source of fine ivory-inlaid goods. In the New Testament it was the home of Barnabas and of Mnason, an early disciple. Believers scattered after Stephen's death preached there, and men from Cyprus were among the first to speak about Jesus to Greeks at Antioch. Barnabas and Saul sailed there from Seleucia at the start of their first missionary journey. After Barnabas and Paul separated, Barnabas returned to the island with Mark. Paul's later voyages passed by it, once sailing in its shelter because of contrary winds.

Cyrene was a Greek city in North Africa, west of Egypt, in the region Acts 2:10 calls the parts of Libya around Cyrene. Easton's Bible Dictionary says Greek colonists founded it about 630 BC and that it later had a large Jewish population. Simon of Cyrene, the father of Alexander and Rufus, was coming in from the country when Roman soldiers forced him to carry Jesus' cross. Jews and proselytes from the area around Cyrene were in Jerusalem at Pentecost, and Acts 6:9 mentions a Jerusalem synagogue of Cyrenians. Men of Cyprus and Cyrene later preached about Jesus to Greeks at Antioch, and Lucius of Cyrene was among the prophets and teachers of the church there. Easton's and Smith's dictionaries link the city with the Tripoli region. The location shown here is the site of its ruins near modern Shahhat in eastern Libya.

Cyrenius was the Roman governor of Syria when the census or registration took place that brought Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem around the time of Jesus' birth (Luke 2:2). Cyrenius is the King James spelling of the Greek form of the Latin name Quirinius, and Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary give his full name as Publius Sulpicius Quirinius. According to Smith's, he was a Roman consul and became governor of Syria in AD 6, after Archelaus was removed. How his governorship fits the date of Jesus' birth has long been discussed. Smith's suggests he served twice as governor, first around 4–1 BC. Easton's proposes that he governed Cilicia, then joined to Syria, before later serving as governor of Syria itself. Smith's connects a later census to the one mentioned in Acts 5:37.

Cyrus was the king of Persia whose decree, issued in his first year, allowed the Jewish exiles to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the temple of the LORD. The Bible presents this as fulfilling a word spoken through Jeremiah (2 Chr 36:22–23; Ezra 1:1–2). He returned the temple vessels that Nebuchadnezzar had carried to Babylon, handing them through his treasurer Mithredath to Sheshbazzar, whom he made governor. He also authorized the supply of cedar from Lebanon for the work. Opponents hindered the rebuilding throughout his reign, and a search for his decree later settled the dispute under Darius. Isaiah names Cyrus as the LORD's "shepherd" and "anointed," who would subdue nations and order Jerusalem rebuilt. Daniel continued into his reign and received a vision in his third year. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as the conqueror of Babylon, about 538 BC, and Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him the founder of the Persian empire.

Dabbesheth was a town on the boundary of the territory given to the tribe of Zebulun. The King James Version spells it Dabbasheth. It appears only once, in the description of Zebulun's border, which went up toward the sea past Maralah, reached Dabbesheth, and then reached "the river that is before Jokneam" (Josh 19:11). That river is probably the brook Kishon, which flows past Jokneam, so Dabbesheth likely lay on the western or southwestern edge of Zebulun's land. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with Dabsheh, a ruined site east of Acre. Some scholars instead place it closer to Jokneam, near the edge of the Jezreel Valley. The location shown here follows the Dabsheh identification. Nothing else is recorded about the town.

Daberath was a city in Lower Galilee, at the western foot of Mount Tabor. Its name probably means "pasture," according to Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. It appears on the line of Zebulun's border, which ran from Sarid past Chisloth-tabor to Daberath and up to Japhia (Josh 19:12). It lay on the boundary between Zebulun and Issachar and belonged to Issachar. It was one of the towns from Issachar given with its pasturelands to the Levites. Joshua 21:28 spells it Dabareh. The surrounding passages assign these towns to the Gershonite clan of Levites, which suggests Daberath went to the Gershonites (Josh 21:28; 1 Chr 6:72). Both Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the modern village of Daburiyya (Deburieh) on the lower western slopes of Mount Tabor. The location shown here follows that identification.

Dagon was the national god of the Philistines. After Samson was captured, the Philistine lords gathered to offer him a great sacrifice, crediting him with their victory (Judg 16:23). Dagon's temple there is usually placed at Gaza, where Samson had been taken. When the Philistines captured the ark of the covenant, they set it beside Dagon's image in his temple at Ashdod. On two mornings the image was found fallen face down before the ark, and the second time its head and hands lay broken off on the threshold. From then on, Dagon's priests and worshippers would not step on that threshold (1 Sam 5:2–5). Saul's head was later fastened in Dagon's temple (1 Chr 10:10). The name is commonly linked to the Hebrew word for "fish," and Easton's and Smith's Bible dictionaries describe the idol as part man, part fish. Hitchcock's Bible Names also gives "corn" as a possible meaning.

Dalaiah was a man of the tribe of Judah, one of the seven sons of Elioenai, and so a member of the royal line of David. He appears only in the genealogy of David's descendants in 1 Chr 3:24. He is the sixth son listed, after Hodaiah, Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub and Johanan, and before Anani. The surrounding genealogy traces this family through Jeconiah (Jehoiachin) and Zerubbabel, which places Dalaiah several generations after the Babylonian exile. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a descendant of the royal family of Judah and gives the meaning of his name as "freed by Jehovah." Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "the poor of the Lord." The name is often spelled Delaiah, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it under that form.

Dalmanutha was a place on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, mentioned only in Mark 8:10. Jesus and his disciples came there by boat after he fed the four thousand. By inference from the following verses, this is where the Pharisees came to argue with him and ask for a sign from heaven. The parallel account in Matt 15:39 says he came instead to "the coasts of Magdala" (Magadan in some manuscripts), and Matthew adds that Sadducees were present too. For this reason Dalmanutha is usually placed near Magdala on the western shore. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both suggest the small valley of 'Ain-el-Barideh ("the cold fountain"), about a mile from Magdala. The exact site is uncertain. The location shown here follows the western-shore identification near Magdala.

Dalmatia was a mountainous region on the eastern shore of the Adriatic Sea, in what is now coastal Croatia. Its name still survives there today. It is mentioned once in the Bible. In 2 Tim 4:10, Paul writes that Titus had gone to Dalmatia, while Demas had left for Thessalonica and Crescens for Galatia. The letter does not say why Titus went. The name first belonged to the land of the Dalmatae, an Illyrian tribe conquered by Rome. It was later used for the southern part of the Roman province of Illyricum and eventually for the whole province. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia thinks Paul probably meant the whole province. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects the region with Paul's own earlier preaching as far as Illyricum, mentioned in Rom 15:19. The location shown here is a point in the central Dalmatian coastal area.

Dalphon was the second of the ten sons of Haman, the Persian official who plotted to destroy the Jews in the reign of King Ahasuerus. He is named only in Esth 9:7, in the list of Haman's sons killed by the Jews in the fortress city of Shushan when the day set for their destruction was turned against their enemies. The surrounding verses go on to describe the bodies of the ten sons being hanged at Esther's request (Esth 9:13–14). His name's meaning is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "swift", the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "crafty", and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the house of caves". Nothing else is recorded about him.

Damaris was a woman of Athens who believed Paul's message after he spoke at the Areopagus, about AD 48 by inference from context. Acts 17:34 names her alongside Dionysius the Areopagite as among those who joined Paul and believed, while others mocked or put off hearing more. Nothing else is recorded about her. That she is one of only two converts named may suggest she was a woman of some standing, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes, comparing the prominent Greek women who believed at Berea. Chrysostom and others, as Smith's Bible Dictionary reports, held that she was the wife of Dionysius, though the verse itself does not say so. Her name is often explained as meaning "heifer" (Easton's Bible Dictionary), perhaps from a related Greek word, while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a little woman."

Damascus was an ancient city of Syria, about 130 miles northeast of Jerusalem, and the capital of the Aramean (Syrian) kingdom (Isa 7:8). It first appears in Abram's pursuit of the eastern kings and as the home of his steward Eliezer. David defeated the Syrians of Damascus and garrisoned the region. Later a rebel band led by Rezon took power there. Its kings, including Benhadad, Hazael and Rezin, alternately fought and allied with Israel and Judah. Then the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser took the city and deported its people to Kir, and Ahaz copied an altar he saw there. Naaman praised its rivers Abana and Pharpar. In Acts, Saul was converted near Damascus, about AD 32 by inference from context, and preached there. He later escaped the governor serving King Aretas. It is the present-day Syrian capital, which the location shown here matches.

Dan was the region allotted to the tribe of Dan, the seventh lot drawn when Joshua divided the land west of the Jordan. It lay between Judah and Ephraim and stretched toward the Mediterranean coast. Its towns included Zorah, Eshtaol, Ir-shemesh, Aijalon, Timnah, Ekron, Eltekeh, Gibbethon, Jehud and Bene-berak, with its border running toward Joppa (Japho). The Danites could not fully hold this land. The Amorites confined them to the hill country and kept them out of the valley, and by the time of the judges the tribe still had no settled inheritance. Judges 18 goes on to tell how part of the tribe moved north and took Laish, which they renamed Dan. That northern city is a separate place from the region described here. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "judgment" or "he that judges." The location shown here marks the tribe's original southern territory in the Shephelah, west of Jerusalem.

Dan was Israel's northernmost town, near the sources of the Jordan below Mount Hermon. Originally called Laish or Leshem, it was captured by members of the tribe of Dan, who renamed it after their ancestor (Josh 19:47; Judg 18:29). Its mention in Abram's pursuit of Lot's captors (Gen 14:14) probably uses the later name for the same area. The phrase "from Dan even to Beersheba" became a standard way of naming the whole land from north to south. Jeroboam set up one of his two golden calves here, and Jehu kept it (1 Kgs 12:29; 2 Kgs 10:29). Ben-hadad of Syria struck the town in Asa's reign, and Jeremiah pictured news of invasion arriving from Dan. "Danjaan" (2 Sam 24:6) is probably the same place. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies the site as Tell el-Kady (Tel Dan), which the location shown here matches.

Dan was a son of Jacob and the first of two sons born to him by Bilhah, Rachel's servant. Naphtali was his full brother, and Easton's Bible Dictionary counts Dan as Jacob's fifth son. Rachel named him, saying that God had judged her and heard her voice, and the name is usually taken to mean "judge" (Gen 30:6). His birth is placed at about 1755 BC, by inference from context. Only one son, Hushim, is recorded for him (Gen 46:23). In Jacob's final blessing he is pictured as a serpent by the road that bites a horse's heels (Gen 49:17). He was the ancestor of the tribe of Dan. Most later uses of the name refer to that tribe or to the northern city of Laish, which the Danites renamed after him (Judg 18:29). That city's name gave rise to the phrase "from Dan to Beersheba" (1 Sam 3:20).

Daniel was the second son of David, born at Hebron during David's reign there. His mother was Abigail, formerly the wife of Nabal the Carmelite, whom David married after Nabal's death (1 Sam 25). He is named Daniel in 1 Chr 3:1, while the parallel list in 2 Sam 3:3 calls him Chileab. Some take the two as names for the same man. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek reading and the shape of the Hebrew text suggest that "Chileab" may have arisen from a copying error in Samuel. The name Daniel means "God is my judge." Apart from his place in these birth lists, nothing more is recorded about him, and he plays no part in the later struggles over David's throne. He is distinct from the prophet Daniel and others who bear the same name.

Daniel was a priest descended from Ithamar, the son of Aaron, and was among the family heads who returned with Ezra from Babylon to Jerusalem (Ezra 8:2). A Daniel also appears among the priests who sealed the covenant drawn up under Nehemiah (Neh 10:6). Smith's Bible Dictionary treats these as two entries but suggests they may be the same man, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists both passages under one person. This entry follows that identification. The name means "God is my judge." He is not the prophet Daniel of the book of Daniel, who lived earlier, during the exile itself.

Daniel was a man of Judah taken to Babylon as an exile, where he was trained with Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah and given the Babylonian name Belteshazzar. He refused the king's food and wine and was noted for understanding visions and dreams. He revealed and interpreted Nebuchadnezzar's dream, was made ruler over the province of Babylon and chief of its wise men, and later read the mysterious writing for Belshazzar. Under Darius he was one of three presidents. When he kept praying toward Jerusalem despite a royal decree, he was thrown into a lions' den and came out unhurt. He lived into the reign of Cyrus. The later chapters of his book record his own visions, and Jesus cites "Daniel the prophet" (Matt 24:15). Ezekiel names a Daniel beside Noah and Job. Some take that Daniel to be an older figure, but this entry treats him as the same man. Several other men share the name.

Dannah was a city in the hill country of Judah, named once in the list of towns given to the tribe of Judah, where it appears just before Kirjath-sannah, also called Debir (Josh 15:49). Nothing else is said about it in the Bible. Its site is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it probably south or southwest of Hebron, though no trace of the name had been found. Easton's Bible Dictionary puts it about 8 miles southwest of Hebron. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with the village of Idhna, about 8 miles west of Hebron, and the location shown here follows the Idhna identification. Easton's gives the meaning of the name as "murmuring," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "judging."

Dara was one of the five sons of Zerah in the tribe of Judah, named with his brothers Zimri, Ethan, Heman and Calcol (1 Chr 2:6). Zerah was a son of Judah and Tamar (1 Chr 2:4), so Dara was Judah's grandson. The brother called Zimri here is probably the same man as the Zabdi named as Zerah's son in Josh 7:1. Dara appears only in this genealogy, and nothing else is recorded about him. Because the names Ethan, Heman and Calcol also appear in 1 Kgs 4:31 alongside a Darda, among the wise men whom Solomon surpassed, many readers take Dara and Darda to be the same person. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Darda is called a son of Mahol there, which leaves the link uncertain. It gives the meaning of Darda as "pearl of wisdom."

Darda was a wise man named, with his brothers Heman and Chalcol and with Ethan the Ezrahite, as a standard against which Solomon's wisdom is measured. 1 Kgs 4:31 calls them "the sons of Mahol" and says Solomon was wiser than all of them. The verse records nothing else about him. The similar list in 1 Chr 2:6, where the name appears as Dara, places him among the sons of Zerah, son of Judah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes both lines of descent. "Sons of Mahol" may name his father, which is the reading this entry follows. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "pearl of wisdom," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "home of knowledge." Rabbinic tradition read the name as "the generation of knowledge," taken to mean the wilderness generation.

Darius was a king of Persia during whose reign the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem resumed and was completed. He is generally identified as Darius I (Darius the Great), who followed Cyrus and Cambyses. Work on the temple had stopped because of local opposition until his second year (Ezra 4:5, 24). In that year the prophets Haggai and Zechariah began to speak, and their messages are dated by his reign (Hag 1:1; Zech 1:1). When Tattenai, the governor west of the Euphrates, wrote to Darius about the building work, the king ordered a search of the royal archives. Cyrus's earlier decree was found, and Darius confirmed it with his own decree that the work go ahead quickly. The temple was finished in the month Adar of his sixth year (Ezra 6:15). This Darius is distinct from Darius the Mede in Daniel and from Darius the Persian in Neh 12:22.

Darius, called "Darius the Persian," was a king of Persia named in Neh 12:22 as the limit of a record. The Levite heads of families, and also the priests, were registered in the days of the high priests Eliashib, Joiada, Johanan and Jaddua, up to his reign. Nothing else is said about him in this passage. Because several Persian kings bore the name Darius, which one is meant is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both identify him most likely as Darius II (Ochus or Nothus), son of Artaxerxes Longimanus, who reigned about 424–405 BC. Both also mention the view that he was Darius III (Codomannus), the last Persian king, who was defeated by Alexander the Great about 336–330 BC. This entry follows the Darius II identification as the more probable one. He should not be confused with Darius the Mede or with the other kings of this name.

Darius, called Darius the Mede, was the son of Ahasuerus and of Median descent. In the Book of Daniel he took over the kingdom of the Chaldeans (Babylon) at about sixty-two years old (Dan 5:31; Dan 9:1). He appointed 120 princes over the kingdom (Dan 6:1). Persuaded by his officials, he signed a binding decree (Dan 6:6–9), and in that account Daniel was thrown into the lions' den. Afterward Darius wrote to all peoples throughout his realm (Dan 6:25). Daniel prospered in his reign and in that of Cyrus the Persian (Dan 6:28), and later visions are dated to his first year (Dan 9:1; Dan 11:1). He is not named outside Daniel, and his historical identity is debated. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he was Astyages, the last Median king. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies him with Gubaru, whom Cyrus appointed governor of Babylon. Several other kings in the Bible share the name Darius.

Darkon was the ancestor of a family counted among the descendants of "Solomon's servants" who returned from exile in Babylon to Judah with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:56; Neh 7:58). Nothing is recorded about Darkon himself, only that his descendants appear in both versions of the list of returning exiles. The context shows that the family belonged to the group called Solomon's servants, which the lists place alongside the temple servants (Nethinim). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the return to about 536 BC, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras gives the name as Lozon. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "scatterer," the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia "carrier," and Hitchcock's Bible Names "of generation" or "of possession."

Dathan was a man of the tribe of Reuben, a son of Eliab and brother of Abiram and Nemuel (Num 26:9). With Abiram and On son of Peleth, he joined Korah the Levite in a rebellion against the leadership of Moses and Aaron in the wilderness (Num 16:1). When Moses summoned Dathan and Abiram, they refused to come (Num 16:12), so Moses went to them with the elders of Israel. The people were told to move away from the tents of Korah, Dathan and Abiram, and Dathan and Abiram stood at the doors of their tents with their wives and children (Num 16:24–27). The earth then opened and swallowed them, their households, their tents and their possessions (Deut 11:6; Ps 106:17). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Eliab was a son of Pallu, son of Reuben. Later passages recall the event as a well-known warning.

The Daughter of Herodias was the young woman who danced at the birthday feast of Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, and pleased him and his guests (Matt 14:6; Mark 6:22). Her mother, Herodias, had been the wife of Herod's brother Philip before marrying Herod. Herod swore to give the girl whatever she asked. According to the surrounding verses in both Gospels, she consulted her mother and, at her prompting, asked for the head of John the Baptist on a dish. Herod regretted his oath but had John beheaded in prison, and the head was brought to her, and she gave it to her mother. The Gospels do not name her. The Jewish historian Josephus names a daughter of Herodias as Salome, and Christian tradition has generally identified the dancer with her.

Daughter of Lot - Older was the elder of Lot's two daughters, called "the firstborn" in Genesis. She escaped with her father and sister when Sodom was destroyed, about 1897 BC by inference from context, and the three of them came to live in a cave. Believing there was no man left to marry them and that their father was old, she proposed to her younger sister that they make Lot drunk and lie with him to preserve his family line (Gen 19:31–34). She went to him first, and he did not know when she lay down or rose. The next day she urged her sister to do the same. She bore a son named Moab, whom the text identifies as the ancestor of the Moabites (Gen 19:37). Because Lot was the father of both sisters' children, her son Moab and her sister's son Ben-ammi were half-brothers to her as well as her sons and nephew.

Daughter of Lot - Younger is the unnamed younger of Lot's two daughters in Genesis 19. When the men of Sodom surrounded Lot's house, Lot offered his two unmarried daughters to them to protect his guests (Gen 19:8). At dawn the angels took Lot, his wife and the two daughters by the hand and led them out before the city was destroyed, about 1897 BC by inference from context. Lot's sons-in-law refused to leave (Gen 19:14). Whether they were engaged to these daughters or married to others is unclear. Lot later left Zoar and lived in a mountain cave with both daughters (Gen 19:30). There, following her older sister's plan, she conceived a child by her father (Gen 19:36). Gen 19:38 says she named her son Ben-ammi, ancestor of the Ammonites. Because Lot fathered both Ben-ammi and her sister's son Moab, both boys were also her half-brothers.

Daughter of Machir is an unnamed woman mentioned once in the genealogy of Judah. Her father Machir was the son of Manasseh, so she belonged to the Joseph tribes. She was the sister of Gilead, and other passages in 1 Chronicles name Peresh, Sheresh and Hammoleketh among Machir's children. According to 1 Chr 2:21, Hezron, a grandson of Judah, married her when he was sixty years old, and she bore him a son, Segub. The next verse says Segub was the father of Jair, who held towns in Gilead. Her marriage linked a line of Judah with Manasseh's territory east of the Jordan. Her own name is not recorded.

Daughter of Meshullam is an unnamed woman mentioned only in Neh 6:18. She was the daughter of Meshullam son of Berechiah and married Johanan, the son of Tobiah. From the surrounding passage (Neh 6:17), this Tobiah is Tobiah the Ammonite, one of Nehemiah's main opponents during the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls. The verse explains that many in Judah were bound by oath to Tobiah because of family ties. He was the son-in-law of Shechaniah son of Arah, and his son had married this woman. Her father is probably the same Meshullam son of Berechiah who repaired sections of the wall in Neh 3:4 and 3:30, so her marriage linked a family active in the rebuilding with Nehemiah's adversary. Nothing else is recorded about her.

The Daughter of Pharaoh was the Egyptian princess who found and adopted the infant Moses. She came down to bathe at the river, probably the Nile, with her maidens, saw a basket among the reeds, and sent her maid to fetch it (Exod 2:5). Moses' sister offered to find a Hebrew nurse, and the princess agreed, paying the child's own mother to nurse him (Exod 2:7–9). When the boy was older he was brought to her and became her son. She named him Moses, saying she had drawn him out of the water (Exod 2:10). Stephen recalls that she raised him as her own son (Acts 7:21), and Hebrews says Moses, when grown, refused to be called her son (Heb 11:24). The text names neither her nor her father. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests she was probably a daughter of Seti I and notes that Josephus calls her Thermuthis. Other daughters of Pharaoh, such as Solomon's wife, are different women.

Daughter of Pharaoh was an Egyptian princess, the daughter of a Pharaoh king of Egypt, whom Solomon married to seal an alliance with Egypt (1 Kgs 3:1). Her father is not named, and several other women in the Bible share this title. Solomon first brought her to live in the city of David while he finished building his palace, the temple and the wall of Jerusalem. He then built her a house of her own, designed like the porch of his palace (1 Kgs 7:8), and she moved up into it, after which he built the Millo (1 Kgs 9:24). According to 2 Chr 8:11, Solomon said his wife should not live in the house of David because places the ark of the LORD had entered were holy. She is named first among the many foreign wives Solomon loved (1 Kgs 11:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that this marriage is the first mention of a link between Israel and Egypt since the Exodus.

Daughter of Putiel is the unnamed woman described in Exod 6:25 as "one of the daughters of Putiel." She married Eleazar, the son of Aaron, and bore him a son, Phinehas. The verse appears in a genealogy of the Levites that lists the heads of their ancestral families. Nothing else is recorded about her, and the Bible gives neither her own name nor any further details about her father Putiel. Her son Phinehas went on to become a prominent priest in later passages such as Num 25:7–13, where he is promised a lasting priesthood.

Daughter of Shuah was a Canaanite woman who became the wife of Judah, son of Jacob. Her own name is not given. She is identified only through her father, Shuah (or Shua), a Canaanite. Judah met her while staying near his friend Hirah the Adullamite and married her (Gen 38:2). She bore him three sons, Er, Onan and Shelah (1 Chr 2:3). According to the surrounding account in Genesis 38, Shelah was born at Chezib, and she died some years later, before the events involving Tamar. The Hebrew phrase in 1 Chr 2:3 can also be read as a name, Bath-shua, meaning "daughter of Shua." Her firstborn son Er is described as evil in the LORD's sight and was put to death (1 Chr 2:3).

David was the son of Jesse of Bethlehem, of the tribe of Judah, and the great-grandson of Obed, son of Ruth (Ruth 4:17). 1 Chr 2:15 lists him as Jesse's seventh son. Samuel anointed him as a youth. He later fled from King Saul, led a band of followers and lived for a time at Ziklag. After Saul's death he became king, first at Hebron and then over all Israel from Jerusalem, the "city of David." His power reached as far as Damascus. The account of his family includes his wife Michal, conflict among his sons Amnon and Absalom, and the succession of his son Solomon. He organized the temple singers and is credited with many psalms. Later kings were measured against him, prophets spoke of a future David, and the New Testament calls Jesus the "son of David." By inference from context, he lived about 1085–1015 BC.

The killing of Goliath by David was a single combat during a standoff between Saul's army and the Philistines in the valley of Elah, in Judah. Goliath, a champion from Gath standing six cubits and a span (roughly nine and a half feet) in heavy bronze armour, challenged Israel morning and evening for forty days to send a man to fight him. David, Jesse's youngest son, had come from Bethlehem with food for his three eldest brothers. Hearing the challenge, he offered to fight, pointing to the lion and bear he had killed while keeping sheep. He refused Saul's armour and went out with his staff, his sling and five smooth stones. His first stone struck Goliath in the forehead, and David cut off the giant's head with Goliath's own sword. The Philistines fled, pursued as far as Gath and Ekron. This entry dates the event to about 1067 BC, by inference from context.

The Death of Abijam marks the end of the short reign of Abijam, king of Judah and son of Rehoboam, who is called Abijah in Chronicles. 1 Kgs 15:8 records it in the standard formula for a king's death: he "slept with his fathers," was buried in the city of David in Jerusalem, and his son Asa became king in his place. The parallel account in 2 Chr 14:1 gives the same details under the name Abijah. The passage does not say how he died. Since 1 Kgs 15:2 gives him a reign of three years, his death falls soon after his accession, about 956 BC by inference from context. Asa's reign follows it.

The Death of Abraham marks the end of the patriarch's life at the age of 175, as Gen 25:7 records. The verses that follow (Gen 25:8–10) say he died in a good old age, was gathered to his people, and was buried by his sons Isaac and Ishmael in the cave of Machpelah. This was the field Abraham had bought from the Hittites, where his wife Sarah was already buried. Machpelah lay near Mamre, which is identified with Hebron. Tradition places the cave at the site now known as the Cave of the Patriarchs in Hebron. By inference from the ages and chronology in Genesis, this entry dates his death to about 1821 BC. That would place it roughly 175 years after his birth, in Isaac's later years.

The Death of Adam is recorded in a single verse, Gen 5:5, which states that Adam lived 930 years in all and then died. It comes in the genealogy running from Adam to Noah, where each entry closes with the words "and he died." The surrounding verses (Gen 5:3–4) say Adam fathered Seth at 130 and lived another 800 years, having other sons and daughters. The text gives no details about how or where he died. This entry places it in the region of Eden. Genesis 3, however, records that Adam was driven out of the garden, so he probably died somewhere outside it. The date of about 3074 BC is an estimate inferred from context, counting 930 years from a creation date of 4004 BC in the traditional chronology associated with Archbishop James Ussher.

The Death of Ahaz was the end of the life and reign of Ahaz, king of Judah, which followed the Reign of Ahaz. The account in 2 Kings says simply that he "slept with his fathers", a common phrase for a king's death, and was buried with his ancestors in the city of David, meaning Jerusalem. His son Hezekiah then became king in his place. The parallel account in 2 Chr 28:27 adds that although he was buried in Jerusalem, he was not placed in the tombs of the kings of Israel. Isa 14:28 dates a prophetic oracle to the year Ahaz died. This entry places his death at about 726 BC, a date inferred from context rather than stated in the text.

The Death of Amaziah marked the end of the reign of Amaziah, king of Judah, dated here to about 810 BC by inference from context. The only verse supplied mentions it in passing. After the king "slept with his fathers," his son Azariah (also called Uzziah) rebuilt the port of Elath and restored it to Judah (2 Kgs 14:22). The surrounding narrative gives the details. A conspiracy formed against Amaziah in Jerusalem. He fled to Lachish, but his pursuers killed him there. His body was carried back on horses and buried with his ancestors in the city of David (2 Kgs 14:19–20; 2 Chr 25:27–28). The people of Judah then made his sixteen-year-old son Azariah king (2 Kgs 14:21).

The Death of Amon was the assassination of Amon, king of Judah, by his own servants, who conspired against him and killed him in his own house (2 Kgs 21:23). It ended a short reign, which the surrounding passage gives as two years (2 Kgs 21:19), and is dated here to about 640 BC by inference from context. The connection with Uzza comes from the following verses, which say Amon was buried in his tomb in the garden of Uzza, the same place his father Manasseh was buried (2 Kgs 21:18, 26). According to 2 Kgs 21:24, the people of the land then killed the conspirators and made his son Josiah king. The parallel account in 2 Chr 33:24–25 tells the same story.

The Death of Arphaxad marks the end of the life of Arphaxad, a son of Shem listed in the genealogy from Shem to Abram. Unlike the genealogy in Genesis 5, the list in Genesis 11 does not use the phrase "and he died." His death is inferred from the statement that he lived 403 years after fathering Salah and had other sons and daughters (Gen 11:13). The nearby verses say he was born two years after the flood and fathered Salah at 35 (Gen 11:10–12), which gives a total lifespan of about 438 years. The date shown here, about 1908 BC, is an estimate inferred from these figures and is not stated in the text. Nothing else is recorded about the circumstances of his death.

The Death of Asa ended the reign of Asa, king of Judah. 1 Kgs 15:24 reports that he "slept with his fathers," the usual phrase for a king's death, and was buried with his ancestors in the city of David in Jerusalem. His son Jehoshaphat succeeded him as king. The verse just before (1 Kgs 15:23) says that in old age he was diseased in his feet. The parallel account in 2 Chr 16:12–14 adds that this illness began in his thirty-ninth year as king and that he died in his forty-first year. It also says he was buried in a tomb he had prepared for himself in the city of David, laid on a bed filled with spices, and honored with a very great burning. The death is dated to about 914 BC, an estimate inferred from context.

The Death of Cainan marks the end of the life of Cainan, an early patriarch in the genealogy from Adam to Noah. Genesis 5:14 records that he lived nine hundred and ten years in all, and then he died. The surrounding genealogy (Gen 5:9–13) presents him as the son of Enos, Adam's grandson, and the father of Mahalaleel. He is also listed as Kenan in 1 Chr 1:2 and appears in Luke's genealogy of Jesus (Luke 3:37). He should not be confused with a second Cainan, son of Arphaxad, named only in Luke 3:36. Adding the ages given in Genesis 5 places his death about 2769 BC. This date and his birth date of about 3679 BC are estimates inferred from context and are not stated in the text. The verse follows the fixed pattern of this genealogy, which gives each patriarch's total years and ends with "and he died."

The Death of David was the end of King David's life and his burial in Jerusalem, recorded in 1 Kgs 2:10, which says he "slept with his fathers," a common biblical phrase for dying. He was buried in the city of David, the old stronghold of Zion that David had captured and made his capital (2 Sam 5:7). The account closes with a summary of his reign: forty years over Israel, seven in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem. The death is dated to about 1015 BC, by inference from context. It closes the reign of David and comes just after his final instructions to his son Solomon (1 Kgs 2:1–9). Solomon then sat on his father's throne. The parallel account in 1 Chr 29:26–28 adds that David died at a good old age, "full of days, riches, and honour."

The Death of Eber marks the end of the life of Eber, a descendant of Shem in the genealogy running from Shem to Abraham. Genesis 11 does not describe his death directly. Unlike the genealogy in Genesis 5, this list does not end each entry with "and he died." Instead it says that after fathering Peleg, Eber lived another 430 years and had other sons and daughters (Gen 11:17). The previous verse says he was 34 when Peleg was born, which gives a total lifespan of about 464 years. That makes him the longest-lived figure in the line after the Flood. His death is placed at about 1817 BC, a date inferred from the chronology of the genealogy rather than stated in the text.

The Death of Eli, Ark Captured was the day the aged priest and judge Eli learned that Israel had lost a battle to the Philistines, and he died on hearing the news. Eli was ninety-eight years old and nearly blind. A man who had fled from the army reached him and reported that Israel had been routed with heavy losses, that his two sons Hophni and Phinehas were dead, and that the ark of God had been taken. When the messenger mentioned the ark, Eli fell backward from his seat beside the gate and broke his neck, for he was old and heavy. The passage notes that he had judged Israel for forty years. The surrounding chapter places the scene at Shiloh. The date of about 1122 BC is an estimate inferred from context, following forty years after the start of his judgeship.

The Death of Enos is recorded in the genealogy of Genesis 5, which lists the descendants of Adam through Seth. Enos, the son of Seth and grandson of Adam, lived 905 years in all, and the text then states simply that he died (Gen 5:11). The surrounding genealogy says he fathered Kenan at ninety and lived 815 years afterward, having other sons and daughters. Like the other entries in this list, his ends with the same closing phrase, "and he died." This entry dates his death to about 2864 BC, an estimate inferred from the genealogy's figures, roughly 905 years after his birth. That date depends on reading the ages in Genesis 5 as a continuous chronology, and other ways of counting give different results.

The Death of Hezekiah was the end of the life and reign of Hezekiah, king of Judah. It is recorded briefly in 2 Kgs 20:21, which says that he "slept with his fathers," the usual biblical phrase for a king's death. His son Manasseh then became king in his place. This entry dates the event to about 697 BC, an estimate inferred from context. It closes the Reign of Hezekiah, which 2 Kgs 18:2 says lasted twenty-nine years. The parallel account in 2 Chr 32:33 adds that he was buried in the most honoured part of the tombs of David's descendants, and that all Judah and the people of Jerusalem honoured him at his death. The text does not give the cause of his death. Earlier, 2 Kgs 20:6 records a promise of fifteen more years of life after his serious illness, so he probably died at the end of that added period.

The Death of Isaac was the end of the patriarch Isaac's life at the age of 180 years, recorded in Gen 35:28–29. The text says he died "old and full of days" and was "gathered unto his people." His sons Esau and Jacob, long estranged, buried him together. The preceding verse, Gen 35:27, places Isaac at Mamre near Hebron when Jacob returned to him, which is why this entry locates his death there. Jacob's later words in Gen 49:31 indicate that Isaac was buried in the cave of Machpelah, beside Abraham and Sarah. Although the account comes at this point in Genesis, Isaac's age suggests he lived on for some years after events told later, such as Joseph being sold into Egypt. This entry dates his death to about 1716 BC, an estimate inferred from context.

The Death of Ishmael was the end of the life of Ishmael, the son of Abraham and Hagar. Genesis records that he lived 137 years, then "gave up the ghost and died" and was "gathered unto his people," a common biblical phrase for joining one's ancestors in death (Gen 25:17). The notice comes at the close of a list of Ishmael's twelve sons and their settlements, just after the account of Abraham's death and burial, which Ishmael attended with Isaac. The date, about 1773 BC, is an estimate inferred from context, counting 137 years from his birth around 1910 BC. The text does not say where or how he died, though the surrounding verses place his descendants in the region from Havilah to Shur, east of Egypt.

The Death of Jacob was the end of the life of the patriarch Jacob, also called Israel, in Egypt. He had lived there seventeen years, and his whole life lasted 147 years. This entry dates his death to about 1689 BC, an estimate inferred from context. Before he died he blessed his twelve sons, the heads of the twelve tribes of Israel, each with his own blessing. He then told them he was about to be 'gathered unto my people.' He asked to be buried with his ancestors in the cave in the field of Machpelah, near Mamre in Canaan, which Abraham had bought from Ephron the Hittite. Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, and Jacob's wife Leah were already buried there. The following verses (Gen 49:33; Gen 50) record that he died, that Joseph had him embalmed, and that his sons carried out his burial request.

The Death of Jared closes the life of Jared, an early patriarch in the line from Adam to Noah. Genesis 5:20 records that he lived 962 years in all and then died. The surrounding genealogy (Gen 5:15–19) names him as the son of Mahalaleel and the father of Enoch. The age given makes him the second-longest-lived person in the genealogy, behind only his grandson Methuselah, whose 969 years appear in Gen 5:27. The Bible gives no details about how his death happened. By inference from the genealogy's chronology, his death is dated here to about 2582 BC, roughly 962 years after his birth in about 3544 BC. These dates are estimates and are not stated in the text.

The Death of Jehoahash was the death and burial of Joash (also called Jehoash), king of the northern kingdom of Israel. This entry's title combines the forms of his name, and he is not to be confused with his father Jehoahaz (2 Kgs 13:10). The account says Joash "slept with his fathers," the usual phrase for a king's death. He was buried in Samaria, Israel's capital, alongside earlier kings of Israel. His son Jeroboam, usually called Jeroboam II, took the throne after him. The same death notice appears again at 2 Kgs 14:16, after the story of Joash's war with Amaziah of Judah. The date of about 825 BC is an estimate inferred from context.

The Death of Jehoahaz marks the end of the reign of Jehoahaz, king of the northern kingdom of Israel. According to 2 Kgs 13:9, he "slept with his fathers," a common biblical way of describing a natural death. He was buried in Samaria, Israel's capital, and his son Joash (also called Jehoash) became king after him. The surrounding chapter identifies this Jehoahaz as the son of Jehu and says he reigned seventeen years (2 Kgs 13:1). By inference from context, his death took place around 840 BC. He should not be confused with Jehoahaz of Judah, the son of Josiah, who was taken captive and died in Egypt (2 Kgs 23:31–34).

The Death of Jehoram marks the end of the reign of Jehoram (also called Joram), king of Judah and son of Jehoshaphat. 2 Kgs 8:24 says he "slept with his fathers" and was buried with them in the city of David, meaning Jerusalem, and that his son Ahaziah became king after him. By inference from context, this happened about 886 BC, after a reign that 2 Kgs 8:17 puts at eight years. The parallel account in 2 Chr 21:18–20 adds that he died in great pain from an incurable disease of the bowels. It also says the people made no burning in his honor, as they had for his ancestors, and that he was buried in the city of David but not in the tombs of the kings. He should not be confused with his contemporary of the same name, Jehoram son of Ahab, king of Israel.

The Death of Jehoshaphat was the end of the life and reign of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah and son of Asa. 1 Kgs 22:50 records it briefly. He "slept with his fathers," the usual phrase for a king's peaceful death, and was buried with his ancestors in the city of David, meaning Jerusalem. His son Jehoram then became king in his place. The parallel account in 2 Chr 21:1 repeats these details, and 1 Kgs 22:42 states that Jehoshaphat reigned twenty-five years in Jerusalem. This entry dates his death to about 889 BC, an estimate inferred from context rather than stated in the text. It closes his reign as one episode in the history of the southern kingdom of Judah.

The Death of Jehu marks the end of the reign of Jehu, the army commander who seized the throne of the northern kingdom of Israel and ended the house of Ahab. The account is brief. It says only that Jehu "slept with his fathers," the usual phrase for a king's natural death. He was buried in Samaria, the royal capital, and his son Jehoahaz succeeded him (2 Kgs 10:35). The next verse, 2 Kgs 10:36, says Jehu reigned over Israel for twenty-eight years. His death began the dynasty of his descendants on Israel's throne, which 2 Kgs 10:30 records had been promised to last four generations. This entry places his death at about 857 BC, a date inferred from context and not stated in the text.

The Death of Jeroboam II marked the end of the long reign of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of the northern kingdom of Israel. 2 Kgs 14:29 records it in the standard formula for a royal death: he "slept with his fathers," with the kings of Israel, and his son Zachariah reigned in his place. This entry dates it to about 784 BC, by inference from context, following a 41-year reign (2 Kgs 14:23). Other chronologies place it several decades later, and the gap between this date and Zachariah's accession in Azariah's 38th year (2 Kgs 15:8) has led some to suppose an interregnum. The later account in 2 Kgs 15:8–12 says Zachariah ruled only six months before Shallum killed him, ending the dynasty of Jehu in its fourth generation, as that passage notes had been promised to Jehu.

The Death of Job is recorded in the closing verses of the book of Job. After his ordeal ended and his fortunes were restored, Job lived another 140 years. He saw his children, grandchildren and descendants to the fourth generation, and then he died "old and full of days" (Job 42:16–17). The text gives no cause of death and no burial place.
