This entry dates his death to about 1580 BC and his birth to about 1720 BC, both estimates inferred from context. The book itself gives no calendar date, and the age-related estimates here do not fully account for the 140 years after his restoration plus his life before it, so the timing of Job's life remains uncertain.

The Death of Joseph was the end of the life of Joseph, son of Jacob, in Egypt at the age of 110. Joseph had lived there with his father's household long enough to see Ephraim's great-grandchildren, and the children of Manasseh's son Machir were raised on his knees. Before he died, he told his brothers that God would surely bring them out of Egypt to the land promised to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. He made the Israelites swear an oath to carry his bones up from Egypt when that happened. After his death he was embalmed and placed in a coffin in Egypt. Later passages record that the oath was kept: Moses took Joseph's bones at the exodus (Exod 13:19), and they were buried at Shechem (Josh 24:32). This entry dates his death to about 1635 BC, an estimate inferred from context.

The Death of Joshua was the end of the life of Joshua son of Nun, Moses' successor and leader of Israel, who is called "the servant of the LORD" and died at the age of 110 (Josh 24:29). It came "after these things," meaning after he had gathered the tribes at Shechem and renewed their covenant with God. He was buried within the boundary of his own inheritance at Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim, on the north side of the hill of Gaash (Josh 24:30). Judges 2:8–9 repeats the notice almost word for word, naming the burial place Timnath-heres, and uses it to mark the passing of his generation. The date shown here, about 1424 BC, is an estimate inferred from context and is not stated in the text.

The Death of Josiah was the killing of Josiah, king of Judah, at Megiddo by Pharaoh-nechoh, king of Egypt. According to 2 Kgs 23:29, Necho was marching north to the Euphrates River against the king of Assyria when Josiah went out to confront him, and Necho killed him at Megiddo as soon as they met. The passage does not say why Josiah opposed the Egyptian advance. The parallel account in 2 Chr 35:20–24 adds that Necho warned Josiah not to interfere, that Egyptian archers wounded the disguised king in battle on the plain of Megiddo, and that his servants carried him back to Jerusalem, where he died and was buried amid national mourning. The event ended Josiah's reign and is dated to about 609 BC, by inference from context.

The Death of Jotham marks the end of the reign of Jotham, king of Judah. According to 2 Kgs 15:38, he "slept with his fathers", the usual phrase for a king's natural death. He was buried with his ancestors in the city of David, the royal burial area in Jerusalem, and his son Ahaz became king in his place. The parallel account in 2 Chr 27:9 records the same burial and succession. Earlier verses in the same chapter say Jotham came to the throne at twenty-five and reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem, so by inference he died at about forty-one. This entry dates his death to about 742 BC, an estimate inferred from context. The event closes Jotham's reign and opens that of Ahaz in the history of the southern kingdom of Judah.

The Death of Lamech was the end of the life of Lamech, the father of Noah, recorded in the genealogy from Adam to Noah. Genesis 5:31 says he lived 777 years in all and then died. This entry dates it to about 2353 BC, an estimate inferred from the ages in the genealogy. The surrounding verses (Gen 5:25–30) identify him as the son of Methuselah and say he fathered Noah at 182, so by inference he died when Noah was 595, about five years before the Flood, which came in Noah's 600th year (Gen 7:6). He should not be confused with the Lamech of Cain's line in Gen 4:18–24, a different person.

The Death of Mahlaleel ended the long life of Mahalaleel, a descendant of Seth in the line of patriarchs between Adam and Noah. Genesis 5 records that he lived 895 years in all and then died (Gen 5:17). The verse follows the chapter's repeated pattern for each generation: the total of a patriarch's years, then the words "and he died." The surrounding genealogy shows that he was the son of Kenan and the father of Jared. This entry dates his death to about 2714 BC and his birth to about 3609 BC. Both dates are estimates reached by inference from the ages given in the genealogy, not dates stated in the text. No other details of his death are recorded.

The Death of Manasseh ended the reign of Manasseh son of Hezekiah, king of Judah. 2 Kgs 21:18 says he "slept with his fathers," the usual phrase for a king's natural death. He was buried in the garden of his own house, called the garden of Uzza, and his son Amon succeeded him. This is unusual, because many earlier kings of Judah are said to have been buried in the city of David. The parallel account in 2 Chr 33:20 also places the burial at his own house. Later in the chapter (2 Kgs 21:26), Amon is buried in the same garden. The garden's exact location is unknown, though it was probably near the royal residence in Jerusalem. By inference from context, the death is dated to about 642 BC, after a reign that 2 Kgs 21:1 gives as fifty-five years.

The Death of Menahem was the end of the reign of Menahem, king of the northern kingdom of Israel, recorded in 2 Kgs 15:22. The text says that he "slept with his fathers," the usual expression for a king's death and burial, and that his son Pekahiah became king after him. Earlier verses in the same chapter say that Menahem took the throne by killing Shallum, reigned ten years in Samaria, and paid heavy tribute to Pul, king of Assyria (2 Kgs 15:14–20). The wording suggests a natural death. If so, he was one of the few kings in Israel's final decades not to be assassinated, though his son Pekahiah was later killed by Pekah (2 Kgs 15:25). This entry dates the event to about 761 BC, by inference from context. Other chronologies place it differently, often around the 740s BC.

The Death of Methuselah is the brief notice in Genesis that Methuselah died after living 969 years (Gen 5:27), the longest lifespan given for anyone in the Bible. It closes his entry in the genealogy from Adam to Noah, which follows a set pattern of age at fatherhood, remaining years, total years, and the words "and he died." The text gives no cause or circumstances. By inference from the surrounding numbers, he died in the year of the flood: he fathered Lamech at 187 (Gen 5:25), Lamech fathered Noah at 182 (Gen 5:28), and the flood came when Noah was 600 (Gen 7:6), which adds up to 969. This entry dates his death to about 2348 BC, an estimate drawn from that genealogical chronology, not a date stated in the text.

The Death of Moses is recorded in Deuteronomy 34. Moses climbed from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, to the top of Pisgah opposite Jericho. From there the LORD showed him the land promised to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, from Gilead and Dan to the western sea, the Negev and Zoar, but told him he would not cross into it. Moses died there in Moab at 120 years old, with his eyesight and strength still intact. He was buried in a valley opposite Beth-peor, and the text notes that no one knows where his grave is. Israel mourned him for thirty days. Joshua son of Nun, on whom Moses had laid his hands, then led the people. The passage ends by saying no later prophet in Israel was like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face. By inference from context, this entry dates his death to about 1452 BC.

The Death of Nahor was the end of the life of Nahor, son of Serug and father of Terah, and so the grandfather of Abraham. He is not the same person as Abraham's brother Nahor. The genealogy in Genesis 11 does not narrate his death or say "and he died," as Genesis 5 does for earlier generations. It is inferred from the stated length of his life. By Gen 11:24 he was 29 when Terah was born, and Gen 11:25 says he lived another 119 years and had other sons and daughters. That gives a lifespan of about 148 years, the shortest of the post-Flood figures listed in that chapter. This entry dates his death to about 2007 BC, a date inferred from the chapter's chronology rather than stated in the text.

The Death of Noah is recorded in a single brief statement at the close of his story: all of Noah's days came to 950 years, and then he died (Gen 9:29). The verse just before it, Gen 9:28, adds that he lived 350 years after the flood. Since Gen 7:6 places the flood in his six-hundredth year, the figures agree. His death follows the account of his drunkenness and his blessing and curse on his sons, and it ends the narrative of his life. The text gives no place or circumstances for his death. This entry dates it to about 1998 BC, by inference from the chronology of Genesis, which would put his birth about 2948 BC. Noah's age matches the long lifespans given for the generations before the flood in Gen 5. His total of 950 years is among the longest recorded there.

The Death of Omri was the end of the reign of Omri, king of the northern kingdom of Israel. The text says only that he "slept with his fathers," a common phrase for a king's death, and was buried in Samaria, and that his son Ahab became king after him (1 Kgs 16:28). The surrounding passage explains the burial place. Omri had bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer and built the city there, making it his capital, and he reigned twelve years in all (1 Kgs 16:23–24). His death opened the reign of Ahab, which the following chapters describe at length. This entry dates the event to about 918 BC, an estimate inferred from context rather than a date given in the text.

The Death of Pekah was the assassination of Pekah son of Remaliah, king of the northern kingdom of Israel, by Hoshea son of Elah. Hoshea organized a conspiracy, struck Pekah down, killed him, and became king in his place. The text dates this to the twentieth year of Jotham son of Uzziah, king of Judah. That is unusual, since 2 Kgs 15:33 gives Jotham a reign of sixteen years, so the year is probably counted from the start of his reign, which continued into his successor's time. The killing ended Pekah's twenty-year reign (2 Kgs 15:27) and came soon after the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser took Galilee and Gilead (2 Kgs 15:29). Hoshea went on to be Israel's last king (2 Kgs 17). This entry dates the event to about 739 BC, by inference from context. Other chronologies place it nearer 732 BC.

The Death of Pekahiah was the assassination of Pekahiah, king of the northern kingdom of Israel, by Pekah son of Remaliah, one of his own captains. Pekah conspired against him and struck him down in Samaria, inside the palace of the king's house. He did it with fifty men of Gilead. The verse also names Argob and Arieh in connection with the killing, though it is unclear whether they were fellow conspirators or royal officials who died alongside the king. Pekah then took the throne in his place (2 Kgs 15:25). The event ended Pekahiah's short reign and his family's hold on the throne. It is dated here to about 759 BC, an estimate inferred from context rather than stated in the text. It was one of several violent changes of ruler in Israel's final decades.

The Death of Peleg closed the life of Peleg, son of Eber and an ancestor of Abraham in the line of Shem. Genesis 11:19 says that after Peleg fathered Reu he lived another 209 years and had other sons and daughters. Unlike the genealogy in Genesis 5, this list does not say outright that he died. His death is inferred from the end of his recorded lifespan. Gen 11:18 says he was 30 when Reu was born, so he probably lived 239 years in all. This entry dates his death to about 2008 BC, an estimate worked out from the genealogy's figures rather than a date given in the text. Gen 10:25 explains his name with the remark that in his days the earth was divided.

The Death of Reu marks the end of the life of Reu, a descendant of Shem in the genealogy of Genesis 11. Gen 11:21 records that Reu lived 207 years after the birth of his son Serug and had other sons and daughters. Unlike the genealogy in Genesis 5, this list does not end each entry with the words "and he died," so his death is inferred rather than narrated. The preceding verse (Gen 11:20) says Reu was 32 when Serug was born, which by inference gives him a total lifespan of 239 years. Counting from his birth, this entry places his death at about 1978 BC, a date estimated from the genealogy's figures and not stated in the text. Nothing is recorded about where or how he died. Elsewhere, Reu is listed as the son of Peleg and an ancestor of Abraham.

The Death of Salah marks the end of the life of Salah, son of Arphaxad and father of Eber, in the line from Shem to Abraham. Genesis 11 does not describe his death directly. Unlike the genealogy in Genesis 5, it does not add "and he died." It says only that Salah lived 403 years after Eber was born and had other sons and daughters (Gen 11:15). The nearby verse Gen 11:14 says he was thirty when Eber was born, so his total lifespan works out to 433 years. This entry dates his death to about 1878 BC and his birth to about 2311 BC, both by inference from the ages given in the genealogy rather than from any date stated in the text. The Greek Septuagint gives different figures for this genealogy, so other chronologies arrive at other dates.

The Death of Saul was the end of Israel's first king in battle against the Philistines on Mount Gilboa, about 1056 BC by inference from context. Badly wounded by archers, Saul asked his armor-bearer to kill him so the enemy could not abuse him. When the frightened armor-bearer refused, Saul fell on his own sword, and the armor-bearer did the same. Saul's three sons and his men died that day, and nearby Israelites abandoned their towns to the Philistines. The next day the Philistines cut off Saul's head, put his armor in the temple of Ashtaroth, and fastened his body to the wall of Beth-shan. Men of Jabesh-gilead, whom Saul had once rescued (1 Sam 11), recovered the bodies by night, burned them, buried the bones at Jabesh and fasted seven days. A parallel account appears in 1 Chr 10; in 2 Sam 1 an Amalekite claims to have killed Saul.

The Death of Serug marks the end of the life of Serug, son of Reu, father of Nahor, and great-grandfather of Abraham in the genealogy from Shem to Abram (Gen 11:20–26). Unlike the genealogy in Genesis 5, this list does not say outright that each man died. Gen 11:23 records only that Serug lived two hundred years after Nahor was born and had other sons and daughters. Gen 11:22 says he was thirty when Nahor was born, so his total lifespan works out to 230 years. Counting from his birth, this entry places his death at about 1955 BC, a date inferred from the genealogical figures rather than stated in the text. The Bible gives no place or circumstances for his death.

The Death of Seth is recorded in the genealogy of Genesis 5, which says that Seth lived 912 years in all and then died (Gen 5:8). Seth was the son of Adam and Eve, born after the death of Abel (Gen 4:25; Gen 5:3). Earlier verses in the same chapter say he fathered Enos at 105 and had other sons and daughters. The notice follows the chapter's set pattern for each ancestor: age at the birth of an heir, years lived afterward, total lifespan, and the words "and he died." Counting the genealogy's ages forward from Adam places Seth's death at about 2962 BC, 912 years after his birth. This date is an inference from context and is not stated in the text.

The Death of Shallum was the killing of Shallum son of Jabesh, king of the northern kingdom of Israel, by Menahem son of Gadi. Menahem came up from Tirzah, an earlier royal city of Israel, to the capital Samaria, struck Shallum down there and took the throne in his place. The surrounding verses explain the background. Shallum had himself seized power by assassinating King Zechariah (2 Kgs 15:10), and he ruled for only one full month in Samaria (2 Kgs 15:13) before Menahem overthrew him. His death ended a very short reign and began Menahem's. This entry places it in about 772 BC, a date inferred from context.

The Death of Shem marks the end of the life of Noah's son Shem, whose line leads to Abraham. Genesis does not narrate his death directly. It says only that Shem lived five hundred years after fathering Arphaxad and had other sons and daughters (Gen 11:11). The verse before it says Shem was a hundred years old when Arphaxad was born, two years after the flood (Gen 11:10). Together these give a lifespan of about six hundred years. This entry dates his death to about 1846 BC and his birth to about 2446 BC, by inference from the genealogical figures in Genesis 11. Such dates are estimates, and they vary with how the biblical chronology is reckoned. By the same figures, Shem would have outlived several of his descendants named in the genealogy.

The Death of Solomon marked the end of the reign of Solomon, son of David and king over all Israel. The account states it briefly: Solomon "slept with his fathers," a common biblical way of saying a king died, and he was buried in the city of David, the oldest part of Jerusalem. His son Rehoboam then became king in his place. The verse just before (1 Kgs 11:42) says Solomon had ruled from Jerusalem over all Israel for forty years, and the parallel account in 2 Chr 9:29–31 repeats these details. This entry dates his death to about 975 BC, an estimate drawn from context. The text itself gives no date. The events that follow show that Solomon's death led directly to the division of the kingdom under Rehoboam.

The Death of Terah was the end of the life of Terah, father of Abram, Nahor and Haran, in the city of Haran. Gen 11:32 states that he lived 205 years and died there. The surrounding passage in Gen 11:31 explains that Terah had left Ur of the Chaldees with Abram, Sarai and his grandson Lot, intending to reach Canaan, but settled in Haran instead. Stephen's speech in Acts 7:4 says that Abram moved on to Canaan after his father died. Reading Gen 12:4 alongside Gen 11:26 raises a question of timing, since Terah would have been still alive when Abram left at age 75. Some explain this by taking Abram as a younger son, and the Samaritan Pentateuch gives Terah's age as 145. This entry follows the 205 years of the Hebrew text and dates his death to about 1921 BC, an estimate inferred from context.

The Death of Tibni ended a period of divided rule in the northern kingdom of Israel. After King Zimri's death, the people split, with half following Tibni the son of Ginath and half following Omri (1 Kgs 16:21). According to 1 Kgs 16:22, Omri's supporters prevailed over Tibni's, Tibni died, and Omri then reigned alone. The text does not say how Tibni died, whether in battle, by execution or otherwise. This entry dates the event to about 925 BC, an estimate inferred from context. The rivalry probably lasted around four years. That is inferred from the parallel notes that Zimri reigned in the 27th year of Asa king of Judah and that Omri began to reign in Asa's 31st year (1 Kgs 16:15, 23).

The Death of Uzziah marked the end of the long reign of Uzziah, king of Judah, who is called Azariah in 2 Kings. According to 2 Kgs 15:7, he "slept with his fathers" and was buried with his ancestors in the city of David, in Jerusalem, and his son Jotham became king in his place. The parallel account in 2 Chr 26:23 adds that he was buried in a field belonging to the royal burial ground rather than among the kings themselves, because he had leprosy. Jotham had already been governing on his behalf during that illness (2 Kgs 15:5). Isaiah dates his vision of the Lord to "the year that king Uzziah died" (Isa 6:1). This entry places the death in about 758 BC, a date inferred from context rather than stated in the text.

The Death of Zachariah was the assassination of Zachariah, king of the northern kingdom of Israel, by Shallum the son of Jabesh. Shallum conspired against him, struck him down publicly "before the people," killed him, and took the throne in his place (2 Kgs 15:10). By inference from context, this happened about 772 BC. The surrounding passage says Zachariah, son of Jeroboam II, had reigned only six months (2 Kgs 15:8). It also presents his death as the end of Jehu's dynasty, fulfilling the promise that Jehu's descendants would sit on Israel's throne to the fourth generation (2 Kgs 15:12; compare 2 Kgs 10:30). The killing opened a period of rapid changes of ruler in Israel. Shallum himself reigned only a month before Menahem killed him (2 Kgs 15:13–14).

The Debates in the Temple were a series of confrontations between Jesus and Jerusalem's religious leaders in the temple courts during Holy Week, about AD 30 by inference from context, recorded in Matthew, Mark and Luke. The chief priests and elders challenged his authority, and he answered with a counter-question about John's baptism. He then told parables of two sons, of wicked tenants who killed the vineyard owner's son, and of a wedding feast, which the leaders recognized as aimed at them. Pharisees asked whether paying tribute to Caesar was lawful, Sadducees posed a riddle about resurrection and a woman married to seven brothers, and a scribe asked which commandment was greatest. Jesus asked in turn how the Messiah could be David's son, citing Psalm 110. Afterward no one dared question him. He warned against the scribes and Pharisees and praised a poor widow's offering at the treasury.

Debir was a Canaanite town in the hill country of Judah, earlier called Kirjath-sepher (Josh 15:15; Judg 1:11) and also Kirjath-sannah (Josh 15:49). Joshua captured it, killed its king and destroyed its inhabitants (Josh 10:38–39), and its king appears in the list of defeated kings (Josh 12:13). It had been home to the Anakim, whom Joshua drove from the area (Josh 11:21). The surrounding passages say Othniel later took the town and won the hand of Caleb's daughter Achsah. Debir became one of Judah's cities and was given with its pasturelands to the priests (Josh 21:15; 1 Chr 6:58). Several places share the name. The site is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary points to a valley about three miles west of Hebron, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia favors edh-Dhaheriyeh, about 11 miles southwest of Hebron. The location shown here follows the edh-Dhaheriyeh identification.

Debir was a place on the northern border of the tribe of Judah, mentioned only in Josh 15:7, where the boundary line ran up toward Debir from the valley of Achor and turned north toward Gilgal, opposite the ascent of Adummim. It is different from the better-known city of Debir (Kiriath-sepher) in the hill country south of Hebron, one of several places with this name. Its exact site is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary links it with a Wadi Dabor near the northwest corner of the Dead Sea. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Thoghret ed-Debr, a pass near Tal'at ed-Damm and the so-called Inn of the Good Samaritan on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho. It also notes that some scholars read the verse as having no place name here at all. The location shown here follows the Jericho-road identification.

Debir was a place on the border of the territory given to the tribe of Gad east of the Jordan. Josh 13:26 names "the border of Debir" alongside Mahanaim in describing Gad's boundary, so it probably lay not far from Mahanaim, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. This Debir is different from the better-known Debir in Judah's hill country, also called Kiriath-sepher. The Revised Version margin reads the name as Lidebir, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the same place as Lo-debar, the town where Mephibosheth lived (2 Sam 9:4). Its exact location is uncertain. The same encyclopedia mentions Ibdar, south of the Yarmuk River, as a possible site. The location shown here is in northern Jordan south of the Yarmuk, which fits that suggestion.

Debir was the king of Eglon, one of five Amorite kings in southern Canaan. Adonizedek king of Jerusalem summoned him, along with the kings of Hebron, Jarmuth and Lachish, to join an alliance against Gibeon after Gibeon made peace with Joshua and Israel (Josh 10:3). Later in the same chapter the alliance is defeated at Gibeon. The five kings flee and hide in a cave at Makkedah, where they are shut in until Joshua returns from pursuing their armies. He then puts them to death and hangs them on five trees (Josh 10:16–26), as Easton's Bible Dictionary summarizes. Debir is named only in Josh 10:3. The other kings are named again later in the chapter, but he is referred to there only as the king of Eglon. His name is the same as that of the Canaanite town of Debir, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives its meaning as "oracle."

Deborah was the nurse of Rebekah, the wife of Isaac. She is named only at her death, recorded while Jacob and his household were at Bethel. She was buried below Bethel under an oak, and the tree was then called Allonbachuth, meaning "oak of weeping" (Gen 35:8). Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies her with the unnamed nurse who left the house of Bethuel with Rebekah when she went to marry Isaac (Gen 24:59). If so, she had served the family for many years and, by inference, was living with Jacob's household in her old age. Her name is usually understood to mean "bee." She is distinct from Deborah the prophet and judge of Israel in the book of Judges, who shares the name.

Deborah was a prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth, who judged Israel in the period before the monarchy. She sat under a palm tree named after her, between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim, and the Israelites came to her to have their disputes decided. She went with Barak to Kedesh, where he gathered ten thousand men of Zebulun and Naphtali, and told him that the honour of defeating Sisera, the Canaanite commander, would go to a woman. At Mount Tabor she gave Barak the signal to attack. Afterward she and Barak sang a victory song (Judg 5), in which she calls herself "a mother in Israel." The victory is dated here to about 1278 BC, an estimate inferred from context. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that "wife" of Lapidoth might also be read as "woman" of Lapidoth. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "bee." Another Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, appears in Genesis.

Decapolis, Greek for "ten cities," was a region mostly east and southeast of the Sea of Galilee, home to a league of largely Greek cities in Roman times. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, following the Roman writer Pliny, list them as Scythopolis (Beth-shean, the only one west of the Jordan), Hippos, Gadara, Pella, Philadelphia (modern Amman), Gerasa (Jerash), Dion, Canatha, Raphana and Damascus. People from the Decapolis were among the crowds who followed Jesus (Matt 4:25). A man Jesus freed from demons went there to tell what had been done for him (Mark 5:20). Jesus later passed through the region on his way back to the Sea of Galilee (Mark 7:31). By inference from the accounts that follow, he healed a crowd and fed four thousand people near there. The region had no fixed borders, and the location shown here marks Damascus, the northernmost city.

Dedan was an Arabian people and region known for trade, according to the STEPBible Proper Names. Ezekiel lists the men of Dedan among the merchants of Tyre, bringing ivory tusks and ebony and trading in saddlecloths for riding (Ezek 27:15, 20). It is also paired with Sheba as a trading people (Ezek 38:13). The prophets include Dedan in judgements on neighbouring nations. Jeremiah names it alongside Tema and Buz (Jer 25:23) and warns its people to flee when disaster comes on Edom (Jer 49:8). Ezekiel says Dedan will fall by the sword along with Edom, from Teman onward (Ezek 25:13). Genesis names a Dedan both among the descendants of Cush and among Abraham's descendants through Keturah, and the people are probably named after one of them. The location shown here is the oasis of Al-Ula in northwestern Saudi Arabia, the usual identification of ancient Dedan.

Dedan (son of Raamah) was a son of Raamah and a grandson of Cush, named with his brother Sheba in the Table of Nations in Gen 10:7 and again in the genealogy of 1 Chr 1:9. He belongs to the line of Ham, since Cush was a son of Ham. Nothing is recorded about his life. He is distinct from another Dedan, a son of Jokshan and grandson of Abraham through Keturah, although the two lists share the names Sheba and Dedan. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects his descendants with the Dedanites mentioned in Isa 21:13 and Ezek 27:15, and suggests they probably settled among the Cushite peoples on the north-west coast of the Persian Gulf. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "low country."

Dedan (son of Jokshan) was a grandson of Abraham through Keturah, whom 1 Chr 1:32 calls Abraham's concubine. His father Jokshan was one of Keturah's six sons, and his brother was Sheba. Genesis names Dedan's sons as Asshurim, Letushim and Leummim. These plural forms are probably the names of tribes or peoples rather than individuals (Gen 25:3). Easton's Bible Dictionary says his descendants settled near the borders of Edom and probably lived as herders. A separate Dedan appears among the descendants of Ham in the table of nations (Gen 10:7). The prophets also mention a people or region called Dedan, and it is not always clear which line they mean. This entry concerns only the son of Jokshan.

Dekar was the father of one of King Solomon's twelve district officers, who is known only as "the son of Dekar" (Hebrew Ben-deker). Nothing is said about Dekar himself, and his son's own name is not given. According to 1 Kgs 4:9, the son of Dekar was responsible for the district that included Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh and Elon-beth-hanan. Smith's Bible Dictionary places this district in the western part of the hill country of Judah and Benjamin. From the surrounding passage, each of these officers supplied food for the king and his household for one month of the year. The name is usually linked to a Hebrew root meaning "to pierce". On that basis Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "a lancer", while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "force".

Delaiah was a priest in the time of David who headed the twenty-third of the twenty-four divisions into which the priests were organized. The divisions were assigned by lot to take turns serving at the sanctuary, and the twenty-third turn fell to Delaiah (1 Chr 24:18). Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is usually explained as meaning "the Lord has drawn up" or "raised," though Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "freed by Jehovah" and Hitchcock's Bible Names "the poor of the Lord." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this priest should not be confused with them.

Delaiah was the ancestor of a family that returned from exile in Babylon to Judah, probably with Zerubbabel. His descendants are listed with those of Tobiah and Nekoda. The total for the three families is 652 in Ezra 2:60 and 642 in Neh 7:62. The surrounding passage (Ezra 2:59; Neh 7:61) groups these families with people who could not show their ancestral house or prove they were of Israelite descent, so by inference their genealogy had been lost. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the return to about 536 BC. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Delaiah as the head of one of the returning bands, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats him as a family ancestor. Smith's gives the name's meaning as "freed by Jehovah." Several other men in the Bible share this name, and it is not known whether this Delaiah is connected with any of them.

Delaiah was the son of Mehetabeel and the father of Shemaiah. He is mentioned only once, in Neh 6:10, as part of his son's lineage. There Nehemiah describes visiting Shemaiah, who was "shut up" in his house and urged Nehemiah to hide inside the temple because enemies were coming to kill him at night. The following verses of the same chapter say that Tobiah and Sanballat had hired Shemaiah to frighten Nehemiah. Nothing is recorded about Delaiah himself, so he probably lived in Jerusalem in the generation before Nehemiah's time. Several other people in the Bible share his name. Reference works explain the name differently: Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "freed by Jehovah," the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "God has raised," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the poor of the Lord."

Delaiah son of Shemaiah was one of the princes, or royal officials, at the court of King Jehoiakim of Judah. He was sitting with the other officials in the scribe's chamber of the palace when Micaiah reported the contents of Jeremiah's scroll, which Baruch had read aloud in the temple (Jer 36:12). The officials then had Baruch read it to them and reported it to the king. When Jehoiakim cut up the scroll and burned it, Delaiah, together with Elnathan and Gemariah, urged the king not to burn it, but he refused to listen (Jer 36:25). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 604 BC. The name, which several people in the Bible share, is explained as "God has raised" by the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and as "freed by Jehovah" by Smith's.

The Deliverance by Barak and Deborah was Israel's victory over Jabin, king of Canaan, and his commander Sisera, dated about 1278 BC by inference from context. Deborah, a prophetess who judged Israel from beneath a palm tree between Ramah and Bethel, told Barak son of Abinoam that Sisera would be drawn to the Kishon River. Barak agreed to go only if she came, and she warned that the honour would go to a woman. Barak led ten thousand men down from Mount Tabor against Sisera's nine hundred iron chariots, and the Kishon swept the enemy away. Sisera fled on foot to the tent of Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite, who killed him with a tent peg. Deborah and Barak then sang a victory song praising the tribes that fought and rebuking those that stayed away, and the land had rest forty years.

The Deliverance by Gideon was Israel's rescue from Midianite oppression under Gideon son of Joash, an Abiezrite of Manasseh, about 1251 BC by inference from context. An angel of the LORD found Gideon threshing wheat in hiding at Ophrah and called him to save Israel, despite his protest that his family was poor and he was the least in it. Gideon tore down the town's altar of Baal, earning the name Jerubbaal, and asked for signs with a fleece. God reduced his army to three hundred men, who surprised the Midianite camp at night with trumpets and broken pitchers, and the camp fled. Ephraim held the Jordan crossings and captured the princes Oreb and Zeeb. Gideon pursued the kings Zebah and Zalmunna and punished Succoth and Penuel for refusing his men bread. Israel offered him hereditary rule, and the land had quiet for forty years.

The Deliverance by Jephthah was the period in which Jephthah the Gileadite freed Israel from Ammonite oppression and then judged Israel for six years (Judg 12:7). It began about 1152 BC, by inference from context. Jephthah, son of Gilead by a harlot, had been driven out by his half-brothers and lived in the land of Tob. When Ammon made war, the elders of Gilead asked him to lead them and promised to make him their head. By messengers he argued that Israel had taken the disputed land from Sihon the Amorite, not from Ammon, and had held it for three hundred years. The king refused to listen. Jephthah made a vow to the LORD, defeated Ammon across twenty cities, and on his return to Mizpeh was met by his only daughter, to whom he fulfilled his vow. He later defeated the Ephraimites, identifying them at the Jordan fords by how they said "Shibboleth."

The Deliverance by Othniel was the first rescue of Israel by a judge recorded in the book of Judges, dated here to about 1410 BC by inference from context. It follows the pattern set out in Judg 2:16–19, where Israel turns to other gods, falls under oppression, cries out, and the LORD raises up a judge to deliver them. After Israel had served Cushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia (eight years, according to Judg 3:8), the people cried to the LORD, who raised up Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother. The Spirit of the LORD came upon him. He judged Israel, went out to war, and defeated Cushan-rishathaim. The land then had rest for forty years, and Othniel died. The surrounding passage explains that the LORD left other nations in the land to test whether Israel would keep his way.

Demas was a companion and co-worker of the apostle Paul. He is named alongside Luke in the greetings that close Paul's letter to the Colossians (Col 4:14), and in Philemon Paul calls him one of his "fellowlabourers," together with Mark, Aristarchus and Luke (Phlm 1:24). Both letters are usually placed during Paul's first imprisonment at Rome, about AD 57 by inference from context, so Demas was probably with Paul there. In a later letter, 2 Timothy, Paul writes that Demas had left him, "having loved this present world," and had gone to Thessalonica (2 Tim 4:10). Nothing more is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests his name is probably a shortened form of Demetrius, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "popular."

Demetrius was a silversmith at Ephesus who made silver shrines for Diana (the Greek Artemis), a trade that brought good profit to the local craftsmen (Acts 19:24). According to Easton's Bible Dictionary, these were small models of the goddess's temple or statue sold to visitors. Seeing Paul's preaching as a threat to this business, he stirred up the craftsmen and set off the riot in Ephesus, about AD 53 by inference from context. The town clerk later calmed the crowd by telling Demetrius and his fellow craftsmen to take any complaint to the courts and the proconsuls (Acts 19:38). The name also appears in 3 John 1:12, where John commends a Demetrius whom everyone speaks well of. Most reference works, including Smith's Bible Dictionary, treat him as a different man. Smith's notes that he could possibly be the silversmith after conversion but considers this very doubtful.

Derbe was a city of Lycaonia in south-central Asia Minor, mentioned only in Acts. Paul and Barnabas fled there with Lystra after a threat at Iconium (Acts 14:6), and Paul went on to Derbe the day after he was stoned at Lystra (Acts 14:20). On a later journey Paul came again to Derbe and Lystra, where he met Timothy (Acts 16:1). Gaius of Derbe was one of Paul's travelling companions (Acts 20:4). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes it as a frontier customs town on a Roman road toward the Cilician Gates, and says its coins honor the emperor Claudius. Its exact site was long uncertain: Smith's Bible Dictionary notes the modern town Divle, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes Ramsay's choice of Gudelisin. The location shown here follows a later identification with the mound of Kerti Hüyük, north of modern Karaman in Turkey.

Destruction, or the City of Destruction, is a name in Isaiah's prophecy about Egypt turning to the LORD. Isa 19:18 says that five cities in Egypt would speak the language of Canaan and swear by the LORD of hosts, and that one of them would be called "the city of destruction." The Hebrew is Ir-ha-Heres, "city of overthrow." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains this as a wordplay on Ir-ha-Cheres, "city of the sun," a name for Heliopolis, which is called On elsewhere in the Bible. It also notes that some Hebrew manuscripts read "city of the sun" directly. Easton's Bible Dictionary likewise treats the name as an ideal title for On, or Heliopolis. Other readings of the name exist, and it is not certain that a literal city is meant. The location shown here follows the Heliopolis identification, an ancient site now within northeastern Cairo.

Diana was the goddess worshipped at Ephesus, called Artemis by the Greeks and Diana by the Romans (Easton's Bible Dictionary). She appears in Acts 19, where the silversmith Demetrius, who made silver shrines for her, stirred up fellow craftsmen against Paul's preaching. He warned that their trade was in danger and that her temple, revered by "all Asia and the world," would be despised. The crowd shouted "Great is Diana of the Ephesians" and kept up the cry for about two hours. The town clerk calmed them by reminding them that Ephesus was the guardian of her worship and of an image said to have fallen from Jupiter. Easton's describes her temple as one of the seven wonders of the ancient world. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the Ephesian goddess differed from the Roman Diana and was closer to eastern goddesses such as Astarte.

Diblaim was the father of Gomer, the woman the prophet Hosea married (Hos 1:3). He is named only in that verse, where Gomer is called "the daughter of Diblaim," and nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a native of northern Israel, where Hosea worked, and the STEPBible proper names index also treats him as Gomer's father. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries instead take Diblaim to be Gomer's mother. This entry follows the view that Diblaim was her father. The name is generally understood to mean "two cakes," probably pressed cakes of figs. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "cluster of figs."

Dibon was a city east of the Jordan, north of the Arnon River, that changed hands between Moab and Israel. An old victory song over Moab mentions it (Num 21:30), which suggests it was originally Moabite. The Gadites and Reubenites named it among the lands they asked Moses for (Num 32:3), and Gad is said to have built or rebuilt it (Num 32:34). Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests this is why it was also called Dibon-gad. Joshua, however, lists it among the cities allotted to Reuben (Josh 13:9, 13:17). By the time of Isaiah and Jeremiah it was Moabite again and appears in their oracles against Moab (Isa 15:2; Jer 48:18, 22). Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the "Dimon" of Isa 15:9 to be the same city. The name was shared by another place in Judah. The location shown here follows the usual identification with the ruins at modern Dhiban in Jordan, about 3 miles north of the Arnon.

Dibon was a town in Judah where some of the people of Judah settled, along with its surrounding villages, after the return from the Babylonian exile (Neh 11:25). It appears in a list with Kirjath-arba (Hebron) and Jekabzeel, which suggests it lay in the south of Judah. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both identify it with Dimonah, a town in Judah's southern territory (Josh 15:22), and Easton's suggests it is probably the modern ed-Dheib. Its exact site is uncertain, and the location shown here is only approximate, in the Negev region of southern Judah. This Dibon is distinct from the better-known Dibon east of the Dead Sea in Moab, which shares the same name.

Dibon-gad was a camping place of the Israelites during their journey toward the plains of Moab, reached after Iim and left for Almon-diblathaim (Num 33:45–46). The name probably means "Dibon of Gad." By inference from Num 32:34, where the tribe of Gad is said to have built Dibon, it is usually taken to be the town of Dibon east of the Dead Sea, which Gad occupied before it later passed to Reuben and then to Moab. The location shown here follows the common identification with modern Dhiban in Jordan, a little north of the Arnon River (Wadi Mujib). The famous Moabite Stone of King Mesha was found there in 1868. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "great understanding" or "abundance of sons."

Dibri was a man of the tribe of Dan, named only as the father of Shelomith. He appears in Lev 24:11, where his daughter is identified as the mother of a man who blasphemed the name of the LORD during the wilderness period and was brought to Moses. The surrounding passage says this grandson's father was an Egyptian, and that the man was stoned outside the camp as punishment. Dibri himself plays no part in the account. He is mentioned only to identify the family and tribe of the offender's mother. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia tentatively gives the meaning of his name as "eloquent," and Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "an orator."

Diklah was one of the thirteen sons of Joktan, a descendant of Shem through Eber, named in the table of nations in Gen 10:27 and in the parallel genealogy at 1 Chr 1:21. His brothers included Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, Hadoram, Uzal, Sheba, Ophir, Havilah and Jobab. The passages give only his name. Like the other names in this list, it probably stands for a tribe or region as well as a person. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both take the name to mean "palm grove" or "place of palms." They suggest it points to a palm-growing district, probably in southern Arabia, where the settlements of Joktan's descendants are generally placed. The exact location is unknown.

Dilean was a town in the lowlands (Shephelah) of Judah, listed among the cities allotted to the tribe of Judah in Josh 15:38, where it is named alongside Mizpeh and Joktheel. It appears nowhere else in the Bible. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "gourd," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia as "cucumber"; Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "that is poor." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the English Revised Version spells it "Dilan" and suggests it probably lay north of Lachish and Eglon, judging from the towns listed with it. Its site has not been identified with certainty, and the location shown here is only a rough placement in the Judean lowlands, west of Hebron.

Dimnah was a city in the territory of the tribe of Zebulun, one of four Zebulunite towns assigned with their surrounding pasturelands to the Levite families of Merari (Josh 21:35). It is named only here, alongside Nahalal. Its name probably means "dung" or "dunghill" (Easton's Bible Dictionary; Smith's Bible Dictionary). The parallel list of Levitical cities in 1 Chr 6:77 gives Rimmon in its place, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Dimnah is probably a copyist's variant of Rimmon, the Zebulunite border town also named Rimmon in Josh 19:13. The location shown here follows that identification, placing it in Lower Galilee near the modern village of Rummana, north of Nazareth. If Dimnah was instead a separate town, its site is unknown.

Dimonah was a town in the far south of Judah, listed among the cities of the tribe near the border with Edom (Josh 15:22). It appears only in this list, between Kinah and Adadah, so nothing more is recorded about it. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests it may be the same place as Dibon, where people of Judah lived after the return from exile (Neh 11:25). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "dunghill." The exact site is unknown. The location shown here is a rough placement in the Negev, in the region east of Beersheba, consistent with the town's place in the list of Judah's southern cities.

Dinah was the daughter of Jacob and Leah, born after Leah's six sons (Gen 30:21), probably about 1750 BC by inference from context. Her name is usually explained as meaning "judged" or "vindicated" (Easton's Bible Dictionary). While Jacob's family was living near the city of Shechem, she went out to see the local women. Shechem, son of the ruler Hamor, violated her and then sought to marry her. Jacob's sons answered deceitfully, agreeing to the marriage if the men of the city were circumcised. On the third day, while the men were still in pain, her full brothers Simeon and Levi attacked the city, killed Hamor, Shechem and all the males, and took Dinah out of Shechem's house. She is later named among Jacob's family who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:15). She is Jacob's only daughter mentioned by name.

Dinhabah was the city of Bela son of Beor, the first king listed among those who reigned in Edom before any king ruled over Israel (Gen 36:32; 1 Chr 1:43). Smith's Bible Dictionary calls it Bela's capital and probably his birthplace. Nothing else is said about it in the Bible. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "robbers' den," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "he gives judgment." Its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests the modern Dibdiba, a little northeast of Petra. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a possible likeness in the name Hodbat et-Teneib, about 8 miles east of Heshbon, though that lies in Moab, and it adds that no satisfactory identification has been proposed. The location shown here, near Petra in southern Jordan, roughly follows Easton's identification and is only approximate.

Dionysius was an Athenian who believed Paul's message when Paul preached in Athens, probably around AD 48 by inference from context. Acts 17:34 names him first among the few who joined Paul, together with a woman named Damaris and others. He is called "the Areopagite," which most likely means he belonged to the Areopagus, the city's council that met on Mars Hill, where Paul had just given his speech earlier in the same chapter. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as an eminent Athenian and explains the name as meaning "devoted to Dionysus," the Greek god of wine. Scripture says nothing more about him. Church tradition, noted in Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, holds that he became the first bishop of Athens. Other traditions say he was martyred, and one links him with Saint Denis of Paris. A set of mystical writings was later circulated under his name, and Smith's dates these to the sixth century.

Diotrephes was a member of a church addressed in the letter of 3 John. The writer says that Diotrephes "loves to have the preeminence" among the believers there and refuses to receive the writer and his companions (3 John 1:9). The following verse, 3 John 1:10, adds that he spoke against the writer with malicious words, refused to welcome traveling fellow believers, stopped others who wanted to welcome them, and put them out of the church. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that his love of preeminence may mean he held some office in the church and was misusing it. Nothing else is known of him. His Greek name means "nourished by Zeus" (Smith's Bible Dictionary), or "nourished by Jupiter" in Hitchcock's Bible Names.

The Disciples first called Christians is the episode in Acts 11:19–30 in which the believers at Antioch in Syria first received the name "Christians." Believers scattered by the persecution after Stephen's death preached at first only to Jews, but some men from Cyprus and Cyrene spoke to Greeks in Antioch, and many believed. The Jerusalem church sent Barnabas, who encouraged them and then went to Tarsus to bring Saul (Paul). The two taught the church there for a whole year, and it was at Antioch that the disciples were first called Christians. Prophets then came from Jerusalem, and one of them, Agabus, foretold a severe famine across the world, which happened in the reign of Claudius. The disciples sent relief to the believers in Judea through Barnabas and Saul. This entry dates the episode to about AD 40, by inference from context.

event: Discourse on the Kingdom and Other Parables
text: The Discourse on the Kingdom and Other Parables is a section of Luke's Gospel (Luke 17:20–18:14) in which Jesus answers the Pharisees' question about when the kingdom of God would come. He says it does not come with visible signs and that it is "within you." He then warns his disciples that the day of the Son of Man will come suddenly, like lightning, as the flood came in Noah's day and fire fell on Sodom in Lot's day, and that one person will be taken and another left. He adds two parables about prayer. In one, a persistent widow wears down an unjust judge. In the other, a Pharisee and a tax collector pray in the temple, and the humble tax collector goes home justified. The preceding account of the ten lepers (Luke 17:11) places Jesus between Samaria and Galilee on his way to Jerusalem. The date is about AD 30, by inference from context.

The Discourse with Pharisees and Saducees was an exchange that followed the feeding of the four thousand, about AD 29 by inference from context. After Jesus crossed by boat to the district of Dalmanutha, Pharisees, joined by Sadducees in Matthew's account, came to test him by asking for a sign from heaven. He replied that they could read the weather from the sky but not the signs of the times, and said no sign would be given except the sign of Jonah. He then left by boat for the other side. On the way the disciples realized they had brought almost no bread, and Jesus warned them to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees (Mark has the leaven of Herod). They took this as a remark about bread, so he reminded them of the leftovers from the two miraculous feedings. Matthew records that they then understood he meant the teaching of these groups.

Dishan was a son of Seir the Horite and one of the Horite chiefs ("dukes" in the King James Version) in the land of Seir, later called Edom. He is named last among Seir's seven sons, after Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon and Ezer, and Timna is also counted among the siblings here. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries call him Seir's youngest son, apparently from this order. His sons were Uz and Aran (Gen 36:28; 1 Chr 1:42). He appears only in the parallel genealogies of Genesis 36 and 1 Chronicles 1, where the Horite clans are listed alongside the descendants of Esau. His name closely resembles that of his brother Dishon. Easton's and Smith's dictionaries give its meaning as "antelope," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a threshing."

Dishon was the fifth son of Seir the Horite, listed with his brothers Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Ezer and Dishan, and with a sister, Timna (Gen 36:21; 1 Chr 1:38). He was one of the Horite chiefs, or 'dukes,' who ruled in the land of Seir, later known as Edom, before and alongside Esau's descendants (Gen 36:30). His sons are named as Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran and Cheran (Gen 36:26). The name was also borne by his nephew, a son of Anah (Gen 36:25), and because the list of Dishon's sons comes right after that mention, which Dishon fathered them is uncertain. This entry follows the reading that makes them sons of Seir's son Dishon. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as 'antelope,' while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives 'fatness' or 'ashes.'

Dishon was a son of Anah and brother of Aholibamah, listed among the Horite clans in the genealogies connected with Esau's family (Gen 36:25). STEPBible's proper names index identifies him as a grandson of Seir the Horite through Anah. His sister is probably the Aholibamah who became one of Esau's wives (Gen 36:2). 1 Chr 1:41 names his sons as Amram, Eshban, Ithran and Cheran. The parallel list in Gen 36:26 gives the same sons but has Hemdan in place of Amram, probably a variant spelling of the same name. The name Dishon was also borne by another Horite, a son of Seir and so probably this man's uncle (Gen 36:21), and the two are easily confused. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "fatness" or "ashes." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Dividing the land is the account in Josh 13–14 of how Israel's territory was allotted among the tribes after the war with the Canaanites, about 1445 BC by inference from context. When Joshua was old, the LORD told him that much land remained unconquered, including the Philistine territory and Lebanon, yet commanded him to divide the land by lot among the nine and a half tribes. The passage recalls that Moses had already given land east of the Jordan to Reuben, Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh, though the Geshurites and Maachathites were never driven out. Levi received no territory, only cities to live in with pasture for their livestock. Eleazar the priest, Joshua and the tribal heads carried out the distribution. At Gilgal, Caleb, then 85, reminded Joshua of Moses' promise at Kadesh-barnea 45 years earlier that he would inherit the land he had walked on as a spy.

Diviners' Oak was a landmark tree near Shechem, mentioned only in Judg 9:37. There Gaal, who had led Shechem in revolt against Abimelech, watched troops approaching the city. One company came down from the high ground, and another came "by the plain of Meonenim," as the King James Version renders it. The Revised Version translates the phrase "the oak of Meonenim." Easton's Bible Dictionary explains that Meonenim means "soothsayers" or "diviners," so the name probably points to a tree linked with divination. Easton's also suggests it may be the same oak at Shechem where Abram camped and where Jacob later buried the household's foreign gods (Gen 35:4), though that identification is uncertain. Its exact spot is unknown. The location shown here places it in the area around Shechem, near modern Nablus.

Dizahab is a place named only in Deut 1:1, in a list of landmarks used to locate where Moses spoke his words to all Israel, east of the Jordan in the wilderness, alongside Paran, Tophel, Laban and Hazeroth. The name is usually understood to mean "region of gold." Its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify it with Dahab, a cape on the western shore of the Gulf of Aqaba in the Sinai Peninsula. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the list seems meant to fix the camp in the plains of Moab, that no place there bears a similar name, and that some names in the list resemble earlier stations of the wilderness journey. It also records Burckhardt's proposal of a harbor called Mina edh-Dhahab on the same gulf. The location shown here follows the Dahab identification on the Gulf of Aqaba.

Dodanim is listed as the fourth son of Javan in the Table of Nations, alongside his brothers Elishah, Tarshish and Kittim (Gen 10:4; 1 Chr 1:7). Since Javan was a son of Japheth (Gen 10:2), Dodanim was Japheth's grandson. As with the other names in this list, Dodanim probably stands for a people descended from him as well as an individual. In the Hebrew text of 1 Chr 1:7, and in the Greek Septuagint and Samaritan versions of Genesis, the name appears as Rodanim (the King James Version reads Dodanim in both places). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia prefers the Rodanim reading and links the people with the inhabitants of the island of Rhodes. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries connect them with the Dardani of Illyricum and the region of Troy. The text itself does not settle the identification, and this entry does not decide between these views.

Dodavah was a man of Mareshah, a town in Judah, known only as the father of the prophet Eliezer. Eliezer prophesied against King Jehoshaphat of Judah for allying himself with Ahaziah king of Israel, announcing that the LORD had broken his works. As a result, the ships the two kings had built were wrecked and never sailed to Tarshish (2 Chr 20:37). The verse does not make clear whether "of Mareshah" refers to Dodavah or to his son, but it is usually taken as the family's hometown. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Dodavah as a man of Maresha in Judah and gives the meaning of his name as "love of the Lord." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives simply "love." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Dodo was a man of the tribe of Issachar, the father of Puah and the grandfather of Tola. Tola arose after Abimelech to defend Israel as one of its judges and lived at Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim (Judg 10:1). Dodo appears only in this genealogical note, and nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him simply as a descendant of Issachar. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "his uncle." Several other men in the Bible share this name, including fathers of warriors in David's army. This Dodo should be kept distinct from them.

Dodo was an Ahohite, the father of Eleazar, who was one of the three chief warriors among David's mighty men. Eleazar stood with David against the gathered Philistines when the men of Israel had withdrawn (2 Sam 23:9; 1 Chr 11:12). "Ahohite" probably refers to descent from Ahoah, a Benjamite family. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies Dodo with Dodai the Ahohite, who commanded the division of David's army that served in the second month, a division of twenty-four thousand men with Mikloth as a leader (1 Chr 27:4). Smith's Bible Dictionary calls this identification probable, and this entry follows it. Some read Dodai there as a scribal shortening of "Eleazar son of Dodai." Several other people in the Bible share the name Dodo. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "his uncle."

Dodo was a man of Bethlehem and the father of Elhanan, one of David's mighty men known as "the thirty." He is mentioned only in the two parallel lists of David's warriors, where his son appears right after Asahel, the brother of Joab (2 Sam 23:24; 1 Chr 11:26). Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is shared by other men in the Bible, and Smith's Bible Dictionary treats this Bethlehemite as a different person from them. This Elhanan should probably also be kept apart from Elhanan the son of Jaare-oregim, who is credited with killing a Philistine giant (2 Sam 21:19). Smith's gives the meaning of the name as "loving," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "his uncle."

Doeg was an Edomite in the service of King Saul, described as the chief of Saul's herdsmen and as set over his servants. He happened to be at Nob, "detained before the LORD," on the day the priest Ahimelech helped David, who was fleeing from Saul. Doeg later reported what he had seen to the king. When Saul ordered him to attack the priests of Nob, Doeg killed eighty-five men who wore the linen ephod. Afterward David told Abiathar, the son of Ahimelech who escaped, that he had known Doeg would inform Saul, and he took responsibility for the deaths of Abiathar's family. The heading of Ps 52 links that psalm with Doeg's report to Saul, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes. The Septuagint describes his job as tending mules, according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia.

Dophkah was a place where the Israelites camped on their journey from Egypt to Mount Sinai. The list of stopping places in Numbers 33 records that they moved there from the wilderness of Sin and then went on to Alush (Num 33:12–13). It is not mentioned anywhere else. The narrative in Exod 17:1 says only that the people travelled from the wilderness of Sin to Rephidim in stages, so Dophkah was probably one of those unnamed stages. Its exact site is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in the southwestern Sinai Peninsula, near the eastern shore of the Gulf of Suez, somewhere in the Wadi Feiran area. Others have linked it with the Egyptian mining district around Serabit el-Khadim. The location shown here is a rough one in southwestern Sinai, close to Easton's placement. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "a knocking."

Dor was an ancient Canaanite royal city on the Mediterranean coast. Its king is listed among those Joshua defeated, and Josh 12:23 places it "in the coast of Dor." Dor and its surrounding towns lay within the areas of Issachar and Asher but were assigned to Manasseh (Josh 17:11; 1 Chr 7:29). Manasseh did not drive out its Canaanite inhabitants, who went on living there (Judg 1:27). Other passages call the area Naphath-dor, the heights or coast of Dor (Josh 11:2), and 1 Kgs 4:11 names it as one of Solomon's supply districts. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as the most southern Phoenician settlement on that coast and identifies it with Tantura, about 8 miles (13 km) north of Caesarea. Smith's Bible Dictionary agrees, citing Jerome's placement of Dor nine miles from Caesarea. The location shown here follows this identification, at the ancient mound near modern Tantura.

Dorcas, also called Tabitha, was a disciple at Joppa, the port town on the Mediterranean coast (modern Jaffa), known for her good works and gifts to the poor (Acts 9:36). Tabitha is Aramaic and Dorcas its Greek equivalent. According to Easton's Bible Dictionary, both mean "gazelle." Among her charities she made coats and garments, which the widows showed to Peter as they wept beside her body in an upper room (Acts 9:39). The wider account in Acts 9 says she fell ill and died while Peter was at nearby Lydda, where he had healed Aeneas, and the disciples sent for him. Peter sent everyone out of the room, knelt and prayed, then said, "Tabitha, arise." She opened her eyes and sat up (Acts 9:40). This happened about AD 38, a date inferred from context. The same chapter reports that many in Joppa came to believe as a result.

Dothan was a town in the hill country north of Shechem, set among good pasture land. Joseph followed his brothers there while they were grazing their father's flocks and found them at Dothan (Gen 37:17). The surrounding chapter tells how they threw him into a pit and sold him to Ishmaelite traders. Centuries later the prophet Elisha was staying in Dothan when the king of Syria learned where he was and sent troops to seize him (2 Kgs 6:13). The name is usually explained as "two wells" or "two cisterns." Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with Tell Dothan, on the southern edge of the Jezreel plain about 5 miles southwest of modern Jenin. The site lay near an old trade route running from Gilead toward the coast and Egypt. The location shown here follows that identification.

Dragon Spring, called the "dragon well" in the King James Version and rendered "Jackal Well" in some modern translations, was a water source near Jerusalem. It is mentioned only once, in the account of Nehemiah's night inspection of the ruined city walls. Going out by the Valley Gate, he passed in front of this spring on his way to the Dung Gate, viewing the broken walls and burned gates (Neh 2:13). That route suggests the spring lay outside the walls, along the western or southern side of the city, probably in or near the valley below. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that some have identified it with the Pool of Gihon, and others have proposed different springs or pools around Jerusalem. This entry follows none of these specific identifications. The location shown here places it only generally within the Jerusalem area.

Drusilla was the Jewish wife of Felix, the Roman governor of Judea. Acts 24:24 records that some days after Paul's hearing before Felix at Caesarea, Felix came with Drusilla, sent for Paul, and heard him speak about faith in Christ. By inference from context, this happened during Paul's custody there, about AD 56. The Bible says nothing more about her. Drawing on the Jewish historian Josephus, Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify her as the youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I, the king of Acts 12, and a sister of Bernice. They say she was first married to Azizus, king of Emesa, and that Felix persuaded her to leave him. Smith's Bible Dictionary adds that he did this through a Cypriot sorcerer named Simon. Easton's states that she and her son died in the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD 79. Her name is traditionally explained as meaning "watered by the dew."

Dumah was one of the twelve sons of Ishmael, the son of Abraham and Hagar, and so a grandson of Abraham. He appears only in the parallel genealogies of Gen 25:14 and 1 Chr 1:30, listed between his brothers Mishma and Massa. His name means "silence." Nothing is recorded of his life. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to be the probable founder of an Ishmaelite tribe in Arabia whose territory carried his name, and connects this with the oracle concerning Dumah in Isa 21:11. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Arabic geographers credited him with founding the oasis town of Dumat al-Jandal, probably the modern al-Jawf in northern Saudi Arabia. It adds that the Isaiah oracle may concern that place. These links between the person, the tribe and the town are traditional inferences, not statements of the biblical text.

Dumah was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed among the towns allotted to the tribe of Judah alongside Arab and Eshean (Josh 15:52). The name means "silence." Smith's Bible Dictionary places it near Hebron and identifies it with the ruins of a village called ed-Daumeh, about six miles southwest of Hebron. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia likewise places it between Hebron and Beersheba at ed-Daume. The location shown here, southwest of Hebron, matches that identification. The same name belongs to other places and to a son of Ishmael elsewhere in the Bible, and those should be kept distinct from this town in Judah.

Dumah is the name given to the subject of a short prophetic oracle in Isaiah, “the burden of Dumah” (Isa 21:11). In it a voice calls to the prophet out of Seir, the hill country of Edom, asking the watchman what remains of the night. The Hebrew name means “silence.” Interpreters differ on what it refers to. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes it as a symbolic name for Edom, which would fit the mention of Seir. The STEPBible proper names index treats it as a city or region in Arabia. That view connects it with Dumah, a son of Ishmael whose descendants lived in northern Arabia (Gen 25:14), and it is often linked with the oasis of Dumat al-Jandal. The location shown here follows the Arabian identification and is only approximate. The same name belongs to other places in the Bible, including a town in Judah.

The Dung Gate was a gate in the wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's day, called the "dung port" in the King James Version at Neh 2:13. Nehemiah passed it during his night inspection of the ruined walls and burned gates. It stood 1,000 cubits (about 450 meters) along the wall from the Valley Gate. It was rebuilt, with doors, locks and bars, by Malchiah son of Rechab, ruler of the district of Beth-haccerem (Neh 3:13–14). At the dedication of the restored wall, one of the two thanksgiving processions marched along the wall toward it (Neh 12:31). Its name probably reflects its use for carrying refuse out of the city, as the STEPBible names data suggests. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in the southern part of the city, facing the valley where rubbish was dumped. Its exact position is uncertain, and the location shown here is approximate.

Dura was the plain in the province of Babylon where King Nebuchadnezzar set up a golden image sixty cubits high and six cubits wide (Dan 3:1). It is mentioned only in this passage. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the meaning of the name as "circle." Its exact location is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes an older identification with a tract below Tikrit on the Tigris, where the name Dur survives. The French scholar Jules Oppert placed it southeast of Babylon near mounds called Duair, where the base of a huge statue was found. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that the name refers to a wall or rampart (Babylonian duru) and so points to an area within Babylon itself. The location shown here is rough and places Dura at or very near the city of Babylon.

East, in the phrases "the children of the east" and "the men of the east," refers to the peoples of the desert lands east of Israel rather than to a single town. In Judges they joined the Midianites and Amalekites in raiding Israel after the crops were sown. They gathered in the valley of Jezreel with camels "without number," and in the account of Gideon's campaign 120,000 of them fell, leaving about 15,000 with Zebah and Zalmunna at Karkor (Judg 8:10). In Ezekiel, God declares that Ammon will be handed over to the men of the east as a possession. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains that the Hebrew term (kedem) means "in front" and covers the lands just east of Palestine: Arabia, Mesopotamia and Babylonia. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies these people as Arab nomad tribes. The location shown here is a rough point east of the Jordan, near modern Amman, and marks a general region rather than an exact site.

East Gate was a gate in Jerusalem mentioned once, in the account of the rebuilding of the city wall under Nehemiah. Shemaiah son of Shechaniah, called its keeper, repaired a section of the wall near the house of Zadok son of Immer (Neh 3:29). Because it had an appointed keeper and appears in the stretch of wall near the temple, it was probably a gate on the east side of the temple area rather than simply an outer city gate. Several gates in the Bible share this name, including the eastern gates of the temple in Ezekiel's vision, so the exact identity is uncertain. The location shown here places it on the eastern side of the Temple Mount, near the site of the later Golden Gate.

East Gate is the King James rendering of a gate of Jerusalem mentioned in Jer 19:2, where God sends Jeremiah to the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, beside this gate's entrance, to proclaim judgment on Judah. The Hebrew name, Harsith, is understood in two ways. The King James Version takes it from a word for "sun," giving "east gate" (its margin has "sun gate"). Modern versions, following the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia's view, read it as "Potsherd Gate." Easton's Bible Dictionary calls it the Potter's Gate, leading to the potter's field. The setting fits the potsherd reading, since Jeremiah breaks a potter's clay jar there. This entry follows the Potsherd Gate reading. The gate probably stood on Jerusalem's southern side, facing the Hinnom Valley, but its exact site is uncertain, and the location shown here places it only generally within the city. It is distinct from other "east gates" in the Bible, such as those of the temple.

East Manasseh (Half-Tribe) was the territory east of the Jordan River settled by half of the tribe of Manasseh. It covered northern Gilead and the former kingdom of Og in Bashan. Moses assigned it after the clans of Machir, Manasseh's son, captured Gilead from the Amorites. Jair took the towns he named Havoth-jair, and Nobah took Kenath (Num 32:39–42; Deut 3:13–15). Josh 13:29–31 describes the territory as running from Mahanaim through all Bashan, including sixty towns of Jair and the cities of Ashtaroth and Edrei. Its people later spread north toward Mount Hermon and fought alongside Reuben and Gad. The Assyrian kings Pul and Tiglath-pileser deported them to Halah, Habor, Hara and the river Gozan (1 Chr 5:18, 23, 26). Ezekiel's vision gives Manasseh a single portion beside Naphtali. The region lies in present-day northern Jordan and southern Syria. The location shown here is a central point near the modern Jordan–Syria border.

Ebal (son of Shobal) was one of the five sons of Shobal, listed with his brothers Alvan, Manahath, Shepho and Onam in Gen 36:23. The parallel list in 1 Chr 1:40 names the same brothers, with Alvan spelled Alian and Shepho spelled Shephi. Shobal was a son of Seir the Horite (Gen 36:20), so Ebal belonged to the Horite clans who lived in the land of Seir. Their genealogy is set alongside the family of Esau. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "stone" or "bare mountain," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "ancient heaps." He is a different person from the Ebal son of Joktan, and the name is also shared by Mount Ebal in Canaan.

Ebal (son of Joktan) was one of the thirteen sons of Joktan, a descendant of Shem through Eber, listed in the Table of Nations. Genesis calls him Obal (Gen 10:28), and the parallel genealogy in Chronicles spells the name Ebal (1 Chr 1:22). In both lists he appears between Hadoram's brother Uzal and his brothers Abimael and Sheba. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests that, like the rest of Joktan's family, he was apparently the founder of an Arab tribe, since many of Joktan's sons bear names linked with peoples or regions of southern Arabia. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "ancient heaps", while Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "stripped bare". He is a different person from Ebal the son of Shobal, a descendant of Seir, and his name is separate from Mount Ebal.

Ebed was the father of Gaal, and is known only through his son, who is called "Gaal the son of Ebed" throughout Judges 9. Gaal came to Shechem with his brothers and won the confidence of its men (Judg 9:26). He then spoke openly against Abimelech, the son of Jerubbaal (Gideon), and urged the city to stop serving him (Judg 9:28). Zebul, the city's ruler, warned Abimelech in secret that Gaal and his brothers were fortifying Shechem against him (Judg 9:30–31), and Abimelech's forces came out of hiding to attack while Gaal stood at the city gate (Judg 9:35). Nothing is said about Ebed himself. His name means "servant," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Hitchcock's Bible Names. The name is shared by other men in the Bible, who are separate people.

Ebed, son of Jonathan, was one of the family heads who came back from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. He belonged to the descendants of Adin and brought fifty males of his family with him (Ezra 8:6). The name means "servant," according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names. Smith's notes that many manuscripts read the name as Eber. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies him with Obeth in the parallel list of 1 Esdras 8:32, in the Apocrypha. Another Ebed, the father of Gaal in the book of Judges, is a different man who shares the name. Nothing more is recorded about this Ebed beyond his place in Ezra's list of returning exiles.

Ebed-melech was an Ethiopian eunuch who served in the royal household of Judah during the last years before Jerusalem fell. The king of the time was Zedekiah, as Jer 38:5 indicates. When officials put the prophet Jeremiah into a muddy dungeon to die, Ebed-melech left the palace and appealed to the king, who was sitting in the Benjamin Gate. The king ordered him to take thirty men and lift Jeremiah out. Ebed-melech fetched old worn-out rags from a storeroom under the treasury, lowered them on cords, and told Jeremiah to pad his armpits with them so the ropes would not hurt him as he was pulled up. Afterward Jeremiah was told to bring him a message from the LORD: disaster was coming on the city, but, as the following verses state, Ebed-melech himself would be spared. His name means "servant of the king," according to Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Ebenezer, meaning “stone of help,” was the name Samuel gave to a memorial stone he set up between Mizpeh and Shen after Israel defeated the Philistines, saying, “Hitherto hath the LORD helped us” (1 Sam 7:12). The name also appears earlier as the place where Israel camped against the Philistines at Aphek before the battle in which the ark of God was captured and taken to Ashdod (1 Sam 4:1; 5:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary treats these earlier uses as naming the spot in advance, so the defeat and the later victory happened in the same area. The exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says no identification is yet possible.
