Easton's records two proposals: Beit Iksa, a prominent height northwest of Jerusalem, or Deir Aban, east of ‘Ain Shems. The location shown here is a rough one near Mizpah and Beit Iksa.

Eber (Heber) was a descendant of Shem in the line from Noah to Abraham. He was the son of Salah and grandson of Arphaxad (Gen 10:24; 1 Chr 1:18). He fathered Peleg at thirty-four and lived another 430 years, having other sons and daughters (Gen 11:16–17). By inference from the genealogy, he was born about 2281 BC. His two named sons were Peleg, so called because "in his days was the earth divided," and Joktan (Gen 10:25). Shem is described as "the father of all the children of Eber" (Gen 10:21), and Easton's Bible Dictionary regards Eber as the founder of the Hebrew people. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links his name, meaning "the other side," to the word "Hebrew." In Balaam's oracle (Num 24:24), "Eber" probably stands for his descendants as a people. Luke 3:35 names him Heber in the ancestry of Jesus.

Eber (a Benjamite) was a son of Elpaal, from the tribe of Benjamin. He appears only once, in the Benjamite genealogy at 1 Chr 8:12, where he is named first among Elpaal's sons, followed by Misham and Shamed. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him the oldest of the three. The same verse says the towns of Ono and Lod were built. The wording leaves it open whether Shamed alone built them or the brothers together did. Later in the chapter (1 Chr 8:17–18), more men are listed as sons of Elpaal, including Zebadiah, Meshullam, Hezeki, Heber, Ishmerai, Jezliah and Jobab. Earlier verses in the chapter trace Elpaal back to Shaharaim and his wife Hushim. This Eber is separate from the Benjamite Eber listed among the sons of Shashak (1 Chr 8:22), and from the ancestor Eber in Genesis. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Eber (Amok Family Head) was a priest who led the priestly family of Amok after the return from exile in Babylon. He is named once, in a list of priestly family heads (Neh 12:20). The surrounding passage places this list in the days of the high priest Joiakim, son of Jeshua (Neh 12:12), which would make Eber's generation the one after the first returnees. Amok himself appears earlier in the same chapter among the priests who came back with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:7). Easton's Bible Dictionary connects Eber with the time of Zerubbabel. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 445 BC. Nothing more is recorded about him. He is different from the better-known Eber of Genesis, the ancestor of Abraham, and from several other men of the same name.

Ebez (spelled Abez in the King James Version) was a town in the territory given to the tribe of Issachar, listed among its cities in Josh 19:20 alongside Rabbith and Kishion. Nothing else is recorded about it. Its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it at the north of the plain of Esdraelon and suggests the ruins of el-Beida, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name seems related to that of the judge Ibzan and regards everything else about it as conjecture. The location shown here follows an identification with Al-Bathan, a site in the hill country northeast of modern Nablus.

Ebiasaph, also spelled Abiasaph, was a Levite of the line of Korah and head of one of the Korahite families. Exodus names him with Assir and Elkanah as a son of Korah (Exod 6:24), and 1 Chr 6:37 calls him Korah's son. The list in 1 Chr 6:22–23, though, places him after Assir and Elkanah, which may make him a later descendant. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that these lists seem to skip names on purpose. His name probably means "my father has gathered." Through his son Assir he was an ancestor of Heman the singer, whose line 1 Chr 6:33–37 traces back to Korah. Through his son Kore he was an ancestor of Shallum and Meshelemiah, Korahite gatekeepers of the sanctuary (1 Chr 9:19). In 1 Chr 26:1 he appears in the short form Asaph, a different person from David's musician of that name.

Ebron was a town on the northern border of the tribe of Asher, listed with Rehob, Hammon and Kanah in the description of Asher's territory reaching toward Sidon (Josh 19:28). The Hebrew name is Ebron, but the King James Version renders it "Hebron," which can be confused with the well-known Hebron in Judah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may be a copyist's variant of Abdon, a Levitical city in Asher (Josh 21:30; 1 Chr 6:74), because the Hebrew letters for "r" and "d" are easily confused. The location shown here follows that Abdon identification. It places the town in western Galilee, probably at Tel Avdon (Khirbet Abdeh), inland from the Mediterranean coast near modern Nahariya. Nothing else is recorded about the town.

Ecbatana, called Achmetha in the King James Version, was a city in the province of the Medes. According to Ezra 6:2, a scroll was found in its royal citadel or palace. The verses that follow show that it recorded King Cyrus's decree for rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem, which was searched for under Darius. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Ecbatana as the old capital of the Median kings, where Cyrus held his court. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds that Persian kings spent their summers there and kept royal archives in its citadel. Greek writers mention more than one Ecbatana, and Smith's Bible Dictionary links one of them with the ruins at Takht-i-Suleiman in northwestern Iran. The Ecbatana of Ezra is usually identified with the ancient city beneath modern Hamadan in western Iran, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Eden was a Levite of the Gershonite clan, the son of Joah son of Zimmah. He is named among the Levites who rose up at King Hezekiah's call to cleanse the temple in Jerusalem and restore its worship after it had been neglected (2 Chr 29:12). The verse lists two Levites from each of the three Levite clans, Kohath, Merari and Gershon, and Eden and his father represent the Gershonites. An Eden also appears in 2 Chr 31:15 among the Levites who helped distribute the temple offerings to the priestly cities under Hezekiah. That may well be the same man, but the text does not say so. The name is shared by several people and is distinct from the garden of Eden. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "pleasure" or "delight."

Eden was a Levite in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He was one of six men who served 'next' to Kore, the Levite placed over the freewill offerings (by inference from the preceding verse, 2 Chr 31:14). Working in the cities of the priests, these men handed out the tithes, contributions and dedicated gifts to their fellow priests and Levites according to their divisions, giving fairly to old and young alike. STEPBible Proper Names describes him as one of the Levites Hezekiah appointed to this task. A Gershonite Levite named Eden, son of Joah, also appears among those who cleansed the temple at the start of Hezekiah's reign (2 Chr 29:12). He may be the same man, but the text does not say so. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as 'pleasure' or 'delight.'

Eden is the region where God planted a garden "eastward" and placed the first man to tend it (Gen 2:8, 15). A river flowed out of Eden to water the garden and then split into four streams (Gen 2:10). After the Fall, Adam was sent out to till the ground, and cherubim with a flaming sword guarded the way to the tree of life (Gen 3:23–24). The prophets later use Eden as a picture of fertility and splendour (Isa 51:3; Ezek 31:9; 36:35; Joel 2:3). Its site has been placed in Armenia, Arabia, Palestine and elsewhere. Easton's Bible Dictionary favours Babylonia, along the Tigris and Euphrates. This entry shows no location and treats the original site as unidentifiable. A separate Eden, "the children of Eden" in Telassar, was a Mesopotamian district conquered by Assyria and a trading partner of Tyre. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with Bit-Adini on the middle Euphrates.

Eder was a Levite, the second of the three sons of Mushi, listed between his brothers Mahli and Jeremoth (called Jerimoth in 1 Chr 24:30). Mushi was a son of Merari, so Eder belonged to the Merarite branch of the tribe of Levi. He appears only in the lists of Levitical families in 1 Chronicles 23–24, which set out the divisions of the Levites for service at the end of David's reign. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as appointed to the Levitical office, and Smith's Bible Dictionary places him in David's time. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name probably means "flock." He is a different person from the Benjamite Eder named elsewhere in Chronicles, and the name is also used for a tower and a town in the Old Testament.

Eder, called the "tower of Edar" in the King James Version, was a place where Israel (Jacob) set up his tent as he traveled south (Gen 35:21). The surrounding passage shows this was soon after Rachel died and was buried on the road to Bethlehem, and Gen 35:22 places Reuben's affair with Bilhah during the stay there. The name means "flock," so the phrase is usually understood as "tower of the flock," probably a watchtower used by shepherds. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it between Bethlehem and Hebron. It also links it with the "tower of the flock" in Mic 4:8, where the phrase points to Bethlehem and the royal line of David. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is in the Bethlehem area. The same name is used elsewhere in the Bible for a different place, a town in southern Judah (Josh 15:21).

Eder was a town in the far south of Judah, listed in Josh 15:21 among the "uttermost cities" of the tribe toward the border of Edom, alongside Kabzeel and Jagur. It belonged to the Negev district of Judah's territory. The name means "flock," and other places in the Bible share it, such as the Tower of Edar near Bethlehem (Gen 35:21). The site has not been securely identified. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that no trace of it had been found. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mentions Khirbet el-Adar, about 5 miles south of Gaza, as a possibility, but itself judges that site probably too far west for a town near Edom. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the Negev southeast of Beersheba, consistent with the town's listing near the Edomite border rather than with any particular ruin.

Edom was the region and nation south and southeast of the Dead Sea, also called the land of Seir, where Esau's descendants, the Edomites, settled (Gen 32:3; 36:43). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "red." Horite clans lived there earlier (Gen 36:21), and Edom had kings before Israel did (1 Chr 1:43). It bordered Judah's southern frontier (Num 34:3; Josh 15:1). Edom's king refused Israel passage during the wilderness journey, so Israel went around it (Num 20:14; Judg 11:18). Saul fought Edom, David garrisoned it, and Solomon built ships at Ezion-geber in Edom on the Red Sea (2 Sam 8:14; 1 Kgs 9:26). Bozrah and Teman were among its places (Isa 63:1; Jer 49:7). Several prophets announced judgment on Edom for its hostility to Judah, and it is also called Idumea (Ezek 25:12; 36:5; Obad 1:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in the rugged hills east of the Arabah. The location shown here is a general point for the wider surrounding area.

Edrei was a city in the territory given to the tribe of Naphtali. It appears only once, in the list of Naphtali's fortified cities, between Kedesh and Enhazor (Josh 19:37). By inference from that list, which runs through the hill country of upper Galilee, it probably lay in the north of Israel, perhaps not far from Kedesh. Its exact site is unknown, and no location is shown here. It should not be confused with the better-known Edrei in Bashan, east of the Jordan, where Israel defeated Og king of Bashan (Num 21:33; Deut 1:4). That Edrei was a separate city in a different region. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a very great mass, or cloud."

Edrei was a city of Bashan, east of the Jordan, and one of the two royal cities of Og, king of Bashan, the other being Ashtaroth. Og came out with his whole army to fight the Israelites under Moses at Edrei and was defeated, and his kingdom passed to Israel. Edrei marked a limit of Og's realm, with Salchah at the other end, and it was later assigned to the clan of Machir son of Manasseh. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with the ruins of Edr'a at the edge of the rocky Lejah region. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia prefers modern Der'a (Daraa) in southern Syria, noted for an ancient underground city, and the location shown here follows that identification. A town of the same name listed among the fortified cities of Naphtali in Josh 19:37 is probably a different place.

Eglah was one of David's wives and the mother of Ithream, his sixth son. Ithream was born while David reigned at Hebron, before he moved his capital to Jerusalem (2 Sam 3:5; 1 Chr 3:3). She appears only in these two parallel lists of David's sons, and she is the only mother in them described specifically as "David's wife." Nothing else is recorded about her family or background. Her name means "heifer" (Easton's Bible Dictionary). Easton's also mentions a Jewish tradition that identifies Eglah with Michal, Saul's daughter. This entry treats her simply as the wife named in the lists.

Eglaim was a place in Moab mentioned only in Isaiah's oracle against Moab. There the cry of mourning over Moab's ruin is said to reach Eglaim and Beer-elim (Isa 15:8). Since the verse speaks of the cry going round the borders of Moab, the two places probably marked distant points of Moabite territory. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take the name to mean "two ponds" and suggest it is the same as En-eglaim of Ezek 47:10. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it possibly in southern Moab and notes that Eusebius's Onomasticon identified it with Agallim, a village eight Roman miles south of Areopolis. It adds that the site cannot now be identified with certainty. The location shown here is approximate, in southern Moab near the southeastern end of the Dead Sea, following the southern Moab view.

Eglath-shelishiyah is a Hebrew phrase in the oracles against Moab in Isa 15:5 and Jer 48:34, where it appears beside Zoar and Horonaim as fleeing Moabites cry out in distress. The King James Version translates it as "an heifer of three years old." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Revised Version and most scholars read it as a place name, while the King James and Septuagint reading takes it as a comparison of the region's strong cities to a young heifer not yet broken to the yoke. Easton's Bible Dictionary follows the heifer reading. This entry treats it as a place, as STEPBible's proper-names list does, describing it as a Moabite city whose destruction Isaiah and Jeremiah foretold. Some have read it as "the third Eglath," implying several towns of that name. Its location is unknown, and no likely site has been identified.

Eglon was a king of Moab during the period of the judges. After the Israelites again did evil, the LORD strengthened him against Israel, and Israel served him for eighteen years (Judg 3:12, 14). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that he allied with Ammon and Amalek and took Jericho, the "city of palm trees," as his base, drawing on the surrounding verse (Judg 3:13). This entry places that subjugation at about 1378 BC, a date inferred from context. When Israel cried to the LORD, Ehud son of Gera, a left-handed Benjamite, was raised up as a deliverer. He brought Eglon a tribute present (Judg 3:15, 17). The text describes Eglon as a very fat man. The continuing account (Judg 3:21–22) records that Ehud killed him with a hidden dagger during a private audience, which ended the Moabite oppression. He is a different figure from the Canaanite city of the same name.

Eglon was a Canaanite royal city in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, near Lachish. Its king, Debir, joined the alliance of five Amorite kings led by Adonizedek of Jerusalem that attacked Gibeon (Josh 10:3–5). After the coalition's defeat, the five kings were brought out of a cave and put to death (Josh 10:23). Joshua then moved from Lachish to Eglon, besieged and destroyed it, and went on to Hebron (Josh 10:34–37). Eglon appears in the list of defeated kings and was later allotted to Judah (Josh 12:12; 15:39). Its exact site is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary finds the name preserved at Khirbet Ajlan, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes Flinders Petrie's preference for Tell Nejileh, southeast of Tell el-Hesi. The location shown here appears to follow the Tell Nejileh identification. The city is distinct from Eglon, the king of Moab.

The Brook of Egypt (the "river of Egypt" in the King James Version) was a seasonal watercourse at the southwestern edge of Israel's land, between Canaan and Egypt. It marked the end of Israel's promised southern border, which ran from Azmon to the Mediterranean (Num 34:5; Josh 15:4), and it bounded Judah's coastal towns beyond Gaza (Josh 15:47). Israelites came to Solomon's seven-day feast from as far as Hamath in the north to this stream in the south (1 Kgs 8:65; 2 Chr 7:8). The king of Babylon later took all of Egypt's holdings from here to the Euphrates (2 Kgs 24:7). Isaiah and Ezekiel also use it as a southern limit (Isa 27:12; Ezek 47:19). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew word means a wadi, a desert valley that is usually dry but subject to sudden floods. This entry follows the usual identification with Wadi el-Arish in northern Sinai. Some have instead linked it with an eastern branch of the Nile.

Egypt was the ancient kingdom of the Nile valley in the northeast corner of Africa. Its usual Hebrew name, Mizraim, is a dual form that Smith's Bible Dictionary links to the country's two parts, Upper Egypt (the valley) and Lower Egypt (the Delta). Abram went there during a famine (Gen 12:10). Jacob's family later settled there (Exod 1:1), and Joseph died there (Gen 50:26). The Israelites were later enslaved, and Moses led them out after the plagues (Exod 10:21; Deut 34:11). That deliverance is recalled throughout Scripture (Lev 11:45; Amos 2:10; Mic 6:4; Jude 1:5). Under the kings, Solomon married Pharaoh's daughter and bought horses from Egypt (1 Kgs 3:1; 2 Chr 1:16). The prophets warned against relying on Egypt and announced judgment on it (Ezek 17:15; Jer 46:25). Joseph and Mary fled there with the infant Jesus (Matt 2:13).

The Egyptian Sea is a body of water named in Isaiah's prophecy that the LORD would "utterly destroy the tongue of the Egyptian sea" and dry up "the river" into seven streams so that people could cross on foot (Isa 11:15). In the context of the chapter, this clears the way for scattered Israelites to return from Egypt and Assyria, and it probably echoes the crossing of the sea in the Exodus. The "river" is usually taken to be the Euphrates. Most interpreters identify the "tongue" of the Egyptian Sea as the Gulf of Suez, the northwestern arm of the Red Sea. Others suggest a branch of the Nile or the Mediterranean coast near Egypt. The location shown here follows the Red Sea identification and is placed only generally in the northern Red Sea.

Egypt's is the possessive form of Egypt, the land along the Nile River in northeastern Africa, used where something is described as belonging to Egypt, such as its rulers, people, or goods. No verses are supplied for this entry, so its exact contexts cannot be described here. By inference from the name, it refers to the same country that appears throughout the Bible as a major neighbour of Israel, a place of refuge and of bondage, and a regional power. The location shown here is a point near modern Cairo, in the area of ancient Heliopolis (biblical On). It stands for the country as a whole rather than a single town.

Ehi was a son of Benjamin, named among the ten sons of Benjamin in the list of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:21). He belonged to the tribe of Benjamin. This entry identifies him with Aharah, whom 1 Chr 8:1 lists as Benjamin's third son, after Bela the firstborn and Ashbel. The Benjamite genealogies differ in their names and order, and some names in Gen 46:21 appear in other lists as later descendants. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both suggest that Ehi may also be the same person as Ahiram, the third son in Num 26:38, and possibly Aher in 1 Chr 7:12. The Tyndale House proper-names index treats Ahiram, Aharah and Ehi as one man. This entry lists Ahiram separately as a brother. Nothing else is recorded about Ehi beyond his name and place in the family.

Ehud son of Gera was a left-handed Benjamite whom the LORD raised up as a deliverer when Israel was under Eglon, king of Moab (Judg 3:15). Sent to deliver Israel's tribute, he hid a two-edged dagger about a cubit long on his right thigh. He then told Eglon, who was alone in his private upper room, that he had a message from God, and stabbed him with his left hand (Judg 3:16, 3:20–21). He locked the doors behind him, escaped to Seirath, and, as the wider account tells it, led Israel to victory over Moab at the fords of the Jordan. The text places this about 1360 BC by inference from context. After his death Israel again did evil (Judg 4:1). This entry treats him as the Ehud of 1 Chr 8:6, whose sons, including Naaman, Ahiah, Gera, Uzza and Ahihud, were family heads at Geba. Because the name belongs to several people, that identification is uncertain.

Ehud was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the seven sons of Bilhan, listed in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:10. His brothers were Jeush, Benjamin, Chenaanah, Zethan, Tharshish and Ahishahar. Bilhan was a son of Jediael, who in the surrounding verses is a son of Benjamin, so Easton's Bible Dictionary describes this Ehud as Benjamin's great-grandson. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is a different person from the better-known Ehud son of Gera, the left-handed Benjamite judge who killed Eglon king of Moab. Whether the Ehud named in a later Benjamite list in 1 Chronicles 8 is the same man is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "he that praises."

Eker was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles. He was one of three sons of Ram, listed after his brothers Maaz and Jamin (1 Chr 2:27). His father Ram was the firstborn of Jerahmeel, which places Eker among the Jerahmeelites, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. Jerahmeel was a son of Hezron and a grandson of Perez, son of Judah (1 Chr 2:9). Nothing else is recorded about Eker. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes his name to mean "a rooting up," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "root." Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "barren, feeble."

Ekron was the northernmost of the five chief Philistine cities, each ruled by its own lord (Josh 13:3). It lay on Judah's northern border and was assigned first to Judah and then to Dan (Josh 15:11, 45–46; 19:43). Judah is said to have taken it (Judg 1:18), but it was later back in Philistine hands. The captured ark of God was sent there, and its people feared it would kill them (1 Sam 5:10). The Philistines then returned the ark with gold offerings (1 Sam 6:16–17). Israel pursued the Philistines to its gates after David killed Goliath (1 Sam 17:52). King Ahaziah sent to consult Baalzebub, the god of Ekron, and Elijah condemned him for it (2 Kgs 1:2–3, 16). Prophets announced judgment on the city (Amos 1:8; Zeph 2:4). Easton's and Smith's dictionaries placed it at the village of Akir. The location shown here follows the later identification with Tel Miqne.

El-bethel, meaning "God of Bethel," is the name Jacob gave to the place where he built an altar after returning from Paddan-aram. Genesis 35:7 explains the name: this was where God had appeared to him when he fled from his brother Esau. That earlier appearance is the vision of the ladder at Bethel described in Gen 28, so El-bethel is the altar site at Bethel, the town once called Luz. The surrounding verses of Gen 35 make the same link when God sends Jacob back to Bethel. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify it with the scene of Jacob's vision. The location shown here lies at or near Bethel, which is commonly identified with the modern village of Beitin, north of Jerusalem.

El-elohe-Israel was the name Jacob gave to an altar he built after returning from Paddan-aram (Gen 33:20). The name means "God, the God of Israel." The preceding verse places the altar on a plot of ground Jacob bought outside the city of Shechem, and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes it as facing the city. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links the name to the night at Peniel, when Jacob received the new name Israel (Gen 32:28). On that reading, Jacob dedicated his first altar in the land to God under the name now tied to his own. The same work notes other readings. The Greek Septuagint has "he called upon the God of Israel," and some scholars read "pillar" instead of "altar." The exact site is unknown. The location shown here places it at ancient Shechem, near modern Nablus.

El-paran was a place at the edge of the wilderness, named once in the Bible as the farthest point reached by Chedorlaomer and his allied kings when they struck the Horites of Mount Seir (Gen 14:6). The text describes it only as being "by the wilderness." By inference from the name and context, that wilderness is probably the Wilderness of Paran, the broad desert south of Canaan. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as "the terebinth of Paran," suggesting a landmark tree or grove. According to the next verse, the kings then turned back toward En-mishpat, or Kadesh. Its exact site is unknown. Some identify it with Elath at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba. The location shown here is only approximate and places it in the Sinai Peninsula, within the general region of the Wilderness of Paran.

Eladah was a descendant of Ephraim, son of Joseph, named once in the Ephraimite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:20. The line runs Ephraim, Shuthelah, Bered, Tahath, Eladah, Tahath, which makes Eladah the son of one Tahath and the father of another. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia spells the name Eleadah. The STEPBible proper-names index describes him as a son of Ephraim, meaning a descendant rather than an immediate son, and as an ancestor of Joshua. That link follows from the same genealogy, which later reaches Nun and his son Joshua (1 Chr 7:27). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "the eternity of God." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Elah was one of the chiefs, called "dukes" in the King James Version, of Edom, the people descended from Esau. He appears in the list of Edomite chiefs at the end of Genesis 36, and the same list is repeated in 1 Chr 1:52. Nothing else is recorded about him. The list may name clan leaders or the clans and districts they headed, since some names in it also appear elsewhere as places. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as the head of a clan and gives the meaning of the name as "oak" or "terebinth." Several other men in the Bible share the name Elah, including a king of Israel and a son of Caleb. They are separate people and should not be confused with this Edomite chief.

Elah was the father of Shimei, one of the twelve officers King Solomon appointed to supply food for the royal household. Shimei was responsible for the territory of Benjamin (1 Kgs 4:18). Elah himself is known only as Shimei's father. The verse gives no details about his life, and it does not say whether he held any office. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as meaning "oak" or "terebinth." Several other men in the Bible are also named Elah, including a king of Israel and the father of King Hoshea. Nothing in the text links this Elah to any of them.

Elah was the son of Baasha and succeeded him as king of Israel after Baasha died and was buried in Tirzah (1 Kgs 16:6). He began to reign in Tirzah in the twenty-sixth year of Asa king of Judah and ruled for two years (1 Kgs 16:8). This entry dates his reign to about 930 BC, an estimate inferred from context; the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it in 888–887 BC. The writer of Kings groups his sins with his father's, saying both led Israel to sin and provoked the LORD with their idols (1 Kgs 16:13), and refers readers to the chronicles of the kings of Israel for the rest of his acts (1 Kgs 16:14). The surrounding verses (1 Kgs 16:9–10) say that Zimri, one of his chariot commanders, killed him while he was drunk in Tirzah. He was the last king of Baasha's line. Several other men in the Bible share the name Elah.

Elah was the father of Hoshea, the last king of the northern kingdom of Israel. He is known only through his son, who is repeatedly called "Hoshea the son of Elah" in 2 Kings. Hoshea conspired against King Pekah, killed him and took the throne (2 Kgs 15:30). He then reigned in Samaria for nine years (2 Kgs 17:1), and in his seventh year Shalmaneser king of Assyria besieged the city (2 Kgs 18:9). Nothing is said about Elah himself, including whether he held any rank. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 729 BC or earlier, an estimate drawn from his son's reign. The name means "oak" or "terebinth" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Several other men in the Bible share the name, among them a king of Israel, and this Elah should not be confused with them.

Elah was a son of Caleb son of Jephunneh, the man who served as one of the spies Moses sent into Canaan. He appears only in the genealogy of Judah at 1 Chr 4:15, which names him second of Caleb's three sons, between his brothers Iru and Naam, and records that his son was Kenaz. His sister Achsah is known from other passages, such as Josh 15:16–17, where Caleb gives her in marriage to Othniel. This Kenaz, Elah's son, is probably a different man from the Kenaz who was Othniel's father, since the name recurs within Caleb's family. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name Elah as meaning "oak" or "terebinth." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a king of Israel, so this Elah should be kept distinct from them. Nothing further is recorded about his life.

Elah, son of Uzzi and grandson of Michri, was a Benjamite named in 1 Chr 9:8. He appears in the list of people who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. Several other Benjamites are named alongside him, among them Ibneiah son of Jeroham and Meshullam son of Shephathiah. By inference from the surrounding passage (1 Chr 9:7–9), he was one of the leading men of the families of Benjamin who settled in the city. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as one of the chiefs of the tribes when the country was resettled. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with the several other men named Elah in the Bible, including a king of Israel. The name is usually taken to mean "oak" or "terebinth."

Elam (son of Shem) was the first-named son of Shem and so a grandson of Noah, listed in the table of nations alongside his brothers Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud and Aram (Gen 10:22). The genealogy in 1 Chr 1:17 repeats the list but also counts Uz, Hul, Gether and Meshech among Shem's sons, where Genesis names them as sons of Aram. The text records nothing about Elam's life. Like several names in this table, his name was also the name of a people and a land. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects him with the country of Elam east of Babylonia, whose capital was Susa and whose inhabitants were the Elamites. It explains the name as meaning "high" or "highland," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives other meanings, including "a young man."

Elam was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named as a son of Shashak in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. He appears in a list of Shashak's sons that includes Ishpan, Heber, Eliel, Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Hananiah, Antothijah, Iphedeiah and Penuel. Nothing is recorded about his life beyond his place in this family line. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a chief man of Benjamin, probably drawing on the summary in the same chapter that calls these men heads of fathers' houses who lived in Jerusalem. Several other people in the Bible share the name Elam, including a son of Shem and the ancestor of a family that returned from exile. This entry concerns only the Benjamite son of Shashak.

Elam was a Levite of the family of Korah, the fifth of seven sons of Meshelemiah, named in the list of temple gatekeepers organized in the time of King David (1 Chr 26:3). His brothers were Zechariah, Jediael, Zebadiah, Jathniel, Jehohanan and Elioenai. The surrounding chapter assigns these Korahite families to guard the gates of the house of the Lord, so Elam probably served as a gatekeeper, as STEPBible's proper-names index describes him. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him in David's reign, about 1014 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Elam, and this one should not be confused with them.

Elam was the ancestor of a family group of Jews who returned to Jerusalem after the exile in Babylon. His descendants, called "the children of Elam," numbered 1,254 in the list of those who came back with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:7; Neh 7:12). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this return to about 536 BC or before. A later group of seventy men from the same family, led by Jeshaiah son of Athaliah, came with Ezra (Ezra 8:7). Members of the family appear again in the dispute over marriages to foreign women. Shechaniah son of Jehiel, one of Elam's descendants, admitted the wrong to Ezra and proposed a remedy (Ezra 10:2), and six men of the family are named among those who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:26). Nothing is recorded about Elam himself. Several other people in the Bible share the name.

Elam was one of the "chief of the people" named in Neh 10:14 among the leaders who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, after the return from exile in Babylon. By inference from the surrounding chapter, this covenant was a written pledge to keep the law of Moses. Nothing else is recorded about him personally. His name appears alongside Parosh, Pahath-moab, Zattu and Bani, which are also the names of large family groups listed among the returning exiles (Ezra 2:3–10; Neh 7:8–15, where "the children of Elam" are counted). So this Elam probably signed as head or representative of the family of Elam rather than as a single individual, though the text does not say so directly. Several people in the Bible share the name, and this entry treats the covenant signer as a separate figure. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "a young man" or "a secret."

Elam was a priest or Levite in Nehemiah's time. He appears only in a list of eight men who took part in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem, where they stood while the singers sang loudly under their overseer Jezrahiah (Neh 12:42). Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of the priests who accompanied Nehemiah at that dedication. The context suggests the group formed part of one of the two thanksgiving processions on the wall, as described in the surrounding passage. Nothing further is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name Elam, and this man should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "a young man" or "a secret," while Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "eternity."

Elam was an ancient country east of Babylonia. The location shown here is in the lowlands and hills of what is now southwestern Iran, around the modern province of Khuzestan. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the name as an Assyrian word meaning "high" and links the people to Elam, a son of Shem (Gen 10:22). In Abraham's day Chedorlaomer king of Elam led a coalition of four kings (Gen 14:1, 9). Shushan (Susa), where Daniel saw a vision by the river Ulai, lay in the province of Elam (Dan 8:2). The prophets describe Elam's archers and chariots (Isa 22:6). Isaiah calls on Elam and Media to attack, by context against Babylon (Isa 21:2). Jeremiah, early in Zedekiah's reign, foretold that Elam's bow would be broken and its people scattered, and later restored (Jer 49:34–39). Ezekiel pictures Elam among the nations slain by the sword (Ezek 32:24).

Elasah was one of the sons, or descendants, of Pashur listed in Ezra 10:22 among the men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra. The surrounding passage places the descendants of Pashur among the priests, so Elasah was probably a priest, as Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him. By inference from the context of Ezra 10, he was among those who agreed to send away their foreign wives during Ezra's reforms after the return from exile in Babylon. Nothing more is recorded about him. His name means "God has made" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Several people in the Bible bear this name, and this Elasah should not be confused with the others, such as the son of Shaphan who carried Jeremiah's letter to the exiles.

Elasah son of Shaphan was one of two men King Zedekiah of Judah sent to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. The other was Gemariah son of Hilkiah. Jeremiah 29:3 says they also carried the letter Jeremiah wrote to the Jewish exiles in Babylon. The mission is undated in the text, and Smith's Bible Dictionary places it about 594 BC. His name means "God has made" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Elasah is probably the son of Shaphan, the royal scribe under King Josiah (2 Kgs 22:3). That would make him a brother of Ahikam, who protected Jeremiah (Jer 26:24), and of Gemariah son of Shaphan, in whose chamber Baruch read Jeremiah's scroll (Jer 36:10). That Gemariah is a different man from the Gemariah son of Hilkiah who travelled with Elasah. The name Elasah is also borne by another person in the Bible.

Elath was a city at the northern tip of the Gulf of Aqaba, an arm of the Red Sea, near Ezion-geber. Moses recalls that Israel passed by way of Elath and Ezion-geber on the route around Edom toward the wilderness of Moab (Deut 2:8). Under the plural form Eloth it appears beside Ezion-geber in Solomon's time (1 Kgs 9:26). Easton's Bible Dictionary says it later broke away from Judah. King Azariah (Uzziah), named in the preceding verse, rebuilt it and restored it to Judah (2 Kgs 14:22). In the reign of Ahaz, Rezin king of Syria took it back and drove out the Jews, and the Syrians settled there (2 Kgs 16:6). Some translations read "Edom" and "Edomites" here instead. Easton's identifies it with the Greek and Roman Elana and the ruin of Aila. The location shown here is at modern Aqaba in Jordan.

Eldaah was the fifth and last-named son of Midian, listed with his brothers Ephah, Epher, Hanoch (Henoch) and Abida in the two genealogies that record him (Gen 25:4; 1 Chr 1:33). Midian was a son of Abraham by Keturah, so Eldaah was Abraham's grandson, and both passages count him among "the children of Keturah." Nothing else is recorded about him. Because Midian gave his name to the Midianites, Eldaah's line was probably one of the clans of that people, though the text does not say so directly. The meaning of his name is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "God has called," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "knowledge of God."

Eldad was one of the elders of Israel in the wilderness, named alongside Medad in Num 11:26–27. Both men were among those whose names had been written down when Moses gathered seventy elders to share the burden of leading the people. They stayed in the camp instead of going out to the tabernacle with the others. Even so, the spirit rested on them, and they prophesied in the camp. A young man ran to tell Moses. In the wider passage, Joshua urged Moses to stop them, but Moses refused and said he wished all the Lord's people were prophets. Easton's Bible Dictionary links the episode to the Gospel accounts in which the disciples tried to stop someone casting out demons in Jesus' name. The name is usually taken to mean "God has loved" or "favored of God."

Elead was a member of the tribe of Ephraim who, along with Ezer, was killed by the men of Gath, described as people born in that land, when they came down to take away their cattle (1 Chr 7:21). The verse is commonly read, as in the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, as describing a cattle raid by the Ephraimites, though its wording could also mean the men of Gath came to take Ephraim's cattle. The genealogy is ambiguous about his exact place in the family. This entry treats him as a son of Ephraim, matching the next verse, in which Ephraim mourns for his sons. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him more generally a descendant of Ephraim. His name is explained as "God has testified" or "witness of God." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Elealeh was a town east of the Jordan, in the pastoral highlands north of the Dead Sea, always mentioned alongside nearby Heshbon. It was among the places in the land taken from the Amorites that Reuben and Gad asked for because it suited their livestock (Num 32:3), and the Reubenites rebuilt it (Num 32:37). By the time of Isaiah and Jeremiah it was held by Moab. In their oracles against Moab, Heshbon and Elealeh cry out so loudly that they are heard as far as Jahaz, and the joyful shouts over their summer fruit and harvest fall silent (Isa 15:4; 16:9; Jer 48:34). The name probably means "God has ascended." Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the ruin el-'Al, about a mile north or northeast of Heshbon (modern Hesban, Jordan), and the location shown here follows that identification.

Eleasah was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in a genealogy of 1 Chronicles. He was the son of Helez, the son of Azariah, and the father of Sisamai, whose son was Shallum (1 Chr 2:39–40). The surrounding passage traces this line through the family of Jerahmeel, a descendant of Judah through Hezron. It begins with the marriage of Sheshan's daughter to his Egyptian servant Jarha (1 Chr 2:34–35), so Eleasah probably belonged to that branch. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "whom God made." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that in Hebrew it is the same name as Elasah, which is borne by other men in the Bible. This Eleasah should not be confused with them.

Eleasah was a Benjamite in the family line of King Saul, named in the genealogy that runs from Saul through Jonathan to later generations (1 Chr 8:37; 9:43). Both lists say that Moza fathered Binea, then name Rapha (called Rephaiah in 1 Chr 9:43), Eleasah and Azel, each followed by "his son." This can be read as a chain of generations, making Eleasah the son of Rapha, as Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible names index read it. It can also be read as a list of Binea's sons, and this entry follows that reading, treating Eleasah as Binea's son and the brother of Rephaiah and Azel. This entry also identifies him with Eshek, the "brother" of Azel, whose sons were Ulam the firstborn, Jehush and Eliphelet (1 Chr 8:39). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat Eshek as a separate descendant of Saul. Nothing else is recorded about him, and other men in the Bible share his name.

Eleazar was the third son of Aaron and Elisheba, and the brother of Nadab, Abihu and Ithamar. He married a daughter of Putiel, who bore him Phinehas. With his father and brothers he was consecrated as a priest. After Nadab and Abihu died childless, he and Ithamar carried on the priestly service, and he was made chief over the Levites who kept the sanctuary. When Aaron was about to die, Aaron's garments were put on Eleazar, and he succeeded him as priest. He stood with Moses at the census, at Joshua's commissioning, and over the Midianite spoils. Later he and Joshua divided Canaan among the tribes at Shiloh. He was buried in the hill country of Ephraim on land belonging to Phinehas. In David's time Zadok's priestly line was traced to him, as was Ezra's later. Several other people in the Bible share his name.

Eleazar was a son of Abinadab of Kiriath-jearim. After the Philistines returned the ark of the LORD and it had been at Beth-shemesh, the men of Kiriath-jearim brought it to Abinadab's house on the hill and consecrated Eleazar to keep it (1 Sam 7:1). The following verse says the ark stayed there twenty years. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that he was set apart to take charge of the ark but would not have been allowed to touch it, comparing the rules for Levitical care of holy objects in Num 3:31 and 4:15. Ahio and Uzzah, who later drove the cart when David moved the ark (2 Sam 6:3), are also called sons of Abinadab. By inference they were Eleazar's brothers. His name means "God is helper." Several other people in the Bible share the name Eleazar.

Eleazar, son of Dodo the Ahohite, was one of the three most prominent warriors among David's mighty men. 2 Sam 23:9 says he was with David when they defied the Philistines gathered for battle after the men of Israel had withdrawn. The verse that follows in that passage describes him striking down Philistines until his hand was tired and stuck to his sword. The parallel account in 1 Chronicles places a similar stand with David at Pasdammim, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia equates with Ephes-dammim. Easton's Bible Dictionary counts him among the three who broke through the Philistine lines to bring David water from the well of Bethlehem, and assigns him to the tribe of Benjamin. "Ahohite" probably refers to descent from Ahoah. His name means "God is helper." He is distinct from several other men named Eleazar, including Aaron's son, the priest.

Eleazar was a Levite of the clan of Merari, the son of Mahli and grandson of Merari, and the brother of Kish (1 Chr 23:21). A further brother, Libni, is named in 1 Chr 6:29, which lists Libni as a son of Mahli. Eleazar died without sons, leaving only daughters, and these daughters married their cousins, the sons of Kish (1 Chr 23:22). The list of Levite divisions repeats that he had no sons (1 Chr 24:28). The marriages within the family probably kept his branch's line and inheritance among Mahli's descendants, a practice that matches the rule for heiresses in Num 36. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "God is helper." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including Aaron's son the priest, but this Eleazar is known only from these brief notes in Chronicles.

Eleazar son of Phinehas was one of the men who received and weighed the silver, gold and temple vessels that Ezra's company brought from Babylon to Jerusalem. On the fourth day after their arrival, the treasure was weighed in the house of God by Meremoth son of Uriah the priest, with Eleazar beside him and the Levites Jozabad and Noadiah (Ezra 8:33). The verse does not make his own status clear. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him a priest who accompanied Ezra from Babylon, Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as working alongside the priests, and Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a Levite. His name means "God is helper." He is distinct from the much earlier Eleazar son of Aaron, whose own son was also named Phinehas. Several other people in the Bible share the name Eleazar.

Eleazar was one of the descendants of Parosh who appear in the list of Israelite laymen who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra (Ezra 10:25). The surrounding chapter records that these men agreed to send away their foreign wives as part of Ezra's reforms after the return from exile in Babylon. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that he was a layman rather than a priest or Levite, which fits the heading "of Israel" under which he is listed. Nothing else is recorded about him. Eleazar was a common name, shared by several people in the Bible, most notably Aaron's son the priest, and this man should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "help of God."

Eleazar was one of the men who took part in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah, about 446 BC by inference from context. He is named in a list of eight who stood with the singers in one of the processions, while the singers sang loudly under their overseer Jezrahiah (Neh 12:42). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe him as a priest, and the STEPBible proper names index calls him a priest or Levite. The verse itself gives no family or title, so his exact role is inferred from the setting of the dedication ceremony. His name means "God is helper." Several other men in the Bible share this name, and nothing further is known of this one.

Eleazar was an ancestor of Jesus named in Matthew's genealogy, the son of Eliud and the father of Matthan (Matt 1:15). Through Matthan he was the grandfather of Jacob and the great-grandfather of Joseph, the husband of Mary. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places him three generations before Joseph. He belongs to the part of the genealogy after the return from exile in Babylon, and as a descendant of David he was of the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in this list. His name means "God is helper" or "help of God," and several other men in the Bible share it, among them Aaron's son, the priest who succeeded him. This Eleazar should not be confused with them.

Elhanan was a warrior of David's time who fought the Philistines. 1 Chr 20:5 calls him the son of Jair and says he killed Lahmi, the brother of Goliath the Gittite, whose spear shaft was like a weaver's beam. The parallel account in 2 Sam 21:19 calls him the son of Jaare-oregim, a Bethlehemite, and places the battle at Gob. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the words "the brother of" in 2 Sam 21:19 were added in the King James Version to match Chronicles, and that the Revised Version leaves them out. It places the exploit late in David's reign, while Smith's Bible Dictionary dates it to about 1020 BC. In both accounts the giant is linked to Goliath, whom David killed in 1 Sam 17. The name means "God has been gracious." Several men in the Bible share it, including Elhanan son of Dodo, one of David's thirty mighty men.

Elhanan, son of Dodo of Bethlehem, was one of David's mighty warriors, listed among "the thirty" (2 Sam 23:24; 1 Chr 11:26). In both lists his name comes right after Asahel, the brother of Joab, so Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as the first named of the thirty. His name means "God has been gracious" or "whom God gave." Nothing more is recorded about his deeds. Several men in the Bible bear this name, including the Elhanan credited with killing a Philistine giant. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some scholars think these may be the same man, while others treat them as separate people. This entry treats the son of Dodo as a distinct person.

Eli was the priest at the sanctuary in Shiloh before Israel had kings, and the father of the priests Hophni and Phinehas (1 Sam 1:3, 9). He first mistook Hannah's silent prayer for drunkenness, then blessed her. He later received her son Samuel, who served under him and whom he taught to answer the Lord's call (1 Sam 1:13–17; 3:8–9). When he was very old and nearly blind, he heard of his sons' misconduct. A man of God, and then Samuel, announced judgment on his house (1 Sam 2:22, 27; 3:12–14). The ark was captured in battle with the Philistines and his sons were killed. The ninety-eight-year-old Eli heard the news by the wayside, and according to 1 Sam 4:18 he fell, broke his neck and died, having judged Israel forty years. By inference from context he died about 1122 BC. Easton's Bible Dictionary traces his line to Aaron's son Ithamar. Solomon's removal of Abiathar fulfilled the word against Eli's house (1 Kgs 2:27).

Eliab son of Helon was the leader of the tribe of Zebulun during Israel's wilderness journey. He is named among the tribal heads who helped Moses take the census (Num 1:9). In the camp arrangement he was captain of Zebulun, which camped alongside Judah and Issachar (Num 2:7). On the third day of the offerings for the dedication of the altar, he brought Zebulun's gifts, including peace offerings of oxen, rams, goats and lambs (Num 7:24, 29). When Israel set out from Sinai, he commanded Zebulun's company (Num 10:16). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives his name's meaning as "God is my father." Several other men in the Bible share the name. The best known is David's eldest brother (1 Sam 17:28), a different person who is not the subject of this entry.

Eliab was a man of the tribe of Reuben, the son of Pallu and the father of Nemuel, Dathan and Abiram (Num 26:8–9). His name means "God is my father" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary. He is remembered almost entirely through his sons Dathan and Abiram, who joined Korah the Levite and On son of Peleth in a revolt against Moses and Aaron (Num 16:1). When Moses summoned them, they refused to come (Num 16:12). Deuteronomy recalls how the earth opened and swallowed Dathan and Abiram along with their households, tents and possessions (Deut 11:6). Deut 11:6 calls Eliab "the son of Reuben," meaning a descendant of Reuben, since Num 26:8 makes him Reuben's grandson through Pallu. Several other men in the Bible share the name Eliab, and this entry concerns only the Reubenite.

Eliab was the firstborn son of Jesse, of the tribe of Judah, and the eldest brother of David. His name means "God is father." When Samuel came to anoint a king from among Jesse's sons, he saw Eliab and assumed he was the LORD's anointed. In the next verse (1 Sam 16:7), God tells Samuel not to judge by appearance or height, and David is chosen instead. Eliab and his brothers Abinadab and Shammah followed Saul to war against the Philistines. When David came to the camp and asked about Goliath, Eliab angrily accused him of pride and of leaving his sheep just to watch the battle. His daughter Abihail became a wife of King Rehoboam. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the Elihu named as David's brother in 1 Chr 27:18 to be Eliab under another name. Several other men in the Bible are also called Eliab.

Eliab was a warrior of the tribe of Gad, listed third among the Gadite leaders who joined David before he became king (1 Chr 12:9). The surrounding passage (1 Chr 12:8–15) describes these Gadites as mighty men trained for war, with faces like lions and as swift as gazelles, who left their tribe and came to David's stronghold in the wilderness while he was hiding from Saul. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries place his joining at that wilderness stronghold, while the Tyndale House proper-names index links it with David's time at Ziklag, where the chapter opens (1 Chr 12:1). Nothing more is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "God is my father." He is one of several men named Eliab in the Bible and should not be confused with David's eldest brother or with the Zebulunite tribal leader of Moses' time.

Eliab was a Levite in the time of King David, one of several men in the Bible with this name, which means "God is my father" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). He is named among the Levites "of the second degree" whom David's chief Levites appointed to serve when the ark of the covenant was brought up to Jerusalem. In that list the whole group is called porters, or gatekeepers (1 Chr 15:18). He was also one of the musicians who played psalteries, stringed instruments, "on Alamoth" (1 Chr 15:20), a musical term whose exact meaning is uncertain. Once the ark was placed in its tent, Eliab was among the Levites who served before it under Asaph, the chief musician, again playing psalteries and harps while Asaph sounded the cymbals (1 Chr 16:5). Nothing further is recorded about him.

Eliada was a son of David born in Jerusalem, one of the sons born after David established himself there. He appears only in the lists of those sons, always between Elishama and Eliphalet, near the end, so that, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes, he is the second youngest (2 Sam 5:16; 1 Chr 3:8). In 1 Chr 3:8 he is counted among nine sons who follow those of Bathsheba. The parallel list in 1 Chr 14:7 calls him Beeliada. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of that form as "the Lord knows," and Eliada means much the same, "God knows." Nothing else is recorded about his life. The name Eliada is also borne by other men in the Bible, who are different people.

Eliada was a Benjamite commander in the army of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. 2 Chr 17:17 calls him "a mighty man of valour" and says he led 200,000 men from the tribe of Benjamin, armed with bow and shield. He appears in a list of Jehoshaphat's military leaders and the troops under each, all of whom served the king in Jerusalem alongside the garrisons stationed in Judah's fortified cities. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 945 BC. The name, usually taken to mean "God knows" or "known by God" (Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "knowledge of God"), is also borne by other men in the Bible, including a son of David, so this Eliada should not be confused with them.

Eliadah was the father of Rezon, a man God raised up as an adversary to King Solomon (1 Kgs 11:23). He is known only through his son. Rezon had fled from his master Hadadezer, king of Zobah, so Eliadah was probably an Aramean of that region, though this is an inference from the passage. Easton's Bible Dictionary places the family among the Arameans of Zobah and describes Rezon as captain of a raiding band that troubled Solomon. Nothing else is recorded about Eliadah himself. His name is sometimes spelled Eliada, and he should not be confused with other men of that name in the Old Testament, such as a son of David.

Eliah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named as one of the sons of Jeroham in the genealogy of 1 Chr 8:27. His brothers were Shamsherai, Shehariah, Athaliah, Jaresiah and Zichri. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him among the chief men of the tribe, in line with the passage's description of these families as heads of their fathers' houses who lived in Jerusalem (1 Chr 8:28). Nothing else is recorded about him. His name means "my God is the Lord" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). It is the same Hebrew name as Elijah, and several other men in the Bible bear it, so he should not be confused with Elijah the prophet or with others of that name.

Eliah was one of the sons of Elam, a family of Israelite laymen, named in the list of men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra (Ezra 10:26). The surrounding chapter describes how these men agreed to put away their foreign wives after the return from Babylon. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "my God is Jehovah," and it is a form of the name Elijah. Several other people in the Bible bear the same name, and nothing further is recorded about this man beyond his place in the list.

Eliahba was one of David's mighty men, the elite group of warriors known as "the thirty." He appears in both lists of these men, in 2 Sam 23:32 and 1 Chr 11:33, and each time he is called "the Shaalbonite." That title probably means he came from Shaalbim (also spelled Shaalabbin), a town in the territory originally given to Dan. Nothing else is recorded about his life or deeds. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of his name as "God hides," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "my God the Father."

Eliakim son of Hilkiah was the official "over the household", the palace administrator, under King Hezekiah of Judah. When the Assyrian army threatened Jerusalem, he led the delegation, with Shebna the scribe and Joah the recorder, that met the Assyrian officer Rabshakeh outside the city wall. He asked Rabshakeh to speak in Aramaic ("the Syrian language") rather than Hebrew, so that the people on the wall would not understand. The officials then went to Hezekiah with their clothes torn and reported his words. Hezekiah sent Eliakim, dressed in sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah. The same events appear in both 2 Kings and Isaiah. In an oracle, Isaiah calls him "my servant Eliakim" (Isa 22:20). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia read that oracle as Eliakim replacing Shebna as palace administrator. Several other people in the Bible share his name.

Eliakim was a priest in Nehemiah's time who took part in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem. He is named first in a group of seven priests who played trumpets in one of the two thanksgiving processions that went around the wall (Neh 12:41). From the surrounding passage, this group probably walked in the company that went with Nehemiah. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the event to about 446 BC. The name means "God raises up" or "God sets up." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including the palace official under King Hezekiah and the son of Josiah who became King Jehoiakim. Nothing more is recorded about this priest.

Eliakim was a descendant of Zerubbabel who appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, in the line of the tribe of Judah. He was the son of Abiud and the father of Azor (Matt 1:13), which makes him a grandson of Zerubbabel, the leader of the return from exile in Babylon. He lived after the exile, but nothing else is recorded about him. Because he and his immediate descendants do not appear in the Old Testament, Matthew's list is the only source for him. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies his father Abiud with a son of Zerubbabel named in other genealogies and calls Eliakim the eldest son, but this rests on harmonizing different lists. The name, meaning "God raises up" or "God sets up," was shared by several people in the Bible, including a palace official under King Hezekiah and a king of Judah later renamed Jehoiakim. This Eliakim is a different person from both.

Eliakim is an ancestor of Jesus named in the genealogy in Luke's Gospel. Luke 3:30 lists him as the father of Jonan, and the list continues in Luke 3:31 by naming his father as Melea. He belongs to the stretch of the genealogy between David and the exile, which runs through David's son Nathan rather than through Solomon. For that reason he is counted among the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he appears nowhere else in the Bible. Several other men in the Bible share his name, including a palace official under King Hezekiah and the king of Judah later renamed Jehoiakim. This Eliakim should not be confused with them. The name means "God sets up" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, or "raised up by God" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary.

Eliam was the father of Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite, who later became King David's wife. He is named when David asks who the woman is and is told she is "the daughter of Eliam" (2 Sam 11:3). In 1 Chr 3:5 he is called Ammiel, and his daughter Bathshua, the mother of Shimea, Shobab, Nathan and Solomon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the two forms as the same two parts of the name in reverse order. Through Solomon, Eliam stands in the line that Matthew traces to Jesus, where Bathsheba appears as "her that had been the wife of Urias" (Matt 1:6). Several men in the Bible share the name. Some readers identify him with Eliam son of Ahithophel, one of David's mighty men (2 Sam 23:34), but neither of the verses here makes that connection.

Eliam was the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite and one of David's elite warriors known as "the thirty," listed in 2 Sam 23:34. His father, Ahithophel, is probably the same Gilonite who served as David's counselor and later joined Absalom's revolt (2 Sam 15:12). "Gilonite" points to the town of Giloh in the hill country of Judah (Josh 15:51). Apart from his place in this roll of mighty men, nothing else is recorded about him. The name is shared by more than one person. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he may be the same Eliam named as the father of Bathsheba in 2 Sam 11:3, which would make Ahithophel Bathsheba's grandfather. This entry treats the warrior separately. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the people of God."

Eliasaph was the leader of the tribe of Gad during Israel's wilderness journey after the Exodus. He was one of the tribal heads named to help Moses take the census at Sinai (Num 1:14), and he served as captain of Gad's camp (Num 2:14). On the sixth day of the dedication of the altar he brought Gad's offering (Num 7:42, 47), and he led Gad's division when the camp set out (Num 10:20). His father is usually called Deuel, but Num 2:14 reads Reuel. Reuel is also the name of Moses' father-in-law, who is elsewhere called Jethro (Exod 2:18). This entry follows that link, which would make Hobab and Zipporah his siblings, although the passages here present him as a leader of Gad. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "God has added." Several other people in the Bible share the name.

Eliasaph son of Lael was a Levite named as chief of the Gershonites, the clan descended from Levi's son Gershon, during Israel's time in the wilderness (Num 3:24). The passage comes from the census and organization of the Levites at Sinai. There the Gershonites were assigned to camp behind the tabernacle on its west side and to care for its curtains, coverings and hangings. As head of the clan, Eliasaph probably oversaw that work. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as "God has added." Several men in the Bible bear the name Eliasaph. He should be kept distinct from Eliasaph son of Deuel (or Reuel), the leader of the tribe of Gad in the same book. Nothing further is recorded about him.

Eliashib was a man of the tribe of Judah, one of the seven sons of Elioenai, named in the genealogy of David's royal line in 1 Chr 3:24. His brothers were Hodaiah, Pelaiah, Akkub, Johanan, Dalaiah and Anani. The genealogy traces this family through King Jeconiah, and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Eliashib as one of the latest descendants of the royal family of Judah. That would place him well after the return from exile in Babylon, by inference from his position near the end of the list. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, usually explained as "God restores," belongs to several other men in the Bible, including a high priest in Nehemiah's time. This Eliashib should be kept distinct from them.

Eliashib was a priest in the time of King David. He gave his name to the eleventh of the twenty-four divisions, or courses, into which the priests were organized to take turns serving at the sanctuary (1 Chr 24:12). By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was the head of a priestly family descended from Aaron, through either Eleazar or Ithamar, and his division's turn of service was set by lot. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary explains as meaning "God restores," belongs to several men in the Bible. Among them are a high priest in Nehemiah's day and men of the return from exile, and this priest should not be confused with them.

Eliashib was the father of Johanan (also spelled Jehohanan), whose chamber at the temple in Jerusalem Ezra entered after rising from before the house of God. There Ezra fasted from bread and water, mourning the unfaithfulness of the returned exiles who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:6). The name means "God restores," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Several men in the Bible share this name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests this Eliashib is probably the same person as the high priest Eliashib of Nehemiah's time, and Neh 12:23 does mention a Johanan son of Eliashib among the Levite heads of families. STEPBible's proper names index likewise describes him as a priest in Ezra's day. The verse itself gives no further detail about him, so the identification remains an inference. In the apocryphal book 1 Esdras he is called Eliasib.

Eliashib was one of the singers among the Levites in the time of Ezra. He is named in Ezra 10:24 in the list of men who had married foreign wives. From the surrounding chapter, this list records those who agreed to send away their foreign wives during Ezra's reforms after the return from exile. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a singer who had married a foreign wife, and gives the meaning of his name as "whom God restores." Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including the high priest Eliashib of Nehemiah's day and other men named in the same list in Ezra 10. This entry concerns only the singer.

Eliashib was one of the sons, or descendants, of Zattu listed in Ezra 10:27. He appears among the Israelite men who had married foreign wives and who agreed, during Ezra's reforms after the return from exile, to send those wives away. The surrounding chapter describes this pledge, and the list he belongs to names those who took part. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary explains as "whom God restores," was borne by several men of this period, including a high priest in Nehemiah's time and others in the same list in Ezra 10. This Eliashib should not be confused with them.

Eliashib was one of several men of this name in the Bible. He appears only in the list of Israelites who had married foreign women during Ezra's reforms after the return from exile. By inference from the surrounding passage, he is named among the 'sons of Bani' (Ezra 10:34), meaning he belonged to the family or clan of Bani. Ezra 10:44 says the men on this list had taken foreign wives, and the wider chapter describes their agreement to send them away. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 458 BC, a date inferred from context. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is usually taken to mean 'God restores' (Smith's Bible Dictionary). Because the name was common, he should not be confused with Eliashib the high priest or the other Eliashibs in the lists of Ezra and Nehemiah.

Eliashib was the high priest in Jerusalem when the city walls were rebuilt under Nehemiah, about 445 BC by inference from context (Smith's Bible Dictionary gives 446 BC). He and his fellow priests rebuilt the Sheep Gate, set up its doors, and consecrated the wall as far as the towers of Meah and Hananel (Neh 3:1). His house stood along the wall, and other builders repaired the sections reaching to its door and to its far end (Neh 3:20–21). Connected passages add more. Neh 12:10 names him as the son of Joiakim and grandson of Jeshua. Neh 13:4–7 says a priest named Eliashib gave Tobiah a room in the temple, and Neh 13:28 says a grandson of Eliashib the high priest married a daughter of Sanballat. The name is shared by several people in the Bible.

Eliashib was a high priest of the Jews after the return from exile, in the time of Nehemiah. He was the son of Joiakim and grandson of Jeshua, and the father of Joiada (Neh 12:10). His name marks a generation in the records of Levite and priestly family heads kept until the reign of Darius the Persian (Neh 12:22). Johanan is called his son in Neh 12:23, probably meaning his grandson or descendant, since Joiada stands between them in the line. One of Joiada's sons married a daughter of Sanballat the Horonite, and Nehemiah drove him away (Neh 13:28). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him with the Eliashib who rebuilt part of Jerusalem's wall near the Sheep Gate (Neh 3:1) and who gave Tobiah the Ammonite a room in the temple (Neh 13:4, 7). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the God of conversion."

Eliashib was a priest in Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time who had charge of the storerooms of the temple and was closely connected with Tobiah, an Ammonite official who had opposed Nehemiah's work (Neh 2:10). According to the surrounding account, while Nehemiah was away at the Persian court, Eliashib cleared a large room once used for storing grain offerings, incense and tithes and gave it to Tobiah. When Nehemiah returned to Jerusalem and learned of it, he threw Tobiah's belongings out and had the rooms purified (Neh 13:5–9). Because the name is shared by several people, his identity is uncertain. Many readers take him to be the high priest Eliashib of Neh 3:1 and 13:28, whose grandson married into Sanballat's family, while others treat him as a separate priest. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the God of conversion."

Eliathah was a Levite, one of the fourteen sons of Heman, and a musician appointed for the temple service in the time of King David (1 Chr 25:4). When the musicians were divided by lot into twenty-four courses, the twentieth lot fell to Eliathah, and his course numbered twelve, made up of him, his sons and his relatives (1 Chr 25:27). Heman was one of the three chief musicians under David, along with Asaph and Jeduthun, according to the surrounding passage in 1 Chronicles 25. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary explain the name as meaning "to whom God will come" or "to whom God comes." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "God has come," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "thou art my God." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Elidad, son of Chislon, was the leader from the tribe of Benjamin named in Num 34:21 among the men chosen to divide the land of Canaan among the tribes. The surrounding passage (Num 34:16–29) presents these leaders as appointed, one from each tribe, to work with Eleazar the priest and Joshua in assigning the territory west of the Jordan. His name is usually taken to mean "God has loved" or "beloved of God." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he may be the same person as Eldad, though the text does not say so. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his appointment to about 1452 BC, an estimate based on context. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Eliel was one of the heads of families in the half-tribe of Manasseh that settled east of the Jordan. In 1 Chr 5:24 he is listed with Epher, Ishi, Azriel, Jeremiah, Hodaviah and Jahdiel, and they are described as mighty men of valour, famous men and heads of their fathers' houses. The surrounding passage places this group in the land from Bashan to Mount Hermon and goes on to tell of their later deportation by the Assyrians. Easton's and Smith's Bible dictionaries identify him only as a chief of eastern Manasseh. The STEPBible name index places him in the time of King David, though the verse gives no date. Smith's dictionary takes the name to mean "to whom God is strength." Several other men in the Bible are also named Eliel, and nothing more is known about this one.

Eliel was a Benjamite listed among the sons of Shimhi in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin in 1 Chr 8:20. His brothers were Jakim, Zichri, Zabdi, Elienai, Zilthai, Adaiah, Beraiah and Shimrath. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a chief man in the tribe of Benjamin, and the surrounding list names the sons of Shimhi as heads of families who lived in Jerusalem. Shimhi is probably the same man called Shema elsewhere in the chapter, by inference from context, though this is uncertain. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's gives the name's meaning as "to whom God is strength." Several other men in the Bible are also called Eliel, and this one should not be confused with them.

Eliel was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8 as one of the sons of Shashak. He appears in a list with his brothers Ishpan and Heber (1 Chr 8:22), alongside Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Hananiah, Elam, Antothijah, Iphedeiah and Penuel. The passage groups these men among the heads of Benjamite families who lived in Jerusalem, so Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Benjamite chief. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, usually explained as "God is my God" or "God is strength," was borne by several other men in the Bible, and this Eliel should not be confused with them.

Eliel the Mahavite was one of David's mighty men, the warriors listed in 1 Chr 11 as the heroes of David's guard. He is named only once, in 1 Chr 11:46, where he appears alongside Jeribai and Joshaviah, the sons of Elnaam, and Ithmah the Moabite. His title "the Mahavite" probably refers to his hometown or clan, but no place called Mahavah or Mahav is mentioned elsewhere, so its meaning is uncertain. Nothing more is recorded about his deeds or family. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "to whom God is strength," and Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "God, my God." Several other men in the Bible share the name Eliel, including another of David's warriors named in 1 Chr 11:47, and this entry concerns only the Mahavite.

Eliel was one of the warriors named in the list of David's mighty men near the end of 1 Chr 11. He appears in 1 Chr 11:47 alongside Obed and Jasiel the Mesobaite, but nothing else is said about him: no father, home town or deeds are given. The name is shared by several people in the Bible. Another Eliel, called the Mahavite, appears in the verse just before, so this list seems to contain two different men of the same name. STEPBible's proper-names index describes this Eliel as coming from Meholah. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean 'to whom God is strength,' while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives 'God, my God.'

Eliel was one of the warriors from the tribe of Gad who joined David before he became king. He is listed seventh among eleven Gadite leaders in 1 Chr 12:11. By inference from the surrounding passage, these men left their tribe east of the Jordan and came to David's stronghold in the wilderness. They are described as skilled with shield and spear and as swift as gazelles, and they crossed the Jordan when it was in flood. Reference works place the episode differently. Smith's Bible Dictionary sets it while David was hiding from Saul in the wilderness of Judah, while Easton's Bible Dictionary connects it with David's stay at Ziklag. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Eliel, which Smith's Bible Dictionary explains as "to whom God is strength."

Eliel was a Levite leader in David's time, chief of the descendants of Hebron, and he led eighty of his kinsmen (1 Chr 15:9). Hebron here is a family name, not the town. Hebron was a son of Kohath, so Eliel belonged to the Kohathite branch of the Levites, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. He was one of the Levite heads David summoned, along with the priests Zadok and Abiathar, when the ark of the covenant was moved from the house of Obed-edom to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:11). From the surrounding chapter, David called these leaders so they could consecrate themselves and carry the ark. His name is usually taken to mean "God is God" or "my God is God."
