Several other men in the Bible are also named Eliel, including some of David's mighty men, and this one should not be confused with them.

Eliel was one of ten overseers appointed in the reign of King Hezekiah to help manage the offerings, tithes and dedicated gifts brought to the house of God. He served under Cononiah and his brother Shimei, who had chief charge of these stores, by the command of Hezekiah and of Azariah, the ruler of the temple (2 Chr 31:13). The surrounding passage places this work in the storerooms of the temple. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper-names index describe him as a Levite, which fits the context, and Smith dates his service to about 726 BC. He is known only from this verse. The name, meaning roughly "my God is God" or "God is strength," is shared by several other men in the Old Testament, including warriors of David, and this Eliel should be kept distinct from them.

Elienai was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. He is listed as one of the nine sons of Shimhi, along with Jakim, Zichri, Zabdi, Zilthai, Eliel, Adaiah, Beraiah and Shimrath (1 Chr 8:19–21). Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a chief man in the tribe, probably by inference from the later statement in the same chapter that the men listed were heads of families who lived in Jerusalem. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "my eyes are toward God," and Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "the God of my eyes." His father Shimhi is probably the same person as the Shema of 1 Chr 8:13, though the identification is uncertain.

Eliezer (Abraham's Steward) was the man in charge of Abram's household, described as "Eliezer of Damascus" (Gen 15:2). Abram named him when he complained to God that he had no children. The following verse shows that, without a son, this servant would inherit Abram's estate, and the TIPNR proper-names index describes him as Abraham's potential heir before Ishmael and Isaac were born. The Revised Version renders "steward" as "possessor" of the house. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he was probably the unnamed senior servant whom Abraham later sent to his family's homeland in Mesopotamia to find a wife for Isaac (Gen 24), though that chapter does not give the servant's name. Hitchcock's Bible Names takes the name to mean "help of my God." No other passage clearly mentions him by name.

Eliezer was the second son of Moses and his wife Zipporah, and the younger brother of Gershom. He was probably born in Midian, where Moses lived after fleeing Egypt. His name means "God is help" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Moses explained it by saying that the God of his father had been his help and had saved him from Pharaoh's sword (Exod 18:4). According to Easton's Bible Dictionary, Eliezer stayed with his mother and brother at the home of Jethro, Zipporah's father, while Moses returned to Egypt, and they rejoined Moses after the exodus. As a descendant of Moses he belonged to the tribe of Levi. He had only one son, Rehabiah, whose descendants became very numerous (1 Chr 23:15–17). A later line of his descendants served among the Levites who looked after the temple treasuries (1 Chr 26:25). Several other people in the Bible share the name Eliezer.

Eliezer was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the nine sons of Becher named in a genealogy in 1 Chr 7:8. His brothers were Zemira, Joash, Elioenai, Omri, Jerimoth, Abiah, Anathoth and Alameth. Becher was a son of Benjamin (1 Chr 7:6), which, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes, makes Eliezer a grandson of Benjamin. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "God is help." Several other people in the Bible share the name, including Abraham's servant and a son of Moses, and they should not be confused with this Eliezer.

Eliezer was one of seven priests who blew trumpets before the ark of God in the time of King David (1 Chr 15:24). The surrounding chapter describes the ark being brought up from the house of Obed-edom to Jerusalem, and he took part in that procession with Shebaniah, Jehoshaphat, Nethaneel, Amasai, Zechariah and Benaiah. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name means "God is help" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Several other men in the Bible share the name Eliezer, including Abraham's servant and a son of Moses, and this priest should not be confused with them.

Eliezer, son of Zichri, was the ruler of the tribe of Reuben during King David's reign. He appears in a list of the chief officers over the tribes of Israel (1 Chr 27:16), a list in which Shephatiah son of Maachah led the neighbouring Simeonites. The context of 1 Chronicles 27, which records David's administrative organization, places him in David's time, as Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also note. Nothing further is recorded about him. The name, meaning "God is help" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, is shared by several other men in the Bible, and this Eliezer should not be confused with them.

Eliezer, son of Dodavah and from Mareshah, was a prophet in the reign of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. He is known only from 2 Chr 20:37. There he condemns Jehoshaphat for joining with Ahaziah, king of Israel, to build ships meant to sail to Tarshish. He announces that the LORD has broken Jehoshaphat's works, and the ships are then wrecked before they can make the voyage. Mareshah was a town in the lowlands of Judah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "help, or court, of my God." Several other men in the Bible share the name Eliezer, and Easton's Bible Dictionary notes others in Ezra and in Luke's genealogy. This prophet should not be confused with them.

Eliezer was one of the leading men Ezra sent for while the returning exiles were camped by the river Ahava on their way from Babylon to Jerusalem (Ezra 8:16). He is named first in a list of men described as "chief men." The surrounding passage explains why Ezra sent for them: on reviewing the group he found no Levites among it, and he sent these leaders to Iddo at Casiphia to bring ministers for the temple. Nothing else is recorded about this Eliezer. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as meaning "help of my God," belongs to several people in the Bible. This one should probably be kept distinct from the Eliezers in Ezra 10 who had married foreign wives, though that cannot be settled from the text.

Eliezer was a priest in the time of Ezra, one of several men of this name in the Bible. He belonged to the family of Jeshua son of Jozadak, the high priest who led the priests home from exile, and he is listed among Jeshua's descendants or relatives who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:18). The next verse, Ezra 10:19, says that these men pledged to send their wives away and offered a ram as a guilt offering. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with the other men named Eliezer, such as the Levite and the layman listed later in the same chapter. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "help, or court, of my God."

Eliezer was a Levite in the time of Ezra, named in a list of Levites who had married foreign women (Ezra 10:23). Judging from the surrounding chapter, this list belongs to Ezra's reform among the Jews who had returned from exile in Babylon. In that reform, men who had taken wives from the surrounding peoples agreed to send them away. Nothing else is recorded about this Eliezer, and he should not be confused with the several other men of the same name in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "help, or court, of my God."

Eliezer (Son of Harim) was an Israelite of the family of Harim, named in Ezra 10:31 alongside Ishijah, Malchiah, Shemaiah, Shimeon and others. The verse belongs to the list of men who had married foreign wives, drawn up during Ezra's reforms after the return from exile in Babylon. By inference from the surrounding chapter (Ezra 10:3, 19, 44), he was among those who agreed to send these wives away. "Son of Harim" probably means that he belonged to the Harim clan rather than that Harim was his own father. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with the several other men named Eliezer in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "help, or court, of my God."

Eliezer was an ancestor of Jesus named only in the genealogy in Luke's Gospel, which traces Jesus' line back through David to Adam. Luke 3:29 lists him as the son of Jorim and the father of Jose. His place in the list falls between David and the Babylonian exile, so he belonged to the tribe of Judah and lived during the period of the kings, by inference from his position in the genealogy. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he is distinct from the several other men in the Bible who share his name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "God is help."

Elihoenai was a son of Zerahiah and a member of the family of Pahath-moab. He led 200 men of that family who returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra (Ezra 8:4). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "my eyes are toward Jehovah" and dates the return to about 459 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists him under the spelling Eliehoenai. He is mentioned only in this one verse, so nothing more is known of him.

Elihoreph was one of King Solomon's scribes, or royal secretaries. He is named with his brother Ahiah among Solomon's chief officials, and both are called the sons of Shisha (1 Kgs 4:3). Shisha is probably the same man as Shavsha, who served as scribe under David (1 Chr 18:16) and is called Seraiah in 2 Sam 8:17 and Sheva in 2 Sam 20:25. This entry follows that identification. If it is correct, the brothers took over their father's office in the royal court. Nothing else is recorded about Elihoreph. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "God is his reward," the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia tentatively suggests "God of autumn," and Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "god of winter, or of youth."

Elihu was an ancestor of the prophet Samuel, the father of Jeroham and grandfather of Elkanah, Samuel's father. In 1 Sam 1:1 his father is called Tohu. The genealogies of the Levites in 1 Chronicles list the same man as Eliab, son of Nahath (1 Chr 6:27), and as Eliel, son of Toah (1 Chr 6:34). Nahath, Tohu and Toah are probably variant forms of one name. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat Elihu, Eliab and Eliel as the same person. 1 Samuel describes the family as living in Ramathaim-zophim in the hill country of Ephraim and calls Elkanah an Ephrathite. The Chronicles genealogy places the line among the Kohathite Levites, which Smith's Bible Dictionary follows, and this entry counts Elihu as belonging to the tribe of Levi. Elihu is known only from these family lists.

Elihu was one of the captains of thousands from the tribe of Manasseh who went over to David as he traveled to Ziklag (1 Chr 12:20). He is named in a list of seven Manassite commanders who joined David's growing force. The surrounding chapter places this after David left the Philistine army, and Smith's Bible Dictionary sets it on the eve of the battle of Gilboa, where Saul died. The name is usually explained as "He is my God" or "my God is He". Several other men in the Bible are also called Elihu, including the young speaker in the book of Job. This Manassite is mentioned only in this one verse, and nothing more is known about him.

Elihu was a Levite in the time of David, one of the sons of Shemaiah listed in 1 Chr 26:7 alongside Othni, Rephael, Obed, Elzabad and Semachiah. The verse calls Elihu and Semachiah among the "strong men" of the family. The surrounding chapter places Shemaiah's family within the household of Obed-edom, which was assigned to guard the gates of the sanctuary. Easton's Bible Dictionary accordingly describes Elihu as one of the temple porters appointed under David, and Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him as a Korahite Levite. Nothing further is recorded about him. His name probably means "He is my God." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including Job's young companion, and they should not be confused with this gatekeeper.

Elihu was a man of the tribe of Judah, described as "one of the brethren of David" and named as the leader of Judah in the list of tribal chiefs under King David (1 Chr 27:18). This entry treats him as a son of Jesse and a brother of David, Eliab, Abinadab, Shammah, Nethaneel, Raddai and Ozem. His exact identity is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the name as another form of Eliab, David's eldest brother (1 Sam 16:6). Others note that 1 Sam 16:10 implies Jesse had eight sons while 1 Chr 2:13–15 names only seven, so Elihu may be the unnamed one. Because "brethren" can also mean a wider kinsman, he may simply have been a relative of David. His name means "he is my God." Several other people in the Bible share the name.

Elihu, son of Barachel the Buzite and of the family of Ram, is the young man who speaks near the end of the Book of Job. He had waited in silence while Job and his three friends argued, because they were older than he (Job 32:4, 32:6). When the friends could find no answer for Job, he became angry with Job for justifying himself rather than God, and angry with the friends as well (Job 32:2, 32:5). He then gave a series of speeches, introduced again at Job 34:1, 35:1 and 36:1, which run through chapter 37. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links the Buzites with Buz, the brother of Uz named in Gen 22:21, and counts four speeches in all. His name is usually explained as "He is my God." Several other men in the Bible share the name Elihu.

Elijah, called Elias in the New Testament, was a prophet from Tishbe in Gilead who confronted King Ahab of Israel, about 910 BC by inference from context. He announced a drought, and a widow at Zarephath fed him from meal and oil that never ran out. He also restored her son to life. On Mount Carmel he challenged the people to choose between the LORD and Baal, and his prayer was answered. The prophets of Baal were killed, and Jezebel's anger drove him to a cave at Horeb. Elisha became his attendant and successor. Elijah later condemned King Ahaziah, called down fire on soldiers sent for him, and parted the Jordan with his mantle before being taken into heaven (2 Kgs 2:11). Malachi foretold his return, which Jesus linked to John the Baptist, and he appeared with Moses at the Transfiguration. Several other men share the name.

Elijah was a man of the family of Harim, one of the men named in the list of those who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra (Ezra 10:21). The surrounding passage places the sons of Harim among the priests, so this Elijah was probably of priestly descent, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a man of priestly rank. By inference from the wider chapter, he was among those who agreed to put away their foreign wives during Ezra's reforms after the return from Babylon. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with the prophet Elijah or with others who share the name, which means "Yah is God" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia.

The Elijah Translated event was the prophet Elijah's departure from the earth, taken up into heaven by a whirlwind without dying, as told in 2 Kgs 2:1–14. Elijah set out from Gilgal with Elisha and traveled to Bethel, Jericho and the Jordan. At each stop he urged Elisha to stay behind, but Elisha refused to leave him. Groups of the sons of the prophets at Bethel and Jericho knew that the LORD would take Elijah away that day, and fifty of them watched from a distance at the Jordan. Elijah struck the river with his rolled-up mantle, and the two crossed on dry ground. Elisha asked for a double portion of Elijah's spirit. A chariot and horses of fire then separated them, and Elijah went up by a whirlwind. Elisha took up the fallen mantle and parted the Jordan himself. This entry dates the event to about 897 BC, by inference from context.

Elika was a Harodite listed among David's mighty men, the group of elite warriors known as "the thirty" (2 Sam 23:25). He is named right after Shammah the Harodite, who came from the same place, probably Harod, the spring or town near which Gideon camped. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that his name does not appear in the parallel list of David's warriors in 1 Chronicles 11. The meaning of his name is uncertain: Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "God is his rejector," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "pelican of God."

Elim was an oasis where the Israelites camped during their journey from Egypt to Mount Sinai. It came after Marah, the camp of bitter water, and stood out for its twelve springs and seventy palm trees (Exod 15:27; Num 33:9). From Elim the people moved on and camped by the Red Sea, then entered the wilderness of Sin, which lay between Elim and Sinai. They reached Sin on the fifteenth day of the second month after leaving Egypt (Exod 16:1; Num 33:10). The name is usually linked to large trees such as terebinths or palms. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify Elim with Wadi Gharandel, on the western side of the Sinai Peninsula about halfway down the Gulf of Suez, where palms and good water are still found. The location shown here follows that traditional identification.

Elimelech was a man of Bethlehem in Judah, described as an Ephrathite, and the husband of Naomi and father of Mahlon and Chilion. His name means "my God is king." During a famine in the days of the judges (Ruth 1:1, the verse just before he is named), he moved his family to the country of Moab, where he died, leaving Naomi with their two sons (Ruth 1:2–3). Both sons later died in Moab as well. Boaz, the wealthy man in whose field Ruth gleaned, belonged to Elimelech's family (Ruth 2:1, 3). After Naomi returned to Bethlehem, Elimelech's parcel of land was put up for redemption, and Boaz bought all that had belonged to Elimelech and his sons in front of the town elders (Ruth 4:3, 9). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries place him in the Hezronite family of the tribe of Judah.

Elioenai was a man of the tribe of Judah, a descendant of David through the royal line of Jeconiah, named in the post-exile genealogy of 1 Chronicles 3. He was the first-listed of the three sons of Neariah, alongside Hezekiah and Azrikam (1 Chr 3:23). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes this order to mean he was the eldest and traces Neariah back to Shemaiah. Elioenai had seven sons: Hodaiah, Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub, Johanan, Dalaiah and Anani (1 Chr 3:24). Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share his name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary renders as "my eyes are toward the Lord."

Elioenai was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named in a list of Simeonite clan leaders in 1 Chr 4:36. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him the head of a Simeonite family. The surrounding passage explains that the men in this list were princes in their families whose households grew greatly (1 Chr 4:38). It also says that in the days of King Hezekiah they moved toward Gedor to find pasture for their flocks and drove out the people living there (1 Chr 4:39–41). On that basis the STEPBible Proper Names index places him in Hezekiah's reign. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Elioenai should not be confused with them. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "my eyes are toward the Lord."

Elioenai was a member of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the nine sons of Becher listed in the genealogy at 1 Chr 7:8. His brothers were Zemira, Joash, Eliezer, Omri, Jerimoth, Abiah, Anathoth and Alameth. Becher was himself a son of Benjamin, which makes Elioenai a grandson of Benjamin. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as the head of one of the families descended from Becher, and it gives the meaning of his name as "my eyes are toward the Lord." Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, and this Benjamite should not be confused with them.

Elioenai was a Levite, the seventh son of Meshelemiah, named in the list of temple gatekeepers in 1 Chr 26:3. His brothers were Zechariah, Jediael, Zebadiah, Jathniel, Elam and Jehohanan. From the surrounding chapter, Meshelemiah's family belonged to the Korahite branch of the Levites. They were among the divisions of doorkeepers organized for the house of the Lord, which by context dates to the later years of King David's reign. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Korahite Levite and one of these doorkeepers. Smith's gives the meaning of his name as "my eyes are toward the Lord." Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Elioenai, and this entry concerns only the son of Meshelemiah.

Elioenai was a priest of the family of Pashur, listed in Ezra 10:22 among the men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra, after the return from exile. The verse itself names him only as one of the sons of Pashur, alongside Maaseiah, Ishmael, Nethaneel, Jozabad and Elasah. His being a priest is inferred from the surrounding passage, which groups these names under the priests who had taken foreign wives and who agreed to send them away in response to Ezra's reforms. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "my eyes are toward the Lord" and suggests he may be the same Elioenai who appears among the priests at the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt wall (Neh 12:41). Several other men in the Bible share this name, so the identification is uncertain.

Elioenai was an Israelite of the family of Zattu, named in Ezra 10:27 in the list of men who had married foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon. The surrounding chapter records that these men agreed to send their foreign wives away at Ezra's call. This would have been around 458 BC, the date Smith's Bible Dictionary gives, inferred from the context of Ezra's reforms. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary explains as "my eyes are toward the Lord," is borne by several other men in the Old Testament, including a priest of the family of Pashhur in the same list and descendants in the genealogies of Chronicles. The man named here should not be confused with them.

Elioenai was a priest who blew a trumpet at the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. In Neh 12:41 he is named among seven priests with trumpets, alongside Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, Michaiah, Zechariah and Hananiah. By inference from the surrounding passage, this group marched in one of the two companies that processed along the wall before gathering at the temple. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, and it is uncertain whether this priest is the same as any of them, such as the priest of the family of Pashhur who had married a foreign wife (Ezra 10:22). This entry treats him as a separate person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "toward him are mine eyes."

Eliphal, son of Ur, was one of David's mighty men, the elite warriors listed in 1 Chr 11:35. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name is usually taken to mean "God has judged" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), though Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a miracle of God." The parallel list of David's warriors in 2 Samuel 23 has Eliphelet the son of Ahasbai, the son of the Maachathite, at the corresponding place. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, following a footnote in the Revised Version, treat the two as the same man, with the names differing between the two lists. This entry presents him under the Chronicles form of the name.

Eliphalet, also spelled Eliphelet, was a son of King David born in Jerusalem after David made it his capital. His name means "God is deliverance" or "God of deliverance" (Easton's Bible Dictionary; Hitchcock's Bible Names). He appears last in each list of David's Jerusalem-born sons, following Elishama and Eliada (called Beeliada in 1 Chr 14:7). In 1 Chr 3:8 he closes a group counted as nine, in addition to the four sons of Bathsheba. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him apparently the last of David's sons. The Chronicles lists also contain an earlier son with a similar name, Eliphelet or Elpalet. This has led some to count two separate sons, while others treat the names as a duplication. This entry treats Elpalet as a separate brother. Nothing is recorded about Eliphalet beyond his name and place in these lists.

Eliphaz was the firstborn son of Esau by his wife Adah (Gen 36:4, 10, 15). His sons Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam and Kenaz became clan chiefs ("dukes") in Edom. His concubine Timna bore him Amalek, who is also counted among the chiefs descended from him (Gen 36:11–12, 15–16). Gen 36:16 names a chief Korah in his line as well. This Korah is distinct from Esau's son Korah by Oholibamah (Gen 36:14), which is why the name appears here both as a son and as a half-brother. The list in 1 Chr 1:36 counts Timna among his sons, probably as a clan name. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him the father of several Edomite tribes. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "God is his strength." Several people share the name. Job's friend Eliphaz the Temanite is a different man, though his title probably links him to the clan of Teman.

Eliphaz the Temanite was one of Job's three friends, with Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite. When they heard of Job's disasters, they arranged to come together to mourn with him and comfort him (Job 2:11). Eliphaz opens each of the three rounds of speeches (Job 4:1; 15:1; 22:1), and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats him as the leading spokesman of the friends. His title links him to Teman, a place in Edom associated elsewhere with wisdom (Jer 49:7). At the end of the book the LORD addresses Eliphaz directly, saying his anger burns against him and his two friends because they had not spoken rightly of him as Job had. The three then did as the LORD commanded, and the LORD accepted Job's prayer for them (Job 42:7, 9). Several other men in the Bible share the name Eliphaz, including a son of Esau.

Elipheleh was a Levite of the "second degree" listed among the gatekeepers (KJV "porters") in 1 Chr 15:18. He was one of the men David's Levite leaders appointed for the music when the ark of the covenant was brought up to Jerusalem, the city of David. In 1 Chr 15:21 he appears with Mattithiah, Mikneiah, Obededom, Jeiel and Azaziah as one of those who played harps "on the Sheminith," a musical term of uncertain meaning, perhaps referring to an eight-stringed instrument or to a lower pitch. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "God will distinguish him." Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him as a Merarite Levite. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Eliphelet son of Ahasbai was one of David's mighty men, the elite group of warriors listed in 2 Sam 23. He appears only once, in that roster (2 Sam 23:34). The King James wording, "the son of Ahasbai, the son of the Maachathite," is usually read as meaning that Ahasbai was a Maachathite, probably from Maacah or the town of Abel-beth-maacah in the far north. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him with "Eliphal the son of Ur" in the parallel list at 1 Chr 11:35, where the names differ. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "God of deliverance" and counts him among the thirty warriors of David's guard. Several other people in the Bible share the name Eliphelet, including sons of David, and they should not be confused with this warrior.

Eliphelet was a Benjamite, the third son of Eshek, and is named after his older brothers Ulam and Jehush in the genealogy of King Saul's family (1 Chr 8:39). Eshek is called the brother of Azel, so by inference from the surrounding list (1 Chr 8:37–38) he and Azel were sons of Eleasah, making Eliphelet a descendant of Eleasah and, further back, of Saul through Jonathan. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both describe him this way. Smith's gives the meaning of his name as "the God of deliverance" and places him before 536 BC. That date is an estimate, not stated in the text. Nothing is recorded about his life beyond his place in this family line. The name Eliphelet is shared by several other men in the Bible, including a son of David and one of David's warriors, and these should not be confused with him.

Eliphelet was one of the descendants of Adonikam who returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. In Ezra's list of family heads who traveled with him, he is named first among "the last sons of Adonikam," alongside Jeiel and Shemaiah, and the three led a group of sixty men (Ezra 8:13). Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of the leaders of this family group and gives the name's meaning as "the God of deliverance." It dates the return to about 459 BC. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name Eliphelet is shared by several other men in the Bible, including a son of David and one of David's mighty men, and this entry refers only to the returning exile.

Eliphelet was one of the descendants of Hashum listed in Ezra 10:33 among the men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra. The list he appears in, in Ezra 10, records those who agreed to put away these wives after Ezra's reforms among the returned exiles in Jerusalem. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "God of deliverance" and dates the episode to about 458 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Eliphelet is shared by several other men in the Bible, including a son of David, and this Eliphelet should be kept distinct from them.

Elisabeth was the wife of Zacharias, a priest of the division of Abia, and the mother of John the Baptist. She was herself descended from Aaron, and the angel Gabriel calls her a relative ("cousin" in the King James Version) of Mary. She lived in the days of Herod, king of Judea. She and Zacharias were elderly and childless because she was barren, until an angel told Zacharias that she would bear a son named John. After she conceived, she kept herself in seclusion for five months. In her sixth month Mary visited her home. When Elisabeth heard Mary's greeting, the child leaped in her womb and she was filled with the Holy Spirit. In due time she gave birth to a son. By inference from context, these events fall around 6–5 BC. Her name comes from the Hebrew Elisheba, meaning "God is my oath" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia).

Elisha, son of Shaphat of Abel-meholah, was a prophet in the northern kingdom of Israel and the successor of Elijah. God told Elijah to anoint him, and Elijah found him plowing and cast his mantle on him. He served Elijah, who "poured water on the hands of Elijah," and asked for a double portion of his spirit before Elijah was taken up. He then parted the Jordan with Elijah's mantle and was recognized by the sons of the prophets as their leader. His recorded deeds include healing Jericho's waters, multiplying a widow's oil, restoring the Shunammite woman's son to life, curing Naaman the Syrian of leprosy, and foretelling the end of the famine in besieged Samaria. He advised kings, told Hazael he would rule Syria, and was visited by King Joash as he lay dying. Luke 4:27 calls him Eliseus. His name means "God is salvation" (Easton's Bible Dictionary).

Elishah was a son of Javan, listed first among his four sons in the Table of Nations, with Tarshish, Kittim and Dodanim as his brothers (Gen 10:4; 1 Chr 1:7). Javan was a son of Japheth, so Elishah was a great-grandson of Noah. The name, like those of his brothers, probably also stands for a people or region descended from him. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects Javan's line with the peoples of Greece and notes a suggestion that Elishah's descendants settled the Peloponnesus, known in part as Elis. Easton's also links him with "the isles of Elishah" in Ezek 27:7, a coastland that supplied blue and purple cloth to Tyre. Others have connected that name with Cyprus or with Carthage in North Africa. The exact identification remains uncertain.

Elishah was a coastal or island region of the Mediterranean, known in the Bible only as a source of fine dyed cloth. In Ezekiel's lament over Tyre, the city is pictured as a splendid merchant ship whose awning was made of blue and purple cloth from "the isles of Elishah" (Ezek 27:7). The name probably goes back to Elishah, a son of Javan in the table of nations (Gen 10:4), whose descendants were linked with the Greek-speaking peoples. Its exact location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects it with Elis and the Peloponnesus in southern Greece. Many scholars instead identify it with Cyprus, often linked with Alashiya, a name for Cyprus in ancient texts outside the Bible. Others have suggested Sicily or southern Italy. The location shown here follows the Cyprus identification.

Elishama son of Ammihud was the leader of the tribe of Ephraim during Israel's journey through the wilderness. When Moses took the census at Sinai, he was named as the man from Ephraim, one of the sons of Joseph, to help with it (Num 1:10). He was captain of Ephraim's camp, which was stationed on the west side and marched under its own standard (Num 2:18; 10:22). On the seventh day of the altar's dedication he brought Ephraim's offering, which included peace offerings of oxen, rams, goats and lambs (Num 7:48, 53). The Ephraimite genealogy in 1 Chronicles lists him as the son of Ammihud (1 Chr 7:26). The next verse names his son Nun and his grandson Joshua, so Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him as Joshua's grandfather. His name means 'God has heard,' and several other men in the Bible share it.

Elishama was one of the sons of King David born to him in Jerusalem. He appears in the list of David's Jerusalem-born children, named next to last, just before Eliada (called Beeliada in 1 Chr 14:7) and Eliphalet (2 Sam 5:16; 1 Chr 14:7). The same list appears a third time in 1 Chr 3:8. His mother is not named, and nothing else is recorded about his life. The surrounding passages place these births after David moved his capital to Jerusalem and took more wives and concubines there. The name means "God has heard" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other people in the Bible share this name, including another Elishama listed earlier among David's sons in 1 Chr 3:6, who is probably the same person called Elishua in the parallel lists. This entry concerns the son named near the end of the list.

Elishama was the father of Nethaniah and the grandfather of Ishmael, the man who killed Gedaliah, the governor the Babylonians left in charge of Judah, at Mizpah in the seventh month after Jerusalem fell (2 Kgs 25:25; Jer 41:1). Both accounts describe the family as "of the seed royal," meaning it descended from the kings of Judah. Elishama is mentioned only to identify his grandson, and nothing else is recorded about him. The name, meaning "God has heard," belongs to several men in the Bible. Some have suggested he may be the same as Elishama the scribe in Jer 36:12, but the text does not make that link. This entry treats him as the grandfather of Ishmael only. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists him separately among the men of this name.

Elishama, son of Jekamiah, was a descendant of Judah who is named only once, in the genealogy at 1 Chr 2:41. This genealogy traces the line of Jerahmeel, a great-grandson of Judah, through Sheshan's daughter and her Egyptian husband Jarha, down to Shallum, Jekamiah and finally Elishama, the last name in the list. Nothing is recorded about his life beyond his place in this family line. The name means "God has heard," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a prince of Ephraim, a son of David and a royal scribe, but this Elishama appears to be a different person from all of them.

Elishama was a priest in the reign of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. He and another priest, Jehoram, were sent with a group of Levites to accompany the king's officials. By inference from the surrounding passage (2 Chr 17:7–9), the group went through the cities of Judah teaching the people from the book of the law of the Lord. He appears only in 2 Chr 17:8, and nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which means "God has heard" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). This Elishama should not be confused with them. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his time to about 912 BC.

Elishama was the scribe, or royal secretary, at the court of King Jehoiakim of Judah. He is one of several men of this name in the Bible. When Baruch's scroll of Jeremiah's prophecies was read in the temple, Micaiah went down to the scribe's chamber in the king's house, where Elishama sat with the other princes (Jer 36:12). After hearing the scroll read, the officials left it in Elishama's chamber and went to report its contents to the king (Jer 36:20). Jehoiakim then sent Jehudi to fetch it from there, and Jehudi read it aloud before the king and his princes (Jer 36:21). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 605 BC. That date is an estimate inferred from context. The name means "God has heard" or "God hears."

Elishaphat, son of Zichri, was one of the five "captains of hundreds" whom Jehoiada the priest brought into a covenant in the seventh year, at the start of the plot to overthrow Queen Athaliah and crown the young Joash king of Judah (2 Chr 23:1). He appears only in this verse. The surrounding chapter describes the plan these commanders carried out, so he probably took part in guarding Joash and in the events that ended Athaliah's reign, though he is not named again. His name means "God is judge" or "whom God has judged" (Easton's Bible Dictionary; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 877 BC.

Elisheba was the wife of Aaron, Moses' brother, and the mother of his four sons, Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar (Exod 6:23). She was the daughter of Amminadab and the sister of Nahshon, so she came from the tribe of Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies her brother Nahshon as the leader of Judah's camp named in Num 2:3. Because Aaron's sons became the priestly line, the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls her the foundress of the entire Levitical priesthood. Her marriage linked the priestly family of Levi with a leading family of Judah. Her name is usually explained as "God is an oath" or "God swears" (Easton's Bible Dictionary), and Hitchcock's Bible Names treats it as the same name as Elisabeth. She is mentioned by name only once in the Bible.

Elishua was a son of David born in Jerusalem after David made the city his capital. He appears only in the lists of David's sons born there, named next to Ibhar and before Nepheg or Elpalet (2 Sam 5:15; 1 Chr 14:5). His mother is not named, but these lists place him apart from the sons born earlier at Hebron, such as Amnon, Absalom and Adonijah. The parallel list in 1 Chr 3:6 gives the name Elishama at the same point. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary treat the two as the same person, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that Elishama there is probably a copyist's misreading of Elishua. This entry follows that identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "God is my salvation." Nothing more is recorded about his life.

Eliud was a man listed in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, in the part of the line that runs from the Babylonian exile down to Joseph. He was the son of Achim and the father of Eleazar, whose son Matthan was the father of Jacob, the father of Joseph (Matt 1:14–15). That makes Eliud the great-great-grandfather of Joseph, four generations before him, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. As a descendant of David in this line, he belonged to the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he does not appear in Luke's genealogy of Jesus. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "God is my praise." Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "God his praise."

Elizaphan, son of Parnach, was the prince, or chief, of the tribe of Zebulun named in Num 34:25. The surrounding chapter lists the tribal leaders whom the LORD appointed to divide the land of Canaan among the Israelites, with Eleazar the priest and Joshua. Elizaphan was to represent Zebulun in that division, which places him late in the wilderness period, as Israel prepared to enter the land. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name means "God has protected" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several people in the Bible bear this name, including a Levite leader of the Kohathites, and this Zebulunite should not be confused with them.

Elizaphan, also spelled Elzaphan, was a Levite of the clan of Kohath and a son of Uzziel, Aaron's uncle, which made him a cousin of Moses and Aaron. Moses called him and his brother Mishael to carry their dead kinsmen out of the camp from before the sanctuary. From the surrounding chapter these were Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu (Lev 10:1–4). In the wilderness census he was appointed chief of the Kohathite families (Num 3:30). His name later stood for a Levite family. In David's time Shemaiah led 200 'sons of Elizaphan' (1 Chr 15:8), and under Hezekiah, Shimri and Jeiel of that line served among the Levites (2 Chr 29:13). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as 'God has protected.' He is distinct from another man of the same name in the Bible.

Elizur, son of Shedeur, was the leader of the tribe of Reuben during Israel's wilderness journey. He was one of the tribal heads chosen to help Moses and Aaron take the census of Israel (Num 1:5). In the arrangement of the camp he was captain of Reuben, whose standard stood on the south side of the tabernacle (Num 2:10), and when the people set out from Sinai he led Reuben's company on the march (Num 10:18). At the dedication of the altar, as prince of Reuben, he brought his tribe's offering on the fourth day, including peace offerings of oxen, rams, goats and lambs (Num 7:30, 35). His name means "my God is a rock," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia.

Elkanah was a Levite of the family of Korah, the son of Izhar. Exod 6:24 names him with Assir and Abiasaph (also spelled Ebiasaph) as the sons of Korah, from whom the Korahite families descended. This entry follows that account in treating him as Korah's son. In 1 Chr 6:22–23 the same names appear in a line of descent, each called "his son," which could make Elkanah a grandson of Korah through Assir. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both prefer that reading. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that he was one of Korah's sons who, according to Num 26:11, did not die when Korah was destroyed. His name is usually explained as "God has possessed" or "God has created." Several other men in the Bible are also called Elkanah.

Elkanah was the father of the prophet Samuel, a man of Ramathaim-zophim in the hill country of Ephraim whose home was at Ramah (1 Sam 1:1; 2:11). The son of Jeroham, he had two wives: Peninnah, who had sons and daughters, and Hannah, who was at first childless. Each year he went up with his household to offer sacrifice, probably at Shiloh, which 1 Sam 1:3 names as the place of worship. He gave portions to Peninnah and her children, comforted the grieving Hannah, and let her stay home until Samuel was weaned. After Samuel was left to serve under Eli the priest, Eli blessed Elkanah and his wife. 1 Sam 1:1 calls him an Ephrathite, while the genealogies in 1 Chr 6:27, 34 place him among the Levites. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes him as a Levite of the line of Heman the singer. Several other men in the Bible share his name.

Elkanah was a Levite of the clan of Kohath, named in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 6 and counted among the ancestors of the prophet Samuel (STEPBible Proper Names). In one list of Kohath's descendants he follows Shaul and is the father of Amasai and Ahimoth (1 Chr 6:25). In the parallel line traced back from Heman the singer, he is the father of Amasai and the son of Joel (1 Chr 6:36). This entry follows the first list in naming Shaul as his father. The two lists are probably variant forms of the same line, with Shaul and Joel standing in the same position. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including Samuel's father and other Elkanahs in the same chapter, so identifying him in each verse depends on context. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "the zeal of God."

Elkanah was a Levite of the clan of Kohath who appears only in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 6. He was the son of Mahath and the father of Zuph. His name is one of several Elkanahs in the same family line, which makes the lists hard to untangle. In 1 Chr 6:26 his son is called Zophai, probably another form of the name Zuph given in 1 Chr 6:35. The second list traces the ancestry of Heman, a temple singer in David's time (1 Chr 6:33), back through the prophet Samuel to Kohath. By inference from that list and from 1 Sam 1:1, which names Zuph as an ancestor of Samuel's father, also called Elkanah, this Elkanah was a distant forefather of Samuel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as "God has possessed."

Elkanah was a Levite named only in a genealogy in 1 Chr 9:16. He was the father of Asa and the grandfather of Berechiah. The surrounding chapter lists the Levites who lived in Jerusalem, and Berechiah's family is described as living in the villages of the Netophathites, probably near Netophah, south of Jerusalem. Nothing else is recorded about Elkanah himself. His name is shared by several other people in the Bible, including the father of Samuel, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats this Elkanah as a separate Levite. The name is usually explained as "God has possessed" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "God-provided" (Smith's Bible Dictionary).

Elkanah was one of the Korahites who joined David at Ziklag, listed with Jesiah, Azareel, Joezer and Jashobeam in 1 Chr 12:6. By inference from the opening of the chapter, these men came to David while he was still kept away from Saul, and they were counted among the warriors who helped him. The surrounding list marks them as skilled fighters, able to use the bow and sling with either hand. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including the father of Samuel, and this Elkanah should be kept distinct from them. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "God-provided," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "God has possessed."

Elkanah was a Levite who, with Berechiah, served as a doorkeeper for the ark of the covenant (1 Chr 15:23). The surrounding chapter shows that he held this post when David brought the ark up to Jerusalem, as one of the Levites the leaders of the tribe appointed to the music and service for that occasion. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he may be the same man as another Levite Elkanah named in Chronicles, but this is uncertain. Several men in the Bible bear this name, which means "God has possessed" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "the zeal of God" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Nothing further is recorded about him.

Elkanah was a high official of Ahaz king of Judah, described as "next to the king" (2 Chr 28:7). The phrase probably means he held the second-highest position at court, a chief minister or deputy to the king. He was killed by Zichri, a warrior of Ephraim, along with the king's son Maaseiah and Azrikam, the governor of the palace. By inference from the surrounding chapter, this happened during the invasion of Judah by Pekah king of Israel, when Judah suffered heavy losses. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 739 BC. The name, which several other men in the Bible also bear, is usually explained as "God has possessed" or "God has created" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Nothing more is recorded about this Elkanah.

Elkosh was the home of the prophet Nahum, known only from his title "Nahum the Elkoshite" at the opening of his book (Nah 1:1). Calling him an Elkoshite probably means he was born in or came from this place, and Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both describe it as his birthplace. Its location is unknown, and several views exist. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in Galilee but notes that nothing definite is known. Smith's Bible Dictionary links it with the modern village of Alqosh (Alkush), north of Mosul in northern Iraq, near the ruins of Nineveh, the city Nahum's prophecy addresses, and mentions that some prefer a village in Galilee. The STEPBible proper names index places it in Judah. No location is shown for it in this entry.

Ellasar was a kingdom ruled by Arioch, one of four eastern kings led by Chedorlaomer of Elam who fought against five kings of the Jordan plain, including the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah, in the days of Abraham (Gen 14:1, 9). Its alongside Shinar and Elam places it somewhere in Mesopotamia, but the Bible gives no further detail. Its location is debated. Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with Larsa, an old Babylonian city on the east bank of the Euphrates between Ur and Erech, now the ruins of Senkereh in southern Iraq. Another view places it in northern Mesopotamia. The location shown here follows the northern view and marks the region around ancient Urkesh, probably modern Tell Mozan in northeastern Syria.

Elmodam was an ancestor of Jesus named only once, in the genealogy given in Luke's Gospel, which traces the line back through Joseph (Luke 3:28). He is listed as the son of Er and the father of Cosam. In Luke's list he belongs to the stretch of names between David and the Babylonian exile, coming through David's son Nathan rather than through the royal line of kings, so he was presumably of the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him, and the period he lived in can only be inferred from his position in the list. Some modern editions spell the name Elmadam, the form used by STEPBible's Tyndale House proper names list. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "the God of measure, or of the garment," while Smith's Bible Dictionary gives simply "measure."

Elnaam was the father of Jeribai and Joshaviah, two men named among David's mighty warriors in the list at 1 Chr 11:46. He is mentioned only in this verse, and nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation, reads the verse differently and counts Elnaam himself as one of the warriors. This entry follows the Hebrew text, which makes him their father. His name is usually explained as meaning "God is delight" or "God his delight" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "God's fairness."

Elnathan was a man of Jerusalem whose daughter Nehushta was the mother of King Jehoiachin of Judah, which made him the king's maternal grandfather (2 Kgs 24:8). His name means "God has given" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia; Hitchcock's Bible Names). He belongs to the genealogy of Jesus through this grandson, since Jehoiachin (Jechonias) appears in the royal line in Matt 1:11–12. Elnathan himself is not named there. Several men in the Bible share this name. Some interpreters identify him with Elnathan son of Achbor, an official under King Jehoiakim mentioned in Jer 26:22 and 36:12, 25. That would fit, because Jehoiakim was Jehoiachin's father, but the text does not confirm it. This entry treats him only as Nehushta's father.

Elnathan was one of the men Ezra sent for while his returning group camped by the river Ahava. Ezra 8:16 names three men called Elnathan: two among the "chief men" and one among the "men of understanding." The verse does not say which of the three this entry refers to. They may be three different people, or the repetition may reflect copying in the text. By inference from the surrounding passage (Ezra 8:15–17), Ezra had found no Levites in his company, so he sent these leaders to Iddo at Casiphia to bring ministers for the temple. Nothing more is recorded about this Elnathan. He is distinct from other men of the same name in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "God hath given" or "the gift of God."

Elnathan was one of the men Ezra summoned at the river Ahava while gathering exiles to return from Babylon to Jerusalem (Ezra 8:16). The name appears three times in this one verse: two Elnathans are listed among the "chief men," and a third is named with Joiarib as one of the "men of understanding," probably teachers. This entry refers to one of these men, but the text gives no way to tell which, and nothing else is recorded about him. By inference from the surrounding passage, Ezra had found no Levites in his company and sent this group to Iddo at Casiphia to bring back ministers for the temple. The name is shared by other people in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "God hath given" or "the gift of God."

Elnathan was one of the men Ezra sent for while his company of returning exiles camped by the river Ahava. The name appears three times in Ezra 8:16: twice among the "chief men" and once, alongside Joiarib, among the "men of understanding." It is unclear which of these three this entry refers to, and some readers treat the repetition as a possible copying error. From the surrounding passage, Ezra had found no Levites among the travelers, so he sent this group to Iddo at Casiphia to bring back ministers for the temple. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as "God hath given," also belongs to other men, such as Jehoiachin's grandfather and the son of Achbor in Jeremiah's time. They are separate people.

Elnathan son of Achbor was a royal official in Judah during the reign of King Jehoiakim. The king sent him to Egypt with other men to bring back the prophet Uriah, who had prophesied against Jerusalem. According to the following verse (Jer 26:23), Uriah was brought back and executed (Jer 26:22). Later Elnathan was among the princes gathered in the scribe's chamber of the palace when Baruch's reading of Jeremiah's scroll was reported to them (Jer 36:12). When Jehoiakim burned the scroll, Elnathan, together with Delaiah and Gemariah, urged him not to, but the king would not listen (Jer 36:25). Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him with Elnathan of Jerusalem, the father of Nehushta and maternal grandfather of King Jehoiachin (2 Kgs 24:8). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats that identification as possible. His name means "God has given." Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Elon was a Hittite whose daughter married Esau, the son of Isaac. Gen 26:34 calls her Bashemath and says Esau married her, along with Judith daughter of Beeri the Hittite, when he was forty years old. The later list of Esau's wives in Gen 36:2 names Elon's daughter as Adah. The two lists of Esau's wives differ in their names, and the passages do not explain this. Most readers take Bashemath and Adah to be two names for the same woman, and this entry follows that view, which is why Adah appears here as his daughter. Esau's wives are described as daughters of Canaan, so Elon was evidently one of the Hittite inhabitants of the land. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "oak" or "strong." Several other people in the Bible share the name Elon.

Elon was the second of the three sons of Zebulun, listed between his brothers Sered and Jahleel among the family of Jacob who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:14). In the census of the tribes taken in the wilderness, he appears as the ancestor of the Elonites, one of the clans of the tribe of Zebulun (Num 26:26). Nothing else is recorded about him. His name probably means "oak" or "terebinth," according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a judge of Israel from the same tribe, but this entry concerns only the son of Zebulun.

Elon was a man from the tribe of Zebulun who judged Israel for ten years (Judg 12:11). He followed Ibzan of Bethlehem and was succeeded by Abdon, as the surrounding verses of Judges 12 show. Easton's Bible Dictionary counts him as the eleventh of the Hebrew judges. The text records no deeds or battles from his time in office, only its length, his death, and his burial at Aijalon in the territory of Zebulun (Judg 12:12). This Aijalon is a different place from the better-known Aijalon in the territory of Dan. His judgeship is dated here to about 1139 BC, an estimate inferred from context. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "terebinth," a kind of tree. Several other people in the Bible share the name Elon, so this entry concerns only the judge.

Elon was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Dan when the land was divided under Joshua. It is named only once, in the list of Danite towns, between Jethlah and Thimnathah (Timnah), near Ekron (Josh 19:43). The name means "oak" or "terebinth." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the same place as Elon-beth-hanan, which belonged to one of Solomon's provision districts along with Shaalbim and Beth-shemesh (1 Kgs 4:9). It also notes Conder's proposal of Beit 'Anan, northwest of Nebi Samwil. The site has not been firmly identified, and the location shown here is an approximate placement within the Danite region in the hills west of Jerusalem.

Elonbeth-hanan was a town listed in the second of King Solomon's twelve administrative districts. Each district was run by an officer who supplied food for the royal household for one month of the year. This district was under the son of Dekar (Ben-deker) and also included Makaz, Shaalbim and Beth-shemesh. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that it is named alongside towns belonging to the tribe of Dan, which places it in the lowlands west of Jerusalem. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "the house of grace or mercy," and Smith's renders it "oak of the house of grace." Some connect it with Elon, a Danite town named in Josh 19:43. Its exact site is uncertain. The location shown here matches the area of the village of Beit Anan, northwest of Jerusalem, which has been proposed because the name is similar.

Eloth was a town on the shore of the Red Sea in the land of Edom, at the northern tip of what is now the Gulf of Aqaba. It is another spelling of Elath, as Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both note. Solomon built a fleet of ships at nearby Ezion-geber, described as lying beside Eloth, and he visited both places (1 Kgs 9:26; 2 Chr 8:17). Later Uzziah king of Judah rebuilt Eloth and brought it back under Judah's control after his father Amaziah died (2 Chr 26:2). The parallel account in 2 Kgs 14:22 records the same event under the name Elath, and 2 Kgs 16:6 says Judah later lost the town in the days of Ahaz. Its exact site is uncertain. It is usually placed near modern Aqaba in Jordan or nearby Eilat in Israel. The location shown here follows the Aqaba identification.

Elpaal was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. He was a son of Shaharaim by his wife Hushim, and the brother of Abitub (1 Chr 8:11). His half-brothers were Shaharaim's sons by another wife, Hodesh. The list credits Elpaal with many sons, including Eber, Misham and Shamed. The clause "who built Ono, and Lod" is usually read as referring to Shamed, though it may cover the family as a whole. Lod is the later Lydda, the modern city of Lod. A second group of sons, including Ishmerai, Jezliah and Jobab, appears in 1 Chr 8:17–18. Beriah and Shema are also counted among his sons here, by inference from how the list runs on. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as the founder of a numerous family. His name is usually explained as "God has wrought" or "God's work."

Elpalet was a son of David, one of the children born to him after he settled in Jerusalem. He is named only in the two lists of David's sons in Chronicles: as Elpalet in 1 Chr 14:5 and as Eliphelet in 1 Chr 3:6, where he follows Ibhar and Elishama (or Elishua). His mother is not named. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "God of deliverance." Both lists also name a later son called Eliphalet or Eliphelet, so David appears to have had two sons with nearly the same name. The parallel list in 2 Samuel 5 names only one, which has led some interpreters to suggest that Elpalet died young and the name was given again to a younger brother. The text does not say this, so it remains an inference.

Elteke (spelled Eltekeh in the King James Version) was a city in the territory of the tribe of Dan. Joshua 21:23 lists it with Gibbethon among the Danite towns given, together with their surrounding pasturelands, to the Levites. By inference from the surrounding passage, it was assigned to the Kohathite clan. The town also appears in Dan's allotment in Josh 19:44. Its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Beit Likia (Beit Liqya), northeast of Latrun in the hills west of Jerusalem, and the location shown here follows that identification. Others place it farther west on the coastal plain near Ekron and connect it with Altaqu, a town named in Assyrian records of Sennacherib's campaign.

Eltekeh was a city in the territory allotted to the tribe of Dan. It is named only in the list of Dan's towns, alongside Gibbethon and Baalath (Josh 19:44). According to Smith's Bible Dictionary, a later passage (Josh 21:23) records that Eltekeh and its surrounding pasturelands were given to the Kohathite Levites as one of the Levitical cities. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "God is its fear" and identifies the site with Beit-Likia, northeast of Latrun, in the hill country west of Jerusalem. Other identifications of the site have been proposed, so its exact location is uncertain. The location shown here follows the Beit-Likia identification.

Eltekon was a town in the hill country of Judah, named in Josh 15:59 in the list of cities given to the tribe of Judah. It appears in a group of six cities with their villages, alongside Maarath and Beth-anoth, and is not mentioned anywhere else in the Bible. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "founded by God." Because Eltekon is listed next to Beth-anoth, that encyclopedia places it a little north of Hebron, while noting that its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is an approximate placement in the Judean hills northwest of Hebron, consistent with that general area. No specific modern site is firmly identified.

Eltolad was a town in the far south of Judah, listed among the cities of the Negev toward the border of Edom in Josh 15:30. It was later assigned to the tribe of Simeon, whose territory lay inside Judah's allotment (Josh 19:4). Both lists place it beside Hormah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes it to be the same place as Tolad in 1 Chr 4:29, with the first part of the name dropped. Smith's Bible Dictionary, reading that passage, says Simeon held the town until the time of David. The name is usually explained as "kindred of God" or, in Hitchcock's Bible Names, "the generation of God." The actual site has not been identified, so any location given for it, including the location shown here, is only approximate.

Eluzai was one of the warriors who came over to David at Ziklag, while David was still keeping away from Saul. He appears only once, in a list of fighting men in 1 Chr 12:5, alongside Jerimoth, Bealiah, Shemariah and Shephatiah the Haruphite. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 12:1–7) describes these men as skilled archers and slingers who could use either hand, and as kinsmen of Saul from the tribe of Benjamin. So Eluzai was a Benjamite, by inference from that context. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name is usually explained as "God is my strength" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia; Hitchcock's Bible Names), though Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "God is my praise."

Elymas was a Jewish sorcerer and false prophet whom Barnabas and Saul (Paul) met at Paphos, on the island of Cyprus, about AD 45 by inference from context. His Jewish name was Bar-jesus, and Acts gives Elymas as the interpretation of that name, meaning "sorcerer" (Acts 13:6, 8). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains Elymas as a Greek form of an Aramaic or Arabic word for a wise man or magician. He was attached to the Roman proconsul (the "deputy") Sergius Paulus, and when the proconsul sought to hear the apostles, Elymas opposed them and tried to turn him away from the faith. The account that follows in Acts 13:9–12 says Paul declared that Elymas would be blind for a time, he was struck blind, and the proconsul then believed.

Elzabad was a warrior from the tribe of Gad, listed ninth among the Gadite fighters who joined David (1 Chr 12:12). The surrounding passage, which is not quoted here, describes these men as skilled with shield and spear and fierce as lions. They left their tribe to join David at his stronghold in the wilderness while he was being hunted by Saul, and they crossed the Jordan when it was in flood. The STEPBible proper names index links his joining David with Ziklag, where the chapter's list of supporters begins. The name means "God has given" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Another man named Elzabad, a Levite gatekeeper of the family of Obed-edom, appears in 1 Chr 26:7 and is a different person.

Elzabad was a Levite named among the sons of Shemaiah in the list of temple gatekeepers in 1 Chronicles 26. He is listed with his brothers Othni, Rephael, Obed, Elihu and Semachiah, and the text notes that his brothers were "strong men" (1 Chr 26:7). By inference from the surrounding chapter, Shemaiah was a son of Obed-edom, so Elzabad belonged to Obed-edom's family of gatekeepers. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe him as a Korahite doorkeeper. The STEPBible name index places this service in the time of David. His name is usually taken to mean "God has given." The name is also borne by a different man, a warrior from the tribe of Gad who joined David (1 Chr 12:12), who should not be confused with this Levite.

Emek-keziz was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Benjamin, listed in Josh 18:21 after Jericho and Beth-hoglah. The King James Version translates the name as "the valley of Keziz." Easton's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "abrupt" or "cut off." It is mentioned only in this list of Benjamin's cities. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it appears between Beth-hoglah and Beth-arabah. For that reason it probably lay in the Jordan plain, perhaps south of Jericho. Its exact site is unknown and the name has not survived in any modern place name. The location shown here is a rough placement in the lower Jordan Valley near Jericho, inferred from its neighbours in the list.

Emmaus was a village about sixty furlongs (roughly seven miles) from Jerusalem, to which two followers of Jesus were walking on the day of his resurrection (Luke 24:13). The following verses of the passage tell how Jesus joined them on the road unrecognized, and they name one of the travelers as Cleopas. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "hot baths." Its site has long been disputed, and Smith's Bible Dictionary considered it still unidentified. Easton's notes proposals at el-Kubeibeh, northwest of Jerusalem, and at Khurbet Khamasa, southwest of the city. Another identification is Emmaus Nicopolis, modern Imwas near Latrun, about 18 miles west of Jerusalem. That distance fits better with the reading of 160 furlongs found in some ancient manuscripts. The location shown here follows the Emmaus Nicopolis (Imwas) identification.

En-dor was a town in the territory of Issachar whose inhabitants and surrounding towns were allotted to the tribe of Manasseh, though Manasseh did not drive out its Canaanite population (Josh 17:11). On the eve of his final battle with the Philistines, King Saul had his servants find a woman there who was a medium, so that he could consult her (1 Sam 28:7). Psalm 83 recalls En-dor as the place where enemies of Israel perished. The previous verse names Sisera and Jabin, linking it with the victory of Deborah and Barak near the Kishon (Ps 83:10). The name probably means 'spring of Dor.' Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the village of Endur on the northern slope of the Hill of Moreh, south of Mount Tabor and near Nain and Shunem. The location shown here follows that identification.

En-gannim was a town in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, listed among the cities allotted to the tribe of Judah in Josh 15:34, where it appears between Zanoah and Tappuah. Its name means "spring of gardens." Nothing else is recorded about it in the Bible. The name is shared by another place, a Levitical town of the same name in the territory of Issachar, which should not be confused with this one. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify this Judean town with the modern site of Umm Jina, near Zanoah, south of the Wadi es-Sarar (the Sorek valley). The location shown here follows that identification, in the hill country west of Jerusalem.

En-gannim, meaning "spring of gardens," was a city in the territory of the tribe of Issachar. It is listed among Issachar's towns in Josh 19:21. It was one of four cities in Issachar given, with their surrounding pasturelands, to the Gershonite Levites (Josh 21:29). The parallel list of Levitical cities in 1 Chr 6:73 has Anem in its place, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the two as the same town. A different En-gannim lay in the lowlands of Judah. Smith's and Easton's Bible Dictionaries identify this town with modern Jenin, at the southern edge of the Jezreel Valley (the plain of Esdraelon), where the road climbs into the central hill country. The location shown here follows that identification. Easton's Bible Dictionary also links it with the "garden house" toward which King Ahaziah fled from Jehu in 2 Kgs 9:27.

En-haddah was a town in the territory given to the tribe of Issachar when the land was divided under Joshua. It is mentioned only once, in the list of Issachar's towns, where it appears next to En-gannim, Remeth and Beth-pazzez (Josh 19:21). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of the name as "swift fountain," and Hitchcock's Bible Names suggests "well of gladness." Nothing else is recorded about it. Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it is probably the village of Kefr Adan, about 3 miles (5 km) west of Jenin, near the En-gannim with which it is listed. Other scholars have proposed sites farther north, closer to Mount Tabor. The location shown here follows the Kefr Adan identification.

En-hakkore was a spring at Lehi in Judah that, according to Judg 15:19, God opened from a hollow place after Samson had killed a thousand Philistines with a donkey's jawbone. Exhausted and thirsty, Samson drank and revived, and he named the spring En-hakkore. The narrator notes that it was still there at Lehi "unto this day." The preceding verse (Judg 15:18) records Samson calling out to God in his thirst, which explains the name. Easton's and Hitchcock's dictionaries render it "spring of him who called," as the Septuagint does. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew could also mean "spring of the partridge." The exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the spring 'Ayun Kara near Zorah, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as unknown. The rough location shown here follows the identification near Zorah.

En-hazor was a city in the territory allotted to the tribe of Naphtali, listed with Kedesh and Edrei in Josh 19:37. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts it among Naphtali's fortified cities, based on the surrounding list, and treats it as a different place from the better-known Hazor. The name means "spring of Hazor" according to Smith's, while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the grass of the well." Its site is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary left it unidentified. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name survives in Hazireh, on the slopes west of Kedesh in upper Galilee, though it notes that no spring has been found there to match the "En" (spring) in the name. The location shown here, in the hills west of Kedesh in northern Galilee, appears to follow that identification.

En-mishpat was an older name for Kadesh, a spring site in the wilderness south of Canaan. It appears only in Gen 14:7, where the four eastern kings led by Chedorlaomer turned back to En-mishpat during their campaign and then struck the country of the Amalekites and the Amorites living in Hazazon-tamar. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as 'fountain of judgment,' and Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the place as Kadesh-barnea, the oasis where Israel later camped during the wilderness years. That link to Kadesh-barnea is an inference from the shared name Kadesh. The location shown here, in northeastern Sinai near the springs often associated with Kadesh-barnea, follows that identification. The exact site of Kadesh is still debated.

En-rimmon was one of the towns in southern Judah where people of Judah settled after returning from exile in Babylon, listed alongside Zareah and Jarmuth (Neh 11:29). The name probably means “spring of the pomegranate.” Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both suggest it is the same place as the “Ain and Rimmon” given to Judah and later to Simeon (Josh 15:32; Josh 19:7; 1 Chr 4:32). That would make it a far southern town near the Negev. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Eusebius described it as a very large village south of Eleutheropolis. It identifies the site with Khirbet Umm er-Rumamin, about 9 miles (15 km) north of Beersheba. The location shown here follows that identification.

En-rogel was a spring just outside Jerusalem that marked a point on the boundary between the tribal territories of Judah and Benjamin (Josh 15:7; Josh 18:16). The boundary ran down the valley of Hinnom past the south side of the Jebusite city to reach it. During Absalom's revolt, Jonathan and Ahimaaz waited at En-rogel so they would not be seen entering the city. A servant girl brought them news, which they carried to David (2 Sam 17:17). Later, Adonijah held a sacrificial feast by the stone of Zoheleth near the spring and invited the king's sons and the men of Judah (1 Kgs 1:9). The name is often explained as "fuller's spring." Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the Gihon spring ("Fountain of the Virgin"). Easton's Bible Dictionary favors Bir Ayyub ("Job's well"), below the meeting of the Kidron and Hinnom valleys. The location shown here follows the Bir Ayyub identification.

En-shemesh, meaning "spring of the sun," was a spring that marked part of the boundary between the tribal territories of Judah and Benjamin. Joshua 15:7 traces Judah's northern border past "the waters of Enshemesh" toward En-rogel, and Josh 18:17 traces Benjamin's southern border the same way, from En-shemesh toward Geliloth near the ascent of Adummim. Because it lay between the ascent of Adummim and En-rogel, it was east of Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives. Easton's, Smith's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia all identify it with the spring known as Ain Haud, about a mile east of Bethany, the last spring on the road down to Jericho. Christians call it the "Apostles' Fountain" because of a tradition from the 15th century that the apostles drank there. The location shown here matches that identification.

En-tappuah, meaning "spring of the apple" (or "apple spring"), was a spring on the border of the tribe of Manasseh. Joshua 17:7 traces Manasseh's boundary from Asher to Michmethah, near Shechem, and then along to the inhabitants of En-tappuah. By inference from the following verse, it was probably the spring of the town of Tappuah. The land of Tappuah belonged to Manasseh, but the town itself, on the border, belonged to Ephraim. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it on the boundary running south, east of Shechem. Both it and Easton's Bible Dictionary identify it with a spring at or near Yasuf, about 3 miles north of Lebonah. The location shown here, south of Shechem, follows that identification with the Yasuf area.

Enaim was a town in Judah where Tamar, dressed as a veiled woman, sat beside the road to Timnah and waited for her father-in-law Judah, because she had not been given to his son Shelah as promised (Gen 38:14). When Judah's friend, the Adullamite named in the surrounding passage, came back to pay her, he asked the local men where the woman by the roadside at this place was. They told him there had been no such woman there (Gen 38:21). The King James Version translates the name as "an open place" and "openly" rather than treating it as a place name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives its meaning as "place of a fountain." Easton's Bible Dictionary and that encyclopedia both take it to be probably the same as Enam (Josh 15:34), a town in the Shephelah lowland between Adullam and Timnah. Its exact site is uncertain, and the location shown here is only a rough placement near Timnah.

Enam was a town in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah. It is listed among the towns allotted to the tribe of Judah, alongside Zanoah, Engannim and Tappuah (Josh 15:34). This is its only mention in the Bible, and nothing is recorded about events there. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "double spring," and Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "fountain" or "open place." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it together with Enaim, the place by the road to Timnah where Tamar sat (Gen 38:14), which suggests the two may be the same town. The exact site of Enam is unknown, and the location shown here is only approximate.

Enan was a man of the tribe of Naphtali and the father of Ahira, who led that tribe during Israel's time in the wilderness.
