He is known only through his son's name, "Ahira the son of Enan," which appears five times in Numbers. Ahira was chosen to help Moses with the census at Sinai (Num 1:15). He served as captain of Naphtali in the camp arrangement (Num 2:29). He brought his tribe's offering on the twelfth day of the altar dedication (Num 7:78, 83) and commanded Naphtali's division on the march (Num 10:27). Nothing is recorded of Enan himself. His name is usually explained as "having eyes" or "having fountains" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "cloud."

Eneglaim was a place on the shore of the Dead Sea, named only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel's vision of the restored land. In that vision a river flows from the temple and turns the salt water fresh, so that fishermen spread their nets along the shore "from Engedi even unto Eneglaim" (Ezek 47:10). Its name probably means "spring of the two calves." The verse marks the two ends of a stretch of shoreline, so Eneglaim was evidently some distance from Engedi, but its exact site is unknown. Smith's Bible Dictionary says it cannot be determined which side of the sea it lay on. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it near the Jordan's mouth, noting Tristram's identification with 'Ain Hajlah and Robinson's with 'Ain Feshkah. The location shown here is rough and follows a different view, placing it near the southern end of the Dead Sea.

Engedi was a town in the wilderness of Judah on the western shore of the Dead Sea, listed among Judah's cities in Josh 15:62. Its name means "fountain of the kid" (Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries), and it is identified with the spring and oasis of modern Ein Gedi (Ain Jidy), which the location shown here matches. David hid in strongholds in the wilderness of Engedi while Saul pursued him. In Jehoshaphat's reign, invaders from Ammon, Moab and Mount Seir gathered there, and 2 Chr 20:2 equates it with Hazazon-tamar, the Amorite settlement attacked by Chedorlaomer in Gen 14:7. The Song of Songs mentions its vineyards and henna blossoms. In Ezekiel's vision of the healed Dead Sea, fishermen spread their nets from Engedi to Eneglaim. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes its warm springs, palm groves and cliff-side caves.

Enoch (son of Cain) was the son of Cain and his wife, and the first of Cain's descendants named in Genesis. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe him as Cain's eldest son. Cain built a city and named it Enoch after him (Gen 4:17). Easton's notes that this is the first city mentioned in Scripture. By inference from Gen 4:16, it stood in the land of Nod, east of Eden, though its location cannot be fixed. The Hebrew sentence could also be read as saying that Enoch himself built the city. This entry follows the usual reading, with Cain as the builder. Enoch was the father of Irad, and through him the ancestor of Mehujael, Methusael and Lamech (Gen 4:18). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "dedicated." He is a different man from Enoch the son of Jared, who appears in Seth's line in Genesis 5.

Enoch (father of Methuselah), also spelled Henoch, was a descendant of Adam through Seth. He was the son of Jared and the father of Methuselah. Jared was 162 when Enoch was born, and Enoch was 65 when Methuselah was born. Genesis says that afterward Enoch "walked with God" for 300 years and had other sons and daughters. His life lasted 365 years, and then "he was not; for God took him" (Gen 5:24). Heb 11:5 explains this as his being taken so that he did not see death, because he had pleased God. Jude 1:14 calls him "the seventh from Adam" and quotes a prophecy of his about the Lord coming with ten thousands of his saints. He also appears in the genealogies of 1 Chr 1:3 and Luke 3:37. Easton's Bible Dictionary distinguishes him from Enoch the son of Cain. Working from the genealogy's figures, this entry dates his life to about 3382–3017 BC.

The Enoch taken up event was the end of Enoch's earthly life, when God removed him instead of letting him die. Enoch was the father of Methuselah. Genesis 5:24 says that Enoch "walked with God: and he was not; for God took him," which breaks the pattern of the surrounding genealogy, where each man's entry ends with his death. Hebrews 11:5 understands the event to mean that Enoch was taken without experiencing death, so that he "was not found." It adds that before this he was known as one who pleased God, and it lists him among examples of faith. By inference from the genealogy, Gen 5:23 gives his lifespan as 365 years, which places the event at about 3017 BC on this entry's chronology. The date is an estimate drawn from context and is not stated in the text.

Enos, also spelled Enosh, was the son of Seth and grandson of Adam. Genesis 4:26 records his birth and adds that at that time people began to call on the name of the LORD. Easton's Bible Dictionary offers two readings of this remark: that people began to call themselves by the Lord's name, setting themselves apart from idolaters, or that they began to call on the Lord in a public and earnest way. Seth fathered Enos at 105. Enos fathered Cainan at 90, had other sons and daughters, and died at 905. By inference from these ages, he was born about 3769 BC and died about 2864 BC. His name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary renders "mortal man," appears in the genealogy of 1 Chr 1:1 and in Luke's genealogy of Jesus (Luke 3:38).

Epaenetus was a Christian living in Rome whom Paul greets in his letter to the Romans, calling him "my wellbeloved" (Rom 16:5). Paul describes him as the "firstfruits" of his region for Christ, meaning one of the first people there to become a believer. The King James Version reads "of Achaia," the Roman province of southern Greece. Many manuscripts instead read "of Asia," meaning the Roman province in western Asia Minor, and the Revised Version follows that reading. Easton's Bible Dictionary considers "Asia" probably correct, and the STEPBible proper names index also calls him the first convert in Asia. His greeting comes right after the greeting to the church that met in the house of Priscilla and Aquila. This suggests he may have been connected with that household, though that is an inference. Nothing more is known of him. His name means "commendable."

Epaphras was a Christian worker from Colossae and a companion of Paul. Paul calls him "our dear fellowservant" and "a faithful minister of Christ," and says the Colossians had learned the gospel from him (Col 1:7). This suggests, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes, that he probably founded the church there. Paul describes him as "one of you," a servant of Christ who prayed earnestly that the Colossians would stand mature and complete in God's will (Col 4:12). The next verse adds that he worked hard for the believers in Laodicea and Hierapolis as well. In the letter to Philemon, Paul calls him "my fellowprisoner" (Phlm 1:23). He was therefore with Paul during his first Roman imprisonment, dated to about AD 57 by inference from context. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that his name is a shortened form of Epaphroditus, but he is usually treated as a different person from the Philippian messenger of that name.

Epaphroditus was a member of the church at Philippi who served as its messenger to the apostle Paul. He carried the Philippians' gift to Paul, which Paul acknowledges as fully supplying his needs (Phil 4:18), and he stayed to look after Paul. Paul calls him "my brother, and companion in labour, and fellowsoldier" (Phil 2:25). The surrounding verses (Phil 2:26–30) say he fell seriously ill, nearly dying, while doing this work, and then recovered. Paul decided to send him home, and by inference he carried the letter to the Philippians with him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places these events during Paul's first imprisonment in Rome. The name, meaning "lovely" or "handsome," was common at the time. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Epaphras is a shortened form of it. Whether he is the same man as Epaphras of Colossae is uncertain, and this entry treats them as separate people.

Ephah is named first among the children of Midian, son of Abraham by his wife Keturah. The others are Epher, Hanoch (also spelled Henoch), Abida and Eldaah (Gen 25:4; 1 Chr 1:33). The name later stands for a people or region descended from this line. Isa 60:6 pairs Ephah with Midian as sources of camels and dromedaries that will come with travellers from Sheba, bringing gold and incense. By inference, the descendants were camel-herding traders in the Arabian desert. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a proposal that Ephah matches an Arab group named in Assyrian records of the 8th century BC. The name probably means "darkness," though Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "weary" or "tired." Several other people in the Old Testament are also called Ephah.

Ephah was a concubine of Caleb, named in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chr 2:46. She bore him three sons, Haran, Moza and Gazez. The same verse adds that Haran fathered a son named Gazez, so the name may belong to both a son and a grandson, or the line may be recorded in two ways. The surrounding chapter traces the descendants of Hezron, so this Caleb is probably Caleb son of Hezron (compare 1 Chr 2:18, 42) rather than Caleb son of Jephunneh, the spy sent by Moses. Several people in the Bible share the name Ephah, including a son of Midian (Gen 25:4) and a man listed just after her in 1 Chr 2:47. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "darkness", and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "weary" or "tired". Nothing else is recorded about her.

Ephah was a child of Jahdai and a member of the tribe of Judah, named only in 1 Chr 2:47. Ephah's siblings were Regem, Jotham, Geshan (also spelled Gesham), Pelet and Shaaph. The verse appears in the genealogy of Caleb's descendants, though it does not say how Jahdai himself was connected to Caleb. The verse groups Ephah among Jahdai's "sons", and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Ephah as a son, while this entry treats Ephah as female. Nothing else is recorded about this person. The name is shared by others, including Caleb's concubine Ephah, mentioned in the previous verse (1 Chr 2:46), who is a different person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "weary" or "tired", and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "darkness".

Ephah was a people and region of northern Arabia, named in Isa 60:6 alongside Midian and Sheba as sources of the camels and dromedaries that would come to Jerusalem bearing gold and incense. STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) describes Ephah as an Arabian tribe known for its camels. Its pairing with Midian fits Gen 25:4 and 1 Chr 1:33, which name Ephah as a son of Midian, so the tribe was probably understood as descended from him and closely linked to the Midianites. Its exact territory is unknown. The location shown here is approximate, placing it in northwestern Arabia near the Gulf of Aqaba, within the general area associated with Midian. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "weary" or "tired."

Ephai was a man from Netophah whose sons were among the Judean army officers who came to Gedaliah at Mizpah after the Babylonians appointed him governor of those left in Judah (Jer 40:8). Netophah was a town near Bethlehem, as its pairing with Bethlehem in Neh 7:26 suggests. Ephai himself is known only through his sons, who are not named. The written Hebrew text spells the name Ophai, while the traditional reading is Ephai. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "gloomy." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia holds that these sons were later killed along with Gedaliah when Ishmael son of Nethaniah murdered the governor and the Judeans with him. That is an inference from Jer 41:3, which does not name them.

Epher was a son of Midian and so a grandson of Abraham through his wife Keturah. He appears second in the list of Midian's five sons, with his brothers Ephah, Hanoch (spelled Henoch in 1 Chr 1:33), Abida and Eldaah, all counted among the descendants of Keturah (Gen 25:4; 1 Chr 1:33). Nothing else is recorded about him, and he is probably named as the ancestor of a clan within the Midianite peoples. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of his name as "calf" or "young deer," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "dust" or "lead." The name is shared by other men in the Bible, including figures in the genealogies of Judah and Manasseh, who are different people from this son of Midian.

Epher was a man of the tribe of Judah, listed as the third of four sons of Ezra in the genealogy of Judah (1 Chr 4:17). His brothers were Jether, Mered and Jalon. This Ezra is a different person from the scribe of the same name, and nothing else is recorded about Epher beyond his place in the family list. The name is shared by several people in the Bible, including a grandson of Abraham through Midian and a head of a family in the half-tribe of Manasseh, so this Epher should be kept distinct from them. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of the name as "calf" or "young deer," while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "dust" or "lead."

Epher was one of the heads of the families of the half-tribe of Manasseh that lived east of the Jordan. In 1 Chr 5:24 he is the first named in a list of seven clan leaders described as mighty men of valour and famous men. The surrounding passage says these eastern tribes later turned from God and were carried into exile by the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser. Easton's Bible Dictionary therefore counts Epher's family among those taken captive. Nothing else is recorded about him. The same name belongs to other people in the Bible, including a son of Midian and a man of Judah, and they should not be confused with him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "dust" or "lead."

Ephes-dammim was the place in Judah where the Philistines camped before the battle in which David fought Goliath. It lay between Shochoh and Azekah, in the hill country west of Bethlehem overlooking the valley of Elah (1 Sam 17:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify it with Pas-dammim, where a later clash with the Philistines took place (1 Chr 11:13). The name is usually explained as "boundary of blood," which Easton's links to repeated fighting there. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests instead that it may come from the deep red color of the local soil. Easton's connects the site with the modern Beit Fased near Shochoh, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia regards the exact spot as undetermined. The location shown here is a point between Shochoh and Azekah, matching the description in 1 Sam 17:1.

Ephesus was a major city of the Roman province of Asia, on the western coast of Asia Minor. Its ruins lie near modern Selçuk in Turkey. The city was known as the guardian of the goddess Diana's worship (Acts 19:35). Paul first stopped there briefly, reasoning in the synagogue before sailing for Jerusalem with a promise to return (Acts 18:19–21). The Alexandrian teacher Apollos also came there. Paul returned on his next journey, and his preaching across Asia stirred opposition. According to Acts 19:24 the image-makers started a riot, by inference from context about AD 53. Paul wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus (1 Cor 16:8; 15:32). Later he called its church elders to meet him at Miletus. Paul's letter to the Ephesians is addressed to believers there, Timothy stayed on there, and Tychicus was sent there. Ephesus heads the seven churches addressed in Revelation. Tradition holds that the apostle John spent his last years there.

Ephlal was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:37, where he is the son of Zabad and the father of Obed. The surrounding list traces the line of Jerahmeel, son of Hezron, so Ephlal belonged to the Jerahmeelite clan within Judah, as Smith's Bible Dictionary also notes. By inference from the wider passage, this line came down from Sheshan, whose daughter married an Egyptian servant named Jarha. Nothing else is recorded about Ephlal beyond his place in this family line. His name is usually explained as meaning "judgment" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "judging" or "praying."

Ephod was a man of the tribe of Manasseh, known only as the father of Hanniel. In Num 34:23 Hanniel son of Ephod is named as the prince, or leader, of the tribe of Manasseh, one of the sons of Joseph. The surrounding chapter shows that these tribal leaders were appointed to help divide the land of Canaan among the Israelite tribes. Nothing else is recorded about Ephod himself. His name is spelled the same as the ephod, the priestly garment often mentioned in the Old Testament, but the text does not link the two.

Ephraim was the second son of Joseph and his Egyptian wife Asenath. He was born in Egypt, probably about 1708 BC by inference from context. Joseph named him because God had made him fruitful "in the land of my affliction" (Gen 41:52), and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "fruitful." According to Gen 48, Jacob adopted Ephraim and his older brother Manasseh as his own sons, crossing his hands to give the younger the greater blessing. Joseph lived to see Ephraim's descendants to the third generation (Gen 50:23). The genealogies name Shuthelah, Becher, Tahan, Ezer, Elead and Beriah among his sons and descendants (Num 26:35; 1 Chr 7:20–23). Most later uses of the name refer to the tribe descended from him, one of the two Joseph tribes (Josh 14:4), or to its central hill country, "mount Ephraim." The prophets, especially Hosea and Isaiah, use Ephraim as a name for the northern kingdom of Israel.

Ephraim was a town near the wilderness where Jesus went with his disciples after he stopped moving openly among the Jews (John 11:54). The surrounding chapter shows that this withdrawal followed the raising of Lazarus and the council's decision to put Jesus to death, so it was probably a retreat to a quieter place before the final Passover, about AD 30 by inference from context. The text says only that Jesus stayed there with his disciples. The site is uncertain. It is commonly identified with the modern village of et-Taiyibeh (Taybeh), northeast of Jerusalem on the edge of the Judean wilderness, and some link it with the Old Testament towns of Ophrah or Ephron. The location shown here follows the et-Taiyibeh identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "fruitful" or "increasing."

Ephraim (Territory) was the land allotted to the tribe of Ephraim, descended from Joseph's son Ephraim, in the central hill country west of the Jordan. Joshua 16 traces its borders. The south ran from the Jordan near Jericho up past Bethel, then west by lower Beth-horon and Gezer to the Mediterranean. The north, shared with Manasseh, followed the brook Kanah to the sea, with Ephraim to the south and Manasseh to the north. Ephraim also held towns inside Manasseh's land, including Tappuah. The Canaanites of Gezer were not driven out but lived under tribute. The hill region, called "mount Ephraim," held Timnath-serah, the town given to Joshua (Josh 19:50). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the phrase as the section of the central range belonging to Ephraim. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "fruitful." The location shown here lies in the central hills north of Bethel, in today's West Bank.

Ephratah, also called Ephrath, was the wife Caleb son of Hezron married after the death of his first wife Azubah. She bore him Hur, who is called her firstborn (1 Chr 2:19, 2:50; 4:4). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary take her to be the grandmother of Caleb the spy, through her son Hur. Her descendants are tied to Bethlehem. Hur is called "the father of Bethlehem," and 1 Chr 2:51 gives that title to Salma, one of Hur's sons. STEPBible's proper-name index therefore treats her, through Hur or Salma, as the founder of the town. This probably explains why Bethlehem was also known as Ephratah, the name used in Mic 5:2. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of her name as "abundance" or "bearing fruit."

Ephrath was the ancient name of the town later called Bethlehem, in the hill country south of Jerusalem. Genesis twice adds the note "which is Bethlehem" to explain the older name, and Smith's Bible Dictionary treats it as the early name of Bethlehem-judah. Jacob's family was traveling south from Bethel and was only a short distance from Ephrath when Rachel went into a hard labor. She gave birth to Benjamin and died, and Jacob buried her beside the road to Ephrath. This was about 1739 BC, by inference from context. Near the end of his life, Jacob recalled burying her there. Some read 1 Sam 10:2 as placing Rachel's tomb farther north, near the border of Benjamin. The location shown here follows the Genesis identification with Bethlehem and matches the modern town of that name.

Ephrathah (spelled Ephratah in the King James Version) is an older name for Bethlehem in Judah. In Ruth 4:11 the elders at the gate bless Boaz with parallel wishes to prosper in Ephratah and be famous in Bethlehem, treating the two names as one place. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that other passages also link the names, such as Gen 35:19 and the form “Bethlehem Ephratah” in Mic 5:2. In Ps 132:6 the psalmist says “we heard of it at Ephratah: we found it in the fields of the wood,” referring to the ark. Easton's reads this as David hearing of the ark in his hometown of Bethlehem and later finding it at Kirjath-jearim, the “forest town.” Some interpreters instead take Ephratah here as the district around Kirjath-jearim. The location shown here follows the Bethlehem identification, about 9 km (5 miles) south of Jerusalem.

Ephron was a Hittite, the son of Zohar, who lived among the people of Heth and owned the field and cave of Machpelah near Mamre in Canaan. When Abraham sought a burial place for his wife Sarah, he asked the Hittites to approach Ephron for him. Ephron answered Abraham publicly at the city gate, before the assembled townspeople. Abraham insisted on paying, and he weighed out four hundred shekels of silver, after which the field, the cave and its trees were formally made over to him (Gen 23:16–17). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes the elaborate courtesy of the exchange and the large sum paid. The site continued to be identified as Ephron's field when Abraham was buried there and when Jacob asked to be buried with his fathers (Gen 25:9; Gen 49:29–30). The name is commonly explained as meaning "fawn-like" (Smith's Bible Dictionary).

Ephron was a place on the boundary between the tribal territories of Benjamin and Judah, west of Jerusalem. Joshua 18:15 describes Benjamin's southern border running from the edge of Kirjath-jearim to the spring of the waters of Nephtoah. The King James wording here does not use the name: where it reads "went out on the west," the place is identified only by inference from the parallel description of Judah's northern border in Josh 15:9, which mentions "the cities of mount Ephron" on the same stretch between Nephtoah and Kirjath-jearim. Several different places in the Bible share the name Ephron, and the exact site of this one is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the hill country west of Jerusalem. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "dust."

Ephron was a town in the hill country north of Jerusalem, one of the places King Abijah of Judah took from Jeroboam of Israel after defeating him, along with its surrounding villages, Bethel and Jeshanah (2 Chr 13:19). The King James Version spells it "Ephrain", and the Hebrew text has both spellings. Its grouping with Bethel suggests it lay near the border between Judah and Israel. Many scholars identify it with the modern village of et-Taiyibeh, northeast of Bethel, and link it with Ophrah and with the Ephraim to which Jesus withdrew in John 11:54. The location shown here follows the et-Taiyibeh identification, though the identification is not certain. The name also belongs to Mount Ephron on Judah's border and to Ephron the Hittite, and should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "dust".

Er was the firstborn son of Judah, born to him by the daughter of Shua, a Canaanite woman. His younger full brothers were Onan and Shelah. Judah arranged his marriage to Tamar. Genesis says Er was wicked in the sight of the LORD and that the LORD killed him, though the text does not describe what he did. He died in Canaan without children, before Jacob's family went down to Egypt. After his death Tamar bore twins, Pharez and Zerah, to Judah himself, so they were Er's half-brothers. Er is still named among Judah's sons in the later genealogies. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "watchful," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "watchman." The name is shared by several people in the Bible; this entry concerns Judah's son.

Er was a son of Shelah, the son of Judah, and so a grandson of Judah within the tribe of Judah. He is named only once, in a genealogy at 1 Chr 4:21, where he is called "the father of Lecah." Lecah was probably a town or clan rather than a single son, since Chronicles often uses "father of" for the founder of a settlement. His brothers were Laadah, the father of Mareshah, along with Jokim, Joash and Saraph. The same verse links Shelah's descendants with families of fine linen workers of the house of Ashbea. He should not be confused with his uncle Er, Judah's firstborn, after whom he was probably named. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "watchman."

Er is a man named only in Luke's genealogy of Jesus. He was the son of Jose and the father of Elmodam (Luke 3:28). Jose appears in the next verse of the list, and some translations render his name as Joshua. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places Er in the seventh generation before Zerubbabel. He belongs to the stretch of Luke's line that runs from David's son Nathan down to Shealtiel and Zerubbabel, so he counts as a member of the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "watchman." He should not be confused with other men called Er, such as Judah's eldest son or Judah's grandson, the son of Shelah.

Eran was a son of Shuthelah and a grandson of Ephraim, belonging to the tribe of Ephraim within the descendants of Joseph. He appears only once, in the census taken in the wilderness (Num 26:36), where he is named as the ancestor of the Eranites, a family or clan within the tribe. In that census, Shuthelah heads the main Ephraimite clan and Eran's family is listed as a branch of it. Bered, his brother, is probably the Bered named in the Ephraimite genealogy at 1 Chr 7:20, which lists him as a son of Shuthelah. Nothing else is recorded about Eran's life. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "watcher" or "watchful."

Erastus was a companion and helper of Paul. While Paul was based at Ephesus, he sent Erastus and Timothy ahead into Macedonia, describing them as two of those who served him, while he himself stayed on in Asia (Acts 19:22). An Erastus described as the city's treasurer (the KJV says "chamberlain") sent greetings to the Christians at Rome in Paul's letter written from Corinth (Rom 16:23). In his last letter Paul notes that Erastus stayed behind at Corinth (2 Tim 4:20). It is uncertain whether these passages refer to one man or more. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the Corinthian treasurer as separate from Paul's travelling companion. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same man might have left a civic office to take up mission work. The link to Corinth in two of the three passages makes a single Erastus plausible. The name means "beloved."

Erech was an ancient city in the land of Shinar (southern Mesopotamia), named in Gen 10:10 as one of the cities where Nimrod's kingdom began, along with Babel, Accad and Calneh. Easton's Bible Dictionary links Ezra 4:9's "Archevites", people settled in Samaria who wrote against the rebuilding of Jerusalem, with Erech, probably as its former inhabitants. The city is the Sumerian and Babylonian Uruk, identified with the ruins of Warka near the Euphrates in southern Iraq, about 120 miles southeast of Babylon. The location shown here matches that site. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Uruk was among the oldest cities of Babylonia, home of the hero-king Gilgamesh and of a major temple to Ishtar. This entry dates the beginning of Nimrod's kingdom to about 1822 BC, an estimate inferred from context.

Eri was one of the sons of Gad, Jacob's son, and so a member of the tribe of Gad. He appears in the list of Jacob's descendants who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:16), and in the wilderness census he is named as the ancestor of the Erites, one of the Gadite clans (Num 26:16). His brothers were Ziphion (Zephon), Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Arodi (Arod) and Areli. The two lists differ slightly in spelling, and Ezbon in Genesis is probably the same person as Ozni in Numbers. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "watchful", while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "my city".

Esar-haddon was a king of Assyria, the son and successor of Sennacherib. According to 2 Kgs 19:37 and Isa 37:38, he came to the throne after his brothers Adrammelech and Sharezer killed their father with the sword while he worshipped in the house of his god Nisroch, then fled to Armenia. Ezra 4:2 records that the people living around Samaria in Zerubbabel's time traced their settlement there to Esar-haddon, who had brought them to the land. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia dates his reign to about 680–668 BC, from Assyrian sources, and describes his rebuilding of Babylon and his conquest of Egypt. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both suggest that Manasseh of Judah was probably brought before him as a prisoner at Babylon, as 2 Chr 33:11 describes, since he was the Assyrian king who ruled from Babylon.

Esau (Edom) was the elder twin son of Isaac and Rebekah and brother of Jacob. He was born red and hairy (Gen 25:25), about 1836 BC by inference from context. He was a hunter and the son Isaac meant to bless, but Jacob received the blessing first (Gen 27:1, 27:30). Genesis 25:30 explains his other name, Edom ("red"), by the red stew for which he sold his birthright. His wives included Adah, Aholibamah and Bashemath, and his sons included Eliphaz, Reuel, Jeush, Jaalam and Korah. Jacob feared him and sent gifts ahead on returning from Haran (Gen 32:19). Esau settled in Seir and became the father of the Edomites (Gen 36:43). His names came to stand for that people. They dealt with Israel at Kadesh, were subdued by David, and are denounced by several prophets (Num 20:14; 2 Sam 8:14; Obad 1:6). Malachi and Paul contrast him with Jacob (Mal 1:2; Rom 9:13).

Esau, used as a place name, stands for the land and people of Edom, the territory settled by the descendants of Esau, Jacob's twin brother. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Esau driving the Horites out of Mount Seir and settling there as a powerful chief in Edom. Gen 36:40 lists the chiefs (dukes) who came from Esau "after their places," tying his name to the districts they held. The prophets use "Esau" as a name for this land and nation. Jer 49:10 says Esau will be stripped bare and his hiding places uncovered, and Obad 1:18 pictures the house of Esau as stubble burned by the house of Jacob. The region lay south-east of the Dead Sea in what is now southern Jordan. The location shown here marks the surrounding area, near ancient Bozrah (modern Buseirah), rather than a single town.

Esek was a well dug by Isaac's servants in the valley of Gerar, in the southern land where Isaac had settled. The herdsmen of Gerar quarreled with Isaac's herdsmen over it, claiming the water as theirs, so Isaac named the well Esek, meaning "contention" or "quarrel" (Gen 26:20). The surrounding narrative shows Isaac then moving on to dig another disputed well, Sitnah, and finally an undisputed one, Rehoboth. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places Esek near Gerar and Rehoboth but notes that the site has not been identified. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the region of Gerar, in the western Negev of modern southern Israel, and does not mark a known site.

Eshan was a town in the hill country of Judah, named only once, in the list of towns allotted to the tribe of Judah (Josh 15:52). The King James Version spells it "Eshean." It appears alongside Arab and Dumah in a group of towns in the uplands around Hebron. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects it with the ruin of es-Simia near Dumah, south of Hebron. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia holds that no satisfactory identification has been found and notes a suggestion that the name may be a variant form of Beersheba. The location shown here lies close to Dumah, south-west of Hebron, and so follows the es-Simia identification.

Eshban was a Horite, one of four sons of Dishon, listed in the genealogy of the people of Seir in Gen 36:26 and repeated in 1 Chr 1:41. His brothers were Ithran and Cheran, and a fourth brother is called Hemdan in Genesis but Amram in Chronicles. Chronicles places this Dishon as a son of Anah. Genesis 36 also mentions a Dishon who was a son of Seir, so which Dishon was Eshban's father is open to question. This entry follows the Chronicles reading. Nothing is recorded about Eshban beyond his name and family. The Tyndale House proper-names index describes him as a Horite chief in the land of Seir. The meaning of his name is uncertain: Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "wise man," the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "thoughtful" or "intelligent," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "fire of the sun."

Eshcol was an Amorite, the brother of Mamre and Aner, who lived near Abram in the area of Mamre, close to Hebron. The three brothers were allies of Abram (Gen 14:13). When Abram went after the kings who had captured his nephew Lot, Eshcol and his brothers went with him. After the victory, Abram refused to keep any of the recovered goods for himself, but he insisted that Aner, Eshcol and Mamre receive their share (Gen 14:24). The name means "cluster of grapes." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and the STEPBible proper-names list connect him with the valley of Eshcol near Hebron, where Moses' spies later cut a large cluster of grapes (Num 13:23). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia presents this link as possible rather than certain. Smith's Bible Dictionary places these events about 1912 BC.

Eshtaol was a town in the lowland (the Shephelah), listed among the cities of Judah (Josh 15:33) and also counted within the inheritance of the tribe of Dan (Josh 19:41). It is almost always named together with neighboring Zorah. Between the two towns lay the "camp of Dan," where the Spirit of the LORD first began to move Samson. His family later buried him there, in the burial place of his father Manoah (Judg 13:25; 16:31). Eshtaol was also one of the home towns of the Danites who sent out five spies and then six hundred armed men in search of new territory (Judg 18:2, 8, 11). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "narrow pass." It notes two proposed sites: the modern Eshwa (Ashu'a), a short distance east of Zorah, and Kustul, east of Kiriath-jearim. The location shown here follows the Eshwa identification.

Eshtemoa the Maachathite is named once, in the genealogy of Judah at 1 Chr 4:19, as a son of Hodiah, the sister of Naham. This entry treats Mered as his father. That is an inference from the surrounding verses (1 Chr 4:17–18), which describe Mered's two wives. On that reading, Ishbah, Miriam and Shammai, the children of Mered's other wife, would be Eshtemoa's half-siblings. The same verse also names the father of Keilah the Garmite among Hodiah's sons. Eshtemoa shares his name with a town in the hill country of Judah, and the town Keilah is mentioned beside him. For that reason he is often understood as the ancestor or founder of the people who settled there, though the passage does not say so directly. The meaning of the label "Maachathite" here is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the bosom of a woman."

Eshtemoa was a town in the hill country of Judah. It was one of the cities given, with its surrounding pasturelands, to the priestly descendants of Aaron (Josh 21:14; 1 Chr 6:57). After David defeated the Amalekites who had raided Ziklag, he sent gifts from the spoil to his friends in Eshtemoa, among other towns where he and his men had moved about (1 Sam 30:28). Josh 15:50 lists it in a shorter form, Eshtemoh, among the towns of Judah's mountain district. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the village of es-Semu'a, about 7 or 8 miles south of Hebron, where ancient remains survive. The location shown here follows that identification. Easton's gives the name's meaning as "obedience." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same name is used of a person in a genealogy of Judah (1 Chr 4:17, 19).

Eshtemoh was a town in the hill country of Judah. It is named once, in the list of towns given to the tribe of Judah, between Anab and Anim (Josh 15:50). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as the same place as Eshtemoa, a spelling found elsewhere. Under that name, connected passages describe it as a town assigned to the priests (Josh 21:14; 1 Chr 6:57) and as one of the places to which David sent spoil after defeating the Amalekites (1 Sam 30:28). The town is commonly identified with the modern village of es-Samu, about 9 miles (14 km) south of Hebron, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Eshton was a man named in the genealogies of the tribe of Judah. According to 1 Chr 4:11, he was the son of Mehir, whose father was Chelub, the brother of Shuah. Eshton fathered Beth-rapha, Paseah and Tehinnah, and Tehinnah is called the father of Ir-nahash. The passage closes by calling this family "the men of Rechah," a place or clan otherwise unknown. Some of these names, such as Beth-rapha and Ir-nahash, look like place names, so the list may record the founders of settlements as well as individual descendants, though the text does not say so directly. Nothing else is recorded about Eshton. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "effeminate," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "uxorious."

Esli was an ancestor of Jesus named only in Luke's genealogy, where he appears as the son of Nagge and the father of Naum (Luke 3:25). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts him as the tenth generation before Joseph, the husband of Mary, and suggests his name probably stands for the Hebrew name Azaliah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "near me" or "he who separates." Because Luke's list places him between Zerubbabel (Luke 3:27) and Joseph, he probably lived in the centuries after the return from the Babylonian exile. As part of the line Luke traces back through David, he belonged to the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him.

The Espousal of Mary was the betrothal of Mary, later the mother of Jesus, to Joseph, a man described as being of the house of David (Luke 1:27). In Jewish custom of the time, betrothal was a binding agreement that came before the couple lived together, which is why Matthew notes that Mary was found to be with child 'before they came together' (Matt 1:18). Luke mentions the betrothal when introducing Mary as the virgin to whom the angel Gabriel was sent, an episode that follows the announcement of John the Baptist's birth to Zechariah. The location shown here is Nazareth, inferred from Luke's statement that Gabriel was sent to a city of Galilee named Nazareth (Luke 1:26). The date of about 6 BC is an estimate inferred from context. Neither passage describes the betrothal itself; both mention it only as the setting for the conception of Jesus.

Esther, also called Hadassah, was a Jewish woman who became queen of the Persian king Ahasuerus. Orphaned as a girl, she was raised in Shushan by her cousin Mordecai, the son of her father Abihail's brother, who took her as his own daughter (Esth 2:7). Gathered among the maidens brought to the palace, she was chosen by the king and crowned in Vashti's place, while keeping her people and family hidden at Mordecai's instruction (Esth 2:17; 2:20). When Haman obtained a decree to destroy the Jews, Mordecai urged her to plead with the king. She approached him uninvited, was received with the golden sceptre, and invited him and Haman to two banquets. At the second she asked for her life and her people's and named Haman as their enemy (Esth 7:3–6). Haman was hanged, and Esther and Mordecai wrote with authority to confirm the observance of Purim (Esth 9:29–32).

Etam was a rocky height in the territory of Judah where Samson went to live after killing many Philistines in revenge for the burning of his wife and her father. Samson stayed at "the top of the rock Etam" (Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the Revised Version reads "cleft"). Three thousand men of Judah came to him there, fearing Philistine reprisals, and asked what he had done. Easton's describes the place as a natural stronghold and identifies it with Beit 'Atab, west of Bethlehem near Zorah and Eshtaol, where a long tunnel under the village may be the cleft. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that a cavern called 'Arak Isma'in, high on the cliffs of the Wady Isma'in, fits the story better. The location shown here is in the hills west of Jerusalem, near both suggested sites. Other places in the Bible share the name Etam.

Etam was a town of the tribe of Simeon, named in 1 Chr 4:32 alongside Ain, Rimmon, Tochen and Ashan as one of the villages where the Simeonites lived. It appears only in this list. The parallel list of Simeon's towns in Josh 19:7 names Ain, Remmon, Ether and Ashan, so Smith's Bible Dictionary links the two passages, and Etam may correspond to the Ether of Joshua. The name is shared by other places in the Bible, including the rock where Samson stayed after fighting the Philistines (Judg 15:8) and a town near Bethlehem in Judah. This entry treats the Simeonite town as a separate place. Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reports Conder's identification with Khirbet Aitun in the hills northwest of Beersheba, and the rough location shown here follows that identification.

Etam was a city of Judah that King Rehoboam built up as a fortified town, listed with Bethlehem and Tekoa in 2 Chr 11:6. The surrounding passage presents it as one of the defensive cities he strengthened after the kingdom divided. Its place in that list suggests it lay near Bethlehem, in the hill country to the south. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Josephus and the Talmud place there the springs that supplied Solomon's pools, Bethlehem and the temple. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with 'Ain 'Atan, a strong spring at the head of the Wadi Urtas. The location shown here is Khirbet el-Khokh, a site in the same area near modern Artas. The name is shared by other places, including the rock of Etam where Samson took refuge (Judg 15:8) and a town of Simeon (1 Chr 4:32). These may be different places.

Eth-kazin was a town on the eastern border of the tribe of Zebulun. Josh 19:13 names it in the description of that boundary, between Gath-hepher (Gittah-hepher) and Rimmon, near Neah. The King James Version spells it Ittah-kazin. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains that this spelling comes from reading the Hebrew ending that means "toward" as part of the name itself, so the town's name is properly Eth-kazin. Its site has not been identified. The location shown here is approximate, in Lower Galilee near Gath-hepher, by inference from its place in the boundary list. Nothing else is recorded about the town.

Etham was the Israelites' second camp after leaving Egypt, reached by a march from Succoth and described as being "in the edge of the wilderness" (Exod 13:20; Num 33:6). From there they turned back toward Pi-hahiroth, before Baal-zephon, and camped before Migdol (Num 33:7). After crossing the sea they traveled three days through the "wilderness of Etham" to Marah (Num 33:8), so the name also covered desert land east of the sea. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Exod 15:22 calls this stretch the wilderness of Shur. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests the name may come from the Egyptian Khetam, "fortress," on Egypt's eastern frontier. The exact site is unknown. The location shown here follows the view that it lay near the north end of the Bitter Lakes, south of modern Ismailia. The stop dates to about 1491 BC, by inference from context.

Ethan the Ezrahite was a man famous for his wisdom. 1 Kgs 4:31 names him first in a list of renowned sages, along with Heman, Chalcol and Darda, the sons of Mahol, to show that Solomon was wiser than all of them. The heading of Psalm 89 names Ethan the Ezrahite as its author. "Ezrahite" probably points to descent from Zerah of Judah, since 1 Chr 2:6 lists Ethan, Heman, Calcol and Dara as sons of Zerah. Easton's Bible Dictionary instead places him in the tribe of Levi, linking him with the Levite singer Ethan of David's time. The name is shared by several people in the Bible, so how these figures relate is uncertain. This entry treats him as the wise man of 1 Kings and the author of Psalm 89.

Ethan was a man of the tribe of Judah, one of the five sons of Zerah listed in 1 Chr 2:6, alongside Zimri (called Zabdi in Josh 7:1), Heman, Calcol and Dara. The STEPBible Proper Names index identifies him as a grandson of Judah, since Zerah was a son of Judah by Tamar (Gen 38:30). His only recorded son was Azariah. The name is shared by several men in the Bible. 1 Kgs 4:31 compares Solomon's wisdom to that of Ethan the Ezrahite, Heman, Chalcol and Darda. Because three of those names match Zerah's sons, some readers take them to be the same family, while others see them as different men, since that verse calls them sons of Mahol. This entry treats Ethan son of Zerah only as the genealogy presents him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "strong."

Ethan was a Levite of the Gershonite branch of the tribe of Levi. He was the son of Zimmah and the father of Adaiah, and he appears in the family line of Asaph, the temple singer (1 Chr 6:42). The other Gershonite genealogy in the same chapter names Zimmah's son as Joah, followed by Iddo, Zerah and Jeaterai (1 Chr 6:21). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both take Joah and Ethan to be the same man, and this entry follows that view. By the same comparison, Iddo probably corresponds to Adaiah. Nothing is recorded about his life beyond his place in these genealogies. Several other men in the Bible are also called Ethan, so he should not be confused with Ethan the Ezrahite or Ethan the Merarite singer.

Ethbaal was king of the Sidonians and the father of Jezebel, who married King Ahab of Israel (1 Kgs 16:31). This marriage is mentioned as the setting for Ahab's turn to serving and worshipping Baal. His name is usually taken to mean "with Baal." Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Josephus calls him king of the Tyrians as well, and identifies him with Eithobalus, who seized the throne of Tyre and ruled for thirty-two years, about 940–908 BC. Easton's Bible Dictionary adds that he was said to have been a priest of Astarte. His link to the royal line of Judah is probably through Athaliah, Ahab's daughter, who married Jehoram of Judah (2 Kgs 8:18, 26). If she was Jezebel's daughter, Ethbaal was an ancestor of the later Davidic kings, though the text does not say directly who her mother was.

Ether was a town in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, listed in the same district as Libnah and Ashan (Josh 15:42). It appears again among the towns given to the tribe of Simeon, whose territory lay within Judah's (Josh 19:7). In that list it is grouped with Ain, Remmon and Ashan as "four cities and their villages." Nothing else is recorded about it. Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Khirbet el-'Atr, an ancient site with cisterns and foundations near Beit Jibrin, whose name is spelled the same way. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the Shephelah. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "abundance," and Hitchcock's Bible Names as "talk."

Ethiopia is the English rendering, through Greek, of the Hebrew name Cush, a land lying south of Egypt along the Nile. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it from Syene at the First Cataract to beyond the meeting of the White and Blue Nile, roughly corresponding to modern Sudan. Smith's Bible Dictionary adds Nubia and northern Abyssinia in its widest sense. The location shown here is in the Nile valley of northern Sudan. In Gen 2:13 the Gihon, a river of Eden, is said to surround the whole land of Ethiopia. Because that passage is set in Eden, the identity of this Cush is uncertain, and it may not be the same African region. In Esther, Ethiopia marks one edge of the empire of Ahasuerus, which stretched from India to Ethiopia over 127 provinces (Esth 1:1; 8:9). Job 28:19 mentions the topaz of Ethiopia as a costly stone.

Ethnan was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:7 as one of the sons of Helah, alongside Zereth and Jezoar. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 4:5–6) explains that Helah was one of the two wives of Ashur, called the father, probably meaning the founder, of Tekoa. Ashur's other wife, Naarah, bore Ahuzam, Hepher, Temeni and Haahashtari, who were Ethnan's half-brothers. Coz, named next in 1 Chr 4:8, is also treated here as a brother, though the text does not state his parentage directly. His name is usually taken to mean "gift" or "hire," as in Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Eubulus was a Christian who sent greetings to Timothy at the close of Paul's second letter to him (2 Tim 4:21). He is named alongside Pudens, Linus, Claudia and "all the brethren." Because the letter is usually understood to have been written while Paul was imprisoned in Rome, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take Eubulus to be a member of the church there. The ISBE adds that his Greek name suggests he was probably a Gentile by birth. The name means "prudent" or "good counselor," according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Nothing more is recorded about him, and this is his only mention in the Bible.

Eunice was the mother of Timothy (called Timotheus in the King James Version) and the daughter of Lois. Paul names her in 2 Tim 1:5, recalling the sincere faith that lived first in Lois, then in Eunice, and then in Timothy. Her name is Greek, meaning "good victory" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Acts 16:1, which tells how Paul found Timothy at Lystra, describes his mother as a Jewish believer and his father as a Greek, so she probably lived in Lystra. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia infers that she came to faith during Paul's first visit to the city. It also connects her with 2 Tim 3:15, which says Timothy had known the scriptures from childhood, and suggests she taught him there. Nothing more is recorded about her.

Euodias was a Christian woman in the church at Philippi. In Phil 4:2 Paul urges her and another woman, Syntyche, to "be of the same mind in the Lord." The appeal suggests the two had disagreed, though the letter does not say what the dispute was about. The next verse, Phil 4:3, speaks of women who "laboured with me in the gospel," and Easton's Bible Dictionary takes this to include Euodias, describing her as one who worked hard alongside Paul. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the name is more accurately spelled Euodia, the form used in the Revised Version and most modern translations. The name is usually explained as meaning "fragrant" or "sweet scent" (Smith's and Hitchcock's Bible Names), while Easton's gives "a good journey." She is mentioned nowhere else in the Bible.

Euphrates is the great river of western Asia, still known by that name, flowing from the mountains of eastern Turkey through Syria and Iraq to the Persian Gulf. Genesis names it as the fourth river of Eden (Gen 2:14). Often called simply "the river" or "the great river," it marks the northeastern limit of the land promised to Abram and Israel (Gen 15:18; Josh 1:4). David fought Hadadezer of Zobah at this border, and Solomon ruled the region west of it from Tiphsah to Gaza. At Carchemish on its banks, Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon defeated Pharaoh Necho (Jer 46:2). Jeremiah hid a linen belt by the river, and he had a scroll weighted with a stone and thrown into it, both as prophetic signs. Revelation describes angels bound at the river and its waters drying up for the kings of the east. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the name as "sweet water" or "the great stream." The location shown here lies on its middle course in eastern Syria.

Eutychus was a young man at Troas whose name means "fortunate" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). While Paul was preaching late into the night to the believers gathered in an upper room, Eutychus sat in a window, sank into a deep sleep, and fell from the third story. He "was taken up dead" (Acts 20:9). The surrounding passage (Acts 20:7–12) relates that Paul went down, embraced him and said his life was in him. The gathering then resumed and continued until daybreak, and the young man was brought away alive. Easton's Bible Dictionary compares the scene to the restorations performed by Elijah and Elisha. The episode is told in the "we" section of Acts, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes as an eyewitness account. It is dated here to about AD 54, an estimate inferred from context.

Eutychus revived refers to the incident at Troas during Paul's third missionary journey when a young man who had fallen to his death was restored to life. On the first day of the week the believers met in a crowded, lamp-lit upper room to break bread, and Paul, who planned to leave the next day, spoke until midnight. Eutychus, sitting in a window, sank into a deep sleep and fell from the third storey. He was picked up dead. Paul went down, lay on him and embraced him, and told the others not to be alarmed, because his life was in him. Paul then went back upstairs, broke bread, ate and talked until daybreak before leaving. The young man was brought in alive, to the great comfort of the group. The surrounding narrative is told in the first person plural, and its narrator is traditionally identified as Luke. The date, about AD 54, is inferred from context.

Eve was the first woman in the Bible, the wife of Adam and the mother of Cain, Abel and Seth. Her creation is described in Gen 2:21–22, where she is formed from Adam's side. Adam named her Eve "because she was the mother of all living" (Gen 3:20), and Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "life" or "living." Genesis 3 tells how the serpent deceived her into eating the forbidden fruit, which she also gave to Adam. Paul refers to this when he warns that the serpent "beguiled Eve through his subtilty" (2 Cor 11:3), and 1 Tim 2:13 notes that Adam was formed first, then Eve. When Cain was born she said, "I have gotten a man from the LORD" (Gen 4:1). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the biblical account of her closes with the birth of Seth.

Evi was one of five kings of Midian killed by the Israelites in the war against Midian near the end of Moses' life. Numbers 31:8 names him first among the five, with Rekem, Zur, Hur and Reba, and says Balaam son of Beor was killed at the same time. Joshua 13:21 recalls the same event when describing the land given to the tribe of Reuben. There Evi and the others are called princes of Midian and "dukes of Sihon," which suggests they were local rulers allied with or subject to Sihon, the Amorite king of Heshbon. According to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, the battle took place while Israel was camped on the plains of Moab. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "desire," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "unjust."

Evil-merodach was a king of Babylon who, in the first year of his reign, released Jehoiachin, the exiled king of Judah, from prison. This happened in the thirty-seventh year of Jehoiachin's captivity, in the twelfth month. 2 Kgs 25:27 gives the twenty-seventh day and Jer 52:31 the twenty-fifth. The verses that follow in both accounts say he spoke kindly to Jehoiachin, gave him a seat above the other kings with him, and provided for him at the royal table for the rest of his life. Reference works identify him as the son and successor of Nebuchadnezzar. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives his Babylonian name as Amel-Marduk, 'man of Marduk,' and says dated tablets show a reign of a little over two years. Easton's Bible Dictionary dates it about 562–560 BC. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionary both report that he was murdered by his brother-in-law Neriglissar, who succeeded him.

The Exodus from Egypt was the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt under the leadership of Moses and Aaron, after 430 years living there (Exod 12:40). God charged the two brothers to bring Israel out (Exod 6:13), and when Pharaoh repeatedly hardened his heart and refused to let the people go, a series of plagues struck Egypt: water turned to blood, frogs, boils, hail, locusts and three days of darkness. The last was the death at midnight, against which each Israelite household killed an unblemished lamb and marked its doorposts with the blood at the first Passover. The people left in haste, carrying their unleavened dough, and the day was to be remembered with the Feast of Unleavened Bread. God then led them away from the nearer road through Philistine territory. This entry dates the departure to about 1491 BC, by inference from context.

Ezbai was the father of Naarai, one of the warriors listed among David's mighty men in 1 Chr 11:37. Nothing else is said about him, and he appears only in this verse. The parallel list in 2 Sam 23:35 has "Paarai the Arbite" at this point, so many readers take Naarai and Paarai to be the same man. By that comparison, "son of Ezbai" in Chronicles may correspond to "the Arbite" in Samuel, though how the two readings relate is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of the name as "shining," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds "blooming."

Ezbon was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, the first named of five sons of Bela, Benjamin's firstborn. In 1 Chr 7:7 he and his brothers Uzzi, Uzziel, Jerimoth and Iri are called heads of their fathers' houses and mighty men of valour, and their family line is counted at 22,034 fighting men. A separate list of Bela's sons in 1 Chr 8:3–5 gives different names, among them Addar, Gera, Abihud, Abishua, Naaman and Ahoah, and those are counted here as his brothers as well. Ezbon does not appear in that second list. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with Ezbon the son of Gad (Gen 46:16). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "hastening to understand," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "working."

Ezekiel was a priest and prophet, the son of Buzi, who received the word of the LORD while living among the Jewish exiles in the land of the Chaldeans by the river Chebar (Ezek 1:3). The book of Ezekiel is attributed to him. Easton's Bible Dictionary places him among the captives taken to Babylon with King Jehoiachin, about 597 BC, and his prophetic activity is dated here to about 593 BC, by inference from context. According to the same dictionary, he had a house in exile, was often consulted by the elders, and lost his wife suddenly. God made Ezekiel himself a sign to the people: what he did, they would do, and when it happened they would know that he was the Lord GOD (Ezek 24:24). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "the strength of God." The time and manner of his death are not recorded.

Ezem was a town in the far south of Judah, in the Negev region, that was later given to the tribe of Simeon. The King James Version spells it Azem in Joshua. It appears in the list of Judah's southernmost towns near the border with Edom (Josh 15:29), again among the towns of Simeon's inheritance, which lay within Judah's territory (Josh 19:3), and among the places where Simeon's descendants lived (1 Chr 4:29). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a bone." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some identify Ezem with Azmon, a point on Judah's southern border. The text gives no further details, and the exact site has not been securely identified. The location shown here is only a rough placement.

Ezer was a Horite chief, one of the sons of Seir the Horite, the native people of the land of Seir, later Edom. He is listed with his brothers Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon and Dishan, and is named among the "dukes" (clan chiefs) descended from Hori (Gen 36:21, 30; 1 Chr 1:38). His sons were Bilhan, Zaavan and Akan. 1 Chr 1:42 spells the last two Zavan and Jakan. Timna appears among his siblings because Gen 36:22 calls her Lotan's sister, which makes her a daughter of Seir by inference. Hitchcock's Bible Names and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of his name as "help." Several other people in the Bible share the name, and this Ezer should not be confused with them.

Ezer was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:4 as one of the sons of Hur, the firstborn of Ephratah and "father of Bethlehem." He is called "the father of Hushah," which may mean he was the ancestor or founder of the town or clan of Hushah rather than the father of a person, a common usage in these lists. The STEPBible proper-names index describes him as the "father or founder" of Hushah. The name probably means "help," as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Hitchcock's Bible Names give it. Several other men in the Bible share the name Ezer, and nothing beyond this single genealogical mention is recorded about him. His relationship to the other sons of Hur listed with him, such as Penuel, rests on the grouping in this genealogy.

Ezer was a son of Ephraim and so a member of the tribe of Joseph. He is mentioned only in 1 Chr 7:21, which says that he and Elead were killed by the men of Gath who were born in that land, because they had come down to take the people of Gath's cattle. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes these men of Gath as the original inhabitants of the land. The wording of the genealogy leaves it slightly unclear whether Ezer was Ephraim's son or a later descendant, but this entry follows the reading that he was Ephraim's own son. The following verses (1 Chr 7:22–23) say that Ephraim mourned many days and later had another son, Beriah, named because of this trouble. His other brothers include Shuthelah, Becher and Tahan. His name means "help" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Several other people in the Bible share the name Ezer.

Ezer was a warrior from the tribe of Gad who joined David while David was an outlaw avoiding King Saul. He is listed first among eleven Gadite leaders in 1 Chr 12:9. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 12:8) describes these Gadites as men of war who crossed over to David at his stronghold in the wilderness. It calls them skilled with shield and spear, with faces like lions and as swift as gazelles on the mountains. Because Ezer is named first, he was probably the chief or most senior of the group. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, meaning "help" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, belongs to several different men in the Bible, and this Ezer should not be confused with the others.

Ezer son of Jeshua was one of the men who rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah after the return from exile. Nehemiah 3:19 calls him "the ruler of Mizpah" and says he repaired a second section of the wall, facing the ascent to the armoury where the wall turned. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify him as a Levite. This probably follows from the surrounding passage, which lists Levites among the builders working on this stretch of the wall. His father Jeshua may be the Levite of that name mentioned elsewhere in Nehemiah, but this is not certain. The name Ezer, meaning "help" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Hitchcock's Bible Names, is borne by several different men in the Bible, and this Ezer is known only from this one verse.

Ezer was one of the men named at the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. He is the last in a list of eight names given in Neh 12:42, alongside Maaseiah, Shemaiah, Eleazar, Uzzi, Jehohanan, Malchijah and Elam. By inference from the context, this group belonged to one of the two great thanksgiving companies that processed on the wall, and it was linked with the singers led by Jezrahiah. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a priest, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a musician in one of those companies. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names takes to mean "a help." The event is usually dated to about 446 BC, an estimate inferred from context.

Ezion-geber was a city and harbour on the Gulf of Aqaba, the northeastern arm of the Red Sea, always named beside Elath (Eloth) in Edomite territory. During the wilderness journey Israel camped there before moving on to Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin, and later passed by it on the way toward Moab. Solomon built a fleet there, and Jehoshaphat's ships, built with the help of an ally to sail for Ophir's gold, were wrecked there before they set out. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries suggest the gulf once reached farther north, placing the city near the spring 'Ain el-Ghudyan, about 10–15 miles up the Arabah valley. The location shown here follows a different view, a site on the present shore at the head of the gulf, near modern Aqaba and Eilat. The name is traditionally explained as "giant's backbone."

Ezra was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:17, where he is the father of Jether, Mered, Epher and Jalon. The same verse goes on to say that "she bare" Miriam, Shammai and Ishbah, the father of Eshtemoa. The verse does not name this woman, and the following verse suggests the children belong to one of Mered's wives, so their exact place in the family is unclear. This Ezra is a different man from the well-known priest and scribe who led returning exiles to Jerusalem. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as meaning "help," a shortened form of Azariah, "the LORD has helped," and notes that the Hebrew spelling here differs slightly from that used for the scribe.

Ezra was a priest and scribe of the tribe of Levi who led a company of Jewish exiles from Babylon to Jerusalem in the reign of Artaxerxes king of Persia, about 459 BC according to Easton's Bible Dictionary. His genealogy calls him the son of Seraiah. Easton's suggests he may have been a grandson, and 1 Chr 6:14–15 makes Seraiah the father of Jehozadak (Josedech). Described as "a ready scribe in the law of Moses," Ezra received a royal letter letting him draw on the treasuries and appoint judges beyond the river. In Jerusalem he mourned the people's marriages to foreign wives and led an oath and an inquiry into the matter. Later, with Nehemiah the governor, he read the law aloud from a wooden platform and led the people in worship. Jewish tradition credits him with writing Ezra and Chronicles.

Ezra was a priest listed among the priests and Levites who came back from Babylon to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and the high priest Jeshua (Neh 12:1). He is distinct from the better-known Ezra the scribe, who arrived later. His name became the name of a priestly family: in the next generation, in the days of the high priest Joiakim, that family was headed by Meshullam (Neh 12:13). An Ezra also took part in the procession at the dedication of Jerusalem's wall (Neh 12:33). The STEPBible proper-names index treats him as the same man, and this entry follows that view, though the long gap in time leaves the identification open. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as a shortened form of Azariah, "the LORD has helped," and links him with the Azariah of Neh 10:2.

Ezri, son of Chelub, was the official in charge of the farm laborers who worked King David's fields and tilled the ground (1 Chr 27:26). He is named in a list of David's stewards, the men who managed the king's property, including his vineyards, olive groves, herds and storehouses. Nothing more is recorded about him. His name probably means "my help" or, in a fuller form, "help of the LORD," as Hitchcock's Bible Names and Easton's Bible Dictionary give it. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his service to about 1014 BC, an estimate drawn from the setting in David's reign. His father Chelub is otherwise unknown and should probably not be confused with the Chelub of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chr 4:11.

The Fasting Question was an exchange in which Jesus was asked why his disciples did not fast, recorded in Matthew, Mark and Luke. Matthew says the disciples of John the Baptist asked it, contrasting their own frequent fasting and that of the Pharisees with the practice of Jesus' followers. Mark and Luke leave the questioners less clearly identified, and Luke adds that John's disciples also made prayers while Jesus' disciples ate and drank. Jesus answered with an image from a wedding: the bridegroom's companions do not fast or mourn while he is with them, but days would come when he would be taken away, and then they would fast. In all three Gospels the episode directly follows the call of Matthew (Levi), so it probably took place at or near Capernaum, about AD 28 by inference from context.

The Feast of Dedication was the winter festival at Jerusalem during which Jesus walked in Solomon's Porch in the temple and was pressed by the Jews to say plainly whether he was the Christ (John 10:22–24). The feast, later known as Hanukkah, marked the rededication of the temple under Judas Maccabeus, as told in 1 Maccabees. Jesus replied that his works done in his Father's name bore witness to him, that his sheep hear his voice and receive eternal life, and that he and the Father are one. His hearers took up stones, charging him with blasphemy for making himself God. He answered by quoting the scripture "Ye are gods" (Ps 82:6) and urged them to believe the works, that the Father is in him and he in the Father. They tried again to seize him, but he escaped. This entry dates the episode to about December AD 29, by inference from context.

The Feast of Tabernacles here is the occasion in John 7 when Jesus went from Galilee to Jerusalem for this annual Jewish festival, about AD 29 by inference from context. Because some sought to kill him, he had stayed in Galilee. His unbelieving brothers urged him to show himself openly. He said his time had not yet come, then went up quietly after them. About the middle of the feast he taught in the temple, defending his sabbath healing by comparing it with sabbath circumcision. The crowds argued over whether he was the Christ or the Prophet. The Pharisees and chief priests sent officers to arrest him, but no one laid hands on him. He also spoke of rivers of living water, which John explains as the Spirit. Nicodemus, named in John 7:50, urged the Pharisees to hear a man before judging him.

The Feeding of Five Thousand was the miracle in which Jesus fed a large crowd with five loaves and two fishes, the only miracle of his ministry recorded in all four Gospels. After the apostles returned from their mission, and after Jesus heard of John the Baptist's death, he withdrew by boat to a remote place near Bethsaida on the Sea of Galilee. Crowds followed, and he taught and healed them. At evening the disciples urged him to send the people away to buy food. Philip reckoned that two hundred pennies' worth of bread would not be enough, and Andrew pointed out a boy with five barley loaves and two small fishes. Jesus had the people sit in groups on the grass, blessed and broke the food, and the disciples distributed it. About five thousand men ate, besides women and children, and twelve baskets of leftovers were gathered. John notes it was near Passover, about AD 29 by inference.

The Feeding of Four Thousand was a miracle in which Jesus fed a large crowd with seven loaves and a few small fish, recorded in Matt 15:32–39 and Mark 8:1–9. The crowd had stayed with him for three days without food, and some had come from far away. When his disciples asked where they could find enough bread in such a remote place, Jesus had the people sit on the ground, gave thanks, broke the bread and fish, and gave them to the disciples to hand out. Everyone ate their fill, and seven baskets of leftovers were collected. Matthew counts four thousand men besides women and children. Afterward Jesus sent the crowd away and left by boat for the region of Magdala. The setting is probably the Decapolis, by inference from Mark 7:31, and the date of about AD 29 is also inferred. It is a separate occasion from the feeding of the five thousand.

Felix was the Roman governor of Judea to whom Paul was sent under guard from Jerusalem, about AD 56 by inference from context. The commander Claudius Lysias addressed him in a letter as "most excellent governor" (Acts 23:24–26). Felix heard the Jewish leaders' charges and Paul's defense but, knowing more about "that way," postponed a decision until Lysias arrived. Later, with his Jewish wife Drusilla, he sent for Paul and heard him speak about faith in Christ. When Paul spoke of righteousness, self-control and coming judgment, Felix trembled and sent him away. Acts 24:26 adds that he hoped Paul would give him money. After two years Porcius Festus replaced him, and Felix left Paul in prison to please the Jews. Smith's Bible Dictionary says Claudius appointed him about AD 53 and that Drusilla was a daughter of Herod Agrippa I.

Field, the "fuller's field" (ESV "Washer's Field"), was a spot just outside Jerusalem where fullers washed and bleached cloth, an activity that needed a steady water supply. It lay beside a highway near the conduit of the upper pool. There Isaiah and his son Shearjashub were sent to meet King Ahaz (Isa 7:3). Years later the Assyrian officials Tartan, Rabsaris and Rabshakeh, sent from Lachish with an army, stood at the same place to confront King Hezekiah's men (2 Kgs 18:17; Isa 36:2). Its exact position is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it west of the city, near the upper pool at the head of the Hinnom Valley. Others place the upper pool north of the city or near the Gihon spring to the east. The rough location shown here follows the western placement near the Hinnom Valley.

The Fig Tree Cursed was an incident during Holy Week, the morning after the Triumphal Entry, probably in AD 30 by inference from context. After visiting the temple, Jesus spent the night at Bethany with the twelve. The next morning, on the way back into Jerusalem across the Mount of Olives, he was hungry. He saw a fig tree in leaf and went to it, but it had nothing on it except leaves. Mark adds that it was not yet the season for figs. Jesus said that no one would ever eat fruit from it again, and his disciples heard him. Matthew reports that the tree withered at once. Mark's account sets the curse before the cleansing of the temple, and the following verses there, not quoted here, describe the disciples seeing the withered tree the next morning.

The First Disciples Gathered is John's account of how Jesus' earliest followers came to him, about AD 27 by inference from context, just after John the Baptist's testimony. When John pointed to Jesus as "the Lamb of God," two of his disciples followed Jesus and spent the day with him. One was Andrew, who then brought his brother Simon. Jesus renamed Simon Cephas, meaning "a stone." The other disciple is unnamed, and by long tradition he is identified as John the Apostle. The next day, as Jesus set out for Galilee, he called Philip of Bethsaida, the hometown of Andrew and Peter. Philip brought Nathanael, who doubted that anything good could come from Nazareth. When Jesus said he had seen him under the fig tree, Nathanael called him the Son of God and King of Israel, and Jesus promised he would see greater things.

The First Missionary Journey was the first extended preaching tour of Barnabas and Paul (then called Saul), recorded in Acts 13–14. After the pair returned from Jerusalem with John Mark (Acts 12:25), the church at Antioch in Syria fasted, prayed, laid hands on them and sent them out. They sailed from Seleucia to Cyprus and preached in the synagogues of Salamis, with John as their helper. At Paphos the governor Sergius Paulus heard them, and a sorcerer who opposed them was struck blind. John left them at Perga in Pamphylia (Acts 13:13). They went on to Antioch in Pisidia, where Paul preached in the synagogue, and then to Iconium, Lystra and Derbe. At Lystra, after Paul healed a man, crowds tried to sacrifice to them, and Paul was later stoned. They returned to strengthen the new disciples and sailed from Attalia back to Antioch. This entry dates the journey to about AD 45, lasting about a year, by inference from context.

The First missionary journey begins with the commissioning of Barnabas and Saul (Paul) by the church at Antioch in Syria. After Barnabas and Saul returned from their errand in Jerusalem, bringing John Mark with them, they were among the prophets and teachers at Antioch, along with Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, and Manaen, who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch. While these leaders were worshipping and fasting, the Holy Spirit told them to set apart Barnabas and Saul for the work to which he had called them. After more fasting and prayer, the church laid hands on the two men and sent them off. The commissioning follows the account of Herod's death and the note that the word of God kept spreading. It is dated to about AD 45, by inference from context.

The First Passover and Temple Cleansing took place early in Jesus' ministry, when he went up to Jerusalem for Passover and found people selling cattle, sheep and doves in the temple, along with money changers.
