He made a whip of cords, drove them out, scattered the coins, overturned the tables, and said his Father's house must not become a marketplace. His disciples recalled the words of Ps 69:9 about zeal for God's house. When the Jews asked for a sign, he said, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." John explains that he meant his body, which the disciples understood after his resurrection. Many believed because of his miracles, though Jesus did not entrust himself to them. The other Gospels describe a similar cleansing in his final week. Some see two events, others one. This entry follows John's placement and dates it to about AD 27, by inference.

The Fish Gate was a gate in the wall of Jerusalem. Its name probably comes from a fish market nearby, perhaps where traders from the coast sold their catch, as Neh 13:16 describes Tyrians doing. King Manasseh, who is the "he" of 2 Chr 33:14 by context, built an outer wall west of Gihon that ran as far as the Fish Gate. After the exile, the sons of Hassenaah rebuilt it, setting its beams, doors, locks and bars. Zephaniah foretold a cry of distress rising from it on the day of the LORD. Nehemiah's account of the rebuilding moves west from the Sheep Gate, so the Fish Gate is usually placed on the city's north side, the direction from which attackers most often approached. Its exact site is uncertain, and the location shown here is approximate.

The Fishers of Men was Jesus' call of his first disciples beside the Sea of Galilee, dated to about AD 27 by inference from context, after his time in Capernaum. Matthew and Mark relate that Jesus saw the brothers Simon Peter and Andrew casting a net and said, "Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men." They left their nets at once. A little further on he called James and John, sons of Zebedee, who were mending nets in a boat. They left their father with the hired servants and followed him. Luke's account, set at the lake of Gennesaret (another name for the same lake), adds that Jesus taught the crowd from Simon's boat and then told him to let down his nets after a fruitless night. The catch broke the nets and nearly sank two boats. Jesus told Simon he would now catch men, and they left everything. Whether Luke describes the same occasion is debated. This entry treats the accounts together.

Forest, more fully the House of the Forest, appears in Isa 22:8 as the place where Judah's armour was stored. Isaiah says that when Judah's defences were laid bare, the people looked to the weapons kept there. By inference from connected passages, this is the House of the Forest of Lebanon, a large hall Solomon built in Jerusalem. 1 Kgs 7:2 describes it as supported by rows of cedar pillars, which probably explains the name. 1 Kgs 10:17 says Solomon placed gold shields in it, which fits its use as an armoury. The building no longer survives, so its exact position is unknown. The location shown here places it within Jerusalem, near the royal and temple quarter. The Hebrew word for "forest" also has its ordinary meaning elsewhere, but this entry concerns only the building.

The Forest of Ephraim was a wooded region where David's troops fought and defeated the army of Israel that had rallied behind his son Absalom (2 Sam 18:6). The fighting spread across the whole countryside, and the text says the forest itself killed more men that day than the sword did (2 Sam 18:8). The surrounding chapter adds that twenty thousand fell and that Absalom was caught by his head in an oak there, where Joab killed him. Because David was at Mahanaim and Absalom had camped in Gilead (2 Sam 17:24–26), the forest probably lay east of the Jordan, even though the tribe of Ephraim's own territory was west of it. How it got the name is uncertain. Some place it west of the Jordan within Ephraim. The location shown here follows the Gilead identification, in the wooded hills of what is now northern Jordan.

The Foretelling the Death and Resurrection was the occasion when Jesus first openly taught his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem, suffer many things from the elders, chief priests and scribes, be killed, and rise again on the third day (Matt 16:21; Mark 8:31; Luke 9:22). It followed Peter's confession, near Caesarea Philippi, about AD 29 by inference from context. Peter took Jesus aside and rebuked him, saying this must not happen. Jesus answered, "Get thee behind me, Satan," because Peter was thinking in human terms rather than God's (Mark 8:33). Jesus then told the disciples and the crowd that anyone who wished to follow him must deny himself and take up his cross, and that whoever saves his life will lose it. He spoke of the Son of Man coming in his Father's glory with the angels, and said some standing there would not die before seeing the kingdom.

Fortunatus was a member of the church at Corinth who, with Stephanas and Achaicus, came to Paul while he was writing 1 Corinthians. Paul says he was glad they had come, because they had supplied what was lacking on the Corinthians' part (1 Cor 16:17). The following verse speaks of their refreshing his spirit. Paul was probably at Ephesus at the time, since he says in 1 Cor 16:8 that he will stay there until Pentecost. Easton's Bible Dictionary adds that the three men probably carried the letter back to Corinth. His name is Latin and means "fortunate" or "blessed." Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that a Fortunatus is named at the end of Clement's first letter to the Corinthians, an early Christian writing outside the Bible, and suggests he may be the same man. He appears only once in the Bible.

Gaal was the son of Ebed. He came to Shechem with his brothers during the rule of Abimelech, the son of Gideon (Jerubbaal), and the men of Shechem put their trust in him (Judg 9:26). He openly challenged Abimelech's right to rule, urging the Shechemites to serve the descendants of Hamor instead (Judg 9:28). Zebul, the city's governor, was angered and secretly warned Abimelech that Gaal was fortifying the city against him (Judg 9:30–31). When Abimelech's men came out of ambush, Gaal at first took them for shadows on the mountains, as Zebul suggested. He then led the Shechemites out to fight but was defeated, and Zebul drove him and his brothers out of Shechem (Judg 9:35–41). Nothing more is recorded of him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "contempt", and Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "loathing".

Gaash was a hill in the hill country of Ephraim. Joshua was buried on its north side, within his own inheritance at Timnath-serah, which Judg 2:9 calls Timnath-heres (Josh 24:30). The "brooks of Gaash" were the home of one of David's mighty warriors, named Hiddai in 2 Sam 23:30 and Hurai in the parallel list at 1 Chr 11:32. These are probably two spellings of the same man's name. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests that these brooks, better understood as seasonal streambeds or wadis, lay at the foot of the hill. The name is often explained as meaning "shaking" or "earthquake." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that no likely identification of the site has been proposed, so the location shown here is only approximate, placed near Timnath-serah in Ephraim.

Gabbai was a man of the tribe of Benjamin named in the list of those who settled in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. In Neh 11:8 he appears with Sallai, following Sallu son of Meshullam, and together they are counted with 928 people. By inference from the context of the chapter, Gabbai and Sallai were leaders or heads of Benjamite families who lived in the city. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as apparently the head of an important Benjaminite family resident at Jerusalem, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him one of the chiefs of the Benjamites there. The name is usually explained as meaning "collector" or "tax gatherer." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Gabbatha was the place in Jerusalem where Pilate sat on the judgment seat to give his verdict at the trial of Jesus. John 19:13 calls it in Greek "the Pavement" and gives Gabbatha as its Hebrew (probably Aramaic) name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take to mean "height" or "ridge." The Pavement was probably a stone-paved or mosaic platform outside the governor's residence, since Pilate brought Jesus out to it. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on the temple mount by the fortress of Antonia, and a long tradition links it with a stretch of Roman paving near the "Ecce Homo" arch. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it on the western hill, by Herod's palace. The location shown here is approximate and follows the temple-mount view.

Gabriel is an angel named in the books of Daniel and Luke, the only angel besides Michael named in the Bible. In Daniel he appears in human form. A voice beside the Ulai river tells him to make Daniel understand a vision, which Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies as the vision of the ram and the goat. Later, while Daniel is praying at the time of the evening offering, Gabriel comes to him swiftly and touches him, and the surrounding passage records his message about the seventy weeks. In Luke he identifies himself as one who stands in God's presence. He is sent to announce good news to the priest Zacharias, which the context shows is the coming birth of John the Baptist. Six months later he is sent to Nazareth in Galilee, to Mary, to announce the birth of Jesus. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Scripture never calls him an archangel. His name is variously explained as "man of God" or "God is my strength."

Gad was the seventh son of Jacob and the first son of Zilpah, Leah's servant, making him the full brother of Asher. He was born in Paddan-aram, about 1753 BC by inference from context. Leah named him, and the King James Version explains the name as "a troop," while Easton's Bible Dictionary prefers "fortune" (Gen 30:11). Little is recorded about Gad himself. He went down to Egypt with Jacob's family along with seven sons, whose names appear in slightly different forms in Gen 46:16 and Num 26:15. Jacob's deathbed blessing plays on his name, saying a troop would attack him but he would overcome in the end. He was the ancestor of the tribe of Gad, a herding tribe that settled in Gilead east of the Jordan. The name is also borne by others, including a prophet of David's time.

Gad was a prophet in David's time, called "David's seer" or "the king's seer" (2 Sam 24:11; 2 Chr 29:25). While David was a fugitive from Saul, Gad told him to leave his stronghold for Judah, and David went to the forest of Hareth. Years later, after David counted the people, Gad brought him the LORD's choice of three punishments: famine, flight from enemies, or plague. When the plague ended, Gad told David to build an altar on the threshing floor of Araunah, called Ornan in Chronicles. Chronicles credits him with a book recording David's acts and a share in commanding the Levites' music in the temple. Jewish tradition holds that Gad and Nathan completed the books of Samuel, which is why this entry names him as a writer of them. He is distinct from Jacob's son Gad and others of that name.

Gad was the territory east of the Jordan given to the tribe of Gad. Moses assigned it to them, along with Reuben and half the tribe of Manasseh, from the conquered kingdoms of Sihon and Og (Num 32:33; Josh 13:8). Joshua 13:24–28 describes it as including Jazer, the cities of Gilead, and half the land of the Ammonites as far as Aroer near Rabbah. It also ran from Heshbon to Mahanaim and took in the Jordan valley towns of Beth-haram, Beth-nimrah, Succoth and Zaphon, up to the Sea of Chinnereth. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it roughly in the center of the land east of the Jordan, north of Reuben and around the Jabbok. The location shown here lies in that part of central Gilead, in present-day Jordan. The Gadites also built Dibon and Aroer farther south (Num 32:34). Jeremiah 49:1 speaks of the Ammonite king taking possession of Gad, and Ezekiel's vision gives Gad a new southern portion (Ezek 48:27–28).

The Gadarene Demoniacs episode is the account of Jesus freeing demon-possessed men after crossing the Sea of Galilee, dated here to about AD 28 by inference from context. Mark and Luke place it in the country of the Gadarenes, opposite Galilee, and describe one man. Matthew says the Gergesenes and mentions two men. The possessed man lived among the tombs, broke every chain used to restrain him, cried out night and day, and cut himself with stones. When Jesus commanded the spirit to leave, it gave its name as Legion, "for we are many." The spirits asked to enter a nearby herd of pigs, about two thousand, which then rushed down a steep bank into the sea and drowned. The herders spread the news, and the frightened local people begged Jesus to leave. The healed man asked to go with him. Jesus sent him home instead, and he told of what Jesus had done throughout the Decapolis.

Gaddi, son of Susi, was the man chosen from the tribe of Manasseh, which is counted here as part of the tribe of Joseph, to be one of the twelve men Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan (Num 13:11). The surrounding chapter shows that each tribe supplied one leader for this mission. Nothing more is recorded about him. By inference from the chapter, he would have been among the ten scouts whose discouraging report led the people to refuse to enter the land, since only Joshua and Caleb are singled out as giving a favorable account. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "fortunate," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "my fortune."

Gaddiel son of Sodi was the man from the tribe of Zebulun among the twelve men Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan (Num 13:10). The surrounding chapter describes the twelve as tribal leaders sent from the wilderness of Paran. Only Joshua and Caleb are named later for urging Israel to go in, so Gaddiel was probably among the ten whose discouraging report turned the people against entering the land, as Numbers 13–14 recounts. He is not mentioned anywhere else. His name is usually explained as "fortune of God" (Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary) or "blessed of God" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia).

Gadi was the father of Menahem, who seized the throne of the northern kingdom of Israel. He is known only from the phrase "Menahem the son of Gadi" in 2 Kgs 15:14 and 15:17, which tell how Menahem came up from Tirzah to Samaria, killed King Shallum son of Jabesh and reigned in his place. Menahem began to reign in the thirty-ninth year of Azariah king of Judah and ruled ten years in Samaria. Nothing else is recorded about Gadi himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "fortunate," and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Gadite, that is, a member of the tribe of Gad, a view probably drawn from the form of the name.

Gaham was a son of Nahor, the brother of Abraham, by Nahor's concubine Reumah. He is named only once, in Gen 22:24, in the list of Nahor's children reported to Abraham after the testing of Isaac. His full brothers and sister were Tebah, Thahash and Maachah. Through Nahor's wife Milcah he had eight half-brothers, among them Huz, Buz, Kemuel and Bethuel, the father of Rebekah. Nothing else is recorded about him, and no descendants are named. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "sunburnt" and dates him to about 1900 BC. Like other dates for this period, that figure is an estimate inferred from context.

Gahar was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants returned to Jerusalem from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel. The "children of Gahar" appear in the list of returning families in Ezra 2:47 and again in the parallel list in Neh 7:49. In both lists they are named next to the family of Giddel. That these families were temple servants, and that they returned under Zerubbabel, comes from the surrounding context of the lists. Nothing else is recorded about Gahar himself. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "lurking-place," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "hiding-place." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same family is called Geddur in 1 Esdras 5:30.

Gaius (of Macedonia) was a man from Macedonia who traveled with the apostle Paul. During the riot in Ephesus, stirred up by the silversmith Demetrius according to the wider account in Acts 19, the crowd seized Gaius and his fellow Macedonian Aristarchus and rushed them into the city's theater (Acts 19:29). Smith's Bible Dictionary and others suggest the mob took them because Paul himself could not be found. The riot took place during Paul's third missionary journey, about AD 53 by inference from context. Nothing more is said of what happened to Gaius. The name Gaius was common, and several men called Gaius appear in the New Testament. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies this Gaius with Paul's host at Corinth (Rom 16:23; 1 Cor 1:14). Others treat them as different people, and this entry follows that view.

Gaius (of Derbe) was one of the companions who travelled with Paul on his last journey toward Jerusalem, at the end of his mission through Macedonia and Greece. Acts 20:4 lists him with Sopater of Berea, Aristarchus and Secundus of Thessalonica, Timothy, and Tychicus and Trophimus of Asia, all of whom went with Paul into Asia. The group probably carried the collection from the churches for the believers in Jerusalem, by inference from the context of Paul's travels. Derbe was a town in Lycaonia in southern Asia Minor that Paul had visited earlier (Acts 14:20). The New Testament names several men called Gaius, including a Macedonian companion of Paul at Ephesus (Acts 19:29), a Corinthian whom Paul baptised (1 Cor 1:14), and the recipient of 3 John. Whether any of them is the same person is uncertain. This entry treats Gaius of Derbe separately. The journey is dated about AD 54, by inference from context.

Gaius was a Christian at Corinth, one of the few people there whom Paul baptized personally, alongside Crispus (1 Cor 1:14). In Rom 16:23 a Gaius sends greetings and is called Paul's host and host of the whole church. Since Paul probably wrote Romans from Corinth, this entry follows the common view that the two references describe the same man, a believer whose home received Paul and served as a meeting place for the congregation. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both take this view. Several other men named Gaius appear in the New Testament, including a Macedonian companion of Paul seized by the crowd at Ephesus and the recipient of 3 John. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects the Corinthian host with the Macedonian traveller. How these figures relate to one another is uncertain. The name, a common Roman one, means "lord" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Gaius was the Christian to whom the letter known as 3 John is addressed. The writer calls himself "the elder" and greets Gaius as "wellbeloved," one whom he loves "in the truth" (3 John 1:1). Christian tradition identifies the elder as the apostle John. Easton's Bible Dictionary places Gaius in Asia Minor. The rest of the letter praises him for staying faithful to the truth and for welcoming travelling Christian workers, as the STEPBible proper-names index also notes. The name was common in the Roman world, and several men called Gaius appear in the New Testament, including companions of Paul in Macedonia, Derbe and Corinth. Whether this Gaius is any of them is uncertain, so this entry treats him as a separate person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "lord" or "an earthly man."

Galal was a Levite named in 1 Chr 9:15 among the Levites who lived in Jerusalem, in a list that by context describes the community resettled there after the Babylonian exile. He appears alongside Bakbakkar, Heresh and Mattaniah, the son of Micah, whose descent is traced back to Asaph. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts Galal himself among the sons of Asaph, and the STEPBible Proper Names index describes him as a Levite musician descended from Asaph. The verse does not state his own ancestry, so that link rests on how the list is read. Smith's dates him to about 536 BC, an estimate drawn from the setting rather than stated in the text. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a roll, a wheel." Several men in the Bible bear the name Galal, and this entry covers only the one in 1 Chr 9:15.

Galal was a Levite, the son of Jeduthun and father of Shemaiah. He appears only in genealogies of the Levites who lived in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. 1 Chr 9:16 names his grandson Obadiah, son of Shemaiah. The parallel list in Neh 11:17 names a grandson Abda, son of Shammua. Shammua and Shemaiah are probably the same person, and Obadiah and Abda the same descendant. Jeduthun is elsewhere known as a leader of temple music, so Galal's family probably served among the temple singers, as the STEPBible Proper Names describes him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia distinguishes him from another Levite named Galal mentioned just before, in 1 Chr 9:15. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a roll" or "a wheel."

Galatia was a region in central Asia Minor, in modern Turkey. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains that its name comes from Gaulish (Celtic) settlers who arrived about 280 BC, and that it became a Roman province in 25 BC. Paul passed through "the region of Galatia" with Phrygia on his second journey (Acts 16:6). He later went through it again, strengthening the disciples (Acts 18:23). He wrote to "the churches of Galatia" (Gal 1:2) and directed them about a collection for the saints (1 Cor 16:1). Crescens later went there (2 Tim 4:10), and Peter addressed scattered believers in Galatia and neighboring provinces (1 Pet 1:1). Scholars differ over whether the name means the old Gaulish territory around Ankara in the north or the larger Roman province, which also included southern cities such as Iconium and Lystra. The location shown here, in the south near Iconium, fits the wider provincial sense.

Galeed was the name Jacob gave to a heap of stones that he and Laban set up as a witness to the agreement between them when they parted (Gen 31:47–48). The name is Hebrew and means "heap of witness." Laban called the same heap Jegar-sahadutha, which Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies as the Aramaic equivalent, reflecting the language of Laban's family in Mesopotamia. Laban declared that the heap would stand as a witness between the two men. Smith's Bible Dictionary places the cairn on Mount Gilead, where the surrounding narrative sets the meeting, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the story may hint at how the name Gilead came to be applied to that region. The exact site is not known. The location shown here places it in the hill country of Gilead, east of the Jordan in present-day northern Jordan.

Galilee was the northern region of the land of Israel; its Hebrew name means "circuit" or "district" (Easton's Bible Dictionary). In the Old Testament it lay in the hill country of Naphtali, where Kedesh was a city of refuge (Josh 20:7). Solomon gave Hiram of Tyre twenty of its cities, and the Assyrian Tiglath-pileser later captured it and deported its people. Isaiah calls it "Galilee of the nations," which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes as a reference to its mixed population. In the New Testament it was a province ruled by Herod as tetrarch. It held Nazareth, Cana and Capernaum. Jesus grew up there and taught and healed throughout it, his first miracle was at Cana, many of his disciples came from there, and after his resurrection he met the eleven on a mountain there. The location shown here is a central point within the region.

Gallim was a town, probably in the territory of Benjamin north of Jerusalem. It was the home of Phalti son of Laish, to whom Saul gave his daughter Michal, David's wife, while David was a fugitive (1 Sam 25:44). The same man is called Paltiel in 2 Sam 3:15. Gallim appears again in Isaiah's description of an Assyrian army advancing on Jerusalem, where it is named alongside Laish (Laishah) and Anathoth as towns crying out in alarm (Isa 10:30). Smith's Bible Dictionary connects this passage with Sennacherib's approach. Its exact site is unknown. Smith's Bible Dictionary says there is no clue to its position. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that many link it with the Gilgal on Judah's northern border. The location shown here follows the view of Easton's Bible Dictionary and Tyndale House that it lay in Benjamin, placing it near Anathoth. Easton's gives the name's meaning as "heaps."

Gallio was the Roman "deputy" (proconsul) of Achaia when Paul was working in Corinth. Some Jews of the city rose up together against Paul and brought him before Gallio's judgment seat. Before Paul could speak, Gallio told the accusers that he would hear them if the case involved a real wrong or crime. The surrounding verses show that he regarded the dispute as a question of their own law and dismissed it. Afterward the Greeks beat Sosthenes, the chief ruler of the synagogue, in front of the court, and "Gallio cared for none of those things." Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him as the elder brother of the philosopher Seneca and notes that contemporaries described him as affable. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia dates his term of office to about AD 51–53.

Gamad is known only from Ezek 27:11, where the Gammadim (the people of Gamad) stood in the towers of Tyre and hung their shields on its walls. They appear next to the men of Arvad in Ezekiel's lament over the city. Whether Gamad was a place or a description of a group is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary reads the word as a term for a class of fighting men, such as "brave warriors," "valorous men," "short-swordsmen" or "daring ones," who defended Tyre's towers. Others take it as the name of a people or town that supplied soldiers to Tyre. The location shown here is rough. It places Gamad on the Syrian coast near Arvad, probably by inference from the two being named together in the verse.

Gamaliel, son of Pedahzur, was the leader of the tribe of Manasseh during Israel's time in the wilderness. He was one of the tribal heads named to help Moses and Aaron take the census of Israel at Sinai (Num 1:10). In the arrangement of the camp he was captain of Manasseh, which camped beside Ephraim on the west side of the tabernacle (Num 2:20). At the dedication of the altar he brought his tribe's offering on the eighth day, the same gifts each tribal leader presented, including peace offerings of oxen, rams, goats and lambs (Num 7:54, 59). When Israel set out from Sinai, he commanded Manasseh's company on the march (Num 10:23). His name means "recompense of God" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary. He is a different person from the Pharisee and teacher of the law named Gamaliel in the New Testament.

Gamaliel was a Pharisee and teacher of the law in Jerusalem in the first century AD, respected by all the people and a member of the council (the Sanhedrin). When the apostles were brought before the council for preaching, he had them sent out briefly and then advised caution (Acts 5:34). The surrounding passage records his argument that if their work was of human origin it would fail, but if it was from God it could not be overthrown. The council followed his advice and released the apostles after a beating, an event dated here to about AD 30 by inference from context. Paul later said he had been brought up in Jerusalem "at the feet of Gamaliel" and trained strictly in the law (Acts 22:3). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify him with the famous rabbi Gamaliel, grandson of Hillel. The name is also borne by an earlier Israelite, a leader of the tribe of Manasseh in Numbers.

event: Gamaliel advises the counsel and Apostles freed
text: Gamaliel advises the counsel and Apostles freed is the episode in which the Jewish council in Jerusalem released the apostles after a trial. Gamaliel, a Pharisee and teacher of the law respected by all the people, had the apostles taken outside and then warned the council to be careful. He pointed to two earlier movements, one led by Theudas with about four hundred followers and one led by Judas of Galilee at the time of the census. Both leaders died and their followers scattered. He advised leaving the apostles alone: if their work was merely human it would fail, but if it was from God the council could not stop it and might find itself fighting God. The council agreed. It had the apostles beaten, ordered them not to speak in Jesus' name, and let them go. They left rejoicing and kept teaching daily in the temple and in homes. By inference from context, this took place about AD 30.

Gamul was a priest whose family received the twenty-second of the twenty-four priestly divisions when the courses of service at the sanctuary were assigned by lot (1 Chr 24:17). The surrounding chapter places this arrangement in the time of King David, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes Gamul as head of that course. Each division took its turn serving at the house of the Lord. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name is usually understood to mean "weaned" (Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary), while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a recompense."

Gareb was one of David's mighty warriors, named in the lists of David's elite fighting men (2 Sam 23:38; 1 Chr 11:40). Both lists call him an Ithrite and place him next to Ira, another Ithrite. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains "Ithrite" as a member of the Ithrite family, one of the clans of Kiriath-jearim (1 Chr 2:53). It also notes that some read the word slightly differently, which would make him a native of the town of Jattir. Nothing else is recorded about his life or deeds. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a scab." The same name appears in Jer 31:39 for a hill near Jerusalem, but that is a place and is separate from this warrior.

Gareb was a hill near Jerusalem, mentioned only in Jer 31:39. In Jeremiah's prophecy of the city's rebuilding, a measuring line would run out over the hill Gareb and then around to Goath, marking a wider boundary for the restored city. By inference from the passage, the hill then lay outside or at the edge of the city. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a scab," and Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it was probably the hill of lepers, which would explain its place outside the city. The STEPBible proper names index describes it as a hill that was to be brought within Jerusalem's future boundaries. Its exact site is unknown. Some place it to the west or northwest of the ancient city, though this is uncertain. The location shown here is a general point within Jerusalem.

Garmite is a name in the tribe of Judah's genealogy at 1 Chr 4:19, which lists the sons of Hodiah, sister of Naham, as "the father of Keilah the Garmite, and Eshtemoa the Maachathite." The wording is obscure, and readings differ. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes "Garmite" to mean a descendant of Gerem, a label attached to Keilah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also treats it as a clan name applied to Keilah, and says the reason is unknown. This entry treats Garmite as a son of Hodiah and Mered and a brother of Eshtemoa. Hodiah's husband is inferred to be Mered from the surrounding verses. Through Mered's other wife, Bithiah, Pharaoh's daughter, he would be a half-brother of Miriam, Shammai and Ishbah (1 Chr 4:17–18). Nothing else is recorded about him.

Gatam was a son of Eliphaz and so a grandson of Esau, since Eliphaz was Esau's son by his wife Adah (Gen 36:10, the verse just before the list). He is named fourth among Eliphaz's sons, after Teman, Omar and Zepho and before Kenaz (Gen 36:11; 1 Chr 1:36). In Gen 36:16 he appears among the "dukes", or clan chiefs, descended from Eliphaz in the land of Edom, alongside his brothers Korah and Amalek. This suggests that Gatam was the ancestor and head of an Edomite clan that bore his name. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him somewhat after 1760 BC, an estimate drawn from context. The meaning of his name is uncertain: Smith's gives "a burnt valley", while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "their lowing" or "their touch". Nothing more is recorded about him.

Gate Miphkad, called the Muster Gate in the ESV, was a gate of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. It is mentioned only once, in the list of workers who rebuilt the city wall after the return from exile. Malchiah, a goldsmith's son, repaired the stretch of wall as far as the house of the temple servants (the Nethinim) and of the merchants, opposite this gate, and up to the upper room at the corner (Neh 3:31). The Hebrew name probably means "appointment" or "mustering," which suggests a place where people were counted or assembled, though the text does not explain its use. Since the list runs around the wall in order, the gate was probably on the east side of the city, north of the temple area and near the wall's northeast corner. Its exact position is uncertain, and the location shown here is an approximate placement within Jerusalem.

The Gate of Benjamin was a gate of Jerusalem in the time of Jeremiah. Its name probably comes from the fact that it faced the tribal territory of Benjamin, which lay north of the city. The passage suggests this, since Jeremiah was arrested there by the guard captain Irijah while leaving the city and was accused of deserting to the Babylonians (Jer 37:13). Jer 20:2 calls it the "high gate of Benjamin" beside the house of the LORD, where the priest Pashur put Jeremiah in the stocks. The king, Zedekiah by inference from context, was sitting in this gate when Ebedmelech came to plead for Jeremiah (Jer 38:7). Zech 14:10 uses it as a landmark marking the extent of a restored Jerusalem. Its exact position is uncertain. The location shown here places it on the north side of the city near the Temple area.

The Gate of Ephraim was a gate in the wall of Jerusalem. When Jehoash (also called Joash), king of Israel, defeated and captured Amaziah, king of Judah, at Beth-shemesh, he came to Jerusalem and broke down a 400-cubit stretch of the city wall, about 600 feet (180 m), from the Gate of Ephraim to the Corner Gate (2 Kgs 14:13; 2 Chr 25:23). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on the side of the city facing the territory of Ephraim, which is the north side. That fits its name, which probably refers to the road leading out toward Ephraim. A gate of the same name appears in Nehemiah's account of the restored city (Neh 8:16; 12:39), probably the same gate, though this is not certain. Its exact position is unknown. The location shown here places it within the northern part of ancient Jerusalem.

The Gate of Ephraim was a gate in the wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's day. It was probably on the north side of the city and was likely named for the road leading north toward the territory of Ephraim. An open street or square lay beside it, and during the Feast of Tabernacles people built booths there along with other public spaces (Neh 8:16). At the dedication of the rebuilt wall, one of the thanksgiving processions passed above this gate on its way past the Old Gate, the Fish Gate and the towers of Hananeel and Meah to the Sheep Gate (Neh 12:39). A gate of the same name appears in earlier accounts of King Jehoash of Israel breaking down Jerusalem's wall (2 Kgs 14:13). Its exact position is uncertain, and the location shown here is only an approximate point within Jerusalem.

The Gate of the Children of the People (called the People's Gate in some modern translations) was a gate of Jerusalem mentioned only in Jer 17:19. The LORD told Jeremiah to stand there, and then in all the gates of the city, to deliver a message about keeping the sabbath. The verse describes it as the gate through which the kings of Judah came in and went out, which suggests it was a main entrance used by the royal court and the general population. Its exact position is not known. Some have linked it with a gate near the palace or the temple, but the text gives no further detail. The location shown here is a general point within ancient Jerusalem rather than a precise site for the gate.

The Gate of the Foundation was a gate in Jerusalem, mentioned once, in the account of the priest Jehoiada's plan to crown the young Joash king in place of Queen Athaliah. Jehoiada divided the priests and Levites on duty into three groups: one at the king's house, one at the Gate of the Foundation, and the rest of the people in the temple courts (2 Chr 23:5). The parallel account in 2 Kgs 11:6 seems to call the same gate "the gate of Sur," so the two names probably refer to one entrance. Its exact position is unknown. Given the setting, it was probably connected with the temple or the royal palace beside it. The location shown here places it generally within Jerusalem near the temple area rather than at an identified site.

The Gate of the Fountain (Fountain Gate in modern translations) was a gate in the wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. It stood near the king's pool and the pool of Siloah (Siloam), by the king's garden and the stairs leading down from the city of David. That places it toward the southern end of the city, probably near the southeast corner where the Kidron and Tyropoeon valleys meet. During his night inspection of the ruined walls, Nehemiah reached this gate and found so much rubble that his animal could not get through (Neh 2:14). Shallun son of Colhozeh, ruler of part of the Mizpah district, rebuilt it, fitting its doors, locks and bars, and repaired the nearby wall of the pool (Neh 3:15). At the dedication of the wall, one procession passed by it and went up the stairs of the city of David toward the Water Gate (Neh 12:37).

The Gate of the Valley, called the Valley Gate in modern translations, was a gate in the wall of Jerusalem. Nehemiah left the city through it at night to inspect the broken walls and burned gates, going past the Dragon Well toward the Dung Gate (Neh 2:13). He then went up along the brook and came back in through the same gate (Neh 2:15). STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) also connects it with King Uzziah, who built towers at the Valley Gate (2 Chr 26:9), and with the rebuilding under Nehemiah, when the gate was repaired along with a stretch of wall reaching to the Dung Gate (Neh 3:13). Its name suggests it opened onto one of the valleys around the city, usually taken to be the Tyropoeon or the Hinnom Valley. The exact site is uncertain. The location shown here places it on the western side of the old City of David.

Gath was one of the five chief cities of the Philistines, and one of the places where some of the Anakim remained after Joshua's conquest (Josh 11:22; 13:3). The Philistines carried the captured ark of God there (1 Sam 5:8). Gath was the home of the giant Goliath and of other men of great stature who fell to David and his servants. While fleeing Saul, David twice took refuge with Achish king of Gath, and six hundred men from Gath later followed him. Shimei went there to bring back runaway servants. David took Gath, and it appears among the cities Rehoboam fortified. Hazael of Syria later captured it, and Uzziah broke down its walls. Its name, meaning "winepress," appears in the saying "Tell it not in Gath" (2 Sam 1:20; Mic 1:10). Several sites have been proposed. The location shown here follows the common identification with Tell es-Safi, given in Easton's Bible Dictionary.

Gath-hepher was a town on the border of the tribe of Zebulun in Lower Galilee. In Josh 19:13 the King James Version spells it Gittah-hepher, in a list of points marking Zebulun's boundary. It is best known as the hometown of the prophet Jonah son of Amittai, who foretold Jeroboam II's restoration of Israel's borders (2 Kgs 14:25). The name is usually explained as "winepress of the pit" or "winepress of the well." Jerome described it as a small village near Sepphoris where Jonah's tomb was shown, and a long local tradition places that tomb at the same spot. Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia all identify Gath-hepher with el-Meshhed, a hilltop village with ancient ruins near Kafr Kanna, a few miles northeast of Nazareth. The location shown here follows that identification.

Gath-rimmon was a city in the territory of the tribe of Dan, listed with Jehud and Bene-berak in Dan's allotment (Josh 19:45). It was later given, with its surrounding pasturelands, to the Levites. By inference from the surrounding passage, it went to the Kohathite clan (Josh 21:24). The parallel list in 1 Chr 6:69 names it alongside Aijalon but places it in a passage about Ephraim's cities. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "press of the pomegranate." Gath-rimmon was apparently in the coastal plain not far from Joppa. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that its exact site is not identified. The location shown here places it east of modern Tel Aviv. The name is shared by another Levitical city in Manasseh (Josh 21:25), which this entry does not describe.

Gath-rimmon was a town in the territory of the half tribe of Manasseh west of the Jordan. Along with Taanach, it was given with its pasturelands to the Levites (Josh 21:25). The name, meaning "press of the pomegranate," is shared with a Levitical city of Dan listed just before it, and Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the name here probably arose from a copying error. The parallel list in 1 Chr 6:70 gives Bileam in its place, which Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take to be Ibleam. Early Greek manuscripts give other names, such as "Baithsa" and "Jebatha." The location shown here follows the Ibleam identification, probably the modern site of Khirbet Belameh near Jenin.

Gaza, called Azzah in some passages (1 Kgs 4:24; Jer 25:20), was a city near the Mediterranean coast in the far southwest of Canaan, on the route toward Egypt. Gen 10:19 names it as a limit of Canaanite territory. Joshua's campaigns reached it, and some Anakim remained there. It was allotted to Judah, which took it (Judg 1:18), but it later appears as one of the five chief Philistine cities (1 Sam 6:17). Samson visited Gaza and was later imprisoned there, blinded and made to grind grain (Judg 16:21). Hezekiah struck the Philistines as far as Gaza, and Amos, Jeremiah, Zephaniah and Zechariah announced judgment on it. In Acts 8:26 Philip was sent to the desert road running from Jerusalem to Gaza, where he met the Ethiopian official, about AD 32 by inference from context. The location shown here is modern Gaza City.

Gazez was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:46. He was a son of Caleb by Ephah, Caleb's concubine, and his full brothers were Haran and Moza. Through Caleb he was related to a large group of other children in the same genealogy, including Mesha, Jesher, Shobab, Ardon, Jahdai and Achsa, and half-brothers such as Hur, Sheber and Tirhanah. The same verse also names a second Gazez, a son of Haran, which would make him this Gazez's nephew. It is not clear whether the verse means two separate men or repeats one name, and this entry treats the son of Caleb as a distinct person. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a passing over."

Gazez, son of Haran, was a member of the tribe of Judah named in the genealogy of Caleb's descendants (1 Chr 2:46). His father Haran was a son of Caleb by Caleb's concubine Ephah, which makes this Gazez Caleb's grandson. The same verse also lists a Gazez among Ephah's own sons, alongside Haran and Moza, so the name appears twice in one line: once for a son of Caleb and once for a son of Haran. Whether these are two different men, an uncle and nephew sharing a name, or a single person mentioned twice is not clear from the text, and this entry treats the son of Haran as a separate individual. Nothing further is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a passing over."

Gazzam was the ancestor or head of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants returned from the Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel. The "children of Gazzam" appear in the list of returning exiles in Ezra 2:48 and again in the parallel list in Neh 7:51, where they are named among other temple-servant families such as those of Rezin, Nekoda and Uzza. Nothing else is recorded about Gazzam himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the return to about 536 BC, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "devouring." Hitchcock's Bible Names instead renders it "the fleece of them." The same family appears as "Gazera" in the apocryphal book 1 Esdras.

Geba, whose name means "hill," was a town in the territory of Benjamin, also spelled Gaba (Josh 18:24). It was given to the Levites (Josh 21:17; 1 Chr 6:60). In Saul's early reign the Philistines kept a garrison there until Jonathan attacked it (1 Sam 13:3). King Asa fortified Geba with stones and timber taken from Baasha's works at Ramah (1 Kgs 15:22; 2 Chr 16:6). The phrase "from Geba to Beersheba" marked the northern and southern limits of Judah (2 Kgs 23:8). Isaiah names it on the route of an invading army approaching Jerusalem from the north (Isa 10:29). Its people returned after the exile (Ezra 2:26; Neh 7:30; Neh 11:31). Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the village of Jeba, about six miles north of Jerusalem and facing Michmash across a gorge. The location shown here follows that identification. Several other biblical places share the name.

Geba is the starting point of David's pursuit of the Philistines after his victory in the valley of Rephaim. He struck them down "from Geba until thou come to Gazer," driving them west toward the coastal plain (2 Sam 5:25). Several places in the Bible share this name. The best-known Geba is a town of Benjamin north of Jerusalem, usually placed at the modern village of Jaba. The parallel account in 1 Chr 14:16, however, reads "from Gibeon" instead of "from Geba," and many readers take the two names to refer to the same starting point. The location shown here follows that Gibeon reading, at the site of el-Jib northwest of Jerusalem. Either way, the route ran from the hill country of Benjamin to Gezer at the edge of the lowlands. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a hill" or "cup."

Gebal was a Phoenician city on the Mediterranean coast, known to the Greeks as Byblos and probably the modern town of Jbeil in Lebanon, north of Beirut. Ezekiel's lament over Tyre says the elders and skilled men of Gebal worked as caulkers on Tyre's ships (Ezek 27:9). In 1 Kgs 5:18 the word the King James Version renders "stonesquarers" is, according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, the Hebrew term for men of Gebal (Gebalites), who helped prepare stone and timber for Solomon's temple. Josh 13:5 also mentions their land. Gebal appears in Ps 83:7 among peoples allied against Israel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes that Gebal to be a separate hill district southeast of the Dead Sea, near Edom. The location shown here follows the Phoenician coastal city. The name probably means "border" or "limit."

Geber was the father of one of the twelve district officers who supplied food for King Solomon and his household. He is known only through his son, whose name is not given in the King James Version. The son was based at Ramoth-gilead and oversaw the towns of Jair in Gilead and the region of Argob in Bashan, which had sixty large walled cities with bronze bars, a district east of the Jordan (1 Kgs 4:13). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Revised Version treats "Ben-geber" ("son of Geber") as the officer's own name. On that reading Geber himself is not really a separate figure. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which means "man" or "strong one," is shared by another person in the same list of officers, so the two should not be confused.

Geber son of Uri was one of the twelve district officers King Solomon appointed to supply food for the royal household, and he is the last named in the list. His district was east of the Jordan in Gilead. It covered the former territory of Sihon king of the Amorites and of Og king of Bashan (1 Kgs 4:19). The verse calls him "the only officer which was in the land." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests this probably means one official was assigned to this large region because it could supply less than the others. That source and Smith's Bible Dictionary place his district probably south of the one held by Ben-geber, who is named earlier in the list (1 Kgs 4:13). The name Geber means "man" or "strong one." Because several people in the Bible share the name, he should be kept distinct from the others.

Gebim was a small town north of Jerusalem, in the territory of Benjamin, named only once in the Bible. In Isaiah's poem of an army advancing on Jerusalem (Isa 10:28–32), usually understood as the Assyrian army, its people gather to flee as the invader approaches (Isa 10:31). The name is usually explained as meaning "cisterns" or "trenches," though Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "grasshoppers." Its exact site is uncertain. The surrounding list of towns runs toward Jerusalem, and Gebim comes after Anathoth and Madmenah and just before Nob. On that basis Smith's Bible Dictionary places it between Anathoth and the ridge of Nob. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it as probably the modern village of el-Isawiyeh, northeast of Jerusalem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes another proposal, Jebia, farther north toward Shechem. The location shown here follows the el-Isawiyeh identification.

Gedaliah was the son of Ahikam and grandson of Shaphan, appointed by Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon to govern the people left in Judah after Jerusalem fell. He was one of several men of this name in the Bible. Based at Mizpah, he received Jeremiah, who had been released from prison into his care. He promised the Judean army captains and their men that it would go well with them if they settled in the land and served Babylon. Jews scattered in Moab, Ammon and Edom then returned to him and gathered a large harvest. Johanan son of Kareah warned him that Ishmael son of Nethaniah had been sent by Baalis king of the Ammonites to kill him, but Gedaliah did not believe it. In the seventh month Ishmael, who was of royal descent, came with ten men, ate with him, and killed him along with the Jews and Chaldeans at Mizpah.

Gedaliah was a Levite musician, one of the six sons of Jeduthun, who served under their father's direction in the worship organized in David's time, prophesying with the harp to give thanks and praise to the LORD (1 Chr 25:3). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives his name as meaning "Yahweh is great." His brothers were Zeri (probably the same as Izri, named later in the chapter), Jeshaiah, Hashabiah, Mattithiah and Shimei. Verse 3 says six but names only five, and Shimei, who appears later in the list, is generally taken as the sixth. When the musicians were divided by lot into twenty-four courses, the second lot fell to Gedaliah, whose group of brothers and sons numbered twelve (1 Chr 25:9). Several other people in the Bible share his name, including the governor of Judah appointed after the fall of Jerusalem. This Gedaliah is mentioned only in these two verses.

Gedaliah was a priest in the time of Ezra, one of the descendants of Jeshua son of Jozadak, the high priest who returned from exile in Babylon. He appears only in Ezra 10:18, in the list of priests found to have married foreign wives. The following verse (Ezra 10:19) says that these men of Jeshua's family pledged to send their wives away and offered a ram as a guilt offering, so Gedaliah was probably among those who made that pledge. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, meaning "the LORD is great" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), was borne by several people in the Bible. This Gedaliah is distinct from the better-known governor of Judah appointed by the Babylonians after the fall of Jerusalem.

Gedaliah son of Pashur was one of the officials in Jerusalem during the reign of King Zedekiah, shortly before the city fell to Babylon. He is named with Shephatiah son of Mattan, Jucal son of Shelemiah and Pashur son of Malchiah as having heard Jeremiah tell the people that those who stayed in the city would die, while those who surrendered to the Chaldeans would live (Jer 38:1). The following verses of the chapter show these officials asking the king to put Jeremiah to death, and Jeremiah being lowered into a muddy cistern. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Gedaliah as one of the nobles who conspired against the prophet. His father Pashur may be the priest Pashur son of Immer who had earlier put Jeremiah in the stocks (Jer 20:1–2), but the text does not say so. Several other men in the Bible share the name Gedaliah.

Gedaliah was an ancestor of the prophet Zephaniah, named in the genealogy that opens the book of Zephaniah. He was the son of Amariah and the father of Cushi, so he was Zephaniah's grandfather (Zeph 1:1). The same verse traces the line back one more generation to Hizkiah. Many readers take Hizkiah to be King Hezekiah of Judah, though the text does not say so. Zephaniah prophesied in the days of King Josiah, so Gedaliah probably lived a couple of generations earlier, in the late eighth or early seventh century BC, by inference from the genealogy. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share his name, including the governor of Judah appointed after the Babylonian conquest, and this Gedaliah should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "God is my greatness."

Geder was a Canaanite city whose king appears among the thirty-one kings west of the Jordan defeated by Joshua and the Israelites. Its only mention is in that list, where it comes next to Debir (Josh 12:13). The name probably means "wall," which may suggest a walled town (Hitchcock's Bible Names; Easton's Bible Dictionary). Its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it may be the same as Gedor in the hill country of Judah (Josh 15:58). Smith's Bible Dictionary links it with the Geder of 1 Chr 4:39. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connects it with Beth-gader (1 Chr 2:51) and with the home of Baal-hanan the Gederite (1 Chr 27:28). The location shown here follows the Gedor identification, a site in the hills north of Hebron, probably modern Khirbet Jedur.

Gederah was a town in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, listed among the fourteen cities of that district in Josh 15:36. The name means "wall" or "fortified place." In 1 Chr 4:23 the King James phrase "among plants and hedges" probably translates two place names, Netaim and Gederah, where potters of the tribe of Judah lived and worked for the king. Josabad "the Gederathite," one of the warriors who joined David (1 Chr 12:4), is likely named after this town or a place of similar name. Because he appears in a group with Benjamite links, some think his home was a different Gederah in Benjamin. STEPBible's name index also links Baal-hanan, one of David's overseers, to Gederah. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions an identification with Jedireh, a ruin near Zorah. The location shown here lies farther west, near the modern Israeli town of Gedera.

Gederoth was a town in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah. It appears in the list of Judah's lowland towns, alongside Beth-dagon, Naamah and Makkedah (Josh 15:41). Its name probably means "sheepfolds" or "walls," as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. During the reign of Ahaz, the Philistines invaded the lowland and the south of Judah. They captured Gederoth, along with Beth-shemesh, Aijalon, Socho, Timnah and Gimzo, and settled there (2 Chr 28:18). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia cites Eusebius, who places a large village called Gedrom 10 Roman miles from Lydda on the road to Eleutheropolis. That points to Katrah (Qatra), southeast of Yebnah. The encyclopedia also suggests a possible link with the Kidron of 1 Maccabees. The location shown here, near modern Gedera, follows the Katrah identification and is approximate.

Gederothaim was a town in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, named in the list of cities given to the tribe of Judah in Josh 15:36, directly after Gederah. The name probably means "two sheepfolds" (Smith's Bible Dictionary) or "place of enclosures" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). The verse closes its group with "fourteen cities," yet fifteen names appear. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may have arisen when a scribe accidentally repeated the preceding Gederah. The Greek Septuagint reads the phrase as "and its cattle shelters" rather than as a separate town. Others treat it as a distinct town. Its site is not known. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the Judean lowland near Gederah.

Gedor was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the sons of Abiel (also called Jeiel) and his wife Maachah. He appears in the two parallel genealogies of the family that settled at Gibeon, listed among his brothers Abdon, Zur, Kish, Baal, Ner, Nadab, Ahio, Zacher (Zechariah) and Mikloth (1 Chr 8:31; 1 Chr 9:37). Nothing is recorded about him beyond his name. The surrounding lists trace King Saul's line through Gedor's brother Ner, so Gedor belonged to the family from which Saul came. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and the STEPBible names list both describe him as an ancestor of Saul, a term used loosely here for a member of Saul's forebears' household. The mention of "Jeroham of Gedor" in 1 Chr 12:7 probably refers to a town of that name rather than to this man.

Gedor was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed in Josh 15:58 with Halhul and Beth-zur among the towns given to the tribe of Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place it a few miles north of Hebron, at Khirbet Jedur, about halfway between Bethlehem and Hebron. The location shown here follows that identification. 1 Chr 12:7 names Joelah and Zebadiah, "the sons of Jeroham of Gedor," among the warriors who joined David. The surrounding passage links that group with Saul's tribe of Benjamin, so Easton's Bible Dictionary takes this Gedor to be a town apparently in Benjamin, probably the same as Geder. Whether the two verses refer to one place or two is uncertain. Several other places in the Bible share the name.

Gedor was a place where clans of the tribe of Simeon went looking for pasture for their flocks, reaching its entrance as far as the east side of the valley (1 Chr 4:39). The surrounding passage says they found good, quiet pasture there, drove out the earlier inhabitants, including the Meunim, and settled in their place, in the days of King Hezekiah (1 Chr 4:40–41). The name is shared by other places in the Bible, and this Gedor's location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary links it with Gederah of Josh 15:36, in the lowland of Judah, or with Gerar, where the patriarchs grazed their flocks. The Greek Septuagint reads "Gerar" here, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia considers that reading probably correct. The location shown here follows the Gederah identification, near modern Gedera in Israel's coastal plain.

Gehazi was the servant of the prophet Elisha, mentioned in three episodes of 2 Kings. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "valley of vision." In the story of the Shunammite woman, he summoned her for Elisha and pointed out that she had no son and that her husband was old. When her child later died, he tried to push her away from the prophet at Mount Carmel. Elisha then sent him ahead with his staff to lay on the boy's face, but the child did not wake. After Elisha refused Naaman's gifts, Gehazi ran after the Syrian commander to take something from him, then told Elisha he had gone nowhere. In the verses that follow (2 Kgs 5:26–27), Elisha declares that Naaman's leprosy will cling to him. Later he described Elisha's deeds to the king, whom Easton's and Smith's dictionaries identify as Joram, just as the Shunammite arrived.

Geliloth was a landmark on the southern boundary of the tribe of Benjamin, where it met the territory of Judah. Josh 18:17 traces the border from En-shemesh toward Geliloth, "over against the going up of Adummim," and then down to the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben. The name means "circles" or "regions." The parallel description of Judah's northern border in Josh 15:7 names Gilgal at the same point, and Easton's and Smith's Bible dictionaries take Geliloth to be that place. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia instead places it on the road climbing from Jericho toward the Ascent of Adummim, about 6 miles (10 km) from Jerusalem, and says no exact site can be fixed. The location shown here, in the Jordan Valley near Jericho, follows the Gilgal identification.

Gemalli was a man of the tribe of Dan and the father of Ammiel, who represented Dan among the twelve men Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan (Num 13:12). He is mentioned only in this one verse, and nothing else is recorded about him. Gemalli therefore belonged to the generation that left Egypt in the exodus, but the text gives no further details of his life. His name is usually linked to the Hebrew word for "camel". The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "camel owner", and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "camel-driver".

Gemariah son of Hilkiah was one of two envoys whom King Zedekiah of Judah sent to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. He traveled with Elasah son of Shaphan, and the two carried Jeremiah's letter to the Jewish exiles in Babylon (Jer 29:3). Easton's Bible Dictionary adds that the mission carried tribute from Zedekiah, and Smith's Bible Dictionary dates it to about 594 BC. His father Hilkiah is often taken to be the high priest of Josiah's reign who found the book of the law (2 Kgs 22). That would explain why this entry places Gemariah in the tribe of Levi and names Azariah as his brother, since 1 Chr 6:13 lists Azariah as a son of Hilkiah. This identification is an inference. He is a different man from Gemariah son of Shaphan in Jer 36. The name means "the LORD has accomplished."

Gemariah, son of Shaphan the scribe, was a royal official (one of the "princes") in Jerusalem during King Jehoiakim's reign. Baruch read Jeremiah's prophecies to the people from Gemariah's chamber in the upper court of the temple, at the entrance of the New Gate (Jer 36:10). His son Michaiah heard the reading and reported it to the officials meeting in the scribe's chamber of the palace, and Gemariah was among them (Jer 36:11–12). When the king burned the scroll, Gemariah, with Elnathan and Delaiah, had urged him not to, but the king refused (Jer 36:25). His father is probably the Shaphan who served as scribe under King Josiah (2 Kgs 22:3), and his brothers Ahikam and Elasah also appear in Jeremiah (Jer 26:24; 29:3). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "Yahweh has accomplished." A different Gemariah, son of Hilkiah, appears in Jer 29:3.

Gennesaret was a district, and by some accounts a town, on the northwestern shore of the Sea of Galilee. After Jesus fed the five thousand and walked on the water, he and his disciples crossed the lake and landed in "the land of Gennesaret" (Matt 14:34; Mark 6:53), where the Healing in Gennesaret took place. Luke calls the Sea of Galilee itself "the lake of Gennesaret" (Luke 5:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary links the name to Chinnereth, a town of Naphtali named in Josh 19:35. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify the land of Gennesaret with the fertile plain now called el-Ghuweir. It runs a little over three miles from Magdala (el-Mejdel) in the south toward Khan Minyeh in the north and is about a mile wide. Josephus praised its fruitfulness. The name is often explained as "garden of the prince." The location shown here lies on that western shore.

Genubath was the son of Hadad, a member of Edom's royal family, and of the sister of Tahpenes, the wife of the Egyptian Pharaoh. His only mention, 1 Kgs 11:20, says that Tahpenes herself weaned him in Pharaoh's house and that he grew up in the royal household among Pharaoh's own sons. The surrounding passage explains how this came about: Hadad had fled to Egypt as a child when David's forces conquered Edom, and there he won Pharaoh's favor and married into the royal family. Genubath was therefore born and raised at the Egyptian court, probably during the later part of David's reign, by inference from context. According to Easton's and Hitchcock's dictionaries, his name means "theft." Nothing more is recorded about his life.

Gera was a member of the tribe of Benjamin. Gen 46:21 lists him among the sons of Benjamin who went down to Egypt with Jacob. The Benjamite genealogy in 1 Chr 8 names Gera again, alongside Shephuphan and Huram. Judg 3:15 calls Ehud, the left-handed deliverer who brought Israel's tribute to Eglon king of Moab, "the son of Gera, a Benjamite." This entry treats these mentions as one person, the father of Ehud. Because the judges' period comes long after Benjamin's sons, "son" there may mean a descendant rather than a direct child. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats Gera as a Benjamite family name and says the Gera of Judges was Ehud's "father, or ancestor." Several people in the Bible bear this name, so the identifications are uncertain.

Gera was the father, or possibly a more distant ancestor, of Shimei, the Benjamite from Bahurim who cursed King David. Gera himself never appears in the narrative. He is named only in the phrase "Shimei the son of Gera." Shimei belonged to the family of the house of Saul and cursed David at Bahurim when the king fled toward Mahanaim (2 Sam 16:5; 1 Kgs 2:8). The surrounding narrative places this flight during Absalom's rebellion. Shimei later met David at the Jordan and fell down before him (2 Sam 19:16, 18). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Gera, meaning "grain," was a family name in the tribe of Benjamin. On that reading, "son of Gera" may mean a descendant of a Benjamite clan ancestor rather than Shimei's immediate father. Several men in the Bible bear this name, and it is uncertain how they relate to one another.

Gera was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, a son of Bela and so a grandson of Benjamin. He is named second among Bela's sons in 1 Chr 8:3, after Addar and before Abihud. The list goes on in 1 Chr 8:4–5 and names a second Gera among the same brothers, which may be a copying repetition or a second person of that name. Other brothers of his appear in a separate list of Bela's sons in 1 Chr 7:7. Gen 46:21 names a Gera as a son of Benjamin himself, and later Benjamites such as Ehud and Shimei are called sons of Gera, so the name seems to have been common in the tribe, perhaps as a family name. Several people therefore bear it, and it is uncertain how they relate. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "pilgrimage, combat; dispute."

Gera was a Benjamite named as one of the sons of Ehud in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin (1 Chr 8:7). He is listed with Naaman and Ahiah. The surrounding passage says Ehud's family were heads of households in Geba and were moved to Manahath (1 Chr 8:6), and 1 Chr 8:7 adds "he removed them". The STEPBible proper names index reads this phrase as an alternative name, Gera or Heglam, and describes him as among those carried into exile. The verse goes on to say that someone "begat Uzza, and Ahihud". The wording is unclear, but this entry counts them among Ehud's sons and so as Gera's brothers. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name was shared by several Benjamites, including a son of Benjamin, the father of the judge Ehud, and the father of Shimei. This Gera should be kept distinct from them.

Gerar was an ancient city in the far south of Canaan, near Gaza, named as a point on the Canaanite border (Gen 10:19). Abraham lived there for a time, and its king, Abimelech, took Sarah after Abraham said she was his sister (Gen 20:1–2). During a later famine Isaac also settled in Gerar, where the local herdsmen quarreled with his men over wells. Abimelech, called king of the Philistines, later came from Gerar with his army commander Phichol to make peace with him (Gen 26:1, 6, 20, 26). Centuries afterward King Asa chased a defeated Ethiopian army as far as Gerar and plundered the surrounding towns (2 Chr 14:13–14). The site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia favored Um Jerrar, southwest of Gaza near the coast. The location shown here matches Tel Haror (Tell Abu Hureira), northwest of Beersheba, which is probably the most widely held identification today.

Gershom was the elder son of Moses and his wife Zipporah, born in Midian while Moses lived there in exile. Moses named him for that exile, saying, "I have been a stranger in a strange land" (Exod 2:22). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as "a stranger here." Gershom and his younger brother Eliezer later came with their mother and Jethro to meet Moses in the wilderness (Exod 18:3). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him as the son Zipporah circumcised on the way to Egypt (Exod 4:24–26), though that passage does not name the child. As a Levite, Gershom's line was counted among the Levitical families, and his son Shebuel (also spelled Shubael) served as chief and as ruler of the treasures under David. The STEPBible names index links him to Jonathan, a priest for the Danites (Judg 18:30). Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Gershom was the father of Jonathan, the man who served as priest to the tribe of Dan at the carved image the Danites set up in their new territory. In Judg 18:30 the King James Version calls Gershom the son of Manasseh, and says Jonathan and his sons kept this priesthood until the land went into captivity. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the Revised Version reads "son of Moses" here instead. On that reading this Gershom would be Moses' son of the same name (Exod 2:22), and Jonathan his descendant. This entry follows the King James wording, which lists Manasseh as his father. Several men in the Bible bear the name Gershom, and nothing more is told about this one. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a stranger here."

Gershom was a priest descended from Phinehas, Aaron's grandson, who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. In Ezra 8:2 he heads the list of family leaders who travelled with Ezra, standing for the priestly line of Phinehas, alongside Daniel for the line of Ithamar and Hattush for the line of David. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him the head of a father's house and places the journey in the reign of Artaxerxes, as the surrounding chapter indicates. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a stranger here." The same name belongs to other people in the Bible, most notably Moses' son, so this Gershom should not be confused with them.

Gershon, also called Gershom in several passages of Chronicles, was a son of Levi and the brother of Kohath and Merari. He is always listed first among Levi's sons, and Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take him to be the eldest. He went down to Egypt with Jacob's family. His sons are named as Libni and Shimei. 1 Chr 23:7 names them Laadan and Shimei, so Laadan is probably another name for Libni. Num 26:59 names Jochebed as a daughter of Levi, which makes her Gershon's sister. His descendants, the Gershonites, formed one of the three main Levite families. In the wilderness they carried the tabernacle's tent, coverings and door hangings under the oversight of Ithamar, using two wagons and four oxen. In Canaan they received thirteen cities, including Golan in Bashan. Under David, Joel led 130 of them, and they served in the temple divisions.

Geruth Chimham was a stopping place near Bethlehem where Johanan and the Judean survivors stayed on their way to Egypt (Jer 41:17). From the surrounding chapter, this was after Ishmael murdered Gedaliah, the governor Babylon had appointed, when the group feared Babylonian reprisal. The Hebrew geruth is usually taken to mean a lodging place, and the King James Version renders it "habitation." Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it to be an inn or khan on land at Bethlehem that David gave to Chimham, probably the son of Barzillai the Gileadite, who went with David to Jerusalem after Absalom's defeat (2 Sam 19:37–40). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes it as a lodging place on the highway to Egypt, though it also notes that Josephus reads the word as "sheep pens." The location shown here is an approximate spot near Bethlehem.

Gesham was a son of Jahdai, named in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chr 2:47. The King James Version spells his name Geshan. He is listed with five brothers, Regem, Jotham, Pelet, Ephah and Shaaph. Smith's Bible Dictionary places this family within the line of Caleb. That fits the surrounding verses, which list Caleb's descendants, though Jahdai's own connection to Caleb is not stated and has to be inferred from where he appears. Nothing else is recorded about Gesham beyond his name and his place in this list.

Geshem, also called Gashmu, was an Arabian who joined Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite in opposing Nehemiah's rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem after the return from exile. When the work began, the three mocked the Jews and accused them of rebelling against the Persian king (Neh 2:19). Once the wall was finished except for its gates, Geshem and Sanballat invited Nehemiah to meet them in a village on the plain of Ono, a proposal Nehemiah understood as a plot to harm him (Neh 6:1–2). Sanballat's open letter then cited Gashmu as the source of a rumor that Nehemiah meant to make himself king (Neh 6:6). Gashmu is generally taken as another form of the same name. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both suggest he was probably the chief of an Arab tribe living south of Judah.

Geshur was a small Aramean kingdom east of the Jordan, called "Geshur in Syria" (2 Sam 15:8). The Israelites did not drive out the Geshurites, who went on living among them (Josh 13:13). In David's time its king was Talmai son of Ammihud. His daughter Maacah married David and was the mother of Absalom (2 Sam 3:3; 1 Chr 3:2). After killing his half-brother Amnon, Absalom fled to his grandfather in Geshur and stayed there three years, until Joab went and brought him back to Jerusalem (2 Sam 13:37–38; 14:23). 1 Chr 2:23 links Geshur and Aram with the capture of the towns of Jair. The name is usually explained as meaning "bridge." Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary place Geshur in the rugged lava region of el-Lejah in northeast Bashan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the Jaulan (Golan) area. The location shown here follows the Lejah identification.

Gether was a son of Aram and a grandson of Shem, named third of Aram's four sons in the Table of Nations alongside Uz, Hul and Mash (Gen 10:23). The parallel genealogy in 1 Chr 1:17 lists him directly among the sons of Shem without naming Aram as his father. In the Chronicles list the brother called Mash in Genesis appears as Meshech. Like the other names in this table, Gether probably stands for both an individual ancestor and the people descended from him. He is mentioned nowhere else in the Bible. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that no satisfactory trace of a people descended from him has been found, so any tribe or region linked to his name remains unknown. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the vale of trial or searching," while Smith's gives "fear."

Gethsemane was a place across the Kidron Valley from Jerusalem, at the foot of the Mount of Olives. Jesus went there with his disciples after the Last Supper and told them to sit while he went on to pray (Matt 26:36; Mark 14:32). The surrounding accounts show it was also where Judas betrayed him and he was arrested, about AD 30 by inference from context. Matthew and Mark call it simply a “place.” John 18:1 calls it a garden across the Kidron, and Luke 22:39 places it on the Mount of Olives and says Jesus often went there. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia derives the name from the Aramaic for “oil press,” which suggests an olive grove. A tradition dating from the 4th century identifies a walled garden of old olive trees just east of the Kidron. Some writers quoted in Easton's Bible Dictionary preferred a more secluded spot farther up the valley. The location shown here roughly follows the traditional site.

Geuel, son of Machi, was the man from the tribe of Gad among the twelve spies Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan (Num 13:15). The surrounding chapter shows that each spy represented one tribe and that most of them returned with a discouraging report. Only Caleb and Joshua are singled out as dissenting, so Geuel was presumably among the others. He is not mentioned anywhere else. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary give his name's meaning as "majesty of God," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "God's redemption."

Gezer was an ancient Canaanite royal city in the foothills west of Jerusalem, between lower Beth-horon and the Mediterranean (Josh 16:3). Its king Horam came to help Lachish and was destroyed by Joshua (Josh 10:33). It marked the western edge of Ephraim's territory and was given with its pasturelands to the Levites. Ephraim did not drive out its Canaanite inhabitants, who stayed on and paid tribute (Josh 16:10; Judg 1:29). David pursued the Philistines as far as Gezer, and a later battle with them was fought there (1 Chr 20:4). The parallel in 2 Sam 21:18 calls the place Gob. A pharaoh captured and burned the city and gave it to his daughter, Solomon's wife, and Solomon then rebuilt it (1 Kgs 9:15–17). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Tell el-Jezer (Tell Gezer), and the location shown here follows that identification.

Giah was a place near Gibeon, mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Sam 2:24. After the battle at the pool of Gibeon, Joab and Abishai chased Abner. At sunset they reached the hill of Ammah, which lay "before Giah by the way of the wilderness of Gibeon." Giah is named only to fix where that hill stood. Its exact site is unknown. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "a waterfall." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint reads it as Gai, matching the Hebrew word for "valley," and suggests the Hebrew form may have come from a copying error.
