The location shown here is a rough placement east of Gibeon, toward the wilderness, based on the verse's description of the route.

Gibbethon was a town in the territory of the tribe of Dan, listed with Eltekeh and Baalath (Josh 19:44) and given with its pasturelands to the Levites (Josh 21:23). Easton's Bible Dictionary specifies the Kohathite clan. By the time of the divided kingdom it belonged to the Philistines. Nadab king of Israel was besieging it when Baasha conspired against him and killed him there (1 Kgs 15:27). Later, Israel's army was again camped against Gibbethon when Zimri seized the throne in Tirzah. The troops made their commander Omri king (1 Kgs 16:16), and he marched from Gibbethon to besiege Tirzah. The name probably means "height" or "hill." Its site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Kibbiah, modern Qibya, about 16 miles southeast of Jaffa. Others favor Tell el-Melat near Gezer. The location shown here follows the Qibya identification.

Gibeah, meaning "a hill," was a town of Benjamin (Josh 18:28), also called Gibeah of Benjamin and Gibeah of Saul. In Judges a Levite stopped there for the night rather than lodge in a foreign city. The men of the town surrounded the house where he stayed and abused his concubine until she died. Israel's tribes then demanded the guilty men, Benjamin refused to hand them over, and after two defeats Israel took and destroyed the town by ambush (Judg 19:12–15; 20:4–37). Gibeah later appears as Saul's home and royal residence (1 Sam 10:26; 15:34; 22:6). The Ziphites came there to report on David's movements, and seven of Saul's descendants were hanged there (2 Sam 21:6). Hosea recalls "the days of Gibeah" (Hos 9:9). Name is shared by several places. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with Tell el-Ful, about 3 miles north of Jerusalem, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Gibeah, a name meaning "hill," was a town in the hill country of Judah. Joshua 15:57 lists it with Cain and Timnah in a district of ten towns, a group that also includes Maon, Carmel and Ziph. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia therefore place it in the uplands southeast of Hebron. Its exact site is unknown, and the location shown here is approximate. 2 Chr 13:2 names Michaiah, daughter of Uriel of Gibeah, as the mother of King Abijah of Judah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats this as probably the same town, and this entry follows that view, though the verse does not say which Gibeah is meant. Because several places in the Bible share this name, this Gibeah should be kept distinct from others, such as the Benjaminite town.

Gibeath-elohim, meaning "hill of God," was a place in the territory of Benjamin. It is named only in 1 Sam 10:5, where Samuel tells the newly anointed Saul that he will come there. He says a Philistine garrison is stationed at the site and that Saul will meet a company of prophets coming down from the high place, playing a lyre, tambourine, flute and harp as they prophesy. The verse also calls it a city. Its identification is uncertain. STEPBible Proper Names places it near Gibeah. Some readers take it to be Gibeah itself, since 1 Sam 10:10 says Saul met the prophets at "the hill." Others link it with Geba, where a Philistine garrison is mentioned in 1 Sam 13:3. The location shown here is only approximate, in the hill country north of Jerusalem.

Gibeath-haaraloth, meaning "hill of the foreskins," was the place where Joshua circumcised the Israelites with flint knives soon after they crossed the Jordan River into Canaan (Josh 5:3). The King James Version translates the name as "the hill of the foreskins" instead of giving it as a proper name. The surrounding chapter places the Israelite camp at Gilgal, and the circumcision is linked there to the naming of Gilgal, so the hill was probably at or near Gilgal in the Jordan Valley east of Jericho. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here, in the plain near Jericho, follows that inference.

Gibeon, also called Gibbar, is the name under which a family group of 95 people appears among the exiles who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel. Ezra 2:20 calls them "the children of Gibbar," while the parallel list in Neh 7:25 gives the same number under the name "the children of Gibeon." This entry treats both names as one ancestor or family head. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Gibbar as the father of some who returned. Because many names in these lists are towns rather than people, "Gibeon" may instead refer to the people of the city of Gibeon, the Hivite town that made a treaty with Joshua. In Nehemiah the name stands near other place names, which makes that reading likely there. Nothing else is recorded about this person.

Gibeon was a large Hivite city, described as greater than Ai and one of the royal cities. Its people made peace with Joshua, and it was the only city that did so (Josh 11:19). When five Amorite kings attacked it for this, Joshua defeated them there, and in that battle he called on the sun to stand still over Gibeon. The city was later assigned to Benjamin and given to the priests. At the pool of Gibeon, Joab's men fought Abner's, and Asahel was killed in that battle. Joab later killed Amasa at the great stone in Gibeon. The tabernacle and the altar of burnt offering stood at its high place, where Solomon sacrificed and received a dream from God. Gibeonites helped rebuild Jerusalem's wall after the exile. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with modern el-Jib, northwest of Jerusalem, and the location shown here matches that identification.

Giddalti was a Levite, one of the fourteen sons of Heman, the king's seer, listed among the musicians David organized for service in the house of the Lord (1 Chr 25:4). When these musicians were divided by lot into twenty-four courses, the twenty-second lot fell to Giddalti. His group of twelve, made up of himself, his sons and his relatives, served in that turn (1 Chr 25:29). The surrounding chapter describes these families as prophesying with harps, lyres and cymbals, so Giddalti was probably one of the temple's instrumental musicians. His name is usually understood to mean "I magnify (God)" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "I have trained up" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). Several of Heman's sons have names that some scholars read together as a line of a psalm or prayer, but the text presents them simply as individuals. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Giddel was the ancestor, or head, of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants returned from the Babylonian exile to Jerusalem and Judah with Zerubbabel. The "children of Giddel" appear in the list of returning temple servants in Ezra 2:47 and again in the parallel list in Neh 7:49. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the name's meaning as "very great." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras gives the name as Cathua. The same name belongs to another man elsewhere in the returnee lists, an ancestor of a family of Solomon's servants, who is a separate person from this one.

Giddel was the ancestor of a family listed among the descendants of "Solomon's servants" who returned from exile in Babylon to Judah with Zerubbabel. His name appears only in the parallel lists of returnees in Ezra 2:56 and Neh 7:58, where the "children of Giddel" are named alongside the families of Jaalah and Darkon. Nothing else is recorded about him. The return is usually dated to about 536 BC, the date Smith's Bible Dictionary gives, by inference from context. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras gives the name as Isdael. The name probably means "great" or "very great." Another Giddel, the head of a family of temple servants, appears in the same lists, so the name belongs to more than one person, and this entry concerns only the ancestor of Solomon's servants.

Gideon, also called Jerubbaal, was a judge of Israel and son of Joash the Abiezrite of Ophrah. While he was threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from the Midianites, an angel of the LORD called him to deliver Israel, and he built an altar there named Jehovahshalom. He tore down Baal's altar by night, rallied his clan, and asked for a sign with a fleece. God reduced his army to three hundred men, who routed Midian with trumpets and broken pitchers. He then pursued and killed the kings Zebah and Zalmunna. He turned down Israel's offer to make his family hereditary rulers (Judg 8:23), but made a gold ephod at Ophrah that became a snare. The land then had forty years of peace, starting about 1251 BC by inference from context. Of his seventy sons, Abimelech killed all but Jotham. Judg 8:20 names Jether as his firstborn. Hebrews calls him Gedeon.

Gideoni was a man of the tribe of Benjamin and the father of Abidan, who led the Benjamites during Israel's time in the wilderness. He is known only as part of his son's name, "Abidan the son of Gideoni." That phrase appears when Abidan is named as Benjamin's representative at the census (Num 1:11), as captain of the tribe in the camp arrangement (Num 2:22), as the prince who brought Benjamin's offering on the ninth day of the altar dedication (Num 7:60, 65), and as commander of the tribe's company when the camp set out (Num 10:24). Nothing is recorded about Gideoni himself. By inference from these passages, he belonged to the generation before the exodus. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "a cutting down," and Hitchcock's Bible Names treats it as the same as Gideon.

Gidom was a place named only in Judg 20:45, in the account of the war between the other Israelite tribes and Benjamin after the outrage at Gibeah. As the defeated Benjamites fled toward the wilderness and the rock of Rimmon, Israel pursued them hard as far as Gidom and killed two thousand of them there. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it between Gibeah and the cliff of Rimmon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes it as the eastward limit of the pursuit from Gibeah toward the wilderness and notes that no modern place name preserving it has been found. Its exact site is therefore unknown. The location shown here is a rough placement in the hill country northeast of Gibeah, between Gibeah and Rimmon, by inference from the passage. The name has been taken to mean "desolation" or "cutting down."

Gihon was the second of the four rivers that flowed out of the garden of Eden, described as winding around the whole land of Cush, rendered "Ethiopia" in the King James Version (Gen 2:13). The name is also used elsewhere in the Bible for a spring near Jerusalem, which is a separate place. The river's location is unknown, and no site is shown here. Interpreters have proposed several identifications. Some link it with the Nile, since Cush is often associated with Africa. Others suggest the Oxus or the Ganges. Easton's Bible Dictionary, reasoning that all four rivers rose near the headwaters of the Euphrates and Tigris, favors the Araxes (the modern Aras), which flows to the Caspian Sea, and takes Cush here as an Asian region. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mentions A. H. Sayce's identification with the Kerkha River east of the Tigris. This entry does not follow any one of these views.

Gihon was a spring just outside Jerusalem, below the City of David. Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet, with Benaiah and the royal guard, brought Solomon there on King David's mule and anointed him king. The crowd's rejoicing as they came back up was heard throughout the city (1 Kgs 1:33, 38, 45). King Hezekiah later blocked its upper outlet and channeled the water straight down to the west side of the City of David (2 Chr 32:30). Manasseh built an outer wall west of Gihon, in the valley (2 Chr 33:14). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the spring called the Virgin's Fountain in the Kidron Valley, which a tunnel links to the Pool of Siloam. The location shown here follows that identification. The same name is also given to a river of Eden (Gen 2:13).

Gilalai was a musician who took part in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. He appears only in Neh 12:36, among the "brethren" of Zechariah who played "the musical instruments of David the man of God" in a procession led by Ezra the scribe. The preceding verse, Neh 12:35, identifies Zechariah as the son of Jonathan and one of the priests' sons with trumpets. That is why Gilalai is counted here as a son of Jonathan and a brother of Zechariah, Shemaiah, Azarael, Milalai, Maai, Nethaneel, Judah and Hanani, though "brethren" could also mean fellow members of a group. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of the priests' sons and dates the event to about 446 BC. The meaning of his name is uncertain: Smith's gives "weighty" and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a wheel."

Gilboa was a mountain range in northern Israel, on the eastern edge of the plain of Jezreel (Esdraelon) above the Jordan valley. It is known almost entirely for one event. Saul camped there with the army of Israel while the Philistines gathered at Shunem, across the valley (1 Sam 28:4). The Philistines killed Saul and Jonathan on Gilboa and hung their bodies on the wall of Beth-shan. The men of Jabesh-gilead later took the bodies away, and David afterward recovered the bones (2 Sam 21:12). In his lament over Saul and Jonathan, David called for no dew or rain to fall on the mountains of Gilboa, where Saul's shield was thrown away (2 Sam 1:21). The name is usually explained as "bubbling spring" (Smith's and Easton's Bible Dictionaries). The range is identified with the modern Jebel Faqu'a, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Gilead was the son of Machir and grandson of Manasseh, of the tribe of Joseph. His family, the Gileadites, formed a major branch of Manasseh (Num 26:29). Numbers 26 lists his sons as Jeezer (elsewhere Abiezer), Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Shemida and Hepher, each the head of a clan (Num 26:30). Through Hepher he was the great-grandfather of Zelophehad, whose daughters asked Moses for an inheritance (Num 27:1; Josh 17:3). The heads of his clans later raised the question of their marriages (Num 36:1). His sister was Hammoleketh, Peresh and Sheresh were his brothers, and another sister married Hezron of Judah (1 Chr 2:21). The region of Gilead east of the Jordan was given to his father Machir (Josh 17:1). The Gilead named as Jephthah's father (Judg 11:2) is probably a later man of the same name, or possibly the clan itself.

Gilead was the father of Jephthah, the judge of Israel described as a mighty warrior. Judg 11:1 says Jephthah's mother was a prostitute and that Gilead fathered him. The next verse, Judg 11:2, adds that Gilead's wife also bore him sons, and that these half-brothers later drove Jephthah away from the family inheritance because of his birth. Nothing else is recorded about Gilead himself. His name is the same as that of the region east of the Jordan and of an earlier descendant of Manasseh, so it is not certain how far the name here refers to a specific individual rather than to the clan or territory Jephthah came from. This entry follows the plain reading, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia does, and treats him as Jephthah's actual father. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the heap or mass of testimony."

Gilead was a man of the tribe of Gad, named only once, in the Gadite genealogy of 1 Chr 5:14. He was the son of Michael and the father of Jaroah, and his line is traced back through Jeshishai and Jahdo to Buz. Through Jaroah he was an ancestor of Huri, Abihail and Abihail's sons, a family the surrounding passage places among the Gadites living east of the Jordan in Bashan and the region of Gilead. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists him as a Gadite, and he shares his name with the land of Gilead and with other men called Gilead, including the better-known descendant of Manasseh. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the heap or mass of testimony." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Gilead was a hilly region east of the Jordan River, also called "mount Gilead" and "the land of Gilead." Jacob headed toward it after fleeing Laban (Gen 31:21), and traders carried balm and spices from it to Egypt (Gen 37:25; Jer 8:22). Its grazing land drew the tribes of Reuben and Gad, and Moses gave part of it to Machir of Manasseh (Num 32:1, 40). The Jabbok River divided it, with half once ruled by Sihon king of the Amorites (Josh 12:2). Jephthah led its people against Ammon, and the prophet Elijah came from there (Judg 11:9; 1 Kgs 17:1). Tiglath-pileser of Assyria took it and deported its people (2 Kgs 15:29). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as about 60 miles long, running from near the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea. That is roughly the hill country of northwestern Jordan, where the location shown here is placed.

Gilgal was Israel's first camp west of the Jordan, on the east border of Jericho, where Joshua set up twelve stones taken from the river (Josh 4:19–20). The text links its name to the LORD "rolling away" the reproach of Egypt (Josh 5:9), and Israel kept the Passover there. It served as Joshua's base during the conquest (Josh 9:6; 10:6–15). Later, Samuel judged Israel there on his yearly circuit. Saul was made king there and later offered sacrifice there without waiting for Samuel, and Samuel killed Agag there (1 Sam 7:16; 11:15; 13:8–12; 15:33). Judah met David there on his return across the Jordan (2 Sam 19:15). Hosea and Amos condemn the worship practised at Gilgal. Several places share the name. Smith's Bible Dictionary places this Gilgal near Jericho, and Easton's Bible Dictionary places it near Shiloh. The location shown here follows an identification with Jaljulia in the Sharon plain.

Gilgal was a place associated with the prophets Elijah and Elisha, distinct from the better-known Gilgal near Jericho in the Jordan valley. Elijah set out from Gilgal with Elisha on the journey that ended with his being taken up into heaven by a whirlwind (2 Kgs 2:1). Elisha later returned there during a famine, when a group of prophets, called the sons of the prophets, were sitting before him and he had his servant cook a stew for them (2 Kgs 4:38). The next verse says the two prophets "went down" to Bethel, so this Gilgal probably lay in the hill country rather than in the low Jordan plain. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with Jiljilia, on a hill north of Bethel. The location shown here follows that identification. The name means "circle" or "rolling."

Gilo, also spelled Giloh, was a town in the hill country of Judah. It appears here only indirectly, in the word "Gilonite" (someone from Gilo), used of Ahithophel, the father of Eliam, one of David's mighty warriors (2 Sam 23:34). Other passages give more about the town. Josh 15:51 lists Giloh among the towns of Judah's hill country. 2 Sam 15:12 says that Absalom sent for Ahithophel, David's counsellor, from his city Giloh when he began his revolt. The exact site is uncertain. It is often identified with Khirbet Jala, a few miles north-west of Hebron, and the location shown here lies in that part of the Judean hills.

Giloh was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed among the cities given to the tribe of Judah in the same group as Debir and Eshtemoa (Josh 15:51). It was the home of Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's counsellor. Absalom summoned him from Giloh while offering sacrifices as his rebellion against David gained strength (2 Sam 15:12). According to 2 Sam 17:23, when Absalom rejected his advice, Ahithophel went home to his city and hanged himself. 2 Sam 23:34 names his son Eliam, also called a Gilonite, among David's mighty men. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a suggestion that the original form of the name was Gilon. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify the site with the ruins of Khirbet Jala, about 7 miles (11 km) north of Hebron, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Gimzo was a town of Judah, mentioned only once in the Bible, near the edge of the Philistine plain. It was one of several towns in the low country and the south of Judah, along with their surrounding villages, that the Philistines captured and settled. The surrounding chapter places this in the reign of King Ahaz (2 Chr 28:18). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the name's meaning as "fertile in sycamores," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "that bulrush." The site is generally identified with the modern village of Jimzu, about 3 to 3.5 miles (5 to 6 km) southeast of Lod (ancient Lydda), on an old route toward Jerusalem, as Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe. The location shown here follows that identification.

Ginath was the father of Tibni, the man whom half the people of Israel tried to make king after the death of Zimri, while the other half followed Omri (1 Kgs 16:21). Omri's supporters prevailed, Tibni died, and Omri became king (1 Kgs 16:22). Ginath is mentioned only to identify his son, and nothing else is recorded about him, including his tribe or home. The setting suggests he lived in the early ninth century BC, an estimate inferred from context. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "protection," while Hitchcock's Bible Names connects it with "a garden."

Ginnethon was a priest named among those who set their seal to the covenant made under Nehemiah, in which the returned community pledged to keep the law (Neh 10:6). The name also appears as a priestly family. Ginnetho, probably a variant spelling, is listed among the priests who came back from exile with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:4). In the next generation, in the days of the high priest Joiakim, Meshullam was head of the priestly house of Ginnethon (Neh 12:16). The covenant signer may have been an individual of that name or someone sealing on behalf of the family, since many names in that list match priestly houses. Which reading applies is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "gardener."

Girgasite (also spelled Girgashite) is listed in the table of nations as a son of Canaan, the son of Ham. He is named with the Jebusite and the Amorite (Gen 10:16; 1 Chr 1:14). Like his brothers, the name stands for a people descended from him rather than for an individual whose life is recorded. Easton's Bible Dictionary counts him as Canaan's fifth son. Later passages name the Girgashites among the peoples living in Canaan before the Israelites, including Gen 15:21, Deut 7:1 and Josh 3:10. Where they lived is not known. Easton's suggests central western Palestine. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a proposed link with the Gergesenes east of the Sea of Galilee (Matt 8:28). It also notes that Josephus said nothing was known of the people.

Gispa was one of two men placed over the Nethinim, the temple servants, in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. Nehemiah 11:21 says the Nethinim lived in Ophel, the hill area south of the temple, and that Ziha and Gispa were in charge of them. Nothing else is recorded about him. Some reference works spell the name Gishpa. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "caress," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "coming hither." A Ziha also appears among the families of Nethinim who returned with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:43), so Gispa's fellow overseer may have belonged to or led that family. This is an inference.

Gittaim was a town to which the people of Beeroth fled, living there as resident foreigners "until this day" (2 Sam 4:3). The verse comes in the account of Rechab and Baanah, Beerothites who killed Saul's son Ish-bosheth. Nehemiah lists Gittaim with Hazor and Ramah among the towns Benjamites settled after the exile (Neh 11:33). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the two mentions are probably the same place, since the Beerothites' refuge need not have lain outside Benjamin. Easton's Bible Dictionary also places it probably in Benjamin and gives the name's meaning as "two winepresses." The exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only approximate, in the lowland west of the Benjamin hill country, near modern Ramla.

Goah was a place near Jerusalem, mentioned only in Jer 31:39, where the King James Version spells it Goath. In Jeremiah's prophecy of the city's future rebuilding, a measuring line goes out over the hill Gareb and then turns around to Goah, marking part of the boundary of the restored city. The surrounding verses describe the city's edges, so Goah was probably a point on the west or south side of Jerusalem, but its exact site is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "a lowing" (the sound of cattle). Because no precise site has been identified, the location shown here simply places it at Jerusalem.

Gob was a place where David's warriors fought two battles against the Philistines. It appears only in 2 Sam 21:18–19. In the first battle Sibbechai the Hushathite killed Saph, one of the descendants of the giant. In the second, Elhanan son of Jaareoregim of Bethlehem killed the brother of Goliath the Gittite, whose spear shaft was like a weaver's beam. The name is usually explained as meaning "pit" or "cistern." Its identity is uncertain. The parallel account in 1 Chr 20:4 names the place Gezer, as Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries note. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mentions that some manuscripts read Nob, while the Syriac and Septuagint versions read Gath, and it favours Gath. The location shown here follows the Gezer identification, at or near Tel Gezer in the low hills between Jerusalem and the coastal plain.

God is the supreme being of the Bible, introduced in its first verse as the creator of the heaven and the earth (Gen 1:1). As Easton's Bible Dictionary notes, the Bible assumes his existence rather than arguing for it. In the King James Version, the Hebrew name Jehovah is usually rendered "LORD" in small capitals, while "God" translates the Hebrew El and Elohim. Other titles include Almighty, Lord of hosts, Father and Judge. Throughout the Old Testament he speaks to Moses, Joshua and the prophets, gives Israel his law, and directs events among the nations, stirring up Cyrus of Persia and handing Jehoiakim over to Babylon (Ezra 1:1; Dan 1:2). In the New Testament Jesus is called the Son of God, and God is spoken of as the Father (Mark 1:1; 1 Pet 1:2). This entry counts Adam and Eve as his children because Genesis presents them as formed directly by him, and Luke 3:38 calls Adam "the son of God."

The cursing of Cain by God followed Cain's killing of his brother Abel. God declared Cain cursed from the ground that had received Abel's blood. When Cain farmed, the soil would no longer yield its strength to him, and he would wander the earth as a fugitive. Cain protested that his punishment was more than he could bear. He said he was being driven from the land and hidden from God's presence, and that anyone who found him would kill him. In response God promised sevenfold vengeance on anyone who killed Cain, and put a mark on him so that no one would kill him. The text does not describe the mark. Cain then left the presence of the LORD and settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden. The date of about 3875 BC is an estimate inferred from the genealogies, not stated in the text.

event: God decides to destroy every living thing
text: The God decides to destroy every living thing episode is the passage in Genesis 6:1–7 that sets the stage for the flood. As people multiplied on the earth, "the sons of God" took wives from "the daughters of men," and their children became "mighty men" of renown. Giants (Nephilim) are also said to have lived on the earth at that time. The identity of the sons of God is debated: some take them as angelic beings, others as men of Seth's line or as rulers, and the passage itself does not say. The LORD declared that his spirit would not strive with man forever and set man's days at 120 years. Seeing that human wickedness was great and that people's thoughts were only evil continually, God regretted making humankind and resolved to wipe out people, animals, creeping things and birds. This entry dates the event to about 2468 BC, an estimate inferred from context.

event: God instructs Noah to build the ark
text: God instructs Noah to build the ark is the episode in Gen 6–7 in which God, seeing the earth corrupt and filled with violence, tells Noah he will destroy all flesh with a flood. Noah, described as a just man who walked with God and found grace with the LORD, is told to build an ark of gopher wood sealed with pitch, 300 cubits long, 50 wide and 30 high, with rooms, a window, a side door and three decks. God promises a covenant with Noah and says he will enter the ark with his wife, his sons Shem, Ham and Japheth, and their wives, along with pairs of every kind of animal and food for all. A further instruction calls for clean animals and birds by sevens and warns that forty days of rain will begin in seven days. Each time, Noah does all that God commands.

event: God makes a covenant with Noah
text: The covenant God made with Noah is the agreement God established after the Flood, when Noah and his family had left the ark. Noah built an altar and offered burnt offerings of every clean animal and bird. The LORD resolved never again to curse the ground or destroy every living thing, and promised that seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, and day and night would not cease. God blessed Noah and his sons, told them to be fruitful and fill the earth, and gave them every living creature for food, with the condition that they not eat flesh with its blood. Because humans are made in God's image, whoever sheds human blood must answer with his own life. God then made his covenant with Noah, his descendants and every living creature, promising that no flood would again destroy the earth. The rainbow in the cloud was given as its lasting sign. This entry dates it to about 2347 BC, by inference from context.

Gog was a descendant of Reuben, named once in a family line in 1 Chr 5:4. The verse traces a line of descent from Joel: Shemaiah his son, Gog his son, Shimei his son. This makes Gog the son of Shemaiah, the grandson of Joel, and the father of Shimei. The surrounding chapter lists the descendants of Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, and Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both identify Gog as a Reubenite. Nothing else is recorded about his life. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "roof" or "covering." Several people in the Bible share this name. This Reubenite is a different figure from the Gog of the land of Magog in Ezek 38–39, a leader of nations who is mentioned again in Rev 20:8.

Gog is the leader addressed in Ezekiel's prophecy as "the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal," of the land of Magog (Ezek 38:2–3; 39:1). Ezekiel is told to prophesy against him. In the latter days, when Israel is living in safety, Gog comes up against the land "as a cloud to cover the land," and God's fury rises against him (Ezek 38:14–18). He and his multitude are then buried in Israel, in a valley east of the sea that is renamed the valley of Hamongog, meaning "multitude of Gog" (Ezek 39:11). Revelation takes up the names: "Gog and Magog" stand for the nations gathered from the four quarters of the earth for a final battle (Rev 20:8). Interpreters differ on whether Gog stands for a historical ruler or a symbolic figure. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "roof; covering." A Reubenite in 1 Chr 5:4 has the same name but is a different person.

Gog is a name that appears with Magog in Rev 20:8, where Satan, released at the end of the thousand years, goes out to deceive the nations in the four quarters of the earth, called "Gog and Magog," and gathers them for battle in numbers like the sand of the sea. The pairing draws on Ezek 38–39, where Gog is a ruler "of the land of Magog" who invades Israel from the far north and is destroyed. In Revelation the two names seem to stand for the hostile nations as a whole rather than for one territory. Treated as a region, its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions a view placing it in the steppes of Central Asia north of the Hindu Kush. The location shown here is a general area north of the Caucasus near the northern Caspian Sea, matching the "north country" of Ezekiel. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "roof; covering."

Goiim is a Hebrew word meaning "nations," treated in some translations as the proper name of a place or people. The King James Version translates it rather than keeping it as a name. In Gen 14:1 and 14:9 Tidal, called "king of nations," is one of four eastern kings, alongside Amraphel of Shinar, Arioch of Ellasar and Chedorlaomer of Elam, who make war against five kings. In Josh 12:23 the "king of the nations of Gilgal" appears among the Canaanite kings defeated by Joshua, listed right after the king of Dor. These two uses probably refer to different peoples: one far to the east, the other in Canaan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Revised Version keeps "Goiim" as a proper name in both passages, and that some identify Tidal's realm with Gutium, a mountain people east of Mesopotamia. No location is shown here, because the site is uncertain.

Golan was a city in Bashan, east of the Jordan, in the territory of the half-tribe of Manasseh. Moses set it apart as one of three cities of refuge east of the river, alongside Bezer of Reuben and Ramoth in Gilead of Gad, where a person who had killed someone accidentally could flee (Deut 4:43; Josh 20:8). It was later given, with its surrounding pasturelands, to the Gershonite families of the Levites (Josh 21:27; 1 Chr 6:71). Scripture says nothing more about it. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that it later gave its name to the district of Gaulanitis, roughly the modern Jaulan (the Golan region). Smith's Bible Dictionary describes the exact site as unknown. The location shown here is east of the Sea of Galilee in southern Syria, near the village of Sahem el-Jolan, a site often proposed for ancient Golan.

Golgotha was the place outside Jerusalem where Jesus was crucified. The Gospels explain the name as "the place of a skull" (Matt 27:33; Mark 15:22), and John notes that Jesus carried his own cross there (John 19:17). The word comes from Aramaic for "skull." Its Latin equivalent gives the familiar name Calvary. Smith's Bible Dictionary offers two explanations of the name: it was a place of executions, or a bare, rounded mound shaped like a skull. Connected passages place it near the city and outside its gate (Heb 13:12), with a garden and tomb close by (John 19:41). The exact site is uncertain. Long tradition places it at the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. Easton's Bible Dictionary favors the skull-like hillock above Jeremiah's Grotto, north of the city. The location shown here is approximate and only places it within Jerusalem, without choosing between these sites.

Goliath was a Philistine champion from Gath whose height is given as six cubits and a span (1 Sam 17:4), about ten and a half feet by the reckoning of Easton's Bible Dictionary. He came out from the Philistine army to challenge Israel, and David heard his words (1 Sam 17:23). David killed him in the valley of Elah, about 1067 BC by inference from context. His sword was later kept wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod at Nob, and the priest gave it to David (1 Sam 21:9; 22:10). Goliath's brother, named Lahmi in 1 Chr 20:5, was killed by Elhanan (2 Sam 21:19). 2 Sam 21:22 describes such warriors as born to 'the giant in Gath.' The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the Goliath of 2 Sam 21:19 as a different, younger man. This entry follows Chronicles in treating Lahmi as his brother.

Gomer (son of Japheth) is the first-named son of Japheth, son of Noah, in the Table of Nations. His brothers were Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech and Tiras, and his sons were Ashkenaz, Riphath and Togarmah (Gen 10:2–3; 1 Chr 1:5–6). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries call him Japheth's eldest son, which follows from his being listed first. In Ezek 38:6 Gomer, together with "the house of Togarmah of the north quarters" and their troops, appears as a people among the forces allied with Gog, so the name stands for a nation as well as an ancestor. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies this people with the Gimirra of Assyrian records and the Cimmerians of Greek writers, northern tribes who moved into Asia Minor in the 7th century BC. Easton's and Smith's go further and trace the Celtic peoples to Gomer. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "complete."

Gomer (wife of Hosea) was the daughter of Diblaim and the wife of the prophet Hosea, whom he married at the beginning of his prophetic work (Hos 1:3). The surrounding passage says Hosea was told to take "a wife of whoredoms" (Hos 1:2), and their marriage serves in the book as a picture of Israel's relationship with God. Gomer bore a son, Jezreel, then a daughter, Lo-ruhamah, and another son, Lo-ammi. Their names were given as signs to Israel (Hos 1:4–9). In Hos 3:1–3 Hosea is told to love an adulterous woman again and buys her back. Many readers, including the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, take this woman to be Gomer, though she is not named there. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of her name as "to finish; complete." She is a different person from Gomer the son of Japheth.

Gomer is a people or land named in Ezek 38:6 as one of the allies of Gog. Gomer and "all his bands" appear alongside the house of Togarmah from the far north, as part of a great army gathered against Israel. The name probably refers to the descendants of Gomer, the son of Japheth, who is named in the table of nations in Genesis 10:2–3 as the father of Ashkenaz, Riphath and Togarmah. That family link would explain why Gomer and Togarmah appear together in Ezekiel. Many scholars connect Gomer with the Cimmerians, known in Assyrian records as the Gimirrai, a people who lived north of the Black Sea and later moved into Asia Minor. That identification is an inference, and no exact location is fixed here. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "to finish; complete."

Gomorrah was a city of the plain of the Jordan, nearly always named alongside Sodom. Genesis lists it at the edge of Canaanite territory (Gen 10:19) and describes the region as well watered before its destruction (Gen 13:10). Its king, Birsha, joined the kings of Sodom, Admah, Zeboiim and Zoar in a failed battle in the Valley of Siddim, after which the invaders carried off the cities' goods (Gen 14:2, 8–11). Because of the great outcry against their sin, the LORD rained sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah, and the land smoked like a furnace (Gen 18:20; 19:24, 28). This is dated to about 1897 BC, by inference from context. Later writers used Gomorrah as a byword for wickedness and total ruin (Isa 1:9; Jer 49:18; Jude 1:7). Easton's Bible Dictionary places the cities near the northern end of the Dead Sea; the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia favors the south. The location shown here follows the southern view.

The Good Samaritan Parable Taught was the occasion when Jesus told the story of a compassionate Samaritan in answer to a lawyer's questions. The lawyer, testing him, asked what he must do to inherit eternal life. Jesus turned the question back to the law, and the lawyer quoted the commands to love God completely and to love one's neighbour as oneself. Seeking to justify himself, he then asked who his neighbour was. Jesus described a man travelling from Jerusalem to Jericho who was robbed, beaten and left half dead. A priest and a Levite saw him and passed by on the other side. A Samaritan bandaged his wounds, took him to an inn, paid for his care and promised to cover any further costs. Asked which of the three had been a neighbour, the lawyer answered, "He that shewed mercy on him," and Jesus told him to do likewise. It is dated about AD 29, by inference from context.

Goshen was a region of Egypt where Jacob and his family settled during the time of Joseph, and where the Israelites lived until the Exodus. Joseph offered it to his family so they could live near him with their flocks and herds (Gen 45:10). Joseph met Jacob there (Gen 46:28–29), and Pharaoh granted it to them as "the best of the land" for their livestock (Gen 47:6). There they prospered and multiplied (Gen 47:27). Exodus says that the plagues of flies and hail spared Goshen (Exod 8:22; 9:26). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place it east of the Nile in the eastern Nile Delta. Easton's links it with Wadi Tumilat, while the encyclopedia connects it with the district around Phakousa. The location shown here, near modern Faqus, follows that second identification. The name is also used for other places, in southern Canaan.

Goshen was a district in southern Canaan, distinct from the better-known Goshen in Egypt where Jacob's family settled. It appears in the summaries of Joshua's conquests as "the country of Goshen", listed with lands stretching from Kadesh-barnea and Gaza to Gibeon (Josh 10:41), and alongside the hills, the south country, the valley and the plain (Josh 11:16). A town named Goshen is also listed among the cities of Judah's southern hill country (Josh 15:51). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the district probably took its name from this town or was linked to it. Easton's Bible Dictionary places the district in the maritime plain of Judah, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as a separate region whose exact site is unknown. The location shown here follows the hill country view and places it southwest of Hebron. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "drawing near".

Gozan was a region in northern Mesopotamia where the king of Assyria settled Israelites deported after the fall of Samaria. They were placed in Halah, in Habor by "the river of Gozan," and in the cities of the Medes (2 Kgs 17:6; 18:11). 1 Chr 5:26 names Reubenites, Gadites and the half tribe of Manasseh among those taken there. Sennacherib's envoys also listed Gozan with Haran, Rezeph and Eden as nations whose gods had not saved them from Assyria (2 Kgs 19:12; Isa 37:12). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia equates it with Assyrian Guzana, Ptolemy's Gauzanitis, west of Nisibis. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it on the Habor, the modern Khabur River, a tributary of the Euphrates. Easton's Bible Dictionary links the "river of Gozan" with the Kizil Ozan. The location shown here follows the Khabur identification, near Tell Halaf in northeastern Syria.

Great Sea is the biblical name for the Mediterranean Sea, which formed the western border of the land promised to Israel. Numbers sets it as the west boundary, and the northern boundary line also starts from it (Num 34:6–7). Joshua uses it to describe the western limit of the land, toward the sunset, and of Judah's territory, with Philistine towns such as Ashdod and Gaza lying along its coast (Josh 1:4; 15:12, 47). Kings ruling the coastal region facing Lebanon are also mentioned (Josh 9:1). In Ezekiel's vision of the restored land, the Great Sea again marks the west side and the starting or ending point of the northern and southern borders, and its abundant fish are compared to those of a healed Dead Sea (Ezek 47:10, 15, 19–20). The STEPBible Proper Names index notes that it is also called the Sea of the Philistines. The location shown here is a general point in the central Mediterranean.

Greece is the land and people of the Greeks, called Javan in Hebrew, whose name the King James Version renders as "Grecia" or "Greece." In Daniel's visions the rough goat stands for the king of Grecia, and its great horn for the first king (Dan 8:21). A prince of Grecia follows the prince of Persia (Dan 10:20), and a rich Persian king stirs up all against the realm of Grecia (Dan 11:2). Smith's Bible Dictionary reads these as a sketch of Alexander and his successors, and Zech 9:13, which sets Zion's sons against Greece's sons, as a prophecy of the Maccabean wars. In Acts 20:2 Paul reaches Greece after passing through Macedonia, so the name there probably means the southern province of Achaia. Paul probably wrote Romans during that stay, about AD 54 by inference from context. The location shown here is a general point in the Greek peninsula.

Gudgodah was a stopping place of the Israelites during their wilderness journey. Deut 10:7 says they traveled there after leaving Mosera, where Aaron died according to the preceding verse, and went on from Gudgodah to Jotbath, described as a land of streams of water. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with Hor-hagidgad, the stop between Bene-jaakan and Jotbathah in the itinerary of Num 33:32, and notes that the Greek Septuagint calls both places Gadgad. The site has not been identified with certainty. The same encyclopedia suggests the old name may survive in Wadi Gudaghid, a tributary of Wadi Jerafeh that runs down into the Arabah valley roughly due west of Petra, though the consonants do not match exactly. The rough location shown here is in that area. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "happiness."

Guni was a son of Naphtali and so a grandson of Jacob through Bilhah, Rachel's servant. He is listed with his brothers Jahzeel, Jezer and Shillem among the family members who went down with Jacob to Egypt (Gen 46:24). In the census of Numbers he appears as the ancestor of the Gunites, one of the clans of the tribe of Naphtali (Num 26:48). The genealogy in 1 Chr 7:13 repeats the list, calling the brothers "the sons of Bilhah" because they descended from her through Naphtali. That verse spells two of the names differently, Jahziel for Jahzeel and Shallum for Shillem. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a garden" or "a covering." The name Guni is also borne by at least one other man in the Bible, so this entry is limited to Naphtali's son.

Guni was a man of the tribe of Gad, named in the Gadite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 5. He was the father of Abdiel and the grandfather of Ahi, who is described as chief of his father's house (1 Chr 5:15). The surrounding passage places these Gadites in the land of Bashan and Gilead, east of the Jordan. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Guni is also borne by another man in the Bible, a son of Naphtali, so the Gadite here should not be confused with him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a garden" or "a covering," while Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "painted."

Gur was a place near Ibleam, in the hill country at the southern edge of the plain of Jezreel. It is mentioned only once, as "the going up to Gur." There Jehu's men struck King Ahaziah of Judah in his chariot as he fled after Jehu killed Joram of Israel. Ahaziah escaped to Megiddo and died there (2 Kgs 9:27). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as an ascent rising from the plain of Jezreel, and Smith's Bible Dictionary calls it a rise in the ground. Easton's and Hitchcock's Bible Names give the name's meaning as "whelp," while Smith's gives "abode." The exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement near Ibleam, which is probably the modern Khirbet Belameh near Jenin.

Gurbaal was a place or district where certain Arabians lived, mentioned only in 2 Chr 26:7. That verse says God helped King Uzziah of Judah against the Philistines, against these Arabians, and against the Mehunims. The name is usually taken to mean "dwelling of Baal," and Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests a temple of Baal probably stood there. The exact site is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it, from the context, somewhere between Palestine and the Arabian peninsula. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the ancient Aramaic paraphrase (the Targum) reads Gerar, perhaps because the Philistines are named just before. It also notes that the link with the Mehunims points eastward, possibly to a sanctuary on a mountain near Petra. The location shown here is approximate and follows the eastern view, placing Gurbaal in the highlands of Edom in southern Jordan.

Haahashtari was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the Chronicles genealogy as one of the four sons of Ashur by his wife Naarah. His brothers were Ahuzam, Hepher and Temeni (1 Chr 4:6). According to the preceding verse, Ashur, called the father of Tekoa, had two wives, Helah and Naarah. Through Helah he had further sons, Zereth, Jezoar and Ethnan, who were Haahashtari's half-brothers. Coz is listed alongside them in the same family. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "a runner," and Smith's Bible Dictionary as "the courier." Smith's allows that the name may refer to a family rather than a single man. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the Hebrew may be a scribal variant of "the Ashurites," a label describing the names before it. This entry treats Haahashtari as an individual son of Ashur.

Habaiah was the ancestor of a priestly family whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon. In the lists of returnees, "the children of Habaiah" appear among the priests, alongside the families of Koz and Barzillai (Ezra 2:61; Neh 7:63). Smith's Bible Dictionary places this return with Zerubbabel. The verses that follow in both lists (Ezra 2:62; Neh 7:64) say these priestly families searched for their genealogical records and could not find them, so they were barred from serving as priests. The STEPBible Proper Names list likewise describes Habaiah's descendants as excluded from the priesthood for lack of records. Nothing is recorded about Habaiah himself beyond his place as the family's ancestor. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "the hiding of the Lord," and Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "whom Jehovah hides."

Habakkuk was a prophet of Judah and the writer of the Old Testament book that bears his name. The book opens by calling its message "the burden which Habakkuk the prophet did see" (Hab 1:1), and its final chapter is a prayer of his set "upon Shigionoth," probably a musical or poetic term (Hab 3:1). The book records his questions to God about injustice and God's answers, including the coming of the Chaldeans (Hab 1:6). That suggests he worked in the years before the Babylonian invasions. Nothing certain is known of his life beyond what the book itself says. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him around the twelfth or thirteenth year of King Josiah, about 630 BC. This entry dates his prophecies to about 607 BC, an estimate inferred from context. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "he that embraces" or "a wrestler."

Habaziniah was the father of a man named Jeremiah and the grandfather of Jaazaniah, who led the Rechabites in the time of the prophet Jeremiah. He is mentioned only once, in a genealogy identifying Jaazaniah when the prophet brought the Rechabite household into a room of the temple and offered them wine, which they refused out of loyalty to their ancestor Jonadab's command (Jer 35:3). His son Jeremiah is a different person from the prophet. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Habaziniah to have been the head of one of the Rechabite families and dates him before 589 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Revised Version spells the name Habazziniah. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Habor was a river in Assyria, and probably also the district around it, where the king of Assyria settled Israelites deported from the northern kingdom. 2 Kgs 17:6 and 2 Kgs 18:11 place the exiles in Halah and in Habor "by the river of Gozan" after the fall of Samaria in Hoshea's ninth year. 1 Chr 5:26 records that Pul and Tiglath-pileser carried the Reubenites, Gadites and half-tribe of Manasseh to Halah, Habor, Hara and the river Gozan. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia read Habor as the river of Gozan itself. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that another river called Khabur flows into the Tigris, but identifies the biblical Habor with the Khabur (ancient Chaboras), a tributary of the Euphrates in modern northeastern Syria. The location shown here follows that Euphrates-tributary identification.

Hachaliah was the father of Nehemiah, the Jewish official who served at the Persian court in Shushan and later became governor of Judah. He is known only through his son, who is identified as "the son of Hachaliah" at the opening of his book and again in the list of those who sealed the covenant. Hachaliah is also counted as the father of Hanani, probably because Nehemiah calls Hanani his brother (Neh 1:2; Neh 7:2), though "brother" there could mean a close relative. Nothing else is recorded about Hachaliah's life. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as "whom Jehovah enlightens," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "who waits for the Lord."

Hachilah was a hill in the wilderness of Judah, near Ziph, where David hid while Saul was pursuing him. The text places it "on the south of Jeshimon" and "before Jeshimon," meaning at the edge of the barren wasteland that falls away toward the Dead Sea (1 Sam 23:19; 26:1). Twice the people of Ziph went to Saul at Gibeah to report that David was hiding there. On the second occasion Saul camped on the hill by the road, while David stayed out in the wilderness nearby (1 Sam 26:3). The surrounding chapter tells how David then entered Saul's camp at night and took the king's spear and water jug. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Easton's Bible Dictionary identify Hachilah with the ridge of Dhahret el-Kolah (Zahrat al Kula) east of Ziph, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Hachmoni was the father of Jehiel, a man who served at King David's court and "was with the king's sons" (1 Chr 27:32). The phrase probably means that Jehiel looked after or tutored the royal princes. He is named alongside Jonathan, David's uncle, who was a counsellor and scribe. Nothing else is recorded about Hachmoni himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests that Hachmoni may have been the founder of a family rather than an immediate father, since the related name "Hachmonite" is also applied to Jashobeam, one of David's mighty men (1 Chr 11:11), whose actual father was Zabdiel. On that view "son of Hachmoni" would mean a member of the Hachmonite family. This entry treats him as Jehiel's father, as the verse reads. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a wise man."

Hadad the son of Bedad was one of the early kings of Edom, listed among the rulers who reigned there before any king ruled over Israel. He succeeded Husham, and his royal city was Avith, a place whose location is unknown. He is remembered for defeating Midian "in the field of Moab" (Gen 36:35; 1 Chr 1:46). After his death, Samlah of Masrekah became king in his place (Gen 36:36; 1 Chr 1:47). The list of Edomite kings in Genesis is repeated almost word for word in 1 Chronicles. Several other men in the Bible share the name Hadad, including a later Edomite prince who opposed Solomon, so this Hadad should be kept distinct from them. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the name may have served as a royal title, much like Pharaoh. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "joy" or "noise."

Hadad was an Edomite of the royal family whom God raised up as an adversary to Solomon (1 Kgs 11:14). As a small child he fled to Egypt with some of his father's Edomite servants. By inference from the surrounding verses (1 Kgs 11:15–16), this was to escape Joab's slaughter of the men of Edom in David's time. In Egypt he won Pharaoh's favor and married the sister of Queen Tahpenes. Their son Genubath was raised in Pharaoh's household (1 Kgs 11:20). When Hadad heard that David and Joab were dead, he asked Pharaoh to let him return to his own country. 1 Kgs 11:25 counts the trouble Hadad caused alongside that of Rezon, who reigned in Syria. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes Hadad as stirring up Edom against Israelite rule. Several other people in the Bible share the name, including a son of Ishmael and an early king of Edom.

Hadad was a king of Edom, the last in the list of Edomite kings who reigned before Israel had a king. He succeeded Baal-hanan son of Achbor. His city was Pau (Pai in 1 Chr 1:50), and his wife was Mehetabel, daughter of Matred and granddaughter of Mezahab. Genesis 36:39 spells his name Hadar, while 1 Chronicles has Hadad. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both take Hadar to be a copyist's variant of Hadad. After his death, 1 Chronicles goes on to list the chiefs ("dukes") of Edom. Easton's places his reign at about the time of Saul. Several other people in the Bible are named Hadad, including an earlier Edomite king, Hadad son of Bedad, in the same list. This Hadad is distinguished by his city and his wife.

Hadad-rimmon is a place named once, in Zech 12:11, where the prophet compares a coming great mourning in Jerusalem to "the mourning of Hadadrimmon in the valley of Megiddon." Its name combines two names of Syrian gods. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take it as a place in the valley of Megiddo and connect the mourning with the lament for King Josiah, who was mortally wounded in battle near Megiddo (2 Kgs 23:29; 2 Chr 35:22–25). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes another view: the name may join two divine names, and the weeping may be ritual mourning for a god such as Tammuz (compare Ezek 8:14). Jerome identified it with Maximianopolis, near Jezreel. Easton's identifies it with the modern village of Rummaneh at the foot of the Megiddo hills, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Hadar was one of the twelve sons of Ishmael, Abraham's son by Hagar. He appears only in the lists of Ishmael's sons, named alongside brothers such as Tema, Jetur, Naphish and Kedemah (Gen 25:15). The parallel list in 1 Chr 1:30 spells his name Hadad. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the two spellings come from a small difference in the Hebrew text, and that the Revised Version reads "Hadad" in both places. Like his brothers, he was probably regarded as the ancestor of an Arabian tribe, by inference from the context of these genealogies, though nothing further is recorded about him or any people descended from him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "power" or "greatness." Ishmael also had a daughter, Bashemath, who married Esau.

Hadarezer, also called Hadadezer, son of Rehob, was king of the Aramean (Syrian) state of Zobah in David's time. Both spellings appear in the text, and Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning "Hadad is help." David defeated him near the Euphrates and also killed twenty-two thousand Syrians of Damascus who came to his aid. David took gold shields from Hadarezer's servants and a great deal of bronze from his cities, Betah and Berothai, which are called Tibhath and Chun in 1 Chr 18:8. Chronicles says Solomon later used this bronze for the temple's bronze sea, pillars and vessels. Toi king of Hamath, who had been at war with Hadarezer, sent gifts to congratulate David. Later Hadarezer brought Syrians from beyond the river to Helam under his commander Shobach. After their defeat, the kings subject to him made peace with Israel. Rezon, who later opposed Solomon, had fled from him.

Hadashah was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Judah. It appears only once, in the list of towns of the Shephelah, the lowland hills of western Judah, where it is named between Zenan and Migdalgad (Josh 15:37). The name means "new." The Mishnah, as reported by the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, calls it the smallest town in Judah. Its site is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests it is probably the Adasa mentioned in the history of the Maccabees, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as unidentified. The location shown here follows an identification with the modern village of Ibdis, in the southern coastal plain of Israel, which fits the town's place in the Shephelah list.

Hadid was a town named with Lod (Lydda) and Ono in the lists of exiles who returned from Babylon. Ezra 2:33 counts 725 people from Lod, Hadid and Ono together, and the parallel list in Neh 7:37 gives 721. Neh 11:34 includes Hadid among the places resettled by people of Benjamin after the return, so it was probably a Benjamite town. The name is usually taken to mean "sharp" or "pointed." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with Adida, a town fortified by Simon Maccabeus according to 1 Maccabees. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that in Eusebius's time a town called Aditha stood east of Lydda. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the ISBE place Hadid at modern el-Haditheh, about 3 miles (5 km) east or northeast of Lydda, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Hadlai was an Ephraimite, known only as the father of Amasa. His son was one of the leaders of the tribe of Ephraim who stood up against the soldiers of the northern kingdom returning from war against Judah. Those soldiers had brought back captives from Judah, and the leaders objected to keeping them (2 Chr 28:12). By context these events fell in the time of Pekah, king of Israel, and Ahaz, king of Judah, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. Nothing else is recorded about Hadlai himself. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "resting," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "rest of God."

Hadoram was a son of Joktan, listed fifth among his thirteen sons in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:27) and again in the parallel genealogy of 1 Chr 1:21. Through Joktan he descended from Shem by way of Arphaxad, Shelah and Eber, making him about the sixth generation after Noah. His brothers included Sheba, Ophir and Havilah, and nothing is recorded about him beyond his name. Like the other sons of Joktan, he is generally taken to stand for a people or tribe as well as an individual. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as the founder of an Arab tribe, while Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that, unlike the territories of several of his brothers, his settlements have not been identified. He should not be confused with Hadoram the son of Tou, king of Hamath, who appears in David's time.

Hadrach was a region in Syria, named only once in the Bible, in Zechariah's oracle that opens "the burden of the word of the LORD in the land of Hadrach," with Damascus as its resting place (Zech 9:1). The following verses group it with Hamath, Tyre and Sidon as targets of the same judgment (Zech 9:2). Its exact location is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with Hatarikka, a land in Assyrian inscriptions that Assyrian kings campaigned against in the 8th century BC, placed north of Lebanon, probably near Hamath. Easton's Bible Dictionary records Rawlinson's suggestion of Edessa. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the name as lost. The location shown here is a rough point at Damascus, reflecting the region's link with that city in the verse rather than a specific identified site.

Haeleph was a town given to the tribe of Benjamin, named once in the list of Benjamin's cities in Josh 18:28. The King James Version spells it Eleph. The Hebrew form includes the definite article, "the Eleph," which gives the spelling Haeleph. It appears in the last group of fourteen cities, alongside Zelah and Jebusi (Jerusalem), so it probably lay in the hill country near Jerusalem. Nothing else is recorded about it. Its exact site is uncertain. The location shown here follows the view that identifies it with Lifta, an abandoned village on the northwestern edge of modern Jerusalem. Other scholars connect Lifta instead with Nephtoah, a spring on the border between Judah and Benjamin.

Hagab was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel, as recorded in the list of returning families in Ezra 2:46. Nothing else is known of him as an individual. His name probably means "locust," according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that his family is listed just after the similar name Hagabah but is missing from the parallel list of returning temple servants in Neh 7:48. The return under Zerubbabel is usually dated to about 536 BC or shortly before, an estimate drawn from context rather than stated in the text.

Hagabah was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Judah with Zerubbabel. His name appears only in the list of returning families, where "the children of Hagabah" are counted among the temple servants (Ezra 2:45). The parallel list spells the name Hagaba (Neh 7:48). According to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, the name means "locust." That work also notes that he is similar to, but listed separately from, Hagab, another ancestor of temple servants named in Ezra's list. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in these lists.

Hagar was an Egyptian slave woman who served Sarai, the wife of Abram (Abraham). Because Sarai had no children, she gave Hagar to Abram as a wife after he had lived ten years in Canaan. When Hagar conceived, she looked down on her mistress, and later she fled from Sarai. On the way, an angel met her and asked where she was going. She bore Abram a son, Ishmael, when Abram was eighty-six, about 1910 BC by inference from context. Later, Sarah saw Ishmael mocking, and Abraham sent Hagar and the boy away with bread and water. They wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba, where the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven and told her that God had heard the boy. In Gal 4:24–25 Paul, spelling her name Agar, uses her in an allegory of the covenant from Mount Sinai.

Haggai was a prophet in Judah after the return from exile in Babylon. The book that bears his name is credited to him. He delivered a series of messages dated to the second year of King Darius of Persia, about 520 BC by inference from context. They were addressed to Zerubbabel the governor, Joshua the high priest, and the people, urging them to resume rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem. The leaders and people obeyed his words, and he assured them that the LORD was with them. He also questioned the priests about ritual uncleanness to make a point about the nation. Ezra pairs him with Zechariah son of Iddo and credits their prophesying with helping the elders finish the temple. Nothing is recorded of his family or tribe, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "feast."

Haggeri is named in 1 Chr 11:38 as the father of Mibhar, one of the mighty men of David listed in that chapter. Nothing else is recorded about him. In the parallel list of David's warriors at 2 Sam 23:36, the corresponding place reads "Bani the Gadite." Smith's Bible Dictionary takes that as the probable original reading, which suggests that "Mibhar the son of Haggeri" may reflect a difference in how the text was handed down. Following the same connection, the STEPBible proper-names index places Haggeri's family in the tribe of Gad. Some reference works, such as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, spell the name Hagri. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "a stranger," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "wanderer."

Haggi was the second son of Gad and a grandson of Jacob. He appears in the list of Jacob's descendants who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:16), where he is named after his brother Ziphion. His other brothers were Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi and Areli. In the census taken in the wilderness (Num 26:15), he is named as the ancestor of the Haggites, one of the clans of the tribe of Gad. Some of his brothers' names differ between the two lists: Ziphion appears as Zephon, Arodi as Arod, and Ezbon is matched in Numbers by Ozni. The name probably means "festive," according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Nothing else is recorded about Haggi or his descendants.

Haggiah was a Levite from the line of Merari, named once in the genealogy of the Levites at 1 Chr 6:30. There he is listed as the son of Shimea and the father of Asaiah. The surrounding verses trace Merari's descendants generation by generation, and the Merarite placement follows from that context, as Smith's Bible Dictionary also notes. Nothing else is recorded about his life. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "the Lord's feast," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "feast of Yah." His son Asaiah may be the Merarite Asaiah who later helped bring the ark to Jerusalem under David, but the text does not make that link directly.

Hahiroth is a shortened form of Pi-hahiroth, the place where the Israelites camped just before passing through the sea after leaving Egypt. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as the same place as Pi-hahiroth. In Num 33:8 the Hebrew text has the short form, though the King James Version renders it "Pihahiroth." That verse records that Israel set out from before it, crossed through the midst of the sea into the wilderness, traveled three days in the wilderness of Etham, and camped at Marah. The earlier accounts place Pi-hahiroth between Migdol and the sea, opposite Baal-zephon (Exod 14:2; Num 33:7). Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is a rough placement near the northern end of the Gulf of Suez, close to modern Suez, which matches one common view of where the crossing took place.

Hakkatan was the father of Johanan, who led the family group descended from Azgad when it returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. Johanan brought 110 men with him (Ezra 8:12). Hakkatan is known only through this mention of his son, and nothing else is recorded about him. Whether he went back to Jerusalem himself is not stated. His name means "the little one" or "the young one" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia; Smith's Bible Dictionary). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras 8:38 gives the name as Akatan.

Hakkephirim is a place named in Neh 6:2, where Sanballat and Geshem invited Nehemiah to meet them in the plain of Ono. Nehemiah understood the invitation as a plot to harm him. The Hebrew word means "the villages," and the King James Version translates it that way ("in some one of the villages"). Some modern translations instead treat it as the proper name of a particular village. Either reading places it in the plain of Ono, a lowland area near the coastal plain, well away from Jerusalem. That distance probably explains why Nehemiah suspected a trap. The exact site is unknown. The location shown here places it near ancient Ono, generally identified with Kafr Ana, near present-day Or Yehuda east of Tel Aviv.

Hakkoz was a priest whose name was given to the seventh of the twenty-four divisions of priests. These divisions were drawn by lot in David's time to take turns serving at the sanctuary (1 Chr 24:10). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as the head of one of these priestly courses, and gives the name's meaning as "the thorn." Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the same name appears as Koz in the King James Version of Ezra 2:61 and Nehemiah 3:4, 21. Those passages concern a later priestly family of that name, so the connection between the two is probably one of family descent. Beyond his place in the order of the priestly courses, nothing more is recorded about him.

Hakupha was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel. "The children of Hakupha" appear in the list of returning families in Ezra 2:51 and again in the parallel list in Neh 7:53. In both lists they are named between the families of Bakbuk and Harhur. The verses give no further details about Hakupha himself, and the name may refer to a family line rather than to a single known individual. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as a family name among the Nethinim and gives its meaning as "incitement." Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "bent," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a commandment of the mouth."

Halah was a region where the king of Assyria resettled Israelites taken captive from the northern kingdom. After Samaria fell in the ninth year of King Hoshea, the deportees were placed in Halah, in Habor by the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes (2 Kgs 17:6; 18:11). Chronicles says Tiglath-pileser had earlier carried Reuben, Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh to Halah, Habor, Hara and the river Gozan (1 Chr 5:26). Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it along the upper Khabur River in present-day northeastern Syria and, like Smith's Bible Dictionary, links it with the district Ptolemy called Chalcitis. Another view connects it with an Assyrian district near Nineveh. The location shown here follows the upper Khabur identification, near the Gozan river named alongside it.

Halhul was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed among the towns allotted to the tribe of Judah alongside Bethzur and Gedor (Josh 15:58). The Bible mentions it only in this list. Its name survives in the modern village of Halhul, a few miles north of Hebron near the road to Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary puts it about 5 miles north-east of Hebron, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives about 4 miles north. The location shown here matches this identification. Easton's records a Jewish tradition that Gad, David's seer, was buried there. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds that the village's mosque is linked to the prophet Jonah by a tradition dating to at least the 14th century. Easton's takes the name to mean "full of hollows", and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "trembling".

Hali was a town on the border of the territory given to the tribe of Asher. It is named only once, in the list of Asher's boundary towns, between Helkath and Beten and alongside Achshaph (Josh 19:25). The Bible says nothing more about it. Its site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says no firm identification is possible, though it suggests the ruin of Khirbet 'Alia, about 13 miles northeast of Acre. The location shown here is only approximate, placing it in western Galilee inland from Acre, the general area of Asher's border towns. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "necklace," and Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "a precious stone" among other meanings.

Hallohesh was one of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the covenant made in the time of Nehemiah, after the return from exile. Nehemiah 10 lists him among the chiefs who pledged to keep the law. Neh 10:24 names him beside Pileha and Shobek. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes him to be the same man as Halohesh of Neh 3:12, whose son Shallum, ruler of half the district of Jerusalem, helped repair the city walls with his daughters. Because the two passages may refer to the same family or to different people, that link is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as "enchanter", while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "the whisperer". Smith's dates the covenant to about 410 BC, an estimate.

Halohesh was the father of Shallum, who helped rebuild the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah. He is named only to identify his son. Shallum, described as ruler of half the district of Jerusalem, repaired a section of the wall with his daughters (Neh 3:12). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the wall repair to about 446 BC, an estimate drawn from context. Nothing else is said about Halohesh himself. A man spelled Hallohesh appears among the leaders who sealed the covenant in Neh 10:24. He may be the same person or a member of the same family, but the text does not say so.

Ham was one of the three sons of Noah. He is always listed between Shem and Japheth (Gen 5:32; 6:10). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take him to be the youngest, pointing to Gen 9:24, while Smith's Bible Dictionary treats him as the second son. He and his wife entered the ark with Noah's family and came out after the Flood, which is dated to about 2348 BC by inference from context. Later, when Noah lay drunk, Ham saw his father's nakedness and told his two brothers. In the account that follows, Noah's curse falls on Ham's son Canaan (Gen 9:25). Ham's sons were Cush, Mizraim, Phut and Canaan, ancestors of peoples traditionally linked with Ethiopia, Egypt, Libya and Canaan. The Psalms use "the land of Ham" as a poetic name for Egypt (Ps 105:23). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "hot."

Ham was a region east of the Jordan where Chedorlaomer and the kings allied with him defeated the Zuzim during their campaign, as described in Gen 14:5. It is named between Ashteroth Karnaim and Shaveh Kiriathaim, which suggests a place in the highlands of Transjordan along the invaders' route south. This name is shared by several places and people in the Bible, including Noah's son. The site of this Ham is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint reads "with them" instead of "in Ham." It also records suggestions that the name comes from "Ammon" or was an old name for Rabbath-ammon. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it probably in Ammonite territory. The location shown here follows the identification with Rabbath-ammon, at modern Amman in Jordan. The name probably means "hot" or "heat."

Ham, as a place name, here refers to Egypt, called "the land of Ham" in several psalms recalling the exodus (Ps 78:51; Ps 105:23, 27; Ps 106:22). The name comes from Noah's son Ham, whose descendants in Gen 10:6 include Mizraim, the Hebrew name for Egypt. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as "hot" or "heat," and Easton's Bible Dictionary notes a link with an Egyptian word meaning "black." Several places share this name. Another Ham appears in Gen 14:5 as the home of the Zuzims, east of the Jordan, and is usually treated as a separate town. The location shown here is in the Nile Delta near modern Cairo, which places it in Egypt rather than at the town east of the Jordan. No verses are attached to this entry, so this identification rests on the coordinates and on those connected passages.

Haman, son of Hammedatha the Agagite, was the chief official of the Persian king Ahasuerus, who placed him above all the other princes (Esth 3:1). When Mordecai the Jew refused to bow to him, Haman resolved to destroy all the Jews in the empire.
