He cast Pur, the lot, to set a date, promised silver to the royal treasury, and sealed a decree with the king's ring. Queen Esther invited him with the king to two banquets. Between them he was made to lead Mordecai through the city in honour. At the second banquet Esther named him as the enemy, and he was hanged on the gallows he had built for Mordecai. His wife was Zeresh, and his ten sons were later killed and hanged. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries read "Agagite" as descent from Amalekite kings. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links it to a region called Agag near Media.

Hamath was a major city of Syria, the capital of a kingdom of the same name, identified with modern Hama on the Orontes River; the location shown here follows that identification. Amos calls it "Hamath the great" (Amos 6:2). Its king Toi sent greetings to David after David defeated Hadadezer (2 Sam 8:9), and Solomon built store cities in its territory (2 Chr 8:4). Jeroboam II of Israel later recovered it (2 Kgs 14:28). Assyria conquered it, and the Assyrian envoys pointed to its fallen king and gods as a warning to Jerusalem (2 Kgs 18:34; 19:13). People from Hamath were resettled in Samaria, where they made the god Ashima (2 Kgs 17:24, 30). Riblah "in the land of Hamath" was where Pharaoh Necho imprisoned Jehoahaz and Nebuchadnezzar judged Zedekiah (2 Kgs 23:33; Jer 52:9). Ezekiel names Hamath on Israel's northern border (Ezek 47:16–17).

Hamath-zobah was a place in Syria that Solomon attacked and overcame, mentioned only in 2 Chr 8:3. The surrounding passage describes his building of cities, and the next verse speaks of store cities he built in Hamath. The name joins Hamath, the major city on the Orontes River, with Zobah, an Aramean kingdom of David's time. Its exact identity is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests it may have been a second Hamath, distinguished from "Great Hamath" by the added name Zobah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that no site of that name is known apart from Great Hamath. It suggests the double name may describe the reach of Solomon's conquests over parts of Zobah, which Hamath had perhaps absorbed. It also notes that one Greek manuscript reads "Beth-zobah." The location shown here follows the identification with Hamath itself, the modern city of Hama in Syria.

Hamathite is the name given to one of the descendants of Canaan, son of Ham, in the Table of Nations. He is named last among Canaan's sons, after Zidon, Heth, the Jebusite, the Amorite, the Girgasite, the Hivite, the Arkite, the Sinite, the Arvadite and the Zemarite. Genesis adds that after these "the families of the Canaanites spread abroad" (Gen 10:18). The same list is repeated in 1 Chr 1:16. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the name as a family or people descended from Canaan rather than a single individual. The form of the name suggests a link with the people of Hamath, a city on the Orontes River in Syria (modern Hama), though the verses do not state this directly. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hammath was one of the fortified cities in the territory given to the tribe of Naphtali. It is listed alongside Ziddim, Zer, Rakkath and Chinnereth (Josh 19:35). The name means "hot springs." Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with the warm baths on the shore of the Sea of Galilee just south of Tiberias. Smith's also suggests that the Levitical city Hammoth-dor in Josh 21:32 is the same place. The location shown here does not follow that identification. It places the city farther northwest, near the present Israel–Lebanon border, so the site remains uncertain. The same Hebrew name appears in 1 Chr 2:55, where the King James Version spells it Hemath and calls it "the father of the house of Rechab." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes that Hemath as a person, an ancestor of the Kenites, rather than this city.

Hammedatha was the father of Haman, the official whom King Ahasuerus of Persia promoted above all his princes and who plotted to destroy the Jews in the book of Esther. He is known only through his son, who is repeatedly called "Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite" (Esth 3:1; 3:10; 8:5; 9:24). The text says nothing about Hammedatha himself. The title "Agagite" may describe the family as a whole, though it is attached to Haman's name, and its origin is not explained in these verses. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the name to be Persian, meaning "given by the moon," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "he that troubles the law." His grandsons, Haman's ten sons, were killed when the Jews defended themselves (Esth 9:10).

Hammelech is named in the King James Version as the father of two men in the book of Jeremiah. His son Jerahmeel was one of three men the king, Jehoiakim by the context of the chapter, ordered to arrest Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet, though they were hidden (Jer 36:26). His son Malchiah owned the muddy cistern in the court of the prison into which Jeremiah was lowered with ropes (Jer 38:6). The Hebrew ha-melekh means "the king," and views differ on whether it is a personal name. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia read it as "the king," as the American Standard Version translates it. On that reading these men were royal sons, possibly of different kings, since Zedekiah reigned by the time of Jer 38. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it as probably a proper name, and this entry follows that view.

Hammoleketh was a woman of the tribe of Manasseh, part of the wider Joseph tribes, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 7. She is called the sister of Gilead, so she was a daughter of Machir, Manasseh's son. Peresh and Sheresh, Machir's sons by his wife Maachah in the preceding verses, were her brothers. 1 Chr 7:18 says she bore Ishod, Abiezer and Mahalah. Her name means "the queen," according to Easton's Bible Dictionary. Her son Abiezer probably gave his name to the Abiezrite clan of Manasseh. That clan appears among Manasseh's family groups in Josh 17:2, and Gideon belonged to it, as Judg 6:11 shows. Nothing else is recorded about her.

Hammon was a city named in the list of towns on the border of the tribe of Asher, alongside Rehob and Kanah and reaching toward Sidon (Josh 19:28). The name probably means "glowing" or "warm," and Smith's Bible Dictionary connects it with warm springs. A Hammon is also listed among the towns with surrounding pasturelands given to the Levites from the tribe of Naphtali (1 Chr 6:76). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible names list take this Naphtali town to be the same as Hammath or Hammoth-dor in Joshua, which would make it a different place from the Asher town. For the Asher town, Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests 'Ain Hamul. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia prefers Umm el-'Amud on the coast about 10 miles south of Tyre, where an inscription to Baal Hammon was found. The location shown here follows that coastal identification.

Hammoth-dor was a city in the territory of Naphtali that was assigned, with its surrounding pasturelands, to the Levites. It was one of three such cities from Naphtali, listed with Kedesh in Galilee, a city of refuge, and Kartan (Josh 21:32). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "dwelling of the warm springs." Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take it to be the same place as Hammath, a fortified city of Naphtali (Josh 19:35). The ISBE also links it with Hammon in the parallel Levitical list (1 Chr 6:76) and places it at the hot springs of el-Hammam, just south of Tiberias on the Sea of Galilee. The location shown here does not follow that identification. It places the city in far western Upper Galilee, near the present Lebanese border. The exact site remains uncertain.

Hamonah, meaning "multitude" or "horde," is the name of a city in Ezekiel's prophecy against Gog, mentioned only in Ezek 39:16. The surrounding passage describes the burial of Gog's defeated army in a valley that would be called Hamon-gog, and says the land would be cleansed in this way. Hamonah is apparently a city near that burial valley, and its name recalls the multitude buried there. Easton's Bible Dictionary treats it as a figurative name for the place of slaughter and burial, while Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe it as a city, the latter placing it near Hamon-gog. No actual site is known. The location shown here is a rough placement east of the Dead Sea, probably based on Ezek 39:11, which puts the burial valley "on the east of the sea."

Hamor was a Hivite, called "prince of the country" around the city of Shechem, and the father of Shechem in the time of Jacob. Jacob bought a field from Hamor's sons for a hundred pieces of money, and Joseph's bones were later buried there. After his son Shechem seized and violated Jacob's daughter Dinah, Hamor went to Jacob to ask for her as Shechem's wife. Jacob's sons replied deceitfully, demanding that the city's men be circumcised. Hamor and Shechem persuaded the men at the city gate to agree. Afterward Jacob's sons, named as Simeon and Levi in the surrounding narrative, killed Hamor, Shechem and the men of the city. Generations later the people of Shechem were still called "the men of Hamor" (Judg 9:28). Acts 7:16 gives his name in Greek form as Emmor. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the name means "donkey."

Hamuel was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named only in the Simeonite genealogy of 1 Chr 4:26. He was the son of Mishma and the father of Zacchur, whose son was Shimei. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him in the family of Shaul, a son of Simeon, which fits the surrounding verses. It gives the meaning of his name as "heat," that is, "wrath, of God." Some reference works, including the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, spell the name Hammuel. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hamul was a son of Pharez (Perez) and a grandson of Judah, and the brother of Hezron. He is listed among the family of Jacob that went down to Egypt (Gen 46:12), so he belongs to the tribe of Judah. In the census taken in the wilderness, his descendants form a clan called the Hamulites (Num 26:21), making him the founder of one of Judah's family groups. The genealogy in 1 Chr 2:5 names him again alongside Hezron. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him the younger son, probably because Hezron is always named first. Pharez was Judah's son by Tamar, as Gen 38 relates. The meaning of his name is usually given as "pitied" or "spared" (Easton's Bible Dictionary; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Nothing else is recorded about his life.

Hamutal was a wife of King Josiah of Judah and the mother of two later kings, Jehoahaz and Zedekiah. She was the daughter of a man named Jeremiah from Libnah, a town in Judah. He is probably not the prophet Jeremiah, who came from Anathoth. She is named only in the standard notices that open the reigns of her sons. Jehoahaz became king at twenty-three and reigned three months in Jerusalem (2 Kgs 23:31). Zedekiah became king at twenty-one and reigned eleven years (2 Kgs 24:18; Jer 52:1). That Josiah was their father comes from the surrounding passages, which call Jehoahaz the son of Josiah and make Zedekiah the uncle of King Jehoiachin. Jehoiakim, whose mother was Zebudah, was by inference their half-brother. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "kinsman of the dew." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it also appears in the form "Hamital."

Hanameel was the son of Shallum and a cousin of the prophet Jeremiah, since Shallum was Jeremiah's uncle. His name is often explained as meaning "God has been gracious" (Easton's Bible Dictionary). The LORD told Jeremiah that Hanameel would come and ask him to buy his field at Anathoth, in the territory of Benjamin, because the right of redemption belonged to Jeremiah as next of kin. Hanameel then came to Jeremiah in the court of the prison and made the offer. Jeremiah took it as the word of the LORD and bought the field for seventeen shekels of silver. The deed of purchase was handed to Baruch son of Neriah in front of Hanameel, the witnesses who signed it, and the Jews sitting in the prison court. By context this happened while the Babylonians were besieging Jerusalem, and the purchase served as a sign that land would again be bought and sold in Judah.

Hanan was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the sons of Shashak listed in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. His brothers named in the same list include Abdon, Zichri, Hananiah, Elam, Antothijah, Iphedeiah, Ishpan, Heber, Eliel and Penuel. 1 Chr 8:28 describes the men of this list as heads of their fathers' houses living in Jerusalem, and on that basis Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him one of the chief people of the tribe. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which means "gracious" or "merciful," is shared by several other men in the Old Testament, and this Hanan should not be confused with them.

Hanan was one of the six sons of Azel, a man of the tribe of Benjamin descended from King Saul through Jonathan's line. He appears only in two nearly identical genealogies, where he is listed last among his brothers Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah and Obadiah (1 Chr 8:38; 1 Chr 9:44). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia call him the youngest son, a reading drawn from his place at the end of the list. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, meaning "gracious," is shared by several other men in the Bible, so he should not be confused with them.

Hanan son of Maachah was one of David's mighty warriors. He appears only once, in the extended list of heroes in 1 Chr 11:43, where he is named alongside Joshaphat the Mithnite. This part of the list goes beyond the parallel roster in 2 Samuel 23, and nothing further is recorded about his deeds or background. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests that "son of Maachah" might mean he came from the Syrian district of Aram-maachah, though Maachah may simply be his father's name, as this entry takes it. The name Hanan means "gracious" or "merciful." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Hanan should not be confused with them.

Hanan was the ancestor or head of a family of Nethinim, the temple servants, whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel. The "children of Hanan" appear in the list of returning families in Ezra 2:46 and again in the parallel list in Neh 7:49. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his name. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the return to about 536 BC, and the name is usually explained as meaning "gracious" or "merciful." Several other men in the Bible are also called Hanan, and this entry refers only to the one named in the temple servants' lists.

Hanan was a Levite in Jerusalem after the return from exile. He was one of the men who, alongside Ezra's public reading of the law, helped the people understand what was being read while they stood in their places (Neh 8:7). A Levite named Hanan also appears among the Levites who put their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time (Neh 10:10). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes this to be probably the same man, since he is listed there with several of the same companions, including Hodijah, Kelita and Pelaiah. This entry follows that identification. Smith's dates the events to about 446 BC. The name means "gracious" or "merciful." Several other men in the Bible are also called Hanan.

Hanan was one of the men who put their seal to the covenant made under Nehemiah, in which the returned exiles in Jerusalem pledged to keep the Law of Moses. He appears only in Neh 10:22, in a list of names with no further details. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary count him among the chiefs or heads of the people, since the verse falls within the list of lay leaders (Neh 10:14–27). STEPBible's Tyndale names list describes him as a Levite. Smith dates the sealing to about 410 BC, an estimate. Several other men in the Bible share the name Hanan, including two more in the same chapter, so he should not be confused with them. The name is usually taken to mean "merciful" or "gracious."

Hanan was one of the men who set their seal to the written covenant made in Jerusalem under Nehemiah, by which the returned exiles bound themselves to keep the Law of Moses. He is named only once, in Neh 10:26, between Ahijah and Anan. That verse falls within the list of the "chief of the people" (Neh 10:14–27), and Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him among the leading laymen who signed. The STEPBible names index describes him as a Levite. This entry follows the lay identification, which places him among the heads of the people. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a Levite named Hanan earlier in the same list (Neh 10:10), so he should not be confused with them. The name is usually explained as meaning "merciful" or "full of grace."

Hanan, son of Zaccur and grandson of Mattaniah, was one of the men Nehemiah appointed as treasurers over the temple storehouses in Jerusalem after the return from exile. He served alongside Shelemiah the priest, Zadok the scribe and Pedaiah the Levite. They were chosen because they were considered trustworthy, and their job was to distribute supplies to their fellow workers. By inference from the context, these supplies were the tithes of grain, wine and oil brought in for the Levites and singers, and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a storekeeper of the provisions collected as tithes. The name means "merciful" or "full of grace," according to Smith's and Hitchcock's dictionaries. Several other men in the Bible are also named Hanan, and this one is known only from Neh 13:13.

Hanan was the son of Igdaliah, mentioned once in the Bible. His name means "gracious" or "merciful." Jeremiah brought the Rechabites into the temple in Jerusalem, to a room belonging to "the sons of Hanan." This room was next to the chamber of the princes and above the chamber of Maaseiah son of Shallum, the doorkeeper (Jer 35:4). The verse calls someone "a man of God," but it is unclear whether this means Hanan or his father Igdaliah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia applies it to Igdaliah. The title may mean a prophet, and Hanan's "sons" may have been his disciples or followers rather than his children, though the text does not say so. The setting of the chapter places him in the time of King Jehoiakim, near the end of the kingdom of Judah. Several other people in the Bible share the name Hanan.

Hanani was a seer in Judah during the reign of King Asa. According to 2 Chr 16:7, he came to Asa and rebuked him for relying on the king of Syria rather than on the LORD, warning that the Syrian army had therefore escaped his hand. The following verses report that Asa was angered and put him in prison. Hanani is also named as the father of the prophet Jehu, who spoke the word of the LORD against Baasha king of Israel and later confronted King Jehoshaphat of Judah. Jehu's writings recorded Jehoshaphat's acts. 2 Chr 19:2 calls Jehoshaphat's challenger "Jehu the son of Hanani the seer," which supports treating the seer and the father as one man. Smith's Bible Dictionary allows that the father may have been a different Hanani, and Easton's Bible Dictionary says he was probably the same. This entry follows the single-person view. The name means "gracious."

Hanani was a Levite musician, one of the fourteen sons of Heman listed in 1 Chr 25:4. Heman was one of the leaders of music in worship during David's reign. When the singers and musicians were divided by lot into twenty-four courses, or rotating groups, for service at the sanctuary, the eighteenth lot fell to Hanani. His group of twelve was made up of him, his sons and his relatives (1 Chr 25:25). His brothers included Hananiah, Mattaniah, Uzziel and Jerimoth, who each led a course of their own. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of his name as "gracious." Several other men in the Bible are also named Hanani, and this one should not be confused with them.

Hanani was a priest from the family of Immer who returned from exile in Babylon and is listed among the men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra. He appears with Zebadiah under the heading "of the sons of Immer" (Ezra 10:20). By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was among those who agreed to send away their foreign wives, and the priests listed alongside him pledged to do so and offered a ram as a guilt offering. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify him as a priest. The name, meaning "gracious," belongs to several men in the Bible, and this Hanani should not be confused with others of the same name, such as the seer of King Asa's time or Nehemiah's brother.

Hanani was a brother of Nehemiah, and so a son of Hachaliah. Neh 1:2 calls him "one of my brethren," a phrase that could mean a close relative in general, but Neh 7:2 calls him "my brother." He came with some men of Judah to Nehemiah, probably at the Persian royal city of Susa named in the surrounding verses. Nehemiah questioned them about the Jews who had survived the exile and about Jerusalem, and their report led to Nehemiah's mission to rebuild the city. After the wall was finished, Nehemiah put Hanani, together with Hananiah the ruler of the palace, in charge of Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes this as charge over the city gates, while Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a governor of the city under Nehemiah. The name means "gracious" and is shared by several other people in the Bible.

Hanani was one of the musicians who took part in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. He is named last in a group of eight "brethren" who played "the musical instruments of David the man of God," with Ezra the scribe leading them in the procession (Neh 12:36). The preceding verse introduces Zechariah son of Jonathan, and the group in Neh 12:36 is called his brethren. This entry treats Hanani as Jonathan's son and Zechariah's brother, though "brethren" may mean kinsmen or fellow musicians rather than full brothers. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a priest, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a priest and chief musician. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which means "gracious."

Hananiah was a son of Zerubbabel, the governor who led Jews back from exile in Babylon. He belonged to the tribe of Judah and to the royal line of David, and probably lived in the late sixth century BC, after about 536 BC, which Smith's Bible Dictionary gives as an estimate. His brother Meshullam and sister Shelomith are named with him, and 1 Chr 3:20 lists five more siblings. 1 Chr 3:21 names his sons Pelatiah and Jesaiah, then lists 'the sons of' Rephaiah, Arnan, Obadiah and Shechaniah. This entry treats all six as his children, though the verse can also be read as a separate list of related families or as a chain of later generations. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him with Joanna in Luke's genealogy of Jesus. His name means 'the Lord has been gracious.' Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Hananiah was a member of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 8:24 as one of the sons of Shashak. His brothers listed with him include Ishpan, Heber, Eliel, Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Elam, Antothijah, Iphedeiah and Penuel. The passage gives no details about his life beyond his place in the family line. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him a chief of Benjamin, and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as the head of a Benjamite house, following the genealogy's summary of these men as heads of fathers' houses. His name means roughly "the Lord has been gracious." It was common in Israel, so he should be kept distinct from the several other men called Hananiah in the Bible.

Hananiah was a Levite, one of the fourteen sons of Heman, who was one of the chief musicians organized under King David. He is listed with his brothers in 1 Chr 25:4. When lots were cast to set the order of service for the temple musicians, the sixteenth lot fell to Hananiah. He served with his sons and relatives, a group of twelve (1 Chr 25:23). The surrounding chapter places this arrangement in David's reign. The name means roughly "the Lord has been gracious" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) and was common in Israel, so this Hananiah should be kept distinct from several others of the same name.

Hananiah was one of the captains of King Uzziah of Judah. 2 Chr 26:11 describes Uzziah's army, which went out to war in organized bands. Jeiel the scribe and Maaseiah the official counted and recorded it, and the whole work was under Hananiah's direction. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him one of Uzziah's military officers, and Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a general. The name, meaning roughly "the Lord has been gracious," was common in Israel, and several different men in the Bible bear it. This Hananiah is known only from this one verse, and nothing more is told about his family or career.

Hananiah was a descendant of Bebai, one of the family groups of Israel, in the time of Ezra. He appears with Jehohanan, Zabbai and Athlai in Ezra 10:28. That verse belongs to the list in Ezra 10 of men who had married foreign wives and who, in response to Ezra's reforms after the return from exile in Babylon, agreed to send those wives away. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of the sons of Bebai who returned with Ezra from Babylon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him a Levite and notes that he also appears in the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:29. Nothing more is recorded about him. His name, meaning roughly "the Lord has been gracious," was common in Israel, and he should not be confused with the several other men called Hananiah.

Hananiah was one of the men who repaired the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah after the return from exile. Nehemiah 3:8 describes him as "the son of one of the apothecaries," a phrase usually understood to mean that he belonged to the guild of perfume or ointment makers. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it this way, calling him one of the perfumers. He worked on the section next to Uzziel, a goldsmith, and the workers in this stretch fortified the city as far as the Broad Wall. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, meaning roughly "the Lord has been gracious," was common in Israel, and several other men called Hananiah appear in the Bible. This one is not clearly identified with any of them.

Hananiah, son of Shelemiah, was one of the men who rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah after the return from exile. Nehemiah 3 lists the builders section by section, and Neh 3:30 says that Hananiah and Hanun, the sixth son of Zalaph, together repaired "another piece." The phrase suggests they took on a second stretch of wall. By inference from the nearby verses, this section lay on the eastern side of the city, near the Horse Gate, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it. That work further suggests the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes he may be the same man as another Hananiah named among the wall builders. His name, common in Israel, means "the LORD has been gracious." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hananiah was the ruler of the palace in Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah. After the city wall was rebuilt, Nehemiah put him in charge of Jerusalem together with Nehemiah's brother Hanani. Nehemiah explains the choice by saying Hananiah was a faithful man who feared God more than many others (Neh 7:2). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes "the palace" to mean the fortress or citadel (the birah) guarding the temple area. Smith's Bible Dictionary connects him with the arrangements for guarding the city gates described in the following verse, and dates his appointment to about 446 BC. The name means "the LORD has been gracious" and was common in Israel, so this man is distinct from the several others called Hananiah in the Bible. Whether he is the same as any other Hananiah named in Nehemiah is uncertain.

Hananiah was one of the men who sealed the written covenant in Nehemiah's time, when the community that had returned from exile in Babylon pledged to keep God's law. He is known only from his name in the list of those who set their seal to it (Neh 10:23), where he appears between Hoshea and Hashub. The surrounding section of the list (Neh 10:14–27) names the leaders of the people. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a Levite. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, meaning "the Lord has been gracious," was common in Israel, and several other men named Hananiah appear in Nehemiah's time. Whether this man is the same as any of them is uncertain.

Hananiah was a priest in the generation after the return from exile in Babylon. Neh 12:12 names him as head of the priestly family of Jeremiah in the days of Joiakim. Joiakim was the high priest who succeeded his father Jeshua, according to Neh 12:10 and 12:26. The family of Jeremiah was probably named after the priest Jeremiah who came back with Zerubbabel and Jeshua (Neh 12:1). It is a different person from the prophet Jeremiah. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Hananiah simply as a priest, son of Jeremiah. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him the head of that priestly course. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which means roughly "the Lord has been gracious."

Hananiah was a priest who blew a trumpet at the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt wall in Nehemiah's time. Neh 12:41 lists him last among seven priests with trumpets, after Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, Michaiah, Elioenai and Zechariah. By inference from the surrounding chapter, this group went with the second of the two thanksgiving choirs that marched along the wall. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, and it is uncertain whether this priest is the same as any of them, so this entry treats him as a separate person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "grace," "mercy," or "gift of the Lord."

Hananiah son of Azur was a prophet from Gibeon who publicly opposed Jeremiah in the temple during the fourth year of Zedekiah king of Judah. Speaking before the priests and the people, he declared in the Lord's name that within two full years God would break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon from the neck of all nations. As a sign, he took the wooden yoke Jeremiah was wearing and broke it. Jeremiah was then told to answer that the wooden yokes would be replaced by yokes of iron, and to tell Hananiah that the Lord had not sent him and that he was making the people trust in a lie. Hananiah died in the seventh month of that same year. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Benjamite and a false prophet. His name is shared by several other people in the Bible.

Hananiah was the father of Zedekiah, one of the princes of Judah during the reign of King Jehoiakim. He is known only through his son, who was among the officials sitting in the scribe's chamber of the royal palace when Micaiah son of Gemariah came to report the reading of Jeremiah's scroll by Baruch (Jer 36:12). Nothing further is recorded about Hananiah himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists him as the father of one of the princes under Jehoiakim. His name means "the LORD has been gracious" and was common in Israel, so he should be distinguished from others called Hananiah. These include the prophet who opposed Jeremiah and Daniel's companion, who was renamed Shadrach. Whether he is connected to any of them is not stated.

Hananiah was the father of Shelemiah and the grandfather of Irijah, the captain of the guard at the gate of Benjamin in Jerusalem. During the Babylonian siege, Irijah arrested the prophet Jeremiah as he was leaving the city and accused him of deserting to the Chaldeans (Jer 37:13). Hananiah is named only in this genealogical note identifying his grandson, and nothing else is recorded about him. The name, meaning "the LORD has been gracious," was common in Israel, and several other men in the Bible bear it. These include the false prophet who opposed Jeremiah, but nothing in the text links this Hananiah with any of them. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him before 589 BC, which fits a grandfather of an officer serving in Zedekiah's reign.

Hanes was a city in Egypt, mentioned only in Isa 30:4. In a passage warning Judah against relying on Egypt for protection, Isaiah describes envoys at Zoan (Tanis) and ambassadors arriving at Hanes, probably Judah's delegation seeking an alliance with Pharaoh. Its location is uncertain. Some identify it with Heracleopolis Magna, a major city of Middle Egypt whose name survives in the modern village of Ihnasya el-Medina near Beni Suef. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both mention this view. Others, following the ancient Aramaic translation, take Hanes to be Tahpanhes, a fortified town on Egypt's eastern frontier in the Nile Delta, closer to Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes this view. The location shown here follows the Heracleopolis identification.

Haniel was a man of the tribe of Asher, named as one of the sons of Ulla alongside his brothers Arah and Rezia in the genealogy of Asher (1 Chr 7:39). Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a chief of the tribe of Asher, probably by inference from the next verse, which calls the descendants of Asher heads of their fathers' houses and leading men. The name is also spelled Hanniel, the form the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia uses. It is usually explained as meaning "grace of God" (Smith's Bible Dictionary) or "the gift of God" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). He should be distinguished from Hanniel son of Ephod, a leader of Manasseh in the time of Moses.

Hannah was one of the two wives of Elkanah and the mother of the prophet Samuel. Her husband loved her and favored her, but she was childless while his other wife, Peninnah, had children (1 Sam 1:2, 1:5). On a yearly visit to the sanctuary at Shiloh she prayed silently in deep distress, and Eli the priest at first thought she was drunk until she explained that she had poured out her soul before the LORD. After the family returned home to Ramah she conceived and bore a son, naming him Samuel because she had asked him of the LORD. She kept him at home until he was weaned, then brought him to Shiloh to remain in the LORD's service. Her song of thanksgiving is recorded in 1 Sam 2:1–10. She later had three more sons and two daughters. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of her name as "favour" or "grace."

Hannathon was a town on the northern boundary of the territory given to the tribe of Zebulun. The boundary description in Josh 19:14 says the border turned around on the north side to Hannathon and ended in the valley of Jiphthahel. This is its only mention in the Bible. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts it among the cities of Zebulun, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "the gift of grace." Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links it with Kefar Hananyah, which the Mishnah names as the northern limit of Lower Galilee, and places it at the modern village of Kefr 'Anan, about 3 miles southeast of er-Rameh. Others place it at Tell el-Bedeiwiyeh, at the edge of the Beth Netofa valley farther south and west. The location shown here follows the Kefr 'Anan identification.

Hanniel was the son of Ephod and the leader, or prince, of the tribe of Manasseh named in Num 34:23. He was one of the tribal leaders chosen to help divide the land of Canaan among the tribes. The surrounding passage shows that these leaders were to work with Eleazar the priest and Joshua in allotting the land west of the Jordan. Manasseh is listed there as one of the two tribes descended from Joseph. The half of Manasseh that had already settled east of the Jordan did not need such a leader, so Hanniel probably represented the western half of the tribe, by inference from the passage. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "grace of God." A different man named Hanniel, from the tribe of Asher, appears in 1 Chr 7:39.

Hanoch was a son of Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, and so a grandson of Jacob. He is named first in every list of Reuben's sons, alongside his brothers Pallu, Hezron and Carmi, which suggests he was the eldest, as Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to be. He appears among Jacob's descendants who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:9), and among the heads of the fathers' houses of Reuben (Exod 6:14). In the wilderness census he is the ancestor of the Hanochites, one of the clans of the tribe of Reuben (Num 26:5). The Reubenite genealogy in 1 Chr 5:3 repeats his name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "dedicated." The same Hebrew name is borne by a son of Midian, a different person.

Hanun was the son of Nahash and succeeded him as king of the Ammonites. When Nahash died, David sent servants to console Hanun, saying he wanted to show kindness to him as his father had shown kindness to David. The Ammonite princes persuaded Hanun that the envoys had really come to spy out the city and overthrow it. Hanun shaved off half of each man's beard, cut their garments off at the buttocks and sent them away. Realizing they had made themselves hateful to David, Hanun and the Ammonites spent a thousand talents of silver hiring chariots and horsemen from Mesopotamia, Syria-maachah and Zobah. The war that followed went against the Ammonites (2 Sam 10). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "favored." The name is also borne by other men in the Bible.

Hanun was a man who, together with the inhabitants of Zanoah, repaired the Valley Gate of Jerusalem during the rebuilding of the city walls under Nehemiah. His group built the gate, set up its doors, locks and bars, and also repaired a thousand cubits (roughly 450 metres) of wall as far as the Dung Gate (Neh 3:13). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this work to about 446 BC. Whether Hanun was a leader of the Zanoah group or simply one of its members is not clear; the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts him among the inhabitants of Zanoah. The name, meaning "favored" or "gracious," is shared by several people in the Bible, including an Ammonite king in David's time and another wall-builder in the same chapter, and this Hanun should be kept distinct from them.

Hanun, the sixth son of Zalaph, was one of the men who repaired the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah after the return from exile. Neh 3:30 says he worked on "another piece", a second section next to the one repaired by Hananiah son of Shelemiah. Smith's Bible Dictionary places this stretch apparently on the east side of the city and dates the work to about 446 BC, a date inferred from context. The phrase "another piece" suggests he had already worked on an earlier section, though the text does not say which. The name, meaning "favored" or "gracious," is shared by several people in the Bible. He is probably distinct from the Hanun who repaired the Valley Gate earlier in the same chapter, and from the Ammonite king of that name in David's time. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hapharaim was a town in the territory given to the tribe of Issachar. It is named only once, in the list of Issachar's towns, alongside Shion and Anaharath (Josh 19:19). By inference from the surrounding list, which also includes Jezreel and Shunem, it lay in or near the Jezreel Valley in lower Galilee. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "searching" or "digging," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "place of a moat." The exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia follows Eusebius, who placed it about 6 miles north of Megiddo, and links it with the ruins of el-Ferriyeh northwest of el-Lejjun. The location shown here places it somewhat farther east, near modern Afula in the Jezreel Valley.

Hara was a region in the Assyrian empire to which Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria deported the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half tribe of Manasseh, along with Halah, Habor and the river Gozan (1 Chr 5:26). It is named only in this verse, and its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it between the Tigris and the Euphrates along the banks of the Khabur, and both Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionary note the suggestion that it is a variant of Haran. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia observes that the parallel accounts in 2 Kgs 17:6 and 18:11 omit Hara and add "the cities of the Medes," and that the Greek translation reads "mountains of the Medes." It suggests that the name may preserve a Hebrew word for "mountains" of Media. The location shown here follows the Khabur valley placement, in present-day northeastern Syria.

Haradah was one of the places where the Israelites camped during their wilderness journey after leaving Egypt. It appears only in the list of stations in Numbers 33, where the people moved to it from Mount Shapher and then on to Makheloth (Num 33:24–25). Easton's Bible Dictionary counts it as the twenty-fifth station of the journey, and the name is usually taken to mean "fear" or "fright." Nothing else is recorded about the place, and Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that its position is uncertain. The location shown here is only a rough estimate, placing it in the highlands east of the Arabah in present-day southern Jordan, near the Petra region.

Haran (brother of Abraham) was a son of Terah and a brother of Abram and Nahor (Gen 11:26–27). He was the father of Lot and of two daughters: Milcah, who married her uncle Nahor, and Iscah (Gen 11:27, 29). Haran died in Ur of the Chaldees, where he was born, while his father Terah was still alive (Gen 11:28). Afterward Terah took Haran's son Lot, along with Abram and Sarai, from Ur toward Canaan (Gen 11:31). Sarah is counted among his siblings because Gen 20:12 describes her as Terah's daughter by a different mother. His place in the birth order is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him the eldest son, while Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat him as the youngest. He is a different figure from the town of Haran, where the family later settled (Gen 11:31).

Haran (son of Caleb) was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:46. He was a son of Caleb by Caleb's concubine Ephah, and his full brothers were Moza and Gazez. The same verse says that Haran in turn fathered a son named Gazez. A brother and a son therefore share the name, and the text gives no further detail to explain this. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both describe him only as Caleb's son by Ephah. The Caleb of this genealogy belongs to the line of Hezron in Judah. He is not to be confused with Haran the brother of Abraham, who shares the name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "mountainous country," and Smith's renders it "a mountaineer." Nothing else is recorded about his life.

Haran (son of Shimei) was a Gershonite Levite listed in David's organization of the Levites. 1 Chr 23:9 names him with Shelomith and Haziel as the three sons of Shimei and counts them among the heads of the families descended from Laadan. From the surrounding chapter, this list belongs to the time when David, in his old age, arranged the Levites for service at the temple, so Haran probably lived during David's reign. It is unclear how this Shimei relates to the Shimei whose four sons appear in the next verse. Many readers take the Shimei of verse 9 to be a descendant of Laadan, distinct from Laadan's brother Shimei. Nothing else is recorded about Haran. He should not be confused with Haran the brother of Abraham. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "a mountaineer," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "mountainous country."

Haran was a city in Upper Mesopotamia where Terah settled with Abram, Sarai and Lot after leaving Ur of the Chaldees on the way to Canaan, and where Terah died (Gen 11:31–32). Abram left Haran for Canaan at seventy-five, taking his household and the possessions gathered there (Gen 12:4–5). By inference from context this was about 1921 BC. Later Rebekah sent Jacob to her brother Laban in Haran to escape Esau, and on arriving he met shepherds from the town (Gen 27:43; 28:10; 29:4). The Assyrian envoy listed Haran among places conquered by Assyrian kings (2 Kgs 19:12; Isa 37:12), and Ezekiel names its merchants among Tyre's trading partners (Ezek 27:23). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on the Balikh River, a tributary of the Euphrates, on the east–west caravan route. It is the modern Harran in southeastern Turkey, which matches the location shown here.

Harbona was one of the seven chamberlains, or court eunuchs, who served in the presence of the Persian king Ahasuerus. He is named third in the list of officials the king ordered, on the seventh day of his feast while he was merry with wine, to bring Queen Vashti before him (Esth 1:10). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the name's meaning as "ass-driver," taking it to be a Persian word. Easton's also identifies him with Harbonah in Esth 7:9, who later told the king about the gallows Haman had built for Mordecai, which led to Haman being hanged on it. The spelling differs slightly, but the same office and court make it probable that he is the same man.

Harbonah was one of the chamberlains (court officials) serving King Ahasuerus of Persia. At the banquet where Queen Esther exposed Haman's plot against the Jews, Harbonah told the king that Haman had built a gallows fifty cubits high for Mordecai, the man whose report had once saved the king's life, and that it stood at Haman's house. The king then ordered Haman hanged on it (Esth 7:9). Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him with Harbona, one of the seven chamberlains whom the king sent to bring Queen Vashti before his guests (Esth 1:10); the spelling differs slightly in the KJV. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "his destruction" or "his sword."

Hareph was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only once, in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:51, as "the father of Bethgader." There he appears alongside Shobal and Salma among the descendants of Caleb. The preceding verse can be read either as "the sons of Caleb the son of Hur" or as listing sons of Hur himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia call Hareph a son of Caleb, while this entry treats him as a son of Hur, which links him with the other sons of Hur named in this genealogy and in 1 Chr 4. In these lists "father of" a town probably means its founder or leading clan head, so Hareph was likely the ancestor of the people of Beth-gader. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "winter" or "reproach." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Harhaiah was the father of Uzziel, who repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall in the time of Nehemiah (Neh 3:8). He is named only in this one verse. The phrase "of the goldsmiths" is usually read as describing Uzziel, and perhaps the family, as belonging to the goldsmiths' guild. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both connect the goldsmith label with Harhaiah. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "heat, or anger, of the Lord" and Smith's Bible Dictionary "the Lord is angry," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "Yah protects." Smith's Bible Dictionary places him before 446 BC, an estimate drawn from the date of the wall rebuilding.

Harhur was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Judah with Zerubbabel. His name appears only in the two parallel lists of returning exiles, where "the children of Harhur" are named between the families of Hakupha and Bazluth (Ezra 2:51; Neh 7:53). The surrounding verses in both lists place these families among the Nethinim, the group who assisted the Levites in the temple. Nothing else is recorded about Harhur himself, and whether he was a single ancestor or the name of a clan is not stated. The name is usually explained as meaning "fever" or "inflammation" (Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also suggests "free-born" and notes a parallel form, Hasour, in the apocryphal 1 Esdras 5:31.

Harim was a priest whose name was given to the third of the twenty-four priestly divisions drawn by lot to serve in turn at the house of God (1 Chr 24:8). Smith's Bible Dictionary places this arrangement in the days of David. The priestly family called the children of Harim, 1,017 strong, appears in the lists of those who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:39; Neh 7:42), and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats them as his descendants. In Ezra's time five priests of this family, Maaseiah, Elijah, Shemaiah, Jehiel and Uzziah, are named among those who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:21). A second group of 'sons of Harim' appears later in the same chapter (Ezra 10:31). By inference from the context, they stand among the lay Israelites listed from Ezra 10:25 on, so they probably belonged to a separate, non-priestly family of the same name.

Harim was the father of Malchijah, one of the men who rebuilt Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah after the return from exile. According to Neh 3:11, Malchijah son of Harim, together with Hashub son of Pahath-moab, repaired a second section of the wall and the Tower of the Furnaces. Nothing else is said about Harim himself. Harim is also the name of a priestly family and of a lay family among the returned exiles, and "son of Harim" may mean a member of one of these families rather than a literal son. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats Harim here as a family name and notes that it is uncertain which family is meant. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "destroyed" or "dedicated to God."

Harim was one of the men who set their seal to the written covenant made in Nehemiah's time, when the people pledged to keep the law of Moses after returning from exile. He appears in Neh 10:27 alongside Malluch and Baanah, in the part of the list that, by context (Neh 10:14), names the leaders of the people rather than the priests or Levites. He may have signed as head of a family that bore the name Harim. The name is shared by several others, including a priest who also sealed the covenant (Neh 10:5) and families named among the returned exiles (Ezra 2:32, 39), so his exact identity is uncertain. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "destroyed" or "dedicated to God."

Hariph was one of the leaders who set their seal to the written covenant made in the time of Nehemiah, when the returned exiles pledged to keep the law of God (Neh 10:19). His name appears in the list of the "chief of the people" who signed after the priests and Levites, beside names such as Anathoth and Nebai. The text gives no personal details about him. Since several names in this list match family names elsewhere, he may have signed on behalf of a clan. Neh 7:24 counts 112 "children of Hariph" among those who returned from exile, and the parallel list in Ezra 2:18 gives the name Jorah at that point. Because the name is shared by more than one person, it is uncertain exactly how this signer relates to that family.

Hariph was the ancestor of a family of 112 people who returned to Jerusalem and Judah from exile in Babylon, in the group listed with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2; Neh 7). Hariph appears in Nehemiah's version of the list (Neh 7:24). The parallel list in Ezra gives the same family, with the same number, under the name Jorah (Ezra 2:18), so the two names are taken to refer to the same family. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes the group as the descendants of Hariph. Nothing else is recorded about Hariph himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also links him to the Hariph who sealed Nehemiah's covenant (Neh 10:19), perhaps as a family head acting for the clan. Because several people share the name, that connection is uncertain.

Harmon is a name that appears in Amos 4:3 in the original Hebrew and refers to the place where the wealthy women of Samaria would be thrown when their city fell. The King James Version does not treat it as a name and translates the word as "the palace." Other translations keep it as the proper name Harmon. The preceding verse in Amos 4 addresses these women as "cows of Bashan" on the mountain of Samaria and warns that they would be dragged out through breaches in the city wall. STEPBible's proper-names index suggests Harmon may be the destination of the exiled Israelites. The meaning of the word and the site it names are uncertain, and some translators connect it with Mount Hermon or a region beyond it. The location shown here is a rough placement near Samaria, the city the prophecy addresses, not an identified site.

Harnepher was a man of the tribe of Asher, named as the second of the sons of Zophah in the Asherite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:36. His brothers listed in the genealogy include Suah, Shual, Beri, Imrah, Bezer, Hod, Shamma, Shilshah, Ithran (Jether) and Beera. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a chief of the tribe of Asher, reflecting the genealogy's description of these men as heads of their fathers' houses and leading men. Nothing further is recorded about him beyond his place in this list. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "panting", while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "the anger of a bull" or "increasing heat."

Harod was a spring where Gideon and his army camped early one morning before routing the Midianites, whose camp lay to the north by the hill of Moreh in the valley (Judg 7:1). The name is usually taken to mean "trembling" or "fear." Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests that Gideon's test of his men by how they drank also happened here. The common identification is Ain Jalud, modern Ein Harod, a large spring at the foot of the northern cliffs of Mount Gilboa on the edge of the Jezreel Valley. The location shown here follows that view. Some scholars have looked instead for the spring near Shechem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also links it with the spring in Jezreel where Saul camped (1 Sam 29:1). Two of David's mighty men, Shammah and Elika, are called Harodites (2 Sam 23:25). This probably refers to a place named Harod, but whether it is the same place is uncertain.

Harosheth-hagoyim, called "Harosheth of the Gentiles" in the King James Version, was the home of Sisera, commander of the army of Jabin, the Canaanite king who reigned in Hazor (Judg 4:2). Sisera gathered his nine hundred iron chariots and his troops from there and marched to the Kishon River to fight Israel (Judg 4:13). After Barak defeated him, Barak chased the chariots and the army all the way back to Harosheth, and Sisera's whole force was killed (Judg 4:16). Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the name as "the smithy of the nations" and suggests that Jabin's chariots may have been made there. It places the city at the pass leading from the plain of Acre into the Jezreel Valley, at the foot of Mount Carmel, and identifies it with el-Harithiyeh. Some scholars instead treat the name as a district rather than a town. The location shown here follows the el-Harithiyeh identification, near the Kishon.

Harsha was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Judah. The "children of Harsha" appear in the list of returnees in Ezra 2:52, and again in the parallel list in Neh 7:54. In both lists the name stands next to Bazluth (Bazlith) and Mehida. The context places them among the groups who came back with Zerubbabel. Nothing else is recorded about Harsha himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the corresponding list in 1 Esdras gives the name as "Charea." The meaning of the name is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "worker" or "enchanter," Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "deaf," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "workmanship" or "a wood."

Harum was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only once, in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chr 4:8. That verse says Coz fathered Anub and Zobebah, and then mentions "the families of Aharhel the son of Harum." This entry follows the reading that makes Harum a son of Coz and a brother of Anub and Zobebah, as the STEPBible proper names index does. The verse itself does not say so directly, and Harum's exact place in the line is unclear. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls this one of the most obscure genealogies of Judah. Harum is remembered as the father of Aharhel, whose descendants formed clans within Judah. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "elevated," and Smith's as "lofty." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Harumaph is named only once in the Bible, as the father of Jedaiah. Jedaiah was one of the men who repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah after the return from exile, and he worked on the part opposite his own house (Neh 3:10). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Harumaph may have been Jedaiah's father or a more distant ancestor, since "son of" can carry either sense. Nothing else is recorded about Harumaph himself. Smith's gives the meaning of the name as "slit-nosed," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "destruction."

Haruz was a man of Jotbah and the father of Meshullemeth, the mother of King Amon of Judah (2 Kgs 21:19). Since Amon was the son of King Manasseh, Meshullemeth was Manasseh's wife, which made Haruz the king's father-in-law and Amon's maternal grandfather. Amon appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, which links Haruz to that line through his daughter. Haruz is named only in this verse, and nothing else is told about him. Jotbah's location is uncertain. Some place it in Galilee, while others connect it with Jotbathah, a camp from the wilderness journey. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates Haruz before 644 BC, an estimate drawn from the timing of Amon's reign. The meaning of his name is given as "eager" in Easton's Bible Dictionary, "zealous" in Smith's, and "careful" in Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Hasadiah was a man of the tribe of Judah, a descendant of the royal line of David through King Jehoiachin (Jeconiah). He appears only in the genealogy at 1 Chr 3:20, as one of a group of five: Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah and Jushab-hesed. This entry follows the reading that these five were sons of Zerubbabel, the leader of the return from Babylon, as Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take it. That would make him a brother of Meshullam, Hananiah and Shelomith, who are listed just before. Easton's Bible Dictionary instead counts him among the sons of Pedaiah, Zerubbabel's father in this genealogy. If he was Zerubbabel's son, he probably lived in the late sixth century BC, an estimate inferred from context. His name means roughly "the Lord is kind" or "favoured by the Lord."

Hasenuah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only in the genealogy of Sallu in 1 Chr 9:7. He was the father of Hodaviah, the grandfather of Meshullam, and the great-grandfather of Sallu. From the surrounding chapter, Sallu appears among the Benjamites living in Jerusalem, probably after the return from exile. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Hasenuah as belonging to one of the chief families of the tribe. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "bristling" or "hated." Other English versions spell the name Hassenuah, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. A similar name, Senuah, appears in the Benjamite list of Neh 11:9, though it is uncertain whether the same family is meant. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hashabiah was a Levite of the clan of Merari, named only in a genealogy in 1 Chronicles. He was the son of Amaziah and the father of Malluch (1 Chr 6:45). The surrounding passage (1 Chr 6:44–47) traces the ancestry of Ethan, one of the Merarite musicians whom David put in charge of the singing at the house of the Lord, so Hashabiah appears as one of Ethan's forebears. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Old Testament share the name, and this entry is distinct from them. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Merarite Levite, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the estimation of the Lord."

Hashabiah was a Levite of the clan of Merari, named only in genealogies. He was the son of Bunni and the father of Azrikam. Through Azrikam and Hasshub he was an ancestor of Shemaiah, one of the Levites who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon (1 Chr 9:14; Neh 11:15). The two lists give the same line from Shemaiah back to Hashabiah. Chronicles traces it to Merari, and Nehemiah adds Hashabiah's father Bunni. Several other people in the Bible share the name, so this Hashabiah should not be confused with them. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the two verses as separate entries, but this entry takes them as one man because the genealogies match. The name is usually explained as meaning "the Lord regards" or "the estimation of the Lord" (Hitchcock's Bible Names).

Hashabiah was a Levite musician, one of the sons of Jeduthun (also called Ethan), who served in the worship arranged in David's time. 1 Chr 25:3 names him among Jeduthun's sons, alongside Gedaliah, Zeri (Izri), Jeshaiah and Mattithiah, who worked under their father's direction as he prophesied with the harp to give thanks and praise the LORD. That verse counts six sons but names only five; the sixth is probably Shimei, who appears later in the same chapter. When the temple musicians were divided by lot into twenty-four groups, the twelfth lot fell to Hashabiah, and his group of sons and relatives numbered twelve (1 Chr 25:19). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 1014 BC and calls him the fourth son of Jeduthun. Several other men in the Bible share this name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "the estimation of the Lord."

Hashabiah was a Levite of the Hebronite clan who, with 1,700 of his relatives described as capable men, served as an officer over Israel west of the Jordan. According to 1 Chr 26:30, they handled both "the business of the LORD" and "the service of the king," which probably means they oversaw religious and royal affairs in that region. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes the Hebronites as descendants of Hebron, son of Kohath, and the surrounding chapter places this appointment among King David's arrangements for the Levites, so he probably served during David's reign. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this one should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the estimation of the Lord."

Hashabiah son of Kemuel was the leader of the tribe of Levi during King David's reign. He appears in 1 Chr 27:16–22, a list of the chief officers over the tribes of Israel, where he is named for the Levites while Zadok is named separately for the Aaronites, the priestly line descended from Aaron. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him prince of the tribe of Levi and dates him to about 1014 BC, an estimate inferred from context. Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Hashabiah, many of them Levites, so this one should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the estimation of the Lord."

Hashabiah was one of the chief Levites in the reign of King Josiah of Judah. He is named in 2 Chr 35:9 with Conaniah, Shemaiah, Nethaneel, Jeiel and Jozabad, who together gave the Levites 5,000 sheep and goats and 500 oxen as Passover offerings for the great Passover Josiah held in Jerusalem. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this feast to about 623 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel account in 1 Esdras calls him Sabias. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Hashabiah, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as "the estimation of the Lord." The text gives no reason to identify this Levite with any of them.

Hashabiah was a Levite of the period after the Babylonian exile. This entry treats him as a single person, though reference works divide these verses among several men of the same name. A Hashabiah was among the Levites recruited to travel from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra, listed with Jeshaiah of the sons of Merari (Ezra 8:19). Ezra then set apart Sherebiah, Hashabiah and ten others to guard the gold, silver and temple vessels on the journey (Ezra 8:24). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary call this second man a chief priest, but since Sherebiah and Hashabiah appear just before as Levites, the same men are probably meant. A Hashabiah also sealed the covenant under Nehemiah (Neh 10:11) and is named among the chief Levites who led praise and thanksgiving in alternating groups (Neh 12:24).

Hashabiah was the ruler of half the district of Keilah, a town in the lowlands of Judah, who repaired a section of the wall of Jerusalem when it was rebuilt under Nehemiah (Neh 3:17). He worked next to Rehum son of Bani, in a stretch of the wall assigned to Levites. STEPBible's proper-name index counts Hashabiah himself among these Levites, although the verse could also be read as simply placing him next to them. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the rebuilding to about 446 BC, an estimate inferred from context. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names renders as "the estimation of the Lord," belongs to several other men in the Bible, mostly Levites. This entry treats the Hashabiah of Neh 3:17 as a separate person, since nothing else is known about him.

Hashabiah was a Levite named in the genealogy of Uzzi, the overseer of the Levites in Jerusalem after the return from exile (Neh 11:22). He was the son of Mattaniah and grandson of Micha, and the father of Bani, whose son Uzzi held that office. The family belonged to the sons of Asaph, the singers who were in charge of the work of the house of God. A brother named Shemaiah is also linked to him, though the verse does not mention him. Nothing else is recorded about Hashabiah himself. His name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names renders "the estimation of the Lord," is shared by several other men in the Bible, mostly Levites, so he should not be confused with them.

Hashabiah was a priest who headed the priestly family of Hilkiah in the generation after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears only in a list of the heads of priestly families (Neh 12:21). By inference from the surrounding passage, that list belongs to the days of Joiakim, the son of the high priest Jeshua, which is how Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Hashabiah, many of them Levites, and this priest should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the estimation of the Lord," and Smith's renders it "whom God regards."

Hashabnah was one of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, a written pledge by the returned exiles in Jerusalem to keep the law of Moses. He appears only once, in the list of signatories at Neh 10:25, where he is named between Rehum and Maaseiah among the "chief of the people," as distinct from the priests and Levites listed earlier in the chapter. Nothing else is recorded about his family or role. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the sealing to about 410 BC and takes the name to mean "whom Jehovah regards," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the silence of the Lord."

Hashabniah was the father of Hattush, a man who helped rebuild the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah after the return from exile. He is known only from Neh 3:10, which places his son's repair work next to that of Jedaiah son of Harumaph. Nothing else is recorded about Hashabniah himself, and he probably lived in the generation before the rebuilding. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "whom Jehovah regards." A similar name belongs to a Levite who led the people in prayer in Neh 9:5. Because this name is shared by more than one person, it is uncertain whether the two are connected, and this entry treats the father of Hattush separately.

Hashabniah was a Levite in Jerusalem after the return from exile, in the time of Ezra and Nehemiah. He is named only once, in Neh 9:5, among the Levites who led a gathering of the people during a public fast and confession of sin. With Jeshua, Kadmiel, Bani, Sherebiah, Hodijah, Shebaniah and Pethahiah, he called on the assembly to stand up and bless the LORD, opening the long prayer recorded in that chapter. The context shows this gathering led to the written covenant the people's leaders sealed (Neh 9:38). Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "whom Jehovah regards" and dates the event to about 410 BC, an estimate drawn from context. The same name belongs to another man elsewhere in Nehemiah, the father of Hattush (Neh 3:10). Whether the two are related is not stated.

Hashbadana was one of the men who stood on Ezra's left hand on the wooden platform when Ezra the scribe read the Law aloud to the people gathered in Jerusalem after the return from exile (Neh 8:4). He is named alongside Pedaiah, Mishael, Malchiah, Hashum, Zechariah and Meshullam, while six others stood on Ezra's right. The text gives no further details about his family or role. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests these men were probably Levites, though the verse does not say so, and many see them as leading men or elders. Smith's and Easton's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of his name as "considerate judge" or "consideration in judging." This is his only appearance in the Bible.

Hashmonah was one of the places where the Israelites camped during their journey through the wilderness after leaving Egypt. The itinerary in Numbers 33 lists it between Mithcah, where they came from, and Moseroth, where they went next (Num 33:29–30). Nothing else is recorded about it. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as “fatness,” counts it as the thirtieth halting place, and places it not far from Mount Hor. Moseroth, the next stop, is probably the same as the Mosera where Deut 10:6 says Aaron died, which fits a location in that area. The exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only approximate and places it in the region east of the Arabah valley, south of the Dead Sea, in present-day southern Jordan.

Hashub, son of Pahath-moab, was one of the men who helped rebuild the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah's leadership. Working alongside Malchijah son of Harim, he repaired a second section of the wall and the Tower of the Furnaces (Neh 3:11). Pahath-moab, meaning "governor of Moab," was the name of a large family that returned from exile, so "son of" here probably means he belonged to that clan rather than being a literal son. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the wall-building to about 446 BC, a date inferred from context. The name Hashub belongs to several people in Nehemiah's time, including another wall-builder who worked opposite his own house and a Levite. It is uncertain whether any of these are the same man as this Hashub.

Hashub was a man who, together with Benjamin, repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall opposite their house during the rebuilding led by Nehemiah (Neh 3:23). The pair worked on the stretch just before Azariah son of Maaseiah, who repaired beside his own house. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several men in the Bible share this name, and another Hashub appears among the wall builders in the same chapter (Neh 3:11). Smith's Bible Dictionary treats this Hashub as a separate person from that one, and this entry does the same. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "esteemed" or "numbered."

Hashub was one of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the written covenant made in Nehemiah's time, after the return from exile in Babylon. In that covenant the community pledged to keep the law of Moses. He appears only in a list of names between Hananiah and Hoshea (Neh 10:23). By inference from the surrounding passage, he belongs to the group described as "the chief of the people," and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him this way. The text says nothing more about him. Several other men named Hashub appear in Nehemiah and 1 Chronicles, including two who helped repair Jerusalem's wall (Neh 3:11, 23). He may be the same man as one of them, but that cannot be confirmed. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "esteemed" or "numbered."

Hashubah was a son of Zerubbabel, the governor who led exiles back from Babylon, and so a descendant of King David through Jehoiachin, in the tribe of Judah. He is named only in the genealogy of David's line at 1 Chr 3:20, where he heads a group of five: Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah and Jushab-hesed. The previous verse lists Meshullam, Hananiah and their sister Shelomith as Zerubbabel's children, so the separate count of five suggests a second group within the family. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes these five as the latter half of Zerubbabel's family, possibly born after the return to Judah. Nothing else is recorded about his life. His name is usually explained as meaning "consideration" or "esteem".

Hashum was the ancestor of a family whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem and Judah with Zerubbabel. The list in Ezra gives their number as 223 (Ezra 2:19). The parallel list in Nehemiah gives 328 (Neh 7:22). The two lists differ in several figures. Ezra 10:33 names seven men of this family, among them Mattenai, Zabad, Eliphelet, Manasseh and Shimei, who had married foreign wives and agreed to put them away during Ezra's reforms. Nothing is recorded about Hashum himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary connects this family with the Hashum who sealed the covenant under Nehemiah (Neh 10:18), but that may be a different man of the same name. Several people in the Bible bear the name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "silence" or "their hasting."

Hashum was one of the men who stood on Ezra's left hand when Ezra the scribe read the Law of Moses from a wooden platform to the assembled people in Jerusalem (Neh 8:4). He is named among thirteen men who flanked Ezra, six on his right and seven on his left, but nothing more is said about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of the priests or Levites, which is an inference from the setting, since the verse gives no title. Several men in the Bible bear this name. A family of Hashum is listed among returning exiles and among those who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah's day, and this Hashum may have been its head or a member of it, though the text does not say so. The reading took place after the return from exile, in the time of Nehemiah.

Hashum was one of the leaders who set their seal to the covenant made in the time of Nehemiah, in which the returned exiles pledged to keep the law of God (Neh 10:18). He appears in the list of the chiefs of the people, between Hodijah and Bezai. The name is also used elsewhere for a family whose members returned from Babylon and for a man who stood with Ezra at the reading of the law. This Hashum was probably the head of that family, signing on its behalf, but this is an inference, and the name is shared by several people, so the link is uncertain. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "silence" or "their hasting."

Hasrah, also called Harhas, was the father of Tikvah (or Tikvath) and the grandfather of Shallum, husband of the prophetess Huldah. He is known only from the account of King Josiah's reign. Hilkiah the priest and the king's officials went to consult Huldah about the book of the law found in the temple. Her husband's family line is given there in two parallel forms. 2 Kgs 22:14 spells the name Harhas, and 2 Chr 34:22 spells it Hasrah. The title "keeper of the wardrobe" follows Hasrah's name in both verses, but the wording does not make clear whether it belongs to him or to Shallum. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it as Hasrah's office and explains it as care of the priestly garments. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hassenaah is named in Neh 3:3 as the ancestor or head of a group called "the sons of Hassenaah." They rebuilt the Fish Gate when Nehemiah restored the walls of Jerusalem, probably around 446 BC, a date inferred from context. The verse says they laid the gate's beams and set up its doors, locks and bars. Nothing else is recorded about Hassenaah as an individual. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name is probably the same as Senaah (Ezra 2:35; Neh 7:38) with the Hebrew definite article added. Senaah appears among the groups of returning exiles, and its context there suggests a place-name. On that view, "sons of Hassenaah" may mean the people of a town rather than the descendants of one man. This entry treats Hassenaah as a male person, while noting that the name may be a place.

Hasshub was a Levite of the clan of Merari, known only as a link in a family line. He was the son of Azrikam and the father of Shemaiah, a Levite listed among those who lived in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile (1 Chr 9:14; Neh 11:15). The two lists trace the same line back to Hashabiah. Chronicles places the family among the sons of Merari, while Nehemiah adds the name Bunni. The King James Version spells his name Hasshub in Chronicles and Hashub in Nehemiah. The name probably means "considerate" or "intelligent," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary. Several other men named Hashub appear in Nehemiah, and one Hebrew lexicon treats two of them as the same person. Whether this Levite is also one of them is uncertain.

Hasupha was the ancestor or head of a family of Nethinim, the temple servants, whose descendants returned to Jerusalem from exile in Babylon. The family appears in the lists of those who came back with Zerubbabel, named second among the temple servants after Ziha and before Tabbaoth (Ezra 2:43). The parallel list spells the name Hashupha (Neh 7:46), and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes the form Asipha in 1 Esdras 5:29. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this first return to about 536 BC. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "uncovered", and Smith's gives "stripped". Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his family's place in these lists.

Hatach was one of the chamberlains of King Ahasuerus of Persia, assigned by the king to attend Queen Esther.
