Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe him as a eunuch, and the name is also spelled Hathach. When Mordecai mourned in sackcloth at the king's gate, Esther sent Hatach to find out what had happened and why (Esth 4:5). He went out to Mordecai in the city square in front of the gate (Esth 4:6). The surrounding passage shows that Mordecai told him about Haman's plot against the Jews and asked that Esther plead with the king. Hatach brought this message back to Esther (Esth 4:9) and then carried her reply to Mordecai (Esth 4:10). He is mentioned only in this exchange. Easton's gives the meaning of his name as "verity," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "he that strikes."

Hathath was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:13 as a son of Othniel and grandson of Kenaz. This Othniel is probably the same Othniel son of Kenaz who captured Debir and later served as Israel's first judge (Josh 15:17; Judg 3:9–11). The King James text names only Hathath as Othniel's son. Meonothai is treated here as his brother because he appears in the next verse, and some ancient translations add his name to verse 13. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of his name as "terror", and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "fearful". Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hatipha was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants, "the children of Hatipha," returned from exile in Babylon. The family appears in the list of returnees recorded in Ezra 2:54 and repeated in Nehemiah 7:56, where it is named last among the temple-servant families, right after the children of Neziah. Smith's Bible Dictionary places this return with Zerubbabel, about 536 BC. Nothing else is known of Hatipha himself, and the name may stand for a clan rather than a single remembered individual. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of the name as "captured" or "captive." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same family appears as "Atipha" in the parallel list in 1 Esdras 5:32.

Hatita was the ancestor of a family of temple gatekeepers ("porters") whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Judah. The "children of Hatita" appear in the list of returnees in Ezra 2:42 and its parallel in Neh 7:45. There they are one of six gatekeeper families, alongside those of Shallum, Ater, Talmon, Akkub and Shobai. The six families together numbered 139 in Ezra and 138 in Nehemiah. The lists place this return under Zerubbabel, which Smith's Bible Dictionary dates to about 536 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes Hatita as the head of a family and notes that the corresponding list in the apocryphal book of 1 Esdras gives the name as "Ateta." Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the name's meaning as "exploration" or "exploring." Nothing else is known about him.

Hattil was the ancestor of a family group listed among the descendants of "Solomon's servants" who returned to Judah from exile in Babylon. His name appears in the parallel lists of returnees in Ezra 2:57 and Neh 7:59, alongside Shephatiah, Pochereth of Zebaim, and Ami (called Amon in Nehemiah). Nothing else is recorded about him. By inference from the surrounding lists, "Solomon's servants" were a hereditary class associated with temple service, probably descended from laborers conscripted under Solomon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same family is called Agia in 1 Esdras 5:34. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "howling for sin."

Hattush was a man of the tribe of Judah, listed as a son of Shemaiah in the royal line of David that ran through King Jehoiachin (Jeconiah) after the exile (1 Chr 3:17–22). His brothers were Igeal, Bariah, Neariah and Shaphat. The verse gives the total as "six" but names only five, a difficulty that has never been settled. Some take the count to include Shemaiah himself. Many readers identify him with the Hattush "of the sons of David" who returned from Babylon with Ezra (Ezra 8:2), which would fit the generations in this genealogy, but that link is an inference. The name is also borne by other men of the same period, including a priest and a wall-builder in Nehemiah, so the identification is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "forsaking sin."

Hattush was a descendant of David named in Ezra 8:2 among the family heads who traveled from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. The surrounding passage places this return in the reign of the Persian king Artaxerxes. He stands in the list beside Gershom, of the priestly line of Phinehas, and Daniel, of the line of Ithamar, as the representative of the royal house of David. He is probably the same Hattush whom 1 Chr 3:22 lists among the descendants of Zerubbabel, in the line of David's heirs after the exile, though that link is an inference. The name is shared by other men of the post-exilic period, including a wall-builder in Nehemiah's day and a priest who signed the covenant, and it is not always clear which mentions refer to the same person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "forsaking sin."

Hattush, son of Hashabniah, was one of the men who helped rebuild the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah after the return from exile. He repaired the section next to Jedaiah son of Harumaph, who worked on the stretch opposite his own house (Neh 3:10). Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Hattush belongs to several men in the Bible, including a descendant of David and a priest who returned with Zerubbabel. This Hattush is identified only by his father's name, and whether he is the same as any of the others is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "forsaking sin."

Hattush was a priest named in the lists of Nehemiah. Neh 12:2 includes him among the priests who came back from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel and Jeshua, and Neh 10:4 names him among those who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's day. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the Tyndale House proper-names index describe him as a priest who returned with Zerubbabel. The two lists are separated by many decades, so the names may refer to a priestly family or to two different men. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a descendant of David who returned with Ezra. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes some doubt about whether that descendant of David and this priest are the same person. This entry treats Hattush as the priest of Nehemiah's lists.

Hauran was a region east of the Sea of Galilee, named only in Ezekiel's vision of the future boundaries of Israel. There it marks part of the northern border, where Hazar-hatticon lies "by the coast of Hauran" (Ezek 47:16). It is also the starting point for measuring the eastern border, which runs from Hauran, Damascus and Gilead down along the Jordan to the Dead Sea (Ezek 47:18). Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "cave-land" and describes Hauran as one of the ancient divisions of Bashan and a very fertile area. Both Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify it with the Greek and Roman province of Auranitis and with the modern Hauran, a plain in southern Syria on the edge of the desert. The location shown here is a general point east of the Sea of Galilee within that wider area.

Havilah (son of Cush) was one of the sons of Cush, the son of Ham, named in the Table of Nations. He appears alongside his brothers Seba, Sabtah, Raamah and Sabtecha in Gen 10:7, and the list is repeated in 1 Chr 1:9. Nimrod is also called a son of Cush in the verse that follows (Gen 10:8). Nothing else is recorded about him. As with many names in this genealogy, his name probably also stands for a people or region descended from him. He should be kept distinct from Havilah the son of Joktan, a descendant of Shem (Gen 10:29), and from the land of Havilah mentioned elsewhere, although some interpreters connect the names. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "circle," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "that suffers pain."

Havilah (son of Joktan) was one of the thirteen sons of Joktan named in the Table of Nations, listed between his brothers Ophir and Jobab (Gen 10:29; 1 Chr 1:23). Joktan was a son of Eber in the line of Shem, which makes Havilah a Semite. He should not be confused with Havilah the son of Cush (Gen 10:7), a Hamite, or with the land of Havilah mentioned elsewhere in Genesis. Nothing is recorded about his life. Like many names in this list, his name probably also stood for a people or region descended from him. By inference from his brothers' names, such as Sheba and Ophir, which are usually connected with southern Arabia, that people was probably located in Arabia. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "that suffers pain" or "that brings forth."

Havilah (of Eden) was a land encircled by the Pison, the first of the four rivers that flowed out from the river of Eden (Gen 2:11). The text describes it as a place where there is gold, and the next verse (Gen 2:12) adds that its gold is good and that bdellium, an aromatic resin, and onyx stone are found there. Its location is unknown, and views differ widely. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it may be the sandy tract along the western border of Babylonia, stretching from the lower Euphrates toward the mountains of Edom. No location is shown here. The same name is used elsewhere in the Bible for other places and for individuals in the genealogies of Genesis, and it is uncertain how, or whether, this Havilah relates to them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "that suffers pain" or "that brings forth."

Havilah (of Arabia) was a region marking one end of the territory of Ishmael's descendants, who lived "from Havilah unto Shur," the area east of Egypt (Gen 25:18). The same phrase reappears when King Saul defeated the Amalekites from Havilah to Shur (1 Sam 15:7), suggesting Havilah was a known boundary on the desert fringe southeast of Israel. Its exact location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in southern Arabia and links it with the tribes named Havilah among the descendants of Cush (Gen 10:7) and of Joktan (Gen 10:29). It cites Kalisch's view that these are one vast country stretching from the Persian Gulf to the Red Sea. The location shown here follows a narrower placement in northwestern Arabia, near the Arabah south of the Dead Sea. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "that suffers pain; that brings forth."

Havvoth-jair was a group of villages east of the Jordan. The name means "tent villages of Jair," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Jair, a descendant of Manasseh, captured the towns during Israel's conquest and named them after himself (Num 32:41). Deut 3:14 links them with the region of Argob in Bashan, reaching to the borders of Geshur and Maacah. Judg 10:4 says the thirty sons of Jair the judge held thirty cities called Havvoth-jair in Gilead. Whether this is the same Jair or a later namesake is uncertain. 1 Chr 2:23 counts the towns of Jair among sixty cities connected with the sons of Machir, the father of Gilead. The exact area is uncertain, with Bashan and Gilead both suggested. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia favors northern Gilead. The location shown here, which is approximate, follows a placement in Gilead.

Hazael was a king of Syria (Aram), ruling from Damascus, in the time of Elisha. God told Elijah to anoint him king over Syria (1 Kgs 19:15), though the anointing itself is not recorded. Hazael first appears as an officer of King Ben-hadad, sent with forty camels' load of gifts to ask Elisha whether the sick king would recover. Elisha wept and foretold both the harm Hazael would do to Israel and his rise to the throne. The next day Ben-hadad was smothered with a wet cloth, and Hazael reigned in his place. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Hazael himself to be the killer. He fought Joram of Israel at Ramoth-gilead, struck Israel throughout its territory, and oppressed it for all of Jehoahaz's reign. He captured Gath and turned toward Jerusalem until Jehoash of Judah paid him off with temple and palace treasure. His son Ben-hadad succeeded him.

Hazaiah was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy of Maaseiah son of Baruch, one of the Judahites who settled in Jerusalem after the return from exile (Neh 11:5). He was the son of Adaiah and the father of Col-hozeh, and so the great-grandfather of Maaseiah. The line traces back through Joiarib and Zechariah to Shiloni. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Shiloni to mean the Shilonites, the descendants of Judah's son Shelah. Hazaiah himself probably lived some generations before Nehemiah's time, by inference from his place in the list. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name means "the LORD sees" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "seeing the Lord" (Hitchcock's Bible Names).

Hazar-addar was a town on the southern border of the land promised to Israel. In Num 34:4 it appears in the list of boundary points: the border ran south of the ascent of Akrabbim, passed on to Zin, went south to Kadesh-barnea, and continued to Hazar-addar and then Azmon. The name means "village of Addar," according to Easton's Bible Dictionary, which identifies it with Addar (or Adar) in the parallel boundary description of Josh 15:3. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as "an imprisoned generation." Easton's places it in the desert west of Kadesh-barnea. Its exact site is unknown, and the location shown here is only a rough placement in the Negev region of southern Israel.

Hazar-enan was a town marking the northeastern corner of the land promised to Israel. In Numbers it is where the northern border ends after Ziphron, and the point from which the eastern border begins, running to Shepham (Num 34:9–10). Ezekiel's vision of the restored land also uses it as a northern boundary point, near the borders of Damascus and Hamath (Ezek 47:17), and places the tribe of Dan's portion at the far north beside it (Ezek 48:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "village of fountains" and mentions two identifications: Ayan ed-Dara in the Anti-Lebanon range, or, more probably, Kuryetein, about 60 miles east-northeast of Damascus. The location shown here follows the second view, the modern town of Al Qaryatayn in Syria.

Hazar-gaddah was a town in the far south of Judah's territory, named only once, in the list of towns allotted to the tribe of Judah in Josh 15:27. It appears among the towns of the Negev near the border with Edom, between Moladah and Heshmon. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on Judah's southern border, midway between the Mediterranean and the Dead Sea. Its name has been explained differently: Easton's gives "village of fortune," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "imprisoned band." The first part, Hazar, commonly means a settlement or enclosure. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is a rough placement in the eastern Negev, southeast of Beersheba, based on its position in the town list.

Hazar-shual was a town in the Negev, in the far south of Judah, always listed near Beersheba. It appears among the southern cities of Judah's allotment (Josh 15:28) and again among the towns given to Simeon within Judah's territory (Josh 19:3). The Simeonites were living there in the time of David, as their genealogy in 1 Chr 4:28 notes. After the return from Babylonian exile, people of Judah settled there again (Neh 11:27). Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the name as "village" or "enclosure of the jackal," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a wolf's house." Easton's identifies it with the ruins of Saweh, halfway between Beersheba and Moladah. The exact site is uncertain. The location shown here, east of Beersheba, fits that general area.

Hazar-susah was a town in the Negev, in the far south of Canaan, assigned to the tribe of Simeon when the land was divided (Josh 19:5). It is listed alongside Ziklag and Beth-marcaboth among the Simeonite towns that lay inside Judah's territory. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "village of the horse." The parallel list of Simeon's towns in 1 Chr 4:31 gives a similar name, Hazar-susim. Easton's also treats it as the same place as Sansannah in Judah's town list (Josh 15:31) and links it with the horse and chariot depots of Solomon's day (2 Chr 1:14). The neighboring name Beth-marcaboth, "house of chariots," fits that connection. The town's exact site is unknown, and the location shown here is only a rough placement in the northern Negev.

Hazar-susim was a town of the tribe of Simeon in the far south of Judah, the Negev region. It appears in 1 Chr 4:31 in a list of Simeonite towns, alongside Beth-marcaboth, Beth-birei and Shaaraim, which the text says were Simeon's cities until the reign of David. The name probably means "village of horses," and it sits next to Beth-marcaboth, "house of chariots," in the list. The parallel list of Simeon's towns in Josh 19:5 gives the name as Hazar-susah, which is generally taken to be the same place. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the Negev near Beersheba, based on the town's place among the other Simeonite towns.

Hazarmaveth was a son of Joktan, a descendant of Shem through Eber, named third among Joktan's thirteen sons in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:26) and in the parallel genealogy of 1 Chr 1:20. His brothers include Almodad, Sheleph, Jerah, Sheba, Ophir and Havilah. Nothing is recorded of his life beyond his place in these lists. His name is usually taken to mean "court of death" or "dwelling of death." Like several of Joktan's sons, he appears to represent both an ancestor and a people or region. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary link the name with Hadramaut, an ancient province and people of southern Arabia on the Indian Ocean coast east of modern Yemen. Smith's notes that the region was known in antiquity for trade with India and Africa.

Hazazon-tamar was a place near the Dead Sea where Amorites lived in the time of Abraham. In Gen 14:7 the eastern kings led by Chedorlaomer struck the Amalekite country and the Amorites living there on their return from Kadesh. Centuries later, in 2 Chr 20:2, messengers told King Jehoshaphat that a great army from beyond the sea was at Hazazon-tamar, which the verse identifies with En-gedi. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as "Hazazon of the palm trees" and takes it to be the older name of En-gedi, possibly preserved in Wady Husasah northwest of Ain Jidy. The same work notes another view placing it at Thamara, perhaps the ruin Kurnub southwest of the Dead Sea on the road from Hebron to Elath. The location shown here follows the En-gedi identification, on the western shore of the Dead Sea. The King James Version spells it Hazezon-tamar in Genesis.

Hazelelponi was a woman of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:3 as the sister of Jezreel, Ishma and Idbash, who are called sons of "the father of Etam." She is one of the few women named in this list, and nothing more is said about her. The Hebrew of the verse is difficult, and this entry follows the reading that places these siblings in the family of Hur. By inference from nearby genealogies, where Hur's descendants include Shobal, Salma, Hareph, Penuel and Ezer (1 Chr 2:50–51; 4:4), she is grouped here with them as Hur's daughter. Whether "father of Etam" refers to a person or to the founder of the town of Etam near Bethlehem is uncertain. Her name is also spelled Hazzelelponi. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "shade coming upon me," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "sorrow of countenance."

Hazer-hatticon, a name meaning "the middle village," is a place named in Ezekiel's vision of the ideal boundaries of the restored land of Israel. It appears in the description of the northern border, listed after Hamath, Berothah and Sibraim, and is said to lie "by the coast of Hauran," meaning at the edge of the Hauran region east of the Jordan (Ezek 47:16). It is mentioned nowhere else, and its exact site is unknown. The STEPBible Proper Names index (Tyndale House) suggests it is probably the same place as Hazar-enan, which the following verse gives as the border's endpoint. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the region of Hamath in present-day central Syria.

Hazeroth was a stopping place of the Israelites in the wilderness after they left Mount Sinai. They traveled to it from Kibroth-hattaavah and stayed there for a time (Num 11:35; Num 33:17). When they left, they camped in the wilderness of Paran, or at Rithmah in the itinerary of Num 33 (Num 12:16; Num 33:18). The account in Num 12, set during this stay, tells how Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses and Miriam was struck with leprosy. Hazeroth is also one of the landmarks used to place Moses' speeches in Deut 1:1. The name probably means "enclosures" or "settlements." Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the spring of 'Ain Hudhera (Ain Khadra), about 30 to 40 miles northeast of the traditional Mount Sinai. The location shown here follows that identification.

Haziel was a Levite in the time of David, named once in the list of Gershonite families that David organized for service. 1 Chr 23:9 calls him one of three sons of Shimei, with his brothers Shelomith and Haran, and says they were heads of the fathers' houses of Laadan. This Shimei is probably a descendant within Laadan's line. He is distinct from the Shimei who was a son of Gershon and is named in the following verse, which is why these men count as Laadan's chiefs. Nothing else is recorded about Haziel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "God sees," and Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "union of God."

Hazo was a son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and his wife Milcah. He appears only once, in the list of Nahor's children reported to Abraham after the near-sacrifice of Isaac (Gen 22:22). His full brothers were Huz, Buz, Kemuel, Chesed, Pildash, Jidlaph and Bethuel, and Bethuel was the father of Rebekah. Nahor also had children by his concubine Reumah: Tebah, Gaham, Thahash and Maachah. Hazo is the fifth son named in the list. Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the meaning of his name as "vision." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he may have been the ancestor who gave his name to a family or clan descended from Nahor.

Hazor was a major Canaanite city in northern Israel, described as formerly "the head of all those kingdoms" (Josh 11:10). Its king Jabin gathered a northern coalition against Joshua, who captured Hazor, killed its people and burned it, the only city of that region he burned (Josh 11:1, 11:13). It was later allotted to Naphtali. In the time of the judges another Jabin, reigning in Hazor, oppressed Israel through his commander Sisera (Judg 4:2). Solomon later fortified it with Megiddo and Gezer, and the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser captured it and deported its people (2 Kgs 15:29). Several other places share the name. Older works placed it near Kedesh, at Khurbet Harrah (Easton's Bible Dictionary) or Tell Khuraibeh (Smith's Bible Dictionary). The location shown here follows the identification with Tell el-Qedah (Tel Hazor), north of the Sea of Galilee.

Hazor was a town in the far south of Judah, listed in Josh 15:23 among the cities of the Negev allotted to the tribe of Judah, between Kedesh and Ithnan. It is one of several places in the Bible with this name and should not be confused with the better-known Canaanite city of Hazor in the north. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests the name should probably be read together with the following word as a single place, Hazor-Ithnan, rather than "Hazor and Ithnan." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the town as unidentified, and its exact site remains uncertain. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the Negev, in keeping with the town's position in the southern list. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "court" or "hay." Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "castle."

Hazor was a town in the far south of Judah, the Negev, named in the list of towns given to the tribe of Judah in Josh 15:25. The verse is hard to divide. The King James Version reads "Hazor, Hadattah, and Kerioth, and Hezron, which is Hazor," but many readers join the names differently. Smith's Bible Dictionary reads "Hazor-Hadattah" ("new Hazor") as one town. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connects this Hazor with Kerioth-Hezron, the town the verse says "is Hazor." So it is unclear whether one or two places called Hazor are meant here. Several other places in the Bible share the name, including another Hazor in the same southern list (Josh 15:23) and the well-known Canaanite city in the north. The exact site is unknown, and the location shown here is only a rough placement in the Negev of Judah.

Hazor was a town in the territory of Benjamin where Benjamites lived after returning from the Babylonian exile. It appears only once, in Nehemiah's list of resettled places, alongside Ramah and Gittaim (Neh 11:33). The name was shared by several places in the Bible, including the better-known Canaanite city of Hazor in the north, so this town should be kept distinct from them. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with Khirbet Hazzur, a ruin a little east of Nebi Samwil, northwest of Jerusalem. The location shown here, which is only approximate, matches that general area. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "court," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "castle."

Hazor is a place or region in Arabia, named in Jeremiah's oracle against Kedar and "the kingdoms of Hazor." It is distinct from the better-known city of Hazor in northern Israel and from the other places of the same name. Jeremiah announces that Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon would strike Kedar and Hazor, the "men of the east." He urges Hazor's inhabitants to flee far off and hide (Jer 49:28, 30) and declares that the place would become a permanent desolation, home only to wild animals (Jer 49:33). The pairing with Kedar suggests a land of Arabian tribes, possibly settled peoples living in unwalled villages rather than nomads. Its exact location is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions a view that it may be Jetor, or Ituraea, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as unidentified. The name probably means "enclosure" or "court."

Hazor-hadattah, meaning "New Hazor," was a town in the far south of the territory allotted to the tribe of Judah. It appears only in Josh 15:25, among the southernmost cities of Judah "toward the coast of Edom" in the Negev. The King James Version prints "Hazor, Hadattah" as two names, but many readers take them as a single compound name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that "hadattah" looks like an Aramaic word, which is unusual in this region. Nothing else is recorded about the town, and its site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary links it with the ruins of el-Hazzarah near Beit Jebrin. Eusebius and Jerome describe a "New Hazor" east of Ashkelon. The location shown here follows a placement in the eastern Negev, matching the verse's setting near the Edomite border, and is only approximate.

event: Healing a Blind Man at Bethsaida
text: The Healing a Blind Man at Bethsaida was a miracle of Jesus recorded only in Mark's Gospel. When Jesus arrived at Bethsaida, people brought a blind man to him and begged him to touch him. Jesus took the man by the hand and led him outside the town. He spat on his eyes, laid his hands on him, and asked whether he could see anything. The man looked up and said he saw people who looked like trees walking around. Jesus then put his hands on his eyes a second time, and the man's sight was fully restored so that he saw everything clearly. Jesus sent him home and told him not to go into the town or tell anyone there. The healing is unusual among the Gospel miracles because it happened in two stages. By inference from context it is dated to about AD 29, following Jesus' exchange with the Pharisees.

event: Healing a Boy with a Demon
text: Healing a Boy with a Demon was an event recorded in Matthew, Mark and Luke, the day after the Transfiguration, when Jesus came down from the mountain (Luke 9:37). A father begged Jesus to help his only son, tormented since childhood by a spirit that made him mute, caused him to foam, and often threw him into fire or water. The disciples had failed to cast it out, while scribes argued with them. Jesus lamented a faithless generation and told the father all things are possible to one who believes. The father replied, "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." Jesus rebuked the spirit, which convulsed the boy and left him seemingly dead, then lifted him up. Privately he said this kind comes out only by prayer and fasting. The mountain is unnamed. This entry places it at Mount Hermon rather than the traditional Mount Tabor, and dates it to about AD 29 by inference.

event: Healing a Crowd near Sea of Galilee
text: The Healing a Crowd near Sea of Galilee was an episode in which Jesus, returning from the region of Tyre and Sidon, came to the Sea of Galilee by way of the Decapolis. Matthew says he went up a mountain and sat down, and great crowds brought him the lame, blind, mute, maimed and many others. He healed them, and the people marveled and praised the God of Israel. Mark's parallel account focuses on one man who was deaf and could hardly speak. Jesus took him aside, put his fingers in his ears, spat and touched his tongue, looked up to heaven, sighed and said "Ephphatha" ("Be opened"). The man immediately heard and spoke plainly. Jesus told them to tell no one, but they spread the news all the more, saying he made the deaf hear and the mute speak. By inference from context, it took place about AD 29, following the healing of the Canaanite woman's daughter.

The Healing a Withered Hand was a miracle Jesus performed in a synagogue on a Sabbath, recorded in Matthew, Mark and Luke. It followed the dispute over his disciples picking grain on the Sabbath. A man with a withered hand, his right hand according to Luke 6:6, was present, and the Pharisees and scribes watched to see whether Jesus would heal him so they could accuse him. Jesus had the man stand in the middle and asked whether it was lawful on the Sabbath to do good or evil, to save life or to destroy it. In Matthew he compared the man to a sheep rescued from a pit. He then told the man to stretch out his hand, and it was restored like the other. The Pharisees left and plotted, with the Herodians in Mark's account, how to destroy him. This entry places the event in Capernaum, which is probable from context, and dates it to about AD 28, also by inference.

The Healing of Blind Bartimaeus was a miracle Jesus performed at Jericho, recorded in three Gospels. Mark names the man Bartimaeus, son of Timaeus, a blind beggar sitting by the road as Jesus left the city with a large crowd (Mark 10:46). Hearing that Jesus of Nazareth was passing, he called out, "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me," and shouted louder when people told him to be quiet. Jesus stopped and had him called. Throwing off his cloak, he came and asked to see. Jesus told him his faith had made him well, and he was healed immediately and followed Jesus. Matthew describes two blind men healed as Jesus left Jericho, with Jesus touching their eyes. Luke places the healing as Jesus approached the city and adds that the people praised God. This entry dates it to about AD 30, by inference from context.

The Healing of the Canaanite Daughter was the episode in which Jesus freed a Gentile woman's daughter from a demon while he was in the region of Tyre and Sidon, recorded in Matt 15:21–28 and Mark 7:24–30. Matthew calls her a woman of Canaan. Mark calls her a Greek, Syrophoenician by birth. She begged Jesus to help, calling him Son of David. At first he did not answer, and his disciples urged him to send her away. Jesus said he was sent only to the lost sheep of Israel and that it was not right to give the children's bread to dogs. She replied that even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from the table. Jesus praised her faith and declared the demon gone. She returned home and found her daughter healed, lying on the bed. This entry dates it to about AD 29, an estimate from context, following the dispute over tradition.

Healing Centurion's Servant is the miracle at Capernaum in which Jesus healed the servant of a Roman centurion without going to the house. Both Matthew and Luke place it soon after the Sermon on the Mount, about AD 28 by inference from context. The servant was paralyzed and near death. In Matthew the centurion comes to Jesus himself. In Luke he sends Jewish elders, who say he loves their nation and built them a synagogue, and then friends. In both accounts the centurion says he is not worthy to have Jesus under his roof. As a man who gives orders and is obeyed, he asks Jesus only to speak the word. Jesus marvels and says he has not found such faith even in Israel. Matthew adds his saying that many will come from east and west to sit with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The servant was found healed that same hour.

The Healing in Gennesaret was the occasion when Jesus and his disciples crossed the Sea of Galilee and landed in the district of Gennesaret, on its western shore. It came right after Jesus walked on the water, and is dated to about AD 29 by inference from context. As soon as they left the boat, local people recognized Jesus. They sent word through the surrounding region and carried the sick on beds to wherever they heard he was. Mark adds that in every village, town, or rural area he entered, people laid the sick in the streets. They begged to touch even the edge of his garment, and everyone who touched it was healed. Both Matthew and Mark tell the event, Matthew in briefer form. Gennesaret is probably the fertile plain on the northwest shore of the lake, south of Capernaum.

Healing Multitudes was an episode in Jesus' Galilean ministry, about AD 28 by inference from context, following his healing of a withered hand. Aware of opposition (the Pharisees' plot in Matt 12:14), Jesus withdrew with his disciples to the Sea of Galilee. Great crowds followed from Galilee, Judea, Jerusalem, Idumea, beyond the Jordan, and around Tyre and Sidon, having heard of his works. He had a small boat kept ready so the crowd would not crush him, as the sick pressed to touch him. He healed them all. When unclean spirits fell before him crying that he was the Son of God, he strictly ordered them not to make him known. Matthew presents this as fulfilling Isaiah's words about God's chosen servant who would not quarrel or cry out. Luke describes a similar scene on a level place, where power went out from him and healed everyone.

The Healing the Leper was a miracle of Jesus in Galilee, told in Matthew, Mark and Luke. Matthew places it right after Jesus came down from the mountain with great crowds following him, while Luke sets it in "a certain city" and describes the man as "full of leprosy." The man knelt or fell on his face before Jesus and said, "If thou wilt, thou canst make me clean." Mark notes that Jesus was moved with compassion. He reached out, touched the man and said, "I will; be thou clean," and the leprosy left him at once. Jesus then strictly told him to tell no one, but to show himself to the priest and offer what Moses commanded for cleansing, as a testimony to them. This entry dates it to about AD 28, during Jesus' first tour of Galilee, by inference from context.

The Healing the Man with Palsy was a miracle of Jesus at Capernaum, told in Matthew, Mark and Luke. It took place about AD 28 by inference from context, soon after he healed a leper. Crowds filled the house where Jesus was teaching, so four men carrying a paralyzed man on a bed went up on the roof, opened it and lowered him down in front of Jesus. Seeing their faith, Jesus told the man his sins were forgiven. Some scribes and Pharisees privately accused him of blasphemy, since only God can forgive sins. Jesus knew what they were thinking and asked whether it was easier to say "your sins are forgiven" or "get up and walk." To show that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, he told the man to take up his bed and go home. The man did so at once, and the amazed crowd praised God.

The Healing of the Woman With an 18-year Infirmity took place while Jesus was teaching in a synagogue on the Sabbath, an event recorded only in Luke's Gospel. A woman who had suffered from "a spirit of infirmity" for eighteen years was bent over and could not straighten herself. Jesus called her to him, told her she was freed from her infirmity, and laid his hands on her. She immediately stood upright and praised God. The ruler of the synagogue objected that healing should be done on the six working days, not on the Sabbath. Jesus answered that each of them would untie an ox or donkey on the Sabbath to lead it to water, so this daughter of Abraham, bound by Satan for eighteen years, should also be set free on that day. His opponents were put to shame, and the crowd rejoiced. It is dated to about AD 29, by inference from context.

Heber was a son of Beriah and a grandson of Asher, the son of Jacob. He and his brother Malchiel appear among Asher's descendants in the list of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:17), and he is named again in the Asherite genealogy of Chronicles (1 Chr 7:31). In the census taken in the wilderness he is the ancestor of a clan called the Heberites within the tribe of Asher (Num 26:45). His children were Japhlet, Shomer, Hotham and their sister Shua (1 Chr 7:32). Shomer is probably the same person as the Shamer named a few verses later in that genealogy. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the name to mean "associate." Several other men in the Bible are also called Heber, and they should not be confused with this Asherite.

Heber the Kenite was the husband of Jael, in the time of the judge Deborah. He descended from Hobab, the father-in-law of Moses, but had separated from the other Kenites and set up his tent by the plain of Zaanaim near Kedesh (Judg 4:11). His household was at peace with Jabin king of Hazor. For that reason the Canaanite commander Sisera, fleeing on foot after his army's defeat, went to the tent of Jael. There she killed him with a tent peg while he slept (Judg 4:17, 21). The Song of Deborah praises Jael as "the wife of Heber the Kenite" (Judg 5:24). The text records nothing Heber himself did beyond his move and his peace with Jabin. Several other men in the Bible share the name Heber, and this entry concerns only the Kenite.

Heber was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:18 as a son of Jehudijah and as "the father of Socho." His brothers were Jered, father of Gedor, and Jekuthiel, father of Zanoah. "Father" here probably means founder or leading figure of the town of Socho (Socoh) in Judah rather than a literal parent. The verse is hard to read, and views on his father differ. This entry names Ishbah, linking him to the family listed in the preceding verse. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and the Tyndale House proper-names index name Mered, the husband of Bithiah, Pharaoh's daughter, and treat Jehudijah as Mered's Judahite wife. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Heber, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes to mean "associate," is shared by several other people in the Bible.

Heber was a man of the tribe of Gad, one of seven kinsmen listed together in the Gadite genealogy of 1 Chr 5:13. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes these seven as heads of Gadite families. The next verse, 1 Chr 5:14, calls the group the sons of Abihail, which is how Heber is identified as Abihail's son and as the brother of Michael, Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Jachan and Zia. According to 1 Chr 5:17, this genealogy was recorded in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel, and the STEPBible proper-names index places him in that period. The Gadites are described as living in Bashan and Gilead, east of the Jordan. Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name Heber, and he should not be confused with them.

Heber was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named as a son of Elpaal in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 8:17. He appears in a list with his brothers Zebadiah, Meshullam and Hezeki, and the family also included Beriah, Shema, Eber, Misham, Shamed, Ishmerai, Jezliah and Jobab. Nothing is recorded about his life beyond his place in this list. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name may stand for a clan or family descended from Elpaal rather than a single individual. The name is usually taken to mean "associate" or "alliance". Several other people in the Bible are also called Heber, including Heber the Kenite, the husband of Jael, and a grandson of Asher. This Benjamite should not be confused with them.

Heber was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, listed as one of the sons of Shashak in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. He is named alongside his brothers Ishpan, Eliel, Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Hananiah, Elam, Antothijah, Iphedeiah and Penuel. Nothing further is recorded about him beyond his place in this family list. By inference from the surrounding passage, Shashak's family was among the Benjamite households living in Jerusalem. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him simply as a Benjamite. Some modern renderings and name lists, such as the STEPBible proper names index, give his name as Eber. He should not be confused with several other men called Heber in the Bible, including Heber the Kenite, the husband of Jael.

Hebron was a Levite, the third of the four sons of Kohath, and so a grandson of Levi. His brothers were Amram, Izhar and Uzziel, and the genealogies list the four of them in the same order (Exod 6:18; Num 3:19; 1 Chr 6:2). He became the head of a Levite family. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that his descendants were called the Hebronites. In David's time, Eliel led eighty men of the sons of Hebron who helped bring the ark of the covenant up to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:9). When David organized the Levites, the family was counted under four heads: Jeriah the first, Amariah the second, Jahaziel the third and Jekameam the fourth (1 Chr 23:19; 24:23). These were probably later descendants and not his immediate sons. Several other people in the Bible share the name Hebron, which is also the name of a well-known town in Judah.

Hebron was a member of the tribe of Judah, listed among the descendants of Caleb the brother of Jerahmeel in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2. His four sons were Korah, Tappuah, Rekem and Shema. The wording of 1 Chr 2:42 is difficult. It names Mesha as Caleb's firstborn and the father of Ziph, then speaks of "the sons of Mareshah the father of Hebron." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Tyndale House's STEPBible name list call Hebron a son of Mareshah. Another reading links him directly to Mesha, and this entry follows that one, treating Mesha as his father. Several names in this list, including Ziph, Mareshah, Hebron and Tappuah, are also towns in Judah, so the genealogy may partly describe the clans that settled them. He is a different person from others in the Bible named Hebron.

Hebron was an ancient city in the hill country of Judah, earlier called Kirjath-arba after Arba, a great man among the Anakim (Josh 14:15). It was said to have been built seven years before Zoan in Egypt (Num 13:22). Abram settled by Mamre at Hebron, and he buried Sarah in the cave of Machpelah there. Isaac and Jacob also lived there. Its king Hoham joined the alliance against Joshua, who took the city. It was given to Caleb, who drove out the sons of Anak, and it later became a priestly city and a city of refuge. David reigned from Hebron over Judah for seven and a half years, and six of his sons were born there. Abner was buried there, and all Israel anointed David king there. Absalom later launched his revolt from Hebron, and Rehoboam fortified it. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the modern city of Hebron (el-Khalil), which matches the location shown here.

Hegai, also spelled Hege in Esth 2:3, was the king's chamberlain at the Persian court of King Ahasuerus. He was keeper of the women in the palace at Shushan. When the king ordered fair young virgins from every province to be gathered so a new queen could be chosen, they were placed in Hegai's custody in the house of the women, and he oversaw their preparations for purification (Esth 2:3, 8). Esther was among those brought to him. When her turn came to go in to the king, she asked for nothing beyond what Hegai advised (Esth 2:15). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries describe him as a eunuch, which is how the Hebrew word rendered "chamberlain" is often understood. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his service to about 474 BC. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives possible meanings of the name, including "meditation."

Helah was one of the two wives of Ashur, the "father of Tekoa," in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah. Her fellow wife was Naarah (1 Chr 4:5). Her sons are named as Zereth, Jezoar and Ethnan (1 Chr 4:7). This entry also counts Coz as her son. He is named in the next verse (1 Chr 4:8), directly after her sons, and is probably read as continuing her line, though the text does not say so outright. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the meaning of her name as "rust." Nothing more is recorded about her beyond this genealogical mention.

Helam was a place east of the Jordan River where David fought and defeated the Syrian (Aramean) army. Hadarezer, king of Zobah, brought Syrian forces from beyond the river, probably the Euphrates, and they gathered at Helam under his army commander Shobach (2 Sam 10:16). David assembled all Israel, crossed the Jordan, and met them there in battle (2 Sam 10:17). The next verse, 2 Sam 10:18, reports that the Syrians fled and Shobach was killed. The site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls it unknown and notes proposals placing it between Damascus and Hamath, or at Aleppo. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions an identification with Alamatta near Nicephorium on the Euphrates. The location shown here is a rough placement east of the Jordan in the region of Gilead, in present-day Jordan.

Helbah was a Canaanite town in the territory given to the tribe of Asher. It appears only in Judg 1:31, in a list of towns whose inhabitants Asher did not drive out, alongside Accho, Zidon (Sidon), Ahlab, Achzib, Aphik and Rehob. The name means "fatness" or "fertile." Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary place it on the plain of Phoenicia, with Smith suggesting it lay not far from Sidon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it may be the same place as Mahalliba, named in Sennacherib's prism inscription, but says the site has not been found. Its exact location therefore remains unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the coastal region of Lebanon, north of Sidon.

Helbon was a place known for its wine, mentioned only in Ezek 27:18. In Ezekiel's lament over Tyre, Damascus is said to have traded with Tyre in "the wine of Helbon, and white wool." The name probably means "fat" or "fertile." Older geographers linked Helbon with Aleppo (Arabic Haleb). Smith's Bible Dictionary, Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia instead place it at the modern village of Halbun, at the head of a fruitful valley on the eastern slopes of the Anti-Lebanon, about 13 miles north-northwest of Damascus, an area still famous for its grapes. The location shown here follows the Halbun identification. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds that ancient inscriptions mention Helbonian wine, including wine received by Nebuchadnezzar, and that the Greek geographer Strabo says the Persian kings prized it.

Heleb, son of Baanah, was a Netophathite, a man from the town of Netophah in Judah, and one of David's mighty warriors (2 Sam 23:29). The parallel list in 1 Chr 11:30 spells his name Heled. This entry also identifies him with Heldai the Netophathite, who served as captain of the twelfth of David's monthly divisions. Each division had 24,000 men and served for one month of the year (1 Chr 27:15). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes this identification as probable, resting on the shared hometown and the closely related names. The phrase "of Othniel" in 1 Chr 27:15 probably means he belonged to the family line of Othniel, the early judge from Judah. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name Heleb as "fatness."

Helech is a name that appears in Ezekiel’s lament over the trading city of Tyre, in a verse describing the foreign soldiers who guarded its walls (Ezek 27:11). The Hebrew word sits alongside “the men of Arvad,” and the King James Version translates it as “thine army,” so the name does not appear in that translation. The STEPBible Proper Names index (Tyndale House) explains that it may be either a place, possibly in Cilicia in what is now southern Turkey, or a term for Tyre’s own army. If it is a place, it was probably another source of the hired defenders who hung their shields on Tyre’s walls. The location shown here is only approximate and sets it beside Arvad, the island city off the Syrian coast (modern Arwad), because the two names appear together in the verse. Its actual identity remains uncertain.

Helek was a son of Gilead and a descendant of Manasseh, son of Joseph. He founded the Helekite family, one of the clans of Manasseh listed in the census taken on the plains of Moab (Num 26:30). His brothers were Abiezer (called Jeezer in Numbers), Asriel, Shechem, Hepher and Shemida. When the land was divided under Joshua, the children of Helek were among the Manassite families who received a share of territory, apparently west of the Jordan, set apart from the portion already given east of the river (Josh 17:2). Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him Gilead's second son, following the order of the Numbers list. His name means "portion" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Nothing else is recorded about him.

Helem was one of the exiles who had come back from Babylon in the time of the prophet Zechariah. Zechariah was told to take silver and gold from him and from Tobijah and Jedaiah, have crowns made, and set one on the head of Joshua the high priest (Zech 6:10–11). The crowns were then to be kept in the temple of the LORD as a memorial to Helem, Tobijah, Jedaiah and Hen the son of Zephaniah (Zech 6:14). The same man appears as Heldai in Zech 6:10. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both take Helem and Heldai to be one person, and this entry follows that view. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint reads Helem as an ordinary word rather than a name. The setting is usually dated to about 520 BC, an estimate drawn from context.

Heleph was a town named as the starting point of the boundary of the territory given to the tribe of Naphtali (Josh 19:33). From Heleph the border ran past Allon, Zaanannim, Adami, Nekeb, Jabneel and Lakum, ending at the Jordan. The name has been taken to mean "exchange" (Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries) or "changing; passing over" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). The town is mentioned only here, and its site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on Naphtali's northern border, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it on the southern border and leaves it unidentified. The location shown here is in present-day southern Lebanon. It probably follows an identification with the village of Beit Lif, whose name may preserve the ancient one, which would put Heleph toward Naphtali's northwestern edge.

Helez was one of David's mighty warriors, listed among "the thirty" of his elite fighting men. In 2 Sam 23:26 he is called "the Paltite," while 1 Chr 11:27 calls him "the Pelonite." The two titles probably refer to the same man, and the difference is most likely a variation in the copying of the name. 1 Chr 27:10 adds that Helez the Pelonite came from the tribe of Ephraim. In David's organization of the kingdom he commanded the division of 24,000 men that served in the seventh month of the year. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "vigor," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "armed; set free." The name Helez is shared by more than one person in the Bible, so this man should be kept distinct from others who bear it.

Helez was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in a genealogy as the son of Azariah and the father of Eleasah (1 Chr 2:39). The genealogy belongs to the line of Jerahmeel, son of Hezron, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places him among the Jerahmeelites. In this line Azariah descends from the Egyptian servant Jarha, who married the daughter of Sheshan (1 Chr 2:34–38). Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "strength." The name is borne by several people in the Bible, among them one of David's mighty men, and this Helez should not be confused with them.

Heli appears in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, where Joseph is called "the son of Heli" (Luke 3:23). The next verse names Heli's father as Matthat, placing him in a line that runs back through David to the tribe of Judah. Matthew's genealogy names Joseph's father as Jacob (Matt 1:16), and this has led to two main readings. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take Heli as Joseph's father in Luke's account. Another long-standing view, followed by the STEPBible proper names index and by this entry, is that Luke traces Mary's line. In that case Heli was Mary's father and Jesus' maternal grandfather, and Joseph was his son-in-law. Smith's Bible Dictionary mentions a further possibility, that he was Mary's grandfather. Nothing else is recorded about him. According to Hitchcock's Bible Names, his name means "ascending."

Heliopolis, Greek for "city of the sun," was an ancient Egyptian city that was a major center for worship of the sun god. In Jer 43:13, Jeremiah warns that the king of Babylon would break the sacred images of "Bethshemesh" ("house of the sun") in Egypt and burn the Egyptians' temples. This Bethshemesh is generally taken to be Heliopolis, which explains the entry's name. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat Heliopolis as the same city called On elsewhere in the Bible. On was the home of Potipherah, priest of On, whose daughter Asenath married Joseph (Gen 41:45). It is probably also the Aven mentioned in Ezek 30:17. The location shown here is in the northeastern suburbs of modern Cairo, near Matariya and Ain Shams, where the city's remains, including a standing obelisk, are found.

Helkai was a priest who headed the priestly family of Meraioth in the days of Joiakim the high priest, in the generation after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears only once, in a list of the heads of priestly families serving under Joiakim (Neh 12:15). By inference from the surrounding passage, Meraioth was one of the priestly houses that had returned with Zerubbabel, and it probably corresponds to the Meremoth named earlier in the same chapter. Nothing more is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests his name may be a shortened form of Hilkiah, meaning "Yah is my portion," while Easton's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "smooth-tongued."

Helkath was a city on the border of the tribe of Asher, listed first among the boundary towns in Josh 19:25, along with Hali, Beten and Achshaph. It was later one of the cities given, with their surrounding pasturelands, to the Levites (Josh 21:31). By inference from the surrounding passage, it went to the Gershonite clan, who received four cities from Asher. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "smoothness" and places the town on Asher's eastern border. It also notes that the parallel list in 1 Chr 6:75 calls it Hukok, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains as a copyist's variant of the same name. The site's exact identification is uncertain, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as unidentified. The location shown here places it in western Galilee, inland and northeast of the plain of Acco.

Helkath-hazzurim was a field at Gibeon, north of Jerusalem, where twelve of Abner's men, fighting for Saul's son Ish-bosheth, met twelve of Joab's men, fighting for David, in a contest of champions. Each man seized his opponent by the head and drove his sword into his side, so they all fell together, and the place took its name from that combat (2 Sam 2:16). The name is usually understood as "field of sword edges" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "field of rock", and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "field of strong men, or of rocks." The duel settled nothing and led to a wider battle that Abner lost. By inference from the surrounding passage, the field lay near the pool of Gibeon, and the location shown here places it at Gibeon, generally identified with the modern village of el-Jib.

Helon was a man of the tribe of Zebulun, known only as the father of Eliab, the leader of that tribe during the wilderness period. He is never mentioned on his own. His name appears only in the phrase "Eliab the son of Helon", which identifies his son in several roles. Eliab is named as Zebulun's representative at the census (Num 1:9) and as captain of the tribe in the camp arrangement (Num 2:7). He brought Zebulun's offering on the third day of the dedication of the altar (Num 7:24, 29), and he led the tribe's company when Israel set out on the march (Num 10:16). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "strong", and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia as "valorous". Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "window; grief."

Heman was a man famous for his wisdom in the time of Solomon. In 1 Kgs 4:31 he is named with Ethan the Ezrahite, Chalcol and Darda, the sons of Mahol, as one of the wise men whom Solomon surpassed. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects him with the Heman listed in 1 Chr 2:6 as a son of Zerah of the tribe of Judah, together with Ethan, Calcol and Dara. On that reading, "Mahol" may name a family or a group rather than a literal father. He is linked to the Psalms because the heading of Ps 88 attributes it to "Heman the Ezrahite," a term probably meaning a descendant of Zerah. Several men in the Bible bear this name, including Heman the Levite singer of David's time (1 Chr 6:33), and some identify the psalm's author with that singer instead. This entry follows the identification with the wise man of 1 Kgs 4:31.

Heman was a son of Zerah and a grandson of Judah, listed in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah with his brothers Zimri, Ethan, Calcol and Dara (1 Chr 2:6). Zimri appears to be the same person called Zabdi in Josh 7:1. Zerah was one of the twin sons of Judah and Tamar. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies this Heman with the Heman of 1 Kgs 4:31, one of the wise men whom Solomon is said to have surpassed. That verse also names Ethan, Calcol and Darda, which closely matches this list of brothers, although it calls them sons of Mahol. The Heman called "the Ezrahite" in the title of Psalm 88 may also belong to this family, but that is uncertain. Several men in the Bible share this name. This Heman should be kept distinct from Heman the Levite, who was a singer in David's time (1 Chr 6:33).

Heman was a Levite of the Kohathite clan, son of Joel and grandson of Shemuel (Samuel), and one of the chief singers in David's organization of worship (1 Chr 6:33). The Levites appointed him with Asaph and Ethan to sound bronze cymbals when the ark was brought to Jerusalem. He and Jeduthun then served with trumpets, cymbals and other instruments to give thanks to the LORD. David set apart the families of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun to 'prophesy' with harps, lyres and cymbals. Heman is called 'the king's seer in the words of God,' and he had fourteen sons and three daughters, who sang under his direction in the house of the LORD. His family sang at the dedication of Solomon's temple, and his descendants Jehiel and Shimei served under Hezekiah. Easton's Bible Dictionary links him with the heading of Psalm 88. Other men named Heman also appear in the Bible.

Hemath was the ancestor from whom a group of Kenites descended, according to the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chr 2:55. That verse names him as "the father of the house of Rechab" and links him to the families of scribes living at Jabez: the Tirathites, Shimeathites and Suchathites. In these lists "father" often means founder, so Hemath may stand for the head of a clan rather than an immediate parent. The surrounding verses place these families among the descendants of Salma, the founder of Bethlehem. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the name, meaning "heat", could refer to either a person or a place. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia spells it Hammath. The house of Rechab is probably the same family as Jonadab son of Rechab and the Rechabites, who appear in 2 Kings 10 and Jeremiah 35. This entry treats Hemath as a man. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hemdan was a Horite, listed first among the sons of Dishon, with his brothers Eshban, Ithran and Cheran (Gen 36:26). He appears in the genealogy of the Horite clans descended from Seir, which Genesis sets alongside the descendants of Esau in the land of Edom. In the parallel list at 1 Chr 1:41 the King James Version calls him Amram. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both explain this as a difference in the Hebrew spelling: the Chronicles name is properly read Hamran, which the Revised Version uses, and it refers to the same man as Hemdan. 1 Chr 1:41 also makes his father Dishon a son of Anah. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the name Hemdan to mean "pleasant." Nothing more is recorded about him beyond these two genealogical entries.

Hena was a city named in the Assyrian taunts sent to King Hezekiah of Judah during Sennacherib's invasion. The Rabshakeh's speech (2 Kgs 18:34) and Sennacherib's letter (2 Kgs 19:13; Isa 37:13) list it with Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim and Ivah as places whose gods and kings could not withstand Assyria, implying it had already been conquered. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Anah on the Euphrates, not far from Sepharvaim, and Smith's Bible Dictionary also suggests Anah. The location shown here follows that identification, in present-day western Iraq. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes other views: that the text may be corrupt, that "Hena and Ivah" may be a Hebrew phrase meaning "he has driven away and overturned," or that the words may be divine names. Its exact identity therefore remains uncertain.

Henadad was a Levite whose descendants formed a family of Levites in the community that returned from exile in Babylon. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "favour of Hadad." When the foundations of the second temple were laid, the sons of Henadad, with their sons and fellow Levites, joined Jeshua and Kadmiel in overseeing the workmen on the house of God (Ezra 3:9). In Nehemiah's time a Levite named Binnui, "of the sons of Henadad," was among those who set their seal to the covenant to keep God's law (Neh 10:9). Nehemiah 3:18 and 3:24 also name Bavai and Binnui, sons of Henadad, among those who repaired Jerusalem's wall. Henadad himself is known only through his descendants. It is not certain whether every mention refers to the same ancestor, though the references are usually taken together as one Levite family.

Henadad is named in Neh 3:18 as the father of Bavai, who helped repair the wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time and is described as ruler of half the district of Keilah. Henadad himself appears only as his son's father here. The phrase "their brethren" links Bavai with the Levites listed just before (Neh 3:17), so Henadad was probably a Levite. The name also appears elsewhere in Nehemiah's era: the sons of Henadad are among the Levites in Ezra 3:9, and a Binnui son of Henadad repairs another section of the wall in Neh 3:24. These may belong to the same Levitical family, but whether they refer to the same Henadad is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "grace of the beloved."

Henadad was the father of Binnui, who repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall in Nehemiah's time, from the house of Azariah to the turning of the wall at the corner (Neh 3:24). Nothing else is said of him personally in this verse. Elsewhere the "sons of Henadad" appear as a Levite family that helped oversee work on the rebuilt temple (Ezra 3:9), and a Binnui "of the sons of Henadad" is named among Levites who sealed the covenant (Neh 10:9). So Henadad was probably the head of a Levite clan, and "son of Henadad" may mean a descendant rather than a direct son. A Bavai son of Henadad also worked on the wall (Neh 3:18). Because the name is shared by several people, how these references relate is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "grace of the beloved."

Henoch was a son of Midian and so a grandson of Abraham through Keturah, the wife Abraham took after Sarah's death. He is listed third among Midian's five sons, with his brothers Ephah, Epher, Abida and Eldaah, in the genealogy of Keturah's descendants (Gen 25:4; 1 Chr 1:33). Genesis spells his name Hanoch, while the King James text of 1 Chronicles has Henoch. In Hebrew it is the same name as Enoch, which Smith's Bible Dictionary glosses as "dedicated." Like his brothers, he was presumably regarded as an ancestor of a Midianite clan or tribe, though the text records nothing about him beyond his place in the family line. He should not be confused with Enoch the son of Cain, Enoch the father of Methuselah, or Hanoch the son of Reuben.

Hepher was a son of Gilead, the grandson of Machir and great-grandson of Manasseh son of Joseph, and the ancestor of the Hepherites, one of the clans of the tribe of Manasseh. He appears among Gilead's sons with Abiezer, Asriel, Helek, Shechem and Shemida, and his descendants received a share of land along with the other Manassite clans. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary call him Gilead's youngest son, since he is named last in Num 26:32. He is best known through his son Zelophehad, who had no sons but five daughters, Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah. These daughters came forward to claim their father's inheritance. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "a digger." Several other men in the Bible share the name Hepher, and they should not be confused with this one.

Hepher was a man of the tribe of Judah, the son of Ashur and his wife Naarah. He is listed second among Naarah's four sons, after Ahuzam and before Temeni and Haahashtari (1 Chr 4:6). The surrounding genealogy (1 Chr 4:5–7) calls Ashur the father of Tekoa and says he had a second wife, Helah, whose sons, including Zereth, Jezoar and Ethnan, were Hepher's half-brothers. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "a digger," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "a well." The same name belongs to other men in the Bible, including a son of Gilead in the tribe of Manasseh and one of David's mighty men, so he should not be confused with them.

Hepher was one of David's mighty warriors, the elite fighters listed in 1 Chr 11, where he is called "the Mecherathite" (1 Chr 11:36). Nothing else is recorded about him. The term Mecherathite appears nowhere else and probably refers to his hometown or clan, though no place called Mecherah is known. The parallel list in 2 Sam 23:34 has no Hepher at this point, and the names there differ, so some readers take "Mecherathite" as a variant of "Maachathite." The name Hepher is shared by other men in the Bible, including a descendant of Manasseh, the father of Zelophehad, and a son of Ashur of Judah. These are separate people. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a digger," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "a well."

Hepher was a Canaanite town whose king appears among the rulers Joshua defeated west of the Jordan, listed next to the king of Tappuah (Josh 12:17). Under Solomon, "all the land of Hepher" formed part of the third administrative district, along with Sochoh, under the son of Hesed based at Aruboth (1 Kgs 4:10). That suggests the town gave its name to a surrounding district, probably in the Sharon plain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia (1915) treats both the town and the district as unidentified. Many later scholars place Hepher at Tell el-Ifshar (Tel Hefer) on the coastal plain north of modern Netanya, and the location shown here follows that identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a digger."

Hephzi-bah was the wife of King Hezekiah of Judah and the mother of his son and successor Manasseh. She is named only once, in the notice of Manasseh's accession, which says he became king in Jerusalem at twelve and reigned fifty-five years (2 Kgs 21:1). As the mother of a Judean king she belongs to the royal line that Matthew's genealogy of Jesus traces through Hezekiah and Manasseh, though she is not named there. Her name means "my delight is in her" (Hitchcock's Bible Names; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). The same word appears in Isa 62:4 as the new name given to restored Jerusalem, in place of "Forsaken," because the LORD delights in her. There it is a symbolic name for the city, not a reference to the queen, as both Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat the two uses separately.

Heres is a place named in Judg 8:13 as the point from which Gideon son of Joash turned back after defeating the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna. The King James Version reads the Hebrew phrase as "before the sun was up," since heres can mean "sun." The Revised Version and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia read it as a place name, "the ascent of Heres," probably a pass or slope Gideon climbed on his way back. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that both the text and the geography are uncertain. The following verses show Gideon going on to Succoth, so Heres was probably east of the Jordan, between the battlefield near Karkor and Succoth. The location shown here is a rough one in that area. A separate "Mount Heres" near Aijalon in Dan, mentioned in Judg 1:35 and discussed by Smith's Bible Dictionary, is a different place.

Heresh was a Levite named in the list of those who lived in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. He appears alongside Bakbakkar, Galal and Mattaniah, a descendant of Asaph (1 Chr 9:15). By inference from the surrounding passage, which lists the priests, Levites and gatekeepers who resettled the city, he belonged to the Levites who served at the house of God. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Levite attached to the tabernacle and dates him to about 536 BC. His name is usually explained as meaning "artificer" or "carpenter" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; Hitchcock's Bible Names). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that ancient Greek manuscripts render the name differently, as Rharaiel or Hares. Nothing else is recorded about him, and his family line is not given.

Hereth (spelled Hareth in the King James Version) was a forest or wooded area in the land of Judah where David went while fleeing from King Saul. The prophet Gad told David to leave "the hold", by inference from the surrounding passage his refuge near Mizpeh in Moab, and go into Judah, so David came to the forest of Hereth (1 Sam 22:5). The Hebrew name probably means "thicket." The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation, reads "city" instead of "forest," and some scholars have suggested "Horesh" as an alternative reading. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests that David's men may have fetched him water from Bethlehem's well while he was here (2 Sam 23:14–17). The site is uncertain. Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both propose the village of Kharas, about 3 miles east of Keilah, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Hermas was a Christian living in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings near the end of his letter to the Romans. He is named in a group with Asyncritus, Phlegon, Patrobas and Hermes, along with "the brethren which are with them" (Rom 16:14), which suggests these men belonged to the same household or house church. Nothing more is said about him in the Bible. The name is a short form of several Greek names, and Hitchcock's Bible Names links it to Hermes. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Origen and other early writers identified him with the author of The Shepherd, a widely respected early Christian book. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia points out that the Muratorian Canon dates that author to about AD 140–155 and that the name was common. This entry treats Hermas simply as the Roman believer Paul greeted.

Hermes was a Christian in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings at the close of his letter to the Romans. He is named in a group with Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas and Patrobas, along with "the brethren which are with them" (Rom 16:14). That wording suggests these men belonged to the same household or house church. Nothing more is known of him from the Bible. His name is the Greek form of the god the Romans called Mercury. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it was one of the most common slave names of the period, so he may have been a slave or a freedman, though the text does not say. Smith's Bible Dictionary records a tradition that he was one of the seventy disciples and later bishop of Dalmatia. He should not be confused with Hermas, who is named beside him in the same verse.

Hermogenes was a Christian named in 2 Tim 1:15, where Paul reminds Timothy that "all they which are in Asia" had turned away from him, Phygellus and Hermogenes among them. His name is Greek and means "born of Hermes" (the god the Romans called Mercury). Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as once Paul's fellow worker in Asia Minor who later abandoned him, probably because of the dangers involved. It is unclear when and where the desertion happened. Some take it as an earlier rejection of Paul's authority in Ephesus. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia favors a different setting: Christians from the province of Asia who were in Rome during Paul's final imprisonment and avoided him, probably out of fear. It notes that the very next verses contrast them with Onesiphorus, who searched for Paul in Rome.

Hermon is a high mountain at the northern edge of the land east of the Jordan, marking the far limit of the territory Israel took from the Amorites, which ran from Aroer on the Arnon to Hermon (Deut 4:48). The Sidonians called it Sirion and the Amorites Shenir (Deut 3:9), and it is also called Sion (Deut 4:48). Hivites lived beneath it in the land of Mizpeh (Josh 11:3). Poets drew on it as an image: its dew stands for blessing (Ps 133:3), it is paired with Tabor (Ps 89:12), and it appears beside Lebanon and Amana (Song 4:8). The plural 'the Hermonites' in Ps 42:6 probably refers to its several summits, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains. It is identified with Jebel esh-Sheikh, the snow-capped southern end of the Anti-Lebanon range, about 9,200 feet high. The location shown here follows that identification. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it was the scene of the transfiguration.

Herod, usually called Herod the Great, was king of Judaea when John the Baptist and Jesus were born (Matt 2:1; Luke 1:5). When wise men from the east came to Jerusalem looking for a newborn king, Herod was troubled. He questioned them privately about when the star had appeared. Warned in a dream, they went home by another route, and Joseph fled with Mary and the child to Egypt. Furious at being outwitted, Herod had every boy aged two and under in and around Bethlehem killed. After his death, about 4 BC by inference from context, his son Archelaus ruled Judaea. Other sons, Herod Antipas and Philip, appear later in the Gospels, and two different sons bore the name Philip. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as an Idumean whom Rome made king, who rebuilt the Jerusalem temple and died at Jericho.

Herod Antipas was a son of Herod the Great, by Malthace according to Easton's Bible Dictionary, and ruled Galilee as tetrarch during the ministry of Jesus (Luke 3:1). He married Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip. When John the Baptist told him the marriage was unlawful, Herod imprisoned him, although he respected John and listened to him gladly. At his birthday feast the daughter of Herodias danced before his guests, and Herod promised her whatever she asked. This led to John's beheading. By inference from context, the imprisonment was about AD 27 and the execution about AD 29. Hearing of Jesus' works, Herod wondered whether John had risen from the dead. Some Pharisees warned Jesus that Herod wanted to kill him. During Jesus' trial, Pilate sent him to Herod, who mocked him and sent him back. Herod and Pilate became friends that day. Manaen, a teacher at Antioch, had been brought up with him.

Herod Agrippa I was the ruler called simply "Herod the king" in Acts 12. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him as a grandson of Herod the Great who eventually ruled his grandfather's whole kingdom. He moved against the church in Jerusalem. He had the apostle James killed (Acts 12:2) and then imprisoned Peter, who was chained between soldiers until an angel freed him. After Peter escaped, Herod questioned the guards, ordered them put to death, and went down from Judea to Caesarea. There the people of Tyre and Sidon, whose food came from his territory, sought peace with him through his chamberlain Blastus. On a set day he sat on his throne in royal robes and gave a speech. Acts 12:23 says an angel then struck him and he died. This entry dates his death to about AD 45 by inference from context, while Easton's gives AD 44.

Herod dies describes the sudden death of Herod Agrippa I, the king who had earlier imprisoned Peter, at Caesarea. The people of Tyre and Sidon had angered him, but because their land depended on his territory for food, they won over Blastus, the king's chamberlain, and asked for peace. On an appointed day Herod put on his royal robes, sat on his throne, and gave a speech to them. The crowd shouted that it was the voice of a god and not of a man.
