Luke records that an angel of the Lord immediately struck him because he did not give glory to God, and that he was eaten by worms and died. The setting at Caesarea comes from the verse just before the passage (Acts 12:19). The date, about AD 45, is an estimate inferred from context. The Jewish historian Josephus also describes Agrippa's death at Caesarea.

Herod imprisons Peter is the episode in which King Herod, identified as Herod Agrippa I, arrested the apostle Simon Peter in Judea, probably in Jerusalem. It happened soon after he had James the brother of John killed (Acts 12:2). Seeing that this pleased the Jewish authorities, he went further and seized Peter during the days of Unleavened Bread. He put Peter in prison under four squads of four soldiers each and planned to bring him out before the people after the Passover, which the King James Version calls "Easter." Meanwhile the church prayed to God for him without stopping. The date of about AD 40 shown here is an estimate inferred from context. The following verses (Acts 12:6–11) go on to describe Peter's release by an angel on the night before Herod meant to bring him out.

Herod kills James refers to the execution of James the brother of John, one of Jesus' twelve apostles, by King Herod, recorded in Acts 12:1–2. Around this time Herod began harassing members of the church, and he had James killed with the sword, which probably means beheading. The text calls the ruler only "Herod the king." He is generally identified as Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, since the same chapter goes on to describe this Herod's death (Acts 12:23). James is the son of Zebedee named in the Gospels (Matt 4:21). The setting is Judea, probably Jerusalem, where Herod next imprisoned Peter after seeing that the killing pleased some of the people (Acts 12:3). It is the only death of one of the Twelve recorded in Acts. This entry dates it to about AD 40, an estimate inferred from context.

Herod slays male children is the episode in which King Herod, probably Herod the Great, ordered the killing of all the children in and around Bethlehem aged two years and under. When the wise men did not return to tell him where the newborn king could be found, Herod realized he had been tricked and became furious. He set the age limit by the time the wise men had told him the star first appeared (compare Matt 2:7). The account follows Joseph and Mary's flight to Egypt with the child Jesus, so the family had already escaped. Matthew presents the killings as fulfilling Jer 31:15, which pictures Rachel weeping in Ramah for her children. Rachel's burial near Bethlehem (Gen 35:19) probably explains the link. The event is dated to about 4 BC, by inference from context. Matthew is the only gospel that records it.

Herodias was the wife of Herod Antipas, the tetrarch of Galilee, and had earlier been the wife of his brother Philip (Luke 3:19). John the Baptist rebuked Herod over this marriage, and Herodias held a grudge against John and wanted him killed but could not do it (Mark 6:19). At Herod's birthday feast her daughter danced and pleased Herod, who promised to give the girl whatever she asked (Matt 14:6; Mark 6:22). The fuller accounts in Matthew 14 and Mark 6 say that, prompted by her mother, she asked for John's head, and John was beheaded in prison. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Herodias as a granddaughter of Herod the Great through his son Aristobulus and a sister of Agrippa I. It says she left Herod Philip to marry Antipas, her step-uncle, and later went with him into exile at Lugdunum in Gaul.

Herodion was a Christian at Rome whom Paul greets in his letter to the Romans, calling him "my kinsman" (Rom 16:11). The word can mean a blood relative, as Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it, or more broadly a fellow Jew, the reading the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia prefers. This entry leaves both possibilities open. His name suggests a link with the family of Herod. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia proposes that he may have been a freed slave of the Herods or a member of the household of Aristobulus, whom Paul greets in the verse just before (Rom 16:10). Aristobulus is often thought to be a grandson of Herod the Great. Nothing more is known about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the letter to about AD 55, an estimate inferred from context.

Hesed was the father of one of Solomon's twelve district officers, who appears in 1 Kgs 4:10 only as "the son of Hesed" (Hebrew Ben-hesed). Nothing is recorded about Hesed himself beyond his son's role. The son was based in Aruboth, and his district included Sochoh and all the land of Hepher. By inference from the surrounding passage, the twelve officers each supplied food for the king's household for one month of the year. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes the son as Solomon's commissary and gives the meaning of the name as "kindness." It dates him to about 995 BC, an estimate drawn from context rather than stated in the text. The locations of Aruboth and Sochoh in this district are uncertain. They probably lay in the hill country or coastal plain west of Samaria, but no firm identification can be made from this single verse.

Heshbon was the royal city of Sihon, king of the Amorites, who had taken the land of the former king of Moab as far as the Arnon (Num 21:26). Israel captured it under Moses and settled in it and its villages (Num 21:25; Deut 2:24–30). The tribe of Reuben rebuilt it (Num 32:37), and it lay on the border between Reuben and Gad (Josh 13:17, 26). It was later assigned to the Levites (Josh 21:39; 1 Chr 6:81). The Song of Solomon mentions its fishpools (Song 7:4). In the prophecies of Isaiah and Jeremiah it appears as a Moabite city facing judgment (Isa 15:4; Jer 48:2, 34), suggesting that Moab had regained it. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it at the ruins of Hesban, about 20 miles east of the Jordan near the northern end of the Dead Sea, in present-day Jordan. The location shown here follows that identification.

Heshmon was a town in the far south of Judah, named once in the list of cities given to the tribe of Judah in the Negev region toward the border of Edom (Josh 15:27). It appears between Hazar-gaddah and Beth-pelet, and nothing else is recorded about it. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "fatness," and Smith's Bible Dictionary as "rich soil." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the site has not been identified and suggests it may have been the original home of the Hasmoneans. Its exact location is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the northern Negev, based on its position in the list of southern towns.

Heth was a son of Canaan, named second after Sidon, the firstborn, in the table of nations (Gen 10:15; 1 Chr 1:13). He is regarded as the ancestor of the Hittites, and in Genesis his descendants appear as "the sons" or "children of Heth," a people living near Hebron in Abraham's time. Abraham bought from them, through Ephron the Hittite, the field and cave of Machpelah as a family burial place. He paid four hundred shekels of silver in a public transaction at the city gate (Gen 23:3–20). Abraham and Sarah were later buried there (Gen 25:10). Rebekah's distress over the "daughters of Heth" whom Esau had married led her to urge that Jacob not take a wife from among them (Gen 27:46). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the name's meaning as "dread" or "terror."

Hethlon was a place on the northern border of the land in Ezekiel's vision of the restored Israel. Ezekiel describes that border as running from the Mediterranean ("the great sea") along "the way of Hethlon" toward Zedad and Hamath, and he uses the same line to mark the northern edge of Dan's portion (Ezek 47:15; 48:1). The site is not mentioned anywhere else. Smith's and Easton's Bible Dictionaries take "the way of Hethlon" to be the pass at the northern end of Lebanon leading to the plain of Hamath, probably the same route as the "entrance of Hamath" in Numbers. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mentions an identification with 'Adlun on the Qasmiyeh River, and also one with Heitala northeast of Tripoli, which would place the route in the Eleutherus valley between the coast and Homs. The location shown here follows that northern, Eleutherus valley identification.

Hezeki was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, listed among the sons of Elpaal in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 8:17. He appears only in this list, alongside brothers such as Zebadiah, Meshullam and Heber. Elpaal is named earlier in the same chapter as a son of Shaharaim and Hushim, which places Hezeki within a Benjamite family line, and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a descendant of Shaharaim. The context suggests the family was linked with towns such as Ono and Lod. Some modern translations spell the name Hizki, following the Hebrew more closely. His name probably means "strong," as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes, and it is related to the name Hezekiah. Nothing else is recorded about his life or deeds.

Hezekiah was king of Judah, the son of Ahaz and Abijah, who succeeded his father on the throne in Jerusalem (2 Kgs 16:20). Easton's Bible Dictionary dates his 29-year reign to about 726–697 BC. He removed the high places and altars and restored temple worship with offerings and music (2 Chr 29:27; Isa 36:7). In his fourteenth year Sennacherib of Assyria took Judah's fortified cities. Hezekiah paid tribute, stripping gold from the temple doors (2 Kgs 18:13, 16). When the Assyrians later threatened Jerusalem, he prayed for deliverance (2 Kgs 19:15). He fell gravely ill, was told by Isaiah to prepare for death, prayed, and recovered (Isa 38:1; 2 Kgs 20:5). He showed his treasures to envoys from Babylon (Isa 39:2). His men copied out proverbs of Solomon (Prov 25:1). His son Manasseh succeeded him, and Matthew lists him as Ezekias in Jesus' genealogy. The name is also borne by other people in the Bible.

Hezekiah was a son of Neariah and a member of the tribe of Judah, named with his brothers Elioenai and Azrikam in 1 Chr 3:23. He appears only in this genealogy. It traces the royal line of David after the exile, through King Jeconiah (Jehoiachin), so Hezekiah was a descendant of David living after the Babylonian captivity. Nothing more is recorded about him. He is a different person from King Hezekiah of Judah and from others who share the name. The Revised Version spells his name "Hizkiah," as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "strength of the Lord."

Hezekiah is a man named in the lists of Jewish exiles who returned from Babylon to Judah, where "the children of Ater of Hezekiah" number ninety-eight (Ezra 2:16; Neh 7:21). The short phrase is read in different ways. It may mean that Ater's family was traced through, or belonged to, a branch called Hezekiah, or that Hezekiah was linked to Ater's line as his son. This entry follows the second reading and lists Ater as his father. The STEPBible proper-names index describes him as an ancestor of returning exiles, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts him among the returned exiles. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with King Hezekiah of Judah or with others who share the name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "strength of the Lord."

Hezion was the father of Tabrimon and the grandfather of Ben-hadad, the king of Syria who ruled from Damascus. He is named only in the genealogy of Ben-hadad, when King Asa of Judah sent silver and gold from the temple and palace treasuries to buy Ben-hadad's help (1 Kgs 15:18). The verse does not say whether Hezion himself was a king, though the context suggests he founded or belonged to the ruling line in Damascus. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he is probably the same person as Rezon, the ruler of Damascus who opposed Solomon (1 Kgs 11:23). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Greek manuscripts render the name as Azein or Azael. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "vision."

Hezir was a priest in the time of King David whose family was given the seventeenth of the twenty-four divisions of priestly service (1 Chr 24:15). The surrounding chapter describes how these divisions were assigned by lot, each taking its turn at the sanctuary. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes the divisions as monthly courses. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls Hezir the head of the seventeenth course, and Smith's gives the name's meaning as "swine." Nothing else is recorded about him. The same name belongs to more than one person in the Bible. A later Hezir appears among the leaders who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah's time, and he is a different man.

Hezir was one of the leaders who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, in which the returned community in Jerusalem pledged to keep the Law of God. His name is the only thing Neh 10:20 records about him, where it appears between Magpiash, Meshullam and others. By inference from its place in the list, he belongs among the "chiefs of the people" who sealed after the priests and Levites. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both describe him as a lay head of the people. Smith's dates the sealing to about 410 BC and gives the meaning of the name as "swine." The name was shared by several people. It also belongs to the head of a priestly division in David's day (1 Chr 24:15), who is a different man.

Hezrai the Carmelite was one of David's mighty men, the elite warriors listed in 2 Sam 23:35. The parallel list in 1 Chr 11:37 gives his name as Hezro, and Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the two forms as the same man. "Carmelite" probably marks him as coming from Carmel, a town in the hill country of Judah near Maon, rather than from Mount Carmel in the north. This is an inference, since the passages do not say which Carmel is meant. Nothing more is recorded about him beyond his place in the list of David's warriors. The neighbouring name also differs between the two lists: Paarai the Arbite in Samuel and Naarai the son of Ezbai in Chronicles. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "an entry or vestibule."

Hezron was a son of Reuben, the firstborn of Jacob. He is named third among Reuben's four sons, after Hanoch and Pallu and before Carmi. He appears in the list of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:9) and in the genealogies of the heads of Reuben's fathers' houses (Exod 6:14; 1 Chr 5:3). In the census taken in the wilderness, his descendants are counted as the Hezronites, one of the clans of the tribe of Reuben (Num 26:6). Nothing else is recorded about his life. The name was shared by others. 1 Chr 2:24, which mentions a Hezron who died in Caleb-ephratah, belongs by context to a different man, the Hezron of the tribe of Judah descended from Perez, and not to Reuben's son. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "enclosed" or "surrounded by a wall."

Hezron was a son of Pharez (Perez), a grandson of Judah, and the brother of Hamul (Gen 46:12; 1 Chr 2:5). He is listed among Jacob's family who went down to Egypt, and his descendants formed the Hezronite clan of the tribe of Judah (Num 26:21). His sons included Jerahmeel, his firstborn, Ram, and Chelubai, who is evidently the Caleb named a few verses later (1 Chr 2:9, 18, 25). At sixty he married the daughter of Machir, the father of Gilead, and she bore him Segub. After Hezron died at Caleb-ephrathah, his wife Abiah bore his son Ashur, the father of Tekoa (1 Chr 2:21, 24). Through Ram he was an ancestor of David (Ruth 4:18–19). He appears as Esrom, the Greek form of his name, in the genealogies of Jesus (Matt 1:3; Luke 3:33). The name Hezron is also borne by other people in the Bible.

Hiel was a man from Bethel who rebuilt the city of Jericho during the reign of King Ahab of Israel. The verse dates it only as "in his days", which by context refers to Ahab (1 Kgs 16:34). His name is usually taken to mean "God lives." The verse says he laid Jericho's foundation "in" his firstborn son Abiram and set up its gates "in" his youngest son Segub, as the LORD had said through Joshua. That word is the curse in Josh 6:26, spoken after Jericho's fall, that whoever rebuilt the city would do so at the cost of his eldest and youngest sons. Interpreters understand Hiel's loss in different ways. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it to mean his sons died while the work went on. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reads it as the sacrifice of the sons as foundation offerings. The text itself does not say how they died.

Hierapolis, meaning "holy city" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, was a city of Phrygia in the Lycus valley of western Asia Minor. Its only biblical mention is in Col 4:13. There Paul says that Epaphras worked hard for the believers in Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis, which implies that a Christian community existed there. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the church was probably founded by Epaphras. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places the city about 6 miles from Laodicea and about 12 from Colossae. It describes the city's hot calcium-rich springs, whose white deposits gave the site its later name, Pambuk Kalessi ("cotton castle"). It also notes a tradition that the evangelist Philip preached and was buried there. The location shown here is the ruined city beside the white terraces of Pamukkale, near modern Denizli in Turkey.

Highway, called the King's Highway in modern translations, was a main road east of the Jordan and the Dead Sea. During their journey toward Canaan the Israelites asked permission to use it. Moses first asked the king of Edom (Num 20:17), and later Israel asked Sihon king of the Amorites (Num 21:22). Each time they promised to keep to the road, not to turn aside into fields or vineyards, and not to drink from the wells until they had crossed the king's territory. The surrounding chapters show that both requests were refused. STEPBible's proper-names index (Tyndale House) describes the King's Highway as an ancient trade route through Edom and Moab. It is generally taken to have run north and south along the high ground east of the Dead Sea. The location shown here is a rough point in that region, in what is now Jordan.

Hilen was a town in the hill country of Judah, named in 1 Chr 6:58 among the cities and their surrounding pasture lands given to the descendants of Aaron the priest. In the parallel list of priestly cities in Josh 21:15, and in the list of Judah's towns in Josh 15:51, the name appears as Holon, and the two are generally taken to be the same place. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it probably west or southwest of Hebron. Its exact site is uncertain, and the location shown here is a point in that general area. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "place of caves."

Hilkiah was the father of Eliakim, the official in charge of King Hezekiah's palace household in Judah. He is known only through his son, who is regularly called "Eliakim the son of Hilkiah." Eliakim, with Shebna the scribe and Joah the recorder, went out to meet the Assyrian officer Rabshakeh at Jerusalem's wall and then reported his words to Hezekiah (2 Kgs 18:18, 26, 37; Isa 36:22). Isaiah also names Eliakim as God's servant who would replace Shebna (Isa 22:20). Nothing is said about Hilkiah himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests his name was given mainly to tell his son apart from others called Eliakim. The name means "Yah is my portion." Several men in the Bible share it, including the high priest under Josiah, who is a different person.

Hilkiah, son of Shallum and a member of the tribe of Levi, was high priest in Jerusalem during the reign of King Josiah of Judah. Josiah sent him silver gathered from the people to fund temple repairs, and while the money was being brought out he found "the book of the law" in the temple. He gave it to Shaphan the scribe, who read it to the king. Hilkiah then led a delegation to consult the prophetess Huldah, removed the objects made for Baal from the temple at Josiah's command, and joined in providing animals for Josiah's Passover. Priestly genealogies name him as the father of Azariah and an ancestor of Ezra (1 Chr 9:11 gives his father as Meshullam). This entry also counts him as the father of Gemariah, Zedekiah's envoy to Babylon (Jer 29:3), although that identification is uncertain. The Hilkiah who was the father of Eliakim in Hezekiah's day (Isa 36:3) is a different man.

Hilkiah was a Levite of the family of Merari, named only in the genealogy of the Levites in 1 Chr 6:45. He was the son of Amzi and the father of Amaziah. The list traces the ancestry of Ethan, one of the Levites David appointed to lead singing at the house of the Lord, and Hilkiah's place in it comes from the surrounding context of the chapter. His name means "the Lord is my portion" (Hitchcock's Bible Names; the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Old Testament share the name, most of them connected with the priesthood, such as the high priest of Josiah's reign. This Hilkiah is a different person, known only as a link in this family line. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hilkiah was a Levite, the second son of Hosah, named in the list of temple gatekeepers organized in David's time (1 Chr 26:11). His brothers were Simri, Tebaliah and Zechariah, and Hosah's sons and relatives numbered thirteen in all. The surrounding chapter places Hosah's family among the descendants of Merari, and Smith's Bible Dictionary accordingly calls Hilkiah a Merarite Levite. The name means "the LORD is my portion," and it is shared by several other men in the Bible, most notably the high priest in the days of King Josiah, who is a different person. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia raises the possibility that the doorkeeper Hosah's family mentioned in 1 Chr 16:38 is connected, but nothing further is recorded about this Hilkiah himself.

Hilkiah was one of six men who stood at Ezra's right hand on the wooden platform when Ezra the scribe read the law to the people gathered in Jerusalem after the return from exile (Neh 8:4). Nothing else is said about him there. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to have been a Levite and probably a priest, and the STEPBible proper-names index calls him a priest. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that he may be the same Hilkiah listed among the priests who returned with Zerubbabel and whose family appears in a later priestly list (Neh 12:7, 21). That identification is uncertain, because the name was common, especially among priestly families. The name means "Yahweh is my portion."

Hilkiah was a priest among those who returned to Jerusalem from exile in Babylon. Nehemiah 12 lists him among "the chief of the priests and of their brethren in the days of Jeshua" the high priest (Neh 12:7). By inference from the opening of the chapter, he was part of the group that came back with Zerubbabel and Jeshua. In the next generation, under the high priest Joiakim, the priestly family named after Hilkiah was headed by Hashabiah (Neh 12:21), so his name continued as the name of a priestly house. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is different from several other men named Hilkiah, including the high priest in King Josiah's time. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "God is my portion."

Hilkiah was a priest from Anathoth in the territory of Benjamin and the father of the prophet Jeremiah (Jer 1:1). His name means "God is my portion" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names and Smith's Bible Dictionary, or "Yah is my portion" in the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. His brother was Shallum. This is inferred from Jer 32:7, which calls Shallum Jeremiah's uncle and names Shallum's son Hanameel as Jeremiah's cousin. Smith's Bible Dictionary places Hilkiah before 628 BC. Nothing else is recorded of him. Several men in the Old Testament share the name, most of them linked with the priesthood. The best known is the high priest who found the book of the law in Josiah's reign. Some interpreters have identified the two, but most treat Jeremiah's father as a separate priest of Anathoth, and this entry follows that view.

Hill Mizar, called Mount Mizar in modern translations, is a hill named only once in the Bible, in Ps 42:6. There the psalmist, feeling downcast, says he will remember God "from the land of Jordan, and of the Hermonites, from the hill Mizar." The setting suggests a spot in the far north, near the sources of the Jordan and the slopes of Mount Hermon. Its exact location is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "smallness" and places it on the eastern ridge of Lebanon. It connects the hill with David's flight from Absalom and suggests it may be the Jebel Ajlun, named "the little" in contrast to the greater heights of Lebanon and Hermon. Some readers take the name as a contrast between a small hill and mighty Hermon. The location shown here is a rough placement in the Hermon region.

Hillel was the father of Abdon, one of the judges of Israel, and is known only from his son's record in Judg 12:13 and 12:15. Both verses call him (or perhaps Abdon, since the Hebrew phrasing allows either reading) a Pirathonite, a native of Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, where Abdon was later buried. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take the title as describing Hillel himself, and this entry follows that reading. Nothing else is recorded about his life. His name means "praising" or "he greatly praised," according to Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. He should not be confused with the famous Jewish teacher Hillel of the first century BC, who does not appear in the Bible.

Hirah was a man from Adullam, a town in the lowlands of Judah, and a friend of Judah son of Jacob. When Judah left his brothers, he turned aside to stay with Hirah (Gen 38:1). It was in this region that Judah married the daughter of Shuah. Later, after his wife died, Judah went up to his sheepshearers at Timnath together with "his friend Hirah the Adullamite" (Gen 38:12). Further on in the same chapter (Gen 38:20), Judah sends his friend the Adullamite to deliver a young goat and recover the pledge he had left with the woman he had met on the way, who was in fact his daughter-in-law Tamar. Hirah cannot find her. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint and the Vulgate call him Judah's "shepherd" rather than his friend. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hiram, called Huram in Chronicles, was king of Tyre in the days of David and Solomon. He sent David messengers, cedar timber, carpenters and masons to build him a house (2 Sam 5:11; 1 Chr 14:1). Described as always a friend of David, he made a league with Solomon. He supplied cedar and fir for the temple, and his builders worked alongside Solomon's, in return for yearly wheat and oil. Solomon later gave him twenty cities in Galilee. They did not please him, yet he sent Solomon 120 talents of gold, and Chronicles speaks of these cities as restored to Solomon. His experienced sailors joined Solomon's fleets to Ophir and Tarshish, bringing back gold, almug wood, precious stones and ivory. This entry names his father as Huram. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Josephus calls him son of Abibal. The same name is also borne by a Tyrian craftsman.

Hiram, also called Huram, was a skilled bronze worker from Tyre whom King Solomon brought to Jerusalem to make the bronze furnishings for the temple. He is a different person from King Hiram of Tyre, Solomon's ally, who sent him. The connected passages say his father was a man of Tyre and his mother a widow, from the tribe of Naphtali according to 1 Kgs 7:14 and of Dan according to 2 Chr 2:14. He made the lavers, pots, shovels, basins, fleshhooks and other vessels, all of polished bronze, and finished the work Solomon gave him. The nearby 1 Kgs 7:46 says the casting was done in clay ground in the Jordan valley between Succoth and Zarethan. The phrase "Huram his father" in 2 Chr 4:16 is explained in Easton's Bible Dictionary as "Huram-abi," either a personal name or a title of respect meaning something like "master."

Hivite is named in the table of nations as a son of Canaan, but the name stands for a people descended from him rather than for one individual (Gen 10:17; 1 Chr 1:15). The Hivites were one of the peoples living in Canaan before Israel arrived. In Jacob's time Hamor the Hivite, father of Shechem, was prince of the region around Shechem (Gen 34:2), and Esau married a descendant of Zibeon the Hivite (Gen 36:2). They appear regularly in lists of nations God promised to drive out before Israel (Exod 23:28; 34:11) and among the peoples whose kings heard of Joshua's victories. One group lived "under Hermon in the land of Mizpeh" in the north (Josh 11:3). Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "villagers" and places them from Hermon south to Gibeon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some passages may confuse Hivite with the similar name Horite.

Hizkiah was an ancestor of the prophet Zephaniah, named at the head of the prophet's genealogy in Zeph 1:1. That verse traces Zephaniah back through Cushi, Gedaliah and Amariah to Hizkiah, which makes Hizkiah the father of Amariah and Zephaniah's great-great-grandfather. The prophecy is dated to the days of Josiah king of Judah, so Hizkiah lived several generations earlier. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him before 635 BC and gives the meaning of his name as "might of Jehovah." His name is a form of Hezekiah, and many interpreters identify him with King Hezekiah of Judah. This would explain why the genealogy is traced so far back, and the generations fit roughly between Hezekiah and Josiah. The verse itself does not call him king, so the identification remains uncertain. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hizkijah was one of the leaders who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's day, a solemn pledge to keep the law of Moses after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears in a list of names in Neh 10:17, between Ater and Azzur. By inference from the surrounding passage, he belongs to the group headed 'the chief of the people', so he was probably a clan or family head rather than a priest or Levite. STEPBible's proper names index describes him as a clan leader among the returned exiles. His name is the same as Hezekiah's, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as 'the strength of the Lord.' Because Ater and Hezekiah are also linked as one family among the returnees in Ezra 2:16, Hizkijah may stand here for that family. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hobab was a Midianite relative of Moses by marriage. Moses invited him to travel with Israel to the land God had promised, saying Israel would treat him well (Num 10:29). In the verses that follow, Hobab at first declines, and Moses presses him to stay because he knows the wilderness camping places. Judg 4:11 names him as the ancestor of Heber the Kenite, which links him to the Kenites who settled among Israel. Num 10:29 calls him the son of Raguel (Reuel), and Moses' father-in-law. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that he has often been identified with Jethro himself. It also notes that the Hebrew word in Judg 4:11 can mean any male relative by marriage, so it may mean brother-in-law there. This entry follows the view that Hobab was a son of Jethro (Reuel) and a brother of Zipporah, which made him Moses' brother-in-law. The name means "beloved."

Hobah was a place near Damascus, the farthest point to which Abram and his servants chased the defeated forces of the eastern kings after a night attack (Gen 14:15). From the surrounding chapter, this was the campaign in which Abram rescued his nephew Lot, who had been taken captive when Sodom was plundered. The verse places Hobah "on the left hand of Damascus." Because ancient Hebrew directions assume a person facing east, the left hand means north, and Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries both read it as north of Damascus. Easton's gives the name's meaning as "hiding-place." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with a site called Choba, about 60 miles northwest of Damascus. The exact site is uncertain. The location shown here places it a short distance from Damascus itself.

Hod was a man of the tribe of Asher, named once in the tribe's genealogy as one of the sons of Zophah (1 Chr 7:37). His brothers in the list include Suah, Harnepher, Beri, Imrah, Bezer, Shamma, Shilshah, Beera and others. Ithran, who appears in the same verse, is generally taken to be the Jether of the next verse. Zophah's sons are traced back to Asher through Helem, so Hod belonged to a family line within one of Asher's clans. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name is usually understood to mean "splendor" or "majesty" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "praise" or "confession."

Hodaiah was a man of the tribe of Judah, listed first among the seven sons of Elioenai in the genealogy of David's royal line (1 Chr 3:24). His brothers were Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub, Johanan, Dalaiah and Anani. The surrounding chapter traces David's descendants through the kings to Jeconiah and on past the exile, so Hodaiah belongs to a late generation of that line, after the return from Babylon. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him at about 406 BC, an estimate inferred from the genealogy. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "the praise of the Lord." Some manuscripts and translations spell the name Hodaviah. Nothing further is recorded about him.

Hodaviah was a leader of the half-tribe of Manasseh that settled east of the Jordan. He appears once, in 1 Chr 5:24, in a list of seven heads of their fathers' houses, described together as mighty men of valour and famous men. The surrounding passage places these clans in the land from Bashan to Baal-hermon and Mount Hermon, and goes on to tell how the eastern tribes were later carried into exile by the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser. The text does not say exactly when Hodaviah lived. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 720 BC, near the time of that exile, while the STEPBible names index places him in the time of King David. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "praise ye the LORD." Several other men in the Bible share this name and should not be confused with him.

Hodaviah was a Benjamite named in the genealogy of Sallu, one of the Benjamites listed as living in Jerusalem. He was the son of Hasenuah and the father of Meshullam, which made him Sallu's grandfather (1 Chr 9:7). The surrounding list in 1 Chronicles 9 records those who resettled in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile, so Hodaviah probably lived some generations before that return. The STEPBible proper-names index places him among the Benjamite families of post-exilic Jerusalem. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary renders "praise ye Jehovah," is shared by several other men in the Bible, and this Hodaviah should not be confused with them. A similar Benjamite genealogy in Neh 11:7 traces Sallu through different ancestors, and it is uncertain how the two lists relate.

Hodesh was a wife of Shaharaim, a man named in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin. She appears only once, in 1 Chr 8:9, which lists her sons Jobab, Zibia, Mesha and Malcham. The next verse, 1 Chr 8:10, continues the list with Jeuz, Shachia and Mirma, so she is counted as the mother of seven sons. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 8:8) says Shaharaim had children in the country of Moab after sending away his wives Hushim and Baara. By inference from that context, Hodesh was probably a later wife and her sons were born in Moab. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of her name as "new moon," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "a table; news." Nothing else is recorded about her.

Hodevah was a Levite whose descendants were among the Levites who returned from exile in Babylon. In the list of returnees, his descendants are counted together with those of Jeshua and Kadmiel, seventy-four in all (Neh 7:43). The parallel list in Ezra 2:40 spells his name Hodaviah, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a further reading, Hodeiah, treating these as minor variations of the same name. Ezra 3:9 names the "sons of Judah" alongside Jeshua and Kadmiel as overseeing the workmen rebuilding the house of God. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies this Judah with Hodaviah, since the two names have nearly the same meaning, "praise." Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Levite who seems to have given his name to an important family. The return is usually dated to about 538 BC, an estimate drawn from context.

Hodiah was a woman of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:19 as the sister of Naham. Her sons were the ancestors of two clans: the father of Keilah the Garmite, and Eshtemoa the Maachathite. The Hebrew of this passage is difficult, and the verse says only "his wife" without naming the husband. This entry takes him to be Mered, who in the previous verse is married to Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh. On that reading Hodiah would be his other, Judahite wife. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies her husband as Ezra (Ezrah) of Judah and takes her to be the same woman as Jehudijah in verse 18. The STEPBible names list gives her husband as Ishbah. Her name is usually understood to mean "majesty of the Lord."

Hodijah was a Levite in Jerusalem in the time of Ezra and Nehemiah. He was one of the Levites who helped the people understand the law when Ezra read it publicly, while the people stood in their places (Neh 8:7). He was also among the Levites who led the people in worship, calling them to stand up and bless the LORD (Neh 9:5). A Levite named Hodijah appears among those who set their seal to the covenant (Neh 10:10), and Smith's Bible Dictionary takes this to be probably the same man. The name is shared by several people in the Bible, and another Levite and a leader of the people with this name appear in the same covenant list, so how many individuals these verses refer to is not certain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "majesty of Jehovah."

Hodijah was a man who set his seal to the covenant made under Nehemiah, in which the returned exiles pledged to keep the Law of God (Neh 10:13). His name falls in the section of the list that names the Levites, which begins at Neh 10:9, before the list of the chiefs of the people at Neh 10:14. By that placement Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him as a Levite. STEPBible's proper-names index describes him as one of the leaders who signed the covenant. The name appears more than once in this period, including another Hodijah earlier in the same Levite list (Neh 10:10), so it is uncertain whether he is the same person as any other Hodijah. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "majesty of Jehovah." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hodijah was one of the leaders who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's day to keep the law of God (Neh 10:18). His name appears in the section of the list that begins at Neh 10:14 with the "chief of the people." By inference from the passage, he was a lay leader, which is how Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him a Levite, and the STEPBible names index places him among the priests. This entry follows the reading of him as one of the heads of the people. The same covenant list names a Levite or Levites called Hodijah earlier (Neh 10:10, 13), and the name is shared by several people in the Bible, so it is uncertain how he relates to them. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hoglah was one of the five daughters of Zelophehad, a descendant of Manasseh son of Joseph through Machir, Gilead and Hepher. Her sisters were Mahlah, Noah, Milcah and Tirzah. In most lists she is named third (Num 26:33; Josh 17:3). Because their father died without sons, the sisters came before Moses to ask for a share of his land (Num 27:1). The surrounding passage records that their request was granted, and Joshua 17 records that they later received land among the families of Manasseh. Under a further ruling, the sisters married their father's brothers' sons, so the inheritance stayed within their tribe (Num 36:11). Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take her name to mean "partridge." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "his festival or dance."

Hoham was the king of Hebron at the time of Israel's conquest of Canaan under Joshua. Adonizedek, king of Jerusalem, sent to him and to the kings of Jarmuth, Lachish and Eglon, calling them to join an attack on Gibeon, which had made peace with Joshua (Josh 10:3). The surrounding chapter describes these five as Amorite kings. Their alliance was defeated, and the kings hid in a cave at Makkedah, where they were afterwards captured and put to death. Hoham is not named again, but he is presumably among those five kings. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of his name as "Jehovah impels." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the same meaning with a question mark, and Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "woe to them."

Holon was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed among the cities given to the tribe of Judah in a group with Goshen and Giloh (Josh 15:51). It was later assigned with its surrounding pasturelands to the Levites, the descendants of Aaron, and is named alongside Debir (Josh 21:15). The parallel list of Levitical towns in 1 Chr 6:58 gives the name as Hilen, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary take to be the same place. Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the ruins of Beit 'Alam, northwest of Hebron, and the location shown here is in that area. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "sandy." The name Holon is also used of a different town in Moab (Jer 48:21), which should not be confused with this one.

Holon was a town of Moab on the "plain country," the high tableland east of the Dead Sea. It appears only in Jeremiah's oracle against Moab, where it is named with Jahazah and Mephaath as places on which judgment has come (Jer 48:21). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it was probably once an important town of that plateau. Its site is unknown, and Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that no identification had been made. The location shown here is only a rough placement on the Moabite plateau, near the other towns listed with it. The name is shared with a different Holon, a town in the hill country of Judah given to the Levites (Josh 15:51; 21:15), which should not be confused with this Moabite town.

The Holy Place is the term used for the sacred space of the tabernacle, the portable sanctuary Israel carried through the wilderness, so it had no fixed location. In Exod 26:33 it names the outer room, separated by a veil from the "most holy" room containing the ark. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes this room as holding the golden lampstand, the table of showbread and the incense altar. Aaron and his sons served there in special garments, and incense and service cloths were made for it (Exod 28:29, 28:43; Exod 31:11; Exod 39:1). In Lev 16, the instructions for the Day of Atonement, the same term refers to the area "within the vail before the mercy seat," which the high priest entered only with prescribed offerings to make atonement (Lev 16:2–3, 16:16). In other passages it apparently means the holy precincts more generally (Lev 16:24; Num 28:7), so its exact reference depends on context.

The Holy Place was the outer room of Israel's sanctuary, lying in front of the inner sanctuary, called the "oracle" or Most Holy Place. Heb 9:2 describes the tabernacle's first room as holding the lampstand, the table and the showbread. In Solomon's temple in Jerusalem, the ends of the ark's carrying poles could be seen from the Holy Place when the ark was installed, and the cloud filled the house as the priests came out (1 Kgs 8:8–10; 2 Chr 5:9–11). Hezekiah ordered the Levites to clear filth from it after its lamps and incense had been neglected (2 Chr 29:5–7). Ezekiel's temple vision uses the term for the sanctuary and nearby priestly areas (Ezek 42:14; 45:4). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the tabernacle's Holy Place as 20 cubits long and says it held the golden incense altar. The term applies to more than one sanctuary. The location shown here is the temple site in Jerusalem.

The Holy Spirit, also called the Spirit of God, the Spirit of the LORD, the Holy Ghost and the Comforter, is God's Spirit as presented throughout the Bible. He moves over the waters at creation (Gen 1:2), comes upon judges such as Othniel, speaks through prophets and David, and carries prophets from place to place (Judg 3:10; 2 Sam 23:2; 1 Kgs 18:12). In the Gospels Mary conceives Jesus by the Holy Ghost, and the Spirit descends on Jesus like a dove (Matt 1:18; John 1:32). Jesus promises the Spirit to his disciples, who receive him at Pentecost. In Acts he guides their preaching and missions. The epistles describe the Spirit as given to believers and dwelling in them (Rom 5:5; 2 Tim 1:14). Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him the third Person of the Trinity. "Comforter" translates the Greek parakletos, which Smith's Bible Dictionary explains as an advocate, helper or strengthener.

The Holy Week is the final eight days of Jesus' life in and around Jerusalem, told in all four Gospels. It runs from his entry into the city to his resurrection, about AD 30 by inference from context. It begins after Mary anoints him. Jesus approaches from Bethphage on the Mount of Olives and rides into Jerusalem on a young donkey. He drives the traders and moneychangers out of the temple, tells parables against the religious leaders, and answers their questions about tribute to Caesar. He predicts the temple's destruction, teaches about the end of the age, and shares a last meal with his disciples, where he foretells his betrayal and Peter's denial. He is arrested and questioned by the high priest, then tried before Pilate, who wants to release him. He is crucified and buried by Joseph of Arimathaea. Early on the first day of the week, women find the tomb empty.

Homam was a son of Lotan and a brother of Hori, listed among the Horites, the people of Seir, in the genealogies of Edom. He appears only in these lists. 1 Chr 1:39 spells his name Homam, while the parallel list in Gen 36:22 gives it as Hemam. Both verses add that Lotan's sister was Timna, so Timna was Homam's aunt. Lotan is named in the same chapter (Gen 36:20) as a son of Seir the Horite, which makes Homam a grandson of Seir. These Horite clans lived in the land of Seir alongside Esau's descendants, which is why they appear in the Edomite records. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "destruction" or "exterminating." Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "making an uproar."

Hophni was one of the two sons of Eli, the priest at Shiloh, and the brother of Phinehas. Both brothers served as priests of the Lord at the sanctuary there (1 Sam 1:3). The surrounding chapter of 1 Samuel describes the brothers as worthless men who abused their office by seizing sacrificial meat and behaving immorally (1 Sam 2:12–17, 22). A man of God then announced judgment on Eli's house, and as a sign of it Hophni and Phinehas would both die on the same day (1 Sam 2:34). When Israel was fighting the Philistines, the ark of the covenant was brought from Shiloh to the camp, and the two brothers went with it (1 Sam 4:4). In the battle that followed the ark was captured and both of them were killed. A messenger brought the news to Eli (1 Sam 4:11, 17). Easton's Bible Dictionary places this battle at Aphek and gives the meaning of the name as "pugilist" or "client."

Hor-haggidgad was a campsite of the Israelites during their wilderness journey. The itinerary in Numbers places it between Bene-jaakan and Jotbathah: the people moved there from Bene-jaakan and went on from it to Jotbathah (Num 33:32–33). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and the Tyndale House STEPBible names list both identify it with Gudgodah in Deut 10:7, where the same sequence of places appears in a different order. The site has not been securely identified. The location shown here is only approximate. It places the camp in the Arabah region south of the Dead Sea, in present-day southern Jordan, which fits its position in the itinerary before Ezion-geber.

Horam was the king of Gezer at the time of Israel's conquest of Canaan under Joshua. When Joshua attacked the city of Lachish, Horam came up with his forces to help defend it. Joshua defeated him and his people, leaving none of them remaining (Josh 10:33). He is mentioned only in this verse, within the account of Joshua's campaign against the cities of southern Canaan. Gezer itself is not said to have been taken at this point, and by inference from the passage Horam fought away from his own city. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "height," and Smith's Bible Dictionary as "mountainous."

Horeb is the mountain called "the mountain of God," where Moses came while tending Jethro's flock (Exod 3:1) and where the Israelites camped during the Wilderness Wanderings. There God made a covenant with Israel, spoke to the people out of the fire, and gave the law that Moses placed in the ark as two stone tablets (Deut 5:2; Deut 4:15; 1 Kgs 8:9). There the people also made and worshipped a golden calf (Ps 106:19). Near Horeb Moses struck a rock to bring out water (Exod 17:6). It lay eleven days' journey from Kadesh-barnea by way of Mount Seir (Deut 1:2). Later the prophet Elijah traveled forty days to reach it (1 Kgs 19:8). Horeb is generally treated as another name for Sinai. Easton's Bible Dictionary sees it as the whole range of which Sinai was one peak. Several sites have been proposed. The location shown here follows the traditional identification with Jebel Musa in southern Sinai.

Horem was a city in the territory allotted to the tribe of Naphtali, named in Josh 19:38 alongside Iron, Migdalel, Bethanath and Bethshemesh. It is one of the nineteen cities with their villages that close the list of Naphtali's towns. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe it as one of Naphtali's fortified or 'fenced' cities, and both give the name's meaning as 'consecrated.' The Bible records nothing else about it. Its exact site is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary, citing the explorer Van de Velde, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggest the modern Hurah, a mound at the south end of Wadi el-Ain, west of Kedesh in upper Galilee. The location shown here, in upper Galilee west of Kedesh, corresponds to that suggestion.

Horesh was a place in the wilderness of Ziph in Judah where David hid while Saul was hunting him. There Saul's son Jonathan came to David, encouraged him, and the two made a covenant before the LORD before Jonathan returned home (1 Sam 23:15–18). The Ziphites then reported to Saul at Gibeah that David was hiding in strongholds there, near the hill of Hachilah south of Jeshimon (1 Sam 23:19). The King James Version does not treat the Hebrew word as a name and translates it "in the wood." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same word means "forest" elsewhere and favors that reading, while the Septuagint renders it "in the New." This entry treats Horesh as a place name, as STEPBible's proper-name index does. The location shown here, south of Hebron near Ziph, probably matches the ruin Khirbet Khoreisa, which is often identified with Horesh.

Hori was a son of Lotan and a grandson of Seir the Horite, among the early inhabitants of the land of Seir before the Edomites. His brother is called Hemam in Gen 36:22 and Homam in 1 Chr 1:39. Both lists also name Timna as Lotan's sister. In Gen 36:30 the name appears in the phrase "the dukes that came of Hori." Since the chiefs listed there (Dishon, Ezer and Dishan) are sons of Seir, that verse probably uses the name for the Horite people as a whole rather than for this individual. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "cave-dweller," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a prince; freeborn." Nothing else is recorded about him. Several people in the Bible share this name.

Hori was a man of the tribe of Simeon, known only as the father of Shaphat. Shaphat was the Simeonite chosen as one of the twelve men Moses sent from the wilderness to explore the land of Canaan (Num 13:5). Nothing else is recorded about Hori himself. He is mentioned only to identify his son, in the way the other spies are named with their fathers. He lived during the wilderness period of Israel's history. Several people in the Bible share this name, and this entry concerns the Simeonite. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the name's meaning as "cave-dweller," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a prince" or "freeborn."

Hormah was a Canaanite town in the far south of Canaan, earlier called Zephath (Judg 1:17). Its name is usually explained as meaning "devoted to destruction" or "banned" (Easton's Bible Dictionary). Israelites who tried to enter the land against Moses' warning were driven back as far as Hormah by Amalekites, Canaanites and Amorites (Num 14:45; Deut 1:44). Israel later destroyed the Canaanite cities there and named the place Hormah (Num 21:3). Judges 1:17 credits Judah and Simeon with destroying Zephath. Its king is listed among the kings Joshua defeated, next to the king of Arad (Josh 12:14). The town was assigned to Judah and also to Simeon (Josh 15:30; 19:4; 1 Chr 4:30), and David sent it a share of spoil (1 Sam 30:30). Its site is uncertain, and some place it nearer Arad. The location shown here follows the identification with Zephath at Sebaiteh (modern Shivta), favored by Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia.

Horonaim was a city of Moab named only in the prophecies of Isaiah and Jeremiah against Moab. It appears with Zoar, Luhith, Heshbon, Elealeh and Jahaz as a place where cries of destruction would be heard as Moab's people fled (Isa 15:5; Jer 48:3, 34). The texts speak of "the way of Horonaim" and "the going down of Horonaim" (Jer 48:5), which suggests it lay on a road descending from the Moabite plateau toward the Dead Sea and the Arabah. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it south of the Arnon on raised ground, and the name is usually explained as "two caverns" or "two hollows." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the site as unidentified but notes a proposal linking it to ruins near Wadi Kerak. The location shown here, near the eastern side of the southern Dead Sea, fits that general area.

Horse Gate was a gate in the wall of Jerusalem near the temple. During Nehemiah's rebuilding of the walls, priests repaired the section from above the Horse Gate, each working opposite his own house (Neh 3:28). This suggests the priests' homes stood close to the temple. Jeremiah mentions "the corner of the horse gate toward the east" as one of the boundaries of a restored city that would be holy to the Lord, alongside the Kidron Valley (Jer 31:40). That points to a position on the eastern side of the city. Many interpreters also link it with the "horses' entry" to the royal palace where Queen Athaliah was killed (2 Kgs 11:16; 2 Chr 23:15), though this is an inference. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it at the west end of a bridge leading from Zion to the temple. The location shown here is within Jerusalem, by the temple area.

Hosah was a Levite of the family of Merari who served as a gatekeeper ("porter" in the King James Version) in David's time. He was appointed with Obed-edom to guard the ark after David brought it to Jerusalem (1 Chr 16:38). In the later list of gatekeeper divisions, his sons are named as Simri, Hilkiah, Tebaliah and Zechariah. Simri was not the firstborn, but his father made him chief. Altogether Hosah's sons and relatives numbered thirteen. When duties were assigned by lot, Hosah and Shuppim received the west side, including the gate Shallecheth by the ascending causeway. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "trusting." A town in Asher's territory (Josh 19:29) has the same name in the King James Version but is unrelated to this man.

Hosah was a town on the boundary of the tribe of Asher, named in the description of Asher's territory in Josh 19:29. The border is traced past Ramah and the fortified city of Tyre, then turns to Hosah before running out to the sea near Achzib. This places Hosah near Tyre on the Phoenician coast. Easton's Bible Dictionary puts it a little south of Sidon. Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint reads the name as Iaseiph, which some link with Kefr Yasif northeast of Acre. It also cites the suggestion that Hosah is the Assyrian Usu, possibly the mainland settlement facing island Tyre, near Ras el-'Ain south of the city. The location shown here is a tentative placement. The same name belongs to a Levite gatekeeper in Chronicles, a different figure.

Hosea was a prophet, the son of Beeri, and the author of the book that bears his name, the first of the minor prophets. His name means "salvation." Hos 1:1 dates his ministry to the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah of Judah and Jeroboam son of Joash of Israel, roughly from about 785 BC onward, by inference from context. Smith's Bible Dictionary estimates a career of about fifty-nine years. Easton's Bible Dictionary, among others, places him in the northern kingdom of Israel, partly because of his familiarity with places in Ephraim. At the start of his prophecy the LORD told him to marry "a wife of whoredoms" as a sign of the land's unfaithfulness. His wife was Gomer, and his children Jezreel, Lo-ruhamah and Lo-ammi carried symbolic names, as the following verses of Hosea 1 relate. In Rom 9:25 Paul quotes him under the Greek form of his name, Osee.

Hoshaiah was a man who took part in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. Nehemiah organized two large thanksgiving choirs that walked in opposite directions along the top of the wall. Hoshaiah walked behind the singers of one of them, leading half of the princes of Judah in the procession (Neh 12:32). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the event to about 446 BC, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he was probably from the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name means "whom the Lord helps" or "the salvation of the Lord." The name is shared by another man in the Bible, the father of Jezaniah or Azariah in the book of Jeremiah, but nothing links the two.

Hoshaiah was the father of Jezaniah, one of the leaders of the Judeans left in the land after the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem. He is known only through his son. In Jer 42:1 Jezaniah son of Hoshaiah comes with Johanan son of Kareah and the army captains to ask Jeremiah for guidance. In Jer 43:2 it is Azariah son of Hoshaiah who joins Johanan in accusing Jeremiah of lying when the prophet warns them not to go to Egypt. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, following the Septuagint, treats Jezaniah and Azariah as probably the same man, and this entry follows that view, making Hoshaiah the father of one son known by two names. The name means "the Lord helps" or "whom the Lord saves." Several people in the Bible share this name, and nothing more is recorded about this Hoshaiah.

Hoshama was one of the sons of Jehoiachin (also called Jeconiah), the king of Judah who was taken captive to Babylon. He appears only in the royal genealogy of 1 Chr 3:17–18, where he is listed among seven sons along with Shealtiel, Malchiram, Pedaiah, Shenazar, Jecamiah and Nedabiah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the list may refer to sons or more broadly to descendants of Jeconiah. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "whom Jehovah hears." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains it as a shortened form of Jehoshama. Nothing more is recorded about his life. By inference from his father's captivity, he was probably born or raised during the exile in Babylon.

Hoshea son of Elah was the last king of the northern kingdom of Israel, not to be confused with others of the same name. He conspired against King Pekah, killed him and took his throne (2 Kgs 15:30). He reigned nine years in Samaria, beginning in the twelfth year of Ahaz of Judah, about 730 BC by inference from context (2 Kgs 17:1). When Shalmaneser king of Assyria came against him, Hoshea submitted and paid tribute. Later he sent messengers to So king of Egypt and stopped the yearly payment, so the Assyrian king imprisoned him (2 Kgs 17:3–4). Shalmaneser besieged Samaria in Hoshea's seventh year, and after three years the city fell and its people were deported to Assyria (2 Kgs 17:6; 18:9–10). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the annals of Tiglath-pileser III claim he appointed Hoshea king.

Hoshea, son of Azaziah, was the officer over the tribe of Ephraim during King David's reign. He appears only once, in the list of tribal rulers in 1 Chr 27:16–22, where each tribe of Israel is assigned a leader. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both describe him as the ruler of Ephraim in David's time. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Hoshea, which Smith's Bible Dictionary glosses as "salvation," was borne by several people in the Bible. These include Joshua son of Nun, another Ephraimite, whose original name was Hoshea, and the last king of the northern kingdom of Israel. This Hoshea should be kept distinct from them.

Hoshea was one of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, a written pledge by the returned exiles to keep the Law of God. His name appears in the list of signatories at Neh 10:23, alongside Hananiah and Hashub, and nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "salvation" and dates the covenant to about 410 BC. The same name belongs to several other people in the Bible, including the last king of the northern kingdom of Israel, the son of Nun (the earlier name of Joshua), and a tribal officer under David. This Hoshea is a separate person, known only from this list.

Hotham was a man of the tribe of Asher, a son of Heber and a brother of Japhlet, Shomer (also spelled Shamer) and their sister Shua (1 Chr 7:32). Heber was a son of Beriah, Asher's son, so Hotham was Asher's great-grandson. This entry follows the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Easton's Bible Dictionary in identifying him with Helem, named in 1 Chr 7:35 as the brother of Shamer. There his sons are listed as Zophah, Imna, Shelesh and Amal. The difference between the two names is probably a variation in how the name was copied, though the identification is an inference from the flow of the genealogy. Smith's Bible Dictionary lists the two names in separate entries. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of Hotham as "a seal." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hothan was a man from Aroer, known only as the father of Shama and Jehiel, two brothers listed among David's mighty warriors in 1 Chr 11:44. The text calls him "the Aroerite" but does not say which Aroer is meant. Towns of that name stood beside the Arnon River east of the Jordan and in the Negev of Judah, so his home cannot be fixed with certainty. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name is spelled Hotham in many modern translations. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains it as meaning "signet ring." He should not be confused with Hotham the Asherite of 1 Chr 7:32, a different man. By inference from the list in which his sons appear, he lived in the time of David, about the late eleventh or early tenth century BC.

Hothir was a Levite, one of the fourteen sons of Heman, whom 1 Chr 25:4 lists thirteenth among his brothers. Heman is called "the king's seer" in the same chapter, and Smith's Bible Dictionary therefore counts Hothir as a Kohathite Levite. He belonged to the families that David set apart for music in the house of God, playing cymbals, psalteries and harps under their fathers' direction. When the musicians were divided by lot into twenty-four groups of twelve, the twenty-first lot fell to Hothir, "he, his sons, and his brethren" (1 Chr 25:28). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "excelling" or "remaining," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "abundance." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hukkok was a town on the boundary of the tribe of Naphtali in Galilee. It appears only once, in Josh 19:34, where Naphtali's border runs west from Aznoth-tabor to Hukkok and then meets Zebulun on the south and Asher on the west. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the village of Yakuk (Yaquq), in the hills west of Wadi el-Amud and northwest of the plain of Gennesaret, about 4 miles (6 km) from the Sea of Galilee. The ISBE notes that this identification seems rather far from Tabor, but it would place the town near where Zebulun and Naphtali met. The location shown here follows the Yakuk identification. A town called Hukok in Asher (1 Chr 6:75) is probably a different place. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "engraver" or "scribe."

Hukok was a city named in 1 Chr 6:75 alongside Rehob, each given "with her suburbs" (its surrounding pasturelands). From the surrounding list, it was one of the towns in the territory of Asher assigned to the Levite family of Gershon. The parallel list of Levitical cities in Josh 21:31 names Helkath in the matching position, and Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat Hukok as another name for Helkath. Easton's Bible Dictionary instead connects it with Hukkok, a town on the border of Naphtali mentioned in Josh 19:34. Its exact site is uncertain. The location shown here places it in western Galilee, within the territory generally assigned to Asher, which fits its listing among Asher's towns.

Hul was the second of the four sons of Aram and a grandson of Shem, named in the Table of Nations alongside his brothers Uz, Gether and Mash (Gen 10:23). The parallel genealogy in 1 Chr 1:17 lists the same names directly after Shem's sons, with Mash appearing as Meshech. By comparison with Genesis, this is probably a shortened form of the list in which Aram's sons follow straight on. Nothing is recorded of Hul as an individual. As with others in the Table of Nations, his name likely also stands for a people descended from him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls that people uncertain in identity and location, while Smith's Bible Dictionary favors the district near the foot of the Lebanon mountains. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "circle," and Hitchcock's Bible Names as "pain" or "infirmity."

Huldah was a prophetess who lived in Jerusalem during the reign of King Josiah. She was the wife of Shallum, keeper of the wardrobe, whose ancestry is given as son of Tikvah, son of Harhas in 2 Kgs 22:14, and as son of Tikvath, son of Hasrah in 2 Chr 34:22. The priest Hilkiah and other officials sent by the king, including Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan and Asahiah, went to consult her. The surrounding chapters show that this was about the book of the law recently found in the temple. She lived in the part of the city the King James Version calls "the college". Easton's Bible Dictionary explains this as the Mishneh, or "second quarter", possibly a district between the inner and outer walls, though its exact location is unknown. Easton's gives the meaning of her name as "weasel". Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the consultation to about 623 BC.

Humtah was a town in the hill country of Judah, named only once in the Bible, in the list of cities allotted to the tribe of Judah (Josh 15:54). It appears in a group of nine towns with their villages that includes Hebron (also called Kirjath-arba) and Zior. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "place of lizards" and notes that Humtah is listed next to Hebron. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it comes between Aphekah and Hebron in the list. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the hills near Hebron, inferred from its position in the town list.

Huppah was a priest in the time of King David. He is named only once, in the list of the twenty-four divisions of priests who took turns serving at the sanctuary. When David organized the priesthood, the lot assigned the thirteenth turn to Huppah (1 Chr 24:13). From the surrounding passage, the divisions were drawn from the descendants of Eleazar and Ithamar, the sons of Aaron. Huppah was probably the head of a priestly family, and his name stood for the course that served in that position. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both give the meaning of his name as "protection." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Huppim was a son of Ir, named with his brother Shuppim in 1 Chr 7:12. Their sister Maachah married Machir, the son of Manasseh (1 Chr 7:15), so the family was linked by marriage to the tribe of Manasseh. The verse naming him sits at the end of a list of Benjamin's descendants, and Ir is probably the same as Iri, a grandson of Benjamin named a few verses earlier (1 Chr 7:7). A Huppim also appears among Benjamin's sons in Gen 46:21, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name is probably a variant of Hupham, whose family is listed in Num 26:39. The same encyclopedia notes that his exact line of descent is hard to establish, and the STEPBible name index places him either as a descendant of Ir or as a son of Machir. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as "a chamber covered" or "the sea-shore."

Hur was a man of the tribe of Judah who assisted Moses during the wilderness journey. In Israel's battle with Amalek he climbed the hill with Moses and Aaron, and when Moses' hands grew heavy, Aaron and Hur held them up on either side until sunset (Exod 17:10–12). When Moses went up Mount Sinai, he left Aaron and Hur with the elders to settle any disputes (Exod 24:14). Through his son Uri, Hur was the grandfather of Bezalel, the craftsman who made the tabernacle and its bronze altar. Chronicles names him as the firstborn son of Caleb and Ephratah and calls him 'the father of Bethlehem.' His descendants included Shobal, founder of Kirjath-jearim. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats Moses' helper and Bezalel's grandfather as possibly two men. This entry follows Josephus, who identifies them as one man and makes him the husband of Miriam, Moses' sister, a view Easton's Bible Dictionary also gives.

Hur was one of five kings of Midian killed by the Israelites in the time of Moses, along with Evi, Rekem, Zur and Reba. Balaam son of Beor was killed in the same campaign (Num 31:8). The surrounding chapter presents this war as Israel's revenge on Midian for the events at Peor, and Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that Phinehas led the Israelite force. Joshua 13:21 lists the same five men as princes of Midian and as "dukes of Sihon," the Amorite king who ruled from Heshbon, so they were apparently local rulers subordinate to or allied with Sihon. They lived in the land later given to the tribe of Reuben. Several other men in the Bible are named Hur, including the companion of Moses and Aaron, and this Midianite ruler should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "liberty," "whiteness" or "hole."

Hur was the father of one of the twelve district officers King Solomon appointed over Israel to supply food for the royal household. He is known only through his son, who is listed in 1 Kgs 4:8 simply as "the son of Hur" (in Hebrew, Ben-hur) and who served in the hill country of Ephraim. Nothing else is recorded about Hur himself. The name is shared by several other people in the Bible, including the Hur who helped Aaron hold up Moses' hands during the battle with Amalek. There is no indication that this Hur is the same man as any of them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "liberty," "whiteness" or "hole."

Hur was the father of Rephaiah, who repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall when the city was rebuilt under Nehemiah, probably in the mid-400s BC by inference from context. He is known only from Neh 3:9, which names him solely to identify his son. The verse calls someone "the ruler of the half part of Jerusalem," meaning half of the district around the city. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes this title to belong to Rephaiah, which fits the pattern of other district rulers named as builders in the same chapter. STEPBible's Tyndale House name list applies it to Hur himself. This entry follows the reading that Rephaiah was the ruler. Nothing else is recorded about Hur, and he should not be confused with the other men of the same name in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "liberty," "whiteness" or "hole."

Hurai was one of David's mighty men, the elite group of warriors listed in 1 Chr 11:32. He is described as being "of the brooks of Gaash," probably meaning the ravines or valleys near Mount Gaash in the hill country of Ephraim, where Joshua was later buried. The parallel list in 2 Sam 23:30 gives his name as Hiddai, and the two forms are generally taken to refer to the same man. The difference probably comes from a copying variation, since the Hebrew letters involved look alike. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explain the name Hurai as meaning "linen-worker" or "linen-weaver." Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in these two lists.

Huram was a member of the tribe of Benjamin who appears in the tribal genealogies, and this entry treats him as the same man called Huppim and Hupham. Genesis lists Huppim among the sons of Benjamin who went down to Egypt with Jacob (Gen 46:21). Numbers names Hupham as the founder of the clan of the Huphamites, listed next to Shupham and the Shuphamites (Num 26:39). In 1 Chr 8:5 Huram appears beside Shephuphan (probably Shupham) in a list that places him among the sons of Bela, Benjamin's firstborn, which would make him Benjamin's grandson. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe Huram as Bela's son. The STEPBible proper names index (Tyndale House) takes Huppim, Hupham and Huram as one descendant of Benjamin, and this entry follows that view. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that his exact line of descent is hard to establish. Several other men in the Bible share the name Huram.

Huram appears only in the phrase "Huram my father's" in 2 Chr 2:13, part of the letter King Huram (Hiram) of Tyre sent to Solomon. There the king says he is sending a skilled craftsman to help build the temple. Read this way, the phrase names the king's own father, also called Huram, as the craftsman's former master, and this entry follows that reading, treating him as the father of Hiram. Nothing else is said about him. The wording is ambiguous, though, and many translations take "Huram my father" (Huram-abi) as the name or title of the craftsman himself. In that case it would not refer to a separate person at all, and the same expression is used of the craftsman in 2 Chr 4:16. Several people in the Bible share the name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "their liberty" or "their whiteness."

Huri was a man of the tribe of Gad, named only once in the Bible, in the Gadite genealogy of 1 Chr 5:14. He was the son of Jaroah and the father of Abihail, whose descendants are listed among the Gadite families living in Gilead and Bashan east of the Jordan. His line is traced back through Jaroah, Gilead, Michael, Jeshishai and Jahdo to Buz. The verse records nothing else about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both give the meaning of his name as "linen weaver." Hitchcock's Bible Names instead suggests "being angry," or links it with the name Huram.

Hushai the Archite was a loyal friend of King David, called "the king's companion" in 1 Chr 27:33. When David fled Jerusalem during Absalom's rebellion, Hushai met him at the top of the Mount of Olives with his coat torn and earth on his head, a sign of mourning. He then returned to the city as Absalom arrived and greeted Absalom as king, claiming loyalty to whoever the LORD and Israel chose. Asked to weigh in after Ahithophel had given his advice, Hushai argued that David and his men were dangerous fighters and that Ahithophel's plan was unwise. Absalom and the men of Israel preferred Hushai's counsel, and he passed both plans to the priests Zadok and Abiathar. "Archite" probably refers to the Archites, a clan or place on the border of Benjamin (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Baanah, one of Solomon's district officers, was probably his son.

Husham was one of the early kings of Edom, listed among the rulers who reigned there before Israel had a king (the list in Gen 36 opens with that note). He came from the land of Teman, or the Temanites, a region of Edom named after Teman, a grandson of Esau. He succeeded Jobab, and when he died he was followed by Hadad son of Bedad, who defeated Midian in the country of Moab and ruled from the city of Avith (Gen 36:34–35; 1 Chr 1:45–46). The list never says Husham was his predecessor's son, so the kingship apparently did not pass from father to son. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "alert."

Hushim was the son of Dan and the only son listed for him among the family members of Jacob who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:23). In the census of the tribes taken in the wilderness he is called Shuham, and his descendants, the Shuhamites, make up the whole of the tribe of Dan's listed families (Num 26:42). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the form Hushim is plural, as though it named a clan rather than a single person, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia likewise treats it as a family name. This entry follows the view that Hushim and Shuham are the same individual, the ancestor of the Danite clan. The name Hushim is also borne by other people in the Bible, including a Benjamite and a wife of Shaharaim, who should not be confused with this son of Dan.

Hushim was a son of Aher, named only in 1 Chr 7:12 in a short list that also mentions Shuppim and Huppim. The verse calls him "the sons of Aher," so Smith's Bible Dictionary notes the name may be plural and may refer to a family group rather than one person. Views differ on his tribe.
