The verse sits within Benjamin's genealogy, and Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat him as a Benjamite. Tyndale House's STEPBible names place him in the line of Dan. That view connects him with Gen 46:23, where Hushim is Dan's son, and it would account for Dan otherwise being missing from this chapter. This entry follows the Danite reading. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is also borne by others, including a wife of Shaharaim (1 Chr 8:8).

Hushim was one of the two wives of Shaharaim, a man listed in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin. The other wife was Baara. According to 1 Chr 8:8, Shaharaim had children in the country of Moab after he had "sent them away." This is usually read to mean that he divorced or dismissed Hushim and Baara, which suggests that Hushim's children were born before that separation. By Shaharaim, Hushim had two sons, Abitub and Elpaal. The verses that follow (1 Chr 8:12–18) trace Elpaal's descendants, among them the builders of Ono and Lod. The name Hushim is shared by other people in the Bible, including a son of Dan (Gen 46:23) and a Benjamite listed in 1 Chr 7:12. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as meaning "hasters."

Huz was the firstborn son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and his wife Milcah. He is named first in the list of Nahor's sons that was reported to Abraham after the binding of Isaac (Gen 22:21). His full brothers were Buz, Kemuel, Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph and Bethuel, the father of Rebekah. Nahor also had sons by his concubine Reumah. Nothing more is recorded about Huz himself. In Hebrew his name is the same as Uz, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats him under that name. STEPBible's proper-name index describes him as an Aramean, which fits his family's links to Aram. Some readers connect his name with the land of Uz, the homeland of Job, but the text does not draw that link. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 1900 BC, an estimate based on context.

Hymenaeus was a man named twice in Paul's letters to Timothy as someone who had turned away from the faith. In 1 Tim 1:20 he is grouped with Alexander among those who had "made shipwreck" of their faith, and Paul says he has "delivered" both "unto Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme." In 2 Tim 2:17 he is paired with Philetus as a teacher whose words spread "as doth a canker." The next verse says they claimed that the resurrection had already happened and were overturning the faith of some. Most readers, including the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, take both passages to refer to the same man. Because Timothy was working in Ephesus, that work places him there by inference. The name comes from Hymen, the Greek god of marriage, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes.

Ibhar was one of the sons born to David in Jerusalem, after David moved his capital there from Hebron. He appears only in the three lists of those sons (2 Sam 5:15; 1 Chr 3:6; 1 Chr 14:5), and in each list his name comes soon after Solomon's. 1 Chronicles 3 distinguishes these Jerusalem-born sons from the children of David's concubines, so Ibhar was probably the son of one of David's wives, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. His mother is not named, and nothing else is recorded about his life. His name means "he chooses" or "chosen," usually understood as "God chooses" (Easton's Bible Dictionary; Hitchcock's Bible Names). As a son of David he belonged to the tribe of Judah.

Ibleam was a Canaanite city with its surrounding towns, lying within the territory of Issachar or Asher but assigned to the tribe of Manasseh (Josh 17:11). Manasseh did not drive out its inhabitants, and the Canaanites went on living there (Judg 1:27). Ibleam later appears in Jehu's revolt. When Jehu killed King Joram of Israel, King Ahaziah of Judah fled and was struck in his chariot "at the going up to Gur, which is by Ibleam." He escaped to Megiddo and died there (2 Kgs 9:27). The name probably also appears as Bileam in 1 Chr 6:70. The site lay near modern Jenin, but identifications differ. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests Jelamah, north of Jenin. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it at the ruin of Bel'ameh, just south of Jenin. The location shown here follows the Bel'ameh identification.

Ibneiah, son of Jeroham, was a man of the tribe of Benjamin. He is named in 1 Chr 9:8 in a list of Benjamites living in Jerusalem. By inference from the context of 1 Chronicles 9, which describes those who settled in the city after the return from the Babylonian exile, he was among the resettled inhabitants of Jerusalem. The STEPBible proper-names index reads the passage this way. He appears in the same verse as Elah son of Uzzi and Meshullam son of Shephathiah. His name means roughly "the LORD builds up" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives his father's name as Jehoram, a variant of Jeroham. He should not be confused with Ibnijah, a similar name in the same verse belonging to an ancestor of Meshullam. Nothing further is recorded about him.

Ibnijah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only in the genealogy at 1 Chr 9:8. He was the father of Reuel, and through him the great-grandfather of Meshullam son of Shephathiah. Meshullam appears among the Benjamites listed as living in Jerusalem, a list that the surrounding chapter connects with the return after the Babylonian exile. Ibnijah himself is named only as an ancestor, so he probably lived some generations before that resettlement, although the STEPBible Proper Names index counts him among the returning Israelites. The same verse names a different man, Ibneiah son of Jeroham, whose name is spelled very similarly in Hebrew. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of Ibnijah's name as "Yah builds up." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Ibri was a Levite of the clan of Merari, named as a son of Jaaziah in the list of Levite families in 1 Chr 24:27. His brothers there are Beno, Shoham and Zaccur. The list belongs to the arrangement of the Levites for temple service in the last years of David's reign, so by inference Ibri's family belonged to that period. The verse itself is difficult. Its phrase "by Jaaziah" may mean that these men were descendants of Merari through Jaaziah rather than his own sons. Nothing more is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "a Hebrew." Hitchcock's Bible Names suggests "passing over" or "being angry."

Ibzan was a judge of Israel from Bethlehem who succeeded Jephthah, as the context of Judg 12:7 indicates, and was buried in his hometown when he died. Judg 12:9 adds that he had thirty sons and thirty daughters, arranged marriages for all of them with people from outside his clan or town, and judged Israel for seven years. His judgeship is placed at about 1146 BC, by inference from context. Easton's Bible Dictionary counts him as the tenth judge and gives his name the meaning "illustrious." Which Bethlehem was his home is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it to be Bethlehem of Zebulun, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the text does not say whether it was that town or Bethlehem of Judah. Jewish tradition in the Talmud identifies Ibzan with Boaz of Bethlehem in Judah. After Ibzan, Elon judged Israel (Judg 12:11).

Ichabod was a son of Phinehas and a grandson of Eli, the priest at Shiloh. He was a brother of Ahitub. His only mention in the verses supplied here is in 1 Sam 14:3, where he identifies Ahiah, who wore the ephod in Saul's camp. Ahiah was the son of Ahitub and so Ichabod's nephew. The fuller account of his birth is in 1 Sam 4:19–22. His mother went into labour when she heard that the ark of God had been captured by the Philistines and that her husband and father-in-law were dead. She named the child as she was dying, saying the glory had departed from Israel. The name is usually explained as meaning "no glory" or "inglorious" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Hitchcock's Bible Names also gives "where is the glory?" Nothing else is recorded of his life.

Iconium was a city in south-central Asia Minor, modern Konya in Turkey, where Paul and Barnabas preached on the first missionary journey. They came there after being driven out of Antioch in Pisidia (Acts 13:51). In the synagogue at Iconium, a great number of Jews and Greeks believed (Acts 14:1). Opposition then forced the missionaries on to Lystra, and Jews from Antioch and Iconium followed them there and stirred up a crowd that stoned Paul (Acts 14:19). Paul and Barnabas later returned through Iconium to strengthen the believers (Acts 14:21). Timothy was well spoken of by the believers there (Acts 16:2), and 2 Tim 3:11 recalls Paul's sufferings in the city. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls it the capital of Lycaonia. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some ancient writers counted it as Phrygian and places it in the Roman province of Galatia.

Idalah was a city in the territory of the tribe of Zebulun. It appears only once, in the list of Zebulun's towns in Josh 19:15, where it is named between Shimron and Bethlehem (the Bethlehem of Galilee, not the Bethlehem of Judah). Nothing else is recorded about it. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it near Zebulun's western border and identifies it with the modern Jeida in the Kishon valley. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Jerusalem Talmud equates it with a place called Churyeh, which the surveyor Conder linked to Khirbet el-Huwwara, south of Beit Lahm (Galilean Bethlehem). Both proposals lie in the same general area of the lower Galilee hills, and the location shown here is a point in that region. The meaning of the name is unclear and has been explained in different ways.

Idbash was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy at 1 Chr 4:3. He is listed with Jezreel and Ishma, and with their sister Hazelelponi, as children of "the father of Etam." Etam was probably a town near Bethlehem, so "father" likely means founder or leader of its settlement. This entry identifies that father as Hur. That is an inference from the surrounding genealogy, where Hur is called "the father of Bethlehem" (1 Chr 4:4) and his other sons, such as Shobal, Salma and Hareph, appear in 1 Chr 2:50–51. On that reading his brothers also include Penuel, Ezer and Uri. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint reads "sons of Etam." The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "stout," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "flowing with honey." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Iddo was the father of Ahinadab, one of the twelve officers King Solomon appointed to supply food for the royal household, each for one month of the year. Ahinadab was responsible for the district of Mahanaim, a town east of the Jordan in Gilead (1 Kgs 4:14). Nothing else is recorded about Iddo himself, and he is mentioned only as Ahinadab's father. Several other men in the Bible share the name Iddo, and there is no clear basis for linking this one with any of them. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "timely." Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia spell the son's name "Abinadab" rather than the "Ahinadab" found in the King James text.

Iddo was the son of Zechariah and the leader of the half tribe of Manasseh in Gilead, the part of the tribe settled east of the Jordan River. He is named once, in a list of the officers over the tribes of Israel during King David's reign (1 Chr 27:21). The surrounding chapter shows these men served as tribal heads in David's administration, and Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his time to about 1014 BC, an estimate drawn from the setting. Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "lovely," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "beloved." Several other men in the Bible share the name Iddo, and this one should not be confused with them.

Iddo was a seer and prophet in Judah whose writings the Chronicler names as sources for the reigns of Solomon, Rehoboam and Abijah. His "visions" against Jeroboam son of Nebat are listed with the works of Nathan and Ahijah as records of Solomon's acts (2 Chr 9:29). A work of Iddo the seer "concerning genealogies" is cited, along with the book of Shemaiah, for Rehoboam's reign (2 Chr 12:15). The "story" of the prophet Iddo is given as the record of Abijah's ways and sayings (2 Chr 13:22). None of these writings has survived, and nothing else is told of his life. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that he has been identified with Oded, the father of the prophet Azariah. Several other men in the Bible share the name Iddo.

Iddo was the grandfather of the prophet Zechariah, through his son Berechiah (Zech 1:1, 7). He is one of several men in the Bible with this name. Ezra twice calls Zechariah "the son of Iddo" (Ezra 5:1; 6:14). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Ezra treats Iddo as Zechariah's father, while Zechariah names him as grandfather. Probably Ezra uses "son" in the broader sense of descendant, or names the better-known ancestor. In the King James wording of Zech 1:1 and 1:7, the title "the prophet" sits beside Iddo's name, though it may instead refer to Zechariah. Nehemiah 12:4 and 12:16 list an Iddo among the priests who returned from exile with Zerubbabel, with a Zechariah later heading his family. By inference this is the same man, which fits the STEPBible description of him as a priest in post-exilic Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "timely" or "lovely."

Iddo was the chief, or leader, of a community at a place called Casiphia in Babylonia during Ezra's return to Jerusalem. When Ezra found no Levites among the people gathered to travel with him, he sent messengers to Iddo and his brethren with instructions to ask them to send ministers to serve in the temple (Ezra 8:17). The following verses report that Levites and temple servants (Nethinim) came in response (Ezra 8:18–20). The wording of the verse is read in two ways. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Iddo himself to be one of the Nethinim. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that an "and" may have dropped out, so that the message went to "his brethren and the Nethinim," and it notes that 1 Esdras calls him Loddeus. Several other people in the Bible share the name Iddo, and this one is mentioned only here. The exact location of Casiphia is unknown.

Iddo was a priest named among those who returned from exile to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel and Jeshua, listed in Neh 12:4. His name later stood for a priestly family: in the next generation, in the days of the high priest Joiakim, that family was headed by Zechariah (Neh 12:16). The STEPBible proper names index likewise treats him as a returning priest whose name passed to a priestly house. Because Ezra and Zechariah call the prophet Zechariah a descendant of 'Iddo', many readers identify this family head with the prophet, though the text here does not say so. Several other men in the Bible share the name Iddo, so the exact links between them are uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of the name as 'decked' or 'adorned'.

Idumea is the Greek form of the name Edom, the land of the descendants of Esau. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the King James Version also uses "Idumea" in Isa 34:5–6 and Ezek 35:15; 36:5, where newer translations have "Edom." In the New Testament it appears once. Mark 3:8 lists it among the regions, along with Jerusalem, the land beyond the Jordan, and the area around Tyre and Sidon, from which great crowds came to Jesus after hearing about what he was doing. By New Testament times the Edomites had settled mainly in the region south of Judea, so Idumea then meant largely that southern area, as the STEPBible names index describes it. The location shown here points to the older Edomite homeland southeast of the Dead Sea, in present-day southern Jordan. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "red" or "earthy."

Igal son of Joseph was the man chosen from the tribe of Issachar to be one of the twelve spies Moses sent from the wilderness of Paran to explore Canaan (Num 13:7). Nothing else is said about him individually. The surrounding chapters show that ten of the spies brought back a discouraging report, while only Joshua and Caleb urged the people to go in. Since he is not named among those two, Igal was presumably one of the ten. His father Joseph is not the patriarch Joseph but an otherwise unknown man of Issachar. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the name to mean "he (God) redeems." Several other men in the Bible share the name Igal, so this entry is limited to the spy from Issachar.

Igal, son of Nathan of Zobah, was one of David's mighty warriors. His name appears in the list of David's champions in 2 Sam 23:36. Zobah was an Aramean kingdom north of Israel, so he was probably of Aramean origin or from a family linked to that region. The parallel list in 1 Chr 11:38 seems to name the same man as "Joel the brother of Nathan," a difference noted by the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. This entry follows the 2 Samuel reading. His name is usually taken to mean "he (God) redeems." Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with others of the same name, such as Igal the spy sent from the tribe of Issachar to explore Canaan.

Igdaliah was the father of Hanan, mentioned once in the Bible, in Jer 35:4. When Jeremiah brought the Rechabites into the temple, he took them to the chamber belonging to "the sons of Hanan, the son of Igdaliah, a man of God." The room was next to the chamber of the princes and above that of Maaseiah son of Shallum, the doorkeeper. The title "a man of God" could apply grammatically either to Hanan or to Igdaliah. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it as describing Igdaliah, as a prophet or holy man, and this entry notes that reading while recognizing the ambiguity. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as the ancestor of a group that had a chamber in the temple in Jeremiah's time, so he probably lived in or before the late seventh century BC. His name means "Yah is great."

Igeal was a man of the tribe of Judah and a son of Shemaiah, named in the genealogy of King David's royal line in 1 Chr 3:22. His brothers were Hattush, Bariah, Neariah and Shaphat. The verse says the sons of Shemaiah were "six" but names only five, a difference the text leaves unexplained. By inference from the surrounding genealogy (1 Chr 3:17–21), he belonged to the generations after Jeconiah and Zerubbabel, so he probably lived in the period after the Babylonian exile. Nothing else is recorded about him. The Revised Version spells his name Igal, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives its meaning as "God redeems." He should be kept distinct from others of a similar name, such as the spy from Issachar (Num 13:7) and one of David's mighty men (2 Sam 23:36).

Iim was a town in the far south of Judah, named once in the list of cities given to the tribe of Judah, between Baalah and Azem (Josh 15:29). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in the south of Judah, and the Tyndale House STEPBible names list places it in the Negev region, in line with the surrounding names in the list. Nothing else is recorded about it, and its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only approximate and lies east of the Jordan rather than in the Negev. A different place called Iim appears in Num 33:45 as a short form of Ije-abarim, a wilderness stopping place near Moab, and should not be confused with this town. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "heaps."

Ijon was a fortified town in the far north of Israel, in the territory of the tribe of Naphtali. It was among the cities struck by the commanders of Ben-hadad of Syria, whom King Asa of Judah had paid to attack Baasha of Israel (1 Kgs 15:20; 2 Chr 16:4). Later, in the days of Pekah king of Israel, the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser captured it along with Abel-beth-maacah, Kedesh, Hazor and the rest of Naphtali, and deported its people to Assyria (2 Kgs 15:29). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia link the name to the Merj Ayun ("meadow of springs"), a fertile plain northwest of Dan in present-day southern Lebanon. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it at el-Khiam, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Tell Dibbin at the north of the plain. The location shown here lies near el-Khiam.

Ikkesh was a man of Tekoa, a town in Judah, and the father of Ira. He is known only through his son. Ira was one of David's mighty men, listed among "the thirty" (2 Sam 23:26; 1 Chr 11:28). He also served as captain of the army division on duty in the sixth month, a division of 24,000 men (1 Chr 27:9). The label "the Tekoite" is attached to Ira's name in each passage, and it probably identifies the family as coming from Tekoa. Nothing else is recorded about Ikkesh himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "crooked," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives it as "perverse." Smith's dates him to before 1046 BC, an estimate based on his son's service under David.

Ilai was an Ahohite and one of David's mighty men, the elite warriors listed in 1 Chr 11:29. In the parallel list at 2 Sam 23:28 the same man appears as Zalmon the Ahohite, so Ilai and Zalmon are taken as two names for one person. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both make this identification. "Ahohite" probably marks him as a descendant of Ahoah, a Benjamite family. The same label is given to other warriors in David's lists. Beyond his place in these rosters, nothing more is recorded about him.

Illyricum was a Roman region on the eastern shore of the Adriatic Sea, northwest of Macedonia, covering much of present-day Croatia, Bosnia and Albania. It appears in the Bible only in Rom 15:19, where Paul says that he had fully preached the gospel of Christ from Jerusalem "round about unto Illyricum," marking it as the farthest point of his work so far. Easton's Bible Dictionary links this to his third missionary journey and to his travel through Macedonia in Acts 20:2, which would have brought him to Illyricum's borders. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that "unto" may mean either up to the frontier or into the region itself. It favors the first reading, since Acts records no travel beyond Macedonia. The province was later known as Dalmatia, the name used in 2 Tim 4:10. The location shown here lies on the Dalmatian coast of modern Croatia.

Imla, also spelled Imlah, was the father of Micaiah, the prophet whom the king of Israel sent for when Jehoshaphat of Judah asked for one more prophet of the LORD to consult before they went to war together (1 Kgs 22:8–9; 2 Chr 18:7–8). Imla himself is known only as part of his son's name. The narrative names the king as Ahab elsewhere in the same account. Kings uses the form Imlah and Chronicles uses Imla. Smith's Bible Dictionary allows that he may have been a more distant ancestor rather than Micaiah's father, and it gives the meaning of the name as "whom God will fill up." Easton's Bible Dictionary renders it "replenisher." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Immer was a place in the land of exile from which some Jews returned to Judah after the Babylonian captivity. It appears only in the parallel lists of Ezra 2:59 and Neh 7:61, alongside Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub and Addan (or Addon). The people who came from these places could not prove their family descent or show that they were of Israel. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both describe Immer as a place in Babylonia, but its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in northern Mesopotamia, near modern Mosul in Iraq. The same name is also borne elsewhere by a priestly family, which is a separate use of the name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "saying" or "a lamb."

Immer was the ancestor of a priestly family that lived in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. He appears in two parallel genealogies of the priests who settled there. 1 Chr 9:12 traces Maasiai back through Meshillemith to Immer, and Neh 11:13 traces Amashai back through Meshillemoth, probably a variant spelling of the same son's name. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats him as the founder of an important priestly family, and links it with the sixteenth course of temple service assigned to Immer in 1 Chr 24:14. Because several people in the Bible bear this name, it is uncertain whether these references all point to one man or to different members of the same family line. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "saying" or "speaking," and Smith's gives "talkative."

Immer was a priest whose name was given to the sixteenth of the twenty-four priestly divisions organized in David's time (1 Chr 24:14). His descendants, the "children of Immer," numbered 1,052 among those who returned from exile in Babylon (Ezra 2:37; Neh 7:40). Two of them, Hanani and Zebadiah, were among the priests who had married foreign wives in Ezra's day (Ezra 10:20). Jeremiah 20:1 names Pashur, the chief officer in the temple who opposed Jeremiah, as "the son of Immer the priest." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats this Immer as a separate priest of Jeremiah's time. This entry groups all these references under one name, since "son of" may simply mark Pashur as a member of Immer's priestly family. Because the name is shared by several people, the exact identification is uncertain.

Immer was the father of Zadok, who repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall opposite his own house during Nehemiah's rebuilding (Neh 3:29). Nothing else is recorded about Immer himself, and he is known only through his son. Several people in the Bible share the name. Immer was also the name of a priestly family that returned from exile in Babylon, and since the priests worked on the neighbouring stretch of wall (Neh 3:28), "son of Immer" here may refer to a member of that family rather than to Immer's immediate son. This is an inference from the context and is not certain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "saying", "speaking" or "a lamb."

Imna was a man of the tribe of Asher, named once in the tribe's genealogy as one of the sons of Helem, alongside his brothers Zophah, Shelesh and Amal (1 Chr 7:35). The verse calls Helem the brother of the man named just before, which by inference from the surrounding genealogy is Shomer (spelled Shamer in 1 Chr 7:34), son of Heber. This entry treats Helem as another name for Hotham, a third son of Heber listed in 1 Chr 7:32, and so gives Imna's father as Hotham. The identification rests on the two names appearing in matching places in the list. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "holding back." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Imnah was the first-named son of Asher, one of the sons of Jacob, and so belonged to the tribe of Asher. His brothers were Ishuah (also spelled Isuah), Isui (Ishuai) and Beriah, and his sister was Serah. He appears in the list of Jacob's descendants who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:17) and in the Chronicler's genealogy of Asher (1 Chr 7:30). In the census of Numbers he is called Jimna, the ancestor of the clan of the Jimnites (Num 26:44). The King James Version spells his name Jimnah, Jimna and Imnah; these are the same Hebrew name. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat him as Asher's firstborn, an inference from his place at the head of each list. The meaning of the name is uncertain, with suggestions including "prosperity" or "good fortune." Another man in the Bible shares this name.

Imnah was a Levite known only as the father of Kore, according to 2 Chr 31:14. Kore was the gatekeeper of the east gate of the temple. During King Hezekiah's religious reforms he was put in charge of the freewill offerings given to God and handed out the Lord's offerings and the most holy gifts. The phrase "the Levite" in that verse could describe either father or son, but both would have belonged to the tribe of Levi. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates Kore's service to about 726 BC and gives the name's meaning as "holding back." Nothing else is recorded about Imnah himself. The same name belongs to other people in the Bible, including a son of Asher (Gen 46:17; 1 Chr 7:30), whose name the KJV also spells Jimnah. This Levite should not be confused with them.

Imrah was a man of the tribe of Asher, one of the sons of Zophah named in the Asherite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:36. His brothers listed there and in the next verse include Suah, Harnepher, Shual, Beri, Bezer, Hod, Shamma, Shilshah, Ithran (or Jether) and Beera. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in this family list. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "stubborn", and Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "a rebel; waxing bitter; changing". Smith's places him sometime after 1445 BC, a date inferred from the genealogy rather than stated in the text.

Imri was a man of the tribe of Judah, descended through Perez (Pharez), the son of Judah. He appears only in a genealogy in 1 Chr 9:4, which names him as the son of Bani and the father of Omri. His great-grandson Uthai is listed among the people who lived in Jerusalem, and the surrounding chapter places that list after the return from exile in Babylon. Imri himself therefore probably belonged to an earlier generation, though STEPBible's proper-names index counts him among those who settled in Jerusalem after the exile. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is shared by at least one other person in the Bible, so this Imri should not be confused with others who bear it. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "speaking," "exalting," "bitter," or "a lamb."

Imri was the father of Zaccur, one of the men who rebuilt a section of Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah after the return from exile. Zaccur worked on the stretch next to the men of Jericho, near the Sheep Gate where the rebuilding began (Neh 3:2). Nothing else is recorded about Imri himself. His name appears only as part of his son's identification, and the verse does not say whether he was still living at the time. Another man named Imri appears in a Judahite genealogy (1 Chr 9:4), and there is no clear evidence that the two are the same person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "speaking" or "exalting".

India is named in the Bible only in the book of Esther, as the eastern limit of the empire ruled by the Persian king Ahasuerus, whose 127 provinces stretched "from India even unto Ethiopia" (Esth 1:1). The same phrase appears when Mordecai's decree is sent to every province in its own script and language (Esth 8:9). The Hebrew name comes from the Indus River. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both take it to mean the lands around the Indus, mainly the Punjab in present-day Pakistan and northwest India, rather than the whole peninsula. Smith's Bible Dictionary adds that Indian goods probably reached Israel earlier through trade, including Solomon's Red Sea voyages. The location shown here is a general marker within the Indian subcontinent, not a specific site.

Iphedeiah was a son of Shashak and a member of the tribe of Benjamin. He appears only in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8, which lists him with Penuel among the sons of Shashak (1 Chr 8:25). The surrounding list also names his brothers Ishpan, Heber, Eliel, Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Hananiah, Elam and Antothijah. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a chief of the tribe, probably reflecting the note at the end of the list that these men were heads of their fathers' houses living in Jerusalem. His name is usually explained as meaning "the Lord frees" or "the Lord redeems" (Smith's and Hitchcock's). Nothing else is recorded about him.

Iphtah, spelled Jiphtah in the King James Version, was a town in the lowland hill country (the Shephelah) of Judah. It appears only once, in the list of towns given to the tribe of Judah, where it is named alongside Ashnah and Nezib (Josh 15:43). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia (1915) places it in the same district group as Libnah, Ether and Ashan, which are listed in the neighboring verse. Nothing else is recorded about the town, and its site has not been identified. The location shown here is only a rough placement within the Shephelah, based on its position in that list, and does not mark a known ruin.

Ir was a descendant of Benjamin, named in 1 Chr 7:12 as the father of Shuppim and Huppim. The verse sits within a genealogy of Benjamin's family. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies him with Iri, a son of Bela, Benjamin's firstborn, who appears a few verses earlier in 1 Chr 7:7. This entry follows that identification. Ir is also counted here as the father of Maachah, the wife of Machir. That rests on 1 Chr 7:15, which says Machir married the sister of Huppim and Shuppim and gives her name as Maachah, so she was probably Ir's daughter. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "watchman," "city" or "vision."

Ir-shemesh, meaning "city of the sun" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary, was a town in the territory given to the tribe of Dan. It is named in Josh 19:41, alongside Zorah and Eshtaol, at the start of the list of Dan's towns. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both connect it with Beth-shemesh ("house of the sun"), and this entry follows that identification. Elsewhere Beth-shemesh appears on the border of Judah (Josh 15:10) and as the town the ark reached when the Philistines returned it (1 Sam 6). The location shown here matches Tel Beth-shemesh, west of Jerusalem in the Sorek Valley. The ISBE also points to the related name Heres.

Ira the Jairite was one of King David's senior officials, named at the end of the list of David's officers in 2 Sam 20:26. The King James Version calls him "a chief ruler about David." The underlying Hebrew word usually means "priest," and Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a priest, either a royal chaplain or a confidential adviser to the king, comparing the similar title given to David's sons in 2 Sam 8:18. The STEPBible name index also lists him as a priest under David. "Jairite" probably marks him as a descendant of, or someone from the towns of, Jair, a clan of Manasseh in Gilead, though the text does not explain the term. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name Ira is shared by several men in the Bible, including two of David's warriors, and they should not be confused with this one.

Ira the son of Ikkesh was a man from Tekoa, a town in Judah south of Bethlehem, and one of King David's mighty warriors known as "the thirty" (2 Sam 23:26; 1 Chr 11:28). In the list of David's monthly army divisions he appears as the captain for the sixth month, in charge of a division of 24,000 men (1 Chr 27:9). Several other men in the Bible share the name Ira, including another of David's warriors, Ira the Ithrite, so he is identified here by his father and hometown. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "watchman."

Ira the Ithrite was one of David's mighty warriors, listed among the Thirty in 2 Sam 23:38 and in the parallel list in 1 Chr 11:40. In both lists he appears next to Gareb, another Ithrite. The Ithrites were probably a family or clan from Kiriath-jearim (1 Chr 2:53). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew could instead be read "Jattirite," meaning a man from the town of Jattir in Judah. It also suggests he may be the same person as Ira the Jairite, David's chief minister, though this is uncertain. Several men in the Bible share the name Ira, and this entry treats the warrior as a separate person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "watchman."

Irad was a son of Enoch and a grandson of Cain, listed in the genealogy of Cain's descendants in Gen 4:18. He was the father of Mehujael, and through him the line continued to Methusael and then to Lamech. Nothing else is recorded about his life. He belongs to the generations before the flood. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "runner" or "wild ass," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "fleet." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint spells his name Gaidad. His name is similar to Jared in the line of Seth (Gen 5:15–20), and some readers compare the two genealogies. This entry treats Irad as a distinct person in Cain's line, as Genesis presents him.

Iram was one of the chiefs (the King James Version says "dukes") of Edom, the people descended from Esau. He is the last name in the list of Edomite chiefs in Gen 36:43, which says these chiefs are named "according to their habitations in the land of their possession." This suggests that Iram may be the name of a clan or district as well as a person. The parallel list in 1 Chr 1:54 repeats the name. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as chief of an Edomite tribe in Mount Seir, and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "belonging to a city." Nothing more is recorded about him, and Smith's notes that no further identification has been found.

Iri was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, a son of Bela and so a grandson of Benjamin. He is named in 1 Chr 7:7 as the last of Bela's five sons: Ezbon, Uzzi, Uzziel, Jerimoth and Iri. They are described as heads of their fathers' houses and mighty men of valour, whose descendants were counted at 22,034. The other brothers grouped with him here, such as Addar, Gera and Naaman, come from a different list of Bela's sons in 1 Chr 8:3–5. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests that the Ir of 1 Chr 7:12 is the same man under a shorter form of the name. Smith's gives the meaning as "belonging to a city," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "fire" or "light." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Irijah was a captain of the guard at the Benjamin Gate of Jerusalem in the last years of the kingdom of Judah. He was the son of Shelemiah and grandson of Hananiah. When the prophet Jeremiah tried to leave the city through that gate, Irijah arrested him and accused him of deserting to the Chaldeans (the Babylonians). Jeremiah denied it, but Irijah would not listen and took him to the princes (Jer 37:13–14). The surrounding verses add that Jeremiah was leaving for the land of Benjamin while the Babylonian siege was briefly lifted, and that the princes then beat him and imprisoned him. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the incident to about 589 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "Yah sees," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "the fear of the Lord."

Irpeel was a town in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. It appears only once, in the list of Benjamin's cities in Josh 18:27, between Rekem and Taralah. By inference from that list, it belonged to the group of Benjamite towns in the hill country north and west of Jerusalem. The name is usually taken to mean "God heals." The site is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary says no trace of it had been found. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be Rafat, a ruin north of el-Jib, the ancient Gibeon. The location shown here follows the Rafat identification, a few miles northwest of Jerusalem.

Iru was a son of Caleb the son of Jephunneh, named in the genealogy of Judah at 1 Chr 4:15 together with his brothers Elah and Naam. Because he is listed first, Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him Caleb's eldest son. Achsah is counted as his sister. By inference from Josh 15:16–17 and Judg 1:12–13, she is the daughter whom Caleb gave in marriage to Othniel. Nothing more is recorded about Iru himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew name may originally have been Ir. On that reading, the final "-u" is the word "and" belonging to the next name in the list. This entry keeps the familiar form Iru.

Isaac was the son of Abraham and Sarah, and his name means "laughter" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. God promised to establish his covenant with Isaac and his descendants (Gen 17:19). Sarah insisted that Ishmael, Hagar's son, should not share Isaac's inheritance (Gen 21:10). At God's command Abraham bound Isaac and laid him on an altar, though the wider account in Gen 22 shows that he was spared (Gen 22:9). He married Rebekah and fathered the twins Esau and Jacob. He lived for a time in Gerar, where his servants dug wells (Gen 26:6, 19), and in old age he blessed his sons (Heb 11:20). He died aged 180 (Gen 35:28), at Mamre according to Gen 35:27. Later scripture often calls God "the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob," and Isaac appears in Jesus' genealogy (Matt 1:2).

The marriage of Isaac and Rebekah was the wedding of Abraham's son Isaac to Rebekah. Gen 25:20 states that Isaac was forty years old when he married her. It identifies her as the daughter of Bethuel the Syrian of Padan-aram and the sister of Laban the Syrian. This entry dates the marriage to about 1856 BC, an estimate inferred from context that places it forty years after Isaac's birth. The fuller account in Gen 24 tells how Abraham sent his servant to his relatives in Mesopotamia to find a wife for Isaac. There the servant met Rebekah at a well. She agreed to return with him, and Isaac took her into his mother Sarah's tent and married her. The verse given here is a later summary that introduces the account of the births of their sons Esau and Jacob.

Isaiah, son of Amoz, was a prophet in Judah whose visions concerned Judah and Jerusalem during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (Isa 1:1). This entry dates his prophecies to about 759 BC, by inference from context. He brought his son Shear-jashub to meet King Ahaz (Isa 7:3). He also had a second son, Maher-shalal-hash-baz, and he walked naked and barefoot for three years as a sign against Egypt and Ethiopia (Isa 20:3). When the Assyrian king Sennacherib threatened Jerusalem, Isaiah told Hezekiah not to be afraid (2 Kgs 19:6, 20). Later he announced Hezekiah's coming death, prescribed a lump of figs for his recovery, and gave the sign of the shadow turning back (2 Kgs 20:7–11). Chronicles credits him with recording the acts of Uzziah and Hezekiah (2 Chr 26:22; 32:32). The New Testament, which calls him Esaias, quotes him often. A tradition says he was martyred under Manasseh (Smith's Bible Dictionary).

Iscah was a child of Haran, the brother of Abram, mentioned only once, in the note on the marriages of Abram and Nahor (Gen 11:29). That verse names Haran as "the father of Milcah, and the father of Iscah," which makes Iscah a sibling of Milcah, Nahor's wife. Lot was also a child of Haran (Gen 11:27), so Iscah was Lot's sibling too, and a niece or nephew of Abram and Nahor. The verse does not state Iscah's sex. Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia all describe Iscah as Haran's daughter. Smith's notes that Jewish tradition identifies Iscah with Sarai, Abram's wife. Nothing else is recorded about Iscah's life. The name's meaning is given as "spy" (Easton's), "one who looks forth" (Smith's), or "he that anoints" (Hitchcock's Bible Names).

Ish-bosheth was a son of Saul who ruled Israel, apart from Judah, after his father's death. Abner, the commander of Saul's army, brought him to Mahanaim, east of the Jordan, and made him king there. He was forty years old and reigned two years, while Judah followed David (2 Sam 2:8–10). Abner and Ish-bosheth's men fought David's forces at Gibeon (2 Sam 2:12–15). When Ish-bosheth accused Abner of taking Saul's concubine Rizpah, Abner answered angrily and, as the following verses tell, went over to David (2 Sam 3:7–8). At David's demand, Ish-bosheth returned Michal, David's wife, taking her from Phaltiel (2 Sam 3:14–15). Rechab and Baanah killed him while he rested at noon and brought his head to David at Hebron. David had them executed and buried the head in Abner's tomb (2 Sam 4:5–12). In 1 Chr 8:33 he is called Eshbaal. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of Ish-bosheth as "a man of shame."

Ishbah was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:17, where he is called "the father of Eshtemoa." Eshtemoa was a town in the hill country of Judah, so "father" here probably means founder or chief of that settlement rather than a literal parent. His name is usually explained as meaning "praising" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). The verse lists him with Miriam and Shammai as children of an unnamed "she." By inference from 1 Chr 4:18, which is generally read as continuing this list, this entry takes her to be Bithiah, Pharaoh's daughter, and his father to be Mered, a son of Ezra. The same passage names Jehudijah as the mother of Jered, Heber and Jekuthiel. The wording of these verses is compressed, and how these people relate to one another is uncertain.

Ishbak was a son of Abraham and Keturah, and the fifth of their six sons. His brothers were Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian and Shuah, and Isaac and Ishmael were his half-brothers. His name appears only in the two lists of Keturah's sons (Gen 25:2; 1 Chr 1:32), and nothing else is recorded about him. 1 Chr 1:32 calls Keturah Abraham's concubine. By inference from the surrounding chapter, Ishbak was among the sons Abraham sent away eastward with gifts, away from Isaac (Gen 25:6). Smith's Bible Dictionary regards him as the ancestor of a tribe in northern Arabia. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that these names probably stand for tribes, though the tribe of Ishbak has not been identified with certainty. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "leaving."

Ishbi-benob was a Philistine warrior described as one of "the sons of the giant" (the Rephaim, in Easton's Bible Dictionary), who tried to kill David during a battle between Israel and the Philistines late in David's reign. 2 Sam 21:16 says his bronze spearhead weighed three hundred shekels, roughly 7.5 pounds (about 3.5 kg), and that he was armed with a new sword when he attacked David, who had grown tired in the fighting. The next verse, 2 Sam 21:17, records that Abishai son of Zeruiah came to David's aid and killed him. After this, David's men swore that David would no longer go out to battle with them. The surrounding passage (2 Sam 21:15–22) names him as one of four men born to the giant in Gath, alongside figures such as Saph (Sippai) and the brother of Goliath. Easton's and Smith's dictionaries take his name to mean "dweller at Nob" or "my seat at Nob."

Ishi was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:31 as the son of Appaim and the father of Sheshan, whose child was Ahlai. The surrounding genealogy places Appaim in the family of Jerahmeel, a son of Hezron and grandson of Judah. Ishi therefore belonged to the Jerahmeelite branch of Judah, or as Smith's Bible Dictionary puts it, "one of the great house of Hezron." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that such genealogies may show membership in Judah either by blood or by adoption. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "salvation," and Smith's gives "salutary." Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Ishi, and this one should not be confused with them.

Ishi was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:20 as the father of Zoheth and Ben-zoheth. That verse is the only mention of him. It follows a list of the sons of Shimon, and the STEPBible Proper Names index takes Ishi to be one of Shimon's sons, though the verse does not say so directly. Nothing more is recorded about his life. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the name's meaning as "salutary," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "salvation." Several other men in Chronicles bear the same name, including a descendant of Judah through Jerahmeel (1 Chr 2:31), a Simeonite (1 Chr 4:42) and a leader of the half-tribe of Manasseh (1 Chr 5:24). This entry treats the Ishi of 1 Chr 4:20 as a separate person.

Ishi was a man of the tribe of Simeon, described in Smith's Bible Dictionary as the head of a Simeonite family. His four sons, Pelatiah, Neariah, Rephaiah and Uzziel, served as captains of a band of five hundred Simeonites who went to Mount Seir (1 Chr 4:42). The next verse, 1 Chr 4:43, says they struck down the surviving Amalekites there and settled in their place. The surrounding passage places these Simeonite movements in the days of Hezekiah, king of Judah (1 Chr 4:41). Nothing else is recorded about Ishi himself. The name means "salutary" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, or "salvation" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Several other men in the Bible share the name Ishi, including figures in the genealogies of Judah and Manasseh, and should not be confused with this Simeonite.

Ishi was one of the heads of ancestral houses in the half-tribe of Manasseh that settled east of the Jordan. In 1 Chr 5:24 he is listed with Epher, Eliel, Azriel, Jeremiah, Hodaviah and Jahdiel, who are described as mighty men of valour, famous men and heads of their fathers' houses. The surrounding passage places this half-tribe in the land from Bashan to Baal-hermon and Mount Hermon, and Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify him as a chief of eastern Manasseh. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary renders "salutary" and Hitchcock's Bible Names "salvation," is also borne by other men in the Bible, so this Ishi should not be confused with others of the same name.

Ishiah was a man of the tribe of Issachar, named in the tribe's genealogy as a son of Izrahiah and grandson of Uzzi. His brothers were Michael, Obadiah and Joel (1 Chr 7:3). The verse counts the group as "five" though it names only four sons. The fifth is probably Izrahiah himself, though Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Ishiah as the fifth of five sons. All of them are called "chief men," meaning heads of their clan. From the surrounding verses, Uzzi descended from Tola, Issachar's son. Smith's Bible Dictionary places this family in the time of David. The name is also spelled Isshiah, and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "whom the Lord lends." Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in Chronicles bear the same or a similar name, and they appear to be different people.

Ishijah was one of the "sons of Harim," a lay family group among the Israelites who had returned from exile. He is named only once, in the list in Ezra 10:31. That list records the men who had married foreign wives and, during Ezra's reforms, agreed to send them away. Nothing else is known about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "whom Jehovah lends." It dates the event to about 459 BC, a date estimated from the context of Ezra's work in Jerusalem. Some reference works, such as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, spell the name Isshijah.

Ishma was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the genealogy of Judah's descendants. 1 Chr 4:3 lists him with Jezreel and Idbash as belonging to "the father of Etam," and names their sister Hazelelponi. "Father of Etam" may refer to the founder or leading figure of the town of Etam rather than a personal name, so the exact relationship is uncertain. This entry follows the reading that places Ishma among the descendants of Hur. By inference from the next verse, 1 Chr 4:4, which closes the list with "these are the sons of Hur," he is grouped with the other men of Hur's line, such as Shobal, Salma and Hareph. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes his name to mean "desolate."

Ishmael (Son of Hagar) was Abraham's first son, born to Hagar, the Egyptian servant of Sarah, when Abram was eighty-six (about 1910 BC, by inference from context). An angel told Hagar to name him Ishmael, meaning "God hears," because the LORD had heard her affliction. At thirteen he was circumcised on the same day as Abraham. God promised that he would father twelve princes and become a great nation, and Genesis lists his twelve sons, beginning with Nebajoth and Kedar, as princes with their own towns. Gen 21 tells how he and Hagar were later sent away and settled in the wilderness of Paran. He and Isaac together buried Abraham in the cave of Machpelah. His daughter married Esau. She is called Mahalath in Gen 28:9 and Bashemath in Gen 36:3, probably the same woman. He died at 137. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes his descendants as the Ishmaelite tribes of northern Arabia.

Ishmael son of Nethaniah, grandson of Elishama and of the royal line, was one of the army captains who came to Gedaliah at Mizpah after the king of Babylon made Gedaliah governor. He is not the son of Abraham who bears the same name. Johanan son of Kareah warned Gedaliah that Baalis king of the Ammonites had sent Ishmael to kill him, but Gedaliah refused to believe it. In the seventh month Ishmael and ten men ate with Gedaliah at Mizpah, then killed him along with the Jews and Chaldean soldiers there. He then killed a group of arriving men and threw their bodies into the pit King Asa had made, sparing ten who offered hidden stores of food. He carried off the remaining people, including the king's daughters, toward Ammon. Johanan overtook him by the great waters of Gibeon and freed the captives, but Ishmael escaped with eight men to the Ammonites.

Ishmael was one of the six sons of Azel, a Benjamite in the family line of King Saul. He appears only in two matching genealogies, 1 Chr 8:38 and 1 Chr 9:44, where his brothers are named as Azrikam, Bocheru, Sheariah, Obadiah and Hanan. The surrounding lists trace this line from Saul through his son Jonathan and then Merib-baal (Mephibosheth), so Ishmael was a distant descendant of Saul, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name, usually understood to mean "God hears," was shared by several other people in the Bible, including Abraham's son by Hagar, and he should not be confused with them.

Ishmael was a man of Judah known only as the father of Zebadiah, who served as "the ruler of the house of Judah" in charge of the king's matters. The context shows this was during the reign of King Jehoshaphat, who appointed judges and officials in Jerusalem (2 Chr 19:11). Ishmael himself is not described, and nothing else is recorded of his life or role. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and the verse does not link him to any of them. The name means "God hears," according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Ishmael son of Jehohanan was one of the captains of hundreds in Judah whom the priest Jehoiada brought into a covenant with him in the seventh year (2 Chr 23:1). By context, the seventh year is that of Queen Athaliah's rule, and the covenant aimed to overthrow her and make the young Joash king, as the rest of 2 Chronicles 23 describes. Ishmael is named alongside Azariah son of Jeroham, Azariah son of Obed, Maaseiah son of Adaiah and Elishaphat son of Zichri. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name, meaning "God hears" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, belongs to several people in the Bible, and this man should not be confused with Abraham's son or with the Ishmael who killed Gedaliah.

Ishmael was a priest, one of the sons (descendants) of Pashur, listed in Ezra 10:22 among the men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra. The surrounding passage shows that those named agreed to send away these wives as part of Ezra's reforms after the return from exile in Babylon. The name means "God hears," according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Several other men in the Bible share the name, most famously Abraham's son by Hagar, but this Ishmael is known only from this list. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same man appears as Ismael in the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:22. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Ishmaiah, son of Obadiah, was the leader of the tribe of Zebulun during King David's reign. He appears only once, in a list of the chief officers over the tribes of Israel (1 Chr 27:16–22), where he is named as the ruler of Zebulun alongside Jerimoth son of Azriel, ruler of Naphtali. The text gives no further details about his life or duties. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him a viceroy of Zebulun under David and Solomon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as the chief of Zebulun's contingent in David's monthly rotation of tribal service, though the surrounding list is usually read as one of tribal leaders rather than military commanders. His name is usually taken to mean "the LORD hears." He should not be confused with Ishmaiah of Gibeon, a mighty man of David mentioned elsewhere in Chronicles.

Ishmerai was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named as one of the sons of Elpaal in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. He is listed alongside Jezliah and Jobab, with other sons of Elpaal such as Eber, Misham, Shamed, Beriah, Shema, Zebadiah, Meshullam, Hezeki and Heber named in the surrounding verses. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts him among the heads of fathers' houses who lived in Jerusalem, following the summary later in the same chapter. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name probably means "the Lord keeps" or "guard, protector," according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia.

Ishod (spelled Ishhod in some translations, as in the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) was a man of the tribe of Manasseh, named only in the Manasseh genealogy of 1 Chr 7:18. His mother was Hammoleketh, and his brothers were Abiezer and Mahalah. The verse calls Hammoleketh "his sister," and the person meant is not certain. From the preceding verse she was probably the sister of Gilead, the son of Machir. STEPBible's proper-names list takes her as the sister of Manasseh. Smith's Bible Dictionary places this family among the Manassites east of the Jordan. His name has been explained as "man of glory" (Smith's Bible Dictionary) or "a comely man" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Nothing else is recorded about him.

Ishpan was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8 as a son of Shashak. His brothers were Heber, Eliel, Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Hananiah, Elam, Antothijah, Iphedeiah and Penuel. The surrounding passage presents these sons of Shashak among the heads of fathers' houses and chief men who lived in Jerusalem. That is noted in a verse just after his own, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reads it the same way. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "he will hide," Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "hid" or "broken in two," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "bald."

Ismachiah was one of ten overseers who served under Cononiah and his brother Shimei during the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. They were appointed by command of the king and of Azariah, the ruler of the house of God (2 Chr 31:13). The surrounding passage shows that their task was to manage the tithes, offerings and dedicated gifts that the people brought to the temple storerooms. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Levite, which fits the context of temple service, though the verse does not say so directly. His name is generally taken to mean "the LORD sustains" or "whom the LORD upholds." He is mentioned only here, and nothing more is known about him.

Ismaiah was a man from Gibeon, called "the Gibeonite," who is named among the warriors who came over to David. 1 Chr 12:4 describes him as "a mighty man among the thirty, and over the thirty," which suggests he was both a member of David's elite group of warriors known as the Thirty and a leader within it. The surrounding chapter lists men who joined David at Ziklag while he was still in hiding from Saul, as Easton's Bible Dictionary also notes. Many of these men were Benjamites, Saul's own kinsmen. His name is also spelled Ishmaiah in some reference works. He is not mentioned in the lists of the Thirty in 2 Samuel 23 or 1 Chronicles 11, and nothing more is known of him.

Ispah, also spelled Ishpah in some versions, was a man of the tribe of Benjamin named among the sons of Beriah in the genealogy of 1 Chr 8:16. His brothers were Michael, Joha, Ahio, Shashak, Jeremoth, Zebadiah, Arad and Ader. Judging from the surrounding passage, his father Beriah was one of the Benjamite family heads linked with Aijalon (1 Chr 8:13), and the men in this list are later described as heads of families living in Jerusalem (1 Chr 8:28). Smith's Bible Dictionary likewise calls Ispah one of the heads of his tribe. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "bald" and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a jasper stone."

Jacob (Israel) was the son of Isaac and Rebekah and the younger twin of Esau. He was born holding his brother's heel, which gave him his name (Gen 25:26), and Gen 32:28 records that God later renamed him Israel. By Leah, Rachel and their servants Bilhah and Zilpah he had twelve sons, the ancestors of Israel's tribes, and a daughter, Dinah. Late in life he moved his household to Egypt, where his son Joseph held office, and he died there (Exod 1:1). By inference from context, this entry dates his life to about 1836–1689 BC. He gave Joseph land near Sychar in Samaria (John 4:5). His two names became names for the whole nation, as in "the children of Israel" and "the house of Jacob" (Jer 2:4; Mic 1:5). God is called "the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob" (Mark 12:26), and Matthew includes him in Jesus' genealogy (Matt 1:2).

Issachar was the region allotted to the tribe of Issachar, named after Jacob's son (Gen 30:18). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as 'reward.' It was the fourth lot drawn when Joshua divided the land. Its border ran by Jezreel, Chesulloth and Shunem, reached Tabor, and ended at the Jordan, and it took in sixteen cities with their villages. This places it mainly in the eastern Jezreel Valley and the hills around it, the area shown here. Manasseh lay to its west and held several towns inside Issachar, including Bethshean, Endor, Taanach and Megiddo. Under Solomon it was one of the administrative districts that supplied the royal household, governed by Jehoshaphat son of Paruah. In Ezekiel's vision of the restored land, Issachar receives a strip between Simeon and Zebulun, and one of the city's southern gates bears its name.

Issachar was the ninth son of Jacob and the fifth borne to him by Leah. Leah named him after her words "God hath given me my hire," so the name is linked to "hire" or "reward" (Gen 30:18). His birth is placed at about 1752 BC by inference from context, probably in Paddan-aram, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes. Little is recorded of him personally beyond the shared story of Jacob's sons, including the family's move to Egypt. He had four sons: Tola, Puah (Phuvah), Jashub (called Job in Gen 46:13) and Shimron. Jacob's deathbed blessing pictured him as a strong donkey lying down between two burdens. He was the ancestor of the tribe of Issachar. The tribe numbered 54,400 fighting men at Sinai and received land by lot in Joshua's day. It later produced the judge Tola and King Baasha. Several other people in the Bible share the name.

Issachar was a Levite of the Korahite line who served as a gatekeeper of the house of the Lord in the time of King David. He is named only once, in the list of gatekeeper families, as the seventh son in a family of eight brothers: Shemaiah, Jehozabad, Joah, Sacar, Nethaneel, Ammiel, Issachar and Peulthai (1 Chr 26:5). The surrounding passage (1 Chr 26:4) presents these brothers as the sons of Obed-edom, and Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify him that way. The list closes by noting that God blessed the family with many sons. His name, probably meaning "reward," is shared with the better-known ninth son of Jacob and the tribe descended from him, who is a different person. Nothing else is recorded about this Issachar.

Isshiah was a Levite named as a son of Uzziel in the lists of Levite families from King David's time. In 1 Chr 23:20 the King James Version spells his name Jesiah and calls him the second son, after his brother Michah. 1 Chr 24:25 calls him Isshiah, again Michah's brother, and names his son Zechariah as head of a family among the Levites. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies this Uzziel as the son of Kohath, making Isshiah a Kohathite. Exod 6:22 names Mishael, Elzaphan and Zithri as sons of Kohath's son Uzziel, which is why they are counted as his brothers here. Because these lists come many generations after Kohath, "son of Uzziel" in Chronicles probably means a descendant of Uzziel's family line rather than a literal son. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Isuah, also spelled Ishuah (and Ishvah in some references), was the second son of Asher and a grandson of Jacob. He appears in two genealogical lists of Asher's children, alongside his brothers Imnah (Jimnah), Isui (Ishuai) and Beriah and their sister Serah (Gen 46:17; 1 Chr 7:30). Genesis places him among the family members who went down to Egypt with Jacob. Nothing else is recorded about him. The clan list of Asher in Num 26:44 names Jimnah, Jesui and Beriah but not Isuah, which may mean that no clan descended from him, though the text does not say so. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "quiet."

Isui was the third son of Asher and a grandson of Jacob. He is named among Asher's sons in the list of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:17), and again in the genealogy of Asher in 1 Chr 7:30, where the King James Version spells his name Ishuai. In the census taken in the plains of Moab, his descendants appear as a clan of the tribe of Asher, the family of the Jesuites, founded by Jesui (Num 26:44). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the Hebrew form as Ishvi and the meaning as "equal," while Smith's Bible Dictionary links the name to ideas of evenness or quiet. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in these family lists, where his brothers were Imnah, Isuah and Beriah, and his sister was Serah.

Italy was the peninsula of southern Europe stretching from the Alps to the strait facing Sicily, the home region of Rome and the heart of the Roman Empire. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that by New Testament times the name covered this whole peninsula, though it had earlier referred only to the far south. Aquila and Priscilla had recently come from Italy to Corinth after the emperor Claudius ordered all Jews to leave Rome (Acts 18:2). When it was decided that Paul should be sent to Italy as a prisoner, he was placed in the custody of a centurion named Julius, who later put him aboard an Alexandrian ship bound there (Acts 27:1, 6), the start of his journey to Rome, about AD 56 by inference from context. The letter to the Hebrews passes on greetings from "they of Italy" (Heb 13:24), probably Christians living in or from Italy.

Ithamar was the fourth and youngest son of Aaron and his wife Elisheba, of the tribe of Levi (Exod 6:23). He was set apart with his father and brothers to serve as a priest. After his older brothers Nadab and Abihu died for offering unauthorized fire, he and Eleazar carried on the priestly office under Aaron, and Moses instructed them about mourning and the offerings. Ithamar oversaw the accounting of the tabernacle materials and directed the Levite clans of Gershon and Merari in their tabernacle service. Under David the priests were divided by lot, with eight chief households from Ithamar's line, represented by Ahimelech, and sixteen from Eleazar's. A descendant named Daniel returned from Babylon with Ezra. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the high priesthood later passed to his family in Eli, for reasons not recorded. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "island of the palm-tree."

Ithiel was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only in the genealogy of Sallu in Neh 11:7. He was the son of Jesaiah and the father of Maaseiah, and he was an ancestor of Sallu several generations back. Sallu was among the Benjamites who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. Ithiel himself probably lived well before that time, by inference from the length of the line. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "God is with me." The same name belongs to a different man, one of those addressed in Prov 30:1, who is not the person described here.

Ithiel was one of two men, together with Ucal, to whom Agur son of Jakeh addressed his sayings in Prov 30:1. The verse names Ithiel twice and gives no details about who he was, though he may have been a pupil or companion of Agur. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "God is with me" and places the discourse at about 900 BC, an estimate rather than a date given in the text. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says the name is only "perhaps" present here, because the Hebrew words can also be divided and read as a phrase rather than as personal names. This entry follows the reading of the King James Version, which treats Ithiel as a person. The name is shared by others in the Bible, including a Benjamite listed in Neh 11:7, who is a different man.

Ithlah (spelled Jethlah in the King James Version) was a town assigned to the tribe of Dan. It appears only once, in the list of Danite towns in Josh 19:42, next to Shaalabbin and Aijalon (Ajalon). That places it in the western foothills toward the coastal plain. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "suspended" or "high" and describes it as a city on the borders of Dan. Nothing else is recorded about it. Its exact site is uncertain. The location shown here follows an identification with the modern village of Bayt Thul, west of Jerusalem, near the other towns named with it.

Ithmah was a Moabite listed among David's mighty warriors in 1 Chr 11:46. He appears in the extended roster of heroes in 1 Chronicles 11, which goes beyond the shorter list in 2 Samuel 23, and nothing else is recorded about him. His Moabite origin is notable because Moab was often at war with Israel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia points out that a man from that nation still ranked among the king's heroes. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "bereavedness," Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "an orphan," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "purity."

Ithnan was a town in the far south of Judah, in the Negev. It appears only once, in the list of towns given to the tribe of Judah, where it is named alongside Kedesh and Hazor (Josh 15:23). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the "Ethnan" mentioned by Jerome, but it notes that the site has not been identified, and Smith's Bible Dictionary likewise reports that no trace of it had been found. Its exact location is therefore unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the Negev region of southern Judah, based on its place in the town list.

Ithran was a Horite, one of the sons of Dishon, listed among the descendants of Seir the Horite, the early inhabitants of the land of Edom. His brothers were Hemdan, Eshban and Cheran (Gen 36:26). The parallel list in 1 Chr 1:41 gives the same names, except that Hemdan appears as Amram, and it makes Dishon the son of Anah. Genesis also has an earlier Dishon who was a son of Seir, so it is not entirely certain which Dishon was Ithran's father. Nothing further is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he was probably the head of a Horite clan, by inference from the list of Horite chiefs in the same chapter. The name is usually taken to mean "excellent" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). A different Ithran, from the tribe of Asher, appears elsewhere in Chronicles.

Ithream was the sixth son of David, born to him by his wife Eglah while David reigned at Hebron (2 Sam 3:5; 1 Chr 3:3). Both lists of David's Hebron-born sons place him last, after Amnon, the son called Daniel or Chileab, Absalom, Adonijah and Shephatiah, each of whom had a different mother. Solomon and David's other sons born later in Jerusalem were his half-brothers. As a son of David, he belonged to the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about his life, and Eglah appears only as his mother. Reference works explain his name differently: the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "residue of the people," Smith's Bible Dictionary "abundance of people," and Hitchcock's Bible Names "excellence of the people."

Ittai the Gittite was a man from Gath, the Philistine city, who served King David during Absalom's rebellion. When David fled Jerusalem, he urged Ittai to go back, since he was a foreigner and an exile. Ittai refused and swore to stay with the king in life or death, so David let him cross over with all his men and their children (2 Sam 15:19–22). Later David divided his army into three parts under Joab, Abishai and Ittai, and charged all three commanders in everyone's hearing to deal gently with Absalom (2 Sam 18:2, 5, 12). Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he commanded the six hundred men who had followed David since his wandering years, and places this muster at Mahanaim. He is not mentioned again. The name is shared by another Ittai, one of David's mighty men, who is a different person.

Ittai, also called Ithai, was the son of Ribai, from Gibeah in the territory of Benjamin, and one of David's mighty warriors. He appears in the list of David's thirty heroes in 2 Sam 23:29, and again in the parallel list in 1 Chr 11:31, where his name is spelled Ithai. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his name, his father, his home town and his place among David's elite fighters. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both identify him as a Benjamite among David's thirty. Several people in the Bible share the name. This Ittai should be distinguished from Ittai the Gittite, the Philistine from Gath who stayed loyal to David during Absalom's revolt.

Ituraea was a region in the far north-east of the Holy Land, mentioned in the Bible only at Luke 3:1. There Luke names it, with Trachonitis, as the territory ruled by Philip, brother of Herod, as tetrarch in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar. It was the land of the Itureans. Smith's Bible Dictionary and others trace that people to Jetur, a son of Ishmael (Gen 25:15). Its exact boundaries are uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it south-east of Mount Hermon, in the district later called Jedur, between Trachonitis, Gaulanitis, Hermon and the plain of Damascus. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the Itureans lived mainly in the Lebanon mountains and the valley of Coele-Syria, perhaps extending south-east of Hermon. It also notes that Luke's two names may overlap. The location shown here follows the identification with the area around the base of Mount Hermon.

Ivvah was a city named by the Assyrian king Sennacherib's officials in their threats against Hezekiah of Judah. They listed it with Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim and Hena as places whose gods and kings had been unable to resist Assyria, so Jerusalem should not expect rescue either (2 Kgs 18:34; 19:13; Isa 37:13). It is often taken to be the same as Avva, one of the places from which the Assyrians resettled people in Samaria (2 Kgs 17:24). Its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on the Euphrates between Sepharvaim and Hena, and some have linked it with Hit on the Euphrates or with Imm near Aleppo. Others have read Hena and Ivvah as names of gods rather than cities. The rough location shown here follows the Euphrates view, placing it on the middle Euphrates in modern Iraq.

Iye-abarim was a campsite of the Israelites during their wilderness journey. They reached it after leaving Oboth. It is described as lying "in the wilderness which is before Moab, toward the sunrising" (Num 21:11) and "in the border of Moab" (Num 33:44). That places it east of the land along Moab's frontier, before Israel moved on toward the Zered Valley. The name probably means "the heaps (or ruins) of the Abarim," after the Abarim range of highlands east of the Dead Sea. The King James Version spells it Ije-abarim. According to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, the shorter name Iyim (Iim) in Num 33:45 refers to the same place. It also notes that the biblical descriptions are too general to fix the site, and no exact identification is known. The location shown here is a rough placement east of the Dead Sea on the edge of Moab.

Iyim (spelled Iim in the King James Version) was a camping place of the Israelites near the end of their wilderness journey. From there they moved on to Dibon-gad (Num 33:45). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says the name means "heaps" and treats it as a short form of Iye-abarim, the stop named in the previous verse (Num 33:44), which places the site "in the border of Moab." Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it simply as one of the wilderness stations. The exact site is unknown. Since the next stop was Dibon-gad, Iyim was probably not far from Dibon, east of the Dead Sea in present-day Jordan. The location shown here is only approximate and lies close to Dibon.

Izhar was a Levite, the second of the four sons of Kohath and a grandson of Levi. His brothers were Amram, Hebron and Uzziel (Exod 6:18; 1 Chr 6:2; 1 Chr 23:12). Since Amram was the father of Moses and Aaron (Exod 6:20), Izhar was their uncle. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "oil." Numbers 3:19 spells it Izehar. His sons were Korah, Nepheg and Zichri (Exod 6:21). Korah later led a revolt against Moses (Num 16:1). Another son or descendant, Shelomith, is named as chief of the Izharite family in David's time (1 Chr 23:18). The singer Heman traced his ancestry back through Izhar (1 Chr 6:38). In 1 Chr 6:22 the son of Kohath who fathered Korah is called Amminadab. This entry treats him as Izhar, and Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the different name arose in copying.

Izrahiah was a man of the tribe of Issachar, named in its genealogy as the son of Uzzi. His four sons were Michael, Obadiah, Joel and Ishiah. The verse counts the group as "five," probably including Izrahiah himself with his sons, and calls them all "chief men," meaning heads of families or clans. The verse before (1 Chr 7:2) names Uzzi as a son of Tola, Issachar's son, so Izrahiah was Tola's grandson, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes.
