Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a chieftain of Issachar. His name is usually explained as meaning "the LORD shines" or "the LORD appears." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Izri was a Levite musician, one of the six sons of Jeduthun, who served in the worship organized under King David. In 1 Chr 25:3 he is called Zeri and is listed among the sons who prophesied with the harp under their father's direction, giving thanks and praise to the LORD. When the musicians were divided by lot into twenty-four groups of twelve, the fourth lot fell to Izri, together with his sons and relatives (1 Chr 25:11). Reference works such as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat Izri and Zeri as two spellings of the same man's name, and this entry follows that view. His role suggests he served in the reign of David, by inference from the surrounding chapter.

Jaakobah was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named once in a list of Simeonite clan leaders in 1 Chr 4:36. By inference from the surrounding passage (1 Chr 4:38–41), these men were princes of their families whose households grew large. In the days of King Hezekiah of Judah they moved toward Gedor to find pasture for their flocks and took the land from its earlier inhabitants. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 710 BC, an estimate drawn from that context. His name is a form of Jacob. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "heel-catcher," and Smith's gives "supplanter." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jaala, also spelled Jaalah, was the ancestor of a family that returned from exile in Babylon to Judah with Zerubbabel, probably around 538–536 BC by inference from context. He is known only as a name in the parallel lists of returnees in Ezra 2:56 and Neh 7:58, where his descendants appear beside those of Darkon and Giddel. The surrounding passage places these families among the descendants of "Solomon's servants," a group counted together with the temple servants (the Nethinim). Smith's Bible Dictionary accordingly calls them descendants of Solomon's slaves, while Easton's Bible Dictionary groups Jaala with the Nethinim. Nothing more is recorded about him or his family. Easton's and Smith's dictionaries give the meaning of the name as "wild she-goat."

Jaalam was a son of Esau (Edom) and his wife Aholibamah, the daughter of Anah. He is named second of her three sons, between his brothers Jeush and Korah, and he was born in the land of Canaan before Esau moved away (Gen 36:5, 14). His half-brothers Eliphaz and Reuel were Esau's sons by other wives. Jaalam is also listed as a "duke," or clan chief, among the Edomites, which suggests a clan descended from him (Gen 36:18). The genealogy in 1 Chr 1:35 repeats his name among Esau's sons. Nothing else is recorded about him. Modern translations spell the name Jalam, and Easton's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "concealer."

Jaanai was a leader of the tribe of Gad, named in the genealogy at 1 Chr 5:12 alongside Joel the chief, Shapham second in rank, and Shaphat. The surrounding passage places these Gadite families in the land of Bashan, east of the Jordan, which is probably where Jaanai lived as well. Nothing else is recorded about him. Most modern translations spell his name Janai, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists him under that form. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "whom Jehovah answers," Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "answering" or "afflicting," and Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "mourner."

Jaar is a possible place name in Ps 132:6. The Hebrew word means "forest" or "wood," and the King James Version translates it that way: "we found it in the fields of the wood." According to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, this is the only verse where it may be a proper name, and the Revised Version margin reads "the field of Jaar." The psalm recalls the search for a dwelling place for the Lord, so "it" probably refers to the ark of the covenant. On that reading, the same encyclopedia suggests Jaar may be a shortened form of Kiriath-jearim ("town of forests"), where the ark stayed for about twenty years before David brought it to Jerusalem. The rough location shown here puts it in the hills west of Jerusalem, in the general area of Kiriath-jearim. Whether the word is a place name at all is uncertain.

Jaasau was an Israelite man named in the list of those who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra, after the return from exile in Babylon (Ezra 10:37). The surrounding list in Ezra 10 groups these men by family. By inference from that context, Smith's Bible Dictionary places him among the descendants of Bani, and he was among those who agreed to send away their foreign wives during Ezra's reforms. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 459 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "whom the Lord made," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "doing" or "my doing." Some versions spell the name Jaasu.

Jaasiel was the son of Abner and the leader of the tribe of Benjamin during the reign of King David. He appears in the list of officers who ruled over the tribes of Israel (1 Chr 27:16–22), where he is named alongside Iddo, leader of the half-tribe of Manasseh in Gilead. His father is probably Abner the Benjamite, Saul's cousin and army commander, as Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him. That would fit a son of Abner being placed over Benjamin, though the verse does not say so. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify him with Jasiel the Mezobaite, one of David's mighty men in 1 Chr 11:47. The ISBE marks that identification as probable. His name is usually explained as meaning "God makes" or "made by God."

Jaazaniah was the son of Jeremiah and grandson of Habaziniah, and a leading member of the Rechabites, a family clan in the days of the prophet Jeremiah (Jer 35:3). His father Jeremiah is a different man from the prophet. When the prophet was told to bring the Rechabites into a chamber of the temple and offer them wine, he took Jaazaniah together with his brothers, his sons and the whole Rechabite household. Since he heads the list, he was probably the clan's chief at the time, as Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him. By inference from the rest of the chapter, he and his family refused the wine out of loyalty to their ancestor's commands, and the prophet held up their faithfulness as an example to Judah. His name means "the Lord hears." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Jaazaniah should not be confused with them.

Jaazaniah, son of Shaphan, was one of the seventy elders of Israel whom the prophet Ezekiel saw in a vision of the Jerusalem temple. He is singled out as standing among them while each man held a censer and a thick cloud of incense rose (Ezek 8:11). The surrounding passage places this scene in a chamber whose walls were covered with images of creeping things, beasts and idols, so the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as offering incense to idols. His father Shaphan is sometimes taken to be Josiah's scribe of that name, but this is not stated and remains uncertain. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jaazaniah, so he should not be confused with the others. The name means "Yah hears" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, or "whom the Lord will hear" in Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Jaazaniah son of Azur was one of the twenty-five men whom the prophet Ezekiel saw in a vision at the east gate of the temple in Jerusalem. He is named there alongside Pelatiah son of Benaiah, and both are called "princes of the people" (Ezek 11:1). In the verses that follow, Ezekiel is told that these men were devising mischief and giving wicked counsel in the city, and he is commanded to prophesy against them. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the vision to about 593 BC. His name means "the LORD hears." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Jaazaniah should not be confused with Jaazaniah son of Shaphan, whom Ezekiel sees in an earlier vision (Ezek 8:11).

Jaaziah was a Levite of the clan of Merari, named only in the list of Levite families in 1 Chr 24:26–27. That list is part of the arrangement of Levites in King David's time. It names Mahli and Mushi as Merari's sons and then gives a line "of Jaaziah," whose sons were Beno, Shoham, Zaccur and Ibri. This entry treats Jaaziah as a third son of Merari alongside Mahli and Mushi. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that he may instead have been a later descendant. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes the Hebrew text here as difficult and mentions a reading in the Greek Septuagint that some connect with the name Uzziah. The meaning of the name is given variously as "comforted by the Lord" (Easton's Bible Dictionary) or "the Lord strengthens" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia).

Jaaziel was a Levite of the second rank whom the Levite leaders appointed, at David's command, as one of the musicians when the ark was brought up to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:18). He is listed among a group of brethren who also served as gatekeepers. In the same passage he appears as Aziel, which Smith's Bible Dictionary takes as a shortened form of the same name. Aziel is named among the Levites who played psalteries (harps) "on Alamoth," a musical term of uncertain meaning (1 Chr 15:20). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "comforted by God." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "God strengthens." That encyclopedia also notes that some scholars, following the Septuagint, read the name as Uzziel. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 1014 BC.

Jabal was a son of Lamech, a descendant of Cain, and his wife Adah. Jubal was his full brother, and Tubal-cain and Naamah, children of Lamech's other wife Zillah, were his half-siblings. Genesis names him as the father of those who live in tents and keep livestock (Gen 4:20). In other words, he is presented as the founder or first practitioner of a nomadic herding way of life, much as Jubal is linked with music and Tubal-cain with metalworking. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the description to mean that he led a wandering life. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give it as "stream," and Hitchcock's Bible Names as "which glides away." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a suggested link with a word for "ram," which would suit a herdsman. He is mentioned only in this one verse.

The Jabbok is a river east of the Jordan, which it joins roughly midway between the Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea. It is generally identified with the modern Zarqa River (Nahr ez-Zerqa, "blue river") in Jordan. Jacob crossed its ford by night with his wives, servants and eleven sons on his way back to Canaan (Gen 32:22). The following verses, Gen 32:24–30, place his wrestling with a mysterious figure there. The river later served as a boundary. The Amorite kingdom of Sihon stretched from the Arnon north to the Jabbok, which marked the border of the Ammonites (Num 21:24; Josh 12:2). Israel took this land but kept away from Ammonite territory along the river (Deut 2:37). It was given to Reuben and Gad (Deut 3:16). Centuries later the king of Ammon claimed the land between Arnon and Jabbok, and Jephthah disputed that claim (Judg 11:13, 22).

Jabesh is a shortened form of Jabesh-gilead, a town east of the Jordan in Gilead, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "dryness." When Nahash the Ammonite besieged it, its men offered to submit to him. The elders asked for seven days to seek help from Israel. When the news reached Saul, he promised relief by the next day (1 Sam 11:1–10). After Saul and his sons died, the valiant men of Jabesh marched all night to Beth-shan, recovered the bodies from the wall, burned them, buried the bones under a tree (an oak in 1 Chr 10:12) at Jabesh, and fasted seven days. By inference, they were repaying Saul's earlier rescue. The name probably survives in the Wadi Yabis in northern Jordan. Proposed sites include Tell Abu al-Kharaz and Tell el-Maqlub. The location shown here lies near the lower wadi toward the Jordan Valley.

Jabesh was the father of Shallum, who killed King Zachariah of Israel and took his throne. Zachariah is named in the surrounding passage and by Easton's Bible Dictionary. Jabesh appears only in the phrase "Shallum the son of Jabesh," which is repeated three times in the account. Shallum began to reign in the thirty-ninth year of Uzziah king of Judah and ruled in Samaria for just one month before Menahem son of Gadi came from Tirzah and killed him. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts Shallum as the fifteenth king of Israel. Nothing else is recorded about Jabesh himself. Some interpreters read "son of Jabesh" as pointing to Shallum's origin in the town of Jabesh in Gilead. This entry treats Jabesh as the name of his father. The name is usually taken to mean "dry" or "dryness."

Jabesh-gilead was a city in Gilead, east of the Jordan River. When it sent no one to the assembly at Mizpah against Benjamin, Israel's forces killed its inhabitants and spared 400 young women, who were given as wives to the surviving Benjamites (Judg 21:8–14). Later Nahash the Ammonite besieged it, and the people were promised help, which by inference from the surrounding chapter came from Saul (1 Sam 11:1, 9). After the Philistines killed Saul, the men of Jabesh-gilead took his and Jonathan's bodies from the wall of Beth-shan and buried them. David praised their kindness and later moved the bones (1 Sam 31:11; 2 Sam 2:4–5; 21:12). The ancient name probably survives in the Wadi Yabis. The exact site is debated. Proposals include ed-Deir and Meriamin near Pella (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). The location shown here lies about five miles south of Pella, broadly following Easton's Bible Dictionary.

Jabez was a place where several families of scribes lived, according to the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles. The verse names three of these families, the Tirathites, the Shimeathites and the Suchathites, and identifies them as Kenites descended from Hemath, the father of the house of Rechab. The site has not been identified. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it probably within Judah's territory. The location shown here is rough, near Bethlehem, probably by inference from the preceding verse (1 Chr 2:54), which lists Bethlehem among the descendants of Salma. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "sorrow" or "trouble." The place should not be confused with the man named Jabez in 1 Chr 4:9–10, though Smith's and other dictionaries note that the shared name may suggest some connection.

Jabez was a man named in the genealogies of Judah, described as more honorable than his brothers. His mother gave him his name because she bore him in sorrow. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains this as wordplay: the Hebrew name sounds like a word meaning "he causes pain," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "sorrow" or "trouble." Jabez prayed to the God of Israel, asking to be blessed, to have his territory enlarged, to have God's hand with him, and to be kept from harm so that it would not grieve him. The same play on sorrow appears in the prayer itself. The text records that God granted his request. His exact place in Judah's family line is not stated, but Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the passage sits within a genealogy connected with Bethlehem.

Jabin was a king of Hazor, a major Canaanite city in northern Canaan, when the Israelites entered the land under Joshua. When he heard of Israel's victories, he sent messages to Jobab king of Madon and to the kings of Shimron and Achshaph to form an alliance against Joshua (Josh 11:1). The rest of Joshua 11 tells how this northern coalition gathered at the waters of Merom and was defeated. Joshua then took Hazor, killed its king and burned the city. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes this battle as the last of Joshua's recorded battles and the crowning act of the conquest, and notes that here Israel first faced Canaanite horses and chariots. The name was also borne by a later king of Hazor who oppressed Israel in the time of Deborah and Barak (Judg 4). Whether the name was a dynastic title or the two were simply namesakes is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "he that understands."

Jabin (king of Hazor) was a Canaanite ruler, also called "king of Canaan," who reigned from Hazor in northern Israel and oppressed the Israelites during the time of the judges. Sisera, based at Harosheth of the Gentiles, commanded his army (Judg 4:2). Judg 4:3 adds that Jabin had nine hundred iron chariots and oppressed Israel for twenty years. This entry dates the oppression to about 1298 BC, by inference from context. Through Deborah, God promised Barak victory over Sisera's forces at the river Kishon. After that defeat, Sisera fled to the tent of Jael, because Jabin was at peace with the house of Heber the Kenite. Israel then pressed on until Jabin was destroyed, and Ps 83:9 later recalls his downfall. He shares his name and city with the king of Hazor defeated by Joshua (Josh 11:1–10). Easton's Bible Dictionary treats the two as separate kings.

Jabneel was a city near the Mediterranean coast that marked the western end of Judah's northern border. That boundary ran north past Ekron, through Shicron and Mount Baalah, then on to Jabneel before reaching the sea (Josh 15:11). The name probably means "God builds." It is very likely the same town as Jabneh, which Uzziah of Judah took from the Philistines and whose walls he broke down (2 Chr 26:6). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Josephus assigns it to the tribe of Dan. Easton's Bible Dictionary says the Greeks later called it Jamnia, and that after Jerusalem fell in AD 70 it became a large city and the seat of a famous school. The location shown here is modern Yavneh, about 11 miles south of Jaffa and a short distance inland. Another Jabneel, a border town of Naphtali in Galilee, is a separate place.

Jabneel was a town named as a landmark on the boundary of the tribe of Naphtali in Josh 19:33. It is listed with Adami and Nekeb along the border line, which ran on to Lakum and ended at the Jordan. The name is usually taken to mean "building of God" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). The same name was also used for a different town on the northern border of Judah, so the two should not be confused. Views on its site differ. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Kefr Yemmah, which it places on the south shore of Lake Merom in the far north. Others place it at modern Yavne'el, in the valley southwest of the Sea of Galilee. Smith's Bible Dictionary puts it in upper Galilee. The location shown here follows the Yavne'el identification.

Jabneh was a Philistine city whose wall was broken down by King Uzziah of Judah. The king is not named in the verse itself, but the surrounding chapter shows it is Uzziah. 2 Chr 26:6 records this campaign alongside his destruction of the walls of Gath and Ashdod and his building of towns in Philistine territory. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "building," while Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "building of God." Both dictionaries identify Jabneh with Jabneel, a town on the northern boundary of Judah near the Mediterranean coast (Josh 15:11). The city was probably the later Jamnia of the Greek period and is generally located at modern Yavne, south of Tel Aviv and inland from the coast. The location shown here follows that identification.

Jachan was a man of the tribe of Gad, named in 1 Chr 5:13 as one of seven kinsmen listed among the Gadites living in Bashan. His brothers were Michael, Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Zia and Heber, and the next verse names their father as Abihail. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe these seven as chief men or leading 'brothers' of Gad. Nothing else is recorded about him. By inference from the surrounding passage, which says the Gadite genealogies were recorded in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel (1 Chr 5:17), the STEPBible names index places him in Jotham's reign. The meaning of his name is uncertain: Easton's gives 'mourner', Smith's 'affliction', and Hitchcock's Bible Names 'wearing out; oppressing'.

Jachin was a son of Simeon and so a grandson of Jacob. He is listed fourth among Simeon's sons in the family that went down to Egypt with Jacob (Gen 46:10), and again in the genealogy of Exod 6:15. In the census of Numbers 26 he appears as the founder of the Jachinites, one of the clans of the tribe of Simeon (Num 26:12). The list in 1 Chr 4:24 gives the name Jarib in the same position. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take Jarib to be the same man, and Smith's Bible Dictionary calls this a possibility. That list also gives his brothers Jemuel and Zohar as Nemuel and Zerah. The name Jachin, meaning "he will establish," was also borne by other people in the Bible.

Jachin was a priest, or a priestly family, listed among those living in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. He appears beside Jedaiah and Jehoiarib (Joiarib) in the parallel lists of 1 Chr 9:10 and Neh 11:10. In Nehemiah the list names those who settled in Jerusalem when part of the returning population was chosen by lot to live in the city. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connect the name with Jachin, head of the twenty-first course of priests in David's time (1 Chr 24:17). On that view, the name here probably refers to the priestly family descended from that head rather than to a single man. The name probably means "he will establish." Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Jachin was the priest whose family was assigned the twenty-first of the twenty-four divisions of priests that took turns serving at the sanctuary, according to the arrangement credited to David in 1 Chronicles 24. The lots for these divisions were drawn among the descendants of Eleazar and Ithamar, the sons of Aaron. Jachin's name appears only in the list itself (1 Chr 24:17), between Jakim and Gamul, and nothing more is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as the head of this twenty-first course. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "he that strengthens and makes steadfast." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a son of Simeon and a priest of Nehemiah's time. Jachin is also the name of one of the bronze pillars at Solomon's temple. This entry refers only to the head of the priestly division.

Jacob was the son of Matthan and the father of Joseph, the husband of Mary, in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matt 1:15–16). He appears only in that list, which traces the royal line from David through Solomon, so he belonged to the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about his life. He is a different man from the patriarch Jacob, son of Isaac, whose name Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as meaning "that supplants" or "the heel." Luke's genealogy names Joseph's father as Heli (Luke 3:23), and the two lists differ for several generations. Some explain this by taking Luke's line as Mary's ancestry, others by a levirate marriage or an adoption that gave Joseph both a natural and a legal father. This entry follows Matthew's account, in which Jacob is Joseph's father.

Jada was a man of the tribe of Judah named only in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 2. He was a son of Onam and a brother of Shammai (1 Chr 2:28). He had two sons, Jether and Jonathan, and the text notes that Jether died without children (1 Chr 2:32). Onam is described in the surrounding verses as a son of Jerahmeel by his wife Atarah, so Jada belonged to the Jerahmeelite line of Judah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes this and calls him a grandson of Jerahmeel. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "knowing." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jadau was one of the descendants of Nebo listed in Ezra 10:43 among the Israelite men who had married foreign wives after the return from exile. The context of Ezra 10 shows that these men agreed, during Ezra's reforms, to send away their foreign wives. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the event to about 459 BC. The spelling of his name varies in the Hebrew text. The King James Version reads Jadau, while the Revised Version reads Iddo and gives "Jaddai" in the margin. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that 1 Esdras 9:35 calls him "Edos." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as "his hand" or "his confession," and Smith's gives "loving."

Jaddua was one of the chiefs of the people who set their seal to the written covenant in Nehemiah's time, when the community returned from exile pledged to keep the law of Moses. His name appears in the list of signers between Zadok and Meshezabeel's group (Neh 10:21). Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, meaning "known" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, is shared by several people in the Bible. These include a later high priest named Jaddua, who is listed among the descendants of Jeshua in Neh 12. This entry concerns only the lay leader who signed the covenant. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the sealing to about 410 BC, an estimate inferred from context.

Jaddua was a priest of the tribe of Levi in the line of high priests that descended from Eliashib, Nehemiah's contemporary. In Neh 12:11 he is called the son of Jonathan. Neh 12:22 lists the succession as Eliashib, Joiada, Johanan and Jaddua, so Jonathan and Johanan are probably the same man. That verse also says the heads of priestly and Levitical families were recorded up to the reign of "Darius the Persian." Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary call Jaddua the last high priest named in the Old Testament. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies this Darius as Darius III, the last Persian king, who was defeated by Alexander the Great. It also links Jaddua with Josephus's account of Alexander entering Jerusalem. His name means "known." Other people in the Bible share the name.

Jadon the Meronothite was one of the men who helped repair the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah. He worked alongside Melatiah the Gibeonite and the men of Gibeon and Mizpah, next to the section rebuilt by the men of Tekoa, on a stretch reaching toward the seat of the Persian governor of the province west of the Euphrates (Neh 3:7). The name probably means "he will judge" or "he will plead." The title "Meronothite" points to a place called Meronoth, but no such place is named elsewhere. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that another Meronothite, Jehdeiah, appears in 1 Chr 27:30, and that the Jewish historian Josephus gives the name Jadon to the unnamed man of God who confronted Jeroboam at Bethel. That figure is a different person from the wall builder. The work is dated to about 446 BC, by inference from context.

Jael was the wife of Heber the Kenite who killed Sisera, commander of the army of Jabin king of Hazor, after the Canaanites were defeated by Barak. Sisera fled on foot to her tent because Heber's household was at peace with Jabin (Judg 4:17). Jael went out, invited him in, told him not to be afraid and covered him with a mantle. While he lay asleep and exhausted, she drove a tent peg through his temples into the ground with a hammer. When Barak arrived in pursuit, she showed him Sisera lying dead (Judg 4:22). The Song of Deborah mentions "the days of Jael" as a time when the roads were deserted, and calls her "blessed above women" for the deed (Judg 5:24). Her name means "mountain goat" according to Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary.

Jagur was a town in the far south of Judah's tribal territory, toward the border of Edom. It appears only once, in the list of the southernmost cities of Judah in Josh 15:21, where it is named alongside Kabzeel and Eder. These towns lay in the Negev, the dry region in the south of the land. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "place of sojourn," and Smith's Bible Dictionary as "lodging." Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "husbandman" or "stranger." The site has not been identified, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the northern Negev, east of modern Beersheba, based on its position in the list of southern towns.

Jahath was a Levite of the Gershonite line, named as the first of four sons of Shimei in the list of Levite families drawn up in David's last years (1 Chr 23:10). His brothers were Zina (called Zizah in the next verse, probably the same person), Jeush and Beriah. Jahath is called the chief, or head, of these families, with Zizah second. Because Jeush and Beriah had few sons, their descendants were counted together as a single father's house (1 Chr 23:11). Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him a grandson of Gershom (Gershon), and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as head of a later house within the family of Gershom. Nothing further is recorded about him. The name Jahath belongs to several other men in the Bible, mostly Levites, and he should not be confused with them.

Jahath was a Levite, the son of Shelomoth, from the clan of the Izharites. He appears only once, in the list of Levite family heads in 1 Chr 24:22. That list belongs to the account of how the Levites were organized for temple service in David's time. Izhar was a son of Kohath, so Easton's Bible Dictionary places Jahath in the family of Kohath. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible bear the name Jahath, including other Levites in the Chronicles genealogies, and he should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "broken in pieces" or "descending," while Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "union."

Jahath was a Levite descended from Merari who lived in the reign of King Josiah of Judah. Together with Obadiah, another Merarite, he was one of the overseers of the workmen repairing the temple in Jerusalem. Zechariah and Meshullam, of the Kohathite line, also supervised the work, and the passage notes that the workmen did their job faithfully (2 Chr 34:12). By inference from the surrounding chapter, this was the temple restoration carried out in Josiah's eighteenth year. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates it to about 623 BC. Nothing more is known about him. Several other men named Jahath appear in Levite and Judahite genealogies, and this one should be kept distinct from them.

Jahaz was a city east of the Jordan, north of the Arnon River, where Sihon king of the Amorites gathered his army and fought Israel when he refused to let them pass through his land (Num 21:23; Deut 2:32). Israel won the battle and took his territory, an event Jephthah later recalled (Judg 11:20). Other passages call the town Jahaza, Jahazah or Jahzah, place it in Reuben's territory, and assign it to the Merarite Levites. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Moabite king Mesha's inscription claims he drove Israel's king out of Jahaz. By the prophets' time it was a Moabite town, named in oracles against Moab (Isa 15:4; Jer 48:34). Its site is uncertain. The location shown here follows the suggestion, reported by that encyclopedia, that it was at the ruins of Umm er-Rasas, north of Dibon.

Jahaziah son of Tikvah was one of the Israelites gathered in Jerusalem when Ezra called on those who had married foreign wives to separate from them after the return from exile. He is named only in Ezra 10:15, along with Jonathan son of Asahel, Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levite. The verse can be read two ways. The King James Version says he and Jonathan "were employed about this matter," which suggests they helped carry out the plan. Many modern translations read the Hebrew as saying they "stood against" it. STEPBible's Tyndale House name index takes that view, describing him as one of four men who opposed Ezra's order, and this entry follows that reading. Modern versions spell his name Jahzeiah, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "the vision of the Lord." Nothing else is known about him.

Jahaziel was one of the warriors who joined David at Ziklag, named in a list alongside Ismaiah the Gibeonite, Jeremiah, Johanan and Josabad the Gederathite (1 Chr 12:4). The surrounding chapter describes these men as coming to David while he was still kept away from Saul, and as kinsmen of Saul from the tribe of Benjamin. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper-names index treat him as a Benjamite. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that he may instead have been from Judah, since the place-name attached to Josabad points toward Judean territory. This entry follows the Benjamite reading of the list. Nothing more is recorded about him. His name is usually explained as "God sees" or "God watches over." Several other men in the Bible bear the same name and should not be confused with this warrior.

Jahaziel was a priest in the time of King David, named with Benaiah as one of the two priests who blew trumpets regularly before the ark of the covenant (1 Chr 16:6). The surrounding chapter places this appointment when David brought the ark to Jerusalem and set it in the tent he had prepared, arranging ongoing worship around it. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia associate him with the ark's removal to Jerusalem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes that major Greek manuscripts of the Septuagint read the name as "Uzziel" here. The name is usually explained as meaning "God sees." Several men in the Bible bear this name, and nothing beyond this single verse connects this priest to any of them.

Jahaziel was a Levite, the third of the four sons of Hebron, with Jeriah, Amariah and Jekameam as his brothers. Hebron belonged to the Kohathite branch of the tribe of Levi, so Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Jahaziel as a Kohathite. He is named only in two lists from the time of David: one dividing the Levites into their family groups for service at the house of the Lord (1 Chr 23:19), and a repeated list of Levitical families (1 Chr 24:23). By inference from that setting, he headed one of the Hebronite family lines in David's reign. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, often explained as "God sees," belongs to several different men in the Bible, and this Jahaziel should not be confused with them.

Jahaziel son of Zechariah was a Levite descended from Asaph, one of the families of temple musicians, who lived during the reign of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. His ancestry is traced through Zechariah, Benaiah, Jeiel and Mattaniah. When Judah faced invasion by the Moabites and Ammonites, the people gathered to seek the LORD, and the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jahaziel in the middle of the assembly. According to the verses that follow (2 Chr 20:15–17), he told Jehoshaphat and the people not to be afraid, because the battle was God's and they would not need to fight it. Easton's Bible Dictionary and other reference works describe him as encouraging the king against the invaders. His name is usually explained as "God sees." Several other men in the Bible share the name Jahaziel.

Jahaziel was the father of a family leader who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. Ezra 8:5 lists "the son of Jahaziel" among the sons of Shechaniah, along with three hundred men who traveled with him. The son's own name is not given in the Hebrew text as it stands. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the verse probably originally read "of the sons of Zattu, Shecaniah the son of Jahaziel," following the parallel list in 1 Esdras 8:32. On that reading Shecaniah is Jahaziel's son, not a more distant ancestor. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the return to before 459 BC. The name is usually explained as "God sees" or "God watches over." Several other men in the Bible share this name, and this Jahaziel is known only from this single verse.

Jahdai was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy of Caleb as the father of six sons: Regem, Jotham, Geshan (also spelled Gesham), Pelet, Ephah and Shaaph (1 Chr 2:47). This entry treats him as a son of Caleb, placing him among Caleb's many children in the same chapter. The verse names no parent for him and comes abruptly among the lists of sons born to Caleb's concubines, so his exact link to Caleb is unclear. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him a descendant of Caleb of the family of Hezron. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes two views: that Jahdai was another wife or concubine of Caleb, or, which it considers more likely, a descendant whose connecting name has dropped out of the text. His name has been explained as meaning "grasper" or "Yah leads." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jahdiel was one of the heads of family in the half-tribe of Manasseh that lived east of the Jordan. He appears only in 1 Chr 5:24, where he is the last of seven named leaders, alongside Epher, Ishi, Eliel, Azriel, Jeremiah and Hodaviah. All seven are described as mighty men of valor, famous men and heads of their fathers' houses. The surrounding verses place this group in the land stretching from Bashan toward Mount Hermon, and they go on to tell of the tribe's later unfaithfulness and its deportation by the Assyrians. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes his name to mean "God gives joy," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives a similar sense, "whom Jehovah makes joyful." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jahdo was a man of the tribe of Gad, named only once, in the genealogy of 1 Chr 5:14. He was the son of Buz and the father of Jeshishai. The line runs from him through Jeshishai, Michael, Gilead, Jaroah and Huri to Abihail, whose sons were Gadite clan leaders living in Gilead and Bashan. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a Gadite, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him a Gileadite, after the region where this branch of Gad lived. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's gives "united", and Hitchcock's Bible Names offers several possibilities, including "his joy".

Jahleel was the third of the three sons of Zebulun, and so a grandson of Jacob and Leah. His brothers were Sered and Elon. He is named among Jacob's descendants who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:14). In the census taken in the plains of Moab he appears as the ancestor of the Jahleelites, one of the three family groups of the tribe of Zebulun (Num 26:26). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that "son" in these lists may refer to a clan as much as to an individual. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "hoping in Jehovah," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "waiting for, or beseeching, or hope in, God."

Jahmai was a man of the tribe of Issachar, one of the six sons of Tola named in the tribal genealogy of 1 Chr 7:2, alongside Uzzi, Rephaiah, Jeriel, Jibsam and Shemuel. The verse calls these sons heads of their father's house and valiant men of might. It adds that in the days of David their descendants numbered 22,600, so Jahmai is probably remembered as the founder or head of a clan within the family of Tola. Tola himself is listed as a son of Issachar in 1 Chr 7:1. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be a shortened form meaning "may Yahweh protect," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "whom Jehovah guards." Hitchcock's Bible Names instead gives "warm" or "making warm."

Jahzah was a town east of the Jordan, in the territory of the tribe of Reuben, that was given with its pasturelands to the Levites. By context, it went to the Merari clan named in the surrounding passage (1 Chr 6:78). Smith's Bible Dictionary treats it as the same place as Jahaz, also spelled Jahaza and Jahazah. Connected passages tie Jahaz to the battle in which Israel defeated Sihon king of the Amorites (Num 21:23). Jeremiah later lists Jahazah among the towns of the Moabite plateau facing judgment, alongside Holon and Mephaath (Jer 48:21). This suggests the town had passed into Moabite hands by his time. Its exact site is uncertain, and several ruins north of the Arnon River have been proposed. The location shown here is on the plateau east of the Dead Sea in modern Jordan, east of Dhiban.

Jahzeel was the first-named of the four sons of Naphtali, and so a grandson of Jacob through Bilhah, Rachel's servant. His brothers were Guni, Jezer and Shillem. He is listed among the members of Jacob's household who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:24). In the census of the tribes taken in the wilderness he appears as the founder of the clan of the Jahzeelites within the tribe of Naphtali (Num 26:48). The genealogy in 1 Chronicles spells his name Jahziel and calls his brothers "the sons of Bilhah," meaning her descendants through Naphtali (1 Chr 7:13). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of the name as "allotted by God" or "whom God allots," while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "God hastens" or "divides." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jahzerah was a priest of the family of Immer, named only in a genealogy in 1 Chr 9:12. He was the son of Meshullam and an ancestor of Maasiai, one of the priests listed among those living in Jerusalem after the return from exile. In that verse his son is Adiel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies him with Ahasai (Ahzai) in the parallel list of Neh 11:13. There the line runs Amashai son of Azareel, son of Ahasai, son of Meshillemoth, son of Immer. On that identification his son would be Azareel, and Meshillemoth would match the Meshullam and Meshillemith of the Chronicles list. This entry follows that identification. Because the two lists differ in their names, the exact family links are uncertain.

Jair, in the phrase "the towns of Jair," is a region of small settlements east of the Jordan, listed in Josh 13:30 as part of the land given to the half-tribe of Manasseh. There they are described as sixty cities in Bashan, in a territory that ran from Mahanaim and took in the former kingdom of Og. The name comes from Jair, a descendant of Manasseh. The connected passages in Num 32:41 and Deut 3:14 say he captured these villages and named them after himself, Havoth-jair ("villages of Jair"). Those passages differ in where they place the towns, Deuteronomy in the Argob district of Bashan and Numbers in Gilead. STEPBible's proper-names index places them in Gilead. The exact extent of the region is uncertain, and the location shown here is only a rough point in northern Gilead.

Jair was the father of Elhanan, a warrior in David's time who killed a brother of Goliath the Gittite during a later war with the Philistines. The incident is recorded twice. 2 Sam 21:19 places the battle at Gob, calls Elhanan a Bethlehemite, and names his father Jaare-oregim. The parallel account in 1 Chr 20:5 names the father Jair and gives the slain giant's name as Lahmi. Both passages describe the giant's spear shaft as being like a weaver's beam. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the longer form as a copying slip: "oregim" means "weavers" and also appears at the end of the same verse in Hebrew, so it was probably repeated by mistake. This entry treats Jaare-oregim and Jair as one man. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is distinct from the other men named Jair in the Bible.

Jair was the son of Segub and a descendant of Judah through Hezron, who held twenty-three cities in Gilead (1 Chr 2:22). He is also called "the son of Manasseh", probably because, as 1 Chr 2:21 explains, his grandfather Hezron married a daughter of Machir son of Manasseh. When Israel was settling the land east of the Jordan, Jair captured small towns in Gilead and named them Havoth-jair, "the villages of Jair" (Num 32:41). He also took the whole region of Argob in Bashan as far as the borders of the Geshurites and Maachathites, and the name Bashan-havoth-jair lasted afterward (Deut 3:14). In Solomon's time, the towns of Jair and the region of Argob belonged to the administrative district of the son of Geber at Ramoth-gilead (1 Kgs 4:13). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a tradition identifying him with the judge Jair of Judg 10:3–4. Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Jair was a man from Gilead, east of the Jordan, who judged Israel for twenty-two years after Tola (Judg 10:3). His judgeship is dated here to about 1192 BC, an estimate inferred from context. The next verse, Judg 10:4, adds that he had thirty sons who rode thirty donkeys and held thirty towns in Gilead known as Havoth-jair. He died and was buried in Camon (Judg 10:5), a place whose location is uncertain but was probably in Gilead. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "my light" or "who diffuses light." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a descendant of Manasseh who captured towns in Gilead and the father of Mordecai. This entry concerns the judge.

Jair was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, known only as the father of Mordecai, the Jew who lived in Shushan, the Persian royal city, in the book of Esther. Esth 2:5 traces Mordecai's line as "the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish," so Jair was the son of Shimei. Some readers take Shimei and Kish to be more distant, well-known ancestors rather than Jair's immediate father and grandfather, since biblical genealogies sometimes skip generations. Nothing else is recorded about Jair's life. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "enlightener." Several other people in the Bible share the name Jair, and this entry concerns only Mordecai's father.

Jairus was a ruler of a synagogue in Galilee who came to Jesus, fell at his feet and begged him to come to his house (Mark 5:22; Luke 8:41). The surrounding accounts in Mark 5 and Luke 8 tell why. His only daughter, about twelve years old, was dying. On the way to the house Jesus healed a woman who had suffered from bleeding, and meanwhile word came that the girl had died. Jesus went in with Peter, James, John and the girl's parents, raised her to life, and told them to give her something to eat. Matthew 9 tells the same story without naming the father. The town is not named in these verses. Easton's Bible Dictionary places the synagogue at Capernaum, while Smith's Bible Dictionary says only that it was probably in a town near the western shore of the Sea of Galilee.

Jakeh was the father of Agur, whose sayings make up Proverbs 30. He is named only once, in the heading of that chapter (Prov 30:1), and nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "pious." The Hebrew of the verse is difficult. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that the word translated "the prophecy" may instead mean "of Massa" or "the Massaite." Massa was the name of an Ishmaelite tribe and its country (compare Gen 25:14; Prov 31:1). On that reading, Jakeh and his son would have belonged to that people rather than to Israel. Whether that is so cannot be settled from the single verse.

Jakim was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the genealogy of Benjamin's descendants in 1 Chr 8:19. He is listed as one of the sons of Shimhi, alongside his brothers Adaiah, Beraiah, Eliel, Elienai, Shimrath, Zabdi, Zichri and Zilthai. Shimhi appears to be the same man called Shimei elsewhere, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes Jakim as a son of Shimei. The passage says nothing more about him beyond his place in the family list. The name probably means "he (God) lifts up" or "God establishes," and it is related to the name Eliakim. Several people in the Bible bear the name Jakim, so this Benjamite should not be confused with others of the same name, such as the priest of that name in David's time.

Jakim was a priest whose name was given to the twelfth of the twenty-four divisions, or courses, into which the priests were organized to take turns serving at the sanctuary (1 Chr 24:12). The assignment was made by lot under David, as the surrounding chapter describes, and he is presumably the head of that family or division. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name probably means "he (God) raises up" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), and it is shared by another man in the Bible, a Benjamite listed in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 8. This entry concerns only the priest.

Jalon was the last-named of the four sons of Ezra listed in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chr 4:17. His brothers were Jether, Mered and Epher. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he appears nowhere else in the Bible. This Ezra is a different man from the later scribe of the same name, and some reference works, including the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, spell his name Ezrah. Placing Jalon in the tribe of Judah follows from the surrounding genealogy, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Easton's gives "lodger", Smith's Bible Dictionary "abiding" and Hitchcock's Bible Names "tarrying" or "murmuring". The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the meaning as unknown.

Jambres is named once in the Bible, in 2 Tim 3:8, where Paul pairs him with Jannes as men who "withstood Moses." Paul uses the two as an example of people who resist the truth, comparing them to false teachers of his own day. The verse gives no further detail, but by inference from the Exodus account, Jannes and Jambres are usually taken to be among Pharaoh's magicians who copied Moses' early signs in Egypt (Exod 7:11, 22). Exodus does not name those magicians. The names seem to come from Jewish tradition, which Paul draws on here. The STEPBible proper-names index describes Jambres as an Egyptian magician who opposed Moses alongside Jannes. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "poverty," "bitter," or "a rebel."

James (Son of Zebedee) was one of the twelve apostles, a fisherman and the brother of John. Jesus called the two brothers while they were mending nets in a boat with their father Zebedee, and they worked as partners with Simon Peter. Jesus gave James and John the name Boanerges, “sons of thunder.” With Peter and John, James belonged to an inner group that Jesus took with him to the raising of Jairus’s daughter, the Transfiguration and Gethsemane, and he was among those who questioned Jesus privately on the Mount of Olives. He and John once asked Jesus to grant whatever they wanted, angering the other ten, and offered to call down fire on a village that rejected Jesus. Herod killed him with the sword, the first recorded death among the Twelve. This entry dates it about AD 40 by inference. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives AD 44, identifies the king as Herod Agrippa and names his mother as Salome.

James (Son of Alphaeus) was one of the twelve apostles chosen by Jesus. He appears in every list of the Twelve, named by his father Alphaeus, which sets him apart from James son of Zebedee. After the ascension he was among the eleven in the upper room in Jerusalem, where Matthias was later chosen to replace Judas Iscariot. This entry treats him as the brother of Thaddaeus. That reading takes the King James phrase "Judas the brother of James" (Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13) to refer to him, with Luke's Judas matching Thaddaeus in the other lists. The Greek can also mean "son of James," as the STEPBible proper-names index takes it. Since Levi is also called son of Alphaeus (Mark 2:14), the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the two may have been brothers. Many identify him with James "the Less" (Mark 15:40), and Easton's Bible Dictionary also identifies him with James the Lord's brother.

James (Brother of Jesus) is named first among the brothers of Jesus, with Joses, Simon and Judas (Matt 13:55; Mark 6:3). This entry treats him as a son of Joseph and Mary. Paul calls him "the Lord's brother" and says the risen Jesus appeared to him (Gal 1:19; 1 Cor 15:7). He became a leader of the Jerusalem church. Peter sent word to him after escaping prison, he spoke decisively at the Jerusalem Council, and Paul reported to him and the elders (Acts 12:17; 15:13; 21:18). Paul names him with Cephas and John as "pillars" (Gal 2:9). He is taken as the author of the letter of James, and Jude calls himself his brother (Jas 1:1; Jude 1:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary instead identifies him with the apostle James son of Alphaeus, "James the Less," a cousin of Jesus. This entry links him to the "Mary the mother of James and Joses" at the cross (Mark 15:40).

Jamin was a son of Simeon and so a grandson of Jacob. He is listed second among Simeon's sons, after Jemuel (called Nemuel in Num 26:12 and 1 Chr 4:24), in the list of Jacob's family that went down to Egypt (Gen 46:10) and again in the family list in Exodus 6:15. His brothers are given as Jemuel, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar and Shaul, though 1 Chr 4:24 gives a shorter list that includes Jarib and Zerah. Zerah is probably another form of Zohar, and Jarib probably another form of Jachin. Jamin founded a clan within the tribe of Simeon, the Jaminites, who were counted in the census in Num 26:12. His name means "right hand" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this entry concerns only Simeon's son.

Jamin was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:27 as one of the three sons of Ram, the firstborn of Jerahmeel. His brothers were Maaz and Eker, and he is listed second, between them. This made him a grandson of Jerahmeel, whose line forms one branch of Judah's descendants in the Chronicles genealogies. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name means "right hand" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Hitchcock's Bible Names also gives "south wind." Several other people in the Bible share the name, including a son of Simeon and a Levite who helped explain the law in Ezra's time. This entry concerns only the Judahite descendant of Jerahmeel.

Jamin was one of the men named in Neh 8:7 who helped the people understand the law when Ezra read it publicly in Jerusalem after the return from exile. He is listed with Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah, Akkub and others, alongside the Levites, while the people stood in their places. The wording leaves open whether these named men were themselves Levites. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper names list treat him as a Levite, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds a question mark and notes that 1 Esdras 9:48 gives the name as Iadinus. His name means "right hand." This is his only mention, and he should be kept distinct from others of the same name, such as the son of Simeon.

Jamlech was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named in a list of Simeonite clan leaders in 1 Chr 4:34. Nothing else is recorded about him personally. The surrounding passage describes these men as princes in their families whose households grew large. According to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, if the account in 1 Chr 4:41 refers back to this list, he lived in the time of King Hezekiah. That verse tells how the Simeonites moved out in search of pasture and took land near Gedor. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "whom God makes king," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia as "may he (God) cause to reign."

Janim was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed among the cities given to the tribe of Judah in Josh 15:53, where the King James Version spells it Janum. It appears in a group of towns with Beth-tappuah and Aphekah, in the uplands around Hebron. Nothing else is recorded about it. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "slumber." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the site as unidentified. The location shown here follows an identification with the modern village of Bani Naim, east of Hebron, which fits the town's place in the Hebron hill-country list.

Janna was an ancestor of Jesus named only in the genealogy in Luke's Gospel (Luke 3:24). He is listed as the son of Joseph and the father of Melchi. This Joseph is several generations before Mary's husband Joseph and is a different man. Janna falls in the stretch of Luke's list between the return from exile and the time of Jesus, and nothing else is recorded about him. Because Luke traces this line back through David, he is counted with the tribe of Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the Revised Version spells the name Jannai and gives its meaning as "flourishing." Hitchcock's Bible Names connects it with Jannes and offers meanings such as "who speaks or answers" or "afflicted."

Jannes is named in the Bible only once, in 2 Tim 3:8, where Paul pairs him with Jambres as men who "withstood Moses." Paul uses the two as an example of people who oppose the truth, comparing them with corrupt men of his own day. The verse does not say who they were. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary identify Jannes and Jambres as Egyptian magicians at Pharaoh's court, linking them by inference with the unnamed magicians of Exod 7, who copied Moses' and Aaron's signs, such as turning rods into serpents. The Old Testament never gives the magicians' names. Paul probably drew the names from Jewish tradition current in his time, which remembered Jannes and Jambres as Moses' chief opponents in Egypt.

Janoah (spelled Janohah in the King James Version) was a city on the boundary of Ephraim's territory. Joshua 16 traces the border east from Michmethah past Taanath-shiloh to Janohah, then down to Ataroth and Naarath, reaching Jericho and ending at the Jordan (Josh 16:6–7). The name probably means "resting place" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Its location is debated. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place this border town at Yanun (Khirbet Yanun), southeast of Nablus, near the Jordan valley. The location shown here is Yanouh in southern Lebanon, a site often connected with another Janoah in Naphtali that Tiglath-pileser captured (2 Kgs 15:29). This entry follows the Yanouh identification. Because several places in the Bible share this name, which references belong to which town is not always certain.

Janoah was a city taken by Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria during the reign of Pekah king of Israel. Its people were deported to Assyria along with those of Ijon, Abel-beth-maachah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead and Galilee (2 Kgs 15:29). The name means "resting place," and it is shared by more than one biblical town, so its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary place it in the north, in the territory of Naphtali, because it is listed with northern towns. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the village of Yanuch, about 6 miles east of Tyre. Another view links it with Yanun, southeast of modern Nablus, the site usually identified with the Janohah on Ephraim's border (Josh 16:6–7). The location shown here follows the Yanun identification.

Japheth was one of the three sons of Noah, usually listed last after Shem and Ham (Gen 5:32; 6:10). He and his wife entered the ark with Noah's family and came out after the Flood (Gen 7:13; 9:18). When Noah lay drunk and uncovered, Japheth and Shem walked backward with a garment and covered him without looking. Noah then said, "God shall enlarge Japheth," adding that he would dwell in the tents of Shem (Gen 9:23, 27). The name probably plays on the Hebrew for "enlarge," though Easton's Bible Dictionary also notes a derivation meaning "beautiful" or "fair." Gen 10:21 can be read as calling either Shem or Japheth the elder, so his birth order is uncertain. His seven sons were Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech and Tiras (Gen 10:2; 1 Chr 1:5). Smith's Bible Dictionary links his descendants with the Mediterranean coastlands, Europe and much of Asia.

Japhia was a town on the boundary of Zebulun's territory. In Josh 19:12 the border runs from Sarid east to Chisloth-tabor, out to Daberath and then up to Japhia. The following verse, not shown here, continues the line on toward Gath-hepher. The verb "goeth up" suggests the town stood on higher ground than Daberath. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the modern village of Yafa, about 1.5–2 miles (2.5–3 km) southwest of Nazareth near the foot of the hills, and the location shown here follows that identification. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds that the Jewish historian Josephus fortified the place during the war with Rome in the first century AD. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "enlightening" or "appearing." This is a different place from Japhia, the king of Lachish, and from Japhia, the son of David.

Japhia was king of Lachish when the Israelites entered Canaan under Joshua. After Gibeon made peace with Israel, Adonizedek king of Jerusalem appealed to him and to the kings of Hebron, Jarmuth and Eglon to join forces against Gibeon (Josh 10:3). The rest of the chapter tells how these five Amorite kings attacked Gibeon, were routed by Joshua, hid in a cave at Makkedah, and were then put to death. Japhia is not named again, but he is probably one of those five kings. The name is shared by other people in the Bible, including a son of David, so this Japhia should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "enlightening" or "appearing."

Japhia was one of the sons of King David born to him in Jerusalem, after David had moved his capital there from Hebron. He appears only in the three lists of these sons (2 Sam 5:15; 1 Chr 3:7; 1 Chr 14:6), always named next to his brother Nepheg. Nothing else is recorded about his life. The lists in Chronicles, though not the one in 2 Samuel, also include a brother Nogah. According to 1 Chronicles 3, the sons born in Jerusalem included Solomon and Nathan, sons of Bathsheba, and the other sons are not assigned to particular mothers there, so Japhia's mother is unknown. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may mean "tall," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "enlightening" or "appearing." The name is also borne by other people in the Bible, including a king of Lachish, and they should not be confused with this son of David.

Japhlet was a man of the tribe of Asher, named in the Asherite genealogy in 1 Chronicles. He was a son of Heber, and his brothers were Shomer (also spelled Shamer) and Hotham, with a sister named Shua (1 Chr 7:32). His own sons were Pasach, Bimhal and Ashvath (1 Chr 7:33). The surrounding verses (1 Chr 7:30–31) make Heber a son of Beriah and grandson of Asher, so Japhlet was a great-grandson of Asher. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains his name as meaning "whom God delivers," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia tentatively gives "he escapes." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jarah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, a descendant of King Saul, named in the genealogy of Saul's family as the son of Ahaz and the father of Alemeth, Azmaveth and Zimri. Through Zimri his line continued to Moza and later generations. The surrounding verses (1 Chr 9:39–41; 8:33–35) trace his ancestry back through Ahaz, Micah and Merib-baal (Mephibosheth) to Jonathan, Saul's son. The same genealogy appears twice. In 1 Chr 8:36 he is called Jehoadah, and in 1 Chr 9:42 Jarah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint and some Hebrew manuscripts read Jadah in the second passage. It suggests this is probably the original form, a shortened equivalent of Jehoadah. His name may mean "honeycomb." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jared was one of the patriarchs before the Flood in the line of Seth, the son of Mahalaleel and the father of Enoch, who in turn fathered Methuselah. Genesis records that his father was 65 when Jared was born, that Jared was 162 when Enoch was born, and that he lived another 800 years and had other sons and daughters. He died at 962 years, the second-longest lifespan recorded in the Bible after Methuselah's. The King James Version spells his name Jered in the genealogy of 1 Chr 1:2, and Luke includes him among the ancestors of Jesus. The name is usually taken to mean "descent" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). That work also notes a proposed link with Irad in Cain's line (Gen 4:18). By inference from the genealogy's figures, his life is dated here to about 3544–2582 BC.

Jaresiah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the Benjamite genealogy as one of the sons of Jeroham (1 Chr 8:27). His brothers are listed in the same passage as Shamsherai, Shehariah, Athaliah, Eliah and Zichri. The list belongs to a register of Benjamite family heads who lived in Jerusalem, according to the surrounding verses of the chapter. Nothing else is recorded about him. Modern translations spell the name Jaareshiah, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats Jaresiah as the King James form of that name. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "whom Jehovah nourishes."

Jarha was an Egyptian servant of Sheshan, a member of the Jerahmeelite clan of the tribe of Judah. Sheshan had daughters but no sons, so he gave one of his daughters to Jarha as his wife, and she bore him a son, Attai (1 Chr 2:34–35). The daughter is not named in these verses. This entry identifies her as Ahlai, by inference from 1 Chr 2:31, where Ahlai is listed as Sheshan's child even though Sheshan had no sons. The genealogy that follows in 1 Chronicles 2 traces a long line of descendants through Attai. For this reason the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes Jarha as the founder of a house within the Jerahmeelites. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him around the time of Eli, but the text itself gives no date. The meaning of his name is unknown.

Jarib was one of the "chief men" Ezra summoned while his company of returning exiles was camped by the river Ahava on the way from Babylon to Jerusalem (Ezra 8:16). The surrounding passage explains why. Ezra had found no Levites among the travelers, so he sent these leaders, along with two "men of understanding," to Iddo at Casiphia to bring back ministers to serve in the Temple (Ezra 8:15–17). The STEPBible names index and Easton's Bible Dictionary both describe him this way. Nothing else is told about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the journey to 469 BC. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives meanings for the name such as "fighting" or "chiding." The same name belongs to other people, including a son of Simeon (1 Chr 4:24) and a priest of the family of Jeshua (Ezra 10:18). Whether that priest is the same man as this Jarib is uncertain.

Jarib was a priest in Ezra's time, one of several men of that name in the Bible. He belonged to the priestly family of Jeshua son of Jozadak, the high priest who had led the return from exile. Ezra 10:18 lists him with Maaseiah, Eliezer and Gedaliah among the priests found to have married foreign wives. The following verse records that these men pledged to send their wives away and offered a ram as a guilt offering. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 459 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies him with Joribus in the parallel account in 1 Esdras 9:19, and explains the name as meaning "he contends" or "he takes our part."

Jarmuth was a Canaanite city in the Shephelah, the low hill country of Judah. Its king, Piram, joined Adonizedek of Jerusalem and the kings of Hebron, Lachish and Eglon in attacking Gibeon after it made peace with Israel. Joshua defeated the five kings, and they were later brought out of the cave where they had hidden. The surrounding narrative says they were put to death. Jarmuth appears among the cities whose kings Joshua defeated and was later allotted to Judah, listed with Adullam, Socoh and Azekah. After the exile, people of Judah settled there again. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with Khirbet el-Yarmuk (Tel Yarmut), about 8 miles north-northeast of Beit Jibrin, and the location shown here follows that identification. Another Jarmuth, in Issachar, is a separate place.

Jarmuth was a city in the territory of Issachar that was given, with its surrounding pasturelands, to the Levites. In Josh 21:29 it is one of four Issachar cities in the list, alongside Engannim. By inference from the surrounding passage, it went to the Gershonite clan of Levites, and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes it that way. The parallel list in 1 Chronicles 6 gives Ramoth in this position, and Josh 19:21 names a Remeth among Issachar's towns, so these are probably the same place under different spellings. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that some have connected it with the Ramah of Samuel. Several places in the Bible share the name Jarmuth. This one is distinct from the Canaanite royal city of Jarmuth in the lowlands of Judah. Its exact site is uncertain, and the location shown here is only a rough position near the Jezreel Valley in Issachar's territory.

Jaroah was a man of the tribe of Gad, named only once, in a genealogy in 1 Chr 5:14. He was the son of Gilead and the father of Huri. The line runs on to Huri's son Abihail, whose descendants were Gadite family heads living in the land of Bashan and Gilead east of the Jordan. This Gilead appears to be a Gadite descendant of Buz, not the better-known Gilead son of Machir of the tribe of Manasseh. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls Jaroah a chief man of Gad and gives the meaning of his name as "moon". The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says the meaning is unknown and notes that the text of this genealogy may not have been preserved accurately. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jashen is a man named in the list of David's elite warriors known as "the thirty" (2 Sam 23:32). The King James text reads "of the sons of Jashen," which suggests that several of his sons served among David's mighty men, as Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it. The parallel list in 1 Chr 11:34 gives the name as Hashem and calls him "the Gizonite." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia offers another reading. It suggests that "sons of" arose from a copying error that repeated the last letters of the word before it. On that reading Jashen, possibly "the Gunite," was himself one of the thirty. This entry treats him as the father named in the King James wording, while noting that the text is uncertain. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is usually taken to mean "sleeping."

Jasher is the name in the title of "the book of Jasher," a lost writing quoted twice in the Old Testament. The name means "upright," and early translations render the title "the Book of the Upright One" or "the Book of Just Ones," so it may describe the book's subject rather than name an author. Nothing else is known of any person called Jasher, and whether one existed is uncertain. The book is cited as the source of the account of the sun standing still during Joshua's battle against the Amorites (Josh 10:13). It is also cited as the source of David's lament over Saul and Jonathan, known as the Song of the Bow (2 Sam 1:18). Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it was probably a national collection of songs praising Israel's heroes. Smith's Bible Dictionary adds that it was probably written in verse and is wholly lost.

Jashobeam was one of David's leading warriors. He is named first among David's mighty men and called a Hachmonite and "the chief of the captains" (some translations read "chief of the three"). He is said to have used his spear against three hundred men, killing them at one time (1 Chr 11:11). The parallel list in 2 Sam 23:8 names this hero Josheb-basshebeth the Tachmonite and gives the number as eight hundred. A Jashobeam son of Zabdiel commanded the first of David's twelve monthly army divisions, with 24,000 men (1 Chr 27:2). This entry treats him as the same man as the chief warrior, as Easton's Bible Dictionary does. Because the name was shared by several people, the identification is not certain. A Korhite Jashobeam who joined David at Ziklag (1 Chr 12:6) may also be the same person, though the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that opinions differ.

Jashobeam was one of five Korahites, listed with Elkanah, Jesiah, Azareel and Joezer, who joined David (1 Chr 12:6). The surrounding chapter describes the men who came to David at Ziklag while he was keeping away from Saul, and STEPBible's proper-names index places this Jashobeam among them. The name belongs to several men in the Bible. This one is usually kept separate from Jashobeam the chief of David's mighty men and commander of a monthly division, though the two are sometimes identified. Here "Korhites" probably means descendants of Korah, the Levite family. Some suggest it could instead refer to a Benjamite place or clan, since the chapter lists Benjamites just before. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the people sitting" or "captivity of the people." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jashub was the third of the four sons of Issachar, and so a grandson of Jacob, listed with his brothers Tola, Puah and Shimron (1 Chr 7:1). In the list of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt he is called Job (Gen 46:13). The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation, reads Jashub there, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. In the census of the tribes in the wilderness he is named as the ancestor of the Jashubites, one of the clans of the tribe of Issachar (Num 26:24). The name is usually taken to mean "he returns." Nothing further is recorded about his life. The same name is borne by at least one other man in the Bible, so the references need to be kept apart.

Jashub was a man of the family of Bani, listed among the Israelites in Ezra's time who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:29). By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was one of those who agreed to send away these wives after Ezra led the returned exiles in confessing intermarriage with neighboring peoples. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 459 BC, an estimate inferred from context. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same man appears as "Jasubus" in the apocryphal book 1 Esdras 9:30. His name is usually explained as meaning "he returns." Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Jashub is also borne by other people in the Bible, among them a son of Issachar, and this entry concerns only the man named in Ezra.

Jasiel the Mesobaite is the last name in the list of David's mighty warriors in 1 Chr 11:47, where he appears alongside Eliel and Obed. The verse gives no further details about him. "Mesobaite" probably refers to his hometown or clan, but the place is otherwise unknown. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "whom God made." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he is probably the same man as Jaasiel son of Abner, whom 1 Chr 27:21 names as leader of the tribe of Benjamin under David. If so, he would be the son of Saul's army commander Abner. That identification rests on the similar names and is not certain, and this entry treats it as a possibility only.

Jason was a resident of Thessalonica who hosted Paul and Silas during their stay there. Jews who rejected Paul's preaching stirred up a mob that attacked Jason's house looking for the missionaries. When they could not find them, they dragged Jason and some other believers before the city rulers. They accused him of harboring men who acted against Caesar's decrees by proclaiming another king, Jesus. The rulers took security from Jason and the others and then released them. By inference, this pledge was linked to the missionaries leaving the city, since they departed that night (Acts 17:10). A Jason is also among Paul's "kinsmen" who send greetings in Rom 16:21. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take him to be probably the same man. Smith's also notes a conjecture that he is the Secundus of Acts 20:4. The name was a common Greek form used by Jews named Joshua.

Jathniel was a Levite, the fourth son of Meshelemiah, named in the list of temple gatekeepers in 1 Chr 26:2. His brothers were Zechariah the firstborn, Jediael, Zebadiah, Elam, Jehohanan and Elioenai. The surrounding verse (1 Chr 26:1) places Meshelemiah's family among the Korahites, the Levite clan descended from Korah. By inference from the context of the chapter, the family served as gatekeepers in the arrangements for temple service made late in David's reign, as the STEPBible Proper Names index also describes him. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 1014 BC, an estimate drawn from context. The meaning of his name is uncertain: Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "whom God gives" and Hitchcock's Bible Names "gift of God", while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "God lives." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jattir was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed with Shamir and Socoh in the territory allotted to the tribe (Josh 15:48). It was later given, with its surrounding pasturelands, to the descendants of Aaron the priest as one of the Levitical cities, alongside Eshtemoa and Hebron (Josh 21:14; 1 Chr 6:57). After defeating the Amalekites, David sent part of the spoil from Ziklag to the people of Jattir, among other towns of Judah (1 Sam 30:27). The name is usually taken to mean "pre-eminent" or "excellent." Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with Khirbet 'Attir, a ruin full of caves at the southern edge of the Judean hills, about ten miles south of Hebron. The ISBE links it with the "very large village Jethira" described by Eusebius. The location shown here matches that general area.

Javan is a distant land named among the nations in Isaiah and Ezekiel. In Isa 66:19 it appears with Tarshish, Pul, Lud and Tubal among faraway peoples, near "the isles afar off," to whom survivors would be sent to declare God's glory. In Ezek 27:13 Javan, Tubal and Meshech are traders who supplied Tyre's market with slaves and bronze vessels. The name is generally taken to mean the Greeks, especially the Ionians of the Aegean coast of Asia Minor. It is probably connected with Javan, son of Japheth, in the table of nations (Gen 10:2). The location shown here is in Ionia, near ancient Ephesus in western Turkey, and represents the wider region rather than one exact site. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "deceiver" or "one who makes sad."

Javan was a son of Japheth and grandson of Noah. He is listed fourth among Japheth's seven sons, alongside Gomer, Magog, Madai, Tubal, Meshech and Tiras, and was the father of Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim and Dodanim (Gen 10:2–4; 1 Chr 1:5, 7). Like many names in this list, Javan also stands for a people and land descended from him. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the Greeks, especially the Ionians, and the name is later used for Greece.
