Isaiah names Javan among distant nations, and Ezekiel lists it among the trading partners of Tyre, dealing in slaves and bronze goods (Isa 66:19; Ezek 27:13). The Javan in Ezek 27:19 trades iron and spices. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take that one to be a separate place, possibly in southern Arabia.

Jazer (also spelled Jaazer) was an Amorite city east of the Jordan. Moses sent men to spy it out, and Israel took its surrounding villages and drove out the Amorites (Num 21:32). Its land was good for cattle, and the tribes of Reuben and Gad asked for it. Gad rebuilt it (Num 32:1, 35), and it marked part of Gad's border (Josh 13:25). It was later given with its pasturelands to the Levites (Josh 21:39). Joab's census team passed toward it (2 Sam 24:5), and in David's fortieth year capable men of the Hebronites were found at 'Jazer of Gilead' (1 Chr 26:31). Isaiah and Jeremiah mention it in their laments over Moab's vineyards (Isa 16:8–9; Jer 48:32). Its site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary favors a ruin about 10 miles west of Amman, while others suggest Yajuz to the north. The location shown here follows a site west of Amman.

Jaziz was a Hagerite (Hagrite) who oversaw King David's flocks, probably sheep and goats. He is named in a list of the officials who managed the king's property, each responsible for a different part of the royal estate, such as the treasuries, fields, vineyards, olive groves, herds, camels and donkeys (1 Chr 27:31). His title, "Hagerite," links him to the Hagrites, a people group, so he was probably not an Israelite by descent, though the passage itself does not say so. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "whom God moves," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls the meaning uncertain. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jeaterai was a Levite of the Gershonite branch, the son of Zerah, named at the end of a line of descent from Gershom in 1 Chr 6:21. He is generally identified with Ethni, son of Zerah, who appears in the ancestry of Asaph the singer in 1 Chr 6:41. There Ethni's son is Malchiah (1 Chr 6:40). The two lists differ in places: Zerah's father is Iddo in one and Adaiah in the other. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the two names in separate entries. The Tyndale House proper-names index identifies them as one man, and this entry follows that view. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of Jeaterai as "searching out." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives Ethni as "gift." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jeberechiah was the father of Zechariah, one of the two reliable witnesses Isaiah chose to attest a written record. The other was Uriah the priest (Isa 8:2). From the surrounding passage, the record was the large tablet inscribed with the words "Maher-shalal-hash-baz." This was a sign that Damascus and Samaria would soon be plundered, and it was later given as the name of Isaiah's son. The events fall in the reign of King Ahaz of Judah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places them around 734 BC, an estimate drawn from context. Nothing else is recorded about Jeberechiah himself, and his name appears only in this verse. It means "the LORD blesses." Some have linked his son with the Zechariah whose daughter Abi was Hezekiah's mother (2 Kgs 18:2), but the text does not make this connection, and it remains uncertain.

Jebus was the city of the Jebusites, identified in the Bible with Jerusalem (Judg 19:10; 1 Chr 11:4). In Joshua's allotment it appears as "Jebusi, which is Jerusalem" among the cities of Benjamin (Josh 18:28). In Judges a Levite traveling home with his concubine passed by Jebus late in the day but refused to lodge in a city of foreigners (Judg 19:10–11). Its inhabitants later told David he could not enter, but he captured the stronghold of Zion, which became the city of David (1 Chr 11:4–5). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as a naturally strong fortress and calls its capture one of David's great achievements. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name Jerusalem is attested centuries before David, so Jebus was probably an alternate name taken from the Jebusites rather than the city's original name. The location shown here is ancient Jerusalem.

Jebusite, as a place name, refers in Josh 15:8 to the city of the Jebusites, which the verse identifies as Jerusalem. The passage describes the northern border of Judah's territory running up the valley of the son of Hinnom along the south side of the Jebusite city, then to the top of the mountain west of the Hinnom valley. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains that the Jebusites were the original inhabitants of Jebus, the older name of Jerusalem. It notes that they were not fully driven out until David captured the city and made it his capital in place of Hebron. The location shown here follows the identification with ancient Jerusalem, near the southeastern hill of the present Old City area, just above the Hinnom valley.

Jebusite is listed in the Table of Nations as a son, or descendant, of Canaan, the son of Ham. He appears alongside the Amorite, the Girgasite and other Canaanite groups (Gen 10:16; 1 Chr 1:14). The name works both as an individual ancestor and as the people who claimed descent from him. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies them as the original inhabitants of Jebus, the city later known as Jerusalem, and notes that they appear often among the nations of Canaan the Israelites were to dispossess. According to the same dictionary, their king Adonizedek was defeated by Joshua (Josh 10:1, 23). The Jebusites held Jebus until David captured it and made it his capital. David later bought from Araunah the Jebusite the site where the temple was afterwards built (2 Sam 24:16–25; 1 Chr 21:24–25).

Jecamiah was a son of Jehoiachin (also called Jeconiah), the king of Judah who was taken captive to Babylon. He is named only once, in the royal genealogy of David's line at 1 Chr 3:18, alongside his brothers Malchiram, Pedaiah, Shenazar, Hoshama and Nedabiah. Shealtiel and Zedekiah also appear among Jehoiachin's sons in the surrounding verses. Since Jehoiachin spent most of his life in exile, Jecamiah was probably born or raised in Babylon, by inference from context. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes these men as adopted into the royal line after Jehoiachin's line failed; this entry follows the plain reading of the genealogy and lists him as Jehoiachin's son. Modern translations spell the name Jekamiah. It is usually explained as meaning "the Lord gathers" or "the Lord establishes." Another man named Jekamiah appears in an earlier genealogy of Judah (1 Chr 2:41) and is a different person.

Jecoliah, also spelled Jecholiah, was a woman of Jerusalem who was the mother of King Uzziah of Judah. Both accounts of Uzziah's reign name her when they record that he became king at sixteen and reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem (2 Kgs 15:2; 2 Chr 26:3). In 2 Kings her son is mostly called Azariah. She was the wife of King Amaziah, Uzziah's father and predecessor. Her name probably means "the Lord is able" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "strong through the Lord" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). Nothing else is recorded about her. She belongs to the royal line traced in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, where her son appears as Ozias or Uzziah (Matt 1:8–9).

Jedaiah was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named only in a genealogy in 1 Chr 4:37. He was the son of Shimri and the father of Allon, and an ancestor of Ziza. The surrounding passage lists Ziza among the Simeonite leaders whose families grew numerous and who moved in search of pasture for their flocks. Jedaiah is therefore known only as a link in that family line, and nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls his father Shimri a chief Simeonite and gives the name's meaning as "invoker of Jehovah." Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "the hand of the Lord" or "confessing the Lord." Several other men in the Bible bear the name Jedaiah, including priests. This entry concerns only the Simeonite.

Jedaiah was a priest who lived in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. Nehemiah 11:10 lists him among the priests who settled in the city and calls him the son of Joiarib. The parallel list in 1 Chr 9:10 names Jedaiah and Jehoiarib side by side rather than as father and son. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him simply as a priest in Jerusalem after the Exile. A Jedaiah also appears next to Joiarib among the priests who returned with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:6). In the next generation, under the high priest Joiakim, a man named Uzzi led the priestly family called by Jedaiah's name (Neh 12:19). The name was shared by several men, including a second priest in the same list, so it is uncertain whether all these passages refer to one person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "the hand of the Lord" or "confessing the Lord."

Jedaiah was a priest who headed the second of the twenty-four priestly divisions. When David's reign organized the priests by lot, the second lot fell to him (1 Chr 24:7). His descendants, described as "of the house of Jeshua," were among the priests who returned from exile in Babylon, numbering 973 (Ezra 2:36; Neh 7:39). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes these returning priests to be the descendants of the same Jedaiah, and this entry follows that view. The link rests on the shared name and priestly role, since the texts do not state it outright. The name is usually explained as meaning "knowing the LORD" (Easton's Bible Dictionary) or "praise the LORD" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). Several other men in the Bible share the name, so not every mention of a Jedaiah refers to this person.

Jedaiah, son of Harumaph, was one of the men who rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah after the return from exile in Babylon. He is mentioned only once. Neh 3:10 says he repaired the section of wall opposite his own house, working beside Hattush the son of Hashabniah. Several workers in this chapter repaired the stretch nearest their homes, so Jedaiah probably lived close to the wall. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name Jedaiah, including priests of the same period, and he should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the hand of the Lord" or "confessing the Lord."

Jedaiah was one of the chief priests who returned from exile to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel and Jeshua. In Neh 12:7 he is the last name in a list of priestly leaders described as "the chief of the priests and of their brethren in the days of Jeshua." The same list already has a Jedaiah in the previous verse, so the text appears to name two different priests with this name, and this entry covers the second. A later list of priestly family heads in the time of the high priest Joiakim (Neh 12:12) names two Jedaiah families. In this one, Nethaneel led the family descended from this Jedaiah (Neh 12:21), while Uzzi led the other. Little else is known about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "the hand of the Lord" or "confessing the Lord."

Jedaiah was one of the exiles who had come back from Babylon in the time of the prophet Zechariah. He is named with Heldai and Tobijah as the people from whom Zechariah was told to take silver and gold on the same day. He was also to go to the house of Josiah son of Zephaniah (Zech 6:10). From this metal crowns were made and set on the head of Joshua the high priest. The crowns were then kept in the temple of the LORD as a memorial to Helem (probably the same man as Heldai), Tobijah, Jedaiah and Hen son of Zephaniah (Zech 6:14). Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a priest in the days of Jeshua the high priest, though the passage itself does not give his office. The name is shared by several other men in the Bible, including priests listed in Chronicles, Ezra and Nehemiah.

Jediael was a son of Benjamin. He is named in 1 Chr 7:6 as one of three sons, alongside Bela and Becher. His son was Bilhan, whose seven sons included Jeush, Ehud and Ahishahar. The clan descended from Jediael was counted by its family heads at 17,200 fighting men fit for war (1 Chr 7:11). His name does not appear in the lists of Benjamin's sons in Gen 46:21 and Num 26:38. Smith's Bible Dictionary records the common view that he is the same person as Ashbel, though it says this is not certain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a suggestion that this list originally referred to Zebulun, with the name read as Jahleel (Gen 46:14). This entry treats him as a son of Benjamin. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which probably means "known of God."

Jediael son of Shimri was one of the warriors listed among David's mighty men in 1 Chr 11:45, where he is named alongside his brother Joha. The verse adds the description "the Tizite," and it is unclear whether this refers to Joha alone or to both brothers. Nothing else is known about the place or family it points to. This part of the Chronicler's list goes beyond the parallel roll of heroes in 2 Samuel 23, so Jediael appears only here in that list. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he is probably the same Jediael of Manasseh who deserted to David at Ziklag (1 Chr 12:20), and STEPBible's proper-names index also places him in the tribe of Manasseh. Several other men in the Bible share this name, so the identification is uncertain. The name is commonly explained as meaning "known of God."

Jediael was a man of the tribe of Manasseh, one of seven "captains of the thousands" of Manasseh who joined David as he went to Ziklag (1 Chr 12:20). By inference from the surrounding passage, this happened when the Philistine leaders sent David away rather than let him fight with them against Saul, and he returned to his base at Ziklag. Smith's Bible Dictionary links this to David's pursuit of the Amalekites in 1 Sam 30:9–10. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "known of God," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the knowledge of God." Several other men in the Bible share the name Jediael, including a descendant of Benjamin, one of David's mighty men, and a Levite gatekeeper. Whether any of them is the same person as this captain is not stated.

Jediael was a Levite, the second son of Meshelemiah, listed among the gatekeepers of the temple in David's time (1 Chr 26:2). His brothers were Zechariah the firstborn, Zebadiah, Jathniel, Elam, Jehohanan and Elioenai. The surrounding passage, 1 Chr 26:1, places Meshelemiah's family among the Korahites, descendants of Asaph, and Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Jediael as a Korahite of the family of Ebiasaph. Nothing more is recorded about him beyond his place in this list of gatekeeping families. His name is usually explained as "known of God" or "God makes known." Several other men in the Bible share the name, so this Jediael should not be confused with them.

Jedidah was the mother of King Josiah of Judah and the daughter of Adaiah of Boscath (2 Kgs 22:1). Her name means "beloved" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "well beloved; amiable"). She is named only once, in the formal note that opens the account of her son's reign. That note records that Josiah became king at eight years old and reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem. By inference from the account of Josiah's father in the preceding chapter, she was a wife of King Amon. Boscath, also spelled Bozkath, is listed in Josh 15:39 among the towns of the lowland of Judah. Josiah appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matt 1:10–11), which places Jedidah among the ancestors in that line, although Matthew does not name her. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates her son's birth to about 648 BC.

Jeduthun (Ethan) was a Levite of the clan of Merari and son of Kishi, also spelled Kushaiah. He was one of the three chief musicians appointed in King David's time, alongside Heman and Asaph (1 Chr 6:44; 15:17, 19). The names Ethan and Jeduthun appear in matching lists of these three leaders, and Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries treat them as probably the same man, as this entry does. He played bronze cymbals, gave thanks before the LORD, and prophesied with the harp (1 Chr 16:41–42; 25:1, 3). His six sons served under his direction, and some were gatekeepers (1 Chr 16:42; 25:3, 6). Shimei, the sixth son, is probably the one named in 1 Chr 25:17. He is called "the king's seer" (2 Chr 35:15). His descendants still served in Solomon's and Hezekiah's days (2 Chr 5:12; 29:14). His name heads Psalm 77, which Smith's takes to indicate his choir.

Jeduthun was a Levite, the father of Galal, known only as an ancestor in the lists of Levites who settled in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. Through Galal his descendants included Obadiah son of Shemaiah (1 Chr 9:16), who is called Abda son of Shammua in the parallel list (Neh 11:17). That list places this family among the Levites connected with the temple's thanksgiving and prayer. Several men in the Bible share the name, so it is uncertain whether this Jeduthun is the same as the musician David appointed to lead worship. Because his descendants appear among the temple singers, that identification is quite possible, but this entry treats him separately. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "his law" or "giving praise."

Jegar-sahadutha was the Aramaic name Laban gave to the heap of stones he and Jacob set up as a witness to the covenant they made when they parted. Jacob called the same heap Galeed, its Hebrew counterpart (Gen 31:47). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names give the meaning as "heap of witness" or "pile of testimony." Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Galeed does not match the Aramaic name exactly. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links the second part of the name to the word for "witness" in Job 16:19. The surrounding chapter places the meeting in the hill country of Gilead, east of the Jordan, which Jacob's party reached after fleeing Haran. The exact site is unknown. The location shown here is a point in northern Gilead, in present-day northern Jordan.

Jehaleleel was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogies of 1 Chr 4:16, which lists his four sons: Ziph, Ziphah, Tiria and Asareel. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that he and his sons appear abruptly in the list, with no stated link to the names around them, so his exact place in Judah's family tree is uncertain. The Tyndale House proper-names index (STEPBible) treats him as a son of Elah, connecting him with the preceding verse, where Elah appears among the sons of Caleb son of Jephunneh. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "praising God." The son named Ziph may be connected with the Judean town of that name, though the verse does not say so. He should not be confused with the Levite Jehalelel of a later period (2 Chr 29:12).

Jehalelel was a Levite of the Merari clan, known only as the father of Azariah. His son was one of the Levites who arose in the time of King Hezekiah to sanctify themselves and cleanse the temple, listed alongside representatives of the other Levite families, the Kohathites and the Gershonites (2 Chr 29:12). Nothing else is recorded about Jehalelel himself, and it is not clear whether he was still living at the time. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "who praises God." A man of Judah with a similar name, spelled Jehaleleel in the King James Version, appears in 1 Chr 4:16. He is a different person.

Jehdeiah was a Levite, a descendant of Amram through Shubael. He appears only in 1 Chr 24:20, in a list of the remaining Levite family heads set out in connection with David's organization of temple service, so he probably lived in or near David's time. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him the representative of Shubael's descendants. Since 1 Chr 23:16 names Shebuel as a son of Gershom, son of Moses, Shubael is probably the same man, which would make Jehdeiah a descendant of Moses. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "may Yahweh give joy." He should not be confused with another Jehdeiah, the Meronothite who managed David's donkeys (1 Chr 27:30).

Jehdeiah the Meronothite was the official in charge of King David's donkeys, one of the overseers of the royal property listed in 1 Chr 27:30. He served alongside Obil the Ishmaelite, who looked after the camels. The title "Meronothite" probably refers to his home town, Meronoth, whose location is unknown. Smith's Bible Dictionary specifies that he had charge of the she-asses, and Easton's Bible Dictionary places his service under both David and Solomon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of the name as "may Yahweh give joy." The same name belongs to another man in the Bible, a Levite of David's time (1 Chr 24:20), so this officer should not be confused with him.

Jehezekel was a priest in the time of King David who received the twentieth of the twenty-four divisions into which the priests were organized for service at the house of the Lord (1 Chr 24:16). These divisions were assigned by lot, each priestly family taking its turn in the temple duties. He is mentioned only in this list. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains his name as "whom God makes strong," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "strength of God." The Hebrew name is the same as that of the prophet Ezekiel, but nothing connects this priest with the prophet, who lived centuries later.

Jehiel was one of the warriors in the list of David's mighty men in 1 Chronicles. He is named with his brother Shama as the sons of Hothan the Aroerite (1 Chr 11:44), and Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of David's guard. "Aroerite" means a man from Aroer. More than one town had that name, including one east of the Jordan near the Arnon and one in southern Judah, so it is uncertain which was his family's home. This part of the Chronicles list has no counterpart in the parallel list of David's warriors in 2 Sam 23, and nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible are also called Jehiel.

Jehiel was a Levite musician in the time of David, one of several men in the Bible with this name. He is listed among the Levites "of the second degree," the second rank of singers and gatekeepers appointed when the ark of the covenant was brought up to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:18). In that procession he was one of the group who played psalteries (harps or lyres) "on Alamoth," a musical term of uncertain meaning, perhaps referring to a high pitch or a particular style (1 Chr 15:20). After the ark was placed in its tent, he was named among the Levites serving under Asaph, the chief musician, in the ongoing worship before the ark (1 Chr 16:5). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "God lives."

Jehiel, also called Jehieli, was a Gershonite Levite of the family of Laadan in David's time. In 1 Chr 23:8 he is named as the chief of Laadan's sons, listed alongside Zetham and Joel. In 1 Chr 26:21–22, however, Zetham and Joel are called "the sons of Jehieli" and are placed over the treasures of the house of the Lord. This entry follows the second passage in treating them as his sons. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains Jehieli as "a Jehielite," meaning a member of Jehiel's family, which may account for the difference between the two lists. When the leaders gave gifts for building the temple, those who had precious stones handed them over to the temple treasury through "Jehiel the Gershonite" (1 Chr 29:8). This was probably the same man, consistent with his family's role over the treasures. Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Jehiel was the son of Hachmoni and one of the officials of King David's court. He is named once, in the list of David's officers in 1 Chr 27:32, where he is said to have been "with the king's sons." Easton's Bible Dictionary takes this to mean he was a tutor in the royal household toward the end of David's reign. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the exact meaning of the phrase is unclear. "Hachmoni" may be a family or clan name rather than a personal one. The related form "Hachmonite" is used of Jashobeam, one of David's mighty men, in 1 Chr 11:11. The same verse also names Jonathan, David's uncle, as a counsellor and scribe. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jehiel, which Smith's Bible Dictionary renders as "God lives."

Jehiel was one of the sons of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, and a younger brother of Jehoram, who succeeded their father on the throne. He is named second in the list of Jehoshaphat's sons, after Azariah and before Zechariah, a second Azariah, Michael and Shephatiah. The verse calls Jehoshaphat "king of Israel," though he ruled the southern kingdom of Judah. Jehiel is one of several people in the Bible with this name. The next verses (2 Chr 21:3–4) say Jehoshaphat gave his younger sons wealth and fortified cities in Judah. Once Jehoram had secured the kingdom, he killed all his brothers. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Jehiel to be among them, and this entry follows that reading. His death in Jerusalem is placed about 889 BC, by inference from context.

Jehiel was a Levite descended from Heman, one of the temple musicians' families. He appears in the list of Levites who answered King Hezekiah's call to purify the temple at the start of his reign (2 Chr 29:14). He is named alongside Shimei as the representatives of the sons of Heman. From the surrounding chapter, these Levites consecrated themselves and then cleansed the house of the Lord, which had been neglected. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 726 BC. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as one who helped Hezekiah in his work of reform. Some reference works, including the STEPBible names list, give his name as Jehuel. Several other men in the Bible are called Jehiel, and nothing more is known of this one beyond this single mention.

Jehiel was one of ten overseers who served under Cononiah and his brother Shimei during the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah (2 Chr 31:13). He was appointed at the king's command and under Azariah, the ruler of the house of God. By inference from the surrounding passage, these men looked after the offerings, tithes and dedicated gifts that the people brought to the temple storerooms. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper names index both identify him as a Levite, and the context of temple service supports this. His name is usually explained as meaning "God lives." Several other men in the Bible are also called Jehiel, and nothing more is recorded about this one.

Jehiel was one of the "rulers of the house of God" in the reign of King Josiah of Judah. Together with Hilkiah and Zechariah, he gave the priests 2,600 small animals and 300 oxen for the Passover offerings at Josiah's great Passover celebration (2 Chr 35:8). The verse counts these three among Josiah's princes who gave willingly to the people, the priests and the Levites. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a prince who gave generously toward restoring the temple sacrifices under Josiah. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these reforms to about 623 BC, an estimate inferred from context. The Hilkiah named beside him is probably the high priest of that name active under Josiah, though the verse does not say so. Nothing else is recorded about this Jehiel, and he should not be confused with the several other men of the same name in the Bible.

Jehiel was the father of Obadiah, a member of the family group descended from Joab. He is named only to identify his son, who led 218 men of that family when they returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra (Ezra 8:9). Nothing else is said about Jehiel himself, and the verse does not say whether he made the journey. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "God lives" and places him before about 459 BC, a date inferred from the timing of Ezra's return. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jehiel, including another Jehiel mentioned in the book of Ezra, so this one should be kept separate from them.

Jehiel was the father of Shechaniah and belonged to the family of Elam, one of the clans who returned from exile with or before Ezra. He is named only as Shechaniah's father, in the account of Ezra's response to marriages between Israelites and foreign women. Shechaniah admitted to Ezra that the people had taken foreign wives and proposed a way forward (Ezra 10:2). Ezra 10:26 lists a Jehiel among the sons of Elam who had married foreign wives. The STEPBible Proper Names index (Tyndale House) treats him as this same man, so Shechaniah may have been confessing a fault within his own family. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "God lives." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and the text says nothing more about this one.

Jehiel was a priest of the family of Harim in the time of Ezra. He is named in Ezra 10:21 alongside Maaseiah, Elijah, Shemaiah and Uzziah. By inference from the surrounding passage, which begins its list with the priests and ends by stating that all these men had taken foreign wives, Jehiel was among those who had married women from outside Israel and agreed to send them away during Ezra's reforms after the return from exile. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 459 BC, an estimate drawn from context. The name means "God lives." Several other men in the Bible are also called Jehiel, and this one is known only from this single mention.

Jehiel was a man of the family of Elam. He is named in Ezra 10:26 in the list of Israelites who had married foreign wives after the return from exile. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was among those who agreed to send away their wives and children in the reform led by Ezra. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the name means "God lives" and describes him as a member of the same family who himself had to part with his wife. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jehiel. They include another Jehiel of the sons of Elam, named a few verses earlier in the same chapter, whose son Shechaniah first proposed the reform. This entry concerns only the man listed in Ezra 10:26. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jehizkiah son of Shallum was one of the leaders of Ephraim in the northern kingdom of Israel during the reign of Ahaz of Judah. His name means "the LORD strengthens," as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes. Along with Azariah, Berechiah and Amasa, he stood up against the soldiers returning from war with captives from Judah (2 Chr 28:12). The surrounding passage shows that Israel's army under Pekah had taken large numbers of Judeans prisoner, and that the prophet Oded warned against keeping them as slaves. These chiefs backed that warning, and the captives were then clothed, fed and taken back to Jericho. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia dates these events to about 734 BC, while Smith's Bible Dictionary gives 738 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jehoaddan was the mother of Amaziah, king of Judah, and the wife of King Joash (also called Jehoash). She came from Jerusalem. She is known only from the notices that open Amaziah's reign, which say he became king at twenty-five and reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem (2 Kgs 14:2; 2 Chr 25:1). Naming the king's mother is a regular feature of these accounts of Judah's kings. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the written Hebrew text of 2 Kgs 14:2 spells her name Jehoaddin, the form used in the Revised Version. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "Jehovah his ornament," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "pleasure, or time, of the Lord." As mother of a king in David's royal line, she belongs to the line that Matthew's genealogy of Jesus follows, although Matthew's list does not name Amaziah.

Jehoahaz was a king of Judah, a son of Josiah and Hamutal, the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah. After Josiah's body was brought back from Megiddo, "the people of the land" anointed Jehoahaz king in Jerusalem at age twenty-three. He reigned only three months, about 609 BC by inference from context. Pharaoh Necho then removed him, made his brother Eliakim king under the new name Jehoiakim, and took Jehoahaz to Egypt, where he died. Jeremiah calls him Shallum and declares that he would never return (Jer 22:11). 1 Chr 3:15 lists Shallum as Josiah's fourth son. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the ages given in Kings make Jehoiakim the elder, so the people chose Jehoahaz over an older brother. His brother Zedekiah, a later king, had the same mother, Hamutal. Several other people in the Bible, including a king of Israel, also bear the name Jehoahaz.

Jehoahaz was king of Israel, the son and successor of Jehu, and the father of Joash (also spelled Jehoash). He is one of several people in the Bible with this name. He began to reign in Samaria in the twenty-third year of Joash king of Judah and ruled seventeen years, roughly 857–840 BC by inference from context. Throughout his reign Hazael king of Syria oppressed Israel and reduced his army to fifty horsemen, ten chariots and ten thousand foot soldiers. Jehoahaz pleaded with the LORD, who heard him because of Israel's suffering. He was buried in Samaria and succeeded by his son, who recovered from Ben-hadad son of Hazael the cities taken from Jehoahaz in war. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that he continued the religious practices of the house of Jeroboam. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the deliverer later given to Israel was probably Jehoash or Jeroboam II.

Jehohanan was a Levite of the family of Korah, the sixth son of Meshelemiah, listed among the gatekeepers of the sanctuary in the arrangements credited to King David (1 Chr 26:3). His brothers were Zechariah, Jediael, Zebadiah, Jathniel, Elam and Elioenai. The surrounding chapter, read in context, places these gatekeepers in David's later reign, about 1000 BC by inference. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as head of one of the divisions of temple porters. His name means "the Lord is gracious" and is the longer form of the name John. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that one Greek textual tradition reads his name as Jehonathan. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jehohanan, and this entry concerns only Meshelemiah's son.

Jehohanan was a military commander in Judah during the reign of King Jehoshaphat. 2 Chr 17:15 lists him among the king's captains and places 280,000 men under him. He is named "next to" Adnah, the chief commander, which suggests he ranked second among the leaders of Judah's troops. The surrounding passage describes these men as soldiers stationed in Jerusalem who served the king, apart from the garrisons in Judah's fortified cities (2 Chr 17:13, 19). Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "whom Jehovah gave" and notes that John is its shortened form. Several other men in the Bible share this name, and nothing in the text links this commander to any of them.

Jehohanan was the father of Ishmael, one of the "captains of hundreds" whom the priest Jehoiada brought into a covenant with him in the seventh year (2 Chr 23:1). The surrounding account shows that this covenant was the plan to overthrow Queen Athaliah and put the young king Joash on the throne of Judah. Jehohanan himself is known only as Ishmael's father, and nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "whom Jehovah gave" and notes that John is a shortened form of it. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this entry refers only to the father of Ishmael.

Jehohanan was one of the descendants of Bebai listed in Ezra 10:28 among the Israelites who had married foreign wives after the return from exile. In the context of Ezra 10, these men agreed to send away their foreign wives during the reforms led by Ezra. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 459 BC. The name means "the Lord has been gracious," and John is a shortened form of it. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:29 gives his name as Joannes. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jehohanan. Nothing more is known of this one beyond his place in this list.

Jehohanan was a priest in Jerusalem after the return from exile, listed as head of the priestly family of Amariah (Neh 12:13). The list he appears in names the heads of priestly families in the days of Joiakim, who was high priest after his father Jeshua. That setting comes from the surrounding verses rather than from Neh 12:13 itself. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 406 BC. The name means "the Lord has been gracious" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), and Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that John is a shortened form of it. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and nothing beyond this single listing is recorded about this one.

Jehohanan was one of the participants in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. He is named in a list of eight men who stood with the singers during the ceremony, while the singers sang loudly under the direction of Jezrahiah (Neh 12:42). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe him as a priest, by inference from the surrounding list of priests and musicians taking part in the celebration. Smith's dates the event to about 446 BC. The name means "the Lord is gracious" or "gift of the Lord," and John is its shortened form. Several other men in the Bible share this name, and nothing more is known about this particular Jehohanan beyond this one mention.

Jehoiachin, also called Jeconiah, Coniah and (in Matthew) Jechonias, was a king of Judah, the son of Jehoiakim and of Nehushta, daughter of Elnathan of Jerusalem. He succeeded his father and reigned in Jerusalem for only three months. 2 Kgs 24:8 gives his age at accession as eighteen, while 2 Chr 36:9 says eight and adds ten days to the reign. He surrendered to Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon and was taken into exile with his mother, wives, officials, nobles and craftsmen, about 598 BC by inference from context. Nebuchadnezzar put Zedekiah, a son of Josiah, on the throne in his place. Jeremiah declared that Coniah and his descendants would be cast out, though another prophet foretold his return. Ezekiel and Esther date events by his captivity. In the thirty-seventh year of his exile, Evil-merodach of Babylon released him from prison. His sons included Shealtiel (Salathiel), and Matthew includes him in the genealogy of Jesus.

Jehoiada was the father of Benaiah, who commanded David's Cherethites and Pelethites and later became Solomon's army commander (2 Sam 8:18; 1 Kgs 2:35). He is known almost entirely through his son's title, "Benaiah the son of Jehoiada." 2 Sam 23:20 calls Benaiah "the son of a valiant man, of Kabzeel," which may describe Jehoiada as a brave man from Kabzeel in southern Judah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some read the phrase as describing Benaiah himself. 1 Chr 27:5 can be read as calling Jehoiada a chief priest. This entry also includes the Jehoiada of 1 Chr 12:27, leader of the Aaronites who joined David with 3,700 men, and treats him as probably the same man. Smith's Bible Dictionary lists them separately. The name means "the LORD knows." Several other biblical men share this name.

Jehoiada, one of several men of this name, was the priest in Jerusalem (the high priest, in Easton's Bible Dictionary) who restored David's line after Queen Athaliah seized Judah's throne. His wife Jehoshabeath, King Jehoram's daughter, hid the infant Joash from Athaliah's massacre. In the seventh year Jehoiada bound the captains and guards by oath in the temple, armed them with King David's weapons, crowned and anointed Joash, and had Athaliah killed outside the temple. He made a covenant binding king and people to the LORD and reorganized the temple services. Joash did right while Jehoiada instructed him, and together they repaired the temple, using a collection chest for funds. Jehoiada died aged 130. Joash later had his son Zechariah killed. This entry takes Jesus' "Zacharias son of Barachias" (Matt 23:35) as that Zechariah, making Barachias another name for Jehoiada. Others link it with the prophet Zechariah son of Berechiah.

Jehoiada son of Benaiah was one of King David's counselors. He is named only in 1 Chr 27:34, in a list of David's officials, where he comes "after Ahithophel" alongside Abiathar, while Joab commanded the army. The preceding verse calls Ahithophel the king's counselor, so Jehoiada probably took over or shared that advisory role, perhaps after Ahithophel joined Absalom's revolt and died. STEPBible Proper Names describes him as Ahithophel's successor as counselor. Elsewhere David's well-known officer is Benaiah son of Jehoiada. This Jehoiada may therefore have been that Benaiah's son, named after his grandfather, though some readers suspect the two names were reversed in copying. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names renders as "knowledge of the Lord."

Jehoiada son of Paseah was one of the men who helped rebuild the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah. Together with Meshullam son of Besodeiah, he repaired the Old Gate. They laid its beams and set up its doors, locks and bars (Neh 3:6). Nothing else is recorded about him. Several people in the Bible share the name Jehoiada, and this one should not be confused with the better-known priest of that name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and other modern references give his name as Joiada, which reflects the Hebrew spelling in this verse. The name means "the Lord knows," and Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "knowledge of the Lord." By inference from the setting of Nehemiah's work, his repairs date to the mid-400s BC.

Jehoiada was a priest mentioned once, in Jer 29:26, in a letter that Shemaiah, a man among the exiles in Babylon, sent to Jerusalem. Shemaiah tells the priest Zephaniah that the LORD has made him priest in place of Jehoiada. The letter says this priest had charge of the officers in the house of the LORD, with authority to put anyone who acted as a self-made prophet into prison and the stocks. By inference from the surrounding chapter, Shemaiah was urging Zephaniah to use that authority against Jeremiah. Who this Jehoiada was is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some identify him with the well-known priest of Queen Athaliah's time, while others hold that nothing more is known of him. It also observes that Zephaniah could not have directly succeeded that earlier priest. This entry treats him as a separate priest of Jeremiah's time. The name means "Yahweh knows."

Jehoiakim, originally named Eliakim, was a king of Judah and the son of Josiah and Zebudah. After Pharaoh Necho of Egypt removed his brother Jehoahaz, Necho made Eliakim king and renamed him Jehoiakim. He taxed the land to pay Egypt's demands. He became king at twenty-five and reigned eleven years in Jerusalem, roughly 609–598 BC by inference. During his reign Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon defeated Egypt at Carchemish and besieged Jerusalem, carrying off temple vessels. Jehoiakim served Babylon for three years and then rebelled. He had the prophet Urijah brought back from Egypt and killed. He also burned the scroll of Jeremiah's prophecies, which Baruch then rewrote. Jeremiah foretold that no one would mourn him and that his body would be thrown out. Kings and Chronicles say he did evil in the sight of the LORD. His son Jehoiachin succeeded him.

Jehoiarib was a priest whose family became the first of the twenty-four divisions, or courses, of priests that took turns serving at the sanctuary. The surrounding chapter describes how, under King David, the priestly descendants of Eleazar and Ithamar were assigned their order of service by drawing lots, and the first lot fell to Jehoiarib, with Jedaiah second (1 Chr 24:7). Easton's Bible Dictionary connects him with the Jehoiarib named among the priests living in Jerusalem in 1 Chr 9:10. A similar name, Joiarib, appears among priestly families after the return from exile in Nehemiah, probably the same priestly house. Because the name may refer to the founding head of the division and also to the division that carried his name, it is uncertain how many separate individuals these mentions involve. Easton's gives the name's meaning as "the LORD defends." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "fighting, or multiplying, of the Lord."

Jehonathan, son of Uzziah, was one of King David's royal officials. He was in charge of the storehouses in the fields, cities, villages and fortified towers (the King James Version says "castles"). Azmaveth son of Adiel oversaw the king's own treasures (1 Chr 27:25). He appears in a list of the stewards who managed David's property. The name means "the Lord has given" and is a longer form of Jonathan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew uses both forms of the name. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and nothing else is known about this one. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his service to about 1014 BC, an estimate based on the period of David's reign.

Jehonathan was a Levite in the reign of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. He was one of nine Levites sent out, together with the priests Elishama and Jehoram and a group of the king's officials, to the towns of Judah (2 Chr 17:8). The surrounding passage, 2 Chr 17:7–9, says they carried the book of the law of the LORD and taught it to the people. Nothing more is recorded about him. His name is a fuller form of Jonathan, meaning "the LORD has given" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, and this Levite should not be confused with them. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the teaching mission to about 910 BC.

Jehonathan was a priest who headed the priestly family of Shemaiah in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. He is named in a list of the heads of priestly families serving in the days of Joiakim the high priest, the son of Jeshua (Neh 12:18). By inference from the surrounding list, Shemaiah here is the name of a priestly house, and an earlier Shemaiah appears among the priests who came back with Zerubbabel. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this generation to some time after 536 BC. The name means "the Lord has given" and is a fuller form of Jonathan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Hebrew sometimes uses both forms for the same person. Several other men in the Bible bear this name. Nothing more is recorded about this one.

Jehoram, also called Joram, was king of Judah, the firstborn son and successor of Jehoshaphat. Several people share the name, including a king of Israel of the same period. He began to reign at thirty-two and ruled eight years in Jerusalem, roughly 893–886 BC by inference from context. On taking power he killed all his brothers and some princes of Israel. Surrounded by the Edomites, he broke out by night with his chariots. Later the Philistines and Arabians attacked him, and raiders killed his older sons, so his youngest son Ahaziah succeeded him. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies his wife Athaliah as a daughter of Ahab and Jezebel. Their daughter Jehoshabeath (Jehosheba), wife of the priest Jehoiada, hid her nephew Joash from Athaliah. Jehoram was buried in the city of David, and Matthew lists him among the ancestors of Jesus.

Jehoram was a priest whom King Jehoshaphat of Judah sent out, along with the priest Elishama and a group of Levites, in the third year of his reign. According to the surrounding passage (2 Chr 17:7–9), the princes, Levites and priests went through the cities of Judah teaching the people from the book of the law of the Lord. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a priest sent to instruct the people. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "exaltation of the Lord." Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with others who share the name, including Jehoshaphat's own son and successor, King Jehoram of Judah, and King Jehoram of Israel.

Jehoshabeath, also called Jehosheba (2 Kgs 11:2), was a daughter of King Jehoram of Judah and sister of King Ahaziah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of her name as "Yahweh is an oath." She was married to Jehoiada the priest, and Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that she is the only recorded case of a royal princess marrying a high priest. When Athaliah had the king's sons killed after Ahaziah's death, Jehoshabeath took Ahaziah's young son Joash and hid him and his nurse in a bedchamber, saving his life. The following verse, 2 Kgs 11:3, says he stayed hidden in the temple for six years. Smith's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggest she may have been Jehoram's daughter by a wife other than Athaliah. This entry follows the view that Athaliah was her mother.

Jehoshaphat, son of Ahilud, was the royal recorder under King David and later under Solomon. He is named in the lists of David's chief officials, alongside Joab as army commander (2 Sam 8:16; 1 Chr 18:15) and Adoram as overseer of forced labour (2 Sam 20:24). He still held the office at the start of Solomon's reign (1 Kgs 4:3). The recorder probably kept the official records of the court. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes the post as a high-ranking state office, something like a chancellor. Baana son of Ahilud, one of Solomon's district governors in 1 Kgs 4:12, is taken here to be his brother, on the inference that the two share the same father. This Jehoshaphat is a different person from King Jehoshaphat of Judah and from others who bear the name, which means "the Lord is judge."

Jehoshaphat son of Paruah was one of the twelve officers King Solomon appointed over Israel, and he was responsible for the territory of Issachar (1 Kgs 4:17). The surrounding list in 1 Kings 4 explains that each of these district officers supplied food for the king and his household for one month of the year. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him Solomon's purveyor, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the same account of his duty. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his father's name. His name means "the Lord is judge" or "Yahweh has judged." He should not be confused with other men of the same name, such as Jehoshaphat king of Judah or Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud, who served David and Solomon as recorder.

Jehoshaphat (Josaphat in Matt 1:8) was king of Judah, the son of Asa and Azubah, who succeeded his father in the fourth year of Ahab of Israel. His reign began about 914 BC, by inference from context. He first strengthened Judah against Israel but later made peace and allied with Ahab, joining him in battle at Ramoth-gilead, where he asked that a prophet of the LORD be consulted. He also joined Jehoram of Israel and the king of Edom against Moab, and Elisha agreed to speak out of regard for him. Chronicles records his wealth, tribute from Philistines and Arabians, his appointment of judges in Jerusalem, and a victory over a great invading army after prayer at the temple. A shipping venture linked with Ahaziah ended when the ships were wrecked. His son Jehoram succeeded him. Several other men in the Bible share this name.

Jehoshaphat was the son of Nimshi and the father of Jehu, who became king of Israel. He is named only in the account of Jehu's anointing and revolt, where Jehu is twice identified as "the son of Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi": once when Elisha sends a young prophet to find and anoint him at Ramoth-gilead (2 Kgs 9:2), and again when Jehu conspires against King Joram (2 Kgs 9:14). Nothing else is recorded about his life. Elsewhere, in 1 Kgs 19:16 and 2 Kgs 9:20, Jehu is called simply "son of Nimshi". As the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes, Jehoshaphat's name is left out there, so Nimshi, Jehu's grandfather, stands as the better-known family name. His name means "the Lord judges." He should not be confused with Jehoshaphat king of Judah or others who share the name.

Jehoshaphat was one of the seven priests who blew trumpets before the ark of God when David had it brought up to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:24). The others named with him are Shebaniah, Nethaneel, Amasai, Zechariah, Benaiah and Eliezer, while Obed-edom and Jehiah served as doorkeepers for the ark. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name means "the Lord judges." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew spelling here is Joshaphat, and the Revised Version renders it that way, so the King James spelling links him in name with other men called Jehoshaphat, including the king of Judah. He should not be confused with them; this entry treats him as a separate priest of David's time.

Jehozabad was one of two royal servants who conspired against King Joash (Jehoash) of Judah and killed him. Joash was buried in the city of David, and his son Amaziah became king (2 Kgs 12:21). His fellow conspirator was Jozachar, also called Zabad, the son of Shimeath. Kings calls Jehozabad the son of Shomer, while Chronicles calls him the son of Shimrith, a Moabite woman (2 Chr 24:26). Smith's Bible Dictionary treats Shomer and Shimrith as the same name. The surrounding passage in 2 Chronicles says the conspiracy came in revenge for Joash's killing of the son of Jehoiada the priest, and 2 Kgs 14:5 records that Amaziah later executed the servants who had killed his father. The name means "Yahweh has bestowed" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other people in the Bible share this name.

Jehozabad was a Levite, the second of the eight sons of Obed-edom named in 1 Chr 26:4–5, whose other sons were Shemaiah, Joah, Sacar, Nethaneel, Ammiel, Issachar and Peulthai. The passage lists the divisions of gatekeepers (porters) organized in David's time. By inference from its opening verse, which introduces the Korahite gatekeepers, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia call him a Korahite. Smith's also connects his family with the south gate of the temple and the storehouse beside it, since that lot later in the chapter falls to Obed-edom and his sons (1 Chr 26:15). His name means "Yahweh has bestowed." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Jehozabad should not be confused with them.

Jehozabad was a military commander under King Jehoshaphat of Judah, named in a list of the king's army leaders. He led 180,000 men equipped for war (2 Chr 17:18). By inference from the surrounding passage, he belonged to the tribe of Benjamin: he is listed "next" to Eliada, a Benjamite commander, and Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify him as a Benjamite. His name means "the LORD has given" or "the LORD has bestowed." Several other men in the Bible share this name, and this entry concerns only the commander in Jehoshaphat's reign.

Jehu son of Hanani was a prophet who delivered the word of the LORD against Baasha, king of Israel, and his house. He condemned Baasha for doing evil and following the ways of Jeroboam (1 Kgs 16:1, 7). That prophecy was fulfilled when Zimri destroyed Baasha's whole family (1 Kgs 16:12). Much later Jehu went out to meet King Jehoshaphat of Judah and rebuked him for helping the ungodly. The context makes clear this meant his alliance with Ahab (2 Chr 19:2). Jehu also wrote an account of Jehoshaphat's acts, which was included in the book of the kings of Israel (2 Chr 20:34). Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests his father was probably the seer Hanani who confronted King Asa (2 Chr 16:7). It also notes that about thirty years separate his two recorded appearances, so he probably began prophesying young. He is distinct from Jehu the king of Israel who shares his name.

Jehu was a king of Israel, the son of Jehoshaphat and grandson of Nimshi; several other people in the Bible share the name. God told Elijah to anoint him king (1 Kgs 19:16–17). While Jehu was an army commander at Ramoth-gilead, a messenger from Elisha anointed him, and his fellow officers proclaimed him king. He drove furiously to Jezreel, shot King Joram with an arrow, and had Ahaziah of Judah struck down. According to Easton's Bible Dictionary, he then had Jezebel thrown from a window. He killed the rest of Ahab's house and, by staging a great sacrifice to Baal, gathered Baal's worshippers and had them killed. He still kept the golden calves at Bethel and Dan. He reigned 28 years in Samaria, was buried there, and was succeeded by his son Jehoahaz. His dynasty lasted four generations. This entry dates his reign to about 886–857 BC, by inference from context. Easton's gives 884–856 BC.

Jehu was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy at 1 Chr 2:38 as the son of Obed and the father of Azariah. The surrounding verses place him in the line of Jerahmeel, a son of Hezron. By inference from 1 Chr 2:34–37, he descended from the marriage of Sheshan's daughter to Jarha, an Egyptian servant, through Attai, Nathan, Zabad, Ephlal and Obed. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as of the house of Hezron. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with other men of the same name, such as the king of Israel or the prophet son of Hanani. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "himself who exists," while Smith's renders it "the living."

Jehu was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named in the genealogy of Simeon's descendants in 1 Chr 4:35. He was the son of Josibiah, the son of Seraiah, the son of Asiel. Several other men in the Bible share his name, and this Jehu should not be confused with the better-known king of Israel. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the Tyndale House proper-names index both identify him as a Simeonite. The surrounding passage lists him among the leaders of Simeonite families whose clans grew large and, in the days of King Hezekiah of Judah, moved toward Gedor in search of pasture for their flocks. By inference, Jehu was one of these clan heads, though nothing is recorded about him beyond his name and ancestry.

Jehu the Antothite was one of the warriors who joined David at Ziklag, named among them in 1 Chr 12:3. The surrounding passage describes these men as Benjamites, Saul's own kinsmen, who were skilled archers and slingers able to use either hand. They came to David while he was still kept away from Saul. "Antothite" probably means he came from Anathoth, a Levitical town in Benjamin north of Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper names list both describe him as one of the Benjamite slingers or archers, and Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him among the chief heroes of Benjamin. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is a different man from the better-known Jehu who later became king of Israel, and from the prophet Jehu son of Hanani. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "himself who exists."

Jehubbah was a man of the tribe of Asher, named only once, in the Asherite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:34, as one of the four sons of Shamer, with his brothers Ahi, Rohgah and Aram. Shamer is probably the Shomer of 1 Chr 7:32, a son of Heber and grandson of Beriah, which would place Jehubbah in the house of Beriah, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia points out that the Hebrew text reads his name in more than one way: the spoken tradition gives "and Hubbah," while the written consonants suggest a form like "Yachbah." It treats the meaning of the name as unknown. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "protected" and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "hiding, binding." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jehud was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Dan, listed in Josh 19:45 alongside Bene-berak and Gath-rimmon. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that it is named between Baalath and Bene-berak in the list of Danite towns, and gives the meaning of the name as "praised." It is not mentioned anywhere else in the Bible. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with el-Yehudiyeh, about 8 miles east of Jaffa on the coastal plain. That site corresponds to the modern Israeli town of Yehud, east of Tel Aviv, and the location shown here follows this identification.

Jehudi son of Nethaniah was an official at the court of King Jehoiakim of Judah, named in Jer 36 when Jeremiah's prophecies were read and destroyed. His ancestry is traced back through Shelemiah to Cushi. The princes sent him to bring Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, with the scroll Baruch had read to the people. Later the king sent Jehudi to fetch the scroll from the room of Elishama the scribe, and Jehudi read it aloud to the king and the princes standing beside him. After Jehudi had read three or four columns, the scroll was cut with a knife and thrown into the fire on the hearth, until all of it was burned. The text says only "he" cut it, and this is usually understood to mean the king. His name means "a Jew." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that his name and the name Cushi ("Ethiopian") may point to a foreign origin.

Jehudijah was a woman named in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chr 4:18 as the mother of three sons: Jered the father of Gedor, Heber the father of Socho, and Jekuthiel the father of Zanoah. These sons are described as founders of towns in Judah. The verse calls her "his wife," and the husband is unclear. This entry follows the reading that makes her the wife of Ishbah, who is the nearest man named in the preceding verse. Tyndale House's STEPBible Proper Names makes her the wife of Mered, who is said in the same verse to have married Bithiah, Pharaoh's daughter. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggest the Hebrew may be a description, "the Jewess," rather than a personal name. If so, it may set her apart from the Egyptian wife. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "the praise of the Lord."

Jehush was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, the second of three sons listed for Eshek, after his older brother Ulam and before his younger brother Eliphelet (1 Chr 8:39). Eshek was the brother of Azel, and the surrounding genealogy traces this family back through Jonathan to King Saul, so Smith's Bible Dictionary calls Jehush a remote descendant of Saul. The verse names Eshek as his father. This entry connects him to Eleasah, the father of Azel in 1 Chr 8:37, and by inference also Eshek's father, so Eleasah appears to stand one generation above Jehush. Some reference works, including the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, treat the name as a form of Jeush. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "to whom God hastens." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jeiel was a chief of the tribe of Reuben, named first among the leaders of his kindred when their family genealogy was recorded (1 Chr 5:7). The surrounding passage traces Reuben's descendants through the line of Joel down to Beerah, whom the Assyrian king Tilgath-pilneser carried into exile. Jeiel and Zechariah are listed as "his brethren", that is, relatives of Beerah, so Smith's Bible Dictionary places Jeiel in the house of Joel. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him simply as a Reubenite chief. Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jeiel, and this Reubenite should not be confused with them.

Jeiel, also called Jehiah, was a Levite in David's time who served when the ark of God was brought to Jerusalem. He is listed among the Levites "of the second degree" and the gatekeepers (1 Chr 15:18). He was one of the musicians who played harps on the Sheminith, probably a term for a musical setting (1 Chr 15:21). He was appointed with Obed-edom as doorkeeper for the ark (1 Chr 15:24), where the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes "Jehiah" as another form of the same name. When Asaph led the music before the ark, Jeiel played psalteries and harps (1 Chr 16:5). That verse names Jeiel twice, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the first Jeiel there to be the Jaaziel of 1 Chr 15:18, a different man. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls this Jeiel a Merarite. Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Jeiel was a Levite of the family of Asaph, named only in the genealogy of Jahaziel in 2 Chr 20:14. He was the son of Mattaniah and the father of Benaiah. Through Benaiah and then Zechariah he was an ancestor of Jahaziel, on whom the Spirit of the LORD came in the assembly during the reign of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. By the line given in the verse he was Jahaziel's great-great-grandfather. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Gershonite Levite, since the Asaphite singers were traced to Gershon, and calls him a forefather of Jahaziel. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jeiel, and this entry concerns only the Asaphite ancestor of Jahaziel.

Jeiel was a scribe in the service of Uzziah, king of Judah. He is mentioned only in 2 Chr 26:11, where he and Maaseiah the ruler took the count of Uzziah's army. That army was organized into bands that went out to war, under the direction of Hananiah, one of the king's captains. Jeiel's task was evidently administrative: recording the numbers of the fighting men. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes these troops as irregular raiding forces and dates the passage to about 803 BC. Nothing else is known about him, including his family. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jeiel, and this one should not be confused with them.

Jeiel was a Levite descended from Elizaphan who served in the time of King Hezekiah. He appears with Shimri in 2 Chr 29:13, in a list of Levites grouped by family. From the surrounding passage, these Levites answered Hezekiah's call to purify themselves and cleanse the temple in Jerusalem after it had been neglected. Elizaphan is known from Num 3:30 as a leader among the Levites in the wilderness period, so the 'sons of Elizaphan' here were probably a Levite family that kept his name. Some references, including the STEPBible proper names index, give the name as Jeuel, an alternative Hebrew reading of the same name. Several other men in the Bible are also called Jeiel, and this one is known only from this single mention.

Jeiel was one of the chiefs of the Levites in the reign of King Josiah of Judah. He is named with Conaniah, Shemaiah, Nethaneel, Hashabiah and Jozabad, and together they gave the Levites 5,000 small animals (sheep and goats) and 500 oxen as offerings for the great Passover that Josiah held (2 Chr 35:9). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this Passover to about 623 BC, and explains the name as meaning "treasured of God," though the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats its meaning as unknown. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jeiel, and nothing more is recorded about this one.

Jeiel was one of the descendants of Adonikam who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. He appears in Ezra's list of family heads who joined the journey. Along with Eliphelet and Shemaiah, he is named among "the last sons of Adonikam," and sixty men of the family went with them (Ezra 8:13). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this return to about 459 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and the Tyndale House proper-names index give the name as Jeuel, following a different reading of the Hebrew text; the King James Version reads Jeiel. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name Jeiel, and this man should not be confused with them.

Jeiel was a man of the family or clan of Nebo, listed among the Israelites in Ezra's time who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:43). The surrounding chapter describes how, after returning from exile in Babylon, these men agreed to send away their foreign wives. His name is the first of seven given for the descendants of Nebo, a group probably named after an ancestor or a home town. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a layman and dates these events to about 459 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:35 gives his name as Juel. Nothing more is known about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jeiel, and this one should not be confused with them.

Jekabzeel was a town in the south of Judah. After the return from exile in Babylon, some of the people of Judah lived there and in its surrounding villages (Neh 11:25). Smith's Bible Dictionary treats it as a fuller form of the name Kabzeel, which earlier passages place among the southernmost cities of Judah toward the border with Edom. By that identification it is the same town as Kabzeel, the home of David's warrior Benaiah. The name is usually explained as meaning "God gathers" or, in Hitchcock's Bible Names, "the congregation of God." Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the Negev region of southern Judah.

Jekameam was a Levite, the fourth son of Hebron, listed after his brothers Jeriah, Amariah and Jahaziel. He appears only in the Levite genealogies of 1 Chronicles, which set out the families of Levi in the setting of David's organization of the Levites for temple service (1 Chr 23:19; 1 Chr 24:23). The same chapter names Hebron as a son of Kohath, so Jekameam probably belonged to the Kohathite branch of the tribe. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as the head of a Levitical house and explains his name as probably meaning "may the kinsman establish." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jekamiah was a man of the tribe of Judah named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:41, where he is the son of Shallum and the father of Elishama. This list belongs to the descendants of Jerahmeel. It traces the line that, according to the earlier verses of the chapter (1 Chr 2:34–35), began when Sheshan gave his daughter in marriage to his Egyptian servant Jarha. Smith's Bible Dictionary accordingly places him in the line of Ahlai. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes his name to mean "may the LORD establish." He is probably a different person from the son of King Jeconiah listed in 1 Chr 3:18, whose name the KJV spells Jecamiah.

Jekuthiel was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the genealogies of 1 Chr 4:18 as "the father of Zanoah." His mother was Jehudijah, and his brothers were Jered, father of Gedor, and Heber, father of Socho. In these lists "father" often means the founder or leading figure of a settlement, so Jekuthiel was probably linked with the town of Zanoah in Judah's territory. The passage is hard to follow, because it does not make clear whose wife Jehudijah was. This entry follows the reading that makes Ishbah, named just before in the same genealogy, his father. The STEPBible proper names index instead treats him as a son of Mered, who is named in the same verse. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the meaning of his name is uncertain, possibly "preservation of God." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "hope, or congregation, of the Lord." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jemima was the first of the three daughters born to Job after his fortunes were restored, at the close of the book of Job. Her sisters were Kezia and Keren-happuch (Job 42:14). The following verses, by connection with this passage, describe Job's daughters as the most beautiful women in the land and say he gave them an inheritance alongside their brothers. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of her name as "dove," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "handsome as the day." Nothing else is recorded about her.

Jemuel was a son of Simeon and grandson of Jacob. He is named first among Simeon's sons in Gen 46:10 and Exod 6:15, and Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to be the eldest. Genesis 46 lists him among Jacob's descendants who went down to Egypt. In Num 26:12 and 1 Chr 4:24 he is called Nemuel, and Numbers names the clan descended from him, the Nemuelites, as one of the families of the tribe of Simeon. His brothers were Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar and Shaul. Some of their names also vary between lists: Zohar appears as Zerah, Jachin as Jarib, and Ohad is left out of the later lists. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that Nemuel is probably the original form of the name. That work treats its meaning as unclear, while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "God's day." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jephthah was a Gileadite warrior and judge of Israel, called a mighty man of valour and the son of Gilead by a harlot. His half-brothers drove him from the family inheritance, and he lived in the land of Tob with a band of followers. When the Ammonites attacked Israel, the elders of Gilead brought him back and made him their head and captain at Mizpeh. His messages to the Ammonite king failed. The Spirit of the LORD then came on him, and he vowed to offer whatever first came out of his house if he won. He defeated Ammon, and his only child, a daughter, came out to meet him. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Judg 11:39 to mean she was sacrificed, while some interpreters hold she was devoted to lifelong virginity. He later fought Ephraim, judged Israel six years (from about 1152 BC, by inference), and was buried in Gilead. Heb 11:32 calls him Jephthae.

Jephunneh was the father of Caleb, the man from the tribe of Judah whom Moses sent with Joshua and ten others to explore Canaan (Num 13:6). He is known only through his son, who is repeatedly called "Caleb the son of Jephunneh": one of the two spies who survived the wilderness years, and the man who received Hebron as his inheritance (Num 14:30; Josh 14:13–14). Caleb is also called "the Kenezite" (Num 32:12; Josh 14:6). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes this to mean the family descended from a Kenaz, probably an Edomite clan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that this clan became part of Judah. This entry also counts a Kenaz among his descendants. The hard-to-read 1 Chr 4:15 places a Kenaz in Caleb's family, as the son of Elah in the King James Version. The name is shared with an unrelated man of Asher (1 Chr 7:38).

Jephunneh was a man of the tribe of Asher, named in the tribe's genealogy as a son of Jether and the brother of Pispah and Ara (1 Chr 7:38). He is listed first of the three, and Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to be the eldest. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is a different person from the better-known Jephunneh, father of Caleb, who belonged to the tribe of Judah. The meaning of the name is uncertain: Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "for whom a way is prepared," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "he that beholds."

Jerah was a son of Joktan, a descendant of Shem through Eber, named in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:26) and in the parallel genealogy in 1 Chr 1:20. He is listed fourth among Joktan's thirteen sons, after Almodad, Sheleph and Hazarmaveth. His brothers included Sheba, Ophir and Havilah. Nothing is recorded of his life. The name means "moon" or "month" in Hebrew. Like his brothers, he is probably meant as the ancestor of a people or tribe, and Smith's Bible Dictionary places that tribe in southern Arabia. No district called Jerah has been identified. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes places named Yurakh in Yemen and Yarach in the Hijaz, along with several Arabian place-names built on the word for "moon." It adds that moon worship in southern Arabia made such names common, so no single location can be fixed.

Jerahmeel was a man of the tribe of Judah, the firstborn son of Hezron (1 Chr 2:9, 25). His brothers included Ram and Chelubai, who is called Caleb in 1 Chr 2:42. By his first wife, who is not named, he had Ram (his firstborn), Bunah, Oren, Ozem and Ahijah. A second wife, Atarah, bore him Onam. The genealogy follows his line through several generations and closes with the words "These were the sons of Jerahmeel" (1 Chr 2:33). His grandsons through Ram were Maaz, Jamin and Eker. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats him as the founder of the Jerahmeelites, a clan in southern Judah mentioned in 1 Sam 27:10. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the mercy, or the beloved, of God." Other people in the Bible share this name and should not be confused with him.

Jerahmeel was a Levite, the son of Kish, named in the list of Levite family heads in 1 Chr 24:29. That list belongs to the account of David organizing the Levites for service at the sanctuary. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him as a Merarite who stood as the representative of the family of Kish. By comparison with 1 Chr 23:21, this Kish was a son of Mahli, the son of Merari. Nothing more is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the mercy, or the beloved, of God." Several other men in the Bible share the name, among them a descendant of Judah and an officer of King Jehoiakim, and they should not be confused with this Levite.

Jerahmeel the son of Hammelech was one of three men King Jehoiakim of Judah ordered to arrest Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet. The other two were Seraiah son of Azriel and Shelemiah son of Abdeel (Jer 36:26). The surrounding chapter places the order after the king had burned the scroll of Jeremiah's prophecies. The arrest failed because, the verse says, the LORD hid them. Hammelech means "the king" in Hebrew, so some translations read "the king's son," which would probably make Jerahmeel a royal prince or official. Jer 38:6 names a Malchiah son of Hammelech, into whose cistern Jeremiah was later lowered, and this entry takes him to be Jerahmeel's brother. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "the mercy, or the beloved, of God." Several other people in the Bible share the name.

Jered was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:18. His mother was Jehudijah, and he is called the "father" of Gedor, which probably means he founded the town or was the ancestor of its people, as Smith's Bible Dictionary explains. His brothers Heber and Jekuthiel are likewise named as fathers of Socho and Zanoah, so the three are linked with towns in Judah. The family lines in this passage are hard to untangle, and his father is identified in different ways. This entry follows the reading that connects him with Ishbah, who is mentioned in the preceding verse (1 Chr 4:17). The STEPBible names index makes him a son of Mered, and Easton's Bible Dictionary connects him with Ezra, also named in that verse. His name is usually taken to mean "descent." He is a different person from Jared, the ancestor of Noah.

Jeremai was a man of the family of Hashum who returned to Judah after the exile and is named in Ezra's list of those who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:33). By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was among those who agreed to send away their foreign wives as part of the reforms led by Ezra in Jerusalem. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a layman and dates the event to about 459 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he appears only in this verse. The meaning of his name is uncertain.
