Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "dwelling in heights," Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "my height" or "throwing forth waters," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls it unknown. That encyclopedia also links him with Jeremias in the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:34.

Jeremiah was a man from Libnah, a town in Judah, known only as the father of Hamutal. Hamutal was the mother of two kings of Judah: Jehoahaz, who reigned three months in Jerusalem, and Zedekiah, who reigned eleven years (2 Kgs 23:31; 2 Kgs 24:18; Jer 52:1). Both kings were sons of Josiah, so Hamutal was Josiah's wife, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes. That made Jeremiah of Libnah the grandfather of these two kings. He is a different person from the prophet Jeremiah and from several other men who share the name. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "exaltation of the Lord."

Jeremiah was one of the heads of families in the half-tribe of Manasseh that lived east of the Jordan. He appears in a single list in 1 Chr 5:24, alongside Epher, Ishi, Eliel, Azriel, Hodaviah and Jahdiel. All of them are described as mighty men of valour, famous men, and heads of their fathers' houses. The surrounding passage places this branch of Manasseh in the land from Bashan to Baal-hermon and Mount Hermon. It also says these Manassites were later carried into exile by the Assyrians, so he probably lived some generations before that deportation. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is a different person from Jeremiah the prophet and from the several other men of the same name in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "exaltation of the Lord."

Jeremiah was one of the warriors who joined David at Ziklag, named in 1 Chr 12:4 alongside Ismaiah the Gibeonite, Jahaziel, Johanan and Josabad the Gederathite. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 12:1–2) describes this group as men who came to David while he was still kept away from Saul, skilled archers and slingers who could use either hand. Easton's Bible Dictionary treats him as a Benjamite slinger, since the list opens with Saul's own tribe. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes he may instead have been from Judah, because nearby names such as "the Gederathite" probably point to towns in Judah. This entry follows the Benjamite view. Nothing more is recorded about him. He is distinct from Jeremiah the prophet and from other men of the same name, including two Gadite warriors listed later in the same chapter.

Jeremiah was a warrior from the tribe of Gad who joined David while he was hiding from King Saul. He appears fifth in a list of Gadite leaders (1 Chr 12:10). The surrounding passage describes these Gadites as skilled fighters who crossed over to David at his stronghold in the wilderness, and it says the least of them was equal to a hundred men (1 Chr 12:8, 14). Easton's Bible Dictionary places his joining in the wilderness, while Tyndale House's proper-names index connects it with David's time at Ziklag. The same list names another Jeremiah as the tenth Gadite (1 Chr 12:13), so the two should be kept apart. Nothing else is recorded about this man. His name is shared with several others in the Bible, most famously the prophet. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "exaltation of the Lord."

Jeremiah was a warrior from the tribe of Gad, listed tenth among the Gadite fighters who joined David (1 Chr 12:13). The surrounding passage describes these Gadites as mighty men skilled with shield and spear who left their tribe to join David at his stronghold in the wilderness, while he was still kept away because of Saul (1 Chr 12:1, 8). It also calls them captains of the army (1 Chr 12:14). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him simply as a Gadite warrior. STEPBible places him among those who joined David while he was fleeing from King Saul. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is one of several men in the Bible named Jeremiah and is distinct from the prophet. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "exaltation of the Lord."

Jeremiah (also Jeremy or Jeremias) was a prophet of Judah, son of Hilkiah, from a priestly family at Anathoth in Benjamin (Jer 1:1). He prophesied from Josiah's reign, beginning about 628 BC by inference from context, until after the fall of Jerusalem, and he lamented Josiah's death (2 Chr 35:25). The priest Pashur put him in the stocks, and priests sought his death for his temple preaching. His scribe Baruch read his prophecies publicly, and King Jehoiakim ordered both men arrested. Under Zedekiah he was imprisoned and cast into a dungeon, rescued by Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, and held in the prison court until the city fell. Freed by Nebuzaradan, he was later taken to Tahpanhes in Egypt, where he kept prophesying. Daniel and Ezra cite his seventy-year prophecy, and Matthew quotes him. Jewish tradition credits him with Jeremiah, Lamentations and Kings. Others in the Bible share his name.

Jeremiah was a priest of the period after the Babylonian exile, named only in Nehemiah. He is listed among the priests and Levites who went up to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel and Jeshua (Neh 12:1). He became the head of a priestly family, and in the days of the high priest Joiakim that family was led by Hananiah (Neh 12:12). A Jeremiah also appears among those who sealed the covenant under Nehemiah (Neh 10:2) and in the procession at the dedication of Jerusalem's walls (Neh 12:34). This entry treats all four mentions as one person. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia instead separates the returnee with Zerubbabel from the covenant signer, and identifies the signer with the man in the procession. The later lists may use the family's name rather than refer to the original priest himself. The name is shared by several people in the Bible, including the prophet.

Jeremiah was a Rechabite, the son of Habaziniah and the father of Jaazaniah. He is mentioned only once, in Jer 35:3, where his son Jaazaniah is named first among the Rechabite household that the prophet Jeremiah brought to the temple in Jerusalem. In the surrounding chapter the prophet set wine before the Rechabites, and they refused it, keeping the command of their ancestor Jonadab son of Rechab. This Jeremiah appears only as a link in his son's lineage, and nothing is said about his own life. He is distinct from the prophet Jeremiah and from several other men of the same name. The name is usually explained as meaning something like "the Lord establishes" or "the Lord appoints." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives it as "exaltation of the Lord."

Jeremoth was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles. He appears in a list of names that ends by calling them the sons of Beriah (1 Chr 8:14). By inference from the surrounding passage, this Beriah is the one who, with Shema, headed the families of Aijalon and drove out the people of Gath. The family probably belonged to the Benjamite leaders said later in the chapter to have lived in Jerusalem, which is how the STEPBible Proper Names describes him. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is shared by several other men in the Bible, so this Jeremoth should not be confused with them. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "heights," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia compares it with the similar name Jeroham in the same genealogy.

Jeremoth, also spelled Jerimoth, was a Levite listed as one of the three sons of Mushi, alongside his brothers Mahli and Eder (1 Chr 23:23). Mushi was a son of Merari, so Jeremoth belonged to the Merarite branch of the tribe of Levi, as Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary note. He appears only in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles, in the lists of Levite families arranged for service in the time of David. The second list gives his name as Jerimoth and counts the brothers among "the sons of the Levites after the house of their fathers" (1 Chr 24:30). Nothing further is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name Jeremoth or Jerimoth, and this Levite should not be confused with them. The name is commonly explained as meaning "heights" or "eminences."

Jeremoth was one of the descendants of Elam listed in Ezra 10:26 among the men who had married foreign wives after the return from exile. The surrounding chapter describes how, under Ezra's leadership, these men agreed to send their foreign wives away, and STEPBible's proper-names index places Jeremoth in this group. He is named alongside Mattaniah, Zechariah, Jehiel, Abdi and Eliah, but nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, and this Jeremoth should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "eminences" or "one that fears death."

Jeremoth was one of the descendants of Zattu listed in Ezra 10:27, alongside Elioenai, Eliashib, Mattaniah, Zabad and Aziza. The surrounding chapter shows that the men in this list had married foreign women after the return from exile in Babylon, in the time of Ezra, and STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) notes that he was among those who agreed to send these wives away. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Old Testament bear the same name, and this Jeremoth should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "eminences" or "one that fears death."

Jeriah was a Levite, the firstborn of the four sons of Hebron, followed by Amariah, Jahaziel and Jekameam. He appears in the lists of Levitical families drawn up when David organized the Levites for service (1 Chr 23:19; 1 Chr 24:23). Through Hebron, a son of Kohath, he belonged to the Kohathite branch of the tribe of Levi, and as firstborn he probably headed the Hebronite house. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify him with Jerijah, named in 1 Chr 26:31 as chief of the Hebronites, a man whose kin were found in Jazer of Gilead in David's fortieth year. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "founded of Yahweh," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "fear, or throwing down, of the Lord."

Jeribai was one of David's mighty men, the elite warriors listed in 1 Chronicles 11. He is named as a son of Elnaam, along with his brother Joshaviah, and the two appear next to Eliel the Mahavite and Ithmah the Moabite in the later part of the roster (1 Chr 11:46). Nothing else is recorded about him. As the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes, his name belongs to the part of the Chronicles list that has no counterpart in the shorter roster of David's warriors in 2 Sam 23. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "whom Jehovah defends," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia considers the meaning uncertain.

Jericho was an ancient walled city on the plain west of the Jordan, north of the Dead Sea, called "the city of palm trees" (2 Chr 28:15). Israel camped in the plains of Moab opposite it before crossing the Jordan. Joshua sent spies there, and Rahab hid them. The city was shut up against Israel, its walls fell after Israel marched around it for seven days, and its king was destroyed. It was assigned to Benjamin. Hiel of Bethel later rebuilt it at the cost of his sons, as Joshua had foretold. Elijah and Elisha stopped there, and a company of prophets lived there. Zedekiah was captured in its plains, and 345 of its people returned from exile. Jesus healed blind Bartimaeus nearby and passed through the town. Easton's Bible Dictionary places the Old Testament city near Elisha's Fountain, at Tell es-Sultan, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Jeriel was a man of the tribe of Issachar, one of the six sons of Tola named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 7:2. His brothers were Uzzi, Rephaiah, Jahmai, Jibsam and Shemuel. The passage calls these sons heads of their father's house and valiant men of might. It also gives the number of their descendants in the days of David as 22,600. Tola himself was a son of Issachar (1 Chr 7:1), so Jeriel belongs to an early generation of the tribe. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "founded of God," Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "people of God," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "fear, or vision of God."

Jerijah was a Levite, the chief of the Hebronites, a family descended from Hebron son of Kohath, during the reign of David. In David's fortieth year a search was made through the family records, and capable, valiant men of this clan were found at Jazer in Gilead, east of the Jordan (1 Chr 26:31). Their recorded duties lay among the tribes east of the river, serving both the king and the worship of God. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary treat him as the same person as Jeriah, named as head of the Hebronites in 1 Chr 23:19 and 24:23. The two spellings are variant forms of one Hebrew name, meaning something like "founded of the LORD." This entry follows that identification.

Jerimoth was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named as one of the five sons of Bela in 1 Chr 7:7, alongside Ezbon, Uzzi, Uzziel and Iri. Bela was Benjamin's firstborn son (1 Chr 7:6). The verse calls these five heads of their fathers' houses and mighty men of valour, and says their descendants were counted at 22,034 in the genealogies. Other passages list Bela's sons differently: 1 Chr 8:3–5 names Addar, Gera, Abihud, Abishua, Naaman and Ahoah, and Num 26:40 names Ard. Those men also count as Jerimoth's brothers here. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that "son" may mean a descendant rather than a direct son. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jerimoth, and this one appears only in this genealogy. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Jerimoth was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the nine sons of Becher listed in the genealogy at 1 Chr 7:8. His brothers were Zemira, Joash, Eliezer, Elioenai, Omri, Abiah, Anathoth and Alameth. Becher himself appears in the same chapter as a son of Benjamin, so Jerimoth was Benjamin's grandson. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as the head of a Benjamite house, and STEPBible's proper-names index spells the name Jeremoth. Smith's gives the meaning of the name as "heights", while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "he that fears or rejects death." Several other men in the Bible are named Jerimoth, and this one should not be confused with them.

Jerimoth was one of the warriors who joined David at Ziklag, named in a list alongside Eluzai, Bealiah, Shemariah and Shephatiah the Haruphite (1 Chr 12:5). The surrounding passage describes these men as kinsmen of Saul from the tribe of Benjamin who came to David while he was still kept away from Saul. They were skilled with both right and left hands in slinging stones and shooting arrows, so Easton's Bible Dictionary calls Jerimoth a Benjamite slinger. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jerimoth, and this one should not be confused with them.

Jerimoth, also spelled Jeremoth, was a Levite and one of the fourteen sons of Heman listed among the musicians David organized for service at the sanctuary (1 Chr 25:4). The surrounding chapter describes Heman's sons as leading worship with cymbals, harps and lyres under their father's direction. When the musicians were divided by lot into twenty-four groups of twelve, the fifteenth lot fell to Jeremoth, who served together with his sons and relatives (1 Chr 25:22). The two spellings almost certainly refer to the same man, since both appear in the same list of Heman's sons. Smith's Bible Dictionary places his service in David's reign, about 1014 BC, a date inferred from context. Several other men in the Bible share this name, and this entry concerns only Heman's son.

Jerimoth son of Azriel was the leader of the tribe of Naphtali in the time of King David. He appears only once, in a list of the chief officers over the tribes of Israel (1 Chr 27:19). The surrounding chapter places this list in David's reign, and by inference he served as the tribe's head or prince within David's administration. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jerimoth, and this one is distinguished from them by his father's name and his tribe. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "heights," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "he that fears or rejects death."

Jerimoth was a son of King David, known only as the father of Mahalath, who married David's grandson King Rehoboam of Judah (2 Chr 11:18). This made Mahalath and Rehoboam cousins. The same verse names Abihail, daughter of David's brother Eliab, alongside Mahalath. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes her as Rehoboam's second wife, while the STEPBible names index connects her to Jerimoth's family; this entry does not decide between these readings. Jerimoth does not appear in the lists of David's sons born in Hebron and Jerusalem (1 Chr 3:1–9; 2 Sam 5:14–16). He was probably the son of one of David's concubines, whose children 1 Chr 3:9 mentions without naming them. His birth in Jerusalem is likewise an inference. Several other men in the Bible share his name. Smith's gives the meaning "heights."

Jerimoth was one of ten overseers who served in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah, working under Cononiah and his brother Shimei. They were appointed by command of the king and of Azariah, the ruler of the house of God (2 Chr 31:13). The surrounding passage describes how the people brought offerings, tithes and dedicated things to the temple, and the overseers helped manage these stores. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify him as a Levite, which fits the setting, since Levites handled the temple chambers. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "heights," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "he that fears or rejects death." Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Jerimoth belongs to several different men in the Bible, and this one should not be confused with the others.

Jerioth is a woman named once, in the genealogy of Judah at 1 Chr 2:18. In the King James wording she appears as a wife of Caleb son of Hezron, alongside Azubah. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls her one of the elder Caleb's wives, distinguishing him from the better-known Caleb son of Jephunneh. Her name is usually taken to mean "curtains" (of a tent). The verse goes on to list the sons Jesher, Shobab and Ardon, but it is unclear whether "her sons" refers to Jerioth or to Azubah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew of this verse is difficult and has been read in other ways: Jerioth as a daughter of Caleb and Azubah, Azubah as the daughter of Jerioth, or Jerioth as another name for Azubah. This entry follows the reading that makes her Caleb's partner. Nothing else is known about her.

Jeroboam son of Nebat and Zeruah, a widow, was an Ephrathite of Zereda who served Solomon and rebelled against him (1 Kgs 11:26). The prophet Ahijah met him outside Jerusalem, and when Solomon sought to kill him he fled to Shishak of Egypt until Solomon's death. After the northern tribes broke with Rehoboam, they made Jeroboam king over Israel, leaving only Judah to David's house. He became the first king of the northern kingdom, from about 975 BC by inference from context, and reigned twenty-two years. Fearing the people would return to David's line, he set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan and appointed priests from outside the Levites. At the Bethel altar a man of God from Judah confronted him. He fought Abijah of Judah and was defeated. His son Abijah died young, and Nadab succeeded him. Later kings are repeatedly measured against "the sins of Jeroboam." A later king of Israel had the same name.

Jeroboam, usually called Jeroboam II, was king of the northern kingdom of Israel. He was the son of Joash (also called Jehoash) and succeeded him on the throne in Samaria (2 Kgs 13:13; 14:16). He began to reign in the fifteenth year of Amaziah of Judah and ruled forty-one years, about 825–784 BC by inference from context (2 Kgs 14:23). Through him Israel was delivered, and he recovered Damascus and Hamath for Israel (2 Kgs 14:27–28). The prophets Hosea and Amos were active during his reign (Hos 1:1; Amos 1:1). Amos foretold that God would rise against his house with the sword, and Amaziah the priest of Bethel reported this to the king as a conspiracy (Amos 7:9–11). At his death his son Zachariah succeeded him but reigned only six months (2 Kgs 14:29; 15:8). He is distinct from the earlier Jeroboam son of Nebat, Israel's first king.

Jeroham was the father of Elkanah and so the grandfather of the prophet Samuel. Samuel's birth to Elkanah and Hannah follows later in the same chapter. 1 Sam 1:1 names Jeroham's father as Elihu and places the family at Ramathaim-zophim in the hill country of Ephraim. The genealogies of 1 Chr 6 list him among the Levite descendants of Kohath, where his father appears as Eliab (1 Chr 6:27) and Eliel (1 Chr 6:34). These are probably variant forms of the same name. The description of Elkanah as an "Ephrathite" has been read as tribal (Ephraimite, as in the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or as referring to where the family lived. This entry follows the Chronicles genealogy in placing him in the tribe of Levi. The name means "may he be compassionate," and some Greek manuscripts render it Jerahmeel. Several other people in the Bible share the name.

Jeroham was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8 as the father of six sons: Shamsherai, Shehariah, Athaliah (here a man's name), Jaresiah, Eliah and Zichri. The list of his sons runs across 1 Chr 8:26–27 and ends with the words "the sons of Jeroham." The verse that follows describes the men in this part of the list as heads of families who lived in Jerusalem, so Jeroham's descendants were probably counted among the Benjamite households there. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as the founder of a Benjamite family known by his name. Several men in the Bible are called Jeroham, and it is uncertain whether this one is the same as any of the others. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "high," "merciful" or "beloved."

Jeroham was the father, or possibly a more distant ancestor, of Ibneiah. Ibneiah appears in 1 Chr 9:8 among the Benjamites who settled in Jerusalem, in a list of residents usually understood as those living there after the return from exile. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper names index both identify this Jeroham as a Benjamite, which fits the context of the surrounding list. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes "son" in the broader sense of descendant and dates him to some time before 588 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as "merciful" or "beloved," belongs to several men in the Bible, including the father of Elkanah and grandfather of Samuel. This Jeroham is generally treated as a separate person.

Jeroham was a priest, known only as an ancestor of Adaiah, one of the priests who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile. Nehemiah 11:12 names him as the son of Pelaliah and traces his line back through Amzi, Zechariah and Pashur to Malchiah. Adaiah appears there among the 822 priests who did the work of the temple. 1 Chronicles 9:12 gives a shorter version of the same line, calling Jeroham the son of Pashur. This is probably the same person, with the intervening generations left out, and Easton's Bible Dictionary also suggests the two passages refer to one man. This entry treats them as the same. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes to mean "may he be compassionate."

Jeroham of Gedor was the father of Joelah and Zebadiah, two of the men who came to David at Ziklag (1 Chr 12:7). By inference from the surrounding passage (1 Chr 12:1–2), these were warriors who joined David while he was still kept away from King Saul. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies Jeroham as a Benjamite, and Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to some time before about 1055 BC. The text itself tells us nothing about Jeroham beyond his sons and his connection with Gedor. Which Gedor is meant is uncertain. A town of that name lay in the hill country of Judah, but the context may point to a place in or near Benjamin. Several other men in the Bible are also called Jeroham, and this one should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "high," "merciful," or "beloved."

Jeroham was a man of the tribe of Dan, known only as the father of Azareel. In the list of tribal leaders under King David, Azareel son of Jeroham is named as the prince, or chief officer, over Dan (1 Chr 27:22). Nothing else is recorded about Jeroham himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Azareel may have been his son or a later descendant. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as meaning "may he be compassionate." Several other men in the Bible share the name Jeroham, including the father of Elkanah and grandfather of Samuel, and this Danite should not be confused with them.

Jeroham was the father of Azariah, one of the captains of hundreds whom the priest Jehoiada brought into a covenant with him in the seventh year of Queen Athaliah's rule (2 Chr 23:1). These commanders helped Jehoiada overthrow Athaliah and place the young Joash on the throne of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about Jeroham himself; he is known only through his son. The name, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders "may he be compassionate," is shared by several men in the Bible, and this Jeroham is distinct from the others. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to some time before 876 BC, and that date is an estimate rather than something the text states.

Jerubbesheth is a name for Gideon, the judge of Israel, used only once, in 2 Sam 11:21. There Joab, sending news of Uriah's death to David, expects the king to recall how Abimelech the son of Jerubbesheth was killed at Thebez when a woman dropped a piece of millstone on him from the wall. The account in Judges 9 calls Abimelech's father Jerubbaal, the name Gideon received after tearing down Baal's altar (Judges 6:32). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both treat Jerubbesheth as another name for Gideon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains that later scribes, reluctant to pronounce the name Baal, sometimes replaced "baal" with "bosheth," meaning "shameful thing." It compares Ish-bosheth, called Eshbaal in 1 Chronicles. Jerubbesheth is therefore probably an altered form of Jerubbaal.

Jeruel was a stretch of wilderness in Judah, named only in 2 Chr 20:16. When Moabites, Ammonites and their allies invaded during the reign of Jehoshaphat, the Levite Jahaziel told the king that the army of Judah would meet them as they came up by the cliff of Ziz, at the end of the valley, before the wilderness of Jeruel. The name is usually explained as meaning “founded by God.” The exact area is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on the ascent from the Dead Sea toward Jerusalem, beyond the wilderness of Tekoa (compare 2 Chr 20:20) in the direction of En-gedi, and links it with the district then called el-Hasasah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mentions a suggestion that the name may be a variant of Jezreel in Judah (Josh 15:56). The location shown here follows Easton's identification, in the Judean wilderness between Tekoa and En-gedi, and is approximate.

Jerusalem, also called Zion, Jebus and Salem, was the chief city of ancient Israel in the hill country of Judah. It is the present-day city of Jerusalem, and the location shown here lies in its Old City. Its Canaanite king Adonizedek opposed Joshua (Josh 10:1). David made it his capital, reigning there thirty-three years over all Israel and Judah, and brought the ark there (2 Sam 5:5; 2 Chr 1:4). Solomon built the temple there, and it remained the seat of Judah's kings until the Babylonian army broke down its walls and carried its people captive (2 Kgs 25:10; Jer 52:29). After Cyrus of Persia ordered the temple rebuilt, exiles returned to restore the city (Ezra 1:2; Neh 1:2). Jesus was presented, taught, tried and put to death there, and it was the first center of the church (Luke 2:22; Acts 1:4). Later writers also speak of a heavenly or new Jerusalem (Heb 12:22; Rev 3:12).

The Jerusalem Council was a meeting of the apostles and elders in Jerusalem, held about AD 46 by inference from context, to decide whether Gentile believers had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. The question arose at Antioch when men from Judea demanded circumcision, and after sharp debate Paul and Barnabas were sent to Jerusalem (Acts 15:1–2). There some believing Pharisees pressed the same demand. Peter recalled how God had given the Holy Spirit to Gentiles who heard the gospel from him, and Barnabas and Paul reported the wonders done among the Gentiles. James then proposed that Gentiles not be burdened, but only asked to avoid food offered to idols, sexual immorality, strangled animals and blood (Acts 15:19–20). A letter to the churches of Antioch, Syria and Cilicia was carried by Judas Barsabas and Silas with Paul and Barnabas, and was received with joy.

Jerusalem's is the possessive form of Jerusalem, the hill city in the Judean highlands that became the capital of Israel and the site of the temple. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that it was also called Salem, Jebus, Ariel and "the holy city." It is first mentioned as Salem in Gen 14:18, and later as Jerusalem under its king Adonizedek in Josh 10:1. David captured it from the Jebusites and made it his capital, Solomon built the temple there, and after the kingdom divided it served as the capital of Judah. Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon destroyed it, it was rebuilt after the exile under Cyrus, as described in Ezra and Nehemiah, and the Romans destroyed it again in AD 70. The location shown here is the Old City of present-day Jerusalem. No verses are attached to this particular form of the name.

Jerushah was the wife of King Uzziah of Judah and the mother of his son and successor, King Jotham. She is named only in the brief notices that open Jotham's reign, which record that he became king at twenty-five and reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem (2 Kgs 15:33; 2 Chr 27:1). 2 Kings spells her name Jerusha. Both passages call her the daughter of Zadok. Nothing more is said about this Zadok, and it is uncertain whether he is connected to any other man of that name. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains her name as meaning "possessed," that is, by a husband. Because Jotham appears as Joatham in the line of descent given in Matt 1:9, Jerushah is, by inference, an ancestor in the genealogy of Jesus, though she is not named there.

Jesaiah was a man of the tribe of Judah, a son of Hananiah, named in the genealogy of David's royal line in 1 Chr 3:21. The verse that follows the line from David through the kings and the exile (1 Chr 3:19) shows Hananiah as a son of Zerubbabel, so Jesaiah was probably Zerubbabel's grandson. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him after 536 BC. The wording of 1 Chr 3:21 is compressed, and the 'sons of' Rephaiah, Arnan, Obadiah and Shechaniah can be read in more than one way. Some read the verse as tracing Jesaiah's family line through these men, which is why STEPBible's name list calls him a descendant of Shecaniah. This entry treats them as Jesaiah's brothers, alongside Pelatiah. His name means 'salvation of the Lord' and is a form of the name also spelled Jeshaiah. Several other men in the Bible bear it.

Jesaiah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only once, as the earliest ancestor in the genealogy of Sallu son of Meshullam (Neh 11:7). Sallu was one of the Benjamites living in Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time, after the return from the Babylonian exile. The genealogy traces Sallu back through Meshullam, Joed, Pedaiah, Kolaiah, Maaseiah and Ithiel to Jesaiah, who was Ithiel's father. Since he stands seven generations before Sallu, Jesaiah probably lived well before the exile. Nothing else is recorded about him. The same Hebrew name, often spelled Jeshaiah in English, belongs to several other men in the Bible, but this Jesaiah is identified only by his place in this family line. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "health, or salvation, of the Lord."

Jeshaiah was a Levite of the line of Moses, the son of Rehabiah and the father of Joram. In 1 Chr 24:21 he appears as Isshiah, the first of Rehabiah's sons. In 1 Chr 26:25 he is part of a line running from Eliezer through Rehabiah, Jeshaiah, Joram and Zichri to Shelomith. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 26:26) names Shelomith as the man over the treasuries of dedicated things. The wider chapter (1 Chr 23:15–17) shows that this Eliezer was a son of Moses, so Easton's Bible Dictionary calls Jeshaiah a Kohathite Levite. Smith's Bible Dictionary places the lists in the reign of David, though Jeshaiah himself may have lived earlier as an ancestor in the line. Several other men in the Bible share this name.

Jeshaiah was a Levite, one of the sons of Jeduthun, the musician who led his sons in prophesying with the harp to give thanks and praise to the LORD (1 Chr 25:3). His name means "salvation of the LORD" or "deliverance of Yah," according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. When the temple singers were divided by lot into twenty-four courses in David's time, the eighth lot fell to Jeshaiah, whose group of sons and relatives numbered twelve (1 Chr 25:15). The list in 1 Chr 25:3 counts six sons of Jeduthun but names only five. Shimei, who is counted among the brothers here, probably supplies the missing name, since he appears in the later list of lots (1 Chr 25:17). Izri is likely the same person as Zeri (1 Chr 25:11). Several other men in the Bible bear the name Jeshaiah.

Jeshaiah, son of Athaliah, was a member of the family of Elam who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. Ezra 8:7 lists him as the head of the Elam family group in that company, with seventy males accompanying him. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the return to about 459 BC. The name means "deliverance of the Lord" or "salvation of the Lord," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that he appears as Jesias (Josias in the King James Version) in the parallel list in 1 Esdras 8:33. His father Athaliah is a man, not to be confused with the queen of the same name. Several other men in the Bible are also called Jeshaiah, and this one is known only from this single verse.

Jeshaiah was a Levite of the family of Merari who travelled with Ezra from Babylon to Jerusalem. Ezra 8:19 names him alongside Hashabiah. The two led a group of their relatives and sons, twenty men in all. The surrounding passage shows that Ezra had sent for Levites to serve at the temple because none had joined his company at first. Jeshaiah and his kinsmen were among those who answered that call. His name means "salvation of the Lord" (Smith's Bible Dictionary) or "deliverance of Yah" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same man appears as "Osaias" in 1 Esdras 8:48. Several other people in the Bible share the name, and this entry refers only to the Merarite of Ezra's time. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Jeshanah was a town of the northern kingdom of Israel. Together with its surrounding villages, it was one of three towns that King Abijah of Judah took from Jeroboam after defeating him. The other two were Bethel and Ephrain (2 Chr 13:19). The name probably means "old." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that most scholars read the same name in place of "Shen" in 1 Sam 7:12, where Samuel set up the stone Ebenezer between Mizpeh and Shen. It also links the town with Isanas, a place mentioned by the historian Josephus. The same work identifies Jeshanah with the modern Ain Sinia (Ein Sinya), about 3¼ miles north of Bethel, a site with a spring and ancient remains. The location shown here follows that identification.

Jesharelah was a Levite musician, one of the sons of Asaph, who led the seventh of the twenty-four divisions of temple musicians organized under King David. In 1 Chr 25:2 he is called Asarelah and is listed with his brothers Zaccur, Joseph and Nethaniah. All of them served under their father's direction and "prophesied according to the order of the king," which the surrounding chapter connects with music on harps, lyres and cymbals. When the duties were assigned by lot, the seventh lot fell to Jesharelah, and his group, made up of his sons and relatives, numbered twelve (1 Chr 25:14). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of the name as "upright toward God." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may stand for a family of musicians as well as an individual.

Jeshebeab was a man whose family was assigned the fourteenth of the twenty-four divisions, or courses, of priests. 1 Chronicles 24 describes these divisions being drawn by lot in David's time so that the descendants of Aaron could take turns serving in the sanctuary. He is mentioned only once, in 1 Chr 6:13 of this list (1 Chr 24:13), and nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary take the name to mean "father's seat". The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that one manuscript of the Greek Septuagint reads the name as "Ishbaal", and another leaves it out. It suggests the Hebrew form may have been altered because the original contained the word "baal".

Jesher was a man of the tribe of Judah, listed as the first of three sons of Caleb the son of Hezron, alongside Shobab and Ardon (1 Chr 2:18). The verse names two women, Caleb's wife Azubah and Jerioth, and its wording leaves it unclear which is the mother of these sons. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both take Azubah to be his mother. Caleb had other sons by other women, including Hur, Mesha and Gazez, so Jesher's wider family appears across the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles 2. Jesher appears only in this one verse, and nothing more is recorded about his life. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "uprightness."

Jeshimon, meaning "the waste" or "desolation," was a barren wilderness in Judah near Ziph. In 1 Samuel it serves as a landmark during Saul's pursuit of David. The hill of Hachilah, where David hid and where Saul later camped, lay south of or "before" Jeshimon (1 Sam 23:19; 26:1, 3), and the wilderness of Maon lay to its south (1 Sam 23:24). The Hebrew word is also an ordinary noun for desert, and Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it may simply mean "the waste" below the plateau of Ziph rather than a proper name. The same term appears in Num 21:20 and 23:28 near Pisgah and Peor, possibly for a district east of the Dead Sea. The location shown here follows Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, which place it in the dry, chalky hills west of the Dead Sea, between the Judean highlands and the shore.

Jeshishai was a man of the tribe of Gad, named only once, in the genealogy of 1 Chr 5:14. He is listed as the son of Jahdo and the father of Michael, in a line of ancestors that runs back to Buz and forward to Abihail son of Huri, whose sons were among the Gadite family heads. The surrounding passage places these Gadites east of the Jordan in Gilead and Bashan. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "descended from an old man," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "aged." That encyclopedia also raises the possibility that the name stands for a family or clan as well as an individual.

Jeshohaiah was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named only once, in a list of Simeonite leaders (1 Chr 4:36). The surrounding passage calls the men in this list princes, or heads, of their families. It says their clans grew large and that in the days of King Hezekiah of Judah they moved toward Gedor in search of pasture, drove out the people living there and settled in their place. So Jeshohaiah probably lived in Hezekiah's reign, around the late 8th century BC by inference from context. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 711 BC and, drawing on the genealogy earlier in the chapter, counts him among the descendants of Shimei. It gives the name's meaning as "whom Jehovah casts down," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the meaning as unknown. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jeshua was a town in Judah where people of Judah settled after returning from the Babylonian exile. It appears only once, in Neh 11:26, in a list of settlements that also includes Moladah and Beth-phelet. Those neighbouring towns lay in the Negev, so Jeshua was probably in the far south of Judah, in the region around Beersheba. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the same place as Shema in Josh 15:26, and possibly Sheba in Josh 19:2. It also proposes Khirbet Sa'weh, a walled ruin on a prominent hill about 12 miles (19 km) east-northeast of Beersheba, as the site. The exact location is uncertain, and the location shown here is only a rough placement in that southern area. The name is the same as Joshua.

Jeshua was a Levite in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He is one of six men named in 2 Chr 31:15 who served "next" to Kore, the Levite placed in charge of the freewill offerings brought to the temple. Based in the cities of the priests, these men had the set duty of handing out portions to their fellow priests and Levites according to their divisions (courses), to the great and the small alike. Context places this in Hezekiah's reform of temple worship, roughly the late 8th century BC; Smith's Bible Dictionary dates it to about 726 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is another form of Joshua, and several other men in the Bible share it, so he should not be confused with the high priest Jeshua who returned from exile.

Jeshua was the ancestor of one branch of the family of Pahath-moab, alongside a second branch descended from Joab. He is mentioned only in the lists of exiles who returned from Babylon to Judah. Ezra 2:6 counts 2,812 descendants of Pahath-moab through Jeshua and Joab, while the parallel list in Neh 7:11 gives 2,818. Here Jeshua and Joab are treated as sons of Pahath-moab, although the lists could also mean more distant descendants. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes the Pahath-moab clan as probably one of the chief families of Judah. Jeshua is another form of the name Joshua. Several other people in the Bible share the name, including the high priest of the return, and they should be kept distinct from this ancestral figure.

Jeshua, son of Azaniah, was a leading Levite after the return from exile in Babylon. His name is a form of Joshua, according to Smith's and Hitchcock's dictionaries. His descendants, counted with those of Kadmiel, numbered seventy-four among the returning Levites. When work on the temple began, he and his sons stood with Kadmiel to direct the workmen. Later, when Ezra read the law, Jeshua was among the Levites who helped the people understand it. He also led public prayer and praise from the stairs, and his name heads the Levites who sealed the covenant in Neh 10:9. Because the name appears over several generations and was shared by others, including the high priest Jeshua, it is uncertain whether every mention refers to the same man. It may sometimes stand for the family he headed, as Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it.

Jeshua was the father of Jozabad, one of the Levites who helped weigh the silver, gold and temple vessels brought from Babylon by Ezra's company. The weighing took place in the house of God in Jerusalem on the fourth day after the group arrived, under the priest Meremoth son of Uriah (Ezra 8:33). He is known only through his son's name, and nothing else is said about him. Because his son is counted among the Levites, Jeshua was probably a Levite himself, and Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him that way. Several men in Ezra and Nehemiah share the name Jeshua, including Levites of the returning exiles, so this Jeshua may be one of them, but the text does not say which. The name is a form of Joshua (Hitchcock's Bible Names).

Jeshua was the father of Ezer, one of the men who repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah after the return from exile. He is mentioned only once, in the list of builders, where Ezer worked on a stretch facing the ascent to the armoury at the angle of the wall (Neh 3:19). The verse calls someone "the ruler of Mizpah," but the wording leaves unclear whether the title belongs to Ezer or to his father Jeshua. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several people in the Bible share the name Jeshua, and it is uncertain whether this man is the same as any of the others. Hitchcock's Bible Names treats the name as a form of Joshua.

Jeshua, son of Kadmiel, was one of the chief Levites named in Neh 12:24, alongside Hashabiah and Sherebiah. With their fellow Levites, these leaders were set in opposing groups to lead praise and thanksgiving in turns, "ward over against ward," following the arrangement attributed to David. The surrounding chapter places this list in the period after the return from exile, and the STEPBible Proper Names index places him in Nehemiah's time and links him with the dedication of Jerusalem's wall. Elsewhere Jeshua and Kadmiel appear side by side as Levite family names, so some readers take "son of" here as a way of linking the two households rather than a literal father and son. This entry follows the wording of the verse. His name is a form of Joshua, according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Several other men in the Bible bear the same name.

Jeshua was a priest whose name is linked here with a priestly family and with the son of Jozadak. In David's arrangement of the priests, the ninth course fell by lot to Jeshua (1 Chr 24:11). Easton's Bible Dictionary treats him as head of that ninth order. After the exile, 973 priests of the house of Jeshua, counted among the descendants of Jedaiah, returned to Jerusalem (Ezra 2:36; Neh 7:39). Ezra 10:18 names Jeshua son of Jozadak, some of whose descendants had married foreign wives. Other passages, such as Ezra 3:2 and Hag 1:1, where he is called Joshua, present this son of Jozadak as the high priest who led the return alongside Zerubbabel. It is uncertain whether the Jeshua of David's time and the son of Jozadak are best treated as one figure or several. This entry combines the references under the father Jozadak.

Jesiah was a Korahite named among the warriors who joined David, listed with Elkanah, Azareel, Joezer and Jashobeam in 1 Chr 12:6. The surrounding chapter describes the men who came to David at Ziklag while he was still in hiding from Saul, so Jesiah was by inference one of these early supporters. Smith's Bible Dictionary places this about 1055 BC, a date estimated from context. Modern translations spell his name Isshiah, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives its meaning as "Yah exists." Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "whom Jehovah lends." The term "Korhites" probably means he descended from Korah the Levite, though some take it to refer to a different Korah of the tribe of Judah or Benjamin. Several other men in the Old Testament bear the name Isshiah, and nothing else is known of this one.

Jesimiel was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named in a list of Simeonite clan leaders in 1 Chr 4:36. The surrounding passage describes these men as princes in their families whose households grew large. In the days of King Hezekiah they moved toward Gedor in search of pasture for their flocks and took over land held by earlier inhabitants (1 Chr 4:38–41). That places him, by inference from context, in the late 8th century BC. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him among the family of Shimei, a Simeonite named a few verses earlier. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "God establishes," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "naming, or astonishment, of God."

Jesse was the father of King David, a man of the tribe of Judah living at Bethlehem, and the son of Obed, grandson of Boaz and Ruth. When God sent Samuel to anoint a king from among his sons, Jesse presented the older sons first and had not called the youngest, David, who was tending the sheep. He later sent David to Saul with bread, wine and a young goat, and sent food to his three eldest sons, Eliab, Abinadab and Shammah, serving in Saul's army. 1 Sam 17:12 says he had eight sons, while 1 Chr 2:13–15 names seven. David is often called "the son of Jesse," sometimes dismissively by opponents. Isaiah speaks of a "root of Jesse," a passage Paul quotes, and Jesse appears in the genealogies of Jesus. According to 1 Sam 22:3, David later sheltered his parents with the king of Moab.

The Jesus' 1st Tour of Galilee was a preaching journey through the towns of Galilee, recorded in Matthew, Mark and Luke. In Mark and Luke it follows the evening of healings at Capernaum, after Peter's mother-in-law was cured. Early the next morning Jesus went out alone to a solitary place to pray. Simon Peter and his companions found him and told him that everyone was looking for him, and the crowds tried to keep him from leaving. Jesus answered that he must preach in other towns too, because that was why he had been sent (Mark 1:38; Luke 4:43). He then preached in synagogues throughout Galilee, proclaimed the kingdom, cast out demons and healed many kinds of illness. Matthew adds that his fame spread through Syria and that great crowds followed him from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea and beyond the Jordan. The date, about AD 28, is inferred from context.

The 2nd Tour of Galilee was a preaching journey in which Jesus traveled through every city and village, announcing the good news of the kingdom of God. It is described briefly in Luke 8:1–3 and follows the account of the sinful woman who anointed him. The twelve disciples went with him, along with several women who had been healed of evil spirits and illnesses. Luke names three of them: Mary Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out; Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod's steward; and Susanna. Many other women also traveled with the group and supported Jesus out of their own resources. The text does not say how long the tour lasted or which towns were visited. This entry places it in about AD 28, an estimate inferred from context, and the region is taken to be Galilee from its setting in Luke's narrative.

Jesus, also called Justus, was a Jewish Christian named by Paul at the close of his letter to the Colossians. Paul sends greetings from him together with Aristarchus and Mark, and says that these men, the only ones "of the circumcision" (that is, Jewish believers) among his fellow workers for the kingdom of God, had been a comfort to him (Col 4:11). Since Paul wrote this letter as a prisoner, Jesus Justus was probably with him during that imprisonment, as the STEPBible Proper Names index also understands it. Nothing more is known of him. His name is the Greek form of the Hebrew Joshua, which Hitchcock's Bible Names renders "savior" or "deliverer," and his Latin surname Justus means "just." The name Jesus was common among Jews of the period and is shared by several people in the Bible, including Jesus of Nazareth.

Jesus Christ is the central figure of the New Testament. "Jesus" is the Greek form of Joshua, meaning "the LORD saves," and "Christ" is the Greek equivalent of "Messiah," meaning "anointed." Matthew traces his descent from Abraham and David through the tribe of Judah (Matt 1:1). He was born in Bethlehem to Mary, the wife of Joseph, about 4 BC by inference from context. He grew up in Nazareth and had brothers named James, Joses, Jude and Simon. After John baptized him, he taught and healed mainly in Galilee and then went to Jerusalem, where he was crucified about AD 30. The Gospels report that he rose on the third day and ascended to heaven (Luke 24:46). John calls him the Word (John 1:1), and apostles such as Paul, Peter, James and Jude call themselves his servants. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him with Old Testament promises such as the Prophet like Moses, Immanuel and the Branch.

Jesus and Nicodemus was a night conversation in Jerusalem between Jesus and Nicodemus, a Pharisee and "ruler of the Jews." It probably took place during the Passover described just before (John 2:23), about AD 27 by inference from context. Nicodemus called Jesus a teacher come from God because of his miracles. Jesus answered that no one can see the kingdom of God without being "born again," or "born of water and of the Spirit," and compared the Spirit to the wind, whose origin cannot be traced. When Nicodemus asked how this could be, Jesus asked how a teacher of Israel did not know these things. Jesus then said the Son of man must be "lifted up" as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so that believers would have eternal life. Interpreters differ on whether John 3:16–21 continues Jesus' words or is the Gospel writer's comment. Nicodemus appears again in John 7:50 and 19:39.

event: Jesus as a child in the Temple
text: Jesus as a child in the Temple is the episode, recorded only in Luke, in which the twelve-year-old Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem after the Passover. His parents went to the feast every year. On the way home, Joseph and Mary assumed he was traveling with their relatives and acquaintances, and they went a full day's journey before they noticed he was missing. They returned to Jerusalem, and after three days they found him in the Temple, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking questions. Everyone who heard him was astonished at his understanding and his answers. When his mother said that she and his father had been searching for him anxiously, he replied that they should have known he must be about his Father's business, a saying they did not understand. This entry dates the event to about AD 9, an estimate inferred from his age.

Jesus ascends to Heaven describes the moment, recorded in Acts 1, when the risen Jesus was taken up from his apostles, the Eleven. When they gathered and asked whether he would now restore the kingdom to Israel, he said the times were set by the Father's authority. He promised instead that they would receive power when the Holy Spirit came on them and would be his witnesses in Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria and to the ends of the earth. As they watched, he was lifted up and a cloud hid him from view. Two men in white then stood beside them and said that this same Jesus would come back in the same way they had seen him go. The next verse, Acts 1:12, places the event on the Mount of Olives (Olivet), and Luke 24:50–51 gives a parallel account near Bethany. The date, about AD 30, is inferred from context.

The calling of Matthew by Jesus is recorded in all three Synoptic Gospels. Passing by the Sea of Galilee, apparently near Capernaum, Jesus saw a tax collector sitting at his tax booth and said, "Follow me," and he got up and followed him. Matthew's Gospel calls him Matthew, while Mark and Luke call him Levi, and Mark adds that he was the son of Alphaeus. The accounts are generally taken as describing the same man. Luke says he left everything and then held a large feast at his house, where many tax collectors and others ate with Jesus and his disciples. The scribes and Pharisees objected to his eating with tax collectors and sinners. Jesus replied that the healthy do not need a doctor, only the sick, and that he came to call sinners to repentance, not the righteous. This entry dates the event to about AD 28, by inference from context.

Jesus Circumsized refers to the circumcision and naming of Jesus when he was eight days old, recorded in Luke 2:21. Following the Jewish practice of circumcising a son on the eighth day (see Gen 17:12 and Lev 12:3), Jesus's parents had him circumcised and gave him the name Jesus. Luke notes that this was the name the angel had given before he was conceived, which points back to Gabriel's message to Mary in Luke 1:31. The event is dated here to about 4 BC, an estimate inferred from context, and it would have lasted a single day. Luke describes it briefly, just before the account of Jesus being presented at the temple in Jerusalem. This entry places it in sequence after Herod's killing of the male children of Bethlehem, an event found only in Matthew's account.

Jesus Growing Up refers to the years Jesus spent in Nazareth after his parents found him in the Temple at Jerusalem at about age twelve. Luke says he went back with Mary and Joseph to Nazareth and was obedient to them, while his mother kept in her heart all that had happened. Luke then sums up this period in one sentence: Jesus grew in wisdom and in stature, and in favor with God and with people. Nothing else is recorded of these years. This entry dates them from about AD 9 and gives them a span of roughly seventeen years, both by inference from context. The span runs until Jesus began his public work, when Luke 3:23 says he was about thirty. Elsewhere, Mark 6:3 calls him "the carpenter," which suggests the trade he followed in Nazareth.

The departure of Jesus from Judea toward Galilee is recorded in all four Gospels and marks the start of his public work in Galilee. Matthew and Mark connect it with the imprisonment of John the Baptist: once Jesus heard that John had been put in prison, he went into Galilee, where Mark says he began preaching the gospel of the kingdom of God (Matt 4:12; Mark 1:14). Luke says he returned "in the power of the Spirit" and that news about him spread through the surrounding region (Luke 4:14). John gives a different reason. The Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John, though it was his disciples who did the baptizing, so Jesus left Judea and passed through Samaria on the way (John 4:1–4). This entry dates the journey to about AD 27, an estimate inferred from context.

The visit in which Jesus meets Martha and Mary is recorded in Luke 10:38–42. While traveling, Jesus entered a village, and a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house. Her sister Mary sat at his feet and listened to his teaching, while Martha was busy with many tasks of serving. Martha asked Jesus whether he cared that her sister had left her to serve alone, and asked him to tell Mary to help. Jesus answered that Martha was anxious and troubled about many things, but only one thing was needed, and Mary had chosen the good part, which would not be taken from her. Luke leaves the village unnamed. It is identified as Bethany by inference from John 11:1, which places Martha and Mary, the sisters of Lazarus, there. Following the order in Luke, the visit comes after the parable of the Good Samaritan, probably about AD 29 by inference from context.

event: Jesus' Message on John the Baptist
text: Jesus' Message on John the Baptist was Jesus' reply to a question sent by the imprisoned John, followed by his public teaching about John (Matt 11:2–19; Luke 7:18–35). John sent two disciples to ask whether Jesus was the one who was to come. Jesus pointed to what they had seen and heard: the blind seeing, the lame walking, lepers cleansed, the dead raised, and the poor hearing the gospel. After they left, he told the crowds that John was more than a prophet. He was the messenger foretold in scripture to prepare the way, and the Elijah who was to come. No one born of women was greater, yet the least in the kingdom was greater than he. Jesus compared his generation to children in the marketplace who rejected both the austere John and the Son of Man who ate and drank. It took place in Galilee, about AD 28 by inference from context, after the raising of a widow's son.

The Jesus Rejected at Nazareth episode took place when Jesus returned to the town where he had grown up and, as was his custom, attended the synagogue on the sabbath. Handed the scroll of Isaiah, he read a passage about one anointed by the Spirit to preach good news to the poor, free captives and give sight to the blind, then declared it fulfilled that day. The listeners admired his words but asked, "Is not this Joseph's son?" Jesus answered that no prophet is accepted in his own country. He recalled that Elijah was sent to a widow of Sarepta in Sidon and that Elisha cleansed only Naaman the Syrian. Enraged, the congregation drove him out of town to the brow of the hill to throw him down, but he passed through them and went away. This entry dates it to about AD 27, by inference from context.

The episode titled Jesus Teaches in Perea covers Jesus' ministry after he left Galilee and came into "Judaea beyond Jordan" (Matt 19:1), the region east of the Jordan known as Perea. It is recorded in Matthew 19–20, Mark 10 and Luke 18. Questioned by Pharisees about divorce, Jesus pointed to God's making humans male and female and said what God has joined, no one should separate. He welcomed little children whom the disciples tried to turn away. A rich young ruler asked how to inherit eternal life, and Jesus told him to sell his possessions and follow him, adding that it is hard for the rich to enter the kingdom. Matthew adds the parable of the vineyard laborers paid equally. Jesus again foretold his death and resurrection in Jerusalem and answered the request for places at his right and left by teaching that greatness means serving. This entry dates it to about AD 30, by inference from context.

The Jesus visits Galilee event is Jesus' return from Judea to Galilee, which all four Gospels record. Matthew and Mark place it after John the Baptist was imprisoned. Mark says Jesus came preaching that the time was fulfilled and the kingdom of God was at hand, calling people to repent and believe. Luke says he returned in the power of the Spirit, taught in the synagogues and became widely known. In John it follows his two-day stay among the Samaritans. Galileans who had seen his deeds at the feast in Jerusalem welcomed him. At Cana a royal official from Capernaum begged him to heal his dying son. Jesus told him his son would live, and the fever left the boy at that same hour, so the man and his household believed. John calls this Jesus' second sign in Galilee. The date, about AD 27, is inferred from context.

The episode of Jesus Walking on Water took place on the Sea of Galilee right after the feeding of the five thousand, in about AD 29 by inference from context. Jesus sent his disciples ahead by boat toward Bethsaida or Capernaum while he dismissed the crowd and went up a mountain alone to pray. Matthew and Mark say he did this after dismissing the crowd, and John says he withdrew because people wanted to make him king. During the night a strong headwind held the boat back. In the fourth watch of the night Jesus came to them walking on the sea. The frightened disciples thought he was a spirit, but he told them, "It is I; be not afraid." Only Matthew records that Peter walked on the water toward him, began to sink, and was caught by Jesus. When Jesus got into the boat the wind stopped, and the disciples worshipped him as the Son of God.

The withdrawal of Jesus to Ephraim was his retreat from public view after the chief priests and Pharisees resolved to put him to death following the raising of Lazarus. John 11:54 says he no longer moved openly among the Jews but went to a town called Ephraim, in a region near the wilderness, and stayed there with his disciples. Ephraim is often identified with the Ophrah of the Old Testament, probably the modern village of et-Taiyibeh northeast of Jerusalem, though the site is uncertain. Meanwhile the Passover was approaching, and many people went up to Jerusalem early to purify themselves. In the temple they looked for Jesus and wondered whether he would come to the feast, because the authorities had ordered that anyone who knew where he was should report it so they could arrest him. By inference from context, the event dates to about AD 30.

Jether was a man of the tribe of Asher, listed in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 7 as the father of Jephunneh, Pispah and Ara. He is probably the same person as Ithran, named in the preceding verse among the sons of Zophah alongside Bezer, Hod, Shamma, Shilshah and Beera. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both make this identification, and this entry follows it. The two names are closely related in Hebrew: Jether is usually explained as meaning "abundance" or "excellence" and Ithran as "excellent." The Asher genealogy describes these families as heads of their fathers' houses and as valiant warriors (1 Chr 7:40), so Smith's Bible Dictionary calls Jether the chief of a family of warriors. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jether.

Jether was the firstborn son of Gideon, the judge who delivered Israel from the Midianites. After Gideon captured the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna, he told Jether to rise and kill them. Jether would not draw his sword, because he was afraid and was still a youth (Judg 8:20). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as the oldest of Gideon's seventy sons. His brothers included Abimelech and Jotham. By inference from Judg 9:5, where Abimelech killed his brothers and only Jotham escaped, Jether probably died in that slaughter, though he is not named there. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "he that excels." Several other men in the Bible share the name Jether, and they should not be confused with this son of Gideon.

Jether, also called Ithra (2 Sam 17:25), was the father of Amasa, whom Absalom made commander of his army in place of Joab. Jether's wife was Abigail, sister of Zeruiah, Joab's mother. The nearby verse 1 Chr 2:16 names Abigail as a sister of David, so Amasa was a nephew of the king and a cousin of Joab. The texts differ on Jether's background: 2 Sam 17:25 calls him an Israelite, while 1 Chr 2:17 calls him an Ishmaelite. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both prefer the reading 'Ishmaelite'. Jether is known only through his son. In 1 Kgs 2:5 and 1 Kgs 2:32, Amasa 'the son of Jether' is remembered as a commander whom Joab killed. The name Jether is shared by several other people in the Bible.

Jether was a man of the tribe of Judah, the son of Jada and the brother of Jonathan. He appears only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:32, which describes Jada as the brother of Shammai and notes that Jether died without children. His line therefore continued through his brother Jonathan. Jada belonged to the family of Jerahmeel, a descendant of Hezron, so the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls Jether a Jerahmeelite. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "he that excels," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "abundance." Several other men in the Bible share the name Jether, and this entry refers only to the son of Jada. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jether was a man of the tribe of Judah, listed in 1 Chr 4:17 as the first of the sons of Ezra, with his brothers Mered, Epher and Jalon. This Ezra appears only in Judah's genealogy and is a different person from the later scribe of the same name. Nothing else is recorded about Jether's life or descendants. The name probably means "abundance" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "he that excels" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other men in the Bible are also called Jether, among them Gideon's eldest son, so this entry concerns only the Judahite named in this genealogy. The verse goes on to say "she bare Miriam, and Shammai, and Ishbah," but it does not name the mother. By inference from the following verse, the children listed there probably belong to Mered rather than to Jether.

Jetheth was one of the chiefs (the King James Version says "dukes") of Edom who descended from Esau. He appears in the list of Edomite chiefs named "according to their families, after their places" (Gen 36:40), which is repeated in 1 Chr 1:51 after the death of King Hadad. Because the list ties each chief to a family and a place, the name may stand for a clan or district as well as an individual. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may be a variant of Jether or Ithran, a Horite name in Gen 36:26. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "a nail", Easton's Bible Dictionary "a peg, or a prince", and Hitchcock's Bible Names "giving". Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jethro was a priest of Midian and the father-in-law of Moses. He is also called Reuel (Exod 2:18) and Raguel (Num 10:29). Smith's and Easton's Bible Dictionaries suggest Reuel was his personal name and Jethro a title. Moses tended Jethro's flocks and was doing so when he came to Horeb, the mountain of God. Later Jethro let him return to Egypt with the words "Go in peace." After the exodus, Jethro brought Moses' wife Zipporah and her two sons to him in the wilderness. He praised the LORD for delivering Israel, offered sacrifices, and ate with Aaron and the elders. His son Hobab was asked to travel with Israel. This entry also identifies him with Deuel, father of Eliasaph, leader of the tribe of Gad. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia instead treat Deuel as a separate Gadite.

Jetur is named in 1 Chr 5:19 as one of the peoples, along with the Hagarites, Nephish and Nodab, against whom the tribes east of the Jordan made war. The surrounding passage identifies those tribes as Reuben, Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh. The name belongs to a people as much as a place. Easton's Bible Dictionary links it to Jetur, one of the twelve sons of Ishmael (Gen 25:15), so this was probably an Ishmaelite tribe living in the lands east of the Jordan. Many scholars connect Jetur with the later region of Ituraea, mentioned in Luke 3:1. The location shown here follows that view, placing it in the hill country around Mount Hermon, in present-day southern Lebanon and southwestern Syria. Its exact territory at the time of this war is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "order," "succession," or "mountainous."

Jetur was one of the twelve sons of Ishmael, Abraham's son by Hagar. He appears only in the lists of Ishmael's sons, between Tema and Naphish (Gen 25:15; 1 Chr 1:31). Nothing is told of his life. His brothers included Nebajoth, Kedar, Adbeel, Dumah and Tema, and his sister Bashemath became a wife of Esau. Like several of Ishmael's sons, Jetur's name also stands for a tribe descended from him. In 1 Chr 5:19 the tribes of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh fight against the Hagrites and Jetur. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary link this people with the Itureans of New Testament times, whose region, Ituraea, is named in Luke 3:1. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "an enclosure." Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "order" or "mountainous."

Jeuel was a man of the tribe of Judah, a descendant of Zerah, son of Judah. He is mentioned only once, in the list of people who lived in Jerusalem (1 Chr 9:6). He is named at the head of the sons of Zerah, who with their relatives numbered six hundred and ninety. By inference from the surrounding passage, which describes the first inhabitants to resettle their towns, this places him among those who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a chief man of Judah. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "snatched away by God," and Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "God hath taken away" or "God heaping up." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jeush was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, listed as the first of the seven sons of Bilhan in 1 Chr 7:10. Bilhan was a son of Jediael, whom the nearby 1 Chr 7:6 names as a son of Benjamin, so Jeush belongs to Benjamin's line a few generations down. One of his brothers was also named Benjamin, after the tribe's ancestor. His other brothers were Ehud, Chenaanah, Zethan, Tharshish and Ahishahar. The following verse describes this family as heads of fathers' houses and mighty men of valour. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the list may originally have belonged to Zebulun, but this entry follows the text's placement among the Benjamites. The name is shared by several other people in the Bible. The same encyclopedia gives its probable meaning as "he protects" or "he comes to help."

Jeush was a Levite, one of the four sons of Shimei listed in David's organization of the Levites (1 Chr 23:10). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place this Shimei among the Gershonites, which fits the surrounding passage. Jeush's brothers were Jahath, the chief, and Zizah (called Zina in 1 Chr 23:10), along with Beriah. Because Jeush and Beriah did not have many sons, the two were counted together as a single father's house in the Levitical reckoning (1 Chr 23:11). The context sets this in David's reign, and Smith's Bible Dictionary dates it to about 1014 BC. The name is probably understood as "he protects" or "he comes to help" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Bible share the name Jeush, so this one should be kept distinct from them.

Jeush was a son of Rehoboam, king of Judah, named alongside his brothers Shamariah and Zaham in the list of Rehoboam's family (2 Chr 11:19). The verse says only that "she" bore these sons, after the preceding verse mentions two wives: Mahalath, a granddaughter of David, and Abihail, daughter of Eliab. Some readers, including Tyndale House's STEPBible names list, take Mahalath as the mother. Others read Abihail as a second mother, and this entry follows that view. His half-brothers Abijah, Attai and Ziza and half-sister Shelomith were children of another wife, Maachah (2 Chr 11:20), and Abijah succeeded Rehoboam as king. Jeush was probably born in Jerusalem, Rehoboam's capital. Nothing more is recorded of him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name means "he protects" or "he comes to help." Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Jeush was a son of Esau (Edom) by his wife Aholibamah, the daughter of Anah. He was born in the land of Canaan with his full brothers Jaalam and Korah. He is named first of the three, and Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him the oldest (Gen 36:5, 14). His half-brothers Eliphaz and Reuel were Esau's sons by other wives (1 Chr 1:35). In the list of Edomite leaders Jeush appears as a "duke," meaning a chief or clan head, among the chiefs descended from Aholibamah (Gen 36:18). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the name to mean probably "he protects" or "he comes to help." Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, so this Jeush should be kept distinct from them.

Jeuz was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. He was one of the sons born to Shaharaim by his wife Hodesh. His full brothers were Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcham, Shachia and Mirma, and Abitub and Elpaal were his half-brothers through Shaharaim's wife Hushim. By inference from the surrounding verses (1 Chr 8:8–9), these sons were born in the country of Moab after Shaharaim had sent away his earlier wives. The STEPBible proper-names index also places his birth in Moab. Jeuz and his brothers are described as "heads of the fathers," meaning leaders of family groups (1 Chr 8:10). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia accordingly treats him as the founder of a Benjamite family. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "counsellor." Nothing else is recorded about him.

The Jewish Trials were the hearings Jesus faced before the Jewish authorities in Jerusalem on the night after his arrest in Gethsemane, about AD 30 by inference from context. He was taken to the house of Caiaphas the high priest, where chief priests, scribes and elders had gathered. They looked for witnesses against him, but the testimony did not agree, including a claim that he would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days. When the high priest put him under oath to say whether he was the Christ, Jesus affirmed it and spoke of the Son of man at the right hand of power. The council called this blasphemy and judged him deserving of death, and he was struck and mocked. Meanwhile Peter, waiting by a fire in the courtyard, three times denied knowing Jesus before the cock crowed, then wept bitterly. At dawn the council met again against him.

Jezaniah son of Hoshaiah, described as "the son of a Maachathite," was one of the Judean army captains still in the field after Babylon captured Jerusalem. When Gedaliah was appointed governor, Jezaniah and his men came to him at Mizpah along with Ishmael, Johanan and others (2 Kgs 25:23, where he is called Jaazaniah; Jer 40:8). After Gedaliah's murder he stood with Johanan and the people when they asked Jeremiah to seek the LORD's guidance (Jer 42:1). When the answer told them not to go to Egypt, Azariah son of Hoshaiah joined Johanan in accusing Jeremiah of lying (Jer 43:2). This entry follows Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia in treating this Azariah as the same man. The ISBE notes that the Greek Septuagint also reads "Azariah" at Jer 42:1.

Jezebel was the daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians, and the wife of Ahab, king of Israel. Her marriage to Ahab is tied to his worship of Baal (1 Kgs 16:31). She fed 450 prophets of Baal and 400 prophets of the groves at her table. She also had the LORD's prophets killed, though Obadiah hid a hundred of them in caves. After Elijah killed the Baal prophets, she threatened his life. When Naboth refused to sell his vineyard to Ahab, she sent letters in the king's name that led to Naboth being stoned. Elijah foretold that dogs would eat her at Jezreel. After Jehu killed her son Joram, she painted her face and looked out of a window at Jezreel. She was thrown down and dogs ate her body. Her sons Ahaziah and Joram ruled Israel, and Athaliah is commonly taken as her daughter. Rev 2:20 uses her name for a false prophetess, by context in Thyatira.

Jezer was the third of the four sons of Naphtali, listed after Jahzeel and Guni and before Shillem. He appears among the members of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:24). In the census taken in the wilderness he is named as the ancestor of the Jezerites, one of the clans of the tribe of Naphtali (Num 26:49). The genealogy in 1 Chr 7:13 repeats the same four brothers, spelling two names slightly differently (Jahziel and Shallum), and calls them "the sons of Bilhah." Bilhah was Naphtali's mother, so the phrase most likely counts them as her descendants through him.
