The name is usually explained as meaning "form" or "purpose" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), though Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "power." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jeziah was an Israelite of the family of Parosh who lived after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears only once, in Ezra 10:25, in the list of men who had married foreign wives. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was among those who agreed to send away these wives during the reforms led by Ezra. Some English versions spell his name Izziah, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists him under that form. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "whom Jehovah expiates." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jeziel was a son of Azmaveth and the brother of Pelet, listed in 1 Chr 12:3 among the warriors who joined David at Ziklag. The surrounding passage, 1 Chr 12:1–2, describes these men as kinsmen of Saul from the tribe of Benjamin, skilled archers and slingers who could use either hand. They came to David while he was still unable to move freely because of Saul. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both explain the name as meaning "assembled by God." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew spelling varies in the text and suggests a meaning of "God gathers." His father Azmaveth may be the same man as Azmaveth the Barhumite, one of David's mighty men, but the text does not say so, and the identification is uncertain. Jeziel is mentioned nowhere else.

Jezliah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named as one of the sons of Elpaal in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 8:18. His brothers listed there include Ishmerai and Jobab, along with Beriah, Shema, Eber, Misham, Shamed, Meshullam, Hezeki, Heber and Zebadiah, all counted among Elpaal's descendants in the surrounding verses. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in this family list. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "whom God will preserve." Some versions and reference works, such as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, spell the name Izliah.

Jezoar was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:7 as one of the sons of Helah, along with Zereth and Ethnan. The surrounding verses (1 Chr 4:5–6) identify Helah as one of the two wives of Ashur, called the father of Tekoa. Through Ashur's other wife, Naarah, Jezoar had the half-brothers Ahuzam, Hepher, Temeni and Haahashtari. Coz, named in the next verse (1 Chr 4:8), is counted here as a full brother, by inference from his place in the list. Nothing else is recorded about Jezoar. The Hebrew spelling of his name varies, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists him under the form Izhar. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "clear" or "white," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "whiteness."

Jezrahiah was the overseer, or leader, of the singers at the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah. He is mentioned only once, in Neh 12:42. That verse comes in the account of two large thanksgiving choirs that processed along the wall and then stood in the temple, where "the singers sang loud, with Jezrahiah their overseer." Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Levite and dates the dedication to about 446 BC. Both points are inferred from the context of the passage rather than stated in it. His name is usually taken to mean "the Lord arises" or "the Lord shines." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists the name under the alternative spelling Izrahiah. Nothing else is recorded about him, including his family.

Jezreel was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:3 as one of those belonging to "the father of Etam," together with Ishma and Idbash and their sister Hazelelponi. "Father of Etam" probably means the founder or leading ancestor of the town of Etam rather than a literal parent. The verses that follow (1 Chr 4:4) close the list as descendants of Hur, the firstborn of Ephratah, so this entry links Jezreel to Hur's family, alongside relatives such as Penuel, Ezer, Shobal and Salma. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as "seed of God." Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with the city and valley of Jezreel or with Hosea's son of the same name.

Jezreel was the first child of the prophet Hosea and his wife Gomer, and the older brother of Lo-ruhamah and Lo-ammi. The LORD told Hosea to give him this name as a sign that he would soon punish the house of Jehu for "the blood of Jezreel" and end the kingdom of Israel (Hos 1:4). The phrase probably refers to the killings Jehu carried out at the city of Jezreel when he seized the throne (2 Kgs 9–10). The name also points to the valley of Jezreel, where Israel's "bow" would be broken (Hos 1:5). Later in the book the same name is used in a hopeful sense. It speaks of a great "day of Jezreel" when Judah and Israel would be reunited under one head (Hos 1:11), and of the land answering Jezreel with grain, wine and oil (Hos 2:22). This draws on the name's meaning, "God sows." Several other people and a city in the Bible share the name.

Jezreel is the name of a city, one of several places in the Bible called Jezreel. Josh 15:56 lists a Jezreel among the towns of the hill country of Judah. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it southeast of Hebron, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls it unidentified. Ahinoam "the Jezreelitess," one of David's wives, was probably from this Judahite town. She went with David to Gath, was captured and recovered at Ziklag, moved with him to Hebron, and bore his firstborn son Amnon there. The verses grouped here also include the Jezreel near which Israel camped by a spring before fighting the Philistines from Aphek. That Jezreel is usually taken as the northern city and valley of that name. The two may be separate places. The location shown here is a rough one in the north, near the eastern Jezreel Valley, and follows that northern placement.

Jezreel was a town on the border of Issachar, named with Chesulloth and Shunem (Josh 19:18). It was part of the territory Abner placed under Ish-bosheth (2 Sam 2:9). King Ahab kept a palace there, and Naboth's vineyard lay next to it (1 Kgs 21:1). Elijah ran ahead of Ahab's chariot to its entrance (1 Kgs 18:46). King Joram went to Jezreel to recover from wounds received fighting the Syrians. There Jehu, seen approaching by the watchman on its tower, killed Joram, had Jezebel thrown down, and wiped out Ahab's house (2 Kgs 9:15–37; 10:11). Hosea later named his son Jezreel, recalling that bloodshed (Hos 1:4). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies the town with the modern village of Zerin, on the northwestern spur of Mount Gilboa above the valley that bears its name. The same name belongs to other places, including a town in Judah.

Jezreel is the place from which news of the deaths of Saul and Jonathan reached Saul's household, according to 2 Sam 4:4. When the report arrived, the nurse of Jonathan's five-year-old son Mephibosheth fled with him, and in her haste he fell and became lame. The verse refers to the area where Saul's army had camped before the battle on Mount Gilboa. By inference from 1 Sam 29:1, which places the Israelite camp by a spring in Jezreel, this was the town and valley of Jezreel in the north, between Mount Gilboa and the hills of Galilee. The location shown here follows that identification, probably at modern Tel Jezreel (Zer'in), overlooking the Jezreel Valley. Several places in the Bible share this name, including a town in the hill country of Judah (Josh 15:56), so which Jezreel a passage means depends on its context.

Jibsam was a man of the tribe of Issachar, one of six sons of Tola listed in the genealogy at 1 Chr 7:2. His brothers were Uzzi, Rephaiah, Jeriel, Jahmai and Shemuel. The verse calls the sons of Tola heads of their father's house and valiant men of might. It adds that in the days of David their descendants numbered 22,600. Tola was a son of Issachar (1 Chr 7:1), so Jibsam was Issachar's grandson. He is mentioned nowhere else. Some reference works, such as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, spell his name Ibsam. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "pleasant," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "their drought, their confusion."

Jidlaph was a son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and his wife Milcah, which made him Abraham's nephew. He appears only once, in the list of Nahor's eight sons by Milcah that was reported to Abraham after the near-sacrifice of Isaac (Gen 22:20–23). In that list he is named just before Bethuel, the father of Rebekah. His full brothers were Huz, Buz, Kemuel, Chesed, Hazo, Pildash and Bethuel. Nahor also had sons by his concubine Reumah: Tebah, Gaham, Thahash and Maachah. Nothing else is recorded about Jidlaph's life or descendants. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take his name to mean "weeping" or "he weeps." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "he that distills water."

Joab, son of Zeruiah and brother of Abishai and Asahel, was David's nephew (1 Chr 2:16 lists Zeruiah among the sisters of Jesse's sons) and the commander of David's army. He led David's men against Abner's forces at the pool of Gibeon, and he and Abishai later killed Abner to avenge Asahel. He commanded campaigns against Ammon and Syria, and during the Ammonite war he carried out David's plan that led to Uriah's death. He brought Absalom back from Geshur but later killed him during Absalom's revolt. After Absalom made Amasa commander in his place, Joab killed Amasa and put down Sheba's rebellion at Abel of Bethmaachah. He objected to David's census but carried it out. He backed Adonijah's bid for the throne, and Solomon had Benaiah kill him at the altar where he had fled. Several other men in the Bible share the name Joab.

Joab was a man of the tribe of Judah, the son of Seraiah, named in the genealogies of 1 Chr 4:14. He is called "the father of the valley of Charashim," which most likely means he founded or led the settlement there rather than being literally a parent. The name means "valley of craftsmen," and the verse explains that its people were craftsmen. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders the place Ge-harashim. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him among the descendants of Kenaz, which fits the surrounding verses, where Seraiah appears as a son of Kenaz. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with the better-known Joab, David's nephew and army commander, or with others of the same name.

Joab was a descendant of Pahath-moab whose family returned from exile in Babylon to Judah. In the lists of returning exiles, the line of Pahath-moab is counted through two branches, Jeshua and Joab. Together these branches numbered 2,812 according to Ezra 2:6 and 2,818 according to the parallel list in Neh 7:11. Joab's name therefore probably stands for a clan or ancestral house rather than an individual who made the journey himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats this Joab as a family of returned exiles. Ezra 8:9 later mentions a group called the sons of Joab, which may be the same family or a related one. This Joab is not the same person as Joab the commander of David's army. Several people in the Bible share the name, which means "the Lord is father."

Joab was the ancestor of a family group whose descendants returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. Ezra 8:9 records that Obadiah son of Jehiel led the "sons of Joab," with 218 men. Joab himself apparently lived well before this return, and his name stands for a clan rather than an individual traveler. Ezra 2:6 and Neh 7:11 list descendants of "Jeshua and Joab" under the family of Pahath-moab among the earlier returnees, and the STEPBible proper names index accordingly treats this Joab as a descendant of Pahath-moab. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with Joab the commander of David's army or with other men of the same name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "paternity" or "voluntary."

Joah son of Asaph was the recorder, a royal official in charge of records, under King Hezekiah of Judah. With Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, and Shebna the scribe, he went out to meet the Rabshakeh, the envoy of the Assyrian king, outside Jerusalem. The three officials asked the envoy to speak to them in the Syrian language (Aramaic), which they understood, rather than in Hebrew in the hearing of the people on the wall. They then returned to Hezekiah with their clothes torn and reported the Rabshakeh's words. The account appears in both 2 Kings and Isaiah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia dates these events to about 701 BC, during the Assyrian siege. His name is usually explained as "the LORD is brother." Other men in the Bible share the name Joah.

Joah was a Levite, the third son of Obed-edom, listed among the temple gatekeepers organized in David's time (1 Chr 26:4). His brothers named in the same list are Shemaiah the firstborn, Jehozabad, Sacar and Nethaneel, and the next verse, 1 Chr 26:5, adds Ammiel, Issachar and Peulthai. This entry also links him to a father named Shimei, which the verse itself does not explain. The surrounding chapter places Obed-edom's family among the divisions of porters (doorkeepers), and Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe Joah as a Korhite (Korahite) doorkeeper. Smith's dates him to about 1014 BC, an estimate. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "Yahweh is brother." Several other men in the Bible share the name Joah, and they should not be confused with this son of Obed-edom.

Joah son of Zimmah was a Levite of the Gershonite clan. He is named among the Levites who rose to act when King Hezekiah called on them to purify the temple, as the surrounding chapter of 2 Chronicles describes. He is listed alongside representatives of the other Levitical clans, Kohath and Merari. The Eden son of Joah named next to him in the same verse was probably his son. A Gershonite genealogy in 1 Chr 6:20–21 also lists a Joah son of Zimmah, which may point to an earlier ancestor with the same name or to names repeated within the family. Several other men in the Bible share the name Joah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "fraternity" or "brother of the Lord."

Joah was a Levite of the Gershonite clan, the son of Zimmah and the father of Eden. He is named in 2 Chr 29:12 among the Levites who arose to act when King Hezekiah called on them to purify the temple at the start of his reign. Father and son are listed together as the Gershonite representatives, alongside leaders from the Kohathite and Merarite clans. A Joah son of Zimmah also appears in an earlier Gershonite genealogy (1 Chr 6:21). That may be an ancestor with the same names, since Levite families often reused names, but how the two relate is uncertain. Several other men in the Bible are also called Joah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "fraternity" or "brother of the Lord."

Joah was the son of Joahaz and one of three officials King Josiah of Judah sent to repair the temple in the eighteenth year of his reign. This came after Josiah had purged the land and the temple. His companions were Shaphan son of Azaliah and Maaseiah, the governor of the city (2 Chr 34:8). Joah is called "the recorder," and Easton's Bible Dictionary takes this to mean the keeper of the state archives. The verse's wording could be read as giving that title to his father, but reference works generally apply it to Joah. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the event to about 623 BC, an estimate drawn from context. His name is usually explained as "the Lord is brother." Several other men in the Bible are also called Joah, and this one should not be confused with them.

Joahaz was the father of Joah, the recorder who served King Josiah of Judah. He is named only once, in 2 Chr 34:8. That verse says that in the eighteenth year of his reign Josiah sent Joah, together with Shaphan the son of Azaliah and Maaseiah the governor of the city, to repair the house of the LORD. Nothing more is recorded about Joahaz himself. Easton's Bible Dictionary treats the name as a shortened form of Jehoahaz, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives its meaning as "Yahweh has grasped." Smith's Bible Dictionary places him before 623 BC, an estimate inferred from the date of Josiah's temple repairs. He should not be confused with the kings named Jehoahaz, who are different people.

Joanna was a man named in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, in the line of the tribe of Judah. Luke 3:27 lists him as the son of Rhesa and the father of Juda, and places him two generations after Zorobabel (Zerubbabel), the son of Salathiel (Shealtiel). He is a different person from Joanna the woman who followed Jesus, though the name is the same in English. The Revised Version spells his name Joanan, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "grace or gift of the Lord." Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him with Hananiah, the son of Zerubbabel listed in 1 Chr 3:19. Smith's Bible Dictionary mentions the same identification as one possible way of reading the line, which would make him Zerubbabel's son rather than his grandson. This entry follows Luke's text and treats him as Rhesa's son. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Joanna was the wife of Chuza, the steward of Herod, probably Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee, as Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary take it. Luke names her among a group of women, including Mary Magdalene and Susanna, who traveled with Jesus during his second tour of Galilee (about AD 28, by inference from context) and supported him and his disciples from their own means (Luke 8:3). The preceding verse says these women had been healed of evil spirits and illnesses. Joanna appears again after the crucifixion. She was with Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and other women who reported to the apostles what they had found at the empty tomb (Luke 24:10). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes both passages to refer to the same woman. The name Joanna is borne by more than one person in the Bible, but only these two verses refer to this Joanna.

Joash was an Abiezrite of Ophrah and the father of Gideon, one of the judges of Israel. He owned the oak at Ophrah where the angel of the LORD appeared while Gideon was threshing wheat in hiding from the Midianites. Judg 6:25 shows that the altar of Baal Gideon tore down belonged to his father. When the men of the town demanded that Joash hand over his son to be killed for this, Joash refused. He replied that anyone who pleaded for Baal should be put to death, and that if Baal were a god he could defend himself. Gideon is repeatedly called "the son of Joash," and was later buried in his father's tomb at Ophrah. The Abiezrites were probably a clan of the tribe of Manasseh (Josh 17:2). Easton's Bible Dictionary treats the name as a shortened form of Jehoash. Several other people in the Bible share the name.

Joash was a man called "the king's son" in the account of King Ahab's final campaign against Ramoth-gilead. When the prophet Micaiah foretold disaster, the king of Israel ordered him taken back to Amon, the governor of the city, and to Joash, to be held in custody (1 Kgs 22:26; 2 Chr 18:25). This entry follows the common view, found in Easton's Bible Dictionary, that he was a son of Ahab, which would make him a brother of Ahaziah and Joram, both later kings of Israel, and of Athaliah. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he was a younger son who held some subordinate authority while his father was alive. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that "the king's son" may also be a title for a royal officer, as it seems to be in Jeremiah. Several other people in the Bible share the name Joash.

Joash, also called Jehoash, was a king of Judah, the son of King Ahaziah and Zibiah of Beersheba. Several other men share his name. When Athaliah killed the royal family, his aunt Jehosheba, wife of the priest Jehoiada, hid the infant and his nurse (2 Kgs 11:2; 2 Chr 22:11). He became king at seven and reigned forty years in Jerusalem, beginning about 879 BC by inference from context. While Jehoiada instructed him he did what was right, and he made the priests use temple money to repair the temple. He paid off Hazael of Syria with the temple and palace treasures. After Jehoiada died, Joash had Jehoiada's son killed, and a small Syrian force later defeated Judah's army. His servants conspired against him and killed him in the house of Millo, about 839 BC. His son Amaziah followed his example. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that Matthew's genealogy of Jesus omits him.

Joash, also called Jehoash, was a king of the northern kingdom of Israel. He was the son of Jehoahaz and grandson of Jehu, and is distinct from several others of the same name, including his contemporary Joash king of Judah. He succeeded his father in Samaria in the thirty-seventh year of Joash of Judah and reigned sixteen years, roughly 840–825 BC by inference from context. When the prophet Elisha lay dying, Joash visited him and wept over him. He defeated Ben-hadad son of Hazael of Syria three times and recovered Israelite cities lost under his father. When Amaziah king of Judah challenged him, Joash answered with a fable of a thistle and a cedar. He then captured Amaziah at Beth-shemesh, went to Jerusalem and broke down 400 cubits of its wall. He was buried in Samaria, and his son Jeroboam, in whose days Hosea and Amos prophesied, succeeded him.

Joash was a man of the tribe of Judah, listed in the genealogy of Shelah, the son of Judah. He is one of several people in the Bible with this name. He appears only in 1 Chr 4:22, which names him alongside Jokim, the men of Chozeba, and Saraph. The verse says that Joash and Saraph "had the dominion in Moab," which suggests they held some authority or settled there, though no details are given. The passage ends by calling these "ancient things," an indication that the record was old even when the Chronicler wrote it. The preceding verse names Er and Laadah as sons of Shelah. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that it is unclear whether Joash was Shelah's son or Jokim's. This entry treats him as a son of Shelah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as "Yahweh is strong" or "Yahweh has bestowed."

Joash was a son of Becher and a member of the tribe of Benjamin, named second among Becher's nine sons in the genealogy at 1 Chr 7:8. His brothers were Zemira, Eliezer, Elioenai, Omri, Jerimoth, Abiah, Anathoth and Alameth. Becher appears in the same chapter as a son of Benjamin (1 Chr 7:6), so Joash was a grandson of Benjamin. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him the head of a Benjamite family and explains the name, a shortened form of Jehoash, as meaning roughly "the LORD hastens to help." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests this genealogy may originally have belonged to the tribe of Zebulun. This entry follows the Benjamite reading of the passage. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with the several other men named Joash in the Bible.

Joash was a son of Shemaah the Gibeathite, from Gibeah, and the brother of Ahiezer. In 1 Chr 12:3 he is listed second, after Ahiezer the chief, among the warriors who came to David at Ziklag while David was still in hiding from Saul. The surrounding passage describes these men as Benjamites, kinsmen of Saul, who were skilled archers and slingers able to use either hand. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both identify him as one of these Benjamite recruits. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some commentators read his father's name as Shemaiah. Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Joash, and this one should not be confused with them.

Joash was one of the officials who managed King David's royal property. In the list of David's stewards he is named as the man in charge of the "cellars of oil," the storehouses of olive oil (1 Chr 27:28). His post sat next to that of Baalhanan the Gederite, who oversaw the olive and sycamore trees in the lowlands, so the two roles probably formed a chain from orchard to storage. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as keeping the royal oil stores under both David and Solomon. Nothing else is recorded about him, including his family or origin. The name Joash, a shortened form of Jehoash, is usually explained as "Yahweh has helped" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other people in the Bible share the name, and this Joash should not be confused with them.

Job was a man of the land of Uz, described as blameless and upright, one who feared God and avoided evil. He regularly offered sacrifices on behalf of his children. When Satan asked whether Job served God for nothing, Job lost his livestock, servants and children and was then struck with painful sores, yet the text says he did not sin or blame God. Three friends, Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, came to comfort him, and a long series of speeches followed in which Job defended his innocence. A younger man, Elihu, then rebuked Job and the friends. The LORD answered Job and afterward said that Job, not his friends, had spoken rightly. Job prayed for them, and his wealth was restored twice over. His later daughters were Jemima, Keren-happuch and Kezia. He lived 140 more years. Ezekiel names him with Noah and Daniel as a righteous man, and James cites his patience.

Job's Trial was the long period of suffering and debate that fills the Book of Job. Job, a man of Uz described as blameless and God-fearing (Job 1:1), was handed over to Satan's power with the single limit that his life be spared (Job 2:6). Stricken with loss and grief, he longed for death and lamented his calamity (Job 3:21; 6:2; 16:16). Friends who came to him argued that he should seek God and that the wicked are always punished (Job 8:5; 18:5; 22:29), while Job insisted on his own righteousness (Job 6:29; 31:22). A younger speaker, Elihu, then rebuked both sides (Job 32:9; 34:37). Finally God answered with questions about creation and about the creatures behemoth and leviathan (Job 38:9, 36; 40:20; 41:24). The book closes with Job dying old and full of days (Job 42:17). This entry dates the events to about 1650 BC, by inference from context.

Jobab (son of Joktan) is the last of the thirteen sons of Joktan named in the Table of Nations, listed after his brothers Ophir and Havilah (Gen 10:29; 1 Chr 1:23). Through Joktan, son of Eber, he belonged to the line of Shem. Nothing is recorded of him beyond his name and place in the genealogy. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as the founder of an Arabian tribe, which fits the setting of Joktan's descendants, who settled in the east (Gen 10:30). The name's meaning is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "a desert," the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "howling," and Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "sorrowful, hated." He should not be confused with the other men named Jobab in the Bible, such as the early king of Edom.

Jobab son of Zerah was one of the early kings of Edom listed in Genesis and 1 Chronicles. He came from Bozrah, an Edomite city, and succeeded Bela as king (Gen 36:33; 1 Chr 1:44). When he died, Husham of the land of the Temanites reigned in his place (Gen 36:34; 1 Chr 1:45). The list places these kings before any king reigned over Israel, so Jobab belongs to a very early period. Nothing more is recorded about his reign. Some have tried to link him with Job of the book of Job, but the text does not make this connection. The name Jobab is shared by several other men in the Bible, and this entry concerns only the Edomite king. Bozrah is usually identified with modern Buseirah in southern Jordan. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "sorrowful, hated", and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "howling".

Jobab was a Canaanite king of Madon, a city in northern Canaan, in the time of Joshua. When Jabin king of Hazor heard of Israel's victories in the south, he sent to Jobab and to the kings of Shimron and Achshaph to form an alliance against Israel (Josh 11:1). The following verses of the same chapter say that these allied kings gathered their forces at the waters of Merom and were defeated by Joshua. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of the northern chieftains routed there. By inference, Jobab is the unnamed "king of Madon" in the list of defeated kings at Josh 12:19. He is named only in Josh 11:1. The same name belongs to several other men in the Bible, including a son of Joktan, an early king of Edom, and some Benjamites. Those are different people.

Jobab was a son of Shaharaim and his wife Hodesh, listed in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin in 1 Chr 8:9. He is named first among Hodesh's sons, followed by Zibia, Mesha and Malcham. The next verse adds Jeuz, Shachia and Mirma. Shaharaim also had sons by another wife, Hushim, including Abitub and Elpaal, who were Jobab's half-brothers. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as the head of a Benjamite house, based on the summary of these sons as heads of fathers' houses. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, among them a descendant of Joktan, an early king of Edom and a king of Madon defeated by Joshua. This Jobab should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "sorrowful, hated."

Jobab was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named as one of the sons of Elpaal in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 8:18. He is listed with Ishmerai and Jezliah. Elpaal's other sons, named in the surrounding verses, include Eber, Misham, Shamed, Beriah, Shema, Zebadiah, Meshullam, Hezeki and Heber. Nothing more is recorded about him beyond his place in this family list. The name Jobab belongs to several different men in the Bible, including a son of Joktan, a king of Edom, a king of Madon, and another Benjamite named in the same chapter as a son of Shaharaim. This entry refers only to the son of Elpaal. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "sorrowful" or "hated."

Jochebed was a daughter of Levi, born to him in Egypt, and the wife of Amram. She was the mother of Aaron, Moses and their sister Miriam (Num 26:59). Exod 6:20 calls her Amram's father's sister. Since Exod 6:18 names Amram as a son of Kohath, she was Kohath's sister and Amram's aunt, as Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary note. Her brothers were Gershon, Kohath and Merari, the heads of the main Levite clans. Her name is usually explained as "the LORD is glory" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). She is probably the unnamed Levite woman of Exod 2:1–10 who hid her infant son for three months and then placed him in a basket among the reeds of the Nile. Moses' birth is dated here to about 1571 BC, by inference from context.

Joed was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only in the genealogy of Sallu in Neh 11:7. He was the son of Pedaiah and the father of Meshullam, and Sallu was his grandson. Sallu appears in the list of Benjamites who settled in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. Joed himself probably lived some generations earlier, since the list traces Sallu's ancestry back through several names. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel list in 1 Chr 9:7 gives Sallu's line without Joed's name. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "for whom the LORD is witness." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Joel was the firstborn son of the prophet Samuel and the brother of Abiah. He was a Levite of the Kohathite line. When Samuel grew old, he appointed Joel and Abiah as judges in Beersheba. The next verse, 1 Sam 8:3, says the brothers took bribes and perverted justice, and this led Israel's elders to ask for a king. In the King James text of 1 Chr 6:28, Samuel's firstborn is called Vashni. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explain that Joel's name probably dropped out of that verse, and that "Vashni" is really the Hebrew word for "and the second." Read that way, the verse names Joel first and then Abiah, and this entry treats the two names as one person. Joel was the father of Heman, a singer whom the Levites appointed in David's time. Several other men in the Bible share the name Joel.

Joel was a leader of the tribe of Simeon, named in a list of Simeonite clan heads in 1 Chr 4:35. Nothing is recorded about his ancestry or family, unlike Jehu, who is named next to him with several generations of forebears. The surrounding passage calls the men on this list princes in their families. It says their households grew large and moved toward Gedor in search of pasture during the reign of Hezekiah king of Judah (1 Chr 4:38–41). By inference, Joel belonged to that generation and took part in the move, though he is not mentioned individually. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Simeonite chief and explains the name as meaning "Jehovah is God". Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "he that wills or commands". Several other men in the Bible are also called Joel, including the prophet. This one is known only from this verse.

Joel was a member of the tribe of Reuben, named in its genealogy at 1 Chr 5:4 as the father of Shemaiah. The verse traces a line of descent from him: Shemaiah, then Gog, then Shimei. The following verses continue the line down to Beerah, a Reubenite prince whom the Assyrian king Tilgath-pilneser carried into exile (1 Chr 5:5–6). The text does not say how Joel was connected to Reuben's sons listed just before (1 Chr 5:3). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that some interpreters make him a son of Hanoch, while others trace his descent through Carmi. His name is usually explained as meaning "the LORD is God." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Joel is known only from this genealogy.

Joel was a man of the tribe of Reuben, named in 1 Chr 5:8 as the father of Shema and the great-grandfather of Bela son of Azaz. Bela's family lived in Aroer and spread as far as Nebo and Baal-meon, east of the Dead Sea. The Reubenite context comes from the surrounding genealogy in 1 Chronicles 5. That chapter also mentions a Joel at 1 Chr 5:4, whose descendants begin with Shemaiah. Some readers take Shema and Shemaiah to be the same person, which would make the two Joels one man, but the text does not settle this. Several other men in the Bible share the name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "he that wills or commands." Beyond his place in this family line, nothing else is recorded about him.

Joel was a man of the tribe of Gad, named first among the Gadite leaders as "the chief" in 1 Chr 5:12. The surrounding passage places these Gadites in the land of Bashan, east of the Jordan. By inference from 1 Chr 5:17, their family records were compiled in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 782 BC, an estimate drawn from that context. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that he may be the same person as the Joel listed among the Reubenites earlier in the chapter, perhaps as head of a clan counted with either tribe. Nothing more is recorded about him. His name is usually understood to mean "the LORD is God." Several other men in the Bible share the name Joel.

Joel was a man of the tribe of Issachar, a son of Izrahiah and grandson of Uzzi, named in the genealogy at 1 Chr 7:3. His brothers were Michael, Obadiah and Ishiah. The verse gives a total of "five" but names only four sons, so the count probably includes Izrahiah himself. All of them are called "chief men," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes Joel as a chief of Issachar. The surrounding verses (1 Chr 7:1–2) trace this family back through Uzzi to Tola, a son of Issachar, and go on to note the large number of fighting men the family produced. His name is usually understood to mean "the LORD is God." Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with other men of the same name, such as the prophet Joel.

Joel, the brother of Nathan, was one of David's mighty men, the elite warriors listed in 1 Chr 11:38. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes his brother to be Nathan of Zobah. The parallel list in 2 Samuel 23:36 has "Igal the son of Nathan" in about the same place. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Codex Vaticanus of the Greek Septuagint reads "son" rather than "brother" in Chronicles, so the two names may refer to the same man. This entry follows the Chronicles wording, which calls him Nathan's brother. The name Joel is commonly taken to mean "the LORD is God." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including the prophet Joel.

Joel was a Levite in the time of David who led the clan descended from Gershom, one of Levi's sons. He is called its chief, at the head of 130 of his kinsmen (1 Chr 15:7). When David prepared to bring the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem, he summoned the priests Zadok and Abiathar together with Joel and the other Levite leaders, Uriel, Asaiah, Shemaiah, Eliel and Amminadab (1 Chr 15:11). From the surrounding chapter, these men were charged with consecrating themselves and carrying the ark. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he is probably the same Joel named among the Gershonite leaders in 1 Chr 23:8 and 26:22, though this is not certain. Several other men in the Bible share the name Joel.

Joel was a Levite of the Gershonite clan, descended from Laadan, who served in the time of King David. He appears in the lists of Levites drawn up when David organized their duties, in the setting of 1 Chr 23:1–6. With his brother Zetham he was in charge of the treasures of the house of the LORD (1 Chr 26:22). The two passages present the family differently. In 1 Chr 23:8, Jehiel, Zetham and Joel are listed together as three sons of Laadan. In 1 Chr 26:22, Zetham and Joel are called sons of Jehieli, meaning Jehiel. This entry follows the second passage and treats Joel as Jehiel's son and Zetham's brother. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes both verses to describe the same man and places him about 1014 BC. Several other men in the Bible are also named Joel.

Joel, son of Pedaiah, was the leader of the half-tribe of Manasseh during David's reign. He appears once, in a list of chief officers over the tribes of Israel (1 Chr 27:20). The verse does not say which half of Manasseh he led. The next verse names a separate leader for the half-tribe of Manasseh in Gilead, east of the Jordan, so Joel probably led the western half. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes this view. The STEPBible proper-names index instead places his rule in Gilead. This entry follows the western reading, based on the surrounding list. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should be kept distinct from the several other men named Joel in the Bible, including the prophet. The name is usually understood to mean "the LORD is God."

Joel, son of Azariah, was a Levite of the Kohathite clan in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He is named among the Levites who responded when Hezekiah called on them to consecrate themselves and cleanse the temple in Jerusalem. He is listed with Mahath son of Amasai as the representatives of the Kohathites, alongside leaders from the Merarite and Gershonite clans (2 Chr 29:12). The surrounding chapter shows these men gathering their fellow Levites to remove what had defiled the temple, so Joel probably helped lead that work. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 726 BC. The name Joel is commonly explained as "the LORD is God" and was borne by several men in the Bible. This Joel is known only from this one verse.

Joel was one of the descendants ("sons") of Nebo listed in Ezra 10:43 among the Israelites who had married foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was among those who agreed during Ezra's reforms to send these wives away. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the episode to about 459 BC, an estimate drawn from context. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same man appears as "Juel" in the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:35. His name is usually understood to mean "the Lord is God." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including the prophet Joel, and nothing more is known of this one beyond his place in the list.

Joel, son of Zichri, was a leader of the tribe of Benjamin in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. In the list of those who settled in the city in Nehemiah's time, he is named as overseer of the Benjamites living there, with Judah son of Senuah second over the city (Neh 11:9). That he belonged to Benjamin is inferred from context, since the verse closes the list of Benjamite families that begins at Neh 11:7. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, usually explained as "the LORD is God" (Smith's Bible Dictionary), was borne by several people in the Bible, including the prophet Joel, and this man should not be confused with them.

Joel, the son of Pethuel, was a prophet to whom "the word of the LORD" came, and the book of Joel bears his name (Joel 1:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary counts him as the second of the twelve minor prophets and notes that nothing is known of his life beyond his book. The Tyndale House proper-names list describes him as a prophet of Judah whose message combined judgment and hope. His date is uncertain. This entry places his prophecies about 820 BC, an estimate inferred from context, though the book itself gives no date. In the New Testament, Peter quoted him on the day of Pentecost, saying the events in Jerusalem were "that which was spoken by the prophet Joel" (Acts 2:16). The name, popularly taken to mean "the LORD is God," is shared by several other men in the Bible.

Joelah was one of the warriors who joined David at Ziklag. In 1 Chr 12:7, Joelah and Zebadiah are called "the sons of Jeroham of Gedor." The surrounding passage lists the men who came to David while he was keeping away from Saul, and by inference from that context Joelah fought alongside him. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the Tyndale House proper-names index describe Joelah as a Benjamite, because the list in this part of the chapter is introduced as Saul's kinsmen. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Joelah may instead have been a Judean, since Gedor was also the name of a town in Judah. Nothing more is recorded. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "Jehovah helps," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "may he avail."

Joezer was one of the Korahites named in the list of warriors who joined David at Ziklag while he was still in hiding from Saul (1 Chr 12:6). He appears alongside Elkanah, Jesiah, Azareel and Jashobeam. The surrounding passage presents these men as part of a group of Benjaminite recruits, kinsmen of Saul, who were skilled with the bow and the sling. The label "Korhites" is not explained here. It may refer to descendants of the Levite Korah, or to a family of Benjamin or Judah with a similar name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that he was perhaps a Judean. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as part of David's bodyguard, and Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him one of David's captains. His name means "the LORD is help." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jogbehah was a town east of the Jordan in Gilead. It appears in the list of towns that the tribe of Gad built or fortified after settling the region (Num 32:35); the preceding verse names Gad as the builder. Later, when Gideon pursued the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna, he went up "by the way of them that dwelt in tents" east of Nobah and Jogbehah and struck their camp while it felt secure (Judg 8:11). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "high." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with the ruins of Ajbeihat, about 7 miles northwest of Amman on the road toward es-Salt, at roughly 3,470 feet above sea level. The name survives in Jubeiha, now a district of north Amman, Jordan, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Jogli was a man of the tribe of Dan, known only as the father of Bukki. In Num 34:22 Bukki son of Jogli is named as the leader of Dan among the tribal representatives chosen to help divide the land of Canaan among the tribes of Israel. Nothing else is recorded about Jogli himself, though he was presumably a Danite of some standing, since his son held this role. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggest his name means "led into exile," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "passing over," "turning back" or "rejoicing."

Joha was a Benjamite, one of the sons of Beriah, named in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin in 1 Chr 8:16. He appears alongside Michael and Ispah. The surrounding verses also list Zebadiah, Arad, Ader, Ahio, Shashak and Jeremoth among Beriah's family. The nearby 1 Chr 8:13 presents Beriah as a family head among the inhabitants of Aijalon who drove out the people of Gath, so Joha probably belonged to that Aijalon clan, by inference from the passage. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name is shared by at least one other man, a son of Shimri listed among David's warriors in 1 Chr 11:45, who is a different person. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "the Lord gives life." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia regards its meaning as uncertain and possibly a form of Joah.

Joha was one of David's mighty warriors, named in the list of his elite fighting men in 1 Chr 11:45. He was the son of Shimri and the brother of Jediael, who appears beside him in the same list. He is called "the Tizite," probably a reference to his hometown or clan, though no place called Tiz or Tizi is otherwise known. The verse's wording leaves it unclear whether the title belongs to Joha alone or to both brothers. This section of the list has no parallel in 2 Samuel 23, and nothing more is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "the LORD gives life," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be a form of Joah. The name Joha is also borne by at least one other man in the Bible, a Benjamite.

Johanan son of Kareah (spelled Careah in 2 Kgs 25:23) was a Judean army captain who, with his brother Jonathan, joined Gedaliah at Mizpah after the Babylonians made Gedaliah governor. He secretly warned Gedaliah that Ishmael son of Nethaniah planned to kill him and offered to kill Ishmael first, but Gedaliah refused and said the report was false. After Ishmael murdered Gedaliah, Johanan and the other captains pursued him and freed the captives taken from Mizpah, though Ishmael escaped to the Ammonites. Johanan then joined the people in seeking guidance from Jeremiah, but he rejected the prophet's warning not to go to Egypt. He and the captains led the remnant of Judah there instead. The connected passage in Jer 43:6–7 adds that Jeremiah went with them to Tahpanhes. Several other men in the Bible share this name.

Johanan was the firstborn son of King Josiah of Judah, named first among Josiah's four sons in 1 Chr 3:15, ahead of Jehoiakim, Zedekiah and Shallum. He is not mentioned anywhere else, and he never became king. When Josiah died, the throne passed to Shallum, called Jehoahaz in 2 Kgs 23:30–31, and later to Jehoiakim and Zedekiah. Why Johanan was passed over is not explained. He may have died young, but that is only a possibility. This entry treats him as a member of the tribe of Judah, born in Jerusalem, and as a full brother of Jehoiakim. That makes Zebudah his mother, since 2 Kgs 23:36 names her as Jehoiakim's mother. Jehoahaz and Zedekiah, whose mother was Hamutal, were his half-brothers. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains his name as "gift or grace of God." Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Johanan was one of the seven sons of Elioenai, listed in the royal genealogy of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chr 3:24. His brothers were Hodaiah, Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub, Dalaiah and Anani. The surrounding chapter traces the line of King David through Jehoiachin and Zerubbabel, so Johanan belongs to the family of David's heirs after the return from exile in Babylon. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him in the line of Zerubbabel's descendants, through Neariah and Shemaiah, and dates him to after 406 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a post-exilic Davidic prince. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his name. The name means "the Lord has been gracious," and several other people in the Bible share it.

Johanan was a member of the tribe of Levi in the high-priestly line descended from Aaron. He appears only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 6, as the son of Azariah and the father of another Azariah (1 Chr 6:9–10). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that his grandfather Ahimaaz was the son of Zadok, the priest of David's time. The genealogy adds that Johanan's son Azariah was the one who served as priest in the temple Solomon built in Jerusalem. Nothing else is recorded about Johanan himself. His name means "Yahweh has been gracious" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). It was shared by several other people in the Bible, so he should be kept distinct from other men called Johanan. In the Hebrew Bible these verses are numbered 1 Chr 5:35–36.

Johanan was one of the warriors who came over to David at Ziklag, named in a list of mighty men in 1 Chr 12:4 alongside Ismaiah the Gibeonite, Jeremiah, Jahaziel and Josabad the Gederathite. The surrounding passage, 1 Chr 12:1–7, describes these men as kinsmen of Saul from the tribe of Benjamin who joined David while he was still hiding from Saul. Smith's Bible Dictionary accordingly calls him a valiant Benjamite. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Johanan, meaning "gift or grace of God" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary, belongs to several different people in the Bible. This Johanan should not be confused with the Gadite warrior of the same name listed later in the same chapter.

Johanan was a warrior of the tribe of Gad, listed eighth among the Gadite fighters who came over to David (1 Chr 12:12). The surrounding passage describes these Gadites as skilled, battle-ready men who separated themselves to join David at his stronghold in the wilderness while he was still a fugitive from Saul. Easton's Bible Dictionary places this in the desert of Judah. STEPBible's proper-names index connects the list with the men who joined David at Ziklag and helped him fight raiding bands. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Johanan should not be confused with them. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "gift or grace of God."

Johanan was the father of Azariah, one of the leading men of the tribe of Ephraim during the reign of Ahaz king of Judah. He is known only through his son, who is named in 2 Chr 28:12 among the Ephraimite heads who stood up against the army returning from war. In the surrounding chapter, that army had brought captives from Judah to Samaria, and these leaders opposed keeping them. Nothing else is recorded about Johanan himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew text spells his name in the longer form Jehohanan, meaning "the Lord has been gracious." Several other men in the Bible share the name Johanan, and this one should not be confused with them.

Johanan, son of Hakkatan, was the head of the family of Azgad among those who returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. He led 110 men of his family on the journey (Ezra 8:12). He is one of several men in the Bible named Johanan, and nothing more is recorded about him. Ezra's return took place in the reign of the Persian king Artaxerxes, as the surrounding chapter states. The name means "the Lord has been gracious" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). The same list in the apocryphal book of 1 Esdras gives his name as Joannes.

Johanan was the son of Eliashib. He owned a chamber at the temple in Jerusalem, to which Ezra withdrew after leaving the house of God. There Ezra fasted, eating no bread and drinking no water, as he mourned the unfaithfulness of the returned exiles who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:6). Nothing else is said of him here. The STEPBible Proper Names index describes him as a priest in Ezra's time. Many interpreters link his father with Eliashib the high priest of Nehemiah's day. Neh 12:23 also speaks of a Johanan son of Eliashib in the high priestly line, possibly a grandson called "son" in a broader sense. Whether these are the same man is uncertain, since the name was common and is shared by several people in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "who is liberal or merciful."

Johanan was the son of Tobiah the Ammonite, one of the chief opponents of Nehemiah during the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls. Nehemiah mentions him only in passing, to explain why many people in Judah were bound by oath to Tobiah. Tobiah was the son-in-law of Shechaniah son of Arah, and Johanan had married the daughter of Meshullam son of Berechiah (Neh 6:18). Earlier in the book, a Meshullam son of Berechiah is named among those who repaired sections of the wall, so these marriages probably tied Tobiah's family to people inside Jerusalem's own leadership. Nothing else is recorded about Johanan himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "gift or grace of God." The name was shared by several people in the Bible, and this Johanan should not be confused with the others.

Johanan was a high priest of the Persian period, the son of Joiada and father of Jaddua. Nehemiah 12:11 calls him Jonathan in the line of high priests, and International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the two names as the same man. His name means "Yahweh has been gracious." He belonged to the priestly line of the tribe of Levi. The heads of Levite and priestly families were recorded in the days of Eliashib, Joiada, Johanan and Jaddua, and the Levite chronicles ran until his time (Neh 12:22–23). Neh 12:23 calls him "the son of Eliashib." Since Neh 12:10 makes Eliashib the father of Joiada, this probably means grandson or descendant. Smith's Bible Dictionary says he succeeded his father as high priest, sometime before 332 BC. Several other people in the Bible share this name.

John the Baptist was a prophet who preached in the wilderness of Judea and baptized people in the Jordan, calling for repentance for the forgiveness of sins. He was the son of the priest Zacharias and Elisabeth, and an angel announced his birth and gave his name. Born about 5 BC by inference from context, he lived austerely, and the people widely regarded him as a prophet. He baptized Jesus, said one mightier than he would baptize with the Holy Spirit, and pointed Jesus out as "the Lamb of God." Some of his own disciples, such as Andrew, followed Jesus. After John rebuked Herod for marrying Herodias, his brother Philip's wife, Herod imprisoned him and later had him beheaded. Easton's Bible Dictionary places his imprisonment and death at the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea. His baptism was still known decades later (Acts 18:25; 19:4).

John the Apostle was a son of Zebedee and brother of James, a Galilean fisherman and partner of Simon Peter, whom Jesus called while he was mending nets with his father. He was one of the twelve apostles, and Jesus surnamed the brothers Boanerges, "sons of thunder." With Peter and James he formed an inner group present at the raising of Jairus's daughter, the Transfiguration and Gethsemane. The Gospels record him forbidding an outsider to cast out demons, offering to call down fire on a Samaritan village, and seeking honor with James. After the ascension he appears with Peter healing a lame man, standing trial before the council, and visiting Samaria. Paul calls him a "pillar" (Gal 2:9). Tradition identifies him with the John exiled on Patmos who wrote Revelation, and with the author of the Gospel and letters of John, and this entry follows that tradition. Easton's Bible Dictionary names his mother as Salome.

John (Relative of the High Priest) was a member of the high priestly family in Jerusalem. He is named only once, alongside Annas the high priest, Caiaphas and Alexander, among those of the high priest's kindred who gathered in Jerusalem when the apostles Peter and John were brought before the council after healing a lame man (Acts 4:6). This was probably about AD 30, by inference from context. He was one of those who questioned and judged the two apostles. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as otherwise unknown. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia records a suggestion by the scholar Lightfoot that he was the Talmudic teacher Johanan ben Zakkai. This entry treats him simply as an otherwise unidentified relative of the high priest. His name means "the grace or mercy of the Lord," according to Hitchcock's Bible Names.

The baptism of Jesus by John took place in the Jordan River, where John the Baptist had been preaching and baptizing. Jesus came from Nazareth in Galilee to be baptized (Mark 1:9). Matthew records that John at first refused, saying he needed to be baptized by Jesus. Jesus answered that it was fitting for them to fulfil all righteousness, and John agreed (Matt 3:14–15). As Jesus came up out of the water, the heavens opened and the Spirit of God came down on him like a dove. A voice from heaven declared him God's beloved Son, in whom he was well pleased. Luke adds that Jesus was praying at the time and that many other people had also been baptized (Luke 3:21–22). The event is dated to about AD 26, by inference from context, shortly after John began his ministry.

John Beheaded refers to the execution of John the Baptist by Herod Antipas, the tetrarch of Galilee, probably about AD 29 by inference from context. At a birthday banquet Herod gave for his officials and the leading men of Galilee, the daughter of Herodias danced and pleased him. He swore to give her whatever she asked, up to half his kingdom. Prompted by her mother, she asked for John's head on a platter. Herod was deeply sorry, but because of his oath and his guests he sent an executioner, who beheaded John in prison and brought the head to the girl, who gave it to her mother. John's disciples buried the body and told Jesus. The earlier verses (Matt 14:3–4; Mark 6:17–18) say John had been imprisoned for objecting to Herod's marriage to Herodias. Later, hearing of Jesus, Herod wondered whether John had risen from the dead.

The prediction of John's birth is the account in Luke 1:5–25 of the angel Gabriel announcing to the priest Zacharias that his wife Elisabeth would bear a son. In the days of Herod, king of Judea, Zacharias, of the priestly division of Abia, was chosen by lot to burn incense in the temple at Jerusalem while the people prayed outside. The couple were old and childless. An angel appeared beside the altar of incense and told him to name the child John. He said John would abstain from wine, be filled with the Holy Ghost from the womb, and go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah. When Zacharias asked for a sign, the angel identified himself as Gabriel and struck him unable to speak until the promise was fulfilled. Elisabeth later conceived and stayed in seclusion for five months. This entry dates the event to about 6 BC, by inference from context.

John's Witness was the testimony John the Baptist gave about Jesus at Bethabara beyond the Jordan, where he was baptizing (John 1:28). It is dated to about AD 27 by inference from context and follows the Temptations of Jesus. Priests and Levites sent from Jerusalem, some of them Pharisees, asked John who he was. He denied being the Christ, Elijah or "that prophet". Instead he called himself the voice crying in the wilderness from Isaiah's prophecy. He said that one coming after him, already standing among them, was greater than he, and that he was not worthy to untie his sandal. The next day John saw Jesus approaching and called him "the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world." He said he had seen the Spirit descend like a dove and remain on Jesus, the sign he had been given, and declared him the Son of God.

The John the Baptist Begins Ministry event marks the start of public preaching by John, son of Zacharias, in the wilderness of Judea, recorded in all four Gospels. Luke dates the word of God coming to him to the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas; this entry places it about AD 26, by inference from context. John called people to repent because the kingdom of heaven was near, and the Gospels identify him with Isaiah's voice crying in the wilderness to prepare the Lord's way. He wore camel's hair with a leather belt and ate locusts and wild honey. Crowds from Jerusalem and Judea were baptized by him in the Jordan, confessing their sins. He warned Pharisees and Sadducees, told tax collectors and soldiers to act fairly, and denied being the Christ, announcing a mightier one coming after him who would baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire.

John the Baptist Imprisoned was the arrest and jailing of John by Herod Antipas, the tetrarch, about AD 27 by inference from context. John had openly told Herod that it was not lawful for him to have Herodias, his brother Philip's wife, whom Herod had married. Luke adds that John also rebuked him for other evils. Herod had John seized, bound and put in prison. Matthew says Herod wanted to kill him but feared the crowds, who regarded John as a prophet. Mark says Herodias held a grudge and wanted him dead, but Herod protected John, knowing him to be a just and holy man, and listened to him gladly. Matthew and Mark tell the story in flashback, when Herod hears of Jesus and fears John has risen from the dead. The Jewish historian Josephus places the imprisonment at the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea.

John the Baptist Witnesses refers to John's last recorded testimony about Jesus in John's Gospel. It is set about AD 27 by inference from context, soon after Jesus met Nicodemus. While Jesus and his disciples were baptizing in the Judean countryside, John was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, where there was plenty of water, before he was put in prison. A dispute about purification arose between John's disciples and others, and the disciples told John that the man he had testified about beyond the Jordan was now baptizing and drawing everyone. John answered that a person receives only what heaven gives. He reminded them that he had said he was not the Christ but was sent ahead of him. He compared himself to the bridegroom's friend, who rejoices at the groom's voice: "He must increase, but I must decrease." Interpreters differ on whether John 3:31–36 continues John's words or is the Gospel writer's comment. The exact site of Aenon is uncertain.

Joiada was a priest of the tribe of Levi in the Persian period, the son of Eliashib the high priest and great-grandson of Jeshua, according to the high-priestly line in Neh 12:10–11. His name means "the LORD knows" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). STEPBible's proper-names index describes him as succeeding his father as high priest. Neh 12:11 names his son as Jonathan, the father of Jaddua, while Neh 12:22 lists Johanan after Joiada among the generations by which Levites and priests were recorded. This entry treats Johanan as his son, probably the same person as Jonathan. Neh 13:28 reports that another of Joiada's sons married a daughter of Sanballat the Horonite, an opponent of Nehemiah, and Nehemiah drove him away.

Joiakim was a high priest of the tribe of Levi in the period after the return from exile. He was the son of Jeshua (called Joshua elsewhere), who was the son of Jozadak, and he was the father of Eliashib, who in turn was the father of Joiada (Neh 12:10). Nehemiah uses his time in office as a point of reference, listing the priests who were heads of families "in the days of Joiakim" (Neh 12:12). It also places a list of Levites in his days alongside the days of Nehemiah the governor and Ezra the priest and scribe (Neh 12:26). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe him as high priest and as his father's successor, which fits his place in the line of high priests. Smith's dates him to before 446 BC. His name means "the LORD raises up."

Joiarib was one of the men Ezra summoned at the river Ahava while gathering the returning exiles for the journey from Babylon to Jerusalem. In Ezra 8:16 he is named with Elnathan as "men of understanding," set apart from the "chief men" listed before them. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders the description as "teacher." Read with the following verse, Ezra sent this group to Iddo at Casiphia to bring Levites to serve in the house of God, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a layman who returned with Ezra. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name, often explained as "the LORD contends" or "the LORD defends," is shared by several other men in the Bible, and it is uncertain whether he is connected with any of them.

Joiarib was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the family line of Maaseiah, one of the Judahites who lived in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile (Neh 11:5). He was the son of Zechariah and the father of Adaiah, and he stood several generations before Maaseiah, whose ancestry runs back through Joiarib to Shiloni. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes "Shiloni" to mean a Shilonite, probably a descendant of Shelah son of Judah. The STEPBible name index instead places this line under Judah's son Perez. Either way, he lived some time before the return, probably in the 6th century BC or earlier, by inference from the length of the line. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia simply call him a Judahite. His name is usually taken to mean "the LORD pleads" or "contends." Several other men in the Bible bear the same name.

Joiarib, also called Jehoiarib, was a priest whose name stands for a priestly family in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. He is listed among the priests who lived in the city (1 Chr 9:10; Neh 11:10) and among the priests who came back with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:6). In the next generation, Mattenai is named as head of the family of Joiarib (Neh 12:19). Neh 11:10 calls Jedaiah "the son of Joiarib," which is why this entry lists Jedaiah as his son. The parallel list in 1 Chr 9:10, however, names Jedaiah and Jehoiarib side by side, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the text should probably read "Jedaiah and Joiarib." Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries call him the founder of one of the priestly courses, linking him with the Jehoiarib of 1 Chr 24:7. Several people in the Bible share this name.

Jokdeam was a town in the hill country of Judah, named once in the list of cities given to the tribe of Judah, alongside Jezreel and Zanoah (Josh 15:56). It belongs to a group of towns that includes Maon, Carmel and Ziph (Josh 15:55–57), which places it in the hills south of Hebron. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls it unidentified and suggests it probably lay south of Hebron. Its exact site is unknown, and the location shown here is only an approximate position in that area. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "crookedness, or burning, of the people."

Jokim was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only once, in the genealogy of Judah at 1 Chr 4:22. He is listed among the descendants of Shelah, the son of Judah, alongside Er, Laadah, Joash and Saraph. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a son of Shelah, while Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe him more loosely as a descendant. The verse that names him also mentions the men of Chozeba and says that Joash and Saraph "had the dominion in Moab." It closes by noting that "these are ancient things," which suggests the compiler was drawing on old records. Nothing else is told about Jokim. His name is usually explained as meaning "the LORD raises up" and is related to the name Jehoiakim.

Jokmeam was a city marking the far edge of the district assigned to Baana son of Ahilud, one of Solomon's officers who supplied provisions for the royal household (1 Kgs 4:12; the surrounding passage describes these officers). The district included Taanach, Megiddo and Beth-shean, reaching to Abel-meholah and "beyond" this city. The King James Version reads "Jokneam" in this verse, while the Revised Version reads "Jokmeam." Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Jokmeam as the Levitical city of Ephraim named in 1 Chr 6:68 and places it somewhere in the Jordan valley, which would suit a boundary running toward Abel-meholah. The location shown here instead follows the Jokneam identification, probably modern Tel Yokneam at the northwestern edge of the Jezreel Valley, not far from Megiddo. Several places share similar names, so the identification is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as "confirmation, or revenge, of the people."

Jokmeam was a city of Ephraim that was given, together with its surrounding pasture lands, to the Levites. In 1 Chr 6:68 it is named alongside Bethhoron. By inference from the surrounding verses, it went to the Kohathite families. The parallel list of Levitical cities in Joshua 21:22 has Kibzaim in this position, so the two names probably refer to the same town. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it somewhere in the Jordan valley, reading the Jokmeam of 1 Kings 4:12 in the Revised Version, which the King James Version spells Jokneam, as the same town. The name is shared by more than one place, and the exact site is uncertain. The location shown here follows the Jordan valley view, placing it north-east of Jerusalem toward the valley. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "confirmation, or revenge, of the people."

Jokneam was a Canaanite royal city whose king appears in the list of kings defeated by Joshua, where it is called "Jokneam of Carmel" (Josh 12:22). It lay on the edge of Zebulun's territory, whose border reached "the river that is before Jokneam," probably the Kishon (Josh 19:11). Zebulun later gave the city and its surrounding pasturelands to the Merarite families of the Levites (Josh 21:34). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with Tell Kaimon (Tell Qeimun, today Tel Yokneam), a steep mound at the eastern end of Mount Carmel above the Kishon valley, about 12 miles southwest of Nazareth. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Eusebius placed it on the road from Legio to Acre, which supports that site. The location shown here follows this identification. The same encyclopedia notes that the "Jokneam" of 1 Kgs 4:12 in the King James Version is better read as Jokmeam, a different place.

Jokshan was the second son of Abraham by Keturah, listed after Zimran and before Medan, Midian, Ishbak and Shuah (Gen 25:2; 1 Chr 1:32). Through Abraham he was a half-brother of Isaac and of Ishmael, the son of Hagar. He fathered Sheba and Dedan, and through Dedan he was the grandfather of the Asshurim, Letushim and Leummim (Gen 25:3). These names appear to stand for peoples or tribes as well as individuals, probably groups living in the Arabian region. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "snarer," and Smith's Bible Dictionary as "fowler." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a suggestion that Jokshan may be another form of Joktan, whose descendants also include a Sheba (Gen 10:25–29). Nothing else is recorded about him beyond these genealogies.

Joktan was the second of the two sons of Eber and the brother of Peleg (Gen 10:25; 1 Chr 1:19). Through Eber he descended from Shem, according to the genealogy in Genesis 10. Peleg's line continues toward Abraham in Gen 11, while Joktan's thirteen sons are listed separately. They are Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah, Ebal, Abimael, Sheba, Ophir, Havilah and Jobab (Gen 10:26–29; 1 Chr 1:20–23). Many of these names match peoples or regions of southern Arabia, such as Sheba and Hazarmaveth (probably modern Hadramaut). Gen 10:30 places their territory between Mesha and Sephar. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes an Arab tradition that Joktan, called Qahtan in Arabic, was the ancestor of the purest tribes of central and southern Arabia. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionary give "little" or "small."

Joktheel was a town in the Shephelah, the low hill country of Judah, listed among the towns given to the tribe of Judah in Josh 15:38. It appears between Mizpeh and Lachish in that list, and Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that it is named just before Lachish. The name has been explained as meaning "subdued by God." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes the site as unidentified. The location shown here is only approximate and places it in the Lachish area, by inference from its position in the town list. The same name was later given to a different place. According to 2 Kgs 14:7, King Amaziah captured Sela in Edom and renamed it Joktheel. That Edomite site should not be confused with this town in Judah.

Joktheel was the new name given to the Edomite stronghold of Selah after it was captured by a king of Judah. 2 Kgs 14:7 says he struck down ten thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt, took Selah in battle, and renamed it Joktheel, a name still in use when the account was written. The surrounding chapter shows that the king was Amaziah. The parallel account in 2 Chronicles 25 describes the same campaign. Selah, meaning "rock," has traditionally been identified with the rock city of Petra in southern Jordan. Others place it at es-Sela, a site farther north near Bozrah. The location shown here follows the Petra identification. A different Joktheel, a town in the lowland of Judah, appears in Josh 15:38 and should not be confused with this one.

Jonadab was a nephew of King David, the son of David's brother Shimeah, also called Shammah, of the tribe of Judah. He was a friend of his cousin Amnon, David's son, and is described as a very shrewd man. He advised Amnon to pretend to be sick so that David would send Amnon's half-sister Tamar to cook for him, which led to her rape. After Absalom had Amnon killed in revenge and a report reached David that all his sons were dead, Jonadab told the king that only Amnon had died and that Absalom had planned it since the assault on Tamar. This entry also identifies him with Jonathan, son of Shimea, who killed a Philistine champion at Gath (described in 2 Sam 21:20 as a huge man with six fingers on each hand). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes he may also be the Jonathan called David's 'uncle' (possibly 'relative'), a counsellor and scribe. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats these men separately.

Jonadab, also called Jehonadab, was the son of Rechab and the ancestor of the Rechabites. When Jehu was moving against the house of Ahab, Jonadab came out to meet him. Jehu asked whether his heart was loyal, took his hand and brought him up into his chariot (2 Kgs 10:15). He went with Jehu into the house of Baal when the Baal worshippers were gathered there (2 Kgs 10:23). Jonadab commanded his descendants never to drink wine and to live in tents. Centuries later, in Jeremiah's time, they were still keeping this command. Jeremiah set their obedience against Judah's failure to listen to God, and announced that Jonadab would never lack a descendant to stand before the LORD (Jer 35:6–19). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as the founder of a tribe bound by this vow. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jonadab.

Jonah, son of Amittai, was a prophet of Israel from Gath-hepher, called Jonas in the New Testament. According to 2 Kgs 14:25, he foretold that Jeroboam II would restore Israel's borders, which places him in or shortly before that king's reign. This entry dates his prophecies to about 825 BC, by inference from context. The book bearing his name tells how God sent him to Nineveh, but he fled by ship from Joppa toward Tarshish. When a storm arose, the sailors cast lots, and the lot fell on him. They threw him overboard, and a great fish swallowed him. He prayed from inside it for three days and nights until it cast him onto dry land. Sent again, he warned that Nineveh would be overthrown in forty days. Angry when the city was spared, he was taught through a gourd vine. Jesus cited "the sign of the prophet Jonas" and the Ninevites' repentance.

Jonan is a man named in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, which traces the line back from Joseph through David's son Nathan (Luke 3:30). He is listed as the son of Eliakim and the father of Joseph, and as a descendant of David he belonged to the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him. Some reference works, including the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, give the name as Jonam, a spelling found in some Greek manuscripts. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests it may be a shortened form of Johanan, meaning "gift or grace of God." It places him before 876 BC, which is a rough estimate drawn from his position in the genealogy.

Jonas was the father of Simon Peter and, by inference, of Andrew, since John 1:40 calls Andrew Simon Peter's brother. He is known only from the way Jesus addressed his son. When Andrew brought Simon to Jesus, Jesus called him "Simon the son of Jona" and gave him the name Cephas (John 1:42). After the resurrection, at a meal by the Sea of Tiberias, Jesus addressed him three times as "Simon, son of Jonas" while asking whether Peter loved him (John 21:15–17). Matthew 16:17 likewise calls Peter "Simon Bar-jona." The name appears in different forms. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note that the Revised Version reads "John" in these passages, following Greek manuscripts that have Ioanes. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that Jonas may be a shortened form of that name, or that he may have had a double name. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jonathan was a Levite, the son of Gershom, who became priest to the tribe of Dan after the Danites set up a carved image in their new city of Dan. According to Judg 18:30, he and his sons held this priesthood until the land was taken into captivity. The KJV calls Gershom "the son of Manasseh." Easton's Bible Dictionary explains that the rabbis changed the name from Moses to Manasseh to spare the lawgiver's memory. On that reading, Jonathan was a grandson of Moses through his son Gershom (Exod 2:22). Easton's also identifies him with the young Levite from Bethlehem in Judah whose story is told in Judges 17–18. That Levite first served as household priest to Micah of Ephraim, and Danite raiders later persuaded him to go with them and carry off Micah's idols. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "given of God." Several other men in the Bible share the name.
