Jonathan was the eldest son of King Saul and his wife Ahinoam, and the close friend of David. He led a thousand men at Gibeah of Benjamin. With only his armor-bearer he attacked a Philistine garrison and killed about twenty men. Not knowing of Saul's oath forbidding food, he ate honey and was condemned when the lot fell on him, though 1 Sam 14:45 records that the people rescued him. Jonathan made a covenant with David and for a time persuaded Saul not to kill him. He later warned David of Saul's hostility with a signal of arrows and encouraged him while he was in hiding. The Philistines killed him at Gilboa together with his brothers Abinadab and Malchishua. David mourned him in a lament, showed kindness to his lame son Mephibosheth for his sake, and reburied his bones with Saul's at Zelah. Several other men share this name.

Jonathan, son of the priest Abiathar, was one of several men in the Bible with this name, which means "given of God" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). During Absalom's revolt, David sent Zadok and Abiathar back to Jerusalem with their sons Ahimaaz and Jonathan, who were to carry news of events in the city to the king. The two waited at En-rogel so they would not be seen entering the city. A servant girl brought them information, and they passed it on to David. When Absalom's servants searched for them, a woman told the pursuers they had crossed the brook, and the men returned to Jerusalem without finding them. Later, at Adonijah's feast, Jonathan arrived with the news that David had made Solomon king. His brother Ahimelech appears elsewhere as a priest (2 Sam 8:17). Easton's Bible Dictionary calls Jonathan the last recorded descendant of Eli.

Jonathan was one of David's mighty men, the elite group of warriors listed in 2 Sam 23 and 1 Chr 11. 1 Chr 11:34 calls him "Jonathan the son of Shage the Hararite," and this entry follows that naming of his father. In the parallel list at 2 Sam 23:32–33 his name is followed directly by "Shammah the Hararite." Some readers, including the STEPBible proper-names index, take this to mean he was the son of Shammah, possibly the same Shammah son of Agee the Hararite praised earlier in that chapter. "Hararite" probably refers to a place or clan whose location is uncertain. Nothing is recorded about his deeds beyond his place on the list. His name means "Yahweh has given" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). He is distinct from Jonathan the son of Saul and from several other men of the same name.

Jonathan was a man of the tribe of Judah, listed in the genealogy of Jerahmeel's descendants in 1 Chronicles. He was a son of Jada, the brother of Shammai, and his brother Jether died without children (1 Chr 2:32). Jonathan's sons were Peleth and Zaza, and the passage closes by counting these among "the sons of Jerahmeel" (1 Chr 2:33). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia therefore calls him a Jerahmeelite. Because Jether left no heirs, this branch of Jada's family probably continued only through Jonathan, by inference from the passage. His name means "the LORD has given" (Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "given of God"). Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with the several other men named Jonathan in the Bible, such as Saul's son.

Jonathan was the father of Ebed, one of the family of Adin, who is named in the list of those who came up from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra (Ezra 8:6). His son Ebed led fifty men of that family on the journey. Jonathan himself is known only as Ebed's father. Nothing is said of his own life, or of whether he lived to see the return. He is one of several men in the Bible named Jonathan, a name meaning "the LORD has given." He is a different person from Saul's son, David's friend. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same list appears in 1 Esdras 8:32.

Jonathan son of Asahel was one of the men named when Ezra dealt with the Israelites who had married foreign wives after the return from exile (Ezra 10:15). He is one of several people in the Bible with this name, which means "the LORD has given." Ezra 10:15 names him with Jahaziah son of Tikvah, and says Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levite helped them. The Hebrew can be read two ways. The King James Version says they were "employed about this matter," meaning they managed the inquiry. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes the other reading, that they stood against the plan, and STEPBible's proper names index takes him as an opponent of the demand to put away foreign wives. This entry follows the King James wording quoted here but notes that both readings are held. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a priest. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jonathan was a priest in the generation after the return from exile in Babylon. He is named once, in a list of the heads of priestly families. Nehemiah 12:14 links him to Melicu, which the surrounding list (Neh 12:12) shows to be a priestly house he represented. By inference from that context, he served while Joiakim was high priest, a generation after Zerubbabel's return. Melicu is probably the same as Malluch, one of the priests who came back with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:2). Nothing else is recorded about him. His name means "the LORD has given." Several men in the Bible share it, and he is a different person from Jonathan the son of King Saul.

Jonathan was the father of Zechariah, one of the men with trumpets at the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt wall in Nehemiah's time. Neh 12:35 places him in a family line running back through Shemaiah, Mattaniah, Michaiah and Zaccur to Asaph, the well-known temple musician. That makes Jonathan the son of Shemaiah and a descendant of Asaph. The following verse, Neh 12:36, names Zechariah's 'brethren': Shemaiah, Azarael, Milalai, Gilalai, Maai, Nethaneel, Judah and Hanani. This entry counts them as Jonathan's sons, although the Hebrew word can also mean kinsmen more broadly. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe this Jonathan as a priest. He appears only in this genealogy, and nothing else is told about him. His name means 'the LORD has given.' He is one of several men in the Bible called Jonathan.

Jonathan was a scribe in Jerusalem during the final years of the kingdom of Judah, in the reign of Zedekiah. His house had been turned into a prison, and the princes who were angry with Jeremiah beat the prophet and confined him there (Jer 37:15). Jeremiah later begged King Zedekiah not to send him back to Jonathan's house, fearing he would die there (Jer 37:20). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also connects him with Jer 38:26, where Jeremiah repeats this plea. The name means "Yahweh has given." Nothing more is recorded about him, and he is distinct from the several other men named Jonathan in the Bible, including Saul's son.

Jonathan was a son of Kareah and brother of Johanan, mentioned once in the Bible. After the Babylonians captured Jerusalem, Jonathan and his brother were among the army officers who came with their men to Gedaliah, the governor at Mizpah (Jer 40:8). This was about 587 BC, a date Smith's Bible Dictionary gives. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a Judahite captain. His brother Johanan becomes prominent in the chapters that follow, but Jonathan is not mentioned again. The parallel list of officers in 2 Kgs 25:23 names only Johanan son of Kareah, so it is uncertain whether Jonathan belongs in the original list. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including Saul's son, the friend of David. The name means "the LORD has given."

Joppa was an ancient seaport on the Mediterranean coast, listed on the border of Dan's territory (called Japho in Josh 19:46). It served as the landing point for cedar from Lebanon, floated down the coast for Solomon's temple and again for the rebuilding of the temple after the exile, then carried up to Jerusalem (2 Chr 2:16; Ezra 3:7). Jonah went down to Joppa to find a ship bound for Tarshish. In Acts, Peter came from nearby Lydda to Joppa after the death of the disciple Tabitha (Dorcas), and many there believed. He stayed many days with Simon, a tanner whose house was by the sea. While praying in Joppa he saw his vision of a great sheet let down from heaven, and messengers from Cornelius came to fetch him from there. Joppa is the modern Jaffa, now part of Tel Aviv, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Jorai was a man of the tribe of Gad, one of seven brothers of the house of their fathers listed in 1 Chr 5:13: Michael, Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Jachan, Zia and Heber. The next verse names their father as Abihail. The surrounding passage places these Gadites in Gilead and Bashan, east of the Jordan. It says their genealogies were recorded in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel, so Jorai probably belongs to about that period. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "whom Jehovah teaches." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a Gadite chief and notes that the name may stand for a clan rather than a single person. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Joram was the son of Toi (spelled Tou in Chronicles), king of Hamath. When David defeated Hadadezer king of Zobah, who had been at war with Toi, Toi sent Joram to David to greet him and congratulate him on the victory. Joram brought gifts of silver, gold and bronze vessels (2 Sam 8:10). The parallel account in 1 Chr 18:10 calls him Hadoram. The name Joram means "the LORD is exalted". Hadoram contains the name of the god Hadad instead, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that many commentators prefer the form Hadoram in 2 Samuel as well. Several other people in the Bible are also named Joram, including kings of Israel and Judah. This Joram is a different person, a prince of Hamath.

Joram was a Levite named in a genealogy in 1 Chr 26:25. He was the son of Jeshaiah and the father of Zichri. The line traces back through Rehabiah to Eliezer, and by inference from the surrounding chapter Eliezer is the son of Moses. The line ends with Shelomith, who appears in the passage as the one in charge of the treasuries of dedicated gifts in the time of David. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Joram as an ancestor of Shelomith. His name is usually explained as meaning "the LORD is exalted." It is a shorter form of Jehoram and is shared by several other people in the Bible, including kings of Israel and Judah. Nothing else is recorded about this Joram.

Joram, also called Jehoram, was a son of Ahab and Jezebel who succeeded his brother Ahaziah as king of Israel. He reigned twelve years from Samaria (2 Kgs 1:17; 3:1), beginning about 897 BC by inference from context. He is distinct from his contemporary Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. Early in his reign he mustered Israel and, with Jehoshaphat and the king of Edom, campaigned against Moab (2 Kgs 3). Later, with his nephew Ahaziah of Judah, the son of his sister Athaliah, he fought Hazael of Syria at Ramoth-gilead. He was wounded there and withdrew to Jezreel to recover. While he was in Jezreel, Jehu, anointed to cut off Ahab's house, conspired against him. Joram rode out to meet Jehu on the plot once owned by Naboth, cried out that there was treachery, and fled, but Jehu shot him through the heart. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that his death ended the dynasty of Omri.

Jordan is the main river of the land of Israel. It flows south from the foot of Mount Hermon, through Lake Huleh and the Sea of Galilee, to the Salt (Dead) Sea. It marked the eastern edge of Canaan, so "this side Jordan" and "beyond Jordan" were standard ways of dividing the land (Josh 15:5; 2 Kgs 10:33). Jacob crossed it with only his staff, and Moses was not allowed to cross it. Israel under Joshua passed over near Jericho while priests carrying the ark stood in the riverbed. Its fords were held in war (Judg 3:28; 12:6), and Jeremiah mentions its swelling. Elijah went to the Jordan before he was taken up. John the Baptist preached throughout the region around it and baptized people in the river. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes its sources near Hermon and its winding descent. The point shown here lies in the upper valley north of the Sea of Galilee.

Jorim is a man named only once in the Bible, in Luke's genealogy of Jesus. Luke 3:29 lists him as the son of Matthat and the father of Eliezer. That places him in the line running from David through Nathan, so he belongs to the tribe of Judah. He lived in the generations between David and the Babylonian exile. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the Greek form of his name to come from the Hebrew Joram or Jehoram. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "whom Jehovah has exalted." Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "he that exalts the Lord."

Jorkeam (spelled Jorkoam in the King James Version) is named once, in the genealogy of Caleb's descendants in the tribe of Judah, where Raham is called "the father of Jorkoam" (1 Chr 2:44). Smith's Bible Dictionary allows that the name could belong to a person descended from Caleb or to a place in Judah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes it as a town, with Raham as its founder, since "father of" in these lists often marks the founder of a settlement. It also suggests that Jorkeam may be the same as Jokdeam, a town in the hill country of Judah listed in Josh 15:56. This entry treats Jorkeam as a city. The location shown here lies in the hills south of Hebron, near the other towns of that district, which fits the Jokdeam identification. The exact site is uncertain.

Josabad the Gederathite was one of the warriors who came to David at Ziklag, while David was still hiding from Saul. He is named among a group of fighters in 1 Chr 12:4. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe him as one of the Benjamite archers. This follows from the surrounding passage, which presents these men as Saul's kinsmen from Benjamin who could use both bow and sling. The epithet "Gederathite" probably refers to his home town, Gederah. Its location is uncertain, but it was likely a place in Benjamin rather than the Gederah of the Judean lowlands. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the name is more properly spelled Jozabad, meaning "whom the Lord bestows." He is not the same person as the other men called Jozabad in Chronicles, Ezra and Nehemiah. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Jose is a man named in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, which traces the line back through David's son Nathan and so belongs to the tribe of Judah. He is called the son of Eliezer, and by inference from the order of the list he was the father of Er (Luke 3:29). Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats Jose as another form of Joses. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek text here reads Iesous, the equivalent of Joshua or Jesus, and that the Revised Version renders it that way. Jose is the King James spelling. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "raised" or "who pardons."

Josedech, also called Jehozadak and Jozadak, was a priest of the tribe of Levi in the high-priestly line, the son of Seraiah (1 Chr 6:14). When Nebuchadnezzar took Judah and Jerusalem into exile, Jehozadak was carried away captive (1 Chr 6:15). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that his father Seraiah was executed at Riblah (2 Kgs 25:18–21) and that Jehozadak never served as high priest himself. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he probably died in Babylon. He is mostly remembered as the father of Joshua (Jeshua), the high priest who returned with Zerubbabel, rebuilt the altar and led the rebuilding of the temple. Haggai and Zechariah address Joshua by his father's name. Ezra 7:1 calls Ezra "son of Seraiah," which is why this entry treats Ezra as his brother. Since Ezra lived much later, the phrase may instead mean a descendant.

Joseph (son of Jacob) was the elder of Jacob's two sons by Rachel, named for her hope that the LORD would 'add' another son (Gen 30:24). His envious brothers sold him into Egypt (Acts 7:9), where he served in an Egyptian officer's house and was later imprisoned. Called to interpret Pharaoh's dreams, he was put in charge of Egypt at thirty, received the Egyptian name Zaphnath-paaneah, and married Asenath, who bore Ephraim and Manasseh. During the famine he provided for his father and brothers, who settled in Egypt. He died there at 110 and was embalmed. Moses later carried his bones out of Egypt, and they were buried at Shechem. His name came to stand for the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh and, in the prophets, for the northern kingdom. This entry dates his life to about 1745–1635 BC, by inference from context.

Joseph was a man of the tribe of Issachar, known only as the father of Igal. Igal was the man chosen from Issachar to be one of the twelve spies Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan, and he is listed in Num 13:7 as "the son of Joseph." Nothing else is recorded about Joseph himself. He lived probably a generation before the wilderness journey, and he should not be confused with the several other men of the same name in the Bible, such as Jacob's son Joseph. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names give the meaning of the name as "increase" or "addition."

Joseph (son of Asaph) was a Levite, one of the four sons of the musician Asaph. With his brothers Zaccur, Nethaniah and Asarelah (called Jesharelah in 1 Chr 25:14), he served under his father's direction among those who "prophesied" in the temple worship, by inference with music, as the surrounding chapter describes, according to the king's arrangement (1 Chr 25:2). That king is David, which places Joseph in David's reign. When the temple musicians were divided by lot into twenty-four courses, the first lot fell to Joseph, making him head of the first division (1 Chr 25:9). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him in these terms. Unlike the leaders of the following courses, the verse does not state the number of his group. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name is commonly explained as meaning "increase" or "addition."

Joseph was one of the Israelite laymen listed in Ezra 10 among those who had married foreign wives after the return from exile. He is named only once, alongside Shallum and Amariah (Ezra 10:42). The surrounding chapter shows that these men agreed to send away their foreign wives during Ezra's reforms. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places him among the sons of Bani, the family group that heads this part of the list. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the episode to about 459 BC, an estimate inferred from context. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with the several other men in the Bible who share his name. According to Hitchcock's Bible Names, the name means "increase" or "addition."

Joseph was a priest who headed the priestly family of Shebaniah in the days of the high priest Joiakim, after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears only in a list of priestly family heads (Neh 12:14). By inference from the surrounding passage, which dates the list to Joiakim's time, he lived in the generation after the first returnees under Zerubbabel, Smith's Bible Dictionary places him some time after 536 BC. The family name Shebaniah probably matches the Shechaniah of Neh 12:3, a variation in spelling between the two lists. Several other people in the Bible share the name Joseph, and this one should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "increase" or "addition." Nothing more is recorded about him.

Joseph (Mary's Husband) was the husband of Mary and the legal father of Jesus, who was 'supposed' to be his son (Luke 3:23). A descendant of David from Nazareth in Galilee, he was engaged to Mary when she was found to be pregnant. Described as a just man, he planned to end the engagement quietly. An angel in a dream then told him to take her as his wife, and he did. He traveled to Bethlehem, where Jesus was born. Later dreams sent him to Egypt to escape Herod and then brought him back. He was with Mary when Jesus was presented at the Temple and on the Passover journey when Jesus was twelve. Matthew names his father as Jacob, while Luke's genealogy lists Heli. Matt 13:55 calls him a carpenter and names James, Joses, Simon and Jude as Jesus' brothers. Easton's Bible Dictionary infers that he died before Jesus' public ministry.

Joseph (of Arimathea) was a rich man from the town of Arimathea who asked for and buried the body of Jesus after the crucifixion, about AD 30 by inference from context. Mark and Luke call him an honourable counsellor, which Easton's Bible Dictionary takes to mean a member of the Sanhedrin, the Jewish ruling council. Luke describes him as a good and just man, and Mark says he waited for the kingdom of God. Matthew and John call him a disciple of Jesus, and John adds that he kept this secret for fear of the Jewish authorities. That evening he went boldly to Pilate and asked for the body. Pilate confirmed the death with the centurion and then released it to him. Joseph wrapped the body in clean linen. Connected passages describe Nicodemus helping him (John 19:39) and the body being laid in Joseph's own new rock-cut tomb. Easton's identifies Arimathea with Old Testament Ramah.

Joseph was an ancestor of Jesus named only in Luke's genealogy, which traces Jesus' line back through David to Adam. He was the father of Janna and, according to the next verse (Luke 3:25), the son of Mattathias. Because the line runs through David, he belonged to the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him some time after 400 BC, a date inferred from his position in the list. He should not be confused with the other men named Joseph in the same genealogy, including Mary's husband at its start (Luke 3:23) and another ancestor further back (Luke 3:30). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "increase" or "addition."

Joseph was an ancestor of Jesus named in Luke's genealogy, which traces the line back from Joseph the husband of Mary through David's son Nathan. He is listed as the son of Jonan and the father of Juda (Luke 3:30). Because this line runs through David, he belongs to the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him, and since several people in the Bible share the name, he should not be confused with the better-known men called Joseph. By inference from his place in the list, between David and the Babylonian exile, he probably lived several generations after David, though the text gives no date. The name is commonly understood to mean "increase" or "addition" (Hitchcock's Bible Names).

event: Joseph and Mary Flee to Egypt
text: The Flight of Joseph and Mary to Egypt took place after the wise men had left. An angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream and told him to take the young child Jesus and his mother to Egypt and stay there until he was told to return, because Herod would search for the child to kill him. Joseph got up and left for Egypt by night with the child and Mary. They stayed there until Herod died. Matthew presents this as fulfilling the prophet's words, "Out of Egypt have I called my son", which are found in Hos 11:1. By inference from context, the flight is dated to about 4 BC, shortly before Herod's death. The text does not say where in Egypt the family stayed or how long they were there.

event: Joseph and Mary return from Egypt
text: The return of Joseph and Mary from Egypt was the family's journey back to the land of Israel after the death of Herod the Great. In Egypt an angel appeared to Joseph in a dream and told him to take the young child Jesus and his mother home, because those who had sought the child's life were dead (Matt 2:19–20). Joseph obeyed and came into the land of Israel. When he heard that Herod's son Archelaus now ruled Judea, he was afraid to settle there. After a further warning in a dream, he turned aside to Galilee (Matt 2:22). The next verse says they settled in Nazareth. The location shown here is Jerusalem, standing for Judea, the region Joseph avoided. The date of about 4 BC is inferred from context, which ties the return to Herod's death.

event: Joseph and Mary return to Nazareth
text: The return of Joseph and Mary to Nazareth is the settling of Jesus' family in the Galilean town of Nazareth after his birth. Luke and Matthew each describe it from a different angle. In Luke, once they had done everything the law required, which is the presentation of Jesus at the temple, they went back to Galilee, to "their own city Nazareth" (Luke 2:39). In Matthew, the family returns from Egypt (Matt 2:13–21). Joseph learns that Archelaus has succeeded his father Herod as ruler of Judea and is afraid to go there. Warned in a dream, he turns aside to Galilee and makes his home in Nazareth, which Matthew presents as fulfilling a prophetic saying that he would be called a Nazarene (Matt 2:22–23). This entry places the event right after the temple presentation, about 4 BC, a date inferred from context.

Joseph imprisoned is the episode in which Joseph's Egyptian master put him in the prison where the king's prisoners were held. The earlier verses of Gen 39 name the master as Potiphar and explain that his wife had falsely accused Joseph. The keeper of the prison soon placed Joseph in charge of the other prisoners. When Pharaoh's chief butler and chief baker were jailed there, each had a dream. Joseph interpreted the butler's as restoration to office within three days and the baker's as execution, and both came true on Pharaoh's birthday. Joseph asked the butler to mention him to Pharaoh, but the butler forgot him. Two full years later, when no Egyptian wise man could explain Pharaoh's dreams, the butler remembered Joseph, who was brought hastily from the dungeon. By inference from context, the imprisonment began about 1718 BC and lasted about three years.

The Promotion of Joseph in Egypt was the moment Pharaoh raised Joseph, son of Jacob, to rule over the whole land of Egypt. It followed Joseph's interpretation of Pharaoh's dreams and his advice to prepare for the coming famine. Pharaoh judged that no one was as discerning and wise as a man in whom the Spirit of God was. He placed Joseph over his house and people, keeping only the throne above him. Pharaoh gave Joseph his signet ring, fine linen garments and a gold chain, and had him ride in his second chariot while people cried "Bow the knee." He also gave Joseph the Egyptian name Zaphnathpaaneah and a wife, Asenath, daughter of Potipherah, priest of On. Joseph was thirty years old at the time. This entry dates the event to about 1715 BC, an estimate inferred from context.

Joseph's brothers go to Egypt is the episode in Gen 42 in which Jacob, hearing there was grain in Egypt during a famine in Canaan, sent ten of his sons to buy food but kept Benjamin at home. Joseph, now governor and in charge of selling grain, recognized them as they bowed before him, though they did not recognize him. Speaking through an interpreter, he accused them of spying, held them for three days, then bound Simeon and demanded they bring their youngest brother as proof. The brothers admitted to one another their guilt over Joseph, and he wept in private. Their money was secretly returned in their sacks, which frightened them. Back in Canaan, Jacob refused to send Benjamin, despite Reuben's offer of his two sons. This entry dates it to about 1707 BC, by inference from context, after the seven years of plenty.

Joseph's brothers return to Egypt is the episode in Genesis 43–45 in which Jacob's sons make a second journey to buy grain during the famine. Joseph, now governor of Egypt, had insisted they bring their youngest brother, Benjamin. Judah pledged himself for the boy, and Jacob reluctantly sent him along with gifts. Joseph hosted the brothers, released Simeon and seated them in birth order. He then had his silver cup hidden in Benjamin's sack and sent his steward to overtake them on the road. Judah pleaded to stay as a slave in Benjamin's place. Joseph then revealed himself, told them five more years of famine remained, and, with Pharaoh's approval, sent wagons and provisions to bring Jacob to Egypt. Jacob at first did not believe it but resolved to go. This entry dates the episode to about 1706 BC, the famine's second year (Gen 45:6), by inference from context.

Joseph sold to Egypt is the episode in which Jacob's other sons sold their younger brother Joseph into slavery. Jacob favored Joseph and gave him a coat of many colors. Joseph's dreams of his brothers' sheaves, and of the sun, moon and eleven stars, bowing to him deepened their hatred. Sent by Jacob from Hebron, Joseph found them at Dothan, where they plotted to kill him. Reuben persuaded them to throw him into a dry pit instead, meaning to rescue him. Judah then proposed selling him, and he was sold for twenty pieces of silver to traders called both Ishmeelites and Midianites. They took him to Egypt and sold him to Potiphar, captain of Pharaoh's guard. The brothers dipped his coat in goat's blood, and Jacob mourned him as killed by a wild animal. This entry dates it to about 1728 BC, by inference from context.

Joses was one of the brothers of Jesus, named with James, Simon and Judas (Jude) when the people of Nazareth questioned Jesus' background. They asked whether he was not the carpenter, or the carpenter's son, whose mother was Mary (Matt 13:55; Mark 6:3). This entry treats Joses as a son of Joseph and Mary. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek of Matt 13:55 reads "Joseph," as the Revised Version renders it. The Gospels also mention a Mary "the mother of James and Joses" among the women who watched the crucifixion from a distance and later saw where Jesus was buried (Matt 27:56; Mark 15:40, 47). Mark calls this James "the less." It is uncertain whether these sons are the same as Jesus' brothers. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia considers it possible, while many readers take this Mary to be a different woman.

Joshah son of Amaziah was a man of the tribe of Simeon. He appears only once, in a list of Simeonite names in 1 Chr 4:34. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 4:38–41) describes the men on this list as leaders of their families. It says that in the days of King Hezekiah, their clans grew and moved toward Gedor in search of pasture for their flocks, driving out the earlier inhabitants and settling there. By inference from that context, Joshah was one of these Simeonite clan leaders in Hezekiah's time, probably the late 8th century BC. Nothing else is recorded about him or his father Amaziah, who is not otherwise identified. The meaning of the name is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "Yahweh's gift", and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "whom Jehovah lets dwell".

Joshaphat the Mithnite was one of the warriors named in the list of David's mighty men in 1 Chr 11:43, where he appears next to Hanan the son of Maachah. His name means "the Lord judges" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary, which describes him as one of David's guard. The title "Mithnite" probably refers to his hometown or clan, but no place called Mithna is known from the Bible, so its meaning is uncertain. He is mentioned only in this verse, which belongs to the later part of the list that has no parallel in 2 Samuel 23, and nothing else is recorded about his deeds or family. He should not be confused with Jehoshaphat or the other men called Joshaphat elsewhere in Scripture.

Joshaviah was a son of Elnaam and a brother of Jeribai. Both brothers are named among David's mighty warriors in the list of 1 Chr 11:46. The verse is ambiguous about the title "the Mahavite," which follows the name Eliel and comes before the two brothers. It may belong to Eliel alone, or Eliel may also have been a son of Elnaam. Nothing else is recorded about Joshaviah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that his name does not appear in the parallel list of David's warriors in 2 Samuel 23, which is shorter and differs in detail. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "whom Jehovah makes dwell," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the seat, alteration, or captivity of the Lord."

Joshbekashah was a Levite, one of the fourteen sons of Heman listed among the musicians organized for temple service in David's time (1 Chr 25:4). When the musicians' duties were assigned by lot, the seventeenth lot fell to him, and he served with his sons and relatives in a group of twelve (1 Chr 25:24). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "a seat in a hard place" and calls him head of the seventeenth course of musicians. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some commentators read the last eight or nine names in the list of Heman's sons, including this one, as the words of a prayer or poetic lines rather than personal names. This entry treats Joshbekashah as a person, as the lot assignment in 1 Chr 25:24 does.

Joshua son of Nun, of the tribe of Ephraim (one of the Joseph tribes), was Moses' young assistant and his successor as leader of Israel. He led Israel's fighters against Amalek (Exod 17:9). He and Caleb alone of their generation survived the wilderness (Num 26:65). Moses laid hands on him and charged him to bring Israel into the promised land (Deut 31:7; 34:9). After Moses died, Joshua led the crossing of the Jordan, circumcised the people, and took Jericho, Ai and Hazor. He also made peace with Gibeon and defeated many Canaanite kings. With Eleazar the priest he divided the land among the tribes, giving Hebron to Caleb. In old age he gathered Israel, and the people pledged to serve the LORD. He died about 1424 BC, by inference from context, at Timnath-heres (Timnath-serah). He is also called Oshea, Jehoshua, Jeshua and, in Acts 7:45, Jesus. Jewish tradition credits him with writing the book of Joshua.

Joshua was a man of Beth-shemesh, called "the Bethshemite," who owned the field where the cart carrying the ark of the LORD stopped after the Philistines sent it back to Israel. The cart halted beside a great stone in his field. The people there split up the wood of the cart and offered the cows that had drawn it as a burnt offering to the LORD (1 Sam 6:14). The ark was set on that stone, called the great stone of Abel, which the writer says was still standing in Joshua's field "unto this day" (1 Sam 6:18). Nothing else is recorded about him, and he is distinct from the better-known Joshua son of Nun and others who share the name. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "saviour" or "whose help is Jehovah."

Joshua was a governor of a city in Judah during the reign of King Josiah, mentioned only in 2 Kgs 23:8. A city gate was named after him, and high places stood at its entrance, on the left as one entered. Josiah broke these down as part of his reforms, when he brought the priests out of the cities of Judah and defiled the high places from Geba to Beersheba. The verse does not name the city. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take it to be Jerusalem and call Joshua its governor, and this entry follows that reading. Smith's dates him to about 628 BC. Nothing else is known of him, and he is distinct from the better-known Joshua son of Nun and others who share the name, which means "the LORD is salvation."

Joshua, also called Jeshua, was the son of Josedech (Jozadak) and the high priest of the Jews who returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel. He is one of several people in the Bible with this name. With Zerubbabel, the governor of Judah, he rebuilt the altar at Jerusalem and began work on the temple. They also refused to let outsiders take part in the building, as King Cyrus had commanded. The prophet Haggai addressed him by name and urged him to be strong and finish the work. In Zechariah's visions he stands before the angel of the LORD in filthy garments, with Satan opposing him, and he is later crowned with crowns of silver and gold. He was the father of Joiakim, who in turn began a line of high priests. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he was probably born in Babylon during the captivity.

Josiah was a king of Judah, the son of Amon and Jedidah. The people made him king at eight years old after his father was assassinated, and he reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem, about 640–609 BC by inference from context. He removed the high places at Bethel and in Samaria, burning bones on the Bethel altar as a man of God had foretold by name in 1 Kgs 13:2. He also put away mediums and idols to carry out the book of the law that Hilkiah the priest found in the temple. In his eighteenth year he held a Passover unmatched since Samuel's day. Jeremiah and Zephaniah prophesied during his reign. He went out against Pharaoh Necho at Megiddo, was shot by archers, and died, and all Judah mourned him. Three of his sons, Jehoahaz (Shallum), Jehoiakim and Zedekiah, later reigned. Matthew lists him as Josias in Jesus' genealogy.

Josiah, son of Zephaniah, was a man living in Jerusalem in the time of the prophet Zechariah, after the return from exile in Babylon. Zechariah was told to go to his house on the same day that Heldai, Tobijah and Jedaiah arrived from Babylon, and to take silver and gold from them to make crowns for Joshua the high priest (Zech 6:10). The crowns were then to be kept in the temple as a memorial, linked to these men and to "Hen the son of Zephaniah" (Zech 6:14). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Hen to be another name for Josiah, and this entry follows that view. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that "hen" means "favor," and that the verse may instead be read as "for the kindness of the son of Zephaniah." The text there is uncertain. Nothing more is known about him.

Josibiah was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named only once, in a genealogy in 1 Chr 4:35. He was the son of Seraiah, the grandson of Asiel, and the father of Jehu. That verse is part of a list of Simeonite clan leaders. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 4:41) places these leaders in the days of King Hezekiah, when they moved to Gedor in search of pasture for their flocks. STEPBible Proper Names follows this reading and counts Josibiah among the Simeonite leaders of Hezekiah's reign, though it is perhaps more exact to say that his son Jehu belonged to that generation. Some English versions spell the name Joshibiah. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it to mean "to whom God gives a dwelling," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the seat, or captivity of the Lord." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Josiphiah was the father, or possibly a more distant ancestor, of Shelomith, who led a group of 160 men back from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra (Ezra 8:10). The name is usually explained as meaning "the Lord adds" or "the Lord will increase." In the Hebrew text the verse is awkward, reading "of the sons of Shelomith; the son of Josiphiah." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that a family name, Bani, fell out of the verse, based on the Greek Septuagint and 1 Esdras 8:36. On that reading, Shelomith son of Josiphiah was head of the Bani family group. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the return to about 459 BC. Nothing else is recorded about Josiphiah himself.

Jotbah was the hometown of Haruz, whose daughter Meshullemeth was the wife of King Manasseh of Judah and the mother of King Amon, who reigned two years in Jerusalem (2 Kgs 21:19). This is its only mention in the Bible, and the verse says nothing more about the place. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "goodness", and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "pleasantness". Its location is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the same as Jotbathah, a stopping place of Israel in the wilderness, in the far south near the Gulf of Aqaba. Other scholars identify it with a site in Galilee. The location shown here follows the Jotbathah identification and is only approximate.

Jotbathah was a desert campsite of the Israelites during their wilderness journey. Numbers lists it between Hor-hagidgad and Ebronah (Num 33:33–34). Deuteronomy calls it Jotbath and describes it as "a land of rivers of waters," a place with streams (Deut 10:7). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "goodness." Because the Numbers itinerary soon reaches Ezion-geber on the Gulf of Aqaba (Num 33:35), the site was probably in the southern Arabah valley, north of the gulf. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says the exact site is unknown. A common suggestion links it to the springs of the southern Arabah, near modern Yotvata in Israel, whose name echoes the biblical one. The location shown here is only approximate and follows that southern Arabah identification, north of the Gulf of Aqaba.

Jotham was the youngest son of Gideon, who is also called Jerubbaal. He was the only one to escape when his half-brother Abimelech killed Gideon's other seventy sons on one stone at Ophrah, because he hid himself. When the men of Shechem made Abimelech king, Jotham stood on the top of Mount Gerizim and called out to them. In the verses that follow (Judg 9:8–15) he told the parable of the trees choosing a bramble as king, which Easton's Bible Dictionary calls the earliest parable. He ended with a curse on Abimelech and Shechem. He then fled to Beer and lived there out of fear of Abimelech. The location of Beer is uncertain. The chapter closes by saying that his curse came upon the men of Shechem. Several other people in the Bible share his name, including a later king of Judah.

Jotham was a king of Judah, the son of King Uzziah (also called Azariah) and Jerushah, the daughter of Zadok, and the father of King Ahaz. When Uzziah was struck with leprosy and lived in a separate house, Jotham took charge of the palace and governed the people on his behalf. He became king at twenty-five, began to reign in the second year of Pekah of Israel, and ruled sixteen years in Jerusalem. By inference from context, his reign began about 758 BC and he died about 742 BC. Chronicles says he grew powerful because he ordered his ways before the LORD and mentions his wars. A genealogy of the Transjordan tribes was recorded in his day. The prophets Isaiah, Hosea and Micah were active during his reign. He was buried in the city of David. He appears as Joatham in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus. Several other people in the Bible share his name.

Jotham was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once as one of the six sons of Jahdai, alongside Regem, Geshan, Pelet, Ephah and Shaaph (1 Chr 2:47). He appears in the genealogy of the descendants of Caleb, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him a Calebite. The verse does not say how Jahdai is connected to Caleb's family. STEPBible's proper-name index takes Jahdai as a wife of Caleb, while Smith's Bible Dictionary simply calls Jotham a son of Jahdai. This entry treats Jahdai as his father. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name means "the LORD is perfect" or "the LORD is upright." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including the son of Gideon and the king of Judah, and he should not be confused with them.

The Journey to Rome begins with Paul, a prisoner, handed over with others to Julius, a centurion of the Augustan cohort, to be taken by sea to Italy. The narrator's "we" places the writer, traditionally Luke, on board, along with Aristarchus of Thessalonica. Their ship from Adramyttium stopped at Sidon, where Julius let Paul visit friends. It then sailed in the shelter of Cyprus against contrary winds and reached Myra in Lycia. There they changed to an Alexandrian ship bound for Italy. Slow progress past Cnidus forced them south of Crete, by Salmone, to Fair Havens near Lasea. The fast had passed, probably the autumn Day of Atonement, so sailing was dangerous, and Paul warned of loss. The centurion trusted the ship's master and owner instead, and most chose to try for Phenice, a Cretan harbor, to winter. This was about AD 56, by inference.

Jozabad was one of the men of the tribe of Manasseh who left Saul's side and joined David while David was on his way to Ziklag. 1 Chr 12:20 names him among the captains of thousands from Manasseh who came over to David. By inference from the surrounding passage, this happened when David had gone with the Philistines toward battle against Saul and was then sent back to Ziklag. The same verse names two men called Jozabad in this group, and it is not clear which one this entry refers to. Several other men in the Bible also bear the name. Hitchcock's Bible Names treats Jozabad as the same name as Josabad. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Jozabad was a man of the tribe of Manasseh and one of the "captains of the thousands" of Manasseh who joined David as he went to Ziklag (1 Chr 12:20). By inference from the surrounding chapter and the account in 1 Samuel 29–30, this happened when David left the Philistine army before its battle with Saul and returned to Ziklag, and these men changed sides to support him. The same verse lists two men named Jozabad among the seven Manasseh commanders, so it is unclear which of the two this entry refers to. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names treats Jozabad as the same name as Josabad. Several other men in the Bible also bear this name.

Jozabad was one of ten overseers who served under Cononiah and his brother Shimei during the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He was appointed by command of Hezekiah and of Azariah, the chief officer of the temple. By inference from the surrounding passage, these overseers helped manage the offerings, tithes and dedicated gifts that the people brought to the temple and that were kept in its storerooms. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him as a Levite and dates his service to about 726 BC, an estimate drawn from context. STEPBible's Tyndale House name list describes his role as helping distribute the contributions to the priests and Levites. Smith's gives the name's meaning as "Jehovah justifies." He is mentioned only in 2 Chr 31:13. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jozabad, and this one should not be confused with them.

Jozabad was one of the chief Levites in the reign of King Josiah of Judah. At Josiah's great Passover, he joined Conaniah, Shemaiah, Nethaneel, Hashabiah and Jeiel in supplying the Levites with animals for the Passover offerings: five thousand sheep and goats and five hundred oxen (2 Chr 35:9). Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary takes to mean "the LORD justifies," is shared by several other men in the Bible, including other Levites, so this Jozabad should not be confused with them.

Jozabad, son of Jeshua, was a Levite in the time of Ezra. After Ezra's group arrived in Jerusalem from Babylon, the silver, gold and temple vessels they had carried were weighed in the house of God on the fourth day. The priest Meremoth son of Uriah did the weighing, together with Eleazar son of Phinehas. Two Levites, Jozabad and Noadiah son of Binnui, assisted them (Ezra 8:33). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 459 BC, an estimate from context. It suggests he is probably the same man as a Levite named Jozabad mentioned elsewhere in Ezra and Nehemiah, but the identification is uncertain because several people share the name. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "Jehovah justifies."

Jozabad was a priest of the family of Pashur who lived in the time of Ezra, after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears only in the list of men who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:22). The verse itself simply names him among the sons of Pashur. The surrounding chapter places this family among the priests, and it records that those listed agreed to send away their foreign wives. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:22 gives his name as Ocidelus. His name is usually explained as meaning "the Lord has bestowed," though Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "Jehovah justifies." Several other men in the Bible share the name Jozabad, so this one should not be confused with the Levites of the same name in Ezra and Nehemiah.

Jozabad was a Levite in the time of Ezra, listed among those who had married foreign women (Ezra 10:23). By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was one of the men who agreed to send away their foreign wives during Ezra's reform after the return from exile in Babylon. The STEPBible Proper Names index describes him the same way. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jozabad, including Levites mentioned elsewhere in Ezra and Nehemiah. Whether this Jozabad is the same as any of them is uncertain, and this entry treats him as a separate person known only from this list. Hitchcock's Bible Names treats the name as the same as Josabad.

Jozabad was one of the Levites who helped the people understand the law when Ezra read it publicly in Jerusalem after the return from exile. He is named in Neh 8:7 among thirteen men, alongside Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah and others, who explained the reading while the people stood in their places. Nothing more is said about him in this passage. The name Jozabad is shared by several men of the same period, including Levites mentioned in Ezra and elsewhere in Nehemiah, such as a Levite who oversaw the outward business of the temple (Neh 11:16). He may be the same man as one of these, but the text does not make the identification, so it remains uncertain.

Jozabad was one of the leading Levites living in Jerusalem after the return from exile, in the time of Nehemiah. Together with Shabbethai, he oversaw the "outward business of the house of God" (Neh 11:16), meaning the outside work of the temple rather than its sacred service inside. Because several men in the Bible share this name, it is uncertain whether he is the same as the Levite Jozabad mentioned elsewhere in Ezra and Nehemiah, such as the one who helped explain the law to the people (Neh 8:7) or the son of Jeshua who received the temple treasures (Ezra 8:33). An identification with one of them is possible but not stated in the text.

Jozadak was the father of Jeshua, a priest whose family is named in Ezra 10:18. That verse lists priests of the sons of Jeshua son of Jozadak, namely Maaseiah, Eliezer, Jarib and Gedaliah, among those found in Ezra's time to have married foreign wives. Other passages call Jeshua son of Jozadak the high priest who returned from exile with Zerubbabel and helped rebuild the altar and temple (Ezra 3:2, 3:8, 5:2; Neh 12:26). By inference, Jozadak is the same man as Jehozadak, the son of the high priest Seraiah, who according to 1 Chr 6:14–15 was carried into exile when Nebuchadnezzar took Judah and Jerusalem. Haggai and Zechariah spell the name Josedech. The verse shown here records nothing about Jozadak himself beyond his being Jeshua's father.

Jubal was a son of Lamech and his wife Adah, in the line of Cain, and the brother of Jabal. His half-siblings were Tubal-cain and Naamah, Lamech's children by his other wife, Zillah. Genesis 4:21 calls him "the father of all such as handle the harp and organ," meaning he was the founder or originator of those who play musical instruments. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains that the Hebrew words translated "harp" and "organ" more properly mean a lyre and a mouth-organ or Pan's pipe, so modern translations often render them "lyre and pipe." Along with his brothers, who are linked with herding and metalworking, Jubal appears in a short list that traces early skills and crafts to Lamech's family. His name has been connected with music; Hitchcock's Bible Names gives it as "a trumpet." He is mentioned only in this one verse.

Jucal, also called Jehucal, was the son of Shelemiah and an official at the court of Zedekiah, the last king of Judah. King Zedekiah sent him with Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah the priest to ask the prophet Jeremiah to pray to the Lord for them (Jer 37:3). Easton's Bible Dictionary places this during the final Babylonian siege of Jerusalem under Nebuchadnezzar. Later Jucal was one of four officials, with Shephatiah, Gedaliah son of Pashur, and Pashur son of Malchiah, who heard Jeremiah tell the people what was coming (Jer 38:1). The verses that follow say these officials urged the king to put Jeremiah to death, and the prophet was then lowered into a cistern. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes both forms of the name to mean probably "Yahweh is able."

Juda is an ancestor of Jesus named in Luke's genealogy, which traces the line back from Joseph through David to Adam. He was the father of Joseph and, according to the next verse (Luke 3:27), the son of Joanna. He belongs to the generations after the Babylonian exile, between Zerubbabel and Joseph the husband of Mary. Nothing else is recorded about him. Many later Greek texts spell the name Joda, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists him under that form. He is not the same as several other people in the Bible with similar names, including Judah son of Jacob, who appears as Juda later in the same genealogy. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him with Abiud in Matthew's genealogy (Matt 1:13). The two lists differ in this section, so that identification is uncertain.

Juda was a man named in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, listed as the son of Joseph and the father of Simeon (Luke 3:30). He appears only in this list, which traces the line from David through his son Nathan. That line places Juda in the tribe of Judah. He lived several generations after David and long before the exile, though no dates are given. Nothing else is recorded about him. Juda is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Judah, which Smith's Bible Dictionary explains as meaning "praised." Several other people in the Bible share the name, and this Juda should not be confused with them. Easton's Bible Dictionary places him in Christ's maternal ancestry, reflecting the view that Luke's genealogy follows Mary's line, as distinct from Matthew's.

Judah was the region of southern Canaan allotted to the tribe of Judah, which later formed the heart of the kingdom of Judah. Joshua 15 traces its borders: south along the wilderness of Zin and the border of Edom past Kadesh-barnea, north through the valley of Achor and En-rogel to Kirjath-jearim, and west to the Mediterranean. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the Dead Sea as the eastern boundary and puts the territory at roughly 45 by 50 miles. The region took in the hill country around Hebron, lowland towns such as Lachish and Libnah, the dry wilderness of Judah south of Arad, and the southern lands reaching to Beersheba. David sheltered there and, after Saul's death, went up to Hebron. Later, 'from Geba to Beersheba' described the kingdom's extent. It broadly matches today's southern West Bank and southern Israel. This entry marks no single point.

Judah (patriarch) was the fourth son of Jacob and Leah. She named him from her words "Now will I praise the LORD" (Gen 29:35). His birth is placed about 1755 BC, by inference from context. When his brothers planned to kill Joseph, Judah persuaded them to sell him instead (Gen 37:26). Genesis 38 tells how he married a Canaanite woman and had three sons, Er, Onan and Shelah. After Er and Onan died, he held Shelah back from their widow Tamar, who later bore Judah twins, Pharez and Zerah. During the famine he pledged himself for Benjamin's safety and became the family's spokesman before Joseph (Gen 43:8). Jacob's blessing promised that the sceptre would not depart from Judah (Gen 49:10). He was the ancestor of the tribe of Judah, whose name later passed to the southern kingdom ruled by David's line. He also appears in the genealogy of Jesus.

Judah was a Levite listed among those who had married foreign women in the time of Ezra (Ezra 10:23). He appears in the roll of priests, Levites and other Israelites who had taken wives from the surrounding peoples. From the surrounding chapter, these men agreed to send away their foreign wives. Nothing else is recorded about him, and because several people in the Bible share the name Judah, it is uncertain whether he can be linked with any other Levite of that name in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the praise of the Lord" or "confession."

Judah son of Senuah was a leader in Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah, after the return from exile. He appears in the list of people who settled in the city, and Neh 11:9 says he was "second over the city," serving under or alongside Joel son of Zichri, the overseer. The surrounding verses, which list descendants of Benjamin, suggest he belonged to that tribe, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him a Benjamite. The Hebrew phrase can mean either that he was second in command over Jerusalem or that he was in charge of the city's second district. His father's name is given in the KJV as Senuah, which the same encyclopedia renders Hassenuah. Several people in the Bible share the name Judah, which Hitchcock's Bible Names takes to mean "the praise of the Lord." Nothing more is recorded about him.

Judah was a man named in the lists of Nehemiah 12. One of several people in the Bible with this name, which means "praised," he appears in Neh 12:8 among the Levites who returned from exile with Zerubbabel, alongside Jeshua, Binnui, Kadmiel, Sherebiah and Mattaniah, who led the thanksgiving songs. A Judah is also named in Neh 12:34 among those who walked in the first procession at the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt wall. This entry treats both mentions as one person. Tyndale House's STEPBible Proper Names describes him as a Levite who helped lead the thanksgiving choir at the dedication. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists the two as separate men, treating the Judah of Neh 12:34 as one of the leaders of Judah. The verses give no further details about him.

Judah was one of the musicians who played at the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. He is named among the "brethren" of Zechariah son of Jonathan. Neh 12:35 makes Zechariah one of the priests' sons with trumpets, and this entry makes Judah and the others with him sons of Jonathan, though "brethren" may simply mean kinsmen or fellow musicians. They played the musical instruments of David, and Ezra the scribe led their part of the procession (Neh 12:36). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him a priest and musician and suggests he may be the same as other men named Judah in Ezra and Nehemiah. Because several people share this name, that identification is uncertain. His name is usually taken to mean "praised."

The Kingdom of Judah was the southern Israelite kingdom that formed when the united monarchy split after Solomon's death. Rehoboam, Solomon's son, kept rule over the Israelites living in Judah's cities, and he gathered the men of Judah and Benjamin in an attempt to win back the northern tribes (1 Kgs 12:17, 21). From his capital at Jerusalem he fortified cities for defence (2 Chr 11:5). Judah later faced threats from its neighbours, including a plot to install the son of Tabeal as king (Isa 7:6). It also faced Sennacherib of Assyria, who captured its fortified cities in Hezekiah's fourteenth year (2 Kgs 18:13). King Josiah removed idolatrous priests and practices from its cities to carry out the law found in the temple (2 Kgs 23:5, 24). The location shown here marks Jerusalem, its capital. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of "Judah" as "the praise of the Lord."

Judas (of Galilee) was a rebel leader mentioned by Gamaliel in his speech to the Jewish council in Acts 5:37. Gamaliel was advising the council on how to deal with the apostles. He said that Judas rose up "in the days of the taxing," drew many people after him, and then perished, and his followers were scattered. Gamaliel names him after Theudas as a second example of a movement that came to nothing once its leader died. The "taxing" refers to a Roman registration or census. STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) describes Judas as leading a revolt against the Roman census held while Quirinius was governor of Syria. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia likewise calls him a Galilean who stirred up rebellion during the enrollment. His name is the Greek form of Judah (Easton's Bible Dictionary).

Judas (Jew of Damascus) was the man in whose house Saul of Tarsus stayed in Damascus after his encounter with the risen Jesus on the road to the city. The Lord told Ananias in a vision to go to the street called Straight and ask at the house of Judas for Saul, who was praying there (Acts 9:11). Saul had been led into Damascus blind, so he was probably lodging with Judas as a guest, by inference from the surrounding passage. Nothing more is known of him. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him a Jew of Damascus, while the STEPBible proper names index describes him as a Christian; the text itself does not say. His name is the Greek form of Judah. Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note that a house traditionally called the "house of Judas" is still pointed out on or near Straight Street.

Judas Barsabas was a leader in the early Jerusalem church who was chosen, along with Silas, to carry the decision of the Jerusalem Council to the believers at Antioch. Acts calls the two men "chief men among the brethren." They travelled with Paul and Barnabas, and the council's letter says they would confirm its contents in person. The council is dated to about AD 46, by inference from context. At Antioch, Judas and Silas, described as prophets, encouraged and strengthened the believers with a long address. The next verse, Acts 15:33, says they were later sent back in peace to those who had sent them. His surname, Barsabas, means "son of Sabas." Because Joseph Barsabas, a candidate to replace Judas Iscariot (Acts 1:23), had the same surname, some suggest the two were brothers, but the text does not say so. The name Judas is the same as Judah.

Judas Iscariot was one of the twelve apostles of Jesus and the one who betrayed him. John calls him the son of Simon (John 6:71), and Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries explain his surname as "man of Kerioth," a town in Judah. The Gospels distinguish him from another apostle named Judas, the brother of James (Luke 6:16; John 14:22). He kept the group's money bag. He went to the chief priests to arrange the betrayal, and at the last supper Jesus identified him by handing him dipped bread. He led an armed crowd to a place where Jesus often met his disciples and singled Jesus out with a kiss. When Jesus was condemned, Judas regretted it and returned the thirty pieces of silver. Matt 27:5 says he then hanged himself, and the apostles later chose someone to take his place.

The Judas Plans Betrayal event was the agreement Judas Iscariot, one of the twelve disciples, made with the chief priests in Jerusalem to hand Jesus over to them. It took place during Holy Week, by inference about AD 30, and followed the Sanhedrin's plot to arrest Jesus. Luke says that Satan entered Judas, who then met with the chief priests and the temple captains to discuss how he might betray Jesus. Mark and Luke say the priests were glad and promised him money. Matthew records Judas asking what they would give him and gives the price as thirty pieces of silver. From then on Judas looked for a suitable opportunity, which Luke describes as a time when the crowds were not present (Luke 22:6).

The Judas' Suicide was the death of Judas Iscariot in Jerusalem after Jesus was condemned, about AD 30 by inference from context, during Holy Week. Seeing that Jesus was condemned, Judas regretted his betrayal and returned the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, saying he had betrayed innocent blood. They replied that this was his concern, not theirs. Judas threw the silver down in the temple, left, and hanged himself. The chief priests judged it unlawful to put the money into the treasury because it was the price of blood, so they used it to buy the potter's field as a burial place for foreigners. It became known as the field of blood. Matthew presents this as fulfilling words spoken through Jeremiah. A different account of Judas' death and the field, called Akeldama, appears in Acts 1:18–19.

Jude was one of the brothers of Jesus, a son of Mary and of Joseph the carpenter. The people of Nazareth name him with James, Joses and Simon when they question where Jesus' teaching came from. Matthew calls him Judas and Mark calls him Juda (Matt 13:55; Mark 6:3). The author of the Letter of Jude calls himself "the servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James" (Jude 1:1). This entry, like the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary, takes him to be this brother of Jesus, with the James he mentions being James the brother of Jesus. Easton's Bible Dictionary instead connects the writer with the apostle Judas, also called Lebbaeus or Thaddaeus. Smith's notes that whether these are the same man is disputed. Through Joseph's family he belonged to the tribe of Judah.

Judea was the southern region of the land of Israel in New Testament times, lying west of the Jordan and south of Samaria, with Jerusalem as its chief city. The name derives from Judah, and Ezra 9:9 speaks of the restored community 'in Judah and in Jerusalem' after the exile. Bethlehem, where Jesus was born, lay in Judea (Matt 2:1; Luke 2:4), which was ruled by Herod and later by his son Archelaus (Luke 1:5; Matt 2:22). Crowds from Judea went out to John the Baptist and followed Jesus (Mark 1:5; Matt 4:25), who travelled between Judea and Galilee (John 4:3). Acts names Judea as a stage in the spread of the apostles' witness (Acts 1:8) and as home to early churches (Acts 9:31; Gal 1:22). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the name was sometimes used for Palestine generally (Acts 28:21).

Judea was the southern region of the land of Israel, centered on Jerusalem, and in the time of Jesus it was the southernmost of the three divisions of Palestine, alongside Samaria and Galilee. In John 3:22, after his conversation with Nicodemus in Jerusalem, Jesus and his disciples went out into the Judean countryside, where he stayed with them for a time and baptized. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that after the Babylonian exile the name could refer to the whole country west of the Jordan. Under Roman rule it covered the former territories of Judah, Benjamin, Dan, Simeon and part of Ephraim, and was governed by a procurator as part of the province of Syria. The location shown here is a representative point at Jerusalem, standing for the surrounding region rather than a single site.

The Judgeship of Abdon was the eight-year period when Abdon son of Hillel, from Pirathon, judged Israel after Elon. The text says little about his rule beyond his family: he had forty sons and thirty "nephews" (the Hebrew word is usually translated "grandsons" in modern versions), who rode on seventy young donkeys. By comparison with the similar note about Jair in Judg 10:4, this was probably a sign of wealth and standing. Abdon died and was buried in Pirathon in Ephraim, in "the mount of the Amalekites." No battles or deliverances are recorded, so he is usually counted among the so-called minor judges. This entry dates the judgeship to about 1129 BC, by inference from context, and places it within the wider period of Philistine dominance that leads into the Samson story.

The Judgeship of Eli was the forty-year period during which Eli led Israel, according to 1 Sam 4:18. Earlier chapters present him as the priest at Shiloh, where the tabernacle stood (1 Sam 1:3, 1:9). This entry places the start of his judgeship at about 1162 BC, an estimate inferred from context. The Greek Septuagint gives twenty years instead of forty, but this entry follows the Hebrew text. His tenure ended in disaster. At ninety-eight and nearly blind, Eli was waiting by the gate when a man who had fled the battle brought news that Israel had been routed by the Philistines. His two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, had been killed and the ark of God captured. When he heard the ark had been taken, Eli fell backward from his seat, broke his neck and died, being old and heavy.

The Judgeship of Elon was the ten-year period during which Elon, a man of the tribe of Zebulun, judged Israel. He followed Ibzan of Bethlehem, and the text records no wars or other deeds for him. It notes only the length of his tenure, his death, and his burial at Aijalon in the territory of Zebulun. This Aijalon in northern Israel is a different place from the better-known Aijalon in the south, in the tribal area of Dan. Elon is one of the so-called minor judges, whose brief entries in Judges give little more than names and years. This entry dates his judgeship to about 1139 BC, an estimate inferred from context. It also places it within the wider period of Philistine dominance over Israel described in the later chapters of Judges.

The Judgeship of Ibzan was the seven-year period during which Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel, following Jephthah. By inference from context, it began about 1146 BC. The account is brief. Ibzan had thirty sons and thirty daughters. He sent his daughters to marry outside his clan and brought in thirty women from outside as wives for his sons, which suggests wide family alliances. No wars or acts of deliverance are recorded for him. When he died he was buried at Bethlehem. Which Bethlehem is meant is uncertain. Some identify it with Bethlehem in Judah, and others with the Bethlehem in Zebulun listed in Josh 19:15, which lay closer to the northern judges of this period. He was followed by Elon the Zebulunite.

The Judgeship of Jair was the 22-year period during which Jair, a man from Gilead east of the Jordan, judged Israel. He followed Tola, and his term is placed here at about 1192 BC, by inference from context. The brief account records nothing about wars or deliverances. It notes that Jair had thirty sons who rode on thirty donkey colts, a sign of wealth and standing. They held thirty towns in Gilead, which were still called Havoth-jair ("the villages of Jair") when the account was written. An earlier Jair, son of Manasseh, is linked to towns of the same name in Num 32:41 and Deut 3:14. Whether the two accounts describe the same settlements is uncertain. Jair died and was buried in Camon, probably a town in Gilead, though its exact site is unknown.

The Judgeship of Samson was the twenty-year period in which Samson judged Israel "in the days of the Philistines" (Judg 15:20). It took place while the Philistines dominated Israel, and Samson led Israel during that rule rather than after it ended. The book of Judges states the length of his judgeship twice, once after his victories over the Philistines and again at his burial, when his brothers and his father's household brought his body up and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of his father Manoah (Judg 16:31). The surrounding chapters, Judges 13–16, tell of his birth to Manoah, his great strength and his conflicts with the Philistines. In this entry the judgeship follows that of Abdon and begins about 1121 BC, a date inferred from context rather than stated in the text.

The Judgeship of Tola was the period when Tola, son of Puah and grandson of Dodo, a man of the tribe of Issachar, led Israel after the death of Abimelech. The text says he arose "to defend Israel," which probably means restoring order after Abimelech's violent rule, though no specific battles or enemies are recorded. Tola lived at Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim rather than in Issachar's own territory, and he judged Israel for twenty-three years. When he died he was buried in Shamir. The exact site of Shamir is not known. This entry places the start of his judgeship at about 1215 BC, an estimate inferred from context. The account is only two verses long, making Tola one of the so-called minor judges, whose careers are summarized briefly without narrative detail. Jair of Gilead followed him as judge.

Judgment, called the Hall of Judgment in modern translations, was a porch or hall in King Solomon's palace complex in Jerusalem. According to 1 Kgs 7:7, Solomon built it to hold his throne, where he sat to hear cases and give judgment, and it was paneled with cedar from one side of the floor to the other. The same structure is also called the porch of the throne. It was one of several connected buildings Solomon put up alongside the temple, and by inference from the surrounding passage it stood near the House of the Forest of Lebanon and his own residence. No remains have been identified. The location shown here is a general placement within the area of Solomon's palace on the hill south of the Temple Mount in Jerusalem. This hall should not be confused with the New Testament "judgment hall" (the Roman praetorium).

Julia was a Christian woman living in Rome. Paul greets her near the end of his letter to the Romans (Rom 16:15). She is named together with Philologus, Nereus and Nereus's sister, Olympas, and "all the saints which are with them." That grouping suggests they belonged to the same household or house church. Because her name is paired with Philologus, Smith's and Easton's Bible Dictionaries take her to be probably his wife. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia allows that she may have been his sister, and notes that the name Julia may point to someone connected with the imperial household. The text itself does not say how she was related to the others. Her name is the feminine form of Julius. Nothing else is recorded about her.

Julius was a Roman centurion of "Augustus' band," usually understood as the Augustan cohort. Paul and some other prisoners were placed in his charge when it was decided they should sail to Italy. By inference from the preceding chapters, the voyage began at Caesarea, where Paul had been held. The next day, at Sidon, Julius treated Paul kindly and let him go ashore to visit friends and be cared for. Later in the same chapter, the centurion (presumably still Julius) at first trusted the ship's master over Paul's warning (Acts 27:11). During the shipwreck he stopped the soldiers from killing the prisoners because he wanted to save Paul (Acts 27:43). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as showing Paul friendly regard in many ways. This entry dates the journey to about AD 56–57, by inference from context. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it around AD 60.

Junia was a Christian at Rome whom Paul greets together with Andronicus in Rom 16:7. Paul calls the two his kinsmen, which may mean blood relatives or simply fellow Jews. He also calls them his fellow prisoners, meaning they had been imprisoned at some point, perhaps with him. He says they became believers in Christ before he did, so they were among the earliest followers. Paul describes them as "of note among the apostles." This is read either as saying they were prominent apostles themselves, the reading the STEPBible names data follows, or that they were well regarded by the apostles. Some translations give the name as the masculine "Junias," but this entry treats Junia as a woman. Because the two are named as a pair, Andronicus is often taken to be her husband or brother, though the verse does not say. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as "belonging to Juno."

Jushab-hesed was a son of Zerubbabel, a member of the tribe of Judah descended from King Jehoiachin's royal line. He appears only once, as the last of a group of five sons listed together, "Hashubah, and Ohel, and Berechiah, and Hasadiah, Jushabhesed, five" (1 Chr 3:20). The verse before names Zerubbabel's other children, Meshullam, Hananiah and their sister Shelomith. Because the five are counted separately, they may have been a distinct group, perhaps born later or to another mother, though the text does not say. His brother Abiud is named only in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders his name "loving-kindness is returned" and suggests it was probably symbolic, like Shear-jashub. That would fit a family living through the return from exile, though this is an inference. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Justus was a man at Corinth described as "one that worshipped God," which probably means a Gentile who attended the synagogue without fully converting, and whose house stood next door to the synagogue (Acts 18:7). When the Jews of Corinth opposed Paul's teaching, Paul left the synagogue and went into Justus's house, apparently using it as his base for preaching during his mission to Corinth, about AD 49 by inference from context. Ancient manuscripts differ on his name. Some read "Justus" alone, while others read "Titius Justus" or "Titus Justus." Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he may be Paul's companion Titus, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a proposal linking him with Tertius (Rom 16:22). This entry treats him simply as the Corinthian host named in Acts 18:7. He is distinct from the other men called Justus in Acts 1:23 and Col 4:11. The name means "just" or "upright."

Juttah was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed with Maon, Carmel and Ziph among the towns given to the tribe of Judah (Josh 15:55). It was later one of the nine cities that Judah and Simeon gave to the Levites, together with its surrounding pasturelands (Josh 21:16). The parallel list of Levitical cities in 1 Chronicles 6 does not name it. Juttah is generally identified with the modern town of Yatta (Yutta), about 5.5 miles (9 km) south of Hebron, and the location shown here follows that identification. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes a tradition that Juttah was the home of Zechariah and Elizabeth and the birthplace of John the Baptist, linking it with the "city of Judah" in the hill country mentioned in Luke 1:39. The name is usually explained as meaning "extended" or "stretched out."

Kabzeel was a city in the far south of Judah's territory, listed first among the tribe's "uttermost cities" toward the border of Edom in the Negeb (Josh 15:21). It was the hometown of Benaiah son of Jehoiada, one of David's mighty men, remembered for killing two champions of Moab and a lion in a pit on a snowy day (2 Sam 23:20; 1 Chr 11:22). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary take it to be the same place as Jekabzeel, which was resettled by people of Judah after the exile (Neh 11:25). The name is usually explained as "gathered by God" or "God gathers." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes the site as unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the Negeb, consistent with the description in Joshua.

Kadesh, also called Kadesh-Barnea, was an oasis in the wilderness of Zin, on the southern edge of Canaan near the border of Edom. In Abraham's time it was also called En-mishpat, and it served as a landmark for his travels and for the well where Hagar met the angel. Kadesh was Israel's main camp in the wilderness. The spies reported back to Moses there, and the people stayed there 'many days.' Miriam died and was buried there. At the 'water of Meribah in Kadesh' the people quarreled over water.
