From Kadesh Moses asked the king of Edom for passage, and when he was refused, Israel moved on to Mount Hor. Easton's and Smith's dictionaries identify the site with Ain Kadeis in northeastern Sinai. Many later scholars prefer the nearby, better-watered spring of Ein el-Qudeirat, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Tahtimhodshi was a region that Joab and the army commanders passed through while carrying out David's census of Israel. It is named after Gilead and before Dan-jaan and the area around Sidon, which places it somewhere in the northeast of the territory being counted (2 Sam 24:6). The name is obscure and has been read in several ways. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains it as "the land of the newly inhabited," a region east of the Jordan and north of Gilead. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes Kitto's suggestion of the upper Jordan valley at the foot of Mount Hermon. Many scholars instead read the text as "the land of the Hittites toward Kadesh," meaning Kadesh on the Orontes River in Syria, and modern translations such as the ESV render it "Kadesh." The location shown here follows the Kadesh-on-the-Orontes identification, probably the modern site of Tell Nebi Mend in western Syria.

Kadesh-barnea was a desert oasis on the southern edge of the promised land, an eleven days' journey from Horeb by way of Mount Seir (Deut 1:2). After leaving Horeb, Israel crossed the wilderness and arrived here (Deut 1:19). From Kadesh-barnea Moses sent spies, including Caleb, to explore Canaan. When the people refused to go up and take the land, a journey of thirty-eight years followed before they crossed the brook Zered (Num 32:8; Deut 9:23; Deut 2:14; Josh 14:6–7). Later it marked a point on the southern border of the land and of Judah's territory, and the southern limit of Joshua's campaigns (Num 34:4; Josh 15:3; Josh 10:41). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with 'Ain el-Kadeis. The location shown here matches nearby 'Ain el-Qudeirat in northeastern Sinai, the larger spring in the same area.

Kadmiel was a Levite whose family returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel. In the lists of returnees his descendants are counted with those of Jeshua and Hodaviah, seventy-four in all (Ezra 2:40; Neh 7:43). When the foundation of the temple was laid, Kadmiel and his sons joined Jeshua in overseeing the workmen on the house of God (Ezra 3:9). The name appears again among the Levites who led the people in confession and praise from the stairs (Neh 9:4–5), among those who sealed the covenant (Neh 10:9), and among the Levites who came up with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:8). Neh 12:24 names a chief Levite, Jeshua the son of Kadmiel. Because the name spans many decades, these later mentions may refer to the family or to a descendant of the same name rather than to one man, as Smith's Bible Dictionary implies. The name is usually explained as "before God."

Kain was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed among the ten cities of a district in the tribe's territory in Josh 15:57, where the King James Version spells it "Cain." The Hebrew word behind it, qayin, is also the name of the Kenite clan. In Balaam's oracle at Num 24:22, the King James Version translates it "the Kenite," while the Revised Version reads "Kain." For this reason Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the town to be a Kenite settlement and connects it with the Kenites' "nest" set in the rock in Balaam's words. The site is usually identified with modern Yaqin (Yukin), on a high hill southeast of Hebron overlooking the wilderness of Judah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats this identification as uncertain. The location shown here follows the Yaqin identification.

Kallai was a priest who headed the priestly family of Sallai in the generation after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears only once, in a list of family heads among the priests (Neh 12:20). By inference from the surrounding passage, this list belongs to the days of Joiakim son of Jeshua the high priest, as Smith's Bible Dictionary and STEPBible's proper-names index also place him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connects him more loosely with the priests who returned with Zerubbabel. The family of Sallai is probably the same as the "Sallu" named among the earlier returning priests earlier in the same chapter. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "swift."

Kamon (spelled Camon in the King James Version) was the town where Jair, one of the judges of Israel, was buried (Judg 10:5). The surrounding verses describe Jair as a Gileadite who led Israel for twenty-two years and whose sons held thirty towns in Gilead, so Kamon is usually taken to have been a town of Gilead, east of the Jordan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the ruins of Kamm or Kumeim in northern Jordan. Easton's Bible Dictionary instead proposes Tell Qaimun (Jokneam) on the southern slopes of Mount Carmel, reasoning that Jair may have lived west of the Jordan while serving as judge. The exact site is uncertain. The location shown here follows the Gilead identification and marks only the general area, not a specific site.

Kanah was a stream, called "the river Kanah" in the King James Version, that marked part of the boundary between the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh. Ephraim's border ran westward from Tappuah to the Kanah and on to the Mediterranean Sea, with Ephraim's land to the south of the stream and Manasseh's to the north (Josh 16:8; 17:9). The Hebrew word usually means a wadi or seasonal torrent bed, and the name means "of reeds." Several other biblical places share the name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with the modern Wadi Qanah, which rises southwest of Shechem and joins the Yarkon (Auja) before reaching the sea north of Jaffa. Easton's Bible Dictionary also mentions a reedy stream entering the sea between Joppa and Caesarea. The location shown here follows the Wadi Qanah identification.

Kanah was a city named in Joshua's description of the territory allotted to the tribe of Asher. It appears in a list of towns running northward toward "great Zidon" (Josh 19:28), so it was probably near the northern edge of Asher's land. The name means "of reeds." It should not be confused with other places of the same name, such as the brook Kanah on the border of Ephraim and Manasseh. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the village of Qana, about 7 miles (11 km) southeast of Tyre in modern Lebanon, where Easton's notes nearby ruins and rock carvings thought to be Phoenician. The location shown here follows a different identification, placing it farther south in Lower Galilee, near the modern village of Kafr Kanna.

Kareah, also spelled Careah in 2 Kgs 25:23, was the father of Johanan and Jonathan, two army captains who joined Gedaliah, the governor Babylon appointed at Mizpah after the fall of Jerusalem. Kareah himself appears only as a name identifying his sons, and nothing is told of his own life. His son Johanan warned Gedaliah that Ishmael son of Nethaniah planned to kill him, but Gedaliah would not believe it. After the murder, Johanan led the captains against Ishmael and recovered the captives he had taken from Mizpah. Johanan later rejected Jeremiah's warning not to go to Egypt and led the remnant of Judah there. According to Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries, the name means "bald."

Karka (spelled Karkaa in the King James Version) was a place on the southern border of the territory given to the tribe of Judah. Josh 15:3 traces that border from Maaleh-acrabbim past Zin and Kadesh-barnea, then on to Hezron and Adar, after which it turns toward Karka. Azmon and the Brook of Egypt follow in the next verse. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it between Adar and Azmon, roughly midway between the Mediterranean and the Dead Sea, and explains the name as meaning "floor" or "bottom." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning as "the pavement" or "ground" and notes that Eusebius mentioned a village in Judah toward the wilderness called Akarka. The same work states that the site cannot now be identified. The location shown here is only a rough estimate in the region west of Kadesh-barnea.

Karkor was the place east of the Jordan where the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna camped with about fifteen thousand men. These were all that remained of the eastern armies after a hundred and twenty thousand had fallen (Judg 8:10). The verses that follow (Judg 8:11–12) describe Gideon going up by the route of the tent-dwellers east of Nobah and Jogbehah, surprising this camp, routing the army and capturing both kings. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "foundation" and places Karkor in the open desert not far beyond Succoth and Penuel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the site as unidentified and suggests it may correspond to a Qarqar mentioned in Assyrian records. The exact site is unknown. The location shown here is a rough placement east of the Jordan, in the region of Succoth and Penuel.

Karnaim is a place named in Gen 14:5 as part of the compound name Ashteroth Karnaim, where Chedorlaomer and his allied kings defeated the Rephaim during their campaign east of the Jordan. The name means "horns," according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Some scholars treat Ashteroth Karnaim as one town. Others see two neighboring sites, Ashtaroth and Karnaim, possibly joined in the name. Some modern translations also read Amos 6:13, which in Hebrew has the word "horns," as a reference to a town called Karnaim. By inference from the surrounding names, it lay in Bashan, in what is now southern Syria. The site is often identified with Sheikh Sa'd, near Tell Ashtarah, and the location shown here falls in that area.

Kartah was a city in the territory of the tribe of Zebulun. It was given, together with its surrounding pasturelands, to the Merarite families of the Levites, and is listed next to Jokneam (Josh 21:34). This is its only mention in the Bible. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary take the name to mean "city," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "calling" or "meeting." The site has not been firmly identified. Easton's Bible Dictionary treats it as the same place as Kattath in Zebulun's boundary list (Josh 19:15), and perhaps also as Kitron (Judg 1:30). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says it may be a variant of Kattath or of Kartan. The location shown here is an approximate point in lower Galilee, within Zebulun's territory.

Kartan was a city in the territory of the tribe of Naphtali, given with its surrounding pasturelands to the Levites. Joshua 21:32 lists it as one of three Naphtalite cities, alongside Kedesh in Galilee, the city of refuge, and Hammothdor. From the surrounding passage, these cities were among those allotted to the Gershonite branch of the Levites. The parallel list in 1 Chr 6:76 appears to give the name as Kiriathaim, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Kartan may be a shortened form of that name. The site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it probably near the northwestern shore of the Sea of Galilee, at the ruined village of el-Katanah. The location shown here is only a rough placement farther west, in the hill country of western Galilee.

Kattath was a city named among the towns in the territory of the tribe of Zebulun, listed with Nahallal, Shimron, Idalah and Bethlehem in Josh 19:15. Nothing else is recorded about it. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the same place as Kitron, where Zebulun did not drive out the Canaanites (Judg 1:30), and Kartah, a town given to the Merarite Levites (Josh 21:34). Its site is uncertain. The Babylonian Talmud identifies it with Sepphoris (modern Tzippori), and the Jerusalem Talmud with Kuteineh, west of the Jezreel Valley. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia looks for it near Shimron, and Easton's Bible Dictionary links it with Kana el-Jelil. The location shown here follows the Sepphoris identification.

Kedar was the second son of Ishmael, listed after the firstborn Nebaioth in the genealogies of Gen 25:13 and 1 Chr 1:29. His name became the name of an Arab tribe descended from him, and most later mentions refer to that people, not to the man himself. The prophets describe Kedar as a people of the eastern desert who kept flocks and traded lambs, rams and goats with Tyre (Ezek 27:21; Isa 60:7). They were known for their archers (Isa 21:17), lived in villages (Isa 42:11), and their dark tents became a figure of speech (Song 1:5). Isaiah and Jeremiah announced a coming judgement on them, with Jeremiah naming Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon (Jer 49:28). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place the tribe in northwest Arabia near the borders of Palestine. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "blackness."

Kedar was the land and people of a nomadic Arab tribe in the deserts east of Israel, named after Ishmael's second son (Gen 25:13). Easton's Bible Dictionary places them in northwestern Arabia, and the rough location shown here lies in that region. The biblical writers knew Kedar for its tents, used as an image in Song 1:5 and as a picture of living far from home in Ps 120:5. They also knew it for its flocks and rams, which its princes traded with Tyre (Ezek 27:21; Isa 60:7), and for its archers (Isa 21:17). Isaiah also mentions villages where Kedar lived in the wilderness (Isa 42:11). Jeremiah treats Kedar as a distant eastern land (Jer 2:10) and foretells that Nebuchadrezzar of Babylon would attack it (Jer 49:28). Isaiah announces that its glory would fail within a year (Isa 21:16). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "blackness."

Kedemah was the last-named of the twelve sons of Ishmael, the son of Abraham and Hagar. He appears only in the two genealogies of Ishmael's descendants (Gen 25:15; 1 Chr 1:31), alongside brothers such as Nebajoth, Kedar, Dumah, Tema and Jetur. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to be the youngest. Nothing else is recorded about his life. The surrounding passage in Genesis presents Ishmael's twelve sons as princes of tribes living in the regions east of Egypt toward Assyria, so Kedemah was probably regarded as the founder of a tribal group of the northern Arabian desert. His name is usually understood to mean "eastward" or "toward the east" (Easton's Bible Dictionary). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links it with the Hebrew word for "the East." A sister, Bashemath, who later married Esau, is also counted among Ishmael's children.

Kedemoth was a town east of the Dead Sea, in the land north of the Arnon that Israel took from Sihon, king of the Amorites. Before the conquest, Moses sent messengers "out of the wilderness of Kedemoth" to Sihon at Heshbon with an offer of peace (Deut 2:26). Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the town gave its name to this stretch of open pasture land. Kedemoth was later listed among the towns given to the tribe of Reuben, next to Jahaz and Mephaath (Josh 13:18). It became one of the cities assigned with their pasture lands to the Levites of the family of Merari (Josh 21:37; 1 Chr 6:79). The name probably means "eastern parts" or "beginnings." Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a suggestion that it was the ruins of Umm er-Rasas. The location shown here lies north-east of Dibon, which fits Easton's Bible Dictionary.

Kedesh, also called Kedesh in Galilee, was a city in the hill country of Naphtali in northern Israel. It was originally a Canaanite royal city whose king Joshua defeated (Josh 12:22). It was allotted to Naphtali and later set apart as a city of refuge for someone who had killed another person. It was also given, with its surrounding lands, to the Levites (Josh 20:7; 21:32; 1 Chr 6:76). Barak gathered the men of Zebulun and Naphtali at Kedesh before the battle with Sisera, and Heber the Kenite camped nearby (Judg 4:9–11). Tiglath-pileser of Assyria captured it in Pekah's reign and deported its people (2 Kgs 15:29). It is usually identified with Tel Kedesh (Kedes), northwest of the Huleh Valley, and the location shown here follows that view. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that some place Barak's Kedesh near the Sea of Galilee instead. Several other places share the name.

Kedesh was a town in the far south of Judah, listed in Josh 15:23 among the cities of Judah's southern district. By the context of the surrounding list, it lay toward the border of Edom in the Negev. Several places in the Bible share this name, and this Kedesh is distinct from the better-known northern towns called Kedesh. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it to be the same as Kadesh or Kadesh-barnea. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes this possibility, pointing out that Kadesh-barnea would otherwise be surprisingly missing from the list. It also mentions another proposal, a site called Kadus south of Hebron. The location shown here follows the Kadesh-barnea identification and places it in the northeastern Sinai, near the springs of the Ein el-Qudeirat area.

Kedesh was a city in the territory of the tribe of Issachar. It was one of the towns, with its surrounding pasturelands, given to the Levites (1 Chr 6:72). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it went to the Gershonite Levites and that the parallel list in Joshua 21:28 names Kishion in its place, so the two names may refer to the same town. Several places in the Bible are called Kedesh. This one should not be confused with Kedesh in Naphtali, the city of refuge in Galilee. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both mention Tell Abu Qades (Abu Kadeis), near Megiddo and Lejjun in the Jezreel Valley, as a possible identification, following the surveyor Conder. The location shown here follows that identification.

Kedesh-naphtali was the hometown of Barak son of Abinoam. Deborah summoned him from there and told him to gather ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun at Mount Tabor to fight the Canaanite forces (Judg 4:6). The name means "Kedesh of Naphtali" and sets it apart from other towns called Kedesh. It was probably the same Kedesh in Naphtali that later passages name as a city of refuge (Josh 20:7) and a Levitical town (Josh 21:32), and that Tiglath-pileser of Assyria captured (2 Kgs 15:29). Its exact site is debated. Many place it at Tel Kedesh in Upper Galilee, northwest of the Huleh Valley. Others suggest a site near the southwest shore of the Sea of Galilee, closer to Tabor, because of the Kedesh mentioned in Judg 4:11. The location shown here follows the Upper Galilee identification.

Kehelathah was one of the places where the Israelites camped during their years in the wilderness after leaving Mount Sinai. It appears only in the list of camps in Numbers 33, where the people moved there from Rissah and then went on to Mount Shapher (Num 33:22–23). The name means "assembly" or "gathering," according to Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Nothing else is recorded about the place, and its site is unknown, as both Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note. The location shown here is only a rough estimate based on its place in the route. It puts the camp in the highlands of present-day southern Jordan, east of the Arabah valley.

Keilah was a walled town in the lowlands of Judah, listed among the cities of Judah's territory with Achzib and Mareshah (Josh 15:44). When Philistines raided its threshing floors, David, after twice asking the LORD, went down with his men, defeated them and rescued the town (1 Sam 23:1–5). The priest Abiathar joined him there with an ephod. Saul saw a chance to trap David inside a town with gates and bars. David asked the LORD and was told that the men of Keilah would hand him over, so he and about six hundred men left, and Saul called off his march (1 Sam 23:6–13). After the exile, two rulers of half the district of Keilah, Hashabiah and Bavai, helped repair Jerusalem's wall (Neh 3:17–18). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with Khirbet Qila, southwest of Bethlehem. Easton's also mentions an alternative site, Khuweilfeh. The location shown here follows Khirbet Qila.

Kelaiah, also called Kelita, was a Levite listed in Ezra 10:23 among the men who had married foreign wives in the period after the return from exile. The surrounding chapter describes Ezra's reform, in which these men agreed to send away their foreign wives, so Kelaiah is understood by inference from context to have been one of those who did so. The verse itself notes that Kelaiah and Kelita are the same man. A Levite named Kelita also appears in Nehemiah, helping explain the law when Ezra read it to the people and later sealing the covenant. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that this may be the same person but says the identification is not certain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "swift messenger of Jehovah."

Kelita was a Levite in Jerusalem in the time of Ezra and Nehemiah. When Ezra read the law to the assembled people, Kelita was one of the Levites who helped them understand what was read while they stood in their places (Neh 8:7). His name appears again among the Levites who set their seal to the covenant made under Nehemiah (Neh 10:10). The surrounding context shows that this list belongs to the Levites. Ezra 10:23 mentions "Kelaiah (the same is Kelita)" among the Levites who had married foreign wives. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats him as the same man and says he returned with Ezra. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "dwarf" and Smith's gives "assembly."

Kemuel was the third son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and his wife Milcah. He is named in the list of Nahor's children that reached Abraham after the near-sacrifice of Isaac (Gen 22:21), where he is called "the father of Aram." His full brothers were Huz, Buz, Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph and Bethuel, the father of Rebekah. Nahor's concubine Reumah bore his half-siblings Tebah, Gaham, Thahash and Maachah. This Aram is probably not the Aram son of Shem in the Table of Nations. Nothing else is recorded about Kemuel's life. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "God hath raised up, or established him." The name is shared by other men in the Old Testament, such as a leader of the tribe of Ephraim and a Levite, who are different people.

Kemuel, son of Shiphtan, was the leader ("prince") of the tribe of Ephraim named in Num 34:24. He is listed among the tribal representatives whom the LORD designated, through Moses, to divide the land of Canaan among the Israelites. From the surrounding passage, these leaders were to work alongside Eleazar the priest and Joshua in assigning the inheritance west of the Jordan. This is his only mention in the Bible. The name is shared by other people, including a son of Nahor and a Levite father of Hashabiah, and should not be confused with them. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "congregation of God," the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "God's mound," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "God hath raised up."

Kemuel was a Levite whose son Hashabiah served as the ruler over the tribe of Levi in the list of tribal leaders from King David's reign (1 Chr 27:17). In that list the Aaronites, the priestly branch of the tribe, are counted separately under Zadok. Nothing else is recorded about Kemuel himself, and he is known only as Hashabiah's father. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Hashabiah as a prince of the tribe in David's time. The Hashabiah named here may be the same as the Hashabiah of the Hebronite clan mentioned in the preceding chapter, but this is uncertain. The name Kemuel is shared by other men in the Bible, including a son of Nahor and a prince of the tribe of Ephraim, and they should not be confused with this Levite. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "God hath raised up, or established him."

Kenath was a city east of the Jordan, in the region of Bashan. Num 32:42 says that Nobah captured Kenath and its surrounding villages and renamed the city Nobah after himself. The surrounding chapter places this among the conquests of Manasseh's descendants east of the Jordan. 1 Chr 2:23 lists Kenath and its towns among sixty cities belonging to the sons of Machir, the father of Gilead. In the King James wording an unnamed "he" takes Geshur and Aram. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reads the verse as Geshur and Aram retaking Kenath from the Israelites. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "possession." Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify Kenath with Qanawat (Kanawat), on the slopes of Jebel al-Druze in southern Syria, a site with extensive Roman remains. Some scholars question this identification, but the location shown here follows it.

Kenaz was a son of Eliphaz and a grandson of Esau, listed in the genealogies of Edom (Gen 36:11; 1 Chr 1:36). His brothers were Teman, Omar, Zepho (or Zephi) and Gatam. Amalek was also a son of Eliphaz, by the concubine Timna according to Gen 36:12, and Korah appears alongside them among the chiefs descended from Eliphaz. Kenaz is named as one of the 'dukes', or clan chiefs, among the descendants of Esau (Gen 36:15). STEPBible's proper-names index treats Kenaz as one of the clans of Edom. A chief named Kenaz also appears in the later list of Edomite chiefs in Gen 36:42, which may refer to the same clan. The name is shared by other people, including the father or ancestor of Othniel in Israel, who should be kept distinct. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as 'this purchase' or 'this lamentation.'

Kenaz was one of the chiefs ("dukes" in the King James Version) of Edom, the people descended from Esau. He is named in the closing list of Edomite chiefs in Gen 36:42, repeated in 1 Chr 1:53. The surrounding passage presents these chiefs by their families and places, so the name may stand for a clan or district as well as a person. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him with Kenaz the son of Eliphaz, Esau's son, who appears earlier in the same chapter among the chiefs descended from Eliphaz. This entry follows that identification, though it is not certain that the two lists name the same man. The name is shared by several people in the Bible, including the father of Othniel and a grandson of Caleb. Smith's gives its meaning as "hunting," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "this purchase" or "this lamentation."

Kenaz was the father of Othniel, the first judge of Israel, and of Seraiah (1 Chr 4:13). He is known only through his sons. Othniel captured a Canaanite city for Caleb and received Caleb's daughter Achsah as his wife. He later delivered Israel from Cushan-rishathaim, after which the land had rest forty years. The phrase "Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother" can be read two ways. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Kenaz to be Caleb's younger brother and so a son of Jephunneh, and this entry follows that reading. Others take the brother to be Othniel himself. Easton's also notes that the family remained prominent down to David's time (1 Chr 27:15). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "this purchase" or "this lamentation." Several other men in the Bible are also named Kenaz.

Kenaz was a descendant of Caleb the son of Jephunneh, named in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah. According to 1 Chr 4:15 he was a son of Elah, which makes him Caleb's grandson, as Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both describe him. The Hebrew of the verse is a little unusual, and Smith's notes an alternative reading in the margin, so the exact wording of the relationship is not entirely certain. Nothing further is recorded about him. The name Kenaz is shared by several people in the Bible, including an Edomite chief descended from Esau and the father or ancestor of Othniel, Caleb's younger kinsman. This Kenaz should be kept distinct from them, though the name's recurrence in Caleb's family is notable, since Caleb himself is elsewhere called a Kenizzite.

Keren-happuch was the third and youngest daughter of Job, named in Job 42:14 alongside her sisters Jemima and Kezia. Her birth came in the closing part of the book, after Job's suffering ended and his fortunes were restored, as the surrounding verses describe. The next verse says no women in the land were as beautiful as Job's daughters and that he gave them an inheritance among their brothers. Her name means "horn of antimony" or "horn of eye-paint," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Easton's Bible Dictionary. It refers to a small horn used to hold the black cosmetic that women applied to the edges of their eyelids. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as "the horn or child of beauty." Nothing else is recorded about her.

Kerioth was a city of Moab, east of the Dead Sea. Jeremiah names it with Bozrah among the Moabite cities facing judgment (Jer 48:24), and Amos announces that fire will devour "the palaces of Kerioth" (Amos 2:2), which suggests it was a prominent town. The name means "the cities," according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Moabite king Mesha's inscription mentions a sanctuary of the god Chemosh at Kerioth. Its location is uncertain. It may be the modern Khirbet el-Qureiyat, between Dhiban and Ataroth. Others take it as another name for Ar of Moab, or identify it with Kir of Moab (modern Kerak). The location shown here follows the Qureiyat identification. Some readers link it to Judas Iscariot, but his Kerioth is usually placed in Judah rather than Moab.

Kerioth-hezron was a town in the far south (the Negev) of the tribe of Judah, listed among Judah's southern cities in Josh 15:25. The verse gives it a second name, Hazor. The King James Version reads the phrase as two places, "Kerioth, and Hezron, which is Hazor," while other readings, followed in this entry, treat it as one compound name, "Kerioth-hezron, which is Hazor." Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both suggest that Judas Iscariot may have come from this town, with "Iscariot" taken to mean "man of Kerioth." Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's places it at the ruins of el-Kureitein, about 10 miles south of Hebron. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, following the explorer Robinson, places it at Kuryatain, about 4.5 miles north of Tel Arad. The location shown here is only approximate and sits in the Negev of southern Judah.

Keros was the ancestor of a family of temple servants, the Nethinim, whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Judah with Zerubbabel. The family appears in the list of returning exiles in Ezra 2:44 and in its parallel in Neh 7:47, placed between the families of Ziha and Siaha (spelled Sia in Nehemiah) and Padon. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both class him among the Nethinim, a group assigned to serve at the temple. The context of the lists supports this, since the surrounding names belong to that section. Nothing is recorded about Keros himself beyond his name and his descendants. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "curved", Hitchcock's Bible Names "crooked", and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia tentatively suggests "fortress."

Keturah was a wife of Abraham, whom he took after the events of Genesis 24. By inference from the order of the narrative, this was probably after Sarah's death, as Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both state. Genesis calls her a wife (Gen 25:1), while 1 Chronicles calls her Abraham's concubine (1 Chr 1:32). She bore him six sons: Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak and Shuah. Her descendants included Jokshan's sons Sheba and Dedan and Midian's sons Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida and Eldaah, all counted as "the children of Keturah." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes her sons to represent Arab tribes south and east of Canaan. Her name is usually understood to mean "incense." Nothing is recorded of her origin or nationality.

Kezia was the second of the three daughters born to Job after his trials ended and his fortunes were restored. Her sisters were Jemima, the eldest, and Keren-happuch, the youngest (Job 42:14). The surrounding verses make her a daughter: Job 42:13 says Job had seven sons and three daughters, and Job 42:15 says no women in the land were as beautiful as Job's daughters, and that their father gave them an inheritance alongside their brothers. Smith's Bible Dictionary also calls her the second daughter. Her name is usually taken to mean "cassia," a fragrant spice related to cinnamon, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives that meaning. Nothing else is recorded about her.

Kibroth-hattaavah, meaning "graves of craving" or "graves of lust," was an Israelite camp in the wilderness and their first stop after leaving the desert of Sinai (Num 33:16). It was named for the people buried there "that lusted" (Num 11:34). The surrounding chapter tells how the Israelites grew tired of manna and demanded meat, then received a great flight of quails and were struck by a plague. From there they moved on to Hazeroth (Num 11:35; 33:17). Moses later listed it with Taberah and Massah as places where Israel provoked the LORD (Deut 9:22). Its exact site is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it probably in the Wady Murrah, about 30 miles northeast of Sinai, and Smith's Bible Dictionary puts it near the Gulf of Aqaba. The location shown here, in the eastern Sinai Peninsula, follows this general identification and is approximate.

Kibzaim was a city in the territory of Ephraim. Along with its surrounding pasture lands, it was given to the Levites. By inference from the surrounding passage, it went to the Kohathite family, together with Shechem, Gezer and Beth-horon, making the "four cities" of Josh 21:22. In the parallel list of Levitical cities, 1 Chr 6:68 gives the name Jokmeam in its place. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries therefore treat the two names as referring to the same town. Easton's and Smith's explain the name as "two heaps", while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "congregation". Kibzaim is not mentioned anywhere else, and its site is uncertain. The location shown here follows an identification with a place called Kabus.

Kidron was a seasonal torrent valley just outside Jerusalem, on its eastern side between the city and the Mount of Olives, according to Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries. David crossed it weeping as he fled from Absalom toward the wilderness (2 Sam 15:23), and Solomon made crossing it the limit of Shimei's confinement (1 Kgs 2:37). Reforming kings used it as a place to destroy and dump objects of idol worship. Asa burned his mother Maachah's idol there, Hezekiah's Levites carried the temple's uncleanness to it, and Josiah burned cult objects and scattered their dust and ashes there, near graves (1 Kgs 15:13; 2 Chr 29:16; 2 Kgs 23:4–12). Jeremiah foresaw its fields made holy. The location shown here lies near Ekron rather than Jerusalem. It matches a different Kidron from 1 Maccabees, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia possibly identifies with the village of Katrah.

Kinah was a town in the far south of Judah, named in Josh 15:22 among the cities of the tribe's southernmost district, toward the border of Edom. It appears only in this list, alongside Dimonah and Adadah, and nothing else is recorded about it. The name resembles the Hebrew word for a lament or dirge. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may instead come from the Kenites, who had settlements in the south. The site has not been firmly identified. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it probably near the Dead Sea in the Wady Fikreh. The location shown here is only approximate and follows a placement in the Negev, west of Arad, consistent with the town's listing among Judah's southern cities.

Kir is the name of a place, meaning "wall" or "enclosure," used in the Bible for what appear to be two different sites. Most mentions refer to a distant land where the Assyrian king took the people of Damascus captive after capturing the city and killing Rezin (2 Kgs 16:9), as Amos had foretold (Amos 1:5). Amos 9:7 also names it as the land the Syrians originally came from. Isaiah lists it with Elam as supplying soldiers (Isa 22:6). Its location is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions a link with Susiana near Elam, and Smith's Bible Dictionary notes proposals in Media or Armenia. Isaiah 15:1 separately speaks of "Kir of Moab," a Moabite stronghold, probably the same as Kir-hareseth. The location shown here follows that Moabite identification, probably the modern town of al-Karak in Jordan.

Kir-hareseth was a fortified city of Moab. In 2 Kgs 3:25 it is the one stronghold left standing when the armies of Israel, Judah and Edom overran Moab, wrecking its cities, fields, wells and trees. Even so, slingers surrounded and attacked it. According to Easton's Bible Dictionary, Mesha king of Moab took refuge there, and from its wall he offered his eldest son as a burnt offering, after which the invaders withdrew (2 Kgs 3:26–27). Isaiah's oracle against Moab later mourns the city's ruined foundations (Isa 16:7). Easton's Bible Dictionary treats the forms Kir-haresh and Kir-heres (Isa 16:11; Jer 48:31, 36) as names for the same place, and identifies it with modern Kerak in Jordan, a town on a steep hill east of the Dead Sea. The location shown here follows the Kerak identification.

Kiriath-arba was the earlier name of Hebron, a town in the hill country of Judah. The name means "city of Arba," and Josh 14:15 explains that Arba was a great man among the Anakim. Sarah died there, and Abraham mourned her (Gen 23:2). Jacob later came there to his father Isaac at Mamre, where Abraham and Isaac had lived (Gen 35:27). Under Joshua it was listed among the towns of Judah and was named one of the cities of refuge (Josh 15:54; 20:7). Judges 1:10 records that Judah attacked the Canaanites living there and killed Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai. After the exile, some people of Judah settled again in Kiriath-arba and its villages (Neh 11:25), so the old name was still in use then. The location shown here is the city of Hebron, known today as al-Khalil in the southern West Bank.

Kiriath-arim was a town whose people are listed among the exiles who returned from Babylon, counted together with those of Chephirah and Beeroth as 743 people (Ezra 2:25). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as a shortened form of Kiriath-jearim, and the parallel list in Neh 7:29 gives that fuller name. Kiriath-jearim was one of the Gibeonite cities and stood on the border of Judah and Benjamin. It is known as the place where the ark of the covenant stayed for twenty years. Its exact site is uncertain. One common view places it at Kiriath el-Enab (Abu Ghosh), about 9 miles (14 km) west of Jerusalem. Another, proposed by C. R. Conder, places it at Khirbet Erma, because the name Erma corresponds to Arim. The location shown here appears to follow the Khirbet Erma identification.

Kiriath-baal, meaning "town of Baal," is an alternative name for Kiriath-jearim, a town of Judah. Both verses that use the name explain it this way. Josh 15:60 lists it with Rabbah among the towns of Judah's hill country. Josh 18:14 places it at the end of a stretch of Benjamin's boundary, where the border with Judah ran west of Jerusalem, and calls it "a city of the children of Judah." Elsewhere the same town is called Baalah (Josh 15:9) and Baale of Judah (2 Sam 6:2). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it under Kiriath-jearim. The Baal name probably reflects an older Canaanite association that was later replaced. The town is usually identified with a site near modern Abu Ghosh, about 13 km (8 miles) west of Jerusalem. The location shown here is only approximate.

Kiriath-huzoth was a town in Moab where King Balak took the prophet Balaam after meeting him, when Balak had summoned Balaam to curse Israel (Num 22:39). The name probably means "city of streets." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint reads "city of villages" and that the two first met at "the city of Moab" (Num 22:36), which it takes to be Kir of Moab. It concludes that Kiriath-huzoth was probably not far from there. According to the next verse, Balak sacrificed there and the following day took Balaam up to the high places of Baal (Num 22:40–41). Its exact site is unknown. Some identify it with Kiriathaim and others with Kerioth. The location shown here is only approximate and places it in the Moabite highlands east of the northern Dead Sea, northwest of modern Madaba.

Kiriath-jearim was a city in the hill country west of Jerusalem. It was one of the four Gibeonite cities that Israel reached in Josh 9:17. It was also called Baalah and Kiriath-baal, and it stood on the boundary between Judah and Benjamin, where it is assigned to Judah. The "Kirjath" listed among Benjamin's towns in Josh 18:28 may be the same place. The Danites camped behind it at a spot they named Mahaneh-dan. After the Philistines returned the ark, the men of the city brought it to the house of Abinadab, where it stayed twenty years until David took it up to Jerusalem. Men of Kiriath-jearim were among those who returned from exile, and the prophet Urijah son of Shemaiah came from there. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Kuriet el-'Enab, about 7.5 miles west-northwest of Jerusalem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia considers its exact position unsettled. The location shown here is approximate.

Kiriath-sannah was another name for Debir, a town in the hill country of Judah allotted to the tribe of Judah. It appears only once, in the list of Judah's towns, where it is named next to Dannah and identified with Debir (Josh 15:49). Elsewhere Debir is also called Kiriath-sepher (Josh 15:15; Judg 1:11), and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats all three names as one place. That work notes that the Septuagint reads this name as "city of books." One explanation is that "sannah" arose as a copying slip for "sepher" ("book"). Another, from the scholar A. H. Sayce, holds that it is an old Canaanite name meaning "city of instruction." Debir's modern site is debated. Some place it at Tell Beit Mirsim and others at Khirbet Rabud, southwest of Hebron. The location shown here matches the Khirbet Rabud identification.

Kiriath-sepher was the earlier name of Debir, a Canaanite town in the hill country of Judah. Both Josh 15:15 and Judg 1:11 say plainly that Debir was formerly called Kiriath-sepher. Caleb, advancing against the town's inhabitants, promised his daughter Achsah in marriage to whoever attacked and captured it. The verses that follow in both accounts name Othniel as the man who took it. The name is often rendered "town of books," and the Greek translation took it that way, though the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes other proposed meanings such as "border-town" or "toll-town." The site is uncertain. The same encyclopedia records a frequent identification with edh-Dhaheriyeh, southwest of Hebron, and a suggestion by Sayce that it lay west of Gath. The location shown here follows the edh-Dhaheriyeh identification.

Kiriathaim (King James Version also "Kirjathaim") was a city east of the Jordan in the uplands of Moab. The Reubenites rebuilt it along with Heshbon and Elealeh, and it was listed in Reuben's territory beside Sibmah. Later it was a Moabite town again: Jeremiah lists it among the Moabite cities facing judgment, and Ezekiel names it with Beth-jeshimoth and Baal-meon as "the glory of the country." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Moabite king Mesha claimed to have fortified it, and connects it with Shaveh-kiriathaim in Gen 14:5. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with el-Kureiyat, about 11 miles southwest of Medeba near ancient Ataroth, and the location shown here follows that identification. The ISBE suggests a site north of the Wadi Zerqa Ma'in instead. The name was also used for other places, including a town in Naphtali.

Kiriathaim was a town in the tribal territory of Naphtali, in Galilee, given with its surrounding pasture lands to the Levites. It is named in 1 Chr 6:76 alongside Kedesh in Galilee and Hammon, among the Naphtali towns allotted to the Levite family of Gershon. The name means "two cities." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia equates it with Kartan, which appears in the matching list of Levitical towns in Joshua 21:32. It should not be confused with the better-known Kiriathaim east of the Jordan, in the land of Reuben and later Moab, which shares the same name. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only an approximate placement in Upper Galilee.

Kish, called Cis in Acts 13:21, was a Benjamite of the family of Matri, described as "a mighty man of power," and the father of Saul, Israel's first king. 1 Sam 9:1 traces his ancestry through Abiel back to Aphiah. The only story told about him is that he sent Saul and a servant to look for his lost donkeys, a search that led Saul to Samuel. Saul's and Jonathan's bones were later buried in Kish's tomb at Zelah in Benjamin. His link to Ner is unclear. 1 Sam 14:51 suggests Kish and Ner were both sons of Abiel, while 1 Chr 8:33 and 9:39 say Ner fathered Kish. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the Kish listed among the sons of Jehiel and Maachah (1 Chr 9:36) as a different man, an uncle of Saul's father. This entry follows the view that he is Saul's father and a brother of Ner and Abdon. Several other biblical men share the name.

Kish was a Levite of the clan of Merari, a son of Mahli and brother of Eleazar, named in the lists of Levite families drawn up in David's time (1 Chr 23:21). His brother Eleazar died without sons, leaving only daughters, and Kish's sons married them (1 Chr 23:22). This probably kept Eleazar's family line and inheritance within the clan, much like the rule for heiresses in Num 36. A later list names Kish's son Jerahmeel, apparently as the head of a Levite family descended from him (1 Chr 24:29). The genealogy in 1 Chr 6:29 names a Libni in Mahli's line, which is why Libni is also counted here as a brother. Several men in the Bible are called Kish, and this Levite is a different person from Kish the Benjamite, father of King Saul. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "a bow."

Kish son of Abdi was a Levite of the clan of Merari in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He is named in 2 Chr 29:12 among the Levites who answered Hezekiah's call. Each of the three Levitical clans, Kohath, Merari and Gershon, is represented in that list by two men, and Kish appears with Azariah son of Jehalelel for the Merarites. The surrounding chapter shows these Levites consecrating themselves and cleansing the temple, so he probably took part in that work. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is not the Benjamite Kish who was the father of King Saul, and the name is shared by several other people in the Bible. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of the name as "bow" or "power."

Kish was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in Esth 2:5 as the father of Shimei and the great-grandfather of Mordecai, the Jew living in Shushan who raised Queen Esther. He appears only in this genealogy, which runs Mordecai, son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists five. Readers differ on how to take the line. Most reference works, including Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary, treat Kish as Mordecai's actual great-grandfather, and this entry follows that reading. Others suggest the names may point to well-known earlier Benjamites, such as Kish the father of King Saul, rather than to immediate ancestors. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "a bow."

Kishi was a Levite of the clan of Merari, the son of Abdi and the father of Ethan, one of the chief singers whom David's Levites appointed to lead music at the house of the Lord. He appears only in genealogies of Ethan. In 1 Chr 6:44 his line is traced back through Abdi and Malluch to Merari, and Ethan stands on the left hand of the singers. In 1 Chr 15:17 the same man is called Kushaiah, a name the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders "bow of Yah." Ethan is widely identified with Jeduthun, another leading musician of David's time, and this entry follows that identification. Nothing more is recorded about Kishi himself.

Kishion was a town in the territory of the tribe of Issachar, listed among the cities of Issachar's allotment (Josh 19:20). It was later given, with its surrounding pasturelands, to the Gershonite Levites (Josh 21:28). The King James Version spells the name "Kishon" in that second passage, though it is the same town and not the Kishon River. The parallel list of Levitical cities in 1 Chr 6:72 has "Kedesh" in its place. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the original form may have been something like Kidshon and notes Conder's proposal to identify the site with Tell Abu Kedes, near Taanach on the southern edge of the Jezreel Valley. The location shown here follows that identification. The name is usually explained as meaning "hardness" (Hitchcock's Bible Names).

Kishon (also spelled Kison) was a river in northern Israel. It was the scene of Deborah and Barak's victory over Sisera, the commander of Jabin's army, who gathered his nine hundred iron chariots there (Judg 4:7, 13). Deborah's song says the river "swept them away," calling it "that ancient river" (Judg 5:21), and Ps 83:9 recalls that defeat. Later Elijah brought the prophets of Baal down to the brook Kishon and killed them there (1 Kgs 18:40), probably close below the spot on Carmel where his sacrifice took place, as Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the modern Nahr el-Muqatta (the Kishon River). It is a seasonal stream that drains the plain of Esdraelon (Jezreel) and enters the Mediterranean near Haifa. When rains flood its deep bed and turn the plain to mud, it would have trapped heavy chariots.

Kitron was a Canaanite city in the territory allotted to the tribe of Zebulun. Judg 1:30 records that Zebulun did not drive out its inhabitants, or those of nearby Nahalol. The Canaanites stayed and lived among the Israelites, but were made to pay tribute. Kitron is not mentioned anywhere else under this name. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggest it may be the same place as Kattath, listed among Zebulun's towns in Josh 19:15. Its location is uncertain. Easton's connects it with Cana of Galilee. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note that the Talmud identifies it with Sepphoris, near the modern village of Saffuriyeh (Zippori) in Lower Galilee. The location shown here follows the Sepphoris identification.

Kittim was a son of Javan and grandson of Japheth, listed with his brothers Elishah, Tarshish and Dodanim in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:4; 1 Chr 1:7). No personal details are given. As with the other names in this list, Kittim stands both for an individual ancestor and for the people descended from him. Elsewhere the Bible uses the name for a coastal or island people of the Mediterranean, such as the "isles of Chittim" in Jer 2:10 and Ezek 27:6. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Josephus linked the name to Kition, an ancient city on Cyprus. On that basis the name is often associated with Cyprus in a narrower sense, and more broadly with the islands and coastlands of the western Mediterranean. Smith's Bible Dictionary points out that the King James Version spells the name Kittim in these two verses and Chittim elsewhere.

Kittim (spelled Chittim in the King James Version) is a coastal land across the sea from Israel, mentioned for its ships. In Balaam's oracle, ships from the coast of Kittim come to afflict Asshur and Eber (Num 24:24). In Daniel's vision, the ships of Kittim oppose a northern king, who then turns back in anger against the holy covenant (Dan 11:30). Many interpreters read this as Roman intervention against the Seleucid king Antiochus IV, though the text does not name either. The name is usually linked with Citium, an ancient town on Cyprus, and Kittim is also listed as a descendant of Javan in Gen 10:4, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes. In later use the term could extend to the western coastlands more broadly. The location shown here follows the identification with Cyprus. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "breaking" or "bruising small."

Koa was a people or region named only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel's allegory of Oholah and Oholibah, where it appears with Pekod, Shoa, the Babylonians, Chaldeans and Assyrians among the horsemen, captains and nobles who would come against Jerusalem (Ezek 23:23). The text gives no further detail, so its identity is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it as a province or place in the Babylonian empire, while Smith's Bible Dictionary notes it might instead be a common noun meaning "prince" or "nobleman." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places the people probably northeast of Babylonia. The location shown here follows an identification with the area of ancient Media, in the region of modern Hamadan in western Iran, and should be treated as approximate.

Kohath was the second of the three sons of Levi, listed among Jacob's family who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:11). He had four sons, Amram, Izhar, Hebron and Uzziel, and lived 133 years (Exod 6:18). Exod 6:20 says Amram married Jochebed, Kohath's sister, which makes Kohath the grandfather of Moses and Aaron. His descendants, the Kohathites, formed one of the three main divisions of the Levites. In the wilderness they camped on the south side of the tabernacle. After Aaron's sons had covered its most holy objects, the Kohathites carried them on their shoulders, without touching them. Korah, who led a rebellion with Dathan and Abiram, was his grandson through Izhar. Under Joshua the remaining Kohathite families received ten cities from Ephraim, Dan and half of Manasseh. Under David the Levites were divided into courses that included Kohath's line. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "assembly."

Kolaiah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only in the family line of Sallu, one of the Benjamites who settled in Jerusalem after the return from exile (Neh 11:7). He was the son of Maaseiah and the father of Pedaiah, and through Pedaiah, Joed and Meshullam he was an ancestor of Sallu. Nothing else is recorded about his life. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him before about 536 BC, the period of the first return from Babylon. By inference from the length of the genealogy, he probably lived some generations before Nehemiah's time. The name, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders "voice of Yah," is also borne by another man in the Bible, the father of the false prophet Ahab mentioned in Jeremiah. That man should not be confused with this Benjamite.

Kolaiah was the father of Ahab, one of two men whom Jeremiah condemned for prophesying lies in the Lord's name to the Jewish exiles in Babylon (Jer 29:21). The Lord declared that Ahab and his companion Zedekiah son of Maaseiah would be handed over to Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon and killed before the exiles' eyes. The next verse says the king roasted them in the fire, and Smith's Bible Dictionary accordingly describes Ahab as burnt by the king of Babylon. Nothing else is recorded about Kolaiah himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "voice of Jehovah" and places him before about 594 BC, a date inferred from context. The same name belongs to a different man, a Benjamite ancestor listed in Neh 11:7, who is distinct from this Kolaiah.

Korah was a son of Esau by his wife Aholibamah, the daughter of Anah and granddaughter of Zibeon. He is listed with his full brothers Jeush and Jaalam, and Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him the third son of this marriage. His half-brothers included Eliphaz and Reuel. Korah was born in the land of Canaan before Esau moved to the hill country of Seir (Gen 36:5). He is also named among the "dukes," or clan chiefs, descended from Aholibamah (Gen 36:18), which suggests that an Edomite clan bore his name. The genealogy in 1 Chr 1:35 repeats his place among Esau's sons. The name, perhaps meaning "baldness," is shared by several men in the Bible. This Korah is distinct from the better-known Levite of that name who rebelled against Moses.

Korah was an Edomite chief (a "duke" in the King James Version) descended from Eliphaz, the son of Esau and his wife Adah. He appears only in Gen 36:16, in a list of the chiefs who came from Eliphaz in the land of Edom, alongside Gatam and Amalek. His name is often taken to mean "baldness" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; Hitchcock's Bible Names). He is not named among the sons of Eliphaz in the genealogy just before (Gen 36:11–12) or in the parallel list in 1 Chr 1:36. Because of this, some interpreters, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes, connect him with another Korah, Esau's son by Aholibamah (Gen 36:14, 18). This entry treats him as a separate chief listed under Eliphaz's line. Several other people in the Bible share the name Korah, including the Levite who rebelled against Moses.

Korah (Levite) was a son of Izhar, grandson of Kohath and great-grandson of Levi. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that Izhar was a brother of Amram, which made Korah a cousin of Moses and Aaron. With the Reubenites Dathan, Abiram and On, he led a revolt in the wilderness against Moses and Aaron. Moses told Korah and his company to bring censers with incense before the LORD so that God would show whom he had chosen. The earth opened and swallowed the rebels' households and Korah's men, and fire consumed 250 men. Their censers became a reminder that only Aaron's descendants could offer incense. Korah's sons did not die. Their descendants, the Korahites, later served as gatekeepers of the tabernacle, and several psalms carry headings naming the sons of Korah. Jude 1:11, using the form Core, points to his rebellion as a warning.

Korah was a man of the tribe of Judah, listed in 1 Chr 2:43 as one of the sons of Hebron, with his brothers Tappuah, Rekem and Shema. He appears only in this genealogy, among the descendants of Caleb. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that this Hebron was the son of Mareshah. Some scholars read names in these Calebite lists as clans or towns as well as individuals, and Hebron and Tappuah are also place names in Judah, so Korah may represent a family group. The text records nothing else about him. He is distinct from other men named Korah, such as the Levite who rebelled against Moses and the son of Esau. The name probably means "baldness," according to Smith's Bible Dictionary.

Kore was a Levite of the Korahite family, listed as the son of Ebiasaph and a descendant of Korah (1 Chr 9:19). His brother was Assir. His sons Shallum and Meshelemiah led families of gatekeepers, or porters, who guarded the entrances of the tabernacle and later the temple (1 Chr 9:19; 26:1). 1 Chr 26:1 calls Meshelemiah one "of the sons of Asaph," probably a shortened form of Ebiasaph. Easton's Bible Dictionary follows that verse in calling Kore "the son of Asaph." Smith's Bible Dictionary places his sons in the reign of David. It also reads "the sons of Kore" in 1 Chr 26:19 as "the sons of the Korhite," referring to the Korahite clan as a whole. Shallum and Meshelemiah may be the same man under two forms of the name, but the text does not say so. Several other people in the Bible are also called Kore.

Kore, son of Imnah, was a Levite who served as gatekeeper at the east gate of the temple during the reign of Hezekiah, king of Judah. As part of Hezekiah's reorganization of temple service, Kore was put in charge of the freewill offerings given to God. He was responsible for distributing the offerings presented to the LORD and the most holy things, apparently to the priests and Levites who depended on them (2 Chr 31:14). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he probably belonged to the same family line as an earlier Kore, a gatekeeper of the Korahite clan. Several men in the Bible bear this name, and this entry concerns only the son of Imnah. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his service to about 726 BC.

Koz was the ancestor of a priestly family whose descendants returned from the Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel. He is named alongside Habaiah and Barzillai in the parallel lists of Ezra 2:61 and Neh 7:63. The verses that follow in both lists (Ezra 2:62; Neh 7:64) say these families searched for their genealogical records but could not find them, so they were barred from serving as priests until their status could be settled. STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) gives the name as Hakkoz, reflecting the Hebrew form with the article. Some connect this family with Hakkoz, head of the seventh priestly division in 1 Chr 24:10, and with Meremoth son of Uriah son of Koz, who later served in the temple (Ezra 8:33; Neh 3:4), but these links are uncertain. Several people in the Bible share this name.

Koz was the father of Urijah and the grandfather of Meremoth, who repaired two sections of Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah. One section lay beside the stretch repaired by Meshullam, and the other ran from the door of the high priest Eliashib's house to its far end. Koz is known only through this family line. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats Koz as the same name as Hakkoz, and the STEPBible name index describes Hakkoz as a priestly name. On that view Koz may be the ancestor of a priestly family rather than Meremoth's literal grandfather. The Hakkoz family appears in Ezra 2:61 among priests who could not prove their descent, and Ezra 8:33 calls Meremoth son of Uriah a priest. Because similar names belong to several people, it is uncertain how closely these passages connect.

Kue is a place from which Solomon obtained horses, mentioned in 1 Kgs 10:28 and the parallel 2 Chr 1:16. The King James Version does not show the name. It translates the Hebrew word as "linen yarn," so the verses speak of horses and linen yarn brought from Egypt. Many later translations read the same word as a place name and render the verses as horses imported "from Egypt and from Kue," with the king's merchants buying them from Kue. STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) treats Kue as a place in this way. Kue is usually identified with Cilicia, the coastal plain of what is now south-eastern Turkey, an area known in the ancient world for horse breeding. The location shown here follows that identification and marks the Cilician plain near modern Adana in general terms rather than a specific site.

Laadah was a man of the tribe of Judah, a son of Shelah and so a grandson of Judah. He appears only once, in the genealogy of Judah's descendants at 1 Chr 4:21, where he is called "the father of Mareshah." His brothers named in the passage and its context are Er, Joash, Jokim and Saraph. Mareshah was also the name of a town in the lowlands of Judah, so "father" here may mean the founder or leading figure of that settlement rather than a literal parent, a common pattern in these Chronicles genealogies. This is an inference, and the text does not settle it. The same verse links Shelah's descendants to families of linen workers of the house of Ashbea. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "to assemble together" or "to testify."

Laadan was a member of the tribe of Ephraim, one of the tribes descended from Joseph, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 7:26. His father was Tahan and his son was Ammihud, whose son was Elishama. The list goes on to Joshua the son of Nun (1 Chr 7:27), so Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Laadan as an ancestor of Joshua. Elishama son of Ammihud is probably the same man who led the tribe of Ephraim in the wilderness (Num 1:10). Nothing else is recorded about Laadan's life. The name is shared by others, including a Levite of the family of Gershon (1 Chr 23:7), who is a different person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "for pleasure," "devouring" or "judgment."

Laadan was a Levite, a son of Gershon (also spelled Gershom) and grandson of Levi. He and his brother Shimei are named as the two founders of the Gershonite families (1 Chr 23:7). STEPBible and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify him with Libni, whom Exodus, Numbers and 1 Chronicles list as Gershon's first son alongside Shimei. His sons were Jehiel the chief, Zetham and Joel (1 Chr 23:8), and 1 Chr 26:21 names the Jehielites among the heads of his line. 1 Chr 23:9 lists a Shimei whose sons were heads of Laadan's houses, and this entry treats that Shimei as Laadan's son, distinct from his brother. The name Jahath is linked to him because 1 Chr 6:43 calls Jahath a son of Gershom. However, 1 Chr 6:20 makes Jahath Libni's son, which is how Smith's reads it. An Ephraimite elsewhere also bears the name Laadan.

Laban was the son of Bethuel and brother of Rebekah. He lived at Haran in Padanaram and is called "the Syrian," that is, the Aramean. Gen 29:5 calls him "son of Nahor," meaning descendant, since Bethuel was Nahor's son. With Bethuel he agreed to Rebekah's marriage to Isaac. Years later Rebekah's son Jacob fled to him. Laban promised Jacob his younger daughter Rachel in return for his service but gave him Leah first, saying local custom required the elder to marry first. He then gave Rachel too, with the maids Zilpah and Bilhah. He urged Jacob to stay, saying the LORD had blessed him for Jacob's sake, and they agreed on wages from the flocks. When Jacob left secretly, Laban pursued him to Gilead, was warned by God in a dream, and searched for his stolen household images. The two then made a covenant marked by a heap of stones.

Laban was a place named in Deut 1:1 as one of several landmarks marking where Moses spoke to all Israel east of the Jordan, in the wilderness. It is listed with Paran, Tophel, Hazeroth and Dizahab. The verse is notoriously hard to interpret, and nothing more is said about Laban in the Bible. Its name probably means "white." Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as a city on the Israelites' desert route and probably the same as Libnah, a wilderness camp listed in Num 33:20. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that this identification seems to rest on Laban being mentioned alongside Hazeroth, which also appears near Libnah in that list. Its actual location is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough approximation in the lowlands west of Jerusalem.

Lachish was a fortified city in the lowlands (Shephelah) of southwestern Judah. Its Amorite king Japhia joined Adonizedek of Jerusalem's coalition against Gibeon. Joshua later took the city on the second day of the siege and defeated Horam of Gezer, who came to help it (Josh 10:3, 10:31–33). It was assigned to Judah, and Rehoboam fortified it (2 Chr 11:9). King Amaziah fled there and was killed (2 Kgs 14:19). Sennacherib of Assyria besieged it and sent his officers from there to Jerusalem (2 Kgs 18:14, 18:17; 2 Chr 32:9). Babylon's army later attacked it as one of Judah's last fortified cities (Jer 34:7), and returning exiles resettled it (Neh 11:30). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes Assyrian palace reliefs that show its siege. Older works identified it with Tell el-Hesy. The location shown here follows the identification with Tell ed-Duweir (Tel Lachish).

Lael was a Levite of the Gershonite branch, known only as the father of Eliasaph. In Num 3:24 his son Eliasaph is named chief of the father's house of the Gershonites, the family responsible under Moses for parts of the tabernacle's coverings and hangings. Since his son held this leading role, Lael was presumably a descendant of Gershon son of Levi, though the text gives no further details of his life or ancestry. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as meaning "belonging to God," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "to God" or "to the mighty." He is mentioned in this single verse and nowhere else in the Bible.

Lahad was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles. He was a son of Jahath and the brother of Ahumai. Through Jahath he descended from Reaiah son of Shobal. The verse ends by calling this line "the families of the Zorathites," so Lahad's descendants were probably counted among the clans linked with Zorah, a town in the lowlands of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about his life. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "oppression," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "praising" or "to confess."

Lahmi was a Philistine warrior, the brother of Goliath the Gittite, killed by Elhanan the son of Jair in one of David's later wars with the Philistines (1 Chr 20:5). Like Goliath, he is described as having a spear whose shaft was as thick as a weaver's beam. The same chapter, together with 2 Sam 21:15–22, groups him with other huge warriors from Gath, including Ishbi-benob, Sippai and an unnamed man of great stature, all called descendants of 'the giant' in Gath. The parallel passage, 2 Sam 21:19, says instead that Elhanan, a Bethlehemite, killed Goliath himself. Many interpreters explain the difference as two ways of reading a similar Hebrew text, since 'Lahmi' closely resembles the word for 'Bethlehemite.' This entry follows the Chronicles account, which presents Lahmi as a separate person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as 'my bread' or 'my war.'

Laish was the father of Phalti, also called Phaltiel. He appears only as the father of the man to whom Saul gave his daughter Michal, David's wife, after David fled from Saul's court (1 Sam 25:44). Later, Saul's son Ishbosheth took Michal back from Phaltiel and returned her to David (2 Sam 3:15). The family is described as being "of Gallim," a town that 1 Sam 25:44 connects with Phalti. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies Laish as a Benjamite, which fits Gallim's probable location in the territory of Benjamin, north of Jerusalem. According to Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names, the name means "lion." He should not be confused with the city of Laish in the far north, which the tribe of Dan captured and renamed Dan. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Laish was a city in the far north of the land, which the tribe of Dan captured and renamed Dan. Five Danite spies found its people living quietly and securely, like the Sidonians, with no ruler to trouble them, far from Sidon and without ties to anyone (Judg 18:7). The Danites later came with the idols and priest they had taken from Micah, struck down the inhabitants, burned the city, rebuilt it, and named it after their ancestor Dan (Judg 18:27, 29). Joshua 19:47 calls the city Leshem. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it near the sources of the Jordan, about 4 miles from Paneas (Banias), and identifies it with Tell el-Qadi, the modern Tel Dan. The location shown here matches that identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a lion."

Laishah was a town north of Jerusalem, named in Isaiah's description of an invading army advancing on the city (Isa 10:30). The King James Version spells it "Laish", but it is a different place from Laish, the northern city later renamed Dan. The verse calls on Gallim to cry out so that Laishah and the "poor" town of Anathoth can hear. That grouping, and the march route described in the surrounding passage, places it near Anathoth and Gallim in the territory of Benjamin. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes Conder's suggestion that it is the village of el-Isawiyeh (modern Isawiya), on the eastern slope north-northeast of the Mount of Olives. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the same identification and places it about a mile northeast of Jerusalem. The location shown here follows the Isawiya identification, though the site is not certain.

Lakkum (spelled Lakum in the King James Version) was a town on the border of the tribe of Naphtali, mentioned only once in the Bible. In Josh 19:33 it is the last place named in a line of border points, after Heleph, Allon to Zaanannim, Adami, Nekeb and Jabneel, just before the boundary is said to reach the Jordan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes it as an unidentified town that apparently lay nearer the Jordan than the others listed. Its exact site is still uncertain. The location shown here is only a rough placement in Lower Galilee, in the area of Mount Tabor, which fits the general course of Naphtali's southern border running toward the Jordan.

The Lame man healed is an event in Acts 3 in which Peter and John cured a man who had been lame from birth at the Jerusalem temple. The two apostles were going up to the temple at the ninth hour, the hour of prayer (about 3 p.m.). The man was carried each day to the gate called Beautiful to beg from people entering. When he asked them for money, Peter told him to look at them and said he had no silver or gold, but in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth the man should rise and walk. Peter took him by the right hand and lifted him, and his feet and ankles immediately grew strong. He jumped up, walked and leaped into the temple with them, praising God. The people recognized him as the beggar from the gate and were amazed. This entry dates the event to about AD 30, an estimate inferred from context.

Lamech (descendant of Cain) was the son of Methusael and belonged to the line of Cain, five generations after Cain himself (Gen 4:18). He took two wives, Adah and Zillah. He is the first man in Genesis said to have more than one wife (Gen 4:19). The verses that follow (Gen 4:20–22) name his children: Jabal and Jubal by Adah, and Tubal-cain and a daughter, Naamah, by Zillah. Lamech is remembered for a short poem spoken to his wives. In it he says he has killed a man for wounding him, and he claims that if Cain is avenged sevenfold, he will be avenged seventy-sevenfold (Gen 4:23–24). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that this has been called "Lamech's sword-song." Smith's Bible Dictionary links it with Tubal-cain's metalworking. He is a different person from Lamech the father of Noah, who belongs to the line of Seth (Gen 5).

Lamech (father of Noah) was a descendant of Seth in the genealogy of Genesis 5, the son of Methuselah and the father of Noah. Methuselah fathered him at 187. Lamech fathered Noah at 182, then lived another 595 years and had other sons and daughters, dying at 777. The next verse, Gen 5:29, records that he named Noah, saying the child would bring comfort from the hard toil of working ground that the Lord had cursed. Comparing his age with Noah's age at the flood (Gen 7:6) suggests he died about five years before the flood. He appears in the lists of 1 Chr 1:3 and in Luke's genealogy of Jesus (Luke 3:36). He is a different man from Lamech the descendant of Cain in Gen 4. The dates sometimes given for him, about 3130–2353 BC, are estimates worked out from the genealogy.

Laodicea was a city of the Roman province of Asia in the Lycus valley, near Colossae and Hierapolis. Writing to the Colossians, Paul speaks of his concern for those at Laodicea who had not seen him in person (Col 2:1) and of Epaphras's zeal for them (Col 4:13). He greets the believers there, along with Nymphas and the church in his house. He asks that his letter be read in Laodicea and that the Colossians read "the epistle from Laodicea" (Col 4:15–16). That letter's identity is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes Ussher's view that it was the circular letter known as Ephesians. Laodicea is the last of the seven churches of Asia addressed in Revelation (Rev 1:11; 3:14). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says Antiochus II founded it, naming it after his wife Laodice. Its ruins, shown here, lie near modern Denizli, Turkey.

Lapidoth was the husband of Deborah, the prophetess who judged Israel in the period of the judges (Judg 4:4). He is named only in this one verse, and nothing else is told about him: no family, tribe, home or role in the events of Deborah's time. His name means "torches" or "lamps." Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that some have read the Hebrew phrase not as "wife of Lapidoth" but as "a woman of a fiery spirit," on the view that Lapidoth is not a personal name at all. This entry follows the common reading of the verse, which treats Lapidoth as a man's name and Deborah's husband.

Lasea was a city on the south coast of the island of Crete, mentioned once in the Bible as lying near Fair Havens, the anchorage where Paul's ship put in after struggling along the coast on its voyage toward Rome (Acts 27:8). That voyage is dated about AD 56, by inference from context. Crete is not named in this verse itself, but the surrounding account of the voyage places Fair Havens on Crete's southern shore. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary report that ruins identified as Lasea were found in 1856 a few miles east of Fair Havens, near Cape Leonda. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that the ship's crew would have had to buy supplies from Lasea if they stayed long, which may help explain why the captain did not want to winter there. No coordinates are shown for this entry.

Lasha was a city named in Gen 10:19 as the furthest point of the Canaanites' territory, listed after Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboim. It apparently marked the southeastern corner of the border, near the region of the Dead Sea. The Bible mentions it nowhere else. Its location is uncertain. Jerome, Eusebius's Onomasticon and the Jerusalem Targum identify it with Callirrhoe, a place known for its hot springs near the eastern shore of the Dead Sea, in the Wadi Zerqa Ma'in area. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries both mention this view. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the site may lie further south, possibly west of the Arabah, and considers a firm identification impossible. The location shown here follows the Callirrhoe identification, east of the Dead Sea in present-day Jordan.

Lasharon was a Canaanite town whose king appears in the list of kings defeated by Joshua west of the Jordan (Josh 12:18). It is mentioned only here, and the verse says nothing more about it. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "the plain." Because the name can also be read as "of the Sharon," some interpreters take it as describing the preceding Aphek, meaning "Aphek in the Sharon plain," rather than as a separate town. Others treat it as its own city in Lower Galilee, near the modern village of Sharona, southwest of the Sea of Galilee.
