The location shown here follows the Sharona identification, which is probably the site of the ancient town, although this remains uncertain.

Lazarus is the poor beggar in the parable Jesus tells in Luke 16 about a rich man and a beggar. He lay at the rich man's gate covered with sores (Luke 16:20). After both men died, the rich man, in torment, looked up and saw Lazarus far off at Abraham's side, "in his bosom" (Luke 16:23). The rich man asked Abraham to send Lazarus to dip his fingertip in water and cool his tongue (Luke 16:24). Abraham replied that the rich man had received good things in his lifetime and Lazarus evil things, but now Lazarus was comforted while the rich man was tormented (Luke 16:25). He is the only named character in any of Jesus' parables. He is distinct from Lazarus of Bethany, the brother of Mary and Martha, whom Jesus raised from the dead in John 11. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "assistance of God."

Lazarus was a man of Bethany, the brother of Martha and of Mary, the Mary who anointed Jesus (John 11:1–2). Jesus loved all three (John 11:5). When Lazarus fell sick and died, Jesus first spoke of his death as sleep and then told his disciples plainly that he was dead (John 11:11, 14). At the tomb Jesus called out, "Lazarus, come forth," and he was raised from the dead. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that he had lain four days in the tomb. Six days before Passover, Lazarus sat at the table at a supper for Jesus in Bethany (John 12:1–2). Crowds came to see him, and the chief priests plotted to kill him as well as Jesus (John 12:9–10). The name is a form of Eleazar, meaning "God helps" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). Another Lazarus, the beggar in Jesus' parable in Luke, is a different figure.

Lazarus Raised form the Dead is the event, recorded in John 11, in which Jesus brought Lazarus of Bethany back to life. Bethany lay about fifteen furlongs (roughly two miles) from Jerusalem. When Lazarus fell sick, his sisters Mary and Martha sent word to Jesus, who waited two more days before returning to Judea, despite his disciples' fear of stoning. On arrival he found Lazarus had been in the tomb four days. Martha and then Mary met him, each saying their brother would not have died had he been there. Jesus told Martha, "I am the resurrection, and the life." Moved and troubled at the mourning, he went to the cave-tomb, had the stone removed, prayed, and called, "Lazarus, come forth." Lazarus emerged still bound in graveclothes. Many onlookers believed, while others reported it to the Pharisees. This entry dates it to about AD 30, by inference from context.

Leah was the elder daughter of Laban and sister of Rachel. She is described as "tender eyed," in contrast to her beautiful sister. Jacob served Laban for Rachel, but Laban gave him Leah on the wedding night instead. Jacob then married Rachel as well and loved her more. Leah bore Jacob six sons, Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar and Zebulun, and a daughter, Dinah. She named several of them in the hope of winning her husband's love. Zilpah, the maid Laban gave her, bore Gad and Asher, whom Leah named. Leah agreed with Rachel to leave Laban's house with Jacob. She was buried in the family tomb with Abraham, Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, which Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies as the cave of Machpelah. Ruth 4:11 recalls Rachel and Leah as the two who built the house of Israel. By inference from context, her children were born about 1758–1750 BC.

The Leaving the Ark was the moment at the end of the Great Flood when God told Noah to go out of the ark with his wife, his sons and his sons' wives. God also told him to bring out every living creature with him, the birds, cattle and creeping things, so that they could breed and multiply on the earth. Noah obeyed, and his family and all the animals left the ark "after their kinds." His sons, named elsewhere in Genesis as Shem, Ham and Japheth, came out with him. The ark had come to rest on the mountains of Ararat, according to the earlier verse Gen 8:4, so this is probably where the departure took place. The event follows the subsiding of the waters. It is dated here to about 2347 BC, a traditional estimate inferred from the biblical chronology rather than stated in the text.

Leb-kamai is a name that appears in the Hebrew text of Jer 51:1, in an oracle where the Lord threatens to raise a destroying wind against Babylon and against those who dwell in Leb-kamai. The King James Version does not keep it as a name. It translates the Hebrew literally as "the midst of them that rise up against me." Many interpreters treat it as a coded name, formed by a letter-substitution cipher (atbash) that reverses the order of the Hebrew alphabet. Decoded this way, Leb-kamai spells Kasdim, the Hebrew word for the Chaldeans. On that reading it is a cryptic name for Chaldea, the region of southern Mesopotamia around Babylon, and it stands parallel to Babylon in the same verse. The location shown here follows that identification and marks the general area of Chaldea in what is now southern Iraq, not one specific site.

Lebanah was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) who returned from exile in Babylon to Judah with Zerubbabel. He is known only from the lists of returning exiles. In Ezra 2:45 his descendants appear between other temple-servant families, alongside those of Hagabah and Akkub. The parallel list in Neh 7:48 spells the name Lebana and places it with Hagaba and Shalmai. Nothing else is recorded about him, and the name probably refers to the founder or head of the family group rather than to someone who made the journey himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "white."

Lebanon, in this entry, refers to the House of the Forest of Lebanon, a large hall Solomon built as part of his palace complex in Jerusalem. The location shown here is Jerusalem. It measured 100 cubits long, 50 wide and 30 high, and rested on four rows of cedar pillars with cedar beams (1 Kgs 7:2). Its name probably comes from its rows of cedar columns, which suggested a forest, and from the cedar timber brought from the Lebanon mountains. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes those mountains as the lofty range of Syria famous for its cedars. Solomon placed 300 shields of beaten gold in the hall (1 Kgs 10:17; 2 Chr 9:16), and all its vessels were pure gold, since silver was thought of little value in his day (1 Kgs 10:21; 2 Chr 9:20).

Lebanon is the mountainous region north of Israel, named in Deuteronomy and Joshua as the northern limit of the land promised to Israel, reaching toward the Euphrates (Deut 1:7; Josh 1:4). Joshua 13:5 also mentions "Lebanon toward the sunrising," which Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify as the eastern Anti-Lebanon range, beside the western Lebanon range proper. The name probably means "white," perhaps from its snow (Jer 18:14) or pale limestone. Lebanon was famous for its cedars and other timber. Hiram's servants cut and floated logs down the coast for Solomon's building works (1 Kgs 5:9; 2 Chr 2:8), and cedar was brought to Joppa again for the second temple (Ezra 3:7). Solomon also built in Lebanon (1 Kgs 9:19). Poets and prophets used its cedars, wine, fragrance and streams as images of height, pride and abundance (Ps 104:16; Isa 2:13; Hos 14:7). The location shown here is in the modern country of Lebanon.

Lebaoth was a town in the far south (the Negev) of the territory assigned to the tribe of Judah. It appears near the end of the list of Judah's southern cities in Josh 15:32, alongside Shilhim, Ain and Rimmon. Its name probably means "lionesses," as Smith's Bible Dictionary explains it. Smith's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat it as probably the same place as Beth-lebaoth, a town later listed among the cities given to Simeon within Judah's land (Josh 19:6). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds that the parallel list in 1 Chr 4:31 gives the name as Beth-biri. The site has not been securely identified. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the northern Negev, north of Beersheba.

Lebbaeus Thaddaeus was one of the twelve apostles chosen by Jesus. Matthew calls him “Lebbaeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus” and Mark calls him Thaddaeus. Luke and Acts list “Judas the brother of James” at the same point in their lists, and the names are generally taken as one man. He is probably the “Judas, not Iscariot” who asked Jesus how he would show himself to the disciples and not to the world (John 14:22). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reads the Greek as “Judas of James,” meaning son of James. This entry follows the King James “brother” and takes that James to be James son of Alphaeus, which makes Alphaeus his father. After the ascension he was with the eleven in the upper room. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him with Jude, author of the epistle, and Smith's Bible Dictionary notes a tradition linking him with the church at Edessa.

Lebo-hamath was a place on the far northern edge of the land promised to Israel. The King James Version translates the Hebrew as "the entering in of Hamath," treating it as the approach to the Syrian city of Hamath. Many modern translations read it as a town name, Lebo-hamath. It marks the northern limit of the land the spies explored (Num 13:21), of Israel's assigned border (Num 34:8; Ezek 47:20), and of the territory still unconquered after Joshua (Josh 13:5; Judg 3:3). It became a standard way to describe Israel's full extent, "from the entering in of Hamath unto the river of Egypt" (1 Kgs 8:65; 1 Chr 13:5). Jeroboam II restored the border there (2 Kgs 14:25). The location shown here follows the view that it was the town name, probably modern Lebweh (Labweh) in Lebanon's northern Beqaa Valley.

Lebonah was a town in the hill country of Ephraim, mentioned only once in the Bible. In Judg 21:19 it serves as a landmark for locating Shiloh, where a yearly feast of the LORD was held: Shiloh lay north of Bethel, east of the highway from Bethel to Shechem, and south of Lebonah. Lebonah therefore stood a short distance north of Shiloh, near the main north–south road through the hills. The name probably means "frankincense," according to Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries. The town is generally identified with the modern village of al-Lubban, south of Nablus near the old road. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it about two miles from Shiloh (Seilun), and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes rock tombs nearby. The location shown here follows the al-Lubban identification.

Lehabim is named in the Table of Nations as a son, or descendant people, of Mizraim, the son of Ham whose name is the Hebrew word for Egypt (Gen 10:13; 1 Chr 1:11). The plural ending suggests a people group rather than a single individual, and the same list gives his siblings as Ludim, Anamim, Naphtuhim, Pathrusim, Casluhim and Caphthorim. Neither passage says anything more about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies the Lehabim with the Lebu (or Rebu) of Egyptian inscriptions, an early people living west of Egypt in North Africa, from whom Libya took its name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia similarly connects them with the Lubim mentioned elsewhere in the Bible, and suggests that one name may be a variant of the other. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "flames".

Lehem is a place that may be named in 1 Chr 4:22, in the genealogy of Shelah son of Judah. The verse lists descendants who ruled in Moab and ends with a name the King James Version prints as one word, Jashubilehem, treating it as a personal name. Other translators divide it, reading it as 'and they returned to Lehem' or treat Lehem as a separate place. On that reading, these men of Judah had some connection with Moab and then came back home. Lehem is often taken as a shortened form of Bethlehem, the Judahite town whose name means 'house of bread.' Ruth's story also links Bethlehem with Moab. The location shown here follows the Bethlehem identification, south of Jerusalem. The verse itself calls these records 'ancient things,' and the exact meaning of the name remains uncertain.

Lehi, meaning "jawbone," was a place in Judah where Samson fought the Philistines. The Philistines camped in Judah and spread out in Lehi, demanding that Samson be handed over. When the men of Judah brought him there bound, the cords fell from his arms and he struck down a thousand Philistines with a donkey's jawbone. Afterward, thirsty, he received water from a hollow place, and he named the spring En-hakkore. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the phrase in Judg 15:19 is better read, as in the Revised Version, "the hollow place that is in Lehi." The nearby verse Judg 15:17 calls the site Ramath-lehi. Its exact location is unknown. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests Beit-Likiyeh near upper Beth-horon. The location shown here is a rough placement in the western hills of Judah, near Samson's home region along the Sorek Valley.

Lemuel was a king whose words open the last chapter of Proverbs. Prov 31:1 calls them a prophecy, or oracle, that his mother taught him. In her advice she addresses him by name and warns that kings and princes should not drink wine or strong drink (Prov 31:4). The ISBE notes that the following acrostic poem on the capable wife (31:10–31) may come from the same source. Nothing else is known of him for certain. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries record that rabbinic commentators identified him with Solomon. Smith's adds that others take him for the chief of an Arab tribe, possibly a brother of Agur (Prov 30:1). The ISBE mentions a proposal to read the word translated "prophecy" as a place name, making him "king of Massa" after Ishmael's son Massa (Gen 25:14). The name is usually explained as "dedicated to God."

The Lepers Healed was an incident in which Jesus cured ten men with leprosy as he traveled toward Jerusalem, passing between Samaria and Galilee. As he entered an unnamed village, the ten met him but kept their distance, calling out, "Jesus, Master, have mercy on us." He told them to go and show themselves to the priests, and they were cleansed on the way. Only one of them, a Samaritan, turned back, praised God loudly, and fell at Jesus' feet to thank him. Jesus asked where the other nine were, noting that only this foreigner had returned to give glory to God, and told him that his faith had made him well. The event is dated to about AD 30 by inference from context, and this entry places it after Jesus withdrew to Ephraim.

Leshem was a town that the tribe of Dan captured when its allotted territory proved too small. According to Josh 19:47, the Danites attacked it, put it to the sword, settled there and renamed it Dan after their ancestor. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats Leshem as another form of Laish, the name used for the same town in the fuller account of the Danite migration in Judges 18. As Dan, it later marked the northern limit of Israel in the phrase "from Dan to Beersheba." The site is generally identified with Tel Dan (Tell el-Qadi), near the springs of the Jordan at the foot of Mount Hermon in northern Israel, and the location shown here matches that identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a name" or "a precious stone."

Letushim was a son of Dedan, who was a son of Jokshan, listed with his brothers Asshurim and Leummim in Gen 25:3. Because Jokshan was one of the sons Abraham had with Keturah, Letushim belongs to Abraham's line through Keturah. He is mentioned only in this one genealogy, and nothing is said about his life. His name has a plural form, as do the names of his brothers, so the entry may name a people or tribe rather than a single man. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats Letushim as a Dedanite tribe of North Arabia. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as the second son of Dedan. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "hammermen" or "filemen."

Leummim was the third of the three sons of Dedan named in Gen 25:3, alongside Asshurim and Letushim. Dedan was a son of Jokshan, and Jokshan was one of the sons Abraham had by Keturah (Gen 25:1–2), which makes Leummim a descendant of Abraham through Keturah. Like the names of his brothers, Leummim has a plural form in Hebrew and means "peoples" or "nations." For this reason Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary take it as the name of a tribe or people rather than of a single individual. Easton's describes Leummim as the head of an Arabian tribe, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places this Dedanite tribe in northern Arabia. The Bible gives no further details about him or his descendants.

Levi (patriarch) was the third son of Jacob and Leah. Leah named him in the hope that her husband would now be "joined" to her (Gen 29:34). With his brother Simeon, he avenged the rape of their sister Dinah by killing the men of Shechem, as Gen 34 relates. Jacob rebuked them for it at the time (Gen 34:30) and again in his final words (Gen 49:5). Levi went down to Egypt with Jacob. His sons were Gershon, Kohath and Merari (1 Chr 6:16). His daughter Jochebed, born in Egypt, became the mother of Aaron, Moses and Miriam (Num 26:59). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes from Exod 6:16 that he died in Egypt aged 137. His birth is placed about 1756 BC, by inference from context. His descendants formed the tribe of Levi, set apart to carry the ark and serve the sanctuary, with no territorial inheritance (Deut 10:8; Josh 13:14).

Levi was an ancestor of Jesus who appears only in Luke's genealogy, which traces Jesus' line back through Joseph (Luke 3:24). He is named as the son of Melchi and the father of Matthat. As part of the line running through David, he belonged to the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about his life. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names takes to mean "associated with him," is shared by several people in the Bible. These include Jacob's son, who founded the tribe of Levi, and another Levi listed further back in the same genealogy. He should not be confused with either of them. Matthew's genealogy follows a different line between David and Joseph and does not mention him.

Levi is one of the ancestors of Jesus listed in Luke's genealogy, which traces the line backward from Joseph. Luke 3:29 names him as the father of Matthat, and the next verse (Luke 3:30) names his own father as Simeon. He belongs to the stretch of the genealogy between David's son Nathan and the exile, so he would have been of the tribe of Judah by descent. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Levi belongs to several people in the Bible. He should not be confused with Levi the son of Jacob, with Matthew the tax collector (also called Levi), or with a second Levi who appears earlier in the same genealogy (Luke 3:24) as the father of a different Matthat. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "associated with him."

Libnah was a Canaanite royal city in the Shephelah (lowland) of Judah, near Lachish. Joshua captured it after Makkedah, killed its king and then moved on to Lachish (Josh 10:29–32, 39; 12:15). It was later assigned to Judah and given, with its pasturelands, to the priestly descendants of Aaron (Josh 15:42; 21:13). It revolted against King Jehoram of Judah at the same time as Edom (2 Kgs 8:22). Sennacherib of Assyria attacked it after leaving Lachish (2 Kgs 19:8). Hamutal, mother of kings Jehoahaz and Zedekiah, was the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah. The name means "whiteness." The site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary favors Arak el-Menshiyeh, and other proposals include Tell es-Safi and el-Benawy. The location shown here is a rough point in the southern Shephelah, close to Tel Burna, which some modern scholars propose. A wilderness camp also bore this name.

Libnah was one of the places where the Israelites camped during their journey through the wilderness after leaving Egypt. The list of stations in Numbers 33 records that they moved from Rimmon-parez to Libnah, and from Libnah went on to Rissah (Num 33:20–21). Smith's Bible Dictionary places it on the stretch of the journey between the wilderness of Sinai and Kadesh. The name probably means "whiteness." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the same place as Laban, mentioned in Deut 1:1. The name Libnah is also borne by other places, including a town in Judah, and this wilderness camp should be kept distinct from them. Its actual site is unknown, and the location shown here is only a rough approximation.

Libni was a Levite of the clan of Merari, named in the genealogy at 1 Chr 6:29 as the son of Mahli and the father of Shimei. The line continues through Shimei to Uzza. His brothers Eleazar and Kish are not named in this verse. A later genealogy, 1 Chr 23:21–22, names Eleazar and Kish as sons of Mahli. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests that this Libni may be the same person as Libni the son of Gershon, named earlier in the chapter, and that something may have dropped out of the text here. That would explain why the names in this list do not match the Merarite lines elsewhere. This entry treats him as the Merarite descendant shown in the verse as it stands. Hitchcock's Bible Names takes the name to mean the same as Libnah, and Smith's gives its meaning as "white."

Libya was the region of North Africa west of Egypt, along the Mediterranean coast. In Ezek 30:5 it is named with Ethiopia, Lydia and other peoples allied with Egypt, who are foretold to fall by the sword with Egypt. The Hebrew name behind this translation is Put, a people usually linked with North Africa. In Acts 2:10, Jews and proselytes from “the parts of Libya about Cyrene” were among the crowd in Jerusalem at Pentecost. By the context of the chapter, they heard the apostles speak in their own languages. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as a large tract along the Mediterranean west of Egypt, with Cyrene as one of its five cities. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Greek and Roman writers used the name for the African continent generally, usually excluding Egypt. The location shown here marks the general region west of the Nile, broadly the eastern part of modern Libya.

The Lifetime of Abraham was the span of 175 years that Genesis gives for the life of the patriarch Abraham (Gen 25:7). It began, by inference from context, about 1997 BC. One fixed point within that span is the birth of his son Isaac, which came when Abraham was a hundred years old (Gen 21:5). Abraham therefore lived about seventy-five more years after Isaac's birth. The verses that follow in Gen 25:8–10 describe his death at a good old age and his burial by his sons Isaac and Ishmael in the cave of Machpelah. Genesis states the overall figure as "a hundred threescore and fifteen years," which marks the close of the Abraham narrative before the account turns to Ishmael's descendants and to Isaac.

The Lifetime of Adam is the span of the first man's life as summarized in the genealogy of Genesis 5. Adam was 130 years old when he fathered Seth, a son described as being in his own likeness and image (Gen 5:3). He lived another 800 years after Seth's birth and had other sons and daughters (Gen 5:4). His whole life lasted 930 years, and then he died (Gen 5:5). This summary opens the line of descent from Adam to Noah, and each later generation is recorded in the same pattern. His life began with the creation of Adam and Eve, placed at about 4004 BC. That date is an estimate inferred by adding up the ages in the biblical genealogies, following the chronology associated with Archbishop James Ussher. Adam's life began in Eden, although Genesis 3 records that he was later sent out of the garden.

The Lifetime of Cainan was the span of the antediluvian patriarch Cainan's life, which Genesis 5 gives as 910 years. He was 70 when his son Mahalaleel was born, and he lived another 840 years afterward, having other sons and daughters, before he died. The account follows the fixed pattern of the Genesis 5 genealogy from Adam to Noah: age at the birth of the named son, the years lived after, and the total lifespan. The earlier verse Gen 5:9 names him as the son of Enosh, and some modern translations spell his name Kenan. Luke's genealogy of Jesus also lists him (Luke 3:37). He is distinct from a later Cainan, son of Arphaxad, in Luke 3:36. The starting date given here, about 3679 BC, is an estimate inferred from the genealogical chronology, not a date stated in the text.

The Lifetime of Eber was the life span of Eber, a descendant of Shem in the genealogy that leads from Noah to Abram. Eber was 34 when his son Peleg was born (Gen 11:16), and he lived 430 years after that, having other sons and daughters (Gen 11:17). That gives a total of 464 years, although the text does not state the sum. This entry places his birth in about 2281 BC, an estimate inferred from the genealogical figures rather than stated in the text. Connected passages add more detail. Gen 11:14 names his father as Shelah, and Gen 10:25 names a second son, Joktan. Gen 10:21 calls Shem the father of "all the children of Eber." Luke's genealogy of Jesus lists him as Heber. Eber's life of 464 years is the longest of the generations after Shem in Genesis 11.

The Lifetime of Enoch was the 365-year span of Enoch's life recorded in the genealogy of Genesis 5. This entry places its start about 3382 BC, an estimate inferred from the chronology of the chapter rather than a date given in the text. Enoch, whom Gen 5:18 names as the son of Jared, became the father of Methuselah at age sixty-five. He then lived another three hundred years, during which he 'walked with God' and had other sons and daughters. His full lifespan was 365 years, far shorter than the others listed in the chapter. Unlike the other entries, his account does not close with the words 'and he died.' Instead it says 'he was not; for God took him.' Later passages take this to mean he did not die: Heb 11:5 says he was taken so that he should not see death, and Jude 14 calls him the seventh from Adam.

The Lifetime of Enos covers the life of Enos, son of Seth and grandson of Adam, as recorded in the genealogy of Genesis 5. At ninety years old he became the father of Cainan (Gen 5:9). He lived another 815 years after that and had other sons and daughters (Gen 5:10). His whole life lasted 905 years, and then he died (Gen 5:11). His descent from Seth is not stated in these verses but comes from the preceding lines of the same genealogy and from Gen 4:26, which also links his time with people beginning to call on the name of the Lord. By inference from the genealogy's figures, this entry dates his birth to about 3769 BC, an estimate rather than a date given in the text.

The Lifetime of Isaac covers the whole life of Isaac, son of Abraham and Sarah, from his birth to his death at 180 years old (Gen 35:28). Before his birth, God told Abraham that Sarah would bear him a son, that he was to name the boy Isaac, and that God would establish an everlasting covenant with Isaac and his descendants (Gen 17:19). When the child was born, Abraham gave him that name (Gen 21:3). His birth is dated here to about 1896 BC, an estimate inferred from context. The span covers the events of his life in Genesis, including his marriage to Rebekah and the births of his sons Esau and Jacob. The account of his death in Gen 35:29 says that Esau and Jacob buried him. Counting from that estimated birth date, his death would fall around 1716 BC, also an inference.

The Lifetime of Ishmael was the span of years lived by Ishmael, the son Hagar bore to Abram. Genesis gives both ends of it. He was born when Abram was eighty-six years old (Gen 16:16), and he died at the age of 137 and "was gathered unto his people" (Gen 25:17). By inference from the chronology of Genesis, his birth falls around 1910 BC, which would place his death about 137 years later, in the late 1700s BC. These dates are estimates drawn from context and are not stated in the text. The surrounding chapters, not cited here, tell of his mother's flight into the wilderness, his place in Abraham's household, and the twelve sons descended from him. This entry covers only the span of his life as the two framing verses record it.

The Lifetime of Jacob covers the life of Isaac's younger son, from his birth to his death in Egypt. Rebekah gave birth to twins. Esau came out first, red and hairy, and his brother followed holding Esau's heel, so he was named Jacob. Isaac was sixty years old at the time (Gen 25:24–26). This entry places the birth at about 1836 BC, by inference from context. Jacob's life ended after he had finished giving his final instructions to his sons. He drew his feet into the bed, died, and "was gathered unto his people" (Gen 49:33). Gen 47:28 states that he lived 147 years, the last seventeen of them in Egypt. Connected passages cover the years in between. They record how he obtained Esau's birthright and blessing, served his uncle Laban, was renamed Israel (Gen 32:28), and fathered the twelve sons whose descendants became the tribes of Israel.

The Lifetime of Jared was the 962-year span of Jared, a patriarch in the genealogy from Adam to Noah in Genesis 5. According to Gen 5:18–20, he was 162 when his son Enoch was born, lived another 800 years, and had other sons and daughters before he died. Earlier verses in the same chapter (Gen 5:15–16) name his father as Mahalalel, and his son Enoch later became the father of Methuselah. The 962 years make Jared the second-longest-lived person in the genealogy, behind only his grandson Methuselah at 969 (Gen 5:27). This entry dates his birth to about 3544 BC, an estimate worked out from the chapter's chain of ages rather than a date stated in the text. Like the other entries in Genesis 5, the account gives only his age at his son's birth, his later years, and his death.

The Lifetime of Job covers the life of Job, the man of Uz whose trials and restoration are told in the book of Job. The closing verses say that after his fortunes were restored he lived another 140 years and saw four generations of his descendants, his sons and his sons' sons. He then died "old and full of days" (Job 42:16–17). Since the 140 years are counted from his restoration, his full lifespan was probably longer. This entry dates his life from about 1720 BC, an estimate inferred from context; the book itself gives no date. A different Job appears in Gen 46:13 as a son of Issachar who went down to Egypt with Jacob. The parallel list in Num 26:24 calls him Jashub. He shares only the name with the Job of Uz.

The Lifetime of Joseph was the span of 110 years that Joseph, son of Jacob, lived, from his birth to his death in Egypt. His mother, who by context is Rachel, gave birth to him after a long wait. She said God had taken away her reproach, and she named him Joseph, expressing the hope that the LORD would add another son (Gen 30:23–24). The verses given here do not describe the middle of his life. The wider Genesis account tells how his brothers sold him into Egypt, where he rose to high office and later brought his family to settle there. Genesis 50:22 records that Joseph lived in Egypt with his father's household and lived 110 years. This entry places his birth at about 1745 BC, an estimate inferred from context rather than a date stated in the text.

The Lifetime of Joshua covers the full life span of Joshua the son of Nun, which Judg 2:8 gives as one hundred and ten years. That verse calls him "the servant of the LORD" and records his death at that age. Its account repeats the notice of his death and burial found in Josh 24:29–30, where he is buried in his own inheritance at Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim. Earlier books present him as Moses' assistant and as the leader who succeeded Moses and brought Israel into Canaan. This entry dates the start of his life to about 1521 BC, an estimate inferred from context rather than stated in the text, so his death would fall around 1411 BC on the same reckoning. The Bible itself gives his age but no calendar dates.

The Lifetime of Lamech was the 777-year life of Lamech, the father of Noah, as recorded in the genealogy of Genesis 5. The earlier verses of that chapter (Gen 5:25) name him as the son of Methuselah, which sets him apart from the other Lamech, a descendant of Cain, in Genesis 4. At 182 he fathered Noah. He gave the boy his name, saying that this son would bring comfort from the hard work of the ground the LORD had cursed. He lived 595 more years and had other sons and daughters before he died at 777. This entry dates his birth to about 3130 BC, an estimate drawn from context. Comparing these figures with Noah's age at the flood (600, Gen 7:6) suggests that Lamech died about five years before the flood.

The Lifetime of Mahlaleel was the 895-year life of Mahalaleel, a descendant of Seth in the genealogy running from Adam to Noah. Genesis 5 records that at sixty-five he became the father of Jared, then lived another 830 years and had other sons and daughters before he died at 895 (Gen 5:15–17). The preceding verses in the same chapter name his father as Cainan (Gen 5:12). His son Jared later became the father of Enoch, so Mahalaleel was Noah's great-great-great-grandfather. Luke's genealogy of Jesus includes him under the spelling Maleleel (Luke 3:37). The dates shown here are estimates inferred from the genealogy's figures: his birth falls about 3609 BC, which would place his death about 2714 BC. The text itself gives only the ages, not calendar dates.

The Lifetime of Methuselah was the 969-year life of Methuselah, the longest lifespan recorded in the Bible. It began about 3317 BC, by inference from context. According to the genealogy in Genesis 5, Methuselah became the father of Lamech at 187. He then lived another 782 years and had other sons and daughters, and he died at 969. The surrounding passage names his father as Enoch (Gen 5:21) and his son Lamech as the father of Noah (Gen 5:28–29). Adding up the ages in this genealogy, with Lamech fathering Noah at 182 and the flood coming in Noah's 600th year (Gen 7:6), places Methuselah's death in the year of the flood. That timing is a calculation from the figures, not something the text states.

The Lifetime of Moses spans the life of the Israelite leader from his birth in Egypt to his death at 120 years old. Exodus 2:2 records that his mother bore a son, saw that he was a fine child, and hid him for three months. Deuteronomy 34:7 states that Moses was 120 years old when he died, and that his eyesight had not dimmed nor his strength faded. The start of this period is placed at about 1571 BC, an estimate inferred from context rather than stated in the text. Connected passages fill in the years between. Moses was raised in Pharaoh's household and later fled to Midian (Exod 2). He returned to lead Israel out of Egypt and through forty years in the wilderness (Exod 3–14; Num 14:33). He died in Moab within sight of the promised land (Deut 34:1–5).

The Lifetime of Nahor covers the 148 years of Nahor, son of Serug and father of Terah, in the genealogy from Shem to Abram. Nahor was 29 when Terah was born, and he lived another 119 years afterward, during which he had other sons and daughters (Gen 11:24–25). The total of 148 years is the sum of these two figures, since this passage does not state it directly. By inference from the chronology of the genealogy, his life ran from about 2155 BC to about 2007 BC. Through Terah, Nahor was the grandfather of Abram. He is distinct from his grandson Nahor, Abram's brother, who is named in the verses that follow (Gen 11:26). Among those listed after the flood in this genealogy, Nahor has the shortest recorded lifespan.

The Lifetime of Noah was the span of 950 years that Genesis gives for Noah's life, from his birth to his death (Gen 9:29). The text marks several points along the way. At five hundred years old he became the father of Shem, Ham and Japheth (Gen 5:32). He was six hundred when the flood came upon the earth (Gen 7:6), and he lived another 350 years after it (Gen 9:28). The three figures agree: 600 years before the flood plus 350 after gives the stated total of 950. This entry dates the start of his life to about 2948 BC, an estimate inferred from the genealogical figures in Genesis rather than a date the text gives. The event follows the Birth of Noah, and Noah is its only participant.

The Lifetime of Peleg covers the life of Peleg, a descendant of Shem in the genealogy that runs from Shem to Abram. Genesis records that Peleg was thirty years old when his son Reu was born, and that he lived another 209 years afterward and had other sons and daughters. That gives a total lifespan of 239 years, although the passage does not state the total itself. By inference from the chronology of the genealogy, his birth falls at about 2247 BC. Elsewhere, Gen 11:16 names his father as Eber. Gen 10:25 explains his name with the remark that "in his days was the earth divided." Peleg's lifespan is noticeably shorter than those of the earlier generations in the list, continuing the pattern of declining ages in this genealogy.

The Lifetime of Reu was the life span of Reu, a descendant of Shem in the genealogy that runs from Noah to Abram. Reu was 32 years old when his son Serug was born. He then lived another 207 years and had other sons and daughters. His total age was 239 years, a figure reached by adding the two numbers given in the text. The passage before this one, Gen 11:18, names Reu as the son of Peleg. He appears again in the genealogy of 1 Chr 1:25 and, as Ragau, in Luke 3:35. This entry dates the start of his life to about 2217 BC. That date is an estimate inferred from the chronology of the genealogy, not a date stated in the text.

The Lifetime of Salah is the span of years given for Salah in the genealogy from Shem to Abram. According to Gen 11:14–15, Salah was thirty when his son Eber was born, and he lived another 403 years afterward, during which he had other sons and daughters. That makes a total lifespan of 433 years, though the passage does not state the total or record his death. Its start is placed at about 2311 BC, an estimate reached by adding up the ages in the genealogy. The surrounding verses identify Salah as the son of Arphaxad (Gen 11:12). Elsewhere his name appears as Shelah (1 Chr 1:18) and, in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, as Sala (Luke 3:35). Eber is often linked to the name "Hebrew," which gives this line its significance in the genealogy.

The Lifetime of Serug was the 230-year life of Serug, one of the descendants of Shem listed in the genealogy of Genesis 11. According to Gen 11:22–23, Serug was thirty years old when his son Nahor was born, and he lived another two hundred years after that, having other sons and daughters. The surrounding genealogy names Reu as his father (Gen 11:20) and places him in the line leading to Abraham: his son Nahor was the father of Terah, who was Abraham's father. Luke's genealogy of Jesus includes him under the Greek form Saruch. This entry dates the start of his life to about 2185 BC, an estimate inferred from the genealogical figures rather than a date stated in the text.

The Lifetime of Seth was the span of 912 years that Genesis assigns to Seth, the son of Adam and Eve born after the death of Abel (Gen 4:25). The genealogy of Genesis 5 records that Seth was 105 when he became the father of Enos (Gen 5:6). He lived another 807 years and had other sons and daughters (Gen 5:7). He then died at the age of 912 (Gen 5:8). Every entry in this genealogy follows the same pattern: the age at which a son was born, the years lived afterward, and the total lifespan. This entry dates the beginning of Seth's life to about 3874 BC and its length to 912 years. The starting date is an estimate worked out from context, and the length comes from the stated total.

The Lifetime of Shem was the span of life of Noah's son Shem, which totals 600 years according to the genealogy in Genesis 11. Shem was 100 years old when his son Arphaxad was born, two years after the flood. He then lived another 500 years and had other sons and daughters (Gen 11:10–11). Adding these figures gives his total age. Unlike the earlier genealogy in Genesis 5, this passage does not state the total or record his death. This entry dates the start of his life to about 2446 BC, an estimate inferred from context rather than stated in the text. Earlier passages such as Gen 5:32 and Gen 6:10 name Shem as one of Noah's three sons, alongside Ham and Japheth, and later Genesis 11 traces the line from Arphaxad down to Abram.

The Lifetime of Terah covers the life of the father of Abram, Nahor and Haran. By inference from context, it began about 2126 BC and lasted about 205 years. Genesis records that Terah was seventy when he fathered his three sons (Gen 11:26). It then opens the account of "the generations of Terah" and notes that his son Haran became the father of Lot (Gen 11:27). Haran died while his father was still alive, in the land of his birth, Ur of the Chaldees (Gen 11:28). Later verses in the same chapter say that Terah took Abram, Sarai and Lot from Ur toward Canaan but settled in a place called Haran. They give his age at death there as 205 years (Gen 11:31–32), which is the source of the length shown in this entry.

event: Light of the World/I am discourse
text: The Light of the World/I am discourse was an extended debate between Jesus and the Pharisees and other Jews in the temple at Jerusalem, recorded in John 8:12–59. It follows the account of the woman caught in adultery and is dated to about AD 29, by inference from context. Jesus began by declaring, "I am the light of the world." The Pharisees objected that his testimony about himself was not valid. He replied that the Father who sent him also bore witness. He spoke in the temple treasury, and no one seized him. Many believed him. The debate then turned to freedom from sin, descent from Abraham, and who his hearers' true father was. His opponents called him a Samaritan possessed by a demon. When Jesus said, "Before Abraham was, I am," they picked up stones to throw at him, but he hid himself and left the temple.

Likhi was a son of Shemida and a member of the tribe of Manasseh, one of the tribes descended from Joseph. He appears only once, in the genealogy of 1 Chr 7:19, which lists Shemida's sons as Ahian, Shechem, Likhi and Aniam. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Shemida as a son of Manasseh and gives the meaning of Likhi's name as "learned." Shemida also appears among the clans of Gilead in the census lists of Numbers and Joshua, which suggests that Likhi belonged to that Manassite family line. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Linus was a Christian at Rome who sent greetings to Timothy through Paul's second letter to him. He is named with Eubulus, Pudens and Claudia among those who joined Paul in greeting Timothy, whom Paul urged to come before winter (2 Tim 4:21). The letter was written during what is usually taken as Paul's last imprisonment in Rome, so Linus was probably one of the believers still in contact with him then. The New Testament says nothing more about him. Early church tradition, beginning with Irenaeus in the second century, identifies this Linus as the first bishop of Rome after the apostles, and Smith's Bible Dictionary follows that view. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, citing Lightfoot, notes that it is safest to say he held some prominent position in the Roman church. His name is Greek, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "net."

Lo-ammi was the third child of the prophet Hosea and his wife Gomer, and their second son, after Jezreel and the daughter Lo-ruhamah. His name means "not my people." God commanded Hosea to give him this name as a sign: "for ye are not my people, and I will not be your God" (Hos 1:9). As Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary explain, the name stood for God's rejection of the kingdom of Israel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia compares it with the symbolic names Isaiah gave his children. Later verses in Hosea (Hos 1:10; 2:23) take up the meaning of the name and promise that those called "not my people" will again be called God's people. Paul quotes this promise in Rom 9:25. Nothing else is known about Lo-ammi himself.

Lo-debar was a town east of the Jordan River in Gilead, home of Machir son of Ammiel. In the context of 2 Sam 9, Jonathan's son Mephibosheth was living in Machir's house there until King David brought him to his court. Later, when David fled from Absalom to Mahanaim, the same Machir of Lo-debar was among those who met him there, alongside Shobi of Rabbah and Barzillai of Rogelim. That grouping suggests Lo-debar lay not far from Mahanaim. The name is often explained as meaning "no pasture." Easton's Bible Dictionary places it north of the Jabbok and takes it as probably the same place as Debir in the boundary list of Josh 13:26. Its site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mentions a village called Ibdar, about 6.5 miles (10 km) east of Umm Qeis in northern Jordan, as a possible match, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Lo-ruhamah was the daughter of the prophet Hosea and his wife Gomer, born after her brother Jezreel and before her brother Lo-ammi. Her name means "not pitied" or "no mercy." God told Hosea to give her this name as a sign that he would no longer show mercy to the house of Israel but would take them away (Hos 1:6). After Gomer weaned her, she gave birth to Lo-ammi (Hos 1:8). Smith's Bible Dictionary describes the name as pointing to the ruin of the northern kingdom of Israel. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that later in the book the name is reversed, when God says he will have mercy on her who had not obtained mercy (Hos 2:23). Nothing else is recorded about her life.

Lod was a town in the lowland west of the hill country, associated with the tribe of Benjamin. 1 Chr 8:12 credits its building, along with Ono and their surrounding villages, to Shamed, a Benjamite descended from Elpaal. After the Babylonian exile, the people of Lod, Hadid and Ono returned together. They numbered 725 in Ezra 2:33 and 721 in Neh 7:37. Neh 11:35 lists Lod and Ono among places resettled by Benjamites and links them with "the valley of craftsmen." The same town appears in the New Testament under its Greek name Lydda, where Peter healed Aeneas (Acts 9:32–35). Smith's Bible Dictionary treats it under that name. It is identified with modern Lod in Israel, southeast of Tel Aviv, which the location shown here matches. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "nativity" or "generation."

Lois was the grandmother of Timothy, Paul's younger companion, and the mother of Eunice, Timothy's mother. She is named only once in the Bible, in 2 Tim 1:5, where Paul recalls Timothy's sincere faith and says it lived first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice. By inference from Acts 16:1, the family lived at Lystra, where Paul met Timothy. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests she probably became a Christian during Paul's first missionary journey (Acts 14), when Eunice and Timothy did. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both connect this verse with 2 Tim 3:15, where Timothy is said to have known the holy scriptures from childhood, and infer that Lois shared with Eunice in teaching him the Jewish Scriptures.

City of the Lord is a title given to Jerusalem in Isaiah 60:14, where the prophet says that those who once oppressed and despised the city will come bowing before it and will call it "The city of the LORD, The Zion of the Holy One of Israel." The pairing with Zion shows that Jerusalem is meant. The chapter describes a future restoration of the city. Its closing verse promises that "a little one shall become a thousand, and a small one a strong nation," and that the Lord will bring this about in his time (Isa 60:22). The same phrase is used of Jerusalem in Psalms such as Ps 48:8 and Ps 101:8. The location shown here is Jerusalem, at the Temple Mount.

The Lord's Prayer Taught is Luke's account of Jesus giving his disciples a model prayer. After Jesus finished praying in an unnamed place, one disciple asked him to teach them to pray, as John the Baptist had taught his own followers. Jesus gave a short prayer addressed to the Father. It asks that God's name be honored, his kingdom come and his will be done, and it asks for daily bread, forgiveness of sins as the one praying forgives others, and deliverance from temptation and evil. He followed it with a parable of a man who, at midnight, persuades a reluctant friend to lend him bread through persistence. He then urged them to ask, seek and knock, arguing that if human fathers give good gifts, the heavenly Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask. A longer form of the prayer appears in the Sermon on the Mount (Matt 6:9–13). The event is dated about AD 29 by inference from context.

Lot was the son of Haran and the nephew of Abraham (Abram). He left Ur of the Chaldees with his grandfather Terah, then went with Abram into Canaan and returned with him from Egypt. Their flocks grew so large that their herdsmen quarreled, and Abram proposed they part. Lot chose the well-watered plain of the Jordan and settled toward Sodom, later living in the city. When invading kings raided Sodom he was carried off, and Abram rescued him. Later two angels came to Sodom, and Lot took them into his house. When the men of the city attacked his door, the angels pulled him inside. They then hurried him, his wife and two daughters out before the cities were destroyed. Jesus later recalled Lot's wife as a warning (Luke 17:32). Lot fled to Zoar and then to a mountain cave. His daughters' sons, Moab and Ben-ammi, were ancestors of the Moabites and Ammonites, called the "children of Lot."

Lotan was the first-named son of Seir the Horite, whose family lived in the land later known as Edom before Esau's descendants settled there (Gen 36:20; 1 Chr 1:38). Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him the eldest son, probably because he heads every list of Seir's sons. His brothers were Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer and Dishan, and his sister was Timna, who is named alongside him in both genealogies (Gen 36:22; 1 Chr 1:39). He had two sons, Hori and Homam. Genesis spells the second name Hemam and Chronicles spells it Homam. Lotan also appears among the Horite chiefs, called "dukes" in the King James Version (Gen 36:29). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "coverer."

Lucifer is the name the King James Version uses in Isa 14:12, where the prophet addresses a figure as "Lucifer, son of the morning" who has fallen from heaven and been cut down to the ground after weakening the nations. The name comes from Latin and means "light-bearer" or "bringing light." Both the name and the epithet "son of the morning" point to a bright star, probably the morning star, the planet Venus. The surrounding passage is a taunt song against the king of Babylon (Isa 14:4), and Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both take the title as describing that king's splendor and his downfall. Smith's Bible Dictionary also notes a long Christian tradition, going back at least to Jerome, that applies the verse to Satan's fall from heaven. This entry follows the reading of the passage as addressed to the king of Babylon and also notes the later tradition.

Lucius was a Christian named twice in the New Testament. Lucius of Cyrene was one of the prophets and teachers in the church at Antioch, alongside Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Manaen and Saul, when that church sent Barnabas and Saul out on their first missionary journey, about AD 45 by inference from context (Acts 13:1). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he was probably one of the men of Cyprus and Cyrene who first preached to Greeks at Antioch (Acts 11:20). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that his name is Latin, while his home town suggests he was a Jew from Cyrene in North Africa. A Lucius also sends greetings in Paul's letter to the Romans, where Paul calls him one of his kinsmen (Rom 16:21). Whether this is the same man is uncertain. Easton's treats them as one person, and Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that some hold this view.

Lud was a son of Shem, and so a grandson of Noah. He is named fourth among Shem's sons in the genealogies of Gen 10:22 and 1 Chr 1:17. His brothers were Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad and Aram. Nothing is recorded about his life. He appears only in these lists, which trace peoples back to Noah's descendants. Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the Tyndale House proper-names index all connect him with the Lydians, a people of western Asia Minor in what is now western Turkey, and present him as their probable ancestor. He is a different figure from the Ludim, whom Gen 10:13 lists among the descendants of Mizraim (Egypt). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "strife."

Lud was a people and land named in the prophets, known especially for their archers. Isaiah lists Lud, "that draw the bow," among distant nations to which survivors would be sent to declare God's glory (Isa 66:19). In Jeremiah, the Lydians who "handle and bend the bow" march with Ethiopians and Libyans in Egypt's army (Jer 46:9). Ezekiel names men of Lud as soldiers serving Tyre (Ezek 27:10) and Lydia among Egypt's allies who would fall by the sword (Ezek 30:5). Where Lud was is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary links it to the Ludim descended from Mizraim (Gen 10:13), an African people west of Egypt. Others connect it with Lud son of Shem (Gen 10:22) or with Lydia in Asia Minor. Hitchcock's Bible Names treats the name as the same as Lod. The location shown here follows that identification, placing it at Lod (Lydda) in central Israel.

Ludim is named as the first of the sons of Mizraim, the son of Ham whose name is the Hebrew word for Egypt, in the table of nations (Gen 10:13; 1 Chr 1:11). His brothers were Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim, Pathrusim, Casluhim and Caphthorim. The name has a plural ending, as do the other names in this list, so it probably refers to a people descended from Mizraim rather than to a single individual. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the Ludim to be probably the same as the people called Lud, who appear alongside African nations as fighters in the Egyptian army in Jer 46:9. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests they lived west of Egypt, perhaps farther than any other people descended from Mizraim. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Luhith was a place in Moab, known for its ascent or climbing road, named only in the parallel prophecies against Moab in Isa 15:5 and Jer 48:5. In both passages, fugitives fleeing destruction go up the ascent of Luhith weeping, while a cry of destruction is heard on the road of Horonaim. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it between Zoar and Horonaim. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Eusebius and Jerome still knew the site, between Areopolis (Rabbath-moab) and Zoar. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it was a route by which refugees could climb from the low ground near the Dead Sea to the Moabite plateau, perhaps the road through Wadi Bene Hammad, though the site cannot be identified with certainty. The location shown here is a rough placement east of the Dead Sea in that general area. The name is often explained as meaning "made of boards."

Luke, also called Lucas, was a physician and companion of the apostle Paul. Paul calls him "the beloved physician" (Col 4:14), lists him among his fellow workers (Phlm 1:24), and in what reads as one of his last letters writes that "only Luke is with me" (2 Tim 4:11). Luke is traditionally held to be the author of the Gospel of Luke and the book of Acts. The "we" passages in Acts suggest the writer joined Paul at Troas, traveled to Philippi, rejoined him later on the journey to Jerusalem, and sailed with him through the shipwreck at Malta to Rome. Smith's Bible Dictionary infers that he was a Gentile, since Paul names him apart from those "of the circumcision" (Col 4:11), and records a tradition that he came from Antioch in Syria. His conversion, later life and death are uncertain.

Luz was the earlier name of the Canaanite city that became Bethel, in the hill country north of Jerusalem. Jacob named the place Bethel after his dream there, though the city was first called Luz (Gen 28:19). He later returned there with his household (Gen 35:6) and told Joseph that God Almighty had appeared to him and blessed him at Luz (Gen 48:3). In Joshua, Luz marks the boundary between Joseph's descendants and Benjamin (Josh 16:2; 18:13), and the house of Joseph scouted it before taking it (Judg 1:23). Because Josh 16:2 speaks of going 'from Bethel to Luz,' some treat them as separate places. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Bethel first named a nearby sanctuary whose name eventually replaced the town's. The location shown here places Luz at Bethel, probably near modern Beitin. A different Luz was later founded in the land of the Hittites (Judg 1:26).

Luz was a city built in "the land of the Hittites" by a man from the older Luz, the Canaanite town that the tribes of Joseph captured and renamed Bethel. By inference from the surrounding passage (Judg 1:23–25), he was the man who showed the Israelite scouts the way into his city and was spared when it fell. He then moved away, founded a new town and gave it his home city's name, which was still in use when Judges was written. The name probably means "almond tree" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia; Hitchcock's Bible Names). Its site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Luweiziyeh, about 4 miles northwest of Banias, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes no satisfactory identification. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the wider Hittite region of what is now southern Turkey and northern Syria.

Lycaonia was an inland region of central Asia Minor, in present-day south-central Turkey around the Konya plain. Acts 14:6 describes Paul and Barnabas fleeing there from Iconium to Lystra and Derbe, "cities of Lycaonia," and the surrounding countryside. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it west of Cappadocia and south of Galatia, and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes it as a mostly treeless, dry plain with salt lakes. Both note that Acts 14:11 mentions a local "speech of Lycaonia," a language different from ordinary Greek whose exact nature is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains that in Paul's day Lycaonia was divided: a western part belonging to the Roman province of Galatia, which held Lystra and Derbe, and an eastern part under a client king. It takes the Lystra and Derbe district to be the part meant in Acts. Paul probably passed through the region again on later journeys (Acts 16:1; 18:23).

Lycia was a mountainous coastal region in the southwest of Asia Minor, opposite the island of Rhodes, in what is now southwestern Turkey. Luke mentions it when describing Paul's voyage to Rome as a prisoner. After sailing past Cilicia and Pamphylia, the ship reached Myra, "a city of Lycia" (Acts 27:5), where Paul was moved onto a grain ship from Alexandria (Acts 27:6). This entry dates the voyage to about AD 56, by inference from context. Lycia's port of Patara also appears on an earlier journey of Paul (Acts 21:1). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Lycia came under Persian, Greek and then Roman control, becoming part of the Roman provincial system under the emperor Claudius. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes it as a stopping place on Paul's travels rather than a scene of his work. The location shown here marks the general region.

Lydda was a town in the coastal plain of Judea, near Joppa. Peter visited the believers living there during a tour of the region (Acts 9:32). There he healed Aeneas, a man paralyzed for eight years, and the residents of Lydda and Saron (Sharon) turned to the Lord (Acts 9:35). Because Lydda was close to Joppa, the disciples there sent two men to bring Peter after Dorcas died, and he raised her to life (Acts 9:38). By context these events date to about AD 38. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify Lydda with Old Testament Lod (1 Chr 8:12; Ezra 2:33) and place it about nine miles from Joppa on a road to Jerusalem. Easton's says it was later rebuilt under the name Diospolis. It is identified with the modern city of Lod in Israel, which matches the location shown here.

Lydia was a woman from the city of Thyatira who sold purple goods and lived in Philippi, where she met Paul during his second missionary journey, about AD 47 by inference from context. She already worshipped God, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes to mean she was a Gentile convert to Judaism. While she listened to Paul, the Lord opened her heart to his message. The next verse, Acts 16:15, records that she and her household were baptized and that she persuaded Paul and his companions to stay at her house. After Paul and Silas were released from prison, they went to her house, met the believers there, encouraged them, and left. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls her the first person in Europe to accept Christianity. Her trade and her ability to host guests suggest she had some wealth. Thyatira lay in the region of Lydia, so her name may simply mean "the Lydian woman."

Lydia's Conversion was the moment at Philippi, during Paul's Second Missionary Journey, when a woman named Lydia became a follower of Jesus. It is dated to about AD 47 by inference from context. On the sabbath, Paul and his companions went outside the city to a riverside where people customarily gathered to pray, and they spoke with the women there. The "we" in the account suggests that the writer, traditionally identified as Luke, was present. Silas and Timothy were also with Paul, by inference from the surrounding chapter. Lydia came from the city of Thyatira, sold purple goods, and already worshipped God. The text says the Lord opened her heart to pay attention to Paul's message. She and her household were baptized. She then urged the missionaries to stay in her house if they judged her faithful to the Lord, and she persuaded them. The event followed Paul's vision calling him to Macedonia.

Lysanias was the tetrarch, or regional ruler, of Abilene, named by Luke among the rulers in power when John the Baptist began preaching. Luke dates that moment to the fifteenth year of the Roman emperor Tiberius, when Pontius Pilate governed Judea, Herod Antipas ruled Galilee and his brother Philip ruled Ituraea and Trachonitis. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places this at about AD 26–28. Easton's Bible Dictionary locates Abilene, the district around the town of Abila, on the eastern slope of the Anti-Lebanon range near Damascus. The historian Josephus mentions an earlier Lysanias who ruled Chalcis and Abilene and was put to death about 36 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that inscriptions point to a later ruler of the same name, probably a descendant, and this entry follows that view. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "that drives away sorrow." Nothing else is recorded about him in the Bible.

Lystra was a city of Lycaonia in south-central Asia Minor, where Paul and Barnabas fled after being threatened at Iconium (Acts 14:6). There Paul healed a man who had been lame from birth (Acts 14:8). According to the wider chapter, the crowd took Barnabas and Paul for the gods Jupiter and Mercury and tried to offer sacrifices to them. Soon afterward Jews from Antioch and Iconium stirred up the people, and Paul was stoned and left for dead. After going on to Derbe, the missionaries came back through Lystra to strengthen the disciples (Acts 14:21). On a later journey Paul found Timothy there, a disciple well spoken of by the believers (Acts 16:1–2). Paul later recalled his sufferings at Lystra (2 Tim 3:11). Smith's Bible Dictionary placed it at the ruins of Bin-bir-Kilisseh. The location shown here follows the identification with a mound near Hatunsaray, south of modern Konya, Turkey.

Maacah (also spelled Maachah) was one of King David's wives and the mother of Absalom, David's third son. She was the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur, a small kingdom probably lying east of the Sea of Galilee. Both lists of David's sons name her, placing Absalom among the sons born to David at Hebron (2 Sam 3:3; 1 Chr 3:2). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Geshur as belonging to the old native population of the region, and the marriage probably formed a political alliance between David and Talmai. Later passages connect this family tie to Absalom's story: after killing his half-brother Amnon, Absalom fled to his grandfather Talmai in Geshur (2 Sam 13:37–38). His sister Tamar (2 Sam 13:1) was probably also Maacah's daughter, though the text does not name her mother. Nothing more is recorded about Maacah herself.

Maacah was a small Aramean (Syrian) kingdom near Geshur, northeast of Israel. When the Ammonites had offended David, they hired Syrian forces that included the king of Maacah and a thousand men (2 Sam 10:6). The parallel account says the king came with his people and camped before Medeba (1 Chr 19:7). In the battle, Maacah's troops stood apart in the open field while the Ammonites lined up at their city gate (2 Sam 10:8), and the narrative goes on to describe Joab defeating them. Eliphelet, one of David's mighty men, was the son of Ahasbai, called 'the Maachathite' (2 Sam 23:34), so his family probably came from this region. Its exact extent is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it east of the Hauran. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia puts it between Geshur and Mount Hermon, probably bordered by the Jordan. The rough location shown here, east of Hermon and south of Damascus, is closer to Easton's view.

Maacath was the homeland of the Maachathites, a people Israel did not drive out when it settled east of the Jordan. Joshua 13:13 says they and the neighboring Geshurites went on living among the Israelites "until this day." Maacath is the same territory called Maachah or Maacah elsewhere. Connected passages place it at the northern edge of Bashan near Mount Hermon, next to Geshur (Deut 3:14; Josh 12:5; 13:11). They also describe it as a small Aramean kingdom whose king later sent troops to help the Ammonites against David (2 Sam 10:6). Its exact borders are unknown. It probably lay in what is now southern Syria, east and southeast of Mount Hermon, toward the Golan and the Hauran. The location shown here is a rough placement in that general region.

Maachah (Daughter of Nahor) is the last-named child of Nahor, Abraham's brother, by his concubine Reumah. She is mentioned only once, in Gen 22:24, at the close of a list of Nahor's descendants. By inference from the surrounding passage (Gen 22:20), this list was reported to Abraham after the episode on Mount Moriah. Her full brothers were Tebah, Gaham and Thahash. Her half-brothers were the eight sons of Nahor's wife Milcah, among them Bethuel, whom the preceding verse names as the father of Rebekah. The verse itself does not state Maachah's sex, and the name is borne elsewhere in the Bible by both men and women. This entry follows Smith's Bible Dictionary in treating her as Nahor's daughter. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "pressed down" or "worn." Nothing further is recorded about her.

Maachah was a wife of Rehoboam king of Judah and the mother of King Abijah, and also of Attai, Ziza and Shelomith. She is called the daughter of Abishalom or Absalom, and also "Michaiah the daughter of Uriel of Gibeah" (2 Chr 13:2). Easton's Bible Dictionary reconciles these by taking Uriel as her father and Absalom's daughter Tamar as her mother, which makes her Absalom's granddaughter. This entry follows that view. Rehoboam loved her more than any of his other wives and concubines, and he made her son Abijah chief among his brothers so that he would become king. She is also called the mother of Asa, Abijah's son. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes this to mean grandmother, a woman who held the rank of king's mother. Asa removed her from that position because she had made an idol in a grove, and he burnt the idol at the brook Kidron.

Maachah was a concubine of Caleb, a member of the tribe of Judah, listed in the genealogies of Judah in 1 Chronicles. According to 1 Chr 2:48, she bore Caleb two sons, Sheber and Tirhanah. The next verse, 1 Chr 2:49, adds that she also bore Shaaph, the father of Madmannah, and Sheva, the father of Machbenah and Gibea. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies this Caleb as the son of Hezron, which matches the surrounding genealogy. Nothing else is recorded about her. Several other people in the Bible share the name Maachah, and she should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "pressed down" or "worn."

Maachah (wife of Machir) was the wife of Machir, a son of Manasseh, and the mother of Peresh and Sheresh (1 Chr 7:15–16). She is named only in this genealogy of the tribe of Manasseh. She is described as the sister of Huppim and Shuppim. An earlier verse, 1 Chr 7:12, calls Huppim and Shuppim "the children of Ir" in a Benjamite list, so this entry gives Ir as her father, by inference from that passage. The Hebrew of 1 Chr 7:15 is difficult, and its wording about who is whose sister is unclear. This entry follows the plain statement of 1 Chr 7:16, which calls Maachah the wife of Machir. She named her son Peresh. His brother Sheresh had sons named Ulam and Rakem. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of her name as "pressed down" or "worn."

Maachah was the wife of Jehiel, the "father of Gibeon," meaning probably its founder or leading settler, in the genealogy of Saul's family in 1 Chronicles (1 Chr 8:29; 9:35). The name is shared by several people in the Bible. The surrounding verses name her sons as Abdon, Zur, Kish, Baal, Ner, Nadab, Gedor, Ahio, Zacher and Mikloth. Her husband appears here as Abiel. By inference, Jehiel is the same man as Abiel, since 1 Sam 9:1 and 14:51 call Kish and Ner sons of Abiel. The STEPBible proper names index identifies her as the mother of Kish, the father of King Saul. However, 1 Chr 9:39 makes Ner the father of Kish and grandfather of Saul, so her son Kish may instead have been Saul's great-uncle. The genealogies leave this uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of her name as "pressed down."

Maachah was the father of Hanan, who appears in the list of David's mighty warriors in 1 Chr 11:43. Nothing more is recorded about him, and the verse gives no clan or hometown, unlike many other names in the list. The name Maachah (also spelled Maacah) is shared by several people in the Bible, both men and women, as well as by a small Aramean kingdom near the upper Jordan. Some take "son of Maachah" to point to a family or regional link with that kingdom, but the text does not say so, and this entry treats Maachah as Hanan's father. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Hanan as one of David's bodyguard. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "pressed down; worn; fastened."

Maachah was a man of the tribe of Simeon, known only as the father of Shephatiah. His son was the ruler of the Simeonites in the list of tribal leaders of Israel in 1 Chr 27:16. That list belongs to the account of David's administration, so Shephatiah served in David's reign, as Smith's Bible Dictionary also notes. Nothing else is recorded about Maachah himself. Several other people in the Bible bear the name Maachah, both men and women, and this one should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "pressed down" or "worn."

Maachah, also called Maoch, was the father of Achish, king of the Philistine city of Gath. He is known only through his son. As Maoch, he is named when David and his six hundred men went over to Achish to escape Saul (1 Sam 27:2). As Maachah, he is named when two of Shimei's servants ran away to Achish early in Solomon's reign (1 Kgs 2:39). The two accounts are several decades apart, so some readers take the two kings named Achish to be different men, perhaps grandfather and grandson. This entry follows Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, which treat Maoch and Maachah as one person, the father of a single Achish. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "oppression." Several other people in the Bible share the name Maachah.

Maadai was one of the descendants of Bani listed in Ezra 10:34 among the men of Israel who had married foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was among those who agreed under Ezra's leadership to send away their foreign wives. "Sons of Bani" here probably means members of the family or clan of Bani rather than his literal sons. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "ornament of Jehovah," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "pleasant" or "testifying."

Maai was a Levite musician who took part in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. He is named only in Neh 12:36, among the "brethren" of Zechariah son of Jonathan, a descendant of Asaph who played the trumpet in the preceding verse (Neh 12:35). This entry treats these men as Jonathan's sons and so as Zechariah's brothers, though the word may simply mean kinsmen or fellow Levites of the Asaph line. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both describe him as an Asaphite. With the others in his group he played "the musical instruments of David the man of God" in the procession led by Ezra the scribe. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "compassionate," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "belly; heaping up." Nothing else is known of him.

Maarath was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed among the cities given to the tribe of Judah in Josh 15:59. It appears in a group of six towns with their surrounding villages, named between Gedor and Beth-anoth. The Bible says nothing more about it. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "desolation." Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify it as probably the modern village of Beit Ummar, about 6 miles (10 km) north of Hebron. The village lies on the watershed just west of the road to Hebron, about a mile from Khirbet Jedur, which is thought to be ancient Gedor. The location shown here follows the Beit Ummar identification.

Maareh-geba was the place near Gibeah from which Israel's hidden ambush broke out against the Benjamites, while the main army drew up at Baal-tamar (Judg 20:33). This was during the war the other tribes waged on Benjamin over the crime committed at Gibeah, as the surrounding chapters relate. The King James Version does not treat the Hebrew as a name and translates it "the meadows of Gibeah." The Revised Version margin gives "the meadow of Geba (or Gibeah)." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia points to a Greek manuscript reading and proposes "to the west of Geba." The Syriac version reads it as "the cave of Geba." This entry treats it as a place name, following the STEPBible proper-names list. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is a rough one near Gibeah, which is commonly identified with Tell el-Ful just north of Jerusalem.

Maaseiah was a Levite of the second rank whom David appointed when the ark was brought up to Jerusalem from the house of Obed-edom. He is listed with his fellow Levites among the gatekeepers ("porters") in 1 Chr 15:18. In 1 Chr 15:20 he is named again among the musicians assigned to play psalteries (harps or lyres) "on Alamoth," probably a musical term for a high register. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a porter for the ark, while Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia emphasise his role as a musician. The two verses together suggest he served in both capacities. His name means "the work of the Lord." Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, and nothing further is recorded about this one.

Maaseiah, son of Adaiah, was one of the "captains of hundreds" whom the priest Jehoiada brought into a covenant with him in the seventh year, according to 2 Chr 23:1. From the surrounding chapter and the parallel account in 2 Kings 11, this was the pact that ended Queen Athaliah's rule and placed the young Joash (Jehoash) on the throne of Judah. Maaseiah is named alongside four other commanders and is not mentioned elsewhere. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him a Levite captain, and the Tyndale House proper-names index describes him as a priest. The name means "work of the Lord" (Hitchcock's Bible Names) and is borne by several other men in the Old Testament, so he should not be confused with the others called Maaseiah.

Maaseiah was an officer in the reign of King Uzziah of Judah. He is called "the ruler", meaning an official, in 2 Chr 26:11. Together with Jeiel the scribe, he kept the count of Uzziah's army, which went out to war in organized bands. Both men worked under Hananiah, one of the king's captains. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he was probably a Levite serving in a semi-military role, comparing the Levite officers of 1 Chr 23:4. His name means "work of the Lord". Several other men in the Bible share this name, and nothing links this officer to any of them. He is mentioned only in this one verse.

Maaseiah was a son of King Ahaz of Judah, called "the king's son" in his only appearance (2 Chr 28:7). This made him a brother of Hezekiah, who succeeded Ahaz as king (2 Kgs 18:1). He was killed by Zichri, "a mighty man of Ephraim," along with Azrikam, the governor of the palace, and Elkanah, who was second to the king. The surrounding passage places this during the war in which Pekah, king of Israel, invaded Judah and inflicted heavy losses. The phrase "king's son" is sometimes read as a title for a royal official rather than a literal son. This entry follows the reading that he was Ahaz's son, as Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia do. The name, meaning "work of the Lord" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), is shared by several other people in the Bible.

Maaseiah was the governor of Jerusalem under King Josiah of Judah. In the eighteenth year of Josiah's reign, after the king had purged the land and the temple of idolatry, he sent Maaseiah with Shaphan son of Azaliah and Joah son of Joahaz, the recorder, to repair the house of the Lord (2 Chr 34:8). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the Hebrew word behind "governor" (sar) is rendered elsewhere in the King James Version as "prince," "chief captain" or "chief ruler," so it denotes a high official of the city. The name means "work of the Lord" and was common in the late monarchy and the exile, so several men in the Bible bear it. This Maaseiah appears only in this verse. The parallel account in 2 Kings 22 names Shaphan but not Maaseiah.

Maaseiah was a priest in Ezra's time, about the mid-5th century BC by inference from context.
