He was one of the descendants of Jeshua son of Jozadak, the high priest who led worship among the exiles who returned from Babylon. Ezra 10:18 lists him first among the priests of Jeshua's family who had married foreign wives. The following verse says these men pledged to send their wives away and offered a ram as a guilt offering. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names interprets as "the work of the Lord." Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that four men called Maaseiah appear in Ezra's list of those with foreign wives, so this one should be kept distinct from the others.

Maaseiah was a priest, one of the descendants of Harim, who is listed among the men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra (Ezra 10:21). He appears in a list of five sons of Harim. The surrounding chapter records that these men agreed to send away their foreign wives. The context places him in the mid-5th century BC, after the return from exile in Babylon. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him among four men of this name who had married foreign wives in Ezra's day. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names gives as meaning "the work of the Lord," was common, and several other people in the Bible bear it. Nothing more is known about him.

Maaseiah was a priest of the family of Pashur. He is listed among the men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra (Ezra 10:22). The surrounding passage in Ezra 10 describes how these men agreed to send away their foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the Tyndale House STEPBible names list both identify him as a priest, and that fits the context, because the sons of Pashur appear in Ezra's list of priestly families. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as meaning "the work of the Lord," was borne by several men in the Bible. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that four men named Maaseiah appear in Ezra's list of those who had married foreign wives, so this one should not be confused with the others.

Maaseiah was one of the descendants of Pahath-moab listed in Ezra 10:30 among the Israelite men who had married foreign women in Ezra's time. The context of Ezra 10 shows that these men agreed to put away their foreign wives after the return from exile. He was a layman, not a priest or Levite, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes, and he appears in a group of eight sons of Pahath-moab. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names gives as meaning "the work of the Lord," was borne by several people in the Bible. Smith's Bible Dictionary lists four men named Maaseiah among those who had married foreign wives in this one chapter, so he should not be confused with the others of the same name.

Maaseiah, son of Ananiah, was the father of Azariah. He is known only from the genealogy given for his son in the list of those who rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah. According to Neh 3:23, Azariah repaired a section of the wall beside his own house, next to the section worked on by Benjamin and Hashub. Since Azariah was active then, Maaseiah probably lived during or shortly before the return from exile in the 5th century BC. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, meaning "the work of the Lord" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), was common in this period, and several other men called Maaseiah appear in Ezra, Nehemiah and elsewhere. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats this Maaseiah as a separate individual, and this entry does the same.

Maaseiah was one of the men who stood at Ezra's right hand on the wooden platform when Ezra the scribe read the law to the people in Jerusalem after the return from exile. He is named alongside Mattithiah, Shema, Anaiah, Urijah and Hilkiah, while another group stood on Ezra's left (Neh 8:4). The verse gives no further detail about his family or role. The STEPBible Proper Names index (Tyndale House) describes him as a Levite who assisted Ezra in reading the law. The name means "work of the Lord" and was common in this period, so several different men called Maaseiah appear in Ezra, Nehemiah and elsewhere. It is uncertain whether this man is the same as any of them.

Maaseiah was one of the men who helped the people understand the law when Ezra read it publicly in Jerusalem after the return from exile, in the time of Nehemiah (Neh 8:7). He is named in a list with Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah and others alongside the Levites, while the people stood in their places. The wording leaves open whether these named men were themselves Levites, but Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper names index both describe him as a Levite, and this entry follows that view. His name means "work of the Lord" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other men in the Bible are called Maaseiah, including some from Ezra's time, so it is uncertain whether this Maaseiah appears anywhere else. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Maaseiah is one of several men of this name in the Bible. This one appears only in Neh 10:25, in the list of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the written covenant made in Nehemiah's time. In that covenant the returned community of Jerusalem pledged to keep the law of Moses. He is named between Rehum and Hashabnah, and nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of the heads of the people whose descendants signed the covenant, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats him as one of those who took part in sealing it. The name means "work of the Lord." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it was common in late monarchic and exilic times, so linking him with any other Maaseiah is uncertain.

Maaseiah, son of Baruch, was a man of the tribe of Judah who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile. He appears in Nehemiah's list of the people who settled in the city, where his ancestry is traced back through Colhozeh, Hazaiah, Adaiah, Joiarib and Zechariah to Shiloni (Neh 11:5). By inference from the surrounding passage, he is named as one of the heads of the Judahite families living in Jerusalem. "Shiloni" is often taken to mean a descendant of Shelah, son of Judah, though Smith's Bible Dictionary links him to the line of Perez. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies him with Asaiah, listed among the Shilonites in the parallel list at 1 Chr 9:5. The name means "work of the Lord" and was shared by several other men in the Bible.

Maaseiah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only in the genealogy of Sallu in Neh 11:7. He was the son of Ithiel and the father of Kolaiah, and so an ancestor several generations back of Sallu son of Meshullam, one of the Benjamites who settled in Jerusalem after the return from exile. The verse gives no further details about his life. His name, often explained as "the work of the Lord" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), was common in the later monarchy and exile, according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, and several different men in the Bible bear it. This Maaseiah should not be confused with the others of the same name, such as those listed in Ezra's time as having married foreign wives.

Maaseiah was a priest in Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah, about the mid-5th century BC by inference from context. He appears only in Neh 12:41, in a list of seven priests who played trumpets at the dedication of the rebuilt city wall. The others were Eliakim, Miniamin, Michaiah, Elioenai, Zechariah and Hananiah. From the surrounding passage, this group probably marched with the thanksgiving company that Nehemiah himself followed around the wall to the temple. His name means "work of the Lord" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Many men in the Bible share the name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts this Maaseiah as separate from another of the same name listed in the very next verse, among the priests and singers of the same ceremony. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Maaseiah was a priest who took part in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. He is named first in a list of eight men, alongside Shemaiah, Eleazar, Uzzi, Jehohanan, Malchijah, Elam and Ezer, who stood at the ceremony while the singers sang loudly under the direction of Jezrahiah (Neh 12:42). The verse itself does not state his role, but the STEPBible Proper Names index identifies him as a priest who sang during the dedication, and the context of the processions in this chapter supports that reading. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name Maaseiah was common, especially among priests and Levites of the period, so he cannot be firmly linked to any other man of that name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "the work of the Lord."

Maaseiah was the father of Zephaniah, a priest in Jerusalem in the last years of the kingdom of Judah. He is known only through his son, who is always identified as "Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah." King Zedekiah twice sent Zephaniah to the prophet Jeremiah, once to ask about Nebuchadnezzar's attack (Jer 21:1) and once to ask Jeremiah to pray for the nation (Jer 37:3). Zephaniah also received letters sent from Babylon to Jerusalem (Jer 29:25). The phrase "the priest" in these verses can be read as describing either the son or the father. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it to refer to Zephaniah, while the STEPBible names index treats Maaseiah himself as a priest. Since priesthood was hereditary, both were probably of priestly families. His name means "work of the LORD." Several other men in the Bible share it.

Maaseiah was the father of Zedekiah, a prophet among the Jewish exiles in Babylon whom Jeremiah condemned. In his letter to the exiles, Jeremiah names Zedekiah son of Maaseiah, together with Ahab son of Kolaiah, as men who prophesied lies in the Lord's name, and he announces that Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon would hand them over and kill them before the exiles' eyes (Jer 29:21). Nothing is recorded about Maaseiah himself beyond his being Zedekiah's father. The name, meaning "work of the Lord" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, was common in the late monarchy and the exile, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. Several other men in the Bible share it, and there is no clear way to link this Maaseiah with any of them.

Maaseiah was the father of Neriah and so the grandfather of two brothers who appear in the book of Jeremiah. One was Baruch, to whom Jeremiah handed the deed of the field he bought at Anathoth (Jer 32:12). The other was Seraiah, who went with King Zedekiah to Babylon in the fourth year of his reign and carried Jeremiah's message against Babylon (Jer 51:59). Nothing else is recorded about Maaseiah himself. The name, meaning "work of the Lord" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, belongs to several men in the Bible. The Hebrew spelling in these verses is Mahseiah, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and STEPBible use that form for him. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a priest, which the two verses here do not state.

Maaseiah, son of Shallum, was an official at the temple in Jerusalem during the reign of Jehoiakim, king of Judah. Jeremiah mentions him while describing where he brought the Rechabites. They were taken into the chamber of the sons of Hanan, which was next to the princes' chamber and above the chamber of Maaseiah (Jer 35:4). He is called "the keeper of the door," one of the officers who guarded the temple threshold. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the title as his. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Levite of high rank and compares 1 Chr 9:19, where a Shallum and his family are keepers of the gates. That connection is suggestive but not certain. His name means "work of the Lord." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and nothing else is recorded about this one.

Maasiai was a priest of the family of Immer who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears in the list of priests in 1 Chr 9:12, where he is called the son of Adiel, and descends through Jahzerah, Meshullam and Meshillemith from Immer. Nehemiah 11:13 names a priest Amashai, son of Azareel, son of Ahasai, son of Meshillemoth, son of Immer, in its list of Jerusalem's residents in Nehemiah's time. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the two as apparently the same man, and this entry follows that view. The two lists name different fathers and intermediate ancestors, though both reach back to Immer. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives his name the meaning "work of the Lord."

Maath is a man named only once, in Luke's genealogy of Jesus (Luke 3:26). He is listed as the son of Mattathias and the father of Nagge. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts him as the twelfth generation before Joseph, the husband of Mary. Since the same list names Zerubbabel a few generations earlier and traces the line back through David, Maath probably lived after the Babylonian exile and belonged to the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "small," and Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "wiping away" or "breaking."

Maaz was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:27. He was the first-listed son of Ram, who was the firstborn of Jerahmeel, and his brothers were Jamin and Eker. Jerahmeel was a son of Hezron and a grandson of Perez, son of Judah, so Maaz belonged to the Jerahmeelite branch of Judah's descendants. This Ram, Jerahmeel's son, is different from Ram the brother of Jerahmeel, who was an ancestor of David. Nothing else is recorded about Maaz. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "wood" or "wooden."

Maaziah was a priest in the time of King David, the head of the twenty-fourth and last of the priestly divisions. According to the surrounding chapter, David organized the descendants of Aaron's sons Eleazar and Ithamar into twenty-four groups, or courses, by casting lots. Each course took its turn serving at the sanctuary, and the final lot fell to Maaziah (1 Chr 24:18). Apart from this assignment, nothing more is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "consolation of Jehovah." A priest with the same name appears in Nehemiah's time as one of those who sealed the covenant (Neh 10:8). He lived centuries later and is generally treated as a different man, though the shared name may reflect the continuing priestly line.

Macedonia was a Roman province north of Greece and the first part of Europe where Paul preached. In a night vision a man of Macedonia begged Paul, "Come over into Macedonia, and help us," and he crossed over to Philippi, described as the chief city of that part of the province (Acts 16:9–12). Paul later sent Timothy and Erastus there and passed through again on his way to Jerusalem (Acts 19:21–22; 20:1–3). Its churches, including those at Philippi and Thessalonica, gave to the poor believers in Jerusalem and supplied Paul's own needs (Rom 15:26; 2 Cor 8:1; 11:9; Phil 4:15). Paul wrote 2 Corinthians during this period, probably from Macedonia. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that it was governed by a proconsul, and Smith's Bible Dictionary places his residence at Thessalonica. The region corresponds broadly to northern Greece today, and the location shown here is near modern Thessaloniki.

Machbanai was a warrior from the tribe of Gad who joined David while David was a fugitive from Saul. He is named only in 1 Chr 12:13, as the eleventh of eleven Gadite leaders. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 12:8–14) describes these Gadites as skilled fighters with faces like lions and as swift as gazelles, and calls them captains of the army. That context suggests Machbanai held a command, though the verse does not say how large. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper names index both connect his coming to David with the period David spent at Ziklag, the setting introduced at the start of the chapter. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "bond of the Lord." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Machbenah was a town in the territory of Judah, mentioned only once, in the genealogy of Caleb's descendants. 1 Chr 2:49 calls Sheva the "father of Machbenah." In these lists "father" often means the founder or leading figure of a settlement, so Machbenah is probably a place name rather than a person. The preceding verse (1 Chr 2:48) names Sheva's mother as Maachah, Caleb's concubine. The same verse links nearby towns such as Madmannah and Gibea to Caleb's family, which points to southern Judah. The exact site is unknown. The location shown here places it in the Judean lowlands (the Shephelah), east of Lachish. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "bond," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "poverty" or "the smiting of his son."

Machi was a man of the tribe of Gad, known only as the father of Geuel. Geuel was the Gadite chosen as one of the twelve men Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan, a group that included Caleb and Joshua (Num 13:15). Nothing else is recorded about Machi himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Syriac Peshitta and some manuscripts of the Greek Septuagint read his name as "Machir." Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "decrease," while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "poor" or "a smiter."

Machir was the firstborn son of Manasseh and a grandson of Joseph, born to Manasseh's Aramean concubine (Josh 17:1; 1 Chr 7:14). Joseph lived to see Machir's children, who were raised on his knees (Gen 50:23). Machir married Maachah. His children included Gilead, Peresh, Sheresh and Hammoleketh, as well as a daughter who married Hezron of Judah. His descendants, the Machirites, traced their line through Gilead, and the daughters of Zelophehad belonged to this family. Machir is called a man of war. His clan took Gilead from the Amorites, and Moses gave them that land and parts of Bashan east of the Jordan. In the Song of Deborah, Machir stands for this branch of Manasseh (Judg 5:14). Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he may have been Manasseh's only son. The name is shared with another man, Machir son of Ammiel, who appears in David's time (2 Sam 9:4).

Machir son of Ammiel was a man of Lodebar, a town east of the Jordan, in whose house Jonathan's lame son Mephibosheth was living when King David looked for surviving members of Saul's family. After Ziba told David where Mephibosheth was, David sent and brought him from Machir's house (2 Sam 9:4–5). Later, when David fled from Absalom's rebellion and reached Mahanaim, Machir was one of three men who came to meet him, along with Shobi of Rabbah and Barzillai the Gileadite. The following verses (2 Sam 17:28–29) say they brought bedding, food and supplies for David and his people. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a powerful chief who served the house of Saul and then David. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "selling" or "knowing." He is distinct from the better-known Machir, son of Manasseh.

Machnadebai was one of the Israelite men listed in Ezra 10:40 among those who had married foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon. The list in Ezra 10 records men who agreed, at Ezra's urging, to send away their foreign wives. By inference from the surrounding verses, he belonged to the group descended from Bani (Ezra 10:34), as Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both understand him. Nothing more is known about him beyond his name in this list. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests "what is like the liberal?", and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "smiter."

Machpelah was a cave, together with the field around it, near Hebron in Canaan, described as lying "before Mamre" (Gen 23:17, 19). The name is usually taken to mean "double," and the Greek Septuagint calls it the "double cave" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Abraham bought the field and cave from Ephron the Hittite as a family burial place and buried Sarah there (Gen 23:9, 19). His sons Isaac and Ishmael later buried Abraham there, about 1821 BC by inference from context (Gen 25:9). Jacob asked to be buried there, noting that Isaac, Rebekah and Leah already lay there (Gen 49:30–31), and his sons carried his body from Egypt to the cave (Gen 50:13). Jewish, Christian and Muslim tradition places the cave beneath the massive walled enclosure known as the Haram in Hebron, which some date to Herod's time (Easton's Bible Dictionary). The location shown here follows that identification.

Madai was one of the seven sons of Japheth, the son of Noah, and a brother of Gomer, Magog, Javan, Tubal, Meshech and Tiras. He appears only in the genealogies of the nations in Gen 10:2 and its repetition in 1 Chr 1:5, and no personal details are recorded. His name is the same Hebrew word used elsewhere in the Bible for the Medes, and he is generally regarded as their ancestor. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that Mada is the name by which the Medes appear on Assyrian monuments. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the list may be naming peoples rather than individual sons, so that the entry means the Medes were counted among Japheth's descendants. The Medes lived in the region south and southwest of the Caspian Sea, in what is now northwestern Iran.

Madmannah was a town in the far south (the Negev) of Judah, listed among the tribe's southern towns between Ziklag and Sansannah (Josh 15:31). In the genealogy of Caleb, Shaaph, a son of Caleb's concubine Maacah, is called "the father of Madmannah" (1 Chr 2:49). This probably means he founded or led the town's settlers rather than that he had a son of that name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that Beth-marcaboth, in the parallel list of Simeon's towns (Josh 19:5), stands for the same place. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the name's meaning as "dunghill." The site is uncertain. Smith's and Easton's identify it with el-Minyay, south-southwest of Gaza. The Palestine Exploration survey proposed Umm Deimneh, about 12 miles northeast of Beersheba. The location shown here follows the Umm Deimneh identification.

Madmen was a town in Moab, mentioned only in Jeremiah's prophecy against Moab, where it is told it will be cut down and pursued by the sword (Jer 48:2). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "dunghill." From the wider context of Jeremiah's oracles, Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the threatened sword to be that of the Babylonians. The Hebrew line contains a wordplay between "Madmen" and the verb for being silenced or cut down. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the initial "M" may have come from repeating the last letter of the word before it, so the name may originally have been "Dimon," another form of Dibon. Otherwise the town is unidentified. The location shown here lies close to Dibon (modern Dhiban, in Jordan), which fits that identification.

Madmenah was a town north of Jerusalem, named only in Isaiah's poetic description of an Assyrian army advancing on the city (Isa 10:31). In that passage, Madmenah "is removed" and the people of nearby Gebim gather to flee, picturing villages emptied in panic as the invader draws near. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it among the Benjamite villages along the northern approach and links the advance to Sennacherib. Easton's Bible Dictionary also puts it in Benjamin, not far north of Jerusalem. It notes that the same Hebrew word appears in Isa 25:10, where it is translated "dunghill." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says the site has not been identified, so its exact location is unknown. The location shown here is a rough placement just north of Jerusalem, inferred from the route described in the passage.

Madon was a Canaanite royal city in the north of the land. Its king, Jobab, was one of the rulers Jabin king of Hazor summoned into a coalition against Joshua (Josh 11:1). The following verses of that chapter describe the allied kings gathering at the waters of Merom and being defeated. Madon's king appears in the list of kings Joshua defeated (Josh 12:19). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "strife" and suggests the ruin Madin, near Hattin, about 5 miles (8 km) west of Tiberias. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that the Hebrew letters for "d" and "r" were confused and that the name should read "Maron," which it identifies with Meiron, northwest of Safed. The location shown here follows the identification near Hattin, west of the Sea of Galilee.

Magadan was a place on the shore of the Sea of Galilee. Jesus sailed there after sending away the crowd he had fed (Matt 15:39). The King James Version reads "Magdala," but the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the better manuscripts read Magadan. In the parallel account, Mark 8:10 names the destination Dalmanutha instead, so the two were probably neighbouring districts on the western shore. Many link Magadan with Magdala, the home of Mary Magdalene. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary treat the names as the same place, or as villages close together, and the name probably comes from the Hebrew word for "tower." The location shown here follows the identification with el-Mejdel (modern Migdal), at the southwest corner of the Plain of Gennesaret, about 3 miles northwest of Tiberias.

Magdiel was one of the chiefs, called "dukes" in the King James Version, of Edom, the people descended from Esau. His name appears near the end of the list of Edomite chiefs given "according to their habitations" in Gen 36:43, and again in the parallel list in 1 Chr 1:54, both times paired with Iram. Because the chiefs are listed by where they lived, the name may stand for a clan or district as well as a person. Nothing more is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "prince of God," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "declaring God" or "chosen fruit of God."

Magog was the second of the seven sons of Japheth, Noah's son, named in the table of nations alongside Gomer, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech and Tiras (Gen 10:2; 1 Chr 1:5). Elsewhere the name refers to a people or land. Ezekiel speaks of "Gog, the land of Magog," whose ruler is chief prince of Meshech and Tubal, and says God will send fire on Magog (Ezek 38:2; 39:6). In Rev 20:8, "Gog and Magog" stand for the nations of the four quarters of the earth gathered for battle. The people's identity is uncertain. Josephus links the Magogites with the Scythians, a view also taken by Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries. Others connect the name with Gyges (Gugu), king of Lydia. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Magog may simply be a variant of Gog.

Magog is a region or people named in Ezekiel's prophecy as "the land of Magog," whose ruler Gog is called the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal (Ezek 38:2). God declares he will send fire on Magog (Ezek 39:6). In Rev 20:8 "Gog and Magog" stand for the nations from the four corners of the earth that are gathered for battle, as numerous as the sand of the sea. Elsewhere, Gen 10:2 and 1 Chr 1:5 list Magog as the second son of Japheth, which suggests the people took their name from him. Its exact location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it to be a Scythian or Tartar people, citing Jerome, who placed such nations beyond the Caucasus and near the Caspian Sea. Another suggestion links the name to the Assyrian "land of Gugu." The rough location shown here follows the Caucasus and Caspian view.

Magpiash was one of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the written covenant made in the time of Nehemiah, when the community that had returned to Jerusalem pledged to keep the law of Moses. He appears only in the list of signers, between Ahiah and Meshullam's neighbours in the list (Neh 10:20), and nothing else is recorded about him. Because the leaders in this part of the list often represent family or clan names, Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him with Magbish, a family whose descendants returned from exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:30). The name may then stand for that family rather than a single individual. Smith's gives the meaning of the name as "moth-killer," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "a body thrust hard together."

Mahalab was a place on the boundary of the tribe of Asher, in the description of that border near Tyre and Achzib in Josh 19:29. The King James Version does not show it as a name. It translates the Hebrew phrase as "from the coast to Achzib," but many modern translations read the same words as "from Mahalab to Achzib." Some scholars identify Mahalab with the town called Mahalliba in Assyrian records, and possibly with Ahlab, a town of Asher named in Judges. These links are inferences and remain uncertain. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here places it inland, southeast of Tyre, in the hills near the modern border between Lebanon and Israel.

Mahalah was a descendant of Manasseh, named once in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles as one of three children of Hammoleketh, along with Ishod and Abiezer (1 Chr 7:18). The verse calls Hammoleketh "his sister." From the surrounding verses, Smith's Bible Dictionary takes this to mean the sister of Gilead, so Mahalah belonged to the Manassite clan of Gilead. The text does not say whether Mahalah was male or female. This entry treats Mahalah as female. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Revised Version spells the name Mahlah. That is the same name as one of Zelophehad's daughters, who seems to be a different person. Smith's gives the meaning of the name as "disease." Nothing else is recorded about Mahalah.

Mahalaleel (line of Seth) was a patriarch who lived before the flood, the son of Cainan and a descendant of Seth. According to Genesis 5, his father was seventy when he was born. Mahalaleel fathered Jared at sixty-five, lived another 830 years, had other sons and daughters, and died at the age of 895. Through Jared he was an ancestor of Enoch, Methuselah and Noah. The Chronicler lists him between Kenan and Jered in the genealogy from Adam (1 Chr 1:2). Luke's genealogy of Jesus, tracing the line back to Adam, uses the Greek form of his name, Maleleel (Luke 3:37). This entry dates his life to about 3609–2714 BC, by inference from the ages given in Genesis.

Mahalaleel was a man of the tribe of Judah, descended from Perez, who appears only in the genealogy of Athaiah in Neh 11:4. He was the father of Shephatiah, and through him an ancestor of Athaiah, one of the people of Judah who lived in Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time after the return from exile. Nothing else is recorded about him, and when he lived is not stated. His name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary renders as "praise of God," is also borne by other people in the Bible, most notably the son of Cainan in the early genealogy of Genesis. This Mahalaleel is a separate, much later individual.

Mahalath was one of the wives of Rehoboam, king of Judah and son of Solomon. She was the daughter of Jerimoth, a son of David, which made her a granddaughter of David and a cousin of her husband. Jerimoth does not appear in the main lists of David's sons, so he may have been the son of a concubine, as 1 Chr 3:9 mentions such sons without naming them. Her birthplace in Jerusalem is inferred from her family's place in the royal household. The verse naming her also names Abihail, a descendant of David's brother Eliab. The next verse (2 Chr 11:19) credits sons to "her," but it is unclear whether this means Mahalath or Abihail. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts her among Rehoboam's eighteen wives. She is a different person from Mahalath the daughter of Ishmael, whom Esau married (Gen 28:9).

Mahanaim was a town east of the Jordan River, near the Jabbok. Its name means "two camps". Jacob gave it the name after meeting God's angels there on his way home (Gen 32:2). It marked a boundary between the lands of Gad and eastern Manasseh (Josh 13:26, 30). It was also given with its pasturelands to the Levites (Josh 21:38; 1 Chr 6:80). After Saul's death, Abner made Saul's son Ishbosheth king there (2 Sam 2:8, 12). Later David took refuge there during Absalom's revolt, and Barzillai and others brought him food and supplies (2 Sam 17:24, 27; 19:32). Under Solomon it was the seat of a district officer (1 Kgs 4:14). The exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the ruin of Mukhumah south of the Jabbok. The rough location shown here places it near the Jabbok a little east of the Jordan Valley.

Mahaneh-dan, meaning "camp of Dan," was a place in the lowlands west of Jerusalem linked with the tribe of Dan. Judg 13:25 places it between Zorah and Eshtaol and says this is where the Spirit of the LORD began to move Samson. Judg 18:12 explains the name: the six hundred Danites who set out from Zorah and Eshtaol to seize Laish camped "behind" Kirjath-jearim in Judah, and the spot was called Mahaneh-dan from then on. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes "behind" to mean west of Kirjath-jearim. Some have thought the two descriptions point to different places, but the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Sorek Valley area west of Kirjath-jearim, where Zorah and Eshtaol stand, fits both. No site with a matching name has been found. The location shown here follows that view and places it between Zorah and Eshtaol.

Maharai the Netophathite was one of David's mighty men, the elite warriors listed in 2 Sam 23:28 and 1 Chr 11:30. His title links him to Netophah, a town near Bethlehem in Judah. He also appears in David's military organization as the tenth of twelve commanders who each served one month of the year in rotation. His division of 24,000 men was on duty in the tenth month (1 Chr 27:13). The same verse describes him as one of the Zarhites, the descendants of Zerah, son of Judah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes this to mean he belonged to the family of Zerah and lived in Netophah. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "impetuous."

Mahath, also called Ahimoth, was a Levite of the clan of Kohath who appears only in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 6. In 1 Chr 6:35 he is the son of Amasai and the father of Elkanah, in the line that runs back from Heman the singer, appointed in David's time, through Samuel's ancestors to Kohath. The parallel list in 1 Chr 6:25 gives the name as Ahimoth and names him with Amasai as sons of an earlier Elkanah. That makes the two brothers there rather than father and son. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the two names as probably the same person, and this entry follows that view. The name Mahath is shared by others, including a Levite in Hezekiah's reign mentioned in 2 Chronicles. Whether that man is connected to this one is uncertain. The ancestor is otherwise known only by name.

Mahath son of Amasai was a Kohathite Levite in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He is named first among the Levites who rose to answer Hezekiah's call to sanctify themselves and cleanse the temple in Jerusalem (2 Chr 29:12). Alongside Joel son of Azariah he represented the Kohathite branch of the tribe of Levi, while others came from the Merarite and Gershonite families. The surrounding chapter describes this cleansing, and in it the Levites removed the defilement that had built up in the temple. The name Mahath is borne by more than one person in the Bible. Whether this Mahath is the same as the Mahath later listed among Hezekiah's temple overseers (2 Chr 31:13) is uncertain, though the shared name and period make it possible. The genealogy of Heman in 1 Chr 6:35 also names a Mahath son of Amasai, an earlier ancestor of the same family line.

Mahath was a Levite in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He was one of ten overseers who worked under Cononiah and his brother Shimei, by order of Hezekiah and Azariah, the ruler of the house of God. By inference from the surrounding passage, their task was to manage the offerings, tithes and dedicated gifts that the people brought and that were stored in the temple chambers. STEPBible Proper Names describes him as a Levite who helped distribute the tithes. Several men in the Bible bear this name. A Mahath son of Amasai, a Kohathite Levite, appears in 2 Chr 29:12 among those who cleansed the temple early in Hezekiah's reign. He may be the same man, though the text does not say so. Hitchcock's Bible Names treats the name as the same as Maath.

Mahazioth was a Levite, one of the fourteen sons of Heman listed in 1 Chr 25:4. Heman was one of the chief musicians appointed in David's time, and his sons served in the music of the house of the Lord. When the musicians were divided by lot into twenty-four courses, the twenty-third fell to Mahazioth, who served with his sons and relatives, twelve in all (1 Chr 25:30). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify Heman's family as Kohathite. Easton's gives the meaning of the name as "visions." Nothing more is recorded about him.

Maher-shalal-hash-baz was a son of the prophet Isaiah and his wife, called "the prophetess" (Isa 8:3). His name means roughly "swift is the spoil, speedy is the prey." Before his birth, the LORD told Isaiah to write the name in large letters on a scroll or tablet (Isa 8:1). When the child was born, Isaiah was told to give him that name. The verses that follow (Isa 8:4) explain it as a sign. Before the boy could say "my father" or "my mother," the king of Assyria would carry off the wealth of Damascus and Samaria. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both read the name as a symbol of the coming Assyrian attack on Syria and Israel, the kingdoms of Rezin and Pekah. He was the brother of Shear-jashub, Isaiah's other son, whose name was also symbolic (Isa 7:3).

Mahlah was one of the five daughters of Zelophehad, of the tribe of Manasseh son of Joseph. Her sisters were Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah. She is usually named first among them, and Smith's Bible Dictionary takes her to be the eldest. Her father had no sons, so the sisters came forward together to claim his inheritance (Num 27:1). The ruling in their favour allowed daughters to inherit when there was no son. A later decision required such heiresses to marry within their father's tribe, and Mahlah and her sisters married their cousins, the sons of their father's brothers (Num 36:11). Their claim was honoured when the land was divided in Joshua's time (Josh 17:3). The name may mean "sickness" or "song"; the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats its origin as doubtful. A Mahlah of the same tribe also appears in 1 Chr 7:18.

Mahli (spelled Mahali in Exod 6:19) was a son of Merari and a grandson of Levi. With his brother Mushi he heads one of the two family branches of the Merarite Levites in the genealogies (Num 3:20; 1 Chr 6:19). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him the founder of the Mahlite family and gives the name's meaning as "a sick or weak one." His sons are named as Eleazar and Kish (1 Chr 23:21), and Eleazar had no sons (1 Chr 24:28). Another line runs through Libni (1 Chr 6:29). 1 Chr 24:26 also names Jaaziah among Merari's sons. In Ezra's day a capable man "of the sons of Mahli" was brought to join the return from Babylon (Ezra 8:18), which shows the family still existed. The name is shared by others, including a nephew of his, a son of Mushi.

Mahli was a Levite of the clan of Merari, the son of Mushi and grandson of Merari, the son of Levi (1 Chr 6:47). His brothers were Eder and Jeremoth (also spelled Jerimoth), and the three are listed as the sons of Mushi among the Levite family heads in David's arrangements (1 Chr 23:23; 24:30). In the genealogy of the temple singer Ethan, Mahli's son is Shamer. The surrounding verses make this clear, though the supplied verse names only Mahli. He shares his name with his uncle Mahli, Merari's other son, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes the repetition. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "sick," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia as "a sick or weak one." Because several men in these Levite lists bear the name, telling them apart depends on the father named in each passage.

Mahlon was a son of Elimelech and Naomi, an Ephrathite from Bethlehem in Judah, and the brother of Chilion. During a famine he went with his family to Moab, where they settled. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes him to be the elder son and gives the meaning of his name as "sickly". The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "invalid". Ruth 4:10 identifies him as the husband of Ruth the Moabitess. Mahlon and his brother both died in Moab, leaving Naomi without her sons or her husband. Later, at the gate of Bethlehem, Boaz bought from Naomi everything that had belonged to Elimelech, Chilion and Mahlon. He also took Ruth as his wife "to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance", so that Mahlon's name would not be cut off. By inference from this, Mahlon died without children.

Mahol is named in 1 Kgs 4:31 as the father of Ethan, Heman, Chalcol and Darda, four men so famous for wisdom that the writer measures Solomon's wisdom against theirs and says Solomon surpassed them. Nothing else is told about Mahol himself. His name means "dance" (Easton's Bible Dictionary; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia compares the phrase "sons of Mahol" with "sons of dance," which has led some to read it as a title for a guild of musicians or singers rather than a family. There is also a puzzle of descent. 1 Chr 2:6 lists men with nearly the same names (Ethan, Heman, Calcol and Dara) as sons of Zerah of Judah, and Ethan is called "the Ezrahite," probably meaning a descendant of Zerah. This entry follows the plain reading of 1 Kings and treats Mahol as their father.

Makaz was a town named only once in the Bible, in the list of Solomon's twelve district officers who each supplied food for the king's household for one month of the year. It belonged to the district of the son of Dekar, together with Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh and Elon-beth-hanan (1 Kgs 4:9). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that those three towns probably match places on the border of Dan (Josh 19:41–42). This suggests Makaz lay in the same area, the low hill country west of Jerusalem. Its site has never been identified, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also reports a suggestion that it may be the same as Me-jarkon in the Danite list. The location shown here is only a rough placement near its companion towns, west of Jerusalem, and does not follow that identification.

Makheloth was one of the places where the Israelites camped during their journey through the wilderness after leaving Egypt. It appears only in the list of encampments in Numbers 33, where the people moved to Makheloth from Haradah and then went on to Tahath (Num 33:25–26). Nothing else is said about it. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names give the meaning of the name as "assemblies" or "congregations." Its actual site is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement, in the region east of the Arabah valley in present-day southern Jordan, inferred from its position in the sequence of wilderness stations.

Makkedah was a Canaanite royal city in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah. After Joshua defeated the five allied Amorite kings at Gibeon, Israel pursued their forces as far as Azekah and Makkedah. The five kings hid in a cave there, and when this was reported, Joshua had them shut inside until the pursuit ended. The Israelite army then returned to Joshua's camp at Makkedah. That same day Joshua captured the city, killed its king and inhabitants, and moved on to Libnah. Makkedah appears in the list of defeated kings and among the lowland towns allotted to Judah. Its site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions Sumeil, near Beit Jibrin, and the Palestine Exploration surveyors proposed el-Mughar, "the caves," near Ekron. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that no certainty is possible. The location shown here lies in the northern lowland area associated with the el-Mughar view.

Malachi was the prophet through whom "the burden of the word of the LORD to Israel" came, as the opening verse of the book bearing his name states (Mal 1:1). His book is the last of the minor prophets and closes the Old Testament in the traditional English order. Nothing is known of his life beyond his book. His name means "my messenger," and some have taken it as a title rather than a personal name, though Easton's Bible Dictionary treats it as his ordinary name. By inference from the issues he addresses, such as corrupt priests and marriages to foreign wives, Easton's places him in the time of Nehemiah, after Haggai and Zechariah, when the rebuilt temple was in use. This entry dates his prophecies to about 442 BC, an estimate from context. Easton's suggests about 420 BC.

Malcham was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, a son of Shaharaim by his wife Hodesh. He appears only in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 8:9, where he is listed with his brothers Jobab, Zibia and Mesha. The next verse adds Jeuz, Shachia and Mirma as further sons of Shaharaim. The surrounding passage says Shaharaim had these sons in the country of Moab after sending away his wives Hushim and Baara, whose sons, including Abitub and Elpaal, were Malcham's half-brothers. Nothing else is recorded about him. The same Hebrew form occurs in Zeph 1:5, but there it is not this man. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it as the national idol of the Ammonites, by whom some in Judah swore. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "their king."

Malchi-shua was one of the sons of King Saul. His name is usually explained as "king of help" (Easton's Bible Dictionary) or "my king saves" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). The genealogies of Saul's family name him among Saul's sons with Jonathan, Abinadab and Eshbaal, also called Ish-bosheth (1 Chr 8:33; 9:39), and an earlier list in 1 Sam 14:49 includes him too. His mother is taken to be Ahinoam, whom 1 Sam 14:50 names as Saul's wife. Armoni and Mephibosheth were half-brothers, sons of Saul by Rizpah (2 Sam 21:8). Malchi-shua was killed by the Philistines together with his brothers Jonathan and Abinadab when they pursued Saul and his sons. The surrounding narrative places this battle on Mount Gilboa, where Saul also died (1 Sam 31:2; 1 Chr 10:2). Nothing else is recorded about him.

Malchiah was a Levite of the Gershonite line, named in the family tree of Asaph, one of the singers David put in charge of music at the sanctuary. In 1 Chr 6:40 he appears as the father of Baaseiah and an ancestor of Asaph through Michael. The next verse names his father as Ethni, son of Zerah. This entry gives his father as Jeaterai, who appears as a son of Zerah in the parallel Gershonite list (1 Chr 6:21). The two names are probably different forms for the same man. Nothing more is recorded about Malchiah beyond his place in this genealogy. The name, also spelled Malchijah, means "the Lord is my king" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Several other men in the Bible share it and should not be confused with this Levite.

Malchiah was a man of Israel, one of the descendants of Parosh, listed in Ezra 10:25 among those who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra. The surrounding chapter describes how, after returning from exile, these men agreed to send away their foreign wives. Nothing else is recorded about him. The same list of Parosh's sons also includes a Malchijah, a closely related form of the name, so the two appear to be different men of the same family line. Several other people in the Bible bear this name or its variants, and this Malchiah should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the Lord my king" or "my counselor."

Malchiah was one of the "sons of Harim", meaning a member of the family or clan descended from Harim, listed in Ezra 10:31. He appears in the list of Israelites who had married foreign wives and who, during Ezra's reforms after the return from exile, agreed to send those wives away. The passage records nothing else about him. The name, also spelled Malchijah, is usually explained as "the Lord is my king" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other men in the Bible share this name, including other members of the same list in Ezra 10, so this Malchiah should not be confused with them.

Malchiah, son of Rechab, was ruler of part of the district of Beth-haccerem in Judah in the time of Nehemiah. During the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls after the return from exile, he repaired the Dung Gate. He rebuilt it and installed its doors, locks and bars (Neh 3:14). This Rechab is probably not the ancestor of the Rechabites, though the text does not say either way. Several other men in the Bible share the name Malchiah (also spelled Malchijah), which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as meaning "the Lord my king." This one is known only from this single verse.

Malchiah was one of the men who repaired the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah's leadership after the return from exile. Neh 3:31 calls him "the goldsmith's son." The phrase can also be read as marking him as a member of the goldsmiths' guild, and the STEPBible proper-names index describes him as a goldsmith himself. His section ran up to the quarters of the Nethinim (temple servants) and the merchants, opposite the Miphkad Gate, and as far as the upper room at the corner. This was probably on the eastern side of the city near the temple area, judging from the other landmarks in the chapter. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the Lord my king." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and nothing further is known about this one.

Malchiah was one of the men who stood beside Ezra the scribe on a wooden platform when Ezra read the book of the Law aloud to the people of Jerusalem. He stood on Ezra's left, with Pedaiah, Mishael, Hashum, Hashbadana, Zechariah and Meshullam (Neh 8:4). The verse does not say what his role was. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper names index describe him as a priest. His name, also spelled Malchijah, is explained in Hitchcock's Bible Names as "the Lord my king." Several other men in the Bible share this name, including others in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah. It is uncertain whether this Malchiah is the same as any of them, so this entry treats him only as the man named in Neh 8:4.

Malchiah, son of Hammelech, was the owner of the dungeon or cistern in the court of the prison in Jerusalem into which Jeremiah was lowered with ropes. It held no water, only mud, and Jeremiah sank into it (Jer 38:6). The name Hammelech means "the king", and many translations render the phrase "Malchiah the king's son", so he was probably a member of the royal family in the last years of Judah. This entry treats Jerahmeel, also called the son of Hammelech, as his brother. Jer 36:26 says Jerahmeel was sent by King Jehoiakim to arrest Baruch and Jeremiah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "the Lord my king". Several other men in the Bible share the name, and how they relate to this Malchiah is uncertain.

Malchiel was a son of Beriah and a grandson of Asher, one of the sons of Jacob. He is named with his brother Heber among Asher's descendants who went down to Egypt with Jacob (Gen 46:17). In the census of the tribes taken in the wilderness he appears as the founder of a clan called the Malchielites (Num 26:45). The genealogies of Chronicles add that he was the father of Birzavith (1 Chr 7:31). Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is usually explained as meaning "God is king" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), or "God is my king, or counselor" in Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Malchijah, also spelled Malchiah, was a priest named only as an ancestor in the genealogy of Adaiah, one of the priests who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile. He was the father of Pashur, and through him an ancestor of Adaiah son of Jeroham (1 Chr 9:12). The parallel list in Nehemiah traces the same line in more detail, naming Pashur's descendants Zechariah, Amzi and Pelaliah before Jeroham, and places Adaiah among the priests who did the work of the temple (Neh 11:12). Several men in the Bible bear this name, so his identity with any other Malchijah is uncertain. He may be connected with the Malchijah whose family headed the fifth priestly division (1 Chr 24:9), and his son may be the Pashur son of Melchiah mentioned in Jer 21:1, but the text does not say so directly.

Malchijah was a priest whose family received the fifth of the twenty-four priestly divisions when lots were cast to organize temple service in David's reign (1 Chr 24:9). The surrounding passage describes David, with Zadok and Ahimelech, assigning the descendants of Aaron to courses that took turns serving. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as the head of the fifth division. His name means "Yah is king," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including priests and laymen of later periods, and this entry refers only to the head of the fifth priestly course.

Malchijah was a descendant of Parosh, one of the Israelite laymen listed in Ezra 10:25. The list in Ezra 10 names men who had married foreign wives after the return from exile. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was among those who agreed to send their wives away during Ezra's reforms. The name means "Yah is king." The same verse names two men of this name among the sons of Parosh. The King James Version spells the first "Malchiah" and the second "Malchijah," and this entry refers to the second. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:26 renders the two names as "Melchias" and "Asibias." Nothing more is recorded about him, and several other people in the Bible share the name.

Malchijah, son of Harim, was one of the men who rebuilt Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah after the return from exile. Neh 3:11 says that he and Hashub son of Pahath-moab repaired "the other piece", a second section of the wall, along with the Tower of the Furnaces. His name means "Yah is king," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Several people in the Bible share this name, and nothing more is told about this one. He may be the Malchiah listed among the sons of Harim in Ezra 10:31, who had married foreign wives, but this is not certain. Harim was also the name of a priestly family and of a lay family among the returned exiles, so it is unclear which Harim was his father or ancestor.

Malchijah was one of the men who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, when the community that had returned from exile pledged to keep the law of God (Neh 10:3). He appears in a list alongside Pashur and Amariah. By inference from the context, this part of the list names priests, and STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) identifies him as a priest. The name means "Yah is king," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Several men in the Bible bear this name, including others in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah, so it is uncertain whether this signatory is the same person as any of them. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Malchijah was one of the people who took part in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. He is named in a list of eight men, alongside Maaseiah, Shemaiah, Eleazar and others, who stood in the procession at the temple while the singers sang loudly under their overseer Jezrahiah (Neh 12:42). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe him as a priest who served among the musicians at this celebration. The verse itself gives only his name, so his precise role is inferred from the context of the dedication ceremony. His name means "Yahweh is king," and it is shared by several other men in the Bible, including other priests and Levites of the same period. Whether he is the same as any of them is uncertain, and this entry treats him as a separate person.

Malchiram was a son of Jehoiachin (also called Jeconiah), the king of Judah who was taken captive to Babylon. He appears only in the genealogy of David's royal line in 1 Chr 3:18, listed after Shealtiel among Jehoiachin's sons, with Pedaiah, Shenazar, Jecamiah, Hoshama and Nedabiah. This makes him a member of the tribe of Judah and a descendant of David. Since Jehoiachin was taken into exile as a young man, these sons were probably born in Babylon, though the passage does not say so. Nothing else is recorded about his life. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "uplifted king."

Malchus was the servant of the high priest whose right ear Simon Peter cut off with a sword when Jesus was arrested (John 18:10). Only John's Gospel gives his name. The setting is the garden across the Kidron valley, identified with Gethsemane in the parallel accounts of Matthew and Mark. The high priest that night was Caiaphas, so Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia call Malchus his servant. Matthew, Mark and Luke also tell of the injury but leave the servant unnamed, and Luke alone adds that Jesus touched his ear and healed him (Luke 22:51). Later in the same chapter, a relative of Malchus, also a servant of the high priest, asks Peter whether he had seen him in the garden with Jesus (John 18:26). The name is usually linked to the Semitic word for "king."

Mallothi was a Levite, one of the fourteen sons of Heman, the singer whom David appointed with Asaph and Jeduthun to lead music in the house of the Lord (1 Chr 25:4). Heman belonged to the Kohathite clan of Levi, so Mallothi was a Kohathite. When the musicians were organized into twenty-four rotating divisions by lot, the nineteenth lot fell to Mallothi, and he headed a group of twelve made up of himself, his sons and his relatives (1 Chr 25:26). He is mentioned nowhere else. His name is usually taken to mean "my fullness" (Easton's Bible Dictionary), though the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "my discourse." The fact list here gives his brother as Shubael, while 1 Chr 25:4 has Shebuel; these are generally understood as variant spellings of the same name.

Malluch was a Levite of the clan of Merari, named in the genealogy of Ethan, one of the singers David appointed to lead music at the house of the Lord. The list traces Ethan's line back through Kishi and Abdi to Malluch, so Malluch was Abdi's father and Ethan's great-grandfather. The same verse names Malluch's father as Hashabiah (1 Chr 6:44–45). The Merarite singers stood on the left hand of Heman, the chief singer. Malluch himself is mentioned only in this genealogy, and nothing more is recorded about him. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take to mean "counsellor," is shared by several other men in the Old Testament, including priests and laymen of Ezra's and Nehemiah's time, who are different people.

Malluch was one of the "sons of Bani" named in Ezra 10:29, in the list of Israelite men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was among those who agreed to send away these wives during Ezra's reforms after the return from exile in Babylon. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links this Bani to the line of Judah (citing 1 Chr 9:4) and identifies Malluch with the Mamuchus of 1 Esdras 9:30. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a man of the sons of Harim in the same list. The name is usually explained as meaning "counsellor" or "reigning."

Malluch was one of the sons of Harim listed in Ezra 10:32 among the Israelites who had married foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon. The list belongs to Ezra's reforms, when those who had taken such wives agreed to send them away. By inference from the surrounding verses (Ezra 10:31), he was counted with the descendants of Harim, as Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both note. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary takes to mean "counsellor," is shared by several other men in the Old Testament, including a priest and a Levite, so this Malluch should not be confused with them.

Malluch was a priest, or the head of a priestly family, of the period after the return from Babylon. He appears among the priests who returned with Zerubbabel and Jeshua (Neh 12:2). His family is listed again in the next generation as "Melicu", whose head was Jonathan in the days of the high priest Joiakim (Neh 12:14). The name also appears among the priests who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah's time (Neh 10:4). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take the signer of the covenant to be probably the same priestly line, and they treat Melicu as another form of Malluch. This entry follows that view. Because several men in the Bible bear this name, the identifications are not certain. The name is usually explained as meaning "counsellor".

Malluch was one of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time. In that covenant the returned community of Jerusalem pledged to keep God's law. His name appears in the list of signers in Neh 10:27, next to Harim and Baanah, among the heads of the people rather than the priests or Levites. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a priest and a Levite, and a Malluch who signed earlier in the same list among the priests. This entry treats the signer in Neh 10:27 as a separate person, but it is uncertain whether he can be linked to any of the others. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "counsellor." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "reigning" or "counseling."

Mamre was an Amorite, the brother of Eshcol and Aner, who lived in the land of Canaan in Abram's time. Abram was living by the "plain of Mamre" (in Hebrew, probably the oaks or terebinths of Mamre), a place evidently named after him or associated with him, when news came that his nephew Lot had been taken captive. Mamre and his brothers were allies of Abram (Gen 14:13), and by inference from the passage they went with him to rescue Lot. Afterward Abram refused any share of the recovered goods for himself but asked that Aner, Eshcol and Mamre receive their portion (Gen 14:24). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as an Amorite chief in alliance with Abraham. The same place, the plains of Mamre, is where the LORD later appeared to Abraham (Gen 18:1). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "rebellious," "bitter," or "set with trees."

Mamre was a place near Hebron in Canaan, closely tied to Abraham and his family. Genesis even equates it with Hebron, also called the city of Arbah (Gen 23:19; Gen 35:27). The cave of Machpelah, which Abraham bought from Ephron the Hittite as a family burial place, lay in a field described as "before Mamre," meaning facing it or east of it. Sarah, Abraham and later Jacob were buried there (Gen 23:17–19; Gen 25:9; Gen 49:30; Gen 50:13). Jacob returned to his father Isaac at Mamre, where Abraham and Isaac had lived. By inference from the surrounding account, Isaac died there, about 1716 BC by inference from context. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the name as the "oak grove" of Mamre, named after Abraham's Amorite ally. Proposed sites include Ballatet Selta west of Hebron, er-Rameh, and Khirbet Nimreh north of it. The location shown here lies a short distance north of Hebron.

The man of great stature was an unnamed Philistine warrior who fought against Israel in a battle at Gath during David's reign. He stood out for his size and for having six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in all (2 Sam 21:20; 1 Chr 20:6). Both accounts say he was born to "the giant" in Gath. The phrase may mean a direct son or more broadly a descendant of a race of giants. This entry treats him as a son, and therefore as a brother of the other giants named in these passages: Goliath, Ishbi-benob, Lahmi and Sippai. The verses that follow in both accounts (2 Sam 21:21; 1 Chr 20:7) say he taunted Israel and was killed by Jonathan, son of David's brother Shimea. His own name is never given.

The man of understanding was a Levite descended from Mahli, son of Merari and grandson of Levi. He was brought to Ezra when Ezra was preparing to lead a group of exiles from Babylon to Jerusalem. By inference from the surrounding chapter, Ezra had found no Levites among the travelers camped by the river Ahava and sent messengers to recruit some, and this man was among those who came. Ezra credits his arrival to the good hand of God (Ezra 8:18). The text gives no personal name. Readers take the phrase in different ways: as describing an unnamed skilled or wise Levite, as a description of Sherebiah, who is named immediately afterward, or as a proper name. This entry treats him as a separate, unnamed person.

Manaen was one of the prophets and teachers in the church at Antioch, named alongside Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene and Saul (Acts 13:1). The verse describes him as having been "brought up with Herod the tetrarch," meaning Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee. The Greek word behind the phrase is often rendered "foster brother," so he was probably raised and educated alongside Antipas, perhaps as a childhood companion at court. He was present at Antioch when Barnabas and Saul were set apart for the work that began the first missionary journey, about AD 45 by inference from context. His name is the Greek form of the Hebrew Menahem, meaning "consoler." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he may have been related to an earlier Manaen, an Essene whom Josephus says befriended Herod the Great. Nothing more is known of him.

Manahath was a son of Shobal and a descendant of Seir the Horite, listed among the early inhabitants of Mount Seir (Gen 36:23; 1 Chr 1:40). His brothers were Alvan, Ebal, Shepho and Onam. In 1 Chronicles some of the brothers' names are spelled differently (Alian for Alvan, Shephi for Shepho). Shobal himself appears in Genesis 36 as one of the sons of Seir and a Horite chief. Nothing more is recorded about Manahath beyond his place in these genealogies. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia regards him as the ancestor who gave his name to one of the ancient clans of Mount Seir that was later conquered and absorbed into Edom. He should be kept distinct from the place called Manahath mentioned elsewhere in 1 Chronicles.

Manahath was a place to which some Benjamite families from Geba were moved. It appears only once, in the genealogy of Benjamin, where the heads of the fathers' houses among the sons of Ehud are said to have been removed from Geba to Manahath (1 Chr 8:6). The verse does not say when or why this happened. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "rest." The Manahathites named among the descendants of Judah in 1 Chr 2:52–54 may be connected with the same place, but that link is uncertain. The location is not described in the text. The location shown here follows the identification with modern Malha (al-Maliha), southwest of Jerusalem, which fits a site within reach of Benjamin and Judah. A different Manahath, an Edomite person, appears in Gen 36:23 and is unrelated.

Manasseh (son of Joseph) was the firstborn of Joseph and his wife Asenath, born in Egypt about 1709 BC by inference from context. Joseph chose the name because God had made him forget his hardship and his father's house (Gen 41:51). When the aged Jacob blessed Joseph's two sons, Joseph placed Manasseh at Jacob's right hand (Gen 48:13). The rest of Gen 48 tells how Jacob crossed his hands and gave the younger Ephraim the greater blessing. According to 1 Chr 7:14, his sons were Ashriel and Machir, and Machir was born to an Aramean concubine. Machir's children were raised on Joseph's knees (Gen 50:23). Manasseh became the ancestor of a tribe of Israel. Half of it settled east of the Jordan in Gilead and Bashan (Num 32:33; Deut 3:13), and half settled west of the Jordan, north of Ephraim (Josh 17:7). In Rev 7:6 he is called Manasses.

Manasseh is named in Judg 18:30 as the father of Gershom and grandfather of Jonathan. Jonathan and his sons served as priests to the tribe of Dan at its carved image until the land went into captivity. Nothing else is said about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that in the Hebrew text a small letter n is written above the name, turning Moses (Mosheh) into Manasseh (Menashsheh). It holds that the name was originally Moses, changed so that Moses' name would not be tied to an idolatrous priesthood. This matches the fact that Moses had a son named Gershom (Exod 2:22), and many modern translations read "Moses" here. This entry follows the King James reading, Manasseh, while noting that identification. He is distinct from Joseph's son Manasseh and from King Manasseh of Judah. The name is usually taken to mean "causing to forget."

Manasseh (son of Hezekiah), also called Manasses, was a king of Judah who succeeded his father Hezekiah at age twelve and reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother was Hephzibah. By inference from context, he reigned from about 697 to 642 BC. Kings describes him leading Judah into idolatry worse than that of the nations driven out before Israel, building altars in the two courts of the temple, and shedding much innocent blood. Later passages blame his sins for Judah's eventual exile. Chronicles adds that Assyrian commanders took him in fetters to Babylon, where he prayed and was restored to his kingdom, acknowledging the LORD as God. He was buried in the garden of his own house, the garden of Uzza. His son Amon succeeded him, and 2 Kgs 21:19 names Amon's mother as Meshullemeth. Matthew lists Manasseh in the genealogy of Jesus.

Manasseh was a man of the family of Pahath-moab, listed in Ezra 10:30 among the Israelites who had married foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon. Context shows that those named in this list agreed, during Ezra's reforms, to send away their foreign wives (the STEPBible Proper Names index describes him as having divorced his). Nothing more is recorded about him. The name, meaning "causing to forget" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, was borne by several people in the Bible, including Joseph's elder son and a king of Judah. This Manasseh is a different and otherwise unknown individual. In the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:31 he appears as Manaseas.

Manasseh was a man of the family or clan of Hashum, one of several people in the Bible with this name. He is named once, in the list in Ezra 10 of men who had married foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon (Ezra 10:33). In context, these men agreed during Ezra's reforms to send away their wives, and STEPBible Proper Names describes him as having divorced his foreign wife. The passage records nothing else about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "forgetfulness" or "he that is forgotten." He should not be confused with Joseph's son Manasseh or King Manasseh of Judah.

Manoah was a man of Zorah from the tribe of Dan and the father of Samson. His wife had been unable to have children until an angel of the LORD appeared to her and promised a son (Judg 13:2). Manoah then prayed for the messenger to come again and teach them how to raise the child. The angel returned, and Manoah asked how the boy should be brought up (Judg 13:8–13). He offered to prepare a young goat for the visitor, but was told to make a burnt offering to the LORD instead. He also asked the visitor's name. When Manoah offered the goat on a rock, the angel rose up in the altar's flame. Only then did Manoah realize who the visitor was, and he feared that he and his wife would die because they had seen God (Judg 13:15–22). Samson was later buried in Manoah's burial place between Zorah and Eshtaol (Judg 16:31). His name is usually taken to mean "rest."

Maon was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of Caleb's descendants in 1 Chr 2:45. He was the son of Shammai and the father of Bethzur. STEPBible's Tyndale House name list places him among the descendants of Caleb, which fits the surrounding list in 1 Chronicles 2. Maon and Bethzur are also the names of towns in the hill country of Judah. Because of this, the names in this passage may represent the founders or forebears of the clans that settled those towns, though the verse itself presents them simply as father and son. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "house" or "place of sin."

Maon was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed with Carmel, Ziph and Juttah among the towns assigned to the tribe (Josh 15:55). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "habitation" and says the town gave its name to the surrounding wilderness. David and his men hid in the wilderness of Maon, south of Jeshimon, when the people of Ziph reported him to Saul, and Saul pursued him there (1 Sam 23:24–25). Maon was also the home of a wealthy man whose flocks grazed at nearby Carmel, where he sheared his sheep (1 Sam 25:2). The following verse names him as Nabal, husband of Abigail. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify Maon with Tell Ma'in, a conical hill about seven miles (11 km) south of Hebron, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Marah was a place in the wilderness where the Israelites camped soon after crossing the sea out of Egypt. They reached it after a three days' journey through the wilderness of Etham, and found that its water was too bitter to drink, which is why the place was called Marah, meaning "bitterness" (Exod 15:23; Num 33:8). The following verses in Exodus, not quoted here, tell how the people complained and Moses threw a tree into the water, which made it drinkable. From Marah they moved on to Elim, a site with twelve springs and seventy palm trees (Num 33:9). The exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary mention the common identification with 'Ain Hawarah, a bitter spring about 47 miles from 'Ayun Musa on the western side of the Sinai Peninsula. The location shown here follows that identification.

Mareal, spelled Maralah in the King James Version, was a town on the boundary of the tribe of Zebulun. Josh 19:11 traces Zebulun's border as it went up westward toward the sea, passing Maralah, reaching Dabbasheth and then the stream that lies before Jokneam. The verse indicates its position on the line of the border but says nothing else about the town. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on Zebulun's southern boundary, gives the meaning of the name as "trembling," and identifies it with the modern village of Ma'lul, about 4 miles (6 km) southwest of Nazareth. The location shown here follows that identification, with Ma'lul at the edge of the hills overlooking the Jezreel Valley. The identification rests on the similar name and a fitting position along the border, so it remains probable rather than certain.

Mareshah was a city in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah. It is listed with Keilah and Achzib among the towns allotted to the tribe (Josh 15:44). Rehoboam later fortified it as one of his defensive cities (2 Chr 11:8). When Zerah the Ethiopian advanced with a vast army as far as Mareshah, King Asa met him in battle in the nearby valley of Zephathah (2 Chr 14:9–10). The prophet Eliezer son of Dodavah, who condemned Jehoshaphat's shipbuilding alliance with Ahaziah, came from Mareshah (2 Chr 20:37). Micah addresses its inhabitants in his lament over the towns of Judah (Mic 1:15). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it at the ruin el-Mer'ash near Beit Jibrin. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, drawing on excavations, locates it at Tell Sandahannah, about a mile south of Beit Jibrin. The location shown here follows the Tell Sandahannah identification.

John Mark was an early Christian from Jerusalem, known by the Jewish name John and the Roman name Mark (Marcus). Believers met to pray at the house of his mother Mary, and Peter went there after his release from prison (Acts 12:12). Col 4:10 links him to Barnabas. The KJV reads "sister's son," while Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him Barnabas's cousin. Barnabas and Saul brought him from Jerusalem, and he assisted them in Cyprus on the first missionary journey, about AD 45 by inference from context. He then left them at Perga and returned to Jerusalem. Paul later refused to take him again, and after a sharp disagreement Barnabas sailed with Mark to Cyprus. Mark was afterward with Paul as a fellow worker, and Paul asked for him as useful in the ministry. Peter calls him "my son." Early church tradition names him as the author of the Gospel of Mark.

Maroth was a town of Judah mentioned only once, in Micah's lament over the towns facing invasion (Mic 1:12). Micah says its people waited anxiously for good, but disaster came from the LORD as far as the gate of Jerusalem. The name means "bitterness" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), and it probably forms part of the wordplay on town names that runs through Mic 1:10–15, contrasting "bitterness" with the good its people hoped for. Easton's Bible Dictionary links the passage to the Assyrian invasion and places Maroth not far from Jerusalem. Smith's Bible Dictionary puts it in the western lowland of Judah, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls it an unknown town, probably in the Philistine plain. Its exact site is uncertain. The location shown here is a rough point in the western lowland, following the lowland identification. Some have suggested it is the same place as Maarath (Josh 15:59).

Marsena was one of the seven princes of Persia and Media under King Ahasuerus. Esth 1:14 names him among the nobles who "saw the king's face" and "sat the first in the kingdom," meaning they had direct access to the king and held the highest rank at court. From the surrounding passage, these seven were among the wise men "which knew the times" whom Ahasuerus consulted when Queen Vashti refused to appear at his feast. Only Memucan is recorded as speaking. Marsena is mentioned nowhere else, and nothing more is known of him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says the origin of his name is unknown but probably Persian. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "worthy," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "bitterness of a bramble."

Martha was a woman of Bethany, the sister of Lazarus and Mary, and one of those Jesus is said to have loved (John 11:5). Luke tells how she welcomed Jesus into her house in an unnamed village.
