She was busy with serving and asked him to tell Mary to help her, and Jesus replied that she was anxious about many things (Luke 10:38–41). John names Bethany as the sisters' town. When Lazarus died, Martha went out to meet Jesus. She said her brother would not have died had he been there, and she affirmed that he would rise at the last day. She objected when Jesus ordered the tomb opened, because Lazarus had been dead four days. Later, at the supper in Bethany where Mary anointed Jesus, Martha served while Lazarus sat at the table (John 12:2). Because the house is called hers, the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia infers that she was the elder sister.

Mary (Mother of Jesus) was the wife of Joseph and the mother of Jesus. While she was engaged to Joseph, a descendant of David, an angel told her she would bear a son, and she accepted, calling herself "the handmaid of the Lord" (Luke 1:38). Matthew and Luke say she conceived by the Holy Spirit before she and Joseph came together. She stayed with her relative Elisabeth for about three months, then travelled with Joseph to Bethlehem, where Jesus was born. She was present when the wise men came and at his presentation in the temple. The Gospels name James, Joses, Simon and Jude as Jesus' brothers, and traditions differ on whether they were Mary's own sons. She stood at the cross and later prayed with the disciples (Acts 1:14). Following Easton's Bible Dictionary, this entry treats Luke's genealogy as hers, making Heli her father. Her name is a form of Miriam.

Mary (sister of Lazarus) was a woman of Bethany who lived with her sister Martha and brother Lazarus, and is one of several women named Mary in the New Testament. When Jesus visited the sisters, Mary sat at his feet listening to him, and he said she had chosen the good part, which would not be taken from her (Luke 10:39, 42). When Lazarus fell ill and died, many Jews came to comfort the sisters. Mary stayed in the house while Martha went to meet Jesus. When Martha called her, she went out quickly, fell at his feet and said that her brother would not have died if he had been there. After Lazarus was raised, many who had come to Mary believed in Jesus. Later, at a meal in Bethany, she anointed Jesus' feet with a pound of costly spikenard ointment and wiped them with her hair. Nothing is known of her later life.

Mary (wife of Cleophas) was one of the women who stood near the cross of Jesus, named in John 19:25 with his mother and Mary Magdalene. The wording can be read as calling her the sister of Jesus' mother, or as listing those two women separately, and it is uncertain which is meant. This entry identifies her with the Mary called the mother of James the less and of Joses in the other Gospels, and with "the other Mary" in Matthew, because she appears in the same group of women. On that view she watched the crucifixion from a distance, saw where Jesus was buried, sat facing the tomb, bought spices with Mary Magdalene and Salome after the Sabbath, and helped report the empty tomb to the apostles. These events are dated to about AD 30 by inference. Hitchcock's Bible Names treats her name as the same as Miriam.

Mary (Mother of John Mark) was a woman of Jerusalem whose house served as a gathering place for the early believers. After an angel freed Peter from prison, about AD 40 by inference from context, he went straight to her house, where many were gathered praying (Acts 12:12). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes this as a sign of a close connection between them. Her son was John, also called Mark, who according to later chapters of Acts travelled with Paul and Barnabas. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify her as Barnabas's sister, drawing on Col 4:10, where the King James Version calls Mark Barnabas's "sister's son". Many modern translations read "cousin" there. Smith's also records a tradition that her house stood on the upper slope of Mount Zion and was where the disciples met at Pentecost. Her name is a form of Miriam.

Mary (of Rome) was a Christian woman whom Paul greets in his letter to the church at Rome, saying that she "bestowed much labour on us" (Rom 16:6). Nothing else is known about her, and she should not be confused with the several other women named Mary in the New Testament. Readings of the verse differ on whom her work served. The King James wording points to Paul and his companions, and Easton's Bible Dictionary describes her as someone who treated Paul with special kindness. Some ancient manuscripts read "on you" instead, and the STEPBible names index (Tyndale House) describes her as a woman who worked hard for the church in Rome. Either way, Paul singles her out for her hard work among the believers he greets by name. Hitchcock's Bible Names treats her name as the same as Miriam.

Mary Magdalene was a follower of Jesus and a leading witness of his death, burial and resurrection. Her name probably reflects her hometown, Magdala on the Sea of Galilee (Easton's Bible Dictionary). Luke lists her among women healed of evil spirits who traveled with Jesus, noting that seven devils had gone out of her (Luke 8:2). She watched the crucifixion (Mark 15:40; John 19:25) and saw where the body was laid (Mark 15:47). After the Sabbath she brought spices and found the stone rolled away from the tomb (Mark 16:1; John 20:1). The risen Jesus appeared first to her. She recognized him when he spoke her name and then told the disciples (Mark 16:9; John 20:16–18). Later tradition linked her with the sinful woman of Luke 7. The Gospels do not make that connection, and this entry treats them as distinct.

The Mary Anoints Jesus event took place at Bethany six days before the Passover, about AD 30 by inference from context. At a supper given for Jesus, Martha served and Lazarus, whom Jesus had raised from the dead, sat at the table. Mary took a pound of very costly spikenard ointment, anointed Jesus' feet and wiped them with her hair, filling the house with its scent. Judas Iscariot objected that the ointment could have been sold for three hundred pence and the money given to the poor. John adds that Judas, who kept the common purse, was a thief. Jesus told them to leave her alone, saying she had kept it for the day of his burial, and that the poor would always be with them but he would not. Crowds came to see both Jesus and Lazarus, and the chief priests plotted to kill Lazarus too. Matt 26 and Mark 14 record a similar anointing at Bethany.

Mary Visits Elizabeth is the episode in Luke's Gospel in which Mary, soon after the angel announced that she would bear Jesus, hurried to a town in the hill country of Judah and entered the house of the priest Zacharias to greet his wife Elisabeth. Earlier in the chapter (Luke 1:36), Elisabeth is called Mary's relative and is said to be six months pregnant. When Mary greeted her, Elisabeth's unborn child leaped in her womb. Filled with the Holy Spirit, Elisabeth loudly blessed Mary and the child she carried and called her "the mother of my Lord." Mary answered with a song of praise, traditionally called the Magnificat after its first word in Latin. It celebrates God's mercy, his humbling of the proud and lifting up of the lowly, and his promise to Abraham. Mary stayed about three months and then returned home. The visit is dated to about 5 BC, by inference from context.

Mash was the fourth son of Aram and a grandson of Shem, listed among the descendants of Noah in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:23). The parallel genealogy in 1 Chr 1:17 gives the name as Meshech and places Aram's sons directly after the sons of Shem, without repeating Aram's name before them. His brothers were Uz, Hul and Gether. Nothing more is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint reads Mosoch in both passages, but it treats Mash as the original form, since Meshech is otherwise the name of a son of Japheth. The name probably also stands for a tribe descended from him. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary connect it with Mons Masius, the mountain range that classical writers placed on the northern edge of Mesopotamia, between the Tigris and Euphrates.

Mashal was a city in the territory of the tribe of Asher that was given, with its surrounding pasturelands, to the Levites (1 Chr 6:74). The surrounding passage assigns Asher's Levitical towns to the Gershonite branch of the Levites. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Mishal in the parallel list at Josh 21:30, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also equates it with Misheal in Asher's boundary list at Josh 19:26. Its site is uncertain. The fourth-century writer Eusebius placed it near Mount Carmel by the sea, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia regards it as unidentified. The location shown here is a rough placement in western Galilee, within Asher's territory. Easton's gives the name's meaning as "entreaty," and Hitchcock's Bible Names as "a parable" or "governing."

Masrekah was a place in Edom, the home of Samlah, who became king of Edom after the death of Hadad (Gen 36:36; 1 Chr 1:47). Both verses come from the list of Edomite kings who reigned before any king ruled over Israel. Nothing more is said about the town, and its site is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "vineyard of noble vines," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "place of choice vines." Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "whistling" or "hissing." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that nothing shows where the place should be sought. The location shown here is only a rough placement within Edomite territory, south of the Dead Sea in present-day southern Jordan.

Massa was a son of Ishmael and so a grandson of Abraham. He appears only in the two genealogies of Ishmael's twelve sons, where he is listed seventh, between Dumah and Hadar (called Hadad in 1 Chr 1:30). His brothers included Nebajoth, Kedar and Tema, and his sister was Bashemath. Nothing is recorded about his life. His name is usually taken to mean "burden" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as the founder of a nomadic Arabian tribe living in the desert toward Babylonia, and Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests his descendants may be the Masani, whom the ancient geographer Ptolemy placed in eastern Arabia. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes an alternative rendering of Prov 31:1 that calls Lemuel "king of Massa," which would point to a tribe or place named after him.

Massah was a place in the wilderness where the Israelites, lacking water, quarreled with Moses and tested the LORD by asking, "Is the LORD among us, or not?" Moses named it Massah, meaning "testing" or "temptation," and also Meribah, meaning "quarreling" (Exod 17:7). The surrounding narrative places the episode at Rephidim, before Israel reached Sinai, when water came from a struck rock. That happened during the wilderness wanderings, about 1491 BC by inference from context. Deuteronomy later recalls Massah as a warning not to test God (Deut 6:16) and lists it with Taberah and Kibroth-hattaavah as places where Israel provoked the LORD (Deut 9:22). Moses' blessing on Levi also mentions it (Deut 33:8). Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is approximate, in the southwestern Sinai Peninsula, following the traditional southern route of the Exodus.

Matred was the daughter of Mezahab and the mother of Mehetabel, who married Hadar (called Hadad in 1 Chr 1:50). Hadar was one of the kings who ruled Edom before Israel had kings, and his city was Pau, or Pai in Chronicles. Matred appears only in this genealogical note, which Genesis and 1 Chronicles repeat almost word for word, and nothing else is recorded about her. The Hebrew phrasing is ambiguous. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint and Peshitta treat Matred as a man, the son of Mezahab, which would make Matred Mehetabel's father. This entry follows the reading of Matred as a woman and Mehetabel's mother. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "expulsion," Smith's Bible Dictionary as "pushing forward," and Hitchcock's Bible Names as "wand of government."

Matri was a Benjamite whose name was carried by a family, or clan, within the tribe of Benjamin, and King Saul belonged to that family. The only mention comes in the account of Saul being chosen king at Mizpah. Samuel had the tribes of Israel come forward, and the choice fell first on Benjamin. Then Benjamin's families came forward and the family of Matri was taken. Finally Saul the son of Kish was taken, but when the people looked for him he could not be found (1 Sam 10:21). Nothing else is recorded about Matri himself. He is probably the ancestor the clan was named after, by inference from the phrase "the family of Matri." Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat the name mainly as the name of the clan. Smith's gives its meaning as "rain of Jehovah," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "rainy."

Mattan was a priest of Baal in Jerusalem, killed in front of Baal's altars when the people of the land tore down the house of Baal (2 Kgs 11:18; 2 Chr 23:17). The surrounding accounts place this in the uprising led by the priest Jehoiada, which removed Queen Athalia and put the young Joash on the throne. The Baal temple and its altars and images were smashed during the same action. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests that Mattan probably came to Jerusalem with Athalia from Samaria, where her family, the house of Ahab, had promoted Baal worship. The name means "a gift." Several other people in the Bible share the name, among them the father of Shephatiah in the time of Jeremiah. This entry concerns only the priest of Baal.

Mattan was the father of Shephatiah, one of the Judean officials in Jerusalem who heard Jeremiah's message to the people during the last years of the kingdom of Judah (Jer 38:1). Nothing more is recorded about Mattan himself. His son Shephatiah was among those who then asked the king to put Jeremiah to death and lowered him into a cistern (Jer 38:4–6), as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. The name means "gift," according to Smith's Bible Dictionary. Several people in the Bible bear the name Mattan, including a priest of Baal killed in Jerusalem in the time of Queen Athaliah (2 Kgs 11:18). Nothing in the text links this Mattan to any of the others, so he is best treated as a separate person.

Mattanah was a stopping place of the Israelites near the end of their wilderness journey, on the route toward the land east of the Jordan. Numbers 21 says they went to Mattanah from the wilderness, right after the song about the well the princes dug at Beer, and then moved on to Nahaliel and Bamoth (Num 21:18–19). The name means "gift." Because of this, some have linked it with the well just described. Its site is unknown, and reference works place it differently. Easton's Bible Dictionary puts it in the Wadi Waleh, between the desert and the borders of Moab. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it southeast of the Dead Sea. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says no clue to its location now remains. The location shown here is only approximate, east of the northern Dead Sea, and follows the general view that it lay in the region north of the Arnon on the edge of Moab.

Mattaniah, son of Micha (or Micah), was a Levite descended from Asaph, the temple musician. He lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile. Nehemiah calls him the leader who began the thanksgiving in prayer, which suggests he directed the temple singers (Neh 11:17; 12:8). His grandfather is named Zichri in 1 Chr 9:15 and Zabdi in Neh 11:17, probably two forms of the same name. A Mattaniah also appears with Bakbukiah among the gatekeepers who guarded the storehouses at the gates (Neh 12:25). Because he is again paired with Bakbukiah, the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes this to be the same man. Since several men in the Bible share the name, some of these identifications are uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "gift, or hope, of the Lord."

Mattaniah was a Levite, one of the fourteen sons of Heman, who led one of the families of musicians organized for temple worship in the time of David (1 Chr 25:4). When lots were cast to set the order of service, the ninth lot fell to Mattaniah, and his group of sons and relatives numbered twelve (1 Chr 25:16). The surrounding chapter describes these musicians as serving with cymbals, harps and lyres. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also connect Heman's sons with sounding the horn, drawn from the reference to lifting up the horn in 1 Chr 25:5. His name is usually explained as "gift of the LORD." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including the original name of King Zedekiah, and this entry concerns only the son of Heman.

Mattaniah was a Levite descended from Asaph. He is named only once, in the family line of Jahaziel, who was moved by the Spirit of the LORD to speak before the assembly of Judah during the reign of King Jehoshaphat (2 Chr 20:14). That verse traces Jahaziel's ancestry back through Zechariah, Benaiah and Jeiel to Mattaniah, which makes Mattaniah the father of Jeiel and an earlier ancestor of Jahaziel. Nothing else is recorded about his life. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him simply as a descendant of Asaph and an ancestor of Jahaziel. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "gift, or hope, of the Lord." Several other men in the Bible are also called Mattaniah, and this one should not be confused with them.

Mattaniah was a Levite descended from Asaph, one of the "sons of Asaph" listed among the Levites who gathered when King Hezekiah ordered the temple in Jerusalem to be cleansed and restored to use (2 Chr 29:13). He is named alongside Zechariah as the representatives of the Asaph family, the line of temple singers. The surrounding chapter shows these Levites sanctifying themselves and then removing the impurities from the house of the Lord at the start of Hezekiah's reforms. His name means "gift of the Lord" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other men in the Bible share the name Mattaniah, including the king better known as Zedekiah and other Levites of the Asaph line. This entry concerns only the Levite of Hezekiah's time.

Mattaniah was one of the "sons of Elam", meaning a member of the family or clan descended from Elam, named in Ezra 10:26. He appears in the list of returned exiles who had married foreign wives during Ezra's reforms. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was among those who agreed to send these wives away (Ezra 10:19, 44). Nothing else is recorded about him. His name means "gift of the Lord" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several people in the Bible share this name, including another Mattaniah listed among the descendants of Zattu in the next verse of the same list, so it is not always clear which mention refers to which man. This entry covers the man counted among the family of Elam.

Mattaniah was a man of the family of Zattu who lived in the time of Ezra, after the return from exile in Babylon. Ezra 10:27 names him among the sons of Zattu, together with Elioenai, Eliashib, Jeremoth, Zabad and Aziza. The surrounding chapter shows that this list records men who had married foreign wives and agreed to send them away during Ezra's reforms, so Mattaniah was probably one of them. His name means "gift of the Lord." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including another Mattaniah in the same list from the family of Elam (Ezra 10:26), so he should be kept distinct from them. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Mattaniah was one of the descendants of Pahath-moab listed in Ezra 10:30 among the Israelite men who had married foreign wives after the return from exile. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was among those who agreed under Ezra's reforms to send away these wives. The STEPBible Proper Names index describes him in these terms. Nothing more is recorded about him. His name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names gives as meaning "gift, or hope, of the Lord," was borne by several other men in the Old Testament. This includes another Mattaniah, a son of a different family, named in the same list of Ezra 10. He should not be confused with King Zedekiah, whose original name was also Mattaniah.

Mattaniah was one of several men of this name in the Bible. This one appears only once, in the list of Israelites who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra (Ezra 10:37). The surrounding list places him among the descendants, or "sons," of Bani. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the Tyndale House STEPBible names index both say that these men sent away their foreign wives at Ezra's command during his reforms after the return from exile. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name means "gift of the Lord," according to Smith's Bible Dictionary, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "gift, or hope, of the Lord." He should not be confused with other men named Mattaniah, such as the king of Judah whose name was changed to Zedekiah.

Mattaniah was a Levite of the family of Asaph, the temple singers. He is named only in genealogies in Nehemiah, as the son of Michaiah (also spelled Micha). Through his son Hashabiah he was an ancestor of Uzzi, overseer of the Levites in Jerusalem after the return from exile (Neh 11:22). Through his son Shemaiah he was an ancestor of Zechariah, who played a trumpet at the dedication of the rebuilt city wall (Neh 12:35). Because he appears several generations above men active in Nehemiah's day, he probably lived somewhat earlier, though the line itself belongs to Nehemiah's period. A Levite called Mattaniah son of Micah, of Asaph's line, also appears in 1 Chr 9:15 and may be the same man. The name is shared by several people in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "gift, or hope, of the Lord."

Mattaniah was the father of Zaccur and the grandfather of Hanan, one of the men Nehemiah appointed to oversee the storehouses of the restored Jerusalem community (Neh 13:13). Hanan served alongside Shelemiah the priest, Zadok the scribe and Pedaiah the Levite. These men were chosen because they were considered trustworthy, and their job was to distribute supplies to their fellow workers. Mattaniah himself is known only through this family line. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Levite, probably by inference from his grandson's role in handling the Levites' share of the offerings. His name means "gift of the LORD." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and it is uncertain whether this Mattaniah is the same as any of them.

Mattatha is a man named once in the Bible, in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, which traces Jesus' ancestry back through David to Adam. He is listed as the son of Nathan, who was a son of King David, and as the father of Menan (Luke 3:31). Because his line runs through David, he belongs to the tribe of Judah. The verse gives no details about his life beyond his place in this line of descent. He appears only in Luke's genealogy, which follows Nathan's branch of David's family rather than Solomon's royal line traced in Matthew. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "his gift."

Mattathah was one of the sons, or descendants, of Hashum named in the list of men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra (Ezra 10:33). By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was among those who agreed to send away these wives during Ezra's reforms after the return from exile, as the STEPBible Proper Names index also notes. He appears in that list alongside Mattenai, Zabad, Eliphelet, Jeremai, Manasseh and Shimei, and nothing more is said about him. The Revised Version spells his name Mattattah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies him with the Mattathias of the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:33, a name the King James Version gives as Matthias.

Mattathias was an ancestor of Jesus named in the genealogy in Luke's Gospel, which traces Jesus' line back through Joseph to Adam. Luke 3:25 lists him as the son of Amos, and the preceding words show he was the father of Joseph. This Joseph is a different person from Joseph, the husband of Mary. Mattathias belongs to the stretch of the genealogy between the return from exile and the time of Jesus, and as part of David's line he was of the tribe of Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him after 406 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name is the Greek form of Mattathiah and is usually explained as meaning "gift of the Lord." Several people in the Bible share this name, including another Mattathias who appears a few generations further on in the same list.

Mattathias was an ancestor of Jesus named in Luke's genealogy, which traces Jesus' line back through Joseph. He was the son of Semei and the father of Maath (Luke 3:26). He belongs to the part of the list between the return from exile under Zerubbabel and the time of Jesus, a stretch whose names appear nowhere else in the Bible, so nothing more is known about him. His place in the tribe of Judah follows from the genealogy, which runs through David and Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the name as the Greek form of Mattathiah, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "the gift of the Lord." Several other men in Luke's genealogy and elsewhere share the name, and this entry covers only the son of Semei.

Mattenai was a man of the clan or family of Hashum who appears in the list of men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra (Ezra 10:33). He is named first among seven men from the sons of Hashum. From the surrounding chapter, these men agreed to send away their foreign wives as part of the reforms Ezra led after the return from exile in Babylon. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name Mattenai is shared by several people in the Bible, including another man in the same list and a priest of Joiarib's family in the days of Joiakim. This entry refers only to the descendant of Hashum.

Mattenai was one of the men of Israel listed in Ezra 10 as having married foreign wives in the period after the return from exile in Babylon. His name appears in a run of names in Ezra 10:37 that, by the arrangement of the list, belongs to the descendants of Bani (Ezra 10:34). STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) describes him as a descendant of Bani who divorced his foreign wife during Ezra's reforms, when the men involved agreed to send away their foreign wives. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including another Mattenai in the same chapter among the sons of Hashum (Ezra 10:33) and a priest of that name in Nehemiah. This entry is about the man listed in Ezra 10:37.

Mattenai was a priest who headed the priestly family of Joiarib in the days of Joiakim, the high priest who succeeded Jeshua after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears only once, in the list of priestly family heads in Neh 12:19. By inference from the surrounding passage, which places this list in Joiakim's time, he lived some decades after the first return, probably in the late sixth or early fifth century BC. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as a shortened form of Mattaniah, meaning "gift of the Lord." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning as "liberal." Nothing else is known about him. The same name belongs to other men in the Bible, including laymen in the time of Ezra who had married foreign wives, and this Mattenai should not be confused with them.

Matthan was an ancestor of Jesus named in Matthew's genealogy, the son of Eleazar and the father of Jacob (Matt 1:15). The next verse makes Jacob the father of Joseph, the husband of Mary, so Matthan was Joseph's grandfather, as Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both note. He belongs to the tribe of Judah through the royal line traced from David. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "gift." Luke's genealogy names a different grandfather of Joseph, Matthat, father of Heli (Luke 3:24). Some interpreters treat Matthan and Matthat as the same man, and others see two separate lines of descent. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia discusses Matthat under this name. Nothing else is recorded about Matthan beyond his place in the list.

Matthat was an ancestor of Jesus named in Luke's genealogy. He was the son of Levi and the father of Heli (Luke 3:24). Since the preceding verse calls Jesus the supposed son of Joseph, who was the son of Heli, Matthat appears as Joseph's grandfather in this line. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him simply as the son of Levi and father of Heli. Matthew's genealogy names a different set of ancestors for Joseph, with Matthan as his grandfather (Matt 1:15), and some readers connect the two names. Nothing more is recorded about him. Luke's list includes another, earlier Matthat, also called a son of Levi (Luke 3:29), so the name belongs to more than one person in the same genealogy. He is counted here with the tribe of Judah because Luke traces this line through David.

Matthat was an ancestor of Jesus named in the genealogy in Luke's Gospel. He is listed as the son of Levi and the father of Jorim (Luke 3:29). This places him in the stretch of the line between David and Jesus that runs through David's son Nathan rather than through Solomon. Because he appears in a lineage traced from David, this entry groups him with the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is shared with at least one other man in the same genealogy, a later Matthat listed as the grandfather of Joseph (Luke 3:24). Easton's Bible Dictionary distinguishes this Matthat as the son of "another Levi," separate from the Levi who appears later in the list.

Matthew, also called Levi, was a tax collector who became one of the twelve apostles of Jesus. While he sat at his tax booth, Jesus told him, "Follow me," and he got up and followed (Matt 9:9). The parallel accounts in Mark and Luke call him Levi, and Mark names his father as Alphaeus (Mark 2:14; Luke 5:27). Easton's Bible Dictionary places his booth at Capernaum. Levi then held a large feast in his house for Jesus, attended by many tax collectors and others (Luke 5:29). Matthew appears in every list of the twelve, where Matt 10:3 calls him "the publican," and he was with the other apostles in the upper room after Jesus' ascension (Acts 1:13). Tradition names him as the author of the Gospel of Matthew. His name is usually explained as "gift of the LORD." The New Testament does not record his later life or death.

Matthias was the disciple chosen to take the place of Judas Iscariot among the twelve apostles. After Jesus' ascension, the believers in Jerusalem put forward two candidates, Joseph called Barsabas (also known as Justus) and Matthias (Acts 1:23). They cast lots, the lot fell on Matthias, and he was counted with the eleven apostles (Acts 1:26). By inference from the surrounding passage, he met Peter's stated requirement of having been with the disciples from John's baptism until the ascension, so that he could serve as a witness of the resurrection. The event is dated to about AD 30, by inference from context. His name probably means "gift of God" (Easton's Bible Dictionary). Nothing more is said of him in the Bible. Later traditions, noted in Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, place his preaching and death variously in Ethiopia, Judea or Jerusalem.

The Matthias replaces Judas event was the choosing of a new apostle to fill the place left by Judas Iscariot. After Jesus ascended, the eleven apostles returned from the Mount of Olives to Jerusalem and gathered in an upper room. With them were Mary the mother of Jesus, his brothers, and other women, about 120 disciples in all. Peter told them that Judas, who had guided those who arrested Jesus, had died in a field afterward called Aceldama, "the field of blood." Quoting the Psalms, he said another must take Judas's office. The replacement had to be a man who had been with them from John's baptism until the ascension, to serve as a witness of the resurrection. Two were put forward, Joseph called Barsabas (surnamed Justus) and Matthias. The group prayed, cast lots, and the lot fell on Matthias, who was counted with the eleven. This entry dates it to about AD 30, by inference from context.

Mattithiah was a Levite, the firstborn son of Shallum the Korahite. He appears in the list of those who resettled in Jerusalem after the exile. There he held a permanent duty over "the things that were made in the pans" (1 Chr 9:31). By inference from the passage, this meant preparing the flat-baked items used in worship, probably the grain offerings cooked on a griddle. The STEPBible proper names index describes him as in charge of baking bread in the temple. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him as the eldest son of Shallum, of the family of Korah. Several other men in the Bible share the name Mattithiah, and this one is known only from this single verse.

Mattithiah (meaning "gift of Yah," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) was a Levite musician in the time of King David and one of the sons of Jeduthun. Several men in the Bible share this name. He and his brothers served under their father, who prophesied with the harp to give thanks and praise to the LORD (1 Chr 25:3). When the temple musicians were divided by lot into twenty-four groups, the fourteenth lot fell to Mattithiah, whose group of sons and relatives numbered twelve (1 Chr 25:21). A Mattithiah also appears among the Levites of the second rank who played harps when the ark was brought to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:18, 21). He was later appointed to minister before the ark under Asaph (1 Chr 16:5). Reference works differ on whether these passages describe one man. This entry treats them as the same person.

Mattithiah was one of the descendants of Nebo listed in Ezra 10:43 among the Israelite men who had married foreign wives in the period after the return from exile. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was one of those who agreed to put away these wives during Ezra's reforms. His name means "gift of Yah" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), and the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:35 gives it as "Mazitias." Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, and this Mattithiah should not be confused with them.

Mattithiah was one of thirteen men who stood on a wooden platform beside Ezra the scribe when Ezra read the book of the law publicly to the people gathered in Jerusalem after the return from exile. He is named first among the six who stood on Ezra's right hand, with Shema, Anaiah, Urijah, Hilkiah and Maaseiah (Neh 8:4). The verse does not give his family, his office or anything else about him. The STEPBible proper names index (Tyndale House) describes him as a Levite who assisted Ezra in the reading. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and it is uncertain whether this Mattithiah is the same as any of them.

Me-jarkon was a place in the territory allotted to the tribe of Dan, named in Josh 19:46 together with Rakkon and the border near Japho (Joppa). The name probably means "waters of Jarkon" or "yellow waters." Views differ on what it was. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it as a river and identifies it with the Nahr el-'Auja, the modern Yarkon River, which rises near Antipatris and flows into the Mediterranean north of Jaffa. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats it as a town near Joppa. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew text of the verse is difficult and that the Greek translation reads it as "from the river Jarkon." This entry follows the river identification, and the location shown here is a rough point on the Yarkon River north of Jaffa.

Mearah was a place near Sidon, mentioned only in Joshua 13:4 in the list of land the Israelites had not yet conquered when Joshua was old. The verse places it "beside the Sidonians" and traces a line from there to Aphek and the border of the Amorites. The Hebrew name means "cave," so it probably referred to a notable cavern or a settlement named after one. The Greek Septuagint omits the name or reads "from Gaza," which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes is too far south. Some scholars suggest the word may be a garbled form of a Sidonian town name. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions two proposed sites: the cave of Jezzin in Lebanon, east of Sidon, or Mogheiriyeh ("little cave"), northeast of Sidon. The location shown here follows the Mogheiriyeh identification.

Meconah (spelled Mekonah in the King James Version) was a town in the south of Judah. It is named only once, in Neh 11:28, in a list of places where people of Judah lived after the return from exile in Babylon. It appears there next to Ziklag along with its surrounding villages, so it was probably near Ziklag. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "a base or foundation." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the site has not been identified, and its exact location remains uncertain. The location shown here is a rough placement in the northern Negev, in the general area associated with Ziklag.

Medad was one of the elders of Israel chosen during the wilderness journey, in the account of the seventy elders whom Moses gathered to share the burden of leading the people. He and another man, Eldad, were among those registered, but they stayed in the camp instead of going out to the tabernacle. The spirit rested on them there as well, and they prophesied in the camp (Num 11:26). A young man ran to report this to Moses (Num 11:27). The following verses, Num 11:28–29, tell how Joshua urged Moses to stop them, and Moses replied that he wished all the Lord's people were prophets. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "affectionate", and notes that later Jewish tradition, including a lost apocalyptic Book of Eldad and Modad, supplied the content of their prophecy.

Medan was a son of Abraham and Keturah, the woman Abraham took after Sarah's death. He is listed third among six brothers: Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak and Shuah (Gen 25:2). 1 Chr 1:32 repeats the list and calls Keturah Abraham's concubine. Through Abraham he was a half-brother of Isaac and Ishmael. Nothing is recorded about his life. The surrounding passage (Gen 25:6) says Abraham gave gifts to the sons of his concubines and sent them away eastward, away from Isaac, so Medan probably settled somewhere east of Canaan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the tribe named after him and its territory remain unidentified. It treats a link with the Midianites as unlikely because Midian appears beside him as a separate brother. The name is usually taken to mean "strife" or "judgment."

Medeba was a city east of the Jordan on the high tableland north of the Arnon River. It first appears in a victory song over the Amorite kingdom of Heshbon, where it marks the limit of the land laid waste (Num 21:30). In the division of land east of the Jordan, the level plain around it, "the plain of Medeba," fell within Reuben's territory (Josh 13:9, 16). In David's time the Ammonites' hired allies, including the king of Maachah, camped before Medeba to fight Israel (1 Chr 19:7). According to Easton's Bible Dictionary, Joab defeated them there. By Isaiah's day it was a Moabite city, mourned in his oracle against Moab (Isa 15:2). Its name may mean "waters of quiet," though the sense is uncertain. It is generally identified with modern Madaba in Jordan, south of Heshbon, which matches the location shown here.

Media was an ancient country in what is now western and northwestern Iran, the homeland of the Medes. In the books of Esther and Daniel it is closely joined with Persia. The Persian king's court included the "seven princes of Persia and Media" (Esth 1:14), royal acts were recorded in "the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia" (Esth 10:2), and Daniel's two-horned ram stands for the kings of Media and Persia (Dan 8:20). Isaiah calls on Elam and Media to besiege, which in context is aimed at Babylon (Isa 21:2), and Jeremiah lists the kings of the Medes among nations made to drink the cup of judgment. Ezra records that the decree of Cyrus was found at Achmetha, the Ecbatana of the Greeks, in the province of the Medes. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that Persia under Cyrus absorbed Media in the sixth century BC. The location shown here is a central point for the region.

Megiddo was a Canaanite royal city on the southern edge of the Jezreel Valley, whose king Joshua defeated (Josh 12:21). It was assigned to Manasseh, but the tribe did not drive out its Canaanite inhabitants (Josh 17:11; Judg 1:27). Deborah's song places the battle against the kings of Canaan 'by the waters of Megiddo' (Judg 5:19). Under Solomon it lay in Baana's district and was among the cities he fortified with forced labor (1 Kgs 4:12; 9:15). King Ahaziah of Judah, wounded by Jehu's men, fled there and died (2 Kgs 9:27). King Josiah was killed at Megiddo confronting Pharaoh Necho, about 609 BC by inference from context (2 Kgs 23:29–30; 2 Chr 35:22). Zechariah recalls a great mourning 'in the valley of Megiddon' (Zech 12:11). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes a minority identification with Mujedd'a near Bethshean. The location shown here follows the el-Lejjun identification (modern Tel Megiddo).

Mehetabeel was the father of Delaiah and the grandfather of Shemaiah, the man who invited Nehemiah to meet him inside the temple and shut the doors because enemies were coming to kill him (Neh 6:10). He is known only from this genealogical note, which identifies Shemaiah by his father and grandfather. His name is usually understood to mean "God does good" or, in Easton's Bible Dictionary, "whose benefactor is God." The following verses show that Shemaiah had been hired by Tobiah and Sanballat to frighten Nehemiah into sinning, but nothing is said about Mehetabeel himself. The name is spelled Mehetabel in some English versions and should not be confused with Mehetabel, the wife of the Edomite king Hadar (Gen 36:39).

Mehetabel was the wife of Hadad, one of the kings who ruled Edom before Israel had a king. She is mentioned only in the list of Edomite kings, where her husband succeeds Baal-hanan son of Achbor and reigns from a city called Pau (Gen 36:39), spelled Pai in the parallel list (1 Chr 1:50). Genesis gives her husband's name as Hadar, while Chronicles has Hadad. The two forms differ by a single letter in Hebrew and are generally taken as the same king. Both passages describe her as the daughter of Matred and the daughter, or granddaughter, of Mezahab. It is unclear whether Mezahab was Matred's father or mother. Her name is usually explained as "God does good" or "favored of God" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). A man in Nehemiah's time bore a related name.

Mehida was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (Nethinim) whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon. "The children of Mehida" appear in the list of returning exiles in Ezra 2:52 and again in the parallel list in Neh 7:54. In both lists they come between the families of Bazluth (Bazlith) and Harsha. The lists connect the returning groups with Zerubbabel, and Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both place this family among those who came back with him. Nothing is recorded about Mehida himself beyond his name, which functions here as a family name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that 1 Esdras 5:32 gives the name as "Meeda" and takes it to mean "renowned," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as "a riddle" or "sharpness of wit."

Mehir was a man in the genealogies of the tribe of Judah, named only in 1 Chr 4:11. He was the son of Chelub, who is described as the brother of Shuah, and he was the father of Eshton. Nothing else is recorded about his life. His place among Judah's descendants comes from the setting of the list in 1 Chronicles 4, which traces the families of Judah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "price" or "hire," and Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "a reward." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes that the Targum of Rabbi Joseph calls him Perug, an Aramaic name with the same meaning.

Mehujael was a descendant of Cain, named in the genealogy of Cain's line in Gen 4:18. He was the son of Irad, the grandson of Enoch son of Cain, and the father of Methusael, whose son was Lamech. That makes him the fourth generation after Cain. Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the meaning of his name as "smitten by God," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "who proclaims God." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes the view that the genealogy of Seth's line in Genesis 5 reworks the same material, so that Mahalaleel there would correspond to Mehujael. This entry treats Mehujael as a distinct person in Cain's line, as Gen 4:18 presents him.

Mehuman was one of the seven chamberlains who served in the presence of King Ahasuerus of Persia, and he is named first in the list in Esth 1:10. On the seventh day of the king's feast, when Ahasuerus was merry with wine, he commanded these seven men to bring Queen Vashti before him, as the following verse goes on to say. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe the chamberlains as eunuchs and give the meaning of the name as "faithful", while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "making an uproar" or "a multitude." Easton's identifies Ahasuerus with Xerxes. Mehuman is not mentioned anywhere else in the Bible, and nothing more is known about him.

Mehunim, also spelled Meunim, is the ancestral name of a family of temple servants (Nethinim) listed among those who returned from the Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:50; Neh 7:52). The name appears only as a family heading, so nothing is known of an individual by this name. It is a plural form, and Easton's Bible Dictionary connects it with the Meunim, or Maonites, a people of the region south and southeast of Judah whom Uzziah defeated (2 Chr 26:7) and who were displaced in Hezekiah's day (1 Chr 4:41). On that view, this family probably descended from Meunite captives or foreigners who had been assigned to serve at the temple. This entry treats Mehunim as the name of a family line among the temple servants.

Melatiah was a man from Gibeon who helped rebuild the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah, after the return from exile in Babylon. Nehemiah 3 lists the groups that repaired each section. Melatiah appears in Neh 3:7 alongside Jadon the Meronothite, among the men of Gibeon and Mizpah. They worked next to the men of Tekoa, near the "throne of the governor on this side the river." This probably refers to the official seat of the Persian governor of the province west of the Euphrates. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name is generally taken to mean "the Lord delivers" or "deliverance of the Lord," as given in Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Melchi was an ancestor of Jesus named in Luke's genealogy, which traces the line back from Joseph. He is listed as the son of Janna and the father of Levi, and he stands a few generations before Joseph, the husband of Mary (Luke 3:24). Nothing else is recorded about him. Another Melchi appears further back in the same genealogy (Luke 3:28), so the name belongs to more than one person, and this entry refers to the one in Luke 3:24. Because Luke's line runs through David, he is counted with the tribe of Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names give the meaning of the name as "my king" or "my counsel."

Melchi was an ancestor of Jesus named only in Luke's genealogy, which traces Jesus' descent back through David's son Nathan rather than through the kings of Judah. He is listed as the son of Addi (Luke 3:28). The neighboring verse makes him the father of Neri, whose son Salathiel (Shealtiel) appears in the generations around the Babylonian exile. By inference, Melchi lived during the later monarchy, a member of the tribe of Judah through David's family. Nothing else is recorded about him. Another Melchi, son of Janna, appears a few generations later in the same list (Luke 3:24), so the two should not be confused. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "my king" or "my counsel."

Melchiah, also spelled Malchiah, was the father of Pashur, an official in Jerusalem during the reign of King Zedekiah. His name means roughly "the LORD is king." He appears only in his son's name. Zedekiah sent Pashur son of Melchiah, with the priest Zephaniah, to consult Jeremiah (Jer 21:1). Pashur son of Malchiah was also among the officials who heard Jeremiah's warnings to the people and, as the following verses tell, had him imprisoned (Jer 38:1). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe Melchiah as a priest. This probably connects him with the priestly Pashur son of Malchijah listed in 1 Chr 9:12. Jer 38:6 names a cistern belonging to "Malchiah the son of Hammelech," into which Jeremiah was lowered. Whether that Malchiah is the same man is uncertain.

Melchisedec, also spelled Melchizedek, was king of Salem and priest of the most high God in Abraham's time. When Abraham returned from defeating the kings who had captured Lot, Melchisedec brought out bread and wine and blessed him (Gen 14:18; Heb 7:1). The next verse, Gen 14:20, adds that Abraham gave him a tenth of the spoils. Nothing is said of his ancestry. Ps 110:4 speaks of one sworn by the LORD to be "a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek." The Letter to the Hebrews quotes this line repeatedly and applies it to Jesus. It contrasts this priesthood with the Levitical priesthood of Aaron and notes that Levi was still in Abraham's body when Melchisedec met him (Heb 7:10–11). Salem is commonly identified with Jerusalem. Easton's and Smith's Bible dictionaries mention an old Jewish tradition that identified him with Noah's son Shem.

Melea was a man named only in Luke's genealogy of Jesus. Luke 3:31 lists him as the son of Menan. His son was Eliakim, named in the preceding verse. He belongs to the line that runs from David through David's son Nathan rather than through Solomon, so he was of the tribe of Judah. Melea is a few generations after Nathan: Nathan, Mattatha, Menan, then Melea. Nothing else is recorded about his life. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "fulness," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "supplying" or "supplied."

Melech was a Benjamite, a descendant of King Saul, named as the second of the four sons of Micah. His brothers were Pithon, Tarea (also spelled Tahrea) and Ahaz. He appears only in the two parallel genealogies of Saul's family (1 Chr 8:35; 1 Chr 9:41). The surrounding verses trace this line from Saul through Jonathan to Merib-baal, the son of Jonathan better known as Mephibosheth, and then to Micah. That makes Melech Mephibosheth's grandson and Jonathan's great-grandson, as Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note. His name means "king." Nothing more is recorded about his life. The line continues through his brother Ahaz rather than through him.

Melita is the island in the Mediterranean where the ship carrying Paul as a prisoner to Rome was wrecked. After the crew and passengers reached shore, they learned the island's name (Acts 28:1). It is the modern Malta, south of Sicily. According to Easton's Bible Dictionary, Paul and his companions stayed there three months before sailing on to Rome in another Alexandrian ship that had wintered at the island. By inference from context, this was probably about AD 57. Tradition places the wreck at St. Paul's Bay on the island's northeast coast, and both Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note how well that site fits the description in Acts. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes the island at that time as a dependency of the Roman province of Sicily. Some older interpreters placed Melita at Mljet (Meleda) in the Adriatic Sea, but this entry follows the Malta identification.

Melzar was an official at the Babylonian court. The chief of the eunuchs put him in charge of Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah, young men from Judah who were being trained for royal service (Dan 1:11). Daniel spoke with him about their food. The verses in between describe a ten-day trial of vegetables and water, so Melzar probably agreed to that test. Afterward he took away the king's food and wine they had been given and fed them pulse, meaning vegetables (Dan 1:16). The King James Version treats Melzar as a personal name. Other readings take the Hebrew word, which has the article ("the melzar"), as a job title. Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "the steward," and Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it means a chief butler. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links it to a Babylonian word for a guardian. This entry follows the King James reading of a named individual.

Memphis was the ancient capital of Lower (northern) Egypt, on the west bank of the Nile about 12 miles south of modern Cairo. The location shown here matches the ruins near the village of Mit Rahina. In the King James Bible it appears as Memphis only in Hos 9:6, where the Hebrew is Moph. Elsewhere it is called Noph, a shortened form of its Egyptian name Men-nofer (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). The prophets name it among Egypt's leading cities in oracles of judgment. Isaiah says its princes are deceived, and Jeremiah and Ezekiel foretell that it will be laid waste, left without inhabitants and stripped of its idols (Jer 46:19; Ezek 30:13). Jeremiah 44:1 also lists Noph among the places where Jews lived in Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the city declined after the Persian king Cambyses attacked it, about 525 BC.

Memucan was one of the seven princes of Persia and Media at the court of King Ahasuerus. These men "saw the king's face" and held the highest rank in the kingdom (Esth 1:14). When Queen Vashti refused the king's summons to appear at his feast, Ahasuerus asked these counsellors what should be done. Memucan spoke for them. He argued that Vashti had wronged not only the king but every prince and people in the provinces, because her example might lead wives everywhere to disregard their husbands (Esth 1:16). He recommended that she be removed as queen and her position given to another, with a royal decree announcing the decision. The king and the princes approved, and Ahasuerus acted on his advice (Esth 1:21). The name is probably of Persian origin, and Easton's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "dignified."

Menahem son of Gadi was a king of Israel. He came up from Tirzah to Samaria, killed Shallum son of Jabesh and took the throne (2 Kgs 15:14). He then attacked Tiphsah and its territory because the town would not open its gates to him, and he ripped open its pregnant women. He began to reign in the thirty-ninth year of Azariah king of Judah and ruled ten years in Samaria, from about 772 to 761 BC by inference from context. When Pul king of Assyria invaded, Menahem paid him a thousand talents of silver to secure his support for his rule. He raised the sum by charging each wealthy man in Israel fifty shekels, and the Assyrian king withdrew. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies Pul with Tiglath-pileser III, whose inscriptions name Menahem of Samaria. His son Pekahiah succeeded him.

Menan is a name in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, which traces Jesus' ancestry back through Joseph. He appears as the son of Mattatha and the father of Melea (Luke 3:31). Since Mattatha was the son of Nathan, a son of King David, Menan was a great-grandson of David through the line of Nathan rather than through Solomon, and so belonged to the tribe of Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the Revised Version spells his name Menna. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he is mentioned nowhere else in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "numbered," "rewarded" or "prepared."

Meonothai was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:14 as the father of Ophrah. This entry treats him as a son of Othniel and a brother of Hathath. The Hebrew text of 1 Chr 4:13 names only Hathath as Othniel's son. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the King James margin, the Latin Vulgate and one Greek manuscript tradition read "the sons of Othniel, Hathath and Meonothai," which links Meonothai to Othniel. Othniel, the first judge, was the nephew of Caleb. Smith's Bible Dictionary says Othniel was the son of Caleb's younger brother. Meonothai's name probably means "my dwellings." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests his son Ophrah may have been the founder of a town of that name. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Mephaath was a city east of the Jordan in the territory given to the tribe of Reuben, listed with Jahazah and Kedemoth among the towns of the tableland (Josh 13:18). It was one of the four Reubenite cities assigned, with their surrounding pasturelands, to the Merarite clan of the Levites (Josh 21:37; 1 Chr 6:79). Centuries later, Jeremiah names it among the towns of the 'plain country' on which judgment falls in his prophecy against Moab, which suggests the area was then under Moabite control (Jer 48:21). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Eusebius and Jerome knew it as the site of a Roman garrison. The location is uncertain. Proposed sites include Tell Jawa, south of modern Amman, and Umm er-Rasas further south. The location shown here follows the Tell Jawa identification.

Mephibosheth, also called Merib-baal, was the son of Jonathan and grandson of King Saul. He was five when news came of Saul and Jonathan's deaths, and his nurse dropped him as she fled, leaving him lame in both feet (2 Sam 4:4). David later brought him to Jerusalem, gave him Saul's land to be farmed by Saul's servant Ziba, and had him eat regularly at the king's table (2 Sam 9:10–13). He had a young son, Micah. During Absalom's revolt Ziba met the fleeing David with supplies and was granted all of Mephibosheth's property (2 Sam 16:1–4). When David returned, Mephibosheth came to meet him unwashed and ungroomed. By his own account Ziba had deceived him, and he told the king to let Ziba take everything (2 Sam 19:24–30). David later spared him because of his oath to Jonathan (2 Sam 21:7). Another son of Saul bore the same name.

Mephibosheth was a son of King Saul by his concubine Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah, and the brother of Armoni. He should not be confused with Jonathan's son of the same name, who was Saul's grandson and whom David spared (2 Sam 21:7). During a famine in David's reign, which the surrounding passage ties to Saul's earlier killing of Gibeonites, David handed seven of Saul's descendants over to the Gibeonites: Mephibosheth, Armoni and five grandsons of Saul. The following verses say the Gibeonites hanged them on a hill at the beginning of the barley harvest, and that Rizpah guarded the bodies until the rains came (2 Sam 21:9–10). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both identify him as one of these seven victims. Through his father Saul he was a half-brother of Jonathan, Abinadab, Malchi-shua, Merab and Michal.

Merab was the elder of King Saul's two daughters, sister of Michal and Jonathan. Her mother was probably Ahinoam, who is named as Saul's wife in the next verse after her own listing. Saul offered Merab to David as his wife on condition that he fight the Philistines, hoping David would die in battle. When the time for the marriage came, she was given instead to Adriel the Meholathite. 2 Sam 21:8 says that Adriel's five sons were born to Michal, and these sons were handed over to the Gibeonites and put to death (2 Sam 21:9). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes Michal's name there as a scribal slip for Merab. An ancient Targum explains that Merab bore the sons and Michal raised them. This entry follows the view that the five sons were Merab's, which is why Michal appears as another name for her.

Meraiah was a priest in the days of Joiakim, the high priest who succeeded his father Jeshua after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears in Neh 12:12 in a list of the heads of the priestly families, where he is named as head of the house of Seraiah. That family is probably named after the Seraiah listed among the priests who came back with Zerubbabel earlier in the same chapter. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connects this house with Ezra, whose ancestry Ezra 7:1 traces through a Seraiah. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "resistance", and Smith's Bible Dictionary as "rebellion". Nothing more is recorded about him.

Meraioth was a priest of the tribe of Levi, descended from Aaron through Eleazar, who appears only in genealogies. He was the son of Zerahiah and the father of Amariah, in the line of high priests that leads to Zadok (1 Chr 6:6–7, 52). The genealogy of Ezra also names him as an ancestor (Ezra 7:3). That list is shortened, since there Azariah follows Meraioth directly. In 1 Chr 9:11 and Neh 11:11, a Meraioth stands between Ahitub and Zadok in the ancestry of a chief officer of the temple. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take this as probably a different, later man of the same name. Others read it as the same ancestor in a compressed list. This entry follows the line in 1 Chronicles 6. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "bitterness" or "rebellious."

Merari was the third son of Levi, listed with his brothers Gershon and Kohath, and one of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:11; Exod 6:16). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "bitter." His sons Mahli and Mushi founded the two Merarite families (Exod 6:19; Num 3:33). 1 Chr 24:26–27 also names Jaaziah, apparently as a further son, though the wording is unclear. In the wilderness the Merarites camped north of the tabernacle under Zuriel. They were responsible for its boards, bars, pillars and sockets, served under Ithamar the priest, and were given four wagons and eight oxen to carry them (Num 3:35–36; 7:8). Under Joshua they received twelve cities from Reuben, Gad and Zebulun. Later descendants served as musicians such as Ethan, as gatekeepers, and as Levites under David, Hezekiah, Josiah and Ezra.

Merathaim is a name used for Babylon or the land of Babylonia in Jer 50:21, part of Jeremiah's prophecy against Babylon. In that verse the LORD commands an attacker to go up against 'the land of Merathaim' and the inhabitants of Pekod, and to destroy them completely. The Hebrew name means 'double rebellion.' Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it as a symbolic name for Babylon, marking a rebellion greater than that of other nations. Smith's Bible Dictionary connects the 'double' with the two captivities Babylon brought on Israel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes Delitzsch's suggestion that it may also echo the Babylonian name Marratu, the 'bitter river' or Persian Gulf, and so refer to southern Babylonia. The location shown here places it at the site of Babylon itself, south of modern Baghdad in Iraq.

Mered was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in a fragmentary genealogy as one of the sons of Ezra (spelled Ezrah in some translations), alongside Jether, Epher and Jalon (1 Chr 4:17). He married Bithiah, described as the daughter of Pharaoh (1 Chr 4:18). The passage is hard to follow, but it probably means that Miriam, Shammai and Ishbah, the father of Eshtemoa, were Bithiah's children. Mered also had a wife called Jehudijah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reads this name as a description, "the Jewess," which sets her apart from the Egyptian wife. It also suggests that the Hodiah of 1 Chr 4:19 is the same woman, whose descendants include Keilah the Garmite. His name means "rebellion." Smith's Bible Dictionary mentions a tradition that identifies him with Caleb and Moses.

Meremoth son of Urijah was a priest in Jerusalem after the exile, from the family of Koz (Smith's Bible Dictionary links this with Hakkoz). When Ezra arrived, Meremoth weighed the silver, gold and temple vessels brought from Babylon, assisted by Eleazar and the Levites Jozabad and Noadiah (Ezra 8:33). During Nehemiah's rebuilding of the wall he repaired two sections, the second running the length of Eliashib's house, probably the high priest named in Neh 3:1 (Neh 3:4, 21). This entry also connects him with the Meremoth who sealed Nehemiah's covenant (Neh 10:5) and with the priest Meremoth listed among those who returned with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:3). That priestly house, later headed by Helkai, appears as Meraioth (Neh 12:15), which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats as a scribal variant. Because Zerubbabel's return came about a century earlier, these mentions may refer to an ancestor or to the family rather than the same man.

Meremoth was a man of the family of Bani who is named in Ezra 10:36 among the Israelites who had married foreign wives after the return from exile. The surrounding list in Ezra 10 records those who agreed to send away these wives in response to Ezra's reforms. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a layman, not a priest or Levite. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:34 appears to give his name as Carabasion. Several other men in the Bible bear the name Meremoth, and this one is distinct from them. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name is usually taken to mean "heights" or "elevations."

Meres was one of the seven princes of Persia and Media at the court of King Ahasuerus. Esth 1:14 describes these men as officials who "saw the king's face" and "sat the first in the kingdom," meaning they had direct access to the king and held the highest rank under him. By inference from the surrounding passage, Meres was among the advisers the king consulted when Queen Vashti refused to appear at his banquet, though only Memucan's advice is recorded. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of Ahasuerus's seven counsellors and gives the meaning of his name as "lofty." Hitchcock's Bible Names offers a different meaning. He is mentioned only in this one verse, and nothing else is known about him.

Meribah (of Kadesh) was a spring at Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin. There the Israelites quarreled with the LORD over a lack of water, and water was provided from a rock, near the end of the desert wanderings. The name means "strife" or "quarrel" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Moses and Aaron were told that, because they rebelled against God's word at the water of Meribah, they would not enter the promised land (Num 20:24; Num 27:14). The surrounding account in Numbers 20 describes Moses striking the rock. Smith's Bible Dictionary distinguishes this place from the Massah and Meribah of Exodus 17 near Rephidim, and calls it Meribah-kadesh. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that some think one place carried both names. Ps 81:7 could refer to either. This entry treats the Kadesh spring as its own place. The location shown here is approximate, in the Kadesh region of northeastern Sinai.

Meribah (of Horeb) was the name Moses gave, along with Massah, to the place near Rephidim where the Israelites quarreled with him over lack of water and tested the LORD by asking, "Is the LORD among us, or not?" (Exod 17:7). The surrounding account in Exodus 17 says water came from a rock at Horeb when Moses struck it, so the site is described as a spring. The name means "quarrel" or "dispute." Moses later recalled the episode in his blessing of the tribe of Levi (Deut 33:8). It belongs to the wilderness wanderings, about 1491 BC by inference from context. It is distinct from the later Meribah at Kadesh in Numbers 20. Its exact location is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests Wady Feiran near Mount Serbal, and the location shown here is a rough placement in that part of southern Sinai.

Meribah-kadesh was the place in the wilderness of Zin where, according to Deut 32:51, Moses and Aaron failed to honor God as holy before Israel. That failure is the reason given for Moses not entering the promised land. The name joins Meribah, meaning “strife” or “quarreling,” with Kadesh. It recalls the episode in Num 20, where the people complained about having no water at Kadesh and Moses struck the rock. Ezekiel calls the same spot “the waters of strife in Kadesh” and uses it as a point on the ideal southern border of the restored land, running from Tamar to Kadesh and then along the brook to the Mediterranean (Ezek 47:19; 48:28). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies Kadesh with Kadesh-barnea at ‘Ain el-Kadeis. The rough location shown here, in northeastern Sinai near the springs of that area, follows this identification.

Merodach-baladan, son of Baladan, was a king of Babylon in the time of Hezekiah, king of Judah. Isa 39:1 records that he sent letters and a gift to Hezekiah after hearing that Hezekiah had been ill and had recovered. The parallel account in 2 Kgs 20:12 gives his name as Berodach-baladan. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that his name appears in Assyrian inscriptions. That dictionary describes two reigns: the first from about 721 to 709 BC, and a short second reign of about half a year after he regained the throne around 702 BC. It dates the embassy to Hezekiah to about 713 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a Chaldean king who fought the Assyrian kings Sargon and Sennacherib for control of Babylon. It suggests the embassy may also have sought an alliance with Judah against Assyria.

Merom, or "the waters of Merom," was a body of water in northern Canaan where a coalition of kings gathered to fight Israel (Josh 11:5). Joshua made a sudden attack on them there and routed them (Josh 11:7). The surrounding chapter names Jabin king of Hazor as the leader of the alliance and says the pursuit went as far as Sidon. The name is usually explained as "height" or "high place." Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with Lake Huleh, a small lake in the upper Jordan Valley about ten miles north of the Sea of Galilee, once ringed by papyrus marsh. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mentions other views: Josephus places the allied camp at Beroth near Kedesh in upper Galilee, and Conder proposed a stream west of Nazareth. The location shown here follows the Lake Huleh identification.

Meroz was a place in northern Israel that is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the Song of Deborah. After the victory of Deborah and Barak over Sisera, the angel of the LORD calls for a bitter curse on Meroz and its inhabitants because they did not come to help in the battle (Judg 5:23). The passage gives no further detail. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the harsh words may mean Meroz lay near the battlefield, so its people could easily have joined the fight or stopped Sisera as he fled. Its site is unknown. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it near the Kishon River, while Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mention a possible identification with el-Murussus, north of the Jezreel Valley near Beth-shean. The location shown here is only approximate and places it in the general area of Mount Tabor.

Mesha was a king of Moab in the time of the kings of Israel. According to 2 Kgs 3:4, he was a sheep breeder who paid the king of Israel a yearly tribute of a hundred thousand lambs and the wool of a hundred thousand rams. The following verses of the same chapter say that after Ahab's death Mesha rebelled against Israel. Jehoram of Israel, joined by Jehoshaphat of Judah and the king of Edom, then invaded Moab and laid it waste. Shut up in Kir-hareseth, Mesha offered his firstborn son as a burnt offering on the city wall, and the invaders withdrew. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him the son of Chemosh-Gad and links him with the Moabite Stone, an inscription found at Dibon that records his exploits. The name is also borne by other people in the Bible.

Mesha was the firstborn son of Caleb, the brother of Jerahmeel, and belonged to the tribe of Judah. He appears only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:42, which calls him "the father of Ziph." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes this to mean he was probably the ancestor of the Ziphites, the people of the town of Ziph in Judah. The verse goes on to mention "the sons of Mareshah the father of Hebron." The STEPBible proper-names index reads Mareshah as Mesha's son and the re-founder of Hebron, and this entry follows that reading in connecting Mesha with Hebron. Some Greek manuscripts give his name as Marisa, which suggests a link with Mareshah. Smith's Bible Dictionary mentions the medieval commentator Kimchi's suggestion that his mother was Caleb's wife Azubah. The name probably means "deliverance." Several other people in the Bible share the name, including the king of Moab.

Mesha was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the sons Shaharaim had by his wife Hodesh. He is named in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles alongside his full brothers Jobab, Zibia, Malcham, Jeuz, Shachia and Mirma. Shaharaim also had sons Abitub and Elpaal by another wife, Hushim, who were Mesha's half-brothers. The surrounding verses place these births in the country of Moab, after Shaharaim had sent away his earlier wives, so Mesha was probably born there. Nothing further is recorded about him. He should not be confused with others of the same name, including Mesha the king of Moab, who rebelled against Israel in the days of Ahab's sons. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "burden" or "salvation". Smith's Bible Dictionary gives it as "freedom".

Mesha is a place named in Gen 10:30 as one end of the territory where the descendants of Joktan lived, which stretched from Mesha toward Sephar, "a mount of the east." The "their" of the verse refers, by context, to Joktan's thirteen sons listed just before it, many of whose names are linked with tribes of Arabia. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Mesha as one of the boundaries of the Joktanites when they first settled in Arabia, and Easton's Bible Dictionary calls it a plain on the borders of Arabia. Its exact site is unknown. Proposals range from northern or northwestern Arabia to the Red Sea coast further south. The location shown here is a rough placement in northwestern Arabia, east of the Gulf of Aqaba, marking the northern end of the Joktanite range. This is distinct from Mesha the king of Moab and from other people of that name.

Meshach was the Babylonian name given to Mishael, one of the young men from Judah taken to Babylon and trained for royal service alongside Daniel, Hananiah (Shadrach) and Azariah (Abednego) (Dan 1:6–7). After their training the king found none like them, and they entered his service (Dan 1:19). Daniel shared with them the matter of the king's dream (Dan 2:17), and at Daniel's request the three were set over the affairs of the province of Babylon (Dan 2:49). When they refused to serve Nebuchadnezzar's gods or worship his golden image, the king had them bound and thrown into a furnace heated seven times hotter than usual. The flames killed the men who carried them, but the three came out unharmed. Nebuchadnezzar then praised their God, forbade anyone to speak against him, and promoted them (Dan 3:12–30). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Mishael perhaps means "who is equal to God?"

Meshech was the sixth son of Japheth and a grandson of Noah, listed in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:2; 1 Chr 1:5). The name also stands for the people descended from him. Ezekiel regularly pairs Meshech with Tubal. They traded slaves and bronze vessels in the markets of Tyre (Ezek 27:13), they appear among the slain nations in the realm of the dead (Ezek 32:26), and Gog of the land of Magog is called their chief prince (Ezek 38:2–3; 39:1). The spelling Mesech appears in Ps 120:5, where the name stands for a distant, hostile people. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries both identify the tribe with the Moschi, who lived in the mountains between the Black and Caspian Seas, on the borders of Armenia. A different Meshech, listed among the sons of Shem, appears in 1 Chr 1:17.

Meshech was a people and land on the far northern edge of the biblical world, named after Meshech son of Japheth (Gen 10:2). Ezekiel lists Meshech with Javan and Tubal as merchants who traded slaves and bronze vessels in the markets of Tyre (Ezek 27:13). His prophecy against Gog calls Gog the "chief prince of Meshech and Tubal" (Ezek 38:2–3; 39:1). In Ps 120:5 the psalmist laments living in Meshech and among the tents of Kedar. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes this as a way of describing distant, hostile foreigners. Easton's identifies Meshech with the Moschi, who lived in the mountains between the Black and Caspian Seas. Others link the name with the Mushki of Assyrian records, in central or eastern Anatolia (modern Turkey). The location shown here follows the general region between the Black and Caspian Seas.

Meshech-Tubal is the pairing of Meshech and Tubal, two peoples named together in Ezekiel's lament over Egypt. In Ezek 32:26 they appear among the fallen nations in the underworld, lying in their graves with the uncircumcised, killed by the sword, though they once spread terror in the land of the living. Elsewhere the two are listed as sons of Japheth (Gen 10:2), as traders in slaves and bronze with Tyre (Ezek 27:13), and as peoples ruled by Gog (Ezek 38:2). They are commonly identified with the Mushku and Tabal known from Assyrian records in eastern Anatolia, though some place them farther north toward the Black Sea and Caucasus. Their exact homeland is uncertain, and the location shown here is an approximate regional placement north of the Caucasus.

Meshelemiah was a Levite of the Korahite clan, son of Kore and descended from Asaph. He headed one of the divisions of gatekeepers (porters) at the sanctuary. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary place him in the reign of David. He had seven sons. Zechariah the firstborn, Jediael, Zebadiah and Jathniel are named here, and Elam, Jehohanan and Elioenai in the following verse (1 Chr 26:3). His sons and relatives together numbered eighteen able men. When lots were cast to assign the gates, the east gate fell to him, under the shorter name Shelemiah. His son Zechariah, described as a wise counsellor, received the north gate. Zechariah is also remembered as keeper of the door of the tabernacle. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia further identifies Meshelemiah with the Shallum of 1 Chr 9:17–31 and the Meshullam of Neh 12:25.

Meshezabeel was the father of Berechiah and the grandfather of Meshullam, one of the men who repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall in Nehemiah's time.
