He is known only from this genealogical note in Neh 3:4, which identifies Meshullam by naming his father and grandfather. Nothing else is said about Meshezabeel himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "delivered by God." The same name belongs to other men in Nehemiah, including a leader who sealed the covenant (Neh 10:21) and the father of Pethahiah (Neh 11:24). Whether any of these is the same person as Meshullam's grandfather cannot be determined from the text.

Meshezabeel was one of the leaders who put their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, when the returned exiles pledged to keep the law of God (Neh 10:21). His name appears among the "chief of the people," the lay heads listed after the priests and Levites. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "delivered by God" and suggests that it may stand for a family rather than a single individual. Nothing else is recorded about him. The same name is borne by other men in Nehemiah, including the grandfather of Meshullam, who helped rebuild the wall (Neh 3:4), and the father of Pethahiah (Neh 11:24). Whether any of these is the same person or belongs to the same family is uncertain.

Meshezabeel was the father of Pethahiah, a man of Judah descended from Zerah, son of Judah (Neh 11:24). He is known only through his son, who served "at the king's hand in all matters concerning the people." This is generally understood to mean that Pethahiah represented the Jews of Jerusalem at the Persian court in the time of Nehemiah. Nothing else is recorded about Meshezabeel himself. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary renders as "delivered by God," is shared by other men in Nehemiah: one is an ancestor of Meshullam, who helped repair the wall, and another sealed the covenant. Whether any of these is the same person as Pethahiah's father is uncertain. This entry treats him as the father of Pethahiah named in this verse.

Meshillemith was a priest, the son of Immer, who appears only as an ancestor in two lists of priests living in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. In 1 Chr 9:12 he is the father of Meshullam and an ancestor of the priest Maasiai. Nehemiah 11:13 spells his name Meshillemoth and names him as an ancestor of Amashai, one of the priestly heads of families in Jerusalem. The two genealogies give different names between him and his descendants, and they are usually taken as parallel versions of the same family line. His father Immer probably stands for the priestly family of that name rather than a single generation. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "recompense." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Meshillemoth was an Ephraimite, known only as the father of Berechiah. His son was one of the leaders of the tribe of Ephraim who stood up against the soldiers of the northern kingdom when they returned from war with captives from Judah (2 Chr 28:12). From the surrounding chapter, this was during Pekah's war against Ahaz of Judah. Berechiah and the other leaders refused to let the captives be brought into Samaria as slaves. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Meshillemoth himself as one of the tribe's chiefs, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the leading role to his son. Both dictionaries say the name means "recompense." A priest in Nehemiah's time had the same name, but he is a different person.

Meshobab was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named first in a list of clan leaders in 1 Chr 4:34. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 4:38–41) describes these leaders as princes in their families whose households grew large. Looking for pasture for their flocks, they went toward Gedor and drove out the earlier inhabitants. The passage places this in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, so Meshobab probably lived in the late 8th century BC, by inference from context. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connects the list with the settlement near Gedor, which some read as Gerar, and with the attack on the Meunites. Nothing else is recorded about him, and his father's name is not given.

Meshullam was the father of Azaliah and the grandfather of Shaphan the scribe, who served King Josiah of Judah. He is named only once, in the genealogy given for Shaphan when Josiah sent him to the house of the LORD in the eighteenth year of his reign (2 Kgs 22:3). Nothing else is recorded about him. Many other men in the Bible bear the same name, especially in the period after the exile, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes, and this one should not be confused with them. The name is usually explained as meaning "devoted" or "resigned" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), "friend" (Smith's Bible Dictionary) or "peaceable" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Since his grandson was active in Josiah's reign, Meshullam probably lived two generations earlier, in the seventh century BC, though this is only an inference.

Meshullam was a son of Zerubbabel and a member of the tribe of Judah. He appears only in the genealogy of David's royal line after the exile in Babylon, where he is listed first among Zerubbabel's children, followed by his brother Hananiah and his sister Shelomith (1 Chr 3:19). The next verse lists five more sons, Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah and Jushab-hesed (1 Chr 3:20). Matthew's genealogy of Jesus names another son of Zerubbabel, Abiud (Matt 1:13), who does not appear in the Chronicles list. Nothing is recorded about Meshullam's life. International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name, meaning "devoted" or "resigned," was very common after the exile, and several other men called Meshullam appear in the Bible. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries both identify this man simply as Zerubbabel's son.

Meshullam was a member of the tribe of Gad, one of seven kinsmen listed together in the Gadite genealogy of 1 Chr 5:13 alongside Michael, Sheba, Jorai, Jachan, Zia and Heber. The following verse in that passage identifies these men as sons of Abihail. The surrounding chapter places the Gadites in Bashan, east of the Jordan, and says their genealogy was recorded in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel. On that basis Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of the chief Gadites in Bashan in Jotham's time. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Meshullam is shared by many people in the Bible, especially after the exile, and this Gadite should not be confused with them. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the name to mean "devoted" or "resigned," while Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "friend."

Meshullam was a Benjamite, one of the sons of Elpaal, named in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin in 1 Chr 8:17. He is listed there alongside Zebadiah, Hezeki and Heber. Other brothers named in the wider list include Eber, Misham, Shamed, Beriah, Shema, Ishmerai, Jezliah and Jobab. The passage also connects Elpaal's family with the towns of Ono, Lod and Aijalon. Nothing further is recorded about him beyond his place in this family list. Several other men in the Bible share the name Meshullam, which Smith's Bible Dictionary takes to mean "friend," and this one should not be confused with them.

Meshullam was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, the son of Hodaviah and the father of Sallu. He appears only in a genealogy in 1 Chr 9:7, which traces Sallu's line back through Meshullam and Hodaviah to Hasenuah. That chapter lists the families who settled in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile, so Meshullam's line was probably among them, and the STEPBible Proper Names index places him with those Jerusalem residents. A similar list in Neh 11:7 also names a Benjamite Sallu son of Meshullam but gives a different line of ancestors, so the two lists may record the same family in different forms. Several other men in the Bible share the name Meshullam, and this one should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "peaceable" or "perfect."

Meshullam son of Shephathiah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin. He appears in the list of people who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. His line of descent is traced back through his father Shephathiah to Reuel and then to Ibnijah (1 Chr 9:8). The surrounding passage names him among the Benjamite heads of families who settled in the city, and Smith's Bible Dictionary likewise places him in Jerusalem after the captivity. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible are also called Meshullam, including another Benjamite in the same chapter, so he should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "peaceable" or "perfect," and Smith's gives "friend."

Meshullam was a priest of the family of Immer, named only in genealogies. In 1 Chr 9:12 he is the son of Meshillemith and the father of Jahzerah, and an ancestor of Maasiai, one of the priests listed among those living in Jerusalem, by context after the return from the Babylonian exile. The parallel list in Neh 11:13 traces Amashai back through Azareel and Ahasai to Meshillemoth, son of Immer. This entry treats the Ahasai of that verse as the same man as Meshullam, since both stand as son of Meshillemith or Meshillemoth. Smith's Bible Dictionary instead matches Ahasai with Jahzerah, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes the Nehemiah list as omitting Meshullam's name. Because the two lists differ in names and order, the exact match is uncertain. Several other men in the Bible share the name Meshullam, which was common after the exile.

Meshullam was a Levite descended from Kohath who helped oversee the repair of the temple in Jerusalem during the reign of King Josiah of Judah. According to 2 Chr 34:12, he and Zechariah, both Kohathites, directed the workmen alongside Jahath and Obadiah, Levites of the line of Merari, and the text says the men did the work faithfully. The same verse mentions Levites skilled with musical instruments, though it does not say whether Meshullam was one of them. Smith's Bible Dictionary allows that the name here may stand for a Kohathite family rather than a single man. This verse is the only mention of him. The name was common, especially after the exile, and belongs to several other men in the Bible who should not be confused with this Levite. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives its meaning as "devoted" or "resigned."

Meshullam was one of the "chief men" Ezra summoned while preparing to lead a group of exiles from Babylon to Jerusalem (Ezra 8:16). According to the surrounding passage, Ezra had camped by the river Ahava and found no Levites among his company. He called for Meshullam and several other leaders and then sent them to Iddo at Casiphia to bring Levites and temple servants for the journey. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both describe him this way. The STEPBible name index sees him as a leader who also helped Ezra teach the Law, which links him with a Meshullam in a later passage, though that identification is not certain. The name was very common after the exile, so he is hard to tell apart from others who bore it. It is usually taken to mean "devoted" or "friend."

Meshullam was a man of Ezra's time named in Ezra 10:15, during the assembly that dealt with Israelites who had married foreign wives after the return from exile. He is mentioned together with Jonathan son of Asahel, Jahaziah son of Tikvah and Shabbethai the Levite. The verse is read in two ways. The King James wording says these men were 'employed about this matter' and that Meshullam and Shabbethai 'helped them,' and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a chief man who helped Ezra end the marriages. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Tyndale House's STEPBible name list take the verse to mean that he opposed Ezra's plan, and the ISBE also counts him as a Levite. This entry follows the opposition reading. The name was common after the exile, so he is probably not the same as other men called Meshullam.

Meshullam was one of the descendants of Bani listed in Ezra 10:29 among the Israelites who had married foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon. The surrounding passage in Ezra 10 records that these men agreed to send away their foreign wives, and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as one who put his wife away. He appears in the list alongside Malluch, Adaiah, Jashub, Sheal and Ramoth. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Meshullam was a very common name after the exile, so he should not be confused with the other men of the same name in Ezra, Nehemiah and Chronicles. The name is usually explained as meaning "devoted" or "resigned"; Smith's gives "friend."

Meshullam son of Berechiah and grandson of Meshezabeel was one of the men who repaired the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah. He is listed working on a section next to Meremoth son of Urijah (Neh 3:4), and later as repairing the stretch opposite his own chamber (Neh 3:30). He is generally taken to be one man named twice, though the second mention could in principle refer to a different section he took on. His daughter married Johanan, son of Tobiah, the Ammonite official who opposed Nehemiah. Nehemiah notes this marriage as one reason many in Judah were bound by oath to Tobiah (Neh 6:18). The name Meshullam was common after the exile and is shared by several other men in the Bible, so he should be distinguished from them.

Meshullam, son of Besodeiah, was one of the people who helped rebuild the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah after the return from exile. Together with Jehoiada son of Paseah, he repaired the Old Gate. They laid its beams and set up its doors, locks and bars (Neh 3:6). Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Meshullam was very common after the exile, and several men called by it appear in Ezra and Nehemiah. This one is set apart from the others by his father's name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the name to mean "devoted" or "resigned," while Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "friend."

Meshullam was one of the men who stood beside Ezra the scribe on a wooden platform when Ezra read the book of the law aloud to the people of Jerusalem after the return from exile. He is the last named of the seven who stood at Ezra's left hand, alongside Pedaiah, Mishael, Malchiah, Hashum, Hashbadana and Zechariah (Neh 8:4). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of the principal Israelites who supported Ezra, and STEPBible's proper-names index identifies him as a priest, though the verse itself does not state his office. The name was very common after the exile, and several other men called Meshullam appear in Ezra and Nehemiah. Whether this Meshullam is the same as any of them is uncertain, so this entry treats him as a separate person known only from this occasion.

Meshullam was a priest in Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah. He appears among the priests who set their seal to the covenant the returned exiles made to keep God's law (Neh 10:7). This entry also identifies him with the Meshullam who took part in the procession at the dedication of the rebuilt city wall, named alongside Azariah and Ezra (Neh 12:33). That identification follows the STEPBible Proper Names index. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia instead treat the two mentions as separate people, and Smith's calls the second one of the princes of Judah. Meshullam was a very common name after the exile, so the link between the two verses is uncertain. The name is usually taken to mean "friend" or "devoted."

Meshullam was one of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, when the community returned from exile pledged to keep the law of God. He appears only in the list of signers, between Magpiash and Hezir (Neh 10:20), and nothing more is recorded about him. The name was very common after the exile, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts many men who bore it. Several of them appear in Nehemiah, including a priest who also sealed this covenant and a man who repaired part of Jerusalem's wall. Whether this signer is the same as any of those others is uncertain, and this entry treats him as a separate person. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "devoted" or "resigned," while Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "friend."

Meshullam was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, the son of Joed and the father of Sallu. He appears only in a genealogy in Neh 11:7, which traces Sallu's descent through Meshullam back to Jesaiah. Sallu is listed among the Benjamites who settled in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile, so Meshullam was probably part of that same family line. STEPBible Proper Names describes him as a Benjamite living in Jerusalem after the exile. A similar list in 1 Chr 9:7 also names a Sallu son of Meshullam, but it traces the line through Hodaviah and Hassenuah, so it is uncertain whether both lists refer to the same man. Several other people in the Bible share the name Meshullam, which Hitchcock's Bible Names takes to mean "peaceable" or "perfect."

Meshullam was a priest in the time after the return from exile in Babylon. He is named only in Neh 12:13, in a list of the heads of priestly families serving in the days of Joiakim, son of Jeshua the high priest (Neh 12:12, by context). There he appears as head of the priestly family of Ezra. This Ezra is probably the priestly clan named among those who returned with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:1), not necessarily Ezra the scribe. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name Meshullam was common in this period and is shared by several other men in Ezra, Nehemiah and Chronicles, so he should not be confused with them. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "friend," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "peaceable" or "perfect."

Meshullam was a priest in the days after the return from exile in Babylon. He was head of the priestly family of Ginnethon (Neh 12:16). The list he appears in (Neh 12:12–21) names the heads of the priestly families during the high priesthood of Joiakim, son of Jeshua, so he probably served in the generation after the first returnees. That setting is inferred from the surrounding passage; Smith's Bible Dictionary and Tyndale House's STEPBible name list place him the same way. The Ginnethon family is probably the same as the Ginnethon who signed the covenant in Neh 10:6. Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible bear the name Meshullam, including other priests and Levites of the same period, so care is needed to tell them apart. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "peaceable" or "perfect."

Meshullam was a gatekeeper in Jerusalem after the return from exile. Nehemiah 12:25 lists him with Mattaniah, Bakbukiah, Obadiah, Talmon and Akkub as porters who kept watch at the storehouses by the thresholds of the gates. The following verse dates this group to the days of the high priest Joiakim, and of Nehemiah and Ezra. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia accordingly places him in Joiakim's time, and the Tyndale House proper-names index describes him as a Levite gatekeeper of Nehemiah's era. The name, which may mean "devoted" or "rewarded," was very common after the exile, so he is hard to distinguish from the other men called Meshullam. Some readers link him with Shallum, head of the gatekeeping families in other lists, but this cannot be confirmed. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Meshullemeth was the wife of King Manasseh of Judah and the mother of his son and successor, Amon. She is named only once, in the notice of Amon's accession, which says he began to reign at twenty-two and ruled two years in Jerusalem (2 Kgs 21:19). She is called the daughter of Haruz of Jotbah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that this is the earliest case in Kings where the queen mother's home town is added to her name, and that her name is the feminine form of Meshullam. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give its meaning as "friend." The location of Jotbah is uncertain. Through her son Amon, father of Josiah, she belongs to the royal line traced in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, which names Manasseh and Amon but not her.

Mesopotamia, meaning "between the rivers," is the Greek name for the land between the Euphrates and Tigris, largely in modern Iraq. In the Old Testament it translates the Hebrew Aram-naharaim, "Aram of the two rivers," which Smith's Bible Dictionary takes to mean chiefly the northwestern part, near the great bend of the Euphrates. Abraham's servant traveled there to the city of Nahor to find a wife for Isaac (Gen 24:10). Stephen recalled that God appeared to Abraham there before he lived in Haran (Acts 7:2). Balaam came from Pethor in Mesopotamia (Deut 23:4). Cushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia, ruled Israel for eight years until a judge, named Othniel in Judg 3:9, defeated him, about 1418 BC by inference from context (Judg 3:8–10). The Ammonites hired chariots from there against David (1 Chr 19:6), and its residents were in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:9). The location shown here marks a general point within the region.

Metheg-ammah is named in the King James Version as a place David took from the Philistines after defeating and subduing them (2 Sam 8:1). The Hebrew phrase probably means "bridle of the mother city," and many readers take it as a figure of speech rather than a town name: David seized control of the Philistines' chief city. The parallel account in 1 Chr 18:1 says instead that David took "Gath and her towns," so Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify that city as Gath. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint reads differently, saying David took "the tribute," and that the Hebrew text may be damaged. If a separate place is meant, its site is unknown, though it would have been in the Philistine plain near Gath. The location shown here follows the Gath identification, probably modern Tell es-Safi.

Methusael was a man in the line of Cain, named only in the genealogy of Gen 4:18. He was the son of Mehujael and the father of Lamech, which makes him the fourth generation after Cain (Cain, Enoch, Irad, Mehujael, Methusael). The following verses (Gen 4:19–24) go on to describe his son Lamech, his two wives and his children. Nothing else is recorded about Methusael himself. His name is usually understood to mean "man of God" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "champion of El; man of God"), while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "who demands his death." He is a different person from Methuselah of Seth's line in Gen 5, although the two names look alike and both genealogies end in a man named Lamech.

Methuselah was the son of Enoch, the father of Lamech, and the grandfather of Noah, listed among the descendants of Seth before the Flood. According to Genesis, Enoch became his father at sixty-five. Methuselah himself became the father of Lamech at 187 and had other sons and daughters. He lived 969 years, the longest lifespan recorded in the Bible. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that he died in the year of the Flood. This follows from adding the ages given in Gen 5:25–28 and Gen 7:6, and it fits the dates used here, about 3317 to 2348 BC, which are estimates inferred from these genealogies. His name is usually explained as "man of the dart" or "man of the javelin." He appears in the genealogy of 1 Chr 1:3, and in Luke's genealogy of Jesus under the Greek form Mathusala.

Mezahab was the father of Matred and the grandfather of Mehetabel, the wife of Hadar (called Hadad in 1 Chr 1:50), the last king listed in the list of Edom's kings. He appears only in this genealogical note, given in both Gen 36:39 and 1 Chr 1:50. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary explain the name as meaning "waters of gold." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Jewish commentators such as Abarbanel took the name to mean he was very wealthy, with gold in his house as plentiful as water. It also mentions that the name may instead refer to a place, possibly the same as Dizahab. The wording "daughter of Matred, the daughter of Mezahab" can be read either way. This entry treats Mezahab as a man, Matred's father, following the dictionaries. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Miamin was an Israelite layman of the family of Parosh who lived in Ezra's time, after the return from exile in Babylon. He is named in the list of men who had married foreign wives and who agreed, at Ezra's urging, to send them away (Ezra 10:25). The verse groups him with six others from the same family: Ramiah, Jeziah, Malchiah, Eleazar, Malchijah and Benaiah. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a layman who put away his foreign wife. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the right hand." The same name, often spelled Mijamin, belongs to other men in the Old Testament, such as a priest in David's time, and these are probably different people.

Mibhar, son of Haggeri, appears in 1 Chronicles' list of David's mighty warriors, the elite fighters who served the king (1 Chr 11:38). He is named right after Joel the brother of Nathan, and nothing more is said about him. The name is often explained as meaning "choice" or "chosen." The parallel list in 2 Sam 23:36 has no Mibhar. At that point it reads "Igal the son of Nathan of Zobah, Bani the Gadite." Easton's Bible Dictionary therefore identifies Mibhar with Bani the Gadite. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that the Chronicles wording arose from a copying change, with "Mibhar" coming from "of Zobah" and "son of Haggeri" from "Bani the Gadite." This entry treats Mibhar as the warrior named in Chronicles while noting that the two lists differ at this point.

Mibsam was one of the twelve sons of Ishmael, Abraham's son by Hagar. He is listed fourth, after Nebajoth, Kedar and Adbeel, in the genealogy of Ishmael's descendants in Gen 25:13, which is repeated in 1 Chr 1:29. Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as the head of an Arab tribe, in line with the way Ishmael's sons are presented as founders of tribal groups. His sister Bashemath (also called Mahalath) later married Esau. The name is usually taken to mean "sweet odor" or "perfume" (Smith's Bible Dictionary, Hitchcock's Bible Names). Another Mibsam, a descendant of Simeon, appears in a separate genealogy, and the two should not be confused.

Mibsam was a descendant of Simeon, named in the genealogy of that tribe in 1 Chr 4:25. He was the son of Shallum and the father of Mishma. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 4:24) traces this line from Simeon through his son Shaul, so Shallum was probably Shaul's son, which would make Mibsam Simeon's great-grandson. Nothing else is recorded about his life. His name is often explained as meaning "sweet smell" or "perfume" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; Hitchcock's Bible Names), though the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia marks this meaning as uncertain. The same name belongs to another man, a son of Ishmael (Gen 25:13; 1 Chr 1:29), who is a different person.

Mibzar was one of the chiefs ("dukes" in the King James Version) of Edom, the nation descended from Esau. He appears only in the closing list of Edomite chiefs, between Teman and Magdiel, in Gen 36:42 and its parallel in 1 Chr 1:53. Nothing else is recorded about him. The surrounding passage says these chiefs are named "according to their families, after their places," so Mibzar may stand for a clan or district as much as for an individual. His name means "fortress." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Eusebius linked the name with Mibsara, a sizeable village under Petra that still existed in his day.

Micah was a man from the hill country of Ephraim during the period of the judges, distinct from the prophet and others of the same name. His mother gave two hundred shekels of silver to a metalworker, who made a carved image and a cast image that were kept in Micah's house. Micah kept a shrine with an ephod and household idols (teraphim) and installed one of his sons as priest. When a young Levite from Bethlehem in Judah passed by, Micah hired him as his priest for ten shekels a year, clothing and food, believing the Lord would now favor him. Danite scouts lodged at his house. Later the Danites carried off his images and his priest, and Micah pursued them but turned back because they were too strong. Easton's Bible Dictionary sees the story as leading into Dan's settlement in the north and illustrating the lawlessness of the age.

Micah was a member of the tribe of Reuben. He appears only once, in the Reubenite genealogy of 1 Chr 5:5, as the son of Shimei and the father of Reaia. The surrounding verses (1 Chr 5:4–6) place him in a line descending from Joel. The line runs through Shemaiah, Gog and Shimei to Micah, then through Reaia and Baal to Beerah, a Reubenite prince whom the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser carried into exile. Nothing else is recorded about Micah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as a shortened form of Micaiah, meaning "who is like Yah?" Several other men in the Bible share the name, including the prophet Micah, and this Reubenite should not be confused with them.

Micah the Morasthite was a prophet of Judah, credited with the book that bears the name. According to Mic 1:1, the word of the Lord came to Micah during the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and concerned both Samaria and Jerusalem. This entry dates the prophecies to about 754 BC, an estimate inferred from context. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes "Morasthite" to mean a native of Moresheth-gath (compare Mic 1:14) and treats Micah as a contemporary of Isaiah. The title also sets this prophet apart from others with the same name, such as Micaiah son of Imlah. Much later, during Jeremiah's trial, Micah's warning from Hezekiah's day was quoted: Zion would be plowed like a field and Jerusalem would become heaps (Jer 26:18). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as a shortened form meaning "who is like Yah?"

Micah, also spelled Micha, was the son of Mephibosheth, who is called Meribbaal in Chronicles, and so was a grandson of Jonathan and a great-grandson of King Saul. He is mentioned as Mephibosheth's young son in the account of David's kindness to Mephibosheth, which also notes that Ziba's household served Mephibosheth (2 Sam 9:12). The genealogies of the tribe of Benjamin name his four sons: Pithon, Melech, Tarea (also spelled Tahrea), and Ahaz (1 Chr 8:34–35; 9:40–41). Through him Saul's family line continued. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as a short form of Micaiah, meaning "who is like Yah?" He is a different man from the Micah of Ephraim in the Book of Judges, whose carved image was taken by the Danites.

Micaiah son of Imlah was a prophet in the northern kingdom of Israel during the reign of Ahab, who is named as the king in the surrounding chapter. His name means "who is like the LORD?" When Ahab and Jehoshaphat of Judah planned to attack Ramoth-gilead, Ahab's prophets all promised victory. Jehoshaphat asked for another prophet, and Ahab named Micaiah, whom he hated for always prophesying evil about him. Told to agree with the others, Micaiah swore to speak only what the LORD told him. He first echoed their words, then foretold disaster. Zedekiah son of Chenaanah struck him, and the king had him held under Amon the city governor. Micaiah declared that if the king returned safely, the LORD had not spoken through him. Easton's Bible Dictionary infers he had already been imprisoned and notes a view that he was the unnamed prophet of 1 Kgs 20:35–42.

Micha (also spelled Micah) was a Levite descended from Asaph, the temple musician, and the father of Mattaniah. Mattaniah led the thanksgiving in prayer among the Levites who settled in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. The two genealogies name Micha's father differently: 1 Chr 9:15 calls him Zichri, while Neh 11:17 calls him Zabdi. This entry follows Zichri. The two names are probably variant forms for the same ancestor. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes the family as Gershonite Levites and gives the name's meaning as "who is like God?" Hitchcock's Bible Names treats it as the same name as Micaiah. Several other people in the Bible share this name, and this Micha should not be confused with them.

Micha was one of the men who set their seal to the written covenant made in the time of Nehemiah, when the returned exiles pledged to keep the law of God. His name appears in a list alongside Rehob and Hashabiah (Neh 10:11). That list falls within the section introduced as the Levites (Neh 10:9), so he was probably a Levite, as Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's gives the meaning of the name as "who is like God?", and Hitchcock's Bible Names treats it as the same name as Micaiah. Several other people in the Bible bear this or a similar name, including a son of Mephibosheth and a Levite of the line of Asaph. Whether this Micha is connected to any of them is uncertain.

Michael was a man of the tribe of Asher and the father of Sethur. He is known only from Num 13:13, which names Sethur as Asher's representative among the twelve men Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan. Nothing else is recorded about Michael himself. His name means "who is like God?" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). It is shared by several other people in the Bible, including the archangel Michael, and this Asherite should not be confused with them.

Michael was a member of the tribe of Gad who lived in the region of Bashan, east of the Jordan. He is listed first among seven kinsmen named in 1 Chr 5:13, alongside Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Jachan, Zia and Heber. The next verse, 1 Chr 5:14, identifies these men as the sons of Abihail. According to 1 Chr 5:17, the Gadite families were recorded in genealogies during the reigns of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him a chief Gadite in Bashan. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "who is like God?" Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name Michael, and this one should not be confused with them.

Michael was a man of the tribe of Gad, named only in a genealogy in 1 Chr 5:14. He was the son of Jeshishai and the father of Gilead. Through Gilead he was an ancestor of Abihail, whose sons were among the Gadite family heads in this list. The genealogy traces his own line back through Jahdo to Buz. The surrounding passage places the Gadites in Bashan, east of the Jordan, and nothing more is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "who is like God?" and counts this Michael as one of several Gadites who bear it. The name is shared by a number of people in the Bible, including other men in Chronicles and the archangel, so this Michael should not be confused with them.

Michael was a man of the tribe of Issachar, named first among the sons of Izrahiah, whose brothers were Obadiah, Joel and Ishiah. He belonged to the line of Uzzi, a descendant of Tola, Issachar's son (1 Chr 7:1–3). The verse calls the group "five", although it names only four sons. Izrahiah himself is probably counted as the fifth, by inference from the passage. All of them are described as "chief men", which points to leaders of family clans within the tribe. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "who is like God?" Several other men in the Bible share this name, and this Michael should not be confused with them.

Michael was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named among the sons of Beriah in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles. 1 Chr 8:16 lists him first in a group with Ispah and Joha. Read with the preceding verses (1 Chr 8:14–15), the same list probably also includes Ahio, Shashak, Jeremoth, Zebadiah, Arad and Ader as sons of Beriah. Nearby verses describe Beriah as a head of a family who lived in Aijalon and drove out the inhabitants of Gath (1 Chr 8:13). Nothing else is recorded about Michael himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "who is like God?" Several other men in the Bible share the name, as does the archangel Michael, and this Benjamite should not be confused with them.

Michael was a man of the tribe of Manasseh and one of the "captains of the thousands" of Manasseh who went over to David as he went to Ziklag (1 Chr 12:20). He is named with six other Manassite commanders, including Adnah, Jozabad and Elihu. The surrounding chapter suggests this happened when David left the Philistine army before the battle in which Saul died, though that timing is inferred from context. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name means "who is like God?" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Michael should not be confused with them.

Michael was a man of the tribe of Issachar, known only as the father of Omri. Omri served as the leader of Issachar in the list of tribal chiefs during King David's reign (1 Chr 27:18). Nothing else is recorded about Michael himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that he may have been Omri's father or a more distant ancestor, since 'son of' can sometimes point to a forebear. The name means 'who is like God?' and is shared by several people in the Bible, including the archangel Michael. This Michael should not be confused with them.

Michael was one of the sons of King Jehoshaphat of Judah, listed among the brothers of Jehoram, who succeeded their father as king (2 Chr 21:2). The verse calls Jehoshaphat "king of Israel," although he ruled the southern kingdom of Judah. His brothers were Azariah, Jehiel, Zechariah, a second Azariah, and Shephatiah. According to 2 Chr 21:4, when Jehoram had established himself on the throne he killed all his brothers with the sword. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries both understand Michael to have died in this way. His death is placed here at about 889 BC in Jerusalem, an estimate inferred from the context of Jehoram's reign. The name means "who is like God?" and is shared by several other people in the Bible, including the archangel Michael, so he should not be confused with them.

Michael was the father, or possibly an earlier ancestor, of Zebadiah, a man of the family of Shephatiah. He is known only from the list of family heads who traveled from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra, where his son Zebadiah is named as leading eighty men of that family (Ezra 8:8). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "who is like God?" and allows that "son of" here may mean a more distant descendant. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a parallel to this list in 1 Esdras 8:34. The verse does not say whether Michael himself made the journey. Several other people in the Bible share the name Michael, and nothing further is recorded about this one.

Michael is the angel described in Daniel as "one of the chief princes," who came to help the heavenly messenger speaking to Daniel when the prince of the kingdom of Persia opposed him for twenty-one days (Dan 10:13). He is called the prince of Daniel's people, the one who stands with that messenger (Dan 10:21), and "the great prince" who will stand up for Israel at a time of unparalleled trouble, when those written in the book will be delivered (Dan 12:1). Jude calls him "the archangel" and says that when he disputed with the devil over the body of Moses, he did not bring a railing accusation but said, "The Lord rebuke thee" (Jude 1:9). In Revelation, Michael and his angels fight against the dragon in a war in heaven (Rev 12:7). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "who is like God?" Other men in the Bible share the name.

Michah was a Levite of the family of Uzziel, a branch of the Kohathite clan. In the lists of Levites arranged in King David's time, he is named as the first, or chief, of the sons of Uzziel, with Jesiah (also spelled Isshiah) second (1 Chr 23:20; 24:25). His son Shamir is named after him (1 Chr 24:24). Elizaphan, Mishael and Zithri are also counted among his brothers. Since those three appear elsewhere as sons of the Uzziel of Moses' generation, "sons of Uzziel" here probably names the clan descended from Uzziel rather than his immediate children. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes his name to mean "who is like God?" and notes that it is a form of Micah. The setting in David's reign is inferred from the surrounding chapters, which describe David organizing the Levites.

Michaiah was a Levite of the family of Asaph, the temple singers, named only in genealogies in Nehemiah. He was the son of Zaccur and the father of Mattaniah. Through Mattaniah he was an ancestor of Zechariah son of Jonathan, who played a trumpet at the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt wall (Neh 12:35). The same line appears in Neh 11:22, where the name is spelled Micha. There his descendant Uzzi son of Bani is named as overseer of the Levites in Jerusalem after the return from exile. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him with the Micha of 1 Chr 9:15, the son of Zichri, an identification that rests on the matching descendant Mattaniah. The name is shared by several people in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names treats it as the same name as Micah.

Michaiah was the father of Achbor, one of the officials whom King Josiah sent to ask the Lord about the Book of the Law found in the temple (2 Kgs 22:12). In the parallel account he is called Micah, and his son is named Abdon rather than Achbor (2 Chr 34:20). The two passages describe the same delegation, so they are taken to refer to the same father and son, recorded under variant names. According to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, Micah is a shortened form of the name, which means "who is like Yah?" Nothing else is recorded about Michaiah himself. His son's place among Josiah's leading officials suggests a family of some standing at court. Several other people in the Bible have the same name, and he should not be confused with them.

Michaiah was one of five princes whom King Jehoshaphat of Judah sent out in the third year of his reign to teach in the cities of Judah (2 Chr 17:7). The verse itself only says "his reign," but the surrounding chapter makes clear the king is Jehoshaphat. The following verses add that Levites and priests went with these princes, and that they taught the people from the book of the law of the Lord as they travelled through the towns of Judah (2 Chr 17:8–9). Nothing else is recorded about this Michaiah. Several other people in the Bible share the name, and he is not known to be any of them. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "who is like God?"

Michaiah was a priest who took part in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. He is named in Neh 12:41 among seven priests who played trumpets with one of the two great thanksgiving choirs that processed along the wall. This is his only mention, and nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "who is like God?". Several other people in the Bible bear the same name or a close form of it (Micaiah, Micah), and this priest should not be confused with them. By inference from the setting, the dedication took place in the mid-fifth century BC, after the wall was completed under Nehemiah.

Michaiah was the son of Gemariah and grandson of Shaphan, and he lived in Jerusalem in the time of King Jehoiakim. He heard Baruch read Jeremiah's scroll of the LORD's words to the people (Jer 36:11). The surrounding passage places that reading in his father Gemariah's chamber in the temple court. Michaiah then went to the royal palace and told the assembled officials everything he had heard (Jer 36:13). According to the following verse, the officials then sent for Baruch to read the scroll to them. His grandfather Shaphan was probably the royal scribe of King Josiah's day, which suggests the family held office at court. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "who is like God?" Several people in the Bible share this name, and this Michaiah appears only in this one episode.

Michal was the younger daughter of King Saul and his wife Ahinoam, and David's first wife. She loved David, and Saul gave her to him after David brought proof that he had killed two hundred Philistines, double the hundred named as the bride-price. When Saul sent men to kill David, Michal warned him, let him down through a window, and laid an image in his bed to deceive the messengers. She then told her father that David had threatened her. While David was a fugitive, Saul gave her to Phalti (Phaltiel) son of Laish of Gallim. After Saul's death, David demanded her return through Ish-bosheth. When David danced before the ark as it entered Jerusalem, she despised him and mocked him, and the account adds that she had no child to the day of her death. 2 Sam 21:8 names Michal as a mother of Saul's grandsons. Easton's Bible Dictionary reads Merab there, and this entry follows that reading.

Michmas is the spelling of Michmash used in the lists of exiles who returned from Babylon, where the men of Michmas number 122 (Ezra 2:27; Neh 7:31). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as another form of that name. Michmash was a town of Benjamin. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it east of Bethel on the road toward Jerusalem (Isa 10:28), on the north side of a steep ravine called "the passage of Michmash" (1 Sam 13:23), facing Geba on the other side. It was the scene of Saul's battle against the Philistines. Easton's identifies it with the modern village of Mukhmas, northeast of Jerusalem, and the location shown here matches that site.

Michmash was a town of Benjamin north of Jerusalem, set on the north side of a steep gorge facing Gibeah and Geba to the south. Saul first held it with two thousand men (1 Sam 13:2). The Philistines then camped there in force (1 Sam 13:5, 16), and their garrison guarded the "passage of Michmash," the crossing of the ravine (1 Sam 13:23). Jonathan's attack across this pass, between two crags facing Michmash and Gibeah, led to a Philistine rout that reached Aijalon (1 Sam 14:5, 31). Isaiah pictures an invader from the north leaving his baggage at Michmash on the way to Jerusalem (Isa 10:28). After the exile Benjamites lived there again (Neh 11:31). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the village of Mukhmas above the Wadi es-Suweinit, about 7 miles north of Jerusalem, and the location shown here matches that site.

Michmethath was a town on the boundary between the tribal territories of Ephraim and Manasseh. It appears only in the boundary lists of Joshua. Ephraim's northern border ran to Michmethath and then turned east toward Taanath-shiloh and Janohah (Josh 16:6), and Manasseh's border ran from Asher to Michmethath, which is described as lying "before Shechem," meaning facing or near that city (Josh 17:7). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on the northern border of Ephraim and Manasseh, not far west of the Jordan, and gives the meaning of the name as "hiding-place." Its exact site is uncertain. The location shown here puts it just south of Shechem, near modern Nablus. That fits the description of it lying before Shechem and matches suggested identifications with ruins in the plain east and southeast of the city.

Michri was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only once in the Bible, as the father of Uzzi and grandfather of Elah. He appears in the genealogy of Elah in 1 Chr 9:8. That verse belongs to a list of Benjamite families who lived in Jerusalem, and it names Elah among the heads of fathers' houses there. The surrounding passage concerns those who settled in the city, usually understood as the community after the return from exile. So Michri was probably an ancestor of returned Benjamite settlers rather than a settler himself, an inference from context. Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "prize of Jehovah." Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "worthy of price," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "selling."

Middin was a town of Judah listed among the six cities “in the wilderness” in the tribal allotment of Joshua 15, named between Betharabah and Secacah (Josh 15:61). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the Hebrew word translated “wilderness” as a specific district, which Easton's Bible Dictionary places west of the Dead Sea near En-gedi. The name has been explained as “measures” (Easton) or “judgment; striving” (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Its site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may survive at Khirbet Mird, a fortified hilltop with ancient cisterns overlooking the el-Buqei'a plateau. It also notes that the Greek reading “Ainon” (springs) could point to the oasis of Ain Feshkha near Qumran. The location shown here lies in the el-Buqei'a basin west of the northern Dead Sea, closer to the Khirbet Mird view than to the coastal springs.

Midian was a son of Abraham by Keturah, one of six brothers, and the father of Ephah, Epher, Hanoch (or Henoch), Abida and Eldaah (Gen 25:2–4; 1 Chr 1:32–33). His name is also used for the people descended from him, the Midianites, and for their land. Moses fled to the land of Midian and married into the family of Jethro, the priest of Midian. Later the elders of Midian joined Moab in hiring Balaam. After the affair at Peor, Israel fought the Midianites and killed five of their kings. In the time of the judges Midian oppressed Israel for seven years until Gideon defeated them, about 1258 BC by inference from context. Later prophets recall "the day of Midian" as a great deliverance. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes the Midianites as Arab herders and traders living mainly in the desert east and south of Palestine.

Midian was a desert region and people south and east of Canaan, named, according to Gen 25:2, after a son of Abraham by Keturah. Moses fled there from Pharaoh, served Jethro, the priest of Midian, and kept his flocks until God sent him back to Egypt. His sons Gershom and Eliezer were probably born there. Later the elders of Midian joined Moab in hiring Balaam against Israel, and Israel killed five Midianite kings. In the time of the judges Midian oppressed Israel for seven years, about 1258 BC by inference from context, until Gideon's three hundred men routed them. Prophets later recalled "the day of Midian." Easton's Bible Dictionary describes the Midianites as Arabian nomads and traders whose pastures reached into Sinai. The location shown here lies east of the Gulf of Aqaba, in modern northwestern Saudi Arabia.

Migdal-el, whose name means "tower of God," was a fortified city given to the tribe of Naphtali. It appears only once, in the list of Naphtali's fortified cities, between Iron and Horem (Josh 19:38). Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the name may come from an ancient tower dedicated to God. The site is uncertain. Eusebius's Onomasticon places it near Athlit on the coast south of Ptolemais (Acre). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that some have linked it with Magdala. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia proposes either Khirbet Mejdel, about 3 miles north of Kedesh, or Mejdel Islim, about 5 miles farther northwest. The location shown here, in the hills of southern Lebanon northwest of Kedesh, follows a northern Galilean identification of this kind, closest to the Mejdel Islim proposal.

Migdal-gad was a town of the tribe of Judah, listed in Josh 15:37 among a group of cities in the lowland (Shephelah), the low hill country and coastal plain toward the west. Its name means "tower of Gad" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, or "tower of fortune" according to Easton's Bible Dictionary. The Bible mentions it only in this list, and its site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggest it was probably the town of el-Mejdel (al-Majdal), a short distance northeast of ancient Ashkelon, within the area of the modern city of Ashkelon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that this would place it very close to the Philistine strongholds. The location shown here follows the el-Mejdel identification.

Migdol, meaning “tower,” is the name of a place on Egypt’s eastern frontier. During the Exodus the Israelites camped before Pihahiroth, “between Migdol and the sea,” facing Baalzephon (Exod 14:2; Num 33:7). Jeremiah names a Migdol as one of the Egyptian towns where Jews lived after the fall of Jerusalem, listing it with Tahpanhes and Noph (Memphis) (Jer 44:1; 46:14). In Ezek 29:10 and 30:6 the KJV reads “the tower of Syene,” but Easton’s Bible Dictionary takes the phrase as “from Migdol to Syene,” meaning from Egypt’s northern border to its southern one. Smith’s Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia distinguish two places: an Exodus campsite near the head of the Red Sea, and a fortified town about 12 miles from Pelusium. The location shown here follows the northern frontier site near Pelusium.

Migron was a place in the territory of Benjamin, north of Jerusalem. In 1 Sam 14:2, Saul stayed with about six hundred men under a pomegranate tree at Migron, on the outskirts of Gibeah, while the Philistines held Michmash. Isaiah 10:28 names Migron in a poetic description of an Assyrian army advancing on Jerusalem: after Aiath it passes Migron, then stores its baggage at Michmash. Because that route seems to place Migron north of Michmash, Easton's Bible Dictionary treats these as two separate places, with the town in Samuel lying to the south. Smith's Bible Dictionary and others take them as possibly one locality. The location shown here, given only roughly, follows the setting near Gibeah in 1 Samuel. The exact site of either is uncertain. Easton's gives the name's meaning as "precipice" or "landslip."

Mijamin was a priest whose name was given to the sixth of the twenty-four divisions of priests that David organized for service at the sanctuary (1 Chr 24:9). The divisions were assigned by casting lots, and each one was named for the head of a priestly family. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as the chief of that sixth course. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as meaning "right hand," also belongs to other men in Ezra and Nehemiah, including a priest who returned from exile and a man who had married a foreign wife. Because those passages fall in a much later period, they probably refer to different people, though a priestly family name could have carried on. This entry covers only the head of David's sixth division.

Mikloth was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, listed in the genealogy of the family of Saul as a son of the founder of Gibeon and his wife Maachah (Easton's Bible Dictionary). Chronicles names that father Jehiel, or Jeiel. This entry follows the view that he is the same man as Abiel, whom 1 Sam 9:1 calls the father of Kish, so Mikloth appears as a brother of Kish, Ner, Abdon, Zur, Baal, Nadab, Gedor, Ahio and Zacher (also called Zechariah). Mikloth became the father of Shimeah, spelled Shimeam in the parallel list, and his family lived in Jerusalem alongside their relatives. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that comparing the two lists shows his name has dropped out of the end of 1 Chr 8:31. The name is shared by others, including a commander under David mentioned in 1 Chr 27:4.

Mikloth was an officer in King David's army, named only in 1 Chr 27:4. David's forces were organized into twelve divisions of 24,000 men, each serving for one month of the year. Mikloth belonged to the division for the second month, which was commanded by Dodai the Ahohite. The verse calls him "the ruler" of that course, and readers have understood his role in two ways. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes him as an officer serving under Dodai, while Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible names index describe him as the leader of the second division. The wording supports his being at least a senior officer of that monthly force. The name Mikloth is also borne by a different man, a Benjamite of Gibeon listed in the family of Saul in 1 Chr 8:32 and 9:37–38, who should not be confused with this officer.

Mikneiah was a Levite of the second rank in David's time. He appears among the brothers appointed to serve alongside the leading musicians Heman, Asaph and Ethan when the ark was brought up to Jerusalem. In 1 Chr 15:18 he is listed with men described as "porters," or gatekeepers. In 1 Chr 15:21 he is named among those who played harps "on the Sheminith," a term of uncertain meaning, probably a musical setting or pitch. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes his name to mean "possession of Jehovah" and describes him as both a gatekeeper of the ark and a member of the musical band. Nothing further is recorded about him.

Milalai was one of the musicians who played at the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. He is named only in Neh 12:36, among the "brethren" of Zechariah son of Jonathan, a descendant of Asaph (Neh 12:35). This group played "the musical instruments of David" in the procession led by Ezra the scribe. This entry treats Milalai as a son of Jonathan and a brother of Zechariah and the others named with him. The Hebrew word for "brethren" can also mean kinsmen or fellow Levites, so the exact relationship is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia call him a Levite musician. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he was probably a Gershonite Levite of the sons of Asaph. The name is explained as "eloquent" in Easton's and as "my talk" in Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Milcah (wife of Nahor) was the daughter of Haran and the wife of Nahor, Abraham's brother. Since Haran was also a brother of Abraham and Nahor, she married her uncle. Her sister was Iscah, and Gen 11:27 names Lot as another child of Haran, making him her brother. After the near-sacrifice of Isaac, Abraham received news that Milcah had borne eight sons to Nahor: Huz, Buz, Kemuel, Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph and Bethuel (Gen 22:21–22). Through Bethuel she was the grandmother of Rebekah. Rebekah is repeatedly identified by this lineage, both when Abraham's servant first meets her at the well and when he retells the story to her family. Hitchcock's Bible Names and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of her name as "queen."

Milcah (daughter of Zelophehad) was one of the five daughters of Zelophehad, a descendant of Manasseh son of Joseph, along with Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah and Tirzah. Her father had no sons (Num 26:33; Josh 17:3). The sisters came together to ask for a share of land in their father's name (Num 27:1), and the surrounding chapter records Moses granting their request. Later, to keep the land within the tribe, Milcah and her sisters married sons of their father's brothers (Num 36:11). Joshua 17 describes the daughters receiving their inheritance among the clans of Manasseh. She is usually named fourth among the sisters, though the order varies. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of her name as "queen." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a view that the sisters' names may also reflect places, with Milcah perhaps linked to a place called Beth-milcah.

Milcom was the national god of the Ammonites, called in 1 Kgs 11:5 "the abomination of the Ammonites." Solomon, influenced by his foreign wives, worshipped Milcom along with Ashtoreth of the Sidonians and Chemosh of Moab, and this is given as a reason the kingdom would be divided after him (1 Kgs 11:33). Solomon had built a high place for Milcom east of Jerusalem, on the right side of what was later called the Mount of Corruption. Centuries afterward King Josiah, the king referred to in 2 Kgs 23:13, defiled it as part of his reforms. The name is usually understood to come from the word for "king." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "their king," and Smith's Bible Dictionary "great king." Both Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat Milcom as closely connected with, or the same as, Molech. Some scholars instead regard the two as separate deities.

Miletus was a seaport on the west coast of Asia Minor, near the mouth of the Meander River, about 36 miles south of Ephesus (Smith's Bible Dictionary). Paul reached it by ship on his voyage toward Jerusalem, sailing past Chios, Samos and Trogyllium (Acts 20:15). This was about AD 54, by inference from context. From Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the church, who came to hear his farewell address (Acts 20:17). Later Paul wrote that he had left Trophimus sick at Miletus, called Miletum in the King James Version (2 Tim 4:20). According to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, Miletus was once a leading Ionian Greek trading city that founded many colonies, then declined after its capture by the Persians. River silt has since pushed the coastline miles away from its ruins, which lie in modern Turkey and include a large theater.

Millo was a fortification within ancient Jerusalem, closely linked with the City of David. It already existed when David took the city, since he built "from Millo and inward" (2 Sam 5:9; 1 Chr 11:8). Solomon raised forced labor to build it alongside the temple, his palace and the city wall, and his work on it is mentioned in the context of Jeroboam's revolt. Hezekiah later repaired it while strengthening Jerusalem's defenses. The name probably means "filling," which suggests an earth-filled rampart or terrace. The Greek Septuagint translates it "Akra," meaning citadel. Its exact position is debated. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on the north side of the city, the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia puts it on the southeastern hill south of the temple, and G. A. Smith suggested a site near Ophel's south end. The location shown here follows a site at the northern end of the City of David ridge, just south of the Temple Mount.

Miniamin was a priest, or the head of a priestly family, in the period after the return from Babylon. Under the spelling Miamin he is listed among the priests who came back with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:5), and Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him a chief priest. A Mijamin appears among the priests who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah's time (Neh 10:7). In the days of the high priest Joiakim, the house "of Miniamin" is named among the priestly families, though the name of its head at that time has dropped out of the text (Neh 12:17). This entry treats the three spellings as one priestly line, as Easton's does. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the covenant signer may have been a descendant of the earlier Miamin. The name, which means "from the right hand," was borne by several people, so these identifications are not certain.

Miniamin was a Levite in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He is named in 2 Chr 31:15 as one of six men who worked under Kore, the official in charge of the freewill offerings (2 Chr 31:14, a verse not quoted here). Stationed in the cities of the priests, these men shared out the gifts and tithes to their fellow priests and Levites by their divisions, giving to old and young alike. The name is thought to mean "from the right hand" or "right hand" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other people in the Bible bear this name, including priests in the time of Nehemiah. This entry covers only the Levite of Hezekiah's day, and nothing more is recorded about him.

Miniamin was a priest who played a trumpet at the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. Nehemiah 12:41 names him among seven priests, Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, Michaiah, Elioenai, Zechariah and Hananiah, who sounded trumpets in one of the two thanksgiving processions that marched around the wall. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names take to mean "from the right hand," belongs to several men in the Bible, including priests of the same period. It is uncertain whether this Miniamin is the same as any of them, so this entry treats him only as the trumpeter at the wall's dedication.

Minni was a kingdom named only in Jer 51:27, where it is summoned with Ararat and Ashchenaz to attack Babylon. The prophet pictures a banner raised and a trumpet blown to gather these northern nations against the city. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Minni as a province of Armenia, under Median rule at that time, and mentions a view that the name Armenia may come from Har-minni, "the mountainous country of Minni." Smith's Bible Dictionary also treats it as part of Armenia. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with the Minnai (Mannaeans) of Assyrian inscriptions, a people closely linked with Armenia or part of it. The exact boundaries are uncertain. The location shown here is approximate and follows the Armenian identification, placing it in the highlands of present-day Armenia.

Minnith was a town east of the Jordan, named as the limit of Jephthah's victory over the Ammonites. He struck them from Aroer as far as Minnith, twenty cities, and on to the "plain of the vineyards" (Judg 11:33). Ezekiel mentions "wheat of Minnith" among the goods Judah and Israel traded to Tyre (Ezek 27:17). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat this as the same place, an Ammonite town known for its wheat. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that some readers do not take the word in Ezekiel as a place name at all. The site is uncertain. Eusebius' Onomasticon mentions a Maanith about 4 Roman miles from Heshbon on the road to Rabbah (modern Amman), and the location shown here follows that identification, placing Minnith near Heshbon on the plateau of modern Jordan.

Miriam was the daughter of Amram and Jochebed of the tribe of Levi, and the sister of Aaron and Moses, born in Egypt (Num 26:59; 1 Chr 6:3). She is probably the unnamed sister who watched over the infant Moses in the Nile (Exod 2:4). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes her to be the eldest of the three. Called "the prophetess," she led the women with timbrels and dancing in a song of triumph after the crossing of the Red Sea. Later she and Aaron spoke against Moses over his marriage to an Ethiopian woman. She became leprous and was shut out of the camp for seven days, and the people did not move on until she was brought back. Deut 24:9 recalls this as a warning, and Micah names her with Moses and Aaron as leaders God sent before Israel. She died and was buried at Kadesh, about 1452 BC by inference from context. Other women in the Bible share her name.

Miriam was a descendant of Judah, named once in the genealogy of Ezrah's family in 1 Chr 4:17. That verse says "she bare Miriam, and Shammai, and Ishbah the father of Eshtemoa," without saying who "she" was. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the latter half of the verse probably belongs after verse 18, which names Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh, as the wife of Mered. This entry follows that reading, treating Miriam as the child of Mered and Bithiah, with Shammai and Ishbah as siblings. This entry treats Miriam as female, though the Hebrew name could also be read as a man's name here, and the same encyclopedia allows for either. Nothing else is recorded about this Miriam. She is distinct from Miriam the sister of Moses and from others who bear the name.

Mirma was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named once in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles. He was one of the seven sons of Shaharaim by his wife Hodesh, and his full brothers were Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcham, Jeuz and Shachia. Through Shaharaim's other wife, Hushim, he had two half-brothers, Abitub and Elpaal. The surrounding verses say Shaharaim had these children in the country of Moab after sending away his earlier wives, so Mirma was probably born there, as Smith's Bible Dictionary also states. Together with his brothers he is called one of the "heads of the fathers," meaning a leader of a family clan (1 Chr 8:10). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "fraud." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Misgab was a place in Moab named in Jeremiah's prophecy against that nation, alongside Nebo and Kiriathaim. All three are described as overthrown, with Misgab "confounded and dismayed" (Jer 48:1). The name means "height" or "fortress." Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the same Hebrew word appears in Isa 25:12, where the King James Version renders it "high fort." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia observes that no site with a similar name has been found, and suggests the word may not be a town name at all but a title for a strong Moabite fortress, perhaps Kir-moab itself. The location shown here follows that identification, placing Misgab at Kir-moab, the modern town of Kerak in Jordan. Its actual site remains uncertain.

Mishael was a Levite of the Kohathite clan, a son of Uzziel and so a cousin of Moses and Aaron, since Uzziel was Aaron's uncle (Lev 10:4). Exodus lists him first among Uzziel's sons, with Elzaphan and Zithri (Exod 6:22). Elzaphan is also spelled Elizaphan, and 1 Chronicles names Michah and Isshiah as further sons of Uzziel. Mishael's one recorded act came after Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu died for offering unauthorized fire. Moses called Mishael and Elzaphan to carry the bodies away from the sanctuary and out of the camp (Lev 10:4). The following verse says they carried them out in their tunics. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the name to mean "who is equal to God?" The same name belongs to other people, including Daniel's companion, who were not this man.

Mishael was one of the men who stood on Ezra's left hand when Ezra read the Book of the Law to the people of Jerusalem from a wooden platform (Neh 8:4). He is named alongside Pedaiah, Malchiah, Hashum, Hashbadana, Zechariah and Meshullam, while six others stood on Ezra's right. Nothing else is recorded about him. The STEPBible proper-names index describes him as a Levite, though the verse itself does not give his tribe or his role. The name is usually taken to mean "who is what God is?" (Smith's Bible Dictionary) or "who is equal to God?" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several people in the Bible share this name, including Daniel's companion, who was renamed Meshach in Babylon. This Mishael belongs to the period after the return from exile and appears to be a different person.

Mishal was a town in the territory of the tribe of Asher. It appears in the list of Asher's towns, where the King James Version spells it Misheal (Josh 19:26). It was later given, with its surrounding pasture lands, to the Levites (Josh 21:30). Smith's Bible Dictionary specifies the Gershonite clan of Levites, and the parallel list in 1 Chr 6:74 calls the town Mashal. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "parables" or "governing." The site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the ancient writer Eusebius placed it near Carmel by the sea, and Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests the coastal site Misalli near Carmel. The location shown here is only a rough placement farther north, in western Galilee near Abdon, the town listed next to it in Josh 21:30.

Misham was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the Benjamite genealogy as one of the sons of Elpaal, alongside Eber and Shamed (1 Chr 8:12). Nothing else is recorded about him. The same verse says that Ono and Lod, with their surrounding towns, were built, but the wording most naturally credits this to Shamed rather than to Misham. Elpaal's other sons, such as Beriah, Shema, Zebadiah, Meshullam and Jobab, appear in the verses that follow. Smith's Bible Dictionary traces this family to Shaharaim, whom an earlier passage in the same chapter names as Elpaal's father (1 Chr 8:8–11). The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "purification," Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "their cleansing" or "their beholding," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "their savior" or "taking away."

Mishma was one of the twelve sons of Ishmael, Abraham's son by Hagar. He appears only in the genealogical lists of Ishmael's descendants, named after his brother Mibsam and before Dumah and Massa (Gen 25:14; 1 Chr 1:30). Nothing else is recorded about his life. The context of Genesis 25, which presents Ishmael's sons as princes of their tribes, suggests he headed one of the Ishmaelite clans. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as the founder of an Arab tribe. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "a hearing," and Hitchcock's Bible Names adds "obeying." The name is shared by several people in the Bible, including a later descendant of Simeon, who should not be confused with this son of Ishmael.

Mishma was a member of the tribe of Simeon named in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 4. The list traces a line through Shallum to Mibsam, and then to Mishma. The sons of Mishma are given as Hamuel, Zacchur and Shimei. Read as a chain of father to son, this makes Hamuel his son and Zacchur and Shimei later descendants. Smith's Bible Dictionary reads Mishma as a brother of Mibsam, while this entry follows the reading of him as Mibsam's son. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "hearing" or "obeying." The same name belongs to another man, a son of Ishmael (Gen 25:14), who is a different person.

Mishmannah was a warrior of the tribe of Gad who joined David's forces. He is named only once, as the fourth in a list of Gadite fighters (1 Chr 12:10). The surrounding passage in 1 Chronicles 12 describes these Gadites as skilled with shield and spear, with faces like lions and as swift as gazelles on the mountains. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary place their joining at Ziklag, where David stayed while fleeing from Saul. The wider chapter also speaks of men coming to David at a stronghold in the wilderness, so the exact setting is drawn from the context of the chapter as a whole. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "fatness." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Mispereth was one of the leaders named among those who came back from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel, the first group of returning exiles. The name appears only in two parallel lists of returnees. Neh 7:7 gives the form Mispereth, while Ezra 2:2 spells it Mispar (Mizpar in some King James printings, according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Both forms are generally taken to refer to the same person, since the two lists match closely, and Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "number." Nothing more is recorded: no family, tribe or later role is mentioned. The name stands alongside figures such as Jeshua, Nehemiah and Mordecai at the head of the list, which suggests, by inference, a position of some prominence among the returning community.

Misrephoth-maim was a place in northern Canaan near the coast, the point to which Israel chased the kings allied with Jabin after Joshua defeated them. The pursuit ran to great Sidon, to Misrephoth-maim, and to the valley of Mizpeh to the east (Josh 11:8). It later appears as a boundary of land still to be taken, the hill country from Lebanon to Misrephoth-maim, which is linked with the Sidonians (Josh 13:6). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "burning of waters," perhaps referring to salt-pans, lime-kilns or glass-works, and Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "hot waters." Easton's identifies it with the ruin of Musheirifeh at the headland of Ras en-Naqura, about 11 miles north of Acre. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests Zarephath near Sidon instead. The location shown here follows the Ras en-Naqura identification, near modern Naqoura in southern Lebanon.

The Mission to Antioch in Pisidia was a stage of Paul and Barnabas's first missionary journey, recorded in Acts 13:13–52. Sailing from Paphos on Cyprus, the group reached Perga in Pamphylia, where John Mark left them and returned to Jerusalem. At Antioch in Pisidia, in the synagogue on the sabbath, the rulers invited them to speak. Paul reviewed Israel's history from Egypt to David, then proclaimed Jesus as David's descendant, crucified and raised from the dead, through whom forgiveness of sins is offered. Many Jews and proselytes followed them, and the next sabbath almost the whole city gathered. Some of the Jews opposed Paul, and he and Barnabas announced that they would turn to the Gentiles, many of whom believed. Opponents then stirred up leading citizens, who expelled the two men. They shook the dust off their feet and went on to Iconium. The date, about AD 45, is inferred from context.

The Mission to Berea was a brief stay by Paul, Silas and Timothy (Timotheus) in the Macedonian town of Berea during Paul's second missionary journey. After the uproar in Thessalonica, the believers there sent Paul and Silas away by night, and on arrival they went to the Jewish synagogue. Acts describes the Bereans as more open-minded than the Thessalonians, because they received the message eagerly and examined the scriptures daily to see whether it was true. Many of the Jews believed, along with a good number of prominent Greek women and men. When Jews from Thessalonica heard of this, they came and stirred up the crowds. The believers then sent Paul toward the sea, while Silas and Timothy stayed behind. His escorts took him to Athens and returned with his instruction for the other two to join him quickly. It is dated about AD 48 and lasted perhaps a month, both by inference from context.

The Mission to Corinth, 1&2 Thess Written, was Paul's long stay in Corinth, in the province of Achaia, after he left Athens on his second missionary journey. He lodged and worked with Aquila and Priscilla, fellow tentmakers who had left Rome when Claudius expelled the Jews, and reasoned in the synagogue every sabbath. After Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, Paul met opposition, turned to the Gentiles, and taught from the house of Justus next door. Crispus, the synagogue ruler, believed with his household, and many Corinthians were baptized. Encouraged by a night vision, Paul stayed a year and six months. When Jews accused him before Gallio, the proconsul dismissed the case as a dispute about their law, and Sosthenes was beaten. Paul's letters to the Thessalonians, which name Silvanus (Silas) and Timothy with him (1 Thess 1:1; 2 Thess 1:1), were probably written here, from about AD 49 by inference from context.

The Mission to Ephesus/1 Cor Written was Paul's long stay in Ephesus, the leading city of the Roman province of Asia, during his third missionary journey. On arrival he met about twelve disciples who knew only John's baptism. He baptized them in the name of Jesus, and when he laid hands on them they received the Holy Spirit.
