He taught boldly in the synagogue for three months, then moved to the lecture hall of Tyrannus for two years, so that people throughout Asia heard his message. Paul performed unusual miracles. The seven sons of Sceva tried to use Jesus' name in exorcism and were overpowered. Many former practitioners of magic then burned their books, worth fifty thousand pieces of silver. Paul sent Timothy and Erastus ahead to Macedonia. By inference from 1 Cor 16:8, he wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus. The date of about AD 53 and the span of about two and a half years are estimates inferred from context.

The Mission to Lystra and Derbe was the stage of Paul and Barnabas's First Missionary Journey that followed their flight from Iconium to these cities of Lycaonia and the surrounding region, where they preached. At Lystra Paul healed a man who had been unable to walk from birth. The crowd, speaking Lycaonian, took the two men for gods, calling Barnabas Jupiter and Paul Mercurius because he did most of the speaking. The priest of Jupiter brought oxen and garlands to offer sacrifice. Barnabas and Paul tore their clothes and urged the people to turn from these things to the living God who made heaven and earth, and they barely stopped the sacrifice. Jews from Antioch and Iconium then turned the people against Paul, who was stoned and dragged out of the city as dead. He got up, and the next day he left with Barnabas for Derbe. The episode is dated to about AD 46, by inference from context.

The Mission to Macedonia and Greece was the stage of Paul's third missionary journey that followed the riot in Ephesus. After the uproar ended, Paul gathered and embraced the disciples, then left for Macedonia, where he encouraged the churches before moving on to Greece. He stayed there three months. When some Jews plotted against him as he was about to sail for Syria, he changed his plans and went back overland through Macedonia. A group traveled with him: Sopater of Berea, Aristarchus and Secundus of Thessalonica, Gaius of Derbe, Timothy, and Tychicus and Trophimus of Asia. They went ahead and waited at Troas. The narrator sailed from Philippi after the Feast of Unleavened Bread, reached Troas in five days, and stayed a week. The shift to "we" and "us" in Acts 20:5–6 is usually taken to mean that Luke rejoined Paul here. This entry dates the mission to about AD 54 and gives it a length of about a year, both inferred from context.

The Mission to Phrygia, Galatia and Asia was a stage of Paul's second missionary journey. Paul, Silas and Timothy traveled through Phrygia and the region of Galatia, but the Holy Spirit prevented them from preaching in the province of Asia (Acts 16:6). When they reached Mysia they tried to enter Bithynia to the north, and again the Spirit did not allow it (Acts 16:7). So they passed by Mysia and went down to Troas, a port on the Aegean coast (Acts 16:8). Timothy's presence follows from the preceding passage, where he joins Paul and Silas at Lystra. The phases are dated here to about AD 47 and given a span of roughly a month, both inferred from context rather than stated in the text. The episode leads directly into Paul's vision at Troas and the crossing into Macedonia that follows in the same chapter.

Mithkah (spelled Mithcah in the King James Version) was one of the places where the Israelites camped during their wilderness journey after leaving Egypt. It appears only in the list of stations in Numbers 33, where the people moved from Tarah to Mithcah and then on to Hashmonah (Num 33:28–29). The name means "sweetness." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it was given because of sweet pasture or water at the site. Nothing else is recorded about the camp, and its exact location is unknown. The location shown here is a rough placement in the desert region south of the Dead Sea, in what is now southern Jordan, by inference from its position in the sequence of stations.

Mithredath was the treasurer of Cyrus king of Persia. Through him Cyrus brought out the vessels that Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the temple in Jerusalem. Mithredath counted them and handed them over to Sheshbazzar, the prince of Judah, so the returning exiles could carry them back (Ezra 1:8). The name is Persian. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explain it as "given by Mithra" or "consecrated to Mithra." Another man named Mithredath appears later in the book of Ezra, a Persian official who wrote against the rebuilding of Jerusalem in the time of Artaxerxes. He is a different person from the treasurer described here.

Mithredath was a man who, along with Bishlam, Tabeel and their companions, wrote a letter to Artaxerxes king of Persia. The letter was written in Aramaic (the "Syrian tongue" of the King James text) and translated (Ezra 4:7). The verse does not give the letter's contents. Its setting among the efforts of local opponents to stop the Jews' rebuilding suggests it opposed the work on Jerusalem, and STEPBible Proper Names says it accused the Jews of rebuilding the city's walls. His name is Persian, meaning "gift of Mithra" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, which calls him perhaps an official. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Persian officer stationed at Samaria. He is probably a different man from Mithredath the treasurer of Cyrus in Ezra 1:8, since the name was borne by more than one person.

Mitylene was the chief city of the island of Lesbos, on its east coast in the Aegean Sea. Paul's ship stopped there near the end of his third missionary journey, as he and his companions travelled toward Jerusalem. The party picked Paul up at Assos, where he had come overland, and sailed on to Mitylene (Acts 20:14). By inference from the next stage of the voyage, which reached a point opposite Chios the following day, they probably spent one night there. This entry dates the voyage to about AD 54, an estimate inferred from context. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Mitylene was a free city in Paul's day and was known for its fine buildings. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes it as having two harbours. The site is the modern town of Mytilene, still the main city of Lesbos, which matches the location shown here.

Mizpah was a place in Gilead, east of the Jordan, named when Laban and Jacob parted and set up a heap of stones as a witness between them, with Laban saying, "The LORD watch between me and thee" (Gen 31:49). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "watchtower." In the time of the judges the Israelites camped at Mizpah against the Ammonites. There the people made Jephthah their leader, and he repeated his terms before the LORD. Jephthah lived at Mizpah, and his daughter came out of his house to meet him when he returned from battle (Judg 11:34). Hosea later named Mizpah, alongside Tabor, as a place where Israel's leaders had been "a snare." Several places share this name. Easton's Bible Dictionary equates this one with Ramath-mizpeh. Its exact site is uncertain, and the location shown here is in northern Jordan near modern Ramtha.

Mizpah, called "the land of Mizpeh" in the King James Version, was a district below Mount Hermon where Hivites lived. It is named in Josh 11:3 among the peoples summoned to join the northern alliance against Joshua. The surrounding chapter shows that this alliance was led by Jabin king of Hazor. Josh 11:8 mentions a "valley of Mizpeh" to the east, to which the defeated forces were chased, and this is probably the same area. The name means "watch-tower," and Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the Hebrew has the article, "the Mizpeh." Several other places in the Bible share this name and should not be confused with this one. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's suggests the modern village of Metulla, whose name also means "the look-out," at the northern tip of Israel, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Mizpah (also spelled Mizpeh, meaning "watchtower") was a city of Benjamin near Jerusalem, one of several places with this name. The tribes of Israel assembled there before the LORD to act against Benjamin and swore oaths there (Judg 20:1; 21:1). Samuel gathered Israel there to fast and confess, defeated the attacking Philistines, and set up the Ebenezer stone nearby. He judged Israel there on his yearly circuit and later called the people there to choose a king. King Asa fortified it with stones taken from Ramah. After Jerusalem fell to Babylon, it became the seat of the governor Gedaliah, whom Ishmael son of Nethaniah murdered there. Men of Mizpah later helped rebuild Jerusalem's wall. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it at Neby Samwil, northwest of Jerusalem. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests Scopus, and many modern scholars favor Tell en-Nasbeh. The location shown here follows the Neby Samwil identification.

Mizpeh was a town in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin, listed in Josh 18:26 beside Chephirah and Mozah among the cities given to Benjamin when the land was divided. The name means "watchtower" or "lookout" and is shared by several places in the Bible, so it should not be confused with the Mizpeh of Gilead, Judah or Moab. This Benjaminite town is probably the same as the Mizpah mentioned elsewhere, where Israel gathered under Samuel (1 Sam 7:5–6) and where Gedaliah later governed after Jerusalem fell (2 Kgs 25:23). Its site is disputed. Many scholars favor Tell en-Nasbeh, about 12 km north of Jerusalem, while others favor Nebi Samwil, a high hill just northwest of Jerusalem. The location shown here follows the Nebi Samwil identification.

Mizpeh was a town in the lowlands, or Shephelah, of Judah, listed among the towns given to the tribe of Judah in Josh 15:38. It appears between Dilean and Joktheel in a group of towns that also includes Lachish and Eglon. The name means "watchtower" or "lookout point" and is shared by several places in the Bible, so this Mizpeh should not be confused with the better-known Mizpeh in Benjamin or the Mizpeh in Gilead. Apart from this one listing, nothing more is recorded about it. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the district around Lachish, inferred from the towns it is grouped with.

Mizpeh, called "Mizpeh of Moab," was a town in Moab where David went while fleeing from Saul. There he asked the king of Moab to let his father and mother stay under his protection until David knew what God would do for him (1 Sam 22:3). David's family ties to Moab through his great-grandmother Ruth, a Moabite, may explain why he turned there, though the text does not say so. The following verse (1 Sam 22:5) records that the prophet Gad told David not to stay in the stronghold but to go to the land of Judah, and he moved to the forest of Hareth. The name, meaning "watchtower," is shared by several biblical places, and this town's exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it was probably the citadel of Kir-Moab, modern Kerak in Jordan. The location shown here follows that identification.

Mizraim was the second-named son of Ham, listed after Cush and before Phut and Canaan in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:6; 1 Chr 1:8). He is named as the ancestor of the Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim, Pathrusim, Casluhim and Caphthorim (Gen 10:13; 1 Chr 1:11). These names appear to stand for peoples rather than single individuals. Elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible, Mizraim is the usual name for Egypt, so he is generally understood as the ancestor, or personification, of the Egyptians. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary explain the word as a dual form, probably referring to the two regions of Upper and Lower Egypt. Easton's adds that the modern Arabic name for Egypt, Misr, comes from the same root. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "tribulations."

Mizzah was a son of Reuel and a grandson of Esau through Esau's wife Bashemath. He is listed as the youngest of Reuel's four sons, with his brothers Nahath, Zerah and Shammah (Gen 36:13; 1 Chr 1:37). Genesis also names him among the "dukes", or clan chiefs, descended from Reuel in the land of Edom (Gen 36:17). This suggests that his name came to stand for an Edomite clan as well as for an individual. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of the name is uncertain: Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "fear", the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "strong" or "firm", and Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "defluxion from the head."

Mnason was a Christian from Cyprus, described as "an old disciple" (an early disciple), who gave lodging to Paul and his companions near the end of Paul's journey from Miletus to Jerusalem, about AD 54 by inference from context. Disciples from Caesarea traveled with Paul's group and brought Mnason along so that the travelers could stay with him (Acts 21:16). The verse does not say exactly where his house was. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary take it to have been in Jerusalem, while others place it at a stop along the road from Caesarea. Easton's understands "old disciple" to mean that he became a believer in the earliest days of the church. Smith's suggests that, as a Cypriot, he may have been a friend of Barnabas, who was also from Cyprus. He is mentioned nowhere else in the Bible.

Moab was the son of Lot by his older daughter and the ancestor of the Moabites (Gen 19:37). His half-brother Ben-ammi, born to Lot's younger daughter, became the father of the Ammonites. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "of his father." Most later uses of the name refer to his descendants and their land east of the Dead Sea, probably in modern central Jordan. Israel camped in the plains of Moab before crossing the Jordan. There Balak king of Moab summoned Balaam, and there Israel mourned Moses. Eglon of Moab oppressed Israel until Ehud's deliverance, about 1360 BC by inference from context. Ruth's story begins in Moab. David subdued the Moabites, who rebelled after Ahab's death. Solomon built a high place for Chemosh, Moab's god. Prophets including Isaiah, Jeremiah, Amos and Zephaniah announced judgment on Moab.

Moab was a country east of the Dead Sea and the Jordan, in present-day Jordan, bordered on the north by the Arnon (Num 22:36). Israel camped in the plains of Moab opposite Jericho before entering Canaan. There Balak king of Moab summoned Balaam, Moses delivered the law, and Israel mourned his death (Num 22:1; Deut 1:5; Deut 34:8). Eglon king of Moab oppressed Israel in the time of the judges (Judg 3:12). Ruth and Orpah were Moabites, and Naomi's family lived there during a famine (Ruth 1:1). David sheltered his parents with Moab's king, later conquered Moab, and made it tributary (1 Sam 22:4; 2 Sam 8:2). It rebelled after Ahab's death (2 Kgs 1:1). Its god was Chemosh (1 Kgs 11:7). Prophets including Isaiah, Jeremiah and Amos spoke oracles against it. Easton's Bible Dictionary links it with the modern Kerak region.

Moadiah was a priest, or a priestly family named after him, in the period after the return from exile. Nehemiah lists Maadiah among the priests who came back from Babylon with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:5). In the next generation, in the days of the high priest Joiakim, Piltai was head of the priestly house of Moadiah (Neh 12:17). Since the two lists run in parallel, Maadiah and Moadiah are generally taken as spellings of the same name. This entry also identifies him with Maaziah, one of the priests who sealed the covenant under Nehemiah (Neh 10:8), as the STEPBible proper-names index does. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat Maaziah under a separate heading. Because the covenant came generations after the first return, the name in Neh 10:8 probably stands for the priestly family rather than the original man.

Moladah was a town in the far south (the Negev) of Judah, listed among the cities of Judah's southern district (Josh 15:26). It was then given to the tribe of Simeon, whose territory lay within Judah (Josh 19:2), and Simeon's descendants are recorded living there (1 Chr 4:28). After the return from exile in Babylon, people of Judah settled there again (Neh 11:26). It is always mentioned close to Beersheba. The name probably means “birth.” Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with el-Milh (Tel Malhata), about 10 miles east of Beersheba. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links it with Malatha, a town Josephus mentions, but notes that Eusebius and Jerome placed Malatha near Jattir, which would point elsewhere. The location shown here follows the general identification east of Beersheba in the eastern Negev.

Molech was a god worshipped by the Ammonites. His name probably means "king" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), and Easton's Bible Dictionary notes he is also called Milcom and Malcham. His worship involved making children "pass through the fire," which is generally understood as child sacrifice. The law in Leviticus forbids this practice, and anyone in Israel who gave a child to Molech was to be stoned. It also warns of judgment on a community that ignored the offence. Solomon built a high place for Molech on the hill facing Jerusalem, which Easton's identifies as the Mount of Olives. The rite was later practiced at Topheth in the valley of Hinnom. A king defiled that site to end the practice, Josiah by inference from the surrounding chapter of 2 Kgs 23. Jeremiah condemned Judah for building high places there to offer sons and daughters to Molech.

Molid was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:29 as the son of Abishur and his wife Abihail and the brother of Ahban. Nothing else is recorded about him. The surrounding genealogy (1 Chr 2:25–28) traces Abishur back through Shammai and Onam to Jerahmeel, so Molid belonged to the Jerahmeelite clan of Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary also places him among Jerahmeel's descendants. Smith's gives the meaning of his name as "begetter," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "nativity" or "generation."

Mordecai was one of the leaders who came back from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel. He appears among them in Ezra 2:2 and again in the parallel list at Neh 7:7, where he is named alongside Jeshua, Nehemiah, Bilshan and others at the head of the register of returning Israelites. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several people in the Bible share this name, and this Mordecai is usually kept distinct from Esther's cousin in the Persian court, who lived in Susa decades later. Both lists date the return to the early years after the exile, probably the late 500s BC by inference from context. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "contrition; bitter; bruising."

Mordecai was a Jew of the tribe of Benjamin, the son of Jair, who lived at Shushan (Susa), the Persian royal city, during the reign of Ahasuerus (Xerxes). He raised his orphaned cousin Esther as his own daughter and continued to guide her after she became queen. While sitting in the king's gate, he exposed a plot by two chamberlains to kill the king. He refused to bow to Haman, and this led Haman to plan the destruction of all the Jews. Mordecai mourned in public and urged Esther to intervene. Haman was then hanged on the gallows he had built for Mordecai. The king gave Mordecai his signet ring, and Mordecai became second only to the king. He sent letters establishing the feast of Purim. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that many have regarded him as the author of the book of Esther. A different Mordecai returned from exile with Zerubbabel.

Moreh (Shechem) was a landmark at the place of Shechem, in the hill country of central Canaan, where Abram first stopped after entering the land (Gen 12:6). The King James Version calls it the "plain of Moreh," but Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note that the Hebrew is better rendered "oak" or "terebinth of Moreh," probably meaning "terebinth of the teacher." Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests Moreh may have been a Canaanite who gave his name to the spot. According to the next verse, Gen 12:7, the Lord appeared to Abram here and he built an altar. The arrival is dated about 1921 BC, by inference from context. Deut 11:30 mentions the "plains of Moreh" near Mounts Ebal and Gerizim. Some treat that as a separate site linked with Gilgal, but this entry follows the view that it is the same place. The exact spot is unknown. The location shown here is near Shechem, by the modern city of Nablus.

Moreh (little Hermon) was a hill in the Valley of Jezreel. It is mentioned only in Judg 7:1, where it marks the position of the Midianite camp. Gideon and his men camped beside the well of Harod, and the Midianites lay north of them, by the hill of Moreh, in the valley. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the name to mean "hill of the teacher." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "stretching." Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the ridge called Little Hermon, Jebel ed-Duhy (today Givat HaMoreh), on the northern edge of the Jezreel plain opposite Mount Gilboa, with Shunem at its western foot. One commentator, Moore, placed the scene near Shechem instead. The location shown here follows the Little Hermon identification. This hill is distinct from the place called Moreh near Shechem that is linked with Abraham.

Moresheth was the hometown of the prophet Micah, a town in Judah. It does not appear by name in these verses but is implied by Micah's title, "the Morasthite," meaning a man of Moresheth. Micah prophesied there during the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah (Mic 1:1). A century later, elders recalled him by this title when they defended Jeremiah, quoting his warning that Jerusalem would become heaps (Jer 26:18). Micah 1:14 mentions a "Moresheth-gath," probably the same town, which suggests it lay near the Philistine city of Gath in the Shephelah, the low hill country west of Judah's highlands. Its exact site is uncertain. The location shown here is approximate and fits the common identification with Tell el-Judeideh (Tel Goded), near modern Beit Guvrin.

Moresheth-gath was a town in the lowland foothills of Judah, named only in Mic 1:14 among the places facing judgment in Micah's lament. There the prophet says Judah will have to give parting gifts to Moresheth-gath, probably meaning it would be lost to an enemy. The name likely means "possession of Gath." Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take it to be Micah's home town, since he is called "the Morasthite" (Mic 1:1; Jer 26:18), and it probably lay near Gath and Mareshah (Mic 1:15). Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Jerome placed it a little east of Eleutheropolis, modern Beit Jibrin. The location shown here, a rough one just east of Beit Jibrin, follows that identification.

Moriah is the land to which God sent Abraham to offer his son Isaac as a burnt offering on one of its mountains (Gen 22:2). This is the only place where the land of Moriah is named, and the passage gives no precise location. Abraham saw the place from a distance on the third day of his journey. A later passage, 2 Chr 3:1, gives the name Mount Moriah to the hill in Jerusalem where Solomon built the temple, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes this temple hill to be the mountain of Isaac's sacrifice, and this entry follows that view. The location shown here is the Temple Mount in Jerusalem. Samaritan tradition places the event on Mount Gerizim, and Smith's Bible Dictionary mentions Moreh near Shechem as another proposed site. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia leaves the question open.

Mortar was a district in or near Jerusalem, mentioned only in Zeph 1:11. The King James Version keeps the Hebrew name, Maktesh, which means "mortar" or "hollow." The name probably describes a basin-shaped hollow in the terrain. Zephaniah tells its inhabitants to wail because its merchants and those who handle silver will be cut off, which suggests it was a trading or money-dealing quarter. The neighboring verse mentions the Fish Gate and the "second" quarter of the city, so Maktesh was probably also a part of Jerusalem. Its exact site is uncertain. Many identify it with the central valley running through the old city, often called the Tyropoeon Valley, and the location shown here places it within Jerusalem in that area. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes a suggestion that it was the quarter where Phoenician traders lived.

Moserah was a campsite of the Israelites during their wilderness journey. They reached it from Beeroth of the children of Jaakan, and Deut 10:6 says Aaron died and was buried there, with his son Eleazar taking over as priest. Other passages (Num 20:28; Num 33:38) place Aaron's death on Mount Hor, so Moserah is usually taken to be the area at or near that mountain. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat it as probably the same place as Moseroth (Num 33:30–31), which that list places before Bene-jaakan rather than after it. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "bond" and links it with el-Tayibeh, a small spring at the foot of the pass up Mount Hor. The location shown here follows the traditional identification of Mount Hor with Jebel Harun near Petra in southern Jordan, and it is only approximate.

Moseroth was one of the places where the Israelites camped during their wilderness journey. They came to it from Hashmonah and moved on from it to Bene-jaakan (Num 33:30–31). The name is usually taken to mean "bonds." Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat it as probably the same place as Mosera (Moserah) in Deut 10:6, where Aaron is said to have died and been buried. In that passage, though, the order is reversed, with Mosera coming after Bene-jaakan. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is a rough placement in the region south of the Dead Sea, in present-day southern Jordan, and should be treated as approximate.

Moses was the Israelite leader and prophet through whom God brought Israel out of Egypt and gave them the law. A Levite, son of Amram and Jochebed and brother of Aaron and Miriam, he was born in Egypt and raised by Pharaoh's daughter, who named him because she "drew him out of the water." He married Zipporah and had two sons, Gershom and Eliezer. With Aaron he confronted Pharaoh, led the people through the wilderness, received the commandments at Sinai (Horeb), and oversaw the building of the tabernacle. He died on Mount Nebo, and his assistant Joshua succeeded him. Later scripture constantly cites "the law of Moses," and Jewish and Christian tradition credits him with the first five books of the Bible. The Gospels record him appearing with Elijah at Jesus' transfiguration. His life is dated, by inference from context, to about 1571–1452 BC.

The Moses Flees Pharaoh episode is the account of how Moses, raised in Egypt, left the country after killing an Egyptian. Once grown, Moses went out to see the forced labor of his fellow Hebrews and saw an Egyptian beating one of them. After checking that no one was watching, he killed the Egyptian and hid the body in the sand. The next day he tried to stop two Hebrews from fighting, and the one in the wrong asked whether Moses meant to kill him as he had killed the Egyptian. Realizing the deed was known, Moses was afraid. When Pharaoh heard of it, he tried to have Moses killed, but Moses fled to the land of Midian and sat down by a well. Stephen's speech in Acts 7:23 and 7:30 puts Moses at about forty at the time and his stay in Midian at forty years. This matches this entry's date of about 1531 BC, an estimate inferred from context.

Most Holy is the innermost room of the tabernacle, the portable sanctuary Israel carried through the wilderness. Exod 26:33 describes how a veil hung under the clasps was to separate it from the outer room, the holy place, and says that the ark of the testimony was to be brought inside behind that veil. Because the tabernacle moved with the people, the room had no fixed location, and no coordinates are given here. Other passages describe the same inner room under the name "most holy place" or "holy of holies", both in the tabernacle and later in Solomon's temple in Jerusalem. By inference from the verse's context, which gives detailed building instructions, it was the part of the sanctuary set apart most completely, closed off from the rest by the veil.

The Most Holy Place was the innermost room of the tabernacle, the portable tent-sanctuary the Israelites carried with them in the wilderness. In the instructions for building the tabernacle, God tells Moses to put the mercy seat on the ark of the testimony inside this room (Exod 26:34). The verse just before it (Exod 26:33) describes a veil hanging between the holy place and the most holy place, separating this inner room from the rest of the tent. Leviticus 16 describes the high priest entering behind the veil on the Day of Atonement, and Heb 9:7 says he went in once a year. Because the tabernacle moved with the people, this room had no fixed site, so no location is shown here. The same name was later given to the inner sanctuary of Solomon's temple in Jerusalem (1 Kgs 6:16), which is a separate place.

The Most Holy Place was the innermost room of the temple, where the ark of the covenant was kept. In Solomon's temple it was an inner chamber, also called the oracle, lined with cedar, twenty cubits square, overlaid with fine gold and closed by gold doors (1 Kgs 6:16; 2 Chr 3:8; 1 Kgs 7:50). Two gold-covered cherubim stood inside, and at the temple's dedication the priests set the ark beneath their wings. 1 Chr 6:49 assigns the work of the place most holy to Aaron and his sons. Ezekiel's visionary temple also has a most holy place measuring twenty cubits square, set within a sacred land allotment. The STEPBible Proper Names index applies the name to the matching room in the tabernacle as well. The location shown here is the Temple Mount in Jerusalem, where Solomon's temple stood.

The Mother of Aholah and Aholibah is an unnamed figure in the allegory the prophet Ezekiel was given in Ezek 23. The passage opens by describing two women who were daughters of one mother (Ezek 23:2). She is never named and takes no action in the story. She serves only to show that the two sisters share the same origin. Later in the same chapter, Ezek 23:4 identifies Aholah as Samaria and Aholibah as Jerusalem, the capitals of the northern and southern kingdoms. By inference from the allegory, the common mother probably stands for the single people of Israel from which both kingdoms came, though the text does not say this directly. Ezek 23:3 places the sisters' early history in Egypt, which suggests that their shared origin is meant to recall the nation's beginnings there.

The Mother of Lemuel is the unnamed woman credited with the teaching recorded in Proverbs 31. Prov 31:1 introduces the chapter as "the words of king Lemuel, the prophecy that his mother taught him." The verses that follow (Prov 31:2–9) appear to give her advice: she warns her son against wasting his strength on women and against kings drinking wine, and urges him to speak up for the poor and judge fairly. Whether the closing poem about the capable wife (Prov 31:10–31) also comes from her is uncertain. Neither she nor Lemuel is identified elsewhere in the Bible. Jewish tradition takes Lemuel to be another name for Solomon, which would make her Bathsheba, but the text does not say so. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that a king's mother held a place of special honor in Israel, as Bathsheba did.

The Mother of the Wife of Simon was the mother-in-law of Simon Peter, the apostle. The three Gospels that tell her story all say she lay sick with a fever in Simon's house, which Luke calls "a great fever" (Luke 4:38). Mark and Luke place this immediately after Jesus left the synagogue, and Mark's wider context sets it in Capernaum. People told Jesus about her and asked him to help (Mark 1:30; Luke 4:38). The accounts go on to say that he healed her, that the fever left her, and that she got up and served them. That evening many other sick people were brought to the house to be healed. The event is dated to about AD 27, an estimate inferred from context. Her name is not given, and nothing else is recorded about her.

The Mother of Zebedee's children was the wife of Zebedee and the mother of the apostles James and John. Matthew records that she came to Jesus with her two sons, knelt before him, and made a request. The following verses (Matt 20:21) say she asked that her sons sit at his right and left hand in his kingdom. In Mark's parallel account (Mark 10:35) James and John make the request themselves. She appears again among the women who had followed Jesus from Galilee and watched his crucifixion from a distance, about AD 30 by inference from context. Where Matthew names her at the cross, Mark 15:40 names Salome, so she is often identified as Salome. Some also infer from John 19:25 that she was the sister of Jesus' mother. Both identifications are inferences, and Matthew never gives her name.

Mount Baalah was a hill on the northern boundary of the tribe of Judah, mentioned only in Josh 15:11. The border line ran from the side of Ekron northward to Shicron, passed along Mount Baalah, and then went out to Jabneel before ending at the Mediterranean Sea. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on the north-western boundary between Judah and Dan. It should not be confused with the town of Baalah (Kiriath-jearim) further east along the same northern border. Its exact site is unknown. By inference from its place in the sequence between Ekron and Jabneel, it was probably a low ridge in the coastal plain, and the location shown here is a rough position in that area, west of Ekron and near Jabneel (modern Yavne).

Mount Baalhermon (ESV Mount Baal-hermon) is a mountain named in Judg 3:3 as one boundary of the territory held by the Hivites of Mount Lebanon. These were among the peoples left in the land after the conquest, and the verse gives their range as running "from mount Baalhermon unto the entering in of Hamath." The name links Baal with Hermon. It is probably Mount Hermon itself or part of it, a view supported by 1 Chr 5:23, which mentions Baal-hermon alongside Senir and Mount Hermon. A closely parallel boundary description in Josh 13:5 reads "from Baal-gad under mount Hermon unto the entering into Hamath," so some take Baal-hermon to be a place at the foot of Hermon, possibly Baal-gad. The location shown here follows the identification with the summit of Mount Hermon, on the modern border of Lebanon and Syria.

Mount Carmel is a mountain ridge in northern Israel. The location shown here is on the ridge that runs northwest to the Mediterranean coast near modern Haifa. At Elijah's request, King Ahab gathered all Israel there, together with 450 prophets of Baal and 400 prophets of the groves who ate at Jezebel's table, for a contest between Elijah and these prophets (1 Kgs 18:19–20). Afterward Elijah climbed to the top of Carmel and bowed to the ground with his face between his knees while Ahab went off to eat and drink (1 Kgs 18:42). Carmel was later linked with Elisha. He went there after leaving Bethel and then returned to Samaria (2 Kgs 2:25). The Shunammite woman traveled to him at Mount Carmel after her son died, which suggests he sometimes stayed there (2 Kgs 4:25). STEPBible's Proper Names describes it as a mountain range.

Mount Ebal is a mountain in central Canaan, standing north of Mount Gerizim with the valley of Shechem between them. It is probably the modern Jebel Eslamiyeh beside Nablus, and the location shown here matches that site. Moses instructed that once Israel entered the land, the blessing was to be placed on Gerizim and the curse on Ebal (Deut 11:29). Six tribes, Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan and Naphtali, were to stand on Ebal for the curses. Large plastered stones were also to be set up there, which the surrounding passage says were for writing the law (Deut 27:4, 13). Joshua later built an altar to the LORD on Ebal and gathered all Israel, half facing each mountain, to carry out this command (Josh 8:30, 33). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives its height as about 3,076 feet. STEPBible's proper-name index also links it with Mount Zalmon.

Mount Ephraim was the name for the hill country of central Israel, the highland region settled by the tribe of Ephraim, rather than a single peak. In Jer 4:15 a voice announcing disaster is heard first from Dan, at the far northern edge of the land, and then from Mount Ephraim, which lies much closer to Jerusalem. By inference from the passage, the two places mark the stages of an invader advancing from the north toward Judah. Other passages use the same phrase for the setting of events in Joshua, Judges and Samuel. Examples include the territory given to the descendants of Joseph in Josh 17:15 and the home of Micah in Judg 17:1. The location shown here places the region in the central highlands around modern Nablus, near ancient Shechem.

Mount Ephron was a hill or mountain range named as a landmark on the northern border of the tribe of Judah, where Judah's territory met Benjamin's. Joshua 15:9 traces the boundary from the spring of the waters of Nephtoah out to "the cities of mount Ephron," and then on to Baalah, also called Kiriath-jearim. The verse suggests the area held several towns. It probably lay between Nephtoah and Kiriath-jearim, west of Jerusalem, by inference from the order of the boundary description. Its exact identity is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests the range on the west side of the Wadi Beit Hanina, northwest of Jerusalem. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the hill country west of Jerusalem and should not be taken as a firm identification.

Mount Gerizim is a mountain in the hill country of Samaria, facing Mount Ebal across the valley of Shechem, near modern Nablus. Before Israel entered Canaan, Moses commanded that the blessing be set on Gerizim and the curse on Ebal (Deut 11:29). Six tribes, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph and Benjamin, were to stand on Gerizim to bless the people (Deut 27:12). Joshua 8:33 records this ceremony, with half of Israel facing Gerizim and half facing Ebal around the ark. Later, Jotham stood on its top and called out his parable to the men of Shechem (Judg 9:7). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives its height as about 3,000 feet and, citing Josephus, says the Samaritans built a rival temple there. The Samaritan woman's mention of "this mountain" as a place of worship (John 4:20) is usually taken to mean Gerizim. A small Samaritan community still worships there.

Mount Gilboa is the mountain where Israel was defeated by the Philistines and King Saul died, about 1056 BC by inference from context. The Israelites fled before the Philistines and fell dead on its slopes. The next day, when the Philistines came to strip the bodies, they found Saul and his three sons lying there (1 Sam 31:1, 8; the parallel account in 1 Chr 10:1, 8). A young man who brought the news to David, identified later in the chapter as an Amalekite, said he had happened upon Saul on the mountain, leaning on his spear as chariots and horsemen closed in (2 Sam 1:6). In the lament that follows, David calls on the "mountains of Gilboa" to have no dew or rain (2 Sam 1:21). The site is generally identified with the ridge still called Mount Gilboa in northern Israel, on the southeastern edge of the Jezreel Valley. The location shown here lies on that ridge.

Mount Gilead is the place named in Gideon's proclamation before his battle with the Midianites. God told him to announce that anyone who was fearful should 'return and depart early from mount Gilead', and 22,000 men left, leaving 10,000 (Judg 7:3). Since Gideon's army was camped by the well of Harod, west of the Jordan, this mountain probably lay in that area rather than in the better-known region of Gilead east of the Jordan. Views differ. Some take the name as an early copying slip for Mount Gilboa, which overlooks Harod. Others take it as a local name for a height near the spring, perhaps echoed in the modern name Ain Jalud. The location shown here follows an identification on the Gilboa ridge near the Harod spring. It is probably separate from the 'mount Gilead' where Jacob and Laban made their covenant, which was east of the Jordan.

Mount Halak was a mountain marking the southern limit of the land Joshua conquered. It is described as the mountain "that goeth up to Seir," meaning it rises toward Seir, the hill country of Edom to the southeast. Its northern counterpart was Baal-gad in the valley of Lebanon under Mount Hermon (Josh 11:17; 12:7). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "smooth" or "bald" and suggests it was a conspicuous landmark visible from a distance. Its exact location is uncertain. Easton's notes that some have identified it with Jebel el-Madura, on Judah's southern frontier near the south end of the Dead Sea. Others link it to a hill called Jebel Halaq, whose Arabic name preserves the biblical one. The location shown here follows a site in the central Negev highlands, probably that Jebel Halaq identification.

Mount Heres was a hill in the territory of Dan, near Aijalon and Shaalbim, where the Amorites held on and refused to leave after Israel's settlement. According to Judg 1:35, the Amorites kept living there, but the tribes descended from Joseph later gained the upper hand and forced them to pay tribute. The Hebrew name, Har-heres, means "sun-mountain." Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it is probably the same place as Ir-shemesh ("city of the sun"), which Josh 19:41 lists among Dan's towns. Because of the shared sun meaning, it is often linked with Beth-shemesh. The exact site is uncertain. The location shown here places it in the low hill country west of Jerusalem, in the area of Beth-shemesh and the Aijalon and Sorek valleys.

Mount Hermon is a prominent mountain marking the northern limit of the land Israel took east of the Jordan, which stretched "from the river Arnon unto mount Hermon" (Deut 3:8; Josh 12:1). Og, king of Bashan, ruled in Mount Hermon (Josh 12:5), and Baalgad "under mount Hermon" marked the northern reach of Joshua's conquests (Josh 11:17; 13:5). The half tribe of Manasseh later spread as far as Hermon (1 Chr 5:23). STEPBible Proper Names notes the alternative names Senir and Sirion (compare Deut 3:9) and links Baal-hermon and Baal-gad with it. It is generally identified with the modern Jabal al-Shaykh on the Syria–Lebanon border, the region's highest peak. The Gospels place the Transfiguration on an unnamed high mountain after Jesus' visit to Caesarea Philippi. Some locate it on Hermon, others on Mount Tabor. This entry follows the Hermon view.

Mount Hor was a mountain on the border of Edom where the Israelites camped after leaving Kadesh during their wilderness journey. Here God told Moses to take Aaron and his son Eleazar up the mountain in full view of the people, and Aaron died there at 123 years old, in the fortieth year after the exodus. From Mount Hor Israel went on by the way of the Red Sea to go around Edom, then camped at Zalmonah. Moses' own death was later compared to Aaron's death on this mountain. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Jebel Harun, a prominent two-peaked mountain near Petra in southern Jordan, and notes another view placing it at Jebel Madurah, west of the Arabah. The location shown here follows the Jebel Harun identification. A different Mount Hor on Israel's northern border appears in Num 34:7–8.

Mount Hor was a mountain marking the northern border of the land promised to Israel. In Num 34:7–8 the line runs from the Mediterranean ("the great sea") to Mount Hor, then on to the entrance of Hamath and Zedad. It is mentioned nowhere else and is a different place from the Mount Hor on the border of Edom where Aaron died. Its exact location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it may be one of the peaks of Lebanon. Others have proposed Mount Hermon or a peak in the coastal mountains farther north. The location shown here is a rough one in the mountains of northwestern Syria, which fits a border running inland from the sea toward Hamath, probably modern Hama.

Mount Horeb is the mountain where the Israelites, after the golden calf incident, stripped off their ornaments as a sign of mourning at God's command (Exod 33:6). Elsewhere in the Bible, Horeb is called "the mountain of God," where Moses saw the burning bush (Exod 3:1). Deuteronomy regularly uses the name Horeb for the place where the law was given, which Exodus calls Mount Sinai, so the two names are generally taken to refer to the same mountain or the same range. The prophet Elijah later traveled forty days to reach Horeb (1 Kgs 19:8). Its location is debated. Proposed sites include several peaks in the southern Sinai Peninsula and some in northwest Arabia. The location shown here follows the traditional identification with Jebel Musa in southern Sinai, near St Catherine's Monastery.

Mount Jearim was a mountain on the northern border of the tribe of Judah. In the description of that boundary, the line ran west from Baalah (Kiriath-jearim) to Mount Seir, then along the north side of Mount Jearim, and down to Beth-shemesh and Timnah (Josh 15:10). The verse equates Mount Jearim with Chesalon, so the name may refer to the ridge on which the town of Chesalon stood. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "forests," probably pointing to a wooded height. Chesalon is commonly identified with the modern village of Kesla, west of Jerusalem, and the location shown here matches that identification. This is the only verse in the Bible that mentions Mount Jearim.

Mount Lebanon is the mountain range of Lebanon, named in Judg 3:3 as the home of the Hivites. They were one of the peoples the Lord left in the land after Joshua's conquest to test the Israelites. The verse places the Hivite territory there, stretching from Mount Baal-hermon to the entrance of Hamath. That suggests the northern hill country beyond Israel's settled tribes. STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) describes it as a range marking the northern border of the Promised Land. It is probably the Lebanon range that runs parallel to the Mediterranean coast in the modern country of Lebanon, west of the Beqaa Valley, with the Anti-Lebanon and Mount Hermon to the east. The location shown here is a point in the central part of the range, northeast of Beirut, standing for the range as a whole rather than a single peak.

Mount Moriah is the hill in Jerusalem where Solomon began building the temple of the LORD. 2 Chr 3:1 identifies it as the place where the LORD appeared to David, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite that David had set aside. The accounts in 2 Sam 24 and 1 Chr 21 describe David buying this threshing floor from Ornan, who is called Araunah in Samuel, and building an altar there after a plague was stopped. Gen 22:2 sends Abraham to offer Isaac on a mountain in "the land of Moriah." Jewish tradition identifies that mountain with the temple hill, though Genesis does not explicitly connect the two, and Samaritan tradition places Abraham's offering on Mount Gerizim instead. The location shown here is the Temple Mount in Jerusalem's Old City, the usual identification of the temple site.

Mount Nebo was a mountain in the land of Moab, facing Jericho across the Jordan, and part of the Abarim range. God told Moses to climb it and look at the land of Canaan that Israel would possess (Deut 32:49). Moses went up from the plains of Moab to Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, and the Lord showed him the whole land, from Gilead as far as Dan (Deut 34:1). Moses died there. By inference from context, this was about 1452 BC. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies Nebo with Jebel Nebah, near the northern end of the Dead Sea on its eastern side, about 5 miles southwest of Heshbon. It describes the mountain as the summit of the Pisgah ridge, about 2,643 feet high, with a commanding view of western Palestine. The location shown here matches that identification, the modern Jebel Nebo in Jordan.

Mount of Esau is a name used only in the book of Obadiah for the mountainous homeland of Edom, the nation descended from Esau. It stands in parallel with Edom in Obad 1:8, where the LORD threatens to destroy the wise men of Edom and understanding from the mount of Esau, and with Teman, an Edomite district, in Obad 1:9. Obadiah says its inhabitants will be cut off by slaughter. He also foretells that people from the south will take possession of it (Obad 1:19) and that deliverers on Mount Zion will judge it (Obad 1:21), setting Esau's mountain against Zion. The name probably refers to the whole highland region of Edom rather than one peak, a view shared by the STEPBible Proper Names index. That region is the high country of southern Jordan, east of the Arabah. The location shown here marks a point in that area.

The Mount of Olives is a ridge east of Jerusalem, separated from the city by the Kidron Valley and named for the olive trees on its slopes (Easton's Bible Dictionary). Zechariah describes it as standing "before Jerusalem on the east" and foresees it splitting in two from east to west, opening a great valley (Zech 14:4). Easton's notes that David crossed it while fleeing Absalom (2 Sam 15:30) and that Solomon built high places for foreign gods there (1 Kgs 11:7). In the Gospels Jesus often stayed there. He taught his disciples about coming events in what is called the Olivet Discourse (Matt 24), and he went there on the night of his arrest. Acts 1:12 links the Ascension to it, and Luke 24:50–51 places that event near Bethany, on its eastern side. Easton's says it rises about 200 feet above the city and is now called Jebel et-Tur. Some passages call it simply "the mount."

The Mount of Olives, also called mount Olivet, is the ridge directly east of Jerusalem, facing the temple across the Kidron Valley. David climbed it weeping and barefoot as he fled from Absalom (2 Sam 15:30). Zechariah foretold that the Lord's feet would stand on it and that it would split from east to west, forming a great valley (Zech 14:4). In the Gospels, Jesus approached Jerusalem by way of Bethphage and Bethany on its slopes, and the crowd of disciples praised God as he came down it (Mark 11:1; Luke 19:37). He sat there with his disciples to speak about the end of the age (Matt 24:3; Mark 13:3), and he often went there, including after the Last Supper (Luke 22:39; Mark 14:26). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the modern Jebel et-Tur, about 200 feet above the city.

Mount Paran is a mountain or highland named only in two poetic passages, both describing God coming from the south to his people. In Moses' blessing the LORD comes from Sinai, rises from Seir and shines forth from Mount Paran (Deut 33:2). Habakkuk's prayer similarly has the Holy One coming from Mount Paran, alongside Teman in Edom (Hab 3:3). The name is probably connected with the wilderness of Paran, where Israel camped after leaving Sinai. Its exact location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it was the hilly upland on the north side of the Paran desert, near the southern edge of the Promised Land. Others place it farther south in the Sinai Peninsula, where the name Wadi Feiran may echo Paran. The location shown here is a rough point in the western Sinai Peninsula, which fits the southern Sinai view.

Mount Perazim, meaning "mountain of breaches," is named only in Isa 28:21. There Isaiah says the LORD will rise up as he did at Mount Perazim and be angry as in the valley of Gibeon, to carry out his "strange work." Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Baal-perazim, where David defeated the Philistines. In 2 Sam 5:20 David names that place for the way the LORD broke through his enemies like breaking waters. Isaiah therefore probably recalls that victory as an example of God acting in judgment, though this time against his own people. The exact site is uncertain. It is usually placed near the Valley of Rephaim, southwest of Jerusalem, where the Philistines had gathered. The location shown here is a rough one in that area, just outside Jerusalem.

Mount Seir was the mountain range given to Esau's descendants, the Edomites, as their homeland (Deut 2:5). It lay on the route from Horeb to Kadesh-barnea (Deut 1:2), and the Israelites travelled around it for many days during their wilderness journey (Deut 2:1). God forbade Israel to take any of its land. In Hezekiah's time some 500 men of Simeon went to Mount Seir (1 Chr 4:42). Under Jehoshaphat, the people of Mount Seir joined Ammon and Moab against Judah and were defeated (2 Chr 20:10, 22). Ezekiel prophesied that Mount Seir and all Idumea (Edom) would be made desolate because it rejoiced at Israel's ruin (Ezek 35:2–15). The location shown here places it in the highlands east of the Arabah, south of the Dead Sea, in present-day southern Jordan. The name is shared with another Mount Seir on Judah's border.

Mount Seir was a hill or ridge on the northern boundary of the tribe of Judah, west of Baalah (Kiriath-jearim). Joshua 15:10 traces the border from Baalah westward to Mount Seir, then along the north side of Mount Jearim (Chesalon), down to Beth-shemesh and on to Timnah. It is a different place from the better-known Mount Seir, the mountain range of Edom south and east of the Dead Sea where Esau settled. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes this Judean Seir as a mountain range lying between the Wady Aly and the Wady Ghurab, in the hill country west of Jerusalem. Its exact identification is uncertain. The location shown here places it in the hills between Kiriath-jearim and Beth-shemesh, which fits the order of landmarks in the boundary description.

Mount Sinai, also called Horeb, is the mountain where the LORD came down in fire and smoke, the mountain quaked, and Moses was called to the summit (Exod 19:18–20). The people were kept back by boundaries set around it (Exod 19:23). There Moses received the two stone tablets, and later a second pair, and came down with his face shining (Exod 31:18; Exod 34:4, 29). Leviticus presents its laws as given there, and later passages look back to it (Lev 27:34; Neh 9:13; Acts 7:38). Paul uses it as a figure of the covenant of bondage, placing it in Arabia (Gal 4:24–25). The giving of the Ten Commandments there is dated to about 1491 BC, by inference from context. Its location is debated. Easton's Bible Dictionary favors Ras Sufsafeh in the southern Sinai Peninsula, while others look to northwestern Arabia. The location shown here follows the southern Sinai identification.

Mount Sion is a name for Mount Hermon, used once in the King James Version. Deut 4:48 explains it directly: "mount Sion, which is Hermon." It marks the northern limit of the land east of the Jordan that Israel took from the Amorite kings Sihon and Og, which stretched from Aroer on the Arnon River in the south up to this mountain. It should not be confused with Mount Zion (sometimes spelled Sion) in Jerusalem, which is a different name in Hebrew. The ESV spells it Sirion, matching Deut 3:9, which, according to Easton's Bible Dictionary, says the Sidonians called Hermon Sirion and the Amorites called it Shenir. The location shown here is the Hermon massif, probably the modern Jebel esh-Sheikh on the border of Lebanon and Syria.

Mount Tabor is a mountain in northern Israel where Barak gathered his army before the battle against Sisera. The prophet Deborah summoned Barak son of Abinoam from Kedesh in Naphtali and told him to march to Mount Tabor with ten thousand men from the tribes of Naphtali and Zebulun (Judg 4:6). When Sisera, commander of the Canaanite forces, learned that Barak had gone up the mountain, he moved his army against him (Judg 4:12). At Deborah's command Barak then came down from Tabor with his ten thousand men and defeated Sisera (Judg 4:14). The location shown here is the isolated, dome-shaped hill rising from the eastern edge of the Jezreel Valley, southwest of the Sea of Galilee, still called Mount Tabor today. Its height and position overlooking the plain probably made it a natural rallying point for the tribes.

Mount Zalmon was a wooded hill near Shechem in central Israel. During the conflict between Abimelech and the people of Shechem, Abimelech led his men up the mountain, cut down a tree branch, carried it on his shoulder, and told his followers to do the same (Judg 9:48). The next verse says they piled the branches against the stronghold where the people of Shechem had taken refuge and set it on fire. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Zalmon as a dark-forested hill south of Shechem, the modern Jebel Suleiman, and connects it with the 'Salmon' of Ps 68:14, where snow on the mountain is used as an image. Other identifications place it on one of the peaks beside Shechem, Mount Gerizim or Mount Ebal. The location shown here follows an identification on or near Mount Ebal, just north of Shechem. The exact site is uncertain.

Mount Zemaraim was a hill in the hill country of Ephraim where King Abijah of Judah stood to address Jeroboam and the army of Israel before a battle between the two kingdoms (2 Chr 13:4). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in the Ephraim highlands north of Jerusalem and notes that the battle that followed ended in a heavy defeat for Jeroboam, who never recovered his strength and died soon after. The hill probably took its name from, or lay near, the town of Zemaraim listed among the cities of Benjamin in Josh 18:22. Its exact site is uncertain. Some place it northeast of Bethel, while others place it closer to the Jordan Valley. The location shown here lies north of Jericho, on the eastern edge of the hill country, and follows the second view.

Mount Zion was one of the hills on which Jerusalem stood, and its name is often used for the city itself, especially as the place where the LORD is said to dwell and reign (Ps 74:2; Isa 8:18; Mic 4:7). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it as the southeastern hill, the stronghold David took from the Jebusites and made "the city of David" (2 Sam 5:7). Later tradition gave the name to Jerusalem's southwestern hill. The location shown here follows the eastern-ridge view, placing it near the Temple Mount. Psalms praise it as the city of the great King and as immovable (Ps 48:2; 125:1). The prophets speak of attacks against it, of a remnant escaping from it, and of deliverance there (Isa 29:8; 37:32; Joel 2:32; Obad 1:17), while Lamentations describes it as desolate (Lam 5:18). In the New Testament it stands for the heavenly Jerusalem (Heb 12:22; Rev 14:1).

Moza was a son of Caleb by his concubine Ephah, listed in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah. His full brothers were Haran and Gazez (1 Chr 2:46). Caleb had other sons by other wives and concubines. Moza is named only once, and nothing more is recorded about him. Opinions differ over which Caleb is meant. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him as Caleb the son of Hezron, which fits the surrounding genealogy. The STEPBible proper-names index takes him to be the well-known spy. This entry follows the genealogy's own setting and leaves the question open. The name Moza is shared by at least one other person, a descendant of Saul in the line of Benjamin (1 Chr 8:36–37), who is a different man.

Moza was a Benjamite descendant of King Saul, named only in the two parallel genealogies of Saul's family in 1 Chronicles. He was the son of Zimri and the father of Binea (1 Chr 8:36–37; 9:42–43). Through Zimri's line he traced back to Ahaz. The earlier verses of the same lists (1 Chr 8:33–35; 9:39–41) show this line running from Saul through Jonathan, Merib-baal (Mephibosheth) and Micah to Ahaz. The two lists differ slightly in detail. Zimri's father is called Jehoadah in one and Jarah in the other, and Binea's son appears as Rapha or Rephaiah. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both describe him simply as a son of Zimri of Saul's posterity. Nothing is recorded about his life beyond his place in the genealogy. The name is also borne by a different man, a son of Caleb in the line of Judah (1 Chr 2:46).

Mozah was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Benjamin. It is named only once, in the list of Benjamin's cities, alongside Mizpeh and Chephirah (Josh 18:26). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that it comes between Chephirah and Rekem in that list. The Hebrew form carries the definite article, "ha-Motsah." Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's take the name to mean "an issuing of water" or "fountain," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "place of hard stone." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the town may be the village of Beit Mizzeh, about 4 miles (6 km) northwest of Jerusalem near Qaloniyeh. The location shown here matches that area, near the modern Motza just west of Jerusalem. The Bible records nothing else about the town.

Mushi was a Levite, the second of the two sons of Merari and so a grandson of Levi. He and his brother Mahli are named as the founders of the Merarite families of the Levites (Exod 6:19; Num 3:20). His descendants were called the Mushites, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes from Num 3:33 and 26:58. 1 Chronicles names his three sons as Mahli, Eder and Jeremoth (Jerimoth), so one son shared the name of Mushi's brother. These sons appear in the lists of Levite houses organized for service in David's time. 1 Chr 24:26 also mentions Jaaziah alongside Merari's sons, which is why he is counted as a brother here, though the verse is difficult. Mushi also appears in a Levite genealogy in 1 Chr 6:47, which by context traces the ancestry of the temple musician Ethan. Easton's gives the meaning of his name as “receding.”

The Mustard Seed and Leaven Teaching was a pair of short parables in which Jesus compared the kingdom of God to two ordinary things. First, it is like a grain of mustard seed that a man sowed in his garden, which grew into a great tree where birds lodged in the branches. Second, it is like leaven (yeast) that a woman hid in three measures of flour until the whole batch was leavened. In Luke's account the teaching follows directly after Jesus healed a woman who had been bent over for eighteen years, on a Sabbath in a synagogue. By inference from context it took place during his journey toward Jerusalem, about AD 29. Matthew and Mark also record the mustard seed parable, and Matthew pairs it with the leaven parable as Luke does, though in a different setting.

Myra was a city of Lycia, on the southwest coast of Asia Minor, where the ship carrying Paul as a prisoner to Rome put in after crossing the sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia (Acts 27:5). The next verse, Acts 27:6, says that at Myra the centurion found a ship from Alexandria bound for Italy and moved the prisoners onto it. That ship was later wrecked at Melita (Malta). The voyage is dated to about AD 56, by inference from context. Easton's Bible Dictionary places the city about 2½ miles from the coast. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it later became a prominent port for ships from Egypt and Cyprus, and that it is linked by tradition with Nicholas, a bishop said to have been buried nearby. The location shown here matches the ruins at the modern town of Demre in southern Turkey.

Mysia was a region in the northwest of Asia Minor, in what is now northwestern Turkey. Paul and his companions reached it on the journey that took them through Phrygia, Galatia and Asia, dated here to about AD 47 by inference from context. From Mysia they tried to go northeast into Bithynia, but the Spirit did not allow them (Acts 16:7). They then passed by Mysia and came down to the coastal city of Troas (Acts 16:8). The verses record no preaching there. According to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, Mysia's boundaries were always vague. It stretched roughly from the Sea of Marmara and the Hellespont south toward Lydia, and after 190 BC it formed part of the Roman province of Asia. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes the name as referring to a people and region rather than an official province. Easton's Bible Dictionary treats Troas as its chief port. The location shown here is approximate.

Naam was one of the sons of Caleb the son of Jephunneh, named with his brothers Iru and Elah in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah (1 Chr 4:15). This Caleb is the man known from Numbers and Joshua as one of the spies sent into Canaan, so Naam probably belonged to the generation that settled in the land under Joshua. His sister Achsah is the daughter whom Caleb gave in marriage to Othniel, according to Josh 15:16–17. Nothing else is recorded about Naam. The same verse names Kenaz as a son of Elah but lists no descendants for Naam. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "pleasantness," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "fair; pleasant."

Naamah (line of Cain) was the daughter of Lamech, a descendant of Cain, and his wife Zillah. She is named only once, in Gen 4:22, where she appears as the sister of Tubal-cain, the forger of bronze and iron tools. Jabal and Jubal, Lamech's sons by his other wife Adah, were her half-brothers. The genealogy gives no details about her life, and why she alone among Lamech's daughters is named is not explained. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that she is one of only four women named in the record before the flood, and that all of them except Eve belong to Cain's line. Her name is usually taken to mean "pleasant" or "lovely." Another Naamah, an Ammonite woman who was the mother of King Rehoboam, is a different person.

Naamah was a wife of King Solomon and the mother of Rehoboam, his successor as king of Judah. Each of the three verses that mention her names her as Rehoboam's mother and calls her an Ammonite, a formula repeated in the official summaries of his reign in 1 Kgs 14:21, 31 and 2 Chr 12:13. She was probably one of the foreign women Solomon married, among whom 1 Kgs 11:1 lists Ammonites. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls her the daughter of the king of Ammon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that an addition in the Greek Septuagint makes her the daughter of Hanun son of Nahash, king of Ammon. Through her son she belongs to the royal line of David, and Rehoboam appears in the genealogy of Jesus in Matt 1:7, though she is not named there. Her name, meaning "pleasant," is also borne by the sister of Tubal-cain in Gen 4:22.

Naamah was a town in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, listed among the cities given to the tribe of Judah in the division of the land under Joshua. It appears in Josh 15:41 in a group of sixteen cities with their villages, alongside Gederoth, Beth-dagon and Makkedah. This is its only mention in the Bible, and nothing else is recorded about it. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "beautiful" or "agreeable." Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that some identify it with Na'aneh, and the location shown here follows that identification, near the modern village and kibbutz of Na'an southeast of Ramla. The town is distinct from the two women named Naamah in the Bible, Tubal-cain's sister and the mother of King Rehoboam.

Naaman was a member of the tribe of Benjamin, a son of Bela and so a grandson of Benjamin. Numbers 26:40 names him with his brother Ard as the sons of Bela and as the founder of the clan called the Naamites. 1 Chr 8:4 lists him among Bela's sons, alongside brothers such as Addar, Gera, Abihud, Abishua and Ahoah. A Naaman also appears among the sons of Benjamin himself in Gen 46:21, in the list of those who went down to Egypt with Jacob. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes this to be the same man, which would mean the genealogies sometimes count a grandson among a patriarch's sons. Smith's gives the name's meaning as "pleasantness." He is a different person from Naaman the Syrian army commander healed of leprosy in 2 Kgs 5.

Naaman was the commander of the army of the king of Syria (Aram), a respected and valiant man through whom the LORD had given Syria victory, but who had leprosy. A young girl taken captive from Israel served his wife and spoke of a prophet in Samaria. Naaman came to the king of Israel with a letter from his own king, then went with his horses and chariot to Elisha's house. He was angry at first that the prophet did not come out to heal him in person. After bathing seven times in the Jordan, as told in 2 Kgs 5:14, he was healed. He asked for two mules' loads of earth and vowed to sacrifice to no god but the LORD. Elisha refused his gifts, but Elisha's servant Gehazi took silver and clothing from him and was struck with Naaman's leprosy. Easton's Bible Dictionary places him under Ben-hadad II. Jesus mentions his cleansing in Luke 4:27.

Naaman was a member of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles as one of the sons of Ehud. He appears with Ahiah and Gera in a list of family members who were "removed" (1 Chr 8:7). The preceding verse, 1 Chr 8:6, explains that Ehud's sons were heads of families in Geba and were carried away to Manahath, so this probably describes a forced relocation of the family group. The wording of 1 Chr 8:7 is difficult. It is unclear who did the removing, and Uzza and Ahihud, grouped here with Naaman's siblings, may instead be the sons of the one who removed them. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is distinct from Naaman the Syrian army commander healed under Elisha. A Benjamite Naaman also appears as a son of Bela in Num 26:40, and the two may be related within the same clan.

Naarah was one of the two wives of Ashur, the father of Tekoa, named in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah. Her fellow wife was Helah. Naarah bore Ashur four sons: Ahuzam, Hepher, Temeni and Haahashtari (1 Chr 4:5–6). Her name means "a girl" or "maiden," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls her the second of Ashur's wives, following the order in which the two are named. "Father of Tekoa" probably means that Ashur founded or led the town of Tekoa rather than that he had a son of that name. Nothing else is recorded about Naarah. She should not be confused with Naarah (or Naarath), a town on the border of Ephraim (Josh 16:7).

Naarah, spelled Naarath in the King James Version, was a town on the southern border of Ephraim's territory. Joshua 16:7 traces this boundary down from Janohah to Ataroth, then to Naarath, and on to Jericho and the Jordan River, which places the town in the Jordan Valley not far from Jericho. It is probably the same place as Naaran, named in 1 Chr 7:28 among the towns of Ephraim. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it north of Jericho on the border between Ephraim and Benjamin. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "young person," and Easton's gives "girl." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Eusebius put it 5 Roman miles from Jericho. It also says no identification is certain, though el-Aujeh, about 5 miles northeast of Jericho, would fit. The location shown here, a few miles north of Jericho, follows that general area.

Naarai son of Ezbai was one of David's mighty men, listed among his warriors in 1 Chr 11:37 directly after Hezro the Carmelite. Nothing else is recorded about him. The parallel list in 2 Sam 23:35 seems to name the same man "Paarai the Arbite." Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both treat Naarai and Paarai as one person. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the original form of his name and description is uncertain. Smith's records the view that the Chronicles form is the correct one. This entry follows the Chronicles form. The name is usually explained as meaning "youthful," though Smith's gives "handmaid."

Naaran was a city named as the eastern limit of the lands held by the descendants of Ephraim, the son of Joseph. 1 Chr 7:28 lists it among their possessions and settlements, with Bethel and its towns, Gezer to the west, and Shechem and its towns. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "boyish" or "youthful" and places the town in Ephraim between Bethel and Jericho. Smith's Bible Dictionary considers it very probably the same place as Naarah, which Josh 16:7 names on Ephraim's border near Jericho. The exact site is uncertain. The location shown here places it in the Jordan Valley north of Jericho, which fits its role as an eastern boundary point.

Nabal was a wealthy sheep owner of the house of Caleb whose flocks grazed near Carmel in Judah, and the husband of Abigail. The text describes him as churlish and evil in his doings, while Abigail was wise and beautiful (1 Sam 25:3). When David, then living in the wilderness, sent ten young men at shearing time to greet him and ask for provisions, Nabal insulted them, asking, "Who is David?" David set out to destroy his household, but Abigail went to meet him with gifts and turned him back, saying that Nabal's name, meaning "fool," suited him. She found Nabal drunk at a lavish feast and told him nothing until morning. When she did, "his heart died within him," and about ten days later the LORD struck him and he died. David then took Abigail as his wife. She is later still called "the wife of Nabal the Carmelite."

Naboth the Jezreelite owned a vineyard in Jezreel beside the palace of Ahab king of Samaria. Ahab wanted it for a vegetable garden and offered a better vineyard or its price in money. Naboth refused to give up the inheritance of his fathers. When Ahab sulked, his wife Jezebel wrote letters in his name to the elders and nobles of Naboth's city. She told them to proclaim a fast and seat Naboth prominently. Two worthless men then falsely accused him of cursing God and the king, and he was taken outside the city and stoned to death. As Ahab went to claim the vineyard, the prophet Elijah (named in 1 Kgs 21:17) was sent to tell him that dogs would lick his blood where they had licked Naboth's. 2 Kgs 9:26 adds that Naboth's sons were also killed. Later, Jehu had the body of Ahab's son Joram thrown onto Naboth's plot.

Nadab was the firstborn of the four sons of Aaron and his wife Elisheba, a man of the tribe of Levi, with Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar as his brothers. He went up Mount Sinai with Moses, Aaron, Abihu and seventy elders of Israel, who were told to worship at a distance. He and his brothers were set apart with their father to serve as priests. Nadab and Abihu later offered "strange fire" with incense in their censers, which the LORD had not commanded, and both died before the LORD in the wilderness of Sinai. Lev 10:2 records that fire came out from the LORD and consumed them. What exactly made the fire "strange" is not spelled out. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it as fire not taken from the altar, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia as fire not authorized by the Law. He had no children, so the priesthood passed through Eleazar and Ithamar.

Nadab was the son of Jeroboam, the first king of the northern kingdom of Israel. He succeeded his father on the throne (1 Kgs 14:20). He began to reign in the second year of Asa king of Judah and ruled Israel for two years (1 Kgs 15:25), about 954 BC by inference from context. While Nadab and the Israelite army were besieging Gibbethon, a town then held by the Philistines, Baasha son of Ahijah, of the tribe of Issachar, conspired against him and killed him there (1 Kgs 15:27). Baasha then took the throne. Easton's Bible Dictionary places Gibbethon in the territory of Dan and notes that Baasha went on to wipe out Jeroboam's whole family (1 Kgs 15:29). The rest of Nadab's acts are said to be recorded in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel (1 Kgs 15:31). Several other men in the Bible share the name Nadab.

Nadab was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 2 as a son of Shammai and brother of Abishur (1 Chr 2:28). His grandfather was Onam, who, according to the surrounding verses (1 Chr 2:25–26), was a son of Jerahmeel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia accordingly places him among Jerahmeel's descendants. Nadab had two sons, Seled and Appaim. Seled died without children (1 Chr 2:30), so the line continued through Appaim, whose descendants are listed in the verses that follow. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is shared by other men, including Aaron's son and a king of Israel, who are different people. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of the name as "noble," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "free and voluntary gift" or "prince."

Nadab was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles as a son of the family settled at Gibeon. His mother was Maachah, and this entry gives his father as Abiel. The fuller list in 1 Chr 9:35 names the 'father of Gibeon' as Jehiel. Nadab appears in two near-identical lists of the sons, which name Abdon as the firstborn, followed by Zur, Kish, Baal, Ner and Nadab, and then others such as Gedor, Ahio, Zacher and Mikloth. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him 'a son of Gibeon.' Nothing else is recorded about him. His name probably means 'noble' or 'generous.' He is distinct from the other men called Nadab in the Bible, such as Aaron's son and the king of Israel who succeeded Jeroboam.

Nagge is a man named only in the genealogy of Jesus in Luke's Gospel, which traces Jesus' ancestry back through Joseph. Luke 3:25 names him as the father of Esli. The next verse, Luke 3:26, makes him the son of Maath. He belongs to the stretch of the list between Zerubbabel and Joseph, so he probably lived in the centuries after the return from exile in Babylon. As a descendant of David, he was of the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he appears nowhere else in the Bible. Modern translations often spell his name Naggai, and Smith's Bible Dictionary cross-references him under that form. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "clearness, brightness, light."

Nahalal was a city in the territory of the tribe of Zebulun. It appears in the list of Zebulun's towns, where the King James Version spells it Nahallal (Josh 19:15). It was later given, with its surrounding pasture lands, to the Levites (Josh 21:35). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia specify the Merarite clan of Levites, as the surrounding passage indicates. Both dictionaries and Easton's Bible Dictionary treat it as the same place as Nahalol, where, according to Judg 1:30, Zebulun did not drive out the Canaanite inhabitants. The name is usually taken to mean "pasture." Its site is uncertain. Easton's and Smith's identify it with Malul, west of Nazareth in the Plain of Esdraelon (Jezreel Valley). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also offers 'Ain Mahil, about 3½ miles northeast of Nazareth. The location shown here follows the 'Ain Mahil identification.

Nahaliel was a valley where the Israelites stopped during the last stage of their journey toward Canaan.
