Numbers lists it between Mattanah and Bamoth (Num 21:19), in the stretch of the route north of the Arnon River, on the borders of Moab east of the Dead Sea. The name is usually taken to mean "torrent valley of God" or "valley of God." Its exact location is uncertain. Eusebius placed it near the Arnon, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests one of the Arnon's tributaries, perhaps Wadi Waleh, or Wadi Zerqa Ma'in farther north. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the ravine of the Zerqa Ma'in, known for the ancient hot springs of Callirhoe near the Dead Sea. The location shown here, on the eastern side of the Dead Sea, appears to follow the Zerqa Ma'in identification.

Nahalol was a Canaanite town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Zebulun. Judg 1:30 says Zebulun did not drive out its inhabitants or those of Kitron. Instead the Canaanites went on living among the Israelites and were made to pay tribute. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats Nahalol as the same place as Nahalal, which Josh 19:15 lists among Zebulun's towns and Josh 21:35 names as a town given to the Levites. Its exact site is uncertain. Proposed identifications include the area of the ruined village of Ma'lul and other sites near the western Jezreel Valley. The location shown here follows an identification with the area of modern Ein Mahil, northeast of Nazareth in Lower Galilee.

Naham was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:19 as the brother of Hodiah. Hodiah is described there as the wife of a man whose name the verse does not repeat. By inference from the surrounding verses, this is probably Mered or Ezra, and Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the husband to be Ezra. The verse goes on to mention "the father of Keilah the Garmite, and Eshtemoa the Maachathite." The wording is hard to follow, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls the passage obscure. Some read it as making Naham himself a Judahite clan leader and father of Keilah. Others take Hodiah's sons to be the founders of Keilah and Eshtemoa, which were towns in Judah. His name means "comfort" or "consolation." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Nahamani was one of the leaders named alongside Zerubbabel and Jeshua at the head of the list of exiles who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem and Judah (Neh 7:7). Counting Zerubbabel, the list has twelve leaders, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as one of these twelve heads of the return. His name is missing from the parallel list in Ezra 2:2, which has only eleven names. The same encyclopedia notes that 1 Esdras 5:8 calls him Eneneus, and gives the meaning of his name as "compassionate." Nothing else is recorded about him beyond this single mention.

Naharai was one of David's mighty men, the warriors named in the lists of 2 Sam 23 and 1 Chr 11. He is called a Beerothite (spelled Berothite in Chronicles), meaning he came from Beeroth, probably the Benjaminite town of that name. Both lists say he was armourbearer to Joab the son of Zeruiah, the commander of David's army. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that some printings of the Authorized Version spell his name Nahari in 2 Samuel. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "snorer", while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "my nostrils" or "hot, anger". Nothing else is recorded about him beyond these two parallel lists.

Nahash was king of the Ammonites in the time of Saul. He besieged Jabesh-gilead, east of the Jordan. When its men offered to make a treaty and serve him, he agreed only on condition that he gouge out every man's right eye, as a disgrace on all Israel (1 Sam 11:1–2). According to the rest of the chapter, the town sent word to Saul, who gathered an army and routed the Ammonites (Easton's Bible Dictionary summarizes 1 Sam 11:1–11). Samuel later recalled that this threat from Nahash was the moment the people insisted on having a king (1 Sam 12:12). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "snake" or "serpent." Several men in the Bible share the name, including an Ammonite king who was later friendly to David. Whether he is this same man or a successor is uncertain, and this entry covers only the king of Saul's day.

Nahash was a king of the Ammonites and the father of Hanun, who succeeded him on the throne. He had shown kindness to David at some point, and when Nahash died, David sent servants to Hanun to comfort him over his father's death (2 Sam 10:2; 1 Chr 19:1–2). The text does not say what that kindness was. Whether he is the same Nahash of Ammon who besieged Jabesh-gilead and was defeated by Saul (1 Sam 11) is uncertain. Many readers take them to be one king, possibly hostile to Saul and so friendly to David, while others think they may be two rulers of the same name. A Shobi son of Nahash from Rabbah, the Ammonite capital, later brought supplies to David (2 Sam 17:27) and may have been his son. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which means "snake" or "serpent" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Nahash was the father of Abigail and Zeruiah, named only once, in 2 Sam 17:25. That verse explains that Amasa, whom Absalom made commander of his army in place of Joab, was the son of Ithra and Abigail, "the daughter of Nahash, sister to Zeruiah Joab's mother." The name means "serpent." Because 1 Chr 2:16 calls Zeruiah and Abigail sisters of David, the son of Jesse, his relationship to David's family is understood in different ways. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests that Jesse's wife was first married to Nahash, which would make the two women David's half-sisters through their mother. A rabbinic tradition treats Nahash as another name for Jesse, and some interpreters take Nahash as the name of Jesse's wife. This entry treats Nahash as a man and the father of the two sisters. He is a different person from Nahash, the king of the Ammonites.

Nahash, whose name means "serpent", was a man of Rabbah, the Ammonite capital, and the father of Shobi. He is named only in 2 Sam 17:27, which tells how Shobi, together with Machir of Lodebar and Barzillai the Gileadite, met David at Mahanaim when David was fleeing from his son Absalom. The following verses describe the supplies they brought. The name is shared by several people in the Bible, and whether this Nahash is the same as Nahash king of the Ammonites, whose son Hanun succeeded him (2 Sam 10:1), is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he may be that king, and some take Shobi to be a brother of Hanun. Tyndale House's STEPBible names also treat him as the Ammonite king. If so, Shobi was a royal son who supported David after Hanun's war with Israel.

Nahath was a Levite in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He was one of ten overseers who served under Conaniah (spelled Cononiah in the King James Version) and his brother Shimei. Hezekiah and Azariah, the ruler of the house of God, appointed them to take charge of the offerings, tithes and dedicated things that the people brought to the temple (2 Chr 31:13). The verse itself does not call him a Levite, but the surrounding passage concerns Levites appointed to this work, and Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both describe him that way. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his service to about 725 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Nahath, which Hitchcock's Bible Names takes to mean "rest," also belongs to other people in the Bible, including a descendant of Esau and a Levite of Kohath's line.

Nahath was a son of Reuel and a grandson of Esau through Esau's wife Bashemath. His brothers were Zerah, Shammah and Mizzah. He is listed first among Reuel's sons, and Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to be the eldest. Genesis 36 names him as one of the "dukes", or clan chiefs, who came from Reuel in the land of Edom, so his line was probably one of the Edomite clans (Gen 36:17). The genealogy in 1 Chr 1:37 repeats his name among Reuel's sons. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "rest". Several other people in the Bible share the name Nahath, and this entry concerns only the Edomite chief.

Nahath was a Levite of the clan of Kohath and an ancestor of the prophet Samuel. His name appears in different forms in the genealogies: Tohu in 1 Sam 1:1, Toah in 1 Chr 6:34, and Nahath in 1 Chr 6:26. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries both describe him as a Kohathite Levite, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the three forms as one person. 1 Sam 1:1 calls him the son of Zuph and the father of Elihu, the great-grandfather of Samuel's father Elkanah. 1 Chr 6:26 lists Nahath as the son of Zophai, which is probably another form of Zuph. His son's name also varies, appearing as Eliel in 1 Chr 6:34. Nothing else is recorded about him. Other men in the Bible share the name Nahath, so the context matters when the name appears.

Nahbi was the son of Vophsi and the representative of the tribe of Naphtali among the twelve men Moses sent from the wilderness to explore the land of Canaan (Num 13:14). He is named only in the list of these spies and does not appear again by name. By inference from the wider chapter, he was among the ten spies who brought back a discouraging report, as opposed to Joshua and Caleb. Numbers 14 records that those ten died by a plague. His name is usually taken to mean "hidden" (Easton's Bible Dictionary; Smith's Bible Dictionary), or "very secret" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Nahor (father of Terah), also spelled Nachor, was the son of Serug and the grandfather of Abraham. Genesis records that Serug fathered him at age thirty, and that Nahor fathered Terah at twenty-nine. He then lived another 119 years and had other sons and daughters, a total lifespan of 148 years (Gen 11:22–25). His life is placed at about 2155–2007 BC, by inference from the genealogy's figures. He appears in the line of descent from Shem to Abraham in 1 Chr 1:26, and Luke lists him as "Nachor" among the ancestors of Jesus (Luke 3:34). He shares his name with his grandson Nahor, Terah's son and Abraham's brother. The "Nachor" named in Josh 24:2 as Terah's son is that grandson, not this man. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "snorting."

Nahor (brother of Abraham) was a son of Terah, born at Ur of the Chaldees, and brother of Abram (Abraham) and Haran. He married Milcah, the daughter of his brother Haran, so his wife was also his niece. Abraham was later told that Milcah had borne Nahor eight sons, among them Bethuel, the father of Rebekah. Gen 22:24 adds four more sons by his concubine Reumah. Nahor's family stayed in Mesopotamia when Abraham moved to Canaan. Gen 24:10 speaks of "the city of Nahor," where Abraham's servant found Rebekah as a wife for Isaac. Rebekah's brother Laban is called "the son of Nahor," meaning his descendant, since he was Bethuel's son. Laban later called on "the God of Nahor" when he made a covenant with Jacob. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary suggest that Nahor may have been older than Abraham, even though he is listed after him.

Nahshon, son of Amminadab, was the leader, or "prince," of the tribe of Judah during Israel's years in the wilderness after the Exodus. His sister Elisheba married Aaron, which made him Aaron's brother-in-law. He was named as Judah's representative at the first census of the tribes. He commanded Judah's army, which camped on the east side of the tabernacle and marched first when the camp moved. When the tabernacle was dedicated, he brought the first of the tribal offerings, on the first day. The genealogies list him in the line from Judah through Ram and Amminadab to his son Salmon (also called Salma), then Boaz, and on to David. Matthew and Luke include him, in the Greek form Naasson, in the ancestry of Jesus. Easton's Bible Dictionary concludes from Num 26:64–65 that he died in the wilderness before Israel entered Canaan.

Nahum was the prophet whose vision is recorded in the book that bears his name, the seventh of the minor prophets. Its opening verse calls the book "the burden of Nineveh" and names him "Nahum the Elkoshite," probably meaning he came from a place called Elkosh (Nah 1:1). Nothing else is known of his life. The site of Elkosh is disputed. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes proposals for Galilee and for Alkush near Mosul in Assyria, and suggests that his imagery and language fit someone living in the land of Israel. His message foretells the fall of Nineveh, the Assyrian capital, so it was written while Assyrian power still stood. This entry dates his prophecies to about 663 BC, an estimate inferred from context; Smith's places him in the reign of Hezekiah. His name is often explained as "comfort" or "consolation."

Nain was a town in Galilee, mentioned in the Bible only once. Luke records that Jesus went there the day after healing a centurion's servant at Capernaum, with many of his disciples and a large crowd (Luke 7:11). Near the town gate he met a funeral procession and raised a widow's only son to life (Luke 7:12–17). Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "green pastures" or "lovely," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "beauty" or "pleasantness." The town is usually identified with the modern village of Nein, on the northwestern slope of the Hill of Moreh (Jebel ed-Duhy, also called Little Hermon), overlooking the plain of Esdraelon (the Jezreel Valley), about 4 miles from Mount Tabor. The location shown here follows that identification. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes ancient tombs cut into the rock nearby.

Naioth was a place in or near Ramah, Samuel's hometown, where David and Samuel stayed together after David escaped from Saul (1 Sam 19:18). Saul learned where David was and sent men after him, then came himself. On the way the Spirit of God came on him, and he prophesied until he reached Naioth (1 Sam 19:22–23). From there David fled again and went to Jonathan (1 Sam 20:1). The nearby verse 1 Sam 19:20 describes a company of prophets there, led by Samuel. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary take Naioth to be the dwellings of a prophetic community, and they give the name's meaning as "dwellings" or "habitations." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the meaning as uncertain. The site of Ramah itself is debated. The location shown here is approximate, near Nebi Samwil northwest of Jerusalem, one proposed site for Samuel's Ramah.

Naomi was the wife of Elimelech, an Ephrathite of Bethlehem in Judah, and the mother of Mahlon and Chilion. The family moved to Moab, where Elimelech died. Her sons married there and, by inference from the story, also died, since Naomi urged her two daughters-in-law to go back to their mothers' homes. Ruth refused to leave her and returned with her to Bethlehem at the start of the barley harvest. When the townspeople greeted her, Naomi asked to be called Mara, which Easton's Bible Dictionary explains as meaning "bitter", because she had gone out full and come back empty. She sent Ruth to glean in the fields of Boaz, a wealthy relative of Elimelech, and advised her in her approach to him. Boaz then bought Elimelech's land from Naomi and married Ruth. Naomi nursed their son Obed, whom the neighbouring women called a son born to Naomi. Obed became the grandfather of David.

Naphath is a place or region named in Hebrew in Josh 17:11, the list of towns that Manasseh held within the territories of Issachar and Asher, including Beth-shean, Ibleam, Dor, Endor, Taanach and Megiddo. The King James Version does not show it as a name and translates the phrase as "even three countries." Other translations read it as "the three heights" or as a name, "Naphath" or "the third is Naphath." The word probably means "height" or "hilly region." It may be linked with Naphoth-dor, the heights of Dor, mentioned elsewhere in Joshua and Kings, but its exact meaning and location are uncertain. STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) describes Naphath as a region in Issachar containing towns that belonged to Manasseh. The location shown here is only approximate and places it near Megiddo, at the edge of the Jezreel Valley.

Naphath-dor was the district surrounding the coastal town of Dor, south of Mount Carmel. The name is usually understood as "the heights of Dor" or "the region of Dor," and the King James Version translates it as "the region of Dor" in 1 Kgs 4:11. There it appears as one of Solomon's administrative districts. The son of Abinadab governed it, and he was married to Solomon's daughter Taphath. The same Hebrew phrase occurs in Joshua's lists of Canaanite territories (Josh 11:2; 12:23), and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes the form in the margin of the Revised Version at Josh 12:23 and refers readers to Dor. Whether "heights" means the slopes of Carmel behind the town or the coastal strip itself is uncertain. The location shown here places it at Dor itself, probably the site of Tel Dor near modern Tantura on Israel's Mediterranean coast.

Naphish was a son of Ishmael, Abraham's son by Hagar. He is named eleventh of Ishmael's twelve sons, next to last, between Jetur and Kedemah, in Gen 25:15 and again in 1 Chr 1:31. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "refreshment." Like his brothers, he was probably regarded as the founder of a tribe named after him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies this tribe with "Nephish" in 1 Chr 5:19. That passage lists Nephish among the Hagrite peoples defeated by the Reubenites, Gadites and half-tribe of Manasseh east of the Jordan. The same work links Naphish with the "Nephusim" listed among the temple servants in Ezra 2:50. These connections rest on the similar names rather than on any direct statement in the text.

Naphish, spelled Nephish in the King James text, was a people or territory east of the Jordan. It is named alongside the Hagarites, Jetur and Nodab as one of the groups that the tribes of Reuben, Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh fought (1 Chr 5:19). The name matches Naphish, a son of Ishmael (Gen 25:15; 1 Chr 1:31), and Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as the father of an Arab tribe. The place is therefore probably the land of that tribe, named after its ancestor. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "refreshment" or "one who rests." The exact location is unknown. The location shown here is an approximate point in the region east of the Sea of Galilee, within the area the eastern Israelite tribes settled.

Naphoth-dor was the district around the Canaanite town of Dor on the Mediterranean coast. Its kings were among those summoned by Jabin king of Hazor to join a northern alliance against Joshua. The King James Version translates the phrase as "the borders of Dor on the west" (Josh 11:2), while the Revised Version margin keeps it as a place name, Naphoth-dor. The Hebrew word is usually understood as "heights" or "hilly district," probably referring to the coastal ridge and lower slopes of Mount Carmel inland from the town, though some take it simply as the region belonging to Dor. The same expression appears elsewhere for the territory of Dor (Josh 12:23; 1 Kgs 4:11). The location shown here marks Dor itself, usually identified with Tel Dor (Khirbet el-Burj) near modern Tantura on the coast south of Carmel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the name under Dor.

Naphtali was the territory in northern Israel allotted to the tribe of Naphtali, which received the sixth lot when the land was divided (Josh 19:32–39). Its border ran along the Jordan on the east, with Zebulun to the south and Asher to the west. It contained nineteen fortified cities, including Hazor, Kedesh and Chinnereth. Its hill country was called mount Naphtali, and Kedesh there became a city of refuge (Josh 20:7). Under Solomon it was one of the supply districts, governed by Ahimaaz. Benhadad of Syria struck it, and Tiglathpileser of Assyria later conquered it and deported its people (2 Kgs 15:29). Isaiah pairs it with Zebulun as an afflicted land in "Galilee of the nations," and Matthew links that passage to Jesus settling in Capernaum. The region took its name from Jacob's son Naphtali. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "that struggles or fights." The location shown here is in upper Galilee, north of the Sea of Galilee.

Naphtali was a son of Jacob and the second son born to him by Bilhah, Rachel's servant, making him the full brother of Dan. Rachel named him to mark her 'great wrestlings' with her sister Leah (Gen 30:8). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as 'that struggles or fights.' He went down to Egypt with his four sons, Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer and Shillem (Gen 46:24; 1 Chr 7:13). Jacob's blessing calls him 'a hind let loose' who 'gives goodly words' (Gen 49:21). Little else is told of him personally. Most later mentions concern the tribe descended from him. It settled in the north, west of the upper Jordan and the Sea of Galilee, with Kedesh among its cities (Josh 19:32; Josh 21:32). Assyria later carried it captive (2 Kgs 15:29). Matthew uses the form Nephthalim (Matt 4:13). His birth is placed about 1754 BC, by inference from context.

Naphtuhim is named as a son of Mizraim in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:13), and again in the matching list in 1 Chr 1:11. He is listed alongside Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Pathrusim, Casluhim and Caphthorim. The plural ending, like those of his brothers, suggests the name stands for a people descended from Mizraim, the ancestor of Egypt, rather than a single individual. Nothing more is recorded about him. Where this people lived is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes several proposals, mostly placing them in Lower Egypt, such as the people around Memphis or the inhabitants of the Nile Delta. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions a link with Napata, far to the south on the Nile. The STEPBible Proper Names index places them in northern Egypt, which is the view most commonly followed.

Narcissus was a man living in Rome whose household Paul greets in Rom 16:11, addressing specifically those members of it "which are in the Lord." The wording suggests that only some of his household were Christians. It also leaves open whether Narcissus himself was a believer, or even still alive, since he himself is not greeted. Narcissus was a common name, especially among slaves and freedmen. Some have identified him with the powerful freedman of that name who served the emperor Claudius and was put to death in AD 54. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes Bishop Lightfoot's view that his slaves would then have passed into the emperor's household while keeping his name. Conybeare and Howson preferred a later favorite of Nero. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries both describe any such identification as quite uncertain, and this entry leaves the question open.

Nathan was a son of King David and Bathsheba, born in Jerusalem. He was one of four sons Bathsheba bore to David, along with Shammua (or Shimea), Shobab and Solomon. 1 Chr 3:5 calls his mother Bathshua the daughter of Ammiel. He should not be confused with Nathan the prophet of David's court. Luke's genealogy of Jesus runs through this Nathan rather than through Solomon, naming Mattatha as his son. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Luke's list to be the genealogy of Mary. Zech 12:12 speaks of the mourning of "the family of the house of Nathan" beside the house of David. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats this as a family name, and it probably refers to this son's descendants, though the reference is not certain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "given."

Nathan was a prophet at the courts of David and Solomon. When David proposed building a house for the ark, Nathan first approved, then brought him a message from the LORD that he received that night (2 Sam 7:2–17). After David's sin with Bathsheba, Nathan confronted him with a parable about a rich man and a poor man, telling him, "You are the man." He later delivered the name Jedidiah for Solomon. When Adonijah claimed the throne, Nathan alerted Bathsheba and David, then joined Zadok the priest in anointing Solomon king at Gihon. Chronicles cites a book of Nathan for the acts of David and Solomon, and links him with David's orders for the Levite musicians. Jewish tradition credits him and Gad with completing the books of Samuel. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies Azariah and Zabud, officials of Solomon called sons of Nathan, as his sons.

Nathan was a man from Zobah connected with one of David's mighty men, the elite warriors listed in 2 Samuel 23 and 1 Chronicles 11. He is not the prophet Nathan or David's son of that name. In 2 Sam 23:36 he is the father of Igal, one of the warriors. The parallel list at 1 Chr 11:38 instead has "Joel the brother of Nathan." The two lists differ, and it is not clear whether Igal or Joel is the original name, or whether Nathan was the warrior's father or his brother. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that one early Greek manuscript reads "son" in the Chronicles verse, which would bring the two lists closer together. This entry records both relationships, Igal as his son and Joel as his brother. Zobah was probably the Aramean kingdom north of Israel. The name Nathan means "given" or "giver."

Nathan was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles as the son of Attai and the father of Zabad. By inference from the surrounding verses (1 Chr 2:34–35), he belonged to the line of Jerahmeel. His grandfather was Jarha, an Egyptian servant of Sheshan who married Sheshan's daughter because Sheshan had no sons. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several men in the Bible share the name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as meaning "given" or "rewarded." Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies this Nathan with the prophet of David's and Solomon's reigns and counts Zabad among the prophet's sons at the royal court. This entry follows the reading of Nathan simply as Attai's son in Judah's family line, as the genealogy itself presents him.

Nathan was one of the "chief men" whom Ezra summoned while the returning exiles were camped by the river Ahava, on their journey from Babylon to Jerusalem (Ezra 8:16). He is listed with Eliezer, Ariel, Shemaiah, several men named Elnathan, Jarib, Zechariah and Meshullam. The following verse shows that Ezra sent this group to Iddo at Casiphia to bring Levites to serve in the temple, because none had joined the company. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a companion of Ezra from Babylon and notes that the same list appears in 1 Esdras 8:44. Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name Nathan, which Hitchcock's Bible Names takes to mean "given." It is uncertain whether this Nathan is the same man as anyone else of that name, such as the Nathan later listed among those who had married foreign wives.

Nathan was an Israelite named in Ezra 10:39 in the list of men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra, after the return from exile in Babylon. Going by the surrounding chapter, he was one of those who agreed to send these wives away. He appears among the descendants of Bani, whose family group heads this part of the list, and nothing more is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:34 gives his name as Nathanias. Several other men in the Bible are also called Nathan, including the prophet in David's court and a son of David. This Nathan is a different person, known only from this single mention. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "given" or "giving."

Nathan-melech was a court official of Judah in the time of King Josiah, mentioned only in 2 Kgs 23:11. He is called a "chamberlain," a word Smith's Bible Dictionary takes to mean a eunuch, and the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation, calls him "Nathan, the king's eunuch." His chamber stood in the precincts near the entrance to the house of the LORD. It serves as a landmark in the account of Josiah's reforms: the horses that earlier kings of Judah had dedicated to the sun were kept near this chamber, and Josiah removed them and burned the chariots of the sun. The text does not say whether Nathan-melech himself took part in this sun worship. His name is usually explained as meaning "gift of the king." Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 628 BC, an estimate drawn from the reign of Josiah.

Nathanael was a disciple of Jesus from Cana in Galilee who appears only in the Gospel of John. His name means "gift of God." Philip told him they had found the one Moses and the prophets wrote about, Jesus of Nazareth. Nathanael asked whether anything good could come out of Nazareth, and Philip answered, "Come and see." Jesus greeted him as "an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile" and said he had seen him under the fig tree before Philip called him. Nathanael then called Jesus the Son of God and the King of Israel. Later he was among the disciples together at the Sea of Tiberias when the risen Jesus appeared (John 21:2). Because John never names Bartholomew, and the other Gospels pair Bartholomew with Philip but never mention Nathanael, he is commonly identified with Bartholomew, as Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries note.

Naum was an ancestor of Jesus who appears only in Luke's genealogy, which traces Jesus' line back through Joseph (Luke 3:25). There he is named as the son of Esli and the father of Amos, which places him in the line of Judah in the generations after the return from exile. Nothing else is recorded about him. Naum is the King James spelling of the name rendered Nahum in some other translations, and according to Smith's Bible Dictionary it means "consolation." He is a different person from the prophet Nahum. Smith's Bible Dictionary estimates that he lived around the time of Antiochus Epiphanes, about 175 BC. That date is worked out by counting generations and is not stated in the text.

Nazareth was a town in Galilee, the home of Joseph and Mary, where the angel Gabriel announced Jesus' birth to Mary (Luke 1:26). Joseph left it for Bethlehem before the birth, and the family returned there afterward (Luke 2:4; Luke 2:39). Jesus was brought up there, and as an adult he read in its synagogue (Luke 4:16) before leaving to live in Capernaum (Matt 4:13). As a result he was widely known as "Jesus of Nazareth," a title used by crowds, by Pilate on the cross, and by the apostles (John 19:19; Acts 2:22). Nathanael's question, "Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?" (John 1:46), suggests the town had little standing, though the reason is debated. Matthew links the name to the prophetic saying "He shall be called a Nazarene" (Matt 2:23). The town is not named in the Old Testament. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the modern town of Nazareth (en-Nasirah), which matches the location shown here.

Neah was a town on the boundary of the tribe of Zebulun. It is mentioned only once, in Josh 19:13. That verse traces Zebulun's eastern border past Gath-hepher and Ittah-kazin to Rimmon, and from there toward Neah. The Hebrew reads "the Neah." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "moved" or "moving," and Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on the east side of Zebulun, not far from Rimmon. Its site has not been firmly identified, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it probably lay north of Rimmon (modern Rummaneh) and may be the same place as Neiel in Josh 19:27, on the border of Asher. The location shown here, in lower Galilee north of Rimmon, appears to follow that northern placement and the possible link with Neiel.

Neapolis, meaning "new city," was a port on the northern shore of the Aegean Sea where Paul and his companions first landed in Europe. They sailed from Troas to Samothrace and reached Neapolis the next day (Acts 16:11), after Paul's vision calling him to Macedonia. It served as the seaport for the inland city of Philippi, about 10 miles away by a road over the coastal ridge. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary add that Paul probably sailed from here again on his last journey toward Troas and Jerusalem (Acts 20:6). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the town originally belonged to Thrace and later fell within the Roman province of Macedonia. Most scholars identify it with modern Kavala in Greece, though some have placed it at Eski Kavala, about 10 miles to the west. The location shown here follows the Kavala identification.

Neariah was a descendant of King David in the royal line of Judah that continued after the Babylonian exile. He was one of the sons of Shemaiah, son of Shechaniah. His brothers were Hattush, Igeal, Bariah and Shaphat. The verse gives the total as six, though it names only five, so Shemaiah himself may be included in the count (1 Chr 3:22). Neariah had three sons, Elioenai, Hezekiah and Azrikam (1 Chr 3:23). Smith's Bible Dictionary places him at about 350 BC, an estimate worked out from the genealogy. Smith's gives the meaning of his name as "servant of Jehovah," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "child of the Lord." Several people in the Bible share the name. One is a Simeonite captain named in 1 Chr 4:42, who is a different man.

Neariah was a son of Ishi and one of four brothers, with Pelatiah, Rephaiah and Uzziel, who led five hundred men of the tribe of Simeon to Mount Seir (1 Chr 4:42). The surrounding passage places this expedition in the days of King Hezekiah of Judah. The following verse says the Simeonites struck down the remaining Amalekites there and settled in their place. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 715 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint gives the name as "Noadiah." Smith's renders the name as "servant of Jehovah" and Hitchcock's Bible Names as "child of the Lord." He should not be confused with another Neariah, a descendant of David in the royal line listed earlier in 1 Chronicles 3.

Nebai was one of the leaders of the people whose names were set to the sealed covenant in Nehemiah's time, when the returned exiles pledged to keep the law of God (Neh 10:19). He appears in a list of "chiefs of the people" alongside Hariph and Anathoth, and nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the name as standing for a family among the heads of the people rather than for a single individual. Since some names in this list match places or clans mentioned elsewhere (Anathoth, for example, is also a town), that reading is possible, but the verse itself does not settle it. The name's meaning is uncertain. Smith's gives "fruitful" and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "budding" or "speaking."

Nebaioth was a pastoral people and their territory in the Arabian desert, mentioned as a place in Isa 60:7. There the rams of Nebaioth, along with the flocks of Kedar, are brought as acceptable offerings on God's altar when the nations come to glorify his house. The name is shared with Ishmael's firstborn son, and Kedar was another of his sons (Gen 25:13). So the tribe is probably understood as descended from him and known for its sheep. Many have identified Nebaioth with the Nabateans, the Arab people whose later capital was Petra in southern Jordan. Others question the link because the two names differ slightly in form. The location shown here follows the Nabatean identification and marks the area around Petra. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "words," "prophecies," or "buds."

Nebajoth, also spelled Nebaioth, was the firstborn son of Ishmael and heads the list of Ishmael's twelve sons, followed by Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam and the others (Gen 25:13; 1 Chr 1:29). His sister married Esau. She is called Mahalath in Gen 28:9 and Bashemath in Gen 36:3, probably two names for the same woman. The name also stands for the tribe descended from him. Isaiah pairs "the rams of Nebaioth" with "the flocks of Kedar" as offerings brought to God's altar (Isa 60:7), which points to a herding people. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note that Josephus and Jerome identified this tribe with the Nabataeans, whose capital was Petra. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds that the two names are spelled with different Hebrew consonants, so the link is uncertain.

Neballat was a town where people of the tribe of Benjamin settled after returning from the Babylonian exile. It appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah's list of Benjamite towns, alongside Hadid and Zeboim and near Lod and Ono (Neh 11:34). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "hidden folly," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "prophecy; budding." Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify it with the village of Beit Nebala (Bayt Nabala), about 4 miles from Lydda (modern Lod). Easton's places it north of Lydda and the encyclopedia northeast. The location shown here follows the Bayt Nabala identification. Its closeness to Lod and Ono fits a setting on the western edge of the hill country, toward the coastal plain.

Nebat was the father of Jeroboam, the first king of the northern kingdom of Israel after it broke away from the house of David. He is known only through the phrase "Jeroboam the son of Nebat," which appears again and again in Kings and Chronicles. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the phrase served to distinguish this Jeroboam from the later Jeroboam son of Joash. Nebat is identified as an Ephrathite, meaning an Ephraimite, from Zereda. His wife was Zeruah, who is described as a widow at the time Jeroboam rebelled against Solomon (1 Kgs 11:26). By inference, Nebat had died by then. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is usually explained as meaning "sight" or "aspect" (Easton's Bible Dictionary).

Nebo was the ancestor or head of a family whose descendants are listed in Ezra 10:43. Seven of them, Jeiel, Mattithiah, Zabad, Zebina, Jadau, Joel and Benaiah, were among the men who had married foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon. By inference from the surrounding chapter, they agreed to send those wives away under Ezra's reform. Nothing else is recorded about Nebo himself. Because Ezra 2:29 and Neh 7:33 also mention people of a place called Nebo, the phrase "sons of Nebo" may refer to people from that town rather than to descendants of one man. This entry treats Nebo as a person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "that speaks or prophesies."

Nebo was a town east of the Jordan, on the plateau north of the Dead Sea, distinct from Mount Nebo and from the Nebo in Judah, though it probably took its name from the nearby mountain. It is listed among the towns of the former Amorite territory that the tribes of Reuben and Gad asked Moses for. Reuben rebuilt it and gave it a new name (Num 32:3, 38), and the Reubenite Bela lived as far as Nebo (1 Chr 5:8). Israel camped in the Abarim mountains "before Nebo" (Num 33:47). By the time of Isaiah and Jeremiah it belonged to Moab, and both prophets name it in oracles of mourning and ruin (Isa 15:2; Jer 48:1, 22). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that King Mesha of Moab claimed to have captured it from Israel. The location shown here follows the identification with Khirbet el-Mukhayyat, near Mount Nebo.

Nebo was a town in Judah whose people returned from the Babylonian exile. The lists of returnees record fifty-two "children of Nebo" (Ezra 2:29), and Nehemiah calls it "the other Nebo" (Neh 7:33), probably to tell it apart from the better-known Nebo in Moab. Ezra 10:43 names seven "sons of Nebo" among the men who, by the context of that chapter, had married foreign wives. The name appears in the lists next to Bethel and Ai, but the verses give no clue to where it was. Reference works suggest different sites. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mentions Beit Nuba, northwest of Jerusalem, or Nuba, south-southeast of Adullam. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it at a village about 7 miles northwest of Hebron. The location shown here follows the Nuba identification, between Adullam and Hebron. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "that speaks or prophesies."

Nebuchadnezzar, also spelled Nebuchadrezzar, was the Chaldean king of Babylon who dominated Judah in its last years. He defeated Pharaoh Necho at Carchemish in Jehoiakim's fourth year and made Jehoiakim his vassal until Jehoiakim rebelled. He carried Jeconiah, the nobles and the craftsmen to Babylon along with the temple vessels, and made Zedekiah king. After Zedekiah also rebelled, he besieged Jerusalem. In his nineteenth year his commander Nebuzaradan destroyed the temple and deported the people, and he put Gedaliah over those who remained. Jeremiah and Ezekiel present him as God's instrument against Judah, Tyre, Egypt and Kedar. In Daniel he has prophetic dreams, sets up a golden image, throws Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego into a furnace, loses his kingdom for a time, and finally praises the King of heaven. Dan 5:18 calls him Belshazzar's father. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as Nabopolassar's son and Babylon's greatest king, who died about 562 BC.

Nebushasban was a Babylonian official who held the title Rabsaris at the time Jerusalem fell to Nebuchadnezzar. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains his name as "adorer of Nebo" or "Nebo saves me". It takes Rabsaris to mean chief chamberlain, while Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it to mean chief of the eunuchs. Smith's also suggests he probably succeeded Ashpenaz, who held the same office in Dan 1:3. He appears only in Jer 39:13. There he is named with Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, Nergalsharezer the Rabmag, and the other princes of the king of Babylon. By the context of the passage, these officials were sent to take Jeremiah out of the court of the prison and hand him over to Gedaliah. The Bible records nothing more about him.

Nebuzar-adan was the captain of the guard serving Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. He arrived in Jerusalem in the fifth month of Nebuchadnezzar's nineteenth year. 2 Kgs 25:8 gives the seventh day and Jer 52:12 the tenth. After the city fell, he took into exile the people still left there and those who had gone over to the Babylonians. He left some of the poorest people in Judah and gave them vineyards and fields to work. He brought Jerusalem's leading men to the king at Riblah. On Nebuchadnezzar's orders he took charge of Jeremiah and released him at Ramah, where the prophet had been bound in chains among the captives. He placed the people who remained, including the king's daughters, in the care of Gedaliah son of Ahikam. In Nebuchadnezzar's twenty-third year he deported 745 more Jews. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains his name as meaning "Nebo has given seed."

Nedabiah was one of the sons of Jehoiachin (also called Jeconiah), the king of Judah who was taken captive to Babylon. He is named only once, in the list of David's royal descendants after the exile, as the last of seven sons in 1 Chr 3:18. His brothers were Shealtiel, Malchiram, Pedaiah, Shenazar, Jecamiah and Hoshama. A Zedekiah is also counted among his brothers, though 1 Chr 3:16 may name him as Jehoiachin's son or as his brother, so the relationship is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him "apparently" a son of Jehoiachin, since the genealogy's wording leaves some room for doubt. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "moved of Jehovah." Nothing else is recorded about his life.

Negeb is the dry region in the far south of Canaan, south of the hill country of Judah. The name comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be dry." The King James Version usually translates it simply as "the south." Abram journeyed through it, and returned there from Egypt before going on to Bethel (Gen 12:9; 13:1–3). Isaac later lived there (Gen 24:62). The spies Moses sent went up through the Negeb toward Hebron, and they reported that Amalekites lived there (Num 13:22, 29). King Arad also lived in this region (Num 21:1). Joshua conquered it (Josh 10:40), and Simeon's inheritance lay within it (Josh 19:8). The Bible names several parts of it, such as the Negeb of Judah and of the Kenites (1 Sam 27:10). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes it as a pastoral land of rolling hills between the Dead Sea and the Mediterranean. Jeremiah lists its cities among those that would be restored (Jer 33:13).

Nehelam is known only through the title "Shemaiah the Nehelamite," given to a prophet among the Jewish exiles in Babylon (Jer 29:24, 31–32). Because of that form, it is usually taken to be the name of Shemaiah's hometown or family, but no place called Nehelam is mentioned anywhere else and its location is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary says the origin of the name is unknown and notes the marginal rendering "dreamer." On that reading the word may describe Shemaiah rather than name a place. Jeremiah's letter says the LORD had not sent Shemaiah, that he led the exiles to trust in a lie, and that he and his descendants would be punished for teaching rebellion against the LORD (Jer 29:31–32).

Nehemiah was one of the leaders who came back from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel. He appears only in the lists of returning exiles, where he is named third, after Zerubbabel and Jeshua, among the men who headed the first return (Ezra 2:2; Neh 7:7). He is a different man from the better-known Nehemiah, the governor who rebuilt Jerusalem's walls. That Nehemiah arrived about a century later, and Smith's Bible Dictionary likewise treats this one as a separate leader of the earlier expedition. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "consolation" or "repentance of the Lord."

Nehemiah, son of Hachaliah and brother of Hanani, was a Jew living in Persia who became governor (Tirshatha) of Judah and is the narrator of the book that bears his name. His account opens at Shushan, the Persian royal residence, in the twentieth year of the king (Neh 1:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies the king as Artaxerxes Longimanus and describes Nehemiah as the royal cupbearer, who obtained leave to go to Jerusalem and rebuild its walls, probably about 446 BC. As governor he stood with Ezra the priest and scribe when the law was read, telling the weeping people that the day was holy and not for mourning (Neh 8:9). He was the first to seal the covenant (Neh 10:1). Later passages remember "the days of Nehemiah the governor" alongside Ezra and Zerubbabel (Neh 12:26, 47). Several other men in the Bible share his name.

Nehemiah, son of Azbuk, was the ruler of half the district of Beth-zur who helped repair Jerusalem's wall in the days of Nehemiah the governor. He is mentioned only once. According to Neh 3:16, he worked on the section running to a point opposite the tombs of David, as far as the artificial pool and the "house of the mighty," probably a barracks or guardhouse for warriors. Beth-zur was a town in the hill country of Judah, south of Jerusalem, and his district appears to have been divided between two officials. He is a different man from Nehemiah son of Hachaliah, the governor who organized the rebuilding, and from others of the same name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "consolation" or "repentance of the Lord."

Nehushta was the mother of Jehoiachin, king of Judah, and the daughter of Elnathan of Jerusalem (2 Kgs 24:8). She was the wife of King Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin's father. Her name is usually taken to mean "bronze" or "copper" (Easton's Bible Dictionary). Her son became king at eighteen and reigned in Jerusalem only three months. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that when Jerusalem fell to Babylon she was taken into exile with her son and his court. Later passages, 2 Kgs 24:12 and Jer 29:2, mention the king's mother among the captives, and she is probably the queen mother addressed in Jer 13:18. Through Jehoiachin, who appears as Jechonias in Matthew's genealogy, she belongs to the royal line traced to Jesus. Her father Elnathan is probably the official of that name in Jehoiakim's court mentioned in Jer 26:22 and 36:12, though this identification is an inference.

Neiel was a town on the boundary of the tribe of Asher, named only once, in the description of Asher's border in Josh 19:27. There it appears after the valley of Jiphthahel and Beth-emek and just before Cabul, so it probably lay near Asher's southeastern edge, close to the territory of Zebulun. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "dwelling-place of God," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "commotion of God." Its exact site is also uncertain. Easton's identifies it with the ruin of Y'anin (Yanin), less than 2 miles north of Cabul (modern Kabul). Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the hilltop village of Mi'ar, halfway between Jiphthahel and Cabul. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the same place as Neah (Josh 19:13). The location shown here follows the Y'anin identification.

Nekoda was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants returned to Jerusalem from exile in Babylon. The family appears in the list of returnees in Ezra 2:48 and again in the parallel list in Neh 7:50, between the descendants of Rezin and those of Gazzam. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes Nekoda as the head of this family of Nethinim. Nothing else is recorded about Nekoda as an individual. The verses do not say whether Nekoda was a man or a woman, and this entry treats Nekoda as female. The same name belongs to a different family in the same lists (Ezra 2:60; Neh 7:62), whose members could not prove their Israelite descent. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "painted" or "inconstant."

Nekoda was the ancestor of a family that returned to Judah from the Babylonian exile but could not prove its Israelite descent. The surrounding passage (Ezra 2:59; Neh 7:61) says these returnees came from places such as Tel-melah and Tel-harsa and could not show their father's house or lineage. The descendants of Nekoda are listed with those of Delaiah and Tobiah, and the three families together numbered 652 in Ezra and 642 in Nehemiah. The text gives no further details about Nekoda personally. The name is shared by another Nekoda, whose descendants were among the temple servants (Ezra 2:48), and the two should be kept apart. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "painted" or "inconstant."

Nemuel was a man of the tribe of Reuben, a son of Eliab and the brother of Dathan and Abiram. He is named only once, in the census list of Reuben's descendants taken in the plains of Moab (Num 26:9). He is listed first among Eliab's sons, and Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to be the eldest. His brothers Dathan and Abiram are remembered for joining Korah's rebellion against Moses and Aaron, but the text says nothing about Nemuel taking part. Nothing more is recorded of him. The same name belongs to a different man, a son of Simeon, in the same census chapter, so the two should be kept apart.

Nepheg was a Levite, a son of Izhar and a brother of Korah and Zichri. He is named only once, in the genealogy of Levi's descendants in Exod 6:21. Izhar was a son of Kohath (Exod 6:18), so Nepheg belonged to the Kohathite clan of the tribe of Levi, as STEPBible Proper Names notes. His brother Korah later led the rebellion against Moses together with Dathan and Abiram (Num 16). Shelomoth, also listed as his brother, is named in 1 Chr 23:18 as the chief of Izhar's descendants, though he may be a later descendant rather than a direct son. Nothing else is recorded about Nepheg. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "sprout" or "shoot." A different Nepheg was one of David's sons born in Jerusalem (2 Sam 5:15).

Nepheg was one of the sons of King David born in Jerusalem, after David had moved his capital there from Hebron. He appears only in the three lists of those sons, each time between Elishua or Nogah and Japhia (2 Sam 5:15; 1 Chr 3:7; 14:6). His mother is not named, and the text records nothing about his life beyond his place among David's children. The Chronicles lists include Nogah next to him, a name missing from the list in 2 Samuel. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of his name as "sprout" or "shoot," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "weak" or "slacked." The name is shared by another man, a Levite who was a son of Izhar and a brother of Korah (Exod 6:21), and he should not be confused with this son of David.

Nephtoah was a spring that marked part of the boundary between the tribal territories of Judah and Benjamin. The boundary descriptions call it "the fountain of the water of Nephtoah" and "the well of waters of Nephtoah." The line ran from the hill near Jerusalem to this spring, then on to the cities of Mount Ephron and to Kirjathjearim (Josh 15:9). Benjamin's southern border is traced in the reverse direction, from Kirjathjearim to the same spring (Josh 18:15). Its location is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the spring at Lifta, about 2 miles (3 km) northwest of Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary also notes another view, based on a Talmudic tradition linking Nephtoah with Etam, which places it at 'Ain 'Atan southwest of Bethlehem. The location shown here follows the 'Ain 'Atan identification.

Nephusim was the ancestor or founder of a family whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem. The family appears in the list of returnees in Ezra 2:50, and the parallel list in Neh 7:52 gives the name as Nephishesim. Both lists place these families in the section naming the Nethinim, or temple servants, so the family was probably one of the groups that served at the temple. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the two spellings as the same name and, following the Hebrew scholar Gesenius, takes Nephishesim as the proper form. STEPBible's proper-name index likewise describes the Nephushesim as a family of temple servants who came back from captivity. Nothing more is recorded about the man himself, and the name may refer to a clan rather than to a single individual.

Ner was a Benjamite of King Saul's family and the father of Abner, the commander of Saul's army (1 Sam 14:50; 2 Sam 2:8). He is almost always named only as Abner's father. 1 Sam 14:50–51 calls Ner Saul's uncle and names his father as Abiel, and 1 Chr 9:36 lists Ner alongside Kish, Saul's father, among the sons of a Benjamite family. This makes Ner and Kish brothers and Saul and Abner first cousins, the view of Easton's Bible Dictionary that this entry follows. Abiel is probably the same man as the Jeiel of 1 Chr 9:35, whose wife was Maachah. 1 Chr 8:33, by contrast, says Ner fathered Kish, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia therefore calls Ner Saul's grandfather. The name means "lamp" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Nereus was a Christian in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings near the end of his letter to the Romans (Rom 16:15). Paul greets him together with his sister, whose name is not given, and with Philologus, Julia, Olympas and "all the saints which are with them." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes this group to have formed a small community or house church. That encyclopedia also notes that the name Nereis appears on an inscription of the period listing servants of the emperor's household. Later church tradition, recorded in Smith's Bible Dictionary, holds that Nereus was beheaded at Terracina, probably in the reign of Nerva. A later account, the Acts of Nereus and Achilleus, calls him a chamberlain of Domitilla, a niece of the emperor Vespasian. Whether that Nereus is the man Paul greets is uncertain. Nothing more about him is recorded in the Bible.

Nergal-sharezer was a Babylonian official, one of the princes of Nebuchadnezzar who entered Jerusalem when it fell and sat in the middle gate (Jer 39:3). The name appears twice in that verse, so Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it to refer to two different officials. One of them carries the title Rabmag, probably meaning a chief of the magi or a senior court officer. Nergal-sharezer the Rabmag was among the officials sent by Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, to have Jeremiah released from the court of the prison (Jer 39:13). The name means "O Nergal, protect the king" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify him with Neriglissar, who later took the Babylonian throne after Evil-merodach, son of Nebuchadnezzar, and reigned about 559–556 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also reports this view. Jerusalem's fall is usually dated about 587 BC.

Neri was an ancestor of Jesus named in Luke's genealogy, where he appears as the father of Salathiel and grandfather of Zorobabel (Zerubbabel) (Luke 3:27). The facts here also name his father as Melchi, as the following verse in Luke states. His line belongs to the tribe of Judah. Luke traces it back to David through David's son Nathan, so Neri probably lived around the time of the Babylonian exile. Matthew 1:12 and 1 Chr 3:17 name Jeconiah, not Neri, as Salathiel's father. Explanations offered for this include adoption, a levirate marriage, or Luke following a different line of descent, and the text does not settle the question. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats Neri as a short form of Neriah, meaning "the LORD is my lamp". Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "my light." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Neriah was the son of Maaseiah and the father of two men named in the book of Jeremiah. He is known only through his sons, who are repeatedly identified as "son of Neriah." One was Baruch, the scribe who wrote down Jeremiah's words on a scroll, read them in the temple, rewrote them after King Jehoiakim burned the first scroll, and later went to Egypt with Jeremiah (Jer 36:4, 36:32; 43:6). The other was Seraiah, described as a "quiet prince," who travelled to Babylon with King Zedekiah in his fourth year (Jer 51:59). Both sons are traced through Neriah to Maaseiah (Jer 32:12; 51:59), which shows they were brothers. Nothing is recorded of Neriah's own life. His name is usually taken to mean "lamp of the LORD" (Smith's Bible Dictionary).

Netaim was a place in Judah where a group of potters lived and worked for the king, mentioned only in 1 Chr 4:23. The King James Version translates the Hebrew word as a common noun, "plants", giving "those that dwelt among plants and hedges." The Revised Version instead reads it as a place name, "the inhabitants of Netaim and Gederah," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia favors that reading. Because Gederah lay in the Judean Shephelah, the lowland foothills west of the Judean hills, Netaim is probably to be sought in the same area. The same encyclopedia notes that no likely site has been identified. The location shown here is a rough placement in the Shephelah and does not mark a known site.

Nethaneel, son of Zuar, was the leader of the tribe of Issachar during Israel's time in the wilderness after the Exodus. He was named as Issachar's representative to help Moses and Aaron take the census of Israel's fighting men (Num 1:8). In the arrangement of the camp, Issachar pitched its tents next to Judah on the east side of the tabernacle, with Nethaneel as its captain (Num 2:5). When the tribal leaders brought gifts for the dedication of the altar, he presented his offering on the second day. It included animals for peace offerings (Num 7:18, 23). When the camp set out from Sinai, he commanded Issachar's division (Num 10:15). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "given of God." Several other men in the Bible bear this name, and this entry concerns only the son of Zuar.

Nethaneel was the fourth son of Jesse of the tribe of Judah, and so a brother of King David. He appears only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:14, which lists Jesse's sons in birth order: Eliab, Abinadab, Shimma (Shammah), Nethaneel, Raddai, Ozem and David. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name, according to Smith's Bible Dictionary, means "given of God" and is the same name as Nathanael. Several other men in the Bible share it. The Chronicles list names seven sons, while 1 Sam 16:10–11 and 1 Sam 17:12 speak of eight. Elihu, described in 1 Chr 27:18 as one of David's brothers, is also counted among the siblings here.

Nethaneel was a priest in the time of David, one of seven priests who blew trumpets before the ark of God when it was brought up to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:24). He is named alongside Shebaniah, Jehoshaphat, Amasai, Zechariah, Benaiah and Eliezer, while Obed-edom and Jehiah served as doorkeepers for the ark. By inference from the surrounding chapter, this was the procession that carried the ark from the house of Obed-edom to the tent David had prepared for it, as Smith's Bible Dictionary also notes. The name means "given of God" and is the same as Nathanael. Several other men in the Bible share this name, and nothing beyond this single mention identifies this priest further.

Nethaneel was a Levite in the time of King David, known only as the father of Shemaiah. In 1 Chr 24:6, Shemaiah recorded the drawing of lots that divided the priestly families of Eleazar and Ithamar into their courses. This was done before the king, the princes, Zadok the priest and Ahimelech son of Abiathar. The verse calls Shemaiah "the son of Nethaneel the scribe," and it can be read two ways. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes "the scribe" to mean Shemaiah. The STEPBible proper-names index applies it to Nethaneel. This entry follows the more common reading, in which Shemaiah was the scribe. Nethaneel is probably a Levite himself, since his son is called one. His name means "given of God." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and nothing links this Nethaneel with any of them.

Nethaneel was a Levite named in 1 Chr 26:4 as the fifth son of Obed-edom, listed after Shemaiah, Jehozabad, Joah and Sacar. The next verse (1 Chr 26:5) adds Ammiel, Issachar and Peulthai as further brothers. The passage falls within the arrangement of the temple gatekeepers' divisions in David's time, so Nethaneel was probably one of the gatekeepers. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a temple porter of the Korahite family. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "given of God," and Hitchcock's Bible Names treats it as the same as Nathanael. Several other men in the Bible bear this name, and this entry concerns only the son of Obed-edom.

Nethaneel was one of the princes of Judah whom King Jehoshaphat sent out in the third year of his reign to teach in the cities of Judah. He is named alongside Benhail, Obadiah, Zechariah and Michaiah (2 Chr 17:7). The king is not named in this verse, but the surrounding chapter makes clear it is Jehoshaphat. The following verses add that Levites and priests went with these princes and that they taught from the book of the law of the Lord, as Easton's Bible Dictionary also notes. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the mission to about 912 BC and gives the name's meaning as "given of God," the same name as Nathanael. Nothing more is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with the several other men of the same name in the Bible.

Nethaneel was a chief Levite in the reign of King Josiah of Judah. He is named only in 2 Chr 35:9, as a brother of Conaniah and Shemaiah. Together with Hashabiah, Jeiel and Jozabad, these leaders of the Levites gave the other Levites five thousand sheep and goats and five hundred oxen as offerings for the great Passover that Josiah held. "Brethren" here may mean fellow Levites rather than brothers by birth. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this Passover to about 628 BC. The name means "given of God" and is the same as Nathanael. Several other men in the Bible share the name, so this Nethaneel should not be confused with them.

Nethaneel was one of the sons, or descendants, of Pashur listed in Ezra 10:22 among the priests who had married foreign wives in the period after the return from exile. The surrounding passage records that these men agreed to put away their foreign wives in response to Ezra's reforms. Pashur's family is grouped with the priestly houses in this list, so Nethaneel was probably a priest, and the STEPBible Proper Names index identifies him that way. Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share this name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names treats as the same as Nathanael, and this Nethaneel should not be confused with them.

Nethaneel was a priest who headed the priestly family of Jedaiah after the return from exile in Babylon. Neh 12:21 lists him in a roll of priestly family heads. By inference from the surrounding passage, this roll belongs to the days of Joiakim the high priest, son of Jeshua, which Smith's Bible Dictionary places about 446 BC. The verse records only his name and the family he represented, so nothing more is known of him. His name means "given of God" and is a form of Nathanael. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Nethaneel should not be confused with them.

Nethaneel was one of the Levite musicians who played "the musical instruments of David" at the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem, in the procession led by Ezra the scribe (Neh 12:36). He is named among the "brethren" of Zechariah son of Jonathan, whom the previous verse (Neh 12:35) traces back to Asaph, the musician of David's time. This entry treats Nethaneel as another son of Jonathan, so Zechariah, Shemaiah, Azarael, Milalai, Gilalai, Maai, Judah and Hanani appear as his brothers. The word "brethren" could also mean kinsmen or fellow Levites more broadly. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Levite of the sons of Asaph, and Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him a priest's son. The dedication probably took place around 445 BC, by inference from context. Several other men in the Bible share this name, which means "given of God."

Nethaniah was the son of Elishama and the father of Ishmael, the man who assassinated Gedaliah, the governor Babylon appointed over Judah after Jerusalem fell. He is known only through his son, who is regularly called "Ishmael the son of Nethaniah." The family is described as "of the seed royal," so Nethaniah belonged to the royal line of Judah (2 Kgs 25:25; Jer 41:1). His son Ishmael came to Gedaliah at Mizpah, killed him and others there, took the remaining people captive, and escaped to the Ammonites. The name means "the Lord has given" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some Septuagint manuscripts read the name as Maththanias. Several other men in the Bible share the name Nethaniah.

Nethaniah was a Levite musician of David's time, one of the sons of Asaph who prophesied under their father's direction "according to the order of the king" (1 Chr 25:2). His brothers are named as Zaccur, Joseph and Asarelah. Asarelah is apparently the same person as the Jesharelah of 1 Chr 25:14. When the temple musicians were divided into twenty-four groups by lot, the fifth lot fell to Nethaniah, and his group of sons and relatives numbered twelve (1 Chr 25:12). The name means "gift of the Lord" or "Yah has given" (Hitchcock's Bible Names; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Bible share this name, and this Nethaniah is distinct from them. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 1015 BC, an estimate drawn from the setting in David's reign.

Nethaniah was a Levite in the reign of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. He is named in 2 Chr 17:8 among nine Levites who went out with two priests, Elishama and Jehoram. The surrounding passage explains why. In the third year of his reign Jehoshaphat sent officials to teach in the cities of Judah, and these Levites and priests went with them, carrying the book of the law of the Lord as they taught the people. Nethaniah is mentioned nowhere else, and nothing more is known about him. Several other men in the Bible share his name, so he should not be confused with them. The name means "given of the Lord" or "Yah has given" (Hitchcock's Bible Names; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his service to about 912 BC, an estimate.

Nethaniah was the father of Jehudi and the son of Shelemiah, and through Shelemiah a descendant of Cushi. He appears only once, in Jer 36:14, as part of his son's lineage. The passage tells how the princes of Judah sent Jehudi to bring Baruch and the scroll he had been reading to the people. The scroll held the words Jeremiah had dictated to him. The surrounding chapter places these events in the reign of King Jehoiakim, so Nethaniah probably lived in the late seventh century BC. Nothing more is recorded about him. His name means "Yah has given" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "the gift of the Lord" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, including the father of Ishmael who killed Gedaliah. This entry treats Jehudi's father as a separate person from them.

Netophah was a town in Judah, closely linked with Bethlehem. It is best known through the men called Netophathites. Two of David's mighty men came from there: Maharai and Heleb (or Heled) the son of Baanah (2 Sam 23:28–29; 1 Chr 11:30). Maharai, of the Zerahite clan, also commanded the division of David's army that served in the tenth month (1 Chr 27:13). After the exile, 56 men of Netophah returned with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:22). Nehemiah's parallel list counts the men of Bethlehem and Netophah together, which suggests the two towns were near each other (Neh 7:26). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a possible link with Nephtoah and an echo of the name at Beit Nettif in the Shephelah. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Conder place the town at Khirbet Umm Toba, northeast of Bethlehem. The location shown here follows the Umm Toba identification.

The New Gate was a gate of the temple ("the LORD's house") in Jerusalem in the time of the prophet Jeremiah. When Jeremiah was accused for prophesying against the temple and the city, the princes of Judah came up from the king's palace and sat at the entry of this gate to hear the case (Jer 26:10). It later served as the setting where Jeremiah's scribe Baruch read Jeremiah's scroll to the people from the chamber of Gemariah, son of Shaphan, in the upper court at the entry of the New Gate (Jer 36:10). That description suggests it opened from the higher inner court of the temple. Its name implies it had been built or rebuilt fairly recently. Some interpreters identify it with the upper gate of the temple that King Jotham built (2 Kgs 15:35), though this is uncertain. The location shown here places it within the temple area in Jerusalem.

Neziah was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants returned from the Babylonian exile to Judah. The "children of Neziah" appear in the list of returning exiles in Ezra 2:54 and again in the parallel list in Neh 7:56, placed between the families of Bazluth and Hatipha. The verses themselves only name the family. The identification with the Nethinim comes from where the name falls in the list, among the temple servants, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. Smith's links this return with Zerubbabel and dates it to about 536 BC, an estimate inferred from context. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same family is called "Nasi" or "Nasith" in 1 Esdras 5:32. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "victory" or "pure," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "conqueror" or "strong." Nothing more is known about Neziah himself.

Nezib was a city in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, named only once, in the list of towns allotted to the tribe of Judah (Josh 15:43). It appears in the same group of towns as Keilah and Mareshah. The name probably means "garrison" or "pillar" (Smith's Bible Dictionary), or "standing-place" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Eusebius and Jerome knew the place and put it on the road from Eleutheropolis (Beit Jibrin) to Hebron, about seven to nine miles from Eleutheropolis. Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia all identify it with the village of Beit Nasib (Beit Nuzib), which has ancient remains. The village lies about 2 miles southwest of Khirbet Kila (Keilah) and roughly 14 miles southwest of Jerusalem. The location shown here matches that identification.

Nibshan was a town in the wilderness of Judah, named only once, in the list of towns allotted to the tribe of Judah (Josh 15:62). It belongs to a group of six wilderness towns, listed between Secacah (Josh 15:61) and the City of Salt, followed by Engedi. This places it in the dry country west of the Dead Sea. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary take the name to mean "soft" or "light soil." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the early church historian Eusebius knew of the place but gave no clue to where it was, and that the site has not been found. Its exact location remains uncertain. The location shown here is approximate and follows Easton's suggestion that it was probably near Engedi, on the western shore of the Dead Sea.

Nicanor was one of the seven men chosen by the whole body of believers in the early Jerusalem church, alongside Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Timon, Parmenas and Nicolas (Acts 6:5). The surrounding passage explains that the seven were appointed to oversee the daily distribution of food so the apostles could devote themselves to prayer and teaching. Tradition calls them the first deacons, and Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Nicanor as one of the seven deacons. The event is dated to about AD 30, by inference from context. His name is Greek and means "conqueror" or "victorious" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Like the other names on the list, it may suggest he came from the Greek-speaking Jewish community whose complaint led to the appointment, though that is an inference. Nothing more is recorded of him. He is a different person from the Syrian general Nicanor in the books of Maccabees.

Nicodemus was a Pharisee and "a ruler of the Jews" who appears only in John's Gospel. He came to Jesus by night, and in the conversation that followed he asked how a grown man could be born a second time and how such things could be (John 3:1–9). Later, when the chief priests and Pharisees were moving against Jesus at the time of the Feast of Tabernacles, Nicodemus, "being one of them," spoke up in their council. The surrounding passage shows him objecting that the law does not judge a man without first hearing him. After the crucifixion he joined Joseph of Arimathea, as the context of John 19 indicates, bringing about a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes for Jesus' burial. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him as a member of the Sanhedrin. His name means "victory of the people" (Hitchcock's Bible Names).

Nicolas was one of the seven men chosen by the early Jerusalem church to serve its members, about AD 30 by inference from context. Acts 6:5 lists him last among the seven, after Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon and Parmenas, and describes him as a proselyte of Antioch. That makes him a Gentile by birth who had converted to Judaism before becoming a follower of Jesus, and the only one of the seven whose non-Jewish origin is noted. The surrounding passage explains that the seven were appointed to oversee the daily distribution of food to widows, so the apostles could focus on prayer and preaching, and that the apostles laid hands on them (Acts 6:1–6). Later tradition calls these men the first deacons. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "victory of the people." Some early church traditions connected him with the Nicolaitans mentioned in Rev 2:6, 15, a link the biblical text itself does not make.

Nicopolis, meaning "city of victory," was the city where Paul planned to spend a winter. In Titus 3:12 he asks Titus to join him there once Artemas or Tychicus arrives to take his place. Several ancient cities had this name, and the letter itself does not say which one is meant. A later note added to the end of the letter calls it Nicopolis of Macedonia, which would be the city in Thrace. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries, following Jerome, favour Nicopolis in Epirus in western Greece. That city was founded by Augustus Caesar to celebrate his victory over Antony at the battle of Actium in 31 BC, and it became the leading city of the region. Its ruins lie a few miles north of modern Preveza. The location shown here follows the Epirus identification. Whether Paul actually reached Nicopolis is not recorded.

The Nile is the great river of Egypt, flowing north through northeast Africa into the Mediterranean Sea. The King James Version never uses the name, and usually calls it simply "the river." Pharaoh dreamed of seven fat and seven lean cows coming up out of it (Gen 41:1–3, 17–18). He later ordered every Hebrew baby boy to be thrown into it (Exod 1:22). Moses struck its waters and turned them to blood, so that the fish died and the Egyptians dug beside it for drinking water (Exod 7:17–24). Frogs later swarmed out of it (Exod 8:3). The prophets use the river as a picture of Egypt's wealth and pride, and foretell that it will dry up (Ezek 29:3, 9; 30:12; Zech 10:11). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take Sihor or Shihor as another name for the Nile (Isa 23:3; Jer 2:18). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats Shihor as a separate stream. This entry follows the first view.

Nimrah was a town east of the Jordan River, named in Num 32:3 among the places in the conquered land of Jazer and Gilead that the tribes of Reuben and Gad asked Moses to give them for their livestock. It appears under this name only here. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both take it to be probably the same place as Beth-nimrah, which Num 32:36 and Josh 13:27 list among the towns built or held by Gad. Easton's links it with the Nahr Nimrin, near one of the Jordan fords not far from Jericho. Smith's places it about ten miles north of the Dead Sea and three miles east of the Jordan. The location shown here follows that identification with the Nimrin area in the Jordan Valley. Easton's and Smith's give the name's meaning as "pure" or "limpid."

Nimrim, called "the waters of Nimrim," was a stream or spring in Moab. It appears only in two prophetic oracles against Moab, which foretell that its waters will be desolate. Isa 15:6 describes the hay withered, the grass failing and nothing green left. Jer 48:34 places it in the same list as Zoar and Horonaim. That pairing suggests a location southeast of the Dead Sea. The name may mean "pure" or "wholesome water"; Easton's Bible Dictionary renders it "stream of the leopards."
