The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Eusebius placed a town of this name near Zoar. It also links the name to Wadi Numeira, which opens onto the Dead Sea. Easton's identifies it as Wady en-Nemeirah, a fertile spot at the southeastern end of the sea. The location shown here follows the Numeira identification on the southeastern shore.

Nimrod was a son of Cush and grandson of Ham. In the list of nations he is the first to become "a mighty one in the earth" (Gen 10:8; 1 Chr 1:10). He was remembered as "a mighty hunter before the LORD," and his name became a proverb (Gen 10:9). The verses that follow, Gen 10:10–12, say his kingdom began with Babel, Erech, Accad and Calneh in the land of Shinar, in southern Mesopotamia. This entry dates that beginning to about 1822 BC, an estimate inferred from context. Those verses then describe the building of Nineveh, Calah and other cities in Assyria. The King James Version credits this to Nimrod, while another rendering credits Asshur. Micah 5:6 mentions "the land of Nimrod" alongside Assyria. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes this as Assyria or Shinar, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes it as Babylonia. Nimrod has not been identified with any known historical king.

Nimrod, in the phrase "the land of Nimrod," is a figurative name for Mesopotamia used in Mic 5:6. There it stands in parallel with "the land of Assyria," in a prophecy that Israel's deliverer would turn back the Assyrian invader and lay waste his land. The name comes from Nimrod, the descendant of Cush whom Gen 10:8–12 describes as a mighty hunter. His kingdom began at Babel and other cities in Shinar, and from there he went into Assyria and built Nineveh. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the land of Nimrod as a name for Assyria, or for Shinar as part of it. Because Micah sets it beside Assyria, the phrase probably covers the wider Mesopotamian realm linked to Nimrod. The location shown here is near ancient Babylon in southern Iraq, matching the Shinar view. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "rebellion," but suggests it is probably an unknown Assyrian word.

Nimrod's kingdom begins in Gen 10:8–12, a brief note within the list of nations descended from Noah's sons. Nimrod, a son of Cush, is described as the first "mighty one" on the earth and a "mighty hunter before the LORD," a phrase that became a saying. His kingdom started with Babel, Erech, Accad and Calneh in the land of Shinar, the plain of southern Mesopotamia. Gen 10:11 can be read two ways. The King James Version says Asshur went out from that land, while many other translations say Nimrod himself went into Assyria. This entry follows the second reading. It links Nimrod with the building of Nineveh, Rehoboth, Calah and Resen, the last described as a great city between Nineveh and Calah. The date of about 1822 BC is an estimate inferred from context, since the text gives no date.

Nimshi was the father of Jehoshaphat and the grandfather of Jehu, the army commander who became king of northern Israel and overthrew the house of Ahab. He is known only through his descendant. The fuller form of Jehu's lineage, "Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi" (2 Kgs 9:2, 14), shows Nimshi to be the grandfather. Elsewhere Jehu is simply called "the son of Nimshi," in the sense of a descendant, when God tells Elijah to anoint him (1 Kgs 19:16), when a watchman recognizes his furious driving (2 Kgs 9:20), and in the Chronicler's account of Ahaziah's death (2 Chr 22:7). That Jehu was usually named after his grandfather suggests Nimshi was the better-known figure of the family, though nothing more is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "rescued from danger."

Nineveh was a great city on the east bank of the Tigris and the capital of the Assyrian empire. Gen 10:11 says Asshur built it, or, in the Revised Version's reading, Nimrod. This entry follows the Nimrod reading. Sennacherib king of Assyria returned to live there after his campaign against Judah (2 Kgs 19:36). God sent Jonah to preach against its wickedness. Described as a city of three days' journey with more than 120,000 people, it fasted and put on sackcloth, from the king down (Jonah 3:3–7; 4:11). Jesus later pointed to its repentance (Matt 12:41). Nahum and Zephaniah foretold its desolation, and it fell to the Medes and Babylonians late in the seventh century BC, about 625 BC according to Easton's Bible Dictionary. The location shown here is the ruin mound of Kuyunjik, opposite modern Mosul in northern Iraq.

Noadiah son of Binnui was a Levite in the time of Ezra. According to Ezra 8:33, on the fourth day after Ezra's group reached Jerusalem from Babylon, the silver, gold and sacred vessels they had brought for the temple were weighed in the house of God. The priest Meremoth son of Uriah did the weighing, with Eleazar son of Phinehas and two Levites, Jozabad son of Jeshua and Noadiah, assisting. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel account in 1 Esdras calls him Moeth son of Sabannus. His name is usually explained as meaning "Yahweh has met" or "meeting with Yahweh." The name Noadiah is shared by others in the Bible, including a prophetess who opposed Nehemiah, but this entry concerns only the Levite. Nothing more is known of him.

Noadiah was a prophetess in Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah, about the mid-400s BC by inference from context. She is mentioned only once, in Nehemiah's prayer asking God to remember Tobiah, Sanballat, Noadiah and "the rest of the prophets" who tried to make him afraid (Neh 6:14). By inference from the surrounding chapter, this happened while Nehemiah was rebuilding Jerusalem's walls, when his opponents were trying to frighten him into stopping the work. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes her as a false prophetess who was bribed by Tobiah and Sanballat to stir up discontent in the city. The text itself says nothing more about what she said or did. Her name, often explained as "meeting with the Lord," is also borne by a Levite man in the time of Ezra (Ezra 8:33), a different person.

Noah was the son of Lamech, who named him with the hope that he would bring comfort from the toil of the cursed ground (Gen 5:29). Described as a just man who walked with God, he found favor with the LORD when the earth was filled with violence (Gen 6:8–13). He built the ark as commanded and entered it with his wife, his sons Shem, Ham and Japheth, and their wives, eight people in all, when the flood came in his six hundredth year (Gen 7:6–13; 1 Pet 3:20). Afterwards he built an altar and offered sacrifices, and God blessed him and made a covenant with all flesh (Gen 8:20; 9:1, 17). He later became drunk, and his son's conduct led to a curse on Canaan (Gen 9:24). He lived 350 years after the flood, and the nations descended from his sons (Gen 9:28; 10:32). Later writers name him as an example of righteousness (Ezek 14:14; Heb 11:7).

Noah (daughter of Zelophehad) was one of the five daughters of Zelophehad, of the tribe of Manasseh son of Joseph. Her sisters were Mahlah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah. Her father had no sons (Num 26:33; Josh 17:3). The sisters came before Moses together to ask for a share of land in their father's name (Num 27:1). The surrounding passages say this request was granted, and that they later received land among their father's kin (Num 27:7; Josh 17:4). To keep that inheritance within their tribe, Noah and her sisters married sons of their father's brothers (Num 36:11). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that her name is spelled differently in Hebrew from that of Noah of the flood, and gives its meaning as "motion." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives it as "movement." Nothing else is recorded about her individually.

event: Noah gets drunk and Canaan is cursed
text: Noah gets drunk and Canaan is cursed is the episode in Genesis set after the flood and God's covenant with Noah, placed about 2346 BC by inference from context. Noah became a farmer, planted a vineyard, drank its wine, and lay drunk and uncovered in his tent. Ham, the father of Canaan, saw his father's nakedness and told his brothers Shem and Japheth outside. They laid a garment across their shoulders, walked in backward, and covered Noah without looking at him. When Noah woke and learned what his younger son had done, he cursed Canaan, Ham's son, declaring that he would be a servant of servants to his brothers. He blessed the LORD God of Shem, asked that God enlarge Japheth and let him dwell in Shem's tents, and said Canaan would serve them both. The passage does not explain why the curse falls on Canaan rather than on Ham himself.

Nob was a city of priests near Jerusalem in the time of Saul. David came there alone while fleeing Saul and was met by the priest Ahimelech son of Ahitub (1 Sam 21:1). Doeg the Edomite saw this and reported it to Saul, who summoned Ahimelech and all the priests of Nob. Afterward the city was put to the sword, its men, women, children and livestock alike (1 Sam 22:9, 11, 19). Nob is later listed beside Anathoth among towns resettled after the exile (Neh 11:32). In Isaiah it is the last halt of an advancing army, a place from which Jerusalem could be seen (Isa 10:32). Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions el-Isawiyeh, the northern summit of the Mount of Olives, and Nebi Samwil. The location shown here follows the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, which places it just north of Jerusalem near the Mount Scopus ridge.

Nobah was an Israelite who captured the town of Kenath and its surrounding villages and renamed it Nobah after himself (Num 32:42). The verse closes an account of the tribe of Manasseh's conquests east of the Jordan, alongside those of Machir and Jair, so by inference from the passage he was probably a leader or clan head of Manasseh. Nothing else is recorded about his family or his life. A place called Nobah, mentioned near Jogbehah in Judg 8:11, may be the same renamed town, although this is uncertain. Kenath is often identified with modern Qanawat in southern Syria. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "that barks or yelps."

Nobah was a town east of the Jordan, named after Nobah, a man who captured Kenath and its surrounding villages and renamed it after himself (Num 32:42). The surrounding chapter places this among the conquests of the eastern half-tribe of Manasseh. Nobah appears again in Gideon's pursuit of the Midianites, who went up by the route of the tent-dwellers east of Nobah and Jogbehah and struck their army (Judg 8:11). Easton's Bible Dictionary treats both mentions as the same place, the renamed Kenath. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Nobah of Judges, being paired with Jogbehah, may have been a separate town further south, perhaps northeast of modern Amman, though no matching site has been found. The location shown here follows the Kenath identification, probably the modern Qanawat in southern Syria. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "that barks or yelps."

Nod was the land where Cain lived after he went out from the presence of the LORD, following his murder of his brother Abel and the curse God pronounced on him. Genesis 4:16 places it "on the east of Eden" and says nothing more about it. The name is usually linked to the Hebrew word for wandering, and Easton's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "exile; wandering; unrest," which fits the earlier sentence in the same chapter that Cain would be a fugitive and a vagabond. Its location is unknown, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia regards the region as undiscoverable, so no site is shown for it here. The date of about 3875 BC sometimes given for Cain's curse is an estimate inferred from the genealogies, not stated in the text.

Nodab was a people or clan east of the Jordan, named once in the Bible. It appears alongside the Hagarites, Jetur and Nephish as an enemy of the tribes of Reuben, Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh, who made war against them (1 Chr 5:19). Jetur and Nephish are listed elsewhere among the sons of Ishmael, so Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take Nodab to be probably an Ishmaelite or Arab tribe as well. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a suggestion that the name is a copyist's variant of Kedemah or Nebaioth, two other sons of Ishmael. It also points to a possible echo of the name in Nudebe, a village in the Hauran region of southern Syria. The exact territory is unknown. The location shown here is only an approximate point in the region east of the Sea of Galilee, where the war took place.

Nogah was one of the sons of King David born to him in Jerusalem, listed between Eliphelet and Nepheg in the two lists of David's Jerusalem-born children (1 Chr 3:7; 1 Chr 14:6). His name means "splendor" or "brightness." Nothing more is recorded about his life. The parallel list in 2 Sam 5:14–16 does not include him, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. That encyclopedia also points out that the same name in its Greek form, Naggai, appears in Luke's genealogy of Jesus (Luke 3:25), though that is a different person. Smith's Bible Dictionary places the births of David's Jerusalem sons roughly between 1050 and 1015 BC, an estimate drawn from context. As a son of David, Nogah belonged to the tribe of Judah.

Nohah was a son of Benjamin, listed as the fourth son in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 8:2. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "rest." This entry identifies him with Naaman, who is named among the sons of Benjamin who went down to Egypt with Jacob in Gen 46:21. The lists of Benjamin's sons differ considerably between Genesis, Numbers and Chronicles, so this match is an inference. Elsewhere a Naaman appears as a grandson of Benjamin through Bela (Num 26:40; 1 Chr 8:4), which suggests that the genealogies arrange the family in different ways. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia proposes that the phrase "a resting-place" in Judg 20:43 should be read as the place name Nohah, possibly where his family settled. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Nohah is a place connected with the tribe of Benjamin. It is not named in the King James text. Some later translations find the name in Judg 20:43, where the KJV says the Israelites trod down the Benjamites "with ease." Nohah is also the name of Benjamin's fourth son (1 Chr 8:2), which suggests a clan settlement named after him. This entry links the place with Manahath, where the heads of the Benjamite families of Geba, descendants of Ehud, were moved (1 Chr 8:6). Both names probably come from a Hebrew root meaning "rest," which supports this connection. The location shown here follows that identification and places it at the traditional site of Manahath, probably modern Malha, southwest of Jerusalem. Its exact identity and location remain uncertain.

Nophah was a place named only once, in an old victory song about Israel's defeat of Sihon king of the Amorites (Num 21:30). The song says the land was laid waste from Heshbon to Dibon and "even unto Nophah, which reacheth unto Medeba," so Nophah was probably in the region north of the Arnon, near Medeba. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls it a city of Moab that the Amorites had taken, and gives the name's meaning as "blast." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew text of this verse is hard to read. The Greek Septuagint renders the line differently, as women kindling a fire against Moab. That encyclopedia also links the name to Nobah, the town later called Kenath (Num 32:42). The location shown here follows that link and places it at Qanawat in southern Syria. Its actual site is uncertain.

The Northern Kingdom (Israel) was the state formed by the ten northern tribes after the death of Solomon. When the tribes heard that Jeroboam had returned, they called him to their assembly and made him king over Israel. Only the tribe of Judah stayed loyal to David's family, according to 1 Kgs 12:20. The next verse adds Benjamin to Judah's side. From then on the Hebrew people were divided into two kingdoms, Israel in the north and Judah in the south. Later passages in Kings describe a series of northern dynasties and a capital that eventually settled at Samaria. 2 Kgs 17 records the kingdom's end when Assyria captured Samaria and deported its people. This entry dates the division to about 975 BC and gives the kingdom a span of roughly 254 years, both estimates inferred from context. Many modern chronologies place the split closer to 930 BC.

Northern Kingdom of Israel was the kingdom formed when the northern tribes rebelled against the house of David and made Jeroboam their king, leaving only the tribe of Judah loyal to David's line (1 Kgs 12:19–20; 2 Chr 10:19). By inference from context, the split happened after Solomon's death, when his son Rehoboam refused to lighten the burdens on the people, and this entry dates it to about 974 BC. The kingdom was usually called simply Israel, and in its later history its capital was Samaria. It ended in the ninth year of King Hoshea, when the king of Assyria took Samaria and deported its people to Halah, Habor by the river of Gozan, and the cities of the Medes (2 Kgs 17:6). This entry dates that to about 720 BC, also by inference. The text presents the exile as the Lord removing Israel, with only Judah left (2 Kgs 17:18). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name Israel as "who prevails with God."

Nun was the father of Joshua, Moses' assistant and successor as leader of Israel. He is known almost entirely through the repeated phrase "Joshua the son of Nun," which appears throughout Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy and Joshua, and later in 1 Kgs 16:34 and Neh 8:17, where the son's name is spelled Jeshua. Num 13:8 places the family in the tribe of Ephraim, one of the two tribes descended from Joseph. The genealogy of Ephraim in 1 Chr 7:27 spells his name Non and names his father as Elishama, with Joshua (Jehoshua) as his son. Beyond this, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes, nothing more is known of him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "fish," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds the sense "fecundity."

Obadiah was the official in charge of King Ahab's household in Israel, one of several men of this name in the Bible. The text says he feared the Lord greatly, and when Queen Jezebel was killing the prophets of the Lord, he hid a hundred of them in caves in two groups of fifty and supplied them with bread and water. During a severe drought, Ahab sent him to search the land's springs and brooks for grass to keep the horses and mules alive, the two men dividing the country between them. On his way Obadiah met the prophet Elijah, recognized him and bowed to the ground. He then went and told Ahab, who came out to meet Elijah. His name means "servant of the Lord" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). He is distinct from the prophet whose book bears the same name.

Obadiah was a man of the tribe of Judah and a descendant of King David, named once in the genealogy of David's royal line in 1 Chr 3:21. This entry treats him as a son of Hananiah, alongside Pelatiah, Jesaiah, Rephaiah, Arnan and Shechaniah. The verse's wording ("the sons of Rephaiah, the sons of Arnan, the sons of Obadiah") is ambiguous, and it may instead list separate Davidic families whose link to Hananiah is not stated. From the surrounding genealogy, Hananiah was a son of Zerubbabel (1 Chr 3:19), which places Obadiah in the generations after the return from exile. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 470 BC. His name means "servant of the Lord." Nothing else is recorded about him, and he is one of several men in the Bible named Obadiah.

Obadiah was a man of the tribe of Issachar, a son of Izrahiah and a grandson of Uzzi, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 7:3. His brothers were Michael, Joel and Ishiah. The verse calls the group "five" while naming only four sons, so Izrahiah himself is probably counted among them, and all five are described as chief men. The verses just before trace Uzzi back to Tola, the firstborn son of Issachar. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him about 1014 BC, an estimate drawn from context. His name means "servant of the Lord" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Obadiah should not be confused with them, including the prophet.

Obadiah was one of the six sons of Azel, listed in the genealogy of King Saul's family in the tribe of Benjamin. His brothers were Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah and Hanan. The same list of Azel's sons appears twice, in 1 Chr 8:38 and again in 1 Chr 9:44. The surrounding verses trace Azel's line back through Jonathan's son Merib-baal to Saul, so Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe Obadiah as a descendant of Saul. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "servant of the Lord." Several other men in the Bible share this name, including the prophet, and this Obadiah should not be confused with them.

Obadiah, also called Abda, was a Levite descended from Jeduthun through Galal who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. In 1 Chr 9:16 he is called Obadiah son of Shemaiah. The parallel list in Neh 11:17 names him Abda son of Shammua, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary treat the two as the same man. The name means "servant of the Lord." Smith's also identifies him with the Obadiah listed among the gatekeepers who guarded the storerooms at the gates in Neh 12:25, and this entry follows that view. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia instead counts that gatekeeper as a separate person. Because several men in the Bible bear the name Obadiah, the identification is not certain.

Obadiah was a Gadite warrior, listed second among the Gadite leaders who came over to David (1 Chr 12:9). The surrounding passage, 1 Chr 12:8–15, describes these men as skilled fighters with faces like lions and as swift as gazelles. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary place their joining at Ziklag, while David was a fugitive from Saul. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him a chief of the Gadites. His name means "servant of the Lord." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including the prophet of the book of Obadiah and the steward of King Ahab's household. Nothing else is recorded about this Obadiah.

Obadiah was a man of the tribe of Zebulun and the father of Ishmaiah, named only in 1 Chr 27:19. The verse belongs to a list of the leaders of the tribes of Israel under King David, where Ishmaiah son of Obadiah is given as the leader for Zebulun. Nothing else is recorded about Obadiah himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia read the verse as making Ishmaiah the tribal chief. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the Tyndale STEPBible names list describe Obadiah himself as a prince or ruler of Zebulun in David's time. This entry follows the reading that Ishmaiah held the office, which matches the wording of the list. The name means "servant of the Lord." Several other men in the Bible share it, including the prophet and a steward of King Ahab, and this Obadiah should not be confused with them.

Obadiah was one of the princes, or officials, of Judah whom King Jehoshaphat sent out in the third year of his reign to teach in the cities of Judah. He is named alongside Benhail, Zechariah, Nethaneel and Michaiah (2 Chr 17:7). The following verses, 2 Chr 17:8–9, say that Levites and priests went with these princes and that they taught the people from the book of the law of the Lord. Nothing else is recorded about this Obadiah. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which means "servant of the Lord" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), and there is no clear link between this official and any of them.

Obadiah was a Levite from the clan of Merari who served as one of the overseers of the workmen repairing the temple in Jerusalem during the reign of King Josiah. 2 Chr 34:12 names him with Jahath, another Merarite, and with Zechariah and Meshullam of the Kohathites as the men who directed the work, which the text says was done faithfully. Other Levites skilled with musical instruments were also involved. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these repairs to about 623 BC. His name means "servant of the Lord." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and nothing further is recorded about this Obadiah.

Obadiah son of Jehiel was a family head of the clan descended from Joab. He returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra during the reign of the Persian king Artaxerxes, bringing 218 men of his family with him (Ezra 8:9). Smith's Bible Dictionary places him in the second caravan of returning exiles, the one Ezra led. His name means "servant of the Lord," according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should be kept distinct from the several other men in the Bible called Obadiah, including the prophet and Ahab's household steward.

Obadiah was one of the men who set their seal to the written covenant made under Nehemiah, in which the returned community in Jerusalem pledged to keep the law of God. His name appears in a list in Neh 10:5. The names in that part of the list (Neh 10:1–8) are followed by the statement "these were the priests," so he was probably a priest. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the name may stand for a priestly family rather than a single individual. The name means "servant of the Lord" and is borne by several different men in the Bible. Nothing further is recorded about this Obadiah, and it is uncertain whether he is the same as any other person of that name.

Obadiah was the prophet whose message makes up the Book of Obadiah, the shortest book in the Old Testament. The book opens by calling itself "the vision of Obadiah" and presents a message from the Lord concerning Edom, the nation descended from Esau, announcing that the nations are being summoned to rise against it in battle (Obad 1:1). Nothing is recorded about his family, home or life. His name means "servant of the Lord" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), and several other men in the Bible share it, including the steward of King Ahab's household. There is no clear basis for identifying the prophet with any of them. The date of his prophecy is uncertain. This entry places it about 585 BC, by inference from context, shortly after the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem, when Edom is often thought to have taken advantage of Judah's fall.

Obed was the son of Boaz and Ruth, the father of Jesse, and the grandfather of King David, a member of the tribe of Judah. When he was born, the women of Bethlehem named him and declared, "There is a son born to Naomi" (Ruth 4:17). The phrase reflects that the child continued the family line of Naomi, Ruth's mother-in-law, whose husband and sons had died earlier in the book. Apart from the story of his birth, Obed appears only in genealogies: those at the end of Ruth and in 1 Chronicles, and both genealogies of Jesus, in Matthew and Luke. Matthew notes that he was born of Ruth. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "servant" or "workman." Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Obed was a man of the tribe of Judah who appears only in a genealogy in 1 Chronicles. He was the son of Ephlal and the father of Jehu, and his line continued through Jehu's son Azariah (1 Chr 2:37–38). The surrounding passage (1 Chr 2:34–35) traces this family through the clan of Jerahmeel. It descends from Sheshan, who had no sons and gave his daughter in marriage to Jarha, his Egyptian servant. Obed was a later descendant of that marriage, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary both note. His name is usually taken to mean "servant" or "worker" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with other men of the same name, such as Obed the grandfather of David.

Obed was one of David's mighty warriors, named near the end of the list of David's heroes in 1 Chronicles 11. He appears alongside Eliel and Jasiel the Mesobaite (1 Chr 11:47). This list continues beyond the parallel roster in 2 Samuel 23, and nothing more is recorded about him, neither his family, his hometown nor any deeds. He is a different man from the better-known Obed, son of Boaz and Ruth and grandfather of David, and from the other men of this name in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a servant" or "workman." Smith's Bible Dictionary places him in David's time, about 1046 BC, a date inferred from his place in the account rather than stated in the text.

Obed was a Levite, one of the sons of Shemaiah, listed among the gatekeepers of the temple in the divisions organized in David's time (1 Chr 26:7). His brothers were Othni, Rephael, Elzabad, Elihu and Semachiah. The verse notes that Elzabad's brothers were strong men. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 26:4–6) makes Shemaiah the firstborn son of Obed-edom, so Obed was probably Obed-edom's grandson. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him this way, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts him among the Korahite doorkeepers. Smith's dates him to about 1017 BC, an estimate drawn from context. His name is usually taken to mean "servant" or "worker" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other people in the Bible are also called Obed, including the grandfather of David. This man is a different person, known only from this one list.

Obed was the father of Azariah, one of the captains of hundreds whom the priest Jehoiada brought into a covenant with him in the seventh year (2 Chr 23:1). That covenant began the uprising that removed Queen Athaliah from the throne of Judah and crowned the young Joash, as the rest of the chapter and the parallel account in 2 Kgs 11 describe. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to sometime before 876 BC. Obed is known only as Azariah's father, and nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names takes to mean "servant" or "workman," belongs to several men in the Bible. This Obed is distinct from the better-known Obed who was the son of Ruth and Boaz and the grandfather of David.

Obil was an Ishmaelite who was in charge of King David's camels. He appears once, in the list of officials who managed the king's property (1 Chr 27:30). Next to him in that list, Jehdeiah the Meronothite oversaw the donkeys. As a descendant of Ishmael, Obil probably came from a people known for desert travel and camel herding, which may explain why he held this post. The meaning of his name is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "camel driver", which fits his role, and Smith's Bible Dictionary similarly renders it "chief of the camels". Hitchcock's Bible Names instead gives "that weeps". Smith's dates his service to about 1050 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Oboth was a camp of the Israelites during their wilderness journey, reached shortly before they came to the borders of Moab. In Num 21:10–11 it is their next stop after the episode of the bronze serpent, and Easton's Bible Dictionary calls it the first camp after that event. The fuller itinerary in Num 33:43–44 places it between Punon and Ijeabarim; counting from that list, the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls it the third camp after Mount Hor. From Oboth the people moved on to Ijeabarim, on the edge of Moab toward the east. The name is usually explained as meaning "water-skins" or "bottles." The exact site is unknown. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests it was probably south of the Dead Sea, near the boundary of Moab and Edom. The location shown here is a rough placement east of the Dead Sea.

Ocran was a man of the tribe of Asher, known only as the father of Pagiel. He appears solely in the phrase "Pagiel the son of Ocran" in the book of Numbers. There his son is named as Asher's representative at the census taken in the wilderness (Num 1:13). Pagiel also led Asher's tribe in the camp around the tabernacle and on the march (Num 2:27; Num 10:26), and he brought Asher's offering on the eleventh day of the altar's dedication (Num 7:72, 77). Ocran therefore probably lived during the Exodus generation or shortly before it, though nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "a disturber," and Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "troubled." Some reference works spell the name Ochran.

Oded was the father of Azariah, the prophet whom the Spirit of God came upon during the reign of King Asa of Judah (2 Chr 15:1). Asa's reign is dated roughly to the late 10th and early 9th centuries BC. In 2 Chr 15:8 the prophecy that moved Asa to take courage, remove the idols from Judah, Benjamin and the captured towns of Ephraim, and restore the Lord's altar is called "the prophecy of Oded the prophet." Since the message in the passage is spoken by Azariah, the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the verse means "the prophecy of Azariah the son of Oded." Others take it to mean that Oded was himself a prophet, which is how STEPBible's names index describes him. His name is usually explained as meaning "restorer" or "sustainer." A different Oded, a prophet in Samaria in the time of Ahaz, appears in 2 Chr 28:9.

Oded was a prophet of the Lord in Samaria during the reign of Ahaz of Judah, when Pekah king of Israel defeated Judah and brought a large number of captives back to Samaria. Oded went out to meet the returning army and told them that God had handed Judah over to them because he was angry with Judah, but that they had killed in a rage that reached up to heaven. The following verses (2 Chr 28:10–15) record him warning them not to enslave their fellow Judeans. Some leaders of Ephraim backed him, and the captives were clothed, fed and taken back to Jericho. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 739 BC. This Oded is distinct from another Oded named as the father of the prophet Azariah in the days of Asa (2 Chr 15:1). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "to sustain, hold or lift up."

Og was the Amorite king of Bashan, the region east of the Jordan, who reigned from Ashtaroth and Edrei. He is described as the last survivor of the remnant of the giants, the Rephaim. His iron bedstead, nine cubits long and four wide (about 13 by 6 feet), was said to be kept at Rabbah of the Ammonites. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some take it to be a basalt sarcophagus. Soon after Israel defeated Sihon, Og led his people out to fight them at Edrei and was defeated and killed. Israel took his sixty cities in the region of Argob, and Moses gave his kingdom to Reuben, Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh, mainly the Machirites. Rahab, the Gibeonites, Nehemiah and the Psalms all later recall his defeat, and his former territory became one of Solomon's administrative districts (1 Kgs 4:19).

Ohad was a son of Simeon and a grandson of Jacob, listed third among Simeon's six sons in Gen 46:10 and Exod 6:15. His brothers were Jemuel, Jamin, Jachin, Zohar and Shaul, the last of whom was the son of a Canaanite woman. Zohar appears as Zerah in later lists. In Genesis he is named among Jacob's family who went down to Egypt. Exodus counts these sons as the founding families of the tribe of Simeon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Ohad does not appear in the list of Simeon's clans in Num 26:12–14, so he probably left no separate clan. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain: Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "united" or "power," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "praising" or "confessing."

Ohel was a son of Zerubbabel and a member of the tribe of Judah, descended through the royal line of David. He is mentioned only once, in the genealogy of 1 Chr 3:20, where he is the second name in a group of five sons: Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah and Jushab-hesed. The preceding verse names Zerubbabel's other children, Meshullam, Hananiah and their sister Shelomith. Counting those two brothers first, Easton's Bible Dictionary calls Ohel the fourth son. Abiud is also counted among his brothers here, because Matthew's genealogy of Jesus names Abiud as a son of Zerubbabel. Why the five sons are listed separately is not explained. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both give the meaning of his name as "tent." Nothing else is recorded about his life.

The Old Gate was one of the gates of Jerusalem rebuilt under Nehemiah after the return from exile. Nehemiah 3:6 records that Jehoiada son of Paseah and Meshullam son of Besodeiah repaired it, laying its beams and setting up its doors, locks and bars. It appears again in Neh 12:39, in the route of the procession at the dedication of the wall. Its name is understood in different ways. The King James Version reads it as the "old gate," while the ESV renders it "Gate of Yeshanah," which may refer to a town called Jeshanah or to an older part of the city. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in the north wall and says it was so called because the Jebusites built it. Its exact position is uncertain. The location shown here is a general point within Jerusalem's north side.

Olivet is another name for the Mount of Olives, a ridge just east of Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary says the Kidron Valley separates it from the city and explains the name from the olive trees on its slopes. Acts 1:12 places it a sabbath day's journey from Jerusalem, probably a walk of under a mile. Bethphage and Bethany lay on or near it, and from there Jesus sent two disciples ahead before entering the city (Luke 19:29). In his last days he taught in the temple by day and spent the nights on the mount (Luke 21:37). The events linked to it here are the cursing of the fig tree, his teaching about that tree, the promise of the Holy Spirit, and his ascension. After the ascension the disciples returned from Olivet to Jerusalem. Easton's identifies it with the modern Jebel et-Tur.

The Olivet Discourse was Jesus' teaching on the Mount of Olives about the temple's coming destruction and the end of the age, given during Holy Week, about AD 30 by inference from context. As he left the temple after his debates there, his disciples pointed out its buildings, and he said not one stone would be left on another (Matt 24:1; Luke 21:6). Mark 13:3 names Peter, James, John and Andrew as those who then asked him privately when this would happen. He warned of false Christs, earthquakes, famines and persecution, spoke of the "abomination of desolation" foretold by Daniel, and urged those in Judea to flee. He described the Son of man sending angels to gather his elect, and told his hearers to watch, since no one knows the day or hour. Matthew's account adds the parables of the ten virgins and the talents and a scene of final judgment.

Olympas was a Christian at Rome to whom Paul sent greetings near the end of his letter to the Romans (Rom 16:15). He is named in a single greeting with Philologus, Julia, Nereus and Nereus's sister, followed by "all the saints which are with them." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes this grouping to suggest that these believers formed a small community of their own, perhaps meeting together, within the early Roman church. The same work treats Olympas as a shortened form of the name Olympiodorus, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "heavenly." Nothing else is recorded about him, and this is his only mention in the Bible.

Omar was a son of Eliphaz, the firstborn son of Esau, which made him a grandson of Esau. He is named second among Eliphaz's sons, after Teman, in the genealogy of Esau's descendants in Gen 36:11, and again in the parallel list in 1 Chr 1:36. His brothers included Zepho, Gatam and Kenaz, and the Chronicles list also includes Amalek. Gen 36:15 calls him a "duke," meaning a chief or clan leader, among the Edomite chiefs descended from Esau, so a clan of Edom probably bore his name. Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "eloquent," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be connected with a Hebrew word meaning "speak."

Omri was a king of Israel, the northern kingdom, and father of Ahab. He was captain of the army besieging Gibbethon when Zimri killed King Elah, and the troops made him king in the camp that same day. He then besieged Tirzah. Half the people backed a rival, Tibni son of Ginath, until Omri's side prevailed and Tibni died. He reigned twelve years, beginning in the 31st year of Asa of Judah (about 929 BC, by inference from context), six of them at Tirzah. By 1 Kgs 16:24 he then built Samaria, where he was buried. The text says he did worse evil than all before him, and Micah later condemns the "statutes of Omri." Athaliah, mother of King Ahaziah of Judah, is called his daughter. Through her he is linked to the royal line of Judah. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the Moabite Stone records him oppressing Moab. Several other men in the Bible share his name.

Omri was a member of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the nine sons of Becher listed in the Benjamite genealogy at 1 Chr 7:8. His brothers were Zemira, Joash, Eliezer, Elioenai, Jerimoth, Abiah, Anathoth and Alameth. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies Becher as a son of Benjamin, which would make Omri a grandson of Benjamin. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in this family list. He is not the same person as Omri the king of Israel, father of Ahab, and the name is shared by several other people in the Bible. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "pupil of Jehovah," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "sheaf of corn."

Omri was a man of the tribe of Judah, descended through Pharez (Perez), who appears only in a genealogy in 1 Chr 9:4. He was the son of Imri, the grandson of Bani, and the father of Ammihud. His grandson Uthai is listed among the people of Judah who lived in Jerusalem. The surrounding passage concerns those who resettled there after the exile, so Omri himself probably lived some generations earlier. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and STEPBible's proper names index connect him with Jerusalem, but the verse places only his descendant Uthai there. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is a different man from Omri the king of Israel and from the other men of this name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "sheaf of corn," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "pupil of Jehovah."

Omri, son of Michael, was the leader of the tribe of Issachar during the reign of King David. He appears in a list of the chief officers over the tribes of Israel (1 Chr 27:16–22), where he is named as the officer for Issachar. The single verse that mentions him gives no further details about his life or duties. He should not be confused with other men of the same name, most notably Omri the later king of Israel and father of Ahab. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 1030 BC, and the name is explained as "pupil of Jehovah" there and as "sheaf of corn" in Hitchcock's Bible Names.

On, son of Peleth, was a man of the tribe of Reuben who joined Korah, Dathan and Abiram when they gathered men to challenge the leadership of Moses and Aaron during the wilderness period (Num 16:1). His name appears only in this opening verse. As Smith's Bible Dictionary notes, he is not mentioned again in the rest of the account of the revolt, and he is absent from the description of its outcome, when the ground swallowed Dathan and Abiram. Whether he withdrew from the rebellion or simply goes unnamed afterward is not stated. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "pain," "force" or "iniquity." The other two verses listed here use "on" only as an ordinary English word and do not refer to him.

On was an ancient city of Lower Egypt, later known by its Greek name Heliopolis ("city of the sun"). In Genesis it appears only as the home of Potipherah, priest of On. Pharaoh gave Potipherah's daughter Asenath to Joseph as his wife, and she bore him Manasseh and Ephraim before the years of famine (Gen 41:45, 50; 46:20). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes the city as the great center of Egyptian sun-worship, once filled with obelisks. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that "Aven" in Ezek 30:17, named with Pibeseth in a prophecy against Egypt, has the same Hebrew consonants as On and is almost certainly the same city. Both dictionaries also connect it with Beth-shemesh in Jer 43:13. The location shown here is the ancient site of Heliopolis, on the northeastern edge of modern Cairo, in the area of present-day Matariya.

Onam was a son of Shobal and a grandson of Seir the Horite. He is named in the list of Seir's descendants given alongside the genealogy of Esau's family in Edom. His brothers were Alvan, Manahath, Ebal and Shepho (Gen 36:23). The parallel list in 1 Chr 1:40 gives the same five names with slight spelling differences, Alian for Alvan and Shephi for Shepho. Shobal's descent from Seir comes from the surrounding verses of the genealogy. Nothing more is recorded about Onam beyond his place in these lists. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "vigorous." The same name belongs to another man in the Bible, a descendant of Judah through Jerahmeel, who should not be confused with this Horite.

Onam was a member of the tribe of Judah, listed in the genealogy of Jerahmeel's family. He was the son of Jerahmeel by a second wife, Atarah (1 Chr 2:26). His brothers Ram, Bunah, Oren, Ozem and Ahijah are named in the preceding verse as Jerahmeel's sons, and were probably his half-brothers by Jerahmeel's first wife. Onam had two sons, Shammai and Jada, and through Shammai the line continued to Nadab and Abishur (1 Chr 2:28). Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "strong" and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia as "vigorous"; the latter suggests the name may be connected with Onan, son of Judah. The name is shared by at least one other person, a Horite descendant of Seir in Edom (Gen 36:23), who should not be confused with this Onam.

Onan was the second son of Judah by the daughter of Shua, a Canaanite woman, and the brother of Er and Shelah. After the LORD put Er to death, Judah told Onan to marry his brother's widow and father children who would count as Er's, a custom later set out in law in Deut 25:5. The widow is named Tamar in Gen 38:6. Onan knew any child would not be counted as his own, so he spilled his seed on the ground to avoid giving his brother an heir. Gen 38:10 says the LORD was displeased and put him to death as well. He died in Canaan before Jacob's family moved to Egypt, and the tribal lists of Judah record his death. His half-brothers Pharez and Zerah were later born to Judah by Tamar. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the meaning of his name as "strong."

Onesimus was a man from Colossae whom the apostle Paul calls "my son," saying he had become his spiritual father while Paul was in prison (Phlm 1:10). Paul's short letter to Philemon is an appeal on his behalf. In that letter Paul asks Philemon to receive him "not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved" (Phlm 1:16) and offers to repay anything he owes (Phlm 1:18). This indicates that Onesimus was Philemon's slave and had left his master, perhaps after some wrong. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a runaway who reached Rome, where Paul was held. Paul sent him back with Tychicus and introduced him to the Colossian church as "a faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you" (Col 4:9), so he was probably a native or resident of Colossae. His name means "useful," and Paul plays on this meaning in Phlm 1:11.

Onesiphorus was a Christian whom Paul remembers warmly in his second letter to Timothy. Paul prays for mercy on his household because Onesiphorus often refreshed him and was not ashamed of his chains. The following verses (2 Tim 1:17–18) add that when he came to Rome he searched hard for the imprisoned Paul until he found him, and that he had served in many ways at Ephesus. Paul's closing greetings ask Timothy to greet his household, alongside Prisca and Aquila. Since Timothy was probably at Ephesus, Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary take Onesiphorus to have been an Ephesian whose home and family stayed there. His name means "bringing profit." Because Paul twice greets his household rather than the man himself, some interpreters, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes, think he may have died by the time of writing, though this cannot be known.

Ono was a town in the coastal lowland, regularly named alongside Lod (Lydda). According to 1 Chr 8:12, Shamed, a descendant of Benjamin through Elpaal, built Ono and Lod with their surrounding towns. After the exile, people from Lod, Hadid and Ono returned with Zerubbabel, numbering 725 in Ezra 2:33 and 721 in Neh 7:37, and Benjamites later settled there. Nehemiah 11:35 lists Lod and Ono with "the valley of craftsmen," which Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests may be the same as "the plain of Ono." In that plain Sanballat and Geshem proposed a meeting with Nehemiah, but he understood they meant him harm. Easton's Bible Dictionary says they asked four times and intended to seize him. Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify Ono with Kefr 'Ana, northwest of Lydda, near present-day Or Yehuda. The location shown here follows that identification.

Ophel was a fortified part of ancient Jerusalem, on the narrow ridge running south from the temple mount between the Tyropoeon and Kidron valleys, according to Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries. The name is usually explained as "hill" or "mound", and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes an argument for "fortress." King Jotham built extensively on the wall of Ophel. Manasseh later enclosed it with an outer wall and raised it to a great height. After the exile, the Nethinim, the temple servants, lived there under Ziha and Gispa. Nehemiah places Ophel near the Water Gate on the east and "the tower that lieth out", and the Tekoites repaired the wall up to it. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that the Chronicler used Ophel for the older stronghold called Zion or the City of David. The location shown here lies on that hill just south of the temple area.

Ophir was a son of Joktan, listed among his thirteen sons in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:29) and again in the genealogy of 1 Chr 1:23. Joktan descended from Shem through Eber, so Ophir belongs to the Semitic line. His brothers included Sheba, Havilah, Jobab, Hazarmaveth and Almodad. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him as the eleventh son. The text records nothing else about him personally. Like several of his brothers, his name probably also stands for a people or region. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connects him with the land of Ophir, the source of the gold that Solomon's ships brought back from Ezion-geber. It places that land most likely in southeastern Arabia, though India and Africa have also been proposed. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "fruitful region."

Ophir was a distant region famous for its fine gold. Solomon's ships, crewed by his servants together with experienced sailors sent by Hiram of Tyre, sailed there and brought back over four hundred talents of gold, along with almug (algum) wood and precious stones (1 Kgs 9:28; 10:11; 2 Chr 8:18). By inference from 1 Kgs 22:48, the voyage began at Ezion-geber on the Red Sea, where Jehoshaphat's later fleet bound for Ophir was wrecked. "Gold of Ophir" became a byword for the finest gold in poetry and prophecy (Job 28:16; Ps 45:9; Isa 13:12). Its location is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it in southern Arabia, linking it to Ophir, son of Joktan, in Gen 10:29. Others have suggested Africa or India. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes the identification with Abhira at the mouth of the Indus, which the location shown here follows.

Ophni was a town in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. It appears only once, in the list of Benjamin's cities in Josh 18:24, where it is named with Chepharhaammonai and Gaba among a group of twelve cities with their villages. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "mouldy". Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "wearisomeness" or "folding together." Smith's Bible Dictionary links Ophni with Gophna, a town Josephus describes as important in the Roman period, and with the modern village of Jifna northwest of Bethel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says Jifna suits the position, about 2½ miles northwest of Bethel. It also notes that the change in the name's first letter makes the link less straightforward. The location shown here follows the Jifna identification.

Ophrah was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the genealogies of Judah as the son of Meonothai (1 Chr 4:14). Nothing else is recorded about him. The surrounding verses suggest Meonothai belonged to the family of Othniel, the son of Kenaz: the preceding verse lists Othniel's sons, and some ancient Greek manuscripts read Meonothai there as well, though the Hebrew text does not. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of his name as "fawn." The same name belongs to two towns in the Old Testament, one in Benjamin and one in Manasseh (the home of Gideon), but this Ophrah is a person and is not connected to either place in the text.

Ophrah was a town in the territory given to the tribe of Benjamin, listed alongside Avim and Parah (Josh 18:23). It is a different place from the Ophrah in Manasseh that is linked with Gideon. In Saul's time, Philistine raiding parties left their camp in three groups, and one of them took the road toward Ophrah and the land of Shual (1 Sam 13:17). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reasons that this group went north, because Saul held the passes to the south. Eusebius and Jerome place Ophrah about five Roman miles east of Bethel. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the ISBE both identify it with the hilltop village of et-Taiyibeh, northeast of Beitin (Bethel), and the location shown here follows that identification. The ISBE also suggests it may be the same place as Ephron (2 Chr 13:19) and Ephraim (John 11:54). The name is usually taken to mean "fawn."

Ophrah was a town of the Abiezrite clan of Manasseh and the home of Gideon. An angel of the LORD appeared there under an oak belonging to Gideon's father Joash, while Gideon threshed wheat in a winepress to hide it from the Midianites (Judg 6:11). Gideon built an altar there called Jehovah-shalom (Judg 6:24). After his victory he placed in Ophrah an ephod made from the spoils, which became a snare to him and his family (Judg 8:27). He was buried there in his father's tomb (Judg 8:32). Later his son Abimelech killed seventy of his brothers there on one stone, and only Jotham escaped (Judg 9:5). Its site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Ferata near Shechem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it nearer the Jezreel plain, and the location shown here follows that view, near modern Afula. A different Ophrah lay in Benjamin.

The Oppression by Ammon and Philistia was an eighteen-year period in the time of the judges, following the judgeship of Jair. After Israel again served Baal, Ashtaroth and the gods of surrounding nations, the LORD gave them into the hands of the Philistines and the Ammonites. The Ammonites pressed hardest on the Israelites east of the Jordan in Gilead, and also crossed the river to fight Judah, Benjamin and Ephraim. When Israel cried out, the LORD reminded them of earlier deliverances and told them to call on the gods they had chosen. The people confessed, put away their foreign gods and served the LORD. The Ammonites then camped in Gilead while Israel gathered at Mizpeh, and Gilead's leaders looked for someone to lead the fight. The following chapter shows this was Jephthah. Its start is placed about 1170 BC, an estimate inferred from context.

Oreb was a prince of Midian during the Midianite oppression of Israel in the time of Gideon. His name means "raven" (Easton's Bible Dictionary). After Gideon's surprise attack routed the Midianite camp, the men of Ephraim captured Oreb and his fellow prince Zeeb. They killed Oreb at a rock that was called "the rock Oreb", probably named after him, and brought the heads of both princes to Gideon across the Jordan (Judg 7:25). When the Ephraimites complained that Gideon had not called them sooner, he calmed them by saying that their capture of Oreb and Zeeb outweighed his own achievement (Judg 8:3). Later writers recalled his defeat as a byword for God's judgment on Israel's enemies. A psalm asks that hostile nobles be made like Oreb and Zeeb (Ps 83:11), and Isaiah compares a coming blow against Assyria to "the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb" (Isa 10:26).

Oren was a man of the tribe of Judah, the third of five sons of Jerahmeel listed in 1 Chr 2:25. His father Jerahmeel was the firstborn of Hezron, and his brothers were Ram, Bunah, Ozem and Ahijah. The facts also name Onam as a sibling. The next verse (1 Chr 2:26) says Jerahmeel had a second wife, Atarah, who was Onam's mother, so Onam was probably Oren's half-brother. Oren appears only in this genealogy, and nothing more is recorded about him or his descendants. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "ash" or "pine," and Smith's Bible Dictionary as "pine tree." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some Greek manuscripts spell the name Aran.

Ornan, called Araunah in 2 Samuel, was a Jebusite living in Jerusalem in David's reign who owned a threshing floor. During the plague sent after David's census, the angel of the LORD stopped beside this threshing floor, and the prophet Gad told David to build an altar there. Ornan was threshing wheat with his four sons when he saw the angel. When the king came, Ornan bowed to the ground and offered the site as a gift, along with oxen for sacrifice, threshing tools for wood and wheat. David refused to offer what cost him nothing and insisted on paying. The accounts give different prices: fifty shekels of silver for the threshing floor and oxen (2 Sam 24:24), and six hundred shekels of gold for "the place" (1 Chr 21:25). Solomon later built the temple on this site on Mount Moriah.

Orpah was a Moabite woman who married into the family of Elimelech and Naomi, an Israelite family from Bethlehem living in Moab. Ruth 1:4 says Naomi's two sons married Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth, and stayed there about ten years. Her husband was Chilion, an inference from Ruth 4:10, which names Ruth as the wife of Mahlon. After both sons died, Orpah set out with Naomi toward Judah. When Naomi urged her daughters-in-law to go back to their own families, Orpah wept, kissed her goodbye and returned to her people, while Ruth stayed with Naomi (Ruth 1:14). The meaning of her name is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "forelock or fawn," Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "gazelle," and Hitchcock's Bible Names links it to the Hebrew word for "neck."

Othni was a Levite, the first named of the sons of Shemaiah in the list of temple gatekeepers organized in David's time (1 Chr 26:7). His brothers were Rephael, Obed, Elzabad, Elihu and Semachiah, and the verse calls members of the family "strong men." Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a "mighty man of valour." The surrounding chapter (1 Chr 26:4) names Shemaiah as the firstborn son of Obed-edom, so Othni was Obed-edom's grandson. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts the family among the Korahite Levites, and the context places him among the gatekeepers assigned to guard the sanctuary. He is mentioned nowhere else. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Easton's and Smith's dictionaries give "lion of Jehovah," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "my time" or "my hour."

Othniel son of Kenaz was a warrior of Judah and the first of Israel's judges. He captured the city that Caleb had promised to reward with his daughter Achsah, and so won her as his wife (Josh 15:17; Judg 1:13). The surrounding verses name the city as Kirjath-sepher, later called Debir. He is called "Caleb's younger brother," which may mean that Othniel himself or his father Kenaz was Caleb's brother. The STEPBible proper names index takes him as Caleb's nephew. After Israel cried to the Lord, Othniel was raised up as a deliverer, about 1410 BC by inference from context. Judg 3:8 names the oppressor as Cushan-rishathaim of Mesopotamia. The land then had rest for forty years. His sons were Hathath and probably Meonothai (1 Chr 4:13). In David's time, the captain Heldai was counted as "of Othniel," apparently a family descended from him.

Ozem was a son of Jesse of the tribe of Judah and a brother of King David. The genealogy in 1 Chronicles names him as the sixth son, listed just before David, the seventh (1 Chr 2:15). His other brothers named there are Eliab, Abinadab, Shammah, Nethaneel and Raddai. A later passage mentions an Elihu as one of David's brothers (1 Chr 27:18). Nothing is recorded about Ozem beyond his name and his place in the family. The accounts in 1 Samuel say Jesse had eight sons (1 Sam 16:10–11; 17:12), while Chronicles lists only seven. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "power," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "that fasts." The name is shared by another man, a son of Jerahmeel in the same tribe (1 Chr 2:25), who is a different person.

Ozem was a man of the tribe of Judah, one of the sons of Jerahmeel, the firstborn of Hezron. He appears only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:25, listed fourth among Jerahmeel's sons after Ram, Bunah and Oren, and before Ahijah. The next verse (1 Chr 2:26) adds that Jerahmeel had another wife, Atarah, who was the mother of Onam, so Onam was probably Ozem's half-brother. Through Hezron, Ozem belonged to the line of Judah's son Perez, and the STEPBible names data call him a nephew of Caleb, Jerahmeel's brother. Nothing else is recorded about him. Another Ozem, a brother of David, appears in the same chapter (1 Chr 2:15), and the two should be kept distinct. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "power," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats its meaning as unknown.

Ozni was a son of Gad and the founder of the Oznite family, one of the clans of the tribe of Gad listed in the census taken in the wilderness (Num 26:16). In the list of Jacob's descendants who went down to Egypt he appears to be called Ezbon (Gen 46:16). The two lists name Gad's sons in matching order, and Ezbon stands where Ozni does, so Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat the names as referring to the same man. This entry follows that identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of Ozni as "an ear" or "my hearkening." His brothers were Zephon, Haggi, Shuni, Eri, Arod and Areli. Nothing further is recorded about him.

Paarai the Arbite was one of David's mighty men, the elite warriors listed in 2 Sam 23. He appears only once, named between Hezrai the Carmelite and Bani the Gadite, and nothing more is recorded about him. The title "Arbite" probably refers to Arab, a town in the hill country of Judah, though this is inferred. The parallel list in 1 Chr 11:37 names "Naarai the son of Ezbai" at this point, and Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia all take Naarai to be the same man, the difference in spelling probably arising in copying. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "opening," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "devotee of Peor."

Paddan is a shortened name for Paddan-aram, the region in upper Mesopotamia where Jacob's relatives lived. It appears in this form only once, in Gen 48:7, where the aged Jacob, blessing Joseph's sons in Egypt, recalls coming back from Padan (the King James spelling) when Rachel died on the road near Ephrath, that is, Bethlehem, and he buried her there. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as a plain and takes it to mean Padan-aram. Other passages in Genesis place Paddan-aram around Haran, where Jacob lived with his uncle Laban and married Rachel and Leah. So this verse probably refers to his journey home from that stay. The exact limits of the region are uncertain. The location shown here marks the general area of Haran, near the modern town of Harran in southeastern Turkey.

Paddan-aram was the region in northern Mesopotamia where Abraham's relatives lived, in Genesis. It was the home of Bethuel and his son Laban, whose sister Rebekah became Isaac's wife (Gen 25:20). Isaac later sent Jacob there to find a wife among Laban's daughters rather than among the Canaanites (Gen 28:2–7). Jacob's sons were born there, except Benjamin, as was his daughter Dinah (Gen 35:26; Gen 46:15). He became wealthy there before returning to Canaan (Gen 31:18; Gen 33:18). The name probably means "field" or "plain of Aram." Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in the district around Haran, and Genesis's other accounts of Jacob's stay call his destination Haran. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also mentions a site near Damascus. The location shown here follows the Haran identification, near modern Harran in southeastern Turkey.

Padon was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants returned from the Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel. His name appears only in the two parallel lists of returning exiles, between the families of Keros and Siaha (Sia in Nehemiah), within the section on the temple servants (Ezra 2:44; Neh 7:47). Nothing else is recorded about him personally, and he probably lived well before the return, since the lists name family groups by their forebears. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of the name as "redemption" and identifies him with the "Phaleas" of 1 Esdras 5:29. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the return of his descendants to before 529 BC.

Pagiel was the son of Ocran and the leader of the tribe of Asher during Israel's time in the wilderness. He is named among the tribal heads who helped Moses take the census of Israel (Num 1:13). In the arrangement of the camp he was captain of Asher, which camped next to Dan, by inference from the context on the north side of the tabernacle (Num 2:27). When the altar was dedicated, each tribal prince brought gifts on his own day, and Pagiel brought Asher's offering on the eleventh day. His gifts matched those of the other princes and included peace offerings of oxen, rams, goats and lambs (Num 7:72, 77). When Israel set out from Sinai, he commanded Asher's troops (Num 10:26). His name is usually explained as "God's intervention" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "God allots" (Easton's Bible Dictionary).

Pahath-moab was the ancestor of a large Jewish family group whose descendants returned from the Babylonian exile. The name means "governor of Moab" according to Easton's Bible Dictionary, or "sheik of Moab" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, which suggests the clan was probably named after an ancestor who held that title. His descendants came back with Zerubbabel through two family lines, Jeshua and Joab, numbering 2,812 in Ezra 2:6 and 2,818 in the parallel list in Neh 7:11. A further 200 males came with Ezra, led by Elihoenai son of Zerahiah. Eight men of this family are named among those who had married foreign wives. Because the name is shared by several people, and later passages such as Neh 3:11 and Neh 10:14 use it for the clan or its head, it is not always clear which individual is meant.

Pahath-moab is named in Neh 3:11 as the father of Hashub, who repaired a section of the wall of Jerusalem and the Tower of the Furnaces in Nehemiah's day. Nothing else is said about him personally. Elsewhere Pahath-moab is the name of a large family group whose members returned from exile in Babylon (Ezra 2:6; Neh 7:11), and a leader of that name joined in sealing the covenant under Nehemiah (Neh 10:14). So "son of Pahath-moab" here may mean a member of that family line rather than a literal son. The name, which probably means "governor of Moab," is shared by several people, and it is uncertain how this figure relates to the others.

Pahath-moab was one of the "chief of the people" who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, when the community in Jerusalem bound itself to keep the law (Neh 10:14). He appears in that list next to Parosh, Elam, Zatthu and Bani. The name means "governor of Moab." Several of the names in this list also appear elsewhere as family names. Ezra 2:6 and Neh 7:11 record a large clan called "the children of Pahath-moab" among the exiles who returned from Babylon. So this signer probably stood for that clan or was its head, rather than being a person known in any other way. Because the name is used for both a family and its leaders, it is not certain which individual is meant here.

Pai was the royal city of Hadad, a king of Edom who reigned after Baalhanan, according to 1 Chr 1:50. The same verse names Hadad's wife as Mehetabel, daughter of Matred. The parallel king list in Genesis 36:39 gives the city's name as Pau and the king's name as Hadar, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the two forms as the same place. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of Pau as "howling" or "sighing." The text gives no clue to where the city stood, and its site has not been identified. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it remains unidentified. The location shown here is only an approximate placement within the territory of Edom, south of the Dead Sea in what is now southern Jordan.

Palal was the son of Uzai and one of the men who repaired the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah after the return from exile. His only mention is in the list of builders in Neh 3:25. His section lay opposite the turning, or angle, of the wall and the tower that projected from the king's upper house, near the court of the prison. Pedaiah the son of Parosh worked on the next section after him. Nothing more is known of his family or later life. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "judge."

Pallu was the second of the four sons of Reuben, Jacob's firstborn. His brothers were Hanoch, Hezron and Carmi, and he appears second in every list of them. Genesis 46:9 spells his name Phallu and places him among the family members who went down to Egypt with Jacob. Exodus 6:14 names him as the head of a father's house within Reuben. In the wilderness census he is the founder of the Palluite clan of the tribe (Num 26:5). His son was Eliab, and the next verse, Num 26:9, names Eliab's sons as Nemuel, Dathan and Abiram, the Dathan and Abiram who later joined Korah's rebellion. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that Peleth in Num 16:1 may be the same man. Smith's Bible Dictionary and that encyclopedia take the name to mean "distinguished".

Palti son of Raphu was the man from the tribe of Benjamin chosen as one of the twelve leaders Moses sent from the wilderness of Paran to explore the land of Canaan (Num 13:9). Each tribe supplied one representative for this mission. By inference from the rest of Numbers 13–14, Palti was among the ten spies who brought back a discouraging report, since only Joshua and Caleb are singled out for urging Israel to enter the land. Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "deliverance from the Lord," and Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "whom Jehovah delivers." He is distinct from Phalti (also spelled Palti in some translations), the man to whom Saul gave his daughter Michal.

Paltiel son of Azzan was the leader ("prince") of the tribe of Issachar named in Num 34:26. He appears in a list of tribal leaders whom the Lord appointed, according to the surrounding passage, to work with Eleazar the priest and Joshua in dividing the land of Canaan west of the Jordan among the tribes. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name is usually explained as meaning "God delivers" or "deliverance of God" (Easton's Bible Dictionary; Smith's Bible Dictionary). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his appointment to about 1450 BC. The same name is also borne by a different man, Michal's husband, called Paltiel in 2 Sam 3:15 and Phalti in 1 Sam 25:44, who should not be confused with this tribal leader.

Pamphylia was a coastal region in the middle of the southern shore of Asia Minor, lying between Lycia to the west and Cilicia to the east, in what is now the area around Antalya in southern Turkey. People from Pamphylia were in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:10). On their first missionary journey, Paul and his company sailed from Paphos on Cyprus to Perga in Pamphylia, and there John Mark left them and went back to Jerusalem (Acts 13:13). Paul and Barnabas passed through Pamphylia again on their return from Pisidia (Acts 14:24). Mark's departure in Pamphylia later led Paul to refuse to take him on another journey (Acts 15:38). Years afterward, the ship carrying Paul to Rome sailed across the sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia to Myra in Lycia (Acts 27:5). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that in Paul's time it was a Roman province.

Paphos was a city on the west coast of Cyprus, visited by Barnabas and Saul (Paul) on their first missionary journey, about AD 45 by inference from context. After crossing the island from Salamis, they met a Jewish sorcerer and false prophet named Bar-jesus there (Acts 13:6). The next verses (Acts 13:7–12) place the Roman proconsul Sergius Paulus at Paphos, which fits Easton's Bible Dictionary's description of it as the island's capital and the governor's residence. From Paphos, Paul and his companions sailed to Perga in Pamphylia, where John left them and returned to Jerusalem (Acts 13:13). Ancient writers used the name for two towns: Old Paphos (modern Kouklia), famous for its temple of Aphrodite, and New Paphos, its harbor about ten miles northwest. Easton's, Smith's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take the city in Acts to be New Paphos, and the location shown here follows that identification.

The Parable of the Winseskins (wineskins) was a pair of short sayings by Jesus recorded in Matthew, Mark and Luke. It immediately follows the question of why his disciples did not fast. No one sews a patch of new, unshrunk cloth onto an old garment, because the patch pulls away and makes the tear worse. No one pours new wine into old wineskins (the King James Version's "bottles"), because the skins burst, the wine is spilled and the skins are ruined. New wine must go into new skins, so that both are preserved. Luke's account calls the sayings a parable and adds that no one who has drunk old wine immediately wants new, because he says the old is better (Luke 5:39). The setting is probably Capernaum, inferred from the surrounding narrative, and the date is about AD 28, also inferred from context.

Parah was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Benjamin. It appears only once, in the list of Benjamin's cities, where it is named between Avim and Ophrah (Josh 18:23). The name probably means "heifer," and Smith's Bible Dictionary calls it "heifer-town." Nothing else is recorded about it. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify it with the ruins of Far'ah in the Wadi Far'ah, about 6 miles (10 km) northeast of Jerusalem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places the site about 3 miles northeast of Anata, ancient Anathoth, on a valley that runs into the Wadi Suweinit. Easton's describes the valley as a branch of the Wadi Kelt. The location shown here follows this Far'ah identification.

Paran was a desert region south of Canaan, usually called "the wilderness of Paran." Ishmael lived there after leaving Abraham's household, and his mother found him a wife from Egypt (Gen 21:21). After leaving Sinai, the Israelites' guiding cloud stopped there, and they camped there after Hazeroth (Num 10:12; 12:16). Moses sent the spies out from Paran, and they reported back at Kadesh within it (Num 13:3, 26). It is also named as a landmark in Deut 1:1. David went there after Samuel's death (1 Sam 25:1). According to the surrounding passage, Hadad the Edomite and his men passed through it from Midian on their way to Egypt (1 Kgs 11:18). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the et-Tih plateau of northeastern Sinai, west of the Arabah. The rough location shown here lies farther south, near Wadi Feiran in southern Sinai, a name often linked with Paran.

Parbar was a structure or area on the west side of the temple precinct in Jerusalem, named only in the list of gatekeepers' posts at 1 Chr 26:18: four guards at the causeway and two at Parbar. The word is rare and its meaning uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it as an open area or suburb west of the temple. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a proposed Persian origin meaning something open to the light, which would suggest a colonnade or portico. It also connects the term to a related plural form at 2 Kgs 23:11, translated "suburbs" in the King James Version. STEPBible's proper-names list describes it as a colonnade or structure on the west side of the temple complex. The location shown here places it at the western side of the Temple Mount, an inference from the word "westward" in the verse.

Parmashta was one of the ten sons of Haman, the official who plotted to destroy the Jews of the Persian Empire. He is named only in the list of Haman's sons in Esth 9:7–10. By context these verses record the men killed by the Jews in Shushan (Susa), the Persian royal city, on the day Haman's decree was reversed, the events remembered at the festival of Purim. His brothers were Parshandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha, Poratha, Adalia, Aridatha, Arisai, Aridai and Vajezatha. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "strong-fisted," Smith's Bible Dictionary "superior," and Hitchcock's Bible Names "a yearling bull." The name is probably Persian. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint renders it Marmasima. Smith's dates his death to about 473 BC.

Parmenas was one of the seven men chosen by the Jerusalem church to take charge of the daily distribution of food to its widows, so that the apostles could devote themselves to prayer and teaching (Acts 6:5). By inference from context, this took place about AD 30. He is named sixth in the list, alongside Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon and Nicolas. His name is Greek, a shortened form of Parmenides according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Like the other six, he probably came from the Greek-speaking Jewish believers whose widows had been overlooked.
