The seven are often called deacons, though the passage does not use that title for them. Scripture does not mention him again. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia record a tradition that he was martyred at Philippi during the reign of the emperor Trajan.

Parnach was a man of the tribe of Zebulun, known only as the father of Elizaphan. In Num 34:25 Elizaphan is named as the prince, or leader, of Zebulun among the tribal representatives chosen to help divide the land of Canaan among the Israelite tribes. Since his son was a leader in the generation that was to enter the land, Parnach probably belonged to the generation that left Egypt, though this is an inference. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain: the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "gifted," while Hitchcock's Bible Names suggests "a bull striking, or struck."

Parosh was the ancestor and head of an Israelite family that returned to Jerusalem from exile in Babylon. The lists of returnees in Ezra 2:3 and Nehemiah 7:8 count 2,172 of his descendants, the largest lay family in those lists. Seven men from this family appear in Ezra 10:25 among those who had married foreign wives in Ezra's time. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds that part of the family came back later with Ezra (Ezra 8:3, spelled "Pharosh" in the King James Version). It also notes that a descendant named Pedaiah helped rebuild the city walls (Neh 3:25), and that the name appears among those who sealed Nehemiah's covenant (Neh 10:14). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "a flea." Several people in the Bible share this name. Nothing is recorded about Parosh himself beyond his descendants.

Parosh was the father of Pedaiah, who repaired a section of the Jerusalem wall in Nehemiah's day. Pedaiah worked next to Palal, near the tower that projected from the king's upper palace by the court of the prison (Neh 3:25). Nothing else is said about Parosh himself. Parosh is also the name of a large family that returned from exile (Ezra 2:3; Neh 7:8), so "son of Parosh" may mean Pedaiah was a member of that clan rather than the son of a man by that name. The text does not settle this. Because several people bear this name, it is uncertain how this Parosh relates to the others. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a flea."

Parosh was one of the chiefs of the people who set their seal to the written covenant made in the time of Nehemiah, in which the returned exiles pledged to keep the law of God (Neh 10:14). He heads the list of lay leaders who signed. Parosh is also the name of a large family that returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:3; Neh 7:8). Because the names that follow in Neh 10:14, such as Pahathmoab, Elam and Zatthu, are also family names from those return lists, this Parosh was probably the head or representative of that clan rather than a separately known individual. STEPBible's proper-names index likewise describes him as a clan leader. Several people in the Bible bear this name, and the text says nothing more about this one. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "a flea."

Parshandatha was one of the ten sons of Haman, the official of the Persian king Ahasuerus who plotted to destroy the Jews. He is named first in the list of Haman's sons in Esth 9:7–10. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary take this placement to mean he was the eldest. The surrounding passage records that the Jews killed the ten sons in Shushan, the Persian royal city, on the day Haman's decree was meant to be carried out. His brothers were Dalphon, Aspatha, Poratha, Adalia, Aridatha, Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai and Vajezatha. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may come from a Persian phrase meaning "given by prayer," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the same meaning. Smith's dates his death to about 473 BC, which is an estimate drawn from context.

Paruah was the father of Jehoshaphat, one of the twelve officers King Solomon appointed over districts of Israel. Jehoshaphat's district was the territory of Issachar (1 Kgs 4:17). The surrounding passage explains that each of these officers supplied food for the king and his household for one month of the year. Nothing else is recorded about Paruah himself; he is known only through his son's name. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of his name as "flourishing," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "blooming." Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his son's service to about 1017 BC, an estimate drawn from the timing of Solomon's reign.

Parvaim was a place or region named as the source of the gold Solomon used to decorate the temple in Jerusalem, mentioned only in 2 Chr 3:6. Its location is unknown, and there are several views. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that some identify it with Ophir, the better-known source of Solomon's gold, but that it is uncertain whether the word is a place name at all. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mention a suggested link to a Sanskrit word meaning "eastern," which would make it a general term for "Oriental regions." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also records proposed sites in Arabia, such as Farwa in Yemen, and a view that it is a shortened form of Sephar (Gen 10:30). This entry gives no location.

Pas-dammim was a place where the Philistines gathered for battle against Israel. A barley field there became the scene of a stand by David and one of his mighty men. By inference from the preceding verse (1 Chr 11:12), that man was Eleazar son of Dodo. The people fled, but the two held their ground (1 Chr 11:13). The parallel list in 2 Sam 23:9–12 describes similar deeds without naming the place. Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia all treat Pas-dammim as the same place as Ephes-dammim, where the Philistines camped between Socoh and Azekah before David fought Goliath (1 Sam 17:1). Easton gives the name's meaning as "border of blood." The location shown here follows that identification, placing it in the Elah Valley area of the Judean lowlands, southwest of Jerusalem.

Pasach was a son of Japhlet and a member of the tribe of Asher. He is named only once, in the genealogy of Asher's descendants, where he is listed first among Japhlet's three sons, followed by his brothers Bimhal and Ashvath (1 Chr 7:33). Japhlet appears in the preceding verse as a son of Heber, which places Pasach in the line of Heber, the grandson of Asher. Nothing else is recorded about his life. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "clearing," Smith's Bible Dictionary "cut off," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia "divider."

Paseah was a son of Eshton, named in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chr 4:12. His brothers were Beth-rapha and Tehinnah, and Tehinnah is called the father of Ir-nahash. The verse closes by calling this family "the men of Rechah," a group or place that is otherwise unknown. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes the passage as an obscure fragment of Judah's genealogies, and nothing more is recorded about Paseah himself. His name is usually explained as meaning "lame" or "limping" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Other men named Paseah appear elsewhere in the Bible, and this one should not be confused with them.

Paseah was the father of Jehoiada (called Joiada in many modern translations), who worked with Meshullam son of Besodeiah to repair the Old Gate of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. They laid its beams and set up its doors, locks and bars (Neh 3:6). Nothing else is said about Paseah himself. He appears only as the father who identifies his son. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "limping," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "passing over; halting." Several people in the Bible share this name, including a man in the genealogy of Judah and the ancestor of a family of temple servants who returned from exile. This entry concerns only the father of the Old Gate repairer. Whether he is connected to either of the others is not stated.

Pashur, son of Malchijah, was a priest and the ancestor of a priestly family that returned from exile in Babylon. The genealogies of Adaiah, a priest who lived in Jerusalem after the return, trace his line back to Pashur. 1 Chr 9:12 gives a short form of the line, and Neh 11:12 gives a longer one that names Pashur's son Zechariah. The family known as the children of Pashur numbered 1,247 among those who came back from exile (Ezra 2:38; Neh 7:41). Later, several of its members were among the priests who had married foreign wives in Ezra's time (Ezra 10:22). Several men in the Bible share this name. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both suggest he may be the Pashur son of Malchiah who served as an official under King Zedekiah (Jer 38:1), but this identification is uncertain.

Pashur was a priest who set his seal to the covenant made in the time of Nehemiah, the written pledge by the returned exiles to keep God's law. He appears in Neh 10:3 among the priests listed after Nehemiah the governor. The verse itself gives only his name, and the priestly role follows from the context of the list. Several men in the Bible bear this name, and they are hard to tell apart. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he may be the same as another Pashur of the same period, probably the head of the priestly family of Pashur whose descendants returned from exile. The name has been explained as meaning "splitter" or "cleaver."

Pashur, son of Immer, was a priest and chief officer in the temple at Jerusalem in the time of Jeremiah. When he heard Jeremiah prophesying disaster, he struck the prophet and put him in the stocks at the upper Gate of Benjamin beside the temple (Jer 20:1–2). On releasing him the next day, Pashur was told by Jeremiah that the LORD had renamed him Magormissabib, meaning "terror on every side" (Jer 20:3). Jeremiah also announced that Pashur and his household would go into captivity, and that he would die and be buried in Babylon along with the friends to whom he had prophesied lies (Jer 20:6). Smith's Bible Dictionary places the episode in the reign of Jehoiakim. He is distinct from Pashur son of Malchiah, another opponent of Jeremiah, since the name is shared by several people in the Bible.

Pashur the son of Melchiah was an official of King Zedekiah of Judah, one of several men in the Bible named Pashur. In Jer 21:1 Zedekiah sent him, together with Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah the priest, to ask Jeremiah to inquire of the LORD. Judging from the following verses, this was during the Babylonian attack on Jerusalem. He is probably the same Pashur son of Malchiah who appears in Jer 38:1, where he is among the officials who heard Jeremiah's warnings and urged the king to have him put to death. He is distinct from Pashur the son of Immer, the priest who had Jeremiah beaten and put in the stocks (Jer 20:1–2). Some link him to the priestly family of Pashur son of Malchijah named in 1 Chr 9:12, though this is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "whiteness."

Pashur is known only as the father of Gedaliah, one of the royal officials in Jerusalem who heard Jeremiah's prophecies during the Babylonian siege in the reign of Zedekiah (Jer 38:1). In the passage that follows, Gedaliah and the other officials urge the king to put Jeremiah to death, and the prophet is lowered into a cistern. Nothing else is recorded about Pashur himself. Several men share this name, and he is distinct from Pashur the son of Malchiah, who is named in the same verse. Some suggest he may be the priest Pashur son of Immer, who had Jeremiah beaten and put in stocks (Jer 20:1–2), but the text does not make the link, and the identification is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "that extends or multiplies the hole" or "whiteness."

Patara was a port city on the southwest coast of Lycia, in what is now southwestern Turkey. It is mentioned once in the Bible, as a stop on Paul's voyage from Miletus to Jerusalem at the end of his third missionary journey, about AD 54 by inference from context. Sailing by way of Cos and Rhodes, Paul's party reached Patara (Acts 21:1). The next verse says they found a ship there crossing to Phoenicia and boarded it, so Patara was where they changed vessels for the open-sea crossing. Easton's Bible Dictionary says this ship brought Paul to Tyre. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes Patara as a wealthy harbor known for an oracle of Apollo and as the birthplace of Saint Nicholas. It places the ruins near the modern village of Gelemiş, and the location shown here matches that site.

Pathros was a region of Egypt, generally identified as Upper Egypt, the southern Nile valley above Memphis. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as the Hebrew form of an Egyptian term meaning "the South land," and Easton's Bible Dictionary contrasts it with Lower Egypt in the north. Isaiah lists it among the distant lands from which a scattered remnant of God's people would be brought back (Isa 11:11). After the fall of Jerusalem, Jews lived there alongside communities at Migdol, Tahpanhes and Noph (Memphis), and Jeremiah addressed them about worshipping other gods (Jer 44:1, 15). Ezekiel calls it Egypt's land of origin, where the Egyptians would return as a lowly kingdom, and also foretells its desolation (Ezek 29:14; 30:14). The Pathrusim of Gen 10:14 are probably its people. The location shown here is a point in the Nile valley standing for the region as a whole.

Pathrusim is named in the Table of Nations as one of the descendants of Mizraim, son of Ham, listed alongside Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim, Casluhim and Caphthorim (Gen 10:14; 1 Chr 1:12). The plural ending marks the name as a people rather than a single individual. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explain it as "the people of Pathros," a branch of the Egyptians, since Mizraim is the Hebrew name for Egypt. Pathros appears elsewhere in the prophets, for example Jer 44:1 and Ezek 29:14, as a region of Egypt where Judeans later lived. It is usually identified with Upper (southern) Egypt, the Nile valley south of the Delta. Nothing else is recorded about the Pathrusim beyond the two parallel genealogical lists.

Patmos is a small, rocky island in the Aegean Sea, off the southwest coast of Asia Minor (modern Turkey), where John says he was staying when he received the visions recorded in the Book of Revelation. It is named only once in the Bible, in Rev 1:9, where John describes himself as a companion of his readers in tribulation and says he was on the island "for the word of God, and for the testimony of Jesus Christ." The verse does not say he was exiled, but early Christian tradition preserved by Irenaeus, Eusebius and Jerome holds that he was banished there under the emperor Domitian, about AD 95, and later returned to Ephesus. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Rome used such islands as places of exile. The island still bears the name Patmos today and belongs to the Dodecanese group of Greece, and a cave there is traditionally shown as the place of John's visions.

Patrobas was a Christian in Rome whom Paul greeted by name at the close of his letter to the Romans. He appears in a group of five men, Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas and Hermes, together with "the brethren which are with them" (Rom 16:14). This suggests, by inference, that they belonged to the same household or house church. Nothing more is said about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name is a shortened form of Patrobius. A wealthy freedman of the emperor Nero with that name was later put to death by Galba, and this Patrobas may have been one of his dependents. Smith's Bible Dictionary likewise observes that the name was borne by members of the imperial household. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "paternal."

Pau was the city of Hadar, one of the kings who ruled Edom before Israel had a king. Genesis lists Hadar as the successor of Baal-hanan son of Achbor and names his wife as Mehetabel, daughter of Matred (Gen 36:39). The parallel list in 1 Chr 1:50 spells the name Pai. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the name's meaning as "bleating." Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that its position is unknown. The location shown here is only approximate. It places Pau in the highlands of ancient Edom, southeast of the Dead Sea in what is now southern Jordan, as the general region where an Edomite royal city would have stood.

Paul, also called Saul, was a Jew born in Tarsus who became the leading missionary of the early church. As a young man named Saul he watched the clothes of those who stoned Stephen and then persecuted believers (Acts 7:58). Jesus appeared to him on the road to Damascus, and Ananias restored his sight (Acts 9:17). With Barnabas he preached in Cyprus and Asia Minor, where the people of Lystra called him the god Mercurius (Acts 14:12). Later, with Silas and Timothy, he founded churches in Macedonia and Greece and worked at Ephesus. He was arrested in the Jerusalem temple and heard by Felix, Festus and Agrippa. He appealed to Caesar, survived a shipwreck, and lived two years under guard in Rome (Acts 28:30). Thirteen New Testament letters bear his name. Hebrews does not name its author, and this entry follows the tradition that Paul wrote it.

Paul and Barnabas part ways in Acts 15:35–39, shortly after the Jerusalem Council, about AD 47 by inference from context. After a period of teaching and preaching in Antioch of Syria, Paul proposed that the two of them revisit the believers in every city where they had preached. Barnabas wanted to take John Mark with them, but Paul refused because Mark had left them in Pamphylia and had not continued with them in the work, an event described in Acts 13:13. The disagreement became so sharp that they separated. Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus, while the following verse (Acts 15:40) says Paul chose Silas and set out on his own. Col 4:10 describes Mark as Barnabas's cousin, which may help explain Barnabas's support for him. Later letters such as 2 Tim 4:11 show Paul speaking well of Mark again.

The imprisonment of Paul and Silas took place at Philippi during Paul's second missionary journey, about AD 47 by inference from context. After Paul drove a spirit of divination out of a slave girl, her owners lost their income. They dragged Paul and Silas before the magistrates and accused them, as Jews, of disturbing the city and teaching customs unlawful for Romans. A crowd joined the attack. The magistrates had the two men stripped, beaten with many blows, and handed to a jailer, who locked their feet in stocks in the inner prison. At midnight, as they prayed and sang, an earthquake shook the prison, opened its doors and loosened every prisoner's chains. The jailer was about to kill himself, but Paul assured him everyone was still there. The jailer asked how to be saved, heard their message, washed their wounds, and was baptized with his household. He then fed them in his home.

The release of Paul and Silas was the end of their imprisonment at Philippi during the Second Missionary Journey, about AD 47 by inference from context. The morning after the jailer's conversion, the city magistrates sent officers to the jail with orders to let the two men go, and the jailer passed the message to Paul. Paul refused to leave quietly. He pointed out that they were Roman citizens who had been publicly beaten and imprisoned without a trial, and he demanded that the magistrates come and escort them out themselves. On hearing that the prisoners were Romans, the magistrates were afraid. They came in person, appealed to them, brought them out, and asked them to leave the city. Paul and Silas first went to Lydia's house, where they met and encouraged the believers, and then left Philippi.

The Paul appeals to Caesar episode took place at Caesarea, about AD 56 by inference from context, when Porcius Festus had newly become governor. On a visit to Jerusalem, Festus heard the high priest and Jewish leaders ask that Paul be brought there, intending to ambush and kill him on the way. Festus kept Paul at Caesarea and invited his accusers to come and present their case. Back at Caesarea, Festus took the judgment seat, and the accusers brought many serious charges they could not prove. Paul answered that he had done nothing against the Jewish law, the temple or Caesar. When Festus, wishing to please the Jews, asked whether Paul would stand trial in Jerusalem, Paul refused. He declared that he stood at Caesar's tribunal and appealed to Caesar. After conferring with his council, Festus ruled that Paul would go to Caesar.

Paul arrested in the Temple was the riot in Jerusalem that ended Paul's freedom at the close of his third missionary journey, about AD 54 by inference from context. Near the end of seven days, which the preceding passage links to a purification rite Paul had joined (Acts 21:26), Jews from Asia saw him in the temple and stirred up the crowd. They accused him of teaching against the people, the law and the temple, and of bringing Greeks inside, because they had seen him in the city with Trophimus, an Ephesian. The crowd dragged Paul out, shut the doors and beat him, intending to kill him. The Roman commander, later named as Claudius Lysias (Acts 23:26), arrived with soldiers, bound Paul with two chains and, unable to learn the facts amid the uproar, had him taken to the fortress, probably the Antonia beside the temple. Soldiers carried him up the stairs as the crowd shouted, "Away with him."

Paul arrives at Rome is the final stage of Paul's voyage to Rome as a prisoner, dated here to about AD 57 by inference from context. After three months on Malta, the party sailed on an Alexandrian ship whose figurehead was Castor and Pollux. They stopped three days at Syracuse, went on to Rhegium, and with a south wind reached Puteoli the next day. There they found believers and stayed seven days before travelling toward Rome. Believers from Rome came out to meet them at Appii Forum and Three Taverns, and Paul thanked God and took courage. At Rome the centurion handed the prisoners over, but Paul was allowed to live by himself with a soldier guarding him. The centurion is Julius, and Aristarchus is among the travellers (Acts 27:1–2). Luke is probably the narrator, by inference from the "we" passages.

event: Paul casts demon out of soothsayer
text: Paul casts demon out of soothsayer is the episode at Philippi, during the Second Missionary Journey, in which Paul freed a slave girl from a spirit of divination. It followed Lydia's conversion. As the missionaries were going to the place of prayer, they met a young woman whose fortune-telling earned her owners a great deal of money. For many days she followed Paul and his companions, crying out that they were servants of the most high God who showed the way of salvation. Troubled by this, Paul turned and commanded the spirit in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her, and it left that same hour. The "we" of the narrative implies that Luke was present, along with Silas and Timothy. The following verses (Acts 16:19–24) tell how the owners, having lost their income, had Paul and Silas beaten and jailed. The date, about AD 47, is inferred from context.

Paul gives his testimony is the speech Paul made in Jerusalem just after his arrest in the Temple, near the end of his third missionary journey (about AD 54, by inference from context). As soldiers led him into the fortress, he spoke Greek to the commander, who had taken him for an Egyptian rebel, and asked to address the crowd. Standing on the stairs, he spoke in Hebrew. He described his upbringing in Jerusalem under Gamaliel, his persecution of believers, and his encounter with Jesus on the road to Damascus. He told how Ananias restored his sight and baptized him, and how he later had a vision in the Temple sending him to the Gentiles. At that word the crowd demanded his death. The commander ordered him examined by scourging, but Paul revealed that he was a Roman citizen by birth, and the soldiers drew back.

Paul goes before Agrippa was a hearing at Caesarea, about AD 56 by inference from context, at which Paul, then a prisoner, spoke before King Agrippa and Bernice. The Roman governor Festus arranged it with great ceremony before military officers and leading citizens. Paul had appealed to the emperor, called Augustus and Caesar, and Festus needed a clear charge to send with him (Acts 25:23–27). Given permission to speak, Paul described his early life as a Pharisee, his persecution of Jesus' followers, his vision of Jesus on the road to Damascus, and his commission to preach to Jews and Gentiles (Acts 26:4–23). Festus interrupted, calling him mad. Paul then appealed to the king's belief in the prophets, and Agrippa replied, "Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian." Afterward the officials agreed Paul had done nothing deserving death or prison. Agrippa remarked that he could have been freed had he not appealed to Caesar.

The episode of Paul going before the Council took place in Jerusalem, about AD 54 by inference from context. It came the day after Paul gave his testimony to the crowd. The Roman commander, wanting to learn exactly why the Jews accused Paul, released him from his chains and set him before the chief priests and their council. Paul declared that he had lived in good conscience before God, and the high priest Ananias ordered him struck on the mouth. Paul called him a "whited wall" but then said he had not known he was the high priest. Seeing that the council held both Sadducees and Pharisees, Paul announced that he was a Pharisee on trial over the resurrection of the dead. The two parties quarreled so violently that the commander had soldiers remove Paul to the fortress. That night the Lord told Paul he must also bear witness in Rome.

event: Paul is shipwrecked by a storm
text: Paul is shipwrecked by a storm is the episode in Acts 27 in which the ship taking Paul as a prisoner to Rome was wrecked, probably about AD 57 by inference from context. After leaving Crete, the ship was caught by a violent wind called Euroclydon and driven past the island of Clauda. The crew braced the hull, feared the quicksands (the Syrtis shoals off North Africa), and threw tackle and cargo overboard. Paul said an angel had promised that no life would be lost. On the fourteenth night, adrift in Adria, the sailors sensed land. Paul stopped them from escaping in the boat and urged all 276 aboard to eat. The ship ran aground and broke apart, but the centurion (Julius, named in Acts 27:1) kept the soldiers from killing the prisoners, and everyone reached land. The "we" narration suggests Luke was aboard, and Acts 27:2 names Aristarchus.

The episode of Paul preaching in Athens was part of his Second Missionary Journey, following his mission to Berea, and is dated to about AD 48 by inference from context. While waiting in Athens for his companions, Paul was troubled by the city's many idols. He debated in the synagogue with Jews and God-fearers and argued daily in the marketplace. Epicurean and Stoic philosophers, curious about his teaching on Jesus and the resurrection, brought him to the Areopagus (Mars' Hill). There Paul pointed to an altar inscribed "To the Unknown God" and spoke of the God who made the world and does not live in temples made by hands. He quoted Greek poets and called all people to repent, citing God's raising of a man from the dead. Some listeners mocked, and others wanted to hear more. A few believed, including Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris.

Paul's First Roman imprisonment was the period Paul spent under guard in Rome awaiting a hearing before Caesar, dated here to about AD 57 by inference from context. Three days after arriving, Paul, still chained, called the leading Jews together. He explained that Roman officials had found no capital charge against him, but Jewish opposition had forced him to appeal to Caesar. They replied that they had received no reports about him. On an appointed day he argued about Jesus from the law and the prophets. Some believed and some did not, and he quoted Isaiah on hearing without understanding, declaring that salvation was sent to the Gentiles. Acts ends with him living two full years in a rented house, receiving visitors and preaching freely. Col 4:10–14 and Phlm 23–24 place Epaphras, Luke and Demas with him as a prisoner, probably during this period.

Paul's Journey to Rome was Paul's voyage as a prisoner from the eastern Mediterranean to Italy, told in Acts 27–28. He and other prisoners were handed to Julius, a centurion of Augustus' band, and sailed by way of Sidon, Myra in Lycia and Fair Havens on Crete. The narrator's "we" places the writer aboard, traditionally identified as Luke, and Acts 27:2 also names Aristarchus. The crew set out late in the season against Paul's warning, was caught by the Euroclydon wind, and drifted fourteen days before running aground on Melita, probably modern Malta. All 276 people aboard reached land. There Paul survived a viper bite and healed the father of Publius. The group later sailed via Syracuse to Puteoli and went on to Rome. Paul lived there under guard, met Jewish leaders, and preached openly. This entry dates the journey to about AD 56, by inference from context.

Paul sent to Felix is the episode in which the Roman commander Claudius Lysias moved Paul from Jerusalem to the governor Felix at Caesarea after learning of a plot to kill him. Soldiers took Paul by night by way of Antipatris, carrying a letter saying he was accused only over questions of Jewish law, with nothing deserving death or prison. Five days later the high priest Ananias arrived with elders and an orator, Tertullus, who accused Paul of stirring unrest, leading the Nazarene sect and profaning the temple. Paul denied the charges, saying he was on trial over the resurrection of the dead. Felix postponed a decision and kept Paul under guard with some freedom. He and his wife Drusilla heard Paul speak, and Felix hoped for a bribe. After two years Porcius Festus replaced Felix, who left Paul in custody. The date, about AD 56, is inferred from context.

Paul speaks to Ephesian Elders describes Paul's farewell address to the leaders of the church at Ephesus, given at Miletus during his third missionary journey, about AD 54 by inference from context. Stopping at Miletus on his way to Jerusalem, Paul sent for the elders (Acts 20:17). He reminded them how he had served among them in Asia, teaching publicly and from house to house and warning them for three years. He said he was going to Jerusalem expecting imprisonment and hardship, and that they would not see him again. He charged them as overseers to care for the church and warned that false teachers would arise from outside and from among them. He pointed to his own manual work and quoted Jesus: "It is more blessed to give than to receive." He then knelt and prayed with them, and they wept and took him to the ship. Luke, whose "we" narrative surrounds the scene, was probably present.

Paul stays at Malta is the episode in Acts 28 that follows the shipwreck on Paul's voyage to Rome as a prisoner, dated here to about AD 57 by inference from context. The survivors learned that the island was called Melita, generally identified with modern Malta. The local people welcomed them with a fire against the rain and cold. When a viper fastened on Paul's hand, the islanders first took him for a murderer pursued by justice. When he shook it off unharmed, they said he was a god. Publius, the island's chief man, lodged the party for three days. Paul prayed for Publius's father, who was sick with fever and dysentery, laid hands on him and healed him, and other sick islanders then came and were healed. The narrator's "us" points to Luke. Acts 27:1–2 names the centurion Julius and Aristarchus as also on board.

Paul visits elders in Jerusalem is the event in which Paul, the day after reaching Jerusalem at the end of his third missionary journey, met James and all the elders of the church there, about AD 54 by inference from context. The narrator writes "us," and Luke, traditionally regarded as the author of Acts, is understood to have been present. Paul reported in detail what God had done among the Gentiles through his work, and the elders praised God. They then warned him that thousands of Jewish believers, zealous for the law, had heard he taught Jews abroad to abandon circumcision and the customs of Moses. To counter this, they asked him to join four men under a vow, pay their costs for shaving their heads, and purify himself with them. They also restated their earlier ruling for Gentile believers, recorded in Acts 15:29. The next day Paul entered the temple with the men.

The writing of Galatians is the occasion when the apostle Paul composed his letter to the churches of Galatia. The letter opens by naming Paul as an apostle sent "not of men, neither by man, but by Jesus Christ, and God the Father" (Gal 1:1), and it is addressed to the churches of the region of Galatia, in what is now central Turkey (Gal 1:2). The date of about AD 49 is an estimate inferred from context. It places the letter soon after Paul and Barnabas returned to Antioch in Syria from their first missionary journey (Acts 14:26–28), and before the Jerusalem council described in Acts 15. Some scholars instead date the letter later, to the mid-50s, during Paul's stay in Ephesus. This entry follows the earlier date.

The Pavement was the place in Jerusalem where Pilate sat on the judgment seat to pass sentence on Jesus. John 19:13 gives its Hebrew (Aramaic) name as Gabbatha. The Greek word behind "Pavement" means a surface paved with stone, and Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests a floor of coloured mosaic stones. Easton's also notes that Roman governors often set up their tribunals in open public places, and places this one probably in front of the governor's judgment hall. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes it as lying outside the Praetorium. Its exact site is uncertain. One traditional view links it to the area of the Antonia Fortress north of the temple. Another places it at Herod's palace in the western part of the city. The location shown here marks only a general point within Jerusalem and does not follow either view.

Pedahel, son of Ammihud, was the leader of the tribe of Naphtali in the list of Numbers 34. The surrounding chapter shows that these tribal leaders were appointed, one from each tribe, to help Eleazar the priest and Joshua divide the land of Canaan among the Israelites. This is his only mention in the Bible. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the meaning of his name as "whom God redeems" or "redeemed of God." His father Ammihud should not be confused with other men of that name in the Old Testament.

Pedahzur was a man of the tribe of Manasseh, known only as the father of Gamaliel, the leader of that tribe during the wilderness period after the Exodus. He appears solely in Gamaliel's identifying phrase "Gamaliel the son of Pedahzur." That phrase is used when Gamaliel is named to help Moses take the census (Num 1:10), when he is set as captain of Manasseh in the camp (Num 2:20), when he brings his tribe's offering on the eighth day of the altar's dedication (Num 7:54, 59), and when he leads Manasseh's company on the march (Num 10:23). Nothing else is recorded about Pedahzur himself. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "rock of redemption," and Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "strong or powerful savior" or "stone of redemption."

Pedaiah was a man from Rumah whose daughter Zebudah became the wife of King Josiah of Judah and the mother of King Jehoiakim, who began to reign at twenty-five and ruled eleven years in Jerusalem (2 Kgs 23:36). Nothing else is recorded about him. Since Jehoiakim was the father of Jeconiah, who appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, Pedaiah stands in that line through his daughter. The location of Rumah is uncertain. Some connect it with Arumah near Shechem, mentioned in Judg 9:41. The name means "Yah redeems" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a son of King Jeconiah in 1 Chr 3:18–19, and they should not be confused with this Pedaiah.

Pedaiah was a son of Jehoiachin (also called Jeconiah), the king of Judah taken captive to Babylon, and so belonged to the royal line of the tribe of Judah. He is named among Jehoiachin's seven sons, alongside Shealtiel, Malchiram, Shenazar, Jecamiah, Hoshama and Nedabiah (1 Chr 3:18). By inference he was born during the Babylonian exile, as the STEPBible proper-names index notes. His sons were Zerubbabel and Shimei (1 Chr 3:19). Elsewhere, as in Ezra 3:2, Zerubbabel is called the son of Shealtiel, Pedaiah's brother. Smith's Bible Dictionary mentions a suggestion that Zerubbabel became Shealtiel's heir because Shealtiel had no children of his own. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes other possible explanations. The name means "the Lord redeems," and several other men in the Bible share it.

Pedaiah was the father of Joel, who led the half-tribe of Manasseh among the tribal rulers listed in King David's administration (1 Chr 27:20). Nothing else is recorded about him. Because the next verse (1 Chr 27:21) names a separate leader for the half of Manasseh in Gilead, Joel's half-tribe was probably the western one, west of the Jordan, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also understands it. The name means "the LORD redeems." Several other men in the Bible are also called Pedaiah, and this one is not clearly identified with any of them.

Pedaiah, son of Parosh, was one of the men who repaired the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah. In the list of builders, his section comes right after that of Palal son of Uzai. Palal worked near the turn of the wall and the tower projecting from the king's upper house by the court of the guard (Neh 3:25). Pedaiah's stretch therefore probably lay in the same area, on the eastern side of the city. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes "son of Parosh" to mean a member of the family of that name. Parosh was a large family that returned from exile in Babylon. Smith's dates the work to about 446 BC, an estimate from context. The name means "the Lord redeems." Several other men in the Bible share it, and this one is known only from this verse.

Pedaiah was one of the men who stood on Ezra's left on the wooden platform when Ezra the scribe read the book of the law aloud to the people of Jerusalem (Neh 8:4). He appears in a group of seven on the left, with six more on the right, but the verse gives nothing else about him: no father, no role and no further actions. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as apparently a priest, while the STEPBible proper names index calls him a Levite. Both views rest on inference from his place beside Ezra at the public reading. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the event to about 445 BC. Hitchcock's Bible Names explains the name as meaning "redemption of the Lord." Several other men in the Bible share this name, and this Pedaiah should not be assumed to be any of them.

Pedaiah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only in the genealogy of Sallu in Neh 11:7. He was the son of Kolaiah and the father of Joed, and he was an ancestor of Sallu, one of the Benjamites who settled in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. The verse traces Sallu's line back several generations, through Meshullam, Joed, Pedaiah, Kolaiah, Maaseiah and Ithiel to Jesaiah. Pedaiah himself therefore probably lived well before the return, although the text gives no dates for him and nothing else is recorded about him. His name means "the Lord redeems" or "redemption of the Lord" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other men in the Bible share the name Pedaiah, and they should not be confused with this one.

Pedaiah was a Levite whom Nehemiah appointed as one of the treasurers over the storehouses during his reforms in Jerusalem. He served with Shelemiah the priest and Zadok the scribe, with Hanan son of Zaccur as their assistant. Nehemiah chose these men because they were considered trustworthy, and their job was to distribute the stored supplies to their fellow Levites and temple workers (Neh 13:13). The context suggests these were the tithes of grain, wine and oil brought to the temple storerooms. His name means "the LORD redeems." Several men in the Bible share this name. Smith's Bible Dictionary considers this Levite to be apparently the same Pedaiah who stood beside Ezra at the public reading of the law, probably the one in Neh 8:4, though the text does not say so directly.

Pekah son of Remaliah was a king of the northern kingdom of Israel. A captain under King Pekahiah, he conspired with Argob, Arieh and fifty men of Gilead, killed Pekahiah in the palace at Samaria and took the throne (2 Kgs 15:25). He is said to have reigned twenty years, from about 759 to 739 BC by inference from context. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that other chronologies make his reign later and shorter. Allied with Rezin king of Syria, he made war on Judah. According to 2 Chr 28:6 he killed 120,000 men in one day, and he besieged Ahaz in Jerusalem without taking it (2 Kgs 16:5; Isa 7:1). In his days Tiglath-pileser of Assyria seized Gilead, Galilee and Naphtali and carried their people captive. Hoshea son of Elah then conspired against him, killed him and reigned in his place. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives his name's meaning as "open-eyed."

Pekahiah was a king of Israel, the son and successor of Menahem. He began to reign in Samaria in the fiftieth year of Azariah (Uzziah) king of Judah and ruled for two years. His other acts were recorded in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel. The surrounding passage adds that he continued the worship practices begun by Jeroboam (2 Kgs 15:24). It also says that Pekah son of Remaliah, one of his captains, conspired with fifty men of Gilead and killed him in the palace at Samaria, then took the throne (2 Kgs 15:25). This entry dates his reign to about 761–759 BC, by inference from context, following Easton's Bible Dictionary. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives 759–757 BC, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that many scholars place it later, after 738 BC. His name is usually explained as "the LORD has opened (the eyes)."

Pekod was a people or district of Babylonia named in two prophetic passages. In Jer 50:21 God orders an attack on the land of Merathaim and on the inhabitants of Pekod, as part of the judgment announced against Babylon. In Ezek 23:23 Pekod appears alongside the Babylonians, the Chaldeans, Shoa, Koa and the Assyrians among the horsemen and nobles whom God would bring against Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it as probably a place in Babylonia. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe it as a name applied to the Chaldeans. Because the word can mean "visitation" or "punishment," some read it in Jeremiah as a symbolic name for Babylon as the city marked for judgment, a wordplay paired with Merathaim. Its exact location is uncertain. The location shown here places it in central Babylonia, near the site of Babylon.

Pelaiah was a son of Elioenai and one of seven brothers, along with Hodaiah, Eliashib, Akkub, Johanan, Dalaiah and Anani, listed in 1 Chr 3:24. That verse comes at the end of the genealogy of David's descendants in 1 Chronicles 3, which traces the royal line of Judah through the kings and on past the exile through Zerubbabel. This places Pelaiah several generations after the return from exile. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to some time after 400 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in this family list. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "the Lord's secret or miracle." The same name belongs to other men in the Bible, including Levites of Ezra and Nehemiah's time, and they should not be confused with this descendant of David.

Pelaiah was a Levite in Jerusalem in the time of Ezra and Nehemiah. He was one of a group of Levites who helped the people understand the law while Ezra read it aloud to the gathered assembly, and the people stood in their places as they listened (Neh 8:7). A Levite named Pelaiah also appears among the Levites who set their seal to the covenant of commitment led by Nehemiah (Neh 10:10). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat these as the same man, and this entry follows that view, though the name is shared by more than one person in the Bible. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that he is called Phalias in 1 Esdras 9:48. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 445 BC. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "the Lord's secret or miracle."

Pelaliah was a member of a priestly family, named only in the genealogy of Adaiah, one of the priests who lived in Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time (Neh 11:12). He was the son of Amzi and the father of Jeroham, which made him Adaiah's grandfather. The line goes back through Zechariah and Pashur to Malchiah. Nothing else is recorded about him. The parallel list in 1 Chr 9:12 gives Adaiah's ancestry more briefly and leaves out Pelaliah, Amzi and Zechariah, a common way of shortening genealogies. The name is usually explained as "the LORD judges" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "judged by Jehovah" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "entreating the Lord."

Pelatiah was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the royal genealogy of 1 Chr 3 as a son of Hananiah. The preceding verse, 1 Chr 3:19, names Hananiah as a son of Zerubbabel, so Pelatiah was Zerubbabel's grandson and a descendant of King David and Solomon, as Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note. He is listed with Jesaiah. The verse then names the sons of Rephaiah, Arnan, Obadiah and Shechaniah. This entry treats these men as Pelatiah's brothers, though the wording can also be read as listing separate family lines. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him after 536 BC, after the return from exile, a date inferred from his descent from Zerubbabel. His name means "the Lord delivers." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and nothing more is recorded about this one.

Pelatiah was a man of the tribe of Simeon, one of the four sons of Ishi, along with Neariah, Rephaiah and Uzziel. The four brothers led a force of five hundred Simeonites to Mount Seir, the hill country of Edom south of the Dead Sea (1 Chr 4:42). The following verse, 1 Chr 4:43, says this band struck down the surviving Amalekites there and settled in their place. Smith's Bible Dictionary places the expedition in the reign of Hezekiah, about 700 BC, by inference from the surrounding context in 1 Chr 4:41. His name means "the Lord delivers." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a descendant of David, a leader who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah's day, and a prince of Jerusalem in Ezekiel's vision. This Pelatiah is known only from this one passage.

Pelatiah was one of the men who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, binding the returned exiles to keep the law of God. He appears among the leaders of the people in that list, beside Hanan and Anaiah (Neh 10:22). Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of the heads of the people and suggests the name may stand for a family rather than a single person. It dates the event to about 440 BC, a date inferred from context. His name means "the Lord delivers" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share this name, and he should not be confused with them.

Pelatiah son of Benaiah was one of the "princes of the people" in Jerusalem whom the prophet Ezekiel saw in a vision. The spirit brought Ezekiel to the east gate of the temple, where he saw twenty-five men, among them Jaazaniah son of Azur and Pelatiah (Ezek 11:1). Ezekiel was told to prophesy against these men, whom the surrounding passage describes as devising mischief and giving wicked counsel in the city. While Ezekiel was prophesying, Pelatiah died, and Ezekiel fell on his face and cried out, asking whether God would make a full end of the remnant of Israel (Ezek 11:13). His name means "the LORD delivers" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Bible share the name Pelatiah; this one is known only from Ezekiel's vision.

Peleg was a son of Eber and brother of Joktan, in the line of Shem. His name means "division," and Genesis explains it by saying that "in his days was the earth divided" (Gen 10:25; 1 Chr 1:19). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links this to the scattering of peoples at Babel in Gen 11:1–9. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries instead see a split within Eber's own family, with Joktan's descendants moving into Arabia. This entry follows the second view. Peleg fathered Reu at thirty and lived another 209 years, 239 in all, having other sons and daughters. Through Reu he was an ancestor of Abraham (Gen 11:20–26). Luke's genealogy of Jesus includes him under the Greek form Phalec (Luke 3:35). By inference from the chronology in Genesis, he lived from about 2247 to 2008 BC.

Pelet was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once as one of the six sons of Jahdai in the genealogy of Judah (1 Chr 2:47). His brothers were Regem, Jotham, Gesham (spelled Geshan in the King James Version), Ephah and Shaaph. The passage does not say how Jahdai fits into the surrounding family line. He appears among the descendants of Caleb, but his exact link to them is left open. Nothing else is recorded about Pelet. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "liberation," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "deliverance." Other men named Pelet appear elsewhere in the Bible, among them a man of Benjamin who joined David at Ziklag and a descendant of Jerahmeel. This entry concerns only the son of Jahdai.

Pelet, son of Azmaveth and brother of Jeziel, was one of the warriors who came to David at Ziklag (1 Chr 12:3). The surrounding passage describes these men as kinsmen of Saul from the tribe of Benjamin who joined David while he was still keeping away from Saul. Easton's Bible Dictionary accordingly calls Pelet a Benjamite. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that "son of Azmaveth" could mean either a native of the town of Azmaveth or a son of the Azmaveth who was one of David's mighty men. The name means "deliverance" or "liberation." Nothing more is recorded about him. Another man named Pelet appears in the genealogy of Judah, so the name refers to more than one person.

Peleth was a man of the tribe of Reuben and the father of On. His son joined Korah, Dathan and Abiram in their rebellion against Moses and Aaron during Israel's time in the wilderness (Num 16:1). Nothing else is recorded about Peleth himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "swiftness." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he is probably the same person as Pallu, a son of Reuben, which would explain why the verse counts On among the "sons of Reuben." The name Peleth is also borne by at least one other man in the Bible, a descendant of Judah, who is a different person.

Peleth was a son of Jonathan and a brother of Zaza, named in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah at 1 Chr 2:33. He belonged to the family line of Jerahmeel, a descendant of Judah through Hezron. In context, his father Jonathan was a son of Jada, who was a son of Onam, but the passage records nothing about Peleth beyond his name and family. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of the name as "swiftness." The same name is borne by another man in the Bible, Peleth the father of On, a Reubenite who joined Korah's rebellion, and the two should not be confused.

Pelusium is the Greek name for the Egyptian city that Ezekiel calls Sin. In his prophecy against Egypt, Ezekiel names Sin as "the strength of Egypt" and says it will suffer fury, fire and great pain, alongside No (Thebes) and Noph (Memphis) (Ezek 30:15–16). Easton's Bible Dictionary explains that both the Hebrew and Greek names mean "clayey" or "muddy," from the clay found there. It takes the phrase "the strength of Egypt" to mean an important fortified city, which fits a stronghold on Egypt's northeastern frontier. Easton's identifies the site with the modern Tineh, where a few red granite columns survive. The ruins are usually located near the eastern edge of the Nile Delta, southeast of modern Port Said, at a site also known as Tell el-Farama. The location shown here is an approximate placement in the surrounding region rather than the exact site.

Peniel, meaning "face of God," is the name Jacob gave to the place where he wrestled through the night before meeting Esau. He named it because, he said, he had seen God face to face and his life had been spared (Gen 32:30). The next verse and later passages use the form Penuel. Judg 8:8–17 says Gideon later tore down the tower of Penuel, and 1 Kgs 12:25 says Jeroboam fortified it. The narrative places it near the Jabbok River (the modern Zarqa) east of the Jordan, and Smith's Bible Dictionary notes it was not far from Succoth. Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mentions Merrill's identification with Tulul edh-Dhahab, twin ruin-covered hills by the Jabbok, and Conder's suggestion of Jebel Osha. The location shown here follows the Tulul edh-Dhahab identification.

Peninnah was one of the two wives of Elkanah, a man from the hill country of Ephraim. The other was Hannah, the mother of Samuel. Unlike Hannah, who was childless, Peninnah had children (1 Sam 1:2). When Elkanah offered sacrifices at the yearly festival, he gave portions to Peninnah and to all her sons and daughters (1 Sam 1:4). The verses that follow describe her as Hannah's rival, who provoked Hannah year after year because Hannah had no children (1 Sam 1:6–7). This is also how the STEPBible proper names list from Tyndale House describes her. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls her Elkanah's second wife. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of her name as "coral" or "pearl" and dates her to about 1125 BC, an estimate drawn from context.

Penuel was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:4 as a son of Hur, the firstborn of Ephratah and "father of Bethlehem." Penuel himself is called "the father of Gedor." In these Judahite lists, "father" of a place usually means its founder or the head of the clan that settled there, so Penuel was probably regarded as the founder of the town of Gedor. That town is probably the Gedor listed among the hill-country towns of Judah in Josh 15:58. His brother Ezer is named alongside him as the father of Hushah. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is shared with a Benjamite in 1 Chr 8:25 and with the place where Jacob wrestled. Hitchcock's Bible Names treats it as the same name as Peniel, usually understood as "face of God."

Penuel was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named as one of the sons of Shashak in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. He appears in a list of eleven brothers that includes Ishpan, Heber, Eliel, Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Hananiah, Elam, Antothijah and Iphedeiah (1 Chr 8:25). The chapter places Shashak's family among the Benjamite heads of households who lived in Jerusalem. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is shared by other people in the Bible, including a man of Judah in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 4, and it is also the name of the place where Jacob wrestled. Hitchcock's Bible Names treats the name as the same as Peniel, usually understood to mean "face of God."

Penuel was a city east of the Jordan River, near Succoth and the Jabbok River, according to Easton's Bible Dictionary. Its name means "face of God," and it is also spelled Peniel. Jacob was passing Penuel at sunrise, limping on his thigh, after wrestling through the night (Gen 32:31). The surrounding passage explains that he named the place because he had seen God face to face. Later, when Gideon was pursuing the Midianite kings, the men of Penuel answered him as Succoth had. The preceding verses show this was a refusal to give his troops bread. Gideon threatened to break down their tower, and on his return he did so and killed the men of the city (Judg 8:8–9, 17). After the kingdom divided, Jeroboam built Penuel, probably fortifying it (1 Kgs 12:25). The location shown here follows a common identification with Tulul edh-Dhahab on the Jabbok, the modern Zarqa River in Jordan.

Peor was a mountain peak in Moab. It was the last of the heights to which King Balak brought Balaam so that he could curse Israel (Num 23:28). The verse says it "looketh toward Jeshimon," the wasteland below. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it in the Abarim range near Pisgah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia records Eusebius's statement that it lay between Livias and Heshbon, and Buhl's identification of it with Jebel el-Mashaqqar. The location shown here is a rough position in that area, northeast of the Dead Sea. In other passages "Peor" is short for Baal-peor, the god worshipped there. "The matter of Peor" refers to Israel's idolatry with the Moabites and Midianites, which Num 31:16 links to Balaam's counsel. It brought a plague on the congregation and was still remembered in Joshua's day (Num 25:18; Josh 22:17). The name is often taken to mean "opening" or "cleft."

Peresh was a son of Machir and his wife Maachah, listed in the genealogy of the tribe of Manasseh, one of the two tribes descended from Joseph. According to 1 Chr 7:16, his mother named him, and his brother was Sheresh. The same verse says “his sons were Ulam and Rakem,” but it does not make clear whether these were the sons of Peresh or of Sheresh. Since Machir was Manasseh’s son (1 Chr 7:14), Peresh was Manasseh’s grandson, and Gilead was his brother. Peresh appears only in this verse, and nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is explained in different ways. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give “dung,” while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives “horseman.”

Perez-uzza, meaning "breach of Uzza," was the name David gave to the place where the LORD struck down Uzza during the first attempt to bring the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem (1 Chr 13:11). The surrounding passage and the parallel account in 2 Sam 6:6–8, which spells it Perez-uzzah, explain that Uzza died after taking hold of the ark when the oxen pulling its cart stumbled. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the threshing floor named Chidon in Chronicles and Nachon in Samuel. Its exact site is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it not far from Kirjath-jearim, where the journey began. The location shown here is only a rough placement on the route toward Jerusalem, close to the city.

Perez-uzzah, meaning "breach of Uzzah," was the name David gave to the place where the LORD struck down Uzzah (2 Sam 6:8). By inference from the surrounding passage (2 Sam 6:6–7), Uzzah had taken hold of the ark of God when the oxen stumbled while it was being carried toward Jerusalem, and he died there. The narrative calls the spot Nachon's threshing floor, and the parallel account in 1 Chr 13:9–11 calls it the threshing floor of Chidon. The name was still in use when the account was written. Its exact site is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it not far from Kirjath-jearim, where the journey of the ark began. The location shown here is only a rough placement near Jerusalem, the destination of the journey.

Perga was a city of Pamphylia on the southern coast of Asia Minor, in present-day Turkey. Paul and his companions reached it after sailing from Paphos on Cyprus during the first missionary journey, about AD 45 by inference from context. At Perga, John (Mark) left the group and went back to Jerusalem, while Paul and Barnabas travelled inland to Antioch in Pisidia (Acts 13:13–14). On their return journey they preached in Perga and then went down to the port of Attalia, from which they sailed back to Antioch in Syria (Acts 14:25). Easton's Bible Dictionary calls it the capital of Pamphylia and places it on the river Cestrus, about 7 miles from the sea. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it was known for the worship of a local goddess identified with Artemis. The location shown here is the ruined site near modern Aksu, east of Antalya.

Pergamum (spelled Pergamos in the King James Version) was a city in the Roman province of Asia, in western Asia Minor. It was home to one of the seven churches to which John was told to send what he saw (Rev 1:11), and it receives its own message from the one "which hath the sharp sword with two edges" (Rev 2:12). According to Easton's Bible Dictionary, the letter that follows says that "Satan's seat" was there. It also rebukes the church for holding the teachings of Balaam and the Nicolaitans, and it names Antipas as a faithful martyr killed in the city. Easton's describes Pergamum as the chief city of Mysia, standing near the Caicus River about 20 miles from the sea, and notes that parchment took its name from the city. The location shown here is the modern Turkish town of Bergama.

Perida was the ancestor of a family listed among the descendants of "Solomon's servants" who returned from exile in Babylon. The family appears in the parallel lists of returnees in Ezra and Nehemiah, where it is named between the families of Sotai and Sophereth. Nehemiah 7:57 spells the name Perida, while Ezra 2:55 has Peruda, a small difference in the Hebrew spelling for the same person. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that he also appears as Pharida in 1 Esdras 5:33. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries place this return under Zerubbabel, which Smith dates to before 536 BC. Nothing else is recorded about Perida himself. The meaning of the name is uncertain: Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "grain, kernel," the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia "recluse," and Hitchcock's Bible Names "separation; division."

Persia was the empire, and originally the homeland, of the Persians, in what is now Iran. In the Bible it appears mainly as the power that followed Babylon. Babylon's captives served there "until the reign of the kingdom of Persia" (2 Chr 36:20), and Cyrus king of Persia proclaimed that the Jews could return and rebuild the temple in Jerusalem. Ezra names the later kings Darius and Artaxerxes, under whom the work was opposed, then finished and carried on. Esther and Daniel pair Persia with Media, as in the two-horned ram of Dan 8:20. Ezekiel lists Persians as soldiers in the army of Tyre and as allies of Gog. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name properly means the province of Fars in southwestern Iran. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes an empire stretching from the Indus to Thrace. The location shown here is a general point in western Iran, near modern Hamadan, representing the wider region.

Persis was a Christian woman in the church at Rome whom Paul greeted near the end of his letter to the Romans (Rom 16:12). He calls her "the beloved Persis" and says she "laboured much in the Lord," a phrase that sets her apart from Tryphena and Tryphosa, named in the same verse, who "labour in the Lord." The past tense may suggest that her work had been done earlier. Nothing more is said about her family, origin or role. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "a Persian woman," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name is attested in Rome for a freedwoman, so she may have come from that background, though the text does not say. Smith's dates the letter to about AD 55.

Simon Peter, also called Cephas and Simeon, was one of the twelve apostles of Jesus and a leading figure in the early church. Son of Jonas and brother of Andrew, he was a fisherman on the Sea of Galilee when Jesus called him (Matt 4:18; John 1:40). With James and John he belonged to an inner group present at the raising of Jairus's daughter and in Gethsemane. He confessed Jesus as the Christ but was sharply rebuked soon after (Mark 8:29; Matt 16:23). During the trials he denied Jesus three times, then wept bitterly. The risen Jesus appeared to him (Luke 24:34; 1 Cor 15:5). In Acts he preached in Jerusalem, healed the sick, was imprisoned by Herod and freed by an angel, and preached to the Gentile Cornelius at Caesarea. Paul stayed with him in Jerusalem and later publicly challenged him (Gal 1:18; 2:14). The letters 1 and 2 Peter bear his name.

Peter and John's Trial was the apostles' hearing before the Jewish leaders in Jerusalem, following Peter's preaching in Solomon's Portico, about AD 30 by inference from context. Priests, the temple captain and Sadducees, angered that they preached resurrection through Jesus, arrested them and held them overnight, yet about five thousand men believed. Next day the rulers, elders and scribes gathered with Annas, Caiaphas, John, Alexander and the high priest's kindred, and asked by what power a lame man had been healed. Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, answered that it was by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom they had crucified and God had raised. Amazed at the boldness of these unschooled men and unable to deny the miracle, the council forbade them to teach in Jesus' name. The apostles replied they must obey God, and were released after further threats, because of the people.

The Peter defends Gentile salvation episode took place in Jerusalem after Peter's visit to the Roman centurion Cornelius in Caesarea, about AD 38 by inference from context. When the apostles and believers in Judea heard that Gentiles had received the word of God, Jewish believers who insisted on circumcision criticized Peter for entering the home of uncircumcised men and eating with them. Peter answered by retelling events in order. He described his vision at Joppa of a sheet full of animals and a voice telling him not to call unclean what God had cleansed, and the arrival of three men from Caesarea. He said the Spirit sent him with them, and six fellow believers went along. As he spoke to Cornelius's household, the Holy Spirit came on them as it had on the first believers. Hearing this, his critics fell silent and praised God for granting Gentiles repentance leading to life.

Peter heals Aeneas and Dorcas describes two miracles performed by the apostle Peter while visiting believers near the coast, about AD 38 by inference from context. At Lydda (probably modern Lod) he found Aeneas, paralyzed and bedridden for eight years, and told him that Jesus Christ healed him. Aeneas rose at once, and the people of Lydda and Saron (the plain of Sharon) turned to the Lord. At nearby Joppa (modern Jaffa), a disciple named Tabitha, also called Dorcas, known for her good works and charity, fell ill and died. The disciples sent two men to fetch Peter, and widows showed him garments she had made. Peter sent everyone out, knelt, prayed, and told her to arise. She sat up, and he presented her alive. Many in Joppa believed, and Peter stayed there many days with Simon, a tanner. The episode follows the account of Saul's early preaching.

Peter meets Cornelius is the account in Acts 10 of the apostle Peter's visit to a Gentile centurion at Caesarea. Cornelius, an officer of the Italian band, was devout, gave alms and prayed constantly. In a vision an angel told him to send to Joppa for Simon Peter, who was lodging with Simon a tanner by the sea. The next day, as the messengers neared Joppa, Peter fell into a trance on the housetop. He saw a sheet full of animals let down from heaven and heard a voice telling him to kill and eat. When he refused, the voice said that what God had cleansed he must not call common. The Spirit then told him to go with the men. At Caesarea, Cornelius had gathered his relatives and friends. Peter told them God had shown him not to call anyone unclean, and Cornelius asked to hear his message. The event is dated here to about AD 38, by inference from context.

Peter preaches at Pentecost is the sermon Simon Peter gave in Jerusalem on the day the Holy Spirit came on the disciples, about AD 30 by inference from context. Standing with the other eleven apostles, he answered the charge that they were drunk by pointing out that it was only the third hour of the day, about 9 a.m. He explained what the crowd was seeing as the fulfillment of Joel's prophecy of the Spirit poured out on all people. He then spoke of Jesus of Nazareth, whom God had shown to be approved by miracles, who had been crucified, and whom God raised from death. Peter quoted David's psalms to argue that Jesus is both Lord and Christ. When his hearers asked what they should do, he told them to repent and be baptized in Jesus' name. About three thousand people were baptized that day.

Peter preaches in Solomon's Portico is the speech Simon Peter gave to a crowd in Jerusalem right after he and John healed a lame man, about AD 30 by inference from context. The colonnade called Solomon's was part of the temple complex, where the preceding healing took place. As the healed man held on to the two apostles, astonished people gathered around them. Peter told them the healing came not from his own power or holiness but through faith in the name of Jesus. He said the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob had glorified Jesus, whom the people had handed over and denied before Pilate, asking for a murderer instead, and whom God raised from the dead. Peter allowed that they and their rulers had acted in ignorance. He urged them to repent so their sins would be wiped away, and he cited Moses' promise of a coming prophet and God's covenant with Abraham.

event: Peter preaches to gentiles in Caesarea
text: The episode of Peter preaching to gentiles in Caesarea is the speech Simon Peter gave in the house of the Roman centurion Cornelius, following their meeting earlier in Acts 10. It is dated to about AD 38 by inference from context. Peter began by saying that God shows no partiality and accepts people from every nation who fear him. He then summarized the story of Jesus of Nazareth: his anointing with the Holy Spirit, his healings, his death on a tree, and his resurrection on the third day, witnessed by chosen followers who ate and drank with him. Peter added that Jesus is appointed judge of the living and the dead, and that whoever believes in him receives forgiveness of sins. While he was still speaking, the Holy Spirit came on the listeners, who spoke in tongues. This astonished the Jewish believers with Peter, and Peter had the gentiles baptized.

Peter's Mother-in-law and Others Healed is an episode recorded in Matthew, Mark and Luke and set in Capernaum, probably in about AD 27 by inference from context. After leaving the synagogue, where he had just freed a possessed man, Jesus went into the house of Simon Peter and Andrew with James and John. Simon's mother-in-law lay sick with a high fever. Jesus took her by the hand and lifted her up. In Luke's account he stood over her and rebuked the fever. The fever left her at once, and she got up and served them. That evening at sunset, people brought the sick and those possessed by demons, and the whole town gathered at the door. Jesus laid hands on the sick and healed many. He cast out demons but would not let them speak, because they knew he was the Christ. Matthew links the healings to Isaiah's words about bearing sicknesses.

Pethahiah was a priest who headed the nineteenth of the twenty-four priestly divisions. These divisions were assigned by lot in the time of David, and each one took its turn serving at the sanctuary (1 Chr 24:16). The surrounding chapter presents the arrangement as part of David's organization of the priests descended from Eleazar and Ithamar. Pethahiah is mentioned only in this list, so nothing else is known about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 1020 BC, an estimate drawn from the context of David's reign. His name is usually explained as meaning "Yahweh opens" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, including a Levite in the time of Ezra and Nehemiah and an official serving the Persian king. This entry refers only to the head of the nineteenth priestly course.

Pethahiah was a Levite in the time of Ezra, named in Ezra 10:23 among the Levites who had married foreign women. In the wider passage, those listed agreed to send away these wives as part of the reform Ezra led after the return from exile in Babylon. Nothing else is recorded about him in this verse. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as "the Lord opening" or "gate of the Lord," belongs to several men in the Bible. They include the head of a priestly division in David's time (1 Chr 24:16) and a Levite who helped lead the people's prayer of confession in Nehemiah's day (Neh 9:5). Because that Levite lived in the same period, he may be the same man as the one in Ezra 10:23, but the text does not say so, and this entry treats the connection as uncertain.

Pethahiah was a Levite in the time of Nehemiah. He was one of eight Levites, along with Jeshua, Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabniah, Sherebiah, Hodijah and Shebaniah, who called the gathered people of Jerusalem to stand and bless the LORD. This took place during the day of fasting and confession that followed the reading of the Law (Neh 9:5). The prayer that follows in the chapter recounts Israel's history. The name is often explained as meaning "the Lord opens" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several men in the Bible bear this name. A Levite named Pethahiah appears among those who had married foreign wives in Ezra 10:23, and some identify him with this man. That link is possible but not certain, and this entry treats only the Levite of Neh 9:5.

Pethahiah, son of Meshezabeel, was a man of the tribe of Judah, from the family of Zerah, Judah's son. He lived in the time of Nehemiah, after the return from exile. Neh 11:24 says he "was at the king's hand in all matters concerning the people." Easton's Bible Dictionary takes this to mean he held some office at the Persian court, and the STEPBible name index describes him as appointed to represent the people before the Persian king. The king in question was probably Artaxerxes, whom Nehemiah served. Nothing more is recorded about him. His name is usually explained as "Yahweh opens" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Bible share the name, so he should not be confused with them.

Pethor was the home town of Balaam son of Beor, the man Balak king of Moab sent for to curse Israel (Num 22:5). It is described as lying "by the river" in the land of Balaam's people, and Deut 23:4 places it in Mesopotamia (Aram-naharaim). "The river" most likely means the Euphrates. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Easton's Bible Dictionary identify Pethor with Pitru, a town mentioned by the Assyrian king Shalmaneser. Pitru stood on the west bank of the Euphrates near its meeting with the Sajur River, a few miles south of Carchemish. That would put it about 400 miles from Moab. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the site as unknown. The location shown here follows the Pitru identification, at a site in northern Syria near the Sajur–Euphrates junction, probably modern Tell Aushariye.

Pethuel was the father of the prophet Joel. He is named only once in the Bible, in the opening line of the book of Joel, where the prophet is introduced as "Joel the son of Pethuel" (Joel 1:1). Nothing else is recorded about him: his tribe, home, and lifetime are not given. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to before 800 BC, but this depends on how the book of Joel itself is dated, which is uncertain. The meaning of his name is also explained in different ways. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give "vision of God," the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "God's opening," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "mouth of God" or "persuasion of God."

Peulthai was a Levite listed as the eighth of the brothers Shemaiah, Jehozabad, Joah, Sacar, Nethaneel, Ammiel and Issachar, in the roster of temple gatekeepers organized in David's time. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 26:4) presents these brothers as sons of Obed-edom, and Easton's, Smith's and the Tyndale House proper-names list all identify him that way. This entry names his father as Shimei, which the passage itself does not do. The verse ends with the note that God blessed Obed-edom with these many sons. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the fuller form of his name as Peullethai and explains it as "my wages". Easton's Bible Dictionary renders it "wages of the Lord", and Hitchcock's gives "my works". Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith dates him to about 1020 BC, an estimate inferred from the setting in David's reign.

Phaltiel was the son of Laish from Gallim and the second husband of Michal, Saul's daughter. After David fled from Saul, Saul gave Michal, who was already David's wife, to him. 1 Sam 25:44 calls him Phalti. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "deliverance of the Lord." Later, after Saul's death, Ishbosheth took Michal away from Phaltiel and returned her to David. The surrounding passage explains that David demanded this as a condition for his agreement with Abner (2 Sam 3:14). The next verse says Phaltiel followed her, weeping, as far as Bahurim, until Abner ordered him to go home (2 Sam 3:16). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes a different Phaltiel, a "captain of the people" in the apocryphal book of 2 Esdras, who is not the same man.

Phanuel was the father of Anna, the elderly prophetess of the tribe of Asher, according to Luke 2:36. He is mentioned only here, to identify his daughter, and nothing else is said about him. Since Anna belonged to the tribe of Asher, he did too. Luke tells how Anna, who had been widowed after seven years of marriage, met the infant Jesus when he was brought to the temple in Jerusalem. Phanuel's name is the Greek form of the Hebrew Penuel and means "face of God" (Easton's Bible Dictionary; Hitchcock's Bible Names). It is the same name Jacob gave the place where he wrestled by the Jabbok. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates Phanuel to about 80 BC, an estimate based on his daughter's great age at the time of Jesus' birth.

Pharaoh (during Abraham's Journey) was the unnamed king of Egypt when Abram (Abraham) went down to Egypt during a famine, about 1921 BC by inference from context. His officials praised the beauty of Abram's wife Sarai to him, and she was taken into his house (Gen 12:15). Abram had presented her as his sister, as the surrounding passage explains.
