The LORD then struck Pharaoh and his household with great plagues because of Sarai (Gen 12:17). Pharaoh summoned Abram and asked why he had not said she was his wife (Gen 12:18). He then had his men send Abram away with his wife and all his possessions (Gen 12:20). The text does not give his name, and "Pharaoh" is a royal title meaning "great house." Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he was probably one of the Hyksos, or "shepherd kings," a foreign Semitic dynasty ruling from Zoan (Tanis).

Pharaoh (of Joseph) was the unnamed king of Egypt during Joseph's years there. His officer Potiphar bought Joseph as a slave (Gen 39:1). In anger he jailed his chief butler and chief baker, whose dreams Joseph interpreted (Gen 41:10). When Pharaoh dreamed of seven thin ears of grain devouring seven full ones, the butler remembered Joseph. Joseph explained that seven years of plenty would be followed by seven years of famine. Pharaoh set Joseph over Egypt and gave him his ring, the name Zaphnathpaaneah and a wife, Asenath (Gen 41:42–45). He later welcomed Joseph's family, sent wagons for Jacob, let them settle in Goshen, and was blessed by Jacob (Gen 47:7). Through Joseph he acquired the land of Egypt and a fifth of its produce. The Bible does not name him. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries suggest Apophis, a Hyksos king, while others place Joseph under Thutmose III.

Pharaoh here is the Egyptian king who oppressed the Israelites in the years before and around the birth of Moses. "Pharaoh" was the title of Egypt's rulers, so the name belongs to several different kings in the Bible. This one set taskmasters over the Hebrews and made them build the store cities of Pithom and Raamses for him (Exod 1:11). When the Hebrew midwives failed to kill newborn boys, he ordered his people to throw every Hebrew son into the river (Exod 1:19, 22). His daughter found the infant Moses in a basket among the reeds (Exod 2:5). Later, when he heard that Moses had killed an Egyptian, he tried to kill him, and Moses fled to Midian (Exod 2:15). His identity is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that he was long thought to be Ahmose I, but it favors Seti I, father of Rameses II.

Pharaoh (of the Exodus) was the king of Egypt who refused to let the Israelites leave their forced labor. When Moses and Aaron demanded their release, he made the work harder, called on his magicians, and repeatedly agreed and then refused as the plagues struck Egypt. After the death of the firstborn he let the people go, then pursued them with his chariots, and his army was drowned in the Red Sea. Later writers recall these signs and his overthrow (Neh 9:10; Ps 136:15), and Paul quotes God's words to him (Rom 9:17). The Bible never gives his personal name, and "Pharaoh" is also used for other Egyptian kings. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests Menephtah (Merneptah), son of Rameses II, or his son Seti II. Smith's Bible Dictionary also mentions Thothmes III. This entry does not settle on one identification.

Pharaoh, a title of the kings of Egypt (meaning "great house" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary), here refers to the Egyptian king of the time of David and Solomon. Solomon made an alliance with him and married his daughter, bringing her to the city of David until his palace, the temple and Jerusalem's wall were finished. He later moved her to a house built for her. This Pharaoh captured and burned the Canaanite city of Gezer and gave it to his daughter as a wedding gift. He also received Hadad the Edomite, who had fled from David. He gave Hadad a house, food and land, and married him to the sister of his queen, Tahpenes. Their son Genubath grew up among Pharaoh's sons. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats Hadad's protector and Solomon's father-in-law as possibly different kings. This entry treats them as one person.

Pharaoh in these passages is the king of Egypt in the time of King Hezekiah of Judah, probably the late eighth century BC. When the Assyrian king Sennacherib threatened Jerusalem, Judah looked to this Pharaoh for help. The Assyrian envoy mocked that hope, calling Egypt a broken reed that pierces the hand of anyone who leans on it (2 Kgs 18:21; Isa 36:6). Isaiah likewise condemned those who went down to Egypt to rely on Pharaoh's strength, warning that it would bring them shame (Isa 30:2–3). He also ridiculed the counsellors of Pharaoh at Zoan (Isa 19:11), probably the same king or one close in time. The Bible does not give this king's personal name, and the title was used for many Egyptian rulers. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him with Sethos, a king named by Herodotus. The nearby account in 2 Kgs 19:9 mentions Tirhakah, king of Ethiopia, marching against Sennacherib.

Pharaoh, in this entry, is the Egyptian king named only once, in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah at 1 Chr 4:18. There his daughter Bithiah is said to have been taken as wife by Mered, a descendant of Judah, and to have borne him sons. The verse gives this king no personal name and no other detail, and it does not say when he reigned. "Pharaoh" was the common title of Egypt's native kings rather than a personal name, and Smith's Bible Dictionary explains it as meaning "the great house." Because the Bible uses the same title for several different rulers, this Pharaoh cannot be securely identified with any other Pharaoh mentioned in Scripture or with a known Egyptian king. Some have suggested that "daughter of Pharaoh" may simply mean an Egyptian woman of high or royal standing, but the text itself says no more.

Pharaoh here is the king of Egypt named in Jeremiah's prophecy of the cup of the Lord's wrath. Jeremiah lists him, together with his servants, princes and all his people, among the nations made to drink it (Jer 25:19). "Pharaoh" was the standard title of Egypt's rulers rather than a personal name, so several different kings in the Bible are called by it. The passage does not name this one. Jeremiah 25:1 dates the prophecy to the fourth year of Jehoiakim king of Judah, and Jer 46:2 names the Egyptian king of that year as Pharaoh-necho, defeated at Carchemish. By inference, the ruler meant here is probably Necho, though the verse itself speaks of Egypt's king only by title. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "that disperses" or "that spoils."

Pharaoh, also called Pharaoh-hophra, was the king of Egypt in the last years of the kingdom of Judah. In Jer 44:30, Jeremiah announces that God would hand him over to those seeking his life, as Zedekiah of Judah had been handed to Nebuchadrezzar of Babylon. The Pharaoh in Ezekiel's oracles is probably the same king, judging by their date and setting. Ezekiel says his great army would not help Zedekiah in the war with Babylon (Ezek 17:17). He pictures Pharaoh as a great dragon claiming the Nile as his own creation, and says his arms would be broken while Babylon's king was strengthened against Egypt. A lament portrays him brought down among the slain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies him with Apries, a grandson of Pharaoh Necho who reigned about 589–570 BC and died after a revolt. Other kings of Egypt are also called Pharaoh.

Pharaoh-nechoh, also called Necho, was a king of Egypt in the late 7th century BC. STEPBible Proper Names identifies him as Neco II. He marched north to the Euphrates to fight at Carchemish, and Josiah king of Judah went out to oppose him. Necho warned Josiah off with words that 2 Chronicles describes as coming "from the mouth of God," but Josiah fought anyway and was killed at Megiddo. The date is about 609 BC, by inference from context. Necho then put Josiah's son and successor Jehoahaz in chains at Riblah in Hamath and imposed a tribute of a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold. He made another son, Eliakim, king in his place, renamed him Jehoiakim, and took Jehoahaz to Egypt, where he died. Jehoiakim taxed the people to pay the tribute. Jer 46:2 records Necho's later defeat by Nebuchadnezzar at Carchemish.

Pharez (also Perez, and Phares in the New Testament) was a son of Judah and Tamar, Judah's daughter-in-law, and the twin brother of Zerah. At their birth his brother's hand appeared first, but Pharez came out ahead, and Tamar named him for this "breach" (Gen 38:29). His sons Hezron and Hamul founded the Hezronite and Hamulite clans, and his descendants were counted as the Pharzites (Num 26:20–21). Ruth 4:12 holds up his house as a model of a flourishing family, and the genealogy that follows traces the line from Pharez through Hezron to David. His descendants stayed prominent: one commanded David's army for the first month, and 468 of them lived in Jerusalem after the exile (Neh 11:6). Matthew and Luke list him among the ancestors of Jesus. His birth is placed at about 1721 BC, by inference from context.

Pharosh is the King James spelling, used only in Ezra 8:3, of the name elsewhere written Parosh. The name belongs to an ancestor whose descendants formed a family group among those who returned from exile in Babylon. In Ezra's list of those who went up with him to Jerusalem, Zechariah led the descendants of Pharosh, and 150 males were registered with him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same family appears as Parosh in other lists. Part of it had already returned with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:3; Neh 7:8). Some of its members had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:25). One descendant, Pedaiah, helped rebuild the city walls (Neh 3:25), and a representative sealed Nehemiah's covenant (Neh 10:14). The same encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "flea." Whether Pharosh was a single historical person or simply the family's name is not stated.

Pharpar was one of the two rivers of Damascus that Naaman, the Syrian army commander, named alongside the Abana when Elisha told him to wash in the Jordan to be healed of his leprosy. Naaman asked whether these rivers were not better than all the waters of Israel, and he went away angry (2 Kgs 5:12). This is the only place the river is mentioned. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the name's meaning as "swift," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "that produces fruit." Both Easton's and Smith's identify Pharpar with the modern Awaj River, which rises on the southeast slopes of Mount Hermon and flows east, south of Damascus, into a marshy lake. Easton's notes that one of its branches is called Wady Barbar, a name it takes to preserve "Pharpar." The location shown here follows the Awaj identification.

Phaseah, also spelled Paseah, was the ancestor of a family of Nethinim, or temple servants, whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon. "The children of Paseah" appear in the list of those who came back with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:49), and the same family is named as "the children of Phaseah" in the parallel list in Neh 7:51. In both lists the family is grouped with the descendants of Uzza and other temple-servant families. Nothing is recorded about Phaseah himself beyond his name. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "lame," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "limping." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also equates this family with "Phinoe" in the corresponding list of 1 Esdras 5:31. This Phaseah is distinct from another Paseah named in the genealogies of Judah.

Phebe (also spelled Phoebe) was a Christian woman whom Paul commended to the believers in Rome at the close of his letter to them. He calls her "our sister" and a servant of the church at Cenchrea, the eastern port of Corinth (Rom 16:1). The Greek word translated "servant" is diakonos, and Easton's Bible Dictionary describes her as a deaconess of that church. The next verse, Rom 16:2, asks the Romans to receive her and help her in whatever she needs, because she had been a helper of many people, including Paul himself. Easton's Bible Dictionary adds that she was probably the one who carried Paul's letter to Rome. This is inferred from the commendation, which reads like an introduction for someone about to arrive. Her name means "shining" or "pure" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Phenice (Phoenix in modern translations) was a harbor town on the south coast of Crete, west of Fair Havens. During Paul's voyage to Rome as a prisoner, about AD 56 by inference from context, most of those aboard advised leaving Fair Havens, which was not suitable for wintering, to try to reach Phenice and winter there. Acts 27:12 describes it as a haven facing toward the southwest and northwest. The following verses (Acts 27:13–14) tell how a storm struck soon after they set sail, so the ship probably never reached it. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with modern Loutro, and the location shown here follows that identification. Some instead place it at the nearby bay of Phineka, just to the west. The name likely comes from the Greek word for palm tree. It is distinct from Phenice meaning Phoenicia, as in Acts 11:19.

Phenicia (Phoenicia in modern spelling; also written Phenice in the King James Version) was the coastal region along the Mediterranean north of Israel, roughly modern Lebanon. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as a narrow strip about 120 miles long, running from the Eleutherus River in the north to Mount Carmel in the south. Its chief cities included Tyre and Sidon, and its people were famous seafarers and traders. The name appears only in Acts. Believers scattered by the persecution after Stephen's death travelled there, preaching only to Jews (Acts 11:19). Paul and Barnabas later passed through Phenicia and Samaria on their way to Jerusalem, reporting that Gentiles had been converted (Acts 15:3). At the end of his third journey, Paul boarded a ship bound for Phenicia (Acts 21:2) and landed at Tyre, according to the following verse.

Phichol was the chief captain, or army commander, of Abimelech, the Philistine king of Gerar. He went with Abimelech to Abraham, who acknowledged that God was with Abraham, and was present when the two made a covenant at Beersheba, after which they returned to the land of the Philistines (Gen 21:22, 32). A commander of the same name later went with Abimelech and Ahuzzath to Isaac to make a similar treaty (Gen 26:26). Because the two episodes are separated by many years, it is uncertain whether this is the same man or a successor bearing the same name or title. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper names index treat him as one person active in the days of both Abraham and Isaac. The meaning of the name is unclear: Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "great," Smith's gives "strong," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the mouth of all."

Philadelphia was a city in the Roman province of Asia, in western Asia Minor, and one of the seven churches addressed in the Book of Revelation (Rev 1:11). Its message begins with Christ described as holy and true, the one who holds "the key of David" and opens and shuts doors that no one else can (Rev 3:7). The name means "brotherly love." Smith's Bible Dictionary says it stood on the lower slopes of Mount Tmolus, about 25 miles southeast of Sardis, and was built by Attalus II, king of Pergamum. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds that it lay on a highway into the interior and was rebuilt after an earthquake in the reign of Tiberius. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that it was repeatedly damaged by earthquakes. The site is the modern town of Alaşehir in western Turkey, and the location shown here matches it.

Philemon was a Christian to whom Paul, writing as a prisoner and joined by Timothy, addressed the short New Testament letter that bears his name. Paul calls him "dearly beloved" and a "fellowlabourer" (Phlm 1:1), which suggests he took an active part in the work of the church. The rest of the letter indicates that a church met in his house, that he owed his faith to Paul, and that Paul wrote to appeal on behalf of Onesimus, a slave of his who had run away and become a Christian. He probably lived at Colossae, by inference from Col 4:9 and 4:17, which link Onesimus and Archippus to that city. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Apphia was his wife and Archippus his son. Later tradition, noted in Smith's Bible Dictionary, makes him bishop of Colossae and a martyr under Nero.

Philetus was a man named by Paul in 2 Tim 2:17, alongside Hymenaeus, as an example of those whose teaching spreads like gangrene ("canker" in the King James Version). The next verse, 2 Tim 2:18, explains that the two had strayed from the truth by claiming that the resurrection had already happened, and that this had upset the faith of some. Several reference works, including Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, take this to mean that they treated the resurrection as purely spiritual or figurative. Since Timothy was then probably at Ephesus, Easton's Bible Dictionary places Philetus there. Hymenaeus also appears without him in 1 Tim 1:20, and Smith's suggests Philetus may have been his follower. Nothing else is known of him. His name is Greek and is usually explained as meaning "beloved" or "amiable."

Phillip the Apostle, usually called Philip, was one of the twelve apostles of Jesus and came from Bethsaida in Galilee, the hometown of Andrew and Peter (John 1:44). Jesus found him and told him to follow, and Philip then brought Nathanael, telling him to "come and see" the one Moses and the prophets wrote about (John 1:43–46). He appears in every list of the Twelve (Matt 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:14). Before the feeding of the five thousand, Jesus asked him where bread could be bought, and Philip replied that two hundred pennyworth would not be enough (John 6:5–7). Some Greeks later approached him asking to see Jesus, and he passed the request on with Andrew (John 12:21–22). At the Last Supper he asked Jesus to show them the Father (John 14:8–9). He was with the apostles in the upper room after the ascension (Acts 1:13). According to tradition noted in Easton's Bible Dictionary, he later preached in Phrygia and died at Hierapolis.

Philip was a son of Herod the Great and the first husband of Herodias. He is mentioned only in connection with the imprisonment of John the Baptist. His brother Herod Antipas, the tetrarch, married Herodias, and John rebuked him for it. That rebuke led Herod to have John bound and put in prison (Matt 14:3; Mark 6:17; Luke 3:19). The Gospels call Herodias "his brother Philip's wife," which shows she was still regarded as Philip's wife when Herod took her. Easton's Bible Dictionary adds that he was the father of Salome, and it calls him Herod Philip I. He is a different person from Philip the tetrarch, his half-brother of the same name, who ruled territories to the north-east. Several other people in the New Testament are also named Philip, including the apostle and the evangelist. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a lover of horses."

Philip was a son of Herod the Great who ruled as tetrarch of Ituraea and the region of Trachonitis. Luke 3:1 names him alongside his brother Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee, to date the start of John the Baptist's ministry to the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, probably around AD 28–29 by inference from context. His territories lay northeast of the Sea of Galilee, roughly in the modern Golan Heights and southern Syria. His other brothers included Archelaus. Another son of Herod also bore the name Philip: the Gospels identify a Philip as the first husband of Herodias (Mark 6:17). Whether that man is the same as the tetrarch has been debated, and this entry treats them as two different people. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "warlike" or "a lover of horses."

Phillip the Evangelist, usually called Philip, was one of the seven men chosen by the Jerusalem church to oversee the daily distribution to the needy (Acts 6:5). He is distinct from Philip the apostle. After the persecution that followed Stephen's death scattered the believers (Acts 8:1), Philip preached Christ in the city of Samaria. Many were baptized after hearing him and seeing his miracles, among them Simon the sorcerer. Directed by an angel to the desert road from Jerusalem to Gaza, he met an Ethiopian official reading Isaiah. He explained the passage as speaking of Jesus and baptized him. The Spirit then carried Philip away. He reappeared at Azotus (Ashdod) and preached through the towns as far as Caesarea. About twenty years later, by inference from context, Paul's company stayed at his house in Caesarea, and Acts 21:9 adds that he had four unmarried daughters who prophesied.

Philip preaches in Samaria is the episode in Acts 8 in which Philip the evangelist, one of the believers scattered from Jerusalem by persecution, took the message about Christ to the city of Samaria. Crowds listened, saw miracles, exorcisms and healings, and many men and women were baptized. Among them was Simon, a sorcerer the people had long regarded as "the great power of God," who also believed, was baptized and stayed close to Philip. The apostles in Jerusalem sent Peter and John, who prayed and laid hands on the new believers so that they received the Holy Spirit. When Simon offered money for this power, Peter rebuked him and urged him to repent, and Simon asked them to pray for him. Peter and John then returned to Jerusalem, preaching in many Samaritan villages. The date of about AD 31 is an estimate inferred from context.

Philippi was a city in eastern Macedonia, described in Acts 16:12 as a leading city of that district and a Roman colony. Paul and his companions stayed there for some days on his first journey into Europe. The events located here include Lydia's conversion, the casting out of a spirit from a fortune-telling slave girl, and the imprisonment and release of Paul and Silas along with the conversion of their jailer. Paul later recalled the shameful treatment he had suffered there (1 Thess 2:2). He passed through Philippi again and sailed from it after the days of unleavened bread (Acts 20:6). He also wrote to the believers there, together with their overseers and deacons (Phil 1:1). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries explain that the city was named after Philip II of Macedon and that it lay inland from its port, Neapolis (modern Kavala). Its ruins are in northeastern Greece.

The Philippian jailer converted is the episode in Acts 16 in which the keeper of the prison at Philippi became a believer during Paul's second missionary journey, about AD 47 by inference from context. After Paul and Silas had been beaten and jailed, they prayed and sang hymns at midnight while the other prisoners listened. A great earthquake shook the prison, opened every door and loosed every prisoner's chains. The jailer woke, assumed the prisoners had escaped, and drew his sword to kill himself, but Paul called out that they were all still there. Trembling, he fell before Paul and Silas and asked what he must do to be saved. They told him to believe on the Lord Jesus Christ and spoke the word of the Lord to his whole household. That same night he washed their wounds, was baptized with all his household, and fed them in his home, rejoicing.

Philistia was the land of the Philistines, the coastal plain along the Mediterranean in southwest Canaan. The Hebrew name, Pelesheth, appears in the King James Version as "Philistia" in the Psalms and as "Palestina" in Exod 15:14 and Isa 14:29–31. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes it as a fertile plain about 40 miles long, between Gerar and Joppa, lying on the main route between Egypt and Syria. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia names its five chief cities as Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath and Ekron. In the Song of Moses its inhabitants are said to tremble at Israel's deliverance from Egypt. Psalms 60 and 108 name it among the neighbouring nations God will triumph over, and Ps 87:4 lists it among the nations whose people are counted as born in Zion. Isaiah warns all Philistia not to rejoice that the rod that struck it is broken.

The Philistine Dominion was a forty-year period during the time of the judges when the Philistines ruled over Israel. Judges 13:1 presents it as a consequence of Israel again doing evil in the sight of the LORD, who delivered them into Philistine hands. Samson's career falls within this period. His parents did not understand that his wish to marry a Philistine woman was a way of seeking an occasion against the Philistines, who at that time had dominion over Israel (Judg 14:4). The men of Judah accepted this rule. Three thousand of them came to Samson at the rock of Etam and protested that the Philistines were their rulers (Judg 15:11). Samson judged Israel for twenty years "in the days of the Philistines" (Judg 15:20). Dating the period to about 1141 BC is an estimate inferred from context.

Philologus was a Christian in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings near the end of his letter to the Romans (Rom 16:15). He is named first in a group that includes Julia, Nereus and his sister, Olympas, and "all the saints which are with them." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that Julia was probably his wife or sister, and that this group may have formed one of the house churches within the Roman Christian community. These are inferences from the way the names are grouped, not statements in the text. The Greek name means "fond of learning" or "lover of words." The same encyclopedia notes that the name appears in inscriptions connected with the imperial household, which may hint that he was a freedman or servant there. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Phinehas (Levite) was the son of Eleazar and a daughter of Putiel, and grandson of Aaron the priest (Exod 6:25). At Shittim, when Israel was drawn into sin with Moab, he took a javelin and acted against the offenders. This turned away God's wrath and stopped the plague (Num 25:7, 11; Ps 106:30). He went with the army against Midian, carrying the holy instruments and trumpets (Num 31:6). Later he led the delegation sent to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh over the altar they had built near the Jordan, and he accepted their explanation (Josh 22:13, 30–32). He held land in the hill country of Ephraim, where Eleazar was buried (Josh 24:33). During the war with Benjamin he stood before the ark and asked the LORD whether to fight (Judg 20:28). He was the father of Abishua and an ancestor of Ezra (1 Chr 6:4; Ezra 7:5).

Phinehas was a son of Eli who served with his brother Hophni as a priest of the LORD at Shiloh (1 Sam 1:3). Several people in the Bible share the name, and this one is distinct from the earlier Phinehas, Aaron's grandson. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia call him Eli's second or younger son. According to 1 Sam 2:12–17, Eli's sons treated the sacrifices with contempt, and a prophet warned Eli that both would die on the same day. When Israel brought the ark of the covenant from Shiloh into battle against the Philistines, the two brothers went with it. The ark was captured, both were killed, and a messenger brought the news to Eli. According to 1 Sam 4:19–22, Phinehas's wife went into labor on hearing of his death, named her son Ichabod, and died. Another son, Ahitub, became the father of Ahiah, a priest in Saul's day.

Phinehas was the father of Eleazar, one of the men who helped weigh the silver, gold and temple vessels in the house of God in Jerusalem on the fourth day after Ezra's company arrived from Babylon (Ezra 8:33). He is known only through his son's name. The verse names Eleazar alongside the priest Meremoth and the Levites Jozabad and Noadiah, so Eleazar was probably of priestly or Levitical family. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats this Phinehas as a Levite of Ezra's time, but notes that the phrase may instead mean that Eleazar belonged to the family of the earlier, well-known Phinehas, grandson of Aaron. This entry treats him as Eleazar's father. Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Phlegon was a Christian living in Rome whom Paul greeted near the end of his letter to the Romans (Rom 16:14). He is named in a group with Asyncritus, Hermas, Patrobas and Hermes, along with "the brethren which are with them." That wording suggests these men belonged to the same household or house church within the Roman congregation. Nothing else about him is recorded in the Bible. His name is Greek and means "burning," according to Easton's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes a later tradition, recorded under the name of Hippolytus, that counts him among the seventy disciples and makes him bishop of Marathon. The New Testament itself does not mention this.

Phrygia was a region in the interior of Asia Minor, in present-day west-central Turkey. People from Phrygia were among the Jews and converts gathered in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:10). On his second journey Paul and his companions went through Phrygia and the region of Galatia after being prevented from preaching in Asia (Acts 16:6). At the start of his third journey he again passed through Galatia and Phrygia in order, strengthening the disciples (Acts 18:23). Its borders were never sharply fixed. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls it an ethnic rather than a political term, since its territory was divided among several Roman provinces. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia distinguishes a Galatian Phrygia, which included Antioch and Iconium, from a larger Asian Phrygia. Easton's Bible Dictionary places Colosse, Hierapolis and Laodicea within it. Because the region was so loosely defined, no single location is shown here.

Phurah was Gideon's servant, who went with him by night to the edge of the Midianite camp before Gideon's attack. God told Gideon that if he was afraid to go down to the camp alone, he should take Phurah with him and listen to what the enemy was saying, so that he would be encouraged to attack (Judg 7:10–11). The two reached the outposts of the armed men in the camp, where, as the following verses tell, Gideon overheard a soldier describing a dream that foretold Midian's defeat. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests Phurah was probably Gideon's armor-bearer, comparing Jonathan's armor-bearer in 1 Sam 14:1. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the word for "servant" literally means "young man" and spells the name Purah. The name is usually taken to mean "branch" or "bough." He is not mentioned anywhere else.

Phut, also spelled Put, was the third of the four sons of Ham listed in the Table of Nations, after Cush and Mizraim and before Canaan (Gen 10:6; 1 Chr 1:8). Through Ham he was a grandson of Noah. Unlike his brothers, he is given no listed descendants. Elsewhere the name stands for a people or land descended from him. Ezek 27:10 names men of Phut, together with Persia and Lud, serving as soldiers in the army of Tyre. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the prophets place Phut in Africa, probably near Egypt, and gives the views that it was Libya or Nubia. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia points out that the Greek translation of the prophets renders it "Libya", and it discusses another common identification with the Egyptian Punt, in the Somali region, perhaps reaching across the Red Sea into Yemen. The exact location remains uncertain.

Phygellus was a believer from the Roman province of Asia, in western Asia Minor, named in 2 Tim 1:15. There Paul tells Timothy that everyone in Asia has turned away from him, and he singles out Phygellus and Hermogenes by name. The verse does not say what the turning away involved: whether they rejected Paul personally, refused to help him, or abandoned his teaching. Easton's Bible Dictionary places the incident during Paul's second imprisonment at Rome, the setting the letter itself suggests. The STEPBible proper names index connects the desertion with Paul's ministry in Asia. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "fugitive." Nothing more is known of him, and the King James Version spells the name Phygellus, while many other translations write it Phygelus.

Pi-beseth was a city of Lower Egypt named only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel's prophecy against Egypt. There its young men, along with those of Aven (On, or Heliopolis), are said to fall by the sword, and the cities are to go into captivity (Ezek 30:17). The name is generally taken to mean "house of Bast," after the Egyptian cat-headed goddess. The Greeks called the city Bubastis. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on the easternmost (Pelusiac) branch of the Nile Delta and identifies its ruins as Tell Basta, near modern Zagazig. The location shown here matches that site. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it about 40 miles north of Memphis. It notes that excavations in 1887–90 found remains from many periods of Egyptian history, along with a large cemetery of sacred cats. It was also home to a major annual festival of the goddess.

Pi-hahiroth was the place in Egypt where the Israelites camped by the sea just before crossing it during the Exodus. God told Moses to have the people turn back and camp before Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, opposite Baal-zephon (Exod 14:2). There Pharaoh's chariots and army caught up with them (Exod 14:9). The list of camps in Numbers places it after Etham (Num 33:7). Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary take the name to mean "place where sedge (or reeds) grows." The site is uncertain, partly because the Suez isthmus has changed since ancient times. Easton's notes that some identify it with Ajrud, a fortress between Etham and Suez. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it on the old shoreline within about ten miles of modern Suez. The location shown here follows this general placement near Suez, close to Ajrud.

Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of Judaea under the emperor Tiberius (Luke 3:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary dates his governorship to about AD 26–36. Luke 13:1 reports that he killed Galileans while they were offering sacrifices. When the Jewish council handed Jesus over to him, about AD 30 by inference from context, Pilate questioned him about being King of the Jews and said repeatedly that he found no fault in him. He sent Jesus to Herod, and the two rulers became friends that day. The crowd kept pressing him and warned that releasing Jesus would make him no friend of Caesar. Pilate then washed his hands in public, had Jesus scourged, and sentenced him to be crucified. He wrote the title placed on the cross, gave Joseph of Arimathaea the body, and allowed a guard at the tomb. Acts and 1 Timothy later recall his part.

Pildash was one of the eight sons of Nahor, Abraham's brother, by his wife Milcah. That makes him Abraham's nephew. He appears only once, in the list of Nahor's children that was reported to Abraham after the near-sacrifice of Isaac (Gen 22:22). His full brothers were Huz, Buz, Kemuel, Chesed, Hazo, Jidlaph and Bethuel. Bethuel later became the father of Rebekah. Nahor also had four children by his concubine Reumah: Tebah, Gaham, Thahash and Maachah. Nothing else is recorded about Pildash. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "flame of fire," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "steely."

Pileha was one of the leaders of the people whose names appear on the sealed covenant made in Nehemiah's time, when the returned exiles in Jerusalem pledged to keep the law of Moses. He is named only once, in a list between Hallohesh and Shobek (Neh 10:24). From context, the list belongs to the leaders who set their seal to the agreement described in the surrounding chapter. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the name may stand for a family rather than a single person, and gives a date of about 410 BC. The name is also spelled Pilha in some reference works, such as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Pillars, called the Hall of Pillars in modern translations such as the ESV and the "porch of pillars" in the King James Version, was one of the buildings in Solomon's palace complex in Jerusalem. According to 1 Kgs 7:6 it measured fifty cubits long and thirty cubits wide, roughly 75 by 45 feet. In front of it stood a further porch with pillars and a "thick beam," which modern versions and the STEPBible Proper Names index render as a canopy. The surrounding verses place it among Solomon's other royal buildings, between the House of the Forest of Lebanon and the Hall of Judgment, though its exact purpose is not stated. It was perhaps an entrance colonnade or waiting hall, but that is an inference. No remains have been identified, so the location shown here is only an approximate position within the area of Solomon's palace and temple in Jerusalem.

Piltai was a priest in the days of Joiakim, the high priest who succeeded his father Jeshua after the return from exile in Babylon. In Neh 12:17 he is named as head of the priestly family of Moadiah, which is probably the same family as Maadiah, listed among the priests who came back with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:5). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives this identification. The surrounding passage lists the heads of priestly houses in Joiakim's generation. A gap in the same verse after Miniamin shows that the name of that family's head has dropped out of the text. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains his name as probably meaning "Yahweh delivers." Smith's dates him to about 445 BC. That date is an estimate drawn from the setting rather than stated in the text. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Pinon was one of the chiefs, called "dukes" in the King James Version, of Edom, the nation descended from Esau. He appears only in the list of Edomite chiefs in Gen 36:41 and its parallel in 1 Chr 1:52, where he is named between Elah and Kenaz. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes such a chief to be the head or founder of a tribe within Edom. The surrounding list in Genesis says these chiefs are named by their families and their places, so Pinon may also be the name of a clan or a district. Some interpreters connect it with Punon, a stopping place of Israel in the wilderness (Num 33:42), though that link is an inference. The meaning of the name is given as "darkness" in Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, and as "pearl" or "gem" in Hitchcock's Bible Names. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Piram was the Amorite king of Jarmuth, a city in the lowlands of Judah, at the time of Joshua's conquest of Canaan. He is named only in Josh 10:3, where Adonizedek king of Jerusalem sends to him and to the kings of Hebron, Lachish and Eglon. The following verses explain why: the five kings joined forces to attack Gibeon because it had made peace with Israel. Joshua came to Gibeon's defense and routed them, and the kings fled and hid in a cave at Makkedah. According to Josh 10:16–26, Joshua later brought them out and put them to death, so Piram was presumably among those killed. The king of Jarmuth also appears in the list of defeated kings in Josh 12:11. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "like a wild ass" or "fleet", while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "indomitable."

Pirathon was a town in the hill country of Ephraim. It was the home and burial place of Abdon son of Hillel, one of the judges of Israel, who was buried there "in the mount of the Amalekites" (Judg 12:15). It was also the hometown of Benaiah the Pirathonite, one of David's mighty men (2 Sam 23:30; 1 Chr 11:31). He served as captain of the division of 24,000 men on duty in the eleventh month and is described as an Ephraimite (1 Chr 27:14). Its site is debated. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it at Fer'on, about 10 miles southwest of Shechem. Smith's Bible Dictionary favors Fer'ata, south of the road from Jaffa to Nablus. The location shown here follows the identification with the modern village of Far'un, near Tulkarm.

Pisgah was a mountain ridge or summit in Moab, east of the Jordan and facing Jericho. Its top marked a stage in Israel's march, overlooking Jeshimon, the desert (Num 21:20). King Balak brought Balaam to the field of Zophim on the top of Pisgah and built seven altars there (Num 23:14). Moses was told to climb it and look in every direction at the land he would not enter (Deut 3:27). Deut 34:1 equates the top of Pisgah with Mount Nebo, where he was shown the land. The springs or slopes of Pisgah bordered the plain above the Dead Sea (Deut 4:49). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take Pisgah as the range at the western edge of the Moab plateau, with Nebo as its summit. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with modern Jebel Siaghah, and the location shown here follows that identification, in present-day Jordan.

Pison (Pishon in modern translations) was the first of the four rivers named in the account of the garden of Eden. A single river flowed out of Eden and divided into four heads, and Pison is described as the one that flows around the whole land of Havilah, a land noted for its gold (Gen 2:11). The surrounding verses add that Havilah also had bdellium and onyx stone. Pison appears nowhere else in the Bible, and its location is unknown, so no site is shown here. Easton's Bible Dictionary lists many proposed identifications, including the Phasis, the Halys, the Indus and the Ganges, and gives the meaning of the name as "the current" or "broad-flowing." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "changing" or "extension of the mouth." This entry does not adopt any one identification.

Pisidia was a mountainous district in southern Asia Minor, north of Pamphylia, in what is now south-central Turkey. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the Taurus range runs through it. Paul and Barnabas crossed it during the First Missionary Journey, about AD 45 by inference from context. After leaving Perga they came to "Antioch in Pisidia" and spoke in the synagogue there (Acts 13:14). On the return leg they passed through Pisidia again before reaching Pamphylia (Acts 14:24), heading back toward Antioch in Syria. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains that Antioch actually lay in the Phrygian part of the Roman province of Galatia, near Pisidia's northern border. It was called "Pisidian" because of that closeness and to tell it apart from other cities named Antioch. Pisidia's borders were never sharply defined, so the location shown here is only approximate.

Pispah was a man of the tribe of Asher, named only once, in the Asherite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:38. He is listed there as one of the three sons of Jether, alongside his brothers Jephunneh and Ara. Nothing else is recorded about his life. Jether is probably the same man called Ithran in the preceding verse (1 Chr 7:37), since the two names are closely related forms. This is an inference from the context of the passage. Pispah's brother Jephunneh shares his name with the father of Caleb, but that Jephunneh belonged to the tribe of Judah and is a different person.

Pithom was an Egyptian city that the enslaved Israelites built for Pharaoh, together with Raamses, as a "treasure" or store city while taskmasters forced them into hard labor (Exod 1:11). It is named only in this verse. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the name as Egyptian Pa-Tum, "house of Tum" (the sun-god Atum), links the city to Rameses II, and suggests it is probably the Patumos mentioned by the Greek historian Herodotus. Smith's Bible Dictionary also connects it with Herodotus's town on Egypt's eastern border. Easton's identifies Pithom with Tell el-Maskhuta in the Wadi Tumilat, west of modern Ismailia near the Suez Canal, where excavations in 1883 found brick ruins taken to be storage buildings. Some scholars instead place it at nearby Tell er-Retaba. The location shown here follows the Tell el-Maskhuta area identification.

Pithon was a Benjamite, the first-named of the four sons of Micah, listed with his brothers Melech, Tarea (also spelled Tahrea) and Ahaz (1 Chr 8:35; 1 Chr 9:41). He appears only in the two parallel genealogies of King Saul's family in 1 Chronicles. The surrounding verses show that his father Micah was the son of Merib-baal, the name Chronicles uses for Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son. That makes Pithon a great-grandson of Jonathan and a descendant of Saul, as Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also note. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "harmless," while Hitchcock's Bible Names suggests "mouthful" or "persuasion."

Place, in this entry, is "the place of a skull," the site outside Jerusalem where Jesus was crucified, called Golgotha in Hebrew (Aramaic). John 19:17 says Jesus went out to it carrying his own cross. The parallel accounts in Matt 27:33 and Mark 15:22 also give the name Golgotha, and Luke 23:33 in the King James Version calls it Calvary, from the Latin word for skull. John 19:20 adds that it was near the city. The reason for the name is not explained. Explanations include a skull-shaped rock formation or its use as a place of execution. Two main sites are proposed. One is the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, the site of long Christian tradition. The other is Gordon's Calvary, north of the Damascus Gate. The location shown here is only a rough point in Jerusalem and does not choose between them.

Place, more fully the Place of a Skull, is the meaning given in the Gospels for Golgotha, the site where Jesus was brought to be crucified (Matt 27:33; Mark 15:22). Both writers translate the Aramaic name for Greek readers. Luke 23:33 calls it simply "the place which is called Calvary," from the Latin word for skull, and John 19:17–20 adds that it was near Jerusalem, outside the city. Why it bore this name is not stated. Suggestions include a skull-shaped rise of ground or a place of execution. Its exact location is uncertain. A tradition going back to the fourth century places it at the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, and some identify it with Gordon's Calvary near the Garden Tomb north of the Damascus Gate. The location shown here is only a rough placement at Jerusalem and does not settle between these views.

Plain refers here to the low, flat country of the lower Jordan Valley around Jericho, just north of the Dead Sea. In Deut 34:3 "the plain of the valley of Jericho, the city of palm trees" is one of the regions Moses viewed before his death, a view that, by the surrounding chapter, he had from Mount Nebo. The view stretched as far south as Zoar. Deut 34:8 uses the related phrase "the plains of Moab" for the lowland on the eastern side of the Jordan, across from Jericho, where Israel mourned Moses for thirty days. The two phrases probably describe opposite sides of the same broad valley floor. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links this term to its entry on the Cities of the Plain, the Jordan lowland associated in Genesis with Sodom and Zoar. The location shown here is the valley near Jericho.

The Plain of Aven (ESV "Valley of Aven") is a place named once in the Bible, in Amos's oracle against Damascus and the Arameans (Syria). The Lord declares that he will break the bar of Damascus, cut off the inhabitant of the Plain of Aven and the ruler of Beth-eden, and send the people of Syria into captivity to Kir (Amos 1:5). Its exact identity is uncertain. The Hebrew word aven means "wickedness" or "idolatry", and the name may be a deliberate play on a place known for its worship. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the Syrian Heliopolis, modern Baalbek in Lebanon. Others take it more broadly as the Beqaa Valley between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon ranges, where Baalbek stands. The location shown here follows the Baalbek identification.

The Plain of Jordan (ESV: Jordan Valley) is the well-watered lowland along the Jordan River that Lot chose when he and Abraham separated. Looking from the hill country near Bethel, Lot saw that it was watered everywhere, like the garden of the LORD and like the land of Egypt, before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen 13:10). He took the whole plain for himself and moved east (Gen 13:11). The separation is dated to about 1920 BC, by inference from context. Because the passage links the plain with Sodom, Gomorrah and Zoar, many place it at the southern end of the valley near the Dead Sea. Others take it to mean the broader valley floor north of the Dead Sea. The location shown here is in the central Jordan Valley, roughly between Jericho and the point where the Jabbok joins the Jordan.

Pochereth was the ancestor of a family listed among the descendants of Solomon's servants who returned from exile in Babylon. He appears only in the parallel return lists in Ezra 2:57 and Neh 7:59, where he is called "Pochereth of Zebaim." The surrounding passage (Ezra 2:55–58) places this group with the temple servants, and Smith's Bible Dictionary connects the family with the return led by Zerubbabel. Nothing else is recorded about him. The phrase "of Zebaim" could point to a place or clan, but it is often read as part of a single compound name, Pochereth-hazzebaim, which many modern translations render as Pokereth-Hazzebaim. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "cutting of the mouth of warfare." It is unclear whether Pochereth was an individual or a name preserved for a family line.

Pontus was a region and Roman province in northern Asia Minor, stretching along the southern coast of the Black Sea, in what is now northern Turkey. Its name comes from the Greek name for that sea, the Pontus Euxinus. Easton's and Smith's Bible dictionaries compare it roughly to the later province of Trebizond. It appears three times in the New Testament. People from Pontus were among the crowd in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:9). Aquila, the Jewish husband of Priscilla whom Paul met in Corinth, was born there (Acts 18:2). Peter addresses his first letter to the scattered believers living in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia (1 Pet 1:1). Together these passages point to a significant Jewish population in the region, and Easton's Bible Dictionary calls it a resort of many Jews of the Dispersion. The location shown here marks the general area of the region rather than a single site.

Pool, called the King's Pool in modern translations, was a pool in Jerusalem that Nehemiah passed during his night inspection of the ruined city walls. After the Fountain Gate he reached the King's Pool, but the rubble was so thick there that the animal he was riding could not get through (Neh 2:14). The text does not describe the pool or give its exact position. Its route places it near the southern or southeastern end of the old city, close to the Fountain Gate. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the Pool of Siloam, perhaps named for its nearness to the "king's garden" mentioned in other passages. The location shown here is in that general area of ancient Jerusalem, within the city rather than at a precisely fixed spot. Several places in the Bible are called simply "pool".

Pool (the ESV spells it Pool of Shelah; the King James Version calls it the pool of Siloah) was a reservoir in Jerusalem next to the king's garden. It sat near the Fountain Gate and the stairs that went down from the City of David. Neh 3:15 says that during Nehemiah's rebuilding of the walls, Shallun son of Colhozeh, ruler of part of the Mizpah district, repaired the Fountain Gate along with the wall of this pool. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the Hebrew name shelah as "the dart" and links it with Shiloah, "sending," in Isa 8:6, and so with the Pool of Siloam. On that basis it probably lay at the southern end of the City of David, the ridge running south of the Temple Mount. The location shown here places it in that area. The word "pool" also names several other places in the Bible.

Poratha was one of the ten sons of Haman, the official of the Persian king Ahasuerus who plotted to destroy the Jews. He is named only once, in the list of Haman's sons in Esth 9:8. The surrounding passage (Esth 9:6–10) records that the Jews killed these ten sons in Shushan the palace on the day set for the Jews' destruction, which became the day the Jews defended themselves. At Esther's request their bodies were afterward hanged (Esth 9:13–14). The meaning of his name is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may come from a Persian word meaning "given by fate," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "fruitful." Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his name and his place among his brothers.

Portius Festus (spelled Porcius in the King James text) was the Roman governor who succeeded Felix in Judea, finding Paul still a prisoner at Caesarea (Acts 24:27). Three days after arriving he went up to Jerusalem but ruled that Paul's case be heard at Caesarea (Acts 25:1–4). Wanting to please the Jewish leaders, he offered Paul a trial in Jerusalem. Paul appealed to Caesar instead, and after consulting his council Festus granted the appeal (Acts 25:9–12). When King Agrippa and Bernice visited, Festus explained the case and arranged a hearing (Acts 25:13–24). During Paul's defence he shouted that much learning had driven Paul mad (Acts 26:24). Agrippa later told him Paul could have been freed had he not appealed (Acts 26:32). This entry dates these events to about AD 56 by inference. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries place his arrival about AD 60 and say he died in office within two years.

Poti-pherah was an Egyptian priest of On, the city later known as Heliopolis, near modern Cairo. His daughter Asenath was given to Joseph as his wife by Pharaoh when Pharaoh raised Joseph to authority over Egypt and gave him the Egyptian name Zaphnathpaaneah (Gen 41:45). Through Asenath, Poti-pherah became the grandfather of Joseph's two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, who were born in Egypt before the years of famine (Gen 41:50; Gen 46:20). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the Hebrew title may mean either priest or prince of On. His name is probably Egyptian, and it is often compared with that of Potiphar, the officer who bought Joseph, though the two are distinct men in the narrative. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Potiphar was the Egyptian official who bought Joseph as a slave. He is described as an officer of Pharaoh and "captain of the guard," a title the King James margin renders "chief of the executioners." Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he probably headed a force that combined military and civil police duties. Joseph's brothers sold him to traders, called both Midianites and Ishmeelites, who brought him down to Egypt and sold him to Potiphar (Gen 37:36; Gen 39:1). The rest of Genesis 39 says Joseph won his trust and ran his household. Potiphar's wife then falsely accused Joseph, and Potiphar had him put in prison. Nothing more is said of Potiphar after this. His name is usually taken to mean "belonging to the sun" or "dedicated to Ra," and it closely resembles Potipherah, the name of Joseph's later father-in-law.

The Prayer and Betrayal in Gethsemane was the night when Jesus prayed in anguish and was then arrested, recorded in all four Gospels and dated about AD 30 by inference from context. After the Last Supper Jesus went with his disciples to Gethsemane on the Mount of Olives, a place he often visited. He withdrew a short distance and prayed that "this cup" might pass from him, yet submitted to his Father's will. Luke describes his sweat falling like great drops of blood. Three times he returned to find the disciples asleep and rebuked Peter for not keeping watch. Judas, who knew the place, then arrived with an armed band sent by the chief priests and Pharisees and identified Jesus with a kiss. Simon Peter drew a sword and cut off the right ear of the high priest's servant Malchus. Jesus told him to put the sword away, healed the ear, and was bound and led away.

Priscilla, also called Prisca (2 Tim 4:19), was the wife of Aquila, a Jew from Pontus. She is never mentioned without him. The couple had recently come from Italy because the emperor Claudius had ordered all Jews to leave Rome. Paul met them in Corinth, about AD 49 by inference from context. The surrounding verse, Acts 18:3, adds that he stayed and worked with them as a fellow tentmaker. Later they sailed with Paul toward Syria, and Acts 18:19 says they remained at Ephesus. There they heard Apollos speak in the synagogue, took him aside, and explained the way of God to him more accurately. Paul calls them his helpers in Christ Jesus. Writing from Asia, he sends greetings from them and from the church that met in their house. As Easton's Bible Dictionary notes, her name sometimes comes before her husband's.

The Prison Gate (ESV "Gate of the Guard") was a gate in Jerusalem mentioned only in Neh 12:39. At the dedication of the rebuilt city wall, one of the two thanksgiving choirs marched along the wall past the Ephraim Gate, the Old Gate, the Fish Gate, the towers of Hananeel and Meah, and the Sheep Gate, then "stood still in the prison gate." Because the procession ended near the temple, the gate was probably close to the temple area in the northeast of the city. The text gives no reason for its name, though it may have been linked to a guardhouse. Its exact identity is uncertain. Some connect it with the "court of the prison" near the king's house (Neh 3:25), and others with the Miphkad or Muster Gate (Neh 3:31). The location shown here places it within Jerusalem near the temple mount.

Prochorus was one of the seven men chosen by the early church in Jerusalem to oversee the daily distribution of food to widows, so that the apostles could give their attention to prayer and teaching. He is named third in the list, after Stephen and Philip (Acts 6:5). The choice is dated here to about AD 30, by inference from context. Nothing more is recorded of him in the Bible. His name is Greek, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he may have been a Hellenist, a Greek-speaking Jew, which fits the context of a complaint from the Greek-speaking widows. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him among the "seven deacons," a traditional title for the group. According to later church tradition, also noted in the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, he became bishop of Nicomedia and died a martyr at Antioch.

The Prophecies of Amos were the messages of Amos, a herdsman from Tekoa, given during the reigns of Uzziah of Judah and Jeroboam son of Joash of Israel, "two years before the earthquake" (Amos 1:1). This entry dates them to about 788 BC, lasting roughly a year, both figures inferred from context. Amos first announced judgment on surrounding nations, including Damascus, the Philistine cities, Edom and Moab, and then on Judah and Israel. He condemned the northern kingdom for exploiting the poor, for luxury such as houses and beds of ivory, and for worship at Bethel, Gilgal, Dan and Beersheba. He called for justice to "run down as waters" (Amos 5:24). He described visions such as locusts. At Bethel, the king's sanctuary, he was told to stop prophesying. The book ends with a promise to rebuild the fallen tabernacle of David and replant the people in their land.

The Prophecies of Daniel is the span of events and visions recorded across the whole Book of Daniel, from about 606 BC over roughly 72 years, by inference from context. It opens when Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem in Jehoiakim's third year and Daniel and his companions are taken into royal service in Babylon (Dan 1:1, 1:19). The narrative chapters tell of Daniel interpreting Nebuchadnezzar's dream of a great image and of a tree, the deliverance of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego from the furnace, the writing on the wall at Belshazzar's feast, and Daniel's survival in the lions' den under Darius. The later chapters record Daniel's own visions: four beasts, a ram and a goat, the seventy weeks, and a long account of kings of the north and south. The book closes with Daniel told to seal the words until the time of the end (Dan 12:4).

The Prophecies of Elijah is the stretch of narrative in 1 and 2 Kings covering the ministry of Elijah the Tishbite from Gilead. This entry dates it to about 910 BC and gives it some thirteen years, both by inference from context. It opens with Elijah telling King Ahab there would be no rain except at his word (1 Kgs 17:1). He was sustained at the brook Cherith, then by a widow at Zarephath, whose son he revived. On Mount Carmel he challenged the prophets of Baal, and the people declared that the LORD is God. Threatened by Jezebel, he complained that he alone was left and was told that seven thousand remained faithful. He pronounced judgment on Ahab's house and foretold the death of Ahab's son, King Ahaziah, who is named in the wider chapter. Elijah then parted the Jordan and was taken up as Elisha watched. The passage also includes Elisha's healing of Naaman.

The Prophecies of Elisha are the accounts in 2 Kings of the ministry of Elisha son of Shaphat, who had served Elijah and took up his role after him. The prophetic groups at Jericho recognized that Elijah's spirit rested on him. He made Jericho's bad water wholesome, foretold victory for the allied kings against Moab, multiplied a widow's oil to pay her debt, promised a son to a Shunammite woman and later restored the boy to life, and made a poisoned pot of stew harmless. He repeatedly revealed the plans of the king of Syria to Israel's king and led blinded Syrian troops into Samaria. During the siege of Samaria he foretold sudden plenty, which came true. He told Hazael that he would harm Israel, and from his deathbed he promised King Joash victory over Syria. Even after his burial, a dead man revived on touching his bones. The entry dates these events from about 897 BC over roughly 59 years, by inference from context.

The Prophecies of Ezekiel were the visions and messages given to the prophet Ezekiel while he lived among the Jewish exiles by the river Chebar in Babylonia, and they make up the whole book that bears his name. By inference from context they began about 593 BC and continued for some 23 years. The book opens with his vision of God and his call to speak to a "rebellious house." Symbolic acts follow, such as drawing Jerusalem on a clay tile, along with warnings of famine, sword and the city's fall. Further oracles condemn Jerusalem's unfaithfulness and announce judgment on neighboring nations, including Ammon, Tyre, Egypt and Edom (Mount Seir). Later prophecies promise that the scattered people will be revived and brought back to their land, and describe an attack by Gog. The book ends with a detailed vision of a new temple, the land divided among the tribes, and a city named "The LORD is there."

The Prophecies of Habakkuk are the oracles and prayer recorded in the book of Habakkuk, dated here to about 607 BC by inference from context. Habakkuk opens by asking why God does not answer his cries about violence and injustice, where the law is slack and the wicked surround the righteous. God replies that he is raising up a fierce, swift invader, named in Hab 1:6 as the Chaldeans (Babylonians). The prophet then asks how a holy God can use a people who sweep up nations like fish in a net. Standing at his watchpost, he receives a vision to write down plainly: the proud will fail, but "the just shall live by his faith." Five woes follow against plunder, violence, drunkenness and idolatry. The book closes with a prayer set to music, recalling God's coming in power from Teman and Paran and ending in trust despite trembling.

The Prophecies of Haggai were four dated messages the prophet Haggai delivered in the second year of King Darius, about 520 BC by inference from context. They were addressed to Zerubbabel, governor of Judah, Joshua the high priest, and the remnant of the people. In the sixth month Haggai rebuked the people for living in finished houses while the LORD's house lay in ruins, and he linked their poor harvests and drought to that neglect. Zerubbabel, Joshua and the people obeyed and began work on the temple within weeks. In the seventh month he encouraged those who thought the new building was nothing compared with the former one, promising that its glory would be greater. In the ninth month he questioned the priests about holiness and uncleanness and promised blessing from that day. A final message declared that God would overthrow kingdoms and make Zerubbabel like a signet. Ezra 5:1 pairs Haggai with the prophet Zechariah.

The Prophecies of Hosea were the messages given to Hosea son of Beeri during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah of Judah and Jeroboam son of Joash of Israel. By inference from context they began about 785 BC and spanned roughly 65 years. They open with Hosea's family: his children receive symbolic names such as Loruhamah, meaning "no mercy," and he buys back a wife for silver and barley. The prophecies compare Israel, often called Ephraim, to an unfaithful wife who goes after other lovers. They condemn idolatry, lying, killing and theft, and they criticize alliances with Assyria. They warn of exile to Assyria and of the sword falling on Israel's cities. They also recall God calling Israel out of Egypt and his care in the wilderness. The book ends with promises of healing, restored love and the reunion of Judah and Israel.

The Prophecies of Isaiah are the messages of Isaiah son of Amoz concerning Judah and Jerusalem, given during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (Isa 1:1). This entry dates them from about 759 BC over roughly 62 years, an estimate inferred from those reigns. Isaiah condemns Judah's leaders for exploiting the poor (Isa 3:14) and warns against relying on Egypt instead of the LORD (Isa 31:1). He addresses the threat from Syria and Ephraim under Ahaz (Isa 7:5) and delivers oracles against Assyria, Damascus, Egypt, Kedar and Tyre. A narrative section tells of the Assyrian challenge to Jerusalem and of Hezekiah showing his treasures to envoys from Babylon (Isa 36:20; 39:4). The later chapters offer comfort, describe a suffering servant (Isa 53:3), call the wicked to return to God (Isa 55:7), and look toward restoration and final judgment (Isa 61:4; 66:24).

The Prophecies of Jeremiah are the messages and narratives that make up the book of Jeremiah, the words of Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, a priest from Anathoth in Benjamin (Jer 1:1). This entry dates them from about 628 BC over some 67 years, by inference from context. The book's final chapter reaches to the Babylonian king's provision for the exiled King Jehoiachin (Jer 52:34). Jeremiah warned Judah that it had forsaken the LORD and called it to amend its ways (Jer 2:17; 7:3). He condemned prophets who spoke lies in God's name (Jer 27:15) and told King Zedekiah he would be handed over to the king of Babylon (Jer 37:17). The book records Baruch reading Jeremiah's scroll, the fall of Jerusalem, the murder of Gedaliah and the flight to Egypt. It also contains oracles against Egypt, Moab, Edom and Babylon, and promises that Israel and Judah would return (Jer 33:11; 50:4).

The Prophecies of Joel are the messages in the book of Joel, given as the word of the LORD to Joel son of Pethuel (Joel 1:1). They open with a locust plague and drought that stripped vines, fig trees and pastures, and Joel calls the elders and all the people to fast and assemble at the temple (Joel 1:14; 2:12–16). The locusts are pictured as an invading army announcing the day of the LORD. God then promises to drive off the northern army, send rain and restore the lost years (Joel 2:20–25), and to pour out his spirit on his people, a passage Peter quotes in Acts 2. The last chapter announces judgment on the nations in the valley of Jehoshaphat, naming Tyre, Sidon, Egypt and Edom, and blessing for Jerusalem. The book gives no date. This entry places it about 820 BC by inference, though many scholars date it after the exile.

The Prophecies of Jonah are the events of the book of Jonah, in which the LORD sent Jonah son of Amittai to cry against Nineveh for its wickedness. Jonah instead fled by ship from Joppa toward Tarshish. When a great storm struck, the sailors cast lots, the lot fell on Jonah, and at his request they threw him overboard, and the sea calmed. A great fish swallowed him for three days and three nights, and he prayed from inside it. Sent a second time, Jonah warned Nineveh that in forty days it would be overthrown. The people and king fasted, wore sackcloth and turned from violence, and God spared the city. Jonah was angry, and God used a gourd that grew and withered to ask him about pity for Nineveh. 2 Kgs 14:25 places Jonah in Jeroboam II's reign. This entry dates the events to about 825 BC, by inference from context.

The Prophecies of Malachi were the messages delivered to Israel by the prophet Malachi, described as "the burden of the word of the LORD" (Mal 1:1). They are dated here to about 442 BC, an estimate inferred from context. Many oracles are framed as dialogues in which God makes a charge and the people answer, "Wherein?" God affirms his love for Jacob over Edom. He rebukes priests who offer blind, lame and sick animals and who have corrupted the covenant of Levi. He condemns marriage to foreign women and the divorce of "the wife of his youth," and calls the nation to bring all the tithes into the storehouse. The prophecies announce a coming day of judgment when the Lord will purify the sons of Levi like a refiner. Those who fear him are recorded in a book of remembrance, and the book closes with the promise that Elijah the prophet will be sent before that great day.

The Prophecies of Micah are the messages of Micah of Moresheth, delivered during the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and concerning both Samaria and Jerusalem (Mic 1:1). By inference from context, this period began about 754 BC and lasted roughly 57 years. Micah announced that Samaria would become a heap of ruins and that the disaster would reach the gate of Jerusalem. He named towns of the Judean lowland such as Maroth, Achzib and his own Moresheth-gath. He condemned those who seized fields and houses, rulers who perverted justice, and the seers and diviners, and he warned that Zion would be plowed like a field. Jer 26:18 recalls this warning being spoken in Hezekiah's day. Alongside judgment, he spoke of a gathered remnant, of nations beating swords into plowshares, of deliverance from Assyria, and of the LORD's faithfulness to Jacob and Abraham.

The Prophecies of Nahum are the oracles in the book of Nahum, called "the burden of Nineveh" and the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite (Nah 1:1). They open by portraying the LORD as slow to anger yet great in power, taking vengeance on his enemies while being a stronghold for those who trust him (Nah 1:2–7). They announce that Assyria's yoke on Judah will be broken and the wicked will no longer invade it (Nah 1:13–15). Chapters 2 and 3 vividly picture an attack on Nineveh: raging chariots, opened river gates, a collapsing palace and fleeing people. The "bloody city" is compared with "No," which had itself gone into captivity, and the king of Assyria is told his wound cannot heal (Nah 3:1, 8–10, 18–19). "No" is usually identified with Thebes in Egypt. This entry places the prophecies from about 663 BC over roughly 48 years, by inference from context.

The Prophecies of Obadiah are the oracles of the shortest Old Testament book, introduced as "the vision of Obadiah" concerning Edom (Obad 1:1). Edom, proud of its high home "in the clefts of the rock," will be brought down, betrayed by its allies, and stripped of its wise men and the warriors of Teman (Obad 1:3–9). The charge is violence against its "brother Jacob": Edom stood aloof, gloated, looted and handed over fugitives when foreigners entered Jerusalem (Obad 1:10–14). The prophecy then widens to the day of the LORD on all nations, promising deliverance on Mount Zion, the regaining of Israel's lands, and a kingdom belonging to the LORD (Obad 1:15–21). Its date is debated. Some link it to Edom's revolt under Jehoram (2 Kgs 8:20–22). This entry follows the view that places it after Babylon took Jerusalem, about 585 BC, by inference from context.

The Prophecies of Zechariah were the messages the prophet Zechariah, grandson of Iddo, received beginning in the eighth month of the second year of Darius (Zech 1:1). By inference this was about 520 BC. The span of about two years shown here is also inferred, reaching to the fourth year of Darius mentioned in Zech 7:1. The book opens with night visions of horses patrolling the earth, a man measuring Jerusalem, a high priest given a clean turban, a lampstand between two olive trees, a flying scroll, wickedness sealed in a measuring basket, and four chariots. When a delegation asks whether to keep fasting, the answer calls for justice and mercy. Later oracles foretell a humble king riding a donkey and describe a rejected shepherd paid thirty pieces of silver. They end with a restored Jerusalem, where the nations come every year to keep the Feast of Tabernacles.

The Prophecies of Zephaniah were messages given to Zephaniah, son of Cushi and a descendant of Hizkiah, during the reign of Josiah king of Judah, dated here to about 610 BC by inference from context. They announce that the great 'day of the LORD' is near, a day of wrath on Judah and Jerusalem for the worship of Baal, the host of heaven and Malcham, and for turning away from the LORD. Princes, judges, prophets and priests are condemned, and silver and gold are said to offer no rescue. The meek are urged to seek the LORD in hope of being hidden. Judgment also falls on Philistine cities such as Gaza and Ashkelon, on Moab, Ammon and the Ethiopians, and on a proud 'rejoicing city' that Zeph 2:13 names as Nineveh. The prophecies close with promises that a humble remnant will be gathered and restored, with the LORD rejoicing over Jerusalem.

Ptolemais was a coastal city south of Tyre where Paul and his companions landed on their voyage from Miletus to Jerusalem. After sailing from Tyre they reached Ptolemais, greeted the believers there and stayed with them for one day before continuing their journey (Acts 21:7). The trip took place about AD 54, a date inferred from context. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains that the city was originally called Accho (Acco in Judg 1:31) and was renamed Ptolemais after Ptolemy Soter when he controlled Coele-Syria. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it was the most prominent town on the Phoenician coast in Maccabean times. The site is generally identified with modern Acre (Akko) in northern Israel, on the bay north of Mount Carmel, and the location shown here matches that identification.

Puah was the second-listed of the four sons of Issachar and a grandson of Jacob. His brothers were Tola, Jashub and Shimron. Genesis 46:13 names him Phuvah among the family members who went down to Egypt with Jacob, and Numbers 26:23 spells his name Pua and calls him the ancestor of the Punites, one of the clans of the tribe of Issachar counted in the wilderness census. 1 Chr 7:1 repeats him in the genealogy of Issachar. Jashub appears as Job in Genesis 46:13. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "mouth" or "splendid." Nothing else is recorded about his life. The name is shared by other people in the Bible, including one of the Hebrew midwives in Egypt and the father of the judge Tola, so he should not be confused with them.

Puah was one of the two Hebrew midwives, together with Shiphrah, whom the king of Egypt addressed when he ordered that Hebrew baby boys be killed at birth (Exod 1:15). The verses that follow (Exod 1:16–21) say the midwives feared God and did not carry out the order, telling Pharaoh that Hebrew women gave birth before a midwife could arrive. God then dealt well with them and gave them households of their own. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes her in these terms, and Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the episode to about 1571 BC, an estimate drawn from context. With only two midwives named, they may have been leaders over others rather than the only midwives, though the text does not say. The name is explained as "splendid" by Smith's and as "mouth" by Hitchcock's Bible Names. Several other people in the Bible bear the same or a similar name, including a son of Issachar and the father of the judge Tola.

Puah was a man of the tribe of Issachar, the son of Dodo and the father of Tola. He is known only from Judg 10:1, which records that his son Tola rose to defend Israel after the time of Abimelech and lived at Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim. Nothing else is said about Puah himself. The name is shared by several people in the Bible. These include one of Issachar's own sons, listed elsewhere among the tribe's founding families, and one of the Hebrew midwives in Egypt. This Puah belongs to a much later generation. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "mouth", "corner" or "bush of hair".

Publius was "the chief man" of the island of Malta when Paul and his companions were shipwrecked there, about AD 57 by inference from context. He owned estates near the place where they came ashore, and he welcomed them and lodged them hospitably for three days (Acts 28:7). His father was sick with fever and dysentery. Paul went in to him, prayed, laid his hands on him and healed him (Acts 28:8). The Greek title translated "chief man" (protos, "first") was probably an official title. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it appears on an inscription from the nearby island of Gozo, and Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Publius to have been the governor. A later tradition says that Publius became the first bishop of Malta and afterward bishop of Athens.

Pudens was a Christian at Rome who sent greetings to Timothy at the close of Paul's second letter to him (2 Tim 4:21). He is named alongside Eubulus, Linus and Claudia, and "all the brethren" who were with Paul when Paul urged Timothy to come before winter. By inference from the letter, he was among those who stayed in contact with Paul during his final imprisonment in Rome. The name is Latin and is usually taken to mean "modest" or "bashful". He is not mentioned anywhere else in the New Testament. Smith's Bible Dictionary records a legend that he hosted Peter, was a friend of Paul, and was martyred under Nero. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a conjecture that Pudens and Claudia were husband and wife, with Claudia possibly a British king's daughter, though it calls this only a supposition.

Pul is a distant nation named only in Isa 66:19. There God says he will send survivors to faraway peoples who have not heard of his fame, listing Pul with Tarshish, Lud, Tubal, Javan and the distant coastlands. The text gives no further detail, so its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it as probably the same as Phut or Put (Gen 10:6; Jer 46:9), an African people. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also treats it as an African country. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes two views: the island of Philae in Egypt, or Libya. The location shown here follows the Libyan identification and places it in eastern Libya, in the region around Cyrene. This place is separate from Pul, the Assyrian king of the same name.

Punon was one of the camps where the Israelites stopped during the last stage of their wilderness journey.
