Numbers lists it between Zalmonah and Oboth (Num 33:42–43), and the verse just before shows Zalmonah was the first stop after Mount Hor, so Punon was the second camp after leaving Mount Hor. The text says nothing more about it. Eusebius and Jerome identified it with Phaeno, or Phinon, a village between Petra and Zoar known for copper mines worked by convicts, as Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note. That site is usually taken to be modern Feinan in southern Jordan. The location shown here is only a rough placement east of the Dead Sea and does not mark the Feinan site. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "precious stone", and Smith's gives "darkness".

Put was a people and land in Africa closely tied to Egypt. Nahum 3:9 lists Put alongside Lubim (the Libyans) as helpers of Thebes, together with Ethiopia and Egypt. In Jer 46:9 the King James Version's "Libyans" probably renders the same Hebrew name. There Put's shield-bearers march with Egypt's army against Babylon. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that Gen 10:6 names Phut as a son of Ham, between Egypt and Canaan. It adds that Ezek 27:10 and 30:5 describe men of Put as mercenaries serving Tyre and Egypt, and that a fragment of Nebuchadnezzar's annals mentions "Phut of the Ionians." The exact location is uncertain. Some identify Put with Libya west of Egypt, and others with Punt on the Red Sea coast of East Africa. The location shown here follows the Libyan identification and is placed in Cyrenaica, in modern eastern Libya.

Puteoli was a port city on the coast of Campania in Italy, on the northern shore of what is now the Bay of Naples. It was the last stop on Paul's voyage to Rome as a prisoner. After sailing from Rhegium with a south wind, his ship reached Puteoli the next day (Acts 28:13). The following verse, Acts 28:14, says believers were found there and Paul stayed with them seven days before going on to Rome by land. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe Puteoli as the main harbor for the grain ships from Alexandria and the usual landing place for travelers to Italy from the eastern Mediterranean. According to Hitchcock's Bible Names, its name refers to sulphur springs, which are common in the volcanic area. It is the modern town of Pozzuoli, near Naples, where remains of the ancient harbor and a large amphitheater survive.

Putiel was the father of the woman whom Eleazar, son of Aaron, married. She bore Eleazar a son, Phinehas, so Putiel was Phinehas's maternal grandfather (Exod 6:25). He appears only in this verse, which closes the genealogy of the Levite family heads. The text gives neither his tribe nor his family. His daughter is not named either; she is described only as "one of the daughters of Putiel," which implies he had more than one daughter. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "God is my fatness," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "contemned by El."

Quartus was a Christian who sent greetings to the believers in Rome at the close of Paul's letter to them (Rom 16:23). Paul names him alongside Gaius, his host, and Erastus, the city treasurer, and calls him simply "a brother." Some translations render the phrase "our brother" or "the brother." Paul was probably writing from Corinth, since Gaius and Erastus are connected with that city elsewhere, so Quartus is generally taken to have been a member of the church there, as Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him. His name is Latin and means "fourth." Nothing else about him is recorded in the Bible. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes a later tradition that he was one of the seventy disciples and afterward became bishop of Berytus, modern Beirut.

The Queen of Sheba was a ruler who travelled to Jerusalem to visit King Solomon after hearing of his fame. She came to test him with hard questions, bringing a large company and camels loaded with spices, gold and precious stones, and she talked with him about everything on her mind (2 Chr 9:1). After seeing his wisdom and the house he had built, she gave him 120 talents of gold and a quantity of spices never matched afterward. Solomon in turn gave her whatever she asked, and she returned to her own country with her servants. The account appears in both 1 Kings 10 and 2 Chronicles 9 with only small differences. Jesus later refers to her as "the queen of the south" (Matt 12:42; Luke 11:31). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Arab tradition calls her Bilqis, and Ethiopian legend names her Maqeda and says she bore Solomon a son.

Raamah was a son of Cush and grandson of Ham, listed in the Table of Nations among Noah's descendants. His brothers were Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Sabtecha and Nimrod, and his sons were Sheba and Dedan (Gen 10:7; 1 Chr 1:9). Like many names in this genealogy, Raamah probably stands both for an ancestor and for the people or region descended from him. Ezek 27:22 later mentions merchants of Sheba and Raamah trading spices, precious stones and gold with Tyre, which suggests a trading people, usually placed in Arabia. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "greatness" or "thunder." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Raamah was a country whose merchants traded with the city of Tyre. Ezekiel's lament over Tyre names them alongside the merchants of Sheba, bringing the finest spices, precious stones and gold to its markets (Ezek 27:22). The pairing with Sheba suggests a land in Arabia, and STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) places it there, though its exact site is unknown. The name probably connects to Raamah son of Cush, whom the table of nations lists as the father of Sheba and Dedan (Gen 10:7; 1 Chr 1:9). By inference, the people descended from him gave their name to the region. The location shown here is only approximate and places Raamah in southwestern Arabia, on the Red Sea coast of modern Yemen. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "greatness" or "thunder."

Raamses was one of the two store cities, along with Pithom, that the Israelites were forced to build for Pharaoh while they were enslaved in Egypt (Exod 1:11). It is very probably the same place as Rameses, the spelling Smith's Bible Dictionary links it to. That city appears as the district where Jacob's family settled (Gen 47:11) and as the starting point of the exodus (Exod 12:37). Its exact site is uncertain. Many scholars identify it with the Egyptian royal city Pi-Ramesse at modern Qantir in the eastern Nile Delta, and others with Tanis. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the eastern Delta, near the Wadi Tumilat and modern Ismailia, and does not settle on any one excavated site.

Rab-mag appears in the King James text as one of the princes of the king of Babylon who came in and sat in the middle gate of Jerusalem when the city fell to Nebuchadnezzar's army in the reign of Zedekiah (Jer 39:3). He is named again among the officials whom Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, sent at the time Jeremiah was released from the prison court (Jer 39:13). The King James text lists Rab-mag as if it were a name, and this entry treats it as a person. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary, however, take it as a title, probably meaning "chief of the magi" or chief prince, held by the Nergal-sharezer named just before it. Smith's Bible Dictionary further suggests this Nergal-sharezer is probably the later Babylonian king the Greeks called Neriglissar.

Rab-saris was one of the high officials of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, who entered Jerusalem when the city fell and sat in the middle gate with the other Babylonian princes (Jer 39:3). He was also among the officials who, with Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, sent to have Jeremiah released from the court of the prison (Jer 39:13). The name means "chief of the eunuchs" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), and Smith's Bible Dictionary says it is probably the title of an office rather than a personal name. Read that way, it may describe the man named just before it in each verse, Sarsechim in Jer 39:3 and Nebushasban in Jer 39:13. Whether both verses refer to the same person is uncertain. The same title is used for an Assyrian officer sent to Hezekiah in 2 Kgs 18:17, a different man from an earlier period.

Rabbah, also called Rabbath of the children of Ammon, was the chief city of the Ammonites, east of the Jordan. Deut 3:11 says the giant iron bedstead of Og, king of Bashan, was kept there. It lay beyond the land given to Gad (Josh 13:25). David sent Joab to besiege it, and David stayed in Jerusalem (2 Sam 11:1; 1 Chr 20:1). Joab took the "royal city" and the "city of waters," probably the lower town by its stream, and then called David to capture the rest (2 Sam 12:26–29). Later Shobi son of Nahash of Rabbah brought supplies to David at Mahanaim. Amos, Jeremiah and Ezekiel foretold its destruction. It is generally identified with modern Amman, Jordan, which the location shown here follows. A separate Rabbah in Judah, named with Kirjath-jearim (Josh 15:60), has an unknown location.

Rabbith was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Issachar, named only once, in the list of Issachar's towns alongside Kishion and Abez (Josh 19:20). The Hebrew form carries the definite article, "ha-Rabbith," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "multitude." Smith's also suggests the town may have stood on Issachar's boundary. Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with the village of Raba, in the southern part of the Gilboa range, north of Ibzaq. The location shown here, in the hills southeast of the Jezreel Valley, follows that identification.

Rabsaris was one of three high officials whom the king of Assyria sent from Lachish to Jerusalem, together with Tartan and Rabshakeh, at the head of a large army against King Hezekiah of Judah. The three came up to Jerusalem and stood by the conduit of the upper pool on the highway to the fuller's field (2 Kgs 18:17). The surrounding narrative names the Assyrian king as Sennacherib. The word is probably a title rather than a personal name. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names give its meaning as "chief of the eunuchs," and Easton's Bible Dictionary renders it "Chief of the Heads," meaning a senior court officer. The same title appears for a Babylonian official at the fall of Jerusalem in Jer 39:3 and 39:13. That is evidently a different man holding a similar office.

Rabshakeh was an officer of the king of Assyria, named in the wider account as Sennacherib (2 Kgs 18:13). During Hezekiah's reign he was sent from Lachish with Tartan, Rabsaris and a large army to demand the surrender of Jerusalem. Standing by the conduit of the upper pool, he spoke for the "great king" and asked what Hezekiah was trusting in. Hezekiah's officials Eliakim, Shebna and Joah asked him to speak in Aramaic ("the Syrian language") rather than Hebrew. He refused and shouted in Hebrew so that the people on the wall would hear. Hezekiah's message to Isaiah described his words as a reproach against the living God. Rabshakeh then rejoined the Assyrian king, who was fighting at Libnah. The same account appears in both 2 Kings and Isaiah. Smith's and Easton's Bible Dictionaries take Rabshakeh as an official title, "chief cupbearer," rather than a personal name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives it the broader sense of chief officer.

Racal (spelled Rachal in the King James Version) was a town in Judah. It appears only in 1 Sam 30:29, in the list of places to whose elders David sent a share of the plunder after he defeated the Amalekites who had raided Ziklag. The surrounding passage describes these as places where David and his men had moved about during his years as a fugitive. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "traffic," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia as "trader." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes that the Greek Septuagint reads "Carmel" here. The two names look alike in Hebrew, and Carmel near Hebron features prominently in David's earlier story with Nabal and Abigail, so many scholars adopt that reading. The location shown here follows the Carmel identification, placing Racal at Carmel, probably the modern Khirbet el-Kirmil south of Hebron. Otherwise the town's location is unknown.

Rachab is a woman named in the genealogy of Jesus in Matt 1:5, where she is the wife of Salmon and the mother of Boaz, who later married Ruth and became the great-grandfather of King David through Obed and Jesse. Rachab is the Greek form of the name Rahab, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Easton's Bible Dictionary both treat the names as the same. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies her with Rahab the harlot of Jericho, who hid the Israelite spies and was spared when the city fell (Josh 2; 6). The Old Testament does not say whom that Rahab married, so her identification with Salmon's wife rests on Matthew's genealogy. This entry follows that identification. She is one of the few women named in Matthew's list, along with Tamar, Ruth and the wife of Uriah.

Rachel (spelled Rahel in Jer 31:15) was the younger daughter of Laban and the wife Jacob loved most. Jacob met her as she came with her father's sheep. He served Laban seven years for her but was first given her elder sister Leah, and then received Rachel as well. Long childless, she envied Leah and gave Jacob her maid Bilhah, whose sons Dan and Naphtali she named. God then opened her womb and she bore Joseph. When Jacob left Laban, Rachel stole her father's household images and hid them by sitting on them. She died giving birth to Benjamin on the way to Ephrath (Bethlehem), about 1739 BC by inference from context, and Jacob set a pillar on her grave. Ruth 4:11 names her with Leah as builders of the house of Israel, and Jeremiah, quoted by Matthew, pictures her weeping for her children.

event: Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin
text: Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin is the episode in Genesis 35 in which Jacob's wife Rachel dies in childbirth on the road from Bethel, a short distance from Ephrath. During a hard labour the midwife told her not to fear, because she would have this son too. This probably echoes Rachel's wish, when Joseph was born, for another son (Gen 30:24). As she was dying she named the boy Benoni, usually understood as "son of my sorrow," but Jacob called him Benjamin, usually understood as "son of the right hand." She was buried on the way to Ephrath, identified as Bethlehem, and Jacob set up a pillar over her grave. The passage then lists Jacob's twelve sons. It notes that the others were born in Paddan-aram, so by inference Benjamin was the only one born in Canaan. This entry dates the event to about 1739 BC, an estimate inferred from context.

Raddai was one of the brothers of David, named in 1 Chr 2:14 as the fifth son of Jesse, of the tribe of Judah. He appears only in this genealogy, between Nethaneel the fourth son and Ozem the sixth, and nothing else is recorded about him. The Chronicles list gives Jesse seven sons, while 1 Sam 16:10–11 implies eight, with David the youngest. Raddai's name does not appear in the Samuel accounts of Jesse's sons, which name only Eliab, Abinadab and Shammah. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "trampling," the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia tentatively suggests "beating down," and Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "ruling; coming down." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes that some Greek manuscripts spell the name differently, for example "Rhaddai" or "Zaddai."

Rahab was a prostitute living in Jericho whose house was where the two spies lodged when Joshua sent them from Shittim to scout the land (Josh 2:1). When the king of Jericho ordered her to hand them over, she hid them and later sent them away by another route (Josh 2:3; Jas 2:25). Because of this, she and everyone in her house were spared when Israel destroyed the city. The spies brought out her father, mother, brothers and the rest of her family, and she went on living among the Israelites (Josh 6:17, 23, 25). Hebrews 11:31 cites her as an example of faith, and James 2:25 as an example of being justified by works. Matt 1:5 names a Rahab as the wife of Salmon and mother of Boaz in Jesus' genealogy. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify her with this woman. The name is spelled differently in Hebrew from the poetic name Rahab used for Egypt.

Rahab is a poetic name for Egypt used in the Psalms and Isaiah, distinct from Rahab of Jericho, whose name is spelled differently in Hebrew. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take it to mean "the proud one" or "insolence." In Ps 87:4 Rahab is listed with Babylon, Philistia, Tyre and Ethiopia among nations whose people will come to know the LORD. In Ps 89:10 and Isa 51:9 God is praised for having broken or cut Rahab in pieces. Smith's Bible Dictionary reads these as references to the defeat of Egypt at the exodus. In Isa 51:9 Rahab stands alongside "the dragon," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also sees in the name an ancient image of a sea monster that became an emblem of Egypt. The location shown here is a general point in Egypt's Nile Delta region, matching the identification with Egypt.

Raham was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only once, in the genealogy of the descendants of Caleb son of Hezron in 1 Chr 2:44. He was the son of Shema and is called "the father of Jorkoam." In these Chronicles genealogies "father" can mean the founder or leading figure of a town or clan, so Jorkoam may have been a settlement rather than a son. The TIPNR proper-names index of Tyndale House allows both readings. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "merciful," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "pity" or "love." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Rakem was a descendant of Manasseh, son of Joseph, named only in the genealogy at 1 Chr 7:16. That verse says that Maachah, wife of Machir, bore a son named Peresh, and that his brother was Sheresh. It then says "his sons were Ulam and Rakem." Grammatically, "his" could point to either brother. This entry follows the reading that Rakem and his brother Ulam were sons of Sheresh, which would make Rakem a grandson of Machir and a great-grandson of Manasseh, within the tribe of Joseph. The Bible records nothing else about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "flower garden" and places him before 1451 BC, a date inferred from his place in the family line.

Rakkath was a fortified city in the territory of the tribe of Naphtali. It appears only once, in Josh 19:35, where it is listed between Hammath and Chinnereth among Naphtali's "fenced cities." Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary take the name to mean "shore," and Smith's places the town on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee. Hammath is generally identified with the hot springs just south of Tiberias, so Rakkath was probably nearby. Rabbinic tradition, noted by Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, holds that Herod Antipas built Tiberias on the site of Rakkath. The encyclopedia adds that Tiberias stood on an older settlement, since builders disturbed ancient graves while digging its foundations. Smith's places Rakkath close to Tiberias rather than on its exact site. The location shown here follows the identification with Tiberias.

Rakkon was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Dan. It is named only once, in Josh 19:46, where it is listed after Me-jarkon and just before the border "before Japho," the coastal city later known as Joppa (modern Jaffa). That placement suggests it lay near the coast at the northwestern edge of Dan's allotment. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Tell er-Rakkeit, on the seashore about 6 miles (10 km) north of Joppa, near the mouth of the river 'Aujeh, probably the modern Yarkon River. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes it as a well-watered place not far from Joppa. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew wording of this verse is difficult and that the Greek Septuagint reads it differently. The location shown here follows the Tell er-Rakkeit identification, north of present-day Tel Aviv.

Ram was a son of Hezron in the tribe of Judah, and a brother of Jerahmeel and Chelubai (Caleb) (1 Chr 2:9). Ashur and Segub, also listed as his siblings, appear later in the same chapter as Hezron's sons by other wives. Ram was the father of Amminadab and the grandfather of Nahshon, who was called prince of the children of Judah (1 Chr 2:10). The genealogy in Ruth 4:19 places him in the line that leads to King David. In the King James New Testament his name appears in its Greek form, Aram, in the genealogies of Jesus (Matt 1:3–4; Luke 3:33). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some texts of Luke read "Arni" here. The name probably means "high" or "exalted." He is a different person from Ram, the son of Jerahmeel and so Ram's nephew, who appears later in 1 Chronicles 2.

Ram was the firstborn son of Jerahmeel, a member of the tribe of Judah known only from the genealogy in 1 Chronicles 2. His father Jerahmeel was the firstborn of Hezron, and his brothers were Bunah, Oren, Ozem and Ahijah. Onam is also counted among Jerahmeel's sons, and according to 1 Chr 2:26 he was born to a second wife named Atarah, so he was probably Ram's half-brother. Ram's own sons were Maaz, Jamin and Eker. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several people in the Bible bear the name Ram. This one should be kept distinct from his uncle Ram, Jerahmeel's brother and a son of Hezron, who appears in the line leading to David (1 Chr 2:9–10; Ruth 4:19). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "elevated" or "sublime."

Ram was the ancestor or founder of the clan to which Elihu belonged. Elihu, the son of Barachel the Buzite, was the young man who angrily answered both Job and his three friends (Job 32:2). Nothing else is recorded about this Ram, and he should not be confused with others of the same name, such as Ram in the line of Judah. The name means "high" or "exalted." Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him with Aram, a nephew of Buz in Gen 22:21. That link fits Elihu's description as a Buzite. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia instead treats the name as possibly that of an obscure Arab tribe, and it notes the medieval rabbinic commentator Rashi's suggestion that Ram stands for Abraham. This entry treats Ram simply as Elihu's clan ancestor, which is all the verse itself states.

Ramah was a city in the territory of Benjamin, listed with Gibeon and Beeroth (Josh 18:25). It lay near Gibeah on the road north from Jerusalem, and Deborah judged Israel between Ramah and Bethel (Judg 4:5; 19:13). Baasha king of Israel fortified it to blockade Asa king of Judah. He later abandoned the work, and Asa used its stones and timber to build Geba and Mizpah (1 Kgs 15:17–22; 2 Chr 16:1–6). Isaiah and Hosea name it among Benjamin's towns facing invasion (Isa 10:29; Hos 5:8). Nebuzaradan released Jeremiah there after he had been taken in chains (Jer 40:1), and Jer 31:15 pictures Rachel weeping in Ramah. Its people returned after the exile (Ezra 2:26; Neh 7:30). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the village of er-Ram, about 5 miles north of Jerusalem, and the location shown here follows that view. Several places share the name. The "Ramath of the south" in Simeon (Josh 19:8) is a separate town.

Ramah was a town on the boundary of the tribe of Asher, named in Josh 19:29 as a landmark where the border turned toward the fortified city of Tyre before running on to Hosah and the sea at Achzib. Its name means "height" and is shared by several other places in the Bible, so this town should not be confused with the better-known Ramah in Benjamin. Its exact position is uncertain because the line of Asher's border cannot be traced with confidence. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes proposals placing it about 3 miles east of Tyre or about 10 miles east-southeast of it. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with Rameh or Ramiyeh, a hilltop village in a basin of fields about 13 miles southeast of Tyre, in present-day southern Lebanon, where ancient cisterns and sarcophagi have been found. The location shown here follows that identification.

Ramah was a fortified city in the territory given to the tribe of Naphtali. It appears only once, in the list of Naphtali's "fenced cities" in Josh 19:36, named between Adamah and Hazor. Several other places in the Bible share the name. According to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, the name means "height," and towns called Ramah generally stood on high ground. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the modern village of er-Rameh (Rameh). The village lies on a mountain slope about 8 miles (13 km) west-southwest of Safed, in Upper Galilee, and about 15 miles (24 km) west of the north end of the Sea of Galilee. The location shown here follows that identification. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that no ancient remains are visible above ground at the site, though it was probably occupied in ancient times.

Ramah was the hometown of Elkanah and Hannah and the home of their son Samuel, the city of Mount Ephraim called Ramathaim-zophim in 1 Sam 1:1. Samuel lived there as judge of Israel and built an altar there. The elders came to him at Ramah to ask for a king, and he returned there after anointing David and after his break with Saul. David fled to Samuel at Naioth in Ramah to escape Saul, and Saul followed and prophesied there. Samuel was buried in his house at Ramah. Several places share this name, and this one's site is disputed. Smith's Bible Dictionary follows the tradition placing it at Nebi Samwil, northwest of Jerusalem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia weighs Beit Rima and Ramallah. The location shown here follows a western identification in the hills northwest of Shiloh, near the modern village of Rantis.

Ramah, in this entry, is the town where King Joram (Jehoram) of Israel, son of Ahab, was wounded by the Syrians while fighting Hazael king of Syria. He went back to Jezreel to recover, and Ahaziah king of Judah (called Azariah in 2 Chr 22:6) went down to visit him there. Several places in the Bible are called Ramah, a name meaning "height." Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia all take this Ramah as a shortened form of Ramoth-gilead, and the verse just before, 2 Kgs 8:28, names Ramoth-gilead as the scene of this battle. The site of Ramoth-gilead east of the Jordan has been placed at several locations. The location shown here follows the identification near modern Ramtha in northern Jordan, by the nearby mound of Tell er-Rumeith.

Ramath-lehi, meaning "hill of the jawbone" or "height of Lehi," was the name Samson gave to the place where he threw away the donkey's jawbone he had used to kill a thousand Philistines (Judg 15:17). The surrounding passage places this at Lehi in Judah, where the Philistines had camped to capture him after the men of Judah handed him over bound. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek translation took the name to mean the "throwing up" of the jawbone, but that the Hebrew follows the pattern of names like Ramath-mizpeh. It also suggests the name Lehi may reflect a jaw-like shape in the landscape. The exact site is unknown. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the Sorek Valley (Wadi es-Sarar), near Zorah and Timnah, and the rough location shown here follows that view.

Ramath-mizpeh, meaning "height of the watchtower," was a town east of the Jordan named in Josh 13:26 as a point on the boundary of the land given to the tribe of Gad, listed between Heshbon and Betonim. Nothing else is said about it in the text, and its identity is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the same as Mizpah of Gilead. Easton's Bible Dictionary links it with the Mizpeh where Jacob and Laban made their covenant and places it at modern es-Salt. Smith's Bible Dictionary equates it with Ramoth-gilead. The location shown here follows the Ramoth-gilead identification and sits near the modern town of Ramtha in northern Jordan.

Ramathaim-zophim was a city in the hill country of Ephraim, named in 1 Sam 1:1 as the home of Elkanah, a descendant of Zuph and the father of Samuel. The name means "the two heights" or "two watchtowers" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), and the "-zophim" part probably recalls Zuph, Elkanah's ancestor. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Ramathaim as a fuller name for Ramah, the town that later passages in 1 Samuel present as Samuel's home, the center of his work, and his burial place. It also links the name to "the land of Zuph" (1 Sam 9:5). Some have connected it with Arimathea of the New Testament. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's notes an identification with Nebi Samwil ("the prophet Samuel"), about 4 or 5 miles northwest of Jerusalem, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Rameses was a city and district in the eastern Nile Delta of Egypt. Genesis calls the area where Joseph settled his father and brothers, at Pharaoh's command, "the land of Rameses," described as the best of the land. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take this to be Goshen, or part of it. The city was the starting point of the Exodus. Israel set out from Rameses toward Succoth on the fifteenth day of the first month, the day after the Passover, with about six hundred thousand men on foot besides children. It is probably the same as Raamses, one of the store cities the Israelites built (Exod 1:11). Its site is debated. Easton's identifies it with Zoan (Tanis), and Smith's also notes Tell Ramsis near Belbeis. The location shown here follows the identification with the Egyptian royal city Pi-Ramesses, near modern Qantir.

Ramiah was an Israelite layman of the family of Parosh who lived in the time of Ezra, after the return from exile in Babylon. He is named first among the sons of Parosh in the list of men who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:25). The surrounding chapter describes how these men agreed to send away their foreign wives, so Ramiah was probably among those who made that pledge. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains his name as meaning "Yah has loosened" or "Yah is high," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "exaltation of the Lord." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:26 gives his name as "Hiermas," which points to a Hebrew form close to Jeremiah.

Ramoth was one of the "sons of Bani" listed in Ezra 10:29 among the Israelite men who had married foreign wives after the return from exile. The context of Ezra 10 shows that those named agreed to send these wives away as part of the reform led by Ezra. Nothing else is recorded about him. The spelling of his name differs between textual traditions. The King James Version follows the form the Hebrew scribes marked to be read aloud, Ramoth. The written Hebrew form gives Jeremoth, which the Revised Versions adopt, according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. That form resembles names found in nearby verses of the same list. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of Ramoth as "eminences" or "high places."

Ramoth, a name meaning "heights" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), was a city in the territory of Issachar given with its surrounding pasturelands to the Gershonite Levites. It is listed with Anem in 1 Chr 6:73. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat it as the same town called Remeth (Josh 19:21) and Jarmuth (Josh 21:29) in the parallel lists of Joshua. The encyclopedia suggests it may be er-Rameh, southwest of Jenin. Its exact site is uncertain, and the location shown here is only a rough placement within Issachar's territory near the eastern Jezreel Valley. Several biblical places share the name. This one should not be confused with Ramoth in Gilead, the Levitical city of the tribe of Gad named a few verses later (1 Chr 6:80).

Ramoth, called "south Ramoth" in 1 Sam 30:27, was a city to which David sent part of the plunder he recovered from the Amalekites, along with Bethel, Jattir and other towns where he and his men had moved about. Its name means "heights" or "high places" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several places in the Bible share this name, so its identity is uncertain. Because the gifts went to the elders of Judah, this Ramoth is probably the "Ramath of the south" listed among the towns of Simeon in Josh 19:8, somewhere in the Negev. Easton's Bible Dictionary instead links it with a Levitical city of Issachar, also called Jarmuth and Remeth. The location shown here lies east of the Jordan, near modern es-Salt in Jordan, an area associated with Ramoth-Gilead, and follows that identification.

Ramoth, called "Ramoth in Gilead," was a city east of the Jordan in the territory of the tribe of Gad. Its name means "heights" or "high places" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Moses set it apart as one of three cities of refuge east of the Jordan, alongside Bezer and Golan (Deut 4:43). Under Joshua it was confirmed as a city of refuge and given to the Levites (Josh 20:8; 21:38). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the place usually called Ramoth-gilead, where King Ahab was mortally wounded fighting the Syrians (1 Kgs 22) and where Jehu was later anointed king (2 Kgs 9). Its site is uncertain. Easton's mentions Reimun near Jerash and a site northeast of es-Salt. The location shown here follows another proposed identification, probably Tell er-Rumeith near modern Ramtha in northern Jordan. Several other places in the Bible share the name Ramoth.

Ramoth-gilead was a fortified city east of the Jordan in the region of Gilead. Under Solomon it was the base of Ben-geber, an officer whose district included the towns of Jair and the region of Argob in Bashan (1 Kgs 4:13). Later the Syrians held it. Ahab of Israel, joined by Jehoshaphat of Judah, marched to retake it despite the prophet Micaiah's warning, and he was mortally wounded there (1 Kgs 22:3–29; 2 Chr 18). His son Joram fought Hazael of Syria at the city and was wounded, while Israel kept hold of it (2 Kgs 8:28; 9:14). There a young prophet sent by Elisha anointed Jehu king (2 Kgs 9:1–4). Other passages name it a city of refuge in Gad. Its site is debated: Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests Reimun or Gerasa (Jerash), and Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests Jel'ad. The location shown here follows the identification with Tell er-Rumeith in northern Jordan.

Rapha was a son of Benjamin, the youngest son of Jacob, and so belonged to the founding generation of the tribe of Benjamin. In the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 8:1–2 he is named as Benjamin's fifth son, after Bela, Ashbel, Aharah and Nohah. This entry identifies him with Rosh, who appears among the sons of Benjamin in the list of Jacob's family that went down to Egypt (Gen 46:21). The identification follows the STEPBible proper-name index from Tyndale House. It is an inference, because the Benjamite lists in Genesis, Numbers and Chronicles differ considerably in their names and order. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of Rapha as "tall" and of Rosh as "head." A different Rapha, a descendant of Saul, appears later in the same chapter (1 Chr 8:37). Nothing else is recorded about this son of Benjamin.

Raphu was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, known only as the father of Palti. Palti was the Benjamite chosen as one of the twelve men Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan (Num 13:9). Raphu is named only in this list of the spies, which identifies each one by tribe and by father, so nothing else is recorded about his life. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of his name as "healed" or "one healed." Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to before 1490 BC, an estimate drawn from the timing of the wilderness journey.

Reaia was a man of the tribe of Reuben, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 5:5. He was the son of Micah and the father of Baal. Placing him among the Reubenites is an inference from the passage, which traces this line from Joel, a descendant of Reuben (1 Chr 5:1–4). It ends with Beerah, a Reubenite prince whom the Assyrian king Tilgath-pilneser carried into exile (1 Chr 5:6). Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Reaia as apparently a prince of his tribe. The verse itself records only his place in the family line. Smith's also notes that the name is the same as Reaiah, which other men in the Old Testament bear. Nothing else is told about him.

Reaiah was a man of the tribe of Judah, a son of Shobal, who is called the father of Kirjathjearim. He appears only in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles. 1 Chr 4:2 names him as the father of Jahath, whose sons Ahumai and Lahad headed the families of the Zorathites. He is probably the same person as Haroeh, listed in 1 Chr 2:52 as a son of Shobal alongside half of the Manahethites. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that "Reaiah" should probably be read in place of "Haroeh" there, though both spellings may be copying variants, and this entry treats the two names as one man. The ISBE also calls him the founding ancestor of a Calebite family. His name means "the Lord has seen" (Hitchcock's Bible Names: "vision of the Lord"). The name Reaiah is also borne by other men in the Bible.

Reba was one of five Midianite rulers killed by the Israelites under Moses, along with Evi, Rekem, Zur and Hur. Balaam son of Beor died in the same campaign (Num 31:8). Numbers calls the five "kings of Midian," while Joshua calls them "princes of Midian" and "dukes of Sihon," the Amorite king who ruled from Heshbon (Josh 13:21). This suggests they were local chiefs living in that region and allied with or subject to Sihon. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names take the name to mean "fourth." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Rebekah was the daughter of Bethuel, granddaughter of Abraham's brother Nahor, and sister of Laban of Padan-aram (Gen 22:23; 25:20). Abraham's servant met her drawing water at a well, and she agreed to go with him to marry Isaac, who loved her and was comforted after his mother's death. The marriage is placed about 1856 BC, by inference from context. She was barren until Isaac prayed for her, and she then bore the twins Esau and Jacob. Isaac favored Esau, but Rebekah loved Jacob. Among the Philistines, Isaac called her his sister because he feared men would kill him for her beauty. When she overheard Isaac promising Esau a blessing, she dressed Jacob in Esau's clothes to obtain it. She later warned Jacob of Esau's plan to kill him and urged Isaac to send him to Laban. Her death is not recorded, but she was buried with Isaac in the family tomb, which Gen 49:30 identifies as the cave of Machpelah.

Recah (spelled Rechah in the King James Version) is a name that appears only once in the Bible, in the genealogy of Judah, where Eshton's descendants Bethrapha, Paseah and Tehinnah are summed up as "the men of Rechah" (1 Chr 4:12). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia (1915) takes Recah as a place but notes that nothing is known about it or where it was. It also notes that early Greek manuscripts read the name differently, as Rhechab or Rhepha. STEPBible's proper-name index reads Recah instead as a person or clan descended from Judah through Caleb. This entry treats it as a place. Its site is unknown, and the location shown here is only a rough placement in the hill country of Judah near Bethlehem, inferred from its place in Judah's genealogy.

Rechab was a son of Rimmon from Beeroth, a town counted as part of the tribe of Benjamin. He and his brother Baanah served Ishbosheth, Saul's son, as captains of raiding bands. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes these as leaders of predatory troops. The two brothers came to Ishbosheth's house in the heat of the day while he lay resting at noon. They entered as though to fetch wheat, stabbed him, and escaped. The surrounding narrative goes on to say that they carried his head to David at Hebron, expecting a reward. David answered them with an oath and ordered them put to death (2 Sam 4:8–12). Several other men in the Bible share the name, among them the father of Jehonadab, from whom the Rechabites took their name. This entry concerns only the son of Rimmon.

Rechab was the father of Jonadab, also spelled Jehonadab. He is known only through his son, who is regularly called "the son of Rechab." Jonadab rode with Jehu in his chariot and went with him into the house of Baal when Jehu destroyed Baal worship in Israel (2 Kgs 10:15, 23). Jonadab's descendants, known after his father as the Rechabites, kept Jonadab's command not to drink wine. Jeremiah held up their obedience as an example, and God promised that Jonadab the son of Rechab would never lack a man to stand before him (Jer 35:6–19). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Rechab as the father of Jehonadab and so the forefather of the Rechabites. 1 Chr 2:55 links the house of Rechab with the Kenites. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "square" or "chariot with team of four horses." Others in the Bible share the name, including a son of Rimmon in 2 Sam 4.

Rechab was the father of Malchiah, who is named in Neh 3:14 as "the ruler of part of Bethhaccerem." Malchiah repaired the Dung Gate when Jerusalem's walls were rebuilt under Nehemiah. He rebuilt the gate and fitted its doors, locks and bars. Rechab himself is known only as part of his son's name. Nothing else is recorded about him, so he probably lived in the generation before the wall-building, which Smith's Bible Dictionary dates to before 446 BC. Several men in the Bible share the name Rechab. Some interpreters link this man with the Rechab whose descendants, the Rechabites, appear in Jeremiah, but the text does not make that connection, and this entry treats him simply as Malchiah's father. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "rider." Hitchcock's Bible Names suggests "square" or "chariot with team of four horses."

Rechah is a name in the genealogy of Judah, mentioned only in 1 Chr 4:12, which closes a short list of descendants with the words "These are the men of Rechah." The men named include Eshton, his sons Bethrapha, Paseah and Tehinnah, and Tehinnah's son Irnahash. This entry treats Rechah as a man and the ancestor of this group. Chelub and Shuah are shown as his children by inference from the preceding verse, 1 Chr 4:11, where Chelub, the brother of Shuah, begins the line that ends with "the men of Rechah." The phrase may instead name a place, since such lists often link families to towns. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it as probably a village in Judah, perhaps Rashiah, about three miles south of Jerusalem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that nothing further is known about it.

The Red Sea is the long arm of the Indian Ocean between Africa and Arabia. At its northern end it splits into the Gulf of Suez and the Gulf of Aqaba on either side of the Sinai Peninsula. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries explain its Hebrew name, Yam Suph, as "sea of weeds" or reeds. It is best known as the water the Israelites crossed on dry ground when leaving Egypt, where Pharaoh's chariots and army drowned (Exod 15:4; Heb 11:29), an event recalled often in later books. The name also covers the Gulf of Aqaba. Israel's wilderness routes went "by the way of the Red sea" around Edom, and Solomon built ships at Ezion-geber on its shore (1 Kgs 9:26). It also marked one limit of Israel's promised borders (Exod 23:31). Easton's places the crossing at the Gulf of Suez. The exact point is uncertain, and the location shown here marks the sea as a whole.

Reelaiah was one of the leading men who returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel. His name appears in the list of those who came back with Zerubbabel and Jeshua in Ezra 2:2. In the parallel list in Neh 7:7 he is called Raamiah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts him among twelve chiefs named at the head of the list, notes that 1 Esdras 5:8 gives the name as Resaias, and says it is almost impossible to decide which form is original, though it leans toward Reelaiah. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of Raamiah as "thunder of the Lord." Nothing more is recorded about him beyond his place among these leaders of the return.

Regem was a man of the tribe of Judah, named first among the six sons of Jahdai in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:47. His brothers were Jotham, Geshan (also spelled Gesham), Pelet, Ephah and Shaaph. The verse sits within the list of Caleb's descendants, so the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a Calebite and the probable founder of a family or clan of that name. Jahdai's own link to Caleb is not stated; by inference from the surrounding verses he belonged to the same line. Nothing else is recorded about Regem. The meaning of his name is uncertain: Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "friend," while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "that stones" or "purple."

Regem-melech was one of the men sent, together with Sherezer and their companions, to pray before the Lord and to put a question to the priests and prophets at the house of God (Zech 7:2). The following verse shows that the question was whether to keep up the fast of the fifth month, which mourned the destruction of the temple. The passage is dated to the fourth year of Darius, while the temple was being rebuilt after the exile. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes the senders as exiled Jews. The Hebrew of the verse is difficult and can also be read to mean that the people of Bethel sent the delegation. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name may mean "friend of the king," so some read it as a title for Sherezer rather than as a second person. This entry treats Regem-melech as a separate individual. Nothing else is known of him.

Rehabiah was a Levite, the only son of Eliezer. By inference from 1 Chr 23:15, which names Eliezer as a son of Moses, he was Moses' grandson, as Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary also state. In 1 Chronicles 23:17 he is called the chief of Eliezer's line and is said to have had very many sons, so his descendants became a Levitical family in their own right. In the later list of Levite family heads, Isshiah is named as the first of Rehabiah's sons (1 Chr 24:21). A line of descent in 1 Chr 26:25 traces Rehabiah, then Jeshaiah, Joram, Zichri and Shelomith, who was a treasurer of dedicated gifts. This entry treats Jeshaiah as his son. Jeshaiah may be the same person as Isshiah, but that is uncertain. The name is usually explained as "the Lord has enlarged" (Easton's Bible Dictionary).

Rehob was the father of Hadadezer, king of Zobah, an Aramean (Syrian) kingdom north of Israel. He is known only through his son. Hadadezer is called "the son of Rehob" when David defeated him as Hadadezer went to recover his border at the Euphrates River (2 Sam 8:3). He is named again in the list of spoil David dedicated, which included spoil taken from Hadadezer (2 Sam 8:12). Nothing else is recorded about Rehob himself, and it is not stated whether he was also a king. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as meaning "breadth" or "space," is shared by other people in the Bible and is also used as a place name. This Rehob should not be confused with them.

Rehob was a Levite named among those who set their seal to the written covenant of Nehemiah's day, in which the returned community of Jerusalem pledged to keep God's law. He appears only in the list of sealers at Neh 10:11, between Micha and Hashabiah. By inference from the surrounding list (Neh 10:9–13), this part of the roll names Levites. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the name may stand for a Levitical family rather than a single man. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with others called Rehob in the Bible, such as the father of Hadadezer king of Zobah. The name is usually taken to mean "breadth" or "open space."

Rehob was a town or district in the far north of Israel. It marked the northern limit of the land searched by the twelve spies, who went from the wilderness of Zin "unto Rehob, as men come to Hamath" (Num 13:21). In David's time Syrians of Rehob were among the troops the Ammonites hired against Israel, drawn up in the field apart from the Ammonite army (2 Sam 10:8). Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it to be probably the same as Beth-rehob, the Syrian place named in 2 Sam 10:6 and near the city of Dan in Judg 18:28. The name means "breadth" or "space" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Smith's Bible Dictionary, following Robinson, puts it near Tell el-Kady (Dan) and Banias. Easton's links it with the castle of Hunin, southwest of Dan, and the location shown here follows that identification. Several other places in the Bible share this name.

Rehob was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Asher, listed in Josh 19:28 with Hebron (probably Abdon), Hammon and Kanah, along the boundary that ran north toward Great Sidon. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it east of Sidon. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is a rough position in the hills of the far north of Asher's territory, near the modern Israel–Lebanon border, matching Kanah and Hammon in the same verse. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as meaning "breadth" or "open space," belongs to several places in the Bible. Another Rehob of Asher appears elsewhere in Joshua, and there is a Rehob in the far north near Lebo-hamath. Whether any of these is the same town as this one is uncertain.

Rehob was a city in the territory of the tribe of Asher in northern Israel. It is listed among Asher's towns in Josh 19:30, and it was one of the cities, with its surrounding pastureland, given to the Levites (Josh 21:31; 1 Chr 6:75). The Gershonite Levites received it, according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Judges 1:31 names Rehob among the towns whose Canaanite inhabitants Asher did not drive out. Several places share the name, which means "breadth" or "open space" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts two separate Rehobs in Asher and suggests that the Levitical city and the one left to the Canaanites may not be the same town. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls the site unknown. The location shown here is approximate, in the hills of western Galilee east of Acco, the modern Acre.

Rehoboam was the son and successor of Solomon; his mother was Naamah, an Ammonite. He became king at forty-one and reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, about 975–958 BC by inference from context. At Shechem, where Israel gathered to make him king, Jeroboam and the people asked for relief from Solomon's burdens. Rehoboam rejected the advice of his father's older counsellors. After his tribute officer Adoram was stoned to death, he fled to Jerusalem, and only Judah, with Benjamin, stayed loyal. His attempt to retake the north was halted by a message through the prophet Shemaiah. He fortified cities in Judah. In his fifth year Shishak of Egypt came against Jerusalem, and Rehoboam made bronze shields to replace the ones lost. He had eighteen wives, loved Maachah most, and made her son Abijah his heir. War with Jeroboam lasted all his reign. Matthew's genealogy of Jesus calls him Roboam.

Rehoboth was a well dug by Isaac after he left the valley of Gerar, the third in a series of wells he opened there. The herdsmen of Gerar had disputed the two earlier wells, Esek and Sitnah (Gen 26:20–21), but no one quarreled over this one. So Isaac named it Rehoboth, meaning "broad places" or "room," saying that the LORD had made room for them and they would be fruitful in the land (Gen 26:22). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary place it at er-Ruheibeh, roughly 16 to 20 miles south or southwest of Beersheba. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also links it with Rubuta in the Tell el-Amarna Letters. The location shown here follows the er-Ruheibeh identification. The name is shared by other biblical places, including Rehoboth "by the river" in Edom and the Assyrian city Rehoboth-Ir, which are separate from this well.

Rehoboth, called Rehoboth-Ir ("Rehoboth City") in some modern translations, was a city in Assyria named in Gen 10:11 alongside Nineveh, Calah and Resen. The verse can be read two ways. Either Asshur went out from Shinar and built these cities, or Nimrod went into Assyria and built them. It belongs to the account of the beginning of Nimrod's kingdom, dated by inference from context to about 1822 BC. The name means "broad places" or "streets." Smith's Bible Dictionary says nothing certain is known of its position. Easton's Bible Dictionary, following the Vulgate, takes the phrase to mean "the public squares of the city," that is, of Nineveh. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links it with the Assyrian Rebit Ninua, "streets of Nineveh," a district near that city, and also mentions the old capital Assur as a possibility. The location shown here follows the identification with the Nineveh area, near modern Mosul in Iraq.

Rehum was one of the leaders who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the Babylonian exile. He is listed among the heads of the returning community in Ezra 2:2, and the parallel list in Neh 7:7 gives the name as Nehum, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes as a copying variant. Neh 12:3 names a Rehum among the priests who went up with Zerubbabel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests this should probably read Harim, the priestly house whose head in the next generation was Adna (Neh 12:15). A Harim also appears among the priests who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah's day (Neh 10:5). This entry treats these names as one figure. Smith's Bible Dictionary instead distinguishes the leader of Ezra 2:2 from the priestly Rehum of Neh 12:3. Because the name is shared by several people, the exact identifications remain uncertain.

Rehum was a Persian official, called "the chancellor," who with Shimshai the scribe and their associates wrote a letter to King Artaxerxes opposing the rebuilding of Jerusalem (Ezra 4:8–9). His title probably means "master of decree" or commander. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a high-ranking officer, and Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he was a kind of lieutenant-governor of the province. The letter was sent on behalf of several peoples settled in Samaria and the region west of the Euphrates. The king replied to Rehum and his companions, and when his answer was read to them, they hurried to Jerusalem and forced the Jews to stop their work (Ezra 4:17, 23). His name means "merciful" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Several other men in the Bible share the name Rehum. This entry concerns the Persian official.

Rehum son of Bani was a Levite who helped rebuild the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah. Neh 3:17 names him at the head of a group of Levites who repaired a section of the wall. Hashabiah, ruler of half the district of Keilah, worked on the section next to theirs. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this work to about 445 BC. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "merciful" or "compassionate." Several other men in the Bible are also called Rehum, including a Persian official who opposed the rebuilding of Jerusalem. This Rehum is known only from this one verse.

Rehum was one of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, a written pledge by the returned exiles to keep the law of God (Neh 10:25). His name appears among the "chief of the people" in the list of signers, alongside Hashabnah and Maaseiah. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the covenant to about 410 BC, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "merciful" or "compassionate." Several other men in the Bible are also named Rehum, including a Persian official in Ezra and a Levite who helped repair the wall of Jerusalem. Whether this signer is the same person as any of them cannot be determined from the text, so this entry treats him as a separate individual.

Rei was a man named once in the Bible, among those who did not side with Adonijah when Adonijah tried to make himself king near the end of David's reign (1 Kgs 1:8). He is listed with Zadok the priest, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, Nathan the prophet, Shimei, and David's mighty men, the group that stayed loyal to David and so backed Solomon's succession. The text gives no further details about him, and his identity is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes several proposals: that he and Shimei were officers of David's bodyguard, or that he was Ira the Jairite, called David's priest in 2 Sam 20:26. It also notes that Josephus omits him and reads the phrase as "David's friend." That encyclopedia suggests he was probably an officer of the royal guard. The name is usually explained as meaning "friendly."

The Reign of Abijam was the three-year rule of Abijam, king of Judah, in Jerusalem. He came to the throne in the eighteenth year of Jeroboam son of Nebat, king of Israel, about 958 BC by inference from context. His mother was Maachah, daughter of Abishalom. The account says he followed the sins of his father Rehoboam and that his heart was not fully devoted to the LORD as David's had been. Even so, for David's sake God kept a "lamp" in Jerusalem by establishing Abijam's son after him. War between Judah and Jeroboam continued through his reign. When he died he was buried in the city of David, and his son Asa succeeded him. The parallel account in 2 Chronicles 13 calls him Abijah and describes a battle he fought against Jeroboam.

The Reign of Ahab was the twenty-two-year rule of Ahab son of Omri over the northern kingdom of Israel, with Samaria as his capital. Ahab succeeded his father Omri, who was buried in Samaria (1 Kgs 16:28). His reign began in the thirty-eighth year of Asa king of Judah (1 Kgs 16:29), which places its start at about 918 BC, by inference from context. The text sums up his rule by saying he did evil in the sight of the LORD more than all the kings before him (1 Kgs 16:30). The chapters that follow in 1 Kings describe his marriage to Jezebel, his promotion of Baal worship, his conflicts with the prophet Elijah and his wars with Aram. He died in battle at Ramoth-gilead (1 Kgs 22).

The Reign of Ahaz was the sixteen-year rule of Ahaz son of Jotham over Judah from Jerusalem. By inference from context it began about 742 BC, in the seventeenth year of Pekah of Israel, when Ahaz was twenty. The text says he did not do right like David, made his son pass through the fire, and sacrificed at high places. When Rezin of Syria and Pekah besieged Jerusalem without taking it, and Rezin drove Judah's people from Elath, Ahaz sent silver and gold from the temple and palace to Tiglath-pileser of Assyria, calling himself his servant. Assyria then took Damascus and killed Rezin. After meeting Tiglath-pileser there, Ahaz had Urijah the priest build a copy of a Damascus altar, moved the bronze altar aside, and dismantled temple furnishings. He was buried in the city of David, and Hezekiah succeeded him. Parallel accounts appear in 2 Chr 28 and Isa 7.

The Reign of Ahaziah was the two-year rule of Ahaziah son of Ahab over the northern kingdom of Israel from its capital, Samaria. It began in the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, about 897 BC by inference from context. The text says he did evil, following the ways of his father, his mother (Jezebel, by inference from earlier chapters), and Jeroboam son of Nebat, and that he served and worshipped Baal as Ahab had. Connected passages add more. 2 Chr 20:35–37 records a failed shipbuilding partnership between him and Jehoshaphat. 2 Kgs 1 tells how he was injured in a fall, sent messengers to consult Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, was confronted by Elijah, and died, leaving his brother Jehoram to succeed him. He should not be confused with the later Ahaziah, king of Judah.

The Reign of Ahaziah (Jehoahaz) was the one-year rule of Ahaziah son of Jehoram over Judah from Jerusalem, dated here to about 886 BC by inference from context. He became king at twenty-two, in the twelfth year of Joram son of Ahab, king of Israel. His mother was Athaliah, called the daughter of Omri, probably meaning his granddaughter, since 2 Kgs 8:18 links Jehoram's wife to Ahab. The text says Ahaziah followed the ways of the house of Ahab, to which he was related by marriage, and did evil in the sight of the LORD. He joined Joram of Israel in war against Hazael of Syria at Ramoth-gilead. When Joram was wounded, Ahaziah went down to visit him at Jezreel. The alternative name Jehoahaz appears in 2 Chr 21:17. According to 2 Kgs 9:27, Ahaziah was killed during Jehu's revolt, which ended his short reign.

The Reign of Amaziah was the 29-year rule of Amaziah son of Joash as king of Judah in Jerusalem, beginning about 839 BC by inference from context. He came to the throne at twenty-five, in the second year of Joash king of Israel. He did what was right, though the high places stayed in use. Once secure, he executed the servants who had killed his father but spared their children, following the law of Moses. He defeated Edom in the Valley of Salt and took Selah, renaming it Joktheel. He then challenged Jehoash of Israel, who warned him off with a parable of a thistle and a cedar. Amaziah persisted, was defeated and captured at Beth-shemesh, and Jehoash broke down part of Jerusalem's wall and carried off temple and palace treasures. Amaziah later fled a conspiracy to Lachish, was killed there, and was buried in Jerusalem. His son Azariah succeeded him.

The Reign of Amon was the short rule of Amon, son of Manasseh, as king of Judah in Jerusalem. It lasted two years, beginning about 642 BC by inference from context. Amon became king at twenty-two. His mother was Meshullemeth, daughter of Haruz of Jotbah. The text says he did evil in the sight of the LORD as his father had done, serving and worshipping his father's idols and forsaking the LORD God of his fathers. His own servants conspired against him and killed him in his house. The people of the land then killed the conspirators and made his son Josiah king. Amon was buried in his tomb in the garden of Uzza. Further acts of his reign are said to be recorded in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah. A parallel account appears in 2 Chronicles 33.

The Reign of Asa was the 41-year rule of Asa as king of Judah in Jerusalem, beginning in the twentieth year of Jeroboam of Israel, about 956 BC by inference from context. Asa is described as doing what was right, like David. He expelled male cult prostitutes, removed idols, deposed his mother Maachah as queen and burned her idol by the Kidron brook, though the high places remained. He also brought dedicated silver and gold into the temple. Throughout his reign he was at war with Baasha of Israel, who fortified Ramah to blockade Judah. Asa sent the remaining temple and palace treasures to Ben-hadad of Damascus, who attacked northern Israelite cities. Baasha then abandoned Ramah, and Asa used its materials to build Geba and Mizpah. Diseased in his feet in old age, he was buried in the city of David and succeeded by his son Jehoshaphat. The parallel account in 2 Chronicles 14–16 gives a fuller narrative.

The Reign of Athaliah was the period when Athaliah, mother of King Ahaziah of Judah, ruled the southern kingdom from Jerusalem after her son's death. When she learned Ahaziah was dead, she tried to wipe out the entire royal family. His sister Jehosheba, daughter of King Joram, rescued his infant son Joash and hid him with his nurse, first in a bedchamber and then in the house of the LORD, for six years while Athaliah ruled the land. The parallel account in 2 Chr 22:10–12 tells the same story. Later verses (2 Kgs 11:4–16) describe how, in the seventh year, the priest Jehoiada brought Joash out, had him crowned, and had Athaliah put to death, ending her rule. This entry dates the start of her reign to about 886 BC and its length to about seven years, both inferred from context.

The Reign of Baasha was the 24-year rule of Baasha son of Ahijah over the northern kingdom of Israel. It began in the third year of Asa king of Judah, about 953 BC by inference from context. Baasha ruled from Tirzah, a city in the hill country later known as Samaria, which is the region shown here. The city of Samaria itself was built later by Omri (1 Kgs 16:24). Shortly before this passage, 1 Kgs 15:27–29 says Baasha took the throne by killing Nadab son of Jeroboam and destroying Jeroboam's family, and 1 Kgs 15:16–17 records his ongoing war with Asa. The text says he did evil and followed the ways of Jeroboam. The prophet Jehu son of Hanani announced that Baasha's family would be swept away like Jeroboam's. His other acts are said to be recorded in the chronicles of the kings of Israel.

The Reign of David was David's forty-year rule as king of Israel, recorded across 2 Samuel. It followed the reign of Saul and formed part of the united kingdom. David began to reign at thirty (2 Sam 5:4). At the LORD's direction he first ruled from Hebron over Judah. There Saul's commander Abner came to make terms with him and was later killed, a death the people understood David had not ordered. David then ruled all Israel from Jerusalem. He brought the ark of the LORD into the city and received God's promise concerning his house. He defeated the Philistines, Moab, Ammon, the Syrians, Zobah and Amalek. His reign was troubled by his affair with Bathsheba and the death of her husband Uriah, by Amnon's wrong against Tamar, and by Absalom's revolt, which ended with Absalom's death. It closed with a census and a plague that was stopped at a new altar. By inference from context, it began about 1055 BC.

The Reign of Elah was the short rule of Elah, son of Baasha, as king of the northern kingdom of Israel. He succeeded his father, who was buried in Tirzah, and began to reign in Tirzah in the twenty-sixth year of Asa king of Judah, ruling for two years (1 Kgs 16:8). Tirzah was then the royal city. The location shown here is Samaria, which probably stands for the northern kingdom as a whole, since the city of Samaria was built later by Omri. Before Elah's accession, the prophet Jehu son of Hanani had announced judgment on Baasha's house (1 Kgs 16:7). The following verses (1 Kgs 16:9–12) report that Zimri, a chariot commander, killed Elah while he was drunk in Tirzah in Asa's twenty-seventh year and destroyed Baasha's family, fulfilling Jehu's word. By inference from these dates, the "two years" were probably partial years. The date of about 930 BC is an estimate inferred from context.

The Reign of Hoshea was the nine-year rule of Hoshea son of Elah over the northern kingdom of Israel from its capital, Samaria. It began in the twelfth year of Ahaz king of Judah, about 730 BC by inference from context. The text says Hoshea did evil in the sight of the LORD, though not to the same degree as the Israelite kings before him. Shalmaneser king of Assyria came against him, and Hoshea submitted as a vassal, paying yearly tribute. When Hoshea sent messengers to So king of Egypt and stopped the payments, the Assyrian king treated this as conspiracy and had him seized and imprisoned. The surrounding chapters add that Hoshea came to power by killing his predecessor Pekah (2 Kgs 15:30). They also say that Samaria fell after a three-year siege in his ninth year and that the Israelites were deported (2 Kgs 17:5–6), which made him Israel's last king.

The Reign of Jeconiah was the brief rule of Jehoiachin, also called Jeconiah, as king of Judah in Jerusalem. This entry dates it to about 598 BC, by inference from context. He came to the throne at eighteen, succeeding his father Jehoiakim, and reigned three months. The parallel account in 2 Chr 36:9 adds ten days. His mother was Nehushta, daughter of Elnathan of Jerusalem, and the text says he did evil as his father had done. During his reign Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon besieged Jerusalem. Jehoiachin surrendered with his mother, servants, princes and officers and was taken to Babylon in Nebuchadnezzar's eighth year. The Babylonians removed the treasures of the temple and palace, cut up Solomon's gold vessels, and deported about ten thousand captives, including warriors, craftsmen and smiths, leaving only the poorest people. Nebuchadnezzar then made Jehoiachin's uncle Mattaniah king and renamed him Zedekiah.

The Reign of Jehoahaz was the seventeen-year rule of Jehoahaz son of Jehu over the northern kingdom of Israel from its capital, Samaria. It began in the twenty-third year of Joash king of Judah, about 857 BC by inference from context. The text says he did evil in the LORD's sight and continued the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat. As a result Israel was handed over to Hazael king of Syria and his son Ben-hadad. Jehoahaz pleaded with the LORD, who saw Israel's oppression and gave them a deliverer, though the people still kept Jeroboam's practices and the sacred grove remained in Samaria. The Syrians so reduced his army that only fifty horsemen, ten chariots and ten thousand foot soldiers were left. Jehoahaz was buried in Samaria, and his son Joash succeeded him.

The Reign of Jehoash was the sixteen-year rule of Jehoash (also called Joash), son of Jehoahaz, over the northern kingdom of Israel from its capital, Samaria. He came to the throne in the thirty-seventh year of Joash king of Judah, about 840 BC by inference from context. The text says he did evil in the Lord's sight and continued in the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat. It notes his military strength, especially his war against Amaziah king of Judah. Later passages describe that war (2 Kgs 14:8–14), as well as his visit to the dying prophet Elisha and his recovery of cities from Ben-hadad of Syria (2 Kgs 13:14–25). When he died he was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel, and his son Jeroboam, usually called Jeroboam II, succeeded him.

The Reign of Jehoiakim was the eleven-year rule of Jehoiakim as king of Judah in Jerusalem, beginning about 609 BC by inference from context. He became king at twenty-five, after the brief reign of Jehoahaz. The preceding passage, 2 Kgs 23:34, says Pharaoh Necho of Egypt made him king and changed his name from Eliakim. His mother was Zebudah, daughter of Pedaiah of Rumah. The text says he did evil in the LORD's sight, as his predecessors had done. During his reign Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up against Judah, and Jehoiakim served him for three years before rebelling. Raiding bands of Chaldeans, Syrians, Moabites and Ammonites were then sent against Judah. The writer links these raids to the sins of Manasseh and the innocent blood he shed in Jerusalem. Babylon took all of Egypt's territory from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates. Jehoiakim died, and his son Jehoiachin succeeded him.

The Reign of Jehoram was the eight-year rule of Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat as king of Judah in Jerusalem, dated here to about 893 BC by inference from context. He began to reign at thirty-two, in the fifth year of Joram son of Ahab, king of Israel. The text also calls him Joram, so the two kings shared a name. 2 Kgs 1:17 dates Israel's Jehoram to Judah's Jehoram's second year, which suggests an overlap or co-regency with his father Jehoshaphat. He married a daughter of Ahab (named Athaliah in 2 Kgs 8:26) and followed the ways of Israel's kings, yet Judah was spared for David's sake. During his reign Edom revolted and set up its own king. Jehoram struck the Edomites at Zair by night but could not reclaim the region, and Libnah also revolted. He was buried in the city of David, and his son Ahaziah succeeded him. 2 Chr 21 gives a parallel account.

The Reign of Jehu was the 28-year rule of Jehu, son of Jehoshaphat and grandson of Nimshi, over the northern kingdom of Israel from Samaria (2 Kgs 10:36). By inference from context it began about 886 BC. A young prophet sent by Elisha anointed Jehu, then an army commander, at Ramoth-gilead and charged him to destroy the house of Ahab. His fellow officers proclaimed him king, and Jehu drove furiously to Jezreel. There he shot King Joram, had Ahaziah of Judah struck down, and ordered Jezebel thrown from a window. At his demand Ahab's seventy sons in Samaria were killed, along with Ahab's remaining relatives and officials. He then gathered Baal's worshippers into their temple, had them slain and tore the building down. Yet he kept the golden calves at Bethel and Dan, and in his days Hazael of Syria took Israelite territory.

The Reign of Jeroboam I was the twenty-two-year rule of the first king of the northern kingdom of Israel. It began after Solomon's death, about 975 BC by inference from context. When the northern tribes made Jeroboam king, only Judah stayed loyal to David's house (1 Kgs 12:20). He feared that worship at the temple in Jerusalem would turn the people back to Rehoboam, so he set up calves at Bethel and Dan, appointed his own priests and began a feast in the eighth month (1 Kgs 12:26–32). A man of God from Judah condemned the Bethel altar and foretold the coming of Josiah. Jeroboam's outstretched hand withered and was then restored. When his son Abijah fell ill, Jeroboam's disguised wife consulted the prophet Ahijah at Shiloh, who announced the end of Jeroboam's house. The boy died as she reached Tirzah, apparently the royal residence. His son Nadab succeeded him (1 Kgs 14:20).

The Reign of Jeroboam II was the forty-one-year rule of Jeroboam son of Joash over the northern kingdom of Israel from its capital, Samaria. He came to the throne in the fifteenth year of Amaziah king of Judah, about 825 BC by inference from context. The text judges that he did evil, continuing the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat. Even so, he restored Israel's border from the entrance of Hamath to the Sea of the Arabah (probably the Dead Sea), as the prophet Jonah son of Amittai of Gath-hepher had foretold. The account explains this as the LORD saving a bitterly afflicted Israel through him. It also notes his military strength and his recovery of Damascus and Hamath for Israel, and refers readers to the chronicles of the kings of Israel for more. At his death his son Zachariah succeeded him.

The Reign of Joash (also called Jehoash) was the forty-year rule of this king of Judah in Jerusalem. He became king at seven, in the seventh year of Jehu of Israel, and his mother was Zibiah of Beersheba. This entry dates its start to about 879 BC, an estimate inferred from context. He did right while the priest Jehoiada instructed him, though the high places stayed in use. He ordered the priests to repair the temple with donated money, but by his twenty-third year nothing had been done. Jehoiada then set up a chest with a hole in its lid beside the altar, and the money collected was paid to carpenters, masons and stonecutters. When Hazael king of Syria took Gath and threatened Jerusalem, Joash bought him off with the temple and palace treasures. His servants Jozachar and Jehozabad later killed him at the house of Millo, and his son Amaziah succeeded him.

The Reign of Johoahaz (Shallum) was the three-month rule of Jehoahaz, son of Josiah, as king of Judah in Jerusalem, about 609 BC by inference from context. He became king at twenty-three, right after Josiah's reign. His mother was Hamutal, daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah. The text says he did evil in the sight of the LORD, as his fathers had done. Pharaoh Necho of Egypt put him in chains at Riblah in the land of Hamath so that he could not reign in Jerusalem. Necho imposed a tribute of a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold, and made Jehoahaz's brother Eliakim king, renaming him Jehoiakim. Jehoahaz was taken to Egypt and died there. Jehoiakim raised the tribute by taxing the people. The name Shallum comes from Jer 22:11 and 1 Chr 3:15, which give it to this son of Josiah.

The Reign of Joram was the twelve-year rule of Joram (also spelled Jehoram), son of Ahab, over the northern kingdom of Israel from its capital, Samaria. It began in the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, about 897 BC by inference from context. He should not be confused with Jehoram of Judah, Jehoshaphat's son, who reigned at about the same time. The text says Joram did evil, though not to the degree of his father and mother. He removed the image of Baal that Ahab had made but kept to the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat. Mesha king of Moab had paid Israel a heavy tribute of lambs, rams and wool, and he rebelled after Ahab's death. In response Joram left Samaria and mustered all Israel. The following verses describe a campaign against Moab with Judah and Edom, and 2 Kgs 9:24 records that Jehu later killed Joram.

The Reign of Josiah was the thirty-one-year rule of Josiah over Judah from Jerusalem, beginning about 640 BC by inference from context. He became king at age eight, succeeding Amon. During repairs to the temple, Hilkiah the high priest found a book of the law, which Shaphan the scribe read to the king. Josiah tore his clothes and sent officials to the prophetess Huldah, who foretold disaster on Jerusalem but said Josiah would not live to see it. He read the book of the covenant to the people, removed vessels and priests devoted to Baal and the host of heaven, defiled Topheth, and destroyed the altar at Bethel and high places in Samaria. He then held a Passover unlike any since the judges. Josiah was killed at Megiddo confronting Pharaoh Necho of Egypt, and his son Jehoahaz was made king.

The Reign of Jotham was the sixteen-year rule of Jotham son of Uzziah as king of Judah in Jerusalem. It began in the second year of Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, and this entry dates its start to about 758 BC, by inference from context. Jotham became king at twenty-five, and his mother was Jerusha, daughter of Zadok. He did what was right in the sight of the LORD, following his father Uzziah's example, though the people still sacrificed and burned incense at the high places. He built the upper gate of the temple. During his reign the LORD began sending Rezin king of Syria and Pekah of Israel against Judah. Jotham was buried in the city of David, and his son Ahaz succeeded him. The parallel account in 2 Chronicles 27 adds further building works and a victory over the Ammonites.

The Reign of Manasseh was the fifty-five-year rule of Hezekiah's son over Judah from Jerusalem. He began at age twelve, about 697 BC by inference from context, and his mother was Hephzibah. 2 Kings presents it as a reversal of his father's reforms. He rebuilt the high places, raised altars to Baal, made an Asherah pole (the KJV "grove"), worshipped the stars, and set up altars and a carved image in the temple courts. He made his son pass through the fire, practiced divination, consulted mediums, and shed much innocent blood in Jerusalem.
