Through the prophets, the LORD announced that Jerusalem would share Samaria's fate and be handed over to its enemies. Manasseh was buried in the garden of Uzza, and his son Amon succeeded him. The parallel account in 2 Chr 33 adds that he was taken captive to Babylon, humbled himself, and was restored.

The Reign of Menahem was the ten-year rule of Menahem son of Gadi over the northern kingdom of Israel from its capital, Samaria. It began in the thirty-ninth year of Azariah (also called Uzziah) king of Judah, about 772 BC by inference from context. The preceding verses (2 Kgs 15:14) say Menahem came to power by killing Shallum. The text judges that he continued in the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat. When Pul king of Assyria invaded, Menahem paid him a thousand talents of silver to secure his throne. He raised the money by taxing every wealthy man in Israel fifty shekels of silver, and the Assyrian king then withdrew. Pul is usually identified with Tiglath-pileser III. Menahem died and was succeeded by his son Pekahiah.

The Reign of Nadab was the short rule of Nadab, son of Jeroboam, over the northern kingdom of Israel. He became king in the second year of Asa king of Judah and reigned two years, about 954 BC by inference from context. Because Baasha's reign began in Asa's third year (1 Kgs 15:33), the two years were probably partial years. The text says he did evil in the sight of the LORD and followed his father's way and the sin by which Jeroboam made Israel sin. The following verses (1 Kgs 15:27–29) tell how Baasha conspired against him and killed him while Israel was besieging the Philistine town of Gibbethon, then wiped out Jeroboam's family. This entry places the reign in Samaria as the northern kingdom's region. The city of Samaria itself was built later by Omri (1 Kgs 16:24), and the royal court of this period was at Tirzah (1 Kgs 14:17).

The Reign of Omri was the twelve-year rule of Omri over the northern kingdom of Israel, beginning in the thirty-first year of Asa king of Judah (about 929 BC, by inference from context). Omri took the throne after his supporters prevailed over those who followed Tibni son of Ginath, and Tibni died. He ruled six years from Tirzah, then bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver, built a city there, and named it Samaria after its former owner. The text says he did evil in the eyes of the LORD, worse than all the kings before him, following the ways of Jeroboam son of Nebat. His other acts and his might are said to be recorded in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel. He was buried in Samaria, and his son Ahab succeeded him.

The Reign of Pekah was the twenty-year rule of Pekah son of Remaliah over the northern kingdom of Israel from its capital, Samaria. It began in the fifty-second year of Azariah (Uzziah) king of Judah, about 759 BC by inference from context. The neighbouring verse 2 Kgs 15:25 says he took the throne by killing King Pekahiah. The narrator judges that he did evil and kept the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat. During his reign the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser captured Ijon, Abel-beth-maachah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, Galilee and all the land of Naphtali, and deported their people to Assyria. Later passages (2 Kgs 16:5; Isa 7:1) describe his alliance with Rezin of Syria against Ahaz of Judah. The reign ended when Hoshea son of Elah conspired against Pekah, killed him and became king. Fitting the twenty years into the timeline of the period is a known chronological puzzle.

The Reign of Pekahiah was the two-year rule of Pekahiah son of Menahem over the northern kingdom of Israel from its capital, Samaria. He came to the throne in the fiftieth year of Azariah (Uzziah) king of Judah, about 761 BC by inference from context. The text judges that he did evil in the sight of the LORD and kept to the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who led Israel into sin. His reign ended violently. Pekah son of Remaliah, one of his own captains, conspired against him and, with Argob, Arieh and fifty men from Gilead, killed him in the palace of the king's house in Samaria. Pekah then took the throne. The rest of Pekahiah's acts are said to be recorded in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel, a source that has not survived.

The Reign of Rehoboam was the rule of Solomon's son over the southern kingdom of Judah from Jerusalem. It began after Solomon's death, about 975 BC by inference from context, and lasted about seventeen years, a figure given in 1 Kgs 14:21. It opened with the kingdom splitting. Rehoboam kept only the Israelites living in the cities of Judah. When he sent Adoram, the officer in charge of forced labor, to the northern tribes, they stoned him to death, and Rehoboam fled by chariot to Jerusalem. The north made Jeroboam its king, leaving only Judah loyal to the house of David. Rehoboam gathered 180,000 warriors from Judah and Benjamin to win the kingdom back. The prophet Shemaiah then delivered God's command not to fight their fellow Israelites, saying the division came from the Lord. The people obeyed and went home.

The Reign of Saul was the period during which Saul ruled as Israel's first king, beginning about 1095 BC and lasting about forty years, both figures estimated by inference from context (Acts 13:21 also gives forty years). Samuel anointed him privately with oil (1 Sam 10:1), and he ruled from Gibeah. He fought the Philistines and the Amalekites (1 Sam 14:48). After he offered a burnt offering before Samuel arrived, and later failed to carry out God's command against Amalek, Samuel told him the LORD had rejected him as king (1 Sam 15:26). David was then anointed. He served Saul, defeated Goliath and grew popular, and Saul tried repeatedly to kill him, while Saul's son Jonathan made a covenant with David. Near the end, Saul consulted a medium at night (1 Sam 28:8). The reign ended when the Philistines defeated Israel and killed Saul's sons, Jonathan among them (1 Sam 31:2).

The Reign of Shallum was the brief rule of Shallum son of Jabesh over the northern kingdom of Israel. According to 2 Kgs 15:10, Shallum conspired against King Zechariah, the last ruler of Jehu's dynasty, struck him down in public, and took the throne. The surrounding passage adds that Shallum became king in the thirty-ninth year of Uzziah, king of Judah, and reigned only a full month in Samaria (2 Kgs 15:13). Menahem son of Gadi then came up from Tirzah, killed Shallum in Samaria, and reigned in his place (2 Kgs 15:14). The date given here, about 772 BC, is an estimate inferred from context. His short reign is one of several violent changes of ruler in Israel's final decades.

The Reign of Solomon was the forty-year rule of David's son over all Israel from Jerusalem, recounted in 1 Kings 2–11. It began about 1015 BC, by inference from context, and followed the Reign of David within the united kingdom. Solomon secured his throne by dealing with Adonijah, Joab and Shimei. At Gibeon he offered a thousand burnt offerings, and God promised him wisdom along with riches and honour. He organized officials and regional governors, and he was known for judging the dispute of two mothers and for composing 3,000 proverbs and 1,005 songs. With cedar and fir timber supplied by Hiram, he built the temple, beginning in his fourth year, and then a palace and a house for Pharaoh's daughter. The queen of Sheba visited his court, and gold flowed in. In old age his foreign wives drew him to other gods, and adversaries such as Hadad the Edomite and Rezon rose against him.

The Reign of Tibni was a period of divided rule in the northern kingdom of Israel, when half the people backed Tibni son of Ginath as king and the other half backed Omri. It followed the death of Zimri, according to the surrounding account in 1 Kings 16. Omri's supporters won, Tibni died, and Omri became sole king. The text does not say how Tibni died. It also gives no length for his claim. Comparing 1 Kgs 16:15, where Zimri reigns in Asa's twenty-seventh year, with 1 Kgs 16:23, where Omri's reign is dated from Asa's thirty-first year, suggests the rivalry lasted about four years, around 929 BC by inference from context. The location shown here is Samaria, though by 1 Kgs 16:24 Omri founded Samaria only later, and Tibni's own base is not named.

The Reign of Uzziah was the 52-year rule of Uzziah, called Azariah in 2 Kings, as king of Judah in Jerusalem. The son of Amaziah and Jecholiah of Jerusalem, he became king at sixteen, in the twenty-seventh year of Jeroboam king of Israel (Jeroboam II). This entry dates the start of his reign to about 810 BC, an estimate inferred from context. He is said to have done what was right in the LORD's sight, as his father had, though the people still sacrificed and burned incense at the high places. The LORD struck him with leprosy, and he lived in a separate house until his death while his son Jotham governed the palace and judged the people. The parallel account in 2 Chr 26 uses the name Uzziah and ties the leprosy to his burning incense in the temple. He was buried in the city of David, and Jotham succeeded him.

The Reign of Zachariah was the brief rule of Zachariah, son of Jeroboam II, over the northern kingdom of Israel from its capital Samaria. According to 2 Kgs 15:8 he became king in the thirty-eighth year of Azariah king of Judah and reigned only six months. The text says he did evil in the sight of the LORD as his predecessors had, continuing the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had led Israel into wrongdoing (2 Kgs 15:9). The following verses say that Shallum son of Jabesh conspired against him, killed him publicly and took the throne, and 2 Kgs 15:12 presents this as the end of Jehu's dynasty in the fourth generation. This entry dates the period from about 784 BC and gives it a span of about eleven years, both estimates inferred from context. The longer span probably reflects chronologies that place an interval between Jeroboam II's death and Zachariah's six-month reign.

The Reign of Zedekiah was the final reign of the kingdom of Judah, lasting eleven years in Jerusalem and beginning about 597 BC, by inference from context. Zedekiah became king at twenty-one, following Jeconiah. The preceding verse, 2 Kgs 24:17, says Nebuchadnezzar installed him and renamed him from Mattaniah. His mother was Hamutal, daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah. The text says he did evil as Jehoiakim had, and that he rebelled against the king of Babylon. In his ninth year Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem. The siege lasted into his eleventh year, when famine left the city without bread. When the wall was breached, Zedekiah and his soldiers fled by night toward the plain, but the Babylonian army overtook him near Jericho and his troops scattered. At Riblah his sons were killed before his eyes. He was then blinded, bound in bronze fetters and taken to Babylon.

The Reign of Zimri was the seven-day rule of Zimri over the northern kingdom of Israel, dated to the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah (about 929 BC, by inference from context). He reigned from Tirzah, then the royal city, while Israel's army was camped against the Philistine town of Gibbethon. When the soldiers heard that Zimri had conspired against the king and killed him, they made Omri, the army commander, king that same day in the camp. The surrounding verses (1 Kgs 16:9–10) say the murdered king was Elah and that Zimri commanded half of his chariots. The verses that follow (1 Kgs 16:17–18) tell how Omri besieged Tirzah and Zimri died when he set the palace on fire around himself. The location shown here is Samaria, the region of the northern kingdom. The city of Samaria itself was founded later by Omri.

Rekem was one of five kings of Midian killed by the Israelites in the time of Moses, along with Evi, Zur, Hur and Reba. Numbers 31:8 records their deaths in Israel's war against Midian, the same campaign in which Balaam son of Beor was killed with the sword. Joshua 13:21 recalls the event when describing the land east of the Jordan. It calls these five "princes of Midian" and "dukes of Sihon", meaning chieftains linked to Sihon, the Amorite king who ruled from Heshbon. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "variegation." The same name belongs to other people in the Bible, including a man of Judah and a town of Benjamin, but this entry concerns only the Midianite king.

Rekem was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2 as one of the four sons of Hebron, alongside Korah, Tappuah and Shema. He was the father of Shammai. Nothing else is recorded about him. This Hebron belongs to the line of Caleb within Judah's genealogy, and some of the names in this list, such as Tappuah, also appear as towns in Judah. For that reason the names may stand partly for clans or settlements as well as for individuals, though the text presents them as father and sons. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "variegation." Several other people in the Bible share the name Rekem, including a Midianite king killed in Moses' time. This entry concerns only the son of Hebron.

Rekem was a city in the territory given to the tribe of Benjamin. It appears only once, in the list of Benjamin's towns in Josh 18:27, where it is named alongside Irpeel and Taralah. These belong to the second group of Benjamite towns, which also includes Jerusalem and Gibeah, so Rekem probably lay somewhere in the hill country north or northwest of Jerusalem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia states that the site is unknown, and no modern identification is firmly established. The location shown here is only a rough placement in that general area. The same name is also borne by a king of Midian and by a descendant of Caleb, but this entry concerns only the Benjamite town. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "friendship," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "vain pictures."

Remaliah was the father of Pekah, the army captain who killed King Pekahiah in Samaria and took the throne of Israel, reigning twenty years (2 Kgs 15:25, 27). Nothing is recorded about Remaliah himself. His name survives only in the phrase "son of Remaliah," used of Pekah in Kings, Chronicles and Isaiah, including the accounts of Pekah's alliance with Rezin of Syria against Judah and King Ahaz. Isaiah repeatedly refers to Pekah only as "the son of Remaliah" or "Remaliah's son" without naming him (Isa 7:4–5, 9; 8:6). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests this may be a contemptuous reference to the family's humble origins. The name is usually explained as meaning "adorned by the Lord" (Easton's Bible Dictionary) or "protected by the Lord" (Smith's Bible Dictionary).

Remeth was a town in the territory of the tribe of Issachar, listed alongside En-gannim, En-haddah and Beth-pazzez in the account of Issachar's inheritance (Josh 19:21). The name probably means "height." Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take it as another form of the Ramoth of 1 Chr 6:73 and the Jarmuth of Josh 21:29, a Levitical town of Issachar. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats it as probably a separate place. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it at the village of er-Rameh, about 11 miles southwest of Jenin (En-gannim). The location shown here is a rough placement farther north, in the eastern Jezreel plain between Jenin and the hills of Lower Galilee, within Issachar's allotment. The exact site remains uncertain.

Rephael was a Levite, a son of Shemaiah, named with his brothers Othni, Obed, Elzabad, Elihu and Semachiah in the list of temple gatekeepers in 1 Chr 26:7. The surrounding passage traces Shemaiah to Obed-edom, and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Shemaiah as Obed-edom's firstborn. The verse calls some of the brothers "strong men", and Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that this family's strength for service made them one of the divisions of porters, or gatekeepers. The Chronicler places these arrangements in the reign of David. The name means "God has healed". The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats Rephael as the founder of a family of gatekeepers and notes that the same name appears as Raphael in later Jewish writings such as Tobit. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Rephah was a member of the tribe of Joseph, listed in the genealogy of Ephraim's descendants (1 Chr 7:25). The verse says only that "Rephah was his son," and the "his" can be read in more than one way. This entry follows the reading that makes him a son of Beriah, the son Ephraim named after the loss of his other sons in the preceding verses, with Resheph and Sherah as his siblings. Smith's Bible Dictionary instead calls him a son of Ephraim. The list that follows him runs through Telah and Tahan and on to Nun and his son Joshua (1 Chr 7:26–27), so Rephah appears as an ancestor of Joshua. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats him as the founder of an Ephraimite family and notes that the Hebrew form of his name may be corrupt. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Rephaiah was a son of Binea in the family line of King Saul, from the tribe of Benjamin. He appears only in the two parallel genealogies of Saul's descendants. He is called Rephaiah in 1 Chr 9:43 and Rapha (Raphah) in 1 Chr 8:37. By inference from the surrounding verses (1 Chr 8:33–36; 9:39–42), his grandfather Moza descended from Saul through Jonathan and Merib-baal, so Rephaiah belonged to a late generation of Saul's line. The text says nothing about his life. This entry treats Eleasah and Azel as his brothers, though the repeated phrase "his son" can also be read as a line of descent, with Eleasah as Rephaiah's son and Azel as his grandson. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of the name as probably "Yah is healing." Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Rephaiah was a man of the tribe of Judah and a descendant of King David, named in the royal genealogy that follows the line after the exile. This entry treats him as a son of Hananiah, alongside Pelatiah, Jesaiah, Arnan, Obadiah and Shechaniah. Hananiah was a son of Zerubbabel, according to 1 Chr 3:19, so Rephaiah belongs to the generations after the return from Babylon. The wording of 1 Chr 3:21 is unclear. It lists "the sons of Rephaiah" as a separate family group, so Rephaiah may have headed a clan connected to Hananiah's line rather than being his direct son. The Greek Septuagint reads the verse as a chain of successive generations. His name probably means "Yah is healing," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Rephaiah was one of four sons of Ishi, a man of the tribe of Simeon. With his brothers Pelatiah, Neariah and Uzziel, he was a captain of five hundred Simeonites who went to Mount Seir (1 Chr 4:42). The surrounding verses place this expedition in the days of Hezekiah, king of Judah, and say that the group struck down the remaining Amalekites who had escaped there and settled in their land (1 Chr 4:41, 43). The name probably means "the LORD heals" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, and this Rephaiah appears only in this one passage.

Rephaiah was a son of Tola and a grandson of Issachar, listed in the genealogy of the tribe of Issachar in 1 Chr 7:2. His brothers were Uzzi, Jeriel, Jahmai, Jibsam and Shemuel. Together they are called heads of their father's house and valiant men of might, and their descendants are said to have numbered 22,600 in the days of David. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name probably means "the LORD heals" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Rephaiah should not be confused with them.

Rephaiah son of Hur was the ruler of half the district of Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah. He repaired a section of the city wall when it was rebuilt after the return from exile (Neh 3:9). His section lay next to that of the men of Jericho and others listed just before him. Another official, Shallum son of Hallohesh, is also called ruler of half the district of Jerusalem (Neh 3:12), so the city was probably divided into two administrative halves. The name probably means "the LORD heals" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the work to about 441 BC. Several other men in the Bible share the name Rephaiah, but this one is known only from this verse. Nothing more is recorded about him or his father Hur.

Rephaim, in the phrase "land of Rephaim," is a name for Bashan, the kingdom of Og east of the Jordan. The King James Version translates it as "the land of giants." Moses gave this region, including the district of Argob, to the half tribe of Manasseh (Deut 3:13). The name comes from the Rephaim, an early people that Easton's Bible Dictionary describes as tall original inhabitants of the land who were later displaced. The Revised Version keeps the Hebrew name here. The nearby verse Deut 3:11 says that Og himself was among the last of the Rephaim, which probably explains why his kingdom carried the name. It is a regional name, not a single town. Bashan covered the high plateau east and northeast of the Sea of Galilee, roughly today's Golan Heights and northern Jordan. The location shown here is an approximate point within that region.

Rephidim was a campsite of the Israelites on their journey from Egypt to Mount Sinai. They reached it after leaving the wilderness of Sin, by way of Alush, and found no water to drink there (Exod 17:1; Num 33:14). The surrounding chapter tells how Moses brought water from a rock, and Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the spot was therefore also called Massah and Meribah. At Rephidim the Amalekites attacked Israel, the first battle after the Exodus (Exod 17:8). From there the people moved on to the wilderness of Sinai and camped before the mountain (Exod 19:2; Num 33:15). The name probably means "rests" or "resting places." The exact site is uncertain. Most older dictionaries place it in Wadi Feiran in southern Sinai, while some prefer Wadi esh-Sheikh. The location shown here follows Easton's Bible Dictionary, which puts it in Wadi Feiran near its junction with Wadi esh-Sheikh.

Resen was an ancient city in Assyria, named in Gen 10:12 as lying "between Nineveh and Calah" and called "a great city." It is one of four cities whose founding follows the account of Nimrod's kingdom. The King James Version credits the building to Asshur, while other readings, noted by the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, credit Nimrod. The name probably reflects an Assyrian word meaning "fountainhead," though Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "bridle." Its exact site is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary favours the ruin mound of Karamless, east of the Tigris. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia prefer the ruins at Selamiyeh, about 3 miles north of Calah (modern Nimrud). The location shown here is only approximate, placed in the Nineveh area near modern Mosul in northern Iraq. The founding is dated to about 1822 BC, an estimate inferred from context.

Resheph was a descendant of Ephraim, one of the tribes descended from Joseph, named once in the Ephraimite genealogy at 1 Chr 7:25. The verse lists him after Rephah. This entry reads him as a son of Beriah, the son Ephraim named after the killing of his sons by the men of Gath (1 Chr 7:21–23), which would make Rephah and Sherah his siblings. The wording leaves open whether 'his son' refers back to Ephraim or to Beriah, and Smith's Bible Dictionary calls Resheph simply a son of Ephraim. The list continues through Telah, taken here as Resheph's son, and on down the line that leads to Joshua (1 Chr 7:27). The name means 'flame' or 'fire-bolt,' and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it is also found in Phoenician as the name of a god. Nothing else is recorded about him.

The Resurrection and Ascension are the events that close the four Gospels, dated here to about AD 30 by inference from context. Early on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene, the other Mary and other women (Mark 16:1 adds Salome) came to Jesus' tomb in Jerusalem, found the stone rolled away, and were told by angels that he had risen. Jesus appeared to Mary Magdalene, to two disciples on the road to Emmaus, one named Cleopas, to Simon, and to the gathered disciples, showing his hands and feet and eating before them. Thomas doubted until he saw him, then said, "My Lord and my God." Jesus sent the disciples to meet him in Galilee, where John 21 places an appearance by the Sea of Galilee, and gave them a commission. He was then taken up into heaven, from the Mount of Olives according to Acts 1:12, and the disciples returned to Jerusalem with joy.

The Return from Second Missionary Journey was Paul's voyage from Corinth back to Syria, told in Acts 18:18–23. After a long stay in Corinth, Paul sailed with Priscilla and Aquila, first cutting his hair at the port of Cenchreae because of a vow. At Ephesus he left the couple and reasoned with the Jews in the synagogue. They asked him to stay longer, but he declined, saying he had to keep a coming feast in Jerusalem, and promised to return if God willed. He landed at Caesarea, "went up" and greeted the church, probably the church in Jerusalem by inference from his stated aim, and then went down to Antioch in Syria. After some time there he travelled through Galatia and Phrygia strengthening the disciples, a move often treated as the start of his third journey. This entry dates the return to about AD 50, an estimate inferred from context.

The Return to Antioch in Syria was the final stage of the First Missionary Journey of Paul and Barnabas. After preaching in Derbe, they retraced their route through Lystra, Iconium and Antioch in Pisidia. There they strengthened the disciples, urged them to keep the faith, warned that they must pass through much hardship to enter the kingdom of God, and appointed elders in each church with prayer and fasting. They then crossed Pisidia into Pamphylia, preached in Perga, went down to the port of Attalia, and sailed back to Antioch in Syria, the church that had sent them out (compare Acts 13:1–3). They gathered the church and reported all that God had done through them, and how he had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles. They then stayed there a long time with the disciples. This entry dates the return to about AD 46, by inference from context.

Reu was a descendant of Shem through Eber, the son of Peleg and the father of Serug, in the family line that leads to Abraham. Genesis records that Peleg was thirty when Reu was born, and that Reu was thirty-two when he fathered Serug. He lived another 207 years and had other sons and daughters, a total lifespan of 239 years. 1 Chr 1:25 repeats his place in the line from Shem to Abraham. In Luke's genealogy of Jesus he appears under the Greek form Ragau, son of Phalec (Peleg) and father of Saruch (Serug). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary both identify Ragau as the same person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "his friend" or "his shepherd." His dates of about 2217–1978 BC are estimates inferred from the genealogical figures.

Reuben was the territory given to the tribe of Reuben, descendants of Jacob's eldest son, east of the Jordan River in what is now central Jordan. Moses assigned it to the tribe by families (Josh 13:15). It ran north from Aroer on the Arnon River (probably the modern Wadi Mujib) across the plain around Medeba, with the Jordan as its western edge (Josh 13:16, 23). The land had been the kingdom of Sihon, the Amorite king who ruled from Heshbon and was defeated by Moses along with the Midianite princes (Josh 13:21). Its towns included Heshbon, Dibon, Kirjathaim, Sibmah, Beth-peor and Beth-jeshimoth, and the Reubenites built or rebuilt several of them (Num 32:37). Four of its cities, Bezer, Jahazah, Kedemoth and Mephaath, were given to the Levites (Josh 21:36–37). The location shown here is a central point on the Medeba plateau, near Heshbon.

Reuben was the firstborn son of Jacob and Leah, named by Leah in the hope that her husband would now love her (Gen 29:32). He was born about 1758 BC, by inference from context. He lay with Bilhah, his father's concubine (Gen 35:22). Jacob's dying words address him as firstborn, and the following verse links his loss of preeminence to that act (Gen 49:3–4). When his brothers plotted against Joseph, Reuben persuaded them not to kill him and tore his clothes on finding the pit empty (Gen 37:21, 29). Later he offered his own two sons as a pledge for Benjamin's safe return from Egypt (Gen 42:37). His four sons, Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron and Carmi, went down with him to Egypt (Gen 46:9). His descendants formed the tribe of Reuben, which settled east of the Jordan alongside Gad and half of Manasseh (Num 32:33).

Reuel was a son of Esau and his wife Bashemath (Gen 36:4, 36:10). Genesis 36:3 identifies this Bashemath as a daughter of Ishmael. His half-brothers were Eliphaz, the son of Adah, and Jeush, Jaalam and Korah (1 Chr 1:35). Reuel had four sons, Nahath, Zerah, Shammah and Mizzah (Gen 36:13; 1 Chr 1:37). Each became a chief (the King James Version says "duke") of a clan descended from Reuel in the land of Edom (Gen 36:17). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "God is his friend." Several other people in the Bible share the name, most notably Moses' father-in-law (Exod 2:18). This entry concerns only the Edomite son of Esau.

Reuel was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only once, in a genealogy in 1 Chr 9:8. He was the son of Ibnijah and the father of Shephathiah, and through Shephathiah he was the grandfather of Meshullam. Meshullam appears in a list of Benjamite family heads living in Jerusalem, a list that the surrounding chapter, by inference from its context, places among the people who settled there after the return from exile. Reuel himself would therefore have lived some generations earlier, though nothing else is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name, including a son of Esau. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of the name as "friend of God."

Reumah was the concubine of Nahor, the brother of Abraham. She is named only once, at the end of the list of Nahor's descendants that was reported to Abraham after the near-sacrifice of Isaac. The surrounding verses list Nahor's eight sons by his wife Milcah first, and then Reumah's four children: Tebah, Gaham, Thahash and Maachah (Gen 22:24). The verse does not give the children's genders. This entry treats Maachah as a daughter, while some reference works, such as the STEPBible proper names list, describe all four as sons. Nothing else is recorded about her. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of her name as "lofty" or "sublime," and Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "elevated." Smith's dates her to about 1870 BC, an estimate drawn from the patriarchal timeline.

Rezeph was a city named in the Assyrian king Sennacherib's taunting message to Hezekiah, delivered during the threat to Jerusalem. It is listed with Gozan, Haran and "the children of Eden" in Telassar as places destroyed by earlier Assyrian kings, whose gods had not saved them (2 Kgs 19:12; Isa 37:12). The point of the list was that Jerusalem's God would not save it either. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies Rezeph with the Rasappa of Assyrian records, a provincial center under Assyrian governors and probably an important trade town. It places the city at Rusafa (Resafa) in northern Syria, northeast of Hamath. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as a fortress near Haran, probably west of the Euphrates. The location shown here follows the Resafa identification, a site south of the Euphrates in present-day Syria.

Rezia was a man of the tribe of Asher, named as one of the three sons of Ulla, alongside his brothers Arah and Haniel, in the Asherite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:39. Nothing else is recorded about him, and Ulla himself is not clearly linked to the earlier names in the list. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "delight." Some reference works, such as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, list him under the spelling Rizia.

Rezin was a king of Syria (Aram) who ruled from Damascus in the time of Jotham and Ahaz, kings of Judah. He first moved against Judah late in Jotham's reign, and then joined Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, in attacking Jerusalem and besieging Ahaz. They could not take the city. Isaiah told Ahaz not to fear these "two tails of smoking firebrands" (Isa 7:4) and called Rezin "the head of Damascus." During the campaign Rezin drove the Jews out of the port of Elath. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a reading in which Elath passed to the Edomites instead. Ahaz then appealed to the king of Assyria, who captured Damascus, deported its people to Kir and killed Rezin. Easton's Bible Dictionary dates this to 732 BC, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him the last king of Damascus.

Rezin was the ancestor of a family of temple servants, the Nethinim, whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Judah with Zerubbabel. The family appears in the list of returnees in Ezra 2:48 and again in the parallel list in Neh 7:50, both times beside the families of Nekoda and Gazzam or Reaiah. The context of the return places this before about 536 BC, a date Smith's Bible Dictionary also gives. Nothing else is recorded about Rezin himself. He is different from Rezin the king of Syria (Aram), who allied with Israel against Judah in the time of Ahaz. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "firm," while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "good-will" or "messenger."

Rezon son of Eliadah was a man who fled from his master Hadadezer, king of Zobah, and whom God raised up as an adversary to Solomon (1 Kgs 11:23). The surrounding passage (1 Kgs 11:24–25) says he gathered a band of men after David defeated Zobah, took Damascus, reigned over Syria, and opposed Israel throughout Solomon's reign. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects his break with Hadadezer to David's victory over Zobah recorded in 2 Sam 8:3–8. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that many scholars identify him with Hezion, named in 1 Kgs 15:18 as the grandfather of Ben-hadad I. If so, Rezon founded the line of Syrian kings at Damascus that later fought against Israel. That identification is uncertain.

Rhegium was a city at the toe of Italy, on the Italian side of the Strait of Messina, where Paul's ship stopped on his journey to Rome (Acts 28:13). After the shipwreck on Malta, the ship sailed by way of Syracuse and then "fetched a compass" to reach Rhegium, probably meaning it tacked or took a roundabout course against unfavorable winds, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains. It waited there one day until a south wind rose, then reached Puteoli the following day. The voyage took place about AD 57, by inference from context. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Rhegium as originally a Greek colony that later prospered under Roman rule, and notes that its coins showed the "twin brothers" who gave Paul's ship its name. It is the modern Reggio di Calabria, which matches the location shown here.

Rhesa was a man named in Luke's genealogy of Jesus as the son of Zorobabel (the Greek form of Zerubbabel) and the father of Joanna (Luke 3:27). Through this line he belongs to the tribe of Judah. He appears in only this one verse, and nothing else is told about his life. Rhesa is not among the sons of Zerubbabel listed in 1 Chr 3:19–20, and Matthew's genealogy traces the line from Zerubbabel through Abiud instead, so his place in the family cannot be checked against other passages. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes a suggestion that "Rhesa" may be a title meaning "head" or "prince" rather than a personal name. This entry treats him as a person, as Luke's wording presents him. Older name dictionaries give different meanings for the name, including "affection" (Easton's Bible Dictionary) and "will" or "course" (Hitchcock's Bible Names).

Rhoda was a servant girl in the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark, in Jerusalem. Her name means "rose." When Peter knocked at the gate after an angel freed him from Herod's prison, she came to answer (Acts 12:13). The surrounding passage (Acts 12:12–15) tells how she recognized his voice and was so overjoyed that she ran inside to tell the gathered believers without opening the door. They told her she was out of her mind, and when she insisted, they said it must be his angel. Peter kept knocking until they let him in. The event is dated here to about AD 40, by inference from context; Smith's Bible Dictionary places it about AD 44. Nothing more is recorded about her.

Rhodes is a large island in the southeastern Aegean Sea, off the southwestern tip of Asia Minor (modern Turkey). It still bears the name today and belongs to Greece. It is mentioned once in the Bible, as a stop on Paul's voyage from Miletus toward Jerusalem at the end of his third missionary journey. Sailing on a straight course, the ship reached Cos, the next day Rhodes, and from there went on to Patara on the Lycian coast (Acts 21:1). The voyage is dated about AD 54 by inference from context. Easton's Bible Dictionary says Paul probably landed there. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe Rhodes as a prosperous maritime and commercial center. Its capital city stood at the island's northeastern end and was famous for the Colossus, a huge bronze statue near the harbor. The name is usually taken to mean "rose."

Ribai was a Benjamite from Gibeah, known only as the father of Ittai, one of David's mighty men. He is named in the two parallel lists of David's warriors, where his son is called Ittai in 2 Sam 23:29 and Ithai in 1 Chr 11:31. Both passages place the family in Gibeah of the tribe of Benjamin, the hometown of King Saul. Nothing else is recorded about Ribai himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "pleader with Jehovah", while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "strife". His lifetime would fall before or during David's reign, by inference from his son's service.

Riblah was a city "in the land of Hamath" in Syria that foreign kings used as a military headquarters during campaigns against Judah. Pharaoh Necho held King Jehoahaz in chains there and imposed tribute on Judah (2 Kgs 23:33). Later Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon based himself at Riblah during the siege of Jerusalem. The captured King Zedekiah was brought before him there, and his sons and the nobles of Judah were killed in front of him. Other leading men brought by Nebuzaradan were also executed there (2 Kgs 25:6, 20–21; Jer 39:5–6; 52:9–10, 26–27). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that "Diblath" in Ezek 6:14 should probably be read as Riblah. The same name appears for a point on Israel's boundary in Num 34:11, which Smith's Bible Dictionary treats as a separate place. The location shown here is the village of Ribleh on the east bank of the Orontes River in western Syria, about 35 miles northeast of Baalbek.

Riblah was a town named as a landmark on the eastern border of the land promised to Israel. In Num 34:11 the boundary runs down from Shepham to Riblah, on the east side of Ain, and then descends to the eastern shore of the Sea of Chinnereth (the Sea of Galilee). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the ancient Riblah on the east bank of the Orontes River in modern Syria, a town on the main caravan road north. Pharaoh Necho camped there after the battle of Megiddo, and Nebuchadnezzar later made it his headquarters during his campaign against Jerusalem. Easton's also links Ain with a nearby spring still called el Ain. The name belongs to more than one place, and some take the border Riblah to be a separate site farther south, since the boundary descends from it toward the Sea of Galilee. The location shown here follows the Orontes identification.

Rimmon, called "the rock of Rimmon" or "the rock Rimmon," was a stronghold toward the wilderness to which the tribe of Benjamin fled after its defeat by the other Israelite tribes in the war over the crime at Gibeah. During the flight, thousands of Benjamites were cut down along the roads. Six hundred men reached the rock and stayed there for four months (Judg 20:47). Later the assembly of Israel sent messengers to these survivors at the rock to make peace with them (Judg 21:13). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "pomegranate" or "exalted." Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies the site with the modern village of Rammun, northeast of Jerusalem and east of Bethel, on the edge of the hill country above a steep drop toward the Jordan valley. The location shown here follows that identification. Several other places in the Bible share the name Rimmon.

Rimmon, a name meaning "pomegranate," was a town in the far south of Judah, in the Negev. It is listed among Judah's southernmost cities (Josh 15:32) and was later assigned to the tribe of Simeon (Josh 19:7; 1 Chr 4:32, spelled "Remmon" in the King James Version of Joshua 19:7). In each list it appears next to Ain, and Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggest the two names may form one place, Ain-Rimmon, "spring of the pomegranate." That would make it probably the En-rimmon of Neh 11:29. Zechariah uses it to mark the southern limit of the land, "from Geba to Rimmon south of Jerusalem" (Zech 14:10). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify it with Umm er-Rumamin, about 13 miles (21 km) southwest of Hebron. Several other biblical places share the name Rimmon.

Rimmon was a town in the territory of Zebulun in Lower Galilee, given to the Merarite Levites as one of their four cities with surrounding pasturelands. In the list at Josh 21:35 the town appears as Dimnah, and many scholars take that name as a copying variant of Rimmon. The parallel list of Levitical cities in 1 Chr 6:77 gives the name as Rimmono, and Josh 19:13 places Remmon-methoar on Zebulun's border, probably the same town. The location shown here follows the identification with the village of Rummana, north of Nazareth. Several other places in the Bible share the name Rimmon, which according to Hitchcock's Bible Names means "pomegranate" or "exalted."

Rimmon was a man of Beeroth, a town counted as part of the tribe of Benjamin, and the father of Baanah and Rechab. His sons were captains of raiding bands serving Ish-bosheth, Saul's son. They went to Ish-bosheth's house in the heat of the day while he lay resting at noon and killed him. They then brought the news to David, who answered them with an oath (2 Sam 4:9). Rimmon himself appears only as part of his sons' identification, "the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite." Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that Beeroth was one of the four Gibeonite cities (Josh 9:17). The name is usually understood to mean "pomegranate." Rimmon is also the name of several places in the Bible and should not be confused with them.

Rimmon-perez (spelled Rimmonparez in the King James Version) was one of the places where the Israelites camped during their wilderness journey from Egypt to Canaan. It is named only in the list of stations in Numbers 33. The Israelites arrived there from Rithmah and moved on to Libnah (Num 33:19–20). Nothing else is recorded about it, and the site has not been identified. The location shown here is only a rough placement. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives two explanations of the name. Following Gesenius, "rimmon" means "pomegranate," so the place may have been named for an abundance of pomegranates. Following Conder, the word comes from a root meaning "to be high," giving the sense "cloven height." The second element, "perez," means "breach."

Rimmono was a town in the territory of Zebulun that was assigned, with its surrounding pasturelands, to the Levite clan of Merari, according to 1 Chr 6:77. The King James Version renders the name as Rimmon, while the Hebrew form is Rimmono. It is probably the same place as the Rimmon (KJV "Remmon-methoar") on Zebulun's boundary in Josh 19:13. The parallel list of Levitical cities in Josh 21:35 gives Dimnah where Chronicles has Rimmono, and many scholars think one name arose from a copying variation of the other. The town is commonly identified with the modern village of Rummanah, at the northern edge of the Beit Netofa Valley in Lower Galilee, north of Nazareth. The location shown here follows that identification.

Rinnah was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:20 as one of the four sons of Shimon, alongside Amnon, Ben-hanan and Tilon. Nothing else is recorded about him, and Shimon himself is not otherwise identified. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint reads the verse differently, taking the "Ben" of Ben-hanan as "son of" and so making Rinnah a son of Hanan. This entry follows the Hebrew text, which lists him as Shimon's son. His name is usually understood to mean "a shout," "song" or "rejoicing" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; Hitchcock's Bible Names). Smith's dates him to about 1300 BC, an estimate from his place in the genealogy rather than anything the text states.

The Riot in Ephesus was an uproar against Paul's preaching during his third missionary journey, dated about AD 53 by inference from context. Demetrius, a silversmith who made silver shrines of the goddess Diana (Artemis), gathered his fellow craftsmen. He warned that Paul's teaching that gods made with hands are no gods threatened both their trade and the honor of Diana's temple. The angry crowd shouted "Great is Diana of the Ephesians," seized Paul's Macedonian companions Gaius and Aristarchus, and rushed into the theatre. The disciples and some friendly officials of Asia kept Paul from going in. The Jews pushed forward a man named Alexander to speak, but when the crowd realized he was a Jew they chanted for about two hours. The town clerk finally calmed them. He pointed out that the accused men had committed no sacrilege and told the craftsmen to use the courts or a lawful assembly. Then he dismissed the crowd.

Riphath was the second of the three sons of Gomer, Japheth's son, listed with his brothers Ashkenaz and Togarmah in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:3) and again in the genealogy of 1 Chr 1:6. Nothing else is recorded about him. Like the other names in these lists, his name was probably understood as the ancestor of a people. The Hebrew text of 1 Chr 1:6 reads Diphath, a spelling the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes, while the King James Version keeps Riphath in both places. Identifications of his descendants vary. Josephus, as cited by the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Easton's Bible Dictionary, linked them with the Paphlagonians on the southern coast of the Black Sea. Smith's Bible Dictionary connects the name with the Rhipaean mountains, which it takes to be the Carpathian range. This entry does not settle between these views.

Rissah was one of the places where the Israelites camped during their wilderness journey from Egypt toward Canaan. It appears only in the list of camping stations in Numbers 33. The people came to Rissah after leaving Libnah and moved on from there to Kehelathah (Num 33:21–22). Nothing else is recorded about it, and its exact location is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the mountainous region east of the Arabah, in present-day southern Jordan, near the area later associated with Edom. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "heap of ruins" or "dew," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "watering," "distillation," or "dew."

Rithmah was a place where the Israelites camped during their wilderness journey from Egypt toward Canaan. It appears only in the list of stations in Numbers 33, where Israel moved there from Hazeroth and went on to Rimmon-parez (Num 33:18–19). The name means "broom," after the white desert broom shrub, according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it as a "valley of broom bushes" near Kadesh and suggests it may be the place of Israel's first encampment in that region. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it probably northeast of Hazeroth. Its exact location is unknown, and the location shown here is only a rough placement.

River, often "the River" in the Hebrew Bible, refers in these passages to the Euphrates, the great river of Mesopotamia. Deut 11:24 names it outright as the northeastern limit of the land promised to Israel. Balaam's hometown of Pethor lay "by the river" (Num 22:5), probably on the Euphrates. In Joshua's farewell speech the King James Version says "the flood". Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that this means the Euphrates, which the Revised Version renders "river". Abraham came from beyond it, and his ancestors served other gods there (Josh 24:3, 14–15). Isaiah pictures Assyria as "them beyond the river" and as its flooding waters (Isa 7:20; 8:7). Later prophets use it as a boundary of future rule (Mic 7:12; Zech 9:10). Because "the river" can mean other rivers elsewhere, the name is shared. The location shown here marks a point on the Euphrates in eastern Syria.

River, in the phrase "beyond the river" (also rendered "on this side the river" in the King James Version), was the Persian name for the region west of the river, which is by inference the Euphrates. Seen from the Persian court, this territory, including Samaria and Judah, lay "beyond" it. The region had its own governor, Tatnai, who questioned the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem and then carried out Darius's orders to support it (Ezra 5:3; 6:13). Royal tribute collected there was used to pay for the work (Ezra 6:8). Artaxerxes instructed its treasurers to supply Ezra and gave Ezra authority over its people (Ezra 7:21, 25). Nehemiah carried royal letters to its governors (Neh 2:7–9). The name is shared by several places, and the location shown here marks Jerusalem as a reference point within the wider region.

River of Arnon is the stream and deep gorge east of the Dead Sea that marked the southern limit of Israel's land beyond the Jordan. Modern versions such as the ESV call it the Valley of the Arnon, because the Hebrew word can mean either a seasonal stream or the ravine it runs through. Israel crossed it to fight Sihon the Amorite king of Heshbon (Deut 2:24). Sihon's land ran from Aroer on its bank to the Jabbok, and the conquered territory east of the Jordan stretched from the Arnon to Mount Hermon. This land was given to Reuben and Gad. A city also stood "in the midst of the river." In 2 Kgs 10:33 it marks the southern edge of the lands that Hazael took from Israel, by inference from the surrounding passage. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as the border with Moab, almost dry in summer, and identifies it with the modern Wadi el-Mujib, which the location shown here follows.

Rizpah, daughter of Aiah, was a concubine of King Saul. After Saul's death, his son Ishbosheth accused Abner, the army commander, of sleeping with her. The verses that follow describe this quarrel as what drove Abner to side with David (2 Sam 3:7). She bore Saul two sons, Armoni and Mephibosheth, who is not the son of Jonathan with the same name. During a famine in David's reign, David handed both sons over to the Gibeonites along with five of Saul's grandsons, and all seven were put to death. Rizpah spread sackcloth on a rock and guarded the bodies from birds by day and wild animals by night, from the start of the harvest until the rain fell. When David heard of it, he had their bones buried with those of Saul and Jonathan, according to 2 Sam 21:12–14. Easton's Bible Dictionary estimates her vigil at about five months and gives her name's meaning as "coal" or "hot stone."

The Rock was a rocky height in the wilderness of Maon, in the hill country of Judah south of Hebron, where David took refuge while Saul was hunting him. After the people of Ziph told Saul where David was, David and his men moved into the wilderness of Maon. There he came down to the rock and stayed. Saul followed, and the connected verses (1 Sam 23:26–28) describe the two forces on opposite sides of the mountain. Saul then broke off the chase when news came of a Philistine raid. The place was therefore named Sela-hammahlekoth, usually translated "Rock of Escape" or "Rock of Divisions." Maon itself was a town of Judah near Carmel and Ziph. Its exact site is uncertain, and the location shown here is only a rough placement near Maon, probably the modern Tell Ma'in.

Rocks, called "the rocks of the wild goats" in the King James Version (Wildgoats' Rocks in the ESV), was a rugged area where Saul searched for David with three thousand chosen men from all Israel (1 Sam 24:2). The surrounding passage places this search in the wilderness of En-gedi, on the western shore of the Dead Sea, and STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) describes it as a rugged area near En Gedi. The name probably refers to the steep cliffs there, where wild goats such as the Nubian ibex still live. In the same episode David found Saul in a nearby cave and spared his life. The exact spot is not known. The location shown here is a rough placement in the En-gedi area.

Rogelim was a town in Gilead, east of the Jordan, and the home of Barzillai the Gileadite. When David fled from Absalom to Mahanaim, Barzillai came from Rogelim with Shobi of Rabbah and Machir of Lodebar to help him. The following verses (2 Sam 17:28–29) list the food and bedding they brought. After the rebellion ended, Barzillai came down from Rogelim again and crossed the Jordan with David to see him over the river. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "fullers" and places the town probably near Mahanaim, while Smith's Bible Dictionary sets it in the highlands east of the Jordan. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "a foot or footman." The exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the Gilead hills east of the Jordan valley.

Rohgah was a man of the tribe of Asher, named only once in the Bible, in the Asherite genealogy at 1 Chr 7:34. He is listed as one of the sons of Shamer, along with his brothers Ahi, Jehubbah and Aram. Shamer is probably the same man called Shomer in 1 Chr 7:32, a descendant of Asher through Heber, so by inference Rohgah belonged to the line of Beriah. Nothing else is recorded about his life or deeds. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew text has a variant written form of the name (rohaghah) alongside the form read aloud (rohgah). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning "clamor," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "filled or drunk with talk."

Romamti-ezer was one of the fourteen sons of Heman, a Levite who led music at the sanctuary in King David's time (1 Chr 25:4). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "exaltation of help," and Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "elevation of help." David's musicians were divided by lot into twenty-four courses for service. Romamti-ezer received the twenty-fourth and last lot, and his group of his sons and his brothers numbered twelve (1 Chr 25:31). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a view held by some commentators: the last eight or nine names in the list of Heman's sons, including this one, may originally have been the words of a poetic prayer rather than personal names. This entry follows 1 Chr 25:31, which treats Romamti-ezer as the head of a course of singers.

The Roman Trials were the hearings of Jesus before the Roman governor Pontius Pilate in Jerusalem during Holy Week, about AD 30 by inference from context. All four Gospels record them. Brought to Pilate by the chief priests and a crowd, Jesus was asked whether he was the King of the Jews and answered, "Thou sayest" (Matt 27:11). Luke adds that Pilate, learning Jesus was a Galilean, sent him to Herod, who mocked him and sent him back. Pilate repeatedly said he found no fault in him and, following a Passover custom, offered to release a prisoner. Urged by the chief priests, the crowd chose Barabbas, who was held for insurrection and murder, and demanded that Jesus be crucified. Soldiers in the Praetorium dressed him in a robe, crowned him with thorns, mocked and struck him, and Pilate handed him over for crucifixion.

Rome was the capital of the Roman Empire, in Italy, and is the modern city of the same name. Visitors from Rome, both Jews and proselytes, were in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:10). The emperor Claudius once expelled all Jews from the city, which brought Aquila and Priscilla to Corinth (Acts 18:2). Paul long intended to visit Rome. He wrote to the believers there before he came (Rom 1:7, 15), and in Jerusalem he was told he must bear witness there too (Acts 23:11). He finally arrived as a prisoner, about AD 57 by inference from context. He was allowed to live by himself under guard (Acts 28:16), and Acts 28:30 says this lasted two years. Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, Philemon and 2 Timothy are traditionally held to have been written there. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as the most celebrated city of its day, with about 1,200,000 inhabitants.

Rufus was a son of Simon of Cyrene, the man who was made to carry Jesus' cross on the way to the crucifixion, and the brother of Alexander. Mark identifies Simon as "the father of Alexander and Rufus" (Mark 15:21). The parallel accounts in Matthew and Luke do not name the sons, so Mark's readers probably knew these two men, by inference from the passage. A Christian named Rufus is greeted by Paul in Rom 16:13, and some interpreters identify him with this Rufus. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the two mentions together. The name was common, however, and the link is uncertain. This entry covers the son of Simon named in Mark. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "red."

Rufus was a Christian in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings at the close of his letter to the Romans, calling him "chosen in the Lord" (Rom 16:13). Paul also greeted Rufus's mother, describing her as "his mother and mine," which suggests she had once cared for Paul like a mother, though the occasion is not recorded. The name means "red" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it was a very common name. Another Rufus appears in Mark 15:21 as a son of Simon of Cyrene, the man who carried Jesus' cross. Because Mark's Gospel is traditionally linked with the church at Rome, the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the two may be the same man, but this cannot be confirmed, and this entry treats the Rufus of Romans on his own.

Rumah was the hometown of Pedaiah, whose daughter Zebudah was the mother of Jehoiakim, king of Judah (2 Kgs 23:36). By inference, she was a wife of King Josiah, Jehoiakim's father. This is the only mention of the place in the Bible, and its location is uncertain. The name probably means "high place" or "elevation." Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggest it may be the same as Arumah near Shechem (Judg 9:41), and note that Josephus appears to call it Arouma. Another view places it in Galilee at Khirbet Rumeh, a few miles north of Sepphoris. Smith's Bible Dictionary prefers identifying it with Dumah in the hill country of Judah (Josh 15:52), a reading the Greek Septuagint supports. The location shown here follows the Arumah identification, in the hills southeast of Shechem (modern Nablus).

Ruth was a Moabite woman who married Mahlon, son of the Bethlehem family of Elimelech and Naomi, who had settled in Moab (Ruth 1:4; Ruth 4:10). After her husband died, she refused to leave her mother-in-law. Her sister-in-law Orpah turned back, but Ruth vowed that Naomi's people and God would be her own (Ruth 1:14–16). The two women reached Bethlehem at the start of the barley harvest (Ruth 1:22). There Ruth gleaned in the fields of Boaz, a relative of Elimelech, who told her to stay with his workers (Ruth 2:2, 2:8). She asked Boaz to act as a near kinsman (Ruth 3:9). He redeemed Naomi's land and married Ruth to keep the dead man's name alive on his inheritance (Ruth 4:5, 4:10). She bore Obed (Ruth 4:13), and Matthew names her in the genealogy of Jesus (Matt 1:5). Her birth date of about 1115 BC is an estimate inferred from context.

Sabtah was the third of the five sons of Cush, son of Ham, named in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:7). 1 Chr 1:9 repeats the list and spells his name Sabta. His brothers were Seba, Havilah, Raamah and Sabtecha. Nimrod is also counted among his brothers because Gen 10:8 says Cush fathered Nimrod, though he is named apart from the list. Nothing else is recorded about Sabtah himself. Many names in this genealogy also stand for the peoples or regions descended from them, so Sabtah probably also represents a people. Its location is uncertain and the verses do not identify it. The meaning of the name is given differently by different reference works: Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "rest," Smith's Bible Dictionary "striking," and Hitchcock's Bible Names "a going about" or "old age."

Sabtecha was a son of Cush and a grandson of Ham, named in the Table of Nations in Gen 10:7 and again in the parallel genealogy in 1 Chr 1:9. He is listed fifth among the sons of Cush, after Seba, Havilah, Sabtah and Raamah, and Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both describe him as the fifth son. Nimrod, also called a son of Cush, is named separately in the following verses. Nothing further is recorded about Sabtecha's life. Like other names in the Table of Nations, his name probably stood for a people or region descended from him, but neither passage says where they lived, and any identification remains uncertain.

Sacar was a Levite, the fourth of the eight sons of Obed-edom listed in 1 Chr 26:4. His brothers named there are Shemaiah, Jehozabad, Joah, Nethaneel, Ammiel, Issachar and Peulthai. The passage appears in the list of the divisions of gatekeepers, or porters, for the house of the Lord, so Sacar is understood to have served as a gatekeeper. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him a temple porter, and STEPBible places his service in the reign of King David. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats him as the founder of a family of gatekeepers. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "wages." Nothing else is recorded about him. He is a different man from Sacar the Hararite, the father of one of David's warriors (1 Chr 11:35).

Sadoc was an ancestor of Jesus named in Matthew's genealogy, the son of Azor and the father of Achim (Matt 1:14). His name is the Greek form of the Hebrew Zadok, which Hitchcock's Bible Names and Easton's Bible Dictionary explain as meaning "just" or "righteous." He belongs to the part of the line that runs from Zerubbabel, after the exile in Babylon, down to Joseph. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe him as a descendant of Zerubbabel, and Smith's places him at about 280 BC, an estimate reached by counting generations rather than a date the text states. Because he comes in the royal line of David, he is counted with the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with the better-known priest Zadok of David's time.

Sahar is a place named in some modern translations of Ezekiel 27:18, in a list of goods that Damascus traded with Tyre: "the wine of Helbon and the wool of Sahar." The King James Version reads the same Hebrew word as an adjective, "white wool," so the place name does not appear there. If it is a place, it was probably a wool-producing district within Damascus's trading area. The STEPBible Proper Names (TIPNR, Tyndale House) states that its exact location is unknown. Some suggest it was the steppe country northwest of Damascus, possibly the region later called es-Sahra. The location shown here is only approximate. It places Sahar in the hills northwest of Damascus, near Helbon, the wine-producing town named in the same verse. This is an inference from the pairing of the two names in Ezek 27:18.

Salah, also spelled Shelah, was a descendant of Shem and the father of Eber in the line that leads to Abraham. In Genesis and 1 Chronicles he is the son of Arphaxad, who fathered him at age thirty-five (Gen 11:12; 1 Chr 1:18, 24). Luke's genealogy of Jesus, which follows the Greek Septuagint, places Cainan between Arphaxad and Salah (Luke 3:35–36), making Salah Arphaxad's grandson. This entry follows that line in naming Cainan as his father. Salah fathered Eber at age thirty and lived another 403 years, having other sons and daughters (Gen 11:14–15). That makes a lifespan of 433 years, placed here at about 2311–1878 BC by inference from the genealogy. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "mission" or "sending," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "sprout."

Salamis was a city on the east coast of the island of Cyprus. It was the first place Barnabas and Saul (Paul) visited on their first missionary journey, about AD 45 by inference from context. There they preached in the Jewish synagogues, with John Mark as their assistant (Acts 13:5). The plural "synagogues" suggests a sizable Jewish community, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. Because it was the harbor nearest the Syrian coast, it was a natural landing point after sailing from Seleucia, according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. That work also describes Salamis as the most populous town of Cyprus in the Greek and Roman periods. Easton's Bible Dictionary links it with modern Famagusta. Smith's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place it a few miles north of that town. The location shown here matches the ancient ruins north of Famagusta.

Salathiel is the Greek form of the name Shealtiel. In Luke's genealogy of Jesus he is named as the son of Neri and the father of Zorobabel (Zerubbabel), placing him in the line of David and the tribe of Judah (Luke 3:27). His name probably means "asked of God." Matthew's genealogy (Matt 1:12) and 1 Chr 3:17 instead call him a son of Jeconiah, the king of Judah taken into exile in Babylon. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the difference by suggesting that Salathiel was the natural son of Neri, a descendant of David's son Nathan, and became heir to the royal line when Jeconiah's line ended. Other explanations have also been offered, such as adoption or a levirate marriage. His son Zerubbabel later led a group of exiles back to Jerusalem, and this entry places Salathiel in the generation of the Babylonian exile.

Salecah (spelled Salchah or Salcah in the King James Version) was a city of Bashan, east of the Jordan River, belonging to the kingdom of Og. It is always named as a boundary point, the far edge of Bashan, as in the phrase "all Bashan unto Salcah" (Deut 3:10; Josh 13:11). Joshua 12:5 lists it among the places where Og reigned. After Israel conquered the region, the territory up to Salecah went to the tribes settled east of the Jordan. Easton's Bible Dictionary assigns it to the half tribe of Manasseh, and 1 Chr 5:11 says the tribe of Gad lived in Bashan as far as Salchah. Easton's also gives the name's meaning as "wandering" and identifies the city with Salkhad, about 56 miles east of the Jordan. The location shown here follows that identification with modern Salkhad, in the Jebel al-Druze area of southern Syria.

Salem was the city ruled by Melchizedek, king and priest of the most high God, who brought out bread and wine to Abraham as he returned from defeating the kings and blessed him (Gen 14:18; Heb 7:1). Hebrews explains the name as meaning "peace," so that Melchizedek was "King of peace" (Heb 7:2). Ps 76:2 sets Salem in parallel with Zion as God's dwelling place, which is why Salem is commonly taken as an older or poetic name for Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both note this view, which Jewish tradition, Josephus and early Christians held. Other traditions place Melchizedek's Salem elsewhere. The Samaritans linked it with Salim east of Nablus, and Jerome placed it near Scythopolis (Beth-shean), as Smith's Bible Dictionary reports. The location shown here follows the Jerusalem identification.

Salim was a place near Aenon, where John the Baptist was baptizing because there was plenty of water there (John 3:23). Salim is named only to show where Aenon was, which suggests it was the better-known town. Its location is uncertain. One view, given in Easton's Bible Dictionary, links it with the Shalem of Gen 33:18, in the hills east of Shechem (modern Nablus), with Aenon in the Wadi Far'ah. Another view follows the fourth-century writer Eusebius, who placed Aenon about eight Roman miles south of Scythopolis (Beth-shean, modern Beisan), near Salim and the Jordan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connects this with Tell Ridhghah and a nearby shrine called Sheikh Selim, close to several large springs. The location shown here follows this Jordan valley identification south of Beth-shean, west of the river.

Sallai was a man of the tribe of Benjamin who lived in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. He is named only in Neh 11:8, in the list of those who settled in the city when its population was strengthened in Nehemiah's time. The surrounding passage identifies the group as Benjamites, which Easton's Bible Dictionary also notes. Sallai appears alongside Gabbai, following a man named Sallu, and the verse gives a combined total of 928 men. It is not clear whether that figure counts the followers of Gabbai and Sallai alone or the Benjamite group as a whole, and it is possible that Sallai names a clan rather than a single person. Nothing else is recorded about him. The priestly family head called Sallai in Neh 12:20 is usually taken to be a different man.

Sallu was a man of the tribe of Benjamin named among the inhabitants of Jerusalem in 1 Chr 9:7. He was the son of Meshullam, and his ancestry is traced back through Hodaviah and Hasenuah. The surrounding chapter lists the families who settled in Jerusalem, which the context suggests was after the return from exile in Babylon. The STEPBible Proper Names index describes him as a Benjamite who lived in Jerusalem. A similar list in Neh 11:7 also names a Benjamite Sallu son of Meshullam, but with a different line of ancestors. He is probably the same man, though the two genealogies do not match exactly. The name Sallu is also borne by others in the Bible, including a priest who returned with Zerubbabel, so care is needed to keep them apart. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Sallu was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, the son of Meshullam, named among those who lived in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. Neh 11:7 gives his ancestry through seven generations: Meshullam, Joed, Pedaiah, Kolaiah, Maaseiah, Ithiel and Jesaiah. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was one of the Benjamite family heads listed among the leaders who settled in the city when its population was being restored. The STEPBible Proper Names index describes him as a Benjamite leader. A parallel list in 1 Chr 9:7 names a Sallu son of Meshullam among the Benjamites in Jerusalem, though it traces a different line of ancestors, so it probably refers to the same man. The name Sallu is also borne by a priest who returned with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:7), a different person.

Sallu was a priest listed among the chief priests who returned from the Babylonian exile in the days of Jeshua the high priest (Neh 12:7), which places him in the first return led by Zerubbabel. A later list of priestly family heads from the next generation names Kallai as head of the house "of Sallai" (Neh 12:20). Sallai is probably the same name as Sallu, used here for the family descended from him, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the two as one priestly family. By inference from the surrounding passage, this later list belongs to the time of the high priest Joiakim, Jeshua's son. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Sallu is also borne by a Benjamite living in Jerusalem, a different person.

Salma was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles as a son of Hur. The surrounding passage makes Hur the firstborn of Ephrathah and a descendant of Caleb (1 Chr 2:50). Salma is called "the father of Bethlehem." This probably means he founded the town or was the ancestor of its people, as the STEPBible Proper Names index takes it. His "sons" are listed largely as places and clans: Bethlehem, the Netophathites, Ataroth (the house of Joab), half of the Manahethites, and the Zorites. These were probably settlements and groups in the Bethlehem area. The same name appears in 1 Chr 2:11 for Salma (Salmon), the father of Boaz of Bethlehem. Whether the two are the same man is uncertain, and this entry treats Salma as the son of Hur. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "peace; perfection."

Salmon, also called Salma, was a man of the tribe of Judah, the son of Nahshon and the father of Boaz. He appears only in genealogies: the line from Judah to David at the end of Ruth, the Judahite lists in 1 Chronicles, and the genealogies of Jesus in Matthew and Luke, which spell his father's name Naasson and his son's Booz. Matthew 1:5 names the mother of Boaz as Rachab. She is commonly identified with Rahab of Jericho, and STEPBible's proper-names index describes Salmon as Rahab's husband. Through Boaz and Ruth he was the great-great-grandfather of King David. Smith's Bible Dictionary links him with Bethlehem, noting that a Salma is called the father of Bethlehem in the line of Caleb (1 Chr 2:51, 54). It suggests this explains why he is also counted among Caleb's descendants, though whether that Salma is the same man is not certain.

Salmone was a landmark on the island of Crete that Paul's ship passed on its voyage to Rome. After slow progress against contrary winds, reaching only the area off Cnidus, the ship sailed under the shelter of Crete "over against Salmone" (Acts 27:7). The voyage is dated about AD 56, by inference from context. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe Salmone as the promontory at the eastern tip of Crete, the modern Cape Sidero. Smith's calls it a bold headland visible from a long distance. The location shown here is not on Crete. It places Salmone as a town in the western Peloponnese of Greece, the region of ancient Elis, where a place of the same name existed. This entry therefore shows that site, while the context of the voyage points to the eastern Cretan cape.

Salome was one of the women who followed Jesus and were present at his death and resurrection. Mark names her among the women watching the crucifixion from a distance, along with Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of James the less and Joses (Mark 15:40). After the Sabbath she and the same two women bought spices to anoint Jesus' body and went to the tomb early on the first day of the week (Mark 16:1). These are the only places she is named. Comparing the parallel list in Matt 27:56, which names "the mother of Zebedee's children" in her place, Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify her as the wife of Zebedee and mother of James and John, the woman who asked for places of honor for her sons (Matt 20:20). They also suggest she was probably the sister of Jesus' mother mentioned in John 19:25. These identifications are inferences, and this entry treats them as probable.

Salt, called the City of Salt in modern translations, was one of six towns in the wilderness of Judah. It is named only once, in the list of Judah's territory, between Nibshan and Engedi (Josh 15:62). Its Hebrew name, Ir ha-Melach, means "city of salt" and probably reflects nearness to the salt deposits of the Dead Sea. The site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary place it probably near the Valley of Salt at the southern end of the Dead Sea. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Tell el-Milh ("the salt hill") on the route from Hebron toward Akaba as a possibility. Some modern scholars identify it with Khirbet Qumran on the northwestern shore. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the wilderness of Judah beside the Dead Sea, near Engedi, the town named next to it in the list.

Salt Sea is the biblical name for the lake now called the Dead Sea, at the southern end of the Jordan valley. It is also called "the sea of the plain" (Deut 3:17; Josh 3:16; Josh 12:3). Gen 14:3 says the vale of Siddim, where the kings gathered for battle in Abraham's day, "is the salt sea," which suggests the valley was later covered by its waters or lay beside them. The sea marked the southeastern corner and eastern edge of the promised land (Num 34:3, 12). It also formed the eastern border of Judah, and its northern bay, where the Jordan enters, marked the line between Judah and Benjamin (Josh 15:2, 5; Josh 18:19). When Israel crossed the Jordan near Jericho, the water flowing down toward it was cut off (Josh 3:16). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the Arabs call it Bahr Lut, the Sea of Lot.

Salu was a man of the tribe of Simeon, known only as the father of Zimri. According to Num 25:14, Zimri was killed together with a Midianite woman during the episode at Shittim, when Israelites joined in the worship of Baal of Peor. The surrounding chapter shows that Phinehas the priest was the one who killed them. The verse calls Zimri "a prince of a chief house among the Simeonites." Grammatically this title could belong to either father or son. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia applies it to Salu, as head of a Simeonite family. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Salu is called Salom in 1 Maccabees 2:26, and the name may mean "weighed." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Samaria, meaning "watch-mountain" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, was the capital city of the northern kingdom of Israel, and its name came to stand for the kingdom and its territory (1 Kgs 13:32). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that King Omri built the city on a hill bought from Shemer. Later kings of Israel reigned there (1 Kgs 22:51; 2 Kgs 13:1; 2 Kgs 15:13), and Ahab built an altar to Baal in it (1 Kgs 16:32). A Syrian siege caused severe famine (2 Kgs 6:25). In Hoshea's ninth year Assyria took Samaria and deported Israel (2 Kgs 17:6; 18:10), as prophets such as Hosea and Micah had warned (Hos 13:16; Mic 1:6). Foreign settlers were later placed in its cities (Ezra 4:10). In the New Testament, Samaria is the region between Judea and Galilee that Jesus passed through (John 4:4). The location shown here marks the region. The ancient city is the modern Sebastia.

Samaria's refers to the city of Samaria, capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, here under a possessive form of its name. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as built by King Omri on a solitary hill a few miles northwest of Shechem, which he bought from Shemer for two talents of silver and made his capital in place of Tirzah (1 Kgs 16:24).
