The same dictionary recounts sieges by Ben-hadad of Syria in the days of Ahab and Jehoram, and a three-year Assyrian siege that ended with the city's capture and the deportation of Israel's tribes (2 Kgs 17:3; 18:9–12). Herod the Great later rebuilt it as Sebaste, and Philip preached there (Acts 8:5). The location shown here is the hill at the modern village of Sebastia, the site Easton's identifies as ancient Samaria. No verses were supplied for this particular form of the name.

The Samaritans Reject Jesus is an episode recorded in Luke 9:51–56. As the time approached for Jesus to be "received up," he set out resolutely for Jerusalem and sent messengers ahead to prepare lodging in a Samaritan village. The villagers refused to receive him because he was clearly heading for Jerusalem. This probably reflects the long-standing hostility between Samaritans and Jews over the proper place of worship. James and John asked whether they should call down fire from heaven to destroy the village, "even as Elias did," recalling Elijah calling down fire on the king's soldiers in 2 Kgs 1:10–12. Jesus turned and rebuked them, saying that the Son of man came not to destroy lives but to save them, and the group went on to another village. The village is not named. Jerusalem appears here as the journey's destination. The date of about AD 29 is inferred from context.

Samgar-nebo was one of the princes of the king of Babylon (Nebuchadnezzar, by the surrounding context) who came in and sat in the middle gate of Jerusalem after the Babylonian army took the city (Jer 39:3). He appears only in this list of officials, alongside Nergal-sharezer, Sarsechim, the Rabsaris and the Rabmag. The name is Babylonian. Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "sword of Nebo," while Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "be gracious, O Nebo" or "cup-bearer of Nebo" and suggests it may be a title of Nergal-sharezer rather than a separate person. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint reads the verse differently, and that some scholars regroup the names, joining "Nebo" to the following Sarsechim to match the Nebushazban of Jer 39:13. This entry treats Samgar-nebo as a distinct Babylonian official, following the order of names in the traditional Hebrew text.

Samlah was one of the early kings of Edom, listed among the rulers who reigned there before any king ruled over Israel. He came from Masrekah, a town whose location is unknown. He succeeded Hadad and was followed by Saul (called Shaul in 1 Chr 1:48) of Rehoboth by the river (Gen 36:36–37; 1 Chr 1:47–48). The list does not present these kings as a father-to-son dynasty, since each is identified by his own home town rather than by descent. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests this points to Edom being a confederacy at the time, with the king's city serving as its chief city. Nothing else is recorded about his reign. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "garment."

Samos is a mountainous Greek island in the eastern Aegean Sea, lying just off the coast of Asia Minor between Ephesus and Miletus. It is still called Samos today, and it belongs to Greece. Acts 20:15 names it as a stop on Paul's voyage south along the coast at the end of his third missionary journey. The ship passed Chios, reached Samos the next day, and arrived at Miletus the day after. The King James text adds that they stayed at Trogyllium, a point on the mainland opposite the island. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that this phrase is missing from the oldest manuscripts. The same work says the island was famous in earlier times for its wealth and became part of the Roman province of Asia in 84 BC. Paul's passage probably took place around AD 54, an estimate based on context.

Samothrace (spelled Samothracia in the King James Version) is a mountainous island in the northern Aegean Sea, off the coast of Thrace and northwest of Troas. Its modern name is Samothraki. Paul and his companions stopped there on his second missionary journey, after a vision called him to Macedonia (Acts 16:11). Sailing from Troas, they made a straight run to Samothrace and reached Neapolis, the port of Philippi, the next day. The verse does not say they went ashore, but ancient ships usually anchored overnight rather than sail in the dark, so they probably stopped there for the night. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the island was famous in the ancient world as a sacred site, the center of the mystery cult of the Cabeiri, and that the statue known as the Victory of Samothrace was found there in 1863.

Sampson destroys Temple of Dagon refers to Samson's final act, when he brought down the temple of the Philistine god Dagon and died with those inside. The Philistine lords had gathered to sacrifice to Dagon and celebrate the capture of Samson, who had been blinded and imprisoned. They brought him out to entertain the crowd and placed him between the pillars. The building was full, with about three thousand people on the roof. Samson asked the boy leading him to let him feel the pillars, then prayed for strength one last time to take revenge for his eyes. Pushing against the two central pillars, he collapsed the house, and the text says he killed more people at his death than during his life. The temple was probably in Gaza, where he had been imprisoned, by inference from the preceding verses. His family buried him near Zorah and Eshtaol. He had judged Israel twenty years. The event is dated to about 1101 BC, by inference from context, during the period of Philistine domination.

Samson was a judge of Israel, the son of Manoah, known for his great strength and his lone fights against the Philistines, who ruled Israel in his day (Judg 15:11). Against his parents' wishes he married a Philistine woman of Timnath. At the wedding feast he posed a riddle, his wife coaxed the answer from him, and she was later given to his companion. In revenge he tied firebrands to foxes' tails and loosed them among Philistine crops. After the Philistines burned his wife and her father, he killed a thousand men with the jawbone of an ass. At Gaza he carried off the city gates. Delilah repeatedly tried to learn the secret of his strength and finally betrayed him. Captured and blinded, he pulled down the pillars of Dagon's temple and died with the Philistines. Hebrews 11:32 lists him among the faithful. Smith's Bible Dictionary places his home at Zorah in Dan.

Samuel was a prophet and the last of Israel's judges, the son of Elkanah and Hannah, of the tribe of Levi (also spelled Shemuel). Hannah named him because she had asked him of the LORD (1 Sam 1:20). As a boy he served under Eli at Shiloh, where the LORD called him by night and revealed himself to him. He later judged Israel at Mizpeh, where the Philistines were routed while he offered sacrifice. In old age he made his sons judges. When the people asked for a king, he anointed Saul, later rebuked him and announced his rejection, and then anointed David. He died at Ramah, mourned by all Israel. Later texts rank him with Moses (Jer 15:1; Ps 99:6). 1 Sam 8:2 names his sons Joel and Abiah, while 1 Chr 6:28 gives Vashni for the firstborn. Jewish tradition credits him with writing Judges, Ruth and the books of Samuel. He lived about 1152–1060 BC, by inference from context.

Sanballat was the leading opponent of Nehemiah when Nehemiah came to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem. He is called "the Horonite". Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take this to mean he came from Horonaim in Moab, while others connect the name with Beth-horon. Easton's Bible Dictionary says he held authority in Samaria. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that papyri from Elephantine in Egypt name a Sanballat as governor of Samaria. With Tobiah the Ammonite and Geshem the Arabian, he was grieved at Nehemiah's arrival, mocked the builders and accused them of rebelling against the king. As the wall neared completion, he repeatedly invited Nehemiah to meet in the plain of Ono, intending him harm. He sent an open letter, and with Tobiah he hired a prophet to frighten him. A grandson of the high priest Eliashib became Sanballat's son-in-law, and Nehemiah drove that man away.

The Sanhedrin Conspiracy was the meeting at which the Jewish religious leaders in Jerusalem plotted to arrest and kill Jesus, two days before Passover, during the final week of his life. Matthew places it right after Jesus finished his teaching on the Mount of Olives, when he told his disciples that he would be betrayed and crucified at the feast. The chief priests, scribes and elders gathered at the palace of the high priest Caiaphas and discussed how to seize Jesus by stealth. They agreed not to act during the feast itself, for fear of a riot among the crowds. Mark and Luke give shorter parallel accounts, and Luke stresses that the leaders feared the people. The date of about AD 30 is inferred from context. The name "Sanhedrin" is not used in these verses but refers to the ruling council these groups made up.

Sansannah was a town in the far south (the Negev) of the territory allotted to the tribe of Judah, listed with Ziklag and Madmannah among Judah's southernmost cities (Josh 15:31). It is named only in this verse. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "palm branch", and Easton's Bible Dictionary adds "thorn bush." Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat it as the same place as Hazar-susah, a city of Simeon (Josh 19:5), and probably Hazar-susim (1 Chr 4:31). This fits the way Simeon's towns lay within Judah's southern lands. Its site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mentions the village of Simsim as one suggestion. The location shown here is only a rough position in the northern Negev, north-east of Beersheba, near the ruin of Khirbet esh-Shamsaniyat, which some scholars have proposed.

Sapphira was a member of the early Jerusalem church and the wife of Ananias. According to Acts 5:1, she and her husband sold a piece of property. The surrounding passage (Acts 5:1–11) says they kept back part of the money while presenting the rest to the apostles as the full price. Ananias died after Peter confronted him with lying to God. About three hours later Sapphira, not knowing what had happened, repeated the same claim about the price and also died. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes her as a partner in both his guilt and his punishment. The event is dated to about AD 30, by inference from context. Her name is Aramaic and is usually taken to mean "beautiful" or "sapphire," as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes, while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "that relates or tells."

Sarah, first called Sarai, was the wife of Abraham and the mother of Isaac. Gen 20:12 calls her Abraham's half-sister, a daughter of Terah by a different mother. She was barren and went with Abraham from Haran into Canaan. Twice, in Egypt and at Gerar, Abraham called her his sister, and she was taken into a ruler's household before being given back. After ten years in Canaan without children, she gave her Egyptian maid Hagar to Abraham, and Hagar bore Ishmael. Conflict between the two women followed. God renamed her Sarah and promised she would have a son. Overhearing the promise in her old age, she laughed. At about ninety she bore Isaac, and she later had Hagar and Ishmael sent away. She died at 127 and was buried in the cave of Machpelah at Hebron. Isa 51:2, Heb 11:11 and 1 Pet 3:6 later recall her. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "princess."

Saraph was a man of the tribe of Judah, listed in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:22 among the descendants of Shelah, Judah's son. This entry treats him as Shelah's son, alongside Er, Laadah, Jokim and Joash. The verse says that Joash and Saraph "had the dominion in Moab." It does not explain what that rule involved. Most readers take it to mean that they held power in Moab or married into it, but the Hebrew is unclear. The chronicler adds that "these are ancient things," which suggests the details came from very old records. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "burning," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "noble one" and links the name to a word for burning or shining. Nothing more is known about him.

Sardis was a city in the Roman province of Asia, in western Asia Minor, and the home of one of the seven churches to which the book of Revelation was addressed (Rev 1:11). The message to its church says it had a name for being alive but was dead, though a few people there had not defiled their garments and would walk in white (Rev 3:1, 3:4). According to Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries, it had been the capital of the kingdom of Lydia, standing at the foot of Mount Tmolus beside the river Pactolus, and was the seat of the wealthy king Croesus. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it was rebuilt after an earthquake in AD 17. Its ruins lie at the village of Sart, near Salihli in western Turkey, which is the location shown here. The STEPBible proper-names index suggests that Sepharad in Obad 1:20 may also refer to Sardis.

Sarid was a town on the southern border of the territory allotted to the tribe of Zebulun. Joshua 19 uses it as the starting point for tracing Zebulun's boundary. From Sarid the border ran eastward toward Chisloth-tabor, then on to Daberath and up to Japhia (Josh 19:10, 12). Smith's Bible Dictionary concludes from this that it lay west of Chisloth-tabor. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may originally have read "Sadid." On that reading it follows Conder in placing the town at Tell Shaddu (Tel Shadud), an artificial mound with good springs in the Jezreel Valley, about 5 miles west of Iksal. The location shown here follows that identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "remaining."

Saron is the Greek form of Sharon used by the King James Version in Acts 9:35. It names the broad coastal plain between the central hill country and the Mediterranean, the district in which Lydda stood. After Peter healed the paralysed Aeneas at Lydda, the people living there and in Saron turned to the Lord. In the Old Testament, Sharon was grazing land. Royal herds under Shitrai the Sharonite fed there in David's time (1 Chr 27:29), and Isaiah pictures it as a fold for flocks (Isa 65:10). The plain was known for its fertility and beauty. It is paired with Lebanon and Carmel (Isa 33:9; 35:2) and recalled in the 'rose of Sharon' (Song 2:1). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes a separate Sharon east of the Jordan (1 Chr 5:16). The location shown here points to the coastal plain in general rather than a single site.

Sarsechim was one of the princes of the king of Babylon who came in and sat in the middle gate of Jerusalem when the city fell to Nebuchadnezzar's army (Jer 39:3). He appears only in this list of Babylonian officials, and nothing else is recorded about him. The text of the verse is difficult, and readings differ. The KJV, followed in this entry, treats Sarsechim as a separate name. STEPBible's Tyndale House names list joins it with the preceding "nebo" to read "Nebu-sar-sekim," a high official in Nebuchadnezzar's army. On that reading, the following word "Rabsaris," meaning chief official or chief eunuch, may be his title. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him "prince of the eunuchs." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests a link with Nebushazban the Rabsaris of Jer 39:13. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "master of the wardrobe."

Satan, a Hebrew word meaning "adversary" or "accuser" (Easton's Bible Dictionary), is the Bible's name for a spiritual opponent of God and of people. In Job he comes before the LORD among the sons of God and, with permission, afflicts Job (Job 1:6–12; 2:7). He provokes David to number Israel (1 Chr 21:1) and stands beside Joshua the high priest to resist him (Zech 3:1–2). In the Gospels he tempts Jesus in the wilderness, and Jesus' opponents call him Beelzebub, prince of the devils, a name Jesus treats as Satan's (Matt 12:24–26). He is said to enter Judas and to fill Ananias's heart to lie (John 13:27; Acts 5:3). Paul describes him hindering, tempting and disguising himself as an angel of light. Revelation identifies him with the dragon, the old serpent and the Devil, cast out to the earth and later loosed after a thousand years (Rev 12:9; 20:7).

Saul, son of Kish of the tribe of Benjamin, was the first king of Israel. Described as unusually tall and handsome, he was pointed out to the prophet Samuel as the man who would reign, and was later chosen by lot from Benjamin (1 Sam 9:2; 9:17; 10:21). His home was Gibeah, called “Gibeah of Saul.” He fought the Philistines alongside his son Jonathan and campaigned against the Amalekites, after which Samuel confronted him over the LORD’s command. David entered his service and killed Goliath, but Saul grew jealous of David’s fame, tried to kill him, and pursued him through the wilderness. Facing a Philistine attack, he consulted a medium at Endor. He was wounded by archers and died on Mount Gilboa, and men of Jabesh recovered his body from Beth-shan. His son Ish-bosheth briefly reigned after him. This entry dates his reign to about 1095–1056 BC, by inference from context.

Saul is converted describes how Saul of Tarsus, later known as Paul (Acts 13:9), turned from persecuting Jesus' followers to becoming one of them, about AD 32 by inference from context. Carrying letters from the high priest authorizing him to arrest believers in the synagogues of Damascus, Saul was nearing the city when a light from heaven surrounded him. He fell to the ground and heard a voice identify itself as Jesus, whom he was persecuting. His companions heard the voice but saw no one. Left blind, Saul was led into Damascus, where he went three days without sight, food or drink. In a vision the Lord sent a disciple named Ananias, despite his fears, to the house of Judas on the street called Straight. Ananias laid his hands on Saul so that he would see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit. Something like scales fell from Saul's eyes, and he was baptized. Paul retells the event in Acts 22 and 26.

The persecution of the church by Saul followed directly on the stoning of Stephen in Jerusalem, about AD 31 by inference from context. Saul, who later became known as the apostle Paul, had approved of Stephen's death. At that time a great persecution broke out against the church in Jerusalem, and all its members except the apostles were scattered through the regions of Judea and Samaria. Meanwhile devout men buried Stephen and mourned him deeply. Saul set out to destroy the church, going from house to house, dragging off both men and women and putting them in prison. Later passages such as Acts 9:1–2 and Gal 1:13 describe how this campaign continued and how Paul himself afterward recalled it.

Saul proclaims Jesus is the account of what Saul (later called Paul) did right after his conversion. In the synagogues of Damascus he preached that Jesus is the Son of God and the Christ. His hearers were amazed, since he had come there to arrest believers. After many days, Jews plotted to kill him and watched the city gates, so disciples lowered him over the wall in a basket by night. Paul describes the same escape in 2 Cor 11:32–33, and Gal 1:17–18 places a stay in Arabia and three years before his Jerusalem visit. That is probably why this entry dates the events to about AD 38, an inference from context. In Jerusalem the disciples feared him until Barnabas brought him to the apostles. Saul spoke boldly and debated with Greek-speaking Jews, who then sought to kill him. Believers took him to Caesarea and sent him to Tarsus, and the churches then had peace and grew.

Sceva was a Jew described as a "chief of the priests" at Ephesus, known only as the father of seven sons who worked as travelling exorcists during Paul's mission there, about AD 53 by inference from context (Acts 19:14). The surrounding passage tells how his sons tried to drive out an evil spirit by invoking "Jesus whom Paul preacheth". The spirit answered that it knew Jesus and Paul but not them, and the possessed man overpowered them, so that they fled wounded. The account led many in Ephesus to give up magic. What his title means is uncertain, since he could not have officiated at the Jerusalem temple while living in Asia Minor. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes him to have headed one of the priestly courses. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he belonged to a high-priestly family or had once led a course.

The Sea of Chinnereth is an Old Testament name for the lake later called the Sea of Galilee, Lake of Gennesaret or Sea of Tiberias. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as the same body of water, and the location shown here matches it, at the modern Lake Kinneret in northern Israel. In Num 34:11 the lake serves as a landmark on the eastern boundary of the land promised to Israel, which runs down to its eastern shore. In Josh 13:27 it marks the northern limit of the territory given to the tribe of Gad in the Jordan Valley. That territory covered the remainder of the kingdom of Sihon king of Heshbon, along the east side of the Jordan up to the edge of the lake. The name is probably linked to the nearby town of Chinnereth.

The Sea of Chinneroth is the name Joshua 12:3 uses for a lake marking part of the eastern boundary of the territory ruled by Sihon, king of the Amorites, which Israel took. The verse traces the border from the plain to this sea and then down to the 'sea of the plain,' the Salt Sea. Its position at the northern end of the Jordan valley, together with related names elsewhere in the Old Testament such as 'the sea of Chinnereth' (Num 34:11; Josh 13:27), identifies it with the freshwater lake later called the Sea of Galilee, Lake of Gennesaret or Sea of Tiberias, the modern Lake Kinneret in northern Israel. The name probably comes from the nearby town of Chinnereth or the surrounding district. The location shown here places it on that lake.

The Sea of Galilee is a freshwater lake in northern Israel, fed by the Jordan River. John also calls it the Sea of Tiberias (John 6:1), and STEPBible's proper-names index notes that it is the lake called Chinnereth in the Old Testament. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as oval, about 12½ miles long and up to 7½ miles wide, lying about 682 feet below the Mediterranean, and full of fish. Jesus was walking along its shore when he saw the fishermen Simon Peter and Andrew casting their net (Matt 4:18; Mark 1:16). He returned to it from the region of Tyre and Sidon by way of the Decapolis (Mark 7:31), went up a mountain near it (Matt 15:29), and crossed it by boat (John 6:1). Easton's also links the lake with Capernaum, the calming of a storm, and Jesus' appearance to his disciples after the resurrection (John 21).

The Sea of Jazer is a body of water named only in Jeremiah's lament over Moab, where the spreading vines of Sibmah are said to reach "even to the sea of Jazer" (Jer 48:32). Jazer was a town east of the Jordan in the region taken from the Amorites. Interpretations differ. Some take the phrase to mean a pool, spring or small lake near Jazer. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia regards "sea" here as a copying slip carried over from the preceding clause. It notes that the parallel passage in Isa 16:8 reads simply "unto Jazer." No lake is known at Jazer, and the town's own site is uncertain. This entry treats the Sea of Jazer as a water feature and places it roughly in the area of Jazer, west of modern Amman. The location shown here is approximate.

The Sea of the Philistines is a name used once in the Bible, in Exod 23:31, where God sets the borders of Israel's promised land from the Red Sea to the sea of the Philistines, and from the desert to the river. By inference from context, it refers to the Mediterranean Sea, specifically the part lying off the southern coast of Canaan, where the Philistines lived. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it as that portion of the Mediterranean directly west of Palestine. Elsewhere the Hebrew Bible usually calls the Mediterranean simply "the sea," "the great sea," or "the western sea." In this verse it serves as the western limit of the land, with the Red Sea as the southern limit and the river, probably the Euphrates, as the eastern. The location shown here is a point in the eastern Mediterranean.

Sea of the Plain is a name used in the King James Version for the body of water at the southern end of the Jordan Valley, which the ESV calls the Sea of the Arabah. Joshua 3:16 identifies it with the Salt Sea. It is the lake known today as the Dead Sea, and the location shown here lies there. When Israel crossed the Jordan opposite Jericho, the water flowing down toward this sea was cut off while the water upstream piled up near the city of Adam (Josh 3:16). It later served as a boundary marker. Jeroboam II restored Israel's territory from the entrance of Hamath in the north to the Sea of the Plain in the south, as the prophet Jonah son of Amittai had foretold (2 Kgs 14:25). The name comes from the Arabah, the deep rift valley in which the sea lies.

The Sea of Tiberias is a name used in John's Gospel for the Sea of Galilee. John 6:1 makes the link explicit, describing Jesus crossing "the sea of Galilee, which is the sea of Tiberias." The name probably comes from the city of Tiberias on its western shore, which was founded in the first century and named after the Roman emperor Tiberius. This is an inference from the name, since the verses do not explain it. Elsewhere the same lake is called the Sea of Galilee, the Lake of Gennesaret and, in the Old Testament, the Sea of Chinnereth. John 21:1 places one of Jesus' appearances to his disciples after his resurrection beside this sea. It is the freshwater lake in northern Israel fed by the Jordan River, and the location shown here marks its centre. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it under the entry for the Sea of Galilee.

The Seaside Parables and Miracle were a day in Jesus' Galilean ministry, recorded in Matthew, Mark and Luke. Jesus left a house and sat by the Sea of Galilee, teaching the crowds only in parables. These included the sower and the four kinds of ground, the wheat and tares, seed that grows by itself, hidden treasure, and a net cast into the sea. Privately he explained them to the twelve and others with them. As he prepared to cross to the other side, he told would-be followers that anyone who looks back after putting a hand to the plough is not fit for the kingdom. During the crossing a storm arose while he slept. The frightened disciples woke him, and he rebuked the wind and waves, bringing calm, then asked why they had no faith. The date, about AD 28, is an estimate inferred from context.

Seba was a distant country and people named in Hebrew poetry and prophecy alongside other far-off lands. In Ps 72:10 its kings, together with those of Sheba, bring gifts to Israel's king. In Isa 43:3 God says he gave Egypt, Ethiopia and Seba as a ransom for Israel. Because it is paired with Egypt and Ethiopia (Cush), it was probably in north-east Africa. Genesis 10:7 names a Seba as a son of Cush, which suggests the people were linked by descent with the Cushites, and Isa 45:14 probably refers to the same people as the Sabeans. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies Seba with ancient Meroe, on the Nile in present-day Sudan. Its exact location is uncertain. The location shown here is only a general one in the Ethiopian highlands, following the broader association with Cush rather than a particular site.

Seba was the first-named son of Cush, the son of Ham, in the table of nations (Gen 10:7; 1 Chr 1:9). His brothers were Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah and Sabtecha. Nimrod is also called a son of Cush in the following verse (Gen 10:8). Seba should not be confused with Sheba, his nephew through Raamah, who is named in the same verse. Like many names in this list, Seba probably stands for a people as well as a person. Later passages mention Seba as a distant land alongside Sheba, Egypt and Ethiopia (Ps 72:10; Isa 43:3), and Isa 45:14 speaks of the Sabeans as tall men. These links point, by inference, to a people in the region of Cush, usually placed in northeast Africa. Its exact location is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a drunkard" or "that turns."

Sebam, spelled Shebam in the King James Version, was a town east of the Jordan River. It appears in Num 32:3 in a list of places in the former kingdom of the Amorites that the tribes of Reuben and Gad asked Moses to give them because the land suited their livestock. The STEPBible proper-names index places it in the territory of Reuben. It is probably the same town as Sibmah, which appears later in the same chapter (Num 32:38) among the towns the Reubenites rebuilt. Later prophets mention Sibmah as a Moabite town known for its vineyards (Isa 16:8–9; Jer 48:32). The exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only approximate, in the hill country near Heshbon and Mount Nebo in present-day Jordan.

Secacah was a town in the wilderness of Judah, the dry, thinly settled land west of the Dead Sea. It is named only once, in Josh 15:61, as one of six towns in this district assigned to the tribe of Judah, listed alongside Betharabah and Middin. The Bible gives no other details about it. Smith's Bible Dictionary says its exact position is unknown, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the ancient name has not survived. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects it with a ruin called Sikkeh east of Bethany, following a proposal by the surveyor Conder, who placed it at Khirbet es-Siqqeh, about 2 miles from Bethany. Other scholars place it closer to the Dead Sea, for example at Khirbet Qumran or in the Buqei'a valley. The location shown here follows the Sikkeh identification near Bethany.

event: Second Foretelling of Death and Resurrection
text: The Second Foretelling of Death and Resurrection was the occasion when Jesus, traveling through Galilee with his disciples, again told them plainly that he would be killed. It came soon after he healed a boy possessed by a demon, while the crowds were still amazed at what they had seen (Luke 9:43). Jesus kept the journey quiet because he wanted to teach his disciples privately (Mark 9:30). He told them that the Son of Man would be betrayed or handed over to men, who would kill him, and that he would rise on the third day. Matthew says the disciples were deeply grieved. Mark and Luke say they did not understand what he meant, that its meaning was hidden from them, and that they were afraid to ask him about it. This entry dates it to about AD 29, an estimate inferred from context. It is called the second foretelling because an earlier prediction of his death had come before it.

The Second Missionary Journey was Paul's second preaching tour in Acts, presented here together with the Jerusalem council that came before it (Acts 15:1–18:23). When teachers from Judea demanded that Gentile converts be circumcised, the apostles and elders, with Peter and James speaking (Acts 15:7, 13), decided to ask only a few abstentions of Gentile believers. They sent Judas Barsabas and Silas to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas. Paul then parted from Barnabas over John Mark, chose Silas, and revisited Lystra and Iconium, where Timothy joined them. A vision called them to Macedonia. The "we" passages suggest that Luke was travelling with them. At Philippi, Lydia was converted, and Paul and Silas were beaten and jailed. The mission went on to Thessalonica, Berea, Athens and Corinth, where Paul met Aquila and Priscilla and was brought before Gallio. It ended by way of Ephesus. The date, about AD 46, and the length, about three years, are inferred from context.

The Second Missionary Journey begins with Paul choosing Silas as his companion and setting out from Antioch in Syria. The local believers commended the two men to the grace of God before they left (Acts 15:40). They then travelled through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches already established there (Acts 15:41). This start follows directly on Paul's sharp disagreement with Barnabas over taking John Mark. As the preceding verses of Acts 15 describe, Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus, while Paul went overland with Silas. Silas had earlier been sent from Jerusalem to Antioch with the apostles' letter, which explains how he came to be available. Cilicia was Paul's home region, centred on Tarsus in what is now southeastern Turkey. The date of about AD 47 and the length of roughly one month are estimates inferred from context.

The Second Quarter was a district of Jerusalem where the prophetess Huldah, wife of Shallum the keeper of the wardrobe, lived when King Josiah's officials, led by Hilkiah the priest, went to consult her (2 Kgs 22:14; 2 Chr 34:22). The King James Version renders the Hebrew word mishneh as "the college," following Jewish commentators who took it as a place of instruction. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains that the word properly means "second." It suggests the district may be the lower city, built after the part on Mount Zion and enclosed by a second wall. Tyndale House's STEPBible names also link it to the "second" district in Zeph 1:10. Its exact boundaries are uncertain. The location shown here places it within the city, just west of the Temple Mount.

Secu (spelled Sechu in the King James Version) was a place on Saul's route to Ramah, known for its "great well." It appears only once in the Bible. Saul stopped there while searching for David, who had fled to Samuel, and asked where the two were. He was told they were at Naioth in Ramah (1 Sam 19:22). By inference from the story, it lay between Saul's home at Gibeah and Ramah. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it is probably the modern Suweikeh, south of Beeroth, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes Conder's identification with Khirbet Suweikeh, south of el-Bireh. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also mentions a Greek reading that takes the phrase as "the cistern of the threshing-floor on the bare hill," possibly a spot within Ramah itself. The location shown here follows the Suweikeh identification.

Secundus was a Christian from Thessalonica who traveled with Paul when the apostle left Greece and headed for the province of Asia, near the end of the journey this entry dates to about AD 54, by inference from context. He is named only once, alongside Aristarchus, another Thessalonian, in a group that also included Sopater of Berea, Gaius of Derbe, Timothy, Tychicus and Trophimus (Acts 20:4). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that this group went ahead and waited for Paul at Troas. It also suggests he may have been one of the delegates carrying the Macedonian churches' gifts to Jerusalem, in which case he probably went with Paul that far. The name is Latin for "second", and the same encyclopedia notes that it appears in a list of Thessalonian city officials on an inscription. Nothing more is known of him.

Segub was the youngest son of Hiel of Bethel, who rebuilt Jericho during the reign of Ahab king of Israel. 1 Kgs 16:34 says Hiel laid the city's foundation at the cost of his firstborn Abiram and set up its gates at the cost of Segub. By inference, both sons died, and the verse presents this as fulfilling what the LORD had spoken through Joshua. The connected passage, Josh 6:26, records Joshua's curse on anyone who rebuilt Jericho: the builder would lose his firstborn at the foundation and his youngest son at the gates. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes two explanations for the deaths. One links them to an ancient practice of foundation sacrifice, and the other suggests an accident during the building work. The text itself does not say how Segub died. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "fortified" or "raised." Another man named Segub appears in Judah's genealogy.

Segub was a man of the tribe of Judah, the son of Hezron by the daughter of Machir, the father of Gilead. Hezron married her when he was sixty years old (1 Chr 2:21). Segub's brothers were Caleb, Jerahmeel and Ram, and Ashur was his half-brother. Segub was the father of Jair, who held twenty-three cities in the land of Gilead (1 Chr 2:22). Because his mother came from Machir's family of the tribe of Manasseh, his line probably explains why his son Jair held towns in Gilead, Machir's territory. Elsewhere Jair is called a son of Manasseh, which reflects this descent. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "fortified" or "raised." Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 1682 BC, an estimate based on context. The name is shared with at least one other man in the Bible, so references to Segub need to be told apart.

Seir was a mountainous region, also called Mount Seir, identified with the country of Edom (Gen 32:3; Gen 36:8). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it along the eastern side of the Arabah, from the southeastern end of the Dead Sea toward the Gulf of Aqaba, in what is now southern Jordan. The location shown here lies within that area. Its earliest inhabitants were the Horites (Gen 14:6; Gen 36:30). The descendants of Esau later destroyed them and settled in their place, and Seir was said to be given to Esau as his possession (Deut 2:12; Josh 24:4). Jacob met Esau on his way back to Seir, and Israel passed by its borders on the journey to Canaan (Gen 33:16; Deut 2:4, 8). Mount Halak, which "goes up to Seir," marked the southern limit of Joshua's conquests (Josh 11:17). Later, King Amaziah of Judah defeated the people of Seir (2 Chr 25:11), and Ezekiel named Seir alongside Moab in an oracle (Ezek 25:8).

Seir was a Horite, the ancestor of the Horite clans who lived in the land later called Edom before the descendants of Esau settled there. Gen 36:20–21 and 1 Chr 1:38 name his seven sons as Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer and Dishan, and describe them as chiefs (“dukes”) of the Horites in the land of Edom. Timna is also counted among his children. Gen 36:22 calls her the sister of Lotan, so she was probably Seir's daughter. The region is called “the land of Seir” (Gen 36:30), and the person and the territory share the name. It is uncertain whether the land was named after him or he after it. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of the chiefs of Edom. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as “hairy” or “goat.”

Seirah (Seirath in the King James Version) was the place Ehud escaped to after he killed Eglon, king of Moab. He got away while Eglon's servants were still waiting outside the locked room, passed beyond "the quarries" (or carved images) near Gilgal, and reached Seirah (Judg 3:26). The name probably means "wooded" or "shaggy," pointing to a forested area. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in the hill country of Ephraim, bordering Benjamin. This fits the next verse in Judges, where Ehud blows a trumpet in the mountains of Ephraim to rally Israel against Moab. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that nothing in the text allows a firm identification, and Eusebius names the place without locating it. The location shown here is a rough placement in southeastern Ephraim, inferred from this context.

Sela, a name meaning "rock," was an Edomite stronghold in the rugged mountains south of the Dead Sea. The King James Version uses it as a name in Isa 16:1, where Moab is told to send lambs from Sela to Zion. Elsewhere it renders the word as "the rock," as in Judg 1:36 and Isa 42:11. According to 2 Kgs 14:7, King Amaziah of Judah captured Sela and renamed it Joktheel. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with Petra, the later Nabatean city in modern southern Jordan, and the location shown here follows that identification. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia instead places the rock of Judg 1:36 and Amaziah's conquest at a fortified cliff near the Ascent of Akrabbim, south-west of the Dead Sea. It allows that Isaiah's references may point to Petra. Which site each passage means remains uncertain.

The Rock of Escape was a rock or cliff in the wilderness of Maon, in Judah southeast of Hebron. There David took refuge while Saul was hunting him (1 Sam 23:25). The surrounding narrative describes Saul and David moving along opposite sides of the same mountain. Just as Saul was closing in, he was called away to fight the Philistines, so he broke off the chase. For that reason the place was named Selahammahlekoth (1 Sam 23:28). The Hebrew name can be understood as "rock of escape" or "rock of divisions" (Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the latter), perhaps referring to the two forces being parted there. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name survives in Wadi Malaki, a steep gorge between Carmel and Maon. The exact site is uncertain, and the location shown here places it in that area of the Maon wilderness.

Seled was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:30 as a son of Nadab and the brother of Appaim. The verse notes that he died without children, so his line did not continue, while the genealogy goes on through his brother Appaim. Nadab belonged to the family of Jerahmeel, and Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia accordingly describe Seled as a Jerahmeelite. Nothing else is recorded about his life. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "exultation," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "affliction; warning."

Seleucia was the seaport of Antioch in Syria, near the mouth of the Orontes River and about 16 miles from Antioch. Barnabas and Saul (Paul), sent out by the Holy Spirit at the start of the First Missionary Journey, went down to Seleucia and sailed from there to Cyprus (Acts 13:4), about AD 45 by inference from context. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries say the city was founded by Seleucus Nicator, the first Seleucid king of Syria, and named after him, and that Pompey made it a free city. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes it as a strongly fortified port and notes that the return voyage in Acts 14:26 probably also passed through it. Its site lies near the coast of modern southern Turkey, close to the village of Çevlik, where extensive ruins, including the old harbor, survive.

Semachiah was a Levite, one of the sons of Shemaiah named in the list of temple gatekeepers in 1 Chr 26:7. His brothers were Othni, Rephael, Obed, Elzabad and Elihu, and the verse describes Elzabad's brothers, who include Elihu and Semachiah, as "strong men." The surrounding chapter places this family among the Korahite gatekeepers organized in the time of David. Shemaiah was a son of Obed-edom (1 Chr 26:4–6), so Semachiah was probably Obed-edom's grandson. His name is usually explained as meaning "the LORD has sustained." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that the same name may lie behind "Ismachiah" in 2 Chr 31:13. Nothing further is recorded about him.

Semei is a man named once, in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, which runs back from Jesus through his ancestors (Luke 3:26). There he is the son of Joseph and the father of Mattathias. This Joseph, son of Juda, is a different person from Jacob's son Joseph and from Mary's husband, and he belongs to the stretch of the list between the return from exile and Jesus' birth. Because the line runs through David, Semei counts as a member of the tribe of Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the name as the Greek form of the Hebrew Shimei, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "hearing" or "obeying." The Revised Version spells it Semein. Nothing else is known about him.

Seneh was one of two sharp rocky crags flanking the pass that Jonathan used to approach the Philistine garrison, the other being Bozez (1 Sam 14:4). The name probably means "thorn" or "acacia," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it came from thorn bushes growing on the rock. From the surrounding narrative, the pass lay at Michmash. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify Seneh as the southern cliff of the gorge now called Wadi es-Suweinit, south of Michmash. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia hears an echo of the old name in that valley's modern name, "valley of the little thorn tree." Smith's Bible Dictionary places the pass about 6½ miles north of Jerusalem. The location shown here follows this gorge identification.

Senir (also spelled Shenir) is a mountain name linked with Mount Hermon, at the southern end of the Anti-Lebanon range. Deut 3:9 says it was the Amorite name for Hermon, which the Sidonians called Sirion. Other passages list Senir alongside Hermon as though they were separate: the half tribe of Manasseh spread from Bashan to Baal-hermon, Senir and Mount Hermon (1 Chr 5:23), and Song 4:8 pairs the peaks of Shenir and Hermon. Ezek 27:5 says the ship planks of Tyre were made from fir trees of Senir. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia therefore suggests Senir may have named a particular part of the range, and notes that medieval Arab geographers used Jebel Sanir for the Anti-Lebanon between Damascus and Homs. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it as the central of Hermon's three summits. The location shown here follows the identification with Mount Hermon itself.

Sennacherib was a king of Assyria who invaded Judah in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah and captured its fortified cities (2 Kgs 18:13; Isa 36:1). While he besieged Lachish, he sent officials to Jerusalem to mock Hezekiah's trust and demand surrender. Hezekiah prayed against him, and Isaiah answered that the prayer had been heard. Sennacherib then withdrew and lived at Nineveh. The surrounding passages (2 Kgs 19:35–37) say an angel struck down his army, and that his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer later killed him, with another son, Esar-haddon, succeeding him. Easton's Bible Dictionary dates his reign from about 705 to 681 BC. This entry also includes Sargon, the Assyrian king whose commander took Ashdod (Isa 20:1). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries treat Sargon as Sennacherib's father and predecessor.

Senuah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin. He is known only as the father of Judah, who was "second over the city" of Jerusalem after the return from exile, serving under the overseer Joel son of Zichri (Neh 11:9). By inference from the surrounding list, Senuah belonged to the Benjamite families who settled in Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "bristling" and notes that the Hebrew form carries the definite article, Hassenuah, which is how some modern translations render it. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia compares 1 Chr 9:7, which names a Benjamite Hasenuah among Jerusalem's inhabitants, possibly the same family. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Seorim was a priest whose name was given to the fourth of the twenty-four divisions of priests. In 1 Chronicles 24, during the reign of David, these divisions were set by lot so that each family would take its turn at service in the sanctuary, and the fourth lot fell to Seorim (1 Chr 24:8). Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe him as the chief of this fourth course and give the meaning of his name as "barley." Hitchcock's Bible Names offers other meanings, such as "gates," "hairs" or "tempests." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats Seorim as the name of a priestly course of the period after the exile, while the STEPBible names index takes him to be a priest of David's time who headed the division. This entry follows the passage's setting in David's reign.

Sephar was a mountain or hill country "of the east" named in Gen 10:30 as the far limit of the land settled by the sons of Joktan, a descendant of Shem. Their territory ran from Mesha toward Sephar. The name may mean "numbering" or "book." Since many of Joktan's sons have names that match towns and tribes of southern Arabia, Sephar is usually identified with a place called Zafar there. Two sites carry that name. One is the inland town south of San'a in Yemen, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes as the traditional royal seat of the Himyarite kings. The other is a coastal town on the Indian Ocean east of Hadramaut, which that encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary prefer. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions the Himyarite capital Zafar. The location shown here follows the inland Yemeni Zafar.

Sepharad is a place named only in Obad 1:20, where it is described as the home of exiles from Jerusalem who would one day possess the cities of the south (the Negev). The verse gives no clue to where it was, and its location has long been uncertain. Jewish tradition, going back to the Targum of Jonathan, identified it with Spain, which is why Spanish Jews are called Sephardim. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links it with Saparda in Assyrian inscriptions, a place set either east of Assyria or in Asia Minor. Others, noted by Easton's Bible Dictionary, identify it with Sardis, the capital of Lydia in western Asia Minor. Jerome took the word to mean "boundary," meaning the exiles scattered to the ends of the earth. The location shown here follows the Sardis identification, near modern Sart in western Turkey.

Sepharvaim was a city whose people the king of Assyria resettled in the cities of Samaria after the Israelites were deported (2 Kgs 17:24). The Sepharvites burned their children in fire to their gods Adrammelech and Anammelech (2 Kgs 17:31). Sennacherib's officials later named it among the cities whose gods and king had failed to stand against Assyria, as a warning to Hezekiah (2 Kgs 18:34; 19:13; Isa 36:19; 37:13). Its location is uncertain. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with Sippar on the Euphrates, southwest of modern Baghdad, and read the name as "the two Sipparas." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that its place in the lists, after Hamath, could point to Syria, and mentions a suggested link with Sibraim near Hamath. The location shown here is a rough placement in central Mesopotamia, following the Babylonian identification.

Serah was the daughter of Asher and a granddaughter of Jacob. She appears in the list of those who went down to Egypt with Jacob, where she is named after her four brothers, Jimnah (Imnah), Ishuah (Isuah), Isui and Beriah, as "their sister" (Gen 46:17). The same list of Asher's children is repeated in the tribal genealogies of Chronicles (1 Chr 7:30). In the census of Israel taken in the wilderness she is again named as Asher's daughter. There the King James Version spells her name Sarah, though the Hebrew name is the same (Num 26:46). She is one of very few women named in these tribal lists, and the text gives no reason for her inclusion. Nothing else is recorded about her. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of her name as "abundance" or "princess."

Seraiah was a Levite priest, the son of Azariah and the father of Jehozadak (also called Josedech), in the high-priestly line recorded in 1 Chr 6:14. He served as chief priest in Jerusalem when the city fell to Babylon in the reign of Zedekiah. The captain of the guard took him prisoner, along with Zephaniah the second priest and the three doorkeepers (2 Kgs 25:18; Jer 52:24). The following verses (2 Kgs 25:21; Jer 52:27) report that he was put to death at Riblah. Ezra the scribe is called "the son of Seraiah, the son of Azariah" (Ezra 7:1). Since Ezra lived long after the exile, this probably means he was a descendant rather than a son. Nehemiah 11:11 names a Seraiah "son of Hilkiah" as ruler of the house of God. The ancestry there overlaps with this line, but it is uncertain whether it refers to the same man or a later namesake.

Seraiah son of Tanhumeth was one of the army captains who came with their men to Gedaliah at Mizpah after the king of Babylon made Gedaliah governor of Judah following the fall of Jerusalem. He is named alongside Ishmael son of Nethaniah, Johanan son of Kareah and Jaazaniah (Jezaniah). In 2 Kgs 25:23 he is called a Netophathite, meaning a man from Netophah, a town near Bethlehem. In the parallel list in Jer 40:8 that label is attached instead to the sons of Ephai, who are named right after him. Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Seraiah, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as "prince of the Lord" and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia as "Yah hath prevailed."

Seraiah was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in its genealogy as a son of Kenaz and brother of Othniel (1 Chr 4:13). He was the father of Joab, described as "the father of the valley of Charashim," a name meaning the Valley of Craftsmen. The text explains the name with the note "for they were craftsmen," so Joab was probably the founder or leading figure of a settlement of skilled workers (1 Chr 4:14). Othniel, his brother, is by inference the same Othniel who appears elsewhere as the first judge of Israel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls Seraiah the younger brother, presumably because he is listed second. The name, which the same work explains as "Yah hath prevailed," is shared by several other men in the Bible. This Joab is distinct from David's commander of the same name.

Seraiah was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named only once, in a genealogy at 1 Chr 4:35. He was the son of Asiel and the father of Josibiah, which made him the grandfather of Jehu. This Jehu appears in a list of Simeonite clan leaders. The surrounding passage places these leaders in the reign of Hezekiah, when they moved to find pasture for their flocks, so Seraiah himself probably lived some generations earlier. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name means something like "the Lord has prevailed" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, or "prince of the Lord" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Several other men in the Bible are also called Seraiah, and this one should not be confused with them.

Seraiah was a priest who returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel and Jeshua. He heads the list of priests and Levites who went up with them (Neh 12:1). In the next generation, under the high priest Joiakim, Meraiah led the priestly family named after him (Neh 12:12). The name Seraiah also appears first among the priests who set their seal to Nehemiah's covenant (Neh 10:2). Because that list comes generations after the return, the name there probably stands for the priestly house rather than the man himself. A Seraiah is also listed among the leaders who came with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:2). This entry treats all these mentions as one figure, following the STEPBible proper names index. Smith's Bible Dictionary instead separates the leader of Ezra 2:2 from the priest. Several other people in the Bible share the name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names renders "prince of the Lord."

Seraiah, the son of Azriel, was one of three men whom the king ordered to arrest Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet, together with Jerahmeel the son of Hammelech and Shelemiah the son of Abdeel (Jer 36:26). The king was Jehoiakim of Judah. The order came after he had burned the scroll of Jeremiah's prophecies that Baruch had written down. The verse says the arrest did not happen because the LORD hid the two men. Nothing else is recorded about this Seraiah. The name is shared by several people in the Bible, and this one is distinct from the others. It is usually explained as meaning "the LORD has prevailed" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), though Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "prince of the Lord."

Seraiah was the son of Neriah and grandson of Maaseiah. He was the brother of Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, whom Jer 32:12 and 36:4 also call a son of Neriah. He travelled with King Zedekiah of Judah to Babylon in the fourth year of Zedekiah's reign. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 594 BC, an estimate drawn from context. The King James Version calls him "a quiet prince." Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the Revised Version renders this "chief chamberlain," and Smith's suggests he was the officer in charge of the royal caravan. Jeremiah gave him a written message announcing Babylon's coming ruin and told him to read it aloud when he arrived. The surrounding passage (Jer 51:60–64) adds that he was then to tie a stone to the scroll and throw it into the Euphrates, as a sign that Babylon would sink and not rise again. Several other men in the Bible share his name.

Sered was a son of Zebulun and so a grandson of Jacob and Leah. His brothers were Elon and Jahleel. He appears in the list of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:14). Because he is named first in both lists, Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him Zebulun's firstborn. In the census taken in the wilderness of Moab, he is named as the ancestor of the Sardites, one of the family groups of the tribe of Zebulun (Num 26:26). Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "fear," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "dyer's vat."

Sergius Paulus was the Roman governor of Cyprus when Barnabas and Saul visited the island, about AD 45 by inference from context. The King James Version calls him the "deputy of the country". The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the title as proconsul, the correct term for the governor of a senatorial province such as Cyprus was then. Acts describes him as "a prudent man" who sent for Barnabas and Saul because he wanted to hear the word of God (Acts 13:7). The surrounding passage, set at Paphos, tells how the sorcerer Elymas, who was with the proconsul, tried to turn him away from the faith and was struck blind. Sergius Paulus then believed, astonished at the teaching of the Lord (Acts 13:8–12). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes an inscription found at Rome bearing his name, which it takes to record a later post he held there.

The Sermon on the Mount is Jesus' longest recorded teaching, given according to Matthew on a mountain to his disciples with crowds nearby. It opens with the Beatitudes, blessings on the meek, the pure in heart and the persecuted. It goes on to Jesus' interpretation of the law, including anger, oaths, retaliation and love for enemies. Teaching on giving, prayer (the Lord's Prayer), fasting, treasure and worry follows, then warnings against judging others, the Golden Rule, a test of teachers by their fruits, and the closing parable of houses built on rock and on sand. Luke gives a shorter parallel with blessings and woes, set on a level place (Luke 6:17). Luke places it right after the choosing of the twelve apostles. This entry dates it to about AD 28, by inference from context. The location shown here is Jerusalem, while tradition places the sermon in Galilee.

Serpent's Stone is the meaning usually given to the "stone of Zoheleth," a landmark beside the spring of En-rogel just outside Jerusalem. There Adonijah, David's son, sacrificed sheep, oxen and fattened cattle and held a feast for his brothers the king's sons and the royal officials of Judah, as part of his bid to take the throne (1 Kgs 1:9). The wider chapter tells how, while they were gathered, Solomon was proclaimed king and Adonijah fled to the altar for safety. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes the place as a rocky ledge near the village of Siloam that overhangs the Kidron Valley and is still known by the Arabic name ez-Zehwell or Zahweileh. The location shown here follows that identification, southeast of the old city near the meeting of the Kidron and Hinnom valleys.

Serug was a descendant of Shem, the son of Reu and the father of Nahor, which makes him the great-grandfather of Abraham through Nahor's son Terah. Reu fathered him at age thirty-two, and Serug fathered Nahor at thirty, then lived another two hundred years and had other sons and daughters (Gen 11:20–23). That gives a lifespan of 230 years, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. 1 Chronicles repeats his place in the line from Shem to Abraham, and Luke's genealogy of Jesus includes him under the Greek form Saruch (Luke 3:35). His name is usually explained as meaning "branch." Taking the ages in Genesis at face value, he would have lived from about 2185 to 1955 BC, an estimate inferred from context. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Seth was the third son of Adam and Eve named in Genesis, born after Cain killed Abel. Eve named him, saying God had appointed her another child in place of Abel (Gen 4:25). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "appointed" or "substitute." Adam was 130 years old when Seth was born (Gen 5:3). At 105 Seth fathered Enos, and in that generation people began to call on the name of the LORD (Gen 4:26). He also had other sons and daughters and died at the age of 912 (Gen 5:6–8). Working from these ages, his life is dated to about 3874–2962 BC. Seth appears as "Sheth" at the head of the genealogy in 1 Chr 1:1, and he is listed in Jesus' ancestry in Luke 3:38. This entry links the "children of Sheth" in Num 24:17 to him. Smith's Bible Dictionary reads that phrase as a common noun meaning "sons of tumult."

Sethur, son of Michael, was the man from the tribe of Asher among the twelve spies Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan (Num 13:13). The surrounding chapter describes the mission: the spies were leaders chosen one from each tribe, and they went from the wilderness of Paran to scout the land and report on it. By inference from Num 13–14, Sethur was one of the ten spies who gave a discouraging report, since only Joshua and Caleb are singled out for urging Israel to go in, and the other ten are said to have died by plague. He is not mentioned anywhere else. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "hidden."

The Seven chosen to serve were seven men appointed by the early church in Jerusalem to oversee the daily distribution of food, about AD 30 by inference from context. As the number of disciples grew, the Greek-speaking believers complained that their widows were being neglected in favour of those of the Hebrew-speaking believers. The twelve apostles gathered the disciples and said they should not leave preaching to wait on tables. They asked the community to pick seven men of good reputation, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, so the apostles could devote themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word. The people chose Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolas, a convert to Judaism from Antioch. The apostles prayed and laid their hands on them. Afterward the word spread, the disciples in Jerusalem increased greatly, and many priests joined the faith.

Shaalabbin was a city in the territory allotted to the tribe of Dan. It appears in Josh 19:42 in the list of Danite towns, next to Ajalon (Aijalon) and Jethlah. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat it as the same place as Shaalbim. If so, it is the town where, according to Judg 1:35, the Amorites held out against Dan. It also lay in one of the districts that supplied provisions to Solomon's court (1 Kgs 4:9). Easton's gives the name's meaning as "place of foxes" and identifies the site with the modern village of Selbit, about 3 miles north of Aijalon. The location shown here follows the Selbit identification.

Shaalbim was a town in the lowland hills west of Jerusalem, in the area allotted to the tribe of Dan. Judg 1:35 says the Amorites held on there, along with Mount Heres and Aijalon, until the house of Joseph grew strong enough to make them pay tribute. Under Solomon it belonged to the administrative district of the son of Dekar, together with Makaz, Beth-shemesh and Elon-beth-hanan (1 Kgs 4:9). It is probably the same place as Shaalabbin in Josh 19:42. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also links it with Shaalbon, the home of Eliahba the Shaalbonite, one of David's mighty men (2 Sam 23:32). Eusebius placed it at Salaba near Samaria. Conder identified it with Selbit, northwest of Aijalon. The location shown here follows the identification with modern Salbit.

Shaalim (spelled Shalim in the King James Version) was a district Saul passed through while searching for his father's lost donkeys. He went through the hill country of Ephraim and the land of Shalisha, then through Shaalim, and then through the land of the Benjamites, without finding the animals (1 Sam 9:4). Nothing else is said about it, and the Hebrew name is often understood to mean "land of foxes." Its location is uncertain because the route of the search is unclear. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it apparently northwest of Jerusalem, perhaps near Shaalabbin in Dan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it lay on the western slopes, possibly east of Lydda, and notes that the name might originally have been "Shaalbim." The location shown here is only approximate and follows the general placement northwest of Jerusalem.

Shaaph was a man of the tribe of Judah, named as the last of six sons of Jahdai in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:47. His brothers were Regem, Jotham, Geshan (spelled Gesham in some lists), Pelet and Ephah. Nothing else is recorded about him. Jahdai's own parentage is not stated, but because his family appears among the descendants of Caleb in 1 Chr 2, he is generally taken to belong to Caleb's line, and STEPBible's proper-names index describes Shaaph as a descendant of Caleb. The name Shaaph is also given to a different man, a son of Caleb by his concubine Maachah, mentioned a few verses later in the same chapter. The two are usually treated as separate people, and this entry covers only the son of Jahdai.

Shaaph was a man of the tribe of Judah, a son of Caleb by Maachah. The surrounding passage identifies Maachah as Caleb's concubine, and Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies this Caleb as the brother of Jerahmeel. 1 Chr 2:49 calls Shaaph "the father of Madmannah." Madmannah was also the name of a town in southern Judah, so "father" here probably means the founder or leading figure of that settlement rather than only a parent. The same verse names his brother Sheva as the father of Machbenah and of Gibea, and his sister as Achsah. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Shaaph is shared by several people in the Bible. Another Shaaph appears just before this one, in the list of Jahdai's sons (1 Chr 2:47), and the two are usually treated as different men.

Shaaraim was a city in the Shephelah, the western lowland of Judah, listed among the towns allotted to Judah in Josh 15:36, where the King James Version spells it Sharaim. After David killed Goliath, the defeated Philistines fled from the Elah Valley area toward Gath and Ekron, and their wounded fell along the road to Shaaraim (1 Sam 17:52). The name means "two gates." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that in this verse the "two gates" might instead refer to the two Philistine cities themselves, as the Greek Septuagint suggests. The exact site is uncertain. Proposals include Tell Zakariya, Khirbet Sa'ireh and, more recently, Khirbet Qeiyafa above the Elah Valley. The location shown here is approximate and places it generally in that western Elah Valley region. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the Shaaraim of Simeon (1 Chr 4:31) as a different place.

Shaaraim was a town listed among the cities of the tribe of Simeon in the far south of Israel. 1 Chr 4:31 says these towns belonged to the Simeonites until the reign of David. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "gates." The parallel list of Simeon's towns in Josh 19:6 has Sharuhen in the same position, so the two names probably refer to the same place. The location shown here follows that identification and places it at Tell el-Far'ah (South), near the Besor stream in the western Negev. The name is shared by a different town in the lowlands of Judah (Josh 15:36; 1 Sam 17:52), which should not be confused with this Simeonite town.

Shaashgaz was a chamberlain, or court official, of King Ahasuerus of Persia, mentioned only in Esth 2:14. He was in charge of the concubines in "the second house of the women." When the king was searching for a new queen, each young woman spent one night with him and then moved the next morning into this second house under Shaashgaz's custody. She did not go to the king again unless he took pleasure in her and called for her by name. By context, he worked alongside Hegai, who kept the women before they were brought to the king (Esth 2:8). Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him a chief eunuch and gives the name's meaning as "servant of the beautiful." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint calls him Gai, the same name it gives Hegai, and that the origin of the name is uncertain.

Shabbethai was a Levite in the time of Ezra, after the Jews returned from exile in Babylon. He is named in Ezra 10:15, in the account of how the community dealt with men who had married foreign wives. The King James Version says Jonathan and Jahaziah were "employed about this matter" and that Meshullam and Shabbethai helped them. Many modern translations read the Hebrew as saying that these men opposed the plan. STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) follows that reading and describes Shabbethai as opposing Ezra's efforts. A Levite named Shabbethai also helps explain the law to the people in Neh 8:7 and oversees outside work for the temple in Neh 11:16. He may be the same man, but this is uncertain, since several people share the name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "my rest."

Shabbethai was one of the men, apparently Levites, who helped the people understand the law when Ezra read it publicly in Jerusalem after the return from exile. Nehemiah 8:7 lists him among thirteen named helpers who explained the reading while the people stood in their places. The STEPBible proper names index treats him as a Levite who assisted in explaining the Law. The name also appears in Ezra 10:15, where a Shabbethai the Levite is linked with the inquiry into foreign marriages, and in Neh 11:16, where a Shabbethai is among the chief Levites in charge of the outside work of the temple. These may be the same man, but the text does not say so, and this entry treats only the Shabbethai of Neh 8:7. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "my rest."

Shabbethai was a Levite who lived in Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah. Nehemiah 11:16 names him with Jozabad among the chief Levites and says the two were in charge of the "outward business of the house of God". This probably means the practical and outside affairs that supported the temple, as distinct from the worship carried on inside it. STEPBible Proper Names describes this as overseeing external affairs. A Levite named Shabbethai also appears in Ezra 10:15, during the dispute over foreign marriages, and in Neh 8:7, among those who helped the people understand the law. He may be the same man, but since the name is shared by several people, that cannot be confirmed. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "my rest".

Shachia was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named once in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles. He was a son of Shaharaim by his wife Hodesh. His full brothers were Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcham, Jeuz and Mirma, and his half-brothers Abitub and Elpaal were sons of Shaharaim by another wife, Hushim (1 Chr 8:8–11). The text calls Shaharaim's sons "heads of the fathers," meaning leaders of family groups within the tribe (1 Chr 8:10). Nothing else is recorded about him. The spelling of his name differs among Hebrew manuscripts and ancient translations, and the Greek and Syriac versions read it as Shabiah, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. Its meaning is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives it as "protection of the Lord."

Shadrach was the Babylonian name given to Hananiah, one of the young men of Judah who served with Daniel at the court of Nebuchadnezzar. The chief of the eunuchs renamed him, along with Daniel (Belteshazzar), Mishael (Meshach) and Azariah (Abednego). After their training, the king found none equal to these four. Daniel shared Nebuchadnezzar's troubling dream with them, and later had Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego appointed over the affairs of the province of Babylon. When the three refused to worship the king's golden image, Nebuchadnezzar had them bound and thrown into a furnace heated seven times hotter than usual. The flames killed the men who carried them, but the three came out unharmed. The king then praised their God, issued a decree protecting his worship, and promoted them. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the name Shadrach as "Aku's command".

Shage the Hararite was the father of Jonathan, one of the warriors listed among David's mighty men in 1 Chr 11:34. The parallel list in 2 Sam 23:32–33 reads "Jonathan, Shammah the Hararite" at the same point. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes this to mean that Shage and Shammah are the same man, and this entry follows that view by treating Shammah as another name for him. On that reading, the original text probably said "Jonathan son of Shammah" in Samuel. The STEPBible name index further links him with Shammah the son of Agee the Hararite, whom 2 Sam 23:11 praises for holding his ground against the Philistines. That would make Shage himself a renowned warrior of David's time, around 1000 BC by inference from context. "Hararite" probably means he came from the hill country, though the exact place is uncertain.

Shaharaim was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "double dawn." The text does not name his father, so his exact place in the family line is uncertain. According to 1 Chr 8:8, he had children in the land of Moab after he had sent away his wives Hushim and Baara. The following verses (1 Chr 8:9–11) name a third wife, Hodesh, who bore him Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcham, Jeuz, Shachia and Mirma, apparently in Moab. They also say that by Hushim he had earlier fathered Abitub and Elpaal. The passage gives no reason for sending away his first wives and no explanation for his time in Moab.

Shahazumah (spelled Shahazimah in the King James Version) was a town on the boundary of the tribe of Issachar. It is named only once, in the description of Issachar's border, which reached Tabor, Shahazumah and Beth-shemesh before ending at the Jordan (Josh 19:22). Its listing between Mount Tabor and the Jordan suggests it lay somewhere along the line between them. The site has not been identified. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it should probably be sought southeast of Mount Tabor. The location shown here is only a rough placement, near the Jordan Valley south of the Sea of Galilee, and should not be taken as a known site.

Shalishah was a district that Saul and his servant passed through while searching for his father Kish's lost donkeys. Their route ran through the hill country of Ephraim, then the land of Shalishah, then the land of Shalim, and finally the territory of Benjamin, without finding the animals (1 Sam 9:4). Its exact location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connect it with the town of Baal-shalishah (2 Kgs 4:42), which may have given the district its name. Both place it northeast of Lydda on the western slopes of the central hill country. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes Conder's identification of Baal-shalishah with Khirbet Kefr Thilth. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the hill country north of Jerusalem, near Benjamin, following the general line of Saul's journey.

Shallecheth was one of the gates of the temple in Jerusalem, on its western side. In the Levites' rotation of gatekeeping duties, the lot for the west, together with this gate "by the causeway of the going up," fell to Shuppim and Hosah (1 Chr 26:16). The name probably means "casting out," and Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it to be a refuse gate. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint renders it with a word for a building with chambers. The causeway is generally understood as an ascent rising from the Tyropoeon Valley to the temple. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies the gate with the Bab al-Silsila, the Chain Gate, in the west wall of the Temple Mount enclosure. The location shown here lies on the western side of the Temple Mount, which matches that identification. The exact site is uncertain.

Shallum son of Jabesh was a king of Israel who took the throne by killing King Zachariah. He conspired against Zachariah, struck him down in public, and reigned in his place (2 Kgs 15:10). The surrounding passage shows that the "him" of that verse is Zachariah. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that this ended the dynasty of Jehu. Shallum began to reign in the thirty-ninth year of Uzziah king of Judah and lasted only a full month in Samaria. Then Menahem son of Gadi came up from Tirzah, killed him, and took the throne (2 Kgs 15:13–14). His other acts and his conspiracy were written in the chronicles of the kings of Israel (2 Kgs 15:15). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests his father's name may point to Gilead. This entry dates his reign to about 772 BC, inferred from context; the ISBE places it about 758 BC. Several other biblical figures share his name.

Shallum was the husband of Huldah the prophetess, who lived in Jerusalem in the reign of King Josiah. He is called the son of Tikvah (Tikvath in Chronicles) and the grandson of Harhas (Hasrah in Chronicles). The title "keeper of the wardrobe" follows these names. It is usually taken to describe Shallum himself, though the wording could also refer to his grandfather. Easton's Bible Dictionary understands the wardrobe as the temple vestments. Shallum is mentioned only to identify Huldah, when Hilkiah the priest and the king's officials went to consult her, by context about the book of the law found in the temple (2 Kgs 22:14; 2 Chr 34:22). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he was probably the uncle of Jeremiah named in Jer 32:7. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shallum.

Shallum was a man of the tribe of Judah named in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 2. He was the son of Sisamai and the father of Jekamiah, whose son was Elishama (1 Chr 2:40–41). By the surrounding context, his line belongs to the descendants of Jerahmeel through Sheshan, whose daughter married his Egyptian servant Jarha. The STEPBible proper-names index likewise places him in Judah's line through Jerahmeel. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in this family list. The name Shallum is shared by several other people in the Bible, including a king of Israel and the husband of the prophetess Huldah, so this Shallum should not be confused with them.
