Shallum was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named only in the Simeonite genealogy of 1 Chr 4:25. He was the son of Shaul and the father of Mibsam, and the line continues through Mibsam's son Mishma. The preceding verse lists Shaul among the sons of Simeon, so Shallum was probably Simeon's grandson, as Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to be. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name Shallum, and this one should not be confused with them. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts at least twelve. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "retribution", while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "perfect" or "agreeable."

Shallum was a Levite in the high-priestly line descended from Aaron. He was the son of Zadok and the father of Hilkiah (1 Chr 6:12–13). Ezra the scribe traced his own ancestry through him (Ezra 7:2). In 1 Chr 9:11 and Neh 11:11 he appears as Meshullam, in genealogies of Azariah and Seraiah, who are each called "the ruler of the house of God". Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat Shallum and Meshullam as the same man and regard him as a high priest. Smith's places him probably in the reign of Amon, which fits his son being the Hilkiah who served as high priest under Josiah. The texts themselves give only his place in the family line. Several other men in the Bible are also named Shallum or Meshullam.

Shallum son of Kore was a Levite of the Korahite family who served as chief of the gatekeepers ("porters") of the sanctuary. 1 Chr 9:19 traces his line through Kore and Ebiasaph back to Korah and says he and his kin guarded the gates of the tabernacle, as their fathers had kept the entry. His firstborn son Mattithiah was in charge of the baked goods made in pans (1 Chr 9:31). "The children of Shallum" appear among the gatekeeper families who returned from exile (Ezra 2:42; Neh 7:45). Easton's Bible Dictionary places him in the reign of David. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies him with the gatekeeper called Meshelemiah or Shelemiah in 1 Chr 26. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shallum.

Shallum was an Ephraimite, known only as the father of Jehizkiah, one of the leaders of Ephraim named in 2 Chr 28:12. Several people in the Bible share this name, and this one is otherwise unknown. His son appears in the account of the war in which Pekah of Israel defeated Ahaz of Judah and brought many captives from Judah to Samaria. Jehizkiah and other heads of Ephraim stood up against the returning soldiers and opposed holding fellow Judeans as captives. From that context, Shallum probably lived around the reign of Ahaz, king of Judah. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as an Ephraimite chief. The text itself gives the leadership role to his son and says nothing further about Shallum.

Shallum was a temple gatekeeper (a "porter" in the King James Version) in Ezra's time. He is listed with Telem and Uri in Ezra 10:24, in the roll of men who had married foreign wives. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both describe him this way. The surrounding chapter records that the men on this list agreed to send away their foreign wives during Ezra's reforms after the return from exile, so Shallum was probably among them. The verse places him among the gatekeepers, right after the singer Eliashib. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that he appears as "Sallumus" in 1 Esdras 9:25. Nothing else is known of him. The name Shallum belongs to several other men in the Bible, including a king of Israel, and this gatekeeper should not be confused with them.

Shallum was one of the Israelites listed in Ezra 10:42 among the men who had married foreign wives in the period after the return from exile in Babylon. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was one of those who agreed to send these wives away during the reforms led by Ezra the scribe. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him among the descendants of Bani, following the family heading earlier in the same list. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Shallum is shared by several other men in the Bible, including a king of Israel, and this Shallum should not be confused with them.

Shallum the son of Halohesh was ruler of half the district of Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah. He took part in rebuilding the city wall after the return from exile, repairing a section next to the stretch worked on by Rephaiah's neighbour in the list (Neh 3:12). The verse notes that his daughters worked alongside him, an unusual detail in a list that otherwise names men. The other half of Jerusalem's district appears to have had its own ruler, by inference from the phrase "the half part." The name Shallum is shared by about a dozen men in the Bible, according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, and this one is mentioned only here. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "retribution," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "perfect" or "agreeable."

Shallum was the uncle of the prophet Jeremiah and the father of Hanameel. He is named only once, in Jer 32:7, where the Lord tells Jeremiah that Hanameel, "the son of Shallum thine uncle," will come and ask him to buy a family field at Anathoth, because Jeremiah held the right of redemption. Shallum is described here as a brother of Hilkiah. Jer 1:1 names Hilkiah, a priest of Anathoth, as Jeremiah's father, so by inference Shallum was his father's brother and belonged to the same priestly family of Anathoth. The following verses in Jer 32 describe Jeremiah buying the field from Hanameel. Several other men in the Bible are called Shallum, and Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests this one may perhaps be the same as one of them. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Shallum was the father, or possibly an earlier ancestor, of Maaseiah. He is mentioned once, in Jer 35:4, when Jeremiah brought the Rechabites into the temple. One of the rooms there is identified as the chamber of Maaseiah the son of Shallum, located below the chamber of the princes. The verse calls one of them "the keeper of the door." The STEPBible proper names index takes this title to belong to Maaseiah, as one of the temple's threshold keepers in Jeremiah's time, and this entry follows that reading. Nothing else is said about Shallum himself. Because several men in the Bible bear this name, his identity is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he may be the same as another Shallum of the period and dates him to about 630 BC. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "perfect" or "agreeable."

Shallun son of Col-hozeh was the ruler of the district of Mizpah who took part in Nehemiah's rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls after the return from exile. According to Neh 3:15, he repaired the Fountain Gate. He rebuilt and roofed it and installed its doors, locks and bars. He also rebuilt the wall of the Pool of Siloah (Shelah) beside the king's garden, as far as the stairs leading down from the City of David. His name means "retribution" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary. Some ancient manuscripts and translations spell it Shallum, but he is mentioned only in this one verse.

Shalmai was the ancestor of a family of Nethinim, the temple servants, whose descendants returned to Jerusalem from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel. He is known only from the two parallel lists of returning exiles (Ezra 2:46; Neh 7:48), where "the children of Shalmai" appear next to the families of Hagab or Hagaba and Hanan. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the return to about 536 BC, an estimate drawn from context. The spelling of the name differs between versions and manuscripts. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the Ezra form as Shamlai and the Nehemiah form as Salmai, while the King James Version reads Shalmai in both places. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as "my garment," and Smith's gives "my thanks." Nothing more is recorded about him.

Shalmaneser was a king of Assyria in the time of Hoshea, the last king of the northern kingdom of Israel. He marched against Hoshea, who submitted as his vassal and paid him tribute (2 Kgs 17:3). In Hoshea's seventh year, which was Hezekiah's fourth, he came up against Samaria and besieged it (2 Kgs 18:9). The surrounding account says the siege lasted three years before the city fell and Israel was exiled (2 Kgs 17:5–6; 18:10–11). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies him as Shalmaneser IV, reigning from about 727 BC. It notes that Sargon claimed the final capture, so Shalmaneser may have died or been deposed during the siege. The "Shalman" who spoiled Beth-arbel in Hos 10:14 may be a shortened form of his name, as Easton's Bible Dictionary holds. Others suggest a Moabite king named Salamanu. This entry follows the identification with Shalmaneser.

Shama was one of David's mighty warriors, named in the list of his heroes in 1 Chr 11:44. He and his brother Jehiel were sons of Hothan the Aroerite, so the family probably came from Aroer. There were two towns of that name, one east of the Jordan on the Arnon River and one in southern Judah, and the verse does not say which is meant. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "obedient" and counts him among David's guard. His name appears in the later part of the Chronicles list, which goes beyond the parallel roster in 2 Samuel 23, and nothing else is recorded about him.

Shamariah was a son of King Rehoboam of Judah, listed with his brothers Jeush and Zaham in 2 Chr 11:19. The preceding verse names two of Rehoboam's wives, Mahalath and Abihail, and the Hebrew does not make fully clear which of them bore these three sons. This entry follows the reading that their mother was Abihail, daughter of Eliab, David's eldest brother. His half-siblings Abijah, Attai, Ziza and Shelomith were Rehoboam's children by Maachah (2 Chr 11:20), and Abijah later succeeded his father as king. Nothing more is recorded about Shamariah. His birth in Jerusalem is inferred from his father's reign there. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "kept by Jehovah", and some versions spell it Shemariah.

Shamed was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 8 as a son of Elpaal, alongside Eber and Misham. The verse credits him with building Ono and Lod with their surrounding towns. It is most naturally read as referring to Shamed alone, though it could include his brothers. Lod is probably the later Lydda of the New Testament, the modern city of Lod in Israel, and Ono lay nearby. Smith's Bible Dictionary holds that his name is properly Shamer or Shemer, and some reference works list him as Shemed. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "destroying", while Smith's gives "keeper". Nothing else is recorded about him.

Shamer was a Levite of the family of Merari, named once in the genealogy of the temple singers at 1 Chr 6:46. In that list he is the son of Mahli and the father of Bani, and his line runs on through Amzi and later generations. By inference from the surrounding passage (1 Chr 6:44–47), he was an ancestor of Ethan, one of the singers David appointed to lead music at the sanctuary, and Mahli was himself a descendant of Merari son of Levi. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "keeper," and Hitchcock's Bible Names adds "thorn" or "dregs." Some resources spell the name Shemer. Several people in the Bible share this name, including an Asherite also called Shamer and the Shemer from whom Omri bought the hill of Samaria. This Levite is distinct from them.

Shamer, also called Shomer, was a man of the tribe of Asher who appears only in the Asherite genealogy of 1 Chronicles. He was a son of Heber, and his brothers were Japhlet and Hotham, with a sister named Shua (1 Chr 7:32). His sons were Ahi, Rohgah, Jehubbah and Aram (1 Chr 7:34). The two spellings occur in neighbouring verses of the same list and are taken to refer to the same person, as Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both note. The name is usually understood to mean "keeper". Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in the family line. Several other men in the Bible bear similar names, so he should be distinguished from them.

Shamgar, son of Anath, was a deliverer of Israel in the period of the judges, mentioned right after the account of Ehud. Judg 3:31 says he killed six hundred Philistines with an ox goad and so also delivered Israel. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that an ox goad was a long, sharp-pointed stick used for driving cattle. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia observes that this verse is the first mention of the Philistines troubling Israel. The Song of Deborah recalls "the days of Shamgar" alongside the days of Jael as a time when the roads were deserted and travellers kept to back paths (Judg 5:6). This suggests he lived shortly before or overlapping with Deborah and Barak, and Easton's treats them as probably contemporaries for a time. Nothing else is recorded about him or his father Anath.

Shamhuth was the commander of the fifth of the twelve army divisions that David organized, each serving in turn for one month of the year. His division served in the fifth month and numbered 24,000 men (1 Chr 27:8). He is called "the Izrahite," probably meaning a descendant of Zerah, a clan of Judah, though the exact sense of the term is uncertain. His name appears only in this verse. Many interpreters identify him with Shammah the Harodite, one of David's mighty men (2 Sam 23:25), also called Shammoth the Harorite (1 Chr 11:27), since several other division commanders in this list also appear among those warriors. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia points readers to its entry on Shammuah for this connection. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "desolation" or "destruction."

Shamir was a town in the hill country of Judah. It appears only in the list of Judah's towns in Josh 15:48, where it is named first in a group alongside Jattir and Socoh. Because the name is shared by several places in the Bible, this Shamir should be kept distinct from others of the same name. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggest Khirbet Somerah, a hilltop site with ancient walls, caves, cisterns and tombs, a few miles northwest of Debir and north of Anab. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it more generally, about eight to ten miles south of Hebron. The location shown here lies in the southern Judean hills, in the region of these proposals. The name may mean "thorn" or "point."

Shamir was a town in the hill country of Ephraim where Tola, son of Puah and a man of the tribe of Issachar, lived while he judged Israel after Abimelech. Tola judged for twenty-three years, then died and was buried at Shamir (Judg 10:1–2). Its exact site is uncertain, and other places in the Bible share the name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mentions a proposal to identify it with Sanur, a strongly placed town on the road from Nablus to Jenin, while noting that Sanur probably lay outside Issachar's territory. The same work observes that one manuscript of the Greek Septuagint, Codex Alexandrinus, reads "Samaria" here instead of Shamir. The location shown here follows the Sanur identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "thorn" or "bush."

Shamir was a Levite, the son of Michah, listed among the descendants of Uzziel in 1 Chr 24:24. The passage is part of a register of Levites who were not priests, set out in connection with the organization of temple service in David's time. Uzziel was a son of Kohath, so Shamir belonged to the Kohathite branch of the tribe of Levi, as Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both note. Smith's describes Michah as Uzziel's firstborn. The name may mean "point" or "thorn." Beyond his place in this genealogy, nothing more is recorded about him. The name Shamir is also used for towns elsewhere in the Old Testament, but those are unrelated to this man.

Shamma was a man of the tribe of Asher, named once in the genealogy of Asher's descendants in 1 Chr 7:37. He was one of the sons of Zophah, listed with his brothers Suah, Harnepher, Beri, Imrah, Bezer, Hod, Shilshah, Ithran and Beera. The Ithran of this verse is probably the same person as the Jether named in the next verse, which would account for Jether among his brothers. Nothing else is recorded about Shamma beyond his place in this family list. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "astonishment."

Shammah was a son of Reuel and a grandson of Esau through Esau's wife Bashemath. He is named third among Reuel's four sons, after Nahath and Zerah and before Mizzah (Gen 36:13; 1 Chr 1:37). In the list of Edom's chiefs he appears as "duke Shammah," one of the clan leaders descended from Reuel in the land of Edom (Gen 36:17). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both describe him as a tribal chief of Edom. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "desolation" or "astonishment." Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shammah, including a brother of David and one of David's mighty men. This Edomite chief is a different person.

Shammah son of Agee the Hararite was one of the three leading warriors among David's mighty men, listed after Eleazar in 2 Sam 23:11. When the Philistines gathered as a raiding troop at a field full of lentils and the Israelites fled, Shammah stood his ground. The next verse (2 Sam 23:12) says he took his stand in the middle of the field, defended it and killed the Philistines, and that the LORD brought about a great victory. Easton's Bible Dictionary counts him among David's three mighty men. "Hararite" probably refers to his home town or clan, though its location is unknown. Several men in the Bible are named Shammah, and it is unclear whether the "Shammah the Harodite" and "Shammah the Hararite" listed later in the same chapter are the same man or relatives. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "loss; desolation; astonishment."

Shammah the Harodite was one of David's mighty warriors, listed among the elite group known as "the thirty" in 2 Sam 23:25. The parallel list in 1 Chr 11:27 calls him Shammoth the Harorite. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes "Harorite" as a copying variant of "Harodite" and suggests he probably came from Harod, the spring where Gideon camped (Judg 7:1). Smith's and Easton's Bible Dictionaries also identify him with Shamhuth the Izrahite, the commander of the fifth monthly division of David's army in 1 Chr 27:8. His name is spelled differently in each passage, and beyond his place in these lists nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shammah, including one of David's brothers and another of David's mighty men. This entry concerns only the Harodite.

Shammah was the third son of Jesse of the tribe of Judah, and an older brother of David. When the prophet Samuel came to Bethlehem to anoint a king, Jesse had Shammah pass before him, but Samuel said the LORD had not chosen him (1 Sam 16:9). He was one of Jesse's three eldest sons, with Eliab and Abinadab, who followed Saul to war against the Philistines (1 Sam 17:13). He is also called Shimeah (2 Sam 13:3) and Shimma (1 Chr 2:13). As Shimeah he was the father of Jonadab, a shrewd friend of Amnon, who later told David that only Amnon, not all the king's sons, had been killed by Absalom's order (2 Sam 13:32). Reference works such as the Tyndale House proper names list also link him to a son Jonathan, named in a later passage. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shammah.

Shammai was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of Jerahmeel, son of Hezron. He was a son of Onam and the brother of Jada, and his sons were Nadab and Abishur (1 Chr 2:28). His brother Jada's line is traced next, through Jada's sons Jether and Jonathan (1 Chr 2:32). Nothing further is recorded about his life. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "desolate." Several other men in the Bible bear the name Shammai, and this one should not be confused with them. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists him first among them and identifies him as a Jerahmeelite.

Shammai was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 2. He was the son of Rekem and the father of Maon, and Maon in turn was the "father of Bethzur" (1 Chr 2:44–45). From the surrounding verses (1 Chr 2:42–43), this line descends from Caleb through Hebron, whose son was Rekem, so Shammai probably belonged to the Calebite clans of southern Judah. Maon and Beth-zur are also the names of towns in the hill country of Judah, so "father of" here may mean the founder or leading figure of a settlement rather than only a parent. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "desolate." The name is shared by other men in the Judahite genealogies, so this Shammai should not be confused with them.

Shammai was a descendant of Judah, named only in the genealogy at 1 Chr 4:17. Several men in the Bible share this name. He was a son of Mered, who was a son of Ezra (often spelled Ezrah). The verse lists him with his sister Miriam and his brother Ishbah, the father of Eshtemoa. The wording here is compressed, and the verse does not say who 'she' is. The next verse, 1 Chr 4:18, identifies these children as the offspring of Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh, whom Mered married. Mered also had children by a wife from Judah, and 1 Chr 4:18–19 links Eshtemoa and 'the Garmite' to that line, which explains the half-siblings shown in this entry. Nothing else is recorded about Shammai. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as 'my name' or 'my desolations.'

Shammua son of Zaccur was the man from the tribe of Reuben chosen as one of the twelve spies Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan (Num 13:4). Each spy represented one tribe, and the surrounding chapter shows the group setting out from the wilderness of Paran. He is not named again. Because only Joshua and Caleb are singled out for urging Israel to enter the land, Shammua was probably among the ten spies who brought back a discouraging report and who, according to Num 14:36–37, died by a plague. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "renowned" and dates the mission to about 1490 BC. Several other people in the Bible share the name Shammua, and this Reubenite should not be confused with them.

Shammua was a priest in the period after the return from exile, named in Neh 12:18 as head of the priestly family of Bilgah. The surrounding passage lists the heads of the priestly houses in the days of Joiakim the high priest, who succeeded Jeshua. By inference from that context, Shammua served in the generation after the first returnees from Babylon. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 500 BC, an estimate rather than a date given in the text. His name is often explained as meaning "renowned." Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a spy sent into Canaan and a son of David, and they should not be confused with this priest.

Shammua was a son of King David, born in Jerusalem after David made the city his capital. He is listed first among the sons born there, ahead of Shobab, Nathan and Solomon (2 Sam 5:14; 1 Chr 14:4). In 1 Chr 3:5 he is called Shimea, and that verse names all four as sons of Bathshua daughter of Ammiel, a variant spelling of Bathsheba. Easton's Bible Dictionary treats Shimea and Shammua as the same person. That makes Shammua a full brother of Solomon and a member of the tribe of Judah. Nothing more is recorded about his life beyond these lists. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shammua, so he should be kept distinct from them.

Shamsherai was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the genealogy of Benjamin's descendants in 1 Chronicles. He is listed first among the sons of Jeroham, alongside his brothers Shehariah, Athaliah, Jaresiah, Eliah and Zichri (1 Chr 8:26–27). The following verse describes the men in this part of the list as heads of their fathers' houses who lived in Jerusalem (1 Chr 8:28), so Shamsherai was probably a family leader there. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "sunlike," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "there a singer or conqueror."

Shapham was a leader of the tribe of Gad who lived in Bashan, east of the Jordan. He is named only once, in the Gadite genealogy at 1 Chr 5:12, where he is listed as "the next" after Joel the chief. This probably means he ranked second in authority among the Gadite families. The surrounding passage says these Gadite records were compiled in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel (1 Chr 5:17). On that basis Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 750 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes another possibility: the lists were written down around that time, but Shapham and Joel may have lived earlier, in Saul's day, and taken part in the war against the Hagrites described in the same chapter. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Shaphan son of Azaliah, grandson of Meshullam, was the scribe, or royal secretary, of King Josiah of Judah. In Josiah's eighteenth year the king sent him to the temple about the money collected for its repair. There the high priest Hilkiah gave him the newly found book of the law. Shaphan read it, reported to the king and read it aloud to him (2 Kgs 22:8–10). He was then one of the group sent to consult the prophetess Huldah. His family remained prominent. His son Ahikam protected Jeremiah, his son Elasah carried Jeremiah's letter to Babylon, and Baruch read Jeremiah's scroll in the chamber of his son Gemariah. His grandson Gedaliah was made governor of Judah by Nebuchadnezzar and was later murdered by Ishmael. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "coney" (rock badger). Other men in the Bible share the name.

Shaphan was the father of Jaazaniah, a man Ezekiel saw in a vision of the Jerusalem temple. Jaazaniah stood among seventy elders of Israel, each holding a censer, as a thick cloud of incense rose from their worship of the images carved on the temple walls (Ezek 8:11). Nothing more is said about Shaphan himself. The name, meaning "rock badger" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, belongs to several people in the Bible. The best known is Shaphan the scribe under King Josiah, whose sons served at court in Jeremiah's time. Some have suggested this Shaphan is the same man, but the verse does not say so. That encyclopedia lists him separately and describes him only as "perhaps" the father of Jaazaniah. This entry treats him as a distinct person.

Shaphat, son of Hori, was the man chosen from the tribe of Simeon as one of the twelve spies Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan (Num 13:5). Each tribe supplied one leader for the mission. By inference from the rest of Numbers 13–14, he was among the ten spies who brought back a discouraging report, since only Joshua and Caleb are singled out for their favorable account. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names gives as meaning "judge," is shared by several other men in the Bible, including the father of the prophet Elisha. This Shaphat should be kept distinct from them.

Shaphat was the father of the prophet Elisha, who succeeded Elijah. He is known only through his son, who is repeatedly called "Elisha the son of Shaphat." The family was from Abel-meholah (1 Kgs 19:16). When Elijah found Elisha, he was plowing with twelve yoke of oxen, which suggests, by inference, that Shaphat's household owned considerable farmland (1 Kgs 19:19). The same patronymic identifies Elisha when he is introduced to King Jehoshaphat (2 Kgs 3:11), and again when the king of Israel vows to have him beheaded (2 Kgs 6:31). Nothing else is recorded about Shaphat himself. The name, meaning "judge" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, is shared by several other people in the Bible, among them the Simeonite spy listed in Num 13:5. This entry concerns only Elisha's father.

Shaphat was a son of Shemaiah and a member of the royal line of Judah, listed among the descendants of David in the genealogy of 1 Chr 3:22. His brothers were Hattush, Igeal, Bariah and Neariah, and his grandfather was Shechaniah. From the surrounding genealogy, which traces David's line through Zerubbabel, he probably lived in the period after the return from exile, as STEPBible's Tyndale House name list also places him. The verse totals the sons as "six" but names only five. Including Shemaiah in the count is one way to reach that number, though the verse does not say so. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, meaning "judge" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, is shared by several other men in the Bible, including the Simeonite spy of Num 13:5.

Shaphat was a leader of the tribe of Gad who lived in Bashan, the region east of the Jordan. He is named in a genealogy of the Gadites, listed fourth among their chief men after Joel the chief, Shapham the next, and Jaanai (1 Chr 5:12). The surrounding passage places these records in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel, so Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 750 BC. His name means "judge" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Several other men in the Bible share the name, among them the Simeonite spy sent out by Moses and the father of the prophet Elisha. Nothing more is recorded about this Gadite.

Shaphat son of Adlai was one of the officials who managed King David's royal property. According to 1 Chr 27:29, he was in charge of the herds of cattle that grazed in the valleys. Another official, Shitrai the Sharonite, looked after the herds that pastured in the plain of Sharon. The verse comes from a list of the stewards who oversaw the king's possessions, which also included vineyards, olive groves, camels and flocks. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Shaphat, which means "judge" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, belongs to several men in the Bible. These include the Simeonite spy sent out by Moses and the father of the prophet Elisha, and this Shaphat should not be confused with them.

Shaphir (spelled Saphir in the King James Version) was a town of Judah named only once, in Micah's lament over the towns of the southwestern lowlands. In Mic 1:11 its inhabitants are told to pass away "having thy shame naked," which probably pictures them being led off as captives. The name probably means "beautiful" or "glittering," and like several other names in the passage it seems chosen for wordplay. Its exact location is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia infers from the nearby mentions of Gath, Achzib and Mareshah that the town lay in southwestern Palestine. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the same encyclopedia connect the name with the villages of es-Suafir, a few miles southeast of Ashdod. Another suggestion links it with the white hill Tell es-Safi. The location shown here follows the es-Suafir identification.

Sharai was an Israelite man named in the list of those who had married foreign wives during Ezra's reforms after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears only in Ezra 10:40, within a group that Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both place among the sons of Bani. By inference from the surrounding passage, he was one of the men who agreed to send away his foreign wife. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 457 BC, an estimate drawn from context. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "releaser," while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "my lord," "my prince" or "my song." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Sharar was a Hararite, the father of Ahiam, one of the warriors listed among David's mighty men (2 Sam 23:33). In the parallel list in 1 Chr 11:35 he is called Sacar. The difference between the two names probably comes from copying of the text, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia regards Sharar as the more likely original reading. The description "Hararite" probably refers to his family or place of origin, perhaps the hill country, though its exact meaning is uncertain. Nothing more is recorded about him beyond his son's place in David's roll of heroes. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of David's heroes, but in both lists it is his son Ahiam who is named among the mighty men.

Sharezer was a son of Sennacherib, king of Assyria, and a brother of Adrammelech and Esarhaddon. While Sennacherib was worshipping in the temple of his god Nisroch, Sharezer and Adrammelech killed him with the sword and fled to the land of Armenia. The Hebrew calls this land Ararat, a mountainous region north of Assyria. Their brother Esarhaddon then became king (2 Kgs 19:37; Isa 37:38). Both accounts place the killing after Sennacherib's failed campaign against Jerusalem in Hezekiah's reign. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as Assyrian for "protect the king." It notes that the Babylonian Chronicle speaks of a single, unnamed son as the murderer. Some scholars, following an ancient writer quoted by Eusebius, read his full name as Nergal-sharezer. A different man named Sharezer appears in Zech 7:2.

Sharon was a district east of the Jordan, distinct from the better-known coastal plain of the same name. 1 Chr 5:16 says the people of Gad lived in Gilead, in Bashan and its towns, and in "all the suburbs of Sharon," meaning its pasture lands, as far as their borders. The Gadites are identified by inference from the surrounding passage. Unlike the coastal Sharon, the Hebrew name here has no definite article. Its location is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes two views. Kittel suggested the name is a scribal variant of "Sirion," another name for Mount Hermon, which would place Sharon in the pasture lands of Hermon. Others take it to mean the tableland of Gilead. The location shown here follows the Hermon identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "his plain."

Sharuhen was a town in the far south of Canaan, listed among the thirteen cities and their villages given to the tribe of Simeon within the territory of Judah (Josh 19:6). It appears by this name only in this verse. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes it to be the same town called Shilhim in the parallel list of Judah's southern towns (Josh 15:32) and Shaaraim in the list of Simeon's towns (1 Chr 4:31). Its site is debated. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Sheriah, a large ruin northwest of Beersheba. The location shown here follows a different identification, Tel Sharuhen (Tell el-Far'ah South), a mound beside the Besor stream in the western Negev, south of Gaza.

Shashai was one of the Israelites listed in Ezra 10:40 among the men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra. Ezra's reforms called for these marriages to be dissolved, and Shashai's name appears in the closing list of those involved. The verse itself gives only his name, between Machnadebai and Sharai. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both place him among the sons of Bani, following the arrangement of the list in that chapter. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds that he is called Sesis in 1 Esdras 9:34. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the episode to about 457 BC, an estimate from context. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "rejoicing," "mercy" or "linen," while Smith's renders it "noble." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Shashak was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. He is listed with Ahio and Jeremoth (1 Chr 8:14). This entry follows Smith's Bible Dictionary in treating him as a son of Beriah. By inference from the surrounding verses, that makes him a descendant of Elpaal, since Beriah appears among Elpaal's descendants and as a family head connected with Aijalon. The list itself does not spell out the relationship, so his exact place in it is somewhat uncertain. Eleven sons are credited to him, including Ishpan, Heber, Eliel, Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Hananiah, Elam, Antothijah, Iphedeiah and Penuel (1 Chr 8:25). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as the founder of a Benjamite family. Smith's gives the meaning of his name as "longing"; Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a bag of linen."

Shaul was one of the early kings of Edom. He came from Rehoboth by the river, succeeded Samlah, and was followed on the throne by Baal-hanan the son of Achbor (Gen 36:37–38; 1 Chr 1:48–49). The King James Version calls him Saul in Genesis and Shaul in Chronicles. He appears in the list of kings who ruled Edom before any king reigned over Israel (Gen 36:31). The identity of "the river" is uncertain. The STEPBible proper-names index takes it to be the Euphrates, which is how the river is usually meant in the Old Testament. Others place Rehoboth by a stream within Edom. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "asked." He is a different person from King Saul of Israel and from others who share the name.

Shaul was a son of Simeon and a grandson of Jacob, named among those who went down to Egypt with Jacob (Gen 46:10). He is described as the son of a Canaanitish woman, which sets him apart from his brothers Jemuel (also called Nemuel), Jamin, Ohad, Jachin (also called Jarib) and Zohar (also called Zerah) (Exod 6:15; 1 Chr 4:24). He became the ancestor of the Shaulites, one of the clans of the tribe of Simeon counted in the wilderness census (Num 26:13). The genealogy in Chronicles continues his line through his son Shallum, as the verse after 1 Chr 4:24 records. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "asked." The same name, usually spelled Saul in English, belongs to several other people in the Bible, including Israel's first king.

Shaul was a Levite of the clan of Kohath who appears in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 6. In 1 Chr 6:24 he closes a line of descent from Kohath that runs through Tahath, Uriel and Uzziah. The parallel ancestry of the singer Heman, which traces back through the prophet Samuel, has a Joel son of Azariah and father of Elkanah at the same point (1 Chr 6:36). For this reason the two names are usually taken as the same man, and this entry follows that view. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests that Joel may be a copying variant of Shaul, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him a Levite ancestor of Samuel. The two lists give his father as Uzziah and as Azariah, which are probably alternate forms of one name. Several other people in the Bible are also called Shaul.

Shaveh-kiriathaim was the place where Chedorlaomer and the kings allied with him defeated the Emim during their campaign in the time of Abraham (Gen 14:5). The name probably means "plain of Kiriathaim." Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "plain of the double city" and takes it to be the valley in or beside which the town of Kiriathaim stood. Kiriathaim appears later as a town east of the Jordan, assigned to Reuben in Num 32:37 and later counted among the cities of Moab in Jer 48:1. Deut 2:10–11 says the Emim were the earlier inhabitants of the land of Moab, which fits that setting. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify the site with el-Qureiyat, about 7 miles north of Dibon in modern Jordan. The location shown here follows that Moabite identification and is approximate. The exact site is not certain.

Shavsha was the royal scribe, or state secretary, under King David. He appears in the lists of David's chief officials alongside the priests Zadok and Abiathar's son, though the name is spelled differently in each list. It is Shavsha in 1 Chr 18:16, Seraiah in the parallel list at 2 Sam 8:17, and Sheva in 2 Sam 20:25. Under Solomon, Elihoreph and Ahiah, "the sons of Shisha," held the same office (1 Kgs 4:3). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take Shisha to be another form of the same name, so this entry treats them as one man whose sons succeeded him. The ISBE notes that his father's name is never given and that his name sounds foreign. It suggests he may have been a non-Israelite, possibly chosen because the office involved correspondence with other nations. Which spelling is original is uncertain. The ISBE describes Shavsha as the generally preferred form.

Sheal was one of the descendants of Bani named in the list of Israelite men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra (Ezra 10:29). The context of Ezra 10 shows that these men agreed to send away their foreign wives as part of Ezra's reforms after the return from exile in Babylon. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "asking," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "request." It also notes that Greek versions spell the name differently, and that the parallel list in 1 Esdras calls him Jasaelus. Nothing else is known about him.

Shealtiel, also called Salathiel, was a son of King Jehoiachin (Jeconiah) of Judah. Matthew places his birth after the deportation to Babylon (1 Chr 3:17; Matt 1:12). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the meaning of his name as "asked of God." He is known almost entirely as the father of Zerubbabel, the governor of Judah who led returning exiles. Zerubbabel rebuilt the altar and began work on the temple in Jerusalem with the high priest Jeshua, and Ezra, Nehemiah and Haggai repeatedly call him "son of Shealtiel." As the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes, 1 Chr 3:19 instead names Shealtiel's brother Pedaiah as Zerubbabel's father. This may reflect adoption or a levirate marriage, or Shealtiel may have been Zerubbabel's grandfather. This entry follows the majority of passages in calling him Zerubbabel's father. Luke 3:27 also lists him among the ancestors of Jesus.

Shear-jashub was a son of the prophet Isaiah. His name means "a remnant shall return." He appears only once, when the LORD told Isaiah to take him along to meet King Ahaz of Judah "at the end of the conduit of the upper pool in the highway of the fuller's field" (Isa 7:3). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that his name, like those of other prophets' children such as his brother Maher-shalal-hash-baz, was symbolic and carried a message. Isaiah later uses the same Hebrew words in Isa 10:21 to announce that a remnant of Israel will return. By inference, the boy's presence at the meeting with Ahaz was itself part of the prophet's message. Nothing more is recorded about his life.

Sheariah was one of the six sons of Azel, a Benjamite descended from King Saul through Jonathan. He appears only in the genealogy of Saul's family, which is given twice in nearly identical words (1 Chr 8:38; 1 Chr 9:44). His brothers were Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Obadiah and Hanan. The surrounding lists trace Azel's line back through Jonathan's son Merib-baal (Mephibosheth) to Saul, so Sheariah belonged to a late generation of Saul's descendants. Nothing is recorded about his life beyond his name and place in the family. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "valued by Jehovah," while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "gate of the Lord" or "tempest of the Lord."

Sheba was a distant kingdom known for its trade in gold, spices, incense and precious stones. Its queen heard of Solomon's fame and came to Jerusalem with a large caravan of camels to test him with hard questions. She gave him a hundred and twenty talents of gold and great quantities of spice, then returned to her own land. Prophets and psalms mention Sheba's gold, its incense and its merchants, who traded at Tyre's markets alongside Raamah and Dedan. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies Sheba with Saba in southern Arabia, the Sabaeans of classical writers, in present-day Yemen. Ethiopian tradition instead links the queen with Ethiopia. The location shown here, near modern Addis Ababa, follows the Ethiopian association. Separately, Josh 19:2 uses "Sheba" for a town in Simeon's territory listed with Beersheba, which is probably a different place.

Sheba (son of Raamah) was a son of Raamah and a grandson of Cush, listed with his brother Dedan in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:7) and again in the genealogy of 1 Chr 1:9. Beyond these two genealogical entries, nothing is recorded about him personally. He is usually understood as the ancestor of a people. Easton's Bible Dictionary says his descendants settled with those of Dedan along the Persian Gulf. He should be kept distinct from Seba, his father's brother, named in the same verse, and from other men called Sheba, including the son of Joktan in the line of Shem (Gen 10:28). Which Sheba gave rise to the kingdom whose queen visited Solomon is uncertain. The name has been interpreted in Hitchcock's Bible Names as meaning "oath" or "repose," among other suggestions.

Sheba (son of Joktan) was one of the thirteen sons of Joktan, a descendant of Shem through Eber, named in the table of nations in Gen 10:28 and again in 1 Chr 1:22. He appears only in these lists, with brothers including Ophir, Havilah, Jobab and Abimael, and nothing is told of his life. Many of Joktan's sons are taken as names of peoples or regions in Arabia. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls Sheba probably the founder of the Sabeans, and the STEPBible proper-names index links him with the ancient kingdom of Sheba in southern Arabia, known for its wealth and trade. The name is shared by others, such as a son of Raamah in the line of Ham (Gen 10:7) and a grandson of Abraham through Jokshan (Gen 25:3). Which of these lines the later kingdom of Sheba descends from is uncertain.

Sheba was a son of Jokshan and a grandson of Abraham through Keturah, whom 1 Chr 1:32 calls Abraham's concubine. His brother was Dedan, whose sons Asshurim, Letushim and Leummim are also named (Gen 25:3). The genealogies list him without any further detail. The name Sheba is shared by several people in the Bible, including a descendant of Shem through Joktan (Gen 10:28) and a descendant of Ham through Cush (Gen 10:7). Those two also have a brother or relative named Dedan, which suggests the names stand for related Arabian peoples or tribes. STEPBible Proper Names connects this Sheba with the peoples of southern Arabia, and the name may be linked to the land of Sheba known from the story of its queen. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "oath" or "captivity."

Sheba, son of Bichri, was a Benjamite who led a revolt against King David soon after Absalom's rebellion. 2 Sam 20:21 also calls him a man of the hill country of Ephraim, probably meaning where he lived. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the setting: a dispute had broken out between Judah and the other tribes over bringing the king back. Sheba blew a trumpet and declared, "We have no part in David," and the men of Israel followed him, while Judah stayed loyal. David feared Sheba would do more harm than Absalom and sent Abishai with the royal troops after him. Joab killed Amasa along the way and took part in the pursuit. Sheba took refuge in the fortified town of Abel-beth-maacah. Joab besieged it until a wise woman persuaded the townspeople to cut off Sheba's head and throw it over the wall, which ended the revolt. Several other people in the Bible share the name Sheba.

Sheba was a member of the tribe of Gad, one of seven brothers listed among the leading families of his father's house in 1 Chr 5:13. His brothers were Michael, Meshullam, Jorai, Jachan, Zia and Heber, and his father was Abihail. The surrounding passage places these Gadites in the land of Bashan, east of the Jordan, and says their genealogies were recorded in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel. STEPBible's Tyndale House name index likewise describes him as a Gadite leader in Bashan in Jotham's time. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible bear the name Sheba, and he should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives possible meanings of the name as "captivity," "old man," "repose" or "oath."

Shebaniah was one of the priests who blew trumpets before the ark of God when David brought it up to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:24). He is listed with Jehoshaphat, Nethaneel, Amasai, Zechariah, Benaiah and Eliezer, while Obed-edom and Jehiah served as doorkeepers for the ark. The verse calls him a priest, as do Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, while Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Levite. The surrounding chapter places the event in David's reign, and Smith's Bible Dictionary dates it to about 1043 BC. Nothing more is known of him. The name Shebaniah is shared by several other men in the Old Testament, mainly Levites of Nehemiah's time, and this Shebaniah should be kept distinct from them.

Shebaniah was a Levite in the time of Ezra and Nehemiah, one of several men of that name in the Bible. When the returned exiles gathered for fasting and confession after the reading of the Law, he was among the Levites who stood on the stairs and cried aloud to the LORD (Neh 9:4). He is also named among the Levites who called the people to stand up and bless the LORD their God for ever (Neh 9:5). His name appears again among the Levites who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah to keep God's law (Neh 10:10). Whether all three mentions refer to one man is not certain, though Smith's Bible Dictionary treats them as the same person. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes the name might stand for a Levitical family rather than an individual. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "increased by Jehovah."

Shebaniah was a priest, or the priestly family named after him, in the period after the return from exile in Babylon. As Shechaniah, he appears in the list of priests who came back from captivity with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:3). The surrounding verse, Neh 12:1, identifies the group. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary take Shechaniah and Shebaniah as the same name, and this entry follows that view. A Shebaniah is also among the priests who set their seal to Nehemiah's covenant (Neh 10:4). In the next generation, under the high priest Joiakim, Joseph was head of the priestly house of Shebaniah (Neh 12:14). Since these lists span several generations, the name probably refers to a family line as well as its founder. Several other men in the Bible bear the name, including Levites, and are distinct from this priest.

Shebaniah was one of the men who set their seal to the written covenant in Nehemiah's time, when the community that had returned from exile pledged to keep the law. He appears in Neh 10:12 in a list of names beside Zaccur and Sherebiah. The surrounding passage places this list among the Levites (Neh 10:9–13), and Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe him as a Levite. Easton's Bible Dictionary and STEPBible call him a priest. This entry follows the Levite reading suggested by the context. The name Shebaniah belongs to several people in the Bible, and another Shebaniah appears among the sealers of the same covenant. Beyond his sealing of the covenant, nothing more is known about him.

Shebarim was a place near Ai, mentioned only in Josh 7:5. When Israel's first attack on Ai failed, the men of Ai chased the Israelites from the city gate as far as Shebarim and struck them down on the descent, killing about thirty-six men. The name probably means "breaks" or "ruins." The Revised Version margin renders it "the quarries," and the Greek Septuagint reads it not as a place name but as "until they were broken," meaning until the rout was complete. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the flight would naturally have run from Ai eastward toward the Israelite camp at Gilgal in the Jordan valley, and that no trace of the name has been found. Its exact site is therefore unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement just east of Ai, along the likely line of retreat.

Sheber was a son of Caleb by his concubine Maachah, named in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah together with his brother Tirhanah (1 Chr 2:48). This Caleb is the son of Hezron listed in the same chapter. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him as Caleb ben-Hezron, as distinct from Caleb son of Jephunneh. The following verse names further children of Maachah, including Shaaph, Sheva and a daughter, Achsa. Sheber's half-brothers through Caleb's other wives and concubines include Hur, Haran, Moza and Gazez. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "breaking," and Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "breaking" or "hope."

Shebna was the scribe, or royal secretary, at the court of King Hezekiah of Judah. When the Assyrian officer called the Rabshakeh came to Jerusalem, Shebna went out to meet him with Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder. The three asked him to speak in Aramaic ("the Syrian language"), which they understood, rather than in Hebrew in the hearing of the people on the wall. They returned to Hezekiah with their clothes torn and reported his words. Hezekiah then sent Shebna, Eliakim and the senior priests, dressed in sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah. The same account appears in both 2 Kings and Isaiah. Isa 22:15–25 speaks of a Shebna who was steward of the palace and was to be replaced by Eliakim. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to be the same man, later serving as scribe. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions the view that the scribe was a different person. This entry covers the scribe.

Shebna was a royal official in Jerusalem, described in Isa 22:15 as the treasurer "which is over the house," meaning he was steward of the king's palace. God sends the prophet Isaiah to deliver a message to him. The verses that follow (Isa 22:16–25) rebuke him for cutting out a grand tomb for himself and announce that he will be removed from office and replaced by Eliakim son of Hilkiah. By context this was during the reign of Hezekiah. A Shebna who served as scribe, or secretary, under Hezekiah appears in 2 Kgs 18:18 and Isa 36:3, while Eliakim is there over the household. Some readers take him to be the same man in a lower post, and others take him to be a different person. Several people in the Bible share this name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "who rests himself" or "who is now captive."

Shecaniah was a priest in the time of King David. He headed the family that received the tenth of the twenty-four divisions into which David divided the priests for their turns of service in the sanctuary (1 Chr 24:11). The surrounding chapter describes how these divisions were assigned by lot among the descendants of Eleazar and Ithamar, sons of Aaron. Nothing else is recorded about him personally, and his division is known by his name. The name Shecaniah is borne by several other men in the Old Testament, including priests and Levites of later periods, and this entry concerns only the head of the tenth priestly course. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "habitation of the Lord."

Shecaniah was one of the men who worked under Kore during the reign of Hezekiah, king of Judah, in distributing the offerings brought to the temple. The verse places him with Eden, Miniamin, Jeshua, Shemaiah and Amariah in the cities of the priests. There they handed out portions to their fellow priests and Levites by their divisions, to old and young alike (2 Chr 31:15). The context shows that the overseers named just before belonged to the Levites. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls Shecaniah one of the priests, while the STEPBible names index calls him a Levite. This entry follows the context of tithe distribution under Hezekiah and leaves his exact rank open. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as "habitation of the Lord." Nothing more is recorded about this Shecaniah.

Shechaniah was a member of the royal line of David, in the tribe of Judah. He appears in the list of David's descendants after the Babylonian exile in 1 Chr 3. This entry treats him as a son of Hananiah, whom 1 Chr 3:19 names as a son of Zerubbabel, and as a brother of Pelatiah, Jesaiah, Rephaiah, Arnan and Obadiah. The wording of 1 Chr 3:21 is compressed, though. It can also be read as naming separate family branches without saying how each one connects to Hananiah. Shechaniah's son was Shemaiah, whose sons were Hattush, Igeal, Bariah, Neariah and Shaphat. The verse counts them as six, although only five names appear. The STEPBible proper names index traces his line back to David through Jeconiah. Several other men in the Bible share this name.

Shechaniah was an ancestor named in the list of family heads who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. Ezra 8:3 lists "the sons of Shechaniah, of the sons of Pharosh," naming Zechariah as the leader of the group, with 150 males registered by genealogy with him. The verse is read here as making Shechaniah a descendant of Pharosh (Parosh), so his line formed a branch within that larger clan. The STEPBible Proper Names index (Tyndale House) follows this reading. Some interpreters instead attach "of the sons of Shechaniah" to the end of the previous verse, which would make this Shechaniah a separate family head. Nothing else is recorded about him, and the name was borne by several other men in the Bible. He should not be confused with the Shechaniah mentioned shortly afterward in Ezra 8:5.

Shechaniah is named in the list of family heads who returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra (Ezra 8:5). The verse reads "of the sons of Shechaniah; the son of Jahaziel," and three hundred males travelled with him. The wording is ambiguous. It can be read as a clan called after an ancestor named Shechaniah, led by a son of Jahaziel, or as Shechaniah himself being the son of Jahaziel and leader of the group. Some ancient versions place a clan name, Zattu, before Shechaniah, which supports the second reading. This entry follows the STEPBible Proper Names index, which treats Shechaniah as a descendant of Jahaziel who returned from exile. Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, and it is uncertain whether he is connected with any of them.

Shechaniah, son of Jehiel and one of the descendants of Elam, spoke for the people when Ezra learned that many returned exiles had married foreign wives. He admitted that they had sinned against God by taking wives from the peoples of the land, but he said there was still hope for Israel (Ezra 10:2). The following verses show him proposing a covenant to send those wives away and urging Ezra to act. A Jehiel of the sons of Elam also appears in Ezra 10:26 among the men who had married foreign wives, which may be his father. This entry also treats him as the Shechaniah whose son Shemaiah repaired part of Jerusalem's wall in Nehemiah's time (Neh 3:29). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes that Shechaniah only as Shemaiah's father. Because several men share this name, it is uncertain whether these two passages refer to the same person.

Shechaniah, the son of Arah, was the father-in-law of Tobiah, the Ammonite official who opposed Nehemiah's rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls. Nehemiah notes that many people in Judah were bound by oath to Tobiah because of this marriage tie. Tobiah's son Johanan had also married the daughter of Meshullam son of Berechiah (Neh 6:18). As Easton's Bible Dictionary notes, Shechaniah is known only as Tobiah's father-in-law. The verse does not say outright that Tobiah's wife was Shechaniah's daughter, but "son in law" implies it, and the STEPBible proper names index reads it that way. Shechaniah was probably a man of some standing in Judah, since the link to his family helped Tobiah win support there. His father Arah may belong to the family of Arah listed among the exiles who returned from Babylon, though this is not certain. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shechaniah.

Shechem was a city in the hill country of central Canaan, later in the territory of Ephraim. Abram stopped there at the plain of Moreh on entering Canaan (Gen 12:6), about 1921 BC by inference from context. Jacob camped before the city on returning from Padan-aram, and his daughter was defiled there by Shechem son of Hamor the Hivite (Gen 33:18; 34:2). Joseph's brothers later pastured flocks there. Under Joshua it became a Levitical city of refuge, the site of a covenant assembly, and the burial place of Joseph's bones (Josh 20:7; 24:1, 25, 32). Abimelech was made king there and later fought its men (Judg 9). Rehoboam went there to be crowned, and Jeroboam rebuilt it as his residence (1 Kgs 12:1, 25). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it between Mounts Ebal and Gerizim at modern Nablus, which the location shown here follows.

Shechem (tower) was a fortified place belonging to the city of Shechem, where the people sheltered during Abimelech's attack on the city. After he had taken and destroyed Shechem itself (Judg 9:45), the men of the tower heard what had happened and gathered in the stronghold of the temple of the god Berith, probably the Baal-berith of Judg 9:4. When Abimelech learned of this, he and his followers each cut a branch, piled the branches against the stronghold, and set it on fire, killing about a thousand men and women. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts the tower, with Beth-millo and the temple of El-berith, among the strongest parts of Shechem's defences. Whether it was a citadel inside the city or a separate stronghold nearby is uncertain. The location shown here places it within Shechem, generally identified with Tell Balata near modern Nablus.

Shechem was the son of Hamor the Hivite, the prince of the region around the Canaanite city that shared his name, when Jacob camped there on his return from Padan-aram (Gen 33:18–19). After Shechem took Jacob's daughter Dinah and lay with her, he asked his father to get her for him as a wife, and he offered Jacob's family whatever they asked (Gen 34:2, 34:4, 34:11). Jacob's sons answered deceitfully that the marriage could happen only if every male in the city was circumcised. Shechem and Hamor persuaded the townsmen to agree, and while the men were still recovering, Simeon and Levi killed Hamor and Shechem and took Dinah from Shechem's house (Gen 34:13, 34:24–26). Later passages recall him as the son of Hamor, from whose family Jacob bought land, and the Greek form of his name appears in Acts 7:16 as Sychem (Josh 24:32; Judg 9:28).

Shechem was a son of Gilead in the tribe of Manasseh and the ancestor of the Shechemite clan. Numbers lists him among Gilead's sons, with Abiezer, Asriel, Helek, Hepher and Shemida, each the founder of a family within Manasseh (Num 26:31). When Joshua divided the land, these six clans received their own allotment, west of the Jordan by inference from the passage, apart from the Makirites who held Gilead and Bashan (Josh 17:2). Through Manasseh he belonged to the wider tribe of Joseph. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "back" or "shoulder." He should not be confused with Shechem the son of Hamor in Genesis, who shares the name, or with the city of Shechem, although the clan may have been linked to that region.

Shechem was a man of the tribe of Manasseh, one of the two tribes descended from Joseph, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 7:19. He was a son of Shemida, and his brothers were Ahian, Likhi and Aniam. Other passages such as Num 26:32 and Josh 17:2 present Shemida as a clan head descended from Gilead, so Shechem probably belonged to the Gileadite branch of Manasseh. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a Gileadite. The same passage lists another Shechem, a son of Gilead, which suggests this Shechem was a namesake within the same family line. Several other people in the Bible share the name, and nothing further is recorded about this one. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "back" or "shoulder," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "portion."

Shedeur was a man of the tribe of Reuben, known only as the father of Elizur. Elizur was the leader of Reuben during the wilderness journey after the exodus from Egypt. He was chosen to help Moses with the census (Num 1:5) and served as captain of Reuben's camp, which was stationed on the south side of the tabernacle (Num 2:10). On the fourth day of the dedication of the altar he brought his tribe's offering (Num 7:30, 35), and he led Reuben's host when the camp set out (Num 10:18). Nothing is recorded about Shedeur himself apart from his son. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "darter of light," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "daybreak" while noting a proposed reading, "Shaddai is flame." Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "light of the Almighty."

Sheep Gate was one of the gates of Jerusalem rebuilt under Nehemiah. Eliashib the high priest and his fellow priests rebuilt it, hung its doors and consecrated it, along with the wall as far as the towers of Meah and Hananel (Neh 3:1). Nehemiah's account of the repairs begins and ends at this gate, with goldsmiths and merchants restoring the stretch between the upper corner and the Sheep Gate (Neh 3:32). At the wall's dedication, one procession passed it before halting at the prison gate (Neh 12:39). The name probably reflects sheep being brought through it toward the nearby temple. In John 5:2, the KJV's "sheep market" beside the Pool of Bethesda is rendered "Sheep Gate" in many modern translations. Easton's Bible Dictionary puts it in the eastern wall, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia puts it near the northeast corner. The location shown here places it generally near the temple area.

Shehariah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only once, in the genealogy of Benjamin's descendants that leads up to the family of Saul. He is listed among the sons of Jeroham, together with his brothers Shamsherai, Athaliah, Jaresiah, Eliah and Zichri (1 Chr 8:26–27, by inference from the surrounding list). The genealogy groups these men among the heads of Benjamite families who lived in Jerusalem. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "dawning of the Lord," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "mourning or blackness of the Lord." Smith's also dates him to about 588 BC, but that date is an estimate and the verse itself gives no indication of when he lived.

Shelah was the third son of Judah and his Canaanite wife, the daughter of Shua. He was born at Chezib, after his brothers Er and Onan (Gen 38:5; 1 Chr 2:3). After Er and Onan died, Judah told their widow Tamar to wait until Shelah was grown, fearing that he too would die. When Shelah came of age, however, Judah did not give him to her as a husband (Gen 38:11, 14). Tamar then disguised herself and conceived Pharez and Zerah by Judah himself. Judah later admitted she had been more in the right, because he had withheld Shelah (Gen 38:26). Shelah is listed among Judah's sons in Jacob's family that went to Egypt (Gen 46:12). He became the ancestor of the Shelanites, a clan of Judah (Num 26:20). His descendants included Er, Laadah and linen-working families of the house of Ashbea (1 Chr 4:21), and, in the following verse, Jokim, Joash and Saraph.

Shelemiah was an Israelite named in the list of men who had married foreign wives in Ezra's time and agreed to put them away (Ezra 10:39). The list groups the men by family, and by inference from its arrangement he belonged to the descendants of Bani, whose names run from Ezra 10:34. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also places him among the sons of Bani and notes that 1 Esdras 9:34 calls him Selemias. Nothing else is recorded about him. A second Shelemiah appears a few verses later in the same list (Ezra 10:41), and the name is borne by several other people in the Bible, so he should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "God is my perfection" or "my peace."

Shelemiah was an Israelite in Ezra's time, named in the list of men who had married foreign wives and agreed to put them away (Ezra 10:41). He appears in a group introduced as descendants of Bani. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him as another of the sons of Bani, which reflects the fact that an earlier Shelemiah is named a verse before. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary explains as "repaid by Jehovah," is shared by several men in the Old Testament, and this Shelemiah should not be confused with the others of that name.

Shelemiah was the father of Hananiah, one of the men who repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah's leadership after the return from exile (Neh 3:30). He is known only as his son's father, and nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shelemiah, and there is no clear way to link this one with any of them. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "repaid by the Lord."

Shelemiah was a priest in the time of Nehemiah, one of several people in the Bible with this name. When Nehemiah reorganized the temple storehouses, he appointed Shelemiah as a treasurer over them, together with Zadok the scribe, Pedaiah of the Levites, and Hanan son of Zaccur, son of Mattaniah, as their assistant. Nehemiah chose them because they were considered faithful, and their job was to distribute the stored supplies to their fellow priests and Levites (Neh 13:13). By inference from the surrounding chapter, this was part of Nehemiah's restoration of the tithes that had been neglected during his absence from Jerusalem. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "repaid by Jehovah," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "God is my perfection" or "my peace."

Shelemiah was the son of Cushi and the father of Nethaniah. He is known only from the genealogy of his grandson Jehudi in Jer 36:14. In the reign of Jehoiakim, the princes sent Jehudi to fetch Baruch and the scroll of Jeremiah's prophecies that Baruch had read aloud to the people. Later in the same chapter, Jehudi reads that scroll to the king. Shelemiah himself plays no part in the story. His name serves to identify Jehudi by listing his ancestry back three generations. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "repaid by Jehovah." Several other men in the Bible are also called Shelemiah, and this one should not be confused with them.

Shelemiah son of Abdeel was one of three men whom the king ordered to arrest Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet, together with Jerahmeel the son of Hammelech and Seraiah the son of Azriel (Jer 36:26). The surrounding chapter shows that the king was Jehoiakim and that the order came after the scroll of Jeremiah's prophecies had been read before him and he had burned it. The arrest did not take place, because, as the verse says, "the LORD hid them." Nothing more is recorded about this Shelemiah. The name was borne by several other men in the Bible, and this one is identified only by his father's name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint leaves his name out of this verse. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the episode to about 604 BC.

Shelemiah was the father of Jehucal, also called Jucal, an official in the reign of King Zedekiah of Judah. He is known only through his son. King Zedekiah sent Jehucal with the priest Zephaniah to ask Jeremiah to pray for the people (Jer 37:3). Later Jucal was one of the officials who heard Jeremiah's message to the people (Jer 38:1). By inference from the next verses, those officials pressed the king to have Jeremiah put to death, which is why Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Shelemiah as the father of one of Jeremiah's accusers. The two verses spell his son's name differently, and according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia the Hebrew form of Shelemiah's name also differs slightly between them. Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share his name.

Shelemiah was the son of Hananiah and the father of Irijah, a captain of the guard in Jerusalem in the last years of the kingdom of Judah. He is known only through his son. At the gate of Benjamin, Irijah stopped the prophet Jeremiah, accused him of deserting to the Chaldeans (the Babylonians), and arrested him (Jer 37:13). The verse names Shelemiah only to identify Irijah, and nothing else is said about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him before about 589 BC, a date inferred from the setting during the Babylonian siege. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shelemiah, and there is no clear way to link this one with any of them. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "repaid by Jehovah."

Sheleph was the second of the thirteen sons of Joktan named in the Table of Nations, listed after Almodad and before Hazarmaveth and Jerah (Gen 10:26; 1 Chr 1:20). Through Joktan he belonged to the line of Shem, by way of Eber. His brothers included Sheba, Ophir and Havilah, names that are elsewhere linked with regions of Arabia. The two verses that mention him give only his name and place in the list. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "a drawing forth." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Sheleph is also the name of a Yemenite tribe or district in southern Arabia, known from Sabean inscriptions and Arabian geographers. On that basis he is probably to be understood as the ancestor or namesake of a people living there, as with several of Joktan's other sons.

Shelesh was a man of the tribe of Asher, named once in the Asherite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:35. He is listed with his brothers Zophah, Imna and Amal as a son of Helem, described there as the brother of Shomer. His father is called Hotham in this entry. The two names are probably the same man: 1 Chr 7:32 lists Hotham as a brother of Shomer (spelled Shamer in 1 Chr 7:34), so Helem in verse 35 appears to be another form of Hotham. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia call him a son of Helem, while the STEPBible proper names index joins the two names. The Greek manuscripts spell his name variously, including Seme and Selles. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "captain" or "prince," and Smith's gives "might." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Shelomi was a man of the tribe of Asher, known only as the father of Ahihud. In Num 34:27, Ahihud is named as the prince, or leader, of Asher among the tribal representatives chosen to help divide the land of Canaan among the Israelite tribes. Nothing else is recorded about Shelomi himself. Since his son served in the generation that was about to enter Canaan, Shelomi probably lived during the wilderness period. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him before about 1450 BC, which is an estimate inferred from context. Smith's also gives the meaning of his name as "peaceful."

Shelomith was an Israelite woman of the tribe of Dan, the daughter of Dibri. She is named only as the mother of the man who blasphemed the name of the LORD and cursed during Israel's time in the wilderness, and who was brought to Moses for judgment (Lev 24:11). The surrounding passage says her son's father was an Egyptian (Lev 24:10) and that the son was later stoned outside the camp at the LORD's command (Lev 24:14, 23). Nothing else is recorded about her. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of her name as "peaceful." Several other people in the Bible share the name Shelomith, and this entry refers only to the mother of the blasphemer.

Shelomith was a daughter of Zerubbabel and a member of the tribe of Judah, listed in the royal genealogy descending from David. 1 Chr 3:19 names her as the sister of Meshullam and Hananiah, and she is the only daughter mentioned among Zerubbabel's children. The next verse, 1 Chr 3:20, names further sons: Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah and Jushab-hesed. Matthew's genealogy of Jesus names another son, Abiud (Matt 1:13). Her father is probably the Zerubbabel who led exiles back from Babylon and served as governor of Judah, so Smith's Bible Dictionary dates her to some time after 536 BC. The same dictionary gives the meaning of her name as "peaceful." Nothing more is recorded about her. Several other people in the Bible share the name Shelomith and should not be confused with her.

Shelomith was a Levite of the clan of Gershon, named in 1 Chr 23:9 alongside Haziel and Haran as the three sons of Shimei. The three are described as heads of the fathers' houses of Laadan, one of the Gershonite family lines. The list appears in David's organization of the Levites for service, which suggests that Shelomith's household had a recognized place in that arrangement. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "peaceful" and identifies this Shelomith as a Gershonite. The STEPBible proper-names index notes the variant spelling Shelomoth. Apart from this single genealogical mention, nothing more is recorded. The name is shared by several other people in the Bible, both men and women. They include a daughter of Zerubbabel and a Levite treasurer in David's time, and they should not be confused with this person.

Shelomith was a Levite in King David's reign, descended from Moses' son Eliezer through a line of descendants: Rehabiah, Jeshaiah, Joram, Zichri and then Shelomith, whose father was Zichri (1 Chr 26:25). The parallel listing in 1 Chr 23:15–17 identifies this Eliezer as Moses' son, as Smith's Bible Dictionary also does. Shelomith and his relatives were in charge of the treasuries of dedicated things. These were gifts that David, the heads of families and the army commanders had set apart, mostly from the spoils of war, to maintain the house of the Lord. Earlier dedications were also placed under his care, including those of Samuel the seer, Saul, Abner and Joab (1 Chr 26:26–28). Some sources spell the name Shelomoth. Several other people in the Bible share this name, so this man should not be confused with them.

Shelomith was a daughter of King Rehoboam of Judah and his wife Maachah, the daughter of Absalom. She is named only once, at the end of the list of Maachah's children, after her brothers Abijah, Attai and Ziza (2 Chr 11:20). Her brother Abijah later succeeded Rehoboam as king. The surrounding passage (2 Chr 11:18–19) names Rehoboam's sons by another wife, Mahalath: Jeush, Shamariah and Zaham, who were Shelomith's half-brothers. As a member of the royal household of Judah, she was probably born in Jerusalem, Rehoboam's capital, though the text does not say so. Nothing else is recorded about her. Several other people in the Bible bear the name Shelomith, and they should not be confused with this daughter of Rehoboam.

Shelomith is named in Ezra 8:10 as the ancestor or head of a family whose descendants returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra.
