The verse says that from the sons of Shelomith came the son of Josiphiah, together with 160 males. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Shelomith simply as one whose sons came back with Ezra, and gives the meaning of the name as "peaceful." A different reading is noted in the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, which follows the Greek of 1 Esdras 8:36 in taking the verse as "of the sons of Bani, Shelomith son of Josiphiah." On that reading Shelomith was the leader of the returning group rather than its ancestor. This entry follows the wording of the verse as it stands. Several other people in the Bible share the name, and this Shelomith should not be confused with them.

Shelomoth was a Levite of the family of Izhar, a branch of the Kohathite clan. In 1 Chr 23:18 he is called Shelomith and described as the chief of the sons of Izhar, in the list of Levite families organized under David. In 1 Chr 24:22 he appears as Shelomoth, head of the Izharites, with Jahath named among his sons. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat the two spellings as the same man. This entry follows that view. Exod 6:21 names Korah, Nepheg and Zichri as sons of Izhar but does not mention Shelomith. Because the Chronicles lists are set in David's time, "son of Izhar" there probably means a descendant and family head rather than an immediate son. The same may be true of Jahath. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Shelumiel, son of Zurishaddai, was the leader of the tribe of Simeon during Israel's time in the wilderness after the exodus. He was named as Simeon's representative when Moses took the census (Num 1:6). In the arrangement of the camp, Simeon camped beside Reuben on the south side, with Shelumiel as its captain (Num 2:12). When the tribal leaders brought gifts for the dedication of the altar, he presented Simeon's offering on the fifth day, including animals for peace offerings (Num 7:36, 41). When Israel set out from Sinai, he commanded Simeon's contingent (Num 10:19). The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "friend of God," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "at peace with God." The Greek Old Testament spells the name Salamiel, and the book of Judith traces Judith's ancestry back to him.

Shem was one of the three sons of Noah, born when Noah was five hundred years old and named first beside his brothers Ham and Japheth (Gen 5:32; 6:10). He and his wife entered the ark and survived the flood (Gen 7:13). When Noah later lay drunk and uncovered, Shem and Japheth walked in backward and covered him, and Noah blessed "the LORD God of Shem," making Canaan his servant (Gen 9:23–27). Gen 10:21 calls him the father of all the children of Eber. Its phrase "the elder" can refer to Shem or to Japheth, and Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Shem as the eldest. His sons were Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud and Aram. Arphaxad was born two years after the flood, when Shem was a hundred, and Shem lived five hundred years more (Gen 11:10–11). Luke lists him as "Sem" in Jesus' genealogy (Luke 3:36). The word "Semitic" comes from his name.

Shema was a town in the far south of Judah, listed in Josh 15:26 among the cities of the tribe's southern district, the Negev, between Amam and Moladah. It appears only in this verse. Its name is often taken to mean "hearing" or "obeying" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary treat it as the same place as Sheba. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some link it with Sheba in the list of Simeon's towns (Josh 19:2). It suggests Shema is probably the same as Jeshua, a town resettled after the exile (Neh 11:26). That encyclopedia tentatively identifies the site with Khirbet Sa'wah, a walled ruin on a hilltop between Khirbet Attir and Khirbet el-Milh. The exact location is uncertain, and the location shown here is only approximate, placing it in the Negev east of Beersheba.

Shema was a man of the tribe of Judah, listed in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 2 as one of the four sons of Hebron, along with Korah, Tappuah and Rekem (1 Chr 2:43). He was the father of Raham, who in turn is called the father of Jorkoam (1 Chr 2:44). Hebron here appears within the line of Caleb, and some of the names in this list, including Hebron, Tappuah and possibly Jorkoam, are also place names in Judah. They may therefore stand partly for clans or settlements as well as individuals, though the text presents them as a family line. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "hearing" or "obeying." Several other men in the Bible share the name Shema, and this one is known only from these two verses.

Shema was a man of the tribe of Reuben, named only in a genealogy in 1 Chr 5:8. He was the son of Joel and the father of Azaz, whose son Bela lived in Aroer and held land as far as Nebo and Baal-meon, east of the Jordan. The verse gives his name only as a link in Bela's ancestry and records nothing else about him. Because the genealogy skips generations, he may be the same person as Shemaiah, listed as a descendant of Joel a few verses earlier in 1 Chr 5:4. This is an inference, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connects the name with Shimei, the form found in some Greek manuscripts. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "hearing" or "obeying." Several other people in the Bible share the name, so he should be kept distinct from them.

Shema was a Benjamite, a son of Elpaal, named in the genealogy of Benjamin's descendants. With Beriah he is listed among the heads of the ancestral families living in Aijalon, and the two of them drove out the inhabitants of Gath (1 Chr 8:13). The verse does not say when or how this happened. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both suggest he is probably the same man called Shimhi or Shimei a few verses later in the list (1 Chr 8:21), whose sons are named there. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "hearing" or "obeying." Several other men in the Bible share the name Shema, and this one should not be confused with them.

Shema was one of the men who stood at Ezra the scribe's right hand on the wooden platform when Ezra read the Law aloud to the people gathered in Jerusalem after the return from exile (Neh 8:4). He is named second among the six who stood on Ezra's right, alongside Mattithiah, Anaiah, Urijah, Hilkiah and Maaseiah, while seven others stood on his left. Nothing more is recorded about him, and the text does not say whether he was a priest, a Levite or a lay leader. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel account in 1 Esdras 9:43 calls him Sammus. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the reading to about 458 BC. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shema, which Hitchcock's Bible Names takes to mean "hearing" or "obeying."

Shemaah was a man of Gibeah, called "the Gibeathite," and the father of Ahiezer and Joash. His sons appear at the head of a list of warriors who came over to David (1 Chr 12:3). The surrounding verses show that this list names Benjamites, Saul's own kinsmen, who joined David at Ziklag while he was still in hiding from Saul. Shemaah was therefore probably a Benjamite, which fits Gibeah, Saul's home town in Benjamin. Ahiezer is called the chief of the group. Nothing else is recorded about Shemaah himself. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the meaning of his name as "rumour." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint reads "son" rather than "sons," making him the father of Joash alone. This entry follows the Hebrew text, which names both men as his sons.

Shemaiah was a prophet, called "the man of God," in the reign of Rehoboam king of Judah. When Rehoboam gathered an army to win back the northern tribes that had broken away under Jeroboam, God's word came to Shemaiah. The surrounding verses (1 Kgs 12:23–24) show that he told the king not to fight, and the troops went home. Later, when Shishak king of Egypt invaded Judah, Shemaiah told Rehoboam and the princes gathered in Jerusalem that because they had forsaken the LORD, the LORD had left them in Shishak's hand. After they humbled themselves, he announced that Jerusalem would not be destroyed, though some deliverance only would be granted. Chronicles names "the book of Shemaiah the prophet" as a record of Rehoboam's acts. Several other men in the Bible share this name, which means "the LORD hears" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia).

Shemaiah was a man of the tribe of Judah, the son of Shechaniah, named in the genealogy of David's royal line in 1 Chr 3:22. The surrounding passage traces this line from Solomon through the kings and on to Zerubbabel and his descendants, so Shemaiah probably lived after the Babylonian exile, by inference from his place in the list. He is credited with five named sons: Hattush, Igeal, Bariah, Neariah and Shaphat. The verse totals "six", which may count Shemaiah himself among the sons of Shechaniah, or may reflect a name lost from the list. The verse also names him twice, once as Shechaniah's son and once as father of the five. His name, according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, means "one who hears or obeys the Lord." Several other men in the Bible share this name, and nothing further is recorded about this one.

Shemaiah was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named only in the genealogy of Ziza in 1 Chr 4:37. He was the father of Shimri and an ancestor of Ziza, five generations later, through Shimri, Jedaiah, Allon and Shiphi. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him as a Simeonite. That follows from the context: the list appears among the Simeonite clan leaders in 1 Chr 4:24–43, who are said to have spread to new pasture lands in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah (1 Chr 4:41). Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as "one who hears or obeys the Lord," belongs to several other men in the Bible, and this Shemaiah should not be confused with them.

Shemaiah was a member of the tribe of Reuben, named in the Reubenite genealogy as the son of Joel and the father of Gog (1 Chr 5:4). The list goes on through Gog to Shimei and later descendants. The passage does not give Joel's own parentage, so how this family line connects to Reuben himself is left unstated. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he is the same man called Shema later in the same genealogy (1 Chr 5:8). Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which means "the LORD hears" (Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "that hears or obeys the Lord"), was common in Israel and was borne by many others, especially priests, Levites and prophets. This Shemaiah should not be confused with them.

Shemaiah son of Hasshub was a Levite of the clan of Merari who lived in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. Both lists of Jerusalem's resettled inhabitants trace his line through Hasshub (spelled Hashub in Nehemiah), Azrikam and Hashabiah. 1 Chr 9:14 places him among the sons of Merari, while Neh 11:15 adds the name Bunni to the line. The two passages are generally taken to describe the same man, and this entry treats them that way. He is one of several people in the Bible named Shemaiah, a name meaning "the Lord hears" and borne most often by priests, Levites and prophets, according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Nothing more is recorded about him beyond his ancestry and his place among the Levites settled in Jerusalem.

Shemaiah was a Levite of the family of Jeduthun, the son of Galal and the father of Obadiah. He appears only in genealogies of Levites who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile. 1 Chr 9:16 names him as Obadiah's father. The parallel list in Neh 11:17 gives the same line under slightly different names, "Abda the son of Shammua, the son of Galal, the son of Jeduthun." For this reason Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat Shammua as another form of Shemaiah and Abda as another form of Obadiah. The context in Nehemiah, which places him among the singers led by Mattaniah, suggests that his family served in the temple music. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shemaiah, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes was common among priests, Levites and prophets.

Shemaiah was a Levite in the time of David, the chief of the family descended from Elizaphan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies this as a clan of the Kohathite branch of the Levites, which matches Num 3:30, where Elizaphan leads the Kohathites. Shemaiah led two hundred of his relatives when David organized the Levites to carry the ark of the covenant from the house of Obed-edom up to Jerusalem. David called for him, along with other Levite leaders and the priests Zadok and Abiathar, and told them to prepare themselves for this task. His name means "the LORD hears." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Shemaiah should not be confused with them.

Shemaiah, son of Nethaneel, was a Levite and scribe in the time of King David. According to 1 Chr 24:6, he wrote down the divisions of the priests as they were assigned by lot. This was done in the presence of the king, the princes, Zadok the priest, Ahimelech son of Abiathar, and the heads of the priestly and Levitical families. Households were drawn alternately for the descendants of Eleazar and of Ithamar, Aaron's two surviving sons. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as the scribe who registered the names of the priestly courses. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the event to about 1014 BC, an estimate inferred from context. His name means "the LORD hears." Several other men in the Bible are also called Shemaiah, and this entry refers only to the scribe of 1 Chr 24:6.

Shemaiah was a Levite, the firstborn of the sons of Obed-edom, listed among the gatekeepers in David's reign (1 Chr 26:4). His younger brothers included Jehozabad, Joah, Sacar, Nethaneel, Ammiel, Issachar and Peulthai. His sons were Othni, Rephael, Obed, Elzabad, Elihu and Semachiah. They are described as mighty men of valour who held leading positions in their father's family, and Elzabad's brothers are called strong men (1 Chr 26:6–7). The surrounding chapter organizes the temple gatekeepers into divisions, so Shemaiah's family probably served in that role. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts him among the Korahite Levites, and Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 1014 BC. The name means "the Lord hears" and is shared by several other people in the Bible.

Shemaiah was a Levite in the reign of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. He is named first in a list of nine Levites who, together with the priests Elishama and Jehoram, went out with a group of royal officials (2 Chr 17:8). The surrounding passage, as Easton's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper-names index describe it, shows that this group was sent through the cities of Judah to teach the people from the Book of the Law. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which means "the Lord hears." It was common among priests, Levites and prophets, so this Shemaiah should not be confused with the others. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his service to about 909 BC.

Shemaiah was a Levite of the family of Jeduthun, one of the temple musicians' families, who lived in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He appears in a list of Levites where he is named with Uzziel as representing the sons of Jeduthun, alongside Jehiel and Shimei of the sons of Heman (2 Chr 29:14). By inference from the surrounding passage, these Levites answered Hezekiah's call to consecrate themselves and cleanse the temple in Jerusalem after a period of neglect. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as one of those who helped purify the temple. His name is usually understood to mean "the Lord hears." Several other men in the Bible share the name, many of them priests, Levites or prophets, and this Shemaiah is known only from this one verse.

Shemaiah was a Levite in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He was one of six men named in 2 Chr 31:15 who served in the cities of the priests and assisted Kore, the keeper of the east gate, who was in charge of the freewill offerings (the preceding verse names Kore). Their task was to share out the offerings and holy things to their fellow priests and Levites by their divisions, giving fairly to great and small alike. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Levite appointed to distribute the offerings of the Lord, and Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his service to about 726 BC. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name, meaning "the LORD hears," was common, especially among priests, Levites and prophets, so he should not be confused with the many other men called Shemaiah.

Shemaiah was a Levite in the reign of King Josiah of Judah. He appears only in 2 Chr 35:9, in the account of Josiah's great Passover. There he is named with his brothers Conaniah and Nethaneel, and with Hashabiah, Jeiel and Jozabad, as one of the chiefs of the Levites. Together these leaders gave the Levites five thousand lambs and young goats and five hundred cattle for the Passover offerings. The surrounding chapter places this Passover in Josiah's reign. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates it to about 628 BC, an estimate drawn from context. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint and 1 Esdras call him Samaias. The name means "the Lord hears." Several other men in the Bible share it, many of them priests, Levites or prophets, and nothing beyond this verse is known of this Shemaiah.

Shemaiah was a member of the family of Adonikam who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. Ezra 8:13 names him with Eliphelet and Jeiel as "the last sons of Adonikam." These three led sixty men of the family. The phrase "the last sons" probably means they came later than the earlier group of Adonikam's descendants who returned under Zerubbabel. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name means "the Lord hears," and it is shared by many people in the Bible, especially priests, Levites and prophets, so this Shemaiah should not be confused with the others. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras gives his name as Samaias.

Shemaiah was one of the "chief men" Ezra sent for while his returning company was camped by the river Ahava on the way from Babylon to Jerusalem (Ezra 8:16). He is named in a group with Eliezer, Ariel, Elnathan, Jarib, Nathan, Zechariah and Meshullam. From the surrounding passage, Ezra had found no Levites among the returning people and sent these leaders to Iddo at Casiphia to bring ministers for the temple. Smith's Bible Dictionary therefore describes Shemaiah as one of Ezra's messengers, and Tyndale House's proper-names index counts him as a Levite summoned to join the return. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel account in 1 Esdras gives his name as "Maasmas" or "Samaias." Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name, which means "the Lord hears."

Shemaiah was a priest of the family of Harim who lived in Ezra's time. He is one of several people with this name. Ezra 10:21 lists him among the sons of Harim. In the wider passage, these men are counted among the priests who had married foreign women, and they agreed to send those wives away at Ezra's urging. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both describe him this way. The ISBE adds that the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:21 calls him "Sameus." Harim was one of the priestly families that returned from exile in Babylon. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name means "the Lord hears" (ISBE).

Shemaiah was an Israelite layman of the family of Harim, listed in Ezra 10:31 among the men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra. The surrounding chapter describes how, after returning from exile, these men agreed to send away their foreign wives, and their names were recorded family by family. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 458 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:32 calls him Sabbeus. The name, meaning roughly "the Lord hears," is shared by many people in the Bible, most often priests, Levites and prophets. This Shemaiah is known only from this single mention and should not be confused with the others.

Shemaiah, son of Shechaniah, was one of the people who rebuilt Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah after the return from exile. He repaired a section next to the one done by Zadok son of Immer (Neh 3:29). He is called the keeper of the east gate, which most readers take to mean that Shemaiah himself held this post. The STEPBible Proper Names index describes him as a Levite who repaired the wall near his house. 1 Chr 3:22 also names a Shemaiah son of Shechaniah among the descendants of David. Some connect the two, but whether they are the same man is uncertain. The name was shared by several people in the Bible, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "that hears or obeys the Lord."

Shemaiah, son of Delaiah and grandson of Mehetabeel, was a man in Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time, during the rebuilding of the city wall. He is described as "shut up", which probably means confined to his house, though the reason is not given. When Nehemiah visited him, Shemaiah urged him to meet inside the temple and shut its doors, warning that enemies were coming at night to kill him. The verses that follow (Neh 6:12–13) say Nehemiah saw that God had not sent him, and that Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him to frighten Nehemiah into acting wrongly and so discredit him. For this reason Easton's Bible Dictionary and the Tyndale House proper-names list call him a false prophet. His name means "heard by the Lord" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary. Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Shemaiah was a priest, or the head of a priestly family, in the period after the return from exile in Babylon. He is listed among the priests who came back with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:6). In the time of the high priest Joiakim, the head of the family of Shemaiah was Jehonathan (Neh 12:18), which suggests the name had come to stand for a priestly house. A Shemaiah also appears among the priests who sealed Nehemiah's covenant (Neh 10:8), and the name occurs in the procession at the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt wall (Neh 12:34). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats all of these as one of the priestly courses, and this entry follows that view. Smith's Bible Dictionary instead takes the Shemaiah of Neh 12:34 as a separate person, one of the leaders of Judah. The name means "the LORD hears," and several other people in the Bible share it.

Shemaiah was a descendant of Asaph, the temple musician, and appears only in a family line in Neh 12:35. There he is named as the son of Mattaniah, the father of Jonathan, and the grandfather of Zechariah. Zechariah was one of the priests' sons who played trumpets in the procession at the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt wall under Nehemiah. Shemaiah himself is not described as taking part, so he probably lived a generation or two before that event. Neh 11:22 names a Hashabiah who was also a son of Mattaniah son of Micha, which is probably how this entry identifies him as Shemaiah's brother. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "the LORD hears." Several other people in the Bible share this name.

Shemaiah was one of the musicians who took part in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. He is named first among the 'brethren' of Zechariah son of Jonathan, a group that played the musical instruments of David while Ezra the scribe led their procession (Neh 12:36). The preceding verse, Neh 12:35, identifies Zechariah as a priest's son who played a trumpet. This entry treats Shemaiah as a son of Jonathan and a brother of Zechariah, Azarael, Milalai, Gilalai, Maai, Nethaneel, Judah and Hanani, though 'brethren' can also mean kinsmen or fellow members of a Levitical guild. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes he may stand for a singer or a clan. His name means 'the Lord hears'. Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Shemaiah was one of the men who took part in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time, about 445 BC by inference from context. He is listed in Neh 12:42 among a group of eight who stood with one of the two thanksgiving processions, just before the singers sang loudly under their overseer Jezrahiah. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify him as a priest. The STEPBible proper-names index treats him as a Levite connected with the singing. The verse itself names him only in the list, without giving his family or exact role. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as "that hears or obeys the Lord," belongs to several people in the Bible, including others in Nehemiah, so this Shemaiah should not be assumed to be any of them.

Shemaiah was the father of Urijah, a prophet who spoke in the name of the LORD against Jerusalem and Judah in the same terms as Jeremiah (Jer 26:20). He is mentioned only to identify his son. The phrase "of Kirjathjearim" most naturally describes the family's home town, Kiriath-jearim, west of Jerusalem. The surrounding chapter places Urijah's preaching in the reign of King Jehoiakim, who had him pursued into Egypt and killed, so Shemaiah probably lived in the late 7th century BC. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to before 608 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders as "the LORD hears." It notes that the name was borne most often by priests, Levites and prophets.

Shemaiah the Nehelamite was a prophet among the Jewish exiles in Babylon who opposed Jeremiah. He is one of several men in the Bible with this name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names takes to mean "one who hears or obeys the Lord." "Nehelamite" probably points to his family or home town, though no such place is otherwise known. Jeremiah was told to deliver a message to him (Jer 29:24). The surrounding verses (Jer 29:25–29) say that Shemaiah had sent letters from Babylon to Zephaniah the priest in Jerusalem, urging him to restrain Jeremiah. In response, Jeremiah sent word to all the exiles that the LORD had not sent Shemaiah and that he had led them to trust in a lie. Because he had taught rebellion against the LORD, he and his descendants would be punished. None of his line would remain among the people, and he would not live to see the good the LORD planned for them.

Shemaiah was the father of Delaiah, one of the royal officials ("princes") gathered in the scribe's chamber of the king's house when Baruch's scroll of Jeremiah's prophecies was reported to them (Jer 36:12). The chapter sets this scene in the reign of King Jehoiakim of Judah, so Shemaiah probably lived in the late seventh century BC. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he is known only through his son. Later in the same chapter, Delaiah is one of the officials who urged the king not to burn the scroll (Jer 36:25). The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as "one who hears or obeys the Lord," was common, and several other men in the Bible are called Shemaiah. This entry refers only to Delaiah's father.

Shemariah was one of the warriors who joined David at Ziklag, named in a list of fighting men in 1 Chr 12:5. The surrounding passage describes these men as kinsmen of Saul from the tribe of Benjamin. They came to David while he was still kept away from Saul's court, and they were skilled with bow and sling. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify him as a Benjamite warrior. His name means "whom the LORD guards" or "kept by the LORD." Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shemariah, so he should not be confused with them.

Shemariah was a man of Israel, a member of the family of Harim, who appears in the list of those who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra. Ezra 10:32 names him alongside Benjamin and Malluch. The preceding verse places this group among "the sons of Harim," and the surrounding chapter describes how these men agreed to send away their foreign wives as part of Ezra's reforms after the return from exile. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a layman rather than a priest or Levite. His name means "kept by the LORD" or "whom the LORD guards." Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shemariah, including one of David's warriors and a son of King Rehoboam, and this entry refers only to the man in Ezra's list.

Shemariah was an Israelite in Ezra's time whose name appears in the list of men who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:41). By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was among those who agreed to send these wives away during the reforms led by Ezra after the return from exile in Babylon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places him among the descendants of Bani, the family group whose list begins earlier in the chapter. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and he should not be confused with them. The name means "the Lord guards" or "kept by the Lord."

Shemeber was the king of Zeboiim, one of the cities of the plain near Sodom. He appears only in Gen 14:2, which lists him among five local kings who went to war against Chedorlaomer of Elam and his allies. The surrounding chapter says these kings had served Chedorlaomer for twelve years and rebelled in the thirteenth. The two sides fought in the Vale of Siddim, where the five kings were defeated. Abram later pursued the victors and brought back the captives and goods that had been taken. Shemeber's name is not repeated when the kings are listed again in Gen 14:8, where he is called only the king of Zeboiim. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "soaring on high," and Hitchcock's Bible Names as "name of the strong." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes A. H. Sayce's comparison of the name with the Assyrian name Sumu-abi.

Shemer was the owner of the hill of Samaria in the northern kingdom of Israel. According to 1 Kgs 16:24 he sold the hill for two talents of silver to a king who built a city on it. From the surrounding passage, that king was Omri. The verse says the city was named Samaria after Shemer, the hill's former owner, and it later became the capital of the northern kingdom. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "guardian" or "thorn." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that Shemer may have been an ancient clan name. It also connects the name Samaria with the idea of a "watch mountain," a reading that sits alongside the verse's statement that the city was named after Shemer.

Shemida (also spelled Shemidah) was a son of Gilead in the tribe of Manasseh, son of Joseph. Through Gilead's father Machir, as Num 26:29 traces the line, he was a great-grandson of Manasseh. He was the ancestor of the Shemidaites, one of the clans of Manasseh counted in the census in the plains of Moab (Num 26:32). When the land was divided under Joshua, his descendants were among the Manassite families who received a share of territory, apparently west of the Jordan, alongside the clans of Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem and Hepher (Josh 17:2). 1 Chr 7:19 names his sons as Ahian, Shechem, Likhi and Aniam. One of these sons shares the name Shechem with one of Shemida's brothers. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "name of knowledge," and Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "wise."

Shemiramoth was a Levite musician in David's time. He was one of the Levites of the second rank appointed to accompany the ark of the covenant when it was brought up to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:18). Among the musicians he played the psaltery, a stringed instrument, "on Alamoth," which probably refers to a higher pitch or register (1 Chr 15:20). After the ark was placed in its tent, he was among those Asaph led in ministering before it with psalteries and harps (1 Chr 16:5). Another Levite named Shemiramoth was sent by Jehoshaphat to teach the Law in Judah (2 Chr 17:8). He is a separate person from a later reign, although the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the name as belonging to a Levitical family. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "the height of the heavens."

Shemiramoth was a Levite in the reign of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. He is named in 2 Chr 17:8 among nine Levites who, together with the priests Elishama and Jehoram, were sent out with the king's officials. The surrounding passage (2 Chr 17:7–9) explains the mission. In the third year of his reign Jehoshaphat sent these men through the cities of Judah to teach the people, taking the book of the law of the Lord with them. Nothing else is recorded about him. The same name belongs to a Levite musician in David's time (1 Chr 15:18; 16:5), who is generally treated as a different person, given the gap of more than a century between them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the height of the heavens."

Shemuel son of Ammihud was the leader from the tribe of Simeon chosen to help divide the land of Canaan among the tribes. He appears in a list of tribal leaders whom the LORD named to Moses, one from each tribe. These leaders were to work with Eleazar the priest and Joshua in assigning the territory west of the Jordan (Num 34:20). Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary takes to mean "heard by God," is the same Hebrew name as Samuel. It is shared by several people in the Bible, so this Shemuel should not be confused with the others who bear it. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the appointment to about 1450 BC, an estimate inferred from context.

Shemuel was a son of Tola and a grandson of Issachar, belonging to the tribe of Issachar. He is listed in 1 Chr 7:2 with his brothers Uzzi, Rephaiah, Jeriel, Jahmai and Jibsam as heads of their father's house. The passage calls them valiant men of might, and says their descendants numbered 22,600 in the days of David. The STEPBible Proper Names index describes him as a leader of Issachar during David's reign, though the verse may simply mean the family's numbers were counted then. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "heard by God." The same name belongs to other people in the Bible, and this Shemuel is known only from this one genealogical list.

Shen was a place named only in 1 Sam 7:12, where Samuel set up a memorial stone "between Mizpeh and Shen" and called it Ebenezer after Israel's victory over the Philistines described in the surrounding chapter. The Hebrew reads "the Shen," meaning "the tooth," and Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it was probably a prominent tooth-shaped rock or crag. Its site is unknown. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek translation (the Septuagint) appears to read a different word, and suggests the name may be Jeshanah (as in 2 Chr 13:19), possibly the modern Ain Sinia north of Beitin. The location shown here is only rough. It places Shen northwest of Jerusalem, near Nabi Samwil, one proposed site of Mizpah, rather than following the Jeshanah identification.

Shenazar (spelled Shenazzar in the Revised Version) was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the royal genealogy of 1 Chronicles. He appears in a list of sons that continues from the previous verse, which names the sons of Jeconiah, also called Jehoiachin, the king of Judah taken captive to Babylon. His brothers included Shealtiel, Malchiram, Pedaiah, Jecamiah, Hoshama and Nedabiah. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him as a son of Shealtiel instead, but this entry follows the reading that makes him a son of Jehoiachin. Because his father was deported, he was probably born during the Babylonian exile, as the Tyndale House proper-names list notes. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Shepham was a landmark on the eastern border of the land promised to Israel, as described in Num 34:10–11. The border ran from Hazar-enan to Shepham, then went down from Shepham to Riblah on the east side of Ain, and continued toward the Sea of Chinnereth (Galilee). The site has not been identified. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it between Hazar-enan and a site near Mount Hermon, probably on one of the bare ridges of the Anti-Lebanon range. It explains the name as meaning a "naked" place, and Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "treeless." Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "fruitful" instead. The same encyclopedia suggests that Zabdi the Shiphmite, David's officer over the vineyards, may have come from here. The location shown here is a rough one in northern Lebanon, near the Riblah on the Orontes River, and it reflects the uncertainty about the site.

Shephathiah was a Benjamite named only in a genealogy, as the son of Reuel and the father of Meshullam (1 Chr 9:8). The verse traces the line back one step further, to Reuel's father Ibnijah. He appears in the list of Benjamites who lived in Jerusalem, which the surrounding passage presents as the city's residents after the return from exile in Babylon. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him simply as the father of Meshullam. His son Meshullam is one of the Benjamite heads of families named there. Nothing else is recorded about Shephathiah. His name is spelled a little differently from the more common Shephatiah, borne by several other men in the Old Testament, and he should not be confused with them.

Shephatiah was the fifth son of David, born to him by his wife Abital. He is named only in the two parallel lists of the sons born to David at Hebron, during the years David ruled from that city before moving to Jerusalem. In both lists he comes after Adonijah, the son of Haggith, and before Ithream, the son of Eglah. The surrounding passage states that these sons were born in Hebron (2 Sam 3:5). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his birth to about 1050 BC, an estimate. Nothing further is recorded about his life. Abital appears only as his mother, and no other children of hers are named. His name means "the Lord has judged" or "judged by the Lord." Several other men in the Bible are also called Shephatiah and should not be confused with this son of David.

Shephatiah the Haruphite was one of the warriors who came to David at Ziklag, listed in 1 Chr 12:5. The surrounding passage describes these men as relatives of Saul from the tribe of Benjamin who joined David while he was still kept away from Saul. They were skilled with both bow and sling, able to use either hand. The title "Haruphite" probably refers to his family or hometown, though its exact meaning is uncertain. His name means "the Lord has judged" (Hitchcock's Bible Names; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Bible share the name, and nothing further is recorded about this one. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the event to about 1054 BC, and that date is an estimate.

Shephatiah son of Maachah was the leader of the tribe of Simeon during the reign of David. He appears only once, in a list of the chief officers over the tribes of Israel (1 Chr 27:16), alongside leaders such as Eliezer son of Zichri over Reuben. The list belongs to the Chronicler's account of how David organized his kingdom near the end of his life. Nothing else is recorded about Shephatiah's life or duties. His name means "the LORD has judged" or "the LORD judges," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Hitchcock's Bible Names. Several other men in the Bible share this name, including a son of David and an official in Jeremiah's time. This Shephatiah is distinguished from them by his father, Maachah, and by his role over the Simeonites.

Shephatiah was one of the sons of King Jehoshaphat of Judah, listed with his brothers Azariah, Jehiel, Zechariah, a second Azariah and Michael in 2 Chr 21:2. Their eldest brother Jehoram succeeded Jehoshaphat as king. The verse calls Jehoshaphat "king of Israel," though he ruled the southern kingdom of Judah. The following verses say that Jehoshaphat gave these sons gifts of silver, gold and fortified cities in Judah, and that after Jehoram secured the throne he killed all his brothers with the sword (2 Chr 21:3–4). Shephatiah probably died in that purge in Jerusalem, about 889 BC by inference from context. His name means "the LORD has judged" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Bible share this name.

Shephatiah was the ancestor of a family whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem and Judah. The lists of returnees who came back with Zerubbabel count 372 members of this family (Ezra 2:4; Neh 7:9). A later group of 80 males from the same family, led by Zebadiah son of Michael, travelled with Ezra (Ezra 8:8). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats these as one family that returned in two stages. Nothing is recorded about Shephatiah himself beyond his name, which means "the Lord has judged." Several other people in the Bible share the name, and this family ancestor should not be confused with them.

Shephatiah was an ancestor whose descendants were listed among the families of "Solomon's servants" who returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem and Judah. His name appears in two parallel lists of returnees (Ezra 2:57; Neh 7:59), next to Hattil, Pochereth of Zebaim, and Ami, who is called Amon in Nehemiah. The surrounding passage groups Solomon's servants with the temple servants and gives a combined total of 392 for both groups (Ezra 2:58), so the size of Shephatiah's own family is not stated. The phrase "Solomon's servants" probably refers to descendants of workers who served King Solomon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that 1 Esdras gives his name as Saphat. The name means "the Lord has judged." Several other men in the Bible share this name, and this one is otherwise unknown.

Shephatiah was a man of the tribe of Judah, descended through Perez, named only in the genealogy of Athaiah in Neh 11:4. He was the son of Mahalaleel and the father of Amariah. Through Amariah he was an ancestor of Athaiah, one of the men of Judah who lived in Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah, after the return from the Babylonian exile. Nothing else is recorded about his life, and when he lived can only be placed some generations before Nehemiah's day, by inference from the length of the family line. His name means "the Lord has judged" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Bible share this name, and this Shephatiah is not clearly linked to any of them.

Shephatiah son of Mattan was an official in Jerusalem during the reign of King Zedekiah, shortly before the city fell to Babylon. He appears in Jer 38:1 with Gedaliah son of Pashur, Jucal son of Shelemiah and Pashur son of Malchiah, a group who heard Jeremiah telling the people to surrender to the Chaldeans. In the verses that follow, these men urged the king to put the prophet to death, and Jeremiah was let down into a cistern. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both describe Shephatiah as one of the princes who opposed Jeremiah this way. His name means "the Lord has judged." Several other men in the Old Testament share the name, and nothing further is known about this one.

Shephelah is a Hebrew name meaning "lowland." It refers to the region of low, rolling hills between the Judean mountains to the east and the coastal plain to the west. The King James Version translates it variously as "vale," "low plains" and "low country." The sycamore-fig trees that grew there in abundance became a byword for plenty, and Solomon was said to make cedars as common as those trees (1 Kgs 10:27; 2 Chr 1:15). David appointed an overseer for its olive and sycamore trees (1 Chr 27:28), and Uzziah kept herds there (2 Chr 26:10). Under Ahaz the Philistines invaded its towns, including Beth-shemesh, Aijalon, Socho and Timnah (2 Chr 28:18). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes hills of soft limestone, usually 500 to 800 feet high, crossed by valleys that gave access from the plain. It notes debate over whether the Philistine plain was included. The location shown here marks the general region.

Shepho was a son of Shobal and a descendant of Seir the Horite, listed with his brothers Alvan, Manahath, Ebal and Onam among the inhabitants of the land of Seir (Gen 36:23). The parallel genealogy in 1 Chr 1:40 spells his name Shephi and gives Alvan as Alian. The surrounding passage in Genesis 36 traces the Horite clans who lived in Seir, later Edom, before and alongside Esau's descendants. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a Horite chief. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "bareness," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "desert." Nothing more is recorded about him beyond his place in these lists.

Sherah (also spelled Sheerah) was a woman of the tribe of Ephraim, one of the Joseph tribes. She is remembered in 1 Chr 7:24 for building Lower and Upper Beth-horon and a town named after her, Uzzen-sherah. This is unusual, because the Bible rarely credits a woman with founding towns. The verse calls her "his daughter," and the surrounding passage leaves unclear whether "his" means Ephraim or his son Beriah. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes her as Ephraim's daughter. The STEPBible name index treats her as his granddaughter through Beriah, and this entry follows that view. On that reading, Rephah and Resheph, named in the following verse, were her brothers. The two Beth-horons are generally identified with the modern villages of Beit Ur et-Tahta and Beit Ur al-Fauqa, northwest of Jerusalem. The location of Uzzen-sherah is unknown.

Sherebiah was a Levite of the period after the exile who came to Jerusalem with Ezra. When Ezra asked for Levites to join his group at the river Ahava, Sherebiah was brought, along with his sons and relatives, eighteen men in all (Ezra 8:18). Ezra then set him apart with Hashabiah and others to carry the silver, gold and vessels given for the temple (Ezra 8:24). Later, in Nehemiah's time, he was among the Levites who helped the people understand the law as Ezra read it (Neh 8:7), and he stood with other Levites to lead the people in confession and praise (Neh 9:4–5). Smith's Bible Dictionary adds that he signed the covenant (Neh 10:12). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name may also refer to a Levite family, since it recurs in later lists. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "singing with the Lord."

Sherebiah was a Levite in the time of Nehemiah. He appears among the Levites who put their seal to the covenant to keep God's law (Neh 10:12, read with the surrounding list of Levites). He is also listed among the chief Levites who led praise and thanksgiving in alternating groups, following the arrangement attributed to David (Neh 12:24). Nehemiah 12:8 names a Sherebiah among the Levites connected with the thanksgiving. The context of that list ties it to those who returned from exile with Zerubbabel, so it may refer to an earlier man or to a family name carried by later Levites. Because several Bible figures share this name, how these mentions relate is uncertain. This entry follows the STEPBible Proper Names index in treating them as one Levite who sealed the covenant and led worship. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "singing with the Lord."

Sheresh was a man of the tribe of Manasseh, one of the tribes descended from Joseph. He is named only once, in the genealogy of Manasseh at 1 Chr 7:16. He was a son of Machir, Manasseh's son, and Machir's wife Maachah, and a brother of Peresh. The verse goes on to say "his sons were Ulam and Rakem." The wording could refer either to Sheresh or to Peresh, but this entry follows the reading that makes Ulam and Rakem the sons of Sheresh. Gilead and Hammoleketh, named elsewhere in the same chapter, are listed here among Machir's children and so as Sheresh's siblings. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "root." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Sherezer (also spelled Sharezer) was a man sent, together with Regemmelech and their men, to the house of God to pray before the Lord (Zech 7:2). The following verse shows that the delegation also asked the priests and prophets whether they should keep mourning and fasting in the fifth month, as they had done for many years (Zech 7:3). By inference from Zech 7:1, this took place in the fourth year of Darius, after the return from exile. Who sent him is unclear. The King James wording leaves the senders unnamed, and Easton's Bible Dictionary describes them as the exiles. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reads the Hebrew as saying that the people of Bethel sent him, and notes that the text is difficult. It also links the name to an Assyrian phrase meaning "protect the king," while Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "prince of fire." He is a different person from Sennacherib's son of the same name.

Sheshai was one of the three sons of Anak, named with his brothers Ahiman and Talmai, who lived at Hebron when Moses sent spies into Canaan (Num 13:22). The Anakim were remembered as people of great size, which is why some reference works call Sheshai a giant. Joshua 15:14 says Caleb drove the three sons of Anak out of Hebron. Judges 1:10 reports that the tribe of Judah attacked the Canaanites of Hebron, formerly called Kirjath-arba, and killed Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai. The two accounts are usually read as describing the same conquest, with Caleb leading Judah's forces. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may have belonged to an old Hebron clan rather than a single person. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "noble," while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "six," "mercy" or "flax."

Sheshan was a man of the tribe of Judah, the son of Ishi and a descendant of Appaim in the Jerahmeelite clan of the genealogy in 1 Chronicles 2. The text says he had no sons, only daughters, and that he gave one of his daughters as wife to his Egyptian servant Jarha. She bore Attai, through whom Sheshan's line is traced for several generations. The same chapter also names Ahlai as Sheshan's child. Because Sheshan had no sons, Ahlai is probably a daughter, perhaps the one who married Jarha, though the text does not say so directly. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify him as a descendant of Jerahmeel son of Hezron. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "lily" or "joy."

Shethar was one of the seven princes of Persia and Media at the court of King Ahasuerus, named in Esth 1:14 alongside Carshena, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena and Memucan. These men "saw the king's face," meaning they had direct access to him, and they held the highest rank in the kingdom. In the surrounding passage the king consults this group of advisers about Queen Vashti's refusal to appear before him, though Shethar himself is not singled out. His name is probably Persian. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give its meaning as "a star," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it has never been satisfactorily explained. Smith's dates him to about 483 BC. That date is an estimate based on the setting of the story in the third year of Ahasuerus's reign, usually identified with Xerxes I. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Shethar-boznai was a Persian official in the province west of the Euphrates ("beyond the river") who, with the governor Tatnai and their associates, challenged the Jews rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem. They asked who had authorized the building and its walls (Ezra 5:3). They then sent a letter to King Darius, joined by companions called the Apharsachites (Ezra 5:6). Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies this king as Darius Hystaspes (Darius I). Darius answered by ordering them to keep away from the work and leave the builders alone (Ezra 6:6). Shethar-boznai and the others promptly carried out the king's instructions (Ezra 6:13). He appears only alongside Tatnai, and his exact office is not stated, though the order of names suggests he ranked below the governor. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his Persian name as "star of splendour."

Sheva was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2. He was a son of Caleb and Caleb's concubine Maachah, whose other sons, Sheber and Tirhanah, appear in 1 Chr 2:48. Shaaph was another of her sons. Sheva is called "the father of Machbenah" and probably also "the father of Gibea" (1 Chr 2:49). In these genealogies "father" often means the founder or leading figure of a settlement, so Machbenah and Gibea were probably towns in Judah. Their sites are unknown. The same verse names Achsah as Caleb's daughter, which links this Caleb with the Caleb whose daughter Achsah appears in the conquest accounts. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "Jehovah contends." This Sheva is a different man from Sheva, David's scribe, in 2 Sam 20:25. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Shibah is the name Isaac gave to a well his servants dug at the place that came to be called Beersheba. The King James Version spells it "Shebah." According to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, the Hebrew word means "seven," and the Greek translation renders it "oath" (one edition reads "well of oath"). That encyclopedia treats Shibah as the name of the original well of Beersheba. The narrative explains that the city's name, Beersheba ("well of the oath" or "well of seven"), comes from this naming (Gen 26:33). In the surrounding passage, the servants report finding water on the same day Isaac made a sworn agreement with Abimelech, which probably accounts for the name. An earlier account (Gen 21:31) links the name Beersheba to an oath between Abraham and Abimelech. The location shown here is at ancient Beersheba, probably Tel Beer Sheva in southern Israel.

Shihor (spelled Sihor in the King James Version) is a body of water named in connection with Egypt. Josh 13:3 uses it as the southwestern starting point of the unconquered Philistine territory, describing it as lying "before Egypt." Isa 23:3, in an oracle about Tyre, speaks of "the seed of Sihor, the harvest of the river" as Tyre's revenue, probably meaning Egyptian grain shipped by sea. Identifications differ. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Shihor in Isaiah (and Jer 2:18) as the Nile, and in Joshua as the "river of Egypt," the Wadi el-Arish. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, following Naville, identifies it with an ancient eastern Nile canal called Shi-t-Hor, "the stream of Horus." The STEPBible proper names list treats it as the Brook of Egypt, marking the southwestern boundary of the Promised Land. The location shown here follows the Wadi el-Arish identification in northern Sinai.

Shihor-libnath was a landmark named on the boundary of the territory of the tribe of Asher, apparently marking with Carmel its western limit (Josh 19:26). It is mentioned only once, and its exact identity is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take it as a river, probably the Nahr ez-Zerqa, the modern Nahal Tanninim ("crocodile river"), which flows from the Carmel range into the Mediterranean just north of Caesarea. The ISBE suggests the name "Shihor" echoes the name of the Nile, perhaps because both streams held crocodiles. Smith's Bible Dictionary instead suggests a small stream south of Athlit, while the Syriac Peshitta and Eusebius treated the name as two separate towns. The location shown here follows the Nahal Tanninim identification.

Shikkeron (spelled Shicron in the King James Version) was a place on the northern border of the territory of Judah. It is mentioned only once, in the boundary description of Josh 15:11. That line ran from the side of Ekron northward to Shikkeron, then passed along to Mount Baalah and on to Jabneel before ending at the Mediterranean Sea. Shikkeron therefore lay in the low country west of the hills, between Ekron and Mount Baalah. The exact site is unknown. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes C. Hauser's suggestion of Tell es-Sellakeh, northwest of the village of Aqir. On that view the boundary would follow a natural course over the ridge to Jabneel. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the general area of Ekron.

Shilhi was the father of Azubah, the mother of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. He is mentioned only in the two parallel notices of Jehoshaphat's accession, which give the king's age as thirty-five and his reign as twenty-five years in Jerusalem (1 Kgs 22:42; 2 Chr 20:31). Since Jehoshaphat was the son of King Asa, Azubah was presumably Asa's wife, which made Shilhi the maternal grandfather of Jehoshaphat. Jehoshaphat appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, which links Shilhi to that line through his daughter. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "armed." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a suggestion that "Shilhi" may be a form of Shilhim, a town in Judah (Josh 15:32), and so could name Azubah's birthplace instead of her father. This entry follows the usual reading of Shilhi as a personal name.

Shilhim was a city in the far south of the territory given to the tribe of Judah. It appears once, in the list of southern towns in Josh 15:32, near Lebaoth, Ain and Rimmon. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "aqueducts," while Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "fountains." Easton's identifies it with Sharuhen, which appears in the parallel list of Simeon's towns in Josh 19:6, and with Shaaraim in 1 Chr 4:31. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that Azubah, mother of King Jehoshaphat and called "the daughter of Shilhi" (1 Kgs 22:42), may have come from this town. The location shown here follows the Sharuhen identification and corresponds to Tell el-Far'ah (South), on the Wadi Ghazzeh southeast of Gaza. That site is the one most often linked with Sharuhen, though the identification remains uncertain.

Shillem was the fourth-named son of Naphtali, one of the sons of Jacob, and so a grandson of Jacob through Bilhah, Rachel's servant. He appears in the list of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt, alongside his brothers Jahzeel, Guni and Jezer (Gen 46:24). In the census taken in the wilderness he is named as the ancestor of the Shillemites, one of the clans of the tribe of Naphtali (Num 26:49). The genealogy in 1 Chr 7:13 lists the same four brothers but gives his name as Shallum, a variant form of the same name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as the youngest son of Naphtali, probably from his place at the end of each list. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "requital" or "retribution." Nothing more is recorded about him.

Shiloah was a gently flowing water supply at Jerusalem, mentioned once in the Bible. In Isa 8:6 the prophet uses "the waters of Shiloah that go softly" as an image of the quiet security God offered Judah. He contrasts it with the people's delight in Rezin, king of Syria, and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies Shiloah with the stream later called Siloam, fed by Jerusalem's only perennial spring, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also treats the two names as the same place. On that view the waters were probably those running from the Gihon Spring along the southeastern hill of ancient Jerusalem toward the Pool of Siloam. The location shown here is in that area, in the old City of David south of the Temple Mount. The exact channel Isaiah had in mind is uncertain.

Shiloh was a city in the hill country of Ephraim where Israel set up the tabernacle after the conquest (Josh 18:1). There Joshua and Eleazar the priest divided the land among the tribes by lot (Josh 18:10; 19:51). The house of God stayed there through the time of the judges. It drew yearly pilgrims and held a feast at which the daughters of Shiloh danced (Judg 18:31; 21:19–21; 1 Sam 1:3). Eli and his sons served there as priests, Hannah brought the young Samuel there, and the LORD revealed himself to Samuel there (1 Sam 1:24; 3:21). The ark was taken from Shiloh into battle and lost to the Philistines (1 Sam 4:3–4). Jeremiah later pointed to Shiloh's fate as a warning to Jerusalem (Jer 7:12; 26:6). Judg 21:19 places it north of Bethel, east of the Bethel–Shechem road. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with modern Seilun, the site shown here.

Shiloni is named in the King James Version as the father of Zechariah and the earliest ancestor in the family line of Maaseiah son of Baruch. Maaseiah was one of the men of Judah who settled in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon, in Nehemiah's time (Neh 11:5). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the word as a clan name, "the Shilonite," rather than a personal name, meaning a descendant of Shelah, son of Judah. The STEPBible proper-names index likewise describes the Shilonites as descendants of Judah living in Jerusalem after the exile. The parallel list of Jerusalem's settlers in 1 Chr 9:5 speaks of "the Shilonites," which fits this reading. This entry treats Shiloni as a male ancestor while noting that the name may be a family designation. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Shilshah was a man of the tribe of Asher, named once in the Bible as one of the sons of Zophah in the genealogy of Asher's descendants (1 Chr 7:37). He appears in a list of brothers that includes Suah, Harnepher, Beri, Imrah, Bezer, Hod, Shamma and Beera. The surrounding verses trace Zophah's line back through Helem and Heber to Asher. Nothing else is recorded about Shilshah's life or deeds. The Greek manuscripts spell his name differently, for example Saleisa in Codex Vaticanus and Codex Alexandrinus, according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "strong," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "three," "chief" or "captain."

Shimea was a Levite of the family of Merari, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 6:30. He was the son of Uzza and the father of Haggiah, and his grandson was Asaiah. The surrounding list (1 Chr 6:29) traces this line from Merari through Mahli, Libni, Shimei and Uzza, so Shimea sits in the middle of a chain of descendants, which Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both describe as Merarite. Nothing else is recorded about his life. STEPBible's proper-names index places him in the time of King David, probably by inference from the later Asaiah who led the Merarites when the ark was brought to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:6), if that is the same man. The name is shared by several other people in the Bible, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links it with the related forms Shammua and Shammah.

Shimea was a Levite named in the family line of Asaph, the singer who stood at the right hand of Heman in the temple music arranged under David. In 1 Chr 6:39 he is the father of Berachiah and so Asaph's grandfather. The genealogy goes on to name his father as Michael, and it traces the line back to Gershom son of Levi, so Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe Shimea as a Gershonite Levite. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several people in the Bible share this name, and this entry covers only the ancestor of Asaph.

Shimeah was a Benjamite, the son of Mikloth, named in the genealogy of the family of Gibeon in 1 Chronicles 8. The verse records that Mikloth fathered Shimeah and that these relatives lived in Jerusalem alongside their kinsmen (1 Chr 8:32). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a descendant of Gibeon, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia as a descendant of Jehiel, the "father" or founder of Gibeon. The parallel genealogy in 1 Chr 9:38 gives his name as Shimeam. According to the STEPBible proper names index he was a nephew of Ner, who appears in the same family list. Nothing else is recorded about him, and his dates are unknown, though Smith's Bible Dictionary tentatively places him around 536 BC. Hitchcock's Bible Names suggests the name means "that hears" or "obeys."

Shimeath was the parent of Jozachar, also called Zabad, one of the two royal servants who conspired against King Joash of Judah and killed him. 2 Kgs 12:21 names the killer simply as "Jozachar the son of Shimeath." The parallel account in 2 Chr 24:26 calls him "Zabad the son of Shimeath an Ammonitess," describing Shimeath as a woman from Ammon. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Tyndale House's proper-names list follow Chronicles and identify Shimeath as his mother. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name in Kings reads as masculine, which makes Shimeath the father there, and suggests that the writer of Chronicles took the name's final letter as a feminine ending. This entry lists Shimeath as male. Nothing else is recorded about Shimeath.

Shimei was a Levite musician, a son of Jeduthun (also identified with Ethan), one of David's chief temple singers. When the singers were divided by lot into twenty-four courses of service, the tenth lot fell to Shimei, who led a group of twelve made up of himself, his sons and his relatives (1 Chr 25:17). Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as chief of the tenth division of the singers. His brothers were Gedaliah, Izri (Zeri), Jeshaiah, Hashabiah and Mattithiah. The Hebrew list of Jeduthun's sons in 1 Chr 25:3 gives the total as six but names only five, so Shimei is probably the missing sixth. The sons linked with him here match the sons of Obed-edom in 1 Chr 26:4–5, and Obed-edom is called a son of Jeduthun in 1 Chr 16:38, so this entry connects Shimei with that family. The connection is uncertain. Several other men in the Bible share his name.

Shimei son of Gera was a Benjamite from Bahurim and a member of Saul's family. When David fled Jerusalem during Absalom's rebellion, Shimei followed him along a hillside, cursing him as a "bloody man" and throwing stones and dust. After Absalom's defeat he hurried down with the men of Judah and fell before David as the king crossed the Jordan. Abishai urged that he be executed, but David swore not to kill him. Near death, David reminded Solomon of Shimei's curse (1 Kgs 2:8). Solomon ordered Shimei to build a house in Jerusalem and never leave it, on pain of death, and Shimei agreed. Three years later he went to Achish at Gath to bring back two runaway servants. Solomon summoned him, charged him with breaking his oath and with his wrongs against David, and had him executed, by Benaiah according to 1 Kgs 2:46. Several other men in the Bible share this name.

Shimei, son of Elah, was an official of David and Solomon. He is one of several men in the Bible with this name. When Adonijah tried to claim David's throne, Shimei was among those who did not side with him, along with Zadok the priest, Benaiah, Nathan the prophet, Rei and David's mighty men (1 Kgs 1:8). A Shimei son of Elah later appears among Solomon's twelve district officers, who supplied food for the king and his household. His district was the territory of Benjamin (1 Kgs 4:18). This entry treats the two mentions as the same man, following Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. The latter suggests that Solomon appointed him because of his loyalty. Smith's Bible Dictionary lists the two separately. The Jewish historian Josephus calls him "the friend of David."

Shimei was a son of Pedaiah and a brother of Zerubbabel, listed in the genealogy of David's royal descendants in 1 Chr 3:19. He belonged to the tribe of Judah. Pedaiah is named in the same genealogy as a son of King Jeconiah (Jehoiachin), so Shimei was a grandson of that king. Several other men in the Bible share his name. Nothing further is recorded of him, and no descendants are listed for him, while the verse goes straight on to name Zerubbabel's children. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 536 BC, the period of the return from exile, which fits his being Zerubbabel's brother. The name is usually taken to mean "renowned" or "one who hears."

Shimei was a man of the tribe of Simeon, the son of Zacchur and a descendant of Simeon through Mishma (1 Chr 4:26). Mishma himself appears in the preceding verse as a descendant of Simeon's son Shaul. Shimei is noted for having an unusually large family of sixteen sons and six daughters. The text contrasts this with his relatives, who had few children, so that the clan as a whole did not grow as large as the tribe of Judah (1 Chr 4:27). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places him in the time of David. It links his many descendants to the Simeonite expansion described later in the same chapter, into Gerar and Mount Seir in Hezekiah's day. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shimei, which possibly means "hear me."

Shimei was a Reubenite named in the genealogy of the tribe of Reuben in 1 Chr 5:4. He was the son of Gog and belonged to the line descended from Joel. The next verse, 1 Chr 5:5, names his son Micah. The list continues down to Beerah, a Reubenite leader whom the Assyrian king Tilgath-pilneser carried into exile. Joel's exact connection to Reuben is not spelled out, but the surrounding passage concerns Reuben's descendants, and Easton's and Smith's Bible dictionaries both identify Shimei as a Reubenite. Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shimei and should not be confused with him. Hitchcock's Bible Names explains the name as meaning "that hears" or "my fame."

Shimei was a Levite of the clan of Merari, named only in the genealogy of the Levites in 1 Chr 6:29. In that list he is the son of Libni and the father of Uzza. Here Libni appears as the son of Mahli, Merari's son, so Shimei belongs to the line descending from Merari through Mahli. This Libni is apparently distinct from the better-known Libni who was a son of Gershon, another of Levi's sons. The verse records nothing about Shimei beyond his place in this line of descent. The name Shimei is shared by several men in the Bible, including other Levites, so he should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "that hears or obeys" or "my reputation."

Shimei the Ramathite was the official in charge of King David's vineyards, according to the list of royal stewards in 1 Chr 27:27. The same verse names Zabdi the Shiphmite as the man responsible for the produce of the vineyards stored in the wine cellars, so Shimei probably oversaw the vines themselves while Zabdi handled the wine. "Ramathite" probably means he came from a place called Ramah, as the Tyndale House STEPBible names list takes it. Several towns bore that name, so his hometown is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts him as a man of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with the other men named Shimei in the Bible, a common name probably meaning "hear me" or "heard."

Shimei was a Levite descended from Heman, one of the temple singers' families. He is named with Jehiel as representing the sons of Heman among the Levites who gathered to purify the temple (2 Chr 29:14). From the surrounding chapter, this took place at the start of King Hezekiah's reign, when the king ordered the Levites to sanctify themselves and clear the temple of what had defiled it. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the event to about 726 BC, an estimate based on context. The same passage lists Shemaiah and Uzziel for the sons of Jeduthun, another musical family. Nothing else is recorded about this Shimei. The name was common, and several other men in the Bible are called Shimei. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "that hears or obeys" or "my fame."

Shimei was a Levite in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah and the brother of Cononiah. When Hezekiah restored temple worship, the people brought in offerings, tithes and dedicated things, which were stored in chambers at the temple. Cononiah was put in charge of these contributions, and Shimei ranked next under him (2 Chr 31:12). Ten other Levites, including Jehiel, Azaziah and Benaiah, served as overseers under the two brothers. They were appointed at the command of Hezekiah and of Azariah, the ruler of the house of God (2 Chr 31:13). Shimei is a common name in the Bible, and Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he may be the same as the Levite Shimei of Heman's family listed just before this passage, though this is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "that hears" or "my fame."

Shimei was a Levite in the time of Ezra, named among those who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:23). He appears in the list of men found to have taken wives from the surrounding peoples after the return from exile in Babylon. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was one of those who agreed to send these wives away, as the STEPBible Proper Names index also states. He is listed with other Levites, including Jozabad, Kelaiah (also called Kelita), Pethahiah, Judah and Eliezer. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Shimei is shared by several other men in the Bible, and this one should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "that hears or obeys" or "my fame."

Shimei was one of the descendants of Hashum listed in Ezra 10:33 among the Israelite men who had married foreign wives. Context shows that these men agreed, at Ezra's call after the return from Babylonian exile, to send those wives away. He appears in the list alongside Mattenai, Mattathah, Zabad, Eliphelet, Jeremai and Manasseh, all of the same family. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him the same way, as one of the family of Hashum who put away his foreign wife at Ezra's command. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Shimei was common and is borne by several other people in the Bible, including others in the same list in Ezra 10. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "that hears or obeys" or "my fame."

Shimei was one of the Israelites named in Ezra 10:38 in the list of men who had married foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon. By inference from the surrounding passage, he was among those who agreed, under Ezra's reforms, to send these wives away. The list groups the men by family, and his name falls in the section headed "of the sons of Bani" (Ezra 10:34). For that reason Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a son of Bani, meaning a member of that family line. It dates the event to about 459 BC, an estimate drawn from context. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Shimei should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "that hears or obeys" or "my fame."

Shimei was a Benjamite named in the family line of Mordecai, the Jew living at the Persian palace in Shushan (Susa). Esth 2:5 traces Mordecai as "the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish," so Shimei was Mordecai's grandfather, or possibly a more distant ancestor. Nothing else is recorded about him. Readers differ on how to take the list. Some treat it as a straight run of generations. Others think it names famous forebears of the tribe, linking Kish with Saul's father and Shimei with the Benjamite Shimei son of Gera, who cursed David. This entry treats him simply as the Shimei of Esther 2:5. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may mean "hear me (God)," and notes that it is shared by many people in the Old Testament.

Shimei, also spelled Shimi, was a son of Gershon and grandson of Levi. The genealogies of the tribe of Levi list him with his brother Libni (Exod 6:17; Num 3:18; 1 Chr 6:17). In 1 Chr 23:7 his brother is named Laadan, apparently another name for Libni or for the same family line. His sons Jahath, Zina, Jeush and Beriah headed divisions of the Gershonite Levites in David's time. Zina appears as Zizah in the following verse. 1 Chr 23:9 also names a Shimei whose sons were heads of Laadan's houses. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes that Shimei to be a copying error for one of Laadan's sons. His descendants formed a Levitical clan, and Zech 12:13 names "the family of Shimei" among the households that mourn apart. Several other men in the Bible share this name.

Shimei was a Levite of the family of Gershon, named once in the ancestry of Asaph, one of the singers David put in charge of music at the house of the Lord (1 Chr 6:39–43). He was the father of Zimmah, and through him an ancestor of Ethan and, several generations later, of Asaph. This entry names his father as Laadan, a Gershonite whose family appears in 1 Chr 23:7–9. The verse that follows in the genealogy (1 Chr 6:43) calls him the son of Jahath, son of Gershom, and Smith's Bible Dictionary follows that reading. Because the names Shimei and Jahath recur among the Gershonite families, the exact relationship is uncertain. Several other men in the Bible share this name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "that hears or obeys" or "my fame."

Shimeon was an Israelite of the family of Harim. He is named in the list of men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra (Ezra 10:31). In the surrounding passage these men agreed to send away their foreign wives after Ezra's reforms in Jerusalem. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 458 BC, a date inferred from context. Shimeon is a laymen's name, not a priest's, since the sons of Harim listed here come after the priests and Levites in the chapter. The name is a form of Simeon and is usually taken to mean "hearing" or "hearkening" (Easton's Bible Dictionary). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:32 gives him as "Simon Chosameus." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Shimhi was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. The verses there list nine sons: Jakim, Zichri, Zabdi, Eliel, Zilthai, Elienai, Adaiah, Beraiah and Shimrath. These families appear to have been counted among the Benjamites living in Jerusalem. In Hebrew his name is the same as Shimei, a common name meaning "famous" or "renowned" according to Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he is the same man as Shema, a son of Elpaal mentioned a few verses earlier in the same chapter. Because several men in this genealogy bear similar names, his exact place in the family line is uncertain. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Shimon was a man named in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chronicles, where his four sons are listed as Amnon, Rinnah, Ben-hanan and Tilon (1 Chr 4:20). Nothing else is recorded about him, and the passage does not say how he connects to the surrounding family lines. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls this an obscure genealogy of Judah.
