STEPBible's proper-name index (Tyndale House) places him among the descendants of Judah through Caleb. Smith's gives the name's meaning as "desert," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "providing well" or "fatness." He should not be confused with Simeon, the son of Jacob, whose name is similar.

Shimrath was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only in the genealogy of Benjamin's descendants in 1 Chr 8:21. He was a son of Shimhi, also spelled Shimei, and the last of nine sons listed. His brothers were Jakim, Zichri, Zabdi, Elienai, Zilthai, Eliel, Adaiah and Beraiah. The STEPBible Proper Names index connects his father with Shimei, son of Elpaal. Nothing else is recorded about his life. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "guard", while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "hearing" or "obedient".

Shimri was a man of the tribe of Simeon, the son of Shemaiah and the father of Jedaiah. He appears only once, in the genealogy of Ziza in 1 Chr 4:37. That list traces Ziza back through Shiphi, Allon and Jedaiah to Shimri and Shemaiah. The surrounding passage presents Ziza as one of the Simeonite clan leaders who, in the days of King Hezekiah, moved into the region of Gedor in search of pasture. Shimri would therefore have lived several generations before Hezekiah's reign. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify him as a Simeonite. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name Shimri, so he should not be confused with them.

Shimri was the father of Jediael and Joha, two men named among the mighty warriors of King David's army in 1 Chr 11:45. The verse adds the description "the Tizite," which may apply to Joha alone or to the whole family. If it applies to the family, it probably points to a home town or clan called Tiz or Tizi, though no such place is otherwise known. Nothing more is recorded about Shimri himself. His sons' service under David places him, by inference, in or just before the time of David's reign. Several other people in the Bible share the name Shimri, and this one should not be confused with them. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "vigilant," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "thorn" or "dregs."

Shimri was a Levite of the family of Elizaphan who took part in cleansing the temple during the reign of King Hezekiah. He is named with Jeiel as the representatives of the sons of Elizaphan among the Levites who prepared themselves and purified the house of the Lord (2 Chr 29:13). Elizaphan was a leader of the Kohathite clan (Num 3:30), so Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Shimri as a Kohathite Levite. Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shimri, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts four in all. This entry concerns only the Levite of Hezekiah's time. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "vigilant."

Shimrith, also called Shomer, was the parent of Jehozabad, one of the royal servants who conspired against and killed King Joash of Judah. The other conspirator was Jozachar, also called Zabad, son of Shimeath. Joash was buried in the city of David, and his son Amaziah became king (2 Kgs 12:21). In 2 Kgs 12:21 the name appears as Shomer, while the parallel account in 2 Chr 24:26 gives the feminine form Shimrith and describes her as a Moabitess. Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take Shimrith to be Jehozabad's mother. Smith also notes that Shomer in Kings could be read as a father's name. This entry treats Shimrith as male, following the Kings reading of Shomer as a father. Nothing else is recorded about this person.

Shimron was a Canaanite city whose king was summoned by Jabin king of Hazor to join a northern alliance against Joshua (Josh 11:1). It was later listed among the twelve cities, with their villages, allotted to the tribe of Zebulun (Josh 19:15). The list of defeated kings in Josh 12:20 names a king of Shimron-meron, which Smith's Bible Dictionary takes to be the city's fuller name. The name is often explained as meaning "watch-post" or "watch-height." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that no identification is certain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and others place it at Semuniyeh, a site about 5 miles (8 km) west of Nazareth on the northern edge of the Jezreel plain, linked with the Simonias of Josephus. A site near Acre, Es-Semeiriyeh, has also been suggested. The location shown here follows the Semuniyeh identification.

Shimron was the fourth son of Issachar, son of Jacob, and the founder of the Shimronite clan in the tribe of Issachar. His brothers were Tola, Puah and Jashub. He appears among those who went down to Egypt with Jacob, where the brother called Jashub elsewhere is named Job (Gen 46:13). The census in the wilderness counts the Shimronites as one of Issachar's families (Num 26:24), and he is listed again in the Chronicles genealogy of the tribe (1 Chr 7:1). Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of his name as "watch" or "watchman," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "watch-height." He is a different figure from the Canaanite town of Shimron in Zebulun's territory.

Shimron-meron was a Canaanite royal city whose king appears among the thirty-one kings Joshua defeated west of the Jordan (Josh 12:20). The verse names it right beside Achshaph, the same pairing found with Shimron in Josh 11:1. Because of this, Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia all suggest it is probably the full name of Shimron, a town later assigned to Zebulun (Josh 19:15). Smith's renders the name "watch-height of Meron." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a Canaanite city, Samsimuruna, in Assyrian inscriptions, which some have linked with this place, and mentions a proposed site at es-Semeiriyeh near Acre. The location shown here follows the identification with Tel Shimron, on the northern edge of the Jezreel Valley west of Nazareth.

Shimshai was a scribe, or secretary, who served alongside Rehum the chancellor in the Persian administration of the province beyond the Euphrates. Together with their companions, a group drawn from several peoples settled in Samaria and the surrounding region, they wrote a letter to King Artaxerxes opposing the rebuilding of Jerusalem by the Jews who had returned from exile. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects this opposition with the rebuilding of the temple, while the letter itself speaks of the city. The king replied to Rehum, Shimshai and their associates in Samaria. When his answer was read to them, they went to Jerusalem in haste and forced the Jews to stop the work. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "sunny," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it appears to come from the Hebrew word for the sun, though its origin is uncertain.

Shinab was the king of Admah, one of the five cities of the plain, in the time of Abraham. Genesis 14:2 names him among the five kings, along with Bera of Sodom, Birsha of Gomorrah, Shemeber of Zeboiim and the king of Bela (Zoar), who were attacked by Chedorlaomer king of Elam and his allies. The surrounding passage explains that these kings had served Chedorlaomer for twelve years and then rebelled, and that they fought and lost in the valley of Siddim (Gen 14:4, 8–10). Shinab is not mentioned again. Later passages such as Deut 29:23 recall Admah as destroyed along with Sodom and Gomorrah. The meaning of his name is uncertain: Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "cooling," Smith's Bible Dictionary "splendor of the father," and Hitchcock's Bible Names "father of changing."

Shinar was the early Hebrew name for the lowland plain of southern Mesopotamia between the lower Tigris and Euphrates, later known as Babylonia. Genesis names it as the land where Nimrod's kingdom began with Babel, Erech, Accad and Calneh, about 1822 BC by inference from context (Gen 10:10). It was also the plain where migrants from the east settled and built Babel and its tower (Gen 11:2). Amraphel king of Shinar joined the eastern kings who fought the cities of the plain (Gen 14:1, 9). The Hebrew behind the 'Babylonish garment' Achan stole is literally 'a garment of Shinar' (Josh 7:21). Later books use the name for the Babylonian realm. Temple vessels from Jerusalem were carried there (Dan 1:2), Isaiah lists it among lands of exile (Isa 11:11), and Zechariah's vision places a house there (Zech 5:11). Easton's Bible Dictionary links the name with Sumer. The location shown here is near ancient Babylon.

Shion was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Issachar. It appears only once, in the list of Issachar's towns in Josh 19:19, where it is named between Hapharaim and Anaharath. The surrounding list also includes Shunem, so the town probably lay in the same area, in the Jezreel Valley region of lower Galilee. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "overturning." Nothing else is recorded about the town, and its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be Khirbet Sha'in, near the spring of 'Ain esh-Sha'in, about 4 miles (6 km) northwest of Mount Tabor. The location shown here matches that identification.

Shiphi was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named only in the genealogy at 1 Chr 4:37. He was the son of Allon and the father of Ziza, and his line is traced back through Jedaiah, Shimri and Shemaiah. The surrounding passage lists Ziza among the Simeonite clan leaders whose families grew numerous. By inference from 1 Chr 4:41, these leaders moved to seize pasture land in the days of King Hezekiah of Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls Ziza a prince of the tribe in that period, which would place Shiphi a generation or so earlier, in the late eighth century BC. Nothing else is recorded about Shiphi himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "abundant," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "multitude."

Shiphrah was one of two midwives, with Puah, whom the king of Egypt addressed during the oppression of the Israelites in Egypt (Exod 1:15). The following verses (Exod 1:16–21) say the king ordered them to kill Hebrew baby boys at birth. Because they feared God, they let the boys live and told Pharaoh that Hebrew women gave birth before a midwife arrived. God treated the midwives well and gave them families of their own. The text calls them the "Hebrew midwives." Most references take this to mean they were Hebrews, though Easton's Bible Dictionary describes them as Egyptian midwives serving the Hebrews. This entry follows the reading that they were Hebrew. Her name is usually understood to mean "beauty" or "fairness" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). The Septuagint renders it Sepphora, the same form it uses for Zipporah, Moses' wife.

Shiphtan was an Ephraimite, known only as the father of Kemuel. Kemuel was the prince, or leader, of the tribe of Ephraim chosen to help divide the land of Canaan among the tribes of Israel (Num 34:24). That verse belongs to the list of tribal leaders who were to work with Eleazar the priest and Joshua in giving out the inheritance. Nothing else is recorded about Shiphtan himself. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of his name as "judicial." Easton's describes him as the Ephraimite prince, though the verse gives that title to his son Kemuel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Greek manuscripts spell the name in forms such as Sabatha and Saphatan.

Shishak was a king of Egypt in the time of Solomon and Rehoboam. When Solomon sought to kill Jeroboam, Jeroboam fled to Shishak in Egypt and stayed there until Solomon died (1 Kgs 11:40). In the fifth year of Rehoboam, Shishak came up against Jerusalem. The Chronicler presents this as the result of Judah's unfaithfulness, announced by the prophet Shemaiah. When the leaders humbled themselves, Jerusalem was spared destruction. Shishak still carried off the treasures of the temple and the palace, including the gold shields Solomon had made. He is generally identified with Sheshonk I, founder of Egypt's Twenty-second Dynasty, whose list of conquests in Palestine is carved on the temple wall at Karnak (Smith's and Easton's Bible Dictionaries). Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests that the invasion was urged by Jeroboam. That link is an inference rather than something these verses state.

Shitrai was a man from Sharon who served King David as the official in charge of the royal herds that grazed in the plain of Sharon, the fertile coastal plain along the Mediterranean (1 Chr 27:29). He is called "the Sharonite," which probably marks him as a native of that region. He appears in a list of stewards who managed David's property, alongside Shaphat son of Adlai, who oversaw the herds in the valleys. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as David's chief shepherd. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "gatherer of money." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Shittim, meaning "the acacias" and also called Abel-shittim (Num 33:49), was the last camp of the Israelites east of the Jordan before they entered Canaan. It lay on the plains of Moab across the river from Jericho. While Israel stayed there, the people began to commit sexual immorality with Moabite women (Num 25:1). From Shittim Joshua secretly sent two spies to view the land and Jericho, and they lodged with Rahab (Josh 2:1). The whole people then moved from Shittim to the Jordan and camped before crossing (Josh 3:1). Micah later recalled the events "from Shittim unto Gilgal," connecting it with Balak and Balaam (Mic 6:5). Josephus placed the camp near Abila, a place of palm trees. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Khirbet el-Kefrain, an area with many acacias, and the location shown here follows that identification, near Tell Kefrein in the Jordan Valley.

Shiza was a man of the tribe of Reuben, known only as the father of Adina. His son Adina appears in the list of David's mighty warriors in 1 Chr 11:42, where he is described as a captain of the Reubenites with thirty men under him. Nothing else is recorded about Shiza himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reads the verse as making Shiza one of David's leading warriors, while Smith's Bible Dictionary and the Tyndale House proper-names index treat the warrior as his son Adina, which matches the plain wording of the verse. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "splendor," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "this gift."

Shoa was a people or region named only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel's allegory of Oholibah (Jerusalem). There it appears with the Babylonians, Chaldeans, Pekod, Koa and Assyrians among the nations whose horsemen, captains and lords would come against the city (Ezek 23:23). Since the text gives no further detail, its identity is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary links the name to Suti or Su, a district in the mountains north-east of Babylonia, in what is now Kurdistan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes Schrader's identification with the Sutu of ancient inscriptions, a people living east of the Tigris. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats Shoa, Pekod and Koa as districts of the Assyrian realm, and some have suggested a place within Babylonia itself. The location shown here follows the view that places Shoa east of the Tigris, roughly in the Zagros highlands of western Iran.

Shobab was a son of King David, born in Jerusalem. He appears only in the three lists of David's Jerusalem-born children (2 Sam 5:14; 1 Chr 3:5; 1 Chr 14:4), where he is named second, after Shammua (called Shimea in Chronicles) and before Nathan and Solomon. 1 Chr 3:5 says these four were the sons of Bathshua the daughter of Ammiel, a form of the name of Bathsheba. That makes him a full brother of Solomon and a half-brother of the sons born to David at Hebron, such as Amnon, Absalom and Adonijah. Nothing else is recorded about his life. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "rebellious," while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "returned" or "turned back." The name Shobab is also borne by at least one other man in the Bible, a descendant of Judah through Caleb, who should not be confused with this son of David.

Shobab was a son of Caleb son of Hezron, of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy at 1 Chr 2:18 together with his brothers Jesher and Ardon. The verse says Caleb had children by Azubah his wife and by Jerioth, then lists "her sons" without making clear which woman is meant. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the Tyndale House proper-names list take Azubah to be Shobab's mother. The other half-brothers counted with him in this entry, such as Hur and Mesha, appear elsewhere in the same chapter as sons of Caleb by other wives. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with Shobab the son of David, a different man who shares the name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "returned" or "turned back," and Smith's gives "rebellious."

Shobach was the commander of the army of Hadarezer (Hadadezer), king of the Syrians of Zobah, in the time of David. After the Ammonites and their hired Syrian allies were beaten by Israel, Hadarezer called up Syrian forces from beyond the river, which Easton's Bible Dictionary takes to be the Euphrates. They gathered at Helam with Shobach leading them (2 Sam 10:16). David defeated them there. Shobach was struck down in the battle and died on the field (2 Sam 10:18). The parallel account in 1 Chronicles spells his name Shophach and tells the same story, though its casualty figures differ: seven thousand charioteers and forty thousand foot soldiers, against seven hundred chariots and forty thousand horsemen in Samuel (1 Chr 19:16, 18). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 1034 BC.

Shobai was the ancestor of one of the families of temple gatekeepers (the "porters" of the King James Version) whose descendants returned to Jerusalem from exile in Babylon. His family is listed with those of Shallum, Ater, Talmon, Akkub and Hatita, and the gatekeepers of these six families together numbered 139 in Ezra 2:42 and 138 in the parallel list at Neh 7:45. Smith's Bible Dictionary places this return with Zerubbabel, before about 536 BC. Nothing further is recorded about Shobai himself. The meaning of his name is uncertain: Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "captors," Smith's Bible Dictionary "glorious," and Hitchcock's Bible Names "turning captivity."

Shobal was a son of Seir the Horite, one of the original inhabitants of the land later known as Edom, and he is listed second among Seir's sons (Gen 36:20; 1 Chr 1:38). His brothers were Lotan, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer and Dishan, and Timna was his sister. He is also named among the Horite chiefs, called "dukes" in the King James Version (Gen 36:29). His sons were Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho and Onam (Gen 36:23). In 1 Chr 1:40 two of these names appear in slightly different forms, Alian and Shephi, probably variant spellings of the same names. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries describe him as the second son of Seir. The name Shobal is shared by several people in the Bible, and this entry concerns only the Horite chief.

Shobal was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles as a son of Hur and as "the father of Kirjathjearim," which probably means the founder or leading figure of that town's clan rather than a literal parent (1 Chr 2:50). The KJV wording of 1 Chr 2:50 can also be read as making him a son of Caleb, as Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it. This entry follows the reading that makes Hur his father. His descendants included Haroeh and half of the Manahethites (1 Chr 2:52). In 1 Chr 4:1–2 he appears among the "sons," meaning descendants, of Judah, as father of Reaiah, whose line produced the Zorathites. Haroeh and Reaiah are probably the same person under variant spellings, though this is inferred. The name Shobal is shared with others, including a Horite chief of Edom, and is not to be confused with him.

Shobek was one of the men who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's day, when the community that had returned from the Babylonian exile formally pledged to keep God's law. He is known only from a single name in the list of signers (Neh 10:24), where he appears between Hallohesh and Pileha. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him among the heads of the people, which matches his place in the part of the list introduced as 'the chief of the people' (Neh 10:14). STEPBible's proper-names index describes him as a Levite. This entry follows the 'heads of the people' reading. Smith's dates the covenant to about 446 BC, an estimate inferred from context. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's gives the meaning of his name as 'free', while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives 'made void; forsaken'.

Shobi was an Ammonite, the son of Nahash of Rabbah, the Ammonite capital. When David fled from his son Absalom and reached Mahanaim, east of the Jordan, Shobi met him along with Machir son of Ammiel of Lodebar and Barzillai the Gileadite of Rogelim. The following verses (2 Sam 17:28–29) say these men brought bedding, bowls and food such as wheat, barley, beans, honey and cheese for David and his people. His father is probably the Ammonite king Nahash whose kindness David remembered (2 Sam 10:2). If so, Shobi was the brother of King Hanun, whose city of Rabbah David later captured, and he may have governed there under David, though the text does not say so. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "captor", while Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "glorious".

Shoham was a Levite of the clan of Merari, named once in the Bible as a son of Jaaziah, alongside his brothers Beno, Zaccur and Ibri (1 Chr 24:27). He appears in the lists of Levitical families that 1 Chronicles places in David's time, when the Levites were organized for service at the sanctuary. Beyond his place in this genealogy, nothing more is recorded of him. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of his name as "onyx," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "keeping back." Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 1043 BC, an estimate inferred from the context of David's reign.

Shua was a woman of the tribe of Asher, the daughter of Heber. She appears only once, in the Asherite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:32, which names her as the sister of Japhlet, Shomer (also spelled Shamer) and Hotham. The verses just before it (1 Chr 7:30–31) make Heber a son of Beriah and a grandson of Asher, which places Shua in the fourth generation from Asher. Women are seldom named in these lists, but the text gives no further details about her. She should not be confused with others in the Bible who bear similar names, such as the Canaanite Shua whose daughter married Judah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "crying" or "saving."

Shuah was a son of Abraham by Keturah, the wife Abraham took after Sarah's death and whom 1 Chr 1:32 calls his concubine. He is named last of her six sons, after Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian and Ishbak, which made him a half-brother of Isaac and Ishmael. Nothing is recorded of his life beyond these two genealogies. Genesis 25:6 says Abraham gave gifts to the sons of his concubines and sent them away eastward, so Shuah was probably among them. The STEPBible proper-names index says his descendants formed a tribe, and many link this people with Bildad 'the Shuhite' in Job 2:11, though that connection is inferred. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as 'wealth', while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers 'ditch' or 'humiliation'. Several other people in the Bible bear the same or a similar name.

Shuah was a Canaanite man whose daughter became the wife of Judah, son of Jacob. According to Gen 38:2, Judah met her while staying near Hirah the Adullamite, married her, and had children with her. 1 Chr 2:3 names their three sons as Er, Onan and Shelah and spells the father's name Shua. His daughter's own name is never given; she is called only "the daughter of Shuah" (Gen 38:12), and her death is recorded before Judah went up to Timnath for the sheepshearing. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "wealth," while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "ditch," "swimming" or "humiliation." Several other people in the Bible share this name, including a son of Abraham by Keturah, but this Shuah is the Canaanite father-in-law of Judah.

Shuah was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only once, in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:11. There he appears as the brother of Chelub, who became the father of Mehir and the grandfather of Eshton. Nothing else is recorded about him. This entry gives his father as Rechah, probably by inference from the next verse, 1 Chr 4:12, which ends the short family list with "These are the men of Rechah." Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the Hebrew form of his name is properly Shuchah, and the STEPBible name index spells it Shuhah. This sets him apart from other men called Shuah, such as the son of Abraham and Keturah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meanings "ditch," "swimming" or "humiliation," while Smith's gives "wealth."

Shual, called "the land of Shual," was a district in the hill country of Benjamin. Its name means "fox," and it appears only in 1 Sam 13:17. During Saul's war with the Philistines, raiders went out from the Philistine camp at Michmash in three companies. One of them turned toward Ophrah, into the land of Shual. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the other bands went west and east and that Israel held the pass to the south, so this band probably headed north. That would place Shual near Ophrah, which is commonly identified with et-Taiyibeh, northeast of Bethel. The district itself has not been identified. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries both suggest it may be the same as the "land of Shalim" through which Saul searched for his father's donkeys. The location shown here is a rough placement north of Michmash.

Shubael, also called Shebuel, was a Levite descended from Moses through Moses' son Gershom. He is named as the chief of the sons of Gershom (1 Chr 23:16) and appears among the descendants of Amram, Moses' father, with a son or descendant named Jehdeiah (1 Chr 24:20). He is described as "ruler of the treasures" (1 Chr 26:24), placed in the setting of David's organization of the Levites for temple service. The text calls him "the son of Gershom," which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes as grandson of Moses. Easton's Bible Dictionary and other reference works treat him as a later descendant, since the lists belong to David's time. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Shubael is probably the original form of the name. Several other people in the Bible bear the same name.

Shubael, also called Shebuel, was a Levite musician and one of the fourteen sons of Heman. He is named fourth among them in 1 Chr 25:4 under the form Shebuel. In the casting of lots that divided the temple musicians into twenty-four rotating groups, the thirteenth lot fell to Shubael, whose group of his sons and relatives numbered twelve (1 Chr 25:20). Heman's sons served under their father in the music of worship, and the surrounding passage describes these musicians as appointed in David's time to prophesy with lyres, harps and cymbals. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that Heman's sons had the duty to "lift up the horn" in the temple service. Several other men in the Bible share this name, including a descendant of Moses, and they should be kept distinct from this son of Heman.

Shunem was a town on the border of the territory of the tribe of Issachar, listed with Jezreel and Chesulloth (Josh 19:18). Before the battle of Gilboa the Philistines camped there while Saul's army camped on Mount Gilboa across the valley (1 Sam 28:4). The prophet Elisha regularly stopped at Shunem, where a wealthy woman gave him meals (2 Kgs 4:8). The surrounding chapter tells how she later gave him a room and how he raised her son. Abishag, who served the aged King David, is called a Shunammite in 1 Kgs 1:3. Eusebius placed a village called Sulem 5 Roman miles south of Mount Tabor, and this points to the modern village of Sulam on the slope of the Hill of Moreh. The location shown here follows that identification. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes a possible alternative site for Elisha's Shunem nearer Samaria.

Shuni was a son of Gad, the son of Jacob, and the ancestor of the Shunite family within the tribe of Gad. He appears in the list of Jacob's descendants who went down with him into Egypt (Gen 46:16). He appears again in the census of Israel taken in the plains of Moab, where his line is counted as the clan of the Shunites (Num 26:15). His brothers were Zephon (Ziphion), Haggi, Ozni (called Ezbon in Genesis), Eri, Arod (Arodi) and Areli. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "fortunate," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "changed" or "sleeping."

Shupham was a son of Benjamin and the founder of a Benjamite clan, the Shuphamites, listed in the census of Num 26:39. His name appears in several forms. Genesis 46:21 calls him Muppim and counts him among the sons of Benjamin who went down to Egypt with Jacob. In 1 Chr 8:5 he appears as Shephuphan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also links him with Shuppim in 1 Chr 7:12. It notes that the original form of the name is almost impossible to recover, and that the name probably means a kind of serpent. Because 1 Chr 8:3–5 lists Shephuphan among the sons of Bela, Smith's Bible Dictionary treats him there as Benjamin's grandson. This entry follows the Genesis and Numbers lists, which make him a son of Benjamin. The difference may reflect a family later counted under Bela's line. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Shuppim was a descendant of Benjamin, named with his brother Huppim as one of "the children of Ir" in the genealogy of 1 Chr 7:12. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Ir to be the same man as Iri, son of Bela and grandson of Benjamin, which would make Shuppim a great-grandson of Benjamin. In 1 Chr 7:15 he and Huppim are named as brothers of Maachah, who became the wife of Machir of the tribe of Manasseh. Apart from these genealogical notes, the text records nothing more about him. The name Shuppim belongs to more than one person in the Bible, and this entry covers only the Benjamite son of Ir.

Shuppim was a Levite gatekeeper at the sanctuary, named with Hosah in the list of gatekeeping divisions drawn up in the time of King David. When duties were assigned by lot, Shuppim and Hosah received the west side, including the gate called Shallecheth by the ascending causeway, with guard posts set opposite one another (1 Chr 26:16). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists him as one of the temple porters. Nothing more is recorded about him. Because the previous verse ends with the Hebrew word for storehouses (asuppim), which looks very similar, some interpreters think the name may have come from a copying repetition. This entry treats Shuppim as a person, as the text reads. The name is shared by others in the Bible, including a Benjamite in the genealogies of 1 Chr 7, who should not be confused with this gatekeeper.

Shur, meaning "wall," was a desert region on Egypt's northeastern edge, between Egypt and southern Canaan. The angel found the fleeing Hagar at a spring "in the way to Shur" (Gen 16:7), and Abraham later lived between Kadesh and Shur (Gen 20:1). It often marks a boundary. Ishmael's descendants lived from Havilah to Shur, "before Egypt" (Gen 25:18). Saul struck the Amalekites as far as Shur (1 Sam 15:7), and David raided peoples living toward it (1 Sam 27:8). After crossing the Red Sea, Israel went three days through the wilderness of Shur without water (Exod 15:22). Smith's Bible Dictionary equates this with the wilderness of Etham. Easton's Bible Dictionary links the name to an Egyptian frontier wall. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places the desert east of the Gulf of Suez. The location shown here, in northwestern Sinai, follows the view of a desert just east of Egypt's border.

Shuthelah was a son of Ephraim and the head of the Shuthalhite family within the tribe of Ephraim (Num 26:35). In the census list of Numbers he heads his brothers Becher and Tahan, and his own son Eran founded the Eranite family (Num 26:36). The genealogy in 1 Chronicles names his son as Bered and traces a line of descendants after him (1 Chr 7:20). Later verses in that chapter mention his brothers Ezer and Elead, killed by men of Gath, and Beriah, born afterward. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the line beginning in 1 Chr 7:20 to lead down to Joshua son of Nun, which would make Shuthelah his ancestor. The name appears again a generation or more later in the same Chronicles list, so more than one man may have borne it. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "plant" or "verdure."

Shuthelah was a man of the tribe of Ephraim, one of the two tribes descended from Joseph, and the son of Zabad. He is named once, in the genealogy of Ephraim's descendants in 1 Chr 7:21. The verse goes on to mention Ezer and Elead, who were killed by the men of Gath when they went down to take the Gathites' cattle. It is not clear whether Shuthelah himself was involved in that raid. The name also belongs to an earlier Shuthelah, a son of Ephraim, who appears in the verse just before (1 Chr 7:20). The repetition suggests the family reused the name, but the two are treated as separate people here. The STEPBible Proper Names index identifies this Shuthelah as Zabad's son. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "plant" or "verdure."

Sia was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants returned from the Babylonian exile to Jerusalem. The "children of Sia" appear in the list of returning families in Neh 7:47, between the families of Keros and Padon. The parallel list in Ezra 2:44 spells the name Siaha. Smith's Bible Dictionary connects the family with the return led by Zerubbabel and notes that the apocryphal book 1 Esdras gives the name as Sud. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "moving" or "help." Nothing else is recorded about Sia himself. He is known only as the founder of this family line.

Sibbechai the Hushathite was one of David's mighty men and a commander in his army. In a battle with the Philistines he killed a descendant of the giants, called Saph in 2 Sam 21:18, where the battle is placed at Gob, and Sippai in 1 Chr 20:4, where it is placed at Gezer. He appears among David's warriors as Sibbecai in 1 Chr 11:29. In the parallel list at 2 Sam 23:27 the same position is held by Mebunnai the Hushathite, which reference works such as Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take as the same man, the difference probably arising from the similar Hebrew spelling of the two names. He was the eighth of the monthly army captains, leading a division of 24,000 in the eighth month, and belonged to the Zarhites, a clan of Judah. "Hushathite" probably refers to his hometown.

Sibmah was a town east of the Jordan in the former territory of Moab, rebuilt by the tribe of Reuben and assigned to it in Joshua's division of the land (Num 32:38; Josh 13:19). It is spelled Shibmah in Num 32:38 and probably appears as Shebam in Num 32:3. The town was famous for its vineyards. Isaiah and Jeremiah, in their laments over Moab, mourn the ruined "vine of Sibmah," whose branches had spread as far as Jazer and beyond. They link it with nearby Heshbon, Elealeh and Jazer, which suggests that by then it was again a Moabite town. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the ruin of Sumieh near Heshbon, where rock-cut winepresses have been found. The location shown here is approximate and places it close to Heshbon.

Sibraim was a place named in Ezekiel's vision of the future boundaries of the land of Israel. It appears in Ezek 47:16 as a landmark on the northern border, listed after Hamath and Berothah and described as lying "between the border of Damascus and the border of Hamath." The verse mentions it only once and gives no further detail. Smith's Bible Dictionary says the name means "twofold hope" and that the site has not been identified. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be Khirbet Sanbariyeh, on the west bank of the Hasbani River about 3 miles southeast of Abil, near the modern Lebanon–Israel border. Its exact location remains uncertain. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the region of Hamath in central Syria, reflecting the verse's description of the area between the territories of Damascus and Hamath.

Sidon (also spelled Zidon) was an ancient Phoenician port city on the Mediterranean coast north of Tyre. It is the modern Saida in Lebanon, and the location shown here marks that site. Genesis names it as the northern limit of Canaanite territory. It lay within the area allotted to Asher, but Asher never drove out its people (Judg 1:31). Its sailors and merchants were known across the sea (Isa 23:2; Ezek 27:8), and Israel at times worshipped its gods (Judg 10:6). Isaiah calls it a mother to Tyre, and Jeremiah, Ezekiel and Joel announce judgment against it. Elijah stayed at Zarephath, a town belonging to Sidon. Jesus travelled into the region of Tyre and Sidon, where he healed a Canaanite woman's daughter (Matt 15:21), and people from there came to hear him. Paul's ship called at Sidon on his voyage to Rome (Acts 27:3).

Sidon the Great was the name used for the Phoenician city of Sidon when describing the northern boundary of the territory of the tribe of Asher. Josh 19:28 lists towns such as Hebron, Rehob, Hammon and Kanah reaching "even unto great Zidon," so the city probably marked the limit of Asher's allotment rather than lying within it. The same phrase, "great Zidon," appears in Josh 11:8, where Joshua pursues the defeated northern kings as far as the city. The title "great" probably reflects Sidon's standing as the leading city of the Phoenician coast. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "hunting" or "fishing." The location shown here is the coastal city of Sidon, the modern Saida in southern Lebanon.

Sidon (Zidon), called "great Zidon" in Josh 11:8, was the leading Phoenician port city on the Mediterranean coast north of Israel. In this passage, after Joshua defeated the northern Canaanite coalition at the waters of Merom, Israel chased the fleeing kings as far as great Zidon, Misrephoth-maim and the valley of Mizpeh, which marked the northwestern limit of the pursuit. The word "great" probably reflects the city's size and standing, or may refer to Sidon together with its surrounding territory. Other passages show Sidon as an ancient and important Canaanite city. The location shown here is the modern city of Saida (Sidon) on the coast of Lebanon, the standard identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "hunting" or "fishing."

Sihon was king of the Amorites, ruling from his city of Heshbon east of the Jordan. He had earlier taken land from the king of Moab as far as the Arnon River, a conquest celebrated in a poem quoted in Num 21:27–29. His territory ran from Aroer on the Arnon to the Jabbok River, the border of Ammon, and included the Jordan valley up to the Sea of Galilee. When Israel asked permission to pass peacefully through his land, Sihon refused. He gathered his army and fought them at Jahaz, where Israel defeated him and took his cities. Moses then gave his kingdom, together with that of Og king of Bashan, to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh. Later writers, including Joshua, Nehemiah and the Psalms, often name Sihon and Og together as the two Amorite kings Israel overcame beyond the Jordan.

Silas, called Silvanus in the New Testament letters, was a leading member of the Jerusalem church and a prophet (Acts 15:22, 32). After the Jerusalem Council, about AD 46 by inference from context, he and Judas Barsabas went with Paul and Barnabas to deliver the council's letter to Antioch and confirm it in person. When Paul and Barnabas parted, Paul chose Silas as his companion for the second missionary journey. At Philippi, after Paul cast a spirit out of a fortune-telling slave girl, her owners had both men seized and jailed. At midnight they prayed and sang, and the jailer came to faith. Silas went on with Paul to Thessalonica and Berea, stayed behind there with Timothy, and later rejoined Paul at Corinth. He is named with Paul and Timothy in 1 and 2 Thessalonians. Smith's Bible Dictionary considers him probably the same Silvanus who carried Peter's first letter (1 Pet 5:12), and this entry follows that view.

Silla is a place named only once, in the account of the murder of King Joash of Judah. His servants conspired against him and killed him "in the house of Millo, which goeth down to Silla" (2 Kgs 12:20). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reads the phrase as "on the way that goeth down to Silla" and infers that Silla lay in a valley below Beth-millo, though nothing more is known of what or where it was. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the Hebrew word may mean "highway" and might not be a proper name at all, while the Septuagint and other ancient versions treat it as one. Smith's Bible Dictionary mentions a suggestion that it refers to the area of the Pool of Siloam. The location is uncertain. The point shown here is a rough placement in Jerusalem, near the Millo.

Siloam was a pool, and evidently also a district, at the southern end of ancient Jerusalem. John explains the name as meaning "Sent" (John 9:7). Jesus put clay on the eyes of a blind man and told him to wash in the pool of Siloam. He did so and came back able to see (John 9:7, 9:11). Jesus also mentioned eighteen people killed when a tower in Siloam fell on them (Luke 13:4). The pool is probably the same as the Shiloah of Isa 8:6 and the Siloah of Neh 3:15. Easton's Bible Dictionary says it was fed by a winding rock-cut tunnel from the spring now called the Gihon or Fountain of the Virgin. A Hebrew inscription describing how the tunnel was dug was found there in 1880 and is probably from Hezekiah's reign. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the name survives in the Arabic Silwan. The location shown here is at the southern tip of the City of David.

Simeon was the second son of Jacob and Leah, named because Leah said the LORD had heard that she was unloved (Gen 29:33). Several other people in the Bible share the name. With his brother Levi he avenged their sister Dinah by killing the men of Shechem, which alarmed Jacob (Gen 34:25, 30), and Jacob's dying words condemn the pair's violence (Gen 49:5). When the brothers went to Egypt for grain during the famine, Joseph kept Simeon bound as a hostage until they returned with Benjamin (Gen 42:24, 36; 43:23). His sons included Jemuel (Nemuel), Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar (called Zerah in Chronicles) and Shaul, whose mother was a Canaanite (Gen 46:10; 1 Chr 4:24). He was the ancestor of the tribe of Simeon, whose inheritance lay within Judah's territory (Josh 19:1, 9). His birth is placed about 1757 BC, by inference from context.

Simeon is an ancestor of Jesus named only in Luke's genealogy, which traces Jesus' line back through Joseph, his legal father (Luke 3:30). He is listed as the son of Juda and the father of Levi. Since Luke's list runs from Jesus back through David's son Nathan, Simeon belongs to a generation after David and before the Babylonian exile, and so to the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is one of several men in the Bible named Simeon and is distinct from Jacob's son Simeon, who appears further back in the same genealogy. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Revised Version spells his name "Symeon." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "that hears or obeys."

Simeon, also called Niger, was one of the prophets and teachers in the church at Antioch, named alongside Barnabas, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen and Saul (Acts 13:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary explains Niger as meaning "black," perhaps describing his complexion. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Simeon was his Hebrew name and Niger a Latin name he also used. The verses that follow describe this group fasting, praying and setting Barnabas and Saul apart for the work they had been called to. Simeon was therefore probably among those who sent them out on the first missionary journey, about AD 45 by inference from context. Easton's notes a suggestion that he was the Simon of Cyrene who carried Jesus' cross. This entry treats him simply as the Antioch teacher. Nothing more is recorded of him. The name Simeon is shared by several other people in the Bible.

Simon Zelotes was one of the twelve apostles chosen by Jesus, about AD 28 by inference from context. Matthew and Mark call him "Simon the Canaanite" (Matt 10:4; Mark 3:18), while Luke calls him "Simon called Zelotes" (Luke 6:15; Acts 1:13). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary explain that "Canaanite" here does not mean a native of Canaan. They take it as an Aramaic term whose Greek equivalent is "Zelotes," meaning "zealot." On this view he probably belonged to the Zealots, a Jewish faction known for strict devotion to the law of Moses, before his call. After Jesus' ascension he was among the eleven apostles gathered in the upper room in Jerusalem, shortly before Matthias was chosen to replace Judas (Acts 1:13). Beyond his place in the apostle lists, the Bible records nothing else about him.

Simon was one of the brothers of Jesus, named alongside James, Joses and Judas (Jude) when people in Jesus' hometown questioned where his teaching came from. They asked, "Is not this the carpenter's son?" and were offended at him (Matt 13:55; Mark 6:3). Matthew lists Simon third among the brothers and Mark lists him last. Nothing more is recorded about him in these passages. Interpreters have long differed on how Jesus' "brethren" were related to him, with some taking them as cousins or as Joseph's sons from an earlier marriage. This entry follows the view that Simon was a son of Joseph and Mary, and so of the tribe of Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that some writers identify him with Symeon, who later led the church in Jerusalem, and others with Simon the Canaanite. The name Simon is shared by several people in the Bible.

Simon, known as "the leper," was a man of Bethany in whose house Jesus was staying or dining shortly before his death. During the meal a woman broke open an alabaster jar of very costly ointment of spikenard and poured it on Jesus' head (Matt 26:6; Mark 14:3). Matthew and Mark do not name the woman. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies her as Mary, drawing on the related account in John 12:1–3, which places an anointing at Bethany in a home connected with Lazarus, Martha and Mary. Simon's title probably describes a past condition, since lepers were kept apart from others under the law. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both suggest he may have been healed by Jesus, though the text does not say so. He should not be confused with the several other men named Simon in the Bible.

Simon was a man from Cyrene, a city on the north coast of Africa in present-day Libya, whom the Roman soldiers forced to carry the cross of Jesus on the way to the crucifixion, about AD 30 by inference from context. Matthew, Mark and Luke all record the incident. Mark and Luke add that he was coming in from the country and passing by when he was seized, and Luke says he carried the cross behind Jesus (Luke 23:26). Mark alone names him as the father of Alexander and Rufus (Mark 15:21), which suggests his sons were known to Mark's readers. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests this Rufus may be the one greeted in Rom 16:13. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that Cyrene had a large Jewish community and suggests Simon may have been among the men of Cyrene who later preached in Antioch (Acts 11:20). He is one of several men in the Bible named Simon.

Simon was the father of Judas Iscariot, the disciple who betrayed Jesus. He is known only through his son, who is repeatedly called "Judas Iscariot, Simon's son" in John's Gospel, including at the last supper when Jesus handed Judas the dipped bread (John 13:26). Nothing else is recorded about his life, home or occupation. Because the surname Iscariot is usually taken to mean "man of Kerioth," Simon probably came from the same place, though this is an inference. The name Simon, a shortened form of Simeon, was common, and several men in the New Testament bear it. Passages such as Mark 1:30 and Luke 5:3 concern Simon Peter, and Luke 7:40–44 concerns a Pharisee named Simon who hosted Jesus. These are different men from the father of Judas described in this entry.

Simon the Sorcerer was a man in a city of Samaria who practised sorcery and amazed the people there, presenting himself as someone great (Acts 8:9). When Philip preached in Samaria, about AD 31 by inference from context, Simon believed and was baptized. He then stayed close to Philip, astonished at the miracles and signs he saw (Acts 8:13). When the apostles came and he saw that the Holy Spirit was given through the laying on of their hands, he offered them money for that power (Acts 8:18). Peter rebuked him sharply, as the surrounding passage records, and Simon asked the apostles to pray to the Lord for him so that what they had spoken would not happen to him (Acts 8:24). The text does not say what became of him afterward. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the term "simony," meaning the buying of spiritual office, comes from his name. He is often called Simon Magus.

Simon the Tanner was a man of Joppa, a tanner by trade, in whose house the apostle Peter stayed for many days after raising Dorcas (Acts 9:43). His house stood by the sea (Acts 10:6, 32). While Peter was lodging there, he had a vision, and the men sent by the Roman centurion Cornelius arrived at the gate asking for Simon's house (Acts 10:17). The angel's directions to Cornelius identify Peter's whereabouts by naming his host, which distinguishes this Simon from Simon Peter himself. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe him as a Christian, an inference from his hosting the apostle. Smith's suggests the seaside location was for the water tanning needed, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds that tanners worked outside town for sanitation and because the trade was ritually unclean for Jews. The events are dated about AD 38, by inference from context.

Simri was a Levite of the family of Merari and a son of Hosah, named in the lists of temple gatekeepers organized in David's reign. Although he was not the firstborn, his father made him chief among his sons (1 Chr 26:10). His brothers were Hilkiah, Tebaliah and Zechariah. Hosah's family is listed among the gatekeeper divisions, so Simri probably served as a gatekeeper too, which is how STEPBible's proper-name index describes him. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the name is properly Shimri and gives its meaning as "vigilant," while Easton's Bible Dictionary renders it "watchman." He is mentioned only in this one verse.

Sin was a wilderness region between Elim and Mount Sinai where the Israelites camped on their journey out of Egypt. They arrived on the fifteenth day of the second month after leaving Egypt (Exod 16:1). Numbers places the stop after a camp by the Red Sea and before Dophkah (Num 33:11–12). Exodus has them leave Sin for Rephidim, where they found no water (Exod 17:1). The rest of Exodus 16 describes the people complaining about food here and receiving quails and the first manna. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the region to be probably the narrow coastal plain of el-Markha, along the eastern shore of the Gulf of Suez in the western Sinai Peninsula. Smith's Bible Dictionary likewise places it between the gulf coast and Wadi Feiran. The location shown here follows this coastal identification. It is a different place from the Egyptian city of Sin mentioned in Ezekiel.

Sinai is the desert region, and the mountain within it, where the Israelites camped after leaving Egypt. They came from Rephidim into the wilderness of Sinai in the third month after the Exodus and camped before the mount (Exod 19:1–2). While they were there, Moses received commands about the offerings, the people were counted, Nadab and Abihu died, and the Passover was kept in the second year (Lev 7:38; Num 1:1; 3:4; 9:5). The people then moved on toward the wilderness of Paran (Num 10:12). Later poetry recalls Sinai as the place the LORD came from, where the mountain shook (Deut 33:2; Judg 5:5; Ps 68:8). Other passages call the same place Horeb. Tradition places the mountain in the southern Sinai Peninsula. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia favors Jebel Musa, and Easton's Bible Dictionary points to the nearby bluff of Ras Sufsafeh. The location shown here marks the region broadly within that peninsula.

Sinite is listed as a son of Canaan in the Table of Nations, named between the Arkite and the Arvadite (Gen 10:17; 1 Chr 1:15). As with most of Canaan's descendants in these lists, the name is in a gentilic form ("the Sinite"). It refers to the ancestor of a people, or to the people themselves, rather than to an individual whose life is described. His brothers include Zidon, Heth, the Jebusite, the Amorite, the Girgasite, the Hivite, the Arkite, the Arvadite, the Zemarite and the Hamathite. Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes the Sinite as an inhabitant of a place called Sin near Arka. Smith's Bible Dictionary places the tribe in the northern part of the Lebanon region. This fits the neighbouring names, which point to towns along the Phoenician coast and in Syria.

Siphmoth was a town in the south of Judah, named once in the Bible (1 Sam 30:28). It was one of the places to which David sent a share of the spoil from Ziklag after he defeated the Amalekites. The surrounding passage presents these gifts as going to towns where David and his men had moved about while living as fugitives from Saul. It is listed between Aroer and Eshtemoa, which places it in the southern hill country of Judah. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the name the meaning "fruitful places." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the site has not been found and suggests that Zabdi the Shiphmite (1 Chr 27:27) probably came from here. Its exact location is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in southern Judah, near Eshtemoa.

Sippai, also called Saph, was a Philistine warrior described as one of "the sons of the giant," that is, a descendant of the Rapha or Rephaim. He was killed by Sibbechai the Hushathite, one of David's warriors, in a battle with the Philistines during David's reign (about 1050 BC by Smith's Bible Dictionary's estimate). 2 Sam 21:18 places the battle at Gob and calls him Saph. The parallel account in 1 Chr 20:4 places it at Gezer and calls him Sippai. The surrounding passage (2 Sam 21:22) groups him with Ishbi-benob, Goliath (or Lahmi, Goliath's brother, in Chronicles) and an unnamed man of great stature as giants born to "the giant in Gath." This may mean a common father or simply a common ancestry. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a suggestion that he was Goliath's son, which the text does not settle. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "threshold."

Sirah was a well or cistern from which Joab's messengers brought Abner back, without David's knowledge, after Abner had left David at Hebron (2 Sam 2:26 is not involved; see 2 Sam 3:26). The following verse, 2 Sam 3:27, says Joab then took Abner aside in the gate of Hebron and killed him in revenge for his brother Asahel. The name is often explained as meaning "turning" or "retiring", and Josephus also refers to it as a well. Since Abner was heading away from Hebron, the well was probably on the road north of the city. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with 'Ain Sarah, a spring and small reservoir about a mile north of Hebron on the road toward Jerusalem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also mentions a stepped cistern called Hammam Sarah near Ramet el-Khalil as another possibility. The rough location shown here follows the 'Ain Sarah identification just north of Hebron.

Sirion was the name the Sidonians (Phoenicians) used for Mount Hermon, while the Amorites called it Shenir (Deut 3:9). The name probably means "breastplate" or "body armor," according to Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary. Psalm 29 pairs Sirion with Lebanon as mountains made to leap like a young wild ox at the voice of the Lord (Ps 29:6). There the Hebrew spelling is slightly different (Shirion). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may refer to the whole Hermon range as seen from the Phoenician coast, not to one part of it. Jer 18:14 is also linked to Sirion, probably because the snowy rock described there is taken to be Hermon, although the King James wording does not name it. The location shown here is the summit of Mount Hermon, on the modern border of Lebanon and Syria.

Sisamai was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:40, where he is the son of Eleasah and the father of Shallum. The surrounding list traces the family line of Jerahmeel through Sheshan, whose daughter married his Egyptian servant Jarha. Smith's Bible Dictionary accordingly describes Sisamai as a descendant of Sheshan in the line of Jerahmeel. Nothing else is recorded about his life. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists him under the alternative spelling Sismai. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "house" or "blindness."

Sisera (army captain) was the commander of the army of Jabin, the Canaanite king who reigned in Hazor, and he lived at Harosheth of the Gentiles (Judg 4:2). He commanded nine hundred iron chariots. When Barak gathered Israel's forces on Mount Tabor at Deborah's urging, Sisera brought his army to the river Kishon, where it was routed and destroyed (Judg 4:13–16). He got down from his chariot and fled on foot to the tent of Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite, whose household was at peace with Jabin. While he lay there, Jael drove a tent peg through his temples, so that he was dead when Barak arrived (Judg 4:22). Deborah's song celebrates his defeat and pictures his mother waiting at a window for his return (Judg 5:28). Later texts recall him as an oppressor of Israel (1 Sam 12:9; Ps 83:9). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes differences between the prose and poetic accounts of his defeat.

Sisera was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (Nethinim) whose descendants returned to Jerusalem from the Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel. He is known only from the parallel lists of returnees in Ezra 2:53 and Neh 7:55, where "the children of Sisera" appear alongside the families of Barkos and Tamah. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is a different person from Sisera, the Canaanite army commander in the book of Judges. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes there is no evidence that this family descended from the earlier Sisera. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the name points to Canaanite captives assigned to humble duties in the temple. The return is usually dated to about 538–536 BC.

Sister of Tahpenes was an unnamed Egyptian woman, the sister of Queen Tahpenes, wife of the Pharaoh who ruled Egypt during the reign of Solomon. Pharaoh gave her in marriage to Hadad the Edomite, a member of Edom's royal family who had fled to Egypt as a boy and won Pharaoh's favour (1 Kgs 11:19). She bore Hadad a son, Genubath. Her sister Tahpenes weaned the child in Pharaoh's house, and Genubath grew up in Pharaoh's household among Pharaoh's own sons (1 Kgs 11:20). Through this marriage Hadad became tied to the Egyptian royal family. Her name is not given, and nothing more is recorded about her.

Sitnah was the second of the wells that Isaac's servants dug in the valley of Gerar. The local herdsmen quarreled with them over it, as they had over the first well, so Isaac named it Sitnah, meaning "enmity" or "hostility" (Gen 26:21). The surrounding passage in Gen 26 gives the setting: the first well was called Esek ("contention"), and Isaac then moved on and dug a third well, which went undisputed and which he named Rehoboth. The site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects it with a place called Shutneh near Rehoboth, about 20 miles (32 km) south of Beersheba. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls the site unknown but notes a similar name, Shutnet er Rucheibeh, for a small valley near Rucheibeh. The location shown here is rough and places Sitnah in the general area of Gerar, northwest of Beersheba.

The Skull was the place outside Jerusalem where Jesus was crucified between two criminals (Luke 23:33). The KJV calls it "Calvary," from the Latin calvaria, which translates the Greek kranion, "skull." The parallel accounts in Matthew, Mark and John give its Aramaic name, Golgotha, "the place of a skull." Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it was probably named for its shape, a low, rounded, bare rise resembling a skull, and notes that Scripture never calls it a hill. Hebrews 13:12 places the crucifixion outside the city gate, and John describes the place as near the city. Its exact site is uncertain. The main traditional candidate is the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, and another proposal is "Gordon's Calvary" near the Garden Tomb north of the Damascus Gate. The location shown here is only a rough placement in Jerusalem and does not settle between these views.

Smyrna was a city on the western coast of Asia Minor, about 40 miles north of Ephesus, and the second of the seven churches in the province of Asia to which the book of Revelation was sent (Rev 1:11). The message to its church opens with Christ described as "the first and the last, which was dead, and is alive" (Rev 2:8). The wider message (Rev 2:8–11) speaks of the church's hardship and poverty. The name means "myrrh." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes Smyrna as a busy harbor and trading center that rivaled Ephesus and Pergamos in Roman times. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that Polycarp, a disciple of the apostle John, later led the church there and was martyred in the second century. The city is the modern Izmir in Turkey, which is where the location shown here is placed.

So was a king of Egypt, named only in 2 Kgs 17:4. Hoshea, the last king of Israel, sent messengers to him and stopped paying the yearly tribute to the king of Assyria. The verse calls this a conspiracy, and probably means Hoshea was seeking Egyptian help against Assyria. When the Assyrian king discovered it, he imprisoned Hoshea. The text does not say whether So answered. His identity is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify him with Shabaka (Sabako), the Ethiopian, or Nubian, ruler who founded Egypt's twenty-fifth dynasty. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that writers have linked him with either the first or the second king of that dynasty. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he may have been regent before taking the throne, and that he was defeated by the Assyrian king Sargon at Raphia about 720 BC.

Soco (spelled Shoco in the King James text) was a town in Judah that King Rehoboam rebuilt and fortified, listed with Bethzur and Adullam among his defensive cities (2 Chr 11:7). The surrounding passage presents these towns as strongholds built after the kingdom divided. Two towns of this name appear in Judah's territory: one in the lowland hills (Josh 15:35), and one in the southern hill country (Josh 15:48). The Rehoboam fortress is usually taken to be the lowland town in the Valley of Elah. That is probably the Shochoh where the Philistines gathered before David fought Goliath (1 Sam 17:1). The location shown here follows that identification. It places Soco at a site commonly linked with Khirbet Abbad (Khirbet Shuweikeh), near Azekah and west of Bethlehem. Its nearness to Adullam in the same list fits this view.

Socoh was a town in the Shephelah, the lowland foothills of Judah. It appears in Judah's tribal allotment beside Jarmuth, Adullam and Azekah (Josh 15:35). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "tents" or "tabernacles." According to STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House), this is the Socoh near which the Philistines gathered before David fought Goliath, described in 1 Sam 17:1 as lying near Azekah, and the town Rehoboam later fortified (2 Chr 11:7). The name is shared by several places, including a second Socoh in Judah's hill country, so not every mention necessarily refers to this town. The location shown here is in the Elah Valley, which fits the usual identification with the ruins called Khirbet Shuweikeh (also Khirbet Abbad).

Socoh was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed in Josh 15:48 alongside Shamir and Jattir among the towns allotted to the tribe of Judah. Several places in the Bible share this name. This one is distinct from the Socoh in the Judean lowland, which was the scene of the Philistine gathering before David fought Goliath. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies the hill-country town with a site about 10 miles southwest of Hebron that bears the name esh-Shuweikeh, the same Arabic name as the lowland Socoh. The location shown here, given only roughly, follows that general area south of Hebron. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "tents" or "tabernacles." Beyond its place in the list of Judah's towns, the Bible records nothing further about this Socoh.

Sodi was a man of the tribe of Zebulun and the father of Gaddiel, mentioned only once in the Bible. Gaddiel was the man chosen from Zebulun as one of the twelve leaders Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan (Num 13:10). Sodi himself is named only to identify his son, and nothing else is recorded about him. By inference from the setting, he belonged to the generation that came out of Egypt, during the wilderness period. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "intimate", while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "my secret".

Sodom was a city of the plain near the Dead Sea. It is named with Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboim at the edge of Canaanite territory (Gen 10:19). Lot settled near it after parting from Abram, and its men are described as exceedingly wicked (Gen 13:12–13). Its king fought in the vale of Siddim, where Lot was taken captive. Abram later rescued him and refused the king's offer of goods (Gen 14:8–22). After two angels visited Lot, the city was destroyed by fire and brimstone from heaven (Gen 19:1–28; Luke 17:29). Prophets and New Testament writers repeatedly use Sodom as a byword for sin and for sudden, total overthrow. Its exact site is unknown. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it south of the Dead Sea, near Jebel Usdum ("Mount Sodom"), while Easton's Bible Dictionary favors the northern end. The location shown here follows the southern identification.

The Destruction of Sodom was God's overthrow of Sodom, Gomorrah and the surrounding plain because of the great outcry against their sin. Before it happened, Abraham pleaded with the LORD to spare Sodom for the sake of any righteous people there, and the LORD agreed to spare it if even ten were found. Two angels came to Sodom, where Lot took them into his house. The men of the city surrounded the house and demanded the visitors, and the angels struck them with blindness. At dawn the angels led Lot, his wife and his two daughters out of the city. Lot's sons-in-law had treated his warning as a joke. Lot was allowed to flee to the small town of Zoar. The LORD then rained fire and brimstone on the cities, and Lot's wife looked back and became a pillar of salt. Abraham saw the smoke rising like a furnace. This entry dates the event to about 1897 BC, by inference from context.

The Sojourn in Canaan and Egypt was the 430-year period that Exod 12:40 gives for the time the Israelites and their ancestors lived as foreigners before the Exodus. Readers count it in two ways. Some take it as time spent in Egypt alone. Others count it from God's promise to Abraham, since Gal 3:17 places the giving of the law 430 years after that promise. The Greek Septuagint and the Samaritan Pentateuch support this second reading by adding "and in the land of Canaan" to Exod 12:40. This entry follows the longer reckoning. It starts the period when Abraham entered Canaan, about 1921 BC by inference from context. On that view it covers the lives of Abraham, Sarah and Lot in Canaan, including Abraham's stay in Egypt during a famine. According to Gen 12, Pharaoh took Sarah into his household there.

Solomon was the son of David and Bathsheba, born in Jerusalem, and was chosen by David from among his many sons to succeed him as king of Israel (1 Chr 3:5; 1 Chr 28:5). According to 2 Sam 12:25, the prophet Nathan gave him the name Jedidiah, "beloved of the LORD." He was made king while David was still alive, even though his half-brother Adonijah was trying to take the throne (1 Kgs 1:10, 37). In his fourth year he began building the temple in Jerusalem (1 Kgs 6:1). He also built a royal palace, with the help of Hiram king of Tyre. His reign was remembered for its wealth, trade and wisdom, which drew the queen of Sheba to visit him (1 Kgs 10:10; Matt 12:42). In old age his foreign wives turned him toward other gods (1 Kgs 11:4). Proverbs and the Song of Solomon bear his name. He reigned about 1015–975 BC, by inference from context, and was succeeded by his son Rehoboam.

Solomon's Portico, also called Solomon's Porch, was a covered colonnade in the temple complex at Jerusalem. After Peter and John healed a man lame from birth, the man held on to them there while a crowd ran together in amazement, and Peter used the occasion to address the people (Acts 3:11). Later the apostles regularly gathered there 'with one accord' while many signs and wonders were done among the people (Acts 5:12). These events are dated to about AD 30, by inference from context. John 10:23 also describes Jesus walking there at the Feast of Dedication. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as a cloister, probably on the eastern side of the temple, and notes that it is not mentioned with Solomon's first temple, though Josephus mentions a porch of that name in Herod's temple. The location shown here places it within the temple area.

The son of Abinadab was one of the twelve officers King Solomon appointed over districts of Israel, each responsible for supplying the royal household with provisions for one month of the year, as the surrounding passage explains. His own name is not given; the Hebrew calls him Ben-abinadab, "son of Abinadab." He governed all the region of Dor, the coastal area around the town of Dor south of Mount Carmel, and he was married to Taphath, a daughter of Solomon (1 Kgs 4:11). This made him the king's son-in-law. Which Abinadab was his father is not stated. Some interpreters suggest he was Abinadab the brother of David, which would make him Solomon's cousin, but the text does not confirm this.

The son of Dekar was one of the twelve district officers King Solomon appointed over Israel. According to 1 Kgs 4:7, each of these officers supplied food for the king and his household for one month of the year. His own name is not given; he is known only as Dekar's son, and some modern translations render the phrase as a name, "Ben-Deker." His district included Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh and Elon-beth-hanan. Judging by the known towns of Shaalbim and Beth-shemesh, this was probably the lowland country west of Jerusalem, in the area once allotted to the tribe of Dan. Nothing else is recorded about him or his father.

Son of Geber (in Hebrew, Ben-geber) was one of the twelve officers King Solomon appointed over Israel. According to 1 Kgs 4:7, each officer supplied food for the king and his household for one month of the year. His personal name is not given. He was based at Ramoth-gilead, east of the Jordan. His district took in the towns of Jair son of Manasseh in Gilead and the region of Argob in Bashan, which is described as sixty large cities with walls and bronze bars. A Geber son of Uri appears a few verses later (1 Kgs 4:19) as the officer over Gilead. Whether he was this man's father, or the two simply share a name, is not stated.

Son of Hesed was one of the twelve district officers King Solomon appointed over Israel. Each officer supplied food for the king and his household for one month of the year, as the surrounding passage explains. His personal name is not given; he is identified only as the son of a man named Hesed. He was based in Aruboth, and his district included Sochoh and all the land of Hepher (1 Kgs 4:10). The exact location of Aruboth is uncertain. By inference from the places named with it, the district probably lay in the central hill country or the Sharon plain west of Manasseh. Hepher was an old Canaanite town whose king Joshua defeated, and Sochoh here is probably a town in that same area, not the better-known Sochoh in Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Son of Hur is the name given to the first of King Solomon's twelve district officers listed in 1 Kgs 4:8. These officers each supplied food for the king and his household for one month of the year. His own personal name is not given. The text identifies him only by his father, Hur, and his district was the hill country of Ephraim, the central highlands of Israel. Many translations render the title as Ben-Hur, since "ben" is the Hebrew word for "son". Nothing else is recorded about him. It is uncertain whether his father Hur is connected with any other Hur mentioned in the Bible.

The son of Joiada is an unnamed priest of the tribe of Levi. He was a grandson of Eliashib the high priest, and Johanan was his brother. According to Neh 13:28 he married a daughter of Sanballat the Horonite, one of Nehemiah's leading opponents. Because of this marriage Nehemiah drove him away from his presence. In the surrounding passage this is one of several steps Nehemiah took against marriages with foreigners and the defiling of the priesthood. The text does not give his name. The Jewish historian Josephus tells a similar story about a priest named Manasseh who married Sanballat's daughter and was expelled from Jerusalem, but Josephus places those events later, so whether the two accounts describe the same man is uncertain.

The sons of Jashen were men listed among David's mighty warriors in 2 Sam 23:32. Their father appears as Jashen there and as Hashem the Gizonite in the parallel list at 1 Chr 11:34, so "Gizonite" probably names the family's home town. Neither passage gives the sons' names or their number. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the two names as the same person, and Smith's Bible Dictionary counts the sons of Hashem as members of David's guard. In both lists the phrase is followed by the name Jonathan. Some readers take Jonathan to be one of these sons, but the wording leaves this uncertain, since 1 Chr 11:34 calls him "the son of Shage the Hararite."

Sopater was a believer from Berea in Macedonia who travelled with Paul. Acts 20:4 lists him first among the companions who went with Paul into Asia as he left Greece for Jerusalem, along with Aristarchus, Secundus, Gaius, Timothy, Tychicus and Trophimus. This entry links him to Paul's mission in Macedonia and Greece, dated about AD 54 by inference from context. The Revised Version adds that he was the son of Pyrrhus, a detail the King James Version omits. Easton's, Smith's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia all take him to be probably the same man as Sosipater, a longer form of the same name. In Rom 16:21 Sosipater, with Timothy, Lucius and Jason, sends greetings to the Christians in Rome, and Paul calls him a kinsman, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia understands as a fellow Jew. This entry follows that identification. His name means roughly "saviour of his father."

Sophereth was the ancestor of a family counted among "the children of Solomon's servants" in the lists of exiles who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem and Judah (Ezra 2:55; Neh 7:57). Smith's Bible Dictionary places this return with Zerubbabel, before about 536 BC. The name appears only in these two parallel lists, which name nothing about Sophereth beyond the family line. In Ezra the Hebrew carries the definite article, so the Revised Version reads "Hassophereth" there, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as "scribe" or "numbering," and Smith's gives "writing." This entry treats Sophereth as female, a reading suggested by the feminine ending of the name. The name may also have been the title of an office, such as a scribe, rather than a personal name, so whether it refers to a single individual is uncertain.

Sosthenes was the chief ruler of the synagogue at Corinth during Paul's mission there. Acts 18:17 records that after Gallio, the Roman governor, refused to hear the Jewish leaders' case against Paul, a crowd of Greeks seized Sosthenes and beat him in front of the judgment seat, and Gallio paid no attention. The text does not explain why he was attacked. Paul later names "Sosthenes our brother" as co-sender of 1 Corinthians (1 Cor 1:1). Whether this is the same man is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls it possible, and the Tyndale House proper names index treats them as one person who later joined Paul's work. Other interpreters see two different men. This entry follows the single-person view. The events at Corinth date to about AD 49–51, an estimate from context. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "savior" or "strong."

Sotai was the ancestor, or founder, of a family counted among "the children of Solomon's servants" in the lists of exiles who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem and Judah (Ezra 2:55; Neh 7:57). The two lists are near-identical, and in both his family is named first in this group, ahead of Sophereth and Peruda (Perida). Solomon's servants were probably descendants of laborers or attendants assigned to royal or temple service in Solomon's time. Smith's Bible Dictionary places this return with Zerubbabel, before about 536 BC, which is an inferred date. Nothing is recorded about Sotai himself beyond his name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "binding," and Smith's gives "changeful."

South is a term the King James Version uses for a region lying to the south, and in these verses it points to two different areas. In Zech 7:7 it describes the populated land around Jerusalem in earlier, prosperous times, when people lived in "the south and the plain".
