This is probably the Negev, the dry southern district of Judah, paired with the lowland foothills to the west. In Matt 12:42 and Luke 11:31, Jesus speaks of "the queen of the south" who came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon's wisdom. By comparison with 1 Kgs 10:1–13, she is the queen of Sheba, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. Her land is commonly placed in southern Arabia, while Ethiopian tradition places it in Ethiopia. No single location is shown for this entry.

The Southern Kingdom (Judah) was the kingdom ruled from Jerusalem by David's descendants after Israel split in two. It began when Solomon died and was buried in the city of David, and his son Rehoboam took the throne (1 Kgs 11:43). According to the account that follows in 1 Kgs 12, the northern tribes rejected Rehoboam and made Jeroboam their king. Rehoboam kept the tribe of Judah, along with Benjamin, and this southern realm took Judah's name. The kingdom is dated here from about 975 BC and lasted roughly 390 years, both figures inferred from context. That span reaches to about 586 BC, when, as 2 Kgs 25 records, the Babylonians captured Jerusalem and took its people into exile. Throughout its history Judah's kings came from David's line, in contrast to the changing dynasties of the northern kingdom of Israel.

Spain was the Roman region occupying the Iberian Peninsula in southwestern Europe, roughly the area of modern Spain and Portugal. It is named in the Bible only in Paul's letter to the Romans, where he tells the believers in Rome that he plans to visit them on his way to Spain. He hopes they will help send him on from there, once he has delivered the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem (Rom 15:24, 28). The New Testament does not record whether he ever made the journey. Easton's Bible Dictionary finds no evidence that he did. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia thinks it probable that he went after being released from his first imprisonment, pointing to Clement of Rome's statement that Paul reached "the extreme limit of the West." Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests that the older name Tarshish may have referred to the same region. The location shown here marks the central part of the peninsula.

Stachys was a Christian living in Rome whom Paul greets near the end of his letter to the Romans, calling him "my beloved" (Rom 16:9). He is named alongside Urbane, whom Paul describes as a helper in Christ. Nothing else is recorded about him, and the letter gives no details of his work or background. His name is Greek and means "ear of grain" (Hitchcock's Bible Names; Easton's Bible Dictionary). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name is uncommon and has been found in inscriptions connected with the Roman imperial household. Paul's affectionate description suggests he knew Stachys personally, though how they met is not stated. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the letter to about AD 56.

Stephanas was a Christian of Corinth whose household was the first in the Roman province of Achaia to accept the gospel. Paul calls it the "firstfruits of Achaia" and says it had devoted itself to serving fellow believers. His household was one of the few Paul baptized personally at Corinth. Stephanas later came to Paul, probably at Ephesus, with Fortunatus and Achaicus, and Paul says they made up for the Corinthians' absence. Paul urged the church to respect and follow such workers. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests these three men brought the Corinthians' letter to Paul and probably carried 1 Corinthians back in reply. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions a suggestion that he was the Philippian jailer of Acts 16. His name means "crown" (Hitchcock's Bible Names).

Stephen was one of the seven men chosen by the early church in Jerusalem to serve the community, described as full of faith and of the Holy Spirit (Acts 6:5). Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him one of the seven deacons and the first Christian martyr. He performed great wonders and miracles among the people (Acts 6:8). Members of the synagogue of the Libertines, along with men from Cyrene, Alexandria, Cilicia and Asia, disputed with him (Acts 6:9). He was seized and brought before the council, where he gave a long speech, the longest in Acts. He was then stoned, praying, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit" (Acts 7:59). Devout men buried and mourned him (Acts 8:2). Saul later recalled standing by, approving his death and guarding the clothes of those who killed him (Acts 22:20). The persecution that followed scattered believers as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch (Acts 11:19).

The Stephen addresses the council event is Stephen's long speech before the Jewish council in Jerusalem, which follows his arrest. When the high priest asks whether the charges against him are true (Acts 7:1), Stephen retells Israel's history. He starts with God's call to Abraham in Mesopotamia and the promise of the land (Acts 7:2–5), then covers Joseph being sold into Egypt and rising to power there (Acts 7:9–10), and Moses, who was rejected by his own people, met God at the burning bush and led Israel out of Egypt (Acts 7:25–36). He recalls the golden calf (Acts 7:41) and the tabernacle, and he states that the Most High does not live in temples made with hands (Acts 7:48–49). He ends by accusing his hearers of persecuting the prophets, betraying the Just One, and not keeping the law (Acts 7:52–53). The date of about AD 30 is an estimate inferred from context.

The seizure of Stephen was his arrest in Jerusalem, shortly after he was chosen as one of the seven appointed to serve the church. Stephen had been doing great wonders and miracles among the people. Members of the synagogue of the Libertines, together with Jews from Cyrene, Alexandria, Cilicia and Asia, argued with him but could not stand against the wisdom and spirit with which he spoke. They then persuaded men to claim he had spoken blasphemy against Moses and God. After stirring up the people, the elders and the scribes, they seized him and brought him before the council. There false witnesses accused him of speaking against the temple and the law, saying he claimed Jesus of Nazareth would destroy the temple and change the customs of Moses. Everyone in the council saw his face look like the face of an angel. The event is dated about AD 30, by inference from context.

Stephen is stoned is the event that ended Stephen's speech before the council in Jerusalem. His hearers were enraged and gnashed their teeth at him. Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looked up and said he saw the heavens opened and Jesus, the Son of man, standing at God's right hand. The crowd shouted, covered their ears, rushed at him together, drove him out of the city and stoned him. The witnesses laid their cloaks at the feet of a young man named Saul. Acts 13:9 shows that this Saul is also called Paul, and Acts 8:1 adds that he approved of the killing. As the stones fell, Stephen prayed, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." He then knelt and cried out, "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge," and died. By inference from context, the event took place about AD 31.

Straight Gate is the name used in this entry for the street called Straight in Damascus, where the Lord told Ananias to go to the house of Judas and ask for Saul of Tarsus, who was praying there after his encounter on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:11). The verse names the street but does not describe it. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as a long, broad street running east to west, about a mile long, and serving as the city's main thoroughfare. It notes that several major cities of Syria and Palestine had colonnaded 'straight streets' through their centers. It is probably the east–west street through the old city of Damascus known in Roman times as the Via Recta, and the location shown here lies in the old city. The events linked to it, Saul's conversion and stay in Damascus, are dated to about AD 32, by inference from context.

Suah was a man of the tribe of Asher, the first named of the sons of Zophah in the Asherite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:36. His brothers listed there and in the following verse include Harnepher, Beri, Imrah, Bezer, Hod, Shamma, Shilshah, Ithran or Jether, and Beera, with Ulla also counted among Zophah's sons in this entry. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in this family list. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "sweeping" and dates him to about 1020 BC, an estimate drawn from the genealogy rather than stated in the text. Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "speaking" or "entreating" as possible meanings.

The Subjugation by Cushan-rishathaim was the first period of foreign oppression recorded in the book of Judges. After the Israelites in Canaan did evil in the LORD's sight, forgot him, and served the Baals and the Asherah poles ("groves"), the LORD in anger "sold them" into the power of Chushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia. Israel served him for eight years. His kingdom is called Aram-naharaim in Hebrew, meaning "Aram of the two rivers," probably the region of the upper Euphrates in what is now northern Syria and Iraq. Nothing more is said about him or how his rule was exercised. The passage that follows (Judg 3:9–11) says Israel cried to the LORD, who raised up Othniel, Caleb's younger brother, to defeat him, after which the land had rest. By inference from context, this entry places the oppression about 1418 BC.

The Subjugation by Eglon was the period when Israel was ruled by Eglon, king of Moab, after the deliverance by Othniel. The text says that Israel again did evil in the sight of the LORD, and that the LORD strengthened Eglon against them. Eglon formed an alliance with the Ammonites and Amalekites, attacked Israel, and took "the city of palm trees." Elsewhere that phrase refers to Jericho (Deut 34:3; 2 Chr 28:15), so the city here was probably Jericho. Israel then served Eglon for eighteen years. By inference from context, this began about 1378 BC. The passage that follows describes how the oppression ended when Ehud the Benjaminite killed Eglon and led Israel against Moab (Judg 3:15–30).

The Subjugation by Jabin was a twenty-year period during the time of the judges when Israel was dominated by Jabin, called king of Canaan, who ruled from the city of Hazor in the north. According to Judg 4:1, it began after the death of the judge Ehud, when Israel again did evil in the sight of the LORD. The LORD then gave them over to Jabin, whose army commander was Sisera of Harosheth of the Gentiles. Jabin's strength lay in nine hundred iron chariots, and he oppressed Israel severely until the people cried out to the LORD. This entry dates its start to about 1298 BC, an estimate inferred from context. The rest of Judges 4 and 5 describes how the oppression ended when Deborah and Barak defeated Sisera. An earlier Jabin of Hazor appears in Joshua 11, which suggests the name may have been a royal title or dynastic name.

The Subjugation by Midian was a seven-year period in the time of the judges when Israel, after doing evil in the sight of the LORD, was handed over to Midian. It began about 1258 BC, by inference from context, and followed the deliverance under Deborah and Barak. Each year, once Israel had sown its crops, the Midianites came in with the Amalekites and other eastern peoples. They arrived with their tents, cattle and countless camels, camped on the land, and destroyed the harvest and livestock as far as Gaza. The Israelites took refuge in mountain dens, caves and strongholds and were left badly impoverished. When they cried out to the LORD, he sent a prophet who reminded them that he had brought them out of Egypt and given them the land, yet they had not obeyed him. The following verses (Judg 6:11 onward) tell how Gideon was called to end the oppression.

Succoth, meaning "booths", was a city east of the Jordan, in the valley near the Jabbok River. Jacob settled there after parting from Esau. He built a house and made booths for his cattle, which gave the place its name (Gen 33:17). It later fell to the tribe of Gad as part of the former kingdom of Sihon (Josh 13:27). During Gideon's pursuit of the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna, the leaders of Succoth refused bread to his weary men. On his return Gideon punished its seventy-seven princes and elders with thorns and briers (Judg 8:5–16). Solomon's bronze temple furnishings were cast in the clay ground between Succoth and Zarethan (1 Kgs 7:46). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with Tell Deir Alla, north of the Jabbok. Some have proposed Sakut, west of the Jordan. The location shown here follows Tell Deir Alla. A different Succoth appears in the Exodus account in Egypt.

Succoth was the first camping place of the Israelites after they left Rameses during the exodus from Egypt (Exod 12:37; Num 33:5). The name means "booths" or "tents." From Succoth they moved on to Etham, at the edge of the wilderness (Exod 13:20; Num 33:6). The departure is dated to about 1491 BC, by inference from context. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests Succoth was reached at the end of the first day's march. Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it in the lower Wadi Tumilat, the valley running east from the Nile Delta, and Easton's Bible Dictionary treats Succoth as another name for Pithom. The location shown here follows the Wadi Tumilat identification, placing it near the valley's eastern end close to Lake Timsah, near modern Ismailia. This Succoth in Egypt is distinct from other places of the same name, such as the Succoth east of the Jordan.

Suph is a place named in Deut 1:1 as a landmark for where Moses addressed Israel: beyond the Jordan, in the wilderness, in the Arabah ("the plain") opposite Suph, among Paran, Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth and Dizahab. The King James Version, following the Septuagint and other ancient versions, translates the word as "the Red sea." Easton's Bible Dictionary judges this the most likely reading, taking Suph as a shortened form of Yam Suph, the Hebrew name of the Red Sea. Other suggestions mentioned there include Suphah (Num 21:14), es-Sufah near Maaleh-acrabbim (Josh 15:3), and Zuph (1 Sam 9:5). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia concludes that no site can be identified with confidence. The location shown here follows the Red Sea reading and marks the general area of the northern Red Sea rather than a specific town.

Suphah is a place named in an old poem quoted in Num 21:14 from "the book of the wars of the LORD," which recalls what God did there and in the brooks of Arnon. The King James Version translates the Hebrew word as "Red sea," while its margin and the Revised Version read it as a place name: "Vaheb in Suphah." Easton's Bible Dictionary places Suphah at the southeastern corner of the Dead Sea, at Ghor es-Safieh, an identification first proposed by the explorer Tristram. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the same as Suph in Deut 1:1 and treats its exact location as still unsettled. Its context near the Arnon points to the region of Moab east of the Dead Sea. The location shown here follows the "Red sea" reading and marks the Red Sea region generally.

Sur was a gate in Jerusalem, connected with the temple or the royal palace, named only in 2 Kgs 11:6. The priest Jehoiada planned to make the boy Joash king and overthrow Queen Athaliah. He divided the guards into three companies, one stationed at the king's house, one at the gate of Sur, and one at the gate behind the guard, so that the house would be secured. The parallel account in 2 Chr 23:5 calls this the "gate of the foundation," and the STEPBible proper-names index likewise suggests it may be the Foundation Gate. Its exact position within the temple and palace complex is not known, and the location shown here marks only the general temple area in Jerusalem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a different Sur in Judith 2:28, a coastal place near Tyre whose site has not been identified.

Susa, called Shushan in the King James Version, was a royal city in the province of Elam, where the Persian king kept a palace or citadel. Daniel saw a vision there beside the river Ulai (Dan 8:2), and Nehemiah was serving there when he heard news of Jerusalem (Neh 1:1). Most of the events of the Book of Esther take place at Susa: King Ahasuerus held court and feasts there, Esther and Mordecai lived there, Haman's decree went out from it, and the Jews of the city defended themselves and then celebrated with feasting (Esth 1:2; 3:15; 9:15–18). Its people, the Susanchites, appear among the groups opposing Jerusalem's rebuilding (Ezra 4:9). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with modern Shush in southwestern Iran, where excavated ruins include a great columned palace hall, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Susanna was one of the women who traveled with Jesus and his twelve disciples in Galilee and supported them from their own resources. She is named only once, in Luke 8:3, alongside Mary Magdalene (named in the preceding verse) and Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod's steward, among "many others" who provided for Jesus. By inference from the surrounding passage, these women had been healed of evil spirits and illnesses. This entry places the mention during Jesus' second tour of Galilee, about AD 28, an estimate inferred from context. Nothing else is recorded about her family or later life. Her name is usually understood to mean "lily," as both Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give it.

Susi was a man of the tribe of Manasseh, named only as the father of Gaddi. Gaddi was the man chosen to represent Manasseh, counted as part of the tribe of Joseph, among the twelve sent by Moses to scout the land of Canaan (Num 13:11). Nothing else is recorded about Susi himself. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "horse," "swallow" or "moth."

Sychar was a town in Samaria where Jesus stopped on his way to Galilee and spoke with a Samaritan woman at Jacob's well. John 4:5, its only mention, places it near the plot of land Jacob gave to his son Joseph, a district traditionally placed just east of Shechem. Its exact identity is debated. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats Sychar as another name for Shechem itself. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the village of 'Askar on the lower slope of Mount Ebal, about a mile north of Jacob's well. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia considers it a separate place east of Shechem and suggests the nearby mound of Tell Balata, which was occupied in New Testament times, noting the name may later have moved to 'Askar. The location shown here follows the view that Sychar was a separate site east of Shechem, near Jacob's well.

Syene was a city on Egypt's southern frontier, on the east bank of the Nile, identified with modern Aswan, which is the location shown here. Ezekiel uses it in prophecies against Egypt to mark the country's full extent. Egypt would be made desolate "from the tower of Syene even unto the border of Ethiopia" (Ezek 29:10), and its allies would fall by the sword there (Ezek 30:6). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as Egypt's southern frontier town, as Migdol was in the north-east, and notes its quarries of red granite, called "syenite." On that reading, many translators take Ezekiel's phrase as "from Migdol to Syene," meaning from one end of Egypt to the other. Some interpreters also connect "the land of Sinim" in Isa 49:12 with Syene, a distant place from which scattered people return. This entry notes that view without settling it.

Syntyche was a Christian woman in the church at Philippi whom Paul names in his letter to that church. He urges her and another woman, Euodias (Euodia in many modern translations), to "be of the same mind in the Lord" (Phil 4:2), which suggests some disagreement between them. In the next verse, Phil 4:3, Paul asks an unnamed "true yokefellow" to help these women, saying they had labored with him in the gospel, so she was evidently one of his co-workers. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia infers that she and Euodia were among the early converts from Paul's first visit to Philippi, described in Acts 16. Her name is Greek and is usually taken to mean "fortunate" or "affable" (Easton's Bible Dictionary). Nothing else is recorded about her.

Syracuse was a major city on the east coast of Sicily, today the Italian city of Siracusa. Paul's ship stopped there for three days on his voyage as a prisoner to Rome (Acts 28:12). By inference from the surrounding passage, the ship had sailed from Malta, and after Syracuse it went on to Rhegium and Puteoli. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that its excellent harbor and fresh water made it a convenient stop for grain ships coming from Africa and Alexandria. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes it as founded by settlers from Corinth in 734 BC on the islet of Ortygia. It became the most powerful Greek city in the western Mediterranean, withstood an Athenian siege in 414 BC, and fell to Rome in 212 BC. It then served as the capital of the Roman province of Sicily.

Syria is the King James name for the region north and northeast of Israel, called Aram in Hebrew. In the Old Testament it usually means the Aramean kingdom ruled from Damascus (1 Kgs 15:18). Its kings Benhadad, Hazael and Rezin repeatedly fought Israel and Judah, besieging Samaria and marching on Jerusalem (1 Kgs 20:1; 2 Kgs 6:24; 2 Kgs 16:5). Naaman commanded its army (2 Kgs 5:1). Israelites worshipped its gods (Judg 10:6), and it traded with Tyre (Ezek 27:16). Amos foretold its people's exile to Kir (Amos 1:5). In the New Testament Syria is a Roman province, governed at one point by Cyrenius (Luke 2:2). Jesus' fame spread through it (Matt 4:24), and Paul strengthened churches there and sailed to and from it (Acts 15:41; Acts 21:3). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that in Roman times it also included part of Palestine. The location shown here is a general point near the modern Syria–Turkey border.

Syrtis was the name of dangerous shallow waters and shifting sandbanks off the north coast of Africa, long feared by sailors. The King James Version renders it "the quicksands" in Acts 27:17, while the Revised Version uses the Greek name. During Paul's voyage to Rome, a violent storm drove his ship south from Crete, and the crew feared being driven onto the Syrtis. They undergirded the hull, lowered the sail and let the ship drift. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries both note that the coast had two such areas, the Greater and the Lesser Syrtis. They take the Greater Syrtis, between Tripoli and Barca near Cyrene, to be the one meant here, since the Lesser lay too far west to threaten the ship. The location shown here follows that view and places it in the Gulf of Sidra (Sirte) off modern Libya.

Taanach was a Canaanite royal city on the southwestern edge of the plain of Esdraelon (Jezreel), almost always named alongside nearby Megiddo. Its king was among those defeated by Joshua (Josh 12:21). Although it lay within Issachar's territory, it was counted to Manasseh (Josh 17:11; 1 Chr 7:29), and it was given to the Levites from the half tribe of Manasseh, spelled "Tanach" in Josh 21:25. Manasseh did not drive out its Canaanite inhabitants (Judg 1:27). The Song of Deborah places the battle against the kings of Canaan "in Taanach by the waters of Megiddo" (Judg 5:19). Under Solomon it belonged to the district of Baana son of Ahilud (1 Kgs 4:12). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it also appears in Egyptian records. It is identified with the modern Ta'annek, about five miles southeast of Megiddo, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Taanath-shiloh was a town marking the eastern border of the territory allotted to the tribe of Ephraim. In Josh 16:6 the boundary runs from Michmethah around eastward to Taanath-shiloh, passes it on the east, and continues to Janohah. It is named only in this verse. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "approach to Shiloh," and Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests Taanath may have been an older Canaanite name to which Shiloh was added. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Eusebius placed a town called Thena about ten Roman miles east of Neapolis (modern Nablus) on the road to the Jordan. It identifies the site with the village of Ta'na, about 7 miles southeast of Nablus and near Yanun, the ancient Janoah. A Jewish tradition in the Talmud instead takes it to be Shiloh itself. The location shown here follows the Ta'na identification, now Khirbat Tana.

Tabbaoth was the ancestor of a family of Nethinim, or temple servants, whose descendants were among the exiles who returned from Babylon to Judah. The family appears third in the list of temple servants, after the families of Ziha and Hasupha, in both versions of the list of returnees (Ezra 2:43; Neh 7:46). Smith's Bible Dictionary places their return with Zerubbabel, before about 536 BC. Nothing is recorded of Tabbaoth himself. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of the name as "rings". The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the family may have been named after a place rather than a person, and notes the same family in 1 Esdras 5:29.

Tabbath was a city in the Jordan valley, mentioned only once in the Bible. When Gideon's three hundred men blew their trumpets and the Midianite army turned on itself, the fleeing host ran toward Beth-shittah in Zererath and to the border of Abel-meholah, "unto Tabbath" (Judg 7:22). Its place in this list suggests it marked one of the farthest points of the retreat, probably near the Jordan crossings. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it south of Beth-shean near the Jordan. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the ridge called Tabaqat Fahil on the eastern side of the river, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that no trace of the name has been found. The location shown here is a rough placement on the west side of the Jordan, south of Beth-shean, matching Easton's description. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "good" or "goodness."

Tabeal was the father of a man whom the kings of Syria and Israel planned to set on the throne of Judah, according to Isa 7:6. The surrounding passage identifies these kings as Rezin of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah, who marched against Jerusalem in the reign of Ahaz. Their plan was to break into Judah and install "the son of Tabeal" as king in place of Ahaz. The name is usually explained as meaning "God is good" (Easton's Bible Dictionary; Smith's Bible Dictionary). Neither Tabeal nor his son is mentioned anywhere else, so who they were is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the son was either an Ephraimite serving with Pekah or a Syrian serving with Rezin, and notes that the Aramaic form of the name points to a Syrian. Some references, such as the Tyndale House proper-names list, use the name Tabeal for the intended king himself.

Tabeel was one of the officials who, together with Bishlam, Mithredath and their companions, wrote a letter to Artaxerxes king of Persia. The letter was written in the Syrian (Aramaic) tongue (Ezra 4:7). The surrounding chapter makes clear that it opposed the Jews who had returned from exile and were rebuilding Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Persian governor of Samaria. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him a Persian official in Samaria and says his name means "good is God." Nothing more is known of him. The name is not unique: a different man, spelled Tabeal in the King James Version, appears in Isa 7:6 as the father of a man Israel and Syria planned to set up as king in Judah.

Taberah was a place in the wilderness where the Israelites camped after leaving Mount Sinai. Its name means "burning" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). It was given that name because "the fire of the LORD burnt among them" there (Num 11:3). The surrounding verses in Num 11:1–2 say the people complained, fire broke out at the edges of the camp, and it died down when Moses prayed. Later, Moses listed Taberah with Massah and Kibroth-hattaavah as places where Israel provoked the LORD to anger (Deut 9:22). Smith's Bible Dictionary places it in the wilderness of Paran. Easton's Bible Dictionary treats it as another name for Kibroth-hattaavah, the next site in Numbers 11, while Deut 9:22 names the two separately. The site has not been identified. The location shown here is a rough estimate in the Sinai Peninsula, northeast of the traditional Mount Sinai.

The Tabernacle Built is the episode in which God gave Moses, on the mountain, detailed instructions for a portable sanctuary where he would dwell among Israel during the wilderness wanderings (Exod 25:9; 29:45). The plans cover the ark holding the testimony, a gold-covered table, a seven-branched lampstand, curtains and boards of acacia wood, the bronze-covered altar, and a linen-walled court. They also cover Aaron's priestly garments, the consecration of Aaron and his sons, the incense altar, the census offering, and the sabbath sign. The same section tells how the people made a golden calf while Moses was away, how Moses destroyed it, and how the people were punished. Moses then pleaded for God's presence to go with them. According to Exod 35–40, the work was carried out afterward and the tabernacle was set up in the second year after leaving Egypt, about 1490 BC by inference from context.

Tabor (town) was a town in the territory of Zebulun that was given, with its surrounding pasturelands, to the Levite families descended from Merari (1 Chr 6:77). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it simply as a town of Zebulun. The parallel list of Levitical towns in Joshua 21 names different towns for Zebulun and does not mention Tabor, so its exact identity is uncertain. It is often linked with Chisloth-tabor, a place on Zebulun's border that Josh 19:12 places near Mount Tabor. The location shown here follows that identification, probably the modern village of Iksal, west of Mount Tabor in lower Galilee. Others connect the name more generally with the area around the mountain itself. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "choice," "purity" or "bruising."

Tabor (Plain) was a landmark Samuel named when giving Saul directions after anointing him king. There Saul would meet three men going up to worship God at Bethel, carrying three young goats, three loaves of bread and a skin of wine (1 Sam 10:3). The King James word 'plain' translates a Hebrew term that the Revised Version, Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary render 'oak', so the place was probably a notable tree, 'the oak of Tabor'. It was on Saul's route home to Gibeah. Because the men were heading to Bethel, it was probably not far from that town. It is distinct from Mount Tabor in Galilee. Easton's suggests it may be the oak below Bethel where Rebekah's nurse Deborah was buried (Gen 35:8). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the site is now unknown. The location shown here is a rough placement near Bethel, north of Jerusalem.

Tabrimon was the son of Hezion and the father of Ben-hadad, the king of Syria who ruled from Damascus. He is named only once, in a genealogy identifying the Ben-hadad to whom King Asa of Judah sent silver and gold from the temple and palace treasuries (1 Kgs 15:18). The following verse and the parallel in 2 Chronicles 16 show that Asa was asking Ben-hadad to break his treaty with Baasha of Israel. The verse does not say whether Tabrimon himself was king, though his place in this line suggests he belonged to the ruling family of Damascus. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "Good is Rimmon." Smith's Bible Dictionary spells it Tabrimmon, explains Rimmon as a Syrian god, and places Tabrimon before 928 BC. This dating is an estimate inferred from Asa's reign.

Tadmor was a city that Solomon built "in the wilderness," listed alongside the store cities he built in Hamath (2 Chr 8:4). Its name probably means "palm tree." Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with Palmyra, the later Greek and Roman name for a great oasis city in the Syrian desert. It sat on caravan routes between the Mediterranean and the Euphrates and is famous for its extensive Roman-era ruins. The location shown here follows that identification, in central Syria about 210 km (130 miles) northeast of Damascus. In the parallel passage, 1 Kgs 9:18, the written Hebrew text reads "Tamar," and the Bible's traditional marginal reading gives "Tadmor." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes this, and Easton's takes Tamar there as a separate town on Israel's southern border. This entry follows the Chronicles reading and the Palmyra identification.

Tahan was a son of Ephraim, Joseph's son, and the ancestor of the Tahanites, one of the Ephraimite clans counted in the census Moses took on the plains of Moab (Num 26:35). In that list he appears with Shuthelah and Becher as heads of Ephraim's families. His other brothers, Elead, Ezer and Beriah, come from the genealogy in 1 Chr 7:20–23, which says Elead and Ezer were killed by men of Gath and that Beriah was born afterward. The same name appears again in 1 Chr 7:25 for a later descendant of Ephraim, so the name belongs to more than one person. The Tahan of 1 Chr 7:25 is probably a separate man, though he may carry the name of his clan's founder. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as “beseeching” or “merciful.”

Tahan was a descendant of Ephraim, son of Joseph, named in the genealogy of Ephraim's line in 1 Chr 7:25. He was the son of Telah, and the following verse continues the line with his son Laadan, which leads in turn to Elishama and eventually to Joshua, son of Nun (1 Chr 7:26–27). This places Tahan among Joshua's ancestors. He is known only from this list, and nothing more is recorded about him. Another Tahan, a son of Ephraim who founded the Tahanite clan, appears in Num 26:35. That is a different person, though the name probably reflects a family tradition within the tribe. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "beseeching" or "merciful."

Tahath was one of the places where the Israelites camped during their wilderness journey. Numbers lists it as the stop after Makheloth and before Tarah (Num 33:26–27). Nothing else is recorded about it, and it appears only in this itinerary. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of the Hebrew name as "below." Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "fear" or "going down." The site has not been identified, and the location shown here is only a rough estimate. It places Tahath in the desert region south of the Dead Sea, in what is now southern Jordan, by inference from its place in the sequence of camps. Tahath is also the name of several people in the Bible, but this entry concerns only the campsite.

Tahath was a Levite of the Kohathite clan, the son of Assir, named in two genealogies of Levi's descendants in 1 Chronicles 6. In the first list, which traces the line of Kohath, he comes after Assir and is followed by his son Uriel, then Uzziah and Shaul (1 Chr 6:24). In the second, which traces the ancestry of Heman the temple singer, he again appears as the son of Assir, son of Ebiasaph, son of Korah (1 Chr 6:37). There the next name, from the preceding verse, is Zephaniah rather than Uriel. The two lists probably refer to the same man and follow different lines of his descendants, though the reason for the difference is not explained. Several other people in the Bible share the name Tahath. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "fear" or "going down."

Tahath was a descendant of Ephraim, son of Joseph, named in the Ephraimite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:20. He was the son of Bered and the father of Eladah. The verse lists the names in a chain joined by "his son," which suggests a single line of descent from Ephraim through Shuthelah and Bered, making Tahath probably Ephraim's great-grandson. The same verse names a second Tahath, a son of Eladah and so probably this Tahath's grandson, likely named after him. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is also borne by other people in the Bible, so the verse should be read carefully to tell them apart. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "fear" or "going down."

Tahath was a descendant of Ephraim, son of Joseph, named in the Ephraimite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:20. He was the son of Eladah and the father of Zabad, and so belonged to the tribe of Joseph through its Ephraim branch. The same verse names an earlier Tahath, son of Bered, as Eladah's father. This Tahath therefore probably shared his name with his grandfather, a common practice in Israelite families. The list continues in the next verse with Zabad and further descendants. Nothing else is recorded about his life. The name is also borne by other people in the Bible, including a Levite of the family of Kohath, and it is the name of a camping place of Israel in the wilderness. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "fear" or "going down."

Tahpanhes was a city in the eastern Nile Delta of Egypt. After Jerusalem fell to Babylon and the governor Gedaliah was murdered, a group of Judeans fled there and took the prophet Jeremiah with them, against his warning (Jer 43:7). At Tahpanhes Jeremiah was told to bury large stones in the brickwork at the entrance of Pharaoh's house, which shows the town had a royal building (Jer 43:8–9). Jews were still living there later (Jer 44:1). Jeremiah also names it with Migdol and Noph (Memphis) in a warning of coming war against Egypt (Jer 46:14). Other passages spell the name Tahapanes and Tehaphnehes. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with Tell Defenneh, the Greek Daphnai, on the old caravan route to Palestine, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Tahpenes was a queen of Egypt, the wife of the Pharaoh who took in Hadad the Edomite. The surrounding passage in 1 Kings 11 shows that Hadad had fled to Egypt as a boy when David's forces struck Edom. Pharaoh favored him so much that he gave him Tahpenes' sister, who is not named, as his wife (1 Kgs 11:19). Their son Genubath was weaned by Tahpenes in Pharaoh's house and grew up among Pharaoh's own sons (1 Kgs 11:20). The text does not name the Pharaoh she was married to. Smith's Bible Dictionary places her around 1000 BC, in the time of David and Solomon, which fits the setting of the passage. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meanings "standard," "flight" or "temptation" for her name, though its origin is probably Egyptian.

Tahrea was a son of Micah in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin that traces the descendants of King Saul. He is listed with his brothers Pithon, Melech and Ahaz (1 Chr 9:41). The earlier copy of the same list spells his name Tarea (1 Chr 8:35), and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats that form as a copyist's slip for Tahrea. The verses just before each list name Micah as the son of Merib-baal (Mephibosheth), son of Jonathan, son of Saul, which makes Tahrea a great-great-grandson of Saul. Smith's Bible Dictionary accordingly calls him a grandson of Mephibosheth. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his name and family. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "cunning", while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "anger" or "wicked contention."

Talmai was one of the three sons, or descendants, of Anak, along with Ahiman and Sheshai. They lived at Hebron when the Israelite spies passed through the hill country of Canaan (Num 13:22). The Anakim were known as men of great size, a reputation reflected in the spies' report in the surrounding chapter. During the conquest, Caleb drove Talmai and his brothers out of Hebron (Josh 15:14). Judges 1:10 says the men of Judah attacked the Canaanites of Hebron, formerly called Kirjath-arba, and killed Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai. The two accounts probably describe the same campaign, with Caleb leading Judah's forces. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the name as possibly that of a clan rather than a single person. Talmai of Hebron is distinct from other men of the same name in the Bible, such as Talmai king of Geshur.

Talmai, son of Ammihud, was king of Geshur in the time of David. Geshur was a small kingdom, described by the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia as Aramean, which probably lay east of the Jordan near the Sea of Galilee. Talmai's daughter Maacah became one of David's wives, and she was the mother of Absalom, David's third son, born at Hebron (2 Sam 3:3; 1 Chr 3:2). After Absalom had his half-brother Amnon killed, he fled to his grandfather Talmai in Geshur, while David mourned for his son every day (2 Sam 13:37). The marriage probably reflects a political alliance between David and the Geshurite king. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests Talmai was a minor ruler dependent on David. The name Talmai is shared by other people in the Bible, including a son of Anak at Hebron (Num 13:22), who should not be confused with this king.

Talmon was a Levite gatekeeper ("porter") at the temple in Jerusalem, named with Shallum, Akkub and Ahiman among the gatekeepers in 1 Chr 9:17. The name also marks a family of gatekeepers: "the children of Talmon" appear among those who returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:42; Neh 7:45). Talmon is listed again with Akkub among the gatekeepers living in Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time (Neh 11:19), and among the porters who guarded the storehouses at the gates (Neh 12:25). Because these mentions span several generations, it is uncertain whether they refer to one man, to several men of the same family, or to the family as a whole. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Talmon as the head of a family of door-keepers whose descendants kept the hereditary office after the exile.

Tamah, also spelled Thamah (and Temah in some modern translations), was the ancestor of a family of temple servants who returned from exile in Babylon. His name appears only in the two parallel lists of returning exiles, in Ezra 2:53 and Neh 7:55. There his descendants are named alongside the families of Barkos and Sisera. The surrounding lists place these families among the Nethinim, the servants assigned to assist at the temple. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes them as returning with Zerubbabel. Nothing else is recorded about Tamah himself, and it is not clear whether he was a real individual or a name used for a family group.

Tamar is a place named among the cities Solomon built, described as "in the wilderness, in the land" (1 Kgs 9:18). The King James Version reads "Tadmor" here, but the written Hebrew text has "Tamar," a name meaning "palm" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Several places in the Bible share this name, so its identity is debated. The parallel account in 2 Chr 8:4 has Solomon building Tadmor in the wilderness, which is generally taken as the oasis city later known as Palmyra in the Syrian desert. Others read the name as Tamar in the far south of Judah, near the Dead Sea, because the neighboring towns in the list (Gezer, Beth-horon, Baalath) lie in Solomon's southern territory. The location shown here follows the Tadmor identification, the site of Palmyra in central Syria.

Tamar was a place marking the southeastern corner of the land in Ezekiel's vision of Israel's future borders. From Tamar the southern boundary was to run to the waters of strife at Kadesh, then along the river (the Brook of Egypt) to the Mediterranean (Ezek 47:19; 48:28). Its name means "palm tree," and several biblical places share it. Because the Dead Sea forms the eastern border in the same passage, Tamar probably lay southwest of the Dead Sea. Its exact site is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests it may be Hazazon-tamar, the old name of En-gedi, or a Thamar mentioned by Eusebius a day's journey south of Hebron. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links it with Thamara, a Roman fortress on the road from Hebron to Elath. The location shown here follows the New Bible Dictionary, which identifies it with Kurnub (ancient Mampsis) in the northern Negev.

Tamar was the daughter-in-law of Judah, married first to his firstborn son Er (Gen 38:6). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives her name's meaning as "palm tree." After Er died, she was given to his brother Onan, who also died (Gen 38:8–10). Judah sent her back to her father's house to live as a widow until his third son, Shelah, grew up, because he feared Shelah might also die (Gen 38:11). Shelah was never given to her. When she heard that Judah was going to Timnath to shear sheep (Gen 38:13), she conceived by him, as the chapter goes on to tell. When told she was pregnant, Judah ordered her burned (Gen 38:24), but then admitted she was more in the right than he was (Gen 38:25–26). She bore twins, Pharez (Perez) and Zerah (1 Chr 2:4), about 1721 BC by inference from context. As Thamar, she appears in Jesus' genealogy (Matt 1:3). Several other women share her name.

Tamar was a daughter of King David and the full sister of Absalom, named in 1 Chr 3:9 alongside David's sons. Her name means "palm tree" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). She is described as beautiful, and her half-brother Amnon became infatuated with her. On the advice of his cousin Jonadab, Amnon pretended to be ill and asked David to send Tamar to prepare food for him. When she brought the cakes into his room, he raped her. Tamar put ashes on her head, tore her richly colored robe, and went away crying. Absalom told her to keep quiet, and she lived desolate in his house. Absalom hated Amnon for what he had done and later had him killed. The same name belongs to other women in the Bible, so this Tamar is distinguished as David's daughter.

Tamar was the only daughter of Absalom, the son of King David, and is described as a woman of beautiful appearance (2 Sam 14:27). She had three brothers. Her name means "palm tree," and the STEPBible Proper Names index notes that she shared it with Absalom's sister Tamar, whose story is told in 2 Sam 13. She was probably born in Jerusalem, where her father lived. This entry identifies her as the wife of Uriel of Gibeah and the mother of Maachah. That link is inferred from connected passages. 2 Chr 13:2 calls Maachah (there spelled Michaiah), the mother of King Abijah, a daughter of Uriel of Gibeah, while 1 Kgs 15:2 and 2 Chr 11:20 call her a daughter of Absalom. These accounts are reconciled if Maachah was Absalom's granddaughter through Tamar. The name Tamar belongs to several women in the Bible.

Tanhumeth was the father of Seraiah, one of the army captains who came with their men to Gedaliah at Mizpah after the king of Babylon made Gedaliah governor of Judah following the fall of Jerusalem. Tanhumeth himself does nothing in the text and appears only as Seraiah's father. In 2 Kgs 25:23 the description "the Netophathite" follows his name, which suggests the family came from Netophah, a town near Bethlehem. In the parallel list in Jer 40:8 the same term is attached instead to the sons of Ephai. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him before about 582 BC, a date inferred from the context of Gedaliah's governorship. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "consolation."

Taphath was a daughter of King Solomon. Her only mention is in the list of the twelve officers who supplied food for Solomon's household. There she is named as the wife of the son of Abinadab, usually called Ben-abinadab, who governed the region of Dor on the Mediterranean coast (1 Kgs 4:11). Marrying the king's daughter to a district governor probably tied that official closely to the royal house. Her sister Basmath was likewise married to another of these officers, Ahimaaz (1 Kgs 4:15), and Rehoboam, who succeeded Solomon as king, was her brother. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates her to about 1000 BC, an estimate drawn from Solomon's reign. The meaning of her name is explained differently: Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "ornament," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "distillation" or "drop."

Tappuah was a city in the central hill country of Canaan whose name means "apple" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). It stood on the border between the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, and the boundary ran west from it to the brook Kanah and on to the Mediterranean (Josh 16:8). The surrounding "land of Tappuah" went to Manasseh, but the town itself belonged to Ephraim (Josh 17:8). Josh 17:7 calls the place En-tappuah, probably referring to a nearby spring. A king of Tappuah also appears among the Canaanite kings defeated by Joshua (Josh 12:17). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that this royal city may or may not be the same border town. Several other places share the name. Its site is uncertain. Khirbet Atuf northeast of Nablus has been suggested. The location shown here follows the view placing it south-southwest of Nablus, probably at Sheikh Abu Zarad near Yasuf.

Tappuah was a town in the Shephelah, the lowland of Judah, listed among the cities given to the tribe of Judah between Engannim and Enam (Josh 15:34). The name means "apple." Several places in the Bible share this name, so the town must be told apart from others called Tappuah. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it to be the Canaanite royal city of Josh 12:17, though that verse does not make clear which Tappuah is meant. Its site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes Tristram's proposal of Artuf, near Zorah, and G. A. Smith's suggestion of Tuffuh west of Hebron. It also raises the possibility that this is the same place as Beth-tappuah (Josh 15:53), and concludes that no fully satisfactory identification has been found. The location shown here is only approximate.

Tappuah was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of Caleb's descendants as one of the sons of Hebron, along with his brothers Korah, Rekem and Shema (1 Chr 2:43). Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "apple" or "swelling." Tappuah is also the name of towns in Judah and on the border of Ephraim (for example Josh 15:34). Several names in this part of the Chronicles genealogy match places in Judah, and Hebron itself is a well-known city. For that reason, the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia puts "son" in quotation marks, which suggests the list may partly describe clans or settlements rather than individual people. This entry treats Tappuah as a person, as the verse presents him.

Taralah was a town in the territory given to the tribe of Benjamin. It appears only once, in the list of Benjamin's cities in Josh 18:27, where it is named between Irpeel and Zelah in a group of towns that ends with Jebus, or Jerusalem. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "reeling." Nothing else is said about the town. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Eusebius's Onomasticon says only that it lay in Benjamin, which suggests the site was already unknown by his time, and it has not been identified since. The location shown here is a rough placement in the hill country west of Jerusalem. It is inferred from the town's place among its listed neighbours and should not be taken as a known site.

Tarshish was a distant seaport and trading center, famous for its ships and wealth. Ezekiel describes it as a merchant supplying Tyre with silver, iron, tin and lead (Ezek 27:12), and Jeremiah mentions beaten silver brought from there (Jer 10:9). Isaiah's oracle on Tyre links the two closely (Isa 23:1–14). Jonah tried to flee to Tarshish by boarding a ship at Joppa (Jonah 1:3). The phrase "ships of Tarshish" is used of Solomon's and Jehoshaphat's fleets, some of which were built at Ezion-geber on the Red Sea (1 Kgs 22:48; 2 Chr 20:36). For that reason Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it sometimes simply means large ocean-going ships. Some have placed Tarshish in India or at Carthage. Smith's and Easton's dictionaries identify it with Tartessus, a Phoenician trading center near the mouth of the Guadalquivir in southern Spain, and the location shown here follows that view.

Tarshish (son of Javan) is named in the Table of Nations as one of the four sons of Javan, alongside Elishah, Kittim and Dodanim (Gen 10:4; 1 Chr 1:7). Since Javan was a son of Japheth, Tarshish was a great-grandson of Noah. Nothing is recorded of him beyond his name. As with his brothers, the name probably stands for a people or region as much as for an individual, and the STEPBible proper-names index links him with the ancient city of Tarshish, the distant seaport mentioned often elsewhere in the Old Testament. That place's location is uncertain, and it is commonly placed somewhere in the western Mediterranean. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "contemplation" or "examination." He is distinct from the other men named Tarshish in the Bible.

Tarshish (Prince of Persia) was one of the seven princes of Persia and Media at the court of King Ahasuerus. Esth 1:14 lists him fourth among these men, who "saw the king's face" and "sat the first in the kingdom." In other words, they had direct access to the king and held the highest rank in his government. Judging from the surrounding passage, he was one of the advisers the king consulted, along with the other princes, about Queen Vashti's refusal to appear at his feast. Memucan spoke for the group on that occasion. Nothing else is recorded about Tarshish, and he should not be confused with the place or the other people of the same name in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "contemplation" or "examination."

Tarsus was the chief city of Cilicia, in southeastern Asia Minor, and the birthplace of the apostle Paul. Paul described himself as a Jew born in Tarsus, "a citizen of no mean city," though he was brought up in Jerusalem under Gamaliel (Acts 21:39; 22:3). When he was converted, the Lord directed Ananias to look for "Saul, of Tarsus" in Damascus (Acts 9:11). Later, when his life was threatened in Jerusalem, believers took him to Caesarea and sent him home to Tarsus, and Barnabas went there to find him and bring him to Antioch (Acts 9:30; 11:25). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries describe it as a wealthy commercial city on the river Cydnus, famous for its schools, which Strabo compared to those of Athens and Alexandria. The location shown here is the modern city of Tarsus in southern Turkey, about 10 to 12 miles from the Mediterranean coast.

Tartan was the title of a senior Assyrian military commander. In the King James Version it reads like a personal name, but the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary explain it as an official rank, Assyrian tartanu or turtanu, probably the commander-in-chief and the highest official after the king. It appears in two passages. In Isa 20:1, Sargon king of Assyria sends the Tartan against the Philistine city of Ashdod, and he captures it. In 2 Kgs 18:17, the king of Assyria, named as Sennacherib in the surrounding narrative, sends the Tartan with the Rabsaris and the Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem with a large army. They stop by the conduit of the upper pool to confront King Hezekiah. Because these events happened under two different kings, the two passages probably refer to two different men who held the same office. Neither man's personal name is known.

Tatnai (also spelled Tattenai) was a Persian governor of the province "on this side the river," meaning the territory west of the Euphrates, in the reign of King Darius. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies this king as Darius Hystaspes and dates the episode to about 520 BC. When the Jews who had returned from exile were rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem, Tatnai came with Shetharboznai and their companions and asked who had authorized the work (Ezra 5:3). They then sent a letter to Darius reporting the building and asking that the royal records be checked (Ezra 5:6). Darius found the earlier decree of Cyrus and ordered Tatnai and his associates to stay away from the work (Ezra 6:6), and by inference from the surrounding passage, to support it from royal revenue. Tatnai and his colleagues promptly carried out the king's instructions (Ezra 6:13).

event: Tax Coin in a Fish's Mouth
text: The Tax Coin in a Fish's Mouth was an episode at Capernaum, recorded only in Matthew. The collectors of a tax asked Peter whether his teacher paid it, and Peter said yes. This tax is commonly understood as the annual half-shekel temple tax, by inference from the passage and from Exod 30:13. When Peter came into the house, Jesus spoke first and asked him whether earthly kings collect taxes from their own sons or from others. Peter answered, "from others," and Jesus replied that the sons are therefore exempt. Even so, to avoid giving offence, Jesus told Peter to go to the sea, cast a hook, and open the mouth of the first fish he caught. There he would find a coin to pay the tax for both of them. The episode follows Jesus' second prediction of his death and resurrection and is dated to about AD 29, by inference from context.

event: Teaching and Healing in Perea to Jerusalem
text: The Teaching and Healing in Perea to Jerusalem is the stretch of Jesus' ministry in which he went through towns and villages, teaching as he made his way toward Jerusalem (Luke 13:22). John 10:40–42 places him beyond the Jordan, where many believed in him. This region east of the river is usually called Perea. During this period he warned that many would find the door shut against them, sent a reply to Herod calling him "that fox," and lamented over Jerusalem. He healed on the Sabbath at a Pharisee's house and taught about humility at feasts, about the great supper, and about counting the cost of following him. He told the parables of the lost sheep, the lost coin and the prodigal son, the unjust steward, and the rich man and Lazarus. He also taught about forgiveness and duty. It followed the Feast of Dedication and is dated to about AD 30, by inference from context.

The Teaching by the Fig Tree was a lesson Jesus gave his disciples during Holy Week, about AD 30 by inference from context. Mark sets it on the morning after the temple was cleansed, when the group passing by saw that the fig tree Jesus had cursed the day before had dried up from the roots. Peter pointed it out, and Matthew records the disciples' amazement at how quickly it had withered. Jesus answered by telling them to have faith in God. Anyone who did not doubt could tell a mountain to be thrown into the sea and it would happen, and whatever they asked in prayer, believing, they would receive. Mark adds that when they prayed they were to forgive others, so that their Father in heaven would forgive them. The spot was probably on the road over the Mount of Olives between Bethany and Jerusalem, which is the location shown here.

The Teachings on Humility/Temptation/Reconciliation were a series of instructions Jesus gave the twelve in a house at Capernaum, recorded in Matthew 18, Mark 9 and Luke 9, following the episode of the tax coin in a fish's mouth. After the disciples argued about who was greatest, Jesus set a child among them and said that whoever humbles himself like a child is greatest, and whoever receives such a child in his name receives him. When John reported stopping a man who cast out demons in Jesus' name, Jesus told them not to forbid him. He warned against causing "little ones" to stumble and urged cutting off whatever causes sin. He told of a shepherd seeking a lost sheep and set out steps for confronting a brother who sins. Answering Peter's question about how often to forgive, he told the parable of the unforgiving servant. The date, about AD 29, is an inference from context.

Tebah was a son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, by Nahor's concubine Reumah. He is named first among her four children, listed with Gaham, Thahash and a daughter, Maachah, in Gen 22:24. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him the eldest of Reumah's sons, probably because his name comes first in the list. Through his father he was a half-brother of the eight sons Nahor had by his wife Milcah, among them Huz, Buz, Kemuel and Bethuel, the father of Rebekah. The list appears in a report brought to Abraham after the episode on Mount Moriah. Nothing else is recorded about Tebah's life. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "slaughter," and Hitchcock's Bible Names offers related senses such as "butchery" or "a cook."

Tebaliah was a Levite, the third son of Hosah, named in the list of temple gatekeepers in 1 Chr 26:11. His brothers Hilkiah and Zechariah appear beside him in that verse. Simri, another brother, appears in the surrounding passage, which says Hosah had thirteen sons and brothers in all. Hosah belonged to the clan of Merari, so Tebaliah was a Merarite, and he served among the gatekeepers organized in the time of David. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 1014 BC, an estimate drawn from context. The name is usually taken to mean "the Lord has dipped" or "purified." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the original form may have been Tobiah, meaning "the Lord is good." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Tehaphnehes is a city in Egypt named in Ezekiel's prophecy against Egypt. There the day would be darkened when God broke 'the yokes of Egypt,' its proud strength would end, a cloud would cover it, and its 'daughters' (probably its dependent towns or its people) would go into captivity (Ezek 30:18). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the name as another spelling of Tahpanhes, the city in the eastern Nile Delta that appears in Jeremiah. There it is where Jewish refugees, Jeremiah among them, fled after the fall of Jerusalem (Jer 43:7–9). Tahpanhes is usually identified with the Greek Daphnae, the modern Tell Defenneh, a frontier site near the route between Egypt and Palestine. The location shown here follows that identification.

Tehinnah was a son of Eshton, named in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chr 4:12 alongside his brothers Beth-rapha and Paseah. He is called "the father of Irnahash," which may mean the founder or chief settler of a town called Ir-nahash ("city of Nahash") rather than the parent of a person. Smith's Bible Dictionary reads it this way. The family group is described as "the men of Rechah," a place or clan that is otherwise unknown. The STEPBible names index places him among the descendants of Chelub in the tribe of Judah, following the surrounding verses of the genealogy. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the verse may refer to a settlement after the exile, though it calls the passage very obscure. His name means "supplication" or "entreaty." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Tekoa was a town in the hill country of Judah, south of Bethlehem on the edge of the wilderness that runs down toward the Dead Sea. Joab brought a wise woman from Tekoa to persuade David, through a staged plea, to allow Absalom to return (2 Sam 14:2–9). Rehoboam fortified it along with Bethlehem and Etam (2 Chr 11:6). Jehoshaphat's army went out into the wilderness of Tekoa before facing an invasion (2 Chr 20:20), and Jeremiah called for a trumpet to be blown there as a warning of disaster coming from the north (Jer 6:1). The prophet Amos was one of the herdsmen of Tekoa (Amos 1:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the ruins of Khirbet Tequ'a, about 6 miles (10 km) south of Bethlehem, and the location shown here matches that site.

Tel-abib was a settlement of Jewish exiles beside the river Chebar in Babylonia. Ezekiel went there to the captives, sat among them, and stayed seven days overwhelmed before beginning his work as a prophet (Ezek 3:15). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as Ezekiel's place of residence. The Hebrew name is usually explained as "hill of barley-ears" or "heap of new grain." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a proposal that it renders a Babylonian name meaning "mound of the flood," but treats this as uncertain. Its exact site is unknown. One older view placed the Chebar in upper Mesopotamia at the Khabur River. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia instead place it in southern Babylonia, the latter linking the Chebar to a canal near Nippur. The location shown here follows the Nippur identification and is only approximate.

Tel-harsha was a town or village in Babylonia, listed among the places from which some Jewish exiles returned to Judah after the exile. The King James Version spells it Telharsa in Ezra 2:59 and Telharesha in Neh 7:61. Both lists name it alongside Tel-melah, Cherub, Addan (or Addon) and Immer, and say that the people who came from these places could not prove their family descent or show that they were of Israel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places this return under Zerubbabel and notes that 1 Esdras 5:36 calls the place Thelersas. The name begins with "tel," a mound marking an old settlement. The actual site is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the lowlands of southern Mesopotamia, in present-day Iraq.

Tel-melah was a town in Babylonia, the home of some Jewish exiles who returned to Judah after the exile. It appears only in the parallel lists of returnees in Ezra 2:59 and Neh 7:61, alongside Tel-harsa, Cherub, Addan and Immer. The people who came from these places could not prove their family descent, so they could not show whether they belonged to Israel. The name probably means "hill of salt" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "heap of salt" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it may have stood on the low, salty ground near the Persian Gulf, and that 1 Esdras 5:36 calls it Thermeleth. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in southern Mesopotamia.

Telah was a descendant of Ephraim, son of Joseph, named once in the genealogy of Ephraim's line in 1 Chr 7:25. He was the son of Resheph and the father of Tahan. The list continues for several more generations and ends with Joshua the son of Nun (1 Chr 7:27), so Telah appears among Joshua's ancestors, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. Because the verse's wording is compressed, it is not entirely clear how each name links to the next. This entry follows the usual reading, which makes Telah Resheph's son. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "vigor", while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "moistening" or "greenness."

Telaim was the place where Saul gathered and counted his army before attacking the Amalekites. According to 1 Sam 15:4, the muster numbered two hundred thousand foot soldiers and ten thousand men of Judah. The name means "young lambs," according to Easton's Bible Dictionary. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionary both suggest it is probably the same as Telem, a town in the far south of Judah listed in Josh 15:24. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint and Josephus read Gilgal instead of Telaim, and that some scholars also find the name in 1 Sam 15:7 and 1 Sam 27:8. The exact site is uncertain. The location shown here follows the Telem identification and places it roughly in the Negev south of Hebron, near Tell el-Milh. That fits a staging point for a campaign against the Amalekites, who lived in the southern desert.

Telassar (spelled Thelasar in 2 Kgs 19:12) was a place where "the children of Eden" lived. Sennacherib's messengers name it in their warning to Hezekiah, listing it with Gozan, Haran and Rezeph as peoples his forefathers had destroyed and whose gods had failed to save them (2 Kgs 19:12; Isa 37:12). The name is usually taken to mean "hill of Asshur," or possibly "hill of Assar," a name of the Babylonian god Merodach. Its location is uncertain. Because it appears alongside cities of western Mesopotamia, some link it with Bit Adini (Beth-eden) between the Euphrates and the Balikh. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in southeastern Assyria, probably in Babylonia. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connects it with Til-Assuri, mentioned in Assyrian inscriptions, which may have lain near the western border of Elam. The location shown here follows that Elam identification and is only approximate.

Telem was a town in the far south of Judah. It appears only once, in the list of cities in the Negeb allotted to the tribe of Judah "toward the coast of Edom" (Josh 15:24), where it is named between Ziph and Bealoth. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both suggest it is probably the same place as Telaim, where Saul gathered his army before fighting the Amalekites (1 Sam 15:4). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds that the Greek Septuagint names a place Thelam in 2 Sam 3:12, possibly the same town. Its exact site is unknown. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes a district called Dhullam south of Tel Malhata (el-Milh) and Aroer (Ar'arah) as a suitable match. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the northern Negev.

Telem was a gatekeeper (a "porter" in the King James Version) at the temple in Jerusalem in the time of Ezra. He is named with Shallum and Uri among the gatekeepers in the list of men who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:24). From the surrounding chapter, these men agreed to send their wives away as part of Ezra's reforms after the return from exile. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both suggest he may be the same person as Talmon, a gatekeeper named in Nehemiah, though this is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras gives his name as Tolbanes. Telem is a different man from the southern town of Telem in Judah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "their dew" or "their shadow."

Tema was an oasis town and tribal territory in northern Arabia, known for its caravans. Genesis traces the tribe to Tema, a son of Ishmael, and Easton's Bible Dictionary and others take the place to be named after him. Job 6:19 pictures the caravans of Tema and Sheba looking in vain for water at dried-up streams. In an oracle about Arabia, Isaiah calls on the people of the land of Tema to bring water and bread to fugitives (Isa 21:14). Jeremiah names Tema with Dedan and Buz among the distant peoples who must drink the cup of God's judgment (Jer 25:23). It is generally identified with the modern oasis of Tayma in northwestern Saudi Arabia, on the old caravan route between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Aqaba. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes the ruins of its ancient city wall. The location shown here follows that identification.

Tema was a son of Ishmael, Abraham's son by Hagar. He appears ninth among Ishmael's twelve sons in the genealogy of Gen 25:13–15, and in the parallel list in 1 Chr 1:29–30. Bashemath was his sister. The surrounding passage describes these twelve sons as princes of their own tribes (Gen 25:16), so Tema was probably regarded as the founder of a people. STEPBible's proper-names index links him with the ancient Arabian city of Tema. That place is mentioned elsewhere for its caravans and its people (Job 6:19; Isa 21:14; Jer 25:23) and is generally identified with the oasis of Tayma in northwestern Saudi Arabia. Nothing else is recorded about Tema himself. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "admiration" or "perfection."

Teman was a region, and probably also a town, in Edom, in what is now southern Jordan. The prophets name it alongside Bozrah and "the mount of Esau," sometimes as a stand-in for Edom itself (Amos 1:12; Obad 1:9). Jeremiah asks whether wisdom has vanished from Teman, which suggests it was known for its wise men (Jer 49:7). Eliphaz "the Temanite" in Job probably came from there. Gen 36:11 names a Teman as Esau's grandson, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the region to be named after him. The name means "south." Several prophets announce its desolation, while Habakkuk pictures God coming from Teman (Hab 3:3). Its exact site is unknown. Eusebius placed a town of that name about 15 miles from Petra. Easton's and Smith's dictionaries place it in southern Edom, and the ISBE argues for the north. The location shown here, near modern Ma'an, follows the southern placement.

Teman was a son of Eliphaz and a grandson of Esau. He heads the list of Eliphaz's sons in both genealogies, alongside Omar, Zepho (Zephi in 1 Chr 1:36), Gatam and Kenaz. Chronicles also lists Timna and Amalek with this group. Because Eliphaz was Esau's firstborn, Teman belonged to the leading line of Esau's descendants. Genesis names him first among the 'dukes', or clan chiefs, descended from Eliphaz. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names explain as meaning 'the south,' was also borne by an Edomite clan and district. STEPBible's proper-names index links that clan with a reputation for wisdom. By inference, later references to Teman in Edom, and to Job's friend Eliphaz the Temanite (Job 2:11), trace back to this line. Since the name refers to more than one person or group, which mentions mean the individual and which mean the clan is not always certain.

Teman was one of the chiefs ("dukes" in the King James Version) of Edom, named in the list of chiefs descended from Esau in Gen 36:42 and repeated in 1 Chr 1:53. He appears between the chiefs Kenaz and Mibzar. The surrounding passage (Gen 36:40–43) says these chiefs are named after their families and their places, so the name may refer to a clan or district as much as to an individual. Several people in the Bible share the name. Earlier in the same chapter a Teman is named as a grandson of Esau through Eliphaz and as a chief, and some readers take the two as the same figure or clan. This entry treats the chief in the closing list separately. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "the south."

Temeni was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:6 as one of the four sons Naarah bore to Ashur. His full brothers were Ahuzam, Hepher and Haahashtari. The preceding verse (1 Chr 4:5) calls Ashur "the father of Tekoa" and says he had two wives, Helah and Naarah. The following verse (1 Chr 4:7) names Helah's sons, Zereth, Jezoar and Ethnan, who were Temeni's half-brothers. Coz, listed in 1 Chr 4:8, is also counted here as a half-brother. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as meaning "a southerner," that is, someone from southern Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him at about 1450 BC, an estimate drawn from the genealogy.

The Temple Cleansed was the occasion during Holy Week when Jesus entered the temple in Jerusalem, drove out those buying and selling there, and overturned the tables of the moneychangers and the seats of the dove sellers. Mark adds that he would not let anyone carry goods through the temple. Quoting Scripture (drawn from Isa 56:7 and Jer 7:11), he said God's house should be a house of prayer but they had made it a den of thieves. Matthew reports that he then healed blind and lame people there, while children shouted "Hosanna to the Son of David," which angered the chief priests and scribes. These leaders began looking for a way to destroy him but feared the crowds, who listened closely to his teaching. In Mark the event follows the cursing of the fig tree. It is dated about AD 30 by inference from context. John 2:13–17 describes a similar act early in Jesus' ministry.

The Temple Presentation of Jesus was the occasion when Joseph and Mary brought the infant Jesus to the temple in Jerusalem after Mary's purification under the law of Moses. They presented him to the Lord, as the law required for a firstborn son, and offered a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons. By inference from Lev 12:2–8, this was about forty days after his birth, and the birds were the offering allowed to those who could not afford a lamb. Simeon, a devout man whom the Holy Spirit had promised would see the Lord's Christ before dying, took the child in his arms, praised God, and told Mary that a sword would pierce her own soul. Anna, an elderly widowed prophetess of the tribe of Asher, also gave thanks and spoke of him to those awaiting redemption. The date is about 4 BC, by inference from context.

The Temptations of Jesus were the testing of Jesus by Satan in the wilderness right after John baptized him, about AD 26 by inference from context. Led by the Spirit, Jesus fasted forty days and was then hungry (Matt 4:1–2; Mark 1:12–13). The devil challenged him to turn stones into bread, to throw himself down from a pinnacle of the temple in Jerusalem, and to worship him in exchange for all the kingdoms of the world. Jesus answered each challenge with "It is written," quoting words found in Deut 8:3, 6:16 and 6:13. The devil, in turn, quoted Ps 91:11–12. Matthew and Luke give the last two tests in a different order. Mark adds that Jesus was with the wild beasts. Matthew and Mark say angels then ministered to him, and Luke says the devil left him "for a season" (Luke 4:13).

The Ten Commandments Given is the event at Mount Sinai in which God spoke the core laws of his covenant to Israel. In the third month after leaving Egypt, the Israelites came from Rephidim and camped before the mountain (Exod 19:1–2). Through Moses, God offered to make them his treasured people, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation, and the people agreed to obey (Exod 19:5–8). After two days of preparation, with washed clothes and limits set around the mountain, the third morning brought thunder, lightning, a thick cloud, a loud trumpet, fire and smoke as the mountain shook (Exod 19:10–18). God then spoke the commandments: no other gods, no images, keeping the Sabbath, honoring parents, and bans on killing, adultery, theft, false witness and coveting (Exod 20:1–17). Deut 5 repeats the list. The date, about 1491 BC, is inferred from context.

Terah (spelled Tarah in the King James Version) was a campsite of the Israelites during their wilderness journey. It appears only in the list of stopping places in Numbers 33, where the people moved from Tahath to Tarah and then on to Mithcah (Num 33:27–28). Nothing else is recorded about the site, and its location is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in present-day southern Jordan. It is inferred from its position in the itinerary, which runs between Sinai and the later camps near Ezion-geber and Kadesh. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "stopping" or "station," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "to breathe" or "scent."

Terah, called Thara in Luke 3:34, was the son of Nahor and the father of Abram (Abraham), Nahor and Haran, whom he fathered after reaching the age of seventy. His son Haran died in Ur of the Chaldees and left a son, Lot. Terah then set out from Ur with Abram, Sarai and Lot, intending to go to Canaan.
