They stopped at Haran and settled there, and Terah died in Haran at the age of 205. Joshua later recalled that Terah's family lived beyond the river, meaning the Euphrates, and served other gods. Genesis 11 calls Sarai his daughter-in-law, but in Gen 20:12 Abraham says she is also his father's daughter by another mother, which is why she is counted among Terah's children. By inference from the genealogy, he lived about 2126–1921 BC. He appears in the genealogies of 1 Chr 1:26 and of Jesus in Luke.

Teresh was one of two chamberlains of the Persian king Ahasuerus who guarded the palace door. Esth 2:21 says he and his fellow doorkeeper Bigthan (also spelled Bigthana) became angry and plotted to harm the king. The following verses, Esth 2:22–23, say that Mordecai, who sat in the king's gate, learned of the plot and told Queen Esther, who reported it to the king. After an inquiry both men were hanged, and the matter was written in the royal chronicles. Later, when the king could not sleep and had the chronicles read to him, he heard the account of Mordecai's report against Teresh and Bigthana (Esth 6:2). This led to Mordecai being honored. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "strictness," and Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "severe."

Tertius was the scribe who wrote down Paul's letter to the Romans, presumably at Paul's dictation. In the middle of the closing greetings he added one of his own, "I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you in the Lord" (Rom 16:22), which is the only mention of him in the Bible. His name is Latin for "third." Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he was probably a Roman. Others have thought he was a Roman Christian living in Corinth, where the letter is generally thought to have been written. Some have identified him with Silas, because the Hebrew word shalish also means "third." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Paul seems to have regularly dictated his letters and added only the closing lines in his own hand (2 Thess 3:17; Col 4:18; 1 Cor 16:21). Nothing more is known about Tertius.

Tertullus was an orator, probably a professional advocate, who came with Ananias the high priest and the elders to present their case against Paul before Felix, the Roman governor (Acts 24:1). The setting was Caesarea, where Paul had been sent, and this entry dates the hearing to about AD 56, an estimate inferred from context. Tertullus opened his speech by praising Felix for the peace and reforms the nation enjoyed under him (Acts 24:2). The following verses (Acts 24:5–6) describe how he went on to accuse Paul of stirring up unrest among Jews throughout the world, of leading the sect of the Nazarenes, and of trying to profane the temple. His name is a diminutive of the Latin Tertius, "third." Smith's Bible Dictionary infers he was of Roman or Italian origin, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Roman names were common among Greeks and Jews, so his background is uncertain.

Thahash was a son of Nahor, the brother of Abraham, and Nahor's concubine Reumah. He appears once, in Gen 22:24, among the four children Reumah bore: Tebah, Gaham, Thahash and Maachah. Through his father he was a half-brother of Nahor's eight sons by Milcah, including Huz, Buz, Kemuel and Bethuel, the father of Rebekah. Nothing further is recorded about his life. The name is also spelled Tahash in some modern translations and reference works. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "badger," while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "that makes haste" or "that keeps silence." Like several of Nahor's sons, his name may also have been carried by a later tribe or clan descended from him, but the text itself does not say so.

Tharshish was a member of the tribe of Benjamin, named in a genealogy as one of the seven sons of Bilhan, who was the son of Jediael (1 Chr 7:10). His brothers were Jeush, Benjamin, Ehud, Chenaanah, Zethan and Ahishahar. The brother called Benjamin shares his name with the tribe's ancestor but is a different person. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats Tharshish as the ancestor who gave his name to a Benjamite family. The surrounding passage lists these descendants of Jediael as heads of their fathers' houses and warriors. Nothing else is recorded about him. The same name, usually spelled Tarshish in English, belongs elsewhere in the Bible to other people and to a distant seaport, but those are unrelated to this man.

The Annuciation was the angel Gabriel's announcement to Mary in Nazareth, a town in Galilee, that she would bear a son. Mary was a virgin engaged to Joseph, a descendant of David. Gabriel greeted her as highly favored. When she was troubled by the greeting, he told her not to be afraid: she would conceive and give birth to a son, to be named Jesus, who would be called the Son of the Highest, receive the throne of David, and reign over the house of Jacob forever. Mary asked how this could happen since she had no husband. The angel replied that the Holy Spirit would come upon her, and that her relative Elisabeth, once called barren, was already six months pregnant. Mary accepted, calling herself the Lord's servant. This entry dates the event to about 5 BC, by inference from context.

The church grows is the title for the summary in Acts 2:42–47 of the life of the first believers in Jerusalem after Peter's sermon at Pentecost, about AD 30 by inference from context. The converts devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching, to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer. Awe came on everyone, and the apostles performed many wonders and signs. The believers stayed together and held their property in common, selling possessions and goods and sharing the proceeds with anyone in need. Every day they met together in the temple and broke bread in their homes, eating with gladness and sincerity. They praised God and were viewed favorably by the people, and the Lord added to the church daily those who were being saved. Although the passage describes an ongoing pattern, it follows directly on the Pentecost account and is set in Jerusalem.

The conspiracy to kill Paul was a plot formed in Jerusalem the day after Paul appeared before the Jewish council, about AD 54 by inference from context. More than forty men bound themselves under a curse not to eat or drink until they had killed him. They asked the chief priests and elders to have the council request that the Roman commander bring Paul down again, supposedly for further questioning, so that they could ambush him on the way. Paul's nephew, his sister's son, heard of the plan, went into the fortress and told Paul. Paul had a centurion take the young man to the commander, who heard him privately and ordered him to tell no one. The verses that follow (Acts 23:23–24) record that the commander, named Claudius Lysias in Acts 23:26, then sent Paul under heavy guard to Governor Felix at Caesarea.

The Demoniac refers to Jesus freeing a man possessed by an unclean spirit in the synagogue at Capernaum on a sabbath day. It is recorded in Mark and Luke and dated here to about AD 27, by inference from context, shortly after Jesus called his first fishermen disciples. While Jesus was teaching, the congregation was astonished that he spoke with authority, unlike the scribes. A man with an unclean spirit cried out, "Let us alone," called Jesus "the Holy One of God," and asked whether he had come to destroy them. Jesus rebuked the spirit, told it to be silent and ordered it out. The spirit convulsed the man and cried aloud before leaving. Luke adds that it threw him down in front of the people but did not hurt him. The crowd marveled that even unclean spirits obeyed Jesus' command, and his fame quickly spread throughout the region of Galilee.

The Fall is the account in Genesis 3 of how Adam and Eve disobeyed God in the garden of Eden. The serpent questioned God's command and told the woman that eating from the forbidden tree in the middle of the garden would not kill her but would make them like gods, knowing good and evil. She ate and gave some to her husband, who also ate. Their eyes were opened, they saw they were naked, covered themselves with fig leaves, and hid from God. Questioned, Adam blamed the woman and she blamed the serpent. God cursed the serpent, announced pain in childbirth for the woman, and cursed the ground so the man would toil until he returned to dust. God clothed them in skins and drove them out, setting cherubim and a flaming sword to guard the tree of life. Its date of about 4004 BC is inferred from context.

The flood subsides is the stage of the Great Flood in which the waters drew back and the earth dried. God remembered Noah and the animals in the ark. He sent a wind over the earth and stopped the fountains of the deep and the rain. After 150 days the waters had gone down, and on the seventeenth day of the seventh month the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat. That region is usually identified with ancient Urartu, in present-day eastern Turkey and Armenia. Mountaintops appeared in the tenth month. Noah sent out a raven, then a dove. The dove came back once with nothing, then with an olive leaf, and the third time did not return. By the first day of Noah's 601st year the ground was dry, and by the second month's twenty-seventh day the earth was dried. Noah's sons Shem, Ham and Japheth were with him (Gen 7:13). By inference from context, this lasted about 220 days, around 2347 BC.

The giant in Gath was the Philistine ancestor of four huge warriors from Gath who fought against Israel and were killed by David and his servants (2 Sam 21:22; 1 Chr 20:8). He is never named. The Hebrew term behind "the giant" (rapha) may refer to one father or, more broadly, to a race of giants. Easton's Bible Dictionary links such giants to the Anakim, from whom Goliath came. This entry treats him as a single person. His descendants were Ishbi-benob, who nearly killed David (2 Sam 21:16); Saph, called Sippai in Chronicles, killed by Sibbechai the Hushathite (2 Sam 21:18; 1 Chr 20:4); and an unnamed man with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot (2 Sam 21:20; 1 Chr 20:6). Goliath and Lahmi are counted among them by inference from the related verses, 2 Sam 21:19 and 1 Chr 20:5.

The Good Shepherd Teaching was a discourse of Jesus in Jerusalem, recorded in John 10:1–21, given about AD 29 by inference from context. It follows the healing of a man born blind, and the audience was probably the same Pharisees from that episode. Jesus first told a figure about a sheepfold: the true shepherd enters by the door, calls his sheep by name, and they follow his voice, while a thief climbs in another way. When his hearers did not understand, he called himself the door of the sheep and then the good shepherd, who lays down his life for the sheep, unlike a hired hand who runs from the wolf. He spoke of other sheep not of this fold, and said he had power to lay down his life and take it up again. The sayings divided the Jews. Some said he had a demon, while others asked whether a demon could open the eyes of the blind.

The Great Flood was the deluge described in Genesis 7–8, which began in the six hundredth year of Noah's life, when the fountains of the deep broke open and rain fell for forty days and nights. Noah, his wife, his sons Shem, Ham and Japheth, and their wives entered the ark with pairs of every kind of animal, and the LORD shut them in. The waters rose above the mountains and prevailed for 150 days, and every living creature on dry land died except those in the ark. The ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat, a region usually identified with eastern Turkey and Armenia. Noah sent out a raven and then a dove, which returned with an olive leaf. By the dates given, those aboard spent just over a year in the ark before God told them to go out. The date of about 2348 BC is inferred from biblical chronology.

The Great Flood begins is the opening stage of the flood in Noah's time, when the waters first came upon the earth. Noah was six hundred years old. On the seventeenth day of the second month of that year, the fountains of the great deep burst open and the windows of heaven were opened. Noah went into the ark with his wife, his sons Shem, Ham and Japheth, and their three wives. The animals, clean and unclean, birds and creeping things, came to him in pairs, male and female, as God had commanded, and the LORD shut him in. The waters came seven days later. Rain fell for forty days and forty nights, and the rising waters lifted the ark above the earth. The date of about 2348 BC is an estimate inferred from the biblical chronology, not stated in the text.

The Holy Spirit comes is the name given here to the event at Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit filled the followers of Jesus, apparently the apostles and those gathered with them, shortly after Matthias was chosen to replace Judas. While they were together in one place, a sound like a rushing mighty wind came from heaven and filled the house. Divided tongues like fire appeared and rested on each of them. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages. Devout Jews and converts from many nations were staying in Jerusalem, and a crowd gathered. They were amazed that these Galileans were speaking of God's wonderful works in each listener's native language. Some asked what it meant, while others mocked, saying the men were drunk on new wine. The date of about AD 30 is inferred from context.

The Holy Spirit is promised describes the moment when the risen Jesus, gathered with his apostles, told them not to leave Jerusalem but to wait for "the promise of the Father," which they had already heard from him (Acts 1:4). He contrasted John's baptism with water with the baptism with the Holy Spirit they would receive "not many days hence" (Acts 1:5). The earlier teaching he refers to is probably his words at the Last Supper about sending the Helper, recorded in John 14–16. The location shown here is Olivet, the Mount of Olives, by inference from Acts 1:12, which says the apostles returned to Jerusalem from there after the ascension. The event is dated to about AD 30, by inference from context. The promise looks ahead to the coming of the Spirit at Pentecost described in Acts 2.

The Last Supper was the final meal Jesus shared with his twelve apostles in Jerusalem before his arrest, during Holy Week, about AD 30 by inference from context. On the first day of the feast of unleavened bread, the disciples prepared the Passover in a large furnished upper room that Jesus directed them to find. During the evening meal he announced that one of them would betray him, and each asked, "Is it I?" Judas, after receiving a piece of bread from Jesus, went out into the night. Jesus took bread and a cup, gave thanks, and called them his body and his blood of the new covenant, telling them to do this in remembrance of him. John's account records him washing the disciples' feet as an example. Luke adds a dispute over who was greatest. Peter insisted he would never deny Jesus. After singing a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.

The Samaritan Woman was the meeting between Jesus and a woman of Samaria at Jacob's well near the town of Sychar, about AD 27 by inference from context, as Jesus traveled from Judea toward Galilee. Tired, Jesus sat by the well at about the sixth hour (around noon) while his disciples went into town to buy food, and he asked the woman for a drink. She was surprised, since Jews had no dealings with Samaritans. Jesus spoke of 'living water,' revealed that she had had five husbands, and discussed whether worship belonged on 'this mountain' (probably Mount Gerizim) or in Jerusalem. When she mentioned the coming Messiah, he told her he was that one. She left her waterpot and told the townspeople, many of whom believed. At their request Jesus stayed two days, and more believed, calling him the Saviour of the world.

The Transfiguation (the Transfiguration) was the event in which Jesus took Peter, James and John up a high mountain, where his face shone like the sun and his clothes became dazzling white. Moses and Elijah appeared and talked with him; Luke 9:31 says they spoke of his coming death at Jerusalem. Peter offered to build three shelters, but a bright cloud covered them and a voice said, "This is my beloved Son… hear him." The frightened disciples then saw Jesus alone. Coming down, Jesus told them to tell no one until he had risen from the dead, and he said that Elijah had already come, which they understood to mean John the Baptist. The Gospels do not name the mountain. Christian tradition points to Mount Tabor, while many favor Mount Hermon near Caesarea Philippi. This entry follows Hermon. It is dated about AD 29, by inference from context.

Thebes was a major city of ancient Egypt, called "No" in the King James Version. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains that its Hebrew name, No-amon, means the abode of the god Amon, and that it long served as the capital of Upper Egypt. It stood on both banks of the Nile, at the site of modern Luxor and Karnak. The location shown here follows that identification. Jeremiah and Ezekiel name it among the Egyptian cities facing judgment. They speak of punishing "the multitude of No" along with Pharaoh and Egypt's gods (Jer 46:25), and of No being "rent asunder" (Ezek 30:14–16). Nahum warns Nineveh by pointing to "populous No," a city set among rivers with water as its defence, which had nonetheless fallen (Nah 3:8). This probably refers to the Assyrian sack of Thebes in the seventh century BC.

Thebez was a town attacked by Abimelech, the son of Gideon (Jerubbaal) who had made himself king at Shechem. Judg 9:50 says he camped against Thebez and took it. By inference from its placement right after the destruction of Shechem, Thebez had probably joined Shechem's revolt against him, as Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests. The following verses (Judg 9:51–54) tell how the townspeople fled to a strong tower inside the city. When Abimelech came near to burn it, a woman dropped a piece of millstone on his head from the wall, and he died there. The incident was remembered long afterward. In 2 Sam 11:21, Joab expects David to cite it as a warning against going too close to a city wall. Easton's, Smith's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify Thebez with the village of Tubas, northeast of Nablus, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Theophilus was the man to whom the Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the Apostles are addressed. The author says he wrote his orderly account so that Theophilus would have it (Luke 1:3). Acts opens by addressing him again and referring back to that "former treatise" about what Jesus did and taught (Acts 1:1). His name means "friend of God" or "loved by God." Luke calls him "most excellent," the same title Paul uses for the Roman governors Felix and Festus (Acts 23:26; 26:25). From this, Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary conclude that he was probably a person of rank, perhaps a Roman official. Some have suggested the name stands for any Christian reader, but the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the title to point to a real individual. Nothing more is known of him, and later traditions about his life are uncertain.

There, rendered in modern translations as "The Lord Is There" (Hebrew Yahweh-shammah), is the name given to the city at the very end of Ezekiel's vision of a restored land. In Ezek 48:35 the prophet gives the city's circumference as eighteen thousand measures, which the surrounding chapter describes as reeds or cubits, and declares that from that day its name will be "The LORD is there." The name marks the city as the place of God's presence, set within the redistributed tribal territories of Ezekiel's closing chapters. Ezekiel does not call this city Jerusalem in the verse, and readers have understood it either as a restored Jerusalem or as an idealized visionary city. The location shown here follows the Jerusalem identification, placing it on the site of the historic city.

Thessalonica was a major city of Macedonia at the head of the Thermaic Gulf, today the Greek city of Thessaloniki. Paul came there on his second missionary journey after passing through Amphipolis and Apollonia, and preached in its Jewish synagogue (Acts 17:1). The uproar that followed, about AD 48 by inference from context, drove him on to Berea. The Bereans were contrasted favourably with the Thessalonian Jews, and some of those Jews followed Paul to Berea to stir up the crowds (Acts 17:11, 13). Aristarchus, Paul's companion on the voyage to Rome, was a Macedonian from Thessalonica (Acts 27:2). The Philippian church sent Paul support more than once while he was there (Phil 4:16), and Demas later left Paul to go there (2 Tim 4:10). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the city was named after Cassander's wife Thessalonica and was a provincial capital under Rome.

Theudas was a man who led a short-lived uprising, mentioned only in the speech of the Pharisee Gamaliel to the Jewish council during the trial of the apostles. Gamaliel recalls that some time earlier Theudas claimed to be someone important and gathered about four hundred followers. He was killed, and his followers were scattered and came to nothing (Acts 5:36). Gamaliel used his case, along with that of Judas of Galilee in the next verse, to argue that a movement of merely human origin would fail by itself. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as leading an insurrection against Roman authority. The historian Josephus tells of a Theudas who led a similar movement under the emperor Claudius, about AD 44. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats Luke's Theudas as a different and earlier man, probably one of the rebel leaders active near the end of Herod the Great's reign. Beyond this nothing is known of him.

The Third Missionary Journey was Paul's third preaching tour in Acts, dated here to about AD 50 and lasting roughly four years, both estimates inferred from context. It centered on Ephesus. Before Paul arrived, Aquila and Priscilla instructed Apollos of Alexandria there, who then went on to Achaia. Paul baptized about twelve disciples who had known only John's baptism, taught daily in the school of Tyrannus for two years, and saw former practitioners of magic burn their books. A riot stirred up by the silversmith Demetrius, whose trade in shrines of Diana was threatened, ended when the town clerk dismissed the crowd. Paul then spent three months in Greece, returned through Macedonia, revived a fallen young man at Troas, and sailed by Assos and Mitylene, hurrying to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost. Later, at Caesarea, he stayed with Philip the Evangelist, and Agabus warned him of arrest (Acts 21:8–11).

The Third Missionary Journey Begins is the opening episode of Paul's third journey as presented in this entry, though it centres on Apollos at Ephesus rather than on Paul. According to Acts 18:23, which comes just before this passage, Paul set out through Galatia and Phrygia. Meanwhile Apollos, a Jew born in Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was eloquent and well versed in the scriptures. He had been taught the way of the Lord and taught it carefully and with zeal, but he knew only the baptism of John. When he spoke boldly in the synagogue, Aquila and Priscilla took him aside and explained the way of God to him more fully. When he wanted to go on to Achaia, the believers wrote ahead urging the disciples there to welcome him. In Achaia he was a great help to the believers and publicly refuted the Jews, showing from the scriptures that Jesus was the Christ. A date of about AD 50 is inferred from context.

Thomas was one of the twelve apostles of Jesus, named in every list of the apostles. His name means "twin," and John's Gospel adds that he was called Didymus, the Greek word for twin. Most of what is known about him comes from John. When Jesus decided to return to Judea after Lazarus died, Thomas urged the other disciples to go too, "that we may die with him." Later he asked Jesus how they could know the way when they did not know where he was going. He was absent when the risen Jesus first appeared to the disciples and, according to John 20:25, refused to believe without touching the wounds. Eight days later Jesus appeared again and invited him to do so, and Thomas answered, "My Lord and my God." He was afterward among the disciples by the Sea of Galilee and among the eleven in the upper room in Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions a suggestion that Thomas, Matthew and James son of Alphaeus were brothers.

Three Taverns was a stopping place on the Appian Way, the main Roman road from the south into Rome. When Paul was being taken to Rome as a prisoner, believers from the city heard he was coming and went out to meet him, some as far as Appii Forum and others at Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, he thanked God and took courage (Acts 28:15). The Latin name, Tres Tabernae, means "three shops," and Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as a halting place for travelers where several roads joined the Appian Way. Accounts of its distance from Rome differ. Easton's gives about 11 miles, while Smith's Bible Dictionary, working from the distances in the ancient Antonine Itinerary, places it near modern Cisterna, about 33 miles from the city. The location shown here follows the Cisterna identification. By inference from context, Paul's arrival there falls around AD 57.

Throne, called the Hall of the Throne in modern translations such as the ESV, was a hall in Solomon's palace complex in Jerusalem where the king sat to give judgment. 1 Kgs 7:7 says Solomon built this "porch for the throne," also called the porch of judgment, and panelled it in cedar from floor to floor. The STEPBible proper-names index treats the Hall of the Throne and the Hall of Judgment as two names for the same room. It was one of several buildings Solomon put up alongside the temple. The throne that stood there was probably the ivory-and-gold throne with six steps described in 1 Kgs 10:18–20, though the text does not say so directly. No trace of the building survives. The location shown here places it within Solomon's palace area on the hill just south of the Temple Mount.

Thyatira was a city in western Asia Minor, in the Roman province of Asia. It was the home city of Lydia, a seller of purple cloth who heard Paul's preaching and responded to it (Acts 16:14). By the context of that chapter, they met at Philippi, where she was evidently trading. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note that Thyatira was famous for its dyeing industry and its trade guilds, which fits Lydia's business. Thyatira was also one of the seven churches of Asia to which the book of Revelation was sent (Rev 1:11). The message to its church is introduced as coming from the Son of God (Rev 2:18). It addresses separately those in Thyatira who had not accepted a certain teaching (Rev 2:24). The city is identified with modern Akhisar in western Turkey, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Tiberias was a city on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, which John's Gospel also calls the Sea of Tiberias after it (John 6:1; 21:1). Its only direct mention in the Bible is John 6:23, where boats come from Tiberias to the area where Jesus had fed the crowd. Smith's Bible Dictionary, drawing on Josephus, says Herod Antipas built the city and named it after the Roman emperor Tiberius. Easton's Bible Dictionary dates its founding to about AD 16, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia to about AD 26. The city had a strong Greek and Roman character, and the Gospels never record Jesus visiting it. After the fall of Jerusalem it became a major center of Jewish learning, where the Mishnah and the Jerusalem Talmud were compiled. The modern city of Tiberias, in Israel, stands at or near the ancient site, which matches the location shown here.

Tiberius was the Roman emperor whose reign Luke uses to date the start of John the Baptist's preaching: "the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar" (Luke 3:1). Luke 3:1 is the only place he is named in the Bible. In the same verse Luke lists the local rulers of the time, including Pontius Pilate as governor of Judea and Herod as tetrarch of Galilee. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary identify him as Tiberius Claudius Nero, the stepson and successor of Augustus, who reigned from AD 14 until his death in AD 37. On that basis Jesus' ministry and crucifixion took place under him. Easton's notes that the "Caesar" mentioned in the Gospel debates about paying tribute, and in Pilate's trial of Jesus (as in John 19:12), would by inference be Tiberius.

Tibhath was a city belonging to Hadarezer (Hadadezer), king of the Aramean kingdom of Zobah. After defeating Hadarezer, David took a great quantity of bronze from Tibhath and from Chun, another of his cities. Solomon later used this bronze to make the bronze sea, the pillars and the bronze vessels of the temple (1 Chr 18:8). The parallel account in 2 Sam 8:8 names the city Betah, which Smith's Bible Dictionary treats as the same place. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the Tubihi named in Egyptian records alongside Kadesh on the Orontes. It places the city on the eastern slopes of the Anti-Lebanon range, within Zobah's territory. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only approximate and places it in the region of the Beqaa Valley in modern Lebanon.

Tibni was the son of Ginath and a rival of Omri for the throne of Israel. After Zimri's brief reign ended in his death, the people of Israel split into two factions: half followed Tibni to make him king, and half followed Omri (1 Kgs 16:21). Omri's supporters eventually prevailed, Tibni died, and Omri became sole king (1 Kgs 16:22). The text does not say how Tibni died. Comparing the date of Zimri's reign in 1 Kgs 16:15 with the start of Omri's reign in 1 Kgs 16:23 suggests the contest lasted about four years. This entry places it at roughly 929–925 BC, by inference from context. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Omri was the army's choice, while Tibni was probably backed by the people of Tirzah. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a man of some standing. These two verses are the only biblical mentions of him.

Tidal was the "king of nations" (Hebrew goyim, sometimes rendered Goiim) named in Gen 14:1 as one of four eastern kings in the days of Abraham, allied with Chedorlaomer king of Elam, Amraphel king of Shinar and Arioch king of Ellasar. Together these four fought against five kings of the cities of the plain, in the battle in the vale of Siddim (Gen 14:9). Genesis says nothing else about him, and what "nations" he ruled is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes goyim as Gutium, a land east of the Tigris and north of Elam. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he led various nomadic tribes. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links his name with Tudhula in a late Babylonian text and with the Hittite royal name Tudhaliya, suggesting he may have been a Hittite ruler, though it treats the identification as uncertain. The Greek Septuagint renders his name Thargal.

Hiddekel is the Hebrew name of the river known as the Tigris. Gen 2:14 lists it as the third of the four rivers flowing out of Eden, describing it as the river that runs east of Assyria, alongside the Euphrates. In Dan 10:4 Daniel was standing beside "the great river, which is Hiddekel" when he received a vision. The Greek Septuagint translates the name as Tigris, and Smith's Bible Dictionary links "Dekel" with Digla, a name the river has carried through the ages, preserved in the modern Arabic Dijleh. The Tigris rises in the mountains of eastern Turkey and flows southeast through Iraq, past the site of Nineveh, to join the Euphrates near the Persian Gulf. The location shown here is a rough point on the modern Tigris in northern Iraq. The river's course in the Eden account may have differed from its present one.

Tikvah, also spelled Tikvath, was the son of Hasrah and the father of Shallum, the husband of the prophetess Huldah. He is mentioned only in her genealogy, in the account of how King Josiah's officials consulted Huldah in Jerusalem after the book of the law was found in the temple (2 Kgs 22:14; 2 Chr 34:22). His father's name appears as Harhas in Kings and Hasrah in Chronicles. Either Shallum or Tikvah's line is described as "keeper of the wardrobe"; the wording does not make clear which. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "hope" and notes that the Chronicles form is properly read Tokhath. It places him before about 632 BC, a date inferred from the time of Josiah. The name Tikvah is also borne by at least one other man in the Bible.

Tikvah was the father of Jahaziah, a man named in Ezra 10:15 during the crisis over Israelite men who had married foreign wives after the return from exile. His son Jahaziah and Jonathan son of Asahel are singled out in that verse. The King James Version says they were "employed about this matter," but many modern translations read the Hebrew as saying they opposed the plan. STEPBible's proper-names index follows the opposing reading. Nothing else is recorded about Tikvah himself. His name means "hope" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). The same name belongs to another man in the Bible, the father-in-law of the prophetess Huldah in the time of King Josiah, who is a different person from this Tikvah.

Tilgath-pilneser is the spelling used in Chronicles for Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, who also appears in 2 Kgs 15:29 and 16:7. He carried the Reubenites, Gadites and half tribe of Manasseh into exile at Halah, Habor, Hara and the river Gozan, among them Beerah, a Reubenite prince (1 Chr 5:6, 26). When Ahaz of Judah turned to him for help, he came but distressed him rather than strengthening him (2 Chr 28:20). This entry identifies him with Pul, who received a thousand talents of silver from Menahem of Israel to secure his throne (2 Kgs 15:19). Easton's Bible Dictionary explains Pul as his throne-name in Babylon, though 1 Chr 5:26 names the two side by side, and some treat them as separate kings. This entry also links him with "king Jareb" (Hos 5:13; 10:6), which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes as an epithet meaning roughly "King Contentious". Whom that title refers to is uncertain.

Tilon was a son of Shimon and one of four brothers, with Amnon, Rinnah and Ben-hanan, named in the genealogies of the tribe of Judah (1 Chr 4:20). Nothing more is recorded about him, and Shimon himself is not otherwise identified or linked to the families around him in the list. Ancient manuscripts and translations spell the name differently, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes Greek forms such as Thilan and Tholeim. The meaning of the name is uncertain: Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "gift," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "murmuring."

Timaeus was the father of Bartimaeus, the blind beggar who sat by the roadside as Jesus left Jericho with his disciples and a large crowd (Mark 10:46). He is named only in this verse, and nothing else is recorded about him. His name appears in Greek form, and the name Bartimaeus is itself a combination of the Aramaic word bar, meaning "son," with his father's name, so it simply means "son of Timaeus." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the Greek name Timaeus to mean "honorable," while Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning "defiled." The parallel accounts of the healing in Matt 20:29–34 and Luke 18:35–43 do not name the blind man or his father.

Timna was a concubine of Eliphaz, Esau's son, and the mother of Amalek (Gen 36:12). 1 Chr 1:39 names a Timna as the sister of Lotan, one of the sons of Seir the Horite. Smith's Bible Dictionary presumes that the two are the same woman, and this entry follows that view, which makes her a daughter of Seir and a sister of Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer and Dishan. That would mean a Horite woman was joined to Esau's line. In the list of Eliphaz's descendants at 1 Chr 1:36, Timna's name appears next to Amalek's, apparently a shortened form of the Genesis account. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name Timna also appears for a chief or clan of Edom, so several figures bear it.

Timnah was a town on the northern border of Judah's territory, near Beth-shemesh (Josh 15:10). Judah went up to Timnah (spelled Timnath in the King James Version) to shear his sheep, and Tamar waited for him by the road leading there (Gen 38:12–14). In Samson's day it was a Philistine town with vineyards. Samson saw a Philistine woman there whom he wanted to marry, and a young lion roared at him near its vineyards (Judg 14:1–5). In the reign of Ahaz the Philistines took Timnah and its villages and settled there (2 Chr 28:18). Several places in the Bible share this name. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the Timnah of Genesis may be a different town in the hill country of Judah, but this entry treats it as the same border town. Older dictionaries placed it at Tibneh, west of Beth-shemesh. The location shown here is the nearby Tel Batash in the Sorek Valley.

Timnah was a town in the hill country of Judah, named in Josh 15:57 alongside Cain and Gibeah as the last of a group of ten cities with their villages assigned to the tribe of Judah. Several places in the Bible share this name. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats this Timnah as distinct from the better-known Timnah on Judah's northern border, the town associated with Samson. Nothing else is recorded about it. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Tibna, near Jeba', and the location shown here, in the hills southwest of Bethlehem, follows that identification. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "portion", while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "forbidding".

Timnah was one of the chiefs, called "dukes" in the King James Version, descended from Esau and listed among the leaders of Edom. He heads the list of chiefs named "according to their families, after their places" in Gen 36:40, and the same list is repeated in 1 Chr 1:51, where it follows the death of King Hadad. Because these chiefs are named by their places, Timnah may be the name of a clan or district as well as a person. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests there was probably a place called Timna in Edom, noting that the early writers Eusebius and Jerome knew of a Thamna there. The name also recalls Timna, Esau's son's concubine and Lotan's sister, mentioned earlier in Genesis 36, though any link is uncertain. Nothing further is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "forbidding."

Timnath-heres was the town in the hill country of Ephraim where Joshua was buried, within the bounds of his own inheritance and on the north side of the hill Gaash (Judg 2:9). The name is usually explained as "portion of the sun." In Joshua 19:50 and 24:30 the same place is called Timnath-serah, with the letters of "heres" reversed. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that scholars differ over which form is original, that the change may have been made to avoid a name suggesting sun worship, and that Jewish and Samaritan tradition treats Heres as the original. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it about 10 miles southwest of Shechem. The site is uncertain. Some identify it with Khirbet Tibnah, others with the village of Kifl Haris, where Jewish and Samaritan tradition locates Joshua's tomb. The location shown here follows the Kifl Haris identification.

Timnath-serah was the city in the hill country of Ephraim that the Israelites gave to Joshua at his request, as the LORD had directed, once the land had been divided among the tribes. Joshua rebuilt it and lived there (Josh 19:50). When he died, about 1424 BC by inference from context, he was buried within the border of his inheritance there, on the north side of the hill of Gaash (Josh 24:30). Judg 2:9 gives the name as Timnath-heres. There are two main proposed sites. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it at Kefr Haris, about 10 miles south-west of Shechem, which matches Jewish and Samaritan traditions of Joshua's tomb there. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia prefers Tibneh, north-east of Lydda, where rock-cut tombs were linked with Joshua as early as Eusebius. The location shown here follows the Kefr Haris (Kifl Haris) identification.

Timon was one of the seven men chosen by the believers in Jerusalem to take charge of the daily distribution of food to the community's widows, so that the apostles could devote themselves to prayer and teaching. He is named fifth in the list, after Stephen, Philip, Prochorus and Nicanor (Acts 6:5). The seven are traditionally called "deacons," though the passage does not use that title. This event is dated to about AD 30, by inference from context. Timon's name is Greek, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "honorable" or "worthy." Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he was probably a Greek-speaking Jew. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that only Nicolas is singled out as a proselyte, which implies Timon was probably Jewish by birth. As Easton's Bible Dictionary observes, nothing further is known of him.

Timotheus, the King James form of Timothy, was a disciple from the Lystra and Derbe area who became one of Paul's closest companions. His mother, Eunice, was a believing Jewish woman and his father was a Greek (Acts 16:1). He joined Paul and Silas on the second missionary journey and stayed behind at Berea before rejoining Paul at Athens and then Corinth (Acts 17:14–15; 18:5). Paul sent him on errands to Thessalonica, Macedonia, Corinth and Philippi, and he travelled with Paul into Asia (1 Thess 3:2, 6; Acts 19:22; 20:4). He is named as co-sender of several of Paul's letters, and Paul calls him his "son in the faith" (1 Tim 1:2), a phrase usually taken to mean Paul had converted him. Two letters, 1 and 2 Timothy, are addressed to him. Heb 13:23 reports his release from custody. Easton's Bible Dictionary records a tradition that he later worked in Ephesus and died a martyr there.

The Timothy Joins Paul and Silas episode took place early in Paul's second missionary journey, when Paul and Silas came to Derbe and Lystra in southern Asia Minor. There they met a disciple named Timothy (Timotheus). His mother was a Jewish believer and his father was a Greek, and the believers at Lystra and Iconium spoke well of him. Paul wanted Timothy to travel with him, so he circumcised him because the Jews in that region all knew his father was Greek. As the group moved through the cities, they passed on the decisions reached by the apostles and elders in Jerusalem for the churches to follow, by inference the decrees of Acts 15. The churches grew stronger in the faith and increased in number daily. The date, about AD 47, and a span of roughly a month are estimates inferred from context.

Tiphsah was a city on the Euphrates River that marked the northeastern limit of Solomon's dominion, with Azzah (Gaza) as the opposite limit in the southwest (1 Kgs 4:24). The name means "ford" or "crossing." Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with Thapsacus, a wealthy town on the western bank of the Euphrates where the main caravan route between east and west crossed the river. The ISBE places it probably at the modern Qal'at Dibse in northern Syria, and the location shown here follows that Euphrates identification. The same name appears in 2 Kgs 15:16, where King Menahem attacks a Tiphsah. The name is shared by more than one place, and some scholars, such as Conder (noted in Easton's), connect that passage with Khurbet Tafsah near Shechem.

Tiphsah was a town attacked by Menahem king of Israel, who struck it, its people and its surrounding territory starting from Tirzah because its inhabitants would not open their gates to him. The text records that he also ripped open its pregnant women (2 Kgs 15:16). The name means "ford" or "crossing." Its location is uncertain, and the name is shared with another place. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects this Tiphsah with the Tiphsah of Solomon's northern boundary (1 Kgs 4:24), the town of Thapsacus on the Euphrates, which would make this a long campaign far from Israel. It also notes Conder's identification with Khirbet Tafsah, about 6 miles west of Shechem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some Greek manuscripts read a name close to Tirzah. The location shown here follows the Khirbet Tafsah identification near Nablus, which fits a town in the region of Tirzah.

Tiras was a son of Japheth and a grandson of Noah. He appears only in the genealogy of the nations descended from Noah after the flood, which names him last among Japheth's seven sons, after Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal and Meshech (Gen 10:2; 1 Chr 1:5). Easton's Bible Dictionary takes this to mean he was the youngest. Nothing else is recorded about him. As with the other names in this list, Tiras was probably understood as the ancestor of a people. Ancient commentators, including Josephus, linked him with the Thracians. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia prefers a connection with the Tursenioi, seafaring peoples of the Aegean coasts sometimes identified with the Etruscans, and mentions a further suggestion that Tiras is the same as Tarshish. Which people the name stands for remains uncertain.

Tirhakah was a king of Ethiopia (Cush) whose army marched out to fight Sennacherib of Assyria during the Assyrian invasion of Judah in the reign of King Hezekiah. When Sennacherib heard that Tirhakah was coming against him, he sent messengers back to Hezekiah with a further demand that Jerusalem surrender (2 Kgs 19:9; Isa 37:9). These two parallel verses are his only mentions in the Bible. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies him with Taharqa, a ruler of Egypt and Cush, called Tarqu in Assyrian inscriptions. It dates his reign from about 693 to 667 BC and says he was later defeated by the Assyrian kings Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal and died in Cush. Because Sennacherib's campaign is usually dated to 701 BC, before that accession, some suggest Tirhakah was acting for an earlier pharaoh, while others think two campaigns have been combined.

Tirhanah was a son of Caleb and his concubine Maachah, named once in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah (1 Chr 2:48). His brother Sheber is named alongside him in the same verse. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies this Caleb as Caleb son of Hezron, which fits the surrounding genealogy of Hezron's descendants. Through his father he had a number of siblings and half-siblings, including Achsa, Hur and Moza, and his mother is also linked with further sons in the following verse. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "favor." Nothing else is recorded about his life or descendants.

Tiria was a son of Jehaleleel, named only in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chr 4:16, where his brothers are listed as Ziph, Ziphah and Asareel. Nothing else is recorded about him. His family belongs to Judah because the list falls within that tribe's genealogy, although the passage does not say how Jehaleleel was connected to the main lines. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "fear" and dates him to about 1451 BC, an estimate rather than a date given in the text. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as "searching out." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some Greek manuscripts leave the name out or spell it differently.

Tirzah was a city in the hill country of central Israel. Its king appears among the Canaanite rulers defeated by Joshua (Josh 12:24). It later served as a royal residence and capital of the northern kingdom. Jeroboam's household lived there (1 Kgs 14:17), and Baasha, Elah, Zimri and Omri reigned from it. Elah was assassinated there by Zimri, who ruled for seven days before Omri besieged the city. According to 1 Kgs 16:18, Zimri then burned the palace over himself. After six years Omri moved the capital to Samaria (1 Kgs 16:23–24). Menahem set out from Tirzah to kill Shallum and seize the throne (2 Kgs 15:14). The Song of Solomon compares the beloved's beauty to Tirzah (Song 6:4). Its site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions Teiasir and Telluza, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds et-Tireh. The location shown here follows the Telluza identification, a village north-east of Nablus.

Tirzah was one of the five daughters of Zelophehad, a descendant of Manasseh son of Joseph through Machir, Gilead and Hepher (Num 27:1; Josh 17:3). Because Zelophehad had no sons, she and her sisters Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah and Milcah came forward about their father's inheritance. By inference from the surrounding passages, they were granted land among his clan in place of male heirs (Num 26:33; Num 27:1; Josh 17:3). Later, the sisters married sons of their father's brothers, which kept the land within their tribe (Num 36:11). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary call her the youngest, since she is usually named last, although Num 36:11 lists her second. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of her name as "pleasing". The same name belongs to the city of Tirzah, a royal city of the northern kingdom (1 Kgs 15:33), which is a separate place.

Tishbe was the hometown of the prophet Elijah, who is called "the Tishbite" when he first appears to tell King Ahab that no dew or rain would fall except at his word (1 Kgs 17:1). The same verse says he was "of the inhabitants of Gilead." Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the Hebrew word for "inhabitants" matches "Tishbite," so the Greek Septuagint reads "Elijah the Tishbite of Tishbi in Gilead." Its location is uncertain. Josephus places it in Gilead, east of the Jordan, and some identify it with el-Ishtib in the Gilead hills, about 22 miles south of the Sea of Galilee. Easton's prefers a Tishbi in Upper Galilee, the territory of Naphtali, mentioned in the apocryphal book of Tobit, from which Elijah would later have moved to Gilead. The location shown here follows the Upper Galilee identification.

Titus was a Greek Christian and a close companion and co-worker of Paul. Paul took him to Jerusalem with Barnabas, and he was not required to be circumcised (Gal 2:1–3). Paul calls him his brother, his partner and fellow helper, and his own son in the common faith (2 Cor 2:13; 8:23; Titus 1:4). Paul sent him to Corinth, where he began the church's collection and was asked to finish it. Paul looked for him anxiously, and Titus later met him in Macedonia and comforted him with news from Corinth (2 Cor 2:13; 7:6–14; 8:6, 16; 12:18). The letter to Titus is addressed to him, and its next verse (Titus 1:5) says Paul had left him in Crete. In Paul's last letter Titus has gone to Dalmatia (2 Tim 4:10). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that he is never named in Acts.

Tob, "the land of Tob", was a district east of the Jordan where Jephthah went after his half-brothers drove him out of his family home. There he gathered a band of "vain men", worthless or reckless followers, who went out raiding with him (Judg 11:3). When the Ammonites made war on Israel, the elders of Gilead came to Tob to bring him back as their commander (Judg 11:5). The story implies that Tob lay not far from Gilead. Smith's Bible Dictionary and others take the "men of Ish-tob" who joined the Ammonites against David (2 Sam 10:6, 8) to be men of this same region. The name means "good". Its location is uncertain. The Talmud links it with the district of Hippos east of the Sea of Galilee, while Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia favour et-Taiyibeh, south of Gadara. The location shown here follows the et-Taiyibeh identification.

Tobadonijah was a Levite whom King Jehoshaphat of Judah sent out with other Levites and with the priests Elishama and Jehoram. He is named only in 2 Chr 17:8, where he is listed last among nine Levites, directly after Adonijah and Tobijah. The surrounding passage (2 Chr 17:7–9) explains that in the third year of his reign Jehoshaphat sent officials, Levites and priests through the cities of Judah to teach the people from the book of the law, so Tobadonijah probably took part in that teaching mission. His name is usually explained as meaning "good is the Lord" or "my Lord is good." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name may have arisen from a copying slip that combined the two names just before it, Tobijah and Adonijah. This entry treats him as a distinct person, as the text presents him.

Tobiah was the ancestor of a family that returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel, probably before about 536 BC by inference from context. His descendants were listed with those of Delaiah and Nekoda, totaling 652 in Ezra 2:60 and 642 in the parallel list at Neh 7:62. The surrounding passage (Ezra 2:59; Neh 7:61) places these families among returnees who could not show their father's house or prove they were of Israelite descent. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat Tobiah as the head or namesake of this family. Nothing else is known of him. The name, meaning "the Lord is good" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, is shared by several people, and this Tobiah is distinct from Tobiah the Ammonite who opposed Nehemiah.

Tobiah, called "the servant" and "the Ammonite," was one of the chief opponents of Nehemiah's rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls. With Sanballat the Horonite and Geshem the Arabian he was angered by Nehemiah's arrival, mocked the work, and jeered that a fox could break down the stone wall (Neh 4:3). He and Sanballat hired a prophet to frighten Nehemiah. Tobiah kept up a correspondence with nobles of Judah and sent letters to intimidate Nehemiah. Neh 6:18 explains these ties: he was son-in-law of Shecaniah, and his son Johanan married the daughter of Meshullam son of Berechiah. Later the priest Eliashib, who was allied to him, gave him a room in the temple courts. When Nehemiah returned to Jerusalem, he threw out Tobiah's belongings. His name means "the Lord is good" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other people in the Bible share the name.

Tobijah was a Levite in the reign of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. He is one of nine Levites named in 2 Chr 17:8, sent out with the officials Jehoshaphat appointed and with the priests Elishama and Jehoram. The surrounding passage says they went through the cities of Judah teaching the people from the book of the law. His name means "the LORD is good," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, which also notes that the Greek Septuagint leaves the name out of this list. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the mission to about 910 BC, an estimate drawn from the chronology of Jehoshaphat's reign. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a returned exile in Zechariah's time and Tobiah the Ammonite who opposed Nehemiah. This Levite is distinct from them.

Tobijah was one of the returned exiles who came from Babylon to Jerusalem in the time of the prophet Zechariah. He is named with Heldai and Jedaiah. Zechariah was told to take silver and gold from these men and make crowns, which were set on the head of Joshua the high priest (Zech 6:10–11). Afterward the crowns were to be kept in the temple of the LORD as a memorial to Tobijah and his companions (Zech 6:14). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint translates his name as a descriptive word rather than as a personal name. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the episode to about 519 BC. The name Tobijah means "the LORD is good" and belongs to several people in the Bible. This Tobijah should not be confused with the others who bear it.

Tochen was a town of the tribe of Simeon, listed in 1 Chr 4:32 with Etam, Ain, Rimmon and Ashan as one of a group of five cities with their villages. It is mentioned only here. The parallel list of Simeon's towns in Josh 19:7 does not include it, but the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint gives a name, Thokka, at that point, and infers that Tochen dropped out of the Hebrew text there. Its name is usually explained as meaning "measure" or "task" (Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary), while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "middle." The site has not been identified. Because Simeon's towns lay within Judah's territory in the south, it probably stood in the Negev region, and the location shown here is only a rough placement.

Togarmah was a son of Gomer and grandson of Japheth, listed with his brothers Ashkenaz and Riphath in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:3; 1 Chr 1:6). The name also refers to a people descended from him, called "the house of Togarmah." Ezekiel describes them trading horses, horsemen and mules in the markets of Tyre (Ezek 27:14). Elsewhere he places them in "the north quarters" as part of the forces gathered with Gog (Ezek 38:6). Their homeland is not stated in the text. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify it with Armenia, the ISBE favouring southeastern Armenia or a region connected with it. The ISBE notes that the Armenians themselves traced their ancestry to a figure they called Thorgom, a form of the name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "which is all bone."

Toi was king of Hamath in the time of David. He is also called Tou in 1 Chr 18:9–10. Hadadezer (Hadarezer), king of Zobah, had been at war with him. When Toi heard that David had defeated Hadadezer's whole army, he sent his son Joram to greet David, to ask after his welfare and to congratulate him on the victory. Joram brought gifts of silver, gold and bronze. The Chronicles account names the son Hadoram. Smith's Bible Dictionary places Hamath on the Orontes River in Syria and describes the gifts as an act of homage to David. Smith's also dates the embassy to about 1036 BC, an estimate rather than a date stated in the text. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "who wanders," while Smith's gives "erring."

Tola was a son of Issachar and the founder of the Tolaite clan within the tribe of Issachar. He is always listed first among Issachar's four sons, alongside Puah (also spelled Phuvah or Pua), Jashub (called Job in Gen 46:13) and Shimron, so Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take him to be the eldest. He appears in the list of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt, and in the wilderness census his descendants are counted as the family of the Tolaites. His six sons, Uzzi, Rephaiah, Jeriel, Jahmai, Jibsam and Shemuel, were heads of households, and in David's day their descendants numbered 22,600 fighting men. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "worm" or "scarlet." The name is shared by others, including the later judge Tola, who also came from Issachar.

Tola was a judge of Israel, the son of Puah and grandson of Dodo, from the tribe of Issachar. He rose "to defend Israel" after the time of Abimelech, and he lived at Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim (Judg 10:1). The next verse, Judg 10:2, says he judged Israel for twenty-three years and was buried in Shamir, and Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that Jair succeeded him. His judgeship is placed about 1215 BC, by inference from context. The name is usually taken to mean "worm" or "scarlet." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia observes that Tola and Puah also appear together as sons of Issachar in the tribal genealogies, and suggests they may have been traditional family names within that tribe. Because several people in the Bible bear this name, this entry covers only the judge.

Tolad was a town where the descendants of Simeon lived, named in a list of their settlements in 1 Chr 4:29 alongside Bilhah and Ezem. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies it with El-tolad, which appears in the parallel town lists of Joshua among the southern towns of Judah (Josh 15:30) and among the towns given to Simeon (Josh 19:4). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in the south of Judah, since Simeon's towns lay within Judah's territory. The surrounding passage says the Simeonites held these towns until the reign of David. The exact site is unknown, and the location shown here is only approximate. Easton's gives the meaning of the name as "productive," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a generation."

Tophel is a place named in Deut 1:1. It is one of several landmarks used to describe where Moses spoke to all Israel east of the Jordan, "between Paran, and Tophel, and Laban, and Hazeroth, and Dizahab." The verse is the only mention of it, and none of the places listed with it has been located with certainty. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify Tophel with Tafileh (et-Tafileh), a town southeast of the Dead Sea on the western side of the Edomite mountains. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it on the caravan road from Petra to Kerak, about 15 miles southeast of the Dead Sea, and notes that some linguistic difficulties make the identification uncertain. The location shown here follows the Tafileh identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "ruin" or "folly."

Topheth (also spelled Tophet) was a site in the Valley of Hinnom, just outside Jerusalem, where people burned their sons and daughters in fire as offerings to Molech (Jer 7:31). King Josiah defiled it as part of his religious reforms so that the practice would stop (2 Kgs 23:10). Jeremiah was sent there to prophesy. He announced that the place would be renamed the Valley of Slaughter, that the dead would be buried there until no room was left, and that Jerusalem itself would be made unclean like Topheth (Jer 19:6–14). The meaning of the name is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia favors "place of burning," while Smith's Bible Dictionary links it to the Hebrew word for a drum and suggests it was once a royal garden. It probably lay at the lower end of the Hinnom Valley, south of the Old City, which is where the location shown here places it.

Tower, the Tower of Hananel ("Hananeel" in the King James Version), was a tower in the wall of Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "God has graciously given." In Nehemiah's rebuilding of the wall, the priests under Eliashib the high priest repaired the section from the Sheep Gate as far as the Tower of Meah and the Tower of Hananel (Neh 3:1). At the dedication of the wall, one procession passed the Fish Gate, the Tower of Hananel and the Tower of Meah on its way to the Sheep Gate (Neh 12:39). These passages place it on the north side of the city, near the Temple area. Jeremiah and Zechariah use it as a boundary marker in prophecies of a rebuilt Jerusalem (Jer 31:38; Zech 14:10). Its exact position is unknown. The location shown here is an approximate point in Jerusalem's northern wall area.

Tower here refers to the Tower of Meah, a tower in the wall of Jerusalem whose name means "the Hundred" (so the ESV calls it the Tower of the Hundred). Why it had that name is not explained, and suggestions such as its height or a company of a hundred soldiers remain guesses. When Nehemiah rebuilt the walls, Eliashib the high priest and his fellow priests rebuilt the Sheep Gate and consecrated the wall as far as this tower and on to the Tower of Hananeel (Neh 3:1). At the dedication of the walls, one of the thanksgiving processions passed by the Tower of Hananeel and the Tower of Meah toward the Sheep Gate (Neh 12:39). These passages place it on the north side of the city, near the temple area, between the Sheep Gate and the Tower of Hananeel. The location shown here follows that northern placement. The same word "tower" is also used for several other towers in the Bible.

Tower, called the "tower of the furnaces" in the King James Version and the Tower of the Ovens in modern translations, was a tower in the wall of Jerusalem. During Nehemiah's rebuilding of the city walls, Malchijah son of Harim and Hashub son of Pahath-moab repaired a section of the wall along with this tower (Neh 3:11). At the dedication of the completed wall, one of the two thanksgiving choirs, with Nehemiah following, passed along the wall from beyond this tower to the Broad Wall (Neh 12:38). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it at the north-western angle of Jerusalem's second wall. It suggests the tower was probably named for being near the bakers' street mentioned in Jer 37:21. The exact site is not known, and the location shown here is an approximate point within the city. Several other towers in the Bible share the general name Tower.

The Tower of Babel was a city and tower built by people who all spoke one language. They had settled on a plain in the land of Shinar, in southern Mesopotamia. Using burnt brick for stone and slime (probably bitumen) for mortar, they set out to build a tower whose top would reach heaven, to make a name for themselves and avoid being scattered across the earth. The LORD came down to see the work and confused their language so they could not understand one another. He then scattered them over the whole earth, and they stopped building the city. The text explains the name Babel by this confusion of language, a play on the Hebrew word for "confuse." Babel is usually linked with Babylon. The date, about 2246 BC, is an estimate inferred from context and is not stated in the passage.

Trachonitis was a rugged, rocky region east of the Jordan and south of Damascus. It is named only in Luke 3:1, which dates the start of John the Baptist's preaching to the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar. At that time Herod's brother Philip ruled Ituraea and the region of Trachonitis as tetrarch. The name means "stony," and both Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries link it with the Old Testament district of Argob. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that ancient writers used the name for two volcanic lava fields. One is the inhabited el-Leja, a triangular area of broken basalt with cultivable soil inside its rough borders. The other is the barren, waterless es-Safa farther east. Easton's identifies Trachonitis with the Lejah, in present-day southern Syria. The location shown here is a general point in the surrounding area of that region.

The Triumphal Entry was Jesus' ride into Jerusalem as crowds gathered for a feast, probably Passover. It is recorded in all four Gospels and dated here to about AD 30 by inference from context. Near Bethphage and Bethany on the Mount of Olives, he sent two disciples to fetch a colt from a nearby village, telling them to say "The Lord hath need of him" if questioned. Matthew adds that the colt's mother came too. The disciples laid their garments on the animal and Jesus rode it. Crowds spread clothes and branches on the road, which John calls palm branches, and shouted "Hosanna," hailing him as the Son of David and the King who comes in the name of the Lord. Matthew and John present the event as fulfilling prophecy. John links the crowd's enthusiasm to the raising of Lazarus and notes the Pharisees' dismay. Luke records that Jesus wept over the city and foretold its destruction.

Troas was a port city on the Aegean coast of Mysia in northwest Asia Minor, a few miles south of ancient Troy. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its full name as Alexandria Troas and notes it was a Roman colony. Paul came down to Troas on his second journey, and from there he sailed straight to Samothrace and Neapolis, bringing the gospel to Macedonia (Acts 16:8, 11). By inference from context, this is where he saw the vision of the man of Macedonia. On a later journey his companions waited for him at Troas, and he stayed there seven days (Acts 20:5–6). The parallel narrative in Acts 20 places the raising of Eutychus there. Paul also describes a door opened for preaching at Troas (2 Cor 2:12), and he left his cloak, books and parchments there with Carpus (2 Tim 4:13). Its ruins, known as Eski Stamboul, lie on the Turkish coast near the location shown here.

Trogyllium was a town and promontory on the western coast of Asia Minor, where the ship carrying Paul stopped between Samos and Miletus on his return from his third missionary journey (Acts 20:15). Smith's Bible Dictionary describes it as the rocky tip of the Mycale ridge, directly opposite the island of Samos, with a nearby anchorage still called St. Paul's port. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the strait between the promontory and Samos is barely a mile wide, and that several early manuscripts lack the words "tarried at Trogyllium." Even so, the ship would have passed the promontory and probably stopped there. The voyage took place about AD 54, a date inferred from context. The location shown here is on the mainland coast facing Samos, in present-day western Turkey.

Trophimus was a Christian from Ephesus, in the Roman province of Asia, who traveled with Paul. He was one of the companions who went with Paul from Greece through Macedonia into Asia near the end of his third missionary journey (Acts 20:4). He went on with Paul to Jerusalem. There, people who had seen the two together in the city assumed that Paul had brought him into the temple. Because Trophimus was evidently a Gentile, that belief set off the riot in which Paul was seized and arrested (Acts 21:29). Paul later wrote that he had left Trophimus sick at Miletus, a coastal city not far from Ephesus (2 Tim 4:20). Easton's Bible Dictionary takes this to refer to a later occasion not recorded in Acts. Some, including Smith's Bible Dictionary, have suggested he was the unnamed brother sent with Titus to Corinth.

Tryphena was a Christian woman in the church at Rome. Paul greets her by name near the end of his letter to the Romans, together with Tryphosa, and describes both as women "who labour in the Lord" (Rom 16:12), that is, active workers in the church. Because the two are named together and their names are similar, some have suggested they were sisters, possibly twins. Smith's Bible Dictionary thinks it more likely they were fellow workers, perhaps serving as deaconesses. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of her name as "delicious" or "delicate." Nothing else is known about her, and the letter is dated about AD 55, by inference from context.

Tryphosa was a Christian woman in the church at Rome whom Paul greets near the end of his letter to the Romans. He names her together with Tryphena and describes the two of them as women "who labour in the Lord" (Rom 16:12), which indicates they were active workers in the congregation. Because their names come from the same Greek root, the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests, following Lightfoot, that they were probably sisters or close relatives. It also notes that both names appear in inscriptions connected with the Roman imperial household, so they may have belonged to it, though the verse does not say so. Her name is commonly linked to the idea of delicacy or luxury, while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "thrice shining." Nothing more is known about her.

Tubal was a region and people in the far north, as seen from Israel. Gen 10:2 names Tubal as a son of Japheth, and the STEPBible Proper Names index treats the nation as his descendants. In Ezekiel, Tubal appears with Javan and Meshech as trading partners of Tyre, dealing in slaves and bronze vessels (Ezek 27:13). It is also listed with Meshech as one of the peoples ruled by Gog, 'the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal,' against whom Ezekiel prophesies (Ezek 38:2–3; 39:1). Isaiah includes Tubal among distant nations that will hear of God's glory (Isa 66:19). Tubal is usually linked with the Tabal of Assyrian records in central Anatolia, or with the Tibareni, whom Greek writers place near the southern Black Sea coast. The location shown here, in northeastern Turkey near the Black Sea, matches the Tibareni identification and is approximate.

Tubal was a son of Japheth and grandson of Noah, named fifth among Japheth's seven sons in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:2; 1 Chr 1:5). Elsewhere in the Bible the name refers to the people descended from him, who are usually paired with Meshech. Ezekiel lists Tubal with Javan and Meshech as traders who sold slaves and bronze vessels in the markets of Tyre (Ezek 27:13). He also counts Meshech and Tubal among the fallen nations in the grave (Ezek 32:26), and calls Gog "the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal" (Ezek 38:2–3; 39:1). Isaiah names Tubal among distant nations that will hear of God's glory (Isa 66:19). Josephus linked the Tubalites with the Iberians, between the Black and Caspian Seas. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia instead identifies them with the Tibarenoi of Greek writers and the Tabali of Assyrian inscriptions, in Asia Minor southeast of the Black Sea.

Tubal-cain was a son of Lamech, a descendant of Cain, and Lamech's wife Zillah. Genesis 4:22 describes him as "an instructer of every artificer in brass and iron," which the Revised Version renders "the forger of every cutting instrument of brass and iron" (Easton's Bible Dictionary). He is the first metalworker named in the Bible. His full sister was Naamah, and his half-brothers Jabal and Jubal, sons of Lamech's other wife Adah, are presented in the surrounding verses as founders of herding and of music. Tubal-cain likewise appears as the originator of a craft, working in copper or bronze and iron. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that many commentators connect the name Tubal with the ancient people of Tubal, known for trade in bronze vessels (Ezek 27:13). Nothing else is recorded about him.

Tychicus was a Christian from the province of Asia and a companion of Paul. He was one of the group who traveled with Paul on the journey from Greece and Macedonia toward Jerusalem (Acts 20:4). Paul calls him "a beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord" and sent him to bring news of Paul's circumstances to the believers at Ephesus and Colossae (Eph 6:21; Col 4:7). By inference, he probably carried those letters. In later letters Paul mentions sending him to Ephesus (2 Tim 4:12) and considered sending him or Artemas to Titus in Crete (Titus 3:12). Easton's Bible Dictionary takes him to have been with Paul at Rome. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he and Trophimus may have been the two brothers who helped Titus with the collection for the believers in Judea. His name means "by chance" or "fortunate."

Tyrannus was a man of Ephesus in whose school, or lecture hall, the apostle Paul taught daily after some members of the synagogue there rejected his message and spoke against it publicly (Acts 19:9). Paul withdrew from the synagogue, took the disciples with him, and carried on his discussions in this hall. The next verse says this went on for two years. The mission is dated to about AD 53, by inference from context. Nothing else is said about Tyrannus himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary presumes he was a Greek and a public teacher of philosophy or rhetoric. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions the view that he was a Jew and that his school was a private synagogue. Whether he was the owner, a teacher there, or simply the man the hall was named after is not stated. The name means "prince" or "ruler."

Tyre was a major Phoenician port city on the Mediterranean coast, about 20 miles south of Sidon, at the modern town of Sur in Lebanon. It is first named as a "strong city" on Asher's border (Josh 19:29). Hiram king of Tyre sent cedar and craftsmen to build David's house and later supplied Solomon (2 Sam 5:11; 1 Kgs 5:1; 2 Chr 2:3). Ezekiel describes it as a wealthy merchant city "at the entry of the sea" (Ezek 27:3). Prophets announced judgment on it for its pride and for selling captives, and Ezekiel mentions Nebuchadnezzar's long siege (Isa 23:1; Amos 1:9; Ezek 29:18). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes a mainland fortress and an island city offshore, famous for its purple dye. In the New Testament people from the region came to Jesus, who also visited it, and Paul stopped there on his way to Jerusalem (Mark 3:8; Matt 15:21; Acts 21:7).

Ucal is named in Prov 30:1 as one of the two people, with Ithiel, to whom Agur son of Jakeh spoke his sayings. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests that, if the names are personal, Ithiel and Ucal were probably disciples or sons of Agur. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "power" or "prevalency." The Hebrew of the verse is obscure, and readings differ. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the ancient Greek translations do not treat the word as a name. Many scholars read it instead as a verb, giving a sense like "I have wearied myself, O God, and am consumed." Some have also linked Ucal with Chalcol of 1 Kgs 4:31. This entry follows the traditional King James reading, which takes Ucal as a person's name.

Uel was one of the descendants of Bani listed in Ezra 10:34 among the men of Israel who had married foreign wives. He appears in the list drawn up during Ezra's reforms after the return from exile in Babylon. By inference from the surrounding chapter, these men agreed to send away their foreign wives. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the event to about 458 BC, an estimate based on context. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name is spelled "Juel" in the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:35. Smith's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take the name to mean "will of God", while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "desiring God". Nothing else is recorded about him.

Ulai was a river beside Shushan (Susa), the royal city in the province of Elam, in what is now southwestern Iran. Daniel saw himself standing by the Ulai in his vision of the ram and the goat (Dan 8:2), and there he heard a man's voice "between the banks of Ulai" telling Gabriel to explain the vision to him (Dan 8:16). Greek and Roman writers called it the Eulaeus. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with the eastern branch of the Choaspes, the modern Karkheh, which once split into two streams about 20 miles above Susa. They read "between the banks" as the land between those two streams. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies the Ulai with the Karkheh itself and notes that the river once ran at the foot of Susa's citadel before shifting its bed westward. The location shown here places the river at Susa.

Ulam was a member of the tribe of Manasseh, one of the two tribes descended from Joseph, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 7. His grandparents were Machir, Manasseh's son, and Machir's wife Maachah. His father was Sheresh, brother of Peresh, and his brother was Rakem. He is recorded as the father of Bedan. The family is summed up as descendants of Gilead, son of Machir. The Hebrew of 1 Chr 7:16 says only that "his sons" were Ulam and Rakem, so the father could be either Sheresh or Peresh. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes him as a son of Peresh and treats the name as a Manassite clan, while this entry follows the reading that makes him Sheresh's son.
