Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is shared by at least one other man in the Bible, so this Ulam should not be confused with others of the same name.

Ulam was a Benjaminite, the firstborn of Eshek, with younger brothers Jehush and Eliphelet (1 Chr 8:39). Eshek was the brother of Azel, whose line the genealogy traces back through Jonathan to King Saul. Smith's Bible Dictionary accordingly calls Ulam a descendant of the house of Saul. Since Azel was the son of Eleasah (1 Chr 8:37), this entry links Ulam to Eleasah, though the verse itself names Eshek as his father. Ulam's sons were remembered as mighty warriors and archers, and his descendants grew to 150 sons and grandsons (1 Chr 8:40). They close the Benjamite genealogy of this chapter. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names explain the name as meaning "porch," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "preceding." The name is shared with at least one other man, a descendant of Manasseh.

Ulla was a member of the tribe of Asher, named in the Asherite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 7 as the father of three sons, Arah, Haniel and Rezia (1 Chr 7:39). The list does not say who Ulla's father was. This entry follows the view, given in Tyndale House's STEPBible proper names, that Ulla is the same man as Shual, one of the sons of Zophah, alongside Suah, Harnepher, Beri, Imrah and others (1 Chr 7:36). On that view his brothers include Beera, Bezer, Hod, Shamma, Shilshah and Jether, the remaining sons of Zophah named in the same passage. Other reference works, such as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, treat Shual and Ulla as two separate Asherites. The meaning of the name Ulla is uncertain. Nothing further is recorded about him beyond his place in the genealogy.

Ummah was a city in the territory given to the tribe of Asher, listed near the end of Asher's boundary description along with Aphek and Rehob (Josh 19:30). It is mentioned nowhere else in the Bible. Its location is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests it was probably 'Alma, in the coastal highlands about five miles east-northeast of Ras en-Nakhura. This entry follows that identification, placing it at the modern village of Alma el Shaab in southern Lebanon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes another view: a slight change to the Hebrew text would make the name read Acco, the coastal city later called Ptolemais, modern Akko. It treats this as a conjecture that many scholars nonetheless accept. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "vicinity", while Smith's gives "union".

The United Kingdom was the period when all twelve tribes of Israel were ruled by a single king, before the nation split into the northern kingdom of Israel and the southern kingdom of Judah. It began when the prophet Samuel poured oil on Saul's head and declared that the LORD had anointed him to be captain over his inheritance (1 Sam 10:1). Saul was followed by David and then by Solomon. Connected passages give each of these kings a reign of about forty years (Acts 13:21; 2 Sam 5:4; 1 Kgs 11:42), which accounts for the roughly 120-year span given here. The kingdom divided after Solomon's death, when the northern tribes rejected his son Rehoboam (1 Kgs 12). The starting date of about 1095 BC is an estimate inferred from context, and other chronologies place it somewhat later.

The United Kingdom of Israel was the single monarchy that ruled all the tribes of Israel under its first three kings, Saul, David and Solomon. It began when the prophet Samuel privately anointed Saul as leader (1 Sam 10:1), after which the people publicly made Saul king at Gilgal (1 Sam 11:15). Later the elders of Israel came to David at Hebron and anointed him king over Israel (2 Sam 5:3), and his son Solomon afterward reigned "over all Israel" (1 Kgs 4:1). The kingdom split after Solomon's death, when the northern tribes rejected his son Rehoboam, as 2 Chr 10:19 records. This entry dates the kingdom to roughly 1094–974 BC, an estimate inferred from context. As a political realm rather than a single site, it has no specific location shown here. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name Israel as "who prevails with God."

Unni was a Levite of the second rank whom the chief Levites appointed, at David's command, as one of the musicians when the ark was brought up to Jerusalem from the house of Obed-edom. He is listed among the brethren of the second degree in 1 Chr 15:18, a group that also included gatekeepers. In 1 Chr 15:20 he appears among those who played psalteries, or harps, set to "Alamoth," a musical term of uncertain meaning that may refer to a higher pitch. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of the doorkeepers, while Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a psaltery player. Both roles fit the two verses. The name is shared by another Levite who returned from exile with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:9), a different man from a much later period. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "afflicted" or "that answers."

Unni was a Levite named in the list of priests and Levites who returned from the Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel, according to Easton's Bible Dictionary. Neh 12:9 says that he and Bakbukiah, "their brethren," stood opposite another group of Levites "in the watches", probably as one side of the antiphonal singing or temple service. The Hebrew text is written as Unno, and the Revised Version uses that spelling. The name is also borne by a different man, a Levite singer appointed in David's time (1 Chr 15:18, 20), as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. Smith's Bible Dictionary allows that the name in Nehemiah may stand for a family descended from the earlier Unni rather than for an individual. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as "poor" or "afflicted". Nothing more is recorded about him.

Uphaz was a place known for its fine gold, mentioned only twice in the Bible. Jeremiah describes idols overlaid with silver from Tarshish and gold from Uphaz (Jer 10:9), and Daniel sees a man in linen whose waist is bound with "fine gold of Uphaz" (Dan 10:5). Its location is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it is probably another name for Ophir, a famous source of gold. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the two names differ by only one consonant, and that Daniel's phrase may instead mean "gold and fine gold." Other proposals place it in southern Arabia or in India, near the Hyphasis River in the Punjab. The location shown here is a general one in India and follows the Indian identification.

Upper Beth-horon was a town on the southern boundary of the tribe of Ephraim. Joshua 16:5 traces Ephraim's border on the east side from Ataroth-addar to "Bethhoron the upper." Its name implies a companion town lower down the slope. Connected passages mention Lower Beth-horon on the same border (Josh 16:3) and record that Sheerah, a descendant of Ephraim, built both towns (1 Chr 7:24). Solomon later fortified both towns (2 Chr 8:5). The two towns stood along the ascent from the coastal lowlands into the hill country, on the route that runs northwest of Jerusalem. Upper Beth-horon is probably the modern village of Beit Ur al-Fauqa, and the location shown here lies in that area.

The Upper Room Discourse is the long farewell address Jesus gave his eleven remaining apostles in Jerusalem on the night of the Last Supper, recorded in John 13:31–17:26. It begins after Judas Iscariot left the meal. It takes its name from the upper room where, according to Mark and Luke, the supper was held. Jesus gave a new commandment to love one another and said he was going to the Father to prepare a place for his followers. He called himself the way, the truth and the life, urged them to abide in him, warned that the world would hate them, and promised the Comforter, the Spirit of truth. Peter, Philip and Judas (not Iscariot) interrupt with questions. His words "Arise, let us go hence" (John 14:31) suggest that part of the discourse may have been spoken after leaving the room. It closes with his prayer for the disciples and for later believers. This entry dates it to about AD 30, by inference.

The Uproar in Thessalonica was a disturbance during Paul's second missionary journey, after he and Silas travelled through Amphipolis and Apollonia to Thessalonica. Following his usual practice, Paul reasoned in the synagogue on three sabbaths, arguing from the scriptures that the Messiah had to suffer and rise from the dead, and that Jesus was the Messiah. Some Jews, many devout Greeks and a number of leading women joined Paul and Silas. Jews who did not believe gathered a mob, set the city in an uproar and attacked the house of Jason, their host. Not finding Paul and Silas there, they dragged Jason and other believers before the city rulers. They accused the missionaries of turning the world upside down and of defying Caesar's decrees by proclaiming another king, Jesus. The rulers took security from Jason and the others and released them. This entry dates the episode to about AD 48, by inference from context.

Ur of the Chaldees was the city where Terah's family lived before setting out for Canaan. Haran, Abram's brother, died there, in the land of his birth, before his father Terah (Gen 11:28). Terah then left Ur with Abram, Sarai and Lot, heading for Canaan, but settled in Haran (Gen 11:31). Later passages describe the LORD as having brought Abram out of Ur (Gen 15:7; Neh 9:7). By inference it was also the birthplace of Abram and his brother Nahor, with Abram's birth placed about 1996 BC, also by inference from context. Its site has long been debated. Ancient tradition placed it at Urfa (Edessa) in northern Mesopotamia, and the Talmud at Erech (Warka). The location shown here follows the identification favoured by Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia: the ruins of Tell el-Muqayyar in southern Iraq, near the Euphrates, an ancient center of moon-god worship.

Ur was the father of Eliphal, one of the warriors listed among David's mighty men in 1 Chr 11:35. He is known only from this single mention, and nothing else is recorded about his life or family. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that his name means "flame" and that the parallel list in 2 Sam 23:34 gives the father's name as Ahasbai. It also points out that the two lists differ at this point, and the relationship between the names is not explained. The person Ur is unrelated to the city of Ur of the Chaldeans, Abraham's original home, which shares the same English spelling.

Urbane was a Christian at Rome whom Paul greets in Rom 16:9, calling him "our helper in Christ." The phrase suggests he had worked alongside Paul or his companions in spreading the faith, though where or when is not stated. His name is the King James spelling of the Latin Urbanus, meaning "of the city" or "refined," and modern translations such as the Revised Version use that form. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes it was a common Roman name and dates the letter to about AD 55. Paul names him alongside Stachys, whom he calls "my beloved," in the long list of greetings that closes his letter to the Romans. Nothing else is known of him.

Uri was a man of the tribe of Judah, the son of Hur and the father of Bezaleel, the craftsman God called by name to make the tabernacle and its furnishings (Exod 31:2; 38:22). He is known only through his son, who is regularly identified as "the son of Uri, the son of Hur". The genealogy in 1 Chr 2:20 records the line Hur, Uri, Bezaleel. By inference from 1 Chr 2:19, Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a grandson of Caleb son of Hezron. His listed brothers, including Shobal, Salma and Hareph, are named as sons of Hur in the Judah genealogies of 1 Chr 2:50–51 and 1 Chr 4:3–4. His name is usually explained as "fiery", or "my light" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Several other men in the Bible share the name Uri.

Uri was the father of Geber, one of the twelve district officers King Solomon appointed to supply food for the king and his household, each for one month of the year. Geber's district was the land of Gilead east of the Jordan, the former territory of Sihon king of the Amorites and of Og king of Bashan (1 Kgs 4:19). Nothing else is recorded about Uri himself, and he is mentioned only through his son. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take to mean "fiery," is shared by other men in the Bible, including the father of Bezalel the craftsman, so this Uri should not be confused with them. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some Greek manuscripts give his name as Adai. He probably lived before or during Solomon's reign, in the tenth century BC, by inference from his son's office.

Uri was a temple gatekeeper (a "porter") in Ezra's time. He is listed with Shallum and Telem among the gatekeepers who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:24). The surrounding chapter describes Ezra's reforms after the return from exile, when men who had taken such wives agreed to send them away. So Uri was probably one of those who made that commitment, as the STEPBible proper names index also describes him. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 458 BC. The name is usually explained as meaning "fiery", and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes it may be a shortened form of Uriah. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including the father of the craftsman Bezalel, and this Uri should not be confused with them.

Uriah the Hittite was a soldier in King David's army, one of David's elite warriors known as the mighty men, and the husband of Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam. While Uriah was away fighting the Ammonites, David took Bathsheba. David then called Uriah back to Jerusalem and urged him to go home, but Uriah slept at the palace door, saying he would not enjoy his house while the ark, Israel and his comrades were camped in the field. David sent him back with a letter telling Joab to put him where the fighting was fiercest and then pull back, and Uriah was killed by archers on the city wall. By inference from the surrounding chapters, the city was probably Rabbah, the Ammonite capital. The prophet Nathan condemned David for killing him and taking his wife, and 1 Kgs 15:5 names this as David's one failing. Matthew's genealogy calls him Urias.

Uriel was a Levite of the clan of Kohath, son of Tahath, named in the Kohathite genealogy of 1 Chr 6:24, where his son is Uzziah. The parallel line of descent for the singer Heman (1 Chr 6:33–38) names Zephaniah son of Tahath, father of Azariah, at the same point. This entry follows the common view, given in the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and in STEPBible, that Zephaniah and Uriel are the same man. On that view his son appears as both Uzziah and Azariah, two names also used interchangeably for a later king of Judah. Because Heman's line runs through Elkanah and Samuel, Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him an ancestor of the prophet Samuel. Nothing else is recorded of him. Several other men in the Bible are also called Uriel, including a Kohathite leader in David's time (1 Chr 15:5).

Uriel was a Levite and the chief of the clan of Kohath in the time of King David. He led a group of 120 of his kinsmen (1 Chr 15:5). When David prepared to bring the ark of the covenant up to Jerusalem, he called for the priests Zadok and Abiathar and for six Levite leaders, with Uriel named first (1 Chr 15:11). From the surrounding passage, these leaders were told to consecrate themselves and to carry the ark properly, after an earlier failed attempt. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as the chief of the Kohathites at the time the ark was brought to Jerusalem. Hitchcock's Bible Names treats the name as having the same meaning as Uriah. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a Kohathite ancestor and a man from Gibeah, and they should be kept distinct from this Uriel.

Uriel of Gibeah was the father of Michaiah, the mother of Abijah, king of Judah, according to 2 Chr 13:2. The parallel account in 1 Kgs 15:2 names Abijah's mother as Maachah the daughter of Abishalom (Absalom), and 2 Chr 11:20–21 calls her Maachah, Absalom's daughter and a wife of Rehoboam. A long-standing way of reconciling these, followed in this entry, holds that Michaiah and Maachah are the same woman. On this view Uriel married Tamar, the daughter of Absalom mentioned in 2 Sam 14:27, which would make Maachah Absalom's granddaughter. Through his grandson Abijah, who appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, Uriel is a maternal ancestor in that line. His name probably means "God is my light." Several other men in the Bible share the name Uriel.

Urijah, also spelled Uriah, was a priest of the period after the return from exile in Babylon. He is known only as the father of Meremoth and the son of Koz. His son Meremoth, called "the son of Uriah the priest," received and weighed the silver, gold and temple vessels that Ezra's company brought to Jerusalem (Ezra 8:33). Meremoth also repaired two sections of Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah, including the stretch beside the high priest Eliashib's house (Neh 3:4, 21). Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies Koz with the priestly family of Hakkoz, head of the seventh course of priests, and dates Urijah to about 458 BC. Nothing more is recorded about him, and he should be kept distinct from several other men in the Bible with the same name.

Urijah, also called Uriah, was a priest in Jerusalem during the reign of King Ahaz of Judah. When Ahaz went to Damascus to meet Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, he saw an altar there and sent its design to Urijah. Urijah built a copy before the king returned (2 Kgs 16:10–11). Ahaz then ordered that the regular morning and evening offerings, the king's sacrifices and the people's offerings all be made on this new "great altar," while the old bronze altar was kept for the king to enquire by. Urijah did everything the king commanded (2 Kgs 16:15–16). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe him as high priest. The "Uriah the priest" whom Isaiah took as a reliable witness (Isa 8:2) is probably the same man, as Smith's Bible Dictionary holds, and this entry follows that view. Other people in the Bible share the name.

Urijah was one of the men who stood beside Ezra the scribe on a wooden platform when Ezra read the law publicly in Jerusalem after the return from exile. He was among six men on Ezra's right hand, with seven more on his left (Neh 8:4). The verse does not say what role these men had. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe him as a priest, and Smith's dates the event to about 458 BC. The name, which Smith's gives as meaning "light of Jehovah," is borne by several people in the Bible, and nothing further is known of this Urijah beyond this single mention.

Urijah, son of Shemaiah of Kirjath-jearim, was a prophet in Judah during the reign of King Jehoiakim. He prophesied in the name of the LORD against Jerusalem and the land of Judah, delivering a message that matched Jeremiah's. When Jehoiakim, his officers and the princes heard his words, the king tried to have him put to death. Urijah fled in fear to Egypt, but he was brought back. The verse between these accounts, Jer 26:22, says Jehoiakim sent Elnathan son of Achbor and other men to fetch him. The king killed him with the sword and threw his body into the common people's burial ground. His story appears in Jeremiah 26 as a contrast to Jeremiah, who was spared when he spoke the same message. Several other men in the Bible share the name Urijah, also spelled Uriah.

The Usurpation by Abimelech was the seizure of power at Shechem by Abimelech, Gideon's (Jerubbaal's) son by a Shechemite concubine, after Gideon's death. Appealing to his kinship with the men of Shechem, he took silver from the house of Baal-berith, hired reckless followers, and killed his seventy half-brothers on one stone at Ophrah. Only the youngest, Jotham, escaped. From Mount Gerizim, Jotham told a fable of trees making a bramble their king and called down mutual fire on Abimelech and Shechem. After three years (Judg 9:22), Shechem turned against him and backed Gaal son of Ebed. Abimelech defeated Gaal, destroyed the city, and burned about a thousand people in the stronghold of the god Berith. Attacking another tower, at Thebez (Judg 9:50), he was struck by a millstone a woman dropped, and he had his armourbearer kill him. This entry dates the episode to about 1218 BC, by inference from context.

Uthai was a man of the tribe of Judah, descended through Perez, who is named among those living in Jerusalem in 1 Chr 9:4. His genealogy runs back through his father Ammihud, then Omri, Imri and Bani, to Perez the son of Judah. The surrounding passage lists people who resettled in Jerusalem, and by inference from that context he was among those who returned after the Babylonian exile. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies him with Athaiah, a Judahite of the line of Perez listed among Jerusalem's residents in Neh 11:4, though the two genealogies differ. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "helpful," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "my iniquity." The name is shared by several people in the Bible, including a head of a family who returned with Ezra (Ezra 8:14), so this Uthai should be kept distinct from them.

Uthai was a descendant of Bigvai who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. In the list of family heads who traveled with Ezra, Uthai and Zabbud are named for the family of Bigvai, with seventy males accompanying them (Ezra 8:14). By inference from the passage, the two probably led their family's group on the journey. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this return to about 459 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the apocryphal book of 1 Esdras calls him "Uthi." The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's gives "helpful," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "my iniquity." The name Uthai is also borne by at least one other man in the Bible, a descendant of Judah who lived in Jerusalem after the exile. This entry concerns only the man who traveled with Ezra.

Uz was a region east of the Jordan, best known as the homeland of Job (Job 1:1). Jeremiah lists "all the kings of the land of Uz" among the peoples made to drink the cup of God's wrath, which suggests it was a territory with several local rulers (Jer 25:20). Lamentations addresses the "daughter of Edom" as living in Uz, linking it with Edom or with land under Edomite control (Lam 4:21). Its exact location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it east or south-east of Israel and north of Edom. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia points to the north-east, citing Josephus, who connects Uz with Trachonitis and Damascus, and Arab tradition, which places Job in the Hauran of southern Syria. The location shown here follows the view that places it near Edom, in what is now southern Jordan.

Uz (son of Aram) was a son of Aram and a grandson of Shem, listed in the Table of Nations with his brothers Hul, Gether and Mash (Gen 10:23). The parallel genealogy in 1 Chr 1:17 names the same four directly after Shem's sons, without the phrase "the children of Aram," and gives Mash as Meshech. By inference from Gen 10:23, the Chronicles list is a shortened form, and Uz is Aram's son rather than Shem's. Nothing else is recorded about him. Like many names in these lists, his may also stand for a people descended from him. Other men named Uz appear elsewhere in Genesis, a son of Nahor and a descendant of Seir, and Job is said to have lived in a "land of Uz." Any link between these and Aram's son is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "counsel" or "words."

Uz (son of Dishan) was a Horite, a descendant of Seir, the people who lived in the land of Seir before the Edomites. He appears only in the genealogies of Gen 36:28 and 1 Chr 1:42, which name him and his brother Aran as the sons of Dishan. Dishan was one of the sons of Seir the Horite and a chief in that land, as the surrounding verses of Genesis 36 show. Easton's Bible Dictionary counts Uz among the Horite chiefs in the land of Edom. The verses themselves record nothing about him beyond his name and family. He is distinct from the other men named Uz in the Bible, such as the son of Aram and the son of Nahor. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "counsel" or "words."

Uzai was the father of Palal, who is known from a single verse. Palal repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall in Nehemiah's time, opposite the turning of the wall and the tower projecting from the king's upper house by the court of the prison (Neh 3:25). Nothing else is said about Uzai himself, and he may not have been alive when his son did this work. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "strong," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats its meaning as unknown. Smith's places him before 446 BC, a date inferred from the period of Nehemiah's rebuilding.

Uzal was a place in southern Arabia that traded with the Phoenician city of Tyre, according to Ezekiel's lament over Tyre. In the King James Version of Ezek 27:19 the name is hidden in the phrase "going to and fro". Many modern translations read the same Hebrew word as "from Uzal", which makes it a source of the bright (wrought) iron, cassia and calamus sold in Tyre's markets. Uzal is also the name of a son of Joktan (Gen 10:27; 1 Chr 1:21). Easton's Bible Dictionary takes him as the founder of an Arab tribe whose name probably passed to their province and chief city. STEPBible's name index suggests a region of Arabia known for fine swords. Arab tradition identifies Uzal with Sanaa, the capital of Yemen, and the location shown here follows that identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "wandering".

Uzal was one of the sons of Joktan, a descendant of Shem, named in the list of nations in Gen 10:27 and again in 1 Chr 1:21. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia count him as Joktan's sixth son. Nothing is recorded about his life beyond his place in these genealogies, where he stands between his brothers Hadoram and Diklah. Like his brothers, he is generally taken as the ancestor of a people of southern Arabia. Easton's Bible Dictionary sees him as the founder of an Arab tribe whose name probably passed to their territory and chief city. Smith's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia link the name with Awzal, the old name of San'a, the capital of Yemen. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also suggests that Ezek 27:19 may mention Uzal as a place, depending on how one obscure Hebrew word is read.

Uzza was a garden in Jerusalem where two kings of Judah were buried. Manasseh was laid to rest "in the garden of his own house, in the garden of Uzza" (2 Kgs 21:18), and his son Amon was buried in his own tomb in the same garden (2 Kgs 21:26). These burials fall in about 642 BC and 640 BC, dates estimated from context. Unlike most earlier kings of Judah, neither is said to have been buried in the city of David. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests the garden was probably near the royal palace or part of its grounds. It notes that the name means "strength," and that Manasseh may have acquired the garden from someone called Uzza. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here simply places it within Jerusalem.

Uzza is the man after whom the "garden of Uzza" in Jerusalem was named. It was the burial place of two kings of Judah. King Manasseh was buried there, in the garden of his own house (2 Kgs 21:18), and his son Amon was later buried in his tomb in the same garden (2 Kgs 21:26). The text says nothing else about Uzza himself. Because the garden belonged to Manasseh's house, it was probably near the royal palace. It may have been named after an earlier owner, or possibly after the Uzzah who died beside the ark in David's time, but neither connection is stated in the text. The name is shared by several other people in the Bible, and this entry refers only to the Uzza of the garden.

Uzza was a Levite of the clan of Merari, named only in a genealogy of the tribe of Levi in 1 Chr 6:29. The list traces a line of descent from Merari's son Mahli through Libni and Shimei to Uzza, who is called Shimei's son. The next verse, 1 Chr 6:30, continues the line with his son Shimea, followed by Haggiah and Asaiah. If this Asaiah is the Merarite leader of David's time mentioned in 1 Chr 15:6, Uzza probably lived a few generations before David, though this is an inference. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, including the man who died after touching the ark, and they should not be confused with this Levite.

Uzza was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, listed in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 8:7. He is counted among the descendants of Ehud, whose family heads lived in Geba and were moved to Manahath (1 Chr 8:6). The verse names Naaman, Ahiah and Gera, says "he removed them," and then that he "begat Uzza, and Ahihud." Because the wording is compressed, it is not clear who the father is. This entry treats Uzza as a son of Ehud, as Smith's Bible Dictionary does, but the "he" of the verse may instead be Gera. STEPBible's Tyndale House names list places his birth in Moab. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary gives as meaning "strength," belongs to several different people in the Bible.

Uzza was the ancestor of a family of temple servants, known as the Nethinim, whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Judah. The "children of Uzza" appear in the list of returning families in Ezra 2:49 and again in the parallel list in Neh 7:51. In both lists they stand among the temple-servant families, next to the descendants of Paseah (spelled Phaseah in Nehemiah). Smith's Bible Dictionary places this return with Zerubbabel, before about 536 BC. Nothing else is recorded about Uzza himself, and the lists probably name him only as the head of a family line. The name means "strength" and is shared by several other men in the Bible, including the man who touched the ark in David's time. This Uzza appears to be a separate person.

Uzzah (spelled Uzza in Chronicles) was a son of Abinadab, in whose house the ark of God had been kept. His brother Ahio is named with him, and another brother, Eleazar, was set apart to keep the ark according to 1 Sam 7:1. When David set out to bring the ark to Jerusalem, Uzzah and Ahio drove the new cart that carried it from Abinadab's house (2 Sam 6:3; 1 Chr 13:7). At the threshing floor called Nachon's in Samuel and Chidon's in Chronicles, the oxen stumbled, and Uzzah reached out and took hold of the ark. The LORD's anger was kindled against him, and he died there beside the ark. David was displeased and named the place Perez-uzzah, meaning 'breach upon Uzzah.' Easton's Bible Dictionary links the event to the law in Num 4:15 forbidding anyone to touch the holy things. His name means 'strength.'

Uzzen-sheerah was a town built by Sheerah, a woman of the tribe of Ephraim, who also built Lower and Upper Beth-horon (1 Chr 7:24). The verse calls her "his daughter." By inference from the surrounding genealogy, Easton's Bible Dictionary takes her to be Ephraim's daughter. The town's name appears to include hers, and it probably stood near the two Beth-horons. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint reads the phrase not as a place name but as "and the sons of Ozan, Sheera," and that no satisfactory identification had been proposed. Some identify the site with the village of Beit Sira, a few miles west of Beth-horon, partly because the names sound alike. The location shown here follows the Beit Sira identification.

Uzzi was a Levite and descendant of Aaron, the son of Bukki and the father of Zerahiah. He appears only in genealogies of the priestly line that runs from Aaron through Eleazar and Phinehas to Zadok (1 Chr 6:5–6, 51). Ezra's ancestry also passes through him (Ezra 7:4). Sources differ on whether he held the high priesthood. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him a high priest. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that, although he was an ancestor of Zadok, he may never have served in that office, and it places him somewhat before Eli. The verses themselves list him only as a link in the family line and record nothing else about him. The name, perhaps meaning "my strength," is shared by several other men in the Bible.

Uzzi was a son of Tola and a grandson of Issachar, listed first among Tola's six sons in the genealogy of the tribe of Issachar (1 Chr 7:2). His brothers were Rephaiah, Jeriel, Jahmai, Jibsam and Shemuel. Together they are called heads of their father's house and valiant men, and the family is said to have numbered 22,600 fighting men in the days of David. Uzzi's son was Izrahiah, whose five descendants, Michael, Obadiah, Joel, Ishiah and Izrahiah himself, are described as chief men (1 Chr 7:3). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats him as the founder of a family within Issachar, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "my strength." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Uzzi is known only from these two verses.

Uzzi was a son of Bela and grandson of Benjamin, named in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin in 1 Chr 7:7. He appears with his brothers Ezbon, Uzziel, Jerimoth and Iri as one of five heads of their fathers' houses. They are called mighty men of valour, and their descendants were counted at 22,034. A separate list of Bela's sons in 1 Chr 8:3–5 gives different names, including Addar, Gera, Abihud, Abishua, Naaman and Ahoah, so those men are also counted among his brothers. The name probably means "my strength" (Hitchcock's Bible Names; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a view that this family may have belonged to the tribe of Zebulun. This entry follows the Benjamite reading of the text. Several other men in the Bible share the name Uzzi.

Uzzi was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, the son of Michri and the father of Elah. He appears only once, in a genealogy in 1 Chr 9:8. The surrounding passage lists the Benjamites who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon, so his son Elah, or the family line traced through him, was probably among those settlers. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a chief in the tribe. Several men in the Bible bear the name Uzzi, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary suggest he may be the same person as another Benjamite Uzzi, though this cannot be confirmed. The name is usually taken to mean "my strength."

Uzzi, son of Bani, was the overseer of the Levites living in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon, in the time of Nehemiah. Neh 11:22 traces his ancestry through Bani, Hashabiah and Mattaniah back to Micha, and links the family to the sons of Asaph, the singers who had charge of the work of the house of God. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Levite. The name probably means "my strength" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Uzzi should not be confused with them. He is known only from this single verse.

Uzzi was a priest who headed the priestly family of Jedaiah in the generation after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears only in a list of the heads of priestly families serving in the days of Joiakim the high priest, son of Jeshua (Neh 12:19). The surrounding passage sets this list in Joiakim's time, and Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 500 BC. The name Uzzi is shared by several other men in the Bible, including a descendant of Aaron, a Levite who oversaw the Levites in Jerusalem, and members of the tribes of Issachar and Benjamin. This entry concerns only the priest of Jedaiah's house. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "my strength."

Uzzi was one of the people named in the procession at the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. In Neh 12:42 he appears in a list of eight men who took part in the ceremony alongside the singers led by Jezrahiah. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both describe him as a priest, which is probably inferred from the surrounding passage, where priests with trumpets are part of the same company. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he may be the same man as the Uzzi who headed the priestly family of Jedaiah in Neh 12:19, and dates the dedication to about 446 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this entry treats him separately. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "my strength."

Uzzia the Ashterathite was one of David's mighty men, the warriors listed in 1 Chr 11. He appears only once, in the part of the list that has no parallel in 2 Samuel 23. His title "Ashterathite" probably means he came from Ashtaroth, a town east of the Jordan in Bashan, and Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him as a native of that place. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains his name as "my strength is Yah". Nothing else is recorded about his family or deeds.

Uzziah was the father of Jehonathan, an official in King David's administration. He is mentioned only once, in a list of David's officers, where his son Jehonathan is said to have overseen the royal storehouses in the fields, cities, villages and fortified towers (1 Chr 27:25). Nothing else is recorded about Uzziah himself. He lived in or shortly before David's reign, and Smith's Bible Dictionary places him about 1053 BC, an estimate drawn from context. Smith's also gives the meaning of the name as "strength of the LORD." Several other people in the Bible share this name, most notably the king of Judah also called Azariah. This Uzziah is a different and otherwise unknown man.

Uzziah was a man of the family of Harim, named among those in Ezra's time who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:21). The surrounding passage lists men who agreed to send these wives away as part of the reforms Ezra led after the return from exile. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a priest. That fits the context, since this section of the list covers the priestly families and Harim appears there among them. Smith's dates the episode to about 458 BC, an estimate drawn from context. Smith's also gives the meaning of his name as "strength of Jehovah." Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with the better-known King Uzziah of Judah or with other men of the same name in the Bible.

Uzziah was a man of the tribe of Judah, known only as an ancestor in a genealogy from the time of Nehemiah. Neh 11:4 names him as the son of Zechariah and the father of Athaiah, one of the Judahites who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile. His line is traced back through Amariah, Shephatiah and Mahalaleel to Perez, the son of Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary links his son Athaiah with the Uthai of the similar list of Jerusalem residents in 1 Chronicles 9. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with King Uzziah of Judah or the other men of this name. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "strength of Jehovah."

Uzziah, also called Azariah (and Ozias in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus), was king of Judah, the son of Amaziah and Jecoliah of Jerusalem. The people made him king at sixteen, and he reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem, roughly 810–758 BC by inference from context. Chronicles describes a strong ruler who received gifts from the Ammonites, built fortified towers in Jerusalem and equipped a large organized army. When he entered the temple to burn incense, the priests opposed him. While he was angry with them, leprosy broke out on his forehead. He lived in a separate house until his death while his son Jotham governed, and he was buried in a field belonging to the royal burial ground. Jotham's mother is named elsewhere as Jerushah. Isaiah, Hosea and Amos prophesied in his days, and an earthquake in his reign was long remembered. Several other people share the name.

Uzziel, whose name means "God is my strength" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary, was a Levite, the fourth son of Kohath, and brother of Amram, Izhar and Hebron. Since Amram was the father of Moses and Aaron, Uzziel was their uncle, and Lev 10:4 calls him "the uncle of Aaron." His sons Mishael, Elzaphan and Zithri are named in Exod 6:22. Moses called Mishael and Elzaphan to carry their dead relatives out of the camp. By inference from the surrounding passage, these were Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu. Elizaphan later became chief of the Kohathite families. Uzziel's line continued as a Levitical clan. Amminadab led 112 of its members in David's time. Michah and Jesiah (Isshiah), named as his sons in Chronicles, were probably later descendants heading branches of the family. Several other people in the Bible share the name.

Uzziel was a man of the tribe of Simeon, one of the four sons of Ishi, along with Pelatiah, Neariah and Rephaiah. The brothers served as captains of a band of five hundred Simeonites who went to Mount Seir, the hill country south and east of the Dead Sea (1 Chr 4:42). The surrounding verses say this happened in the days of King Hezekiah of Judah. They also say the Simeonites struck down the surviving Amalekites there and settled in their place (1 Chr 4:41–43). Smith's Bible Dictionary accordingly dates him to Hezekiah's time. His name means "God is my strength." Several other men in the Bible are also called Uzziel, and this one appears only in this passage.

Uzziel was a member of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the five sons of Bela, who was Benjamin's firstborn (1 Chr 7:6; Gen 46:21). His name means "God is my strength" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). In 1 Chr 7:7 he and his brothers Ezbon, Uzzi, Jerimoth and Iri are called heads of their fathers' houses and mighty men of valour, and their descendants numbered 22,034 in the genealogical count. The other brothers listed with him, such as Addar, Gera, Abishua, Naaman and Abihud, come from the separate list of Bela's sons in 1 Chr 8:3–5, which does not name Uzziel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes the view of the scholar Curtis that this passage may originally have described a family of Zebulun. This entry follows the Benjamite reading of the text. Several other men in the Bible share the name Uzziel.

Uzziel was a Levite and one of the fourteen sons of Heman, one of the leading musicians in David's time. He is named third among Heman's sons in 1 Chr 25:4. The same man is called Azareel in the list of the twenty-four groups of temple musicians chosen by lot, where the eleventh lot fell to him, with his sons and relatives making a group of twelve (1 Chr 25:18). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both treat the two names as one person, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that one major Greek manuscript of the Septuagint reads Azarael in verse 4 as well. The name Uzziel means "God is my strength." Several other people in the Bible share this name, so he should not be confused with them. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Uzziel was a Levite descended from Jeduthun, one of the families of temple musicians. He lived in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He and Shemaiah represented the sons of Jeduthun among the Levites who gathered to purify the temple at the start of Hezekiah's reforms (2 Chr 29:14). By inference from the surrounding passage, he took part in clearing out the uncleanness from the house of the Lord and reporting the work to the king. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 726 BC. His name means "God is my strength." Several other men in the Bible are also called Uzziel, and this one is mentioned only here.

Uzziel, son of Harhaiah, was a goldsmith who helped repair the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah's leadership after the return from exile (Neh 3:8). His section lay next to other workers. Beside him, Hananiah, son of one of the perfumers, also worked, and the builders in that stretch strengthened Jerusalem as far as the Broad Wall. His name means "God is my strength." Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he was probably a priest, taking "of the goldsmiths" to mean a priestly guild responsible for making and repairing the sacred vessels. It dates the work to about 446 BC, an estimate inferred from context. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia simply calls him a goldsmith. Several other men in the Bible share the name Uzziel, and nothing else is known about this one.

Vajezatha was one of the ten sons of Haman, the official who plotted to destroy the Jews in the Persian Empire. He is named only once, in the list of Haman's sons in Esth 9:9. The surrounding passage, Esth 9:6–10, records that the Jews killed these ten sons in Shushan (Susa), the Persian capital, on the day set for the attack against them. His brothers were Parshandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha, Poratha, Adalia, Aridatha, Parmashta, Arisai and Aridai. Nothing else is recorded about him. Some modern translations spell the name Vaizatha. The meaning of the name is uncertain. It is probably Persian, and older reference works give differing explanations: Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests "purity" or "worthy of honour," Smith's Bible Dictionary "strong as the wind," and Hitchcock's Bible Names "sprinkling the chamber."

The Vale of Hebron ("Valley of Hebron" in modern versions) was the valley around the town of Hebron, in the hill country of southern Judah. It is named only once, in Gen 37:14, where Jacob sends his son Joseph out from this valley to check on his brothers and the flocks. Joseph then travels north to Shechem, and from there to Dothan, where his brothers sell him. By inference from the passage and from earlier chapters of Genesis, which place Abraham and Isaac near Hebron and Mamre, this valley was where Jacob's family was living at the time. The location shown here marks the general area surrounding Hebron rather than a precise spot, since the text does not say which of the valleys near the town is meant. Hebron is identified with the present-day city of Hebron (al-Khalil) in the West Bank.

The Vale of Siddim was a valley where the kings of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim and Bela (Zoar) gathered and fought the invading eastern kings led by Chedorlaomer (Gen 14:3, 8). The text identifies it with the Salt Sea, the Dead Sea, which suggests the valley later came to lie under its waters or beside them. It was full of slime pits, probably pits of bitumen or asphalt. The kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fell into them as they fled, and the survivors escaped to the hills (Gen 14:10). Easton's Bible Dictionary places the valley at the south end of the Dead Sea, between Engedi and the cities of the plain. It notes that some locate the cities of the plain at the north end instead. The location shown here follows the southern identification, near the southern basin of the Dead Sea.

The Valley of Achor was a valley near Jericho where Joshua and the Israelites brought Achan, his family, his livestock and the goods he had taken, and stoned them. They raised a great heap of stones over him, and the place kept its name from that event. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "trouble." The valley later marked part of the northern border of Judah's territory, which ran up from it toward Debir and Gilgal. Isaiah and Hosea both mention it in promises of restoration, as a resting place for herds and as "a door of hope." Easton's suggests the name had become proverbial for trouble, so these passages picture trouble turned to blessing. Its exact location is uncertain. Proposals include the Buqeia plain west of the Dead Sea and the Wadi Qelt, which Easton's names. The location shown here follows the Wadi Qelt identification, southwest of Jericho.

The Valley of Aijalon is the valley named in Joshua's command during the battle in which the LORD gave the Amorites over to Israel: "Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon; and thou, Moon, in the valley of Ajalon" (Josh 10:12). It is the only verse that names the valley itself. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects it with the town of Aijalon, which was assigned to Dan, later given to the Levites, and lay near the border between Judah and Israel. Easton's identifies the town with modern Yalo, at the foot of the Beth-horon pass. By inference, the valley is the broad lowland west of Gibeon through which the fleeing Amorites would have passed on their way down from the hill country. The location shown here places it in that lowland, near Yalo.

The Valley of Baca is a valley mentioned only in Ps 84:6, a psalm about longing for God's house. It describes travelers who pass through the valley and make it a place of springs, while rain fills the pools. The Hebrew name is usually connected either with weeping or with a kind of balsam tree that grows in dry ground, so the Revised Version renders it "valley of weeping" with "balsam trees" in the margin. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests three possibilities: an actual valley somewhere in Palestine, any one of the valleys pilgrims crossed on their way to the sanctuary on Zion, or a figurative "valley of weeping." Its exact location is uncertain. The location shown here places it just outside Jerusalem, following the view that it was a real valley on the pilgrims' approach to the city.

The Valley of Beracah was a valley in Judah where King Jehoshaphat and his people gathered on the fourth day after their enemies were destroyed, and there they blessed the LORD. The place was named for that act, since Beracah means "blessing," and the name was still in use when Chronicles was written. By inference from the surrounding chapter, the gathering followed the defeat of the Moabites, Ammonites and people of Mount Seir, who turned on one another, and three days spent collecting the spoil. Judah's army had set out into the wilderness of Tekoa (2 Chr 20:20), so the valley probably lay in that region. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it not far from Engedi and identifies it with the valley of Bereikut. The location shown here follows that identification, at a site between Bethlehem and Hebron near Tekoa.

The Valley of Elah was the valley where Saul and the army of Israel camped and lined up for battle against the Philistines (1 Sam 17:2, 19). It was the scene of David's fight with Goliath. Later the priest at Nob reminded David that he had killed Goliath there and gave him Goliath's sword, which had been kept wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod (1 Sam 21:9). According to 1 Sam 17:1, the Philistines camped between Socoh and Azekah in Judah, which places the valley in the Shephelah, the low hills southwest of Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the modern Wadi es-Sunt and connects the name Elah ("terebinth") with the large terebinth trees that still grow there. The location shown here follows that identification.

The Valley of Gerar was the valley near the city of Gerar where Isaac camped and lived after leaving the city itself (Gen 26:17). In the surrounding passage, Abimelech, king of the Philistines at Gerar, had asked Isaac to move away because he had grown too powerful. In this valley Isaac then reopened wells his father Abraham had dug and dug new ones, which led to disputes with the local herdsmen. The valley was probably a seasonal stream bed (a wadi) with groundwater suitable for wells and pasture. Gerar lay in the western Negev, between Gaza and Beersheba, but its exact site is debated. Proposals include Tel Haror (Tell Abu Hureira) and Tell Jemmeh. The location shown here lies along the stream valley now usually called Nahal Gerar (Wadi esh-Sheria), probably the valley meant in the text.

The Valley of Gibeon was the low ground around the town of Gibeon, north of Jerusalem. It is named only in Isa 28:21, where the prophet warns that the LORD will rise up in anger as he did at Mount Perazim and in the valley of Gibeon, to do his "strange work" against his own people. The verse recalls a well-known past victory, and two connected passages are possible references. Mount Perazim points to David's defeat of the Philistines at Baal-perazim (2 Sam 5:20), and the parallel account of his second victory says he struck them from Gibeon to Gezer (1 Chr 14:16). Others connect it with Joshua's victory at Gibeon, when the sun stood still (Josh 10:10–14). The site is not described further. The location shown here is the area around Gibeon, generally identified with the modern village of al-Jib.

The Valley of Hamongog, meaning "valley of the multitude of Gog," is a place named in Ezekiel's prophecy against Gog. Ezekiel says that God would give Gog a burial ground in Israel, in "the valley of the passengers on the east of the sea." There Gog and all his army would be buried, and the place would then be called Hamongog (Ezek 39:11). Travelers passing through the land who found a human bone were to set up a marker beside it until the buriers carried it to this valley (Ezek 39:15). The text does not give a clear location. Many take "the sea" to be the Dead Sea, and some link "the passengers" (Hebrew 'obrim) with the Abarim region east of it. Others read "the sea" as the Mediterranean. The location shown here is a rough one on the eastern side of the Dead Sea, following the Dead Sea reading.

The Valley of Hinnom, also called the valley of the son of Hinnom, was a valley just south of Jerusalem, which Joshua identifies with the Jebusite city. It formed part of the border between the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, running past the southern side of the Jebusite city, below the mountain facing it to the west, and down to En-rogel (Josh 15:8; 18:16). After the exile it marked the northern limit of Judah's settlements, which stretched from Beersheba to this valley (Neh 11:30). Other passages, such as 2 Kgs 23:10 and Jer 7:31, place Topheth, a site of child sacrifice, in this valley. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as a deep, narrow ravine below Mount Zion and notes that its name, shortened in Greek to Gehenna, later came to stand for the place of the wicked. It is generally identified with the modern Wadi er-Rababi, which curves around the west and south of Jerusalem's Old City. The location shown here follows that identification.

The Valley of Jehoshaphat is the place where, in Joel's prophecy, God says he will gather all nations to judge them for scattering his people Israel and dividing his land (Joel 3:2, 12). The name means "the LORD judges," which fits the scene, and the same passage calls it "the valley of decision" (Joel 3:14). The Bible gives no geographical details, and views differ on whether it was a real place. Some take the name as symbolic. Others connect it with the Valley of Berachah, where King Jehoshaphat celebrated a victory (2 Chr 20:26). A long-standing Jewish, Christian and Muslim tradition identifies it with the Kidron Valley, between Jerusalem's Temple Mount and the Mount of Olives, where many graves have been placed in expectation of the final judgement. The location shown here follows the Kidron Valley identification.

The Valley of Jericho was the lowland surrounding the city of Jericho, which Deut 34:3 calls "the city of palm trees." It appears once, in the account of Moses viewing the promised land from Mount Nebo just before his death. As he looked out, the Lord showed him the south and "the plain of the valley of Jericho" stretching as far as Zoar. By inference from the setting, this is the broad, low-lying part of the Jordan Valley on the west side of the river, just north of the Dead Sea. Mount Nebo stood opposite it across the Jordan. The location shown here is the area around ancient Jericho, near the modern town of Jericho in the lower Jordan Valley. The verse does not mark the valley's exact limits.

The Valley of Jezreel was a valley in northern Israel that took its name from the town of Jezreel. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as an offshoot of the Plain of Esdraelon, running east toward the Jordan between Mount Gilboa and the hill of Moreh, the area now often called the Harod Valley. The name was later applied to the whole plain. The location shown here is a rough point near the town itself. Its Canaanite inhabitants had iron chariots, which the tribes of Joseph gave as a reason they could not take the lowlands (Josh 17:16). The Midianites, Amalekites and peoples of the east camped there before Gideon defeated them (Judg 6:33). Easton's also places Saul's death in battle against the Philistines in this area (1 Sam 31). Hosea foretold that God would break Israel's bow in the valley (Hos 1:5).

The Valley of Jiphthahel (Iphtahel in some modern translations) was a valley in lower Galilee that marked part of the boundary between the tribes of Zebulun and Asher. It appears only in the boundary lists of Joshua. Zebulun's northern border ran past Hannathon and ended at this valley (Josh 19:14). Asher's border, running eastward, reached Zebulun and the valley, north of Beth-emek and Neiel, before going on to Cabul (Josh 19:27). It was therefore a meeting point of the two tribal territories. Its exact identification is uncertain. Because Hannathon lies nearby, it is often taken to be one of the wadis draining westward from the hills of lower Galilee. Some identify it with Wadi el-Malik (Nahal Zippori), and others with a stream near the Beit Netofa plain. The location shown here is in that area, northwest of Nazareth.

The Valley of Lebanon was a valley beneath Mount Hermon where the town of Baal-gad stood. It marked the northern limit of the land Joshua conquered, which stretched south to Mount Halak on the way up to Seir (Josh 11:17; 12:7). The kings of this territory west of the Jordan were defeated, and the land was divided among the tribes of Israel. The verses give no further detail. It is commonly taken to be the southern end of the broad valley between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon ranges, now called the Beqaa in Lebanon. Some place it more narrowly in a side valley along Hermon's western slopes, such as the Wadi et-Teim. The location shown here sits in the Hermon area, matching the valley's description as lying under the mountain.

The Valley of Mizpeh was a valley in the far north of Canaan, named in Joshua 11:8 as one of the places to which Israel chased the northern kings after defeating them at the waters of Merom. The pursuit went in several directions: northwest to Sidon and Misrephoth-maim, and eastward to the valley of Mizpeh. The verse gives no further detail. Because Josh 11:3 places Hivites "under Hermon in the land of Mizpeh," the valley is probably the same region, lying below Mount Hermon. Its exact site is uncertain. Some place it in the Marj Ayun (the biblical Ijon area) in southern Lebanon, and others in the valleys running along the western foot of Hermon. The location shown here lies near the northern end of the Hula Valley, close to modern Metula, which fits a placement just south of Marj Ayun.

The Valley of Rephaim was a valley just southwest of Jerusalem, on the border between the tribes of Judah and Benjamin. The boundary descriptions in Josh 15:8 and Josh 18:16, where the King James Version calls it "the valley of the giants," place it at the north end near the valley of Hinnom, and this entry also links it with that name. Philistine armies twice spread out in this valley to attack David after he became king, and both times he defeated them (2 Sam 5:18, 22; 1 Chr 14:9). They camped there again while David was at the cave of Adullam, at harvest time (2 Sam 23:13). Isaiah compares coming judgment to gleaning grain there, which suggests it was known as farmland (Isa 17:5). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it west and southwest of Jerusalem and identifies it with el-Bukei'a. The location shown here matches that general area.

The Valley of Salt was a valley near the border between Judah and Edom where two Israelite kings won battles against the Edomites. In David's reign, 18,000 men were struck down there. 2 Sam 8:13 says they were Syrians, while the parallel account in 1 Chr 18:12 says they were Edomites and credits the victory to Abishai son of Zeruiah. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that some interpreters therefore take the 2 Samuel text to refer to Edom as well. The heading of Ps 60 links Joab with a victory over Edom there. Later, King Amaziah of Judah killed 10,000 Edomites in the valley and then captured Selah, which he renamed Joktheel. Easton's places the valley in the Arabah south of the Dead Sea, while others identify it with Wadi el-Milh east of Beersheba. The location shown here follows the southern Dead Sea identification.

The Valley of Shaveh was the place where the king of Sodom went out to meet Abram as he returned from defeating Chedorlaomer and the kings allied with him (Gen 14:17). The text identifies it with the "king's dale," which is probably the same King's Dale where Absalom later set up a pillar for himself (2 Sam 18:18). The next verse says Melchizedek, king of Salem, also met Abram, which suggests the valley lay near Salem, usually taken to be Jerusalem. Its exact site is uncertain. A common view places it in or near the Kidron Valley just east of Jerusalem, and the rough location shown here follows that identification near the city. It is distinct from Shaveh-kiriathaim (Gen 14:5), a similar name for a different place east of the Jordan.

The Valley of Shaveh, also called the King's Dale (ESV King's Valley), was a valley where the king of Sodom went out to meet Abram after Abram defeated Chedorlaomer and his allied kings (Gen 14:17). The following verse has Melchizedek, king of Salem, bringing out bread and wine at the same meeting, so the valley was probably near Salem, usually understood as Jerusalem. Centuries later, Absalom set up a pillar for himself in the King's Dale because he had no son to carry on his name, and it became known as Absalom's place (2 Sam 18:18). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies the valley with the Kidron, beside Jerusalem, and the location shown here follows that view, placing it in the Kidron Valley east of the Old City. It should not be confused with Shaveh Kiriathaim, a different place named in the same chapter.

The Valley of Shittim is a valley named only once in the Bible, in Joel's prophecy of a future day when a fountain will flow from the house of the Lord and water it (Joel 3:18). The name means "valley of acacias." Acacias grow in dry ground, so the image is probably of water reaching a parched place. Its location is uncertain. Some link it with Shittim, the camp of Israel on the plains of Moab east of the Jordan, across from Jericho, where Israel stayed before entering Canaan (Num 25:1; Josh 2:1). Others take it as a dry valley running from the Jerusalem area down toward the Dead Sea, such as the Kidron, or as a symbolic name for any arid valley. The location shown here follows the association with Shittim on the plains of Moab, northeast of the Dead Sea.

Valley of Slaughter is the name Jeremiah said would replace the names Tophet and the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, the valley just outside Jerusalem. In two nearly identical prophecies (Jer 7:32; Jer 19:6), the LORD declares that the days are coming when the place will no longer be called by its old names but by this new one, because so many dead will be buried at Tophet that no room will remain. It is therefore not a separate location but a prophetic renaming of the Hinnom Valley. That valley is generally identified with the Wadi er-Rababi, which curves along the western and southern sides of Jerusalem's Old City, and the location shown here lies in that area. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the name together with its entries on the Valley of Hinnom and Topheth.

The Valley of Sorek was the valley where Delilah lived, the woman Samson loved after his exploits at Gaza (Judg 16:4). The name probably means "choice vine," according to Easton's Bible Dictionary, which suggests the valley was known for its vineyards. It is generally identified with the modern Wadi es-Sarar (Wadi Surar), a seasonal stream bed that drains the western Judean hills and runs northwest toward the Mediterranean. Easton's places its mouth about eight miles south of Joppa and traces its course past Makkedah and Jabneel. The location shown here lies in the lowlands west of the hill country, near the old border between Judah and Philistine territory. That setting fits the story, in which the Philistine rulers approach Delilah, though the text itself does not say whether she was a Philistine.

The Valley of Succoth was a valley east of the Jordan River, named after the town of Succoth. It appears only in a poetic oracle repeated in Ps 60:6 and Ps 108:7, where God declares that he will divide Shechem and measure out the valley of Succoth. The pairing probably sets a place west of the Jordan beside one to the east, together standing for the land being allotted. The town itself, according to Easton's Bible Dictionary, is where Jacob built a house and shelters for his cattle after meeting Esau. It is also the town whose leaders refused to help Gideon, and the area near where bronze work for Solomon's temple was cast. Easton's identifies it with Tell Deir Alla, a mound in the plain north of the Jabbok River, and the location shown here matches that site. The valley is probably the surrounding stretch of the Jordan Valley.

The Valley of the Passengers (ESV "Valley of the Travelers") is a valley named in Ezekiel's prophecy against Gog as the place where Gog and all his multitude would be buried. It is described as lying "in Israel… on the east of the sea," and the passage says it would "stop the noses of the passengers," probably meaning that the dead would block or overwhelm those travelling through. It would then be renamed the Valley of Hamon-gog, meaning "the multitude of Gog" (Ezek 39:11). Its location is uncertain. "The sea" is usually taken to be the Dead Sea, and some interpreters connect the Hebrew word for "passengers" with the Abarim mountains east of it. Others place the valley on a route east of the Mediterranean or the Sea of Galilee. The location shown here follows the view that it lay east of the Dead Sea, in the region of Moab.

The Valley of the Son of Hinnom was a valley beside Jerusalem, also called the valley of the children of Hinnom. It contained Topheth, a site of high places where people burned their sons and daughters in fire as offerings to Molech and Baal (Jer 7:31; 32:35). By inference from the surrounding chapters, kings Ahaz and Manasseh sacrificed their children there (2 Chr 28:3; 33:6), and Josiah later defiled Topheth to end the practice (2 Kgs 23:10). Jeremiah was sent there to announce that it would be renamed the valley of slaughter and filled with burials (Jer 7:32; 19:2, 6). Josh 15:8 places it on Judah's northern boundary. It is usually identified with the modern Wadi er-Rababi, which curves along the west and south of Jerusalem's Old City; the location shown here follows that view. Its Hebrew name, Ge-Hinnom, gave rise to the later term Gehenna.

The Valley of Zeboim was a valley in the territory of Benjamin. It is mentioned only in 1 Sam 13:18. During Saul's war with the Philistines, raiding parties went out from the Philistine camp at Michmash. One went toward Bethhoron, and another took the road along the border that overlooked the Valley of Zeboim toward the wilderness. The wilderness there is probably the barren country sloping down to the Jordan Valley. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it near Gibeah and identifies it with a ravine north of Jericho called Wady Shakh-ed-Dub'a, meaning "ravine of the hyena." The location shown here follows the identification with Wadi ed Dubba, in the hills east of Michmash toward Jericho. This valley is a different place from Zeboiim, one of the cities of the plain near Sodom, although the two names look alike in English.

The Valley of Zephathah was a valley at Mareshah in the lowland of Judah, where King Asa drew up his army against Zerah the Ethiopian (2 Chr 14:10). By inference from the surrounding passage, Asa defeated Zerah's large force there and pursued it as far as Gerar. Mareshah is generally identified with Tel Maresha, near modern Beit Guvrin, so the valley was probably one of the broad wadis running through the low hills near that town. The exact valley is uncertain. The Greek Septuagint reads the phrase as "the valley north of Mareshah" instead of giving a place name, and some have connected the name with the Wadi es-Safiyeh in the same district. The location shown here places the valley just north of Mareshah, which fits both readings.

The Valley of Zered was a valley or stream course east of the southern end of the Dead Sea where the Israelites camped during their wilderness journey, after leaving the border of Moab and before moving on to the Arnon (Num 21:12). The KJV spells it "Zared." Deut 2:13–14 calls it the brook Zered and marks its crossing as the end of thirty-eight years of wandering. Lying between Edom and Moab, it probably formed a boundary between the two, by inference from these passages. Easton's Bible Dictionary links it with the "brook of the willows" (Isa 15:7) and the "river of the wilderness" (Amos 6:14), and names Wady el-Aksy as one identification. It is more commonly identified with the Wadi al-Hasa in modern Jordan, which flows into the southeastern Dead Sea. The location shown here follows the Wadi al-Hasa identification.

Vaniah was an Israelite named in the list of men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra and agreed to send them away (Ezra 10:36). He is listed among the descendants of Bani, a family group whose members appear in Ezra 10:34–42. This would place him in Jerusalem after the return from exile, about 458 BC by inference from context, a date Smith's Bible Dictionary also gives. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew text of the name is uncertain and that Greek manuscripts spell it in several different ways. The meaning of the name is also unclear: Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "Jehovah is praise," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "nourishment, or weapons, of the Lord."

Vashti was the queen of the Persian king Ahasuerus, whom the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies with Xerxes. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains her name as meaning "beautiful." While the king held a great feast, she hosted a feast for the women in the royal house. When the king sent his chamberlains to bring her before his guests wearing the royal crown so that he could show off her beauty, she refused, and he was furious. His adviser Memucan argued that her refusal wronged the whole empire and would encourage wives everywhere to despise their husbands. He proposed an unalterable decree that she never again come before the king and that her royal position go to another. The king agreed, and Esther was later crowned queen in her place. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests Vashti was a lesser wife given the title of queen. This entry follows the narrative's consistent title of "queen," as does the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia.

The Visiting Capernaum event was a brief stay Jesus made in the town of Capernaum, on the northwestern shore of the Sea of Galilee, soon after turning water into wine at the wedding in Cana. According to John 2:12, he went down to Capernaum with his mother, his brothers and his disciples, and they stayed there only a few days. The phrase "went down" fits the geography, since Cana lay in the hills and Capernaum sat lower, by the lake. John gives no details of what happened during the visit. The surrounding context suggests it was a short pause before Jesus traveled to Jerusalem for the Passover (John 2:13). The date of about AD 27 and the length given here are estimates inferred from context, not stated in the text.

Vophsi was a man of the tribe of Naphtali and the father of Nahbi, who represented Naphtali among the twelve men Moses sent to scout the land of Canaan (Num 13:14). He appears only in this list of the scouts and their fathers, and nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "rich", Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "fragrant", and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls the meaning unknown. That encyclopedia also notes that the Hebrew text of the name may be doubtful, since early Greek manuscripts of the Septuagint read it differently, as Iabei or Iabi. By inference from the setting of the scouting mission in the wilderness period, he lived before the Israelites entered Canaan.

The Voyage from Miletus to Jerusalem was the final stage of Paul's third missionary journey. After leaving the Ephesian elders, Paul and his companions, including the narrator of the "we" passages, traditionally identified as Luke, sailed by Coos and Rhodes to Patara, where they boarded a ship bound for Phenicia. Passing Cyprus, they landed at Tyre and stayed seven days with disciples who urged Paul through the Spirit not to go to Jerusalem. They continued to Ptolemais, then Caesarea, staying with Philip the evangelist, whose four unmarried daughters prophesied. There the prophet Agabus bound his own hands and feet with Paul's belt, foretelling that Paul would be bound in Jerusalem and handed to the Gentiles. Paul declared himself ready to die for the Lord Jesus. Disciples from Caesarea escorted him to Jerusalem to lodge with Mnason of Cyprus, and the believers welcomed them. By inference from context, the journey took about a month, around AD 54.

The Voyage to Miletus was the leg of Paul's third missionary journey that carried him by sea along the coast of Asia from Troas, where Eutychus had just been revived, to Miletus. The narrator's companions sailed ahead to Assos while Paul chose to go there on foot, and they took him on board there (Acts 20:13–14). The writer uses "we", which is traditionally taken to mean Luke was in the party. They stopped at Mitylene on Lesbos, passed Chios, reached Samos, stayed at Trogyllium, and arrived at Miletus the next day (Acts 20:15). Paul deliberately sailed past Ephesus so as not to lose time in Asia, because he hoped to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost (Acts 20:16). By inference from context, the trip took about a week, around AD 54. Assos and Miletus lie on the western coast of modern Turkey.

Waheb is a place named in a short poem that Num 21:14 quotes from the Book of the Wars of the LORD, a lost collection of songs. The Hebrew text reads something like "Waheb in Suphah, and the brooks of Arnon." The King James Version does not show Waheb as a name. It renders the line as "What he did in the Red sea," reading the Hebrew as a verb and taking Suphah as the Red Sea. Many modern translations instead treat Waheb as a place name. Because the poem goes on to the Arnon valleys, Waheb was probably a site near the Arnon, on the border of Moab, and STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) places it possibly in Moab. Its exact location is unknown. The location shown here is rough and follows the reading that links the line with the Red Sea.

The War with Canaanites was Israel's campaign under Joshua to conquer Canaan after crossing the Jordan, recounted in Josh 4–12. From a base camp at Gilgal, where memorial stones from the Jordan were set up and the men were circumcised, Israel took Jericho and burned it. An initial defeat at Ai was traced to Achan's taking of forbidden spoil, and Ai then fell to an ambush. The Gibeonites tricked Israel into a treaty by posing as travelers from far away, with worn-out clothes and moldy bread. Five southern kings led by Adonizedek of Jerusalem attacked Gibeon. Joshua defeated them and took Makkedah, Lachish, Eglon and other southern cities. In the north he took Hazor, the head of a coalition of kingdoms. Joshua 12 lists thirty-one defeated kings, though some Anakim remained in Gaza, Gath and Ashdod. The campaign's start, about 1451 BC, and its length of about seven years are estimates inferred from context.

The Water covers the earth episode is the stage of the Great Flood when the waters rose to their height and stayed there. Genesis says the waters increased greatly and the ark floated on their surface. They covered all the high hills under heaven, rising fifteen cubits (roughly 7 meters) above the mountains. Every living creature on dry land that breathed died, including birds, livestock, wild animals, creeping things and people. Only Noah and those with him in the ark survived. Those were his sons Shem, Ham and Japheth and the family members named elsewhere in the flood account. The waters prevailed on the earth for 150 days. This followed the start of the flood, and it is dated here to about 2348 BC, by inference from the biblical chronology rather than from any date given in the text.

The Water Gate was a landmark on the east side of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. Neh 3:26 places it opposite the area of Ophel where the temple servants (the Nethinim) lived, near a projecting tower. Its name probably reflects a route down to the Gihon Spring in the Kidron Valley below, though the text does not say so. In front of it was an open square, where the people gathered and asked Ezra the scribe to bring out the book of the law of Moses. He read it aloud there from morning until midday to men, women and all who could understand. During the Feast of Tabernacles that followed, people built booths in this same square. Neh 12:37 mentions it again in the procession at the dedication of the wall. The location shown here places it on the eastern slope of the City of David.

The Water to Wine miracle was the first sign Jesus performed, at a wedding in Cana of Galilee. Jesus, his disciples and his mother were guests, and when the wine ran out his mother told him. He answered that his hour had not yet come, but she told the servants to do whatever he said. Six stone water jars, used for Jewish purification rites and each holding two or three firkins (roughly 20 to 30 gallons), stood nearby. Jesus had the servants fill them to the brim with water and then draw some out for the master of the feast. Not knowing where it came from, he tasted it and told the bridegroom that he had saved the good wine until last, against the usual custom. John calls this the beginning of Jesus' miracles, says it revealed his glory, and records that his disciples believed in him. It is dated about AD 27, by inference from context.

The Way of Holiness is the name Isaiah gives to a highway he foresees in the prophecy of Isa 35. In his description it is a road on which the unclean will not travel. It is meant for those who walk it, and even the simple will not lose their way on it (Isa 35:8). The surrounding chapter pictures the desert blooming and the redeemed returning to Zion with singing, so the highway is a road leading back to Jerusalem. The STEPBible proper-names index describes it as a prophesied highway reserved for the redeemed and leading to Zion. It is a road in a prophetic vision, not a known physical route.
