The location shown here is only a rough placement at Jerusalem, its destination, and does not mark an actual road.

West Manasseh was the territory of the half of the tribe of Manasseh that settled west of the Jordan River, in the central hill country of Canaan. The other half held Gilead and Bashan east of the Jordan (Josh 17:1, 17:5–6). The western lot went to the clans of Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Hepher and Shemida, and the daughters of Zelophehad also received land there (Josh 17:2–4). Its border ran from near Shechem to the Kanah brook, which divided it from Ephraim to the south. It reached the Mediterranean on the west and touched Asher and Issachar to the north and east (Josh 17:7–10). Some Ephraimite towns lay inside it (Josh 16:9). Manasseh also claimed cities such as Beth-shean, Taanach, Megiddo and Dor, but could not drive out their Canaanite inhabitants and later made them pay tribute (Josh 17:11–13; Judg 1:27). This area is roughly the northern Samaria hills of today.

The Widow's Son Resurrected was the raising of a dead young man by Jesus at the town of Nain, recorded only in Luke's Gospel. It took place the day after Jesus healed a centurion's servant, about AD 28 by inference from context. Jesus arrived at the town gate with his disciples and a large crowd just as a funeral procession was coming out. The dead man was the only son of a widow, and many townspeople were with her. Jesus felt compassion for her and told her not to weep. He touched the bier, the bearers stopped, and he said, "Young man, I say to you, arise." The man sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him back to his mother. Everyone was struck with fear and praised God, saying that a great prophet had arisen among them. Reports of the event spread through Judea and the surrounding region.

The Wife of Ezekiel was the unnamed wife of the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the Jewish exiles in Babylon. She is mentioned only once: Ezekiel says he spoke to the people in the morning, his wife died that evening, and the next morning he did as he had been commanded (Ezek 24:18). The surrounding passage (Ezek 24:15–24) explains the command. God told Ezekiel he would take away "the desire of thine eyes" with a sudden stroke and that he must not mourn openly for her. His restraint was to serve as a sign to the exiles: when Jerusalem's temple, the object of their own desire, was destroyed, they too would be stunned beyond customary mourning. The STEPBible Proper Names index likewise describes her sudden death as a sign to Israel. Her name, age and family are not recorded.

Wife of Simon was the wife of the apostle Simon Peter. She is never named, and she appears only indirectly: the Gospels mention her when Jesus came to Simon's house and found her mother lying sick with a fever (Matt 8:14; Mark 1:30; Luke 4:38). Luke and Mark place this visit right after Jesus left the synagogue, and the surrounding passages set it in Capernaum, where Mark describes the home as the house of Simon and Andrew. By inference, her mother was living in the household. Nothing else is recorded about her in these accounts. Paul's later remark in 1 Cor 9:5 that Cephas (Peter) took a believing wife with him on his travels probably refers to her, which would suggest she accompanied him in his later work.

The Wilderness Wanderings were the journeys of the nation of Israel, led by Moses and Aaron, that followed the Exodus from Egypt. This passage covers the opening stage. God led the people by a roundabout desert route, guided by a pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night (Exod 13:18, 22). Pursued by Pharaoh's chariots, they crossed the Red Sea on dry land while the Egyptians drowned, and Moses and the people sang a song of victory (Exod 14:21–29; 15:1). They then found bitter water at Marah, were fed with manna in the wilderness, and complained of thirst at Massah and Meribah, where Joshua fought Amalek (Exod 15:23; 16:14; 17:7, 10). At the mount of God, Moses' father-in-law Jethro advised him on judging the people (Exod 18:5, 13). Numbers and Deuteronomy continue the wanderings over about forty years, beginning around 1491 BC by inference from context.

Willows, or the Brook of the Willows, was a stream named in Isaiah's lament over Moab. Isaiah pictures the Moabites, fleeing disaster, carrying the wealth they had stored up away across this brook (Isa 15:7). The name probably comes from the willows or poplars that grew along watercourses in the region. The text does not say where it was. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it on Moab's southern boundary and calls it Wady el-Aksa. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes it as a stream running from Moab to the Jordan or the Dead Sea and notes that it is generally identified with the brook Zered, probably the modern Wadi al-Hasa. STEPBible's proper-names list also treats it as a boundary of Moab, possibly near the Zered. The location shown here is only a rough placement on the east side of the Jordan Valley, so the brook's exact site remains uncertain.

The Wise Men Visit Herod was the arrival in Jerusalem of wise men from the east, after Jesus' birth in Bethlehem, asking where the newborn King of the Jews was, since they had seen his star and had come to worship him. King Herod was troubled by the news, and so was all Jerusalem. He gathered the chief priests and scribes and asked where the Christ was to be born. They answered Bethlehem of Judea and quoted a prophecy that a ruler of Israel would come from there (Matt 2:6, from Mic 5:2). Herod then met the wise men privately, questioned them closely about when the star had appeared, and sent them to Bethlehem. He told them to search carefully for the child and report back so that he could also come and worship him. The date of about 4 BC is inferred from context, around the end of Herod's reign.

The Wise Men Visit Jesus was the occasion when the wise men from the east, after meeting King Herod in Jerusalem, found the young Jesus at Bethlehem. The star they had seen in the east went ahead of them and stopped over the place where the child was, and they were overjoyed when they saw it. Entering the house, they found the child with his mother Mary, bowed down and worshipped him, and opened their treasures to give him gold, frankincense and myrrh. Warned by God in a dream not to go back to Herod, they returned to their own country by a different route. The passage speaks of a house and a "young child" rather than a newborn, which suggests the visit came some time after the birth. This entry dates it to about 4 BC, an estimate inferred from context, and treats it as a single day's event.

The Woe to Chorazin and Bethsaida was a rebuke Jesus spoke against the Galilean towns where most of his miracles had been done, because their people had not repented. He declared that if Tyre and Sidon had seen the same works, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes, so judgment would be more bearable for them. He said Capernaum would be brought down rather than exalted, and that even Sodom would have survived had it seen such works. Matthew places the rebuke right after Jesus' words about John the Baptist, about AD 28 by inference from context. The passage goes on with Jesus thanking the Father for revealing these things to the humble rather than the wise, saying that only the Son truly knows the Father, and inviting the weary to take his yoke and find rest. A similar woe appears in Luke 10:13–15, in a different setting.

The Woes and Parables with Pharisees is the name this entry gives to a stretch of Jesus' teaching in Luke 11:37–13:9. It begins when a Pharisee invites Jesus to dine. Jesus criticizes the Pharisees for cleaning the outside of the cup while being full of greed inside, and he pronounces woes on them and on the lawyers for burdening others and hindering those seeking knowledge. Afterward they watch him closely, hoping to catch him in his words. Jesus then warns his disciples against hypocrisy and fear and refuses to settle a family inheritance dispute. He tells the parable of the rich fool, urges trust in God's care for ravens and lilies, and calls for watchful, faithful servants. When Peter asks whom the parable is for (Luke 12:41), Jesus answers with the image of the faithful steward. The passage ends with a call to repent and the parable of the barren fig tree. This entry dates it to about AD 29, by inference from context.

The Woman Caught in Adultery is an episode in John's Gospel set in the temple at Jerusalem, about AD 29 by inference from context, just after the Feast of Tabernacles. After a night on the Mount of Olives, Jesus was teaching in the temple when the scribes and Pharisees brought him a woman caught in the act of adultery. They said the law of Moses required such a person to be stoned (compare Lev 20:10; Deut 22:22–24) and asked his view, hoping to find grounds to accuse him. Jesus stooped and wrote on the ground, then said that whoever among them was without sin should throw the first stone. The accusers left one by one, beginning with the eldest. Jesus told the woman that he did not condemn her either, and sent her away telling her to sin no more. The passage (John 7:53–8:11) is missing from many early manuscripts of John.

Yiron was a fortified town in the territory of the tribe of Naphtali, spelled "Iron" in the King James Version. It appears only once, in the list of cities given to Naphtali when the land was divided among the tribes (Josh 19:38). It is named alongside Migdalel, Horem, Beth-anath and Beth-shemesh, near the end of a list that totals nineteen cities with their villages. Nothing else is recorded about it. The site is generally identified with the modern village of Yaroun in southern Lebanon, close to the present border with Israel, and the location shown here follows that identification. STEPBible's proper-names index, from Tyndale House, likewise treats it as a Naphtali town known only from this allotment list.

Zaanan was a town of Judah named only once in the Bible, in Micah's lament over the towns of the Shephelah, the low hill country west of Jerusalem (Mic 1:11). Micah says that the inhabitant of Zaanan "came not forth." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that this is wordplay: the town's name sounds like the Hebrew verb for "to go forth," so the people of a town whose name suggests going out stay shut in. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning "place of flocks." Both Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggest it is probably the same place as Zenan, a town in the lowland of Judah listed in Josh 15:37. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is a rough placement in the Judean Shephelah, consistent with that identification.

Zaanannim was a place on the border of the tribe of Naphtali, listed among the boundary points of that tribe's territory in Josh 19:33. It is probably the same place as the "plain of Zaanaim" near Kedesh, where Heber the Kenite, who had separated from the rest of the Kenites, pitched his tent (Judg 4:11). Later in the same chapter Sisera flees to the tent of Heber's wife Jael. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the Revised Version reads "as far as the oak" of Zaanaim instead of "plain." It places the site north-west of Lake Merom (the Huleh basin), near Kedesh. Easton's also records another view, based on the Septuagint and the Talmud, that reads the name as Bitzanaim and identifies it with ruins called Bessum between Tiberias and Mount Tabor. The location shown here follows the identification near Kedesh in upper Galilee, and it is only approximate.

Zabad, also called Jozachar, was one of the two royal servants who conspired against King Joash of Judah and killed him. 2 Chronicles names him Zabad, son of Shimeath, an Ammonite woman. His fellow conspirator was Jehozabad, son of Shimrith, a Moabite woman (2 Chr 24:26). The parallel account in 2 Kgs 12:21 calls him Jozachar son of Shimeath and says the two men struck the king down. Joash was buried in the city of David, and his son Amaziah succeeded him. The surrounding verse in Chronicles (2 Chr 24:25) explains that the conspiracy followed the death of Zechariah son of Jehoiada. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Jozachar to be probably the more accurate form of the name. Several other men in the Bible are also named Zabad, and this entry concerns only Joash's assassin.

Zabad was a man of the tribe of Judah, listed in the genealogy of the Jerahmeelite clan in 1 Chronicles. He was the son of Nathan and the father of Ephlal, whose son was Obed (1 Chr 2:36–37). By inference from the surrounding verses, his line traces back to Sheshan, a Jerahmeelite who had no sons and gave his daughter in marriage to Jarha, his Egyptian servant. Their son Attai was Nathan's father, which makes Zabad Sheshan's great-great-grandson. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may be a shortened form of Zebadiah, meaning "the Lord has given." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "dowry" or "endowed." Several other men in the Bible share this name, and nothing beyond his place in this family list is recorded about this Zabad.

Zabad was a descendant of Ephraim, son of Joseph, named in the Ephraimite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:21. He was the son of Tahath and the father of Shuthelah, several generations after Ephraim. The same verse goes on to mention Ezer and Elead, who were killed by the men of Gath when they came down to take the local people's cattle. It is unclear whether this killing involves Zabad himself. The Tyndale House proper-names index (STEPBible) reads it that way, treating him as a son of Ephraim killed by the men of Gath. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the text of this genealogy is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may be a shortened form of Zebadiah, meaning "Yahweh has given," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "dowry" or "endowed." Several other men in the Bible share the name Zabad.

Zabad, son of Ahlai, was one of David's mighty warriors. He appears only in the Chronicler's list of David's valiant men, where he is named right after Uriah the Hittite (1 Chr 11:41). The parallel list in 2 Samuel 23 ends with Uriah and does not include him. Easton's Bible Dictionary links his father Ahlai to the "children of Sheshan" in the genealogy of Judah (1 Chr 2:31). If that link holds, Zabad came from the Jerahmeelite clans of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about his life or deeds. Several other men in the Bible share the name, so he should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "dowry" or "endowed."

Zabad was one of the descendants of Zattu listed in Ezra 10:27 among the Israelite men who had married foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon. The surrounding chapter describes how, at Ezra's urging, these men agreed to send away their foreign wives. Zabad appears with Elioenai, Eliashib, Mattaniah, Jeremoth and Aziza in the group from the family of Zattu. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a layman and dates the event to about 458 BC, an estimate drawn from context. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "dowry" or "endowed," while Smith's renders it "gift." Several other men in the Bible share this name. This Zabad is known only from this single list.

Zabad was one of the descendants of Hashum named in Ezra 10:33. He appears in the list of men who had married foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was among those who agreed to send these wives away during the reforms led by Ezra. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this event to about 458 BC, an estimate drawn from context. His name is usually taken to mean "gift" or "endowed." Several other men in the Bible share the name Zabad, and he should not be confused with them. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Zabad was one of the descendants of Nebo listed in Ezra 10:43 among the Israelite men who had married foreign wives. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was one of those who agreed under Ezra's reforms after the return from exile to put away these wives. Nebo here is probably a family or clan name, possibly tied to the town of Nebo in Judah's territory, rather than his literal father. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "gift," and Hitchcock's Bible Names as "dowry" or "endowed." Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Zabad is shared by several other men in the Bible, including others in the same list in Ezra 10, so this Zabad should be kept distinct from them.

Zabbai was a descendant of Bebai, one of the Israelites in Ezra's time who had married foreign wives. Ezra 10 lists the returned exiles who agreed to put away these wives. Zabbai is named there with Jehohanan, Hananiah and Athlai, all "of the sons of Bebai" (Ezra 10:28). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 458 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras gives his name as Jozabdus. The meaning of the name is uncertain: Smith's gives "pure" and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "flowing." Several people in the Bible bear the name Zabbai, and this one is known only from this verse.

Zabbai was the father of Baruch, one of the men who repaired Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah. Baruch worked "earnestly" on the section running from the turning of the wall to the door of the house of Eliashib the high priest (Neh 3:20). Nothing else is recorded about Zabbai himself. He lived before the rebuilding, which Smith's Bible Dictionary places shortly before 446 BC. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that a marginal reading gives the name as "Zaccai." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "flowing", and Smith's as "pure." The name is also borne by another man in the same period: a Zabbai listed in Ezra 10:28 among those who had married foreign wives. Whether he is the same person as Baruch's father is uncertain, and this entry treats only the father of Baruch.

Zabbud was one of the descendants of Bigvai who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. Ezra 8:14 names him together with Uthai as heads of the Bigvai family group, which brought seventy men on the journey. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "given", and Easton's Bible Dictionary as "gift". The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew text has two readings at this verse: the written form is Zabbud, while the traditional marginal reading is Zakkur (Zaccur). The STEPBible proper names index follows the Zaccur reading. Smith's dates the return to about 459 BC. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Zabdi was a man of the tribe of Judah, the son of Zerah and the grandfather of Achan through his son Carmi (Josh 7:1, 7:18). When the lot was cast to find who had taken the forbidden plunder from Jericho, it fell first on the family of the Zarhites and then on Zabdi, before narrowing to his household and to Achan (Josh 7:17–18). He is probably the same man as Zimri, listed in 1 Chr 2:6 as one of the five sons of Zerah alongside Ethan, Heman, Calcol and Dara. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both make this identification, and the latter explains the difference in spelling as an easy confusion of similar Hebrew letters. This entry follows that view. The name is shared by several other people in the Bible, and Zabdi may be a more distant ancestor of Achan than the genealogy's simple "son of" wording suggests.

Zabdi was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the sons of Shimhi named in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 8:19–21. His brothers were Jakim, Zichri, Elienai, Zilthai, Eliel, Adaiah, Beraiah and Shimrath. The passage records only his name and family. It belongs to the list of Benjamite households that leads up to the family of King Saul later in the same chapter. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "my gift," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "gift of the LORD" and notes that he was possibly a descendant of Ehud. Several other men in the Bible are also called Zabdi, and this one should not be confused with them.

Zabdi, called "the Shiphmite," was one of King David's officials. He was in charge of the produce of the royal vineyards that went into the wine cellars (1 Chr 27:27), while Shimei the Ramathite oversaw the vineyards themselves. The title "Shiphmite" probably points to his hometown or clan, perhaps Shepham or Siphmoth, though neither link is certain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may mean "gift of the LORD" or "my gift" and relates it to the New Testament name Zebedee. It also notes that one ancient Greek manuscript of the Septuagint gives the name as Zachrei, probably a form of Zichri. Several other men in the Bible share the name Zabdi, and this entry concerns only David's steward.

Zabdiel was the father of Jashobeam, the officer who commanded the first of the twelve monthly divisions of King David's army. Jashobeam's division served in the first month of the year and numbered twenty-four thousand men (1 Chr 27:2). Nothing else is recorded about Zabdiel himself. His name is usually explained as meaning "my gift is God" or "gift of God" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). This Jashobeam is probably the same man as the chief of David's mighty men named in 1 Chr 11:11, who is called there a Hachmonite. The name Zabdiel is borne by more than one person in the Bible, and this entry concerns only the father of David's commander.

Zabdiel was the overseer of a group of 128 priests, described as "mighty men of valour," who lived in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile (Neh 11:14). The name means "my gift is God" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. The King James Version calls him "the son of one of the great men," but the Hebrew can also be read as a proper name, Haggedolim, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes from the marginal reading. On that reading his father was a man named Haggedolim. That the men under him were priests follows from the surrounding list in Nehemiah 11, which groups them with the priestly families settled in the city. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name is shared by other people in the Bible, and this entry concerns only the overseer in Nehemiah's time.

Zabud was a son of Nathan and an official at the court of King Solomon. He was a brother of Azariah, who was in charge of the district officers (1 Kgs 4:5). The King James Version calls Zabud "principal officer" and "the king's friend." Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the Hebrew word translated "principal officer" can mean "priest." It also describes "king's friend" as a trusted advisory post, one held earlier by Hushai the Archite under David (2 Sam 15:37; 1 Chr 27:33). His name means "given" or "gift," according to Easton's and Smith's dictionaries. Some interpreters take his father Nathan to be the prophet Nathan, while others think he was David's son Nathan. The text does not say which, so the identity remains uncertain. Zabud is mentioned only in this one verse.

Zaccai was the ancestor of a family whose descendants, 760 in number, returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem and Judah. The figure is the same in both lists of returning families (Ezra 2:9; Neh 7:14). Both lists place this return under Zerubbabel's leadership, and Smith's Bible Dictionary dates it to before 536 BC. Nothing else is recorded about Zaccai himself, and it is unclear whether the name refers to one individual or serves as a family or clan name. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "pure." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links the name to Zabbai, though the connection between the two is uncertain.

Zacchaeus was a rich chief tax collector at Jericho whom Jesus met while passing through the town on his way to Jerusalem, about AD 30 by inference from context (Luke 19:2). The wider passage says he was short and climbed a sycamore tree to see Jesus over the crowd. When Jesus reached the spot, he called Zacchaeus by name, told him to come down quickly, and said he must stay at his house that day (Luke 19:5). Zacchaeus then stood and announced that he would give half his goods to the poor and repay fourfold anyone he had cheated by false accusation (Luke 19:8). Jesus followed the meeting with the parable of the pounds. Smith's Bible Dictionary infers that Zacchaeus was a Jew, from his name and from Jesus calling him a son of Abraham. Easton's Bible Dictionary links his wealth to Jericho's profitable customs trade.

Zacchur was a member of the tribe of Simeon, named in the Simeonite genealogy of 1 Chr 4:26. He belonged to the family line of Mishma: he was the son of Hamuel and the father of Shimei. The context suggests this Shimei is the man noted in the following verse for having sixteen sons and six daughters, though the single verse here does not state it directly. Nothing else is recorded about Zacchur himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him simply as a Simeonite of the family of Mishma. His name is sometimes spelled Zaccur, a name also borne by several other men in the Old Testament who are distinct from this Simeonite.

Zaccur was a man of the tribe of Reuben and the father of Shammua. Shammua was the Reubenite among the twelve men Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan (Num 13:4). Zaccur is known only through this one mention as his son's father, and nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this entry is distinguished from them by his link to Shammua and the tribe of Reuben. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names give the meaning of the name as "mindful."

Zaccur was a Levite of the clan of Merari, named as one of the sons of Jaaziah alongside Beno, Shoham and Ibri. He appears only in the list of Levite families in 1 Chr 24:27, part of the record of how the Levites were organized for service in David's time. Jaaziah is himself described as a son of Merari, so Zaccur's line forms one branch of the Merarite Levites. Nothing further is recorded about his life. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "mindful." Several other men in the Bible bear the name Zaccur, and this one should not be confused with them.

Zaccur was a Levite, the first-named of the sons of Asaph, David's chief musician. He and his brothers Joseph, Nethaniah and Asarelah (called Jesharelah in 1 Chr 25:14) served under their father's direction and "prophesied" with music by the king's order (1 Chr 25:2). When David's musicians were divided by lot into twenty-four courses, the third lot fell to Zaccur, whose group of sons and kinsmen numbered twelve (1 Chr 25:10). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as chief of one of these courses of singers. Nehemiah 12:35 names a Zaccur son of Asaph as an ancestor of Zechariah, a trumpeter at the dedication of Jerusalem's wall, and Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to be the same man. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which Smith's gives as meaning "mindful."

Zaccur, son of Imri, was one of the builders who repaired the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah after the return from exile. Nehemiah 3 lists the work section by section around the city, and Zaccur's stretch lay next to the portion built by the men of Jericho, near the Sheep Gate at the start of the list (Neh 3:1–2). Nothing more is said about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the rebuilding to about 446 BC. Several other men in the Bible bear the name Zaccur, and this one is distinguished by his father's name. Smith's and Hitchcock's Bible Names give the meaning of the name as "mindful."

Zaccur was one of the men who set their seal to the written covenant made in Nehemiah's time, when the returned community of Jerusalem pledged to keep the law of God. His name appears in Neh 10:12 alongside Sherebiah and Shebaniah. By inference from the surrounding passage, which groups the signers as leaders, priests and Levites, he falls within the list of Levites. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him as a Levite, and this entry follows that view. Some reference works describe him instead as a priest. Nothing else is recorded about him, and several other men in the Bible share his name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as “mindful.”

Zaccur, son of Mattaniah, is known only as the father of Hanan, whom Nehemiah appointed as an assistant to the treasurers over the temple storehouses, alongside Shelemiah the priest, Zadok the scribe and Pedaiah the Levite (Neh 13:13). These men were chosen because they were considered trustworthy, and their job was to distribute supplies to their fellow workers. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Zaccur to have been a Levite and allows that Hanan may have been his descendant rather than his immediate son. The verse itself does not say which group his family belonged to. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "mindful." Several other men in the Bible are also named Zaccur, and this one should not be confused with them.

Zachariah was a king of the northern kingdom of Israel and the son of Jeroboam (Jeroboam II), whom he succeeded on the throne (2 Kgs 14:29). He began to reign in Samaria in the thirty-eighth year of Azariah king of Judah, and he ruled for only six months (2 Kgs 15:8). The surrounding verses (2 Kgs 15:9–10) say he did evil as his fathers had done and that Shallum son of Jabesh conspired against him, killed him publicly and took the throne. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that his death ended the dynasty of Jehu, and it holds that about ten years passed between his father's death and his accession. Other records of his reign were kept in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel (2 Kgs 15:11). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "memory of the Lord."

Zacharias was a priest of the division of Abia (Abijah) in the days of Herod, king of Judaea, and the husband of Elisabeth, who was also of priestly descent. Both were old and childless. While he served in the temple, an angel told him his prayer had been heard and that Elisabeth would bear a son to be named John. Zacharias asked how he could know this, given their age. The people outside wondered why he stayed so long in the temple. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that he was struck mute for his unbelief until the child was born. When relatives wanted to name the baby Zacharias after his father, he confirmed the name John, was filled with the Holy Ghost, and prophesied. His son grew up to be John the Baptist. The name is the Greek form of Zechariah and is shared by others in the Bible, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes.

Zacharias, also called Zechariah, was the son of Jehoiada the priest and lived in the reign of King Joash of Judah. After Jehoiada's death, the Spirit of God came on him. He stood above the people and warned that because they had forsaken the LORD, the LORD had forsaken them (2 Chr 24:20). The next verses say the people stoned him in the temple court at the king's command. Jesus refers to the killing of a Zacharias 'between the temple and the altar' and pairs him with Abel (Matt 23:35; Luke 11:51). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that 2 Chronicles is the last book of the Hebrew Bible, so he was seen as its last recorded martyr, as Abel was the first. Matthew calls him 'son of Barachias.' Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests Barachias may have been his grandfather, and some early Greek writers linked this Zacharias to John the Baptist's father. This entry follows the identification with Jehoiada's son.

Zacher was a Benjamite listed among the sons of the founder of Gibeon and his wife Maachah in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles. He appears in 1 Chr 8:31, and the parallel list in 1 Chr 9:37 calls him Zechariah. The father is named Jehiel or Jeiel in the surrounding verses. This entry identifies him with Abiel, who in 1 Sam 9:1 is the father of Kish. His brothers included Abdon, Zur, Kish, Baal, Ner, Nadab, Gedor, Ahio and Mikloth. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says he lived in Gibeon and, as a brother of Kish, was an uncle of King Saul. Nothing is recorded about him beyond his place in these family lists. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "memorial."

Zadok, son of Ahitub, was a Levite priest descended from Aaron's son Eleazar who served as one of the two chief priests under King David, alongside Abiathar. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him with the valiant young Zadok who joined David at Hebron (1 Chr 12:28). During Absalom's revolt he and the Levites carried the ark out of Jerusalem, but David sent them back, and Zadok's son Ahimaaz carried news to the king. When Adonijah claimed the throne, Zadok stayed loyal and, at David's order, anointed Solomon king at Gihon with oil from the tabernacle. Solomon then put him in Abiathar's place. Chronicles also places him before the tabernacle at Gibeon. His descendants, 'the house of Zadok', later held the chief priesthood, and Ezekiel names the sons of Zadok as the priests allowed to minister at the altar. Several other men in the Bible share this name.

Zadok was the father of Jerushah (also spelled Jerusha), the mother of King Jotham of Judah. Both accounts of Jotham's reign name her as "the daughter of Zadok" when they introduce the king, who began to reign at twenty-five and ruled sixteen years in Jerusalem (2 Kgs 15:33; 2 Chr 27:1). Since Jotham was the son of King Uzziah (also called Azariah), Jerushah was Uzziah's wife, which made Zadok the king's father-in-law and Jotham's maternal grandfather. Through Jotham, who appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, Zadok is connected to that line. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with the better-known priest Zadok of David's time or the other men of the same name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "just" or "justified."

Zadok was a priest of the tribe of Levi who appears only in genealogies of the high-priestly line. He is named as the son of Ahitub and the father of Shallum (1 Chr 6:12). He is a later member of the line, distinct from the better-known Zadok of David's time. Ezra traces his own descent through him (Ezra 7:2). Two parallel lists name his son Meshullam rather than Shallum, probably another form of the same name. Through that son he is an ancestor of Hilkiah and of the priests Azariah and Seraiah, each called "the ruler of the house of God" (1 Chr 9:11; Neh 11:11). These two lists also place Meraioth between Zadok and Ahitub. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Meraioth's name there as a copyist's insertion, and it suggests this second Zadok may himself have entered the list by copying. Nothing further is recorded about him. His name means "just" or "righteous."

Zadok, son of Baana, was one of the men who repaired a section of the wall of Jerusalem during the rebuilding led by Nehemiah after the return from exile. He is mentioned only in Neh 3:4, which lists him among the workers on the north side of the city, next to Meremoth son of Urijah and Meshullam son of Berechiah. Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Zadok, including the priest of David's time and another Zadok who also helped repair the wall (Neh 3:29). This Zadok is distinguished by his father's name. According to Hitchcock's Bible Names, the name means "just" or "justified."

Zadok was the son of Immer, one of the people who rebuilt Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah after the return from exile. Nehemiah 3:29 says he repaired the section opposite his own house, working next to Shemaiah son of Shechaniah, the keeper of the east gate. Immer was the name of a priestly family (1 Chr 24:14; Ezra 2:37), and the verse just before says priests repaired the wall above the Horse Gate, each opposite his house (Neh 3:28). Zadok was therefore probably a priest, though this is inferred rather than stated. Nothing else is known about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, most famously David's priest, and this Zadok should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "just" or "justified."

Zadok was one of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the covenant made in the time of Nehemiah, when the community in Jerusalem pledged to keep the law of God. He appears only once, in the list of signatories in Neh 10:21, between Meshezabeel and Jaddua. Since he is named among the chiefs of the people rather than among the priests or Levites, he was probably a lay leader. Nothing else is known about him. The name was shared by several men in the Bible, including the well-known priest of David's time and other later figures, so he should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "just" or "justified."

Zadok was a scribe in Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah. He was one of several men Nehemiah appointed as treasurers over the storehouses, alongside Shelemiah the priest, Pedaiah of the Levites, and Hanan son of Zaccur. They were chosen because they were considered faithful, and their job was to distribute supplies to their fellow workers. From the wider passage, these were probably the tithes of grain, wine and oil brought in for the Levites and temple staff (Neh 13:13). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes the arrangement as a scribe set over the temple treasuries together with a priest and a Levite. Several other men named Zadok appear in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah, and it is uncertain whether this scribe is the same as any of them. The name means "just" or "justified," according to Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Zaham was a son of King Rehoboam of Judah, named only in 2 Chr 11:19 along with his brothers Jeush and Shamariah. The preceding verse lists two of Rehoboam's wives, Mahalath and Abihail, and the Hebrew leaves unclear which of them bore these sons. This entry follows Smith's Bible Dictionary in taking Abihail, daughter of Eliab, as his mother. The next verses (2 Chr 11:20) name Rehoboam's children by Maachah, Abijah, Attai, Ziza and Shelomith, who were Zaham's half-siblings. His birth in Jerusalem is inferred from Rehoboam's reign there. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain: Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "fatness," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "crime" or "impurity." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Greek manuscripts spell the name Zalam or Rhoollam.

Zair was a place mentioned only in 2 Kgs 8:21, where King Joram of Judah went with all his chariots during a campaign against the Edomites, who had revolted from Judah's rule. Surrounded by the Edomites, he attacked by night and struck them and their chariot commanders, and the people fled to their tents. The name probably means "little." The parallel account in 2 Chr 21:9 has "with his princes" in place of "to Zair," which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes as a copying variant of the same words. The site has not been firmly identified. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it probably east of the Dead Sea. Other suggestions link it with Mount Seir, with the town of Zoar (Smith's Bible Dictionary), or with ez-Zuweirah near the southern Dead Sea (Conder). The location shown here puts it just south of the Dead Sea, on a likely route into Edom.

Zalaph was the father of Hanun, who is mentioned only once, in Neh 3:30. That verse calls Hanun "the sixth son of Zalaph" and lists him among the people who repaired the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah after the return from exile. Hanun worked on "another piece" of the wall, next to Hananiah son of Shelemiah. Nothing else is recorded about Zalaph himself. The verse implies that he had at least six sons, but it does not say whether he was still living when the wall was rebuilt. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the name to mean "caper-plant." Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "wound," and Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "shadow" or "shaking."

Zalmon was a hill or mountain near Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim. It appears in Ps 68:14, where the King James Version spells it "Salmon": when the Almighty scattered kings, it was "white as snow in Salmon." The meaning of this verse is difficult. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that the scattered kings are pictured like snowflakes blown across the mountain in winter. The same mountain appears in Judg 9:48, where Abimelech and his men cut branches on Mount Zalmon and used them to set fire to the stronghold of Shechem. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it to be the southern peak of Mount Gerizim, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Mount Ebal, whose Arabic name may echo Zalmon. The location shown here follows the Mount Ebal identification.

Zalmonah was one of the places where the Israelites camped during their wilderness journey. It was the first stop after Mount Hor, where Aaron died, and the stop before Punon (Num 33:41–42). The Bible gives no other details about it. Its exact site is unknown. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it on the east side of Edom, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name points to a gloomy valley leading up to the Edomite plateau. The location shown here is only a rough placement on the highlands east of the Dead Sea. The name is usually explained as meaning "shady" (Easton's Bible Dictionary) or "gloomy" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia).

Zalmunna was one of two kings of Midian, always named together with Zebah, whom Gideon pursued and killed. While chasing them east of the Jordan, Gideon asked the men of Succoth for bread for his exhausted troops. Their leaders refused, mockingly asking whether he already had the kings in his hand, and Gideon threatened to punish them on his return. The two kings were at Karkor with about fifteen thousand men, all that remained of the eastern armies after a hundred and twenty thousand had fallen. Gideon attacked, routed the host and captured both kings, then showed them to the men of Succoth. When questioned, they admitted killing men at Tabor who resembled Gideon, whom he identified as his brothers. Gideon killed them and took the ornaments from their camels' necks. Ps 83:11 later recalls Zebah and Zalmunna as examples of defeated enemy princes.

Zanoah was a town in the Shephelah, the low hill country of Judah. It appears in the list of towns given to the tribe of Judah (Josh 15:34), grouped with Eshtaol and Zorah. After the return from exile, Jews settled again in Zanoah and its villages, alongside towns such as Adullam, Lachish and Azekah (Neh 11:30). When Jerusalem's walls were rebuilt, Hanun and the people of Zanoah repaired the Valley Gate, hung its doors, fitted its locks and bars, and rebuilt a thousand cubits of wall as far as the Dung Gate (Neh 3:13). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the modern ruin of Zanu'a, about 10 miles west of Jerusalem, and the location shown here follows that identification. Another town of the same name stood in the hill country of Judah, so the name refers to more than one place.

Zanoah was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed with Jezreel and Jokdeam among the cities given to the tribe of Judah (Josh 15:56). The name was also used for another Zanoah in Judah's western lowland, so the two should be kept distinct. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connects this hill-country town with 1 Chr 4:18, where Jekuthiel is called the "father" (probably the founder) of Zanoah. It identifies the site with Zanuta (Zenuta), a ruin on a hill about 12 miles south of Hebron. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it about 10 miles southwest of Hebron. The location shown here follows the Zanuta identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "forgetfulness" or "desertion."

Zaphon was a town in the Jordan Valley east of the Jordan, listed among the towns given to the tribe of Gad. It was part of the rest of the former kingdom of Sihon king of Heshbon, named alongside Beth-aram, Beth-nimrah and Succoth (Josh 13:27). The name means "north." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that in Judg 12:1, where the KJV says the men of Ephraim "went northward" to confront Jephthah, the Hebrew can be read as "to Zaphon," which would make the town the meeting place. The ISBE identifies Zaphon with Amathus, the modern Tell 'Amateh, near the Jabbok. Another view places it at Tell el-Qos, in the Jordan Valley north of the Jabbok. The location shown here follows the Tell el-Qos identification. The same Hebrew word also appears elsewhere as a general term for the north.

Zarephath was a Phoenician town belonging to Sidon, on the coast between Tyre and Sidon. During the drought in Elijah's time, God sent the prophet there, saying a widow had been commanded to feed him. At the city gate he found her gathering sticks and asked her for water (1 Kgs 17:9–10). The following verses of the chapter tell how her flour and oil did not run out and how Elijah raised her son. Jesus referred to this episode in Luke 4:26, where the town appears under its Greek name, Sarepta, and is noted as a non-Israelite city to which Elijah was sent. Obadiah names Zarephath as the northern limit of Canaanite land that returning Israelite exiles would possess (Obad 1:20). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with modern Sarafand in Lebanon, about 8 miles south of Sidon, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Zarethan was a town in the Jordan Valley, spelled Zaretan and Zartanah in the King James Version. When Israel crossed the Jordan opposite Jericho, the river's waters piled up far upstream at the city of Adam, which lay beside Zarethan (Josh 3:16). In the list of Solomon's districts, it helps mark the territory of Baana son of Ahilud, where Beth-shean is described as lying by Zartanah below Jezreel (1 Kgs 4:12). According to 1 Kgs 7:46, Solomon's bronze temple furnishings were cast in the clay ground between Succoth and Zarethan. The parallel account in 2 Chr 4:17 reads Zeredah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the site has not been positively identified, and one proposal points to the peak of Kurn Sartabeh west of the river. The location shown here follows the identification with Tell es-Saidiyeh, a mound on the east side of the Jordan Valley north of the Jabbok.

Zatthu was one of the chiefs of the people listed among those who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah's time, recorded in Neh 10:14 between Elam and Bani. The Revised Version spells the name Zattu. The names around it (Parosh, Pahath-moab, Elam, Zatthu, Bani) follow the order of family groups that returned from exile in Ezra 2:3–10 and Neh 7:8–15. This suggests that Zatthu here probably stands for the head or representative of the Zattu clan rather than a single individual otherwise known. By the same connection, members of this family appear in Ezra 10:27 among those who had married foreign wives. Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "a sprout", and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "olive tree".

Zattu was the ancestor of a large Israelite lay family that returned from exile in Babylon to Judah with Zerubbabel. Ezra's list gives the descendants of Zattu as 945 (Ezra 2:8). Nehemiah's parallel list gives 845 (Neh 7:13), probably a copying difference between the two lists. In Ezra's later reform, six men of this family, Elioenai, Eliashib, Mattaniah, Jeremoth, Zabad and Aziza, are named among those who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:27). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the family's head appears as Zatthu among the leaders who sealed Nehemiah's covenant (Neh 10:14), and that the Greek Septuagint reads the name in Ezra 8:5. Easton's Bible Dictionary likewise takes Zatthu to be probably the same name. Nothing is recorded about Zattu himself beyond his family.

Zavan, also spelled Zaavan, was a son of Ezer and brother of Bilhan and Akan (called Jakan in 1 Chr 1:42). He appears only in the genealogy of the Horites, the people who lived in the land of Seir before the Edomites. In Genesis 36 Ezer is listed among the sons of Seir the Horite and as one of the Horite chiefs, so Zavan was a grandson of Seir. Genesis gives the name as Zaavan (Gen 36:27), while 1 Chronicles has Zavan (1 Chr 1:42). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible names index describe him as a Horite chief. Easton's Bible Dictionary counts him among the "dukes of Edom" and gives the meaning of his name as "terror." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia considers the meaning uncertain but notes a possible root meaning "to tremble." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Zaza was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of the Jerahmeelites in 1 Chr 2:33. He and his brother Peleth were sons of Jonathan, and the verse closes the list with "These were the sons of Jerahmeel," meaning the descendants of Jerahmeel. Jerahmeel was a great-grandson of Judah through Perez and Hezron, as the earlier verses of the same chapter set out, so Zaza belonged to a branch of Judah's clan of Hezron. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "plenty," Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "belonging to all," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as unknown, noting that Greek manuscripts of the Septuagint spell it Ozam or Ozaza.

Zebadiah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 8 as one of the sons of Beriah. His brothers listed there include Arad, Ader, Michael, Ispah, Joha, Ahio, Shashak and Jeremoth. Beriah appears in 1 Chr 8:12–13 as a son of Elpaal, so STEPBible Proper Names describes Zebadiah as a grandson of Elpaal. Beriah and his brother Shema are described there as heads of families in Aijalon. Nothing is recorded about Zebadiah beyond his name. The name means "the Lord is my portion" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other men in the Bible share it, including another Benjamite listed a few verses later in 1 Chr 8:17. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that this second listing may be a copying repetition of the first, but this entry concerns the son of Beriah.

Zebadiah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named as one of the sons of Elpaal in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 8:17. His brothers include Beriah, Eber, Heber, Hezeki, Ishmerai, Jezliah, Jobab, Meshullam, Misham, Shamed and Shema. Some of these names, such as Beriah and Shema, appear in the surrounding verses of the same list, which suggests that they headed related family groups. Nothing further is recorded about him beyond his place in this list. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "portion of the Lord." Several other men in the Bible share the name Zebadiah and should not be confused with this Benjamite.

Zebadiah was a son of Jeroham of Gedor and the brother of Joelah. He is named once, in 1 Chr 12:7, at the end of a list of warriors who joined David at Ziklag while David was still hiding from Saul. By inference from the surrounding passage (1 Chr 12:1–7), these men were relatives of Saul from the tribe of Benjamin and were skilled with bow and sling, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes Zebadiah as a Benjamite recruit. The STEPBible proper names list instead counts him among the Gadites, whose list begins in the following verse. This entry follows the Benjamite reading. Gedor may be the town of that name in Judah, but this is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "portion of the Lord." Several other men in the Bible share this name.

Zebadiah was the third son of Meshelemiah, listed in 1 Chr 26:2 after his brothers Zechariah and Jediael and before Jathniel. His younger brothers Elam, Jehohanan and Elioenai are named in the following verse. The surrounding chapter, 1 Chr 26:1, identifies Meshelemiah as a Korahite among the gatekeepers of the house of the Lord. Easton's Bible Dictionary therefore describes Zebadiah as a Korahite porter, or gatekeeper, of the sanctuary. The wider context places these gatekeeping divisions in the time of David. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this entry refers only to Meshelemiah's son. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "portion of the Lord."

Zebadiah was the son of Asahel, the brother of Joab, and he followed his father as commander of the fourth division of King David's army. Each division served for one month of the year, and the fourth division of 24,000 men was on duty in the fourth month (1 Chr 27:7). The verse says Zebadiah held the post "after him," meaning he succeeded Asahel. Since Asahel was killed by Abner during the war between David and the house of Saul (2 Sam 2:23), the son probably took over his father's place in the listing rather than serving alongside him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "portion of the Lord." Several other men in the Bible share this name, and this Zebadiah should not be confused with them.

Zebadiah was a Levite in the reign of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. He is named among nine Levites whom the king sent out, together with the priests Elishama and Jehoram, to accompany his officials (2 Chr 17:8). The surrounding passage describes this group as traveling through the cities of Judah teaching the people from the book of the law of the Lord. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes the effort as a system of national education. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with the several other men in the Bible who share his name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "portion of the Lord."

Zebadiah, son of Ishmael, was "the ruler of the house of Judah" during the reign of King Jehoshaphat. When Jehoshaphat set up judges in Jerusalem, he put two men over them. Amariah the chief priest was in charge of "all matters of the LORD", and Zebadiah was in charge of "all the king's matters" (2 Chr 19:11). The Levites served under them as officers. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes Zebadiah's role to mean judging civil cases, the "controversies" mentioned in the surrounding passage, as distinct from religious ones. Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share his name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "portion of the Lord."

Zebadiah was the son of Michael, from the family of Shephatiah, and one of the family heads who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. Ezra 8:8 lists him at the head of eighty men from his clan. The surrounding chapter places this list among those who went up with Ezra in the reign of the Persian king Artaxerxes. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same man appears as "Zaraias" in the parallel list of 1 Esdras. His name is usually explained as meaning "portion of the Lord" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other men in the Bible share the name Zebadiah. This one is known only from this single verse.

Zebadiah was a priest of the family of Immer in the time of Ezra, after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears with Hanani in the list of men who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:20). By inference from the surrounding passage, the priests named in this list agreed to send away their foreign wives and offered a ram as a guilt offering, as Ezra 10:19 states for the first group of priests. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies him with "Zabdeus" in the parallel account of 1 Esdras 9:21. Several other men in the Bible share the name Zebadiah, and this one is mentioned only here. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "portion of the Lord."

Zebah was one of two kings of Midian, always named with Zalmunna, who led the eastern invaders defeated by Gideon in the time of the judges. As Gideon chased them east of the Jordan, the leaders of Succoth refused his exhausted men bread, doubting he would ever capture the kings (Judg 8:5–7). Zebah and Zalmunna were camped at Karkor with about fifteen thousand survivors when Gideon routed their army and took them alive (Judg 8:10–12). Easton's Bible Dictionary places Karkor probably in the Hauran. Asked about men they had killed at Tabor, the kings said each resembled a king's son. The next verse (Judg 8:19) shows these were Gideon's brothers. Gideon then killed both kings himself and took the ornaments from their camels' necks (Judg 8:21). Ps 83:11 later recalls their fate. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "victim" or "sacrifice."

Zebedee was a Galilean fisherman and the father of James and John, two of Jesus' twelve apostles (Matt 10:2). He appears in person only once, at the calling of his sons, about AD 27 by inference from context. Jesus found James and John in a boat with their father, mending nets, and when he called them they left Zebedee in the boat with the hired servants and followed him (Matt 4:21; Mark 1:19–20). The mention of hired servants suggests a family business of some size, and Luke 5:10 describes the sons as partners with Simon Peter. Elsewhere Zebedee is named only to identify his sons, the "sons of Zebedee." His wife, "the mother of Zebedee's children," asked Jesus for places of honor for them and was present at the crucifixion (Matt 20:20; 27:56). Comparing Matt 27:56 with Mark 15:40, Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies her as Salome.

Zebina was one of the "sons of Nebo" listed in Ezra 10:43 among the men who had married foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon. In the context of Ezra 10, these men agreed to put away those wives as part of the reforms led by Ezra. "Sons of Nebo" probably refers to people descended from, or associated with, a town called Nebo in Judah, by inference from the similar lists of returnees elsewhere in Ezra and Nehemiah. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "purchase," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia as "bought." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes that his name does not appear in the parallel list in 1 Esdras or in the Codex Alexandrinus manuscript of the Greek Septuagint.

Zeboiim was one of the cities of the plain, almost always named alongside Admah and grouped with Sodom and Gomorrah. Genesis 10:19 lists it among the places marking the edge of Canaanite territory. It had its own king, Shemeber, who joined the kings of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah and Bela (Zoar) in battle against an alliance of eastern kings in the Vale of Siddim. Deuteronomy 29:23 counts it among the cities the LORD overthrew, leaving the land barren, and Hosea 11:8 uses it as a byword for that destruction. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "deer" or "goats." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it should not be confused with Zeboim in 1 Sam 13:18. The site has never been identified. Scholars place the cities of the plain near either the northern or southern end of the Dead Sea, and the location shown here follows the southern view.

Zeboim was a town resettled by people of the tribe of Benjamin after the return from the Babylonian exile. It appears only once, in a list of settlements in Neh 11:34, between Hadid and Neballat. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as inhabited by Benjamites after the Captivity. Its location is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reasons that, because it is listed beside Hadid and Neballat, it lay in the coastal lowland near Lydda (modern Lod), and it notes that the site is lost. The location shown here is instead near the southern end of the Dead Sea, the region associated with the similarly named Zeboiim, one of the cities of the plain mentioned with Sodom and Gomorrah in Genesis. This entry follows that Dead Sea placement, though the two names may refer to different places.

Zebudah was a wife of Josiah, king of Judah, and the mother of King Jehoiakim. 2 Kgs 23:36 names her when recording that her son became king at twenty-five and reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. She was the daughter of Pedaiah of Rumah, a town whose location is uncertain. Her name means "given" or "endowed" (Easton's Bible Dictionary; Hitchcock's Bible Names), and the Hebrew text spells it Zebidah, the form used by the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. This entry also lists Johanan as her son. 1 Chr 3:15 names a Johanan as Josiah's firstborn but does not name his mother, so linking him to Zebudah is an inference. She belongs to the royal line that Matthew's genealogy of Jesus traces through Josiah (Matt 1:10–11).

Zebul was the ruler of the city of Shechem and the officer of Abimelech, son of Jerubbaal (Gideon), during Abimelech's rule there (Judg 9:28, 30). When Gaal son of Ebed stirred up the Shechemites against Abimelech, mocking both him and "Zebul his officer," Zebul grew angry. By inference from the surrounding verses (Judg 9:31–33), he secretly warned Abimelech, who was living at Arumah, and urged him to come against the city. As Abimelech's troops approached, Zebul at first told Gaal that he was only seeing the shadows of the mountains. Then he challenged Gaal to back up his boasts and go out and fight (Judg 9:36, 38). After Gaal was defeated, Zebul drove him and his brothers out of Shechem (Judg 9:41). The name is usually taken to mean "habitation" (Hitchcock's Bible Names; Easton's Bible Dictionary).

Zebulun was the territory allotted to the Israelite tribe descended from Jacob's son Zebulun. It lay in what was later called lower Galilee, and the location shown here is in the hills near Nazareth. Jacob's blessing links Zebulun with the sea and with ships, reaching toward Sidon (Gen 49:13). In Joshua it received the third lot. Its border ran from Sarid toward Chisloth-tabor, Daberath and Japhia, north to Hannathon and the valley of Jiphthah-el. It held twelve cities, including Nahalal, Shimron and a Bethlehem, probably the northern town of that name. It bordered Asher and Naphtali. Isaiah pairs the lands of Zebulun and Naphtali as afflicted regions, and Matthew applies that passage to Jesus living at Capernaum. In Ezekiel's vision, Zebulun has a portion between Issachar and Gad and a city gate on the south side. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "dwelling" or "habitation."

Zebulun was the tenth son of Jacob and the sixth and last son born to Leah. At his birth Leah said that now her husband would dwell with her, and the name is usually taken to mean "dwelling" or "habitation" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Nothing is recorded of his personal life beyond his three sons, Sered, Elon and Jahleel, who went down with Jacob to Egypt and became the founders of the tribe's clans. Jacob's blessing foresaw Zebulun living by the sea, with his border reaching toward Sidon. His descendants formed the Tribe of Zebulun, which received land in Galilee and fought alongside Naphtali under Barak against Sisera. The New Testament uses the Greek form Zabulon, and Matthew places Capernaum within the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali. The birth date of about 1751 BC is an estimate inferred from context.

Zechariah, spelled Zachariah in 2 Kgs 18:2, was the father of Abi, also called Abijah, who was the mother of King Hezekiah of Judah. That made him Hezekiah's maternal grandfather. He is mentioned only in the parallel notices that open the accounts of Hezekiah's reign. Both state that Hezekiah became king at twenty-five and reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. Nothing else is recorded about him, including his tribe, his position, or when he lived beyond being a generation before Hezekiah. The name means roughly "the Lord remembers" and was very common in the Old Testament, so he should not be confused with the many other men called Zechariah. Because Hezekiah appears in the line of kings in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matt 1:9–10), this Zechariah is counted among Jesus' ancestors through Hezekiah's mother.

Zechariah was a leader in the tribe of Reuben, named alongside Jeiel among the chief men of their families when the tribe's genealogy was recorded (1 Chr 5:7). The surrounding passage suggests he was a kinsman of Beerah, the Reubenite prince whom the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser carried into exile (1 Chr 5:6). Later in the same chapter, the Reubenite genealogies are said to have been recorded in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel (1 Chr 5:17), which places him in the eighth century BC. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 740 BC, and the STEPBible proper names index places him in Jotham's reign. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share his name, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes to mean "the LORD remembers."

Zechariah was a Levite of David's time, the firstborn son of Meshelemiah (also called Shelemiah), with brothers Jediael, Zebadiah, Jathniel, Elam, Jehohanan and Elioenai. He served as gatekeeper at the entrance of the tabernacle. When lots were cast for the temple gates, his lot fell to the north gate, and he is described as "a wise counsellor." This entry also includes a Zechariah listed among the Levites of the second rank who played harps (psalteries) when the ark was brought to Jerusalem and who served next to Asaph in the worship that followed, as well as a priest named Zechariah who blew trumpets before the ark. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary treat the gatekeeper, the musician and the trumpeter as possibly different men. The name was common and was understood to mean "Yah remembers."

Zechariah was a Levite, a son of Isshiah, named once in 1 Chr 24:25. He appears in a list of Levite families from the time of King David, when the priests and Levites were organized into divisions for temple service. His father Isshiah was the brother of Michah. By inference from the surrounding passage and 1 Chr 23:20, both were descendants of Uzziel, a son of Kohath, so Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary describe Zechariah as a Kohathite Levite. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Zechariah was very common, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes it was understood to mean "Yah remembers." He should not be confused with the many other men in the Bible who share the name.

Zechariah was the fourth son of Hosah, a Levite of the family of Merari, according to Smith's Bible Dictionary. He is named only in 1 Chr 26:11, where he is listed after his brothers Simri, Hilkiah and Tebaliah, and the verse counts Hosah's sons and relatives together as thirteen. The surrounding chapter lists the divisions of gatekeepers for the house of the Lord. By inference from that context, Zechariah served as a gatekeeper with his father's family in the time of David. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also places him in David's time. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name was common in the Old Testament, so he should not be confused with the many other men called Zechariah, including another Levite gatekeeper named in the same chapter.

Zechariah was the father of Iddo, who served as the leader of the half-tribe of Manasseh in Gilead, east of the Jordan. He appears only once, in a list of tribal leaders from the time of King David (1 Chr 27:21), and he is named only to identify his son. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take him to be a Manassite of Gilead, a reasonable inference since his son led that half-tribe. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Merarite Levite. If Iddo was active under David, Zechariah probably lived in the generation before. Several other men in the Bible share the name Zechariah, which is commonly understood to mean "the Lord remembers," and this one should not be confused with them.

Zechariah was one of the princes, or royal officials, of Judah whom King Jehoshaphat sent out in the third year of his reign to teach in the cities of Judah (2 Chr 17:7). He is named with four other princes: Benhail, Obadiah, Nethaneel and Michaiah. The verses that follow (2 Chr 17:8–9) say Levites and priests went with these princes and taught the people from the book of the law of the Lord. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia ties this teaching to establishing the law and suggests Zechariah served mainly as a judge. Nothing else is recorded about him. Because many men in the Old Testament share this name, he should not be confused with the prophet Zechariah or with others called Zechariah. The name is usually taken to mean "the Lord remembers."

Zechariah was a Levite of the family of Asaph, known only as the father of Jahaziel. 2 Chr 20:14 traces Jahaziel's ancestry through Zechariah, son of Benaiah, back through Jeiel and Mattaniah to Asaph. The verse names him only in this line of descent. It was his son Jahaziel on whom the Spirit of the Lord came before the assembled people during the reign of King Jehoshaphat, when Judah faced invasion. Zechariah would have lived a generation or so earlier, probably in the ninth century BC, by inference from that setting. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name, very common in the Old Testament, was understood to mean "Yah remembers" or "Yah is renowned." Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Zechariah was one of the sons of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, and a member of the tribe of Judah. He is the third of seven sons named alongside his brother Jehoram, who became king after their father (2 Chr 21:2). His other brothers were Azariah, Jehiel, a second Azariah, Michael and Shephatiah. The verse calls Jehoshaphat "king of Israel," but he ruled the southern kingdom of Judah from Jerusalem. The next verses say that once Jehoram had secured the throne, he killed all his brothers with the sword (2 Chr 21:4). Zechariah was therefore probably killed in Jerusalem, about 889 BC by inference from context. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the name to mean "Yah remembers" or "Yah is renowned." Several other people in the Bible share this name.

Zechariah was a man of God who guided King Uzziah of Judah in the early years of his reign. 2 Chr 26:5 says Uzziah sought God "in the days of Zechariah," describing Zechariah as one "who had understanding in the visions of God," and adds that as long as the king sought the Lord, God made him prosper. By inference from the passage, Zechariah's influence lasted as long as he lived, and the king's later decline came after his time. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary call him a prophet and the king's counsellor. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew phrase may instead mean he "instructed" the king in the fear of God, a reading also followed by the STEPBible names index. Nothing else is known of him. He should not be confused with the many other men of this common name.

Zechariah was a Levite of the family of Asaph, one of the Levites named in 2 Chr 29:13 who answered King Hezekiah's call at the start of his reign. He and Mattaniah are listed together as the representatives of the sons of Asaph, the guild of temple singers descended from David's musician Asaph. From the surrounding narrative, these Levites sanctified themselves and helped cleanse the temple in Jerusalem after it had been neglected. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 727 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which probably means "the LORD remembers," was very common, and this Zechariah should not be confused with the prophet or the many others who bore it.

Zechariah was a Levite of the Kohathite clan who helped oversee the repair of the temple during the reign of King Josiah of Judah. According to 2 Chr 34:12, he and Meshullam, also a Kohathite, were given charge of directing the workmen and keeping the work moving. They served alongside Jahath and Obadiah, Levites of the Merarite clan, who also acted as overseers. The same verse says the workmen did their job faithfully and mentions other Levites skilled with musical instruments. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this work to about 628 BC. The context of 2 Chr 34 places the repair in Josiah's eighteenth year. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Zechariah, probably meaning "the LORD remembers," was very common, and several other men in the Bible share it.

Zechariah was one of three "rulers of the house of God" in the reign of King Josiah of Judah, named alongside Hilkiah and Jehiel. When Josiah held his great Passover, these temple officials gave the priests 2,600 small animals and 300 oxen for the Passover offerings, matching the generosity of the king and his princes. Smith's Bible Dictionary places this about 628 BC, though the date is an estimate. His exact role among the temple leadership is not stated. Since Hilkiah was the high priest at this time, Zechariah was probably a senior priest or temple official as well, by inference from the passage. The name Zechariah, meaning roughly "the LORD remembers," was very common, and this man is distinct from the prophet and from the many others who bear it. He appears only in 2 Chr 35:8.

Zechariah was a prophet to the Jews who had returned from exile, and the author of the book that bears his name. He calls himself the son of Berechiah and grandson of Iddo the prophet (Zech 1:1), while Ezra calls him simply “the son of Iddo.” Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests that Berechiah may have died early, leaving Iddo as the head of the family. His prophecies are dated from the eighth month of the second year of King Darius of Persia (about 520 BC, by inference from context) to the fourth year of Darius. Alongside Haggai, he spoke to the people of Judah and Jerusalem, and Ezra credits the two prophets' preaching with the elders' success in rebuilding and finishing the temple. Easton's and Smith's dictionaries describe him as being of priestly descent. Several other men in the Bible share his name.

Zechariah was the head of the family of Parosh (spelled Pharosh in the King James Version) among those who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. Ezra 8:3 lists him with 150 males of his family who were registered by genealogy and travelled with him. The verse also mentions "the sons of Shechaniah", and it is unclear whether this phrase belongs with Zechariah's line or with the family listed before. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the return to about 450 BC, an estimate drawn from context. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which probably means "the LORD remembers", was very common in the Old Testament, and this Zechariah should be kept distinct from the many others who bore it.

Zechariah, son of Bebai, was one of the family heads who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. Ezra 8:11 lists him at the head of the descendants of Bebai, leading twenty-eight males. "Son of Bebai" probably means a descendant of the Bebai clan rather than a direct son, since the line of Bebai had already returned in the earlier wave of exiles. The STEPBible proper-names index describes him that way. The name Zechariah, usually understood as "the Lord remembers," was very common, and this man should not be confused with the many others who bear it. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Zechariah was one of the leading men whom Ezra summoned at the camp by the river before setting out from Babylon to Jerusalem. Ezra 8:16 names him among a group of "chief men" called together with Eliezer, Ariel, Shemaiah, Meshullam and others. The following verses explain that Ezra sent this group to Iddo at Casiphia to bring back Levites to serve in the temple, since none had joined the returning company. Nothing else is said about this Zechariah. The name was common, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he is probably the same man as one of the Zechariahs listed earlier in the chapter as heads of returning families, either of the descendants of Pharosh or of Bebai. The name is usually understood to mean "the LORD remembers."

Zechariah was a man of the family of Elam, listed in Ezra 10:26 among the Israelites who had married foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon. The surrounding chapter shows that in Ezra's time these marriages were judged a breach of the law, and the men named agreed to send their foreign wives away. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 458 BC, an estimate drawn from the context of Ezra's mission. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same list appears in 1 Esdras 9:27. It also explains the name as probably meaning "Yah remembers" or "Yah is renowned." Zechariah was a very common name, and this man should not be confused with the prophet Zechariah or the many others who bore it.

Zechariah was one of the men who stood beside Ezra the scribe when Ezra read the Law aloud to the people gathered in Jerusalem after the return from exile. Ezra stood on a wooden platform built for the occasion. Zechariah was among the seven men on his left, along with Pedaiah, Mishael, Malchiah, Hashum, Hashbadana and Meshullam (Neh 8:4). The verse gives no further detail about him. The STEPBible proper-name index identifies him as a Levite, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia considers him almost certainly the same man as an earlier Zechariah of Ezra's time. The name is very common in the Old Testament and is generally understood to mean "Yah remembers," so it is uncertain whether he appears anywhere else.

Zechariah was a man of the tribe of Judah, descended from Perez, who appears only in a genealogy in Neh 11:4. He was the son of Amariah and the father of Uzziah, and through Uzziah he was the grandfather or ancestor of Athaiah, one of the Judahites who settled in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him simply as an ancestor of Athaiah, whom some identify with Uthai. Nothing else is recorded about his life. The name Zechariah, often taken to mean "the LORD remembers," was very common in the Old Testament and belongs to many different men, so this Zechariah should not be confused with others of the same name.

Zechariah was a man of the tribe of Judah named in the genealogy of Maaseiah, one of the people who lived in Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time (Neh 11:5). He was the son of Shiloni and the father of Joiarib, and he stood several generations back in Maaseiah's line. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Shiloni may also be read as "the Shilonite," a clan label rather than a personal name. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the family as descendants of Perez, while the Tyndale House proper-names list connects them with Shelah, son of Judah. The comparable list in 1 Chr 9:5 mentions "Shilonites," which points to the Shelah connection. This entry gives Shiloni as his father's name, as it appears in the verse. Several other men in the Bible share the name Zechariah, which was common in the Old Testament.

Zechariah was a man named only in a priestly genealogy in Neh 11:12. He was the son of Pashur and the father of Amzi, and through Amzi an ancestor of Adaiah son of Jeroham.
