Adaiah was one of the priests living in Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time, among the 822 who "did the work of the house," meaning the temple. The line runs back through Pashur to Malchiah. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Zechariah as a priest, which fits his place in this priestly family. He probably lived several generations before the return from exile, judging by his position in the list, and nothing more is recorded about him. The shorter parallel genealogy in 1 Chronicles 9 traces Adaiah through Jeroham directly to Pashur and Malchijah and leaves out the intermediate names, including Zechariah. Several other people in the Bible share the name Zechariah.

Zechariah was the head of the priestly family of Iddo in the days of Joiakim, the high priest who succeeded Jeshua after the return from exile in Babylon. He is named only once, in Neh 12:16, in a list of priestly family heads of that generation. The list's context (Neh 12:12) places him in Joiakim's time, probably the late sixth or early fifth century BC. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he may be the same man as Zechariah the prophet, whom Zech 1:1 calls a grandson of Iddo and Ezra 5:1 calls a son of Iddo. The text does not confirm this, and several other men in the Bible share the name.

Zechariah, son of Jonathan, took part in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. Neh 12:35 places him among the priests' sons who went with trumpets in the procession and traces his ancestry through Shemaiah, Mattaniah, Michaiah and Zaccur back to Asaph, the musician of David's time. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia therefore counts him among the temple musicians of the Asaph line. The next verse, Neh 12:36, names the men with him, Shemaiah, Azarael, Milalai, Gilalai, Maai, Nethaneel, Judah and Hanani, as "his brethren" who played "the musical instruments of David." The word may mean brothers or, more broadly, kinsmen. This Zechariah is one of many men of that name in the Old Testament and is known only from this occasion.

Zechariah was one of the priests who played trumpets at the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt wall in Nehemiah's time, in the mid-5th century BC (Smith's Bible Dictionary dates it to 446 BC). He is listed with Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, Michaiah, Elioenai and Hananiah, a group of priestly trumpeters who, by inference from the surrounding passage, marched with the second of the two thanksgiving processions, the one Nehemiah joined. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him with Zechariah son of Jonathan, a trumpeter named in Neh 12:35. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists him simply as a trumpeter at the dedication. Nothing more is recorded about him. Zechariah was a very common name in the Old Testament, and it is uncertain whether he appears anywhere else.

Zechariah, son of Jeberechiah, was one of two people Isaiah called on as reliable witnesses, together with Uriah the priest (Isa 8:2). From the surrounding passage, they witnessed Isaiah writing the name Maher-shalal-hash-baz on a large tablet, a name later given to the prophet's son. This made the record public and attested before the events it foretold. Nothing else is said about him. Several men in the Bible share his name. Some suggest he may be the Zechariah whose daughter Abi was the mother of King Hezekiah, which would make him a contemporary of King Ahaz, but the text does not make this link. Hitchcock's Bible Names treats the name as the same as Zachariah.

Zedad was a town marking the northern border of the land of Israel. It appears in the border Moses described for the promised land, which ran from Mount Hor to the entrance of Hamath and then out to Zedad (Num 34:8). It appears again in Ezekiel's vision of the restored land, on the northern boundary running from the Mediterranean by way of Hethlon toward Zedad (Ezek 47:15). Ancient versions spell the name differently, and this has led to two proposed sites. Some scholars read it as "Zerad" and place it at Khirbet Serada in the Merj Ayun valley of southern Lebanon. Others read "Zedad" and identify it with Sadad, a village in central Syria between Riblah and Qaryatayn, northeast of Baalbek. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia favours Sadad. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls the identification uncertain. The location shown here follows the Sadad identification.

Zedekiah, originally named Mattaniah, was the last king of Judah. A son of Josiah and Hamutal, he was placed on the throne by Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon in place of his nephew Jehoiachin (Coniah), and Nebuchadnezzar renamed him. He began reigning at twenty-one, about 597 BC by inference from context, and ruled eleven years in Jerusalem. The prophet Jeremiah urged him to submit to Babylon. Zedekiah consulted him repeatedly, sometimes in secret, yet also kept him confined. Zedekiah rebelled against Babylon, and Jerusalem was besieged until his eleventh year, when the city was broken into. He fled by night but was captured in the plains of Jericho and brought to Riblah. There his sons were killed before his eyes, he was blinded, and he was taken in chains to Babylon and imprisoned until his death. Several other people in the Bible share this name.

Zedekiah son of Chenaanah was a prophet at the court of Ahab king of Israel. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him a false prophet. When Ahab and Jehoshaphat of Judah consulted the prophets about going to war against the Syrians at Ramoth-gilead, Zedekiah made horns of iron and declared in the LORD's name that with them Ahab would push the Syrians until they were destroyed. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes him to be the leader and spokesman of the 400 court prophets. When the prophet Micaiah foretold disaster, Zedekiah struck him on the cheek and mockingly asked which way the Spirit of the LORD had gone from him to speak to Micaiah. The story is told both in 1 Kings 22 and in its parallel, 2 Chronicles 18. His name means "the LORD is my righteousness." Several people share the name. He is distinct from Zedekiah the last king of Judah, whose blinding is recorded in Jer 39:7.

Zedekiah was a descendant of the royal line of Judah, named only in the genealogy of David's descendants at 1 Chr 3:16. The verse lists the sons of Jehoiakim as "Jeconiah his son, Zedekiah his son," and the wording can be read two ways: Zedekiah as a son of Jeconiah, or as a second son of Jehoiakim and so Jeconiah's brother. This entry follows the first reading, which the STEPBible Proper Names index also takes, making him a son of Jeconiah (also called Jehoiachin). On that reading his brothers are the sons of Jeconiah listed in the following verses, among them Shealtiel, Malchiram, Pedaiah, Shenazar, Jecamiah, Hoshama and Nedabiah. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is probably distinct from King Zedekiah, Judah's last king, who was a son of Josiah. His name means "the Lord is my justice."

Zedekiah son of Maaseiah was a prophet among the Jewish exiles in Babylon, one of several men in the Bible with this name, which means "the Lord is my justice" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). In Jeremiah's letter to the exiles, the Lord condemns him and Ahab son of Kolaiah for prophesying lies in his name, and declares that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon will kill them in front of the people. Their fate was to become a curse used by the exiles: "The LORD make thee like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia understands their message as a promise of an early return from captivity, and draws on the next verse, Jer 29:23, which also charges them with adultery. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 595 BC.

Zedekiah son of Hananiah was one of the princes, or royal officials, of Judah during the reign of King Jehoiakim. He is mentioned only once, among the officials gathered in the scribe's chamber of the king's house when Micaiah son of Gemariah came to tell them about the scroll of Jeremiah's prophecies that Baruch had been reading to the people (Jer 36:12). The surrounding chapter shows that the officials then had Baruch read the scroll to them and reported its contents to the king. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places this in the fifth year of Jehoiakim, following Jer 36:9. Several other men in the Bible share the name Zedekiah, including the last king of Judah, and this man should not be confused with them. The name means "the Lord is my righteousness."

Zeeb was one of two princes of Midian, always named alongside Oreb, during the Midianite invasion of Israel that Gideon defeated. His name means "wolf" according to Easton's Bible Dictionary. After the Midianites were routed, the Ephraimites captured both leaders and killed Zeeb at a winepress that took his name, the "winepress of Zeeb." They brought his head and Oreb's to Gideon across the Jordan (Judg 7:25). When the Ephraimites complained that Gideon had not called them sooner, he calmed them by pointing out that God had given these princes into their hands (Judg 8:3). Psalm 83 later recalls Oreb and Zeeb in a prayer that Israel's enemies might meet the same end (Ps 83:11). Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he was caught at a later stage of the fighting, probably at a ford farther down the Jordan.

Zela (spelled Zelah in the King James Version) was a town in the territory of Benjamin. It is listed among the cities given to that tribe, next to Jerusalem (Josh 18:28). The family tomb of Kish, Saul's father, was there. David had the bones of Saul and Jonathan brought to this tomb and buried in it (2 Sam 21:14). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "slope" or "side" and suggests the town was probably Saul's birthplace. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint translates the word as "side" in 2 Samuel rather than treating it as a place name. It also suggests Zela may be the Zilu mentioned in the Tell el-Amarna Letters. The site has not been identified, so the location shown here is only a rough placement in Benjamin's territory near Jerusalem.

Zelek was an Ammonite listed among David's mighty men, the elite warriors named in 2 Sam 23 and 1 Chr 11. He appears only in these two parallel lists, identified simply as "Zelek the Ammonite," which shows that David's renowned fighters included men of foreign origin. Nothing else is recorded of his deeds or family. In both lists his name comes just before Naharai the Beerothite, who is described as armourbearer to Joab son of Zeruiah. The Hebrew wording could be read as applying that title to Naharai alone, and this entry follows that reading, so Zelek is not himself called Joab's armourbearer. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives it as "cleft," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as unknown.

Zelophehad was a man of the tribe of Manasseh. He was the son of Hepher, of the family of Gilead, and descended through Machir from Manasseh son of Joseph (Num 27:1; Josh 17:3). He had no sons, only five daughters: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah (Num 26:33). Num 27:3 says he died in the wilderness. His daughters asked Moses for their father's share of the land, and the request was granted, so his inheritance passed to them (Num 27:7). Later the leaders of Gilead's families worried that the land would pass to another tribe if the daughters married outside it. It was ruled that the daughters should marry within their father's tribe (Num 36:2, 6), and they married sons of their father's brothers (Num 36:10–11). Smith's Bible Dictionary reads 1 Chr 7:15 as making him Hepher's second son.

Zelzah was a place named only once in the Bible, where Samuel told Saul he would meet two men by Rachel's tomb on the border of Benjamin. They would tell him that his father's lost donkeys had been found and that his father was now worried about him (1 Sam 10:2). Nothing else is said about it, and no similar name has been found in the region. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint reads the phrase as "leaping greatly" rather than as a place-name, and that the Hebrew text may be damaged. Its location depends on where Rachel's tomb stood. Gen 35:19 places the tomb near Bethlehem, while Saul's route here may suggest a site farther north. The location shown here follows Smith's Bible Dictionary, placing Zelzah near the traditional tomb south of Jerusalem. The name has been explained as meaning "shadow" (Smith's) or "noontide" (Hitchcock's).

Zemaraim was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Benjamin. It is listed in Josh 18:22 between Beth-arabah and Bethel, in the group of Benjamin's eastern towns near the Jordan valley. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the ruins of es-Samra, about 4 miles (6 km) north of Jericho, and the location shown here follows that identification. Others, noted in the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, think it lay closer to Bethel, perhaps south of that town. Smith's Bible Dictionary and other works connect the town with Mount Zemaraim in the hill country of Ephraim. According to 2 Chr 13:4, King Abijah of Judah stood on that mountain to speak to Jeroboam's army. The hill probably took its name from the town and lay nearby. The name is often explained as meaning "double fleece" or "wool."

Zemarite is the name of a Canaanite people listed among the descendants of Canaan, son of Ham, in the table of nations (Gen 10:18; 1 Chr 1:16). Like the other names in the list, such as the Amorite, Hivite and Jebusite, it stands for a tribe or clan rather than a single individual, and here it is treated as a son of Canaan. It appears between the Arvadite and the Hamathite, which suggests a home in the north, along the Phoenician coast. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia link the name to Zemar, or Sumur, an important Phoenician city mentioned in the Amarna letters. They place it probably at the village of Sumra on the coast between Tripoli and Arvad. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that older interpreters placed the tribe at Emesa, modern Homs. Beyond the genealogies, the Bible says nothing more about them.

Zemira was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, the first named of the nine sons of Becher listed in 1 Chr 7:8. His brothers were Joash, Eliezer, Elioenai, Omri, Jerimoth, Abiah, Anathoth and Alameth. Becher was himself a son of Benjamin, according to the surrounding genealogy in 1 Chronicles 7 and Smith's Bible Dictionary, which makes Zemira a grandson of Benjamin. Nothing is recorded about him beyond his place in this family list. The meaning of his name is given differently in the reference works. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains it as "vine-dresser," Smith's Bible Dictionary as "a song," and Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "song," "vine" or "palm."

Zenan was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Judah. It is named only once, in the list of towns of the Shephelah, the lowland hill country between the Judean highlands and the coastal plain. There it appears in a group of sixteen towns alongside Hadashah and Migdal-gad (Josh 15:37). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat it as probably the same place as Zaanan, mentioned in Mic 1:11 among towns of the same region. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement within the western Judean lowlands, near the other towns of its group. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "coldness," "target" or "weapon."

Zenas was a Christian named only once in the Bible, in Paul's letter to Titus. Paul calls him "the lawyer" and asks Titus to help him and Apollos on their journey with care, making sure they lacked nothing (Titus 3:13). The Greek verb translated "bring" in the King James Version usually means "send on" or "equip for travel," so Paul may have meant that Titus should supply them for a journey rather than bring them to him. It is unclear what kind of lawyer Zenas was. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes him to have been an expert in the Jewish law of Moses before becoming a Christian. Others, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes, allow that he may have been a practitioner of Roman civil law. The name is Greek, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be a short form of Zenodorus. Nothing more is known of him.

Zephaniah son of Maaseiah was a priest in Jerusalem during the reign of Zedekiah, the last king of Judah. He held the rank of "second priest," below the chief priest Seraiah. Zedekiah sent him twice to the prophet Jeremiah: once with Pashur son of Melchiah to inquire of the LORD as Babylon threatened the city (Jer 21:1), and once with Jehucal to ask Jeremiah to pray for them (Jer 37:3). Shemaiah, a prophet among the exiles in Babylon, wrote to Zephaniah urging him to restrain Jeremiah, but Zephaniah read the letter aloud to Jeremiah (Jer 29:24–29). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to have been an overseer of the temple. After Jerusalem fell, the Babylonian captain of the guard seized him with Seraiah and others, and 2 Kgs 25:21 says they were put to death at Riblah. He is distinct from the prophet Zephaniah and others who bore the name.

Zephaniah was a prophet of Judah and the author of the book that bears his name, the ninth of the twelve Minor Prophets. Zeph 1:1 identifies him as the son of Cushi and traces his family back four generations through Gedaliah and Amariah to Hizkiah (Hezekiah). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes this Hezekiah to be the well-known king of Judah, which would make Zephaniah a member of the royal family, though the verse does not call him king. He prophesied during the reign of Josiah son of Amon. This entry places his prophecies about 610 BC, an estimate inferred from context. Smith's Bible Dictionary judges it more likely that he spoke before Josiah's eighteenth year. Smith's gives the meaning of his name as "hidden by the LORD." Several other men in the Bible share the name, so references to Zephaniah need to be read in context.

Zephaniah was the father of Josiah, a man living in Jerusalem after the return from Babylon. In Zech 6:10 the prophet Zechariah is told to go to Josiah's house with Heldai, Tobijah and Jedaiah, who had come from the captivity, and to make crowns from their silver and gold. Zech 6:14 gives the crowns as a memorial in the temple to Helem, Tobijah, Jedaiah and "Hen the son of Zephaniah." Hen is usually taken as another name for Josiah, though the word may instead mean "kindness." Smith's Bible Dictionary treats Zephaniah as Hen's father too, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia allows that one or more fathers may be meant. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls Josiah a priest. The name, meaning "the LORD has treasured" or "hidden," was shared by several people. This Zephaniah is not the prophet of that name.

Zephath was a Canaanite city in the south of the land. According to Judg 1:17, the tribes of Judah and Simeon fought together, killed its Canaanite inhabitants, destroyed the city completely, and renamed it Hormah. The new name probably plays on the Hebrew idea of something devoted to destruction, and Hormah also appears in earlier wilderness accounts such as Num 21:3. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the meaning of the name Zephath as "watchtower" or "beacon." Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions an identification with the pass of es-Sufah but prefers S'beita, the ancient town of Shivta in the Negev desert of southern Israel. The location shown here follows the S'beita identification.

Zepho was a son of Eliphaz, Esau's firstborn, and so a grandson of Esau. He is listed with his brothers Teman, Omar, Gatam and Kenaz (Gen 36:11). He also appears among the "dukes", or clan chiefs, descended from Esau, which makes him one of the early tribal leaders of Edom (Gen 36:15). The parallel genealogy in 1 Chr 1:36 spells his name Zephi. Amalek, born to Eliphaz's concubine Timna, and Korah, who is named among the chiefs of Eliphaz, are counted as his brothers. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "watch-tower." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Zephon was a son of Gad, one of the sons of Jacob, and the ancestor of the Zephonites, a clan of the tribe of Gad. Genesis names him Ziphion in its list of Gad's sons who went down to Egypt with Jacob (Gen 46:16). Numbers, in the census of Israel taken in the wilderness, gives the name as Zephon (Num 26:15). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat the two forms as the same person. His brothers were Haggi, Shuni, Ozni, Eri, Arod and Areli. Ozni appears to correspond to the Ezbon of Genesis, and Arod to Arodi. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "watch," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia tentatively suggests "gaze." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Zer was a fortified city in the territory given to the tribe of Naphtali, mentioned only once, in the list of Naphtali's fenced cities in Josh 19:35, where it is named between Ziddim and Hammath, alongside Rakkath and Chinnereth. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "flint", while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "perplexity." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint reads this verse differently, as "the fortified cities of the Tyrians," which reflects a Hebrew wording that does not contain the name Zer. The site has not been identified. Because it is listed with Hammath and Chinnereth, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place it near the western or southwestern side of the Sea of Galilee. The location shown here is only a rough placement within Naphtali's hill country in Galilee, and it lies to the north and west of that lakeside area.

Zerah (also spelled Zarah, and Zara in Matt 1:3) was a son of Judah by his daughter-in-law Tamar and the twin brother of Pharez (Perez). At their birth his hand appeared first and the midwife tied a scarlet thread on it, but Pharez was born ahead of him, so Zerah counts as the younger twin (Gen 38:27–30). He is listed among Judah's five sons, with his half-brothers Er, Onan and Shelah, in the household that went down to Egypt with Jacob. He headed the Zarhite clan of Judah. 1 Chr 2:6 names his sons as Zimri, Ethan, Heman, Calcol and Dara. Zabdi, named as his son in Josh 7:1, is probably the same man as Zimri. Through Zabdi, Zerah was the ancestor of Achan, whose theft at Jericho brought wrath on Israel. His descendants also appear among those living in Jerusalem after the exile. Other biblical figures share the name.

Zerah was a son of Reuel and a grandson of Esau through Esau's wife Bashemath. His brothers were Nahath, Shammah and Mizzah (Gen 36:13; 1 Chr 1:37). He is named among the "dukes," or clan chiefs, descended from Reuel in the land of Edom (Gen 36:17). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "rising (of the sun)." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including the father of Jobab, a king of Edom (Gen 36:33). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists that Zerah as a separate person from this chief, and this entry treats them as distinct. Nothing more is recorded about him beyond these genealogies.

Zerah was the father of Jobab, who followed Bela as king of Edom in the period before Israel had kings (Gen 36:33; 1 Chr 1:44). The verses describe him as "of Bozrah," a major Edomite city probably at modern Buseirah in southern Jordan. The wording could also be read as calling Jobab himself a man of Bozrah. The STEPBible Proper Names index takes Zerah to be from Bozrah and counts him among the Edomite royal line. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a son of Judah and an Edomite chief descended from Esau, and it is uncertain whether this Zerah is the same person as any of them. Hitchcock's Bible Names treats the name as the same as Zarah, which it explains as meaning "east" or "brightness."

Zerah was a Levite of the Gershonite clan named in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 6. In one list he is the son of Iddo and the father of Jeaterai, in a line descending from Gershom (1 Chr 6:21). In another he is the son of Adaiah and the father of Ethni, in the ancestry of Asaph, the singer appointed by David (1 Chr 6:41). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the Tyndale House STEPBible names index treat these as the same man, which suggests that Iddo and Adaiah are two forms of one name and that Jeaterai and Ethni may also correspond. This entry follows that identification, though the two lists do not match exactly. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary explains as meaning "rising" of the sun.

Zerah the Ethiopian (or Cushite) led a huge army against the kingdom of Judah. 2 Chr 14:9 credits him with a host of "a thousand thousand" and three hundred chariots, and says he advanced as far as Mareshah in the Judean lowlands. The surrounding passage shows the invasion came in the reign of King Asa, who met him in battle near Mareshah, routed his army and took a great deal of plunder. His identity is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he was probably the Egyptian king Osorkon II, a successor of Shishak. Others see him as a Cushite ruler or general from the region south of Egypt. This entry identifies him only as the Ethiopian commander named in the text. Several other men in the Bible share the name Zerah.

Zerah, also called Zohar, was one of the sons of Simeon, the son of Jacob, and so belonged to the tribe of Simeon. Genesis and Exodus list him as Zohar among Simeon's six sons, alongside Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin and Shaul (Gen 46:10; Exod 6:15). In the census of Numbers and in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles he appears as Zerah, and Numbers names him as the founder of the Zarhite family within Simeon (Num 26:13; 1 Chr 4:24). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary treat Zohar and Zerah as two forms of the same name, and this entry follows that view. Nothing more is recorded about his life. Several other men in the Bible are also named Zerah.

Zerahiah was a priest of the tribe of Levi, descended from Aaron through Eleazar, in the high-priestly line recorded in 1 Chronicles. He was the son of Uzzi, grandson of Bukki, and the father of Meraioth (1 Chr 6:6, 51). Ezra the scribe traced his ancestry through him (Ezra 7:4). His name is usually explained as meaning "the Lord has risen." Nothing is recorded of his life beyond these genealogies. The lists in 1 Chr 9:11 and Neh 11:11 name a "Meraioth, the son of Ahitub" in the ancestry of the chief priests. Following STEPBible's Tyndale House name index, this entry treats that Ahitub as another name for Zerahiah, since Zerahiah's son was Meraioth. The fuller list in 1 Chronicles 6 also has a later Ahitub, the father of Zadok, so the identification is uncertain. Several other people in the Bible share the name Zerahiah.

Zerahiah was the father of Elihoenai, of the family of Pahath-moab. He is mentioned once, in Ezra's list of family heads who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. That list names Elihoenai as leading two hundred men of his clan (Ezra 8:4). Zerahiah himself is known only as Elihoenai's father, and nothing more is recorded about him. Whether he was alive at the time of the return is not stated. The name means "the Lord has risen" or "the Lord has come forth." It was borne by more than one person in the Bible, including a priestly descendant of Aaron in the line of Ezra. This entry concerns only the man of the Pahath-moab family. Some reference works, such as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, describe him as a family head among the returning exiles.

Zered was a brook or stream valley that the Israelites crossed near the end of their journey through the wilderness, on their way past Edom and Moab. Moses records the command to cross it and notes that 38 years had passed between leaving Kadesh-barnea and crossing the Zered. By then the whole generation of fighting men had died, as the LORD had sworn (Deut 2:13–14). Num 21:12 mentions Israel camping in the valley of Zared, probably the same place. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify it with the Wadi el-Hasa, which flows into the Dead Sea near its southeastern end and lay between Moab and Edom. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia instead places it among the streams feeding Wadi Kerak, farther north. The location shown here follows the Wadi el-Hasa identification.

Zeredah (spelled Zereda in the King James Version) was the hometown of Jeroboam son of Nebat, an Ephraimite and an official of Solomon who rebelled against the king (1 Kgs 11:26). Jeroboam later became the first king of the northern kingdom of Israel. The verse calls him an Ephrathite, which here means a man of the tribe of Ephraim, so the town probably lay in the hill country of Ephraim. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in the north of Mount Ephraim and suggests it may be the same place as Zaretan, Zererath or Zartanah, which are mentioned elsewhere near the Jordan Valley. The name is similar to that of other biblical places, and its exact site is uncertain. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the central hill country, near Shechem. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "ambush," and Easton's renders it "the fortress."

Zeredah, spelled Zeredathah in the King James text of 2 Chr 4:17, was a place in the Jordan plain. King Solomon had the bronze furnishings of the temple cast in the clay ground between Succoth and this town. The parallel account in 1 Kgs 7:46 names the place Zarthan (Zarethan), and Easton's Bible Dictionary treats the two names as the same site. It adds that Solomon set up the foundries here where Hiram made the great bronze castings. The same name is also used for other places, most notably Zeredah in Ephraim, the home town of Jeroboam (1 Kgs 11:26). That town is a separate place from this one in the Jordan valley. The location shown here is in the Jordan valley near Succoth, probably at the modern Tell es-Sa'idiyeh east of the river. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "ambush" or "change of dominion."

Zererah (spelled Zererath in the King James Version) was a place or district in the Jordan Valley. It is mentioned only in Judg 7:22, where the Midianite army, thrown into confusion by Gideon's three hundred men, fled toward Beth-shittah "in Zererath" and on toward the border of Abel-meholah and Tabbath. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it may be the same as Zereda or Zeredathah. Zeredathah in 2 Chr 4:17 corresponds to Zarethan in the parallel 1 Kgs 7:46, a site near the Jordan. Easton's also notes that some identify it with Zahrah, about 3 miles west of Beth-shean. The location shown here lies in the central Jordan Valley south of Beth-shean, near the river. That fits the link with Zeredathah and Zarethan, and it fits the Midianites' flight eastward toward the Jordan.

Zeresh was the wife of Haman, the chief official of the Persian king in the book of Esther. When Haman came home angry that Mordecai would not honor him, he gathered his friends and Zeresh (Esth 5:10). She and the friends advised him to build a gallows fifty cubits high and ask the king the next morning to have Mordecai hanged on it, and Haman had it built (Esth 5:14). After Haman was forced to honor Mordecai publicly, he told Zeresh and his friends what had happened. She and his wise men warned him that if Mordecai was a Jew, Haman would not prevail against him but would surely fall (Esth 6:13). The meaning of her name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take it as Persian for "gold", while Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "star of Venus".

Zereth was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:7 as one of the sons of Helah, together with Jezoar and Ethnan. The surrounding verses identify Helah as one of the two wives of Ashur, described as the father (that is, probably the founder or leading figure) of Tekoa. Ashur's other wife, Naarah, bore Ahuzam, Hepher, Temeni and Haahashtari, who were Zereth's half-brothers. Coz, mentioned in the next verse, is also counted here as one of Zereth's brothers, though the passage does not state his parentage clearly. Nothing else is recorded about Zereth's life or descendants. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "splendor," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia regards its meaning as unknown.

Zereth-shahar was a town given to the tribe of Reuben, east of the Dead Sea. It is mentioned only once, in the list of Reuben's cities, where it is named with Kiriathaim and Sibmah and placed "in the mount of the valley" (Josh 13:19). The STEPBible Proper Names take this to mean a mountain or height in the plain beside the Dead Sea. The name is usually understood to mean "splendor of the dawn." Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that the ancient name may survive at the hot springs near Machaerus, on the eastern shore, but holds that no firm identification is possible. The location shown here follows that general area, near the hot springs at ez-Zara (ancient Callirrhoe) on the east coast of the Dead Sea.

Zeror was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only in the family line of Kish in 1 Sam 9:1. He was the son of Bechorath and the father of Abiel, which makes him the great-grandfather of Kish. The next verse names Kish's son as Saul, so Zeror was an ancestor of Israel's first king. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint gives his name as Ared, and it cross-refers him to Zur, a Benjamite in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles. Some readers link the two names, though this is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "a bundle" and dates him to about 1730 BC. Any date for him can only be estimated from his place in the genealogy.

Zeruah was the mother of Jeroboam son of Nebat, the servant of Solomon who rebelled against the king and later became the first king of the northern kingdom of Israel. 1 Kgs 11:26 names her and calls her a widow, so Nebat had evidently died by the time Jeroboam rose against Solomon. The family was from Zereda, in the hill country of Ephraim. She is mentioned nowhere else in the Hebrew text. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some Greek manuscripts leave her name out of this verse. A longer Greek passage after 1 Kings 12:24 calls Jeroboam's mother Sareisa and describes her as a harlot. The meaning of her name is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "stricken," Smith's Bible Dictionary "full breasted," and Hitchcock's Bible Names "leprous" or "hornet."

Zerubbabel was a descendant of David's royal line who led the first group of Jewish exiles from Babylon back to Jerusalem and directed the rebuilding of the temple. He is usually called the son of Shealtiel, though 1 Chr 3:19 names Pedaiah as his father. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains that "son" here means grandson or nephew. With Jeshua the high priest, he rebuilt the altar and began the temple work. He refused help from the peoples whom Esarhaddon had settled in the land. In the second year of Darius, the prophets Haggai and Zechariah addressed him as governor of Judah and urged him to finish the house. Haggai called him God's chosen signet. Matthew lists him among the ancestors of Jesus. Easton's identifies him with Sheshbazzar, who brought back the temple vessels and laid the foundation. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia thinks they were more probably two different governors. This entry follows the identification.

Zeruiah was the sister of David and the mother of Joab, Abishai and Asahel, three leading commanders of David's army (1 Chr 2:16). Her sister was Abigail, mother of Amasa. 2 Sam 17:25 calls Abigail a daughter of Nahash, while Chronicles counts both women as sisters of Jesse's sons. This entry therefore treats Zeruiah as David's half-sister, probably through a shared mother. Her husband is never named, and her sons are almost always identified by her name: "Joab the son of Zeruiah" and "Abishai the son of Zeruiah." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests this may reflect her husband's early death or her own prominence. That work also notes that, by inference from 2 Sam 2:32, he was buried at Bethlehem. David twice complains about "ye sons of Zeruiah" when they press for harsh action (2 Sam 3:39; 16:10; 19:22).

Zetham was a Levite of the Gershonite clan in the time of David, mentioned only in 1 Chronicles. In 1 Chr 23:8 he is listed with Jehiel and Joel as one of the three sons of Laadan. In 1 Chr 26:22 he and his brother Joel appear as "sons of Jehieli" and are placed over the treasures of the house of the LORD. The two passages can be read differently. Zetham may be Jehiel's brother and a son of Laadan, or Jehiel's son and Laadan's grandson. This entry follows the second reading and treats Jehiel as his father. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a proposal by the scholar Curtis that 1 Chr 26:22 should read "Jehiel and his brethren, Zetham and Joel." Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "olive planter."

Zethan was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the seven sons of Bilhan, who was a son of Jediael. His brothers were Jeush, Benjamin, Ehud, Chenaanah, Tharshish and Ahishahar. He appears only once, in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:10, which sets him within a family of fighting men counted in the tribe's records. Nothing else is recorded of him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "olive," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "olive tree." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes that the commentator Curtis regarded this list as originally belonging to Zebulun. This entry follows the passage as it stands, which places Zethan among the Benjamites.

Zethar was one of the seven chamberlains, or eunuchs, who served in the presence of King Ahasuerus of Persia. He is named only once, in a list with Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, Abagtha and Carcas. On the seventh day of the king's feast, when Ahasuerus was merry with wine, he gave these seven men a command. The next verse (Esth 1:11) says that the command was to bring Queen Vashti before him wearing the royal crown. Nothing else is recorded about Zethar. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "star", Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "he that examines or beholds", and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a comparison with a Persian word meaning "conqueror". Smith's dates the event to about 453 BC.

Zia was a man of the tribe of Gad, one of seven kinsmen listed together in the Gadite genealogy of 1 Chr 5:13, alongside Michael, Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Jachan and Heber. The next verse names these men as sons of Abihail. The surrounding passage places the Gadites in the land of Bashan east of the Jordan, and 1 Chr 5:17 says their genealogies were recorded in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel. Nothing else is known of him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may stand for a Gadite clan rather than a single person, and STEPBible describes him as a clan leader. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "fear," Smith's Bible Dictionary "motion," and Hitchcock's Bible Names "sweat" or "swelling."

Ziba was a servant of the house of Saul who, when David asked whether anyone of Saul's family survived, told him of Jonathan's lame son Mephibosheth, living in the house of Machir at Lodebar. David gave Mephibosheth all of Saul's property and ordered Ziba, with his fifteen sons and twenty servants, to farm the land for him. During Absalom's revolt Ziba met the fleeing David with two donkeys, bread, raisins, summer fruit and wine. He claimed that Mephibosheth had stayed in Jerusalem hoping to regain his grandfather's kingdom, and David then gave Ziba everything that belonged to Mephibosheth. When David returned, Ziba and his household crossed the Jordan ahead of him. Mephibosheth then told David that Ziba had deceived him (2 Sam 19:26–27), and David ordered the two to divide the land. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Ziba's report to have been a slander.

Zibeon was a Hivite whose descendant Aholibamah (Oholibamah) became one of Esau's wives. Genesis calls her "the daughter of Anah the daughter of Zibeon," which makes Zibeon her grandfather through Anah (Gen 36:2). Through Aholibamah, Zibeon was the ancestor of Esau's sons Jeush, Jaalam and Korah (Gen 36:14). The Hebrew wording leaves it open whether "daughter of Zibeon" refers to Aholibamah or to Anah. This entry treats Anah as Zibeon's child, and the STEPBible proper-names index likewise calls him Oholibamah's grandfather. The name is shared by more than one person. Later in the same chapter a Zibeon son of Seir the Horite has a son named Anah (Gen 36:20, 24), and many readers take him to be the same man, described there as a Horite rather than a Hivite. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "iniquity that dwells."

Zibeon was a son of Seir the Horite, one of the original inhabitants of the land of Seir, later Edom. His brothers were Lotan, Shobal, Anah, Dishon, Ezer and Dishan, and Timna was his sister. He is listed among the Horite chiefs ("dukes" in the King James Version). His sons were Ajah, also spelled Aiah, and Anah. This Anah is remembered for finding "the mules" in the wilderness while tending his father's donkeys, a phrase some translations render as "hot springs." Genesis 36:2 also names a Zibeon the Hivite as the father of Anah, whose daughter Aholibamah married Esau. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both take him to be this same Horite Zibeon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "hyena"; Smith's gives "robber."

Zibia was a Benjamite, one of the sons born to Shaharaim by his wife Hodesh. He is named only once, in the genealogy of Benjamin's descendants in 1 Chr 8:9, alongside his full brothers Jobab, Mesha and Malcham. The list continues in the next verse with Jeuz, Shachia and Mirma, who are also Hodesh's sons. Shaharaim had earlier fathered Abitub and Elpaal by another wife, Hushim, so they were Zibia's half-brothers. The surrounding passage places these births in the country of Moab, after Shaharaim had sent away his earlier wives, and the STEPBible Proper Names index follows this reading. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take the name to mean "gazelle," the ISBE marking this as uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "roe." Nothing else is recorded about his life.

Zibiah was a woman from Beersheba, in the far south of Judah, and the mother of King Joash (also called Jehoash) of Judah. She is named only in the formal introductions to her son's reign, which say he became king at seven years old, in the seventh year of Jehu of Israel, and reigned forty years in Jerusalem. Her husband was King Ahaziah of Judah. Connected passages such as 2 Kgs 11:1–3 explain that after Ahaziah's death the young Joash was hidden from Queen Athaliah until he could be crowned. Through her son she belongs to the royal line of David that is traced in the genealogies of Jesus. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes her name to mean probably "gazelle" and notes that some Greek manuscripts give it as Abia. Nothing else about her is recorded.

Zichri was a Levite, a son of Izhar and a brother of Korah and Nepheg, named in the genealogy of Levi's descendants in Exod 6:21. Since Izhar was a son of Kohath (Exod 6:18), Zichri belonged to the Kohathite branch of the tribe of Levi, and the Korah named as his brother is the one who later led a rebellion against Moses (Num 16:1). Chronicles names another son of Izhar, Shelomith or Shelomoth (1 Chr 23:18; 1 Chr 24:22), who would also have been Zichri's brother. Nothing else is recorded about Zichri himself. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "that remembers," and Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "memorable." Several other men in the Bible share the name Zichri, and this entry concerns only the son of Izhar.

Zichri was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 8 as one of the sons of Shimhi. His brothers were Jakim, Zabdi, Elienai, Zilthai, Eliel, Adaiah, Beraiah and Shimrath. The passage says nothing about his life. It only places him within a Benjamite family line, and Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Benjamite chief. The STEPBible name index (Tyndale House) treats his father Shimhi as the same person as Shimei and places the family among the descendants of Shaharaim. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 1440 BC, an estimate inferred from the genealogy and not stated in the text. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "that remembers." Several other men in the Bible are also called Zichri, and this entry concerns only the son of Shimhi.

Zichri was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the sons of Shashak named in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. He appears in a list of eleven brothers: Ishpan, Heber, Eliel, Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Hananiah, Elam, Antothijah, Iphedeiah and Penuel. The surrounding verses (1 Chr 8:22–25) close the list by calling them the sons of Shashak, and the chapter later describes them as heads of families living in Jerusalem (1 Chr 8:28). Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "memorable," and Hitchcock's Bible Names as "that remembers." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including another Benjamite in the same chapter (1 Chr 8:27), so this Zichri should be kept distinct from them.

Zichri was a Benjamite, one of the sons of Jeroham named in the genealogy of Benjamin's descendants in 1 Chr 8:27. His brothers listed with him are Shamsherai, Shehariah, Athaliah, Jaresiah and Eliah. The surrounding genealogy places this family among the Benjamites. STEPBible's proper-name index traces Jeroham's line back to Shaharaim, a descendant of Benjamin. Nothing else is recorded about Zichri beyond his place in this family list, and the passage is mainly concerned with heads of families who lived in Jerusalem. The name Zichri, meaning "memorable" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary, belongs to several different men in the Bible, including other Levites and Benjamites. This one should not be confused with them.

Zichri was a Levite of the family of Asaph, the temple musician, and the father of Micah (spelled Micha in Nehemiah). He appears only in the genealogy of his grandson Mattaniah, who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile. Mattaniah was the one who led the thanksgiving in prayer (1 Chr 9:15; Neh 11:17). The parallel list in Neh 11:17 gives Zichri's name as Zabdi. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary also link him with the Zaccur named in Mattaniah's line at Neh 12:35. "Son of Asaph" may mean a later descendant rather than a direct son, since genealogies often skip generations. Zichri himself is known only through these lists, so he probably lived some generations before Nehemiah's time. Several other men in the Bible share the name Zichri, including Levites mentioned in Exod 6:21 and 1 Chr 26:25.

Zichri was a Levite named in the line of Eliezer, son of Moses, in 1 Chr 26:25. The verse lists the descendants in order: Rehabiah, Jeshaiah, Joram, Zichri and Shelomith. Each is called "his son," so this entry reads Zichri as the son of Joram and the father of Shelomith. The surrounding passage concerns the Levites who guarded the temple treasuries, and the next verse names this Shelomith and his brothers as keepers of the dedicated treasures. On that basis the STEPBible Proper Names index describes Zichri as connected with the temple treasury in David's time. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him before about 1043 BC, an estimate drawn from context. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as "that remembers."

Zichri was the father of Eliezer, who served as ruler of the tribe of Reuben in the list of tribal leaders recorded for the reign of King David (1 Chr 27:16). Nothing else is said about Zichri himself, but he was probably a Reubenite, since his son led that tribe. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary takes to mean "memorable," is borne by several different men in the Bible, and this Zichri should not be confused with the others of the same name. By inference from the reign of David, he lived around the late eleventh century BC, a date estimated from context rather than stated in the text.

Zichri was the father of Amasiah, one of the army commanders of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. He is known only from 2 Chr 17:16, which names his son as a man who "willingly offered himself unto the LORD" and who led two hundred thousand fighting men. The surrounding passage lists the military leaders of Jehoshaphat's reign, so by inference Zichri lived in Judah in the generation before that king's time. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Zichri is shared by several men in the Bible, and this one is not clearly linked to any of the others. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts him as the fourth person of that name and describes the meaning of the name as uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "that remembers."

Zichri was the father of Elishaphat, one of the captains of hundreds whom the priest Jehoiada brought into a covenant with him in the seventh year of Athaliah's rule (2 Chr 23:1). Jehoiada made this pact to overthrow Queen Athaliah and put the young Joash on the throne of Judah. The rest of 2 Chr 23 tells that story. Zichri himself is known only as Elishaphat's father, and nothing more is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to some time before 876 BC. The name means "memorable" according to Smith's, and "that remembers" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Several other men in the Bible are also called Zichri, and there is nothing to connect this one with any of them.

Zichri was a warrior of the tribe of Ephraim, called "a mighty man of Ephraim," who fought in the army of the northern kingdom of Israel when it invaded Judah during the reign of King Ahaz. In that campaign he killed three members of the Judean court: Maaseiah, described as the king's son; Azrikam, the governor of the palace; and Elkanah, who was second in rank to the king (2 Chr 28:7). The surrounding chapter places this war under Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, and Smith's Bible Dictionary dates it to about 734 BC. The meaning of his name is uncertain, though it is often explained as "memorable" or "remembering." Several other men in the Bible share the name Zichri, and this one is mentioned only in this single verse.

Zichri was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only as the father of Joel, who served as overseer of the Benjamites living in Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time (Neh 11:9). The tribe is inferred from the surrounding list, which records the Benjamites who settled in the city after the return from exile. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Zichri as the "father or ancestor" of Joel, since "son of" in such lists can also mean a more distant descendant. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names takes to mean "that remembers," is borne by several different men in the Old Testament, and this Zichri should not be confused with the others.

Zichri was a priest who headed the priestly family of Abijah in the days of Joiakim the high priest, the son of Jeshua, after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears only in Neh 12:17, in a list of the heads of priestly families in Joiakim's time. The surrounding passage places this list after the generation of priests who came back with Zerubbabel, so Zichri probably served in the generation after the first return. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 480 BC, an estimate drawn from context rather than stated in the text. Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, and this Zichri should not be confused with them. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "memorable."

Ziddim was a fortified city in the tribal territory of Naphtali, listed first among that tribe's "fenced cities" alongside Zer, Hammath, Rakkath and Chinnereth (Josh 19:35). It is mentioned only in this allotment list, so nothing more is known of its history. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "sides", and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "the declivities". Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with Kefr Hattin (Hattin), about 5 miles west or northwest of Tiberias, near the slopes of the Horns of Hattin above the Sea of Galilee. The location shown here follows that identification. Its listing beside Chinnereth and Rakkath fits a site in the region west of the lake.

Zidkijah was one of the men who set their seal on the written covenant made in Jerusalem under Nehemiah after the return from exile. He is named immediately after Nehemiah the governor (the Tirshatha), which places him first among the other signatories (Neh 10:1). His name means "justice of the Lord" or "the Lord is righteous." Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper-names index treat him as a priest, or the head of a priestly family. Some readers instead take him as a leading official ranked with Nehemiah, because the list of priests appears to begin with the next name in the following verse. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists him under the more common form of the same name, Zedekiah.

Zidon, also spelled Sidon, was the firstborn son of Canaan, a grandson of Noah through Ham, according to the table of nations (Gen 10:15; 1 Chr 1:13). His brothers included Heth and the ancestors of the Jebusites, Amorites, Girgasites, Hivites, Arkites, Sinites, Arvadites, Zemarites and Hamathites. Nothing is told of his life beyond his place in these genealogies. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects him with the Phoenician coastal city of Sidon, about 25 miles north of Tyre, saying the city took its name from him. The STEPBible proper-names list likewise treats him as the ancestor of the Sidonian people. In this reading the person stands at the head of a people and a city that appear often in later biblical history. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "hunting" or "fishing."

Ziha was the ancestor of a family of Nethinim, the temple servants, whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem. They head the list of Nethinim in the record of returning exiles in Ezra 2:43, and the same list appears again in Neh 7:46. Smith's Bible Dictionary places this return under Zerubbabel, about 536 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also links the name to a Ziha who oversaw the Nethinim in Neh 11:21. Because several people bear this name, it is uncertain whether that overseer is the family's ancestor, a later member of the family, or a different man. The meaning of the name is unclear. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "brightness" or "drought," and Smith's gives "parched."

Ziha was one of two leaders over the Nethinim, the temple servants, who lived on Ophel in Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah. Neh 11:21 names him together with Gispa as the men in charge of them. Ophel was the raised area of Jerusalem near the temple, which made it a convenient home for people who served there. Nothing else is recorded about him. The same name appears in Ezra 2:43 and Neh 7:46, at the head of a family of Nethinim who returned from exile in Babylon. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the name here is probably the same as that family's. Ziha may therefore have been a later leader descended from that family, or the family name may be used for its head, but this is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "brightness" or "drought."

Ziklag was a town in the Negev, the southern region of Judah. It is listed among Judah's towns (Josh 15:31) and among those given to Simeon (Josh 19:5; 1 Chr 4:30). Later it was held by the Philistines, and Achish, king of Gath, gave it to David, after which it belonged to the kings of Judah (1 Sam 27:6). While David lived there, warriors from several tribes joined him (1 Chr 12:1, 20). Amalekites raided and burned it (1 Sam 30:1, 14). David recovered the captives and sent some of the spoil to the elders of Judah (1 Sam 30:26). At Ziklag he heard of Saul's death and had the messenger killed (2 Sam 1:1; 4:10). It was resettled after the exile (Neh 11:28). The site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions 'Asluj and Khirbet Zuheilikah. The location shown here follows a site north of Beersheba, near Tel Halif.

Zillah was one of the two wives of Lamech, a descendant of Cain, the other being Adah (Gen 4:19). She bore Tubal-cain, described as an instructor of every craftsman in bronze and iron. Naamah is named as Tubal-cain's sister and is generally taken to be Zillah's daughter as well (Gen 4:22). Zillah and Adah are the wives Lamech addresses in his short poem about killing a man who had wounded him (Gen 4:23). Her name is often explained as meaning "shadow" or "shade", a link to the Hebrew word for shadow that the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives as possible. Lamech's marriage to two wives is the first mention of more than one wife in the Bible.

Zilpah was the maidservant whom Laban gave to his daughter Leah when Leah married Jacob. When Leah stopped having children, she gave Zilpah to Jacob as a wife, a common way for a childless or no-longer-bearing wife to gain children through her servant. Zilpah bore Jacob two sons, Gad and then Asher, both born in Paddan-aram, about 1753 and 1752 BC by inference from context. Gad and Asher became the ancestors of two of the tribes of Israel. Genesis 37:2 calls Zilpah and Bilhah Jacob's wives and places the young Joseph with their sons while tending the flocks. The list of those who went down to Egypt counts sixteen descendants through Zilpah (Gen 46:18). The meaning of her name is uncertain: Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "drooping" and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "a trickling."

Zilthai was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named among the sons of Shimhi in the Benjamite genealogies of 1 Chronicles. He appears only in a list of his brothers, which by context runs from 1 Chr 8:19 to 8:21: Jakim, Zichri, Zabdi, Elienai, Zilthai, Eliel, Adaiah, Beraiah and Shimrath. Nothing else is recorded about his life. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "shady," and Hitchcock's Bible Names as "my shadow." The same name belongs to more than one person in the Bible. A different Zilthai, a leader from the tribe of Manasseh, is named among the men who joined David at Ziklag (1 Chr 12:20). He should not be confused with this Benjamite.

Zilthai was one of the men of the tribe of Manasseh who went over to David as he traveled to Ziklag, and he is listed among the captains of thousands from Manasseh (1 Chr 12:20). The surrounding passage places this when David had marched with the Philistines against Saul and was then sent back by the Philistine lords, probably the episode told in 1 Sam 29–30. Nothing more is recorded about him beyond his name and rank. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "shady," and Hitchcock's Bible Names as "my shadow." The name is shared by another man, a Benjamite listed in a genealogy (1 Chr 8:20), who is a different person. The STEPBible Proper Names list spells this captain's name Zillethai.

Zimmah was a Levite of the clan of Gershom, named in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles. In the line of the singer Asaph he appears as the son of Shimei and the father of Ethan (1 Chr 6:42). The following verse makes Shimei a son of Jahath, son of Gershom. In the list of Gershom's descendants, a Zimmah is called the son of Jahath, son of Libni (1 Chr 6:20). Smith's Bible Dictionary treats these as possibly the same man, which would mean one list omits a generation. This entry follows the identification as Shimei's son and Ethan's father. The name is shared by more than one person in the Bible, so other mentions may refer to different individuals. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "thought" or "wickedness," and Smith's gives "purpose."

Zimmah was a Levite of the Gershonite clan, known only as the father of Joah. His son Joah was among the Levites who arose during the reign of King Hezekiah to help cleanse and purify the temple in Jerusalem (2 Chr 29:12). Zimmah is named only to identify his son, and the verse says nothing about his own life. The name was used by several men. Gershonite genealogies elsewhere also list a Zimmah, and one of them likewise has a son named Joah (1 Chr 6:20–21, 42). This may reflect repeated family names within the clan, but how these men are connected is uncertain. The STEPBible proper-names index links this Zimmah to the temple cleansing under Hezekiah and describes him as of the line of Asaph. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "thought" or "wickedness."

Zimran was a son of Abraham and Keturah, the woman Abraham took after Sarah's death. He is listed first among her six sons, followed by Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak and Shuah (Gen 25:2; 1 Chr 1:32). This made him a half-brother of Isaac and Ishmael. Genesis calls Keturah Abraham's wife, while 1 Chronicles calls her his concubine. Gen 25:6 says that Abraham gave gifts to the sons of his concubines and sent them away eastward, away from Isaac. That probably included Zimran. As Smith's Bible Dictionary notes, no descendants of his are recorded. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "celebrated," Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "song" or "vine," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia derives it from a word for wild sheep or goat. That encyclopedia also mentions a proposed link with the "Zimri" of Jer 25:25 and with places in Arabia.

Zimri was a people or country whose kings appear in Jeremiah's list of nations made to drink the cup of God's wrath. It is named alongside Elam and the Medes (Jer 25:25), right after the kings of Arabia and the "mingled people" of the desert. Nothing else is known about it, and its location has not been identified. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both suggest the name may be connected with Zimran, a son of Abraham and Keturah (Gen 25:2), whose descendants probably lived in Arabia. That would link Zimri with the Arabian peoples in the preceding verse. The location shown here is only a rough placement in southwestern Iran, near ancient Elam, which reflects its pairing with Elam and the Medes in the same verse.

Zimri, son of Salu, was an Israelite leader of a prominent family within the tribe of Simeon. He was killed together with a Midianite woman during the episode at Baal-peor, when many Israelites joined in Moabite and Midianite worship while camped near the Jordan (Num 25:14). The surrounding chapter says that Phinehas, grandson of Aaron, killed the pair with a spear. The next verse names the woman as Cozbi, daughter of a Midianite chief. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the event to about 1450 BC, and any such date is an estimate inferred from context. Several other men in the Bible share the name Zimri, including a later king of Israel who reigned for seven days. This entry concerns only the Simeonite.

Zimri was a king of the northern kingdom of Israel who held the throne for only seven days, about 929 BC by inference from context. He commanded half the royal chariots. He plotted against King Elah, son of Baasha (named in 1 Kgs 16:8), and killed him while Elah was drunk at the house of his steward Arza in Tirzah, in the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah. He then wiped out Baasha's whole family, which the text presents as fulfilling the word of the prophet Jehu. The army, which was besieging the Philistine town of Gibbethon, responded by making its commander Omri king. When Omri took Tirzah, Zimri went into the palace, set it on fire over himself and died. His name later served as a byword for killing one's master, when Jezebel used it to greet Jehu (2 Kgs 9:31). Several other men in the Bible share this name.

Zimri was a Benjamite and a descendant of King Saul, named in the two genealogies of Saul's family in 1 Chronicles. He was a son of Ahaz's son, the brother of Alemeth and Azmaveth, and the father of Moza. The father's name differs between the lists: 1 Chr 8:36 calls him Jehoadah and 1 Chr 9:42 calls him Jarah. These are probably two forms of the same name, and this entry follows the Jarah form. Both lists trace the line from Saul through Jonathan and Merib-baal (Mephibosheth) to Micah and Ahaz. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify him as Saul's descendant. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with other men called Zimri, such as the short-reigning king of Israel.

Zin was a desert region on the southern edge of Canaan, usually called the wilderness of Zin. Kadesh lay within it (Num 20:1; 33:36), and the Israelites camped there during their wanderings. Miriam died and was buried at Kadesh in Zin. It was also where the dispute at the waters of Meribah took place, which is given as the reason Moses and Aaron could not enter the land (Num 27:14; Deut 32:51). The spies sent from Kadesh explored the land starting from Zin (Num 13:21). Zin also marked the southern boundary of the promised land and of Judah's territory, next to Edom (Num 34:3; Josh 15:1). Smith's Bible Dictionary places it between the Arabah and the plateau of et-Tih, south of the Dead Sea. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with the uplands north and northwest of the wilderness of Paran, in the modern Negev. It is distinct from the wilderness of Sin.

Zin was a point on the southern border of the promised land, later the southern boundary of Judah's territory. Both border descriptions place it between the ascent of Akrabbim and Kadesh-barnea (Num 34:4; Josh 15:3). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as a town in the far south of Judah, on the line dividing it from Edom, and notes that its exact site has not been found. It probably lay somewhere between Wadi el-Fiqra and Ain Qadis, the likely sites of Akrabbim and Kadesh-barnea. The location shown here is a rough placement along that route. The name is shared with the wider Wilderness of Zin. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes that wilderness as the southeastern corner of the desert et-Tih and distinguishes it from the Wilderness of Sin. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "buckler" or "coldness."

Zion was originally the fortified stronghold of the Jebusite city of Jerusalem, which David captured and renamed the city of David (2 Sam 5:7; 1 Chr 11:5). Solomon later brought the ark up from there to his new temple (1 Kgs 8:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary places this first Zion on the southeastern hill of Jerusalem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name later seems to have shifted to the temple hill, and that in Christian times it came to be used for the southwestern hill. In the Psalms and Prophets, Zion often appears alongside Jerusalem as a name for the whole city and its people, frequently called the "daughter of Zion" (Ps 102:21; Amos 1:2; Zeph 3:14). It is described as the LORD's holy hill and dwelling place (Ps 2:6; Joel 3:21), and the New Testament quotes such passages (Matt 21:5; 1 Pet 2:6). The location shown here treats Zion as Jerusalem as a whole.

Zion's is the possessive form of Zion, used in phrases such as "for Zion's sake" (Isa 62:1). Zion was one of the hills on which Jerusalem was built. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as the south-eastern hill, which David captured from the Jebusites and where he built a citadel and palace, so that it became known as "the city of David" (2 Sam 5:7; 1 Chr 11:5). In later Old Testament books the name often stands for Jerusalem as a whole, and sometimes for the people of Israel (Ps 87:2; Ps 51:18). In the New Testament it can refer to the people of God or to the heavenly city (Heb 12:22; Rev 14:1). Later tradition gave the name "Mount Zion" to Jerusalem's south-western hill. The location shown here follows the eastern identification and lies on the ridge near the Temple Mount and the City of David.

Zior was a town in the hill country of Judah, named once in the Bible in the list of cities given to the tribe of Judah (Josh 15:54). It appears as the last of a group of nine cities with their villages that also includes Hebron, so it probably lay in the same district near Hebron. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "littleness," and Smith's Bible Dictionary as "smallness." Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the modern village of Si'air, about 4.5 miles north-northeast of Hebron. The encyclopedia describes it as a sizable village with farmland, a nearby spring, and rock-cut tombs that point to an ancient settlement. The location shown here follows the Si'air identification.

Ziph was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed with Maon, Carmel and Juttah among the towns of Judah's tribal territory (Josh 15:55). It is best known from David's flight from Saul. David stayed in strongholds and a wood in the nearby wilderness of Ziph, and Saul searched for him there day after day (1 Sam 23:14–15). On a later occasion Saul brought three thousand chosen men into the same wilderness to hunt him (1 Sam 26:2). Rehoboam later fortified Ziph as one of the defended cities of Judah (2 Chr 11:8). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with Tell Zif, a prominent hill about 4–5 miles southeast of Hebron, and the location shown here follows that identification. The name is shared with at least one other town in Judah, which is a separate place.

Ziph was a town in the far south of Judah, in the Negev, listed among the cities given to the tribe of Judah near the border of Edom. It is named between Ithnan and Telem in Josh 15:24 and does not appear again in the biblical narrative. It is distinct from the better-known Ziph in the hill country of Judah, near Hebron, where David hid from Saul. The name is shared by several places, so care is needed in telling them apart. The site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it probably at the pass of Sufah, while Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia regard its location as unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the Negev, consistent with its listing among Judah's southern towns.

Ziph was a son of Jehaleleel, named in the genealogy of Judah's descendants together with his brothers Ziphah, Tiria and Asareel (1 Chr 4:16). Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Ziph is also used for a town and wilderness in Judah, where Saul searched for David (1 Sam 26:2). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that two towns in Judah bore the name. Whether this man is connected with any of those places is not stated. Because the Chronicles genealogies sometimes list clan founders whose names match towns, a link is possible, but it remains uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Greek manuscripts differ on the name. Codex Alexandrinus reads Ziphai, while Codex Vaticanus has the quite different form Ameachei.

Ziphah was a son of Jehaleleel and a descendant of Judah, named only once, in the genealogy of Judah's clans in 1 Chr 4:16. His brothers were Ziph, Tiria and Asareel. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the name is a feminine form of Ziph, the brother listed just before him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may have come about through a copyist accidentally repeating the previous name, Ziph. Both names may also be connected with the town of Ziph in the hill country of Judah, since Chronicles often lists towns and clans as "sons" in its genealogies, though the verse itself does not say so.

Ziphron was a place named on the northern border of the land promised to Israel, listed in Num 34:9 just before Hazar-enan, where that border ended. The verse gives no further detail, so its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it south-east of Hamath. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as the same place as Sibraim, which appears in Ezekiel's description of Israel's northern border. The location shown here is a rough placement in the Syrian interior east of Homs, matching the general idea that the border ran eastward from the Hamath region toward the desert. Easton's gives the name's meaning as "sweet odour." Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "falsehood of a song" or "rejoicing."

Zippor was the father of Balak, the king of Moab who, alarmed by Israel's victories over the Amorites, sent for Balaam son of Beor to curse Israel (Num 22:2–4; Josh 24:9). Zippor is known only through his son, who is repeatedly called "Balak the son of Zippor" in the account in Numbers, and again in later recollections of the episode by Joshua and by Jephthah (Judg 11:25). Balaam addresses Balak with the same formula in one of his oracles (Num 23:18). Nothing is said about Zippor's own life, and the text does not state whether he was himself a king. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that it is not known whether he was the "former king of Moab" mentioned in Num 21:26. His name means "bird," with "sparrow" offered as a more specific sense by Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries.

Zipporah was the wife of Moses and a daughter of Jethro, the priest of Midian, who is also called Reuel (Exod 2:18). After Moses fled Egypt and settled with her family, her father gave her to him in marriage (Exod 2:21). She bore him two sons, Gershom and Eliezer (Exod 2:22; 18:3–4). On the journey back to Egypt, when the Lord sought to kill Moses, Zipporah circumcised her son with a sharp stone and called Moses "a bloody husband" (Exod 4:24–26). Moses later sent her back to her father, and Jethro brought her and the sons to him in the wilderness (Exod 18:2–6). Num 10:29 calls Hobab the son of Reuel, which probably makes him her brother. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives her name's meaning as "bird." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia thinks the "Cushite woman" of Num 12:1 is probably Zipporah, though others take her to be a second wife.

Zithri was a Levite, the son of Uzziel, named with his brothers Mishael and Elzaphan in the genealogy of Levi's descendants in Exod 6:22. Since Uzziel was a son of Kohath (Exod 6:18), Zithri belonged to the Kohathite clan. His brother Elzaphan is also called Elizaphan (Num 3:30). Isshiah and Michah are listed here as his siblings because 1 Chr 23:20 names Micah and Jesiah (Isshiah) as sons of Uzziel. Nothing else is recorded about Zithri. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the name in the form Sithri. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains it as "the Lord protects", and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "to hide".

Ziz was the ascent or cliff, called the "cliff of Ziz" in the King James Version, by which the invading armies of Moab, Ammon and their allies climbed toward Judah in the time of King Jehoshaphat. In 2 Chr 20:16 the people of Judah are told to go down against the enemy the next day and to find them at the end of the valley, before the wilderness of Jeruel. From the surrounding chapter, the invaders had gathered at Hazazon-tamar, identified with En-gedi, so Ziz was probably a pass leading up from the Dead Sea shore toward Tekoa. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it as the En-gedi pass itself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links the name with the Wadi Hasasa (Easton's Bible Dictionary gives Tell Hasasah), north of En-gedi. The location shown here follows that Wadi Hasasa identification.

Ziza was a man of the tribe of Simeon, the son of Shiphi, and his ancestry is traced back through Allon, Jedaiah, Shimri and Shemaiah (1 Chr 4:37). He appears in a list of Simeonite clan leaders. The verses that follow (1 Chr 4:38–43) describe how these leaders, whose families had grown large, moved toward Gedor in search of pasture in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary therefore call him a Simeonite prince or chief, and Smith's places him in Hezekiah's reign, roughly the late 700s BC, a date inferred from that context. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may be an affectionate shortened form. Several other people in the Bible share the name Ziza, and this one should not be confused with them.

Ziza was a son of King Rehoboam of Judah and his wife Maachah, who is called the daughter of Absalom (2 Chr 11:20). His full brothers were Abijah and Attai, and his sister was Shelomith. Through Rehoboam's other wife Mahalath he had the half-brothers Jeush, Shamariah and Zaham. He belonged to the tribe of Judah and was probably born in Jerusalem, Rehoboam's capital. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Maachah to be Absalom's granddaughter rather than his daughter, since in Hebrew usage "daughter" can refer to a more distant descendant. Ziza is mentioned only in this list of Rehoboam's children, and nothing more is recorded about him. His brother Abijah was the son Rehoboam chose to succeed him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Ziza and should not be confused with him.

Zizah was a Levite of the Gershonite branch, the second son of Shimei. His brothers were Jahath, the chief, and Jeush and Beriah (1 Chr 23:10–11). He appears in the list of Levite family heads that David organized for service. The same man is called Zina in 1 Chr 23:10 and Zizah in the next verse. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint and Vulgate read "Ziza" in both verses, as does one Hebrew manuscript in verse 10. It suggests that Zina is a variant spelling of the same name. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "abundance." Nothing more is recorded about him.

Zoan was an ancient city in the eastern Nile Delta of Egypt, known to the Greeks as Tanis and probably the modern village of San el-Hagar. The location shown here follows that identification. Num 13:22 notes that Hebron was built seven years before Zoan. The Psalms set God's wonders in Egypt in "the field of Zoan," which ties the city or its surrounding plain to the events of the exodus. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take this to mean that Pharaoh held court there during his dealings with Moses. Both also link Zoan with the Hyksos capital Avaris, and Easton's with the city of Rameses. Isaiah speaks of the "princes of Zoan" as Pharaoh's foolish counsellors and mentions Judah's envoys there.
