The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains this by the city's role as a royal capital around 800 to 700 BC. Ezekiel foretells that Zoan will be set on fire.

Zoar was a small city in the plain of the Jordan, earlier called Bela (Gen 14:2, 8). Its king joined the kings of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim in battle in the vale of Siddim. When Sodom was destroyed, Lot fled to Zoar, and Genesis ties the name, meaning "little," to that episode (Gen 19:22–23). He later left it out of fear and lived in a mountain cave with his daughters (Gen 19:30). Zoar marks the limit of the land Moses viewed before his death (Deut 34:3), and Isaiah and Jeremiah name it as a refuge in their oracles against Moab (Isa 15:5; Jer 48:34). Its site is debated. Josephus, Eusebius and medieval sources place it at the southern end of the Dead Sea. Easton's Bible Dictionary and others favor Tell esh-Shaghur north of the sea. The location shown here follows the southern view, probably near modern Safi in Jordan.

Zobah was an Aramean (Syrian) kingdom north of Israel in the time of Saul, David and Solomon. Saul fought "the kings of Zobah" (1 Sam 14:47), suggesting it then had several rulers. Under David it was ruled by Hadadezer son of Rehob, whom David defeated as Hadadezer went to secure his border at the Euphrates. David also struck down the Syrians of Damascus who came to help him and took spoil from Zobah. The Ammonites later hired troops from Zobah against David. Rezon, who fled from Hadadezer, became an adversary of Solomon. Igal, one of David's mighty men, was from Zobah. Its exact extent is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it from the eastern slopes of Lebanon toward the Euphrates, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it between Hamath and Damascus along the Anti-Lebanon. The location shown here follows that area, roughly between modern Homs and Baalbek.

Zobah-Hamath is the area named in 1 Chr 18:3, where David defeated Hadarezer (Hadadezer), king of Zobah, "unto Hamath" while he was going to establish his rule by the Euphrates. The phrase probably describes the stretch of Aramean territory reaching from the kingdom of Zobah north toward Hamath, the city usually identified with modern Hama on the Orontes River in Syria. Zobah itself is generally placed in the region north of Damascus, around the Beqaa Valley, though its exact extent is uncertain. The location shown here is an approximate point in central Syria, south-east of Homs, representing the surrounding region rather than a specific town. A similar name, Hamath-zobah, appears in 2 Chr 8:3 as a place Solomon captured. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls it a fortress of Zobah and notes that some take it to be distinct from Hamath, though this is uncertain.

Zobebah was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of Judah's descendants as a son of Coz (1 Chr 4:8). The same verse names Anub as another son of Coz and mentions the families of Aharhel son of Harum, which is why Harum is also counted among Coz's children. Nothing further is recorded about Zobebah's life or descendants. The Hebrew form of the name carries the definite article ("ha-Zobebah"), and its meaning is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives it as "the slow." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some scholars would read the name as "Jabez," the figure who appears in the next verse, 1 Chr 4:9. This entry treats Zobebah as a distinct son of Coz, as the verse reads.

Zohar was the father of Ephron the Hittite, the man from whom Abraham bought the field and cave of Machpelah near Mamre as a family burial place. He is known only through his son: Abraham asks the people of the land to plead with "Ephron the son of Zohar" on his behalf when seeking a grave for Sarah (Gen 23:8), and the same description is used when Isaac and Ishmael later bury Abraham in that cave (Gen 25:9). Nothing else is recorded about him. Since Ephron is called a Hittite, Zohar was presumably a Hittite too, one of the people living around Hebron in Abraham's day. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "white" or "bright", and Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "light". The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia regards the meaning as uncertain. The same name is borne by other men elsewhere in the Old Testament.

Zoheth was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles as one of the sons of Ishi, along with Ben-zoheth (1 Chr 4:20). He appears only in this single verse, and nothing further is recorded about him. His place in Judah's line comes from the surrounding chapter, which lists the descendants of Judah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that Ben-zoheth, meaning "son of Zoheth," may have been his son rather than his brother, and that a name following it may have dropped out of the text. This entry follows the plain reading of the verse, which treats the two as brothers. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary tentatively gives "snatching," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "separation" or "amazing."

Zophah was a man of the tribe of Asher, named in the tribe's genealogy in 1 Chronicles. He is listed as a son of Helem, alongside his brothers Imna, Shelesh and Amal (1 Chr 7:35). This Helem is usually taken to be Hotham, son of Heber, mentioned a few verses earlier. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the Tyndale House proper-name index both make this identification, and this entry follows it. Zophah had a large family. Suah, Harnepher, Beri and Imrah are among the sons named in 1 Chr 7:36, and the list of his descendants continues in the following verses. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him a chief of Asher, which fits the genealogy's description of these men as heads of their fathers' houses. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain.

Zophar the Naamathite was one of Job's three friends, with Eliphaz the Temanite and Bildad the Shuhite. When they heard of Job's troubles, they arranged to come together from their own homes to mourn with him and comfort him (Job 2:11). Zophar speaks twice in the debate that follows (Job 11:1; 20:1). He does not give a third speech, as Eliphaz and Bildad do. At the end of the book, God tells the three friends to offer sacrifices and have Job pray for them. They do as commanded, and the LORD accepts Job's prayer (Job 42:9). Easton's Bible Dictionary takes "Naamathite" to mean a man from an unknown place called Naamah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia doubts it was the Naamah in Judah, since Job and his other friends came from outside Israel. The meaning of his name is uncertain; suggestions include "sparrow" and "chirping."

Zophim, or "the field of Zophim," was a place at the top of Pisgah in Moab. Its name means "field of watchers" or "lookouts," which suggests a high vantage point. King Balak of Moab brought the prophet Balaam there and built seven altars, offering a bull and a ram on each, in the hope that Balaam would curse Israel from that spot (Num 23:14). From the surrounding passage, it was Balaam's second viewpoint over the Israelite camp, and in place of a curse he again spoke a blessing. The exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects it with Tal'at es-Safa, an ascent leading up to the ridge of Mount Nebo from the north. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests it may be the place later called Mizpah of Moab. The location shown here is on the Pisgah–Nebo ridge, east of the northern end of the Dead Sea in present-day Jordan.

Zorah was a town in the low hill country (the Shephelah) west of Jerusalem. It appears among the towns of Judah under the spelling Zoreah (Josh 15:33) and is later listed in the inheritance of Dan, alongside Eshtaol (Josh 19:41). It was the home of Manoah, Samson's father (Judg 13:2). The Spirit of the LORD began to move Samson in the camp of Dan between Zorah and Eshtaol, and he was buried there in his father's tomb (Judg 13:25; 16:31). Zorah and Eshtaol also sent out the five Danite spies and then the 600 armed men who moved north (Judg 18:2, 8, 11). Rehoboam later fortified it (2 Chr 11:10). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the village of Sur'ah on a hill above the Valley of Sorek, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Zorobabel is the Greek form of the name Zerubbabel. He appears in Luke's genealogy of Jesus as the son of Salathiel and the father of Rhesa (Luke 3:27), in the line that runs back through Neri to David and the tribe of Judah. STEPBible Proper Names identifies him with Zerubbabel, the descendant of David who led exiles back from Babylon and governed Judah during the rebuilding of the temple (Ezra 2:2; Hag 1:1). This entry follows that identification. Matthew's genealogy also names Zorobabel son of Salathiel, but it traces Salathiel to Jechonias rather than Neri and gives the son as Abiud (Matt 1:12–13). 1 Chr 3:19 calls Zerubbabel a son of Pedaiah. Because of these differences, some interpreters treat Luke's Zorobabel as a different man of the same name. How the lists relate is uncertain.

Zuar was a man of the tribe of Issachar, known only as the father of Nethaneel, who led that tribe during the wilderness period after the exodus. Each of his five mentions comes in the phrase "Nethaneel the son of Zuar." They describe Nethaneel as the tribe's representative at the census (Num 1:8), as captain of Issachar's camp next to Judah (Num 2:5), as the prince who brought the tribe's offering on the second day of the altar's dedication (Num 7:18, 23), and as commander of Issachar's host when Israel set out from Sinai (Num 10:15). Nothing else is recorded about Zuar himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of his name as "littleness" or "little one."

Zuph was the district Saul and his servant reached while searching for his father's lost donkeys. There Saul proposed turning back so his father would not start worrying about them instead (1 Sam 9:5). The next verse shows that a town in this district held the seer Samuel, and Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Samuel's city, Ramah. Easton's suggests the region was named after Zuph, an ancestor of Samuel's father Elkanah (1 Chr 6:35; compare 1 Sam 1:1, where Elkanah is from Ramathaim-zophim). Its exact extent is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it in Benjamin near its northern border, Tyndale House's proper-names index places it in Ephraim, and Smith's Bible Dictionary tentatively links it with Soba, west of Jerusalem. The location shown here is a rough one in the hill country northwest of Jerusalem, near the area traditionally associated with Samuel's Ramah.

Zuph, also called Zophai, was a Levite of the Kohathite line and an ancestor of Elkanah, the father of the prophet Samuel. He appears in the genealogy that opens 1 Sam 1:1, where Elkanah of Ramathaim-zophim in the hill country of Ephraim is traced back through Jeroham, Elihu and Tohu to Zuph. The Levite genealogies in 1 Chronicles name him as the son of an earlier Elkanah and the father of Nahath (1 Chr 6:26, 35). Nahath there probably corresponds to Tohu in 1 Samuel, by comparing the two lists. The town name Ramathaim-zophim, and the "land of Zuph" in 1 Sam 9:5, probably come from his name or his clan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some scholars read the word in 1 Sam 1:1 as "Zuphite," a clan name, rather than as a personal name. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "honeycomb."

Zur was a Midianite leader, the father of Cozbi. Num 25:15 describes him as "head over a people, and of a chief house in Midian," so he was a tribal chief with a prominent family. His daughter Cozbi was the Midianite woman killed with the Israelite Zimri during the episode at Peor, when Israel was struck by a plague. The surrounding account (Num 25:6–8, 14) tells how Phinehas killed them both. Zur is probably the same man named in Num 31:8 as one of the five kings of Midian killed in Israel's later war against Midian. Josh 13:21 also lists him among the Midianite princes linked with Sihon. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "stone" or "rock." Several other people in the Bible share the name, including a Benjamite in the line of Saul (1 Chr 8:30).

Zur was one of five kings of Midian killed by the Israelites in their war against Midian in the time of Moses. The others were Evi, Rekem, Hur and Reba, and Balaam son of Beor was killed in the same campaign (Num 31:8). Josh 13:21 recalls the same five as princes of Midian and describes them as dukes, or subordinate chiefs, of Sihon king of the Amorites, living in his country. Num 25:15 names a Zur, head of a leading family in Midian, as the father of Cozbi, the Midianite woman killed alongside Zimri by Phinehas. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies that Zur with this king. His name means "rock." Several other men in the Bible share the name, so this entry covers only the Midianite leader.

Zur was a Benjamite who lived at Gibeon, the second son listed after the firstborn Abdon in the family of the founder of Gibeon and his wife Maachah (1 Chr 8:30; 9:36). His father is named here as Abiel. The Chronicles genealogy calls the father of Gibeon Jehiel (1 Chr 9:35), and Abiel is the name given to Saul's ancestor in 1 Sam 9:1, so this entry treats the two as the same man. Zur's brothers included Kish, Baal, Ner, Nadab, Gedor, Ahio, Zacher and Mikloth, and so he belonged to the same clan from which King Saul came. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a suggestion that he may be connected with Zeror in 1 Sam 9:1. Nothing more is recorded of him. His name means "rock," and several other people in the Bible share it.

Zuriel, son of Abihail, was the chief of the Merarite families of the tribe of Levi during Israel's time in the wilderness after the Exodus. He is named only once, in the census and arrangement of the Levites at Mount Sinai. There Moses is told that the Merarites, under Zuriel's leadership, were to camp on the north side of the tabernacle (Num 3:35). By inference from the surrounding chapter, his clan was responsible for carrying and caring for the tabernacle's structural parts, such as its boards, bars, pillars and sockets. His name means "my rock is God" (Smith's Bible Dictionary), and the same element appears in other names of that period, such as Elizur and Zurishaddai. His father, Abihail, should not be confused with others of that name.

Zurishaddai was a man of the tribe of Simeon, known only as the father of Shelumiel. Shelumiel was chosen to help Moses count Israel in the wilderness (Num 1:6) and served as captain of the Simeonites. He led them when they camped beside the tribe of Reuben (Num 2:12) and when they set out on the march (Num 10:19). On the fifth day of the offerings for the dedication of the altar, he presented Simeon's gifts (Num 7:36, 41). By inference, Zurishaddai himself belonged to Simeon and lived in the generation before the exodus. Nothing more is recorded about him. His name means "my rock is the Almighty" (Smith's Bible Dictionary), which combines the Hebrew word for rock with Shaddai, a title for God.
